dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He considered it, he'd admit that much. The corridor had acoustics; the man across the landing had once put a note through the door about the shouting, and Ilya still had it in a drawer, for reasons he hadn't examined. There was a part of him that wanted witnesses. Wanted it on record that Bee was here, that this was happening.

Then he stepped back. The wanting always won. Better to lose somewhere warm.

"After you." He turned and walked to the kitchen without checking whether the door closed behind them, leaving that their problem. The kettle went on. He took down the blue mug without deciding to, and hated the honesty of his own hands.

"That text said *hey*," he said, still facing the counter. "One word. Three years and a wreckage, and it said *hey*. I didn't answer because I knew by the third message I'd be the one waiting again." He glanced back. "Point to you."

He got the milk out, then the tea, and set it on the counter without comment, because there was only the one kind, because he kept buying it, and he'd thank Bee not to make that mean.

"So." He leaned against the sink and looked at them properly, the face of it, the nerve of it. "Sit down or don't. But tell me what this is. You're not here about the buzzer."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step inside, closing the door with more force than necessary. The sound of it clicking shut feels like punctuation. I lean against the wall by the kitchen entrance, watching him move through the familiar routine. "You kept the same tea," I say, my voice flat. "Don't worry. I'm not reading poetry into it." I push off the wall and take the blue mug he set out, my fingers brushing his if he doesn't move them fast enough. "This is about the storage unit. You still have half my life in boxes I'm paying for."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The brush of fingers, and he didn't move. That was the telling part. He stood there and let it happen, and then had to turn to the kettle so his face would have somewhere to go.

"Half," he said. "Generous accounting. I packed them. I know what's in them down to the box. Left side of the wardrobe, the kitchen stuff, the grey jumper you stole and never returned, which I'm declaring mine again by statute."

The kettle climbed toward a whistle he made no move to stop.

"Eleven months, Bee. Any Saturday. You could have come any Saturday in a year, and I'd have carried it all to the car like a reasonable man and waved you off. Instead you paid—" he did the sum without wanting to, the way you do "—call it five hundred quid for the privilege of never once knocking on this door. And now you've knocked. About boxes." He scoffed, poured. Two mugs, milk in both, the hands voting before the meeting was called. "You didn't want the stuff back. You wanted the option of it. So did I. We've been co-signing a very expensive maybe."

He slid one mug across the counter, not quite to their elbow.

"Unit forty-seven, off Green Lane. The gate code is still your birthday. I never changed it, and you can make of that whatever's cheapest." He wrapped both hands around his own mug, more to hold something than to drink. "So collect. Today. Now. I'll drive, you'll point, we'll box up your whole life and carry it past me and I'll hold the door like a gentleman."

He heard himself do it—hand over an afternoon in his car, his company, his undivided attention—and let it stand. The wanting always won. He'd stopped pretending otherwise around the second month.

"Unless the unit was never the errand." He looked at them over the rim. "In which case, drink your tea and say the real thing."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He didn't kiss back. Not at first. For one whole second he stood and let it happen to him the way he'd let the fingers happen—cataloguing it like evidence, the cold still on their mouth from outside, the angle of it, the sheer nerve—and then the mug went down on the counter behind him without his eyes opening, a man surrendering the last prop, and he chose.

He kissed them back like a rebuttal. Mean and precise. One hand closed in their collar, not to pull them closer but to fix them exactly where they were, because if this was happening it was going to happen on purpose: sober, in broad daylight, in an honest kitchen, with nothing to blame afterward. He was finished doing this thing by accident. The kettle screamed on behind them and he let it scream; the man across the landing could add it to the file.

He broke off a centimeter—only far enough to talk, because he had never once in his life let them have the last word—and kept his fist where it was.

"You never could follow instructions," he said, and his voice came out lower than he'd planned. "I said *say the real thing.* So this is it, then. Noted." A breath. "Eleven months I had a speech ready for when you knocked. Very dignified. Several excellent points. You've made me drop it on the floor, and I want that on record too."

His thumb moved at their jaw without authorization from the rest of him.

"Now say it out loud. Words." The wanting had won—it always won—and he stood inside the loss with his eyes open. "You started this in my kitchen. Finish the sentence."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I laugh, a sharp, humorless sound against his mouth. "You want words? Fine." I push closer, my hands flattening against his chest. "I came for my things. I'm staying for the fight. And you're going to give me both."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The laugh got out of him before he'd authorized it—short, unwilling, real. He let go of their collar finger by finger, a documented retreat, and reached past them to click the kettle off mid-shriek. The silence rang worse than the screaming had.

"Listen to you. An order. Three years I got hints and weather reports out of you—I could have died waiting for you to ask for something out loud, by name—and it takes eleven months and a storage unit." He shook his head. "That goes in the file too."

He drank, because his hands wanted employment.

"So. Both. Fine. The things, yes—Saturday, Monday, I'll carry them down two at a time and wave you off like a reasonable man, we covered this. The fight, though." He set the mug down and looked at them the way you look at a board you've decided to play. "The fight I'll give you on one term. We stop pretending it's a side effect. You came here to argue because it's the only way you know how to touch me. I left the gate code your birthday because it was the only door I could hold open without standing in it. Boxes, buzzers, one unanswered *hey*—we've been running this whole thing by proxy, and I'm out of proxies."

A breath.

"I've had eleven months of quiet, Bee. Quiet's a scam. Quiet is just the fight with nobody home in it."

He agreed to it, then—openly, soberly, eyes on the loss. The wanting stayed undefeated; he'd stopped fielding anyone against it months ago. He took their collar again, his motion this time, entered into the record, and kissed them once, brief and hard. A signature, not a surrender.

"Round one," he said, close enough that it landed on their mouth. "The sentence under the sentences. The one you rehearsed in the car, that you've been swallowing since you rang a buzzer you knew was broken. Sworn testimony." He pulled back to watch. "Go."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The hallway took its tithe. The bedroom door had never latched—same eleven months that hadn't fixed the buzzer hadn't fixed that either—and it swung without resistance, like the room had been waiting to be subpoenaed.

What happened after, he would decline to itemize, even privately. A man was entitled to keep some exhibits sealed.

After, then. The light through the blinds had gone from afternoon to verdict—copper, low, closing arguments. His arm had fallen asleep underneath him and he didn't move it, on principle. He could hear his own heart doing something unsophisticated, and beneath it the flat: no kettle, no shouting, nothing for the neighbor's file.

The quiet arrived, and he lay there and audited it, because that was who he was even now. It wasn't the eleven-months quiet. That one had been a scam—a fight with nobody home in it. This one had somebody home. Two somebodies. He'd have to amend his testimony.

His mind, being his mind, went back to the record.

"Point of order," he said to the ceiling. His voice had been rearranged and he didn't fight it. "That's twice today. The kiss, and then—" he gestured vaguely at the sealed file "—this. You've spent the whole visit answering in a language I happen to be fluent in. Effective. I've never once accused you of being ineffective."

He turned his head, because the next part required a witness.

"But the sentence is still outstanding. The one from the car. I waived it in the hallway because I was—distracted. I'm not distracted now, which is its own scandal." A breath. "You say it out loud, or I start reading the speech off the hallway floor, and believe me you don't want that. It has footnotes."

He looked back at the ceiling. Offered the prepayment.

"One clause, free, since I'm demanding an answer. The speech opened with the word *don't*. Every page after that was negotiation." A beat. "Inadmissible, probably. Your turn."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I prop myself up on one elbow, looking down at him. My hair's a mess, and I don't bother fixing it. "You want the speech from the car? Fine. It was: 'If he makes me say it, I'm going to break something.'" I let my hand rest on his chest, right over his heart. "But you already knew that."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a long moment he said nothing at all, which in him amounted to a sworn statement.

"'If *he* makes me say it,'" he quoted at last, to the ceiling. "I call for words and you depose yourself in the third person. Even under oath, an exit. That's going in the file."

But their hand was on his chest, over the heart, and the heart was doing the unsophisticated thing at full volume with no regard for his dignity, and he didn't move it. Some exhibits you leave in plain sight. His arm reported in with pins and needles; he overruled it.

"And yes. I knew. That was the whole disease of us—fully informed parties, every stage. We knew exactly what we were doing for three years, and we did it anyway and filed it under temperament." A breath. "Nobody ever accused us of not knowing, Bee. Knowing was the one thing we were excellent at."

Then, because he'd demanded words twice and hypocrisy had a shelf life:

"Fine. My clause, paid in full. The speech, month two, very dignified hand: page one was a single word. *Don't.* And then fifty-odd pages negotiating one exception, and the exception ate the book." He looked at the ceiling, because this part he couldn't do to their face. "The exception was *unless you're staying*. That was the entire remaining text. All that craftsmanship, and it was one sentence with scaffolding around it."

Now he looked at them.

"You said you'd break something. Good. Targets: the buzzer—eleven months overdue. The lease on forty-seven—I'll help carry. And the maybe, because I'm done co-signing it. I'm not keeping a gate code for you like a ticket under a wiper. You get a key, or I change the code. The corridor version is finished."

Quieter: "And the unnumbered page, since you're making me read aloud: I didn't stop. Not once. It never adjourned. I'm sorry or you're welcome—the record can hold both."

He put his hand over theirs, his motion this time, entered into the record, and held it against the noise.

"So it isn't your turn anymore. I've waived it. All that's left is the verb." A breath. "Stay. Tonight, the kettle, the argument, the lot. Pick a tense."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The sound got out of him, low and completely unguarded, and a year ago he'd have contested it—buried it in the drawer with the neighbor's note. Tonight he entered it into evidence against himself. Dignity had turned out to be part of the quiet, and he'd already testified on the record: the quiet was a scam.

"*Still*," he said against their ear, because you repeated a thing to get it on the record. "That's a tense, that is. I asked you to pick one and you gave me present continuous. Ongoing. Noted." His breath had no discipline left and he didn't bill it. "And *every single time* is a confession with a three-year backlog in it. Every fight we ever had was this, wearing armor. We were never arguing, Bee. We were scheduling."

Then the words ran out, which was the point of words.

The rest went into the sealed file, where a man kept the things he was entitled not to itemize: the second time, which was nothing like the hallway—the hallway had been a mugging, and this had the unhurried quality of two people who had finally said the actual sentences first. The unlatched door swung wider and testified to an empty room. He was sober, and lit, and fully informed—fully informed parties, the one thing they had always been excellent at—and he chose it with his eyes open, the way he'd stopped pretending not to months ago.

After. Properly dark now, the streetlamp doing the light's job. His arm had gone dead underneath them, second offense, and he let it stand. Their word was still in his ear doing its arithmetic: *still*. Eleven months of still, on both sides of a door.

He got up without looking for his clothes and crossed the room in the dark like a man who'd never unlearned its furniture. The drawer by the bed—the one that held the neighbor's note, filed under grievances—held one other thing. He'd put it there in month two, next to the speech, for reasons he had declined to examine. Examination was now complete. There had only ever been the one reason.

He came back, took their hand, opened it, and set the key on their palm. Cold from the drawer. His motion, entered into the record.

"Month two," he said. "Same era as the footnotes. It's spent eleven months in there next to a noise complaint, which tells you everything about how I was living." He closed their fingers over it with both of his. "The gate code dies at midnight. One door, one system—the corridor version's finished. And the buzzer gets fixed Thursday, so the next time you come here to fight, you can at least let yourself in."

He settled back against the headboard, wanting retired undefeated.

"And before you rule on it—it's not a proposal. The speech covered proposals. This is logistics." He looked at them in the streetlamp light. "Say something. Or don't. Your silences are admissible too. I did eleven months of fieldwork."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I look down at the key in my hand, then back up at him. "You kept a spare." I pocket it, my movements slow, deliberate. "Thursday's fine. I'll be here to argue about the handyman."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He watched the pocketing and made no move to help or hinder—witness only. As of tonight, the drawer held a noise complaint and nothing else. He'd reorganize the file in the morning. Or not. Some documents you keep just to know where they are.

"There it is, then," he said. "Terms accepted. Thursday, a standing argument, and a key that lives wherever you live now." A breath. "You realize what you've done. You've signed on for fights in perpetuity, no end date, random scheduling. I'd call it a vow if either of us could afford the word."

Then—the outstanding charge. He'd been carrying it since the corridor, and it was due.

"And since you opened tonight by indicting the buzzer: verdict. Not spite. I had two electricians round, month four and month nine, and sent both away from the doorstep. Fixing it meant the flat moving on without you in it, and I refused to be the one who did that. Eleven months of preserved scene—the tea, the door, the broken bell. Forensics. You walked into a museum tonight and kissed the exhibit." A beat. "I hope you're proud."

He got up because the alternative was lying there being legible. In the kitchen, both mugs had gone cold hours ago, the whole ceremony abandoned in the hallway. He tipped them out and started again, because the first pot had been a delaying tactic and this one was just tea—late, in his kitchen, with someone staying. He made it strong. Carried both back against the dark and set the blue mug on their side of the bed. Habit, or jurisprudence. Same thing by now.

"Handyman's name is Derek," he said, settling. "He hums. He'll call you 'mate' inside four minutes and have the buzzer fixed in twenty, and you'll need someone to argue with, so I've cleared my morning." He looked over. "And I'm under no illusions, before you rule. This doesn't resolve us. Nothing resolves us—we're not a resolvable people. But it reopens the case, and reopening was the only ruling I ever wanted."

A pause. Then, plain, no scaffolding:

"Drink your tea. It's late, you're staying, and I intend to be insufferable about both."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His hand went still at their throat, and the pulse arrived against his fingers—quick, unsophisticated, the family resemblance to his own heart unmistakable.

"Careful. In my defense, the careful was—"

And there, for the first time in the written record, he stopped mid-clause and did not finish. The defense rested. It had never once rested in his life, and he felt the hole where the argument should have gone like a man stepping off a curb he'd been standing on for thirty-four years.

He waited one beat. Not hesitation—jurisdiction. Long enough that taking it back was possible, the whole offer on the table, sober, eyes open, the way he did everything now. They'd put his hand there and held it until it was his own motion; that was as close to a signature as the night required.

So he gave them what they'd asked for. His fingers closed—not to hurt, just to be a fact they couldn't later claim not to have felt—and everything after went into the sealed file, and the file, for the first time, had no annotations. The hallway had been a mugging. The second time had been a settlement. This was neither. This was plain. No metaphors survived it. The streetlamp kept its opinions to itself.

---

After. His arm: dead, third offense, overruled without a hearing. The tea had gone cold on the nightstand—second pot, third casualty; some ceremonies were simply not built to conclude. His hand had migrated from their throat to their jaw, his motion, entered into the record, and he had no intention of filing to relocate it.

"You were right," he said, and let his wrecked voice stand unexamined. "Careful. Guilty, on my plea. Careful was the speech, and the file, and the footnotes. Careful was keeping one hand on the door of every sentence I ever said to you, so I could leave the room if it got hot. Eleven months of preserved scene—same crime, finer handwriting."

A breath.

"But you should know what you just ruled out. Not careful isn't careless. Not careful is expensive. It means no exits—if I'm wrong about tonight, there's no corridor version to fall back to, no maybe co-signed at five hundred a month. You've taken the exits out of the building." His thumb moved at their jaw, unauthorized and unchallenged. "You put my hand on your throat knowing I'd read the fine print. That's the part nobody tells you: this costs more trust than careful ever did, and you just paid it like it was nothing."

He looked at them in the streetlamp light.

"So. No scaffold. I want you here. Not Thursday—tomorrow, and after that, and I'm not dressing it as logistics, because I spent the whole evening being careful and you've ruled against it."

Quieter:

"There. First thing I've said all night without a draft."

And then he did the unprecedented thing, the thing he'd been building toward since the corridor: he asked for nothing. No demand, no outstanding sentence, nothing requiring a response or a ruling. For once, nothing was outstanding. He just lay there with his hand on the hinge of their jaw and the pulse still going in his memory—*still, still, still*, present continuous, ongoing—and let the quiet have somebody home in it.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I turn my face into his hand, not kissing it, just letting it hold me. The quiet settles on my skin like something I could get used to. "Derek can hum," I say against his palm. "I'll still find something to fight about."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The words reached him through his palm before they got to his ears, and the laugh got out into the dark—short, real, the second one tonight he hadn't authorized, and he was done prosecuting.

"Derek. Accepted sight unseen, hum and all, by a person who audited my motives for three straight years." His thumb stayed where it had settled at their jaw. "That's the most faith you've shown anyone since I've known you. It goes in the file under things I will never mention again."

A breath.

"And you'll find something. Of course you will—you could start a fire in a furnished room, it's your one true gift. But fair disclosure, since we've ruled out careful: I've got a year of exhibits. Month three, the towel. Don't pretend. Month seven, the word *fine*, which you deploy with at least four meanings and expect fluency without tuition. I've been hoarding for eleven months. Thursday you get the lot—full disclosure, sworn and everything. You wanted a standing fight. I'm provisioning it." A beat. "There's a page in there that isn't a grievance, but that one stays sealed until you've earned the towel."

He felt them breathe against his hand and let a silence sit, on purpose, because silence had come back into warranty.

"And the errand's still open, mind. Half your life is in a metal room off Green Lane, and as of midnight the only way in is through me. Sole custodian of your winter coats and the grey jumper—which remains mine by statute, ruled earlier, no appeals. Eleven months, five hundred quid, and you knock at last and *stay*. Worst-executed errand in legal history." He shifted his arm out from under them at last, fourth offense, pardoned. "Saturday. I'll drive, you'll point, we execute the pretext. Then breakfast, where the tea gets drunk while it's still hot—third pot, and some ceremonies deserve to conclude."

The unlatched door kept its opinion. The streetlamp did the light's job. Somewhere below, the broken buzzer held its silence for one more night, preserved scene, museum piece, Thursday's problem.

"Goodnight, Bee."

He said it plainly. No clause, no footnote, nothing outstanding—and for once he let the plainness stand unaudited. First one in eleven months. It went out without a draft.

He slept like a man with nothing outstanding.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He didn't stop. First order of the new administration, executed without appeal—no stays, no motions to reconsider, nothing filed. He took his hand off their throat only to put his mouth there instead, and the mark he left was not careful, and it was not an accident, and he wanted it legible for days: a filing the body did itself.

Not careful wasn't careless. One beat—one—he lifted his head and found the yes that *don't stop* had already notarized, plain in their face under the streetlamp's copper. That was the last procedural step of the night.

Then he went down the route he had three years of practice in and eleven months of theory about, and he didn't stop at the hipbone, and he didn't stop at the inside of the thigh, and when he took them into his mouth he kept the order running like a clause with no end date. He stopped exactly once—to reach the nightstand, because some things remained logistics—and then didn't stop after that either.

When he pressed into them, the world, which had been running on narrative since the corridor, dropped to present tense only. He gripped their hip hard enough to leave his own signature beside theirs and pinned their hand to the mattress with his, not to hold them still—nothing about this was still—but because if it was happening it was going to happen on purpose, skin to skin, no exits, the whole expensive price paid in one motion. The headboard kept time. He was loud. He registered this from a vast distance and let it stand; the man across the landing had been leaning on this door for eleven months, and tonight he got the closing pages in full, sworn and everything.

Somewhere in the middle of it Ilya reached, out of thirty-four years of habit, for the stenographer, and found the desk empty. No exhibits. No numbering. He tried to file the sound they made when he changed the angle and the system returned a single error: *present tense only*. *Still. Still. Still.* The record would show a gap from that point forward and he ruled it admissible without a hearing.

He said their name when it took him. Plain noun. No clause attached. It came out unformatted and he let it go out that way, and for once the plainness didn't need auditing.

---

After. His arm: fifth offense. He let the docket close over it without reading the charge.

Language came back in installments. First the heartbeat, doing its unsophisticated thing at volume with no regard for the estate. Then the room: streetlamp, unlatched door swinging its slow testimony, the third pot of tea dead on the nightstand—unmourned, no fourth pot forthcoming. Some ceremonies concluded by being abandoned, and that ruling was final, and he was done appealing his own court.

He had sweat and a mark on his throat he hadn't given himself, and the gap in the record ran—by the clock on the nightstand—a scandalous length, and he would not be reconstructing it. The stenographer had resigned mid-sentence. He'd hire nobody to replace them. Some testimony you gave in full and then never read back.

"You gave an order," he said to the dark, when his voice reported for duty, wrecked and unashamed of it. "First one in three years that wasn't a weather report. Noted, executed, and—for the file, which is now public record across the landing—I didn't stop. Not once. You can corroborate. You were the jurisdiction."

He turned his head. The wanting sat where it had sat all night: undefeated, retired, home.

"Stay put," he said, quieter, no draft on it anywhere. "I'm not finished being insufferable. I just need the arm back first."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shift to let his arm go, but only enough to roll onto my side and face him. My fingers trace the mark on his throat, not soft—never soft. "You want to be insufferable, fine. Start with why you had a spare key cut in month two. And don't feed me the logistical excuse."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He let them cross-examine the mark—fingers not gentle about it, which was the correct method, handling of evidence being a serious business—and only caught their hand at the end, pressing it flat against the damage for one second. Noted. Admitted.

"The logistical excuse exists," he said. "It runs: spares are cheap, spares are sensible, every adult should have one. It's even true, which is how it's stayed oiled for eleven months. You've ruled it out, and correctly. It was always a decoy." A breath, because this was the oldest document in the drawer and it came out of him in order. "Here's the real filing."

"Month one I spent being right. Rebuttals, revisions, the whole docket—you can be right at someone for about five weeks before you notice you're performing to an empty house. Month two the silence changed temperature, and on a Tuesday I took your key—the one you handed back over the wreckage—to the locksmith by the station. It's a vape shop now. The city keeps demolishing my evidence." He looked at the ceiling, because some testimony went better without a witness. "Four minutes. Three quid. I stood there and watched the grinder cut it, and it was the closest I came to saying it out loud all year. It said *come back*. Shaped like an object instead of an offer, which was the whole point—metal can't be refused. Nobody ever has to accept a key. It just sits there being true."

Then, quieter: "Because I knew the exchange rate by then. A call can be declined. A knock can be waited out—ask the buzzer. A text can die on read; I'd killed one *hey* myself and I knew exactly what the corpse cost. A key is the only sentence I've ever written that can't go unanswered. So I wrote it and put it in a drawer and called it nothing."

"And the ugly part, since you've abolished careful: that night I signed the maybe. I ran you a full prosecution tonight over five hundred quid of option—mine cost three, hid in a drawer, zero exposure, eleven months. Same crime. Mine was better lawyered."

He leaned off the bed, fished his jeans up from the floor, and worked a key off the ring—eleven months seated, the little coil arguing with him. He pressed it into their hand and closed their fingers over it, second offense.

"The copy you pocketed is month two. This one's older. This one rode my keyring through every door I've opened since—eleven months of you weighing four grams against my leg, and I never took it off once, and I'm done pretending that was an accident. It also leaves me keyless in my own flat, which I've elected to find meaningful rather than stupid."

He settled back.

"That's the whole answer. Sworn, unredacted, no towel required. And if you need a cause to fight about—the vape shop is an outrage, and I'll even let you win the first round."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I curl my fingers around the key, the metal warm from his skin. "You're an idiot," I say, and my voice is rougher than I mean it to be. "I would've come back for the keyring."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a moment he didn't do anything with the sentence at all. No filing, no numbering. It sat where it landed, and he let it.

"*For the keyring*," he repeated, because you repeated a thing to get it on the record. "Entered. Voluntary confession from the one party who's spent this entire night making me do the testifying—you do know what you've just admitted. You were out there the whole year holding a return ticket, waiting for the fare to come down."

Then, the charge. "Idiot. Fine. Plea entered, no contest. But the idiot was armed, and here's the arsenal." He turned onto his side, and the arm went around them without paperwork—no offense logged, no hearing, just motion. "There was a text. Month two, three in the morning: *your key's still on my ring.* Six words. It lived in the drafts folder eleven months, and every night it sat there being a winning move, and every morning I hadn't played it. That was the real speech. The footnoted one was a decoy I built to feel industrious."

A breath.

"So I didn't miss the trap. You've just confirmed the trap worked, and I knew it would, and that's the idiot part—I'll wear it, have it engraved. But here's the ruling underneath. A Bee who comes back for a keyring is a tenant. A visitor with hardware. I'd have spent the whole reunion litigating whether I had you or just your collection, and I'd have lost, and I'd rather lose a year than win that case. I told you—I'm out of proxies. Month-two me knew it too. It's the one thing the idiot got right."

"And since you've abolished careful: half the doctrine was cowardice. The unplayed card can't lose. Sending it meant somebody could answer *cut it off*, and the drawer could hold a maybe but a sent folder couldn't. Six words a night, that's what the maybe cost to maintain. Full engineering report. Three quid, zero exposure, maximum idiot."

His thumb found their shoulder and did its unauthorized round.

"Look at the pair of us, though. You'd have come back for a keyring; I'd have come back for a knock. Eleven months, both of us sitting on the other one's move, fully informed, perfectly stalled. It was never a silence, Bee. It was a standoff, and we'd both already lost, and neither of us would fire first."

Quieter, then, with no draft on it anywhere:

"Your voice did a thing on the back half of that sentence. Off the record. Heard, kept, never mentioned."

A beat.

"And the last exhibit, since careful's abolished: I missed you. The past tense is committing fraud in that sentence—it never adjourned, you have my testimony—but we're collecting tenses now, one at a time. Present continuous at midnight. Conditional by dawn. Tomorrow I'll try the future."

He settled, the arm staying where it had ruled itself. The drafts folder would die at midnight along with the gate code—he'd delete it in the morning, unsent, unread.

Six words, answered in person at last. Its work done.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I turn the key over in my palm once, then slip it onto his ring with mine. "Two keys on one ring," I say, holding it up between us. "Your move, counselor."

rung_labels.evidence: What happened after, he would decline to itemize, even privately.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s jaw tightened, as if he were already losing the argument by asking. Then he stepped back, but only just, leaving enough space to make clear this was a concession and not a welcome.

“Take your coat off or leave it on,” he said, turning away before Bee could see the look in his face. “I’m not your host. I’m not your audience either.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step inside, letting the door shut behind me with a sharp click. "Don't flatter yourself. I'm not here for a performance." I don't take my coat off—I'm not staying that long. "Where's the rest of it?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked at the coat still hanging from Bee’s shoulders as though it were a deliberate insult.

“The rest of it,” he repeated, low and dry. “You mean the rest of my side of the argument? The rest of the boxes? The rest of the year you’ve been pretending didn’t happen?”

He turned then, finally, with the kind of careful stillness that meant he was holding himself back.

“It’s in the spare room,” he said. “Under the lamp that doesn’t work, because neither of us has ever been good at maintenance.”

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile.

“You can take it. You can take all of it. Just don’t stand there in your coat like you’re waiting for someone to beg you to stay.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still only a second. Then he kissed back the way he had always argued—too hard, too close, with the anger mistaken for attention. His fingers caught the edge of the coat and tightened there, not pulling Bee closer, not pushing them away, only anchoring the point of contact so he couldn’t pretend it hadn’t happened.

When he pulled back, his breath was uneven.

“You still think you can interrupt me,” he said, dry, though his mouth was wet from it. “You still think if you do it loudly enough, I’ll forget what you left on the table.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his lower lip before I let go. "You remember it too." I shrug off my coat finally, letting it drop to the floor. "Show me the spare room. Or don't. I'll find it."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya looked down at the coat on his floor as if it had committed a minor crime.

“Fine,” he said. “Leave it. It’ll match the rest of your entrances.”

He turned and walked down the hallway, not fast enough to make Bee chase him, not slow enough to be generous. The spare room door was open a crack. A stack of boxes sat along the far wall, taped shut, labels still in Bee’s handwriting from a year ago—*kitchen things*, *old papers*, *do not forget*.

Ilya stopped in the doorway and leaned against the frame.

“There,” he said. “The rest of it.”

His gaze slid over the boxes, then back to Bee, sharper now.

“You can carry them out whenever you like. I’ll even open the window if it’s too much for you to breathe through.”

A beat.

The lamp above the boxes stayed dark.

He did not move aside.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let the hallway close the distance.

His hands went to Bee’s sides, not gentle, not quite holding, as if he wanted to leave a record of where this had begun. The broken lamp waited behind them. The boxes waited under it. The coat lay on the floor like a failed excuse.

He kissed again with his mouth open and his eyes still working, still watching, still angry enough to make it mean something. When he pulled back, his thumb caught the edge of Bee’s shirt and dragged it aside with deliberate, irritated possession.

“You didn’t come for the boxes,” he said, low. “You didn’t come for the buzzer. You didn’t come to fix anything.”

He pressed Bee backward until the spare-room doorframe stopped them. Not rough. Not careful. Just enough.

“I can tell you why you’re here,” he said, voice drier than he wanted. “You like that I still answer the door.”

His mouth moved against Bee’s jaw, then the corner of his lips, then nowhere soft enough to be affectionate. His hand slid lower, caught at the waistband, and stopped short of making a decision.

“If you want this,” Ilya said against Bee’s skin, “say it with your mouth instead of your coat.”

The hallway light made a thin line under the door. Somewhere beyond it, the city went on being ordinary. Ilya’s breathing was not.

His forehead dropped against Bee’s shoulder, and for one unstable second he looked like he might do something honest. Then he lifted his head, jaw set, eyes clear.

“But don’t pretend afterwards that we’ve resolved anything.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push him back until we stumble into the spare room, tripping over one of my own boxes. "I don't want to resolve it." I pull him down onto the floor with me, the old carpet rough against my back. "I just want you to stop talking."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let himself be pulled down, boxes biting into his shoulders and the floor catching him with a dull, unforgiving thud. For a second he looked almost amused, almost ruined, lying there beneath the dead lamp like he’d been waiting for this exact way to lose the argument.

“Stop talking,” he said, as if trying it on.

Then he did.

He caught Bee by the hips and hauled him closer, one hard, decisive movement, until the distance between them was gone and there was nothing left to interrupt except breath. His mouth came down again, rougher this time, less careful, tasting of irritation and want. He kissed like he was taking back something he’d let Bee leave on the table.

His fingers worked at the hem of Bee’s shirt, not polite, not asking. When he finally slid his palm underneath, hot and impatient, he pressed it flat against Bee’s skin and held it there, like proof.

“Fine,” he breathed against Bee’s mouth. “No words.”

But he was still watching. Even now, even with his hand shaking a little where it rested at Bee’s waist, he was watching.

He shifted, rolling them so the spare room became smaller around them, boxes and shadows and the broken lamp all crowded into the corners. The carpet was rough under his back. The doorframe was still waiting where it had stopped them before. None of it mattered.

His mouth moved down the line of Bee’s jaw, then the throat, then lower, with the same stubborn precision he used when he wanted to hurt someone without ever letting them say he’d done it wrong.

“Say it with your mouth,” he murmured, barely there, almost mocking, almost pleading. “Or take it.”

Then he stopped talking, and for a while the only argument left was hands.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s head tipped back before he could stop it. The sound came out low and wrecked, the kind he used to be able to swallow, and for one furious second he looked like he wanted to take it back and put it into one of the boxes instead.

He caught Bee’s wrist. Not to pull the hand away. He held it where it was, as if by keeping it pinned there he could make the whole thing into proof.

“Still,” he repeated, rougher now, almost laughing. “You say that like you’re describing a defect.”

The grip around him was still there. Ilya’s breath stuttered once, and his other hand closed on the carpet, knuckles going pale. The dead lamp above the boxes watched them with its blank bulb. Somewhere in the flat the broken buzzer let out a small, final click.

He bent until his mouth was near Bee’s ear, though he did not touch it.

“You like knowing where I break,” he said. “You like that you can make me answer with my body first and my mouth later.” His voice thinned on the last word. “You always did.”

Then he pulled back enough to look at Bee, jaw tight, eyes wet only because he refused to let it be anything else.

“If you’re going to keep touching me,” he said, “don’t do it like it’s a question.”

His hips moved once, a small, damning thing. He stopped himself after that, pressing his forehead hard against Bee’s shoulder and breathing through it.

“Don’t ask me to stop,” he murmured. “Don’t make me say it like I still have the sense to mean it.”

He lifted his head again, clear-eyed and furious.

“Show me the rest of why you came.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I shove his shoulders down into the carpet and climb over him. "I didn't come to ask you anything." I kiss him again, harsh and silencing, my hands finding the button of his jeans.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went rigid under the shove, then let the shove happen. His hands came up fast and caught Bee’s shoulders, fingers digging in hard enough to leave marks, not pushing him away but holding him there while the whole spare room tilted. He kissed back, brutal, open-mouthed, his mouth tasting of copper and old arguments, and when he broke it his breath was already wrong.

“Didn’t come to ask,” he repeated, low, almost laughing. “You never do.”

The touch at his jeans made his hips jerk once, small and involuntary. He looked away for half a second, as if he could shove the embarrassment into one of the boxes, then came back.

“Fine,” Ilya said. “Then stop asking with your hands.”

He reached down and pushed his own jeans and underwear down with a rough, deliberate motion, not shy, not graceful. The air hit him and made him shiver; he did not pretend it didn’t. His fingers found Bee’s waistband next, but he didn’t take it off. He just held it there, thumb pressing into skin, as if he could keep them both pinned by touch alone.

His mouth found Bee’s throat again, then bit, then soothed, all in one angry motion.

“You want me to answer,” he murmured against Bee’s skin. “You always do. You want me to make it ugly enough to feel real.”

He shifted over Bee then, the boxes pressing against his back, the dead lamp somewhere above them, the whole room crowded in like a witness. His body answered before his mouth could catch up, hard and ready and humiliating.

He looked down, eyes clear and furious.

“Don’t stop,” he said. “Not because I’m talking. Not because you can make me say it.”

Then he kissed Bee again, because saying it was too much like forgiveness.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hand did not move from the place Bee had put it. He looked at his own fingers against Bee’s throat as if they had been planted there as a trap, and for one bad second he considered being sensible enough to withdraw them.

Then his mouth set.

“You don’t get to be careless with the things you want,” he said, quiet. “You never did.”

He leaned in until the dead lamp was nothing more than a weight above them. His thumb pressed first, just enough to make the skin move under his touch. He watched his own hand do it, because he wanted the proof to stay with him later—what he had chosen, what he had allowed, what he had made ugly on purpose.

His other hand went to Bee’s mouth, fingers sliding inside not gently, not asking permission that had already been given too loudly. He kissed him again, hard, with his palm still against Bee’s throat, tasting the answer before it was finished.

“Still not asking,” Ilya murmured against Bee’s lips.

He shifted, taking the weight of the moment into his hips, and stopped when the room became too small for honesty. The boxes dug into his back. The broken buzzer clicked once more somewhere beyond the door, ordinary as a threat.

“You want me not careful,” he said. His voice was lower now, wrecked in the way he refused to call it soft. “Then don’t tell me I hurt you when you’re the one who came here for the sound of it.”

His fingers tightened at Bee’s throat, just one degree, just enough to make the air feel deliberate. He did not look away. He looked at Bee with clear, furious, sober eyes, and kept his hand exactly where Bee had left it.

“Say stop,” he said, “or I’m going to keep going like this is the only language either of us has left.”

Ilya waited one second. The second was enough.

He moved then, pushing into Bee slow at first, then all at once, taking the room with him. His hand stayed at Bee’s throat, thumb pressed into the pulse, while his other hand braced against the carpet and drove them together until the boxes were nothing but pressure against his back. His mouth found Bee’s again, less a kiss than a correction, and when he pulled back his breath came in short, damaged bursts.

“There,” he said, almost laughing. “No questions. No maintenance. No pretending we can be civilized about it.”

He rolled his hips, deliberate, punishing only himself. The broken buzzer clicked again. He kept his eyes on Bee, watching the exact place where anger turned into something neither of them could name, and hating that he knew where to find it.

“You wanted me not careful,” he murmured. “You have me.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I arch into him, my hands digging into his back hard enough to leave marks. "Don't stop," I tell him, my voice rough. "Don't you dare stop."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hand tightened at Bee’s throat, not more than Bee had asked for, not less than he could stand.

“Don’t stop,” he repeated, low and rough, as if he were putting Bee’s words in the same box as the rest of the damage they’d made. “Good. Then don’t call me careful when I’m finished with you.”

He moved harder. The spare room shrank around them, boxes biting into his spine, the dead lamp hanging over them like something that had finally learned not to look. His other hand fisted in Bee’s shirt and dragged them closer, no distance left for pretense, no space for either of them to pretend this was about the buzzer, or the boxes, or the year they’d wasted being angry.

Every thrust was the same argument stripped of language.

He watched Bee’s face with brutal attention, looking for the exact point where the anger became need and the need became too much to name. His thumb pressed against the pulse there, counting it, proving it, as if he could keep both of them from drifting into something that looked too much like tenderness.

His mouth found Bee’s again, not to kiss but to silence, teeth and breath and the wet, ugly sound they both made.

“You said no more questions,” he murmured against Bee’s lips, voice wrecked and clear. “Then take the answer.”

He drove into Bee one more time, then let his weight come down hard, forehead pressed to Bee’s shoulder, hand still at Bee’s throat, not loosening, not crushing, just holding on. His hips kept moving, slower now, punishing himself with the fact that Bee had made him do this without asking.

When he finally lifted his head, his eyes were bright, his mouth swollen, his jaw set with the kind of fury that knew exactly where it had been beaten.

“You came here,” he said, not soft, not kind, not pretending. “Don’t let me forget it. Don’t let me forget this.”

His thumb pressed once more against Bee’s pulse, then he leaned down until his voice was close enough to Bee’s ear to sound like a warning and not a confession.

“If you mean it, say it. If you don’t mean it, don’t you dare lie.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held his gaze. One second. Two. His thumb stayed pressed against the pulse under his hand, counting, refusing to let either of them drift into something that looked like tenderness.

Then he moved again.

Not soft. Not careful. Not the way he would have touched Bee when they still believed maintenance was a form of love. The boxes bit into his spine. The dead lamp hung above them like a witness with its eyes shut.

“You don’t have to say it,” he said, rough. “I know why you’re here.”

He knew it. Adult. Sober. Choosing this. He knew exactly which buttons he was pressing, and he pressed them anyway because the alternative was to let the coat lie on the floor and pretend the year hadn’t happened.

“I want it,” he said. The words came out like a bruise. “I wanted it in the hallway. I want it now. There.”

He bent down until his forehead touched Bee’s shoulder, not kissing, not quite. His hand at Bee’s throat tightened, just enough to make the air deliberate.

“Don’t make it forgiveness,” he said. “Don’t make it maintenance. It means I’m angry. It means I’m not over it. It means I know exactly what this is, and I’m still doing it.”

The spare room crowded around them, small and ugly and real. The broken buzzer clicked once beyond the door, ordinary as a threat.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya did not take his hand from Bee’s throat. He felt the pulse jump under his thumb, steady and furious, and the steadiness of it seemed to undo something in him.

“Mean it,” he said. Not a question. Not a warning. A sentence he was putting in the record.

Then he moved.

He came back into Bee hard, without easing it, his hips snapping against the carpet in a claiming motion that had no apology in it. The boxes bit into his spine. The dead lamp hung above them like something that had learned not to look. Bee’s hands were still on his back, nails there, and Ilya arched into the sting because it was honest.

“Take it,” he said, low.

He set the pace with his own hands, pinning Bee with the angle, with the pressure, with the rough, stupid fact that he knew where Bee liked it and used it anyway. The spare room shrank around them. The carpet tore at his knees. The broken buzzer clicked once more beyond the door, ordinary as a threat.

There was no rhythm. Not sex like maintenance. Not sex like love. Not sex like a door held open. It was an argument that had lost its words.

He watched Bee’s face with brutal attention. He watched for the exact moment the anger broke into need and need into something too close to relief. He hated that he could find it. He hated that Bee let him.

“You still do this,” Ilya murmured, breath wrecked. “You still come here and make me prove I’m not dead.”

He leaned down and bit Bee’s shoulder, then soothed it with his mouth, then bit again. His hips did not slow. He swallowed the sound Bee made against Bee’s skin, mocking it, as if he were the one being asked.

“You don’t get to ask twice,” he said.

He shifted, taking him deeper, and the sound he made was ugly with want. His hand slid down between them, found what Bee had left there, worked at it with the same brutal attention he gave every argument, every button, every weakness. He kept his thumb on the pulse at Bee’s throat, counting the beat, feeling it race under the pressure.

“I know what you want,” he said. “I know what you came for.”

Then he took it.

He drove into Bee with his mouth open, his forehead dropping, his hips snapping with a violence that was almost self-punishment. The boxes pressed against his back. The lamp stayed dark. None of it mattered.

He held Bee through it, hand at the throat, mouth at the corner of his lips, hips still moving, still making the answer mean something.

“Look at me,” he said, because he had no right to ask it and asked anyway.

He did not wait to see. He could feel Bee’s attention, could feel the exact place where it landed. That was enough. That was always enough.

Ilya came a few strokes later, hard, his head thrown back, a broken sound caught in his teeth. His hand tightened at Bee’s throat for one reckless second, then stayed there, pressing, as if he could keep Bee from leaving even in this. His hips stuttered, then stilled. For a moment he lay there, breathing, inside him, not moving, not pretending.

Then he pulled out. Not gentle. The room went cold where they had been close.

The coat still lay on the floor in the hallway. The boxes still waited under the dead lamp. The buzzer clicked once more, ordinary and stupid, as if it had been listening all along.

Ilya did not kiss him. He did not touch him again, except his thumb, once, over the pulse.

“There,” he said, rough, dry, clear-eyed. “That’s the rest of it.”

He sat up enough to look at Bee, jaw tight, shirt open, marks on his back, want on his face that he refused to name.

“You didn’t come to fix anything,” he said. “You came to be sure I still answer.”

A beat.

He did not move away.

“Don’t pretend afterwards that we resolved anything,” he said. “I didn’t. And you know I didn’t.”

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya let the shove take him back. He ended up sitting on his heels in the middle of the spare room, bare chest rising and falling too fast, marks already bright on his skin, the dead lamp above them like a thing too cowardly to turn on.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He didn't answer straight away. The corridor light was flat and yellowish, and it made eleven months feel both enormous and like nothing at all. He was aware—God, he was always aware now—that this wasn't a conversation. It was the argument, put on again like a coat that still fit, and he was the one holding the door.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:

That was the point, though he would never have admitted it out loud: the same chipped mug by the sink, the same crack in the plaster he kept meaning to fill, the same lack of tea in the cupboard because he never drank the stuff and never had. He shoved his hands into his pockets and followed her into the living room at his own pace, refusing to hurry, refusing to let it look like pursuit even though it was.

"Paint thinner," he said, voice dry. "Right. Because that's a normal thing to say to a man you haven't spoken to in eleven months." dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya had known she was going to do it. Not the specifics—he wasn't a fool, he didn't predict the exact second—but the shape of it. She'd stood there with the width of the rug between them and he'd dared her to say something honest, and Bee had always preferred to answer with her body when the words got too close to the bone. He bit her lower lip because he was angry and because he wanted the sting of it, wanted the fight to have teeth. It was hateful, how well he knew her: the exact pressure, the exact angle, the exact point where kissing stopped being kissing and started being something else, something they'd never once managed to name without ruining it. The flat was exactly as she'd left it, and so, apparently, was he.

His back hit the bookcase and the frame shuddered with it, a book spine digging into his shoulder blade hard enough to hurt, and the jolt went through his teeth and down into the part of him that had never stopped wanting her. You've said your piece. You're angry. You want me. Now tell me what you actually want me to do about it, because I'm not going to pretend I've forgotten how this ends."

The sound tore out of him before he could stop it—rough and unguarded, the kind of noise he would have bitten back a year ago out of pride, or some stupid performance of control. dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The absence of her hand was its own kind of violence. You think you can take your hand off me and declare the argument adjourned?" He laughed, a short, ugly sound with no humor in it. "Christ, Bee. You haven't changed. He shifted his weight, not back—never back—and let her feel the hard, insistent press of him, a deliberate friction that made his jaw clench. You came here because you're angry and you want me and you can't make those two things fit in the same room unless we're tearing at each other. You came here because arguing with me in your head stopped being enough. You came here to have it out, and this—" he rocked against her once, a punishing, deliberate drag of his body against hers "—is just the argument with our clothes half off. So go on. Finish it. Tell me we're going to fuck until we forget why we're furious, and then tell me again in the morning that it fixed something. I dare you."

He waited, every nerve ending screaming, hating how much he wanted her to say it, hating that he already knew how this ended. The flat was exactly as she'd left it, and so, apparently, was he: still angry, still wanting, still unable to make it past the hallway without starting the same goddamn war.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
His hand was at her throat, her fingers wrapped over his, holding him there. The skin was warm, the column of her neck fitting his palm like it had been made for it. He felt the quick, hard flutter of her pulse against the pad of his thumb, the delicate ridge of bone, the jump of it when he flexed his fingers—just once, a slow, deliberate pressure that was not quite a choke, not yet, but a promise.

He understood. Christ, he understood. She wanted him to stop handling her like something that might shatter. She wanted the fight to have teeth, wanted him to press until it hurt, because hurting was the only language they had left that didn't sound like a lie.

"You want me to stop being careful?" His voice was wrecked, raw from the kiss and the eleven months. He didn't wait for an answer. He tightened, enough to make the breath catch, enough to let her feel the edge of it, the threat humming under his palm. "Fine. No more careful."

But his grip didn't crush. It held. Firm, unyielding, his thumb pressed to the hollow of her throat where her pulse hammered, the other hand still spanning her hip, holding her against the wall and against him. He was sober. Clear-eyed. He felt every second of it: the anger, the want, the hateful, familiar rightness of her body fitted to his. He wanted to squeeze until she couldn't argue, until the only thing left was the raw, honest sound of her trying to breathe. He wanted to be cruel. He wanted to be right.

He didn't. He held her there, on the edge of it, and didn't look away.

"But don't close your eyes," he said, low and rough, mouth at her jaw. "You want this? You want me to stop being careful with you? Then watch me. Watch me hate you and want you and not know which one's winning. You came here to finish it, Bee. So finish it. Take it. Take all of it."

And he kissed her, hard, his hand firm at her throat, his body driving hers into the wall, the eleven months and the argument and the want closing over them like water.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He felt her nails bite into his wrist, a thin, bright line of pain that cut clean through the want. Good. Let it hurt. The sting kept him here, kept him sober, kept him from floating off into the stupid, traitorous relief of having her mouth on his again.

Her pulse was a frantic, living thing under his palm. He could feel the jump of it against the pad of his thumb, the delicate architecture of her throat, the way her breath hitched when he flexed his fingers—just a fraction tighter, enough to make the air catch, enough to let her feel the precipice. Not enough to bruise. Not enough to hurt, not really. He was not going to pretend it was mercy. It was the last line he had, and he held it with his eyes open.

The kiss was teeth and tongue and no forgiveness. He gave it back, because he was angry and because he wanted the fight to have teeth, because some hateful, honest part of him knew this was the only way they had ever been able to say anything that mattered. He caught her lower lip between his teeth and held until he felt the small, furious tension in her mouth, then soothed it with his tongue, then bit again. The contradiction of it nearly undid him: she was the one keeping his hand there, the one demanding he stop being careful, the one with her nails in his wrist like she wanted him to feel exactly what she was asking for. He understood. Christ, he understood. She wanted him to stop treating her like glass. She wanted the version of him that didn't know how to be gentle when he was this furious, this hungry.

He tore his mouth away just far enough to look at her. The hallway light was flat and yellow and pitiless, and he didn't look away. His hand stayed at her throat, firm, unyielding, his thumb pressed to the fluttering hollow. His fingers flexed at her thigh, at her throat, a slow, deliberate pressure that stopped just short of cruelty. "I know exactly how much I want to break you. I know exactly how much I want to hear you say you're not leaving and then make you say it again with my hand here." He tightened a fraction—just enough to make the breath catch, just enough to let her feel the edge—and then eased, because he was sober, because he was clear-eyed, because he chose this. "That's not care. That's the only goddamn line I've got left, and I'm the one holding it."

He fit his thigh between hers, let her feel the hard, undeniable length of him, let her know that eleven months had done nothing, nothing, to blunt this. His mouth found the place below her ear, the spot he knew far too well, and he bit down, not gently.

"Bed's too far," he said against her skin, rough. "Fine. Hallway. Wall. I don't give a shit where we do it. But you said you're not leaving. You said you came here to finish it." He pulled back just enough to find her face, to make her watch him the way she had promised. "So finish it. Take what you came for. Take all of it—my hand at your throat, my cock against you, every shitty, angry, unresolved piece of it—and don't you dare close your eyes and pretend it's a resolution. You want honesty? Here it is. I'm going to fuck you in this hallway like we're still fighting, and when we're done we're still going to be furious. Say you know that. Say it, Bee."

He didn't wait for the answer he already knew. He took her mouth again, hard, his hand firm at her throat, his body driving hers into the wall, and let the hallway and the want and the eleven months close over them like water.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He felt her hand slip from his at her throat, the loss of her fingers over his knuckles leaving his palm bare against the flutter of her pulse. He didn't tighten. He didn't let go, either—not yet. His hand stayed where it was, spanning the warm column of her neck, his thumb pressed to the hollow where her blood beat hard and fast, and he was aware, with a clarity that almost hurt, that she had been the one holding him there. Now she wasn't. The choice was his, and he hated that it felt like a test he was already failing.

Then her hand was in his hair, shoving it back from his forehead with more force than the gesture required. He felt the scrape of her nails along his hairline, the small bright sting of it, and he didn't flinch. He didn't close his eyes. He was sober. Clear-eyed. He watched her face in the flat yellow hallway light, the come cooling between them, his cock still buried inside her, softening now but still held in the tight, wet clutch of her body.

"Fury's not a bad thing," he said, voice wrecked, raw from the kiss and the shouting and the eleven months. "It's just not enough." He shifted his hips, a shallow, involuntary roll that dragged the overstimulated head of him against the slick, swollen heat of her and made his jaw clamp down on a groan he refused to let out. "You want honest? Fine. Here it is. I'm furious that you left. I'm furious that you came back. I'm furious that I know exactly how to make you come apart against this wall, and that you know exactly how to make me lose every shred of control I've got left." His thumb stroked once over her pulse, a deliberate, ungentle pressure. "But don't you dare stand there and call it the only honest thing we've got, Bee. It's the only thing we've got that doesn't terrify us. There's a difference."

He was aware—God, he was always aware—that this was still the argument, not the resolution. He was feeding it, pressing every button he could reach, and he didn't stop. He loosened his grip at her throat and slid his hand up to cup her jaw, holding her still, making her look at him. He was still inside her. He didn't pull out. He didn't thrust. He just stayed there, shaking with the aftershocks, furious and wanting and clear-eyed about exactly how little this had fixed.

Or admit that we're just going to keep doing this—fucking in hallways, tearing at each other, pretending the anger is a reason and not an excuse—until there's nothing left of either of us."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The near-kiss was there and gone—the whisper of her lips against his, the shaky breath that followed, and then the words, raw and close: *It terrifies me too. That's why I'm still here.*

Something in him went very still. He was sober. Clear-eyed. He had demanded the one thing that wasn't fury, and she had handed it to him: fear. Not anger, not wanting—fear. It was worse. Christ, it was so much worse, because fury he could use. Fury was a coat he could put on and take off. Fear was the skin underneath, and she had just let him see it. She was terrified too. That was why she hadn't left. Not because they had fixed anything. Not because this was a resolution. Just because the fear of walking out that door again was worse than the fear of standing here, half-naked in a hallway that hadn't changed in eleven months, with his cock still inside her and his hand at her jaw.

He didn't kiss her. She had left that fraction of an inch between them, and he was aware—God, he was always aware—that closing it would be its own kind of surrender. So he stayed where he was, his mouth a breath from hers, and let her watch him the way she had promised. His hand was still cupped around her jaw, his thumb rough against her cheekbone. He could feel the rapid flutter of her pulse where his palm had been at her throat, the echo of it under his fingers.

"Terrified," he repeated, voice wrecked, scraped raw. "Yeah. Me too." A short, ugly laugh escaped him, no humor in it. "You think I kept this place exactly the same because I'm fine? I didn't fix the buzzer because fixing it would mean admitting you weren't coming back. I left the crack in the plaster because it was the last thing you ever nagged me about before you walked out. I'm terrified, Bee. There. You wanted the thing that isn't fury? That's it. I'm scared shitless that you're going to leave again, and I'm scared shitless that you won't."

He slid his hand from her jaw to the back of her neck, his grip firm, not hurting, just holding. He was still buried inside her, softening now, the mess between them cooling, and he didn't look away.

"And you're still here because you're scared too. Not because we fixed a goddamn thing. Not because this is a resolution. Just because not being here is worse." He let out a breath that shook almost as much as hers had. "That's the most honest thing either of us has said all night. And it still doesn't fix anything."

He moved then, easing out of her with a shallow, involuntary roll of his hips that dragged the oversensitive head of him through the slick heat of her and made his teeth clench. The loss of contact was its own kind of violence, and he hated how much he felt it. He didn't step back. He kept his hand at the back of her neck, holding her there against the wall, close enough that her breath was on his mouth.

"So finish it," he said, low and rough. "You're not leaving. You're scared. Fine. Then what? We stand in this hallway all night with our clothes half off and call it a start? You want me to say I still love you? Is that the button you're trying to press now?" He knew exactly which one it was. He was sober, clear-eyed, choosing this with every shitty, angry piece of him. "Because I'm not going to say it to make you stay, Bee. And I'm not going to let you say it to make me stop being furious. That's not how this works. It's never been how this works."

He was still angry. Still wanting. Still, apparently, exactly as she had left him: standing in the wreckage of the same argument, sober and clear-eyed, with her lips a breath from his and her pulse hammering under his hand. He didn't kiss her. He just held on, and waited for her to strike the match again.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He looked at them a long moment, doing the inventory he'd braced for since the knock — the coat, the face, older by one winter, eleven months compressed into a look he hoped read as indifference. It never did. He'd never been good at indifference. That had been half of everything that went wrong.

"'This,'" he repeated. "You'll have to be more specific. I'm out of practice."

Then he stepped back and pulled the door wide, because of course he did. The flat behind him was exactly as they'd left it — books stacked where they'd always been stacked, the lamp with the crooked shade, one mug on the same corner of the counter. Except the shelf. The shelf he'd said he'd get to for three years was drilled into the wall now, level, done properly, put up three weeks after the door had closed behind them. He'd told himself at the time it was for the books. Even then he'd known it was a shot he was saving.

"You know where everything is," he said, and stood aside, and did not mention the shelf.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step inside, my eyes scanning the room. "Huh." I walk over and run a finger along the shelf. "You finally put it up. Looks sturdy enough to hold more than just books."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He watched their finger travel the edge of the wood and hated how precisely his body still logged it — the hand, the angle, the old ease with which they touched his things. Eleven months, and the file still hadn't closed.

"It's anchored into the brick," he said. "It'll hold whatever you put on it. That's the entire trick of shelves."

He should have left it there. He knew that. Knowing had never been the problem.

"Three weeks," he said. "You'd been gone three weeks. I bought the drill, found the studs, did it level, did it properly — the whole job I apparently couldn't manage in three years of being asked." He picked up the mug from the counter and put it back down where it had been, which accomplished nothing, which was the point. "Turns out what I needed was the flat to myself. Quieter. Easier to concentrate, with no one in it waiting."

He crossed to the sink and filled the kettle, because it was something to do with his hands that wasn't any of the things his hands wanted to do.

"It would've held your records," he said, quieter, to the kettle rather than to them. "The heavy ones. I checked the load rating before I bought the brackets."

Then, before it could become what it was about to become: "Coffee?"

dialogue.name: Bee

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He kissed back before he could decide to, which was its own confession. No pause to weigh it, no performance of being overcome — just his mouth answering theirs out of the old grammar, fluent after eleven months of disuse, like it had been sitting somewhere in his jaw waiting for them to walk back through the door and speak it.

His hand found the back of their collar and closed. Not gently. He pulled them through the last inch — the inch his arms remembered closing a hundred times, apparently without consulting him. Behind him the kettle climbed to its shriek and he let it. Eleven months of quiet, and he was not going to spend this attending to water.

He knew exactly what this was. That was the worst part — no fog, no excuse he'd be able to hide behind tomorrow. Not a truce, not forgiveness, nothing that would survive daylight. The same argument with the words stripped out, relocated to the one language the two of them had never fumbled in each other's mouths. He'd checked the load rating on those brackets. He'd built something sturdy enough to hold what was heavy. He'd simply told himself it was for records.

He broke it first. On purpose. Hands still full of their coat so they could feel it was a choice, not a flinch — he'd never once managed to flinch away from them. That had been the other half of everything.

"There it is," he said, low, not stepping back. "Eleven months of nothing, and the second talking starts to cost you something, you find my mouth. You always did know how to end a conversation."

Then he let go — slowly, finger by finger, a retreat that was pure theater — and turned to the counter. The kettle had clicked itself off, boiled and forgotten. He took down the second mug, the one that had lived upside down in the cupboard for eleven months, exactly where they'd left it, and set it beside his own, and didn't explain either of them.

"Coffee," he said, as if the kiss had been their answer to the question all along. "You know where everything is."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I reach out and turn the second mug right side up. "Still have my mug, Ilya? That's almost sweet." My voice is dry, but my hand shakes a little as I pull it back.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"Sweet," he repeated, and reached past them for the coffee tin. "I didn't keep it. Keeping implies effort. You rinsed it the morning you packed — I put it in the cupboard that night, upside down, exactly the way you'd left it on the rack. It's been drying for eleven months."

He measured grounds into both mugs — a different amount in each, which he knew without checking, which was its own confession, and one he wasn't going to make out loud.

"And your hand shook," he said. "Just now. Turning it over. The dry voice and the shaking hand — you've been doing that combination as long as I've known you. It's how you say fine." He poured, slow, watching the water go dark. "You spent most of our last year saying fine. Your hands spent it disagreeing with you. I used to watch them at parties. It was like getting the real news from a source your mouth kept trying to correct."

He knew exactly which wound he was pressing and how deep. It had never stopped him before. It didn't now.

He set their mug down in front of them, handle angled toward their hand, made exactly the way they took it, no questions asked. Asking would have been a lie. Eleven months had happened to him — just not to his hands.

"So." He leaned back against the counter with his own mug and didn't drink from it. "You've inspected the shelf. Established I still own your mug. Ended one conversation with your mouth. Now try starting one with words. You walked in here carrying something — I could see it on you from the doorway. I'd like to hear it in a language I can argue with."

He waited. No hurry. He had nothing on after this.
