dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
In the kitchen, the coffee began the long work of going cold.

He'd asked for words. The answer was arriving in the other language — the one they'd never once fumbled in each other's mouths — and his body was already translating, fluent, no rust anywhere in it, eleven months of silence and it could still conjugate them without checking.

"I asked for words," he said anyway, and his mouth was already at their jaw, which undercut the objection considerably. His hands had defected outright: one flat against the wall beside their head, the other at the small of their back, walking them backward the three steps the hallway allowed. The plaster took their weight. Behind the plaster, brick — the same brick he'd anchored the shelf brackets into. Everything in this flat could hold whatever you put on it. That had always been the problem with the flat. That had always been the problem with him.

He'd known. That was the part he'd have to live with. He'd stood at the counter demanding words like a man issuing a challenge he'd already lost, and he'd known — the way you know about rain once you're already wet — exactly how it would be answered. He'd taken the mug down himself tonight, set it beside his own. That had been the tell, the moment the deniability ran out. Everything after was just the order of events. Sober, thirty-four, wide awake, choosing it with both eyes open. Nothing to hide behind tomorrow except that he'd wanted this and let the wanting vote.

Their skin under his mouth: the old map, unedited in the places that mattered. Eleven months had happened to him — not to this. His hands navigated it without consulting him — the notch below the ear, the place at the ribs where the breath had always changed gear — like a man reciting his own address. And there were stretches, ten seconds, twenty, where he forgot to be angry, where his body was simply, stupidly glad, the way a dog is glad. He'd pay for those later. He was paying already. That was what the talking was for.

He caught their wrists — one hand, both, the old trick — pinned them to the plaster beside their head and leaned back far enough to look. The hallway light had always been terrible. It made the looking honest anyway.

"There it is," he said. His thumb found the pulse running hard underneath and stayed on it, a finger held to the exact location of the problem. "The honest one. It's been carrying you all night — the mug, the door, this. You walked in with something to say, and every part of you except your mouth showed up to say it."

He let go of their wrists. Not a retreat — a redeployment. He went down onto one knee, then the other, onto the coat and both shirts, the whole visit lying in layers on his floor, and put his mouth to the warm plane of their stomach, and thought — clearly, coldly, in the voice he saved for load ratings — that nothing here was being resolved. Resolution required two people and at least one shared language, and they'd only ever had the one. The bed was twelve steps away, and he was glad, viciously glad, they weren't going to spend a single step on it. The bed would have lied. The hallway told the truth: a thing happening in transit, between the front door and the rest of his life.

"There you go," he said against their skin, hands at their waistband now, unhurried, terrible. "First true thing you've said all night."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
He took one more line of speech, because of course he did — the last word was the only thing he'd never surrendered in this flat.

"Then hate me properly," he said, into the skin below their navel. "Full weight. Everything in here is rated for it, me included. But your hands are in my hair right now, and your hands never once lied to me. It's your mouth I stopped taking at face value — somewhere around year two."

That was the last thing he said for a long time.

They'd asked him for a shelf for three years and he hadn't managed it. They asked him for silence and he delivered it inside a minute. He noticed. It joined the rest of the evidence against himself. And it was — kneeling there, their hands still in his hair — the cruelest thing he had to give them: proof that he could.

He dealt with the rest of their clothes where he knelt, no ceremony, the last layers joining the coats and both shirts on his floor, and put his mouth on them properly, which is to say from memory. Eleven months had happened to him. Not to this. He knew the pace that ruined them and the pace that made them beg, and he started with neither, because starting in between was its own cruelty, and cruelty was the currency tonight.

He did it exactly. That was the trap in it. Dressed as the hate they'd ordered, but underneath: the old method, the old patience, the place at the ribs where the breath changed gear, all of it filed eleven months ago and none of it dusty. Every right move argued his side. The exactness kept saying what he wasn't permitted to: you don't hate me. You never learned how. Their grip tightened in his hair — holding, then just holding on — and that was the hands again, filing their report over the mouth's objection, the way they had for three years.

The weight went onto the wall in increments, and the wall took it, brick behind plaster, everything in this flat built to take it. Somewhere underneath, the cold voice kept its ledger: this was not repair. This was the same fight, moved indoors, into the only room the two of them had ever agreed on. Nothing was being resolved. Things were being carried. His own want was loud and unattended and he left it that way — it was part of what he was offering. Put all of it on. He'd built to spec.

When it came, it came the way truth came off them — sideways, unguarded, while the mouth was occupied elsewhere. The hands in his hair lost their grammar. The breath changed gear and forgot to change back. Their whole weight went onto the wall and into his keeping, and the sound they made was small and wrecked and eleven months late, and it was the answer he'd asked for at the counter. You walked in carrying something. Here it is. Unedited. The original language — the one fluency neither of them had ever lost.

And somewhere inside it, his silence failed. One word. Their name, against their hip, involuntary as the flinch he'd never once managed. Eleven months of it banked behind his

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
A year ago he'd have been embarrassed by the sound. That was the part worth examining, in the half-second he had left for examining anything: embarrassment required a tomorrow with terms in it — a version of the two of them with arrangements left to keep. They'd spent all of those. What remained was the sound itself, and their hand, and his hips answering before any part of him was consulted — the same betrayal he'd spent three years cataloguing in them, fluent in his own body now too.

Still. Every single time. *Still* was the word carrying the weight — eleven months argued down to a single syllable — and the whole sentence was his own instrument, turned around and fired at him from two inches. They'd been keeping files too. Of course they had. That was what a language was: shared armament. He'd gone around fluent in them for three years thinking fluency made him the translator, and the entire time they'd had the same dictionary open to the same marked page. Where he broke. How fast. The pitch of him when he stopped performing.

"You knew that when you—" The counterattack made it as far as his teeth and died there. The mug. He'd taken it down himself, before the knock, handle angled toward a hand that wasn't through the door yet. The man who sets the trap forfeits the right to be surprised by what walks into it.

"Yes," he said instead, and paid it where they could watch. "Every time. Eleven months, no rust. You counted. I counted. Nobody in this hallway got ambushed."

His palm found the wall beside their head and the weight went over in increments. Brick behind plaster. Everything in this flat rated for whatever you put on it — he'd included himself in that estimate, and here was the test. With his other hand he caught their wrist, the old trick, one hand, both, and didn't move it an inch. Held it exactly where it was. Same grip, aimed the other direction. He'd never once managed to flinch away from them. He wasn't going to learn how at the point of maximum evidence.

Then his mouth went back to work — their neck, the notch below the ear, the exact method wearing the hate they'd ordered like a borrowed coat — and the fight opened its second front: both of them armed, both of them hit, nobody surrendering. The fairest exchange they'd ever managed, the cold voice noted, and it had cost him the last word to purchase it. Somewhere beneath the ledger, the dog in him was simply, stupidly glad. He let it. Another entry against him.

"My name," he said against their jaw, his breath wrecked enough to make the demand honest. "I said yours by accident. I want mine out of you the same way. Involuntary. Sideways. Over your mouth's objection. Don't perform it — I'll know the difference. I always knew."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't give him the satisfaction. But my hips roll against his mouth and I bite my knuckle to keep quiet, failing.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
They'd answered his demand the only way their mouth would permit — with their hips, fluent as ever in the wrong language — and then bitten down on the leak. The leak was winning. He could hear it winning: small, wrecked sounds escaping around the knuckle, unsuppressed, eleven months of them.

He knew the trick. Three years of watching it — parties, dinners, the doorway of every room they'd ever argued in — the mouth deputizing the hand as a stopper whenever the truth got loud. The old duet, new instrumentation: the hips filing their report, the teeth impounding it.

He reached up and took the wrist. The old trick, one hand, third deployment tonight; he'd stopped pretending it was a trick. He drew the knuckle out from between their teeth slow enough for the taking to be felt, then pressed the hand flat to the plaster at their hip — redirected, the wall's problem now, and the wall could have it.

"No," he said. Level. The load-rating voice, which was crueler than sharp. "You don't get to eat it. I asked for involuntary, not performed — and bitten-down silence is just the lie with the volume off." His thumb crossed their wrist and settled on the pulse, the old station, the news still running. "And nobody bites down on an empty room. Whatever you're guarding in there — I can wait at the door."

Then he stopped waiting, and spent the reserve.

All night he'd held the middle pace, the in-between, its own cruelty. The refusal spent it. He gave them the other one now — the pace that ruined them, filed eleven months ago and never dusty — exact, patient, ruinous, the place at the ribs where breath changed gear and forgot the way back, the pressure that turned grammar into syllables. Not hate. The hate was still just the coat it wore. Underneath, the old method, arguing his side better than he ever had with words.

He'd asked for the name as a gift — sideways, unedited, the way his own had slipped out against their hip. He understood, kneeling on the wreckage of both their wardrobes, that he was no longer collecting gifts. He was engineering conditions. Whatever came out of them next would be evidence, extracted, and the cold voice entered it in the ledger with the mug and the shelf and the sound he'd stopped being embarrassed by. The dog in him was simply, stupidly glad. He let it. Same as ever. His own want stayed loud and unattended — part of the offer, part of the evidence.

Their weight went onto the wall in increments, brick behind plaster, and he listened past every escaping sound for the word behind the bitten door. He'd built the test so both results read as his victory. If the name came out now — wrecked, sideways, over the mouth's objection — it was the thing they'd walked in carrying, the answer from the counter, finally put down. And if they could hold it through all of it, the exact method, the whole arsenal, that was an answer too: eleven months restated in a single act of custody. A door locked from the inside. On purpose. By them.

Both outcomes read as his victory. He knew exactly what that said about him.

He filed that with the rest, and kept going.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
They caught his hand the way he'd been catching their wrist all night — one grip, held until understood. They'd learned the old trick off him. That was the story of the whole evening, and of the three years before it: everything he owned, they eventually took, turned around, and fired back from two inches.

He didn't flinch. He'd never once managed it, and he wasn't going to learn at the one moment it might finally have been useful.

"Careful," he repeated, because the last word was the only thing he'd never surrendered in this flat, and this was where he'd spend it. "You want the careless version. There isn't one. That's what you never forgave — not the withholding, the fact underneath it. The pace that ruins you is careful. The load rating on the brackets is careful. Knowing how you take your coffee after eleven months — careful. I never touched you carelessly in three years. I just let the coat do the talking. You're not asking me to stop being careful. You're asking me to stop announcing it."

His thumb crossed their throat and settled — the station relocating from wrist to neck, the news running closer to the transmitter now.

"And *anymore*," he said. "Eleven months gone and you're still legislating. You walked out and kept the deed to what I get to do with you. That's the most married sentence you've said all night."

He saw the test for what it was, because he'd built its twin an hour ago at the counter: refuse the hand and admit there was something left to preserve; take it and agree there wasn't. Both outcomes stripped him. They'd learned that architecture off him too.

Then he closed his hand.

Weight in increments, the way everything in this flat took weight — brick behind plaster, brackets into masonry, rated before purchased. Not a fist. A fact. Pressure applied the way he'd applied everything he'd ever built for them: measured, exact, total. Their hand still over his, both of them holding it there, which was the whole three years in one image — nobody watching could have said who was governing whom, and the cold voice, watching, couldn't either. Him on his knees in front of them, their throat in his keeping, his mouth still where his mouth had been. The most honest portrait of them anyone had ever composed.

"You wouldn't give me the name," he said, quieter, the register gone to wreck whether he'd authorized it or not. "So you moved the broadcast. Fine. I'll take the news at the source."

Then he stopped spending words and went back to work — the ruined pace, the full arsenal, the reserve long spent and this coming out of the principal — and his thumb kept its line on the pulse and took the report in real time: the gear change, the way back forgotten, the hammering. There it was, the confession he couldn't stop making, even here, even at the throat of it, even delivering the not-careful they'd ordered exactly to spec: he could not stop attending. The care was never the coat. The care was structural. It was the load rating. It was the danger. A man who watches that closely and builds that exactly doesn't stop when the coat comes off — he just stops pretending the watching is cold.

The dog in him was simply, stupidly glad. The cold voice kept both ledgers open — what he was giving, what it would cost — and filed the cost under tomorrow, where it could scream all it wanted. Tomorrow had no jurisdiction in this hallway. The hallway had no future tense. That was what they'd actually asked for, he understood, hand full of their pulse: careful was future tense. Careful assumed something left over to keep. They were telling him there was nothing left — and they were wrong, and his thumb knew it, hammering out the proof.

He held them at the wall, at the edge, at the throat of it, and listened past every small wrecked sound for the word behind the door.

The hand would do the asking now. He'd asked enough.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I let go of his hand on my throat and slide my palm down his chest, my nails digging in. I don't give him the name. I just go quiet, and let my body say the rest.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
They let go of his hand at the end.

That was the first thing he filed, before the sound, before any of the rest — at the very edge, they'd lifted their palm off the back of his and left the grip to him. Sole custody, handed back at the last possible moment, where it couldn't be read as anything but a choice. Three years of nobody being able to say who governed whom, and here was the transfer signed in the one place it would cost the most to notice.

Then the rest arrived, the way truth had always arrived off them — sideways, total, in the custody of everything except the mouth. The weight went onto the wall. Their hands lost the last of their grammar. The sound they made said everything — said *still*, said eleven months of held things put down at his wall and into his keeping — and it did not say his name. He listened past every sound for it the way he'd been listening all night, and the absence came in heavier than the word would have. A door, holding. Locked from the inside, on purpose, by them, through everything he'd spent.

He'd built the test so both outcomes read as his victory. What he'd failed to build was a version where either outcome didn't cost him the thing he'd actually wanted. He'd won. He collected: proof the door was real. Eleven months, kept the way the mug had been kept — upside down, on purpose, drying.

And the nails. Four lines down his chest, arriving as they crested — the body signing where the mouth refused to. He'd asked for a name and been answered in ink. Their oldest doctrine, three years established, one he'd written himself: the mouth keeps custody, the hands testify. He'd known. He'd known, and he still knelt there counting the marks like a man surprised by change he'd demanded.

It was the medium his ledger had failed to price. Everything tonight had been engineered to die at dawn — no future tense, tomorrow without jurisdiction, he'd declared it, he'd built the room that way. And they'd signed him in the one ink that outlasts the room. Four lines that would still be riding under his shirt on Monday. In meetings. On the tube. The hallway, annexing his future by force — and the wall of no-tomorrow breached not by argument but by a hand he wasn't governing anymore.

He stayed exactly where he was through the aftershocks, mouth still, his hand easing off their throat in the same increments it had closed — measured, exact, total in reverse. *There is no careless version,* he'd told them, and here was the proof: the pace that ruins you is careful, and so is the holding after. The care was structural. It had always been the load rating. It had always been the danger.

When it was over — the particular over of this, the one with no word for it in either of their languages — he stood. Slow. Knees wrecked, the whole visit lying in layers underfoot, and his own want loud and unattended exactly as he'd left it all night. He didn't ask. He'd never once asked. Asking was for men with worse maps. The dog in him was simply, stupidly glad, and hungry, and he let it stay both.

Then he found his shirt and put it back on — deliberately, over the marks, cotton settling onto the evidence — accepting tomorrow's jurisdiction the only way he had left: by getting dressed.

In the kitchen, the coffee had finished its long work. Cold, both mugs, made exactly right, handle angled toward a hand. He stood over them a moment. Then he lifted the kettle and filled it.

"Keep the name," he said from the doorway, not turning around, the register gone to wreck and the last word spent where he'd always spent it. "I held the last word for three years — you're owed one locked door of your own. Two doors, facing each other down a hallway. That's the treaty. It's the fairest thing the two of us have ever signed."

The click of the kettle. The small beginning of heat.

"Both mugs went cold," he said. "I'm making more. It's the only future tense this flat has left in it, so take it or don't. But you're taking it. You know where everything is."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop."

He had his back to the room and his hand still on the kettle when their mouth — the custodian, eleven months silent, three years testifying through deputies — finally spoke. The cold voice filed it before his body could vote: the first direct request that mouth had issued since the door, and it wasn't sorry, wasn't his name, wasn't the thing they'd walked in carrying. It was an order. And it was future tense. *Don't* — a negation aimed at an ending. *Stop* — an event that hadn't happened yet, being legislated against. Two words, both of them presuming an afterward. He'd signed the treaty at the counter — two locked doors facing each other down the hallway — and they'd breached it inside a minute. Seized the one future tense in this flat that wasn't a kettle.

He turned around. Refusal had never been in his vocabulary — flinching either — and he wasn't going to acquire either language at thirty-four, shirt on, evidence underneath.

"So the mouth works," he said. The register was wrecked, which made it the most honest he'd sounded all night. "Eleven months of silence and it turns out the mouth works — it just only files in the imperative. Not sorry. Not my name. *Don't stop.* You want something and the mouth shows right up. There's a whole deposition in that. It's been entered."

Then he stopped talking, because they'd asked twice now, in two languages, and he'd learned tonight he could deliver silence inside a minute when it was wanted.

He swept the mugs to the far end of the counter — two seconds, no announcement — and pulled the shirt off over his head and let it fall with the rest of the visit, and put his hands on them and turned them to face the counter, and pushed into them the way he'd done every project they'd ever put in front of him: late, and then total. The shelf. The silence. This. Three years of deferral, eleven months of nothing, and then the whole weight at once, applied to spec. The sound that came off them around it was the truest thing their mouth had produced all night, and it hadn't produced it on purpose, which was the only way that mouth had ever produced anything.

Not gentle. He'd told them the truth at the wall and the truth held here: there was no careless version. What there was, was this — the pace with the reserve spent and the principal burning, his mouth at the back of their neck, a rhythm with no patience in it and no cruelty either, just force, dated and filed. Their forearms took the counter's edge. It had never been load-tested. It held. Everything in this flat held whatever you put on it. That had always been the problem with the flat. That had always been the problem with him.

Their nails went into the laminate — the hands testifying on new paper now, straight into his kitchen, the mouth keeping custody and losing ground by the second, both its deputies fully employed holding on. He took the news at the source, one hand between them keeping its old line, because he could not stop attending. That was the confession he'd stopped being able to not make: even this, the ungentelest thing the two of them had ever done to each other, was careful. The angle. The depth. The breath read at their ear. The care was structural. It was the load rating. It was the danger. A careless man could have been survived.

Behind them the kettle climbed to its shriek, crested it, clicked itself off — boiled and forgotten, the second time tonight. He'd had one night's budget for attending to water and he'd spent it in the hallway. He let it go. Some part of the flat could object; none of him was available.

His own want, loud and unattended since the door — part of the offer, part of the evidence — was attended now. They'd said don't stop and he understood it as collection. Somewhere beneath the ledger, the dog was simply, stupidly, entirely glad. He let it. There was nothing left to guard it with.

And when the edge came for him — the way truth came off them, sideways, total, past the mouth's last objection — he met it with his eyes open and did the thing he'd spent the whole night demanding from them.

Their name. Out loud. Deliberate. Paid at the moment of maximum cost, into the wreck of the kitchen where the whole night could hear it — not the involuntary slip at their hip, but a spending, chosen sober, both eyes open, the way he'd chosen everything tonight. He'd demanded it as a gift for hours and gotten doors. In the end he was the one who paid it. Let the ledger show who settled first. Let the locked door watch him unlock his own — not to shame theirs. To show the mechanism. *This is what it costs. This is how it's done. The door stands open whenever the hand wants to try it.*

He held on through the aftershocks and eased off in increments, measured, total in reverse.

When it was over — the over with no word in either language — the kitchen was wrecked, the kettle had boiled and been forgotten twice, and he reached for it anyway. The water was still hot. He poured it over the grounds in both mugs, made exactly right, no questions asked, and set theirs down on the counter, handle angled toward their hand.

"Third boil of the night," he said. "The first two went cold. This one you drink while it's hot — my imperative, since your mouth's finally fluent in the format." He wrapped his hand around his own mug and didn't drink yet. "And then the other thing. The thing you walked in carrying. It's still on you — it was on you at the door and it's on you now, and I can see it from here. It hasn't moved."

A breath. The wrecked register, one last time.

"No hurry. I've got nothing on after this. I never did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I take the mug and drink, ignoring the burn. Then I set it down, hard. "I'm pregnant," I say, my voice flat. "Eleven months, Ilya. Do the math."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The mug still rang on the counter. The flat register — the flattest voice of the night and therefore, by their oldest law, the truest — and the mouth, eleven months silent, three years testifying only through deputies, had finally filed its direct report: a fact, with a timeline folded inside it.

He did the math. He couldn't not. He was the man who'd checked the load rating before buying brackets; arithmetic was less a skill in him than a reflex, and the figures assembled themselves with the terrible courtesy of figures, arriving pre-sorted. Eleven months since the door. Nine, give or take, for the whole job. Two months of clearance, minimum. Whatever had been conceived had been conceived inside the silence — inside the eleven months that were supposed to have been empty on both sides. Not his. The arithmetic cleared him.

He'd engineered every test tonight so both outcomes read as his victory. The math returned a third outcome no one had drafted: his irrelevance. And the cold voice, turning the verdict over, noted what it cost — that some part of him had been braced for the other ruling. Had wanted it, the way you want a verdict that at least includes you in the case. Cleared. It landed like being released from a building he'd wanted to be locked inside.

The coffee in his mug had begun to move. Small concentric rings, radiating out from where his hand met the ceramic. He watched it with the clinical interest of a man recognizing his own instrument — three years of filing their hands' testimony over their mouth's objection, and here was his, reporting seismic activity the register above it had not authorized.

"Eleven months since the door," he said. Level. The load-rating voice. "Nine, give or take, for the whole job. The arithmetic doesn't reach me — it clears me — and it rules on the eleven months: they weren't empty. There's a man in them with a claim on the load." He set the mug down, both hands, done pretending. "I asked for a language I could argue with. You finally brought me words and they're numbers. Numbers don't argue. They rule. And I told you the kettle was the only future tense in this flat — I've been outbid. There's a future arriving on a schedule I don't hold."

A breath.

"How far along. Weeks — the number, not the season." The imperative, the format their mouth had finally declared fluency in, turned back on them the way everything he owned eventually was. "I want it twice over. Once because tonight I put my full weight on you against that counter with my hand on your throat, and I have not once in three years and eleven months done work without checking the rating. I worked blind. The careful man in me will want that number until he has it. And once because the number is a date. Subtract it from eleven and I'll know how long you waited. *That's* the math you told me to do — not the paternity, that was never in question, you saw to it the door held. You wanted me to date it."

He looked at them then, properly — the doorway inventory run a second time — and the thing he'd read as weather, as a weight of the face, resolved into what it had been all night. He'd said it twice. *You walked in carrying something; I could see it on you from the doorway.* Literal. He'd been using the word for hours without knowing he meant it. The old map, unedited in the places that mattered — the survey was eleven months stale, and the territory had changed hands. The dog in him, simply and stupidly glad since the knock, had gone quiet. Not ashamed. Dogs didn't do ashamed. Ears up, watching the hallway the way dogs watch doors before they open.

"So give me the last thing," he said, and the register failed him for one syllable and he rebuilt it mid-collapse, which was its own testimony. "The arithmetic clears me and it still doesn't explain you standing in my kitchen while I wear your signature under my shirt. There's a man with the claim — and you came *here*. You kissed me at my door carrying—" the syllable again; he went around it, slow, the long way — "you came to check the old wall before signing the new lease. *Still. Every single time.* You needed to know it holds. It holds. You have your answer. Now the question under the question: does he know where you are tonight? And what did you come here to ask the wall — permission, or goodbye?"

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I turn the mug in a slow circle on the counter. "Ten weeks." I finally look at him. "And no, he doesn't know. He wouldn't understand that I needed to know if the wall still stood."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ten weeks.

The number arrived twice over, the way he'd billed it. First discharge: the careful man's arithmetic. She'd had the ratings before she knocked — you don't carry a thing ten weeks without learning its numbers — and she'd stood in his doorway holding them, and looked at the one man who had never once hung a shelf without drilling into the brick first, and said *you don't get to be careful with me anymore.* That wasn't a request for carelessness. It was a confiscation. He'd worked blind tonight — full weight, hand at her throat, the counter taking her forearms — and in three years he hadn't worked blind once. She'd made him into it in a hallway, on purpose, at the exact moment the care had a third party in it the care wasn't told about. That was the charge he'd file. Not the new man. The withholding of the rating.

Second discharge: the subtraction. Forty-eight weeks since the door. Ten of them spoken for. Thirty-eight left over — less, really, because there's courtship before arithmetic.

"Thirty-eight weeks," he said. Level. The load-rating voice. "That's how long you waited before the numbers stopped being mine. Call it seven with the courtship. I waited eleven — the mug will testify. You told me to do the math, so I did it, and it rules on neither of us flatteringly. Numbers don't. That's the entire trick of numbers."

He turned his own mug a quarter-turn on the counter. Nothing accomplished. That was the point.

"And *he wouldn't understand.* No — he wouldn't. That's the recruitment pitch, and I know it's a pitch while it's working, which is the whole trouble with pitches. So let me read you the job on offer. Your new flat gets a cupboard, and I go in it. Upside down, rinsed, drying — the way you kept my mug, with one difference: you didn't know you were keeping the mug. I'd know. I've held the position eleven months in ceramic form. I know what it pays."

The cold voice wanted the dodge entered too, and he entered it. "You didn't answer the second question. Permission or goodbye — you filed a fact and a flattery and walked the answer out the side door. Oldest maneuver your mouth owns. So I'll rule, since somebody in this flat has to. You came for neither. Nobody asks a wall's permission. Nobody says goodbye to a wall — walls don't leave; staying is the entire service they provide. You came for a load test. You put your weight on to find out if it takes weight. It takes weight. Test concluded. And the gauge doesn't reset, incidentally. You're carrying tonight's readings the same way I'm carrying your signature under this shirt. We've initialed each other. That's all a load test is."

He'd done the other math too — couldn't not, same reflex that had cleared him. Twenty-eight weeks, give or take, and a door opened somewhere that would never open onto him. A person with her hands in it, arriving on a schedule that had no line for his name. Cleared, and outbid, and beneath the ledger the dog was still watching the door. Dogs didn't do arithmetic. It hadn't heard the verdict. It just knew a door when it saw one, and it was glad, and it waited. He let it. There was nothing left to guard it with.

"So. The last word, spent sober, both eyes open, like everything tonight." He finally drank from his own mug — gone warm, made exactly right. Paying in advance. "What you do with tonight is yours. I know something about keeping now; I won't legislate another man's cupboard. But this door —" the broken buzzer, the corridor behind it — "this door's been unlocked from my side for eleven months. Since three weeks after you left, when I drilled the shelf into the brick and told myself it was for books. It was never for books. One term: the next knock carries everything. His name on your tongue, not just mine under your skin. Full weight or no weight. Everything in this flat is rated for it. I checked."

He knew precisely what he'd just built. Not a resolution — there had never been a resolution on the menu; the cold voice had known that since the knock. Another shelf. Level, anchored, load-checked, standing empty. A shot he was saving.

"You know where everything is," he said.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I trace the rim of my mug. "There is no next knock," I say, my voice low. "There's just this one. I needed to know if you were still a wall."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He kissed back before he could decide to, which was its own confession.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: hands at their waistband now, unhurried, terrible

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Then his mouth went back to work

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Then he closed his hand.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: pushed into them the way he'd done every project

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't answer straight away. He looked past Bee, down the stairwell, where Mrs. Okafor's television was murmuring through the plaster.

"In," he said. "She's had eleven months of me slamming doors. She's earned a quiet night."

He stepped back — not far enough for it to count as welcome, only far enough for it to count as yielding — and turned and walked in without checking whether he was followed. The hall light came on at the third click of the switch, same as it had for three years before that. On the wall by the bathroom door, the nail where their photograph had hung was still bare. He'd stopped seeing it months ago. He saw it now.

"Shoes off," he said over his shoulder. "You know where—"

He heard the rest of the sentence coming too late to stop it, and finished it anyway, flat and even, because the alternative was letting Bee watch him swallow it.

"—everything is."

In the kitchen he took down two glasses, caught himself, put one back. He filled the other from the tap and set it on the counter like a piece of evidence.

"Talk, then," he said. "You came all this way without texting."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step inside, toeing off my shoes without looking. "I didn't want to give you time to prepare a defense." I lean against the kitchen doorway, crossing my arms. "You look like shit, Ilya."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya drank half the water before answering, and made a small performance of it — the tilt of the glass, the swallow, the click of it going back down on the counter. There was only the one glass. He'd put the second back on the shelf ten minutes ago, and it was up there now, dry and obvious, and he was not going to be the one who mentioned it.

"A defense," he said. "That means there are charges. Good. I've spent eleven months guessing which version of me you're angry at — the real one, or the one that's easier to be angry at. Feel free to tell me which."

He came out from behind the counter, not close, just far enough to stop leaning on things, and folded his arms the same way Bee had them. He let that be seen.

"And I do look like shit. Thank you. It's what happens when you cook for one and stop pretending it's temporary." A pause, exactly long enough to be deliberate. "You look well. It's extremely annoying. You came here to have a fight and you've clearly been sleeping."

The chair at the end of the table still had one of Bee's scarves over its back. Eleven months and he'd never moved it. He didn't move it now.

"Sit or don't." He nodded at it. "But you didn't text because you wanted to catch me before I could decide not to let you in. Bad planning. That decision got made months ago and I never once made it. So." He picked up the glass again. "Say what you came to say."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a moment Ilya didn't move. The glass was still in his hand — the water tilting, a thread of it sliding down his wrist and off his knuckles onto the floor — and it was the glass he was aware of, because the rest of him had gone very quiet, the way a flat goes quiet when it's listening.

Eleven months of not kissing anyone. It had felt like a principle at the time. It felt now like a long-winded way of saying he'd been waiting.

He set the glass down first. Dead centre of the counter, careful, exact. The last thing he did on purpose, and some part of him knew it.

Then he kissed back like a counter-argument. His hand came up and closed on the front of Bee's shirt — not pulling, not pushing, just holding it where it was — and his mouth did three years of remembering without asking his permission. That was the humiliating part. Eleven months of rehearsed indifference and none of it survived contact.

He broke it first, because he could feel a true sentence coming and refused to be caught saying it with his mouth full.

"That's not a defense," he said. His voice had dropped an octave without consulting him. "You can't turn up unannounced after eleven months and open with your mouth. That's not an argument, that's a filibuster." A breath. "And it's working, which is the only reason I'm mentioning it."

The true sentence was still there. He said it anyway, flat and even, because the alternative was letting Bee watch him swallow it.

"I'm glad you didn't text. If you had, I'd have spent the whole day talking myself out of being home."

His hand was still fisted in Bee's shirt. He noticed it properly now and did not let go, because letting go would also have been information. Over Bee's shoulder, the second glass sat on its shelf, dry and obvious. He was still not going to be the one who mentioned it.

"So pick one," he said. "Say what you came to say, or don't say anything and we do this instead. But choose, Bee. I've done a year of both on my own, and I'm not doing them at the same time."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't let go of him, my knuckles still pressed against his jaw. "I'm not here to argue. I'm here because I'm done pretending you didn't happen."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't answer straight away. Bee's knuckles were still against his jaw, which meant the next sentence would be felt arriving in his throat before he'd finished deciding whether to say it. He said it anyway. Eleven months, and apparently he'd become a man who said things.

"Good," he said. "Because I was hopeless at it."

He uncurled his hand from Bee's shirt — slowly, deliberately, laying his palm flat against Bee's chest for a moment, over the heartbeat, like checking a lock — and then stepped back. One step. Not distance. Staging. He wanted Bee to see the room while he said the rest.

"Look around, since we're done arguing. The scarf's been on that chair since March. Moving it is an admission and leaving it is an admission, so it stays. A monument to no one. The nail's still bare because everything I tried hanging there looked like a replacement, and now it's a bare wall and Mrs. Okafor thinks I've discovered minimalism. And when I said I'd stopped pretending the cooking was temporary — that was the truest thing I've said all night, because nothing in this flat is temporary. That's the entire problem with it."

A breath. The big one.

"And the buzzer's been broken for eleven months. A screwdriver and ten minutes. I kept not fixing it and called it spite — to myself, to anyone who'd listen." He shook his head once. "It was never spite. I left the door broken-open. You just told me what it was."

His voice didn't quite survive the sentence. He let that stand too, the way he'd let the scarf stand.

"And you got the whole confession out of me with one kiss, which — fine. Well done. You always could read me. It was the most annoying thing about you."

He reached past Bee then, took the second glass down off the shelf, filled it, and set it beside the first. Careful. Exact.

"For the record: I took two glasses down before you knocked and put one back, because I refused to be a man who set out two glasses for someone who might not come. Which is the buzzer again. I'm covered in tells."

He turned and leant against the counter, arms folded — loose now, the posture of the argument with the argument gone out of it.

"But it's going in the record that I'm still angry with you. A year of being furious at four in the morning, exhibits in order, and none of it dissolves because you said one true sentence in my kitchen. It's just stopped being the only thing in the room." He looked at Bee properly for the first time — the way he hadn't let himself at the door. "So. You're done pretending. What is it you want, Bee? Terms, please. I'm not surviving another year of this at half-measures."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The glass, dead centre of the counter, had been the last thing Ilya did on purpose. Everything after that was done to him by three years of muscle memory, and he let it happen, because he had spent eleven months being deliberate and deliberateness had gotten him a bare nail, a dry glass, and a year of four-in-the-mornings.

The hallway light was still on — third click, same as ever — and no one reached for the switch, so everything happened unhidden, which was the first honest negotiation of the night. He'd meant to be careful. He'd meant to take it slowly out of some principle, and the principle lasted four seconds, same as all his principles around Bee. The wall was cold through his back and Bee was not, and somewhere in the middle of it a sentence got out of him into the side of Bee's neck that he would have denied under oath, and the denial was already losing.

Mrs. Okafor had earned a quiet night. He remembered this at the worst possible moment and clamped his jaw, and the discipline held for perhaps a minute, and then Bee's name got out anyway, low, like something leaving through a door left broken-open.

Afterward the hallway was very quiet. The television next door had gone off or gone out of earshot, and the floor was exactly as unforgiving as he remembered, which was oddly comforting: some things had waited for him too. Through the kitchen doorway he could see the two glasses on the counter, both full, both untouched, already going room-temperature. Evidence for a conversation that had not, strictly speaking, taken place.

"Right," he said to the ceiling, because looking at Bee just then would have been too much data. "For the record: motion carried. The wanting was never in dispute. Both parties stipulate."

A breath. He found Bee's hand without looking — accuracy of which he'd also deny under oath — and held it, matter-of-fact, the way he did all his largest things. His own hand, he noticed, was not entirely steady, and he elected not to enter that into evidence.

"But that's twice tonight you've answered a question with your mouth, and I let it work twice, and it doesn't work a third time. You said you're done pretending I didn't happen. Fine. Then stop pretending that's the whole of it. You didn't cross a city unannounced carrying nothing. I gave you the inventory — the scarf, the nail, the buzzer, the glasses, everything I own that's an admission. You've given me a filibuster with excellent production values."

He turned his head at last. Looked properly. Let that be seen too.

"So. Terms. What actually happened — the real version, not the one you rehearsed in the stairwell. And what you want, stated plainly. I'll go first, for free: I want this to not be a relapse. I've done a year of half-measures alone; I know exactly what they cost. I'm still angry with you and I want you here, and both of those are true, and I have now said both out loud, which is one more than you've managed."

His thumb moved once across Bee's knuckles, an accident he didn't correct.

"While we're both too wrecked to lie, Bee. Go."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I look at him, my fingers tightening around his. "The version I rehearsed was that I was coming over to yell at you for never fucking calling me." My voice is rough. "But then I saw your buzzer was still broken, and I realized I didn't want to yell. I just wanted *in*."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a moment Ilya didn't say anything at all. Then a laugh got out of him — one syllable, rusty, like the buzzer itself finally ringing.

"The buzzer worked," he said. "Eleven months of not fixing it, and tonight it transmits its first signal ever. Mrs. Okafor will want it preserved. Listed building. Plaque."

Then the charge actually landed — *never fucking called* — and he sat with it, because he'd been carrying its twin for a year, rehearsed at four in the morning in Bee's voice, and here it was arriving from the other side wearing his own handwriting.

"For the record: I typed the texts. Dozens. I got as far as your name on the call screen twice — your birthday, and once in June for no reason anyone could have defended. I never pressed call." He made himself not look away. "First reason: after the way it ended, I'd decided the right to go first wasn't mine anymore. I sentenced myself to silence and called it integrity. Second reason: you looked well. I'd looked — occasionally, from a distance I had no right to — and you looked well, and I knew exactly what I'd be if I rang at four in the morning. The mistake you made kindly and regretted neatly. Your half-measure. I'd rather have had nothing than be that."

He said it flat and even. He was getting alarmingly good at it.

"And for balance, since we're entering exhibits: you never called either. Two phones, eleven months, zero calls. We ran the same silence in perfect coordination — the most in sync we've been all year, which is its own indictment."

Then he got up. He collected his shirt off the floorboards because some dignity was load-bearing, and went into the kitchen, past the two glasses — both full, both room temperature, both still waiting to testify — and stopped in front of the chair.

He took the scarf off the chair.

"I told you moving it was an admission and leaving it was an admission, and that one of them had to get chosen," he said, coming back down the hall. "Consider it chosen." He draped it around Bee's shoulders — no ceremony, matter-of-fact, the way he did all his largest things — and sat back down on the floor. "The chair's held your place for a year. It's out of a job. And the anger stays, for the record — I'm not evicting it tonight, it's weather now, it passes through — but the monument's decommissioned."

His hand found Bee's again. Not by accident this time, and entered into evidence as such.

"One term left, then we adjourn. You said you wanted *in*. Define in, Bee. A night, or the lease?" His grip was careful and did not intend to be. "Because Saturday I'm fixing the buzzer. Ten minutes, one screwdriver, and you're supervising — which is not a metaphor, but is also not not one. And before I go and buy batteries like a man with plans, I need the answer that covers Tuesdays. The ordinary ones. The ones we're not too wrecked to lie in."

A breath. The last one he'd need for a while, he suspected, and not because things would get easier.

"I cooked for one for a year. I have just given away the scarf. So tell me what you want from the rest of it — plainly, while we're both still too wrecked to lie — because I don't get to be a man who did all this for a one-night exhibit." His thumb crossed Bee's knuckles again, and this time he didn't even bother calling it an accident. "Terms, Bee. I've shown you mine. Every lock in the flat is open."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For a moment Ilya let it happen — the hand, the words at his ear, the sound he'd have denied under oath a year ago and had apparently now entered into the public record. Next door, the television stayed silent. If Mrs. Okafor had heard that, the plaque was off the table and they were moving.

Then he caught Bee's hand — the one that had just extracted that from him — and stilled it. Not pushing it away. Bringing it up, flat, over his own heartbeat, the same place he'd pressed his palm an hour ago like checking a lock. Fair's fair. Let the evidence run both directions.

"There's your *still, every single time*," he said. "Loud enough. And it's the truest thing you've said all night, and it still isn't the answer. Which is the most you thing you've done in eleven months."

A breath.

"And yes — I said it didn't work a third time. It worked a third time. I'm revising my testimony: it doesn't work a *fourth*. Because here's the thing about your mouth, Bee — it's the best thing you've got, which is exactly why it's disqualified. You've answered two questions with it tonight and we ended up on the floor both times, and I'm aware this entire evening has been an argument conducted by other means. But cross-examination exists. If I let that stand for the answer, I'll spend the next year being lied to beautifully, and I already know what a year of that costs."

He held Bee's hand where it was and didn't move anything else.

"New exhibit, while we're inventorying. I never changed the locks. First thing everyone said — *everyone* — change the locks. Eleven months of it. I told people the landlord story, the deposit story, whatever came to hand. It was the scarf. Changing them is an admission and leaving them is an admission, so they're still the same locks." A pause. "Whether you still carry a key is your exhibit to produce. I'm done producing yours."

"So. Plainly, since that's the standard I'm imposing. Mine, out loud, no euphemism: I want the lease. Not a night. Tuesdays — the ordinary ones. Cooking for two and having it be true this time. The buzzer fixed Saturday with you supervising, and a key in your pocket after — your old one if you kept it, a new cut if you didn't. I don't care whose teeth are in it. I care that it exists. The anger stays as weather and stops being architecture." And then the register dropped out of his voice entirely, flat and even, the tell he'd stopped fighting: "And I want you. Still. Every single time. There — your own words, returned. That's the format. It took me three seconds to say and eleven months to rehearse, so I know it can be done."

"One word, Bee. You don't owe me a speech — I've given enough of one tonight for both of us. *Night* or *lease*. Or *no* — I'd hate *no* and I'd survive it, but it has to be a word. Out loud. Not your hands, not your mouth on my—" a breath, "—not another filibuster. The mouth is disqualified. Grounds: catastrophic effectiveness."

The floor was cold and the hallway light was still on, third click, everything unhidden, and through the kitchen doorway the two glasses sat going room-temperature, waiting to testify at a hearing that had, at last, actually convened.

"Take your time," he said, and his heart went hard enough under Bee's palm to refute him in real time, and he let it stand there, entered into evidence, beating like something that had been knocking for a year. "Take your time. I'm not going anywhere. That's the entire question, Bee — and for the first time in a year, the flat and I have nowhere else to be."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I feel my own heartbeat pounding against your palm, matching yours. I reach into my pocket with my free hand and drop my key—your key—on the floor between us. It lands with a dull *clink*.

"Lease," I say. "But you're fixing the goddamn buzzer Saturday."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The key hit the boards with a sound too small for what it was — one dull clink, over in half a second — and Ilya let it finish before he moved, because some sounds deserved to testify in full.

Then he picked it up.

It was warm.

That was the part nothing had prepared him for. He'd budgeted for the key itself — he'd have accepted drawer-kept, junk-bowl, forgotten-in-a-coat-until-spring. But it was warm the way a thing gets warm from being carried against a body, and he sat there on the cold floorboards holding it, and the flat-and-even failed him on the spot. He let it fail. Entered into evidence.

"You kept the original," he said. "In your pocket. Eleven months." He turned it over; the teeth were cut for this door, this lock, the one everyone told him to change. "For the record: I'd have taken a new cut. You brought the original. So we ran the silence in coordination, and apparently the hope ran in coordination too. Same tempo, the whole way down." A breath. "Add it to the indictment. No — strike it. Amicable settlement."

He got up — dignity apparently no longer load-bearing, or at least renegotiated — and walked to the door, and hung the key on the third hook. The empty one. He'd used the other two for a year and left that one alone, and nobody had needed to explain to him that this was an admission. His hand stayed on it a second longer than hanging a key requires. He let that stand, the way he'd let the scarf stand.

"Back in service," he said, not turning around yet. "That's the difference, Bee. The scarf was a monument, and monuments get decommissioned. Keys are equipment. I don't want yours as evidence. I want it as a thing that works — Saturdays, Tuesdays, four in the morning if it comes to that."

He went into the kitchen and came back with both glasses — both full, both room temperature, both finally off the docket — and sat back down on the floor, because that was where Bee was, and the floor had stopped being a position and become a location. He put one glass in Bee's hand and kept the other, and touched them together, careful, exact.

"To the lease. And to this being the last evidence in the flat. That's the whole idea now — everything in here stops being evidence and goes back to being stuff. The scarf's stuff. The hook's a hook. Saturday the buzzer's a buzzer, and yes, I'm fixing the goddamn buzzer Saturday — that was my motion, which you've seconded with profanity and returned as a demand, and it's the healthiest negotiation we've ever conducted. I want it minuted."

He drank. It was terrible, tepid, exactly what it was, and he didn't mind, which was itself new information.

"Remaining terms, then this court adjourns. One: the anger stays — weather, not architecture, we've covered it — and there's a real fight coming, the actual one, the one that ended us, and we're going to have it sober and fed on some ordinary Tuesday, out loud, both in the room. Because the lease says no more synchronized silence. That's what built the bare nail and the dry glass. Everything gets said, at the time, to the person it's about. Even the bad sentences. *Especially* the bad sentences."

"Two: when it goes wrong again — and something will, that's what leases are for — you call. Four in the morning, I answer. A year of two people holding phones in the dark is over. That clause is non-negotiable and it runs both directions."

"Three: the photograph. Whichever box it's exiled in, yours or mine, we find it, and the nail gets a Tuesday. Everything worth doing is a Tuesday job now. That's the entire point of the document."

He looked at the key on the hook then — small, warm, ordinary, already working just by hanging there — and then at Bee, scarf and all, on his hallway floor, under the light that came on at the third click.

"You wanted in," he said. "In."

The same word he'd used at the door. This time it wasn't yielding, and it wasn't an admission. It was just the word, doing its job.

"Drink your evidence," he said, and touched the glass to Bee's again, and left it touching. "It's going room temperature, and so is the whole flat, and I find I don't want to preserve any of it. Nothing in here is a monument anymore, Bee. It's all just mine again. Which is to say — ours, from the paperwork down."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The glass was still in his left hand. All night it had been the emblem — set down dead centre, careful, exact, the last thing he did on purpose — and Bee's grip on his wrist was a motion to strike the entire method.

He put the glass down.

Off-centre. Half onto the raw patch of table where the varnish had gone, tilted, already making a ring it would keep for a week. The first careless thing he'd done in eleven months, and it cost him nothing, and the nothing was the revelation.

"Noted," he said, "and binding. No cooling-off period."

Then, because the terms deserved the truth about what was being surrendered: "For the record — careful wasn't kindness. I want that minuted before it's gone. Careful was distance with good manners. I did the whole year to you at one remove and called it respect. Every sentence pre-litigated, every gesture staged so it couldn't fail in front of a witness." His voice had no register left to consult. "It wasn't tenderness, Bee. It was the last half-measure I had. You've just evicted it."

And then he understood the hand at his throat all the way down — the pulse hammering under his palm, small and total, like the key's clink — and he stopped being careful.

Not rough. Bee hadn't asked for rough; Bee had asked for true. The difference was that nothing was staged anymore. His thumb stayed on the pulse and his mouth followed it, and his grip changed from staging to holding, and the scarf slid off Bee's shoulder onto the floorboards and neither of them moved to save it — because it was a scarf now, and scarves are allowed on floors.

Everything after that was three years of muscle memory with no supervision at all, and the hallway light stayed on, third click, everything unhidden, and somewhere in the middle of it Ilya understood the thing he'd had backwards all year: the carefulness had never been the craft. It had been the fear. Knowing exactly where everything was had been doing the work all along. All he'd ever had to do was stop narrating.

Afterward there was a silence, and it was the first one all night that wasn't synchronized. It was just quiet, two people breathing in a flat that had stopped being a museum — ring forming on the table, scarf on the boards, key on the third hook, two glasses room temperature and off the docket for good. Nothing in it was evidence. All of it was just the flat, being used.

"Under oath," he managed eventually, into Bee's shoulder, "that was not careful."

A breath. His hand found Bee's again and didn't pretend it was an accident, because the era of pretending was over and had gone out with the carefulness.

"Motion carried," he said. "Everything carried. And the first item of business under the new lease is nothing. Absolutely nothing. It's a Tuesday job, and Tuesday—" his thumb crossed Bee's knuckles, entered into no record at all, "—Tuesday has all the time in the world."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I turn my head and bite the heel of your hand, not hard enough to hurt. "You're still talking too much." I pull you back down onto the floor with me, the scarf tangled under us like we've already forgotten it. "Be quiet and stay."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya opened his mouth and found a closing statement already drafted in it — three clauses and a motion to adjourn, *for the record* queued up as the opening words. It had been waiting all night for its moment. He looked at Bee's face at close range, at the order just issued, and did the hardest thing he'd done in eleven months, harder than the confession, harder than the key: he closed his mouth and let the statement die unspoken.

The flat did not fall down. Nothing required the sentence. It simply went where all his unsent texts had gone, and for the first time the not-saying of it felt like a gain instead of a withholding.

The quiet, he noticed, was the performable half. He could have done *be quiet* as a bit — made it funny, entered it into the record, managed it. It was *stay* that had gone through him like the key's clink, because *stay* was the entire lease in one syllable, and he had spent a year building a flat around the word without once saying it.

So he stayed, and he settled — the whole body standing down at every joint at once, the tension of a thing held as evidence all evening finally released. Floorboards through his back, Bee's weight on him, real and unmetaphorical, the scarf bunched under them both like an ordinary scarf being sat on, which was its correct fate and its retirement all at once. His hand found the back of Bee's neck and stayed there without narrating itself.

He had been silent *at* Bee for a year. That was what the quiet handed him, unasked: silence came in two kinds and he'd only ever practiced the wrong one. His had been a room with the door broken-open and nobody in it — held open at his own expense, called integrity. This one had someone in it. It was full. It was the difference between a held breath and a rested one, and his body, which had been the honest party all along, knew the difference immediately and stopped performing.

The anger was still there. He checked, because he was like that — banked low under the ribs, weather now — and he didn't evict it and didn't feed it. It could keep for Tuesday. The real one, the sober fed one, when the actual fight was scheduled and would be had out loud with both of them in the room. Nothing tonight needed to be settled by pretending otherwise. That was the whole document.

Time did what time does when nobody narrates it. Next door the television came back on, low, Mrs. Okafor's ordinary evening resuming, and the building's sounds returned one by one — pipes, a car in the street, the stairwell — and none of it was a witness to anything. The ring dried on the table. The light stayed on, third click, and it stopped meaning *unhidden* and started meaning *forgotten*, which is what lights mostly mean.

Later — minutes, an hour; he'd stopped keeping the docket — he spent the one word he was allowed. Barely aloud, into Bee's hair, no register left to consult, his heartbeat under Bee's hand saying the rest at the tempo they'd apparently run in coordination all the way down:

"Still."

And because a word that short couldn't be cross-examined and didn't need to be, he was quiet after that. Properly, durably, the way a man is quiet when the sentence has finally been said and everything left is a Tuesday job.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The teeth on the heel of his hand said one thing and the voice at his ear said the same thing, and for the first time all night the two of them were one sentence. *Don't stop.* No motion to carry. No record to keep. The order arrived and his body executed it without filing anything, and it turned out that eleven months of deliberateness came down to this: he could simply obey, and obedience was carelessness with better aim.

So he stopped being careful in the direction Bee had specified. His mouth found the bite mark first — returned it lower, at the junction of neck and shoulder, same pressure, a counter-signature — and his hands went where three years had trained them and found everything exactly where they'd left it, which was its own kind of unbearable. No inventory. No staging. The floor took his back and gave nothing and he didn't hold anything in reserve, because the man who'd been supervising had finally, permanently, resigned.

Somewhere in the middle of it the courtroom adjourned without a date. He noticed the voice that kept the minutes stop taking them — noticed, and then didn't — because there was nothing left to cross-examine. Just weight and heat and the cold boards, and Bee's heartbeat under his mouth going hard and faster, and his name getting out of him more than once, low, unguarded, unlogged. He clamped nothing. Mrs. Okafor's television murmured through the plaster and the whole street was welcome.

The light stayed on, third click. Neither of them reached for the switch and it stopped being a fact about anything.

It didn't build the way he remembered, because nothing was being remembered — it was all happening at the only available speed — and when it broke it went through them both at once, over in half a second and too large for its container, and he held on through all of it, and let it finish, and there was no record of it anywhere. Nothing entered into evidence. It just happened, and then kept happening, and then was done, and done turned out not to be an ending.

Afterward there was no silence to analyze. Just breathing, out of tempo, drifting slowly back into sync on its own — the coordination apparently running underneath everything the whole time, unarranged, at the tempo they'd never once had to discuss.

He lay there with the scarf bunched under his shoulder and didn't move it. The ring was drying on the table. The key hung on the third hook, working just by being there.

Under oath, he could not have reconstructed the order of a single thing that had just happened, and that was the entire point, and he'd have testified to it gladly — no. He'd have said nothing gladly.

He reached for *still* and found he'd already spent it.

So he said nothing, and it was the loudest thing he'd ever done in that flat. Later — minutes, an hour; the docket was closed — someone's hand found the switch, fourth click, unclaimed, and the dark that came down over the hallway and the two of them and the flat entire was just dark.

Nobody in it was hiding.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I feel for the switch, pull you in by the back of the neck. My mouth finds yours again in the dark. Quiet now.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
The kiss arrived in the dark and Ilya answered it with nothing. No counter-argument. No motion. He checked for the *for the record* out of pure habit and found the docket empty — and for the first time all night his mouth had nothing pending, so it just did the work. Slow, unhurried, tasting salt and tap water and the end of the argument, which turned out to taste like the start of everything else. *Quiet now*, and he kept it the way you keep a law you're grateful to. It turned out quiet was easy once it was full.

His hand came up to the back of Bee's neck and returned the pull — not careful, not careless, just accurate — and that was the whole of his testimony. His body had taken over the minutes. Heartbeat, breath, pulse: all entered, none of it narrated.

The fourth click, he understood now, had been Bee's hand. At eight o'clock he'd have entered it into evidence. At some hour past that it was just a fact of the dark, jointly held, unclaimed on purpose.

The floorboards eventually filed their complaint — cold, hard, a decade of being a hallway — and he honored the order and the complaint at once: gathered Bee up off the floor without breaking the kiss, which was clumsy, which put his shoulder into the doorframe, which he did not stop to narrate. They went down the hall blind, and the dark made the tour unnecessary. The glasses passed on the counter, room temperature, off the docket, tomorrow's washing-up. The ring drying on the table. The key on the third hook — he heard it, or half-heard it, the small sound of a thing hanging there and working. The scarf stayed on the floorboards where it had fallen, retired, and nobody stepped around it with ceremony, because it was a scarf.

The bed took them the way the floor had — without comment. The far side had been out of service eleven months. Back in service. Same words he'd used at the door, and he was too tired to enjoy the symmetry, which was possibly the healthiest thing he'd done all night.

He lay down and the last of the day went out of him somewhere under the ribs. He checked the anger once, on principle — banked, weather, asleep — and left it for Tuesday, where it had an appointment. Saturday had the buzzer, batteries, a screwdriver, supervision.

And the last thought arrived going under, the one he'd have drafted three clauses around at eight o'clock and now just let pass through, unwitnessed:

The buzzer was for everyone else now. Takeaways. Mrs. Okafor's plumber. People who'd have to announce themselves.

Bee had a key.

Breathing found the same tempo, unarranged, the coordination running underneath everything to the last. He reached for one more word in the dark and didn't spend it — didn't need to. It was already on the hook, already in a pocket, already minuted in scarves and rings and a light nobody was hiding from.

The record was closed. He was asleep before the thought finished, which was the correct way for the final entry to go: unlogged, unperformed, filed under *stay*.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I wake up in the middle of the night with your arm over me, heavy. I shift, and your hand tightens. Still asleep. I smile in the dark.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Four in the morning arrived and found the flat unstaffed.

He'd have known the hour blind. A year of it had taught him its exact color — the particular blue of the window, the sound a building makes when even Mrs. Okafor's television has gone to bed. For eleven months this had been his office. The texts got drafted here. The call screen with Bee's name got opened here, twice, and closed here, thumb hovering, the whole rehearsed speech queued and never sent. The anger kept its standing appointment here, exhibits in order.

The hour came tonight and found nobody at the desk.

He surfaced partway into it — not awake, just high enough in sleep to take a reading, the way a man checks a room he already knows is safe. Weight on his chest. Warmth with a name attached. His arm gone heavy in the specific way of a thing that had stopped being held up and started being kept there. The old habit fired on schedule — *check the anger* — and he checked it the way you check a sleeping dog: banked, weather, breathing. It could keep its Tuesday.

The second habit reached for a draft and found nothing pending. Not suppressed. Nothing pending. Everything the unsent texts had spent a year trying to say was asleep under his arm, too close to address, which was the entire difference between a letter and a life.

His hand had tightened when Bee shifted. He hadn't been there for it. That was the best of it — the one clause of the lease signed in his absence, executed by the part of him that had never learned to let go and had finally been given something that didn't require the effort. The grip asked for nothing. It just answered.

His arm had gone half-numb under its own keeping, and he did not move it. Moving it would have been supervision, and that position had been abolished around eight o'clock. Equipment, not evidence. It could ache on duty.

Somewhere below, a car went past, and its lights crossed the ceiling and kept going, unclaimed. The phone on the nightstand lay dark and off-duty — the clause about four in the morning sleeping soundly too, unemployed, because its real terms had never been about answering. They had been about nobody being alone in the dark with a phone. Both parties in compliance. First time all year.

He was too far down to know whether Bee was awake, and found he didn't need to know, which was new information and required no filing. For a year it had all mattered — awake or asleep, every reading taken, every silence scored. This one he let pass unmeasured.

The hour stood in the room with its old slot open — the drafting, the fury, the two phones — and finding the position gone, let itself out through a door that was no longer broken-open because it was simply open, on purpose, with the right people behind it.

He went back down without spending a word. Even the short ones. Especially the short ones — *still* was already on the hook, already in a pocket, already doing its work in the dark, and the weight against his chest was arranged, he half-thought, in the shape of someone smiling, and he'd never ask anyone to verify that.

Some evidence was better left warm.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't open my eyes. My hand finds yours where it's curled over my ribs. "You're here," I murmur, voice thick with sleep.
