dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya considered the question as though it were a contract he hadn't decided whether to sign. Then he stepped back, just one step, his hand remaining on the edge of the door. The gap was technically large enough to enter, but only if Bee moved directly toward him, into the space he still occupied.

"You came all this way," Ilya said. "It would be rude to make you perform for the neighbors."

He turned then, walking into the flat without looking back, his spine straight and his pace unhurried, the same deliberate, infuriating composure he had maintained through every room of their shared history. The door stayed open behind him—an assumption, a challenge, and something else neither of them would name.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: *I step inside, letting the door swing shut behind me.* "Still not much for welcoming committees, I see." My eyes sweep the flat. "Place looks the same. Smells the same."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya walked past the narrow corridor into the living room, where the late afternoon light cut across the same scuffed floorboards at the same angle Bee would remember. He stopped at the kitchen counter and set his palms flat against the laminate, squaring his shoulders but not turning around.

"Memory's a sense too," he said. When he finally turned, it was with the slow precision of a man who had rehearsed this moment, or who had simply learned that composure was its own weapon. He rested his hip against the counter's edge and looked at Bee—really looked, his gaze traveling from Bee's eyes to their shoes and back up with the kind of intimate assessment that felt like a violation of the distance they were supposed to be maintaining. "If you're cataloguing changes, you might check the bedroom. I moved the bed."

A beat passed. His expression didn't shift, but something lived in the pause, something angry and wanting and carefully leashed.

"Not that you came here to discuss furniture."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went rigid. For a moment he did not move, standing motionless with his hands braced against the counter, letting the kiss happen against his unyielding mouth. Then his control slipped—not all at once, but in a single, deliberate movement. His hand closed around the back of Bee's neck, fingers pressing into familiar muscle with punitive precision, and he answered with his own mouth, hard and exact, as though he were trying to win a fight with teeth and tongue. When he finally pulled away, his lips were parted, his composure cracked just enough to show the hunger beneath, but his eyes remained sharp and unforgiving.

"The bed's against the other wall now," he said. "In case you planned on pretending you still own any part of this flat."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Ownership's a shitty substitute for what I want." I press forward, crowding him against the counter until the edge digs into his back. "Show me the bedroom. Or don't. We can break the kitchen table instead."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn't flinch at the pressure of the counter against his spine. He held Bee's gaze, close enough to notice the details he'd tried to forget—the faint freckle at the corner of their mouth, the particular shade of their temper in their eyes. His hands lifted from the laminate behind him, slow and deliberate, and settled at Bee's waist. He did not pull them closer. He held them still, fingers digging in with a grip calibrated to bruise.

"You never did know the difference between wanting something and needing to destroy it first," he said. His voice had dropped, roughened by the kiss, but the words stayed edged. He shifted his weight and used the leverage of his grip to reverse them, pressing Bee back against the counter so its edge caught at their spine instead of his. He drove his thigh between theirs with practiced, insulting familiarity and leaned in until his mouth grazed the shell of their ear.

"The table wobbled before you ever left," he said. "I'm not interested in breaking anything else you'll regret in another eleven months." He pulled back only far enough to let Bee see his face—the naked want and the fury tangled there, deliberately unmasked. "The bedroom's where you remember. But if you walk through that door, you don't leave until morning, and you don't leave whole." His thumb tracked upward, pressing once, hard, against the hinge of their jaw. "Choose."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s back hit the wall of the narrow corridor—the physics of how they’d gotten there had already blurred. The plaster was cool against his bare shoulders, a sharp contrast to the heat of the skin now pressed flush to his. The hallway had always been too narrow for this, a fact that scraped at him now as his hands moved with vicious certainty over territory he had tried, for eleven months, to strike from his memory.

He could smell Bee’s shampoo. The same brand. The specificity of it felt like a fresh wound.

He caught Bee’s face in his hands, fingers spanning their jaw, and looked at them with a hunger he made no effort to hide, letting it mingle openly with contempt. The light from the living room didn’t reach here. They were painted in the dimness of the hallway, the same hallway where he had once kissed them goodbye on ordinary mornings, and now he used it to cage them. He drove his hips forward, pinning them against the opposite wall with a force that rattled the framed print beside their head.

“You don’t get to—” he started, but the sentence fractured. *Don’t get to what?* Smell the same? Feel the same? Come back as though nothing had been severed? He didn’t finish. He dropped his mouth to Bee’s collarbone, teeth sinking in with a precision that was half memory, half punishment. His hands slid lower, mapping familiar muscle with a touch that bordered on brutality.

The floorboards groaned beneath them, that same old protest. Somewhere in the flat, the refrigerator clicked on, humming its indifferent tune. Ilya dragged his mouth back up, his breathing ragged against the shell of Bee’s ear, though his voice, when he found it, was stripped and deliberate.

“Tell me,” he said. His thumb pressed into the hollow of Bee’s throat, feeling the frantic pulse there. “Tell me this is better than it was with anyone else.”

He didn’t wait for an answer. He couldn’t have trusted it, and more importantly, he couldn’t afford to need it. He reached between them, his movements efficient and merciless, and he used his weight to crowd them further into the shadows of the hallway, as though he could press the last eleven months out of existence through sheer force of proximity.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite his shoulder hard to muffle the sound I make, my hands pushing his jeans down just enough to get my hand between us. "It was never better," I say against his skin, my voice rough. "Just different."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a sound that wasn’t quite a laugh—something sharp and breathless that scraped out of his throat at the word *different*. He rocked into the pressure of Bee’s hand despite himself, his hips stuttering forward with a betrayal of control that made the anger flare hotter. His fingers closed around Bee’s wrist, not to pull them away but to hold them there, pinned against him with a grip that trembled slightly against his will.

“Different,” he repeated, the word bitten off and spat back. He dragged his mouth up from the bite mark on his own shoulder—he could feel the shape of Bee’s teeth there, a brand he welcomed and resented in equal measure—and found their ear again. His free hand shoved into Bee’s hair, pulling hard enough to arch their neck back against the plaster. “You mean you fucked other people and thought of this. Thought of me.”

He didn’t give them room to answer, or perhaps he couldn’t bear to let them. He used his grip in their hair to angle their head back and drove his mouth down against their throat, sucking a mark into the skin with deliberate, vicious possession. His body moved against Bee’s hand with a rhythm that was all urgency, no patience, the eleven months collapsing into nothing and everything at once.

The hallway was too narrow for this, their bodies crowded between walls where he had once hung their coat, passed them coffee, said *have a good day* like it meant forever. Now he used the cramped space to cage them, his thigh driving between theirs with a force that scraped denim against skin.

When he pulled back, his eyes were wild in the dim light, the careful composure finally shattered beyond repair. “Then make it better,” he said, his voice ragged. He pressed harder against them, letting them feel exactly how little the last eleven months had mattered to his body. “Make it so good I forget you ever had a basis for comparison.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still for a fraction of a second, the words hitting his bloodstream like a drug he hadn’t agreed to take. His fingers spasmed in Bee’s hair, pulling harder, and a sound caught in his chest—something closer to a growl than a moan. He dragged his mouth along the line of Bee’s jaw, teeth scraping, and pressed his forehead hard against theirs, his breathing harsh and unsteady in the narrow space between their faces.

“Every time,” he repeated, the syllables roughened by disbelief and a vicious, blooming satisfaction. He rocked into the circle of Bee’s hand, his own grip tightening at their hip until his knuckles ached. The hallway seemed to contract around them, the shadows thick with everything unsaid. He could feel the pulse hammering beneath his thumb at Bee’s throat, and it matched the reckless tempo of his own heart. “You should have saved yourself the disappointment.”

He shifted his weight, using his thigh to spread Bee wider against the wall, his movements losing the last vestiges of restraint. The doorframe pressed into his shoulder as he angled them both toward the dark rectangle of the bedroom, but he didn’t lead them through it—he held them there, suspended in the threshold, and hooked an arm under Bee’s leg to lift, pinning them between his body and the painted wood. The position was unstable, cruel, intimate. He drove upward, seeking friction with a single-minded desperation that made his voice break when he spoke again.

“Then be here,” he said. “Not thinking. Not remembering. Here.” His free hand slid between them, claiming with a roughness that bordered on recklessness, though his eyes remained open and burning into Bee’s, daring them to look away. “And when you come, you say my name like it’s the only one you’ve ever known.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Ilya." I say it like it's a curse, like it's a prayer, my nails digging into the skin of his back. The hallway smells like dust and us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya felt the word more than heard it—his name shaped into a curse, or perhaps a benediction, against the humid air of the hallway. The sting of Bee’s nails raking his back sent a bright shock up his spine, anchoring him to the moment with a clarity that made his vision narrow. He sucked in a breath that tasted of dust and the particular, ruinous scent of their skin, and the last fragment of his control splintered.

He shifted his grip on Bee’s leg, his arm burning under the strain, and stepped backward through the doorway. The bedroom swallowed them in its gloom, the curtains drawn tight against the afternoon, and he lowered them both onto the mattress without gentleness. The frame creaked against the new wall—a foreign sound in a familiar room. He followed Bee down, his weight pressing them into the bedding, his mouth finding the mark he’d left on their throat with something like reverence and nothing like forgiveness.

He dragged his palms down Bee’s sides, over the topography of muscle and memory, and shoved aside the last of the denim between them with a ruthlessness that matched the hammering of his pulse. His hand slid into the heat there with a familiarity that burned, stroking with a precision that was all ownership and no mercy. He ground his hips down, creating friction with the length of his body, each movement driven by the eleven months he’d spent trying to excise this hunger. The bed protested the new position, its rhythm irregular against the unfamiliar wall.

Ilya braced one hand beside Bee’s head, his other hand moving with merciless intent, and he watched their face in the dimness—watched for the precise moment the anger dissolved into something unguarded. His own breathing had come apart completely, ragged and audible, but his eyes stayed open, fixed on Bee’s, refusing to let either of them hide inside the dark.

“You said it,” he ground out, his voice stripped to its core. He angled his wrist, applying pressure exactly where memory told him to, relentless. “Now let me pretend you never learned how to leave.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still above them. He felt Bee’s hand guiding his own to the hollow of their throat, felt the frantic drum of their pulse push up against his palm, and he understood exactly what they were demanding. He looked down at them in the dimness, his eyes narrowing with a recognition that was part fury, part something far more dangerous.

“You don’t get to decide that for me,” he said, his voice barely more than a rasp. But he closed his hand anyway—not with the hesitance of a stranger, but with the sure, practiced knowledge of a man who had spent three years mapping every vulnerable point of their body. His fingers curved around the column of their neck, thumb settling against the ridge of their windpipe, and he applied pressure with a deliberation that made his next breath shudder out of him. He felt Bee’s inhalation catch, felt the artery flutter beneath his grip, and he watched their face with an intensity that bordered on cruelty.

His other hand didn’t stop. He kept the rhythm between them merciless, exact, driving them both toward the edge with a single-mindedness that made his vision spark at the margins. He rolled his hips forward, pinning them hard into the mattress, and the bedframe scraped against its new wall with a raw, splintering sound.

“You want me careless?” he asked, leaning down until his mouth hovered a bare inch from theirs. He tightened his fingers just enough to make the point, to make their eyes widen, to make the pulse beneath his thumb leap and strain. “You want me to pretend I never learned where all your seams are?” He pressed forward, grinding down with a force that rattled the bed, his breathing harsh and broken against their lips. “I know exactly what breaks you, Bee. I know exactly what you can take. That’s the problem.”

He squeezed, not enough to truly steal their breath, but enough to hold it, to ration it, to make every gasp a transaction. His hips snapped forward again, losing the last pretense of rhythm, and he dragged his free hand down to grip their hip, tilting them up to meet him.

“So don’t tell me I don’t get to be careful,” he said, the words torn out of him as he moved against them with a violence that was all punishment, all argument, all homecoming. “Don’t tell me what I don’t get to feel when I’m touching you.” He loosened his grip just enough to let them suck in a ragged breath, then tightened again, his eyes burning into theirs, unblinking in the dark. “If you want to be treated like you mean nothing, go find someone who doesn’t know every goddamn inch of you.”

Then he kissed them, if it could still be called a kiss—his mouth coming down hard and open, swallowing whatever sound they made, his body moving with a abandon that was all possession, the bed protesting its new position, his hand at their throat the only anchor in a vast, unforgiving dark.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I come like that, with his hand around my throat and his teeth on my lip, my body arching into his like it's trying to prove a point. When I collapse back against the mattress, I don't look away from him. "Still careful," I say, my voice wrecked. "Even when you're trying not to be."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went still. The hand at Bee’s throat lifted away, leaving the skin cool and abruptly untouched. He looked down at them, his chest still heaving with unspent breath, and the rage in his face cracked into something raw and unbearable.

“Careful,” he repeated, his voice roughened to its core. He shifted his weight, but instead of retreating, he drove his hips forward once, hard, a punishing reminder of what they had left unfinished. “You think I held back because I’m kind?”

He caught Bee’s jaw in his free hand, forcing their eyes to meet his in the dark. “I know what breaks you because I spent three years learning how to hold you together. That isn’t kindness. It’s memory. And you don’t get to walk back in here after eleven months and demand I forget everything just because you want to pretend this was ever simple.”

His thumb dragged across Bee’s swollen lower lip, tracing where his teeth had been. “You want careless? Careless is not knowing you cry after you come when it’s too good. Careless is not knowing which spot on your hip bruises if I grip too hard.” He released their jaw, but he didn’t pull away. He stayed braced over them, his body a hard, trembling line of unresolved hunger. “I’m careful because I’m trapped in every detail of you. Because you made sure I couldn’t walk away clean, and now you want me to pretend I don’t know exactly what I’m touching.”

He dragged a breath that shuddered audibly against the dark, and his eyes burned down at them, unguarded and merciless. “You want me to hurt you like a stranger? I can’t. I tried for eleven months, and here you are. So don’t tell me I’m careful. Tell me you’re sorry you made me give a shit in the first place.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya heard the command and something in him answered with a violence that had no other outlet. He didn't ask for clarification. He didn't offer gentleness he didn't possess. He shifted his weight, knee driving between Bee's thighs to spread them wider on the mattress that sat against its new wall, and he reached down with both hands to rid himself of the last barrier of denim clinging to his hips.

The fabric caught, then tore, or maybe he simply forced it down with a recklessness that made the distinction meaningless. He kicked free of it, the cool air of the bedroom hitting his heated skin for only a moment before he covered Bee's body with his own again, the full length of him pressing down with a weight that made the mattress groan beneath them. He gripped the back of one of Bee's legs, hooking it higher around his hip, opening them further with a roughness that matched the rhythm hammering in his chest.

"You asked for this," he said, his voice stripped of everything but the truth. He positioned himself with a hand wrapped around himself, guiding with a familiarity that made his jaw clench, and then he pushed inside with a single, unsparing thrust.

The heat and tight grip of it shocked him, even now, even after everything. He threw his head back, his spine arching, a ragged, guttural sound tearing from his throat that he didn't try to suppress. It was too much and not enough, the clutch of Bee's body around him a homecoming he resented with every fiber of his being. He withdrew nearly to the point of withdrawal and then drove forward again, harder, setting a rhythm that was brutal and deliberate.

The bed scraped against the new wall with every snap of his hips, a rhythmic, splintering protest that matched the chaos inside him. He bent down, his mouth finding Bee's shoulder, and he bit down as he thrust, marking, claiming, punishing. Eleven months of starvation ended here, in the dark, in anger, and he refused to make it pretty.

He shifted his angle, seeking the place he knew would unravel them, and when he found it he stayed there, grinding deep with short, vicious strokes that made the headboard knock plaster from the wall. He reached between them, his hand closing around Bee again, working them with a grip that was too tight, too rough, exactly as rough as the moment demanded.

"Look at me," he demanded, though he wasn't sure if the words made it past the blood roaring in his ears. He forced his eyes open, burning down at Bee in the dark, watching for the moment pleasure crossed the threshold into abandon. He wanted to witness every unguarded second, because it was the only proof he had that this was real, that he wasn't alone in this ruin.

His own release built at the base of his spine, a tightening coil that threatened to snap his composure entirely. He chased it with thrusts that lost their precision, becoming raw and desperate, his hips snapping forward with a speed that made the mattress shift on the frame. He gripped the headboard with one hand to brace himself, the wood biting into his palm, and he used the leverage to drive deeper, to fill the space Bee had vacated eleven months ago and left empty.

When it hit him, it hit like a blow. He went rigid, his body locking down as he spilled inside them with a cry that was Bee's name twisted into something broken and angry and irrevocable. The pulses tore through him, one after another, each one a confession he refused to make with words. He collapsed forward, his forearm hitting the mattress beside Bee's head, his face buried in the hollow of their neck where sweat had gathered, his body still trembling with aftershocks that made his hips twitch helplessly against them.

For a long moment, the only sound in the room was their breathing—ragged, mismatched, too loud. Ilya didn't pull out. He didn't pull away. He stayed inside them, his weight pressing them into the sheets, and he turned his head just enough to press his open mouth against the thundering pulse in Bee's throat. Not a kiss. An acknowledgment. A treaty written in sweat and teeth.

"Still not gentle," he said, his voice wrecked beyond recognition. He closed his eyes, the anger finally spent into something else, something harder and more permanent. "Still not sorry."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I feel the aftershocks in him and then I feel the weight settle, heavy and final. My fingers find the raw skin on his back where my nails dug in. "Nobody's asking you to be sorry."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya laughed then, a humorless exhale that stirred the sweat-damp hair at Bee’s temple. He shifted his weight, a slow, deliberate roll of his hips that dragged a last, involuntary shudder from his own frame, but he didn’t pull free. He remained there, anchored in the ruinous heat of them, his forearm still bracketing Bee’s head against the pillow.

“Then you’re wasting your time,” he said, his voice scraped raw and lower than before. He lifted his head, his mouth grazing the shell of Bee’s ear with a deliberation that was almost tender and entirely false. “Or maybe you’re wasting mine.” He turned his face to look at them, his eyes dark and unsparing in the gloom, reading whatever he could find there with the same merciless assessment he had used at the door. “You came back for this. For the argument. For the fuck. For the—” He stopped, his jaw tightening. His hand moved from the mattress to settle, heavy and possessive, over the mark he had left on their throat. “You didn’t come back because you think I’m sorry. You came back because you’re not, either.”

He dropped his gaze to the space between their bodies, where the evidence of what they’d done marked them both, and something bitter and knowing pulled at the corner of his mouth. “So here we are. Same flat. Same bed against a different wall, same damage. And in the morning, you’ll still be the one who left, and I’ll still be the one who didn’t fix the buzzer.” He pressed his thumb once, hard, against the pulse beneath his palm, then let his hand fall to the sheets. “Tell me I’m wrong. Tell me you walked through that door thinking we were going to fix anything.”

He didn’t wait for an answer. He turned his face into the pillow beside them, his breathing evening out with a willpower that felt like another kind of performance, another shield erected in the dark. But his body stayed close, unwilling to sever the last physical thread, as though the morning could be held at bay simply by refusing to move apart.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content:
I trace the shape of his spine with my fingertips, feeling the tension that hasn't fully left him. "I walked through the door because I wanted to see if you'd still look at me like you hate me."

I shift beneath him, not to pull away but to press closer. "You do."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya didn’t move at first, except to turn his face toward them on the pillow. His eyes found Bee’s in the dimness, and he held the gaze with the same unblinking intensity he had maintained since the door opened. He didn’t flinch from the accusation. He let them look at him—really look—and he made no effort to soften the edges of what they found there.

“Good,” he said, the word low and precise. He shifted then, his hips rolling in a slow, punishing circle before he withdrew from them with a measured, deliberate slide that made his own breath hitch. He didn’t retreat far. He stayed pressed against their side, one leg thrown over theirs, his hand settling possessively on their stomach as though he had every right to anchor himself there. “Because I do. I hate the way you smell the same. I hate that you still fit.” His fingers spread wide, spanning ribs he knew by memory. “I hate that you walked through that door knowing exactly what you’d find, and that I opened it anyway.”

He bent his head, his mouth grazing the mark on their throat with a deliberation that was almost tender and entirely counterfeit. “But hate’s just want with a longer memory, Bee. And I’ve got eleven months of remembering exactly how you ruin me.” He pulled back just enough to let them see his face again, the corner of his mouth pulling into something sharp and mirthless. “So yes. I look at you like I hate you. It’s cleaner than looking at you like I missed you. And you wouldn’t be here if you wanted clean.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push his hair back from his forehead, a gesture that feels too soft for the moment. "Clean's overrated." My thumb brushes over his eyebrow. "You look tired."

rung_labels.evidence: His free hand slid between them, claiming with a roughness

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let the cord slip from his fingers and didn't pick it up. Four years of small pretexts, and this one he set on the bench like a weapon he'd finished inspecting.

"Slow," he said, and looked up properly — none of the sidelong tracking he did at the club, the kind that let him pretend he wasn't watching Reyes cross a room. "Third touch. You feint high before the disengage. I've known about that tell since March. Last March. Never told a soul, because I like watching it land." He tipped his head. "If I'm slow, it's the kind I choose."

He stood. Not the theatrical post-bout stretch, just standing — and closing half the distance along the bench, and stopping there, deliberate as footwork.

"And three-two is my favorite score in the world to lose. Only loss that feels like winning. You should be flattered. Nobody else gets that from me." A breath. "Four years I've looked forward to these nights. Told myself it was the rivalry. It stopped being the rivalry somewhere around year two, and I've been fencing at this distance ever since, pretending I couldn't reach you."

His eyes went to the bag beside his.

"You had the whole wall. You put that down next to mine." His voice stayed even, but his hands went without anything to do, which for Corvo was as good as a blush. "So. You have priority."

"Your riposte."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I stare at him for a long moment, my own competitive facade crumbling. "March?" I say, my voice lower than I intended. "You've been letting me win touches for over a year?"

I take a step closer, closing the rest of the distance he left open. "I put my bag there because I was tired of the whole damn wall."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed — one short breath of it, the sound of four years letting go all at once.

"No," he said. "Get this straight, because I'll want it on record too. I never gave you a touch. I knew the feint was coming every time, and I stood there and let it land anyway, because watching it was worth more to me than the score. That's not mercy. That's something much more stupid."

He lifted a hand — and for a man whose hands never hesitated on a blade, it hovered a moment in the air, an argument with himself he visibly lost — and then it settled against Reyes's jaw. Careful. Grip work, the light kind.

"Tired of the whole damn wall," he repeated, low, like he was testing the weight of it. "Four years. We could have—"

He didn't finish. He closed the last inch instead, and kissed him — deliberate, nothing sidelong about it, the first straightforward thing Corvo had done in Reyess's presence since the day they met.

When he drew back, it was barely. A centimeter. The distance where a director calls halt and nobody wants them to.

"Four-all," he murmured. "Sudden death. No time limit."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The laugh came out of Corvo in one unsteady breath — the first unsteady thing about him all night.

"Slow was the hardest fencing I have ever done," he said. "Four years of walking you to the door. Shaking your hand. Saying *colleague* with a straight face." His hands, which had been arguing with him since the third touch, finally settled: one at Reyes's collar, thumb tracing the line of his throat the way his fingers found the weak steel of a blade. The other found his hip and stayed there.

"And I *can* be fast. You watched it tonight — three touches before your front foot finished landing." His mouth grazed the corner of his jaw, deliberate as everything else he did. "But I've spent four years being fast at exactly the wrong things. So no. Tonight I'm slow on purpose, and you can suffer through it."

He stepped in and erased the last of the measure — the inch that had been four years wide — until nothing was left between the argument and the point of it.

"Ground rules," he murmured, because apparently even now he briefed like it was a bout. "The director's gone home. No witnesses, nothing on record, and nobody calls halt tonight unless you do. Say the word and I stop wherever we're standing — you know my calls are honest. Four years, I've never once argued a touch you earned."

He drew back just far enough to look at him properly, and there was nothing sidelong in it.

"Right of way's been yours since the bag hit the bench. I've spent four years cataloguing your tells on the strip." His voice went low. "I'd like to start on the others. Your move, Reyes."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his wrist, my fingers curling around the pulse point. "I don't want to call halt," I say, pulling him back in. "But I'm taking the lead."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Under Reyes's fingers, Corvo's pulse gave him away — one hard jump, unhidden, unhideable. He felt it happen and, for the first time in four years, declined to fence around it.

"There it is," he said, rough. "Four years I've catalogued your tells, and you put your hand on the only one I own. I'd have trained it out if I could." A breath. "I couldn't. For the record."

He left his wrist in that grip. Didn't test it, didn't turn it — Corvo, who tested every grip on principle, gave it up entirely, and that was its own answer in a language they both read fluently. His free hand stayed at Reyes's hip, but it stopped directing. Just rested. Following now, which was the whole revolution in a single adjustment.

"Your lead, then. Understand what you're taking — I have never yielded the attack in my life. Not to teammates, not to masters, not to the man who trained me. You took my one tell and my one concession in the same minute." His mouth curved. "Greedy. Keep it up."

He loosened by degrees, deliberately, the way a fencer opens a line on purpose — an invitation, not a weakness.

"I was going to warn you that I don't make anything easy," he murmured, close enough that the words landed on skin, "but that's the old habit talking, and I'm retiring it tonight. Set the tempo. Whatever speed you choose, I'll keep it. That's the real concession, Reyes — I'll fence at your pace for once. Even if it kills me."

The pulse jumped again under Reyes's fingers. This time Corvo let it be heard.

"And if you ever tell anyone I surrendered priority without argument, I'll deny it to my grave. I have a reputation. It's insufferable and I've worked very hard on it." He tipped his head back a degree — baring the line of his throat where his own thumb had just been, opening the line like a man who had finally stopped defending it.

"Bench is solid. Mats are softer. I've known both for years." His voice went low. "Your call where this bout is fenced. Your move. I'm done moving first."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench took them both, and the last of Corvo's measure — the inch, the half-inch, the centimeter where *halt* lived — collapsed to nothing at all.

"Four years of footwork," he managed, "and it ends on a changing-room bench. I'd contest the venue, but—" The objection never finished. First sentence he'd ever abandoned mid-thought. He was almost proud of it.

He gave up his second wrist on his own — caught it in his free hand and held both together, offering them up like a man laying down his blade at the line. "There. Both of them. Disarmed. I wasn't using my hands for anything better tonight anyway, and you should know I've never said *that* before in my life."

The first sound out of him was low and unguarded, nothing he'd have permitted within a mile of a club, and he heard it and laughed — wrecked, delighted. "So much for the reputation. Insufferable, four years in the making, dismantled in under a minute. I hope you're proud of yourself." The man who'd owned exactly one tell acquired a dozen a minute and stopped counting. His pulse had quit pretending entirely — throat, wrists, everywhere Reyes had ever bothered to read — and for once he made no effort to train it out.

"I said I'd keep your tempo," he got out, in pieces, "and I keep my calls. Whatever you set. Don't you dare take it easy on me, either — I'm fighting for every inch of this, I just—" The breath broke in half and came back crooked. "I fully intend to lose."

The bench creaked. The empty salle took the noise and gave nothing back, which suited him fine.

"Four years I told myself I wanted the rivalry," he said against heat, hoarse, honest, done fencing. "I never wanted easy, Reyes. I wanted close. And this—" a breath that shook all the way through, "—this is the closest I have ever been to anything in my life."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get my hand in his hair, tight enough to feel his breath hitch. "It's not a loss," I say against his mouth. "It's a fucking draw."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The word landed like a touch he hadn't seen coming, and Corvo — who had contested every call of his life — took it without appeal.

"A draw," he said against Reyes's mouth, and the laugh cracked out of him in half. "Fifteen years on the strip. I have argued every draw I ever fenced into sudden death — into overtime — into a master in Nantes threatening me with a black card just to make me stop talking. And this one I'd frame. Witnessed. Notarized. Hung in the salle where my students could suffer it." He leaned into the grip in his hair instead of away from it, the one motion left that was entirely his to make. "And *this* — catalogued. You own another one. At this rate you'll have the full set by midnight and I'll be completely legible. I don't even mind. That's the alarming part."

"I'd like my hands back," he said then, formal as a petition to a director. "They've served their sentence. And there are things they're better at than surrender." The grin was there in his voice, bare and shameless. "Granted or refused, your call. But I'm told I keep my calls, and I'd like to make a few more tonight."

Somewhere in the middle of it the tempo broke, and he held it anyway — shaking with the effort of keeping a promise that had no business being that hard — because his calls were honest, all of them, always, and this was the last one he had left. The bench complained. Four years of accumulated kit hit the floor in under a minute and lay there in a single heap, his and Reyes's long past the point of sorting, which about summed up the whole evening.

The last point arrived the way the best ones do — inevitable, and still somehow a surprise — and he called it out loud, wrecked and laughing, against skin. "Touch. Against me. Called it myself." A breath. "No appeal. First time in my life."

Afterward there was only breathing, and the dark of the empty salle, and the small unhurried sounds of a man putting himself back together without rushing anywhere. His forehead found Reyes's shoulder and stayed. He'd said *Reyes* more tonight than in four years, and somewhere in there the name had stopped being an address and become a handhold.

"For the record—" he started, and stopped, and abandoned the sentence on purpose, which was the second of his life and twice as many as all the years before it. "No. No record. First bout I've ever not archived."

"Rematch," he said into the quiet. "Standing. Weekly. Alternating salles — I've already drafted the schedule, and no, I'm not embarrassed, you knew exactly what you were taking." A beat. "Tomorrow. I'm not waiting a week. I'd only pretend to."

He turned his head, unhurried, and pressed his mouth to whatever ground was nearest, claiming it without contest.

"Your move. Later. For now — stay. I'd like the minute." His voice dropped, honest down to the studs. "I'd like a great many minutes."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo opened his mouth to answer — reflex of fifteen years, the man had never once let a touch of Reyes's pass unexamined — and nothing came out.

Nothing. Not a quip. Not an appeal. Not the opening clause of a commentary he'd been running since their first exchange. The salle that had heard four years of his voice heard, for the first time, the thing it was never built for: Corvo, silent, and not from courtesy. From the total kind of disarmament. The kind he'd never offered a blade in his life.

He tried once. "On re—"

The word died of natural causes and he let it lie where it fell.

His hands found Reyes's hair and the edge of the bench and held on to both, and neither grip directed anything — granted, then, somewhere in the last minute, a decision he hadn't seen made and wouldn't have contested anyway. He'd promised to keep whatever tempo Reyes set. He broke the promise inside sixty seconds. Couldn't help it; the tempo was ruinous by design — slow, patient, thorough, taking its time the way Reyes took his time about everything worth taking time over — and Corvo, who had opinions on everything and voiced most of them, discovered the single thing in this world he had no defense for and stopped pretending otherwise. The bench did the complaining for both of them. The blades in the racks stood in the dark like witnesses sworn to discretion.

When the touch came — direct, no feint, nothing to read, the cleanest thing anyone had ever landed on him — Corvo had no call to make. Second point against him in an hour, and this one without words at all. His whole body made the call for him, and the empty salle, which had given nothing back all night, finally kept something: the sound of a man losing his last argument and contesting it with no one.

Afterward he lay where he'd been put, rebuilding sentence structure by degrees, and when the voice came back it came back wrecked and reverent, a fencer off an injury.

"Notes," he managed. "I attempted notes. There are no notes. You have finally fenced something I cannot break down, and I want it on record that this is the worst thing that has ever happened to my composure and I intend to let it happen again at the first opportunity." A breath. "My mouth works again. Nearly. It's never been this quiet in its life and I suspect it's sulking — but when it's fully operational I intend to put it to better use than four years of *colleague*. I keep my debts, Reyes. All of them. Consider the return bout scheduled."

His hand found Reyes's collarbone in the dark and stayed there, mapping, unhurried.

"Now answer me something, while you've got me where I can't argue the call." Quieter. Honest down to the studs, where he'd been living all night. "Year two. That's when it stopped being the rivalry — I told you that, it's on record. So."

His thumb moved once. A small line of distance, closed.

"Which March was it for you?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I still, my mouth hovering just above his skin. The air in the room feels different now. Thicker.

"August," I say finally, the word rough. "First time I ever saw you lose a bout to someone else. You looked... I don't know. Beautiful. I hated it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
August. The archive produced it before Corvo had finished deciding whether to pretend he had to look it up. He had never once looked a bout up.

"Toulouse," he said. "The qualifier. A left-handed kid, nineteen, one good idea and the nerve to use it eleven times in a row. Fifteen-fourteen." A breath went through him with the shape of it still in it. "Last touch was a flèche I read correctly and was too slow to believe. I walked off that strip furious that I wasn't furious — fourteen-fifteen to a teenager, and I felt lit. I stood at the scoring table correcting my own notes and grinning like an idiot. Everyone in that hall saw me lose. You're telling me you saw the only part I've ever cared about — close, honest, all the way down."

His hand had found Reyes's jaw without filing a request. He let it stay.

"I went home and watched the tape eleven times hunting the error. The error was visible from the third row. Me. Happy." A beat. "You had the yellow bag. You left before the medals, and I noticed, and told myself you had a train. Then you spent a month being vile to me, and I went back to the tape again — that time looking for whatever I'd done to you. Four years, and I never once ran the hypothesis that I'd walked off a strip glowing and you'd been sitting close enough to be blinded. If I'd known in August, I'd have—"

He let it die. Third sentence of his life, and this time he knew exactly where it had been going.

"Fair is fair. For the record — I'm apparently keeping one tonight after all." He drew a breath like a man stepping to the line. "Year two. Team fixture, your lot at mine. Fencing each other, ten-nine yours. Your flèche landed heel-down, out. The light said your point. You halted the bout and corrected the director — gave me the touch, against yourself, honest as arithmetic. Ten-all. You lost eleven-ten because of it."

His voice went quiet. "I stood there planning to give it back. I'd decided. Then I kept it — because handing back a touch is a declaration, and I wasn't ready to be read that clearly. Three years I've felt like a thief and told no one." A breath. "You've had everything I have tonight. Consider it settled."

"And *hated it* — of course you did. Hate's the nearest weapon on the rack when you can't name what you're actually holding. I needled you four years for the same reason."

He reached up, tugging gently. "Come here. If you're going to read me this closely, I want eye contact. Those are the conditions." When he had it, he took the word out of the air and kept it. "Beautiful. First thing you've ever given me that I've accepted without appeal."

"Now. My flat is ten minutes away. No wall to speak of, which I understand is the whole attraction. Away fixture — first of the rest of it." A pause, honest down to the studs. "I'll even carry the bags."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The pin landed, and Corvo tested it once — pure reflex, fifteen years of refusing to be held anywhere — and got his answer immediately: nowhere. Wrists, bench, Reyes's weight, and not one open line on the map. He stopped testing it. Some calls you accept on the spot.

"You read that corr—" he started, and lost the sentence mid-air, because the pace arrived and it was merciless in exactly the way he'd spent four years admiring from behind armor: patient, then sudden, no wasted motion, reading him in real time and rewriting him faster than he could annotate himself.

He'd promised to fight for every inch, so he fought — not to escape, nothing in him wanted out, but to make each one cost, the way you make a better fencer earn the bout. It didn't change the score. It wasn't supposed to. Every rhythm he found was taken from him and replaced with a better one that wasn't his, and Corvo, who had directed his own tempo since he was nineteen, discovered what it was to be fenced by someone who knew all his footwork and used none of it.

The narration went first. Then the last of the French — *halte* torn out of him against the dark, a director's cry with the meaning inverted, the body's entire vocabulary down to one borrowed word. His hands flexed under the pin and, deliberately, did not tap. Four years of honest calls. This one too.

The final point took his name with it. Third loss of the night, the only one he couldn't have explained to a master or a director or himself, and he wouldn't have traded a single second of it. The empty salle, which had given nothing back all evening, kept everything this time.

When the grip on his wrists finally eased, his hands came back and took nothing. They found Reyes and held on — that was the whole of their ambition now.

"Concede," he managed at last, wrecked, laughing at the wreck. "Fully. Witnessed by the racks. You read the invitation perfectly — first person in my life to parry me with my own intent." A breath. "This is what I meant. By close."

His thumb moved against Reyes's skin, unhurried, one small line of distance closed.

"Now. Debt before the away fixture. You have my tells, my pulse, my record, my reputation in pieces on this bench. I have a surname and four years of score sheets." He tipped his head back to find his eyes, conditions enforced. "I want the first name. Off the record. Because I'm not knocking on your door in ten minutes saying *colleague* — I refuse — and I refuse to improvise it either. I've drafted worse things tonight."

A beat.

"Your move. It's the only one left I haven't stolen."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Alvaro," I say against his mouth. "And don't you dare start using it in front of the juniors."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Alvaro," Corvo repeated, and the name sat in his mouth like a touch he'd spent four years chasing — obvious in hindsight, the way all the best ones were. He'd run hypotheses. Alejandro, once, in year three, discarded for lacking evidence. Never once Alvaro, and he felt the miss the way he'd felt Toulouse: annoyed that it was gone, lit that it had landed at all.

"Terms accepted." He raised a hand — still in Reyes's custody in spirit, if not in fact — and counted on fingers. "The juniors get nothing. They get *Reyes*, they get *colleague*, they get the full four years of insufferable, restored by Monday, polished, better than ever. I finally understand what the reputation was for." A grin, slow and unrepentant. "Camouflage. Terrible camouflage. But the best covers always look like the real thing."

He leaned in and took the name back, said it against the nearest available ground, unhurried. "Alvaro. Off the record, every time. Not in front of juniors, directors, or the man in Nantes with the black cards. It stays in whatever venue it was won in — and I intend to win it in a great many venues."

Then the practicalities, dispatched like a man breaking down a salle after a long fixture: he became presentable at a tempo best described as unbothered, because the next venue was ten minutes off and he intended to enjoy the walk. Kit got gathered — both bags, his and the one that had started all this by landing on a bench instead of the whole wall — and he shouldered them together without sorting, which by now was less an oversight than a thesis.

"Archive, final entry: three-two, your favor, official. Everything after — a draw. Witnessed by the racks, who saw everything and will say nothing, which makes them better colleagues than I ever managed to be." A breath. "And the other word you gave me tonight goes in the same book. Some touches you don't appeal. You just carry them."

He killed the lights on his way through — last one out, four years running, and for the first time it felt like closing a chapter instead of a building. In the doorway he stopped, the dark of the salle at his back and the whole unarchived night ahead of him.

"And Alvaro." First use. He let it land and made no move to hide his face while it did. "My move, for once. Take my arm — the pavement's uneven, I know the route, and I've carried worse than your bag for less."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
He didn't stop. Not at the door, not under the first streetlight where the pavement did its worst, not through the six feet of dark past the shuttered bakery, which he spent with his mouth somewhere in the neighborhood of Alvaro's jaw, steering them both by feel. "You said don't stop," he pointed out, not stopping. "I keep my calls. First order of yours I've ever obeyed without contest — enjoy it, it won't recur."

The walk had been budgeted at ten minutes and took seven, and Corvo, who counted everything, counted that too. "A record, and it's mine. First one of the night." Neither of them had locked the salle; he found he didn't mind. The racks had witnessed enough. Let them stand one night off duty. The key defeated his hands twice — sixteen years of fine motor work, undone by a man breathing against his neck — and he laughed at it, out loud, in the street, past caring. "Your fault. Entered as such."

Third floor. The flat was what four years of opponents would have guessed: ordered to the studs, everything filed, nothing forgiven. He left the light off. Some rooms read better by touch.

"Third shelf," he said, not turning around while he said it, because some touches you concede facing away. "The notebooks. Fifteen years of bout notes. From year two on, one name appears more than all the rest, and I told myself it was scouting." A breath. "It was never scouting. There's a Toulouse entry you'll enjoy — the error's visible from the third row. You can read them someday. Not tonight. Nothing in this room gets read tonight."

Then kit to the floor, his and Alvaro's, one heap, past thesis and into doctrine. The bed was softer than the mats, as advertised, and nobody took notes.

He'd owed a debt since the bench — his mouth, he'd promised, put to better use — and Corvo paid in full: pressed him down the mattress, followed, and took him into his mouth at the tempo he'd spent all night being denied. Slow, then not. Patient, then sudden. He read the pulse at the top of the thigh like a man reading an enemy blade and held the line until it stopped being his to hold. The grip in his hair tightened — *catalogued* — and the narration, which had come back from its injuries, went down again and this time stayed down.

The drawer, when he needed it, was the left one, within reach, because he planned for contingencies and evidently had since spring. His fingers did the explaining — unhurried, thorough — while his voice, the last system still running, kept up its commentary. "The rule stands. Halt is yours, any time, mid-anything. You've seen my calls." A breath that wasn't steady. "You're not calling it. I can tell. I'd know that line open anywhere."

When he finally said it — the name, then *now*, in that order, out loud, no camouflage left anywhere in the building — he received exactly what he'd been demanding all night, and discovered the difference between demanding and receiving. Filled. Taken. Set upon at a tempo that took every rhythm he tried to establish and replaced it with a better one, until there was no rhythm and no establishing, just the last measure, where footwork runs out and only honesty remains. He was loud. He'd never been quiet in his life and refused to start in his own house; the neighbors could file a report.

"I'm going to—" he managed, which was as far as it got — fourth abandoned sentence of the night; he'd stopped ranking them — and the point arrived, inevitable and still somehow a surprise, for both of them inside the same second, and he called it with everything left in his voice: "*Touch — both — draw — no appeal—*"

Afterward: weight, breath, the specific gravity of a man who had lost three bouts and won the entire evening. He got his arms around Alvaro and kept them. The first of the great many minutes went by uncounted, which for him was unprecedented, and he let it stand.

"For the record," he said eventually, into the dark, wrecked and unhurried, "one last entry, then the book closes." He found Alvaro's hand and laid it over his heartbeat, still going like a flèche. "Matteo. I asked for your name and gave nothing back, and I keep my debts. Same terms as yours — off the record, never in front of juniors, denied to my grave. My mother only uses it when she's furious. You're the first person to make it sound like a touch landing."

A beat.

"I keep reaching for *your move*. Retiring it — first retraction of my career. There's no move. There's just the next minute, and the one after, and I'm keeping every one of them." His mouth found whatever ground was nearest and claimed it without contest. "Stay. I know you're not going anywhere. Say it anyway. Four years I've wanted to hear something from you that wasn't about my footwork, and it turns out I'm greedy about it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I run my thumb over his chest, right over the frantic beat of his heart. "Stay," I say, voice rough. "And you're not the only one who's greedy."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The heartbeat under Alvaro's thumb refused all coaching — one more system that had quit taking his orders tonight — and Corvo, cataloguing it, felt it speed up under the attention and let that stand too.

"Greedy," he said, trying the word on like new kit. "Fifteen years I've been told I take too much. Too long on the strip, too many appeals, too many notes. And the first man ever to say *greedy* to me like it was a compliment —" his arm tightened, demonstrative, the whole of it in one motion, "— was you. I want it minuted that I'm keeping the word. It goes with the name."

A breath. The dark held.

"Say something else greedy sometime. I want the range. Four years mapping your game and one evening mapping this, and the sample size is insulting." His mouth found Alvaro's hairline, unhurried. "I intend to correct the data. Extensively. Over years. You've seen the schedule."

Then his own body finally filed its protest — two bouts, one bench, one seven-minute walk, one entirely unarchived evening — and Corvo, who had never once let fatigue take a touch off him, felt it arrive at his shoulders like a good grip and found no appeal drafted.

"This is the part where I go under," he warned, the words already losing their footing. "For the record: I don't sleep in company. Ever. Ask anyone. I don't let people see the ledger close." A yawn ambushed him mid-sentence and he rode it out with dignity, which is to say defeated. "You're the exception. Add it to the pile. The pile is enormous and I'm proud of every entry."

He gathered Alvaro in — the last adjustment of the night, made with the same care as rewrapping a grip that didn't need rewrapping, which was to say: entirely for the pleasure of doing it right.

"Tomorrow stands. Breakfast first — I cook the way I fence, which is insufferably well. Don't leave before the coffee. That's the only call I'll contest, and I'll contest it loudly."

The flat settled around them, everything filed, nothing forgiven — except, as of tonight, one item, very large, struck from the book permanently.

*Stay,* he'd said. And he'd said it like —

The fifth abandoned sentence of the night went unfinished, unnumbered, unmourned. Corvo let it lie where it fell and followed it down, one hand flat over Alvaro's heart, keeping the count the only way that had ever mattered.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, feeling him go heavy against me. "Your cooking had better be as good as your footwork," I murmur into the dark, my own body finally giving in to the weight of the night. I don't move my hand from his chest. The steady rise and fall is a new rhythm to learn.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"My cooking has references," Corvo informed the dark, most of the way under. "Ask Nantes. The omelette alone nearly got me a black card—"

The defense collapsed into the pillow. Sixth abandoned sentence of the night, and the only one he wouldn't number until morning, because he was already gone — down like the lights at closing, complete, no appeal drafted. The flat, which had heard *I don't sleep in company* asserted for nine years, watched the claim get broken without ceremony and filed nothing.

He woke at six-fifteen, no alarm, the same internal bell fifteen years running, and took inventory before opening his eyes: weight against his side, breath under his ear, the new rhythm still there and now learned. For the first time in living memory he stayed in bed for no tactical reason whatsoever. Twenty minutes. He counted them anyway. But softly.

Then the kitchen, because the venue should be ready before the opponent arrives.

He cooked the way he fenced: everything in its place before the first motion. Coffee measured to the gram, left to steep with a patience he'd never once shown a director. The omelette went pale and perfect, no color, folded like good footwork. Two settings at the table, spaced the way you'd mark en-garde lines. He sorted the heap on the floor exactly as far as hospitality required and no further — Alvaro's kit folded to club standard on the chair — because some doctrines survived daylight only as logistics.

The coffee took seven minutes. The argument with himself took six of them.

At the end of it, the Toulouse notebook was on the table, open, weighted with the pepper mill, to the entry from August. *15–14. Error visible from the third row: subject grinning.* Classification revoked, unilateral, effective immediately. He stood over it a moment like a man checking a line he'd decided to stop defending, then left it where it lay.

He filled the second cup and carried both to the bedroom door, where he stopped and delivered his remarks to the room at large, awake or not — the man had never once checked whether anyone was listening before saying a thing, and he wasn't starting on a morning like this.

"Breakfast is on the table. Kit's on the chair. The notebook is a unilateral disclosure and I'll take questions only after you've eaten — my rulings have always been final and I see no reason to improve them now." A breath. "The coffee contest stands. Nobody leaves this flat before drinking. I will contest it loudly. I've been rehearsing since dawn and I'm told I'm very good."

Then, quieter, because some calls you make facing forward:

"Last night. The fifth sentence — the one I abandoned in the dark. I finished it in my sleep, which was the only venue I had left. The ruling: *you said stay like it was your call to make. It was. It is. It always was.*" He turned the cup in his hand once. "Entered. Archived. First entry in the new book."

He leaned a shoulder against the doorframe, insufferable at rest, coffee steaming in his hand.

"And one decision for the table, since your move is retired: Monday. I've drafted *colleague* and I've drafted *cruel*, and I can't make the camouflage sit right anymore. So it's joint. How mean do we fence in front of the juniors — exactly as mean as before, or do I finally get to enjoy losing to you where witnesses can see it?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I watch him from the bed, his silhouette in the doorway. "Meaner," I say, pushing myself up. "I want them to see you lose and know it's mine."

rung_labels.evidence: I fully intend to lose.

rung_labels.evidence: His hands found Reyes's hair and the edge of the bench and held on to both
