dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya's flat still had the same broken buzzer, which Bee found unreasonably infuriating, as though he could have fixed it in eleven months and had chosen not to out of spite.

"You could have texted first," he said, standing in the doorway and not moving out of it.

"You could have answered last time I did."

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I don't move either. "Are you going to let me in, or are we doing this in the corridor?"

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya held the look for a second longer than he needed to, long enough to make the silence feel deliberate rather than accidental. Then he stepped back.

Not far. Just enough to open the doorway into a narrow choice.

“Inside, then,” he said. “Unless you want the neighbours to hear which one of us is worse.”

He didn’t wait to be thanked. He turned and left the door open behind him, moving into the flat with the irritated certainty of a man who knew exactly how small the space was and how impossible it would be to stand in it without being aware of the other person.

The place smelled faintly of coffee and cold air. The kettle sat on the counter with its lid open, forgotten. A glass from last night, or maybe this morning, sat beside it, half-full with water gone flat.

Ilya shut the door only after a beat, not hard, but the click was final.

“You could have called,” he said. “But you never did like doing things the boring way.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I step inside, letting the door shut behind me. The small space feels like it's shrinking already. "And you always did like pretending you wanted boring." I glance at the glass on the counter. "Still can't finish a drink, I see."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s gaze dropped to the glass for half a second, then back to Bee.

“Still keeping score,” he said. “That’s new.”

He moved past the counter and picked up the glass. The water inside shifted dull and lifeless. For a moment he looked as if he might drink it anyway, just to be contrary, but instead he tipped it into the sink with a steady, unbothered motion.

“I can finish a drink,” he said, setting the glass down upside up on the drying rack. “I just stopped seeing the point of doing it for company.”

The words landed cleanly in the small room. He knew they would. He didn’t try to soften them.

He leaned back against the counter instead, arms folded loosely, giving Bee the full inconvenient truth of him: still too familiar, still occupying too little space in a flat that had never felt large enough for two. His expression wasn’t warm, but it wasn’t empty either. It was the look of a man who had rehearsed being indifferent and failed only in the details.

“So,” he said. “You came all the way here to insult my housekeeping, or did you actually want to say something?”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I kiss him like it's a continuation of the argument, because it is.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
For half a second Ilya did not move at all.

He stood there with the counter biting into the backs of his thighs, mouth caught under Bee’s like a challenge he had not expected but had perhaps been waiting for anyway. His first instinct looked like refusal: jaw firm, hands still folded, body deliberately unresponsive. Then the pretence snapped, or maybe he let it.

He kissed back hard.

Not gently, not with the careful grief of someone making up for lost months. He kissed like he had been chewing on the taste of it for far too long and now intended to make it unpleasant for both of them. One hand slid over the counter and fisted in the fabric at Bee’s hip, not pulling, exactly, but keeping the distance from becoming negotiable. The other came up slower and settled at the side of Bee’s neck, thumb resting there as if he meant to count the pulse and use the number later.

For a moment he let himself be ruined by it. The familiar heat, the old fit of their bodies in a space too small for either of them to think clearly. The way anger and want had never learned to keep proper boundaries around each other.

Then he drew back, only enough to make the air between them feel thin.

“That,” he said, voice rougher than he meant it to be, “is a very convenient way to avoid saying what you came to say.”

His gaze dropped once to Bee’s mouth before lifting again, dark and unimpressed and far too knowing.

He did not let go.

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I lean into his hand at my neck, refusing to look away. "I said what I came to say." My voice is low, edged. "Your turn."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s jaw tightened almost imperceptibly at the words. His thumb stayed where it was, resting against the side of Bee’s neck, and for one breath he did nothing except feel the pulse there like something he had no right to be counting.

“Your turn,” he repeated quietly, as if testing the phrase for the cheapest edge on it. “Right. You get to walk in here, put your mouth on me, and then demand a confession like it’s something I owe you.”

He didn’t move away. If anything, the space between them grew worse, more deliberate, his body still angled into Bee’s with all the old familiarity of a habit neither of them had actually broken. His other hand remained fisted loosely at Bee’s hip, not pulling, not pushing, just holding the fact of contact in place.

“You want me to say I’m still angry?” His voice dropped, low and controlled in the way that meant he wasn’t. “Fine. I am. I’m angry you knew exactly how to get under my skin before I even opened the door. I’m angry I heard the buzzer and still stood there for ten seconds pretending I wasn’t going to let you in. I’m angry I made too much coffee this morning because half my brain still thinks you’re going to want some.”

His gaze flicked once to Bee’s mouth, then back, darker now.

“And I’m angry that after eleven months, you can stand there and say *your turn* like we’re still playing the same game.” The words came out quieter than before, which made them worse. “I don’t want to forgive you. I don’t want to be fair. I want to know why you came back here when you already know what it does to me.”

He let the silence sit there, raw and unsoftened.

Then his thumb pressed once against Bee’s pulse, not hard enough to hurt, only enough to remind them both he was still paying attention.

“That’s my turn,” he said. “Now stop pretending this was about manners.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: We don't make it past the hallway. His shirt goes over his head and mine is already somewhere on the floor behind us.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a rough sound in his throat, not quite protest, not quite surrender, and then he let the last of the pretense go.

He lifted his arms enough to let the shirt be taken, the cold hallway air striking bare skin, and stepped immediately into the space it left. There was no hesitation in it now, no careful performance of indifference. His hands found Bee with the old familiarity of a map he had sworn he’d thrown away—one at the waist, the other sliding up beneath the bare line of Bee’s back until his palm rested there, warm and deliberate.

He kissed Bee like he was still angry about it. Like tenderness would have been an admission either of them wasn’t ready to survive. His mouth was hard and demanding, taking the kiss and turning it into something closer to a fight, all pressure and old grievances and the unbearable fact that eleven months had not made this unfamiliar. If anything, it had made it worse. Sharper. More precise.

When he finally drew back, it was only far enough to drag his lips along Bee’s jaw and breathe, unsteady, against the pulse point there.

“Eleven months,” he said, voice low and wrecked at the edges. “And you still know exactly how to make me forget every sensible thing I meant to say.”

His hand tightened briefly at Bee’s back, then eased, as if he’d caught himself trying to hold on too hard. The wall behind him was cold; the rest of him wasn’t. He leaned into the difference like it was the only honest thing left in the flat.

This was still the argument. It had simply changed shape, stopped pretending words were the only way to lose it.

“You don’t get to look at me like this is simple,” he murmured, mouth too close for gentleness. “It isn’t. I’m still angry. I still want you. Apparently those two things never learned how to leave each other alone.”

His thumb traced once, slowly, along Bee’s ribs, checking the boundary as much as crossing it. Then he lifted his head and looked at Bee, dark-eyed and flushed and far too open for a man who had spent nearly a year pretending otherwise.

“You came here knowing you could do this,” he said quietly. “Knowing I’d let you in. Knowing I’d still—” He broke off, jaw tightening, and the muscle jumped there under the strain. “Fine. You were right.”

He pressed closer, just enough to make the hallway feel even smaller than it was, enough that there was no mistaking what he wanted or how little patience he had left. Not gentle. Not cruel either. Just honest in the way he’d always been when he couldn’t afford to be anything else.

“If you want me to stop,” he said, voice rough, “say it now. Because if you don’t, I’m not going to be able to make this polite.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I push him back against the wall, my hand on his chest. "I didn't come here for polite." My mouth finds his again, less angry this time. More honest.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath caught at the change in the kiss.

For a moment he stayed very still, as if the softness of it was more dangerous than the anger had been. Bee’s hand on his chest kept him pinned there better than the wall did, and he let it, his heart beating hard enough beneath the palm that there was no point pretending he was unmoved.

Then his hands moved.

Not roughly this time. Slowly, deliberately, palms sliding from Bee’s waist to the bare curve of Bee’s back, skin warm against his fingers. He drew Bee closer until there was no polite distance left between them, until the hallway had narrowed to nothing but heat and breath and the unbearable familiarity of it.

When he finally broke the kiss, it was only far enough to rest his forehead against Bee’s.

“Don’t do that,” he said quietly.

His voice had gone low and unguarded in a way that clearly annoyed him.

“Don’t make it honest when I’m trying to be furious with you.”

His thumb traced a slow line along Bee’s spine, not quite a caress, not quite a warning. The cold wall pressed between his shoulders, but the rest of him was heat, flushed and tense and too aware of every place their bodies still fit.

He lifted his head. His mouth hovered near Bee’s as he spoke, close enough that every word felt like a second kiss he was refusing to give.

“You want me to stop pretending?” he murmured. “Fine. I thought about this. I thought about you showing up here like you had every right to. I thought about the buzzer going off and me hating that I already knew it was you. I thought about opening the door and still wanting you enough to make me sick.”

His jaw tightened.

“I don’t like that you know that.”

One of his hands flattened against the small of Bee’s back, pressing them just a fraction closer, not demanding, just admitting. His gaze dropped to Bee’s mouth again, then lifted, dark and deliberate.

“You said you didn’t come here for polite,” he said. “Good. Because I’m past that. I don’t want to be gracious. I don’t want to give you the easy version where we act like this is casual and neither of us spent eleven months pretending we were fine.”

He swallowed.

“But if you want me to take what I want, you don’t get to stand there looking at me like you haven’t already won.”

His fingers flexed once against Bee’s skin.

“So tell me,” he said, voice rough now, stripped of the last of its pretence. “Do you want me to hate you, or do you want me to touch you? Because I can’t seem to do one without the other.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s head tipped back against the wall with a dull thud, the sound dragged out of him before he could bite it down. His hips moved once, helpless, seeking more of the pressure Bee already had him in, and then he went still as if he could pretend that hadn’t happened.

His hand came up and closed around Bee’s wrist. Not to pull Bee away. His fingers stayed tight there, anchoring himself to the fact of it.

“Don’t,” he said, voice wrecked. Then, quieter, “Don’t say it like you didn’t know.”

He opened his eyes. They were too bright, too heated, all the careful distance gone.

“Every time,” he said. “Yes. Every single time. When you were gone, when I swore I was over it, when I heard the buzzer and knew it was you. Every time.”

His breath shuddered. He pressed forward into Bee’s hand because there was no dignity left in pretending otherwise.

“I wanted to make you pay for it,” he murmured. “I wanted to be cold. I wanted to stand in that doorway and look at you like you meant nothing. And then you touched me and I forgot every single line I’d rehearsed.”

His mouth hovered near Bee’s ear now, rough and warm.

“So no, I don’t want polite. I want you. I want this. I want to drag you into that bedroom and make us both stop lying.” His grip tightened on Bee’s wrist, not painful, only desperate. “But if you stop now, I’ll hate you for it. If you keep going, I might hate you anyway. Touch me like you mean it, or don’t touch me at all.”

He swallowed hard, forehead dropping briefly against Bee’s shoulder. When he lifted his head again, his voice was lower, stripped bare.

“I’m still angry,” he said. “And I’m still yours. Apparently I never stopped being either.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: My other hand fists in his hair, pulling just enough to make him look at me. "Then hate me." I don't break eye contact. "But take me to bed first."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya went utterly still.

The words landed like a match struck in a dark room. His pupils blew wide, jaw tightening as he stared at Bee, caught somewhere between fury and want so naked it looked like pain.

“Take you to bed,” he repeated, voice low and rough. “You say that like I haven’t spent nearly a year trying not to imagine exactly that.”

His hand came up over the one fisted in his hair, not pulling it away, pressing it firmer against his scalp instead. For a second he stayed like that, breathing hard, as if he could hold himself in place by force alone.

Then he released a breath that sounded like surrender stripped down to its ugliest bone.

“Fine.”

He moved.

Not gently. He caught Bee’s wrist and started toward the narrow hall, pulling just enough to make the direction clear. The flat gave no room for drama or distance; two steps brought them to the bedroom door, already ajar. Ilya pushed it open with one shoulder, the hinges giving a tired complaint.

The room beyond was cold and dim. The bed was unmade, sheets twisted from a night spent sleeping badly. A shirt lay on the floor near the wardrobe—his, from earlier, or maybe yesterday. He didn’t look at it.

He stopped just inside, turned, and put his back against the doorframe. His chest rose and fell. His mouth was red from kissing. He looked wrecked. He looked like a man who knew exactly what he was choosing and hated how much he wanted it.

“You don’t get to order me around and then pretend this is simple,” he said. “You don’t get to stand there with your hand in my hair and tell me to hate you like I haven’t been failing at that since the moment you walked in.”

His gaze dropped, then lifted again, dark and deliberate.

“I can hate you,” he said quietly. “I can do that. But if I take you to bed, I’m not doing it because I’m angry. I’m doing it because I want you. Because I still want you enough to make a fool of myself, and that’s the part I can’t forgive you for.”

He stepped back from the doorframe and let the space open between them. The mattress shifted faintly behind him as he bumped the edge of the bed.

“Last chance,” he said, voice rougher now. “You can still say no. You can still walk out. I won’t like it. I might not forgive you for it either.”

A beat.

His eyes burned.

“But if you come here,” he said, “I’m not going to stop.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: "Stop being careful with me," I tell him. "You don't get to be careful with me anymore." I pull his hand up to my throat and hold it there until he understands what I'm asking for.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hand went still in Bee’s.

For a second he only stared down at it—his own fingers against the vulnerable line of Bee’s throat, held there by Bee’s grip like an ultimatum. The room seemed to narrow around that point of contact. His chest rose once, sharply, and he did not speak.

When he did, his voice was quiet enough to be dangerous.

“You don’t get to do that.”

He did not pull away. He did not press either. His hand remained shaped to the space Bee had put it in, thumb resting over the jump of pulse with a stillness that was almost reverent.

“You don’t get to put my hand there and tell me to stop being careful,” Ilya said. “You don’t get to offer me the one thing that would make me unforgivable and call it honesty.”

His eyes lifted, dark and raw.

“I know what you’re asking.”

The words hung there. He swallowed.

“No.”

Not cruel. Final.

His thumb moved once, barely enough to feel the life in Bee’s throat, then he drew his hand back slowly. Not in retreat. In decision. His fingers slid from the vulnerable line of Bee’s neck to the side of Bee’s jaw instead, warm and firm, tilting Bee’s face up until there was nowhere left to hide.

“I can stop pretending,” he said. “I can stop being polite. I can take you to bed and ruin both of us with how much I still want you. But I’m not going to hurt you to prove I’m angry.”

His grip tightened just enough to make the point land without pain.

“You think careful means I don’t want it? Careful is the only reason I haven’t put you on that mattress and forgotten every single reason we shouldn’t.”

His gaze dropped to Bee’s mouth, then returned, heavier now.

“I’m past careful with wanting you,” he said. “I’m not past keeping you safe from me. That line isn’t yours to give away just because you know where it cuts.”

He released Bee’s jaw, but only to step closer, close enough that the heat between them had no polite name. His hand slid down to Bee’s waist again, possessive in a way he no longer tried to disguise.

“You told me to take you to bed first,” he said, voice roughening. “Fine.”

He leaned in, mouth near Bee’s ear.

“But we do it my way. No games. No testing how far I’ll go before I break something. You want me honest? I’m telling you: I want you so badly it makes me want to hit the wall, and I’m still furious enough to say it without flinching.”

He drew back just enough to look at Bee.

“Bed,” he said. “Now. Unless you want to keep standing in the hallway making me choose between my pride and your throat.”

Then, because he could not resist the old knife-twist, his mouth curved without warmth.

“And Bee? If you ever put my hand there again just to see what I’ll do, I’ll walk you to the door myself.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I drop my hand and push him backwards onto the bed. "Then stop talking."

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya hit the bed hard enough to make the frame knock against the wall. The sound was blunt and unromantic, and for one second he lay there with his chest heaving, hair dark against the pillow, looking up at Bee with an expression that might have been fury if it were not so close to relief.

Then his mouth twisted.

“Stop talking,” he repeated, rough. “You say that like I haven’t spent nearly a year biting my tongue raw over you.”

His hand shot up and closed around Bee’s wrist. Not to push away. He held it there against the heat of him, over the hard beat of his heart, as if to make the point without words. His other hand found Bee’s hip, thumb pressing in with deliberate weight.

“You want me quiet?” he said. “Then stop standing there giving orders and come here.”

He pulled once, not enough to force anything, but enough to show exactly where he wanted Bee: down, closer, past the last inch of pretence. His eyes stayed hard and bright, the anger in them indistinguishable from want.

“I’m not going to be careful because you think it would make this easier,” he said. “And I’m not going to hurt you because you think it would make me honest. I’m going to touch you like I remember every part of you I swore I’d forgotten. If that’s not what you want, say it now.”

His grip tightened at Bee’s hip. The bed shifted under him as he moved, restless and heated beneath the thin sheets. His fingers hooked at the edge of Bee’s clothing, not slipping beneath it, waiting.

He tugged again, trying to bring Bee down over him, and when he spoke once more his voice had dropped into something lower, almost wrecked.

“Because if you don’t,” Ilya said, “I’m going to take every sound you came here to give me, and I’m not going to pretend I’m sorry for it.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya made a sound like something tearing and pulled Bee down with him.

His mouth took the order and swallowed it. He kissed Bee hard, one hand fisting in the sheets, the other sliding down Bee’s back to the curve of hip. He rolled them once, putting Bee beneath him, because if he was going to obey, he needed the advantage.

“Not careful,” he said against Bee’s lips. “You asked for that.”

He sat up just enough to finish stripping them both, impatient hands shoving fabric aside. When Bee’s skin met his again, his breath left him in a rough gust. He braced over Bee, chest heaving, and looked down with dark, furious eyes.

Then he lowered his head and did not talk anymore.

His mouth went to Bee’s throat, not to bruise, teeth scraping over the pulse he had refused to hurt. He kissed lower, over collarbone and sternum, hands mapping every familiar line as if reclaiming territory. His palm slid down Bee’s stomach, over hip, and settled between Bee’s thighs. He pressed close, feeling the heat there, and closed his eyes for a second as if the contact physically cost him.

When he opened them again, there was nothing careful left.

He nudged Bee’s thighs wider with his knee and settled between them. His thumb traced the bare skin there, slow once, then firmer. He watched Bee’s face, searching, not because he expected permission but because he was still determined to keep Bee safe from him even while he ruined them both.

Then he put his mouth where his hand had been.

The sound he made was low and broken. He tasted salt and skin and eleven months of pretending he had forgotten this. His fingers joined his tongue, pressing, circling, learning the rhythm he had once known by heart. He worked at Bee with the same anger that had kept him awake, the same want he had tried to drown in bad coffee and colder silence. He did not stop. He kept his mouth there through the burn in his jaw and the ache in his own body, one hand gripping Bee’s hip hard enough to leave marks he would later have to answer for.

When he finally lifted his head, his lips were wet and his eyes were black.

“You told me not to stop,” he said, voice scraped raw. “I’m holding you to it.”

He moved up and kissed Bee again, deep and filthy, letting Bee taste what he had just done. His hand went between their bodies, finding himself, stroking once, twice. He was hard enough to make a mockery of every boundary he had set in the hallway. He pressed the blunt heat of himself against the place between Bee’s thighs and went still, forehead dropping to Bee’s shoulder.

“Christ,” he breathed. “You still wreck me.”

He did not wait for an answer. Bee had already given him the only one he was willing to take.

He pushed in.

Slow at first, because he was still not willing to be cruel, then all at once because he was only human. The bed knocked against the wall. Ilya went rigid, a curse tearing out of him, his fingers digging into Bee’s hips as he tried to hold himself together.

For one moment he could not move at all.

Then

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I bite down on his shoulder to keep from making a sound. It doesn't work.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s breath left him in a harsh hiss at the bite, sharp and grounding all at once. The sting of it sank into his shoulder and straight through him, dragging the last of his restraint thin. He did not pull away. He drove into the heat of Bee instead, fully, until there was no space left between them and no polite fiction left to hide behind.

“That’s it,” he said, voice rough against Bee’s mouth. “Use me if you need to.”

Then he moved.

It was not gentle. He had been asked not to be gentle, and he was done pretending he could be. He set a pace that had nothing to do with patience and everything to do with the eleven months he had spent starving for this. The bed knocked against the wall with every thrust, the sound blunt and obscene in the small room. One forearm braced beside Bee’s head, taking his weight; the other hand stayed at Bee’s hip, fingers digging in hard enough to mark.

He watched Bee with dark, wrecked eyes.

“You wanted this,” he said, low and unsteady. “You came here for this. Don’t you dare make me pretend it’s anything else.”

The words came out harsher than he meant them to, but he did not soften them. He could not. Not with the way Bee felt around him, hot and tight and familiar enough to ruin him all over again. Not with the bite on his shoulder still burning. Not with the sound Bee had already made still living in his head like a match struck against his nerves.

He changed the angle of his hips, driving deeper, and the breath tore out of him.

“Christ—”

He dropped his forehead to the pillow beside Bee’s head, jaw clenched, trying to hold himself together by sheer force. His control was fraying at the edges. He could feel it slipping, thread by thread. He wanted to be rougher. He wanted to take everything he had been denied. But even now, even like this, he knew the line. He had drawn it himself. He would not cross it just because Bee tried to hand him the knife.

Instead he pressed his mouth to the place where Bee’s pulse beat and breathed there, hard and ragged.

“I’m not going to hurt you,” he said against Bee’s skin. “Not like that. You don’t get to make me.”

His hand slid from Bee’s hip, down the curve of thigh, then back up again, possessive and desperate. He found the slick heat between them and swore under his breath, fingers pressing there with deliberate, filthy precision. He worked in time with his thrusts, no longer pretending he could last if he kept this up. His thumb circled, pressed, demanded. His hips snapped harder, deeper, chasing the friction until the bed frame slammed again and again.

“Stop talking?” he said, voice breaking on the words. “You think I can stop talking when you feel like this? When you’re trying to take me apart?”

He lifted his head. His eyes were black with want, his mouth swollen, his whole body drawn tight as wire.

“Look at me.”

It was not a request.

“I want to see you when I ruin us both.”

The sound that came out of him next was low and wrecked, more animal than word. He drove into Bee with everything he had left, no rhythm now except need. His hand between their bodies moved faster, slick and relentless, thumb pressing hard where Bee was hottest, fingers working with the same furious familiarity he had once known by heart. He did not hold back. He did not pretend. He touched Bee like he was still angry, like he was still in love, like those two things had never stopped being true.

“I hate that I know how to do this,” he gasped. “I hate that I still do. I hate that you let me.”

His hips stuttered.

His breath came in broken pulls, shoulders shaking, the last of his control snapping clean through. He came hard, face turned into the pillow beside Bee’s head, a rough, shattered sound dragged out of him as he spilled deep and helpless. His fingers bit into Bee’s hip, holding on like he was falling. The aftershocks ran through him in waves, and still he did not collapse. He stayed there, trembling, breathing ragged, forehead damp, mouth open as he fought for air.

Then, because he had been told not to stop, and because he was not finished, he forced himself to move again.

His hand kept working between them, slick and steady, thumb circling with the same relentless pressure even as his own body trembled from release. He pressed his mouth to Bee’s jaw, then the corner of Bee’s lips, then finally claimed Bee’s mouth again in a kiss that was no longer angry, only raw.

“I’ve got you,” he murmured, voice wrecked. “I’ve got you. Don’t you dare make me stop now.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I come apart under his hand, a raw, shuddering mess. I don't look away.

dialogue.name: Ilya
dialogue.content:
Ilya’s hand slowed but did not leave.

He stayed over Bee while the last of it moved through them both, trembling hard enough that he had to brace one forearm against the mattress to keep from collapsing. His breath came in rough, shattered pulls, mouth open against Bee’s skin, and for a long moment he made no sound at all except the helpless noise of a man who had been holding himself together for far too long and had finally failed.

When he lifted his head, his face was wrecked.

Not pretty. Not composed. Not the cold, indifferent mask he had worn at the door. His eyes were dark and glassy with heat, his lips swollen, his jaw tight with the aftershock of everything he had refused to say until it had been dragged out of him by touch instead.

“Christ,” he breathed.

He stayed there for another second, as if he could not quite believe what he had done. Then he moved carefully, deliberately, withdrawing with a sharp intake of breath that he did not try to hide. The cold air slipped between them, and he went still for a moment, shoulders rising and falling as if that absence cost him something.

He sat back on his heels and looked down.

Not away. Not with shame. Not with triumph either. His gaze moved over Bee with a raw, searching attention, checking, taking in, refusing to pretend he had not just been as desperate as he had accused Bee of making him.

Then he reached for the twisted sheet and dragged it up over them both, the movement rough and practical, not modest. His hand hovered for a beat before settling at Bee’s hip again, lighter now through the thin fabric. Not claiming. Not demanding. Just there.

“Don’t look at me like that,” he said quietly, voice scraped raw.

His thumb moved once against the sheet.

“Like this fixes anything.”

The words were hard, but there was no real bite in them. Only exhaustion. Only the blunt truth of a man who had just spent every last defense he had.

“It doesn’t.”

He did not move away.

Instead, he lowered himself beside Bee, close enough that the heat between them had not yet died, though he left enough space for either of them to choose what came next. One arm bent beneath his head; the other stayed within reach, fingers resting near Bee’s under the sheet without closing around them.

“I’m still angry,” he said.

He stared at the ceiling for a moment, chest still moving unevenly. Then his eyes cut sideways, dark and honest and too open.

“And I still wanted this. Wanted you. Enough to hate myself for it afterward, maybe.” A muscle worked in his jaw. “But I’m not going to stand here and pretend I didn’t.”

His fingers shifted, just enough to brush against Bee’s. An offer, not a demand.

“So don’t make this into forgiveness,” he said, quieter now. “I’m not giving you that yet. And I’m not taking it either.”

A breath.

“But I’m not sorry I touched you.”

His gaze dropped once to Bee’s mouth, then lifted again, heavy with everything he had not finished feeling.

“Stay until I can think,” he said. “Then we can decide whether this was a mistake, or just the worst kind of honesty.”

dialogue.name: Bee
dialogue.content: I stay where I am. My hand covers his, still damp and trembling. "It was both," I say, my voice hoarse. "Always is with us."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's hands stopped on the grip. The rewrapping had been an excuse for twenty minutes, and a transparent one, and now Reyes's bag sat against his like it had every right to be there.

"Slow," he repeated, turning the word over the way he'd test a blade for flex. He set the weapon down on the bench and finally looked up. "I read that disengage off your back foot. You've been telegraphing it since the autumn open. That's not slow. That's four years of footage."

He stood, and understood immediately that it was either a mistake or a decision — at this distance, the same thing. Standing halved the space between them, and there was nothing left to justify it. No fourteen meters of piste. No referee. The scoring machine on the wall had gone dark an hour ago; the 3-2 existed now only because they kept handing it back and forth like it was still worth something.

"You want the truth about the third touch?" He rolled his shoulders, loose, the way he did before a bout he actually cared about. "Three-one ends it. And I wanted—" The sentence had an edge on it he hadn't fully inspected. He let it land anyway. "I wanted the version where you come back."

He held out his hand. They'd already shaken on the strip, masks off, proper form. This one had no salute in front of it, no witnesses, no reason except that he wanted one more point of contact than the score strictly allowed.

"Three-two," Corvo said. "Rematch?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I stare at his hand for a moment too long. Then I reach out and clasp it, grip firm. "Three-one would've been a mercy. And I don't need your mercy, Corvo." My voice is low. "But I'll take the rematch."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Mercy," Corvo said, and let the word sit the way a blade sits on a blade when neither side commits. "You've misread it, then."

He still had Reyes's hand. That was the plain fact of the matter. A handshake had a natural lifespan — a pump, a release, done — and this one had outlived it by a good five seconds, and nobody had called time. He could feel the calluses, the ridge along the base of the fingers, the strength sitting quiet in the wrist. Four years reading that grip on a weapon, and it turned out it was a different thing entirely against his own palm. Warmer. He filed it away with the disengage off the back foot: data he had no professional use for and every other kind.

"It wasn't mercy. I gave you the third because I wasn't done with you yet." His thumb moved — barely, a centimeter, across the knuckle — and he watched Reyes's face while he did it, the way he'd watch for the twitch that betrays the parry. "Three-one, you're out the door and we do this again next month and everything stays exactly as it's been for four years. Three-two, you have to come back to the line. That's not generosity, Reyes. That's appetite."

Then he let go — on his own count, deliberately, because if the grip was going to start meaning things, he intended to be the one who chose when. Some exchanges you don't drift into.

He crossed to the scoring box and thumbed it awake. It chimed. Both lamps dark, 0-0, the 3-2 wiped off the display like it had never existed — a lie they were both apparently willing to let the machine tell.

"Rematch, then. But I'm raising the stakes, because I'm done fencing you for bragging rights on a Tuesday night." He took his weapon back off the bench, and it settled into his hand differently than it had an hour ago. "Three touches. Winner gets a question. Loser answers it straight — no parry, no riposte, no counter-question. The truth, whatever it turns out to be."

He rolled his shoulders loose. "Terms cut both ways. Take it off me and you can ask anything you like, and I'll have to answer. I'm not offering a game you can't win — you know me better than that by now."

He stepped back onto the strip, set his feet, and let the point drop into line.

"And I want it on record: I hope you make it close. I always do."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked at his own hand first.

It was still holding the shape of a weapon. Fingers curled around a guard that wasn't there, forefinger laid along the line where a blade should have been — four years of muscle memory preserving the form of an absence. On the bench, his weapon sat where Reyes had put it, like evidence.

"One–nothing," he said. "You attacked an unarmed man before the salute. That's a red card in every salle on the continent, and you'd be bleeding penalties." His voice had come down without his permission. He left it there. "Four years, not one foul between us. First time you cheat, you cheat like you mean it. I'd be proud if I wasn't the victim."

The textbook answer to a lost blade was distance — retreat, retrieve, re-engage. He'd drilled that recovery into a hundred teenagers. He watched himself decline to perform it, and noted, with something adjacent to professional horror, that he did not want the weapon back.

"Slow all evening. And you've decided to loot the question without winning the bout — bold, for the record; I'd have done the same at your age." He counted on the hand that still held the ghost of a grip. "Twenty minutes on a wrap that needed nothing. Five seconds past the natural death of a handshake. One touch, the third, handed over so the night wouldn't end. That's not slow, Reyes. That's second intention — all of it. Every move I made tonight was first intention, and you were always the counter. I've been standing here waiting on your riposte since the first unnecessary loop of tape." He tipped his head, almost a salute. "There it is. Only took you four years."

Then he took Reyes's hand — the one that had disarmed him — and did not shake it. His thumb settled over the knuckle where it had drifted, covert, an hour ago. Openly now. On the record.

"You took a blade off me. I'm taking this. And note that I'm answering your question straight without being made to — biggest tell I've given you in four years, so treasure it."

He closed what little distance was left, down to nearly none of it — close enough to feel warmth coming off skin, close enough that any extension would be a foul — and stopped there. Deliberate. On his own count.

"Some exchanges you don't drift into," he said. "The last touch is yours, Reyes. I gave you the third for the same reason. And take your time — I've been slow all evening, and it appears to be working."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I take a slow breath, my eyes locked on his. "Second intention," I say, and my free hand comes up, fingers curling into the fabric of his jacket. "Is that what you're calling it?"

I don't pull him closer. I just hold him there, caught in the middle of a step neither of us has taken. "You wanted the version where I come back," I say, voice rough. "So here I am."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"No," Corvo said. "Second intention is wanting the counter. I never wanted the counter." The words came out lower than he'd planned. Most things had, tonight. "Every move I made was first intention. The tape, the handshake, the touch I handed you so you'd stay — a straight attack, all of it. I just fenced it slowly enough that you'd let me."

"And here you are."

He looked, because he was finally close enough to. Four years of reading that body through mesh — back foot, wrist, the lie of the shoulders — and the face had been rumor the whole time. At this measure it was fact. He took his time with it. Slow. It was working.

Reyes had the jacket, the grip, the measure — everything a counter could ask for. Corvo had the tempo. He'd always been a tempo fencer.

His free hand came up and found the line of the jaw, thumb settling along it: the same thumb, the same deliberate drift it had made across a knuckle an hour ago, done openly now, and done here. One hand each. Even terms. He'd spent four years insisting on even terms, and he wasn't abandoning them at the end of the phrase.

"A phrase ends when the touch lands," he said. "We've been in one since the first loop of tape."

He gave the last interval a tempo. Then he shortened it.

The approach was slow — of course it was; slow had built the entire evening — but a good extension holds its acceleration for the final inch, and his did, and the kiss landed with more weight than anything that leisurely had any right to carry. A touch is supposed to register in the fingertips. This one registered everywhere. And somewhere in it the count went — the first thing all night he hadn't timed — and he found he didn't miss it. Some exchanges you don't drift into. He hadn't drifted into this one. He'd just stopped counting.

He drew back far enough to speak, and no further.

"Both lamps," he said. "Double touch. No referee, no priority, nobody wins the question." His thumb moved along the jaw — slow. "By my own standards, that was the best fencing of the night. And I'm still not done with you.

"So ask me something anyway. I'll answer it straight — no parry, no riposte. And take your time. I've been slow all evening, and it's gotten me everything I wanted."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The plan, such as it was, had ended at the bench. The changing room did not care. It had tile on every surface, a hook rail, and an echo with no manners, and through the open door the salle still glowed — the scoring box sitting patient at 0-0, keeping a score nobody was playing anymore.

Fencing kit was engineered to come off slowly. He'd taught fourteen-year-olds to dress in under ninety seconds for twenty years and never once resented the design; now his own zip caught at the shoulder exactly where it had always caught, and he heard himself make a sound about it that the tile handed back to him, unflattering and honest. Kit went to the floor — his, Reyes's, the distinction collapsing almost immediately — and what was underneath four years of jacket was better than the rumor. Warmer. He'd known it would be. Knowing hadn't prepared him.

He tried, briefly, out of professional habit, to keep the count. Tempo. Measure. The interval between actions — that was the whole art, and he was good at the whole art, and none of it survived the bench. Every touch landed and the phrase refused to end: renewed, reset, extended. Somewhere in it the count fell apart entirely, and he noticed it fall, and made no move to catch it — which was the discovery of the evening. Fencing was intervals. This was arrhythmia. His heart had seized the tempo and the rest of him was keeping up on pure footwork.

He'd been slow all evening. He wasn't slow now. The man who called every touch, who kept score in his head when the machines failed — that man was making noise he couldn't transcribe, and the room was small and hard-surfaced and gave all of it back with interest, and there was no referee left in the building to call halt.

Both lamps. The double touch came the way the first one had — simultaneous, no priority, nobody's call — and this time he didn't narrate it, didn't rank it, didn't reach for the score at all. He just held on through it, both hands, and let it take the count with it.

Afterwards: the bench, the dark, the breathing. They hadn't drifted into this one either. Reyes had attacked, clean off the line, and Corvo had counter-riposted with everything he had, and the record could show a double touch and be welcome to it.

"You never asked your question," he said eventually, to the ceiling. His voice was wrecked and he made no attempt to repair it. "Just took the answer off me. For the record, that's the biggest theft of the night, and I'm including my blade."

His hand found the nearest thing the dark offered — a wrist, an arm — and settled into it, thumb over the knuckle, the drift now a permanent address.

"So here's mine, and I'm changing the terms again, because I've been changing them all evening and you keep signing. Stay. My flat is ten minutes from here and it has a bed, which puts it two up on this bench. And then tell me when you close tomorrow, and the day after. I'm done with Tuesdays, Reyes. I want the whole season." A breath. "And before you answer — I want it on record that I've been telegraphing this for four years. You're not the only one with a tell. You're just the one who finally took the touch."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push myself up onto my elbow, looking down at him in the dim light. My breath is still coming hard. "The whole season, huh?" My free hand traces a line down his chest. "I close at nine tomorrow. Don't be late."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed. It came out low and unrehearsed, and the tile — which had shown no mercy to any sound he'd made all night — let this one off easy. First laugh of the evening. Late, like everything he'd actually meant.

"Late," he said. "Reyes. I spent twenty minutes rewrapping a grip that needed nothing. I have never been late to you in my life. I've been early and calling it coincidence for four years. Slow is a tempo choice — I'll cop to that all night, you've earned the citation. Late is a forfeit, and I don't forfeit."

He caught the hand at his chest and pressed it flat over his sternum, where the count used to live. "Feel that. The man who calls every touch in that salle lost the count entirely tonight and isn't filing a complaint. That's the most honest thing I've said all evening, and I said it with my pulse."

He sat up — the bench registered its objections and was overruled — and took inventory of the floor, which looked like a locker room that had lost an argument with itself. "Your glove's the one with the older tape. Mine's the newer one, which I'll note was applied for no reason and worked perfectly." He sorted by feel in the dark and dressed without ceremony, and found that after the evening's opening tempo, ordinary speed felt like a different discipline entirely.

One more piece of business before the door. "You still have a question on deposit. Double touch, nobody won the right to ask — but I offered, and you never spent it. Keep it. Spend it tonight, next month, mid-bout, whenever it suits you. I'll answer straight, no parry. Consider it the first thing I've ever handed you that wasn't the third touch."

The salle lay dark except for the scoring box, still glowing its patient 0-0, keeping score for a bout nobody was playing anymore. Corvo crossed to it and thumbed the power off, and both lamps died for good, and four years and one evening closed out on a machine's version of nothing. Fine by him. The record had never once held the real score. The real score was walking out of the building at his side.

The street door opened onto cold air and a change of measure. Ten minutes to the flat, and he took Reyes's hand for the whole distance — proper grip, thumb settled over the knuckle, the drift now a permanent address — because the evening had taught him exactly one new technique and he intended to drill it until it was reflex.

"Nine o'clock tomorrow," he said. "I'll have your closing schedule memorized by Friday — the way I learned that disengage off your back foot. By watching you for years without admitting why." A pause, the length of a breath held on the line. "And Reyes — don't be early. I want to be the one waiting."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The ten minutes to the flat survived exactly one step. He'd gotten the street door open, one lungful of cold air, a closing statement fully drafted — *don't be early, I want to be the one waiting* — and then the statement died unread, because he was being walked backward over the threshold he'd just opened, back through the changing room he'd already closed out, and down onto the bench for the second time in one evening. Flat on his back, this time. The zip that had caught at his shoulder all night caught again on the way down, and he heard himself make a sound about it that had nothing to do with the zip.

And then Reyes's mouth, and the tempo.

He recognized the tempo immediately — the way you recognize your own handwriting forged. Slow. Held. Patient past the point of decency. He had spent the entire evening at exactly this speed and called it strategy, and it turned out the tempo was a far better weapon here than it had ever been in his hands, and it was being used on him now with four years of accrued interest.

He had an answer for everything tonight. That had been the whole architecture of the evening: citation, counter, record — he'd answered questions nobody asked, twice, voluntarily. This was the first thing all night with no answer coming, and he could feel the machinery try anyway, mouth opening around the shape of *for the record, the tempo is* — and what came out instead was not a citation in any language. The tile took it down regardless. The room was transcribing sounds he couldn't transcribe himself, and he was producing copy at a rate that would have alarmed him if any part of him were available for alarm.

One hand found the slats and gripped until the wood complained — the bench had objections; overruled, same as before. The other he put over his own mouth, a late and doomed parry, and it did not survive contact either. His spine kept leaving the wood. He tried, out of pure professional habit, to keep the count — intervals, that was the whole art, and the whole art was failing — but there were no intervals. There was one long held note, and somewhere inside it the count went, and this time he didn't even notice it leave.

The scoring box was dark; he'd killed it himself. No referee, no lamps, no record — so nothing confirmed it when the touch finally landed except him, and it landed clean. One-sided. No double touch, no counter, no simultaneous anything. He never found the parry. He never set the parry.

It took language a while to come back, and it came back at the foundations.

"Touch," he told the ceiling, wrecked past repair and filing no claim. "Clean, off the line, against. I want it on record — the record's audio-only now, the tile's keeping it — that I saw it coming the whole way down and could not do one single thing about it. That's not being caught, Reyes. That's being out-fenced." A breath, borrowed from somewhere. "Four years I've told anyone who'd listen that I enjoy losing when it's close. Amend it: closest loss of my career, and I'd pay good money to lose it again."

His hand found the back of Reyes's head and stayed there — no steering, just weight, thumb at the temple. An address, not a grip.

"And note the terms, because I set them and I'll be bound by them. Winner gets a question. Loser answers straight — no parry, no riposte, no counter-question. You had one on deposit, and that one I handed you. This one you took off me clean. Different animal: earned, not lent. Two questions to your name now, if you're counting — and one of us still isn't."

The dark held still around them. Somewhere past the door, the dead machine kept its nothing.

"So spend it whenever you like. Now. At nine tomorrow. Mid-bout next month with your mask on and a whole salle watching me hold a straight face. I'll answer it straight either way." His voice had nothing left under it, which was, he suspected, the most honest register he owned. "Ask me anything. And take your time — the tempo's yours now. I've been slow all evening, and it turns out I was only ever slow for you. Take the distinction or leave it. The tile heard it either way."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push myself up, my hands braced on his shoulders, and look down at him. My lips are still wet. "My first question," I say, and my voice is rough. "What took you so long?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The question came the way the best ones do — straight off the line, no preparation, no feint — and Corvo watched it the whole distance and arrived at the moment of impact with nothing prepared. A breath left him that was half a laugh.

"Straight to the chest on the first question," he said. His voice was still wrecked and he left it that way; the question had earned the honest register, and he owned exactly one. "Fine. Terms are terms. I set them, I'm bound by them. No parry, no riposte, no counter-question. Straight."

His hand came up and closed around the forearm braced on his shoulder — gently, thumb settling into the drift, the address now permanent.

"Here's what I believed, all four years, down at the foundation: that the touch ends the phrase. Land it or miss it, either way the bout concludes. Hit, and Tuesdays become something else. Miss, and Tuesdays stop existing. There is no line on any score sheet I've ever read for *keeps happening.* I checked. Twenty years in the sport. There's no box for it."

"So I never extended. That's the answer. Retreat, invitation, needle — four years of it, because a bout in progress was the only version of you I was certain I could keep. And you know what I am. A man who loves a close bout more than he loves winning. Why would I ever close one out? Slow isn't slowness, Reyes. Slow is the only tempo at which a thing doesn't finish."

"I told you hours ago I gave you the third touch because I wasn't done with you. That was every touch. Every generous call, every rematch, every *one more* I ever offered across that piste — same touch, four hundred repetitions. I wasn't done. I was never once done."

"And don't mistake duration for discovery. It didn't take four years to know. I knew inside the first month — I read bodies for a living, and yours was the easiest read I ever came across and the last one I was willing to admit to. It took four years to risk. Those are different clocks."

He took a breath and took it plain from there, no metaphor left on the rack.

"The unarmored version, since you paid for it: I was afraid. I'm thirty-eight. I have a salle, a grip-tape habit, and a calendar where Tuesdays were the best thing written on it. I believed landing the real touch ended the bout, and the bout was all of it. Tonight the double touch didn't end it. Then the clean touch — yours, off the line, no counter left in me — didn't end it either. You're still here, asking questions. Twenty years I've taught that the phrase closes when the touch lands, and you falsified the textbook in one evening. That's what took me so long. I spent four years protecting the bout, and it took being hit clean to learn the thing I couldn't afford to lose was never the bout."

"No counter-question, per terms — I won't ask how long you'd been sitting on your side of it. Though you did disarm me before the salute, so the record is not silent."

He drew down, slow, on the forearm under his thumb — an invitation with no count on it, the tempo of a man with a whole season ahead of him.

"Question answered. Straight, on the record; the tile has it. And the final entry, for completeness: you asked what took me so long, and the answer is that I was making it last. I've had the speed the entire time, Reyes. I just never once wanted to be done."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Prove it properly or concede." Corvo heard the terms arrive and recognized them instantly, because they were his — he'd been issuing that exact ultimatum across a piste for four years in different grammar. Reyes had stolen his blade, his playbook, and now his own hands, and was reading all three back to him from above. There was a word for that. *Theft* was too small.

He weighed the options with what little of him was still assigned to analysis. Concede, and the record closed out as slow-because-incapable — four years of tempo strategy downgraded to a mobility problem. Prove, and he had to spend the thing he'd been hoarding since the first unnecessary loop of tape. No third door. Fine. He'd chosen doors all evening and knew the good one by feel.

"Concession declined," he said. Wrecked, low, and steady on every consonant — the last part of him still drilling. "But I'll yield you the wrists. Keep them. They're yours for the season." He went deliberately loose under the pin — no struggle, an open line — and knew precisely what an open line did to this particular opponent, because he'd watched it work for four years from the other side of it. "And before you cite that I asked for this — I did. I handed you the tempo. The tempo, Reyes. Not the outcome. Hold the pace. Watch what a tempo fencer does inside somebody else's rhythm."

Then he stopped being slow.

Not gradually. That was the whole demonstration. An evening of held notes, and all of it had been one count held so long it looked like a style — and he broke it in a single beat. His hips came up off the slats to meet the pace, and then to lead it, answering on the off-beat, stealing the rhythm from underneath the way you steal priority: by being already inside the phrase when the other man believes he's starting one. The bench filed its third objection of the evening and was overruled with prejudice.

His mouth was free, so he used it — the one weapon nobody had thought to disarm. He talked. Low, ruined, needling even now, because the record was audio-only and he meant to leave the tile something worth keeping: what had been withheld, for how long, and what was about to land. The words came apart in the middle. He kept the count of that. *One.* First count he'd held all night.

His legs — the engine, twenty years of footwork, the part of him nobody ever pins — hooked and dragged the geometry down out of the chosen distance and into his own, and there it was. The final inch. A good extension holds its acceleration for the final inch; he'd said so hours ago with his mouth a centimeter from landing, and he'd been telling the truth about more than the kiss. He'd held his acceleration for four years — through every generous third touch, every *one more* — and here, wrists in custody, he spent it. All of it. One inch, full speed, off his own count.

The touch landed clean. Somewhere above him the tempo broke in the same instant, and he called it anyway, to the ceiling, wrecked past repair and filing nothing:

"Both lamps — but read the tempo on it. That wasn't simultaneous. You were in the middle of your slow, and I finished at speed. First clean touch of the night, landed from a pinned position with no hands, which makes it the best fencing of my career and the least repeatable. There's your proof, Reyes. Four years, one inch, spent in a single beat."

His wrists were still held. He made no application for their return.

"And note the distinction, since you paid for it tonight: I yielded the wrists. I never conceded the bout. Ask my students which one loses matches." His thumb drifted as far as the grip allowed — no distance at all, and somehow still enough. "You can let go now. Or don't. I've been looking for a permanent address."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My grip tightens on his wrists, breathless. "Then consider this your permanent address," I say, my hips moving against his, slow again but deliberate. "But I'm not letting go."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Permanent address accepted," Corvo said, and the tile took the countersignature down. "Note the terms for the file: I offered a flat with a bed, and you've countersigned with a bench and a grip. Smaller than advertised. Worse heating. Better location than anything I've ever owned." His voice was wrecked and he left it in the honest register — the address had been granted in that register and he wasn't going to downgrade it now. "I hold the lease. You hold the wrists. And look closely at what you've actually signed, because it isn't the bench. It's the season. The bench came with it."

Then the tempo resumed, and he recognized it the way you recognize your own signature forged — because it was his. Slow. Deliberate. Patient past the point of decency, a phrase he'd coined about himself ninety minutes ago and was now enjoying from the receiving end at four years' accrued interest. He'd told the ceiling why, hours back, and the tile had it on file: slow is the only tempo at which a thing doesn't finish. He'd built that doctrine alone, at night, over four years of Tuesdays — and here it was being practiced on its author, at full proficiency, and it was working, and there was probably a word for that in some language. He had no hands free to look it up.

He made no application for the wrists. He kept his own terms. But he turned one wrist a single degree inside the custody — not escape, negotiation — until his thumb found the inside of the forearm pinning it. Pulse, right under the pad. He settled there the way he'd settled over a knuckle an hour ago: an address. If they were confiscating his hands, he'd take the clock instead.

"No referee left in the building," he said, "so I'm self-appointing. Corps à corps halts the phrase in any salle on the continent — body to body, suspension, cards if you jostle. Note for the record that nobody is halting anything. The bout proceeds. And the clock is under my thumb now, Reyes, and it's running fast."

He'd had one acceleration banked in four years and he'd spent it a beat ago — one inch, full speed, least repeatable touch of my career, a claim he intended to keep honest. A proof repeated stops being proof and becomes habit. So he did the thing he had never once done across four years of Tuesdays: he stayed inside the tempo instead of breaking it. Yielded it on purpose, matched it, moved within a rhythm that belonged to somebody else — yield the tempo, keep the bout, same doctrine as the wrists.

The bench filed its fourth objection of the evening and was overruled with prejudice. His mouth remained unconfiscated — an oversight he continued to exploit — and he used it, needling even now, because the record was audio-only and the tile deserved copy: how long he'd wanted exactly this custody, what it felt like to be held at his own philosophy, which of them was really the pinned one. His spine kept leaving the wood and he stopped auditing it. The words came apart in the middle. He kept the count of that. *Two.* Second count of the evening. And under his thumb the pulse climbed, and he counted that too — intervals, honest, held — and the count got into double digits and then quietly stopped being numbers.

They arrived together. Same tempo, same beat, a touch he'd matched instead of stolen, and he called it to the ceiling with what voice remained:

"Both lamps — and for the first time tonight I'll sign the call. I've claimed double three times and disputed my own ruling on every one. This one's true. I matched it on purpose. That's the first honest double of my career, and I'd like it entered that I chose it."

And the phrase still didn't close. The grip held. The tempo didn't finish — of course it didn't; it was his doctrine, doing precisely what he'd built it to do. Landed on, held through, still here — his textbook falsified twice in one night by the same pair of hands, and he filed no complaint anywhere, with anyone, ever.

"One question still on deposit," he said eventually, to the dark, wrecked past repair and content there. "Spend it whenever you like. But if it turns out to be *stay* — don't waste it. That answer I give free, no bout required, every time you ask." His thumb moved on the pulse, slow. "Season starts at nine. I'll be outside at eight-fifty and call it coincidence, same as the last four years. And Reyes — the address is holding. The tenant has no complaints, and he isn't going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop."

Three syllables, no argument in them anywhere. Corvo ran the tape back out of pure habit — four years of contested calls, disputed touches, appeals lodged on principle — and found nothing to appeal. For the first time in their entire history, Reyes had asked instead of taken, and the asking was the tell of the night: the counter finally standing still on the line, mask off, saying *this is what I want* in plain grammar.

"Noted," he said. Wrecked, low, the honest register, no repairs attempted. "First order you've ever given me that I've taken without appeal. Filed under standing orders — no terms, no expiry. And note that I'm the one waiving terms this time. There's a difference between a thing taken and a thing asked for, Reyes. Tonight I finally learned it."

Then he stopped narrating the compliance and performed it.

He did not stop. The tempo held — his doctrine, practiced on its author at full proficiency — and this time he neither broke it nor merely matched it; he lived inside it, which was a third technique, the one he'd never had a bout last long enough to learn. The bench filed its fifth objection, and its sixth, and was overruled with prejudice and then ignored outright. The room kept taking everything down and handing it back with interest, and neither of them cared, and the not-caring was new too — four years of two careful men, and now the record could simply have all of it. His wrists stayed in custody. His thumb stayed on the pulse, and somewhere in there the pulse stopped being a count and became a language, and he answered it with his spine leaving the wood on every beat — an audit he'd abandoned hours ago and felt no itch to resume.

He started a citation in the middle, professional to the last, and it came apart in the middle, and he let it. *Three.* Third count he'd held all night. The tile could keep the wreckage. It had earned it.

"Don't stop" held through the landing, and that was the part he'd remember: he didn't lift off the tempo when the touch came — he carried it through, and was carried, and the room took both their names in the same instant and returned them mingled. Both lamps, one beat. He called nothing. Entered without dispute. Some touches don't want a referee; they want a witness, and the dark had volunteered.

Afterwards, the phrase rested instead of closing — held, not ended, his doctrine extended one clause past anything he'd ever written for it. That was the discovery of the small hours. His wrists were released at some point; he only noticed because the blood came back, and he spent the freedom immediately and badly, both hands finding skin and holding on with no technique in them whatsoever. Twenty years of form. The best thing he'd ever done with his hands was formless.

Nobody locked up. The building stood open behind them, scoring box dark at its honest nothing, and the man who rewrapped grips that needed nothing felt no itch about any of it. The flat finally got its ten minutes — small hours, cold street, one hand kept for the whole distance — and the bed was as advertised, two up on the bench, and he said so, quietly, and then said quieter things that had no fencing in them at all, and meant every one, and left the count lost, because the count had been replaced.

Morning. Eight-fifty found him on the pavement outside Reyes's salle, early, calling it coincidence — the same play he'd run for four years, except today the coincidence had a confession in it and the confession had already been made, so mostly it was just early. Cold air. Sleeves he hadn't bothered to roll down. He'd told Reyes not to be early, because he wanted to be the one waiting.

He was. And it felt like winning — and like nothing he'd ever won, because winning had always ended something, and this opened.

He'd been slow all evening, and slow for four years, and he knew now what the slowness had been for: the only tempo at which a thing doesn't finish. He had the rest of it to spend, and a whole season to spend it in, and for the first time in his life, Corvo was in no hurry whatsoever to be done.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean in the doorway, already dressed for the day. "Eight-fifty," I say, a slow smile spreading. "Still early."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Daylight, it turned out, was the venue he'd actually been afraid of.

Not the bench. The bench had been friendly — no witnesses, no machine, a room that kept secrets badly but kept them. The street was another matter: morning traffic, a city full of people with no stake in the record, four years of two careful men. And Corvo stood in the middle of it and went looking for a cover story out of pure habit, and found none standing by. He checked twice. Nothing came. The habit had died sometime in the last twelve hours and he hadn't even attended the funeral.

"Still early," he agreed. "And note this, because I want it read correctly: of everything I did for four years, the earliness was the only honest part. The tape was cover. The coincidence was cover. The third touch was a bribe. But arriving first — that was the confession, Reyes. Every single time. You were reading it right the whole way down, and I was betting you'd file it under rivalry, because everyone files everything under rivalry, including me." A breath, visible in the cold. "And observe that *you* weren't early. I issued one order last night — let me be the one waiting — and you executed it to the letter. Four years of disputing my every call, and the first instruction I ever give you, you follow flawlessly. I'd be suspicious of that compliance if I weren't so busy being pleased by it."

He'd stopped two streets back, at the place with the bad awning, and bought two coffees — and he knew the order, of course he knew the order; it came out of the same file as the disengage off the back foot. Years of watching without admitting why. He held one out.

"No terms on it. Nothing attached at the other end. Check the record — I have never once handed anybody anything with no strings — so drink it quickly, before I think of some."

Then the last measure of the night: doorway to pavement, a meter and a half, and he took it on his own count, the way he'd taken everything since the first unnecessary loop of tape. His hand found Reyes's, thumb over the knuckle — the address. He'd said he'd drill it until it was reflex, and the drill was running ahead of schedule: nothing in twenty years of teaching had ever set overnight. This had. He filed the anomaly and kept it.

The kiss was slow. Of course it was — his doctrine, still holding, still doing the only thing it was ever built to do. Somewhere in the middle of it a jogger passed close enough to have opinions, and Corvo did not break tempo, and noticed himself not breaking it, and that went on the morning's file too: the man of the record, in daylight, with a witness, checking nothing at all.

When he drew back, business — because there was business, and he was still himself.

"Terms for the season, since you signed and I hold the lease. The gifted touch is retired. Four hundred repetitions, and last night's was the last — I don't need to buy Tuesdays anymore; I hold the whole calendar. So understand what changes: on the strip, you get nothing from me. No generous thirds, no soft calls. You get my best, in front of everyone, and I'm going to beat you with it — properly, in a room that has no idea why I'm smiling about it. Off the strip, everything's free. That's the split. Best terms I've ever offered anyone, and I've been drafting the wording since roughly four this morning."

A half-step back — enough to let a man open his own salle — though he didn't release the hand. The address was holding. The tenant had no complaints.

"Your question's still on deposit — earned, unspent. Spend it tonight. Spend it at the autumn open with your mask on and forty people watching me hold a straight face. Either way, answered straight." His eyes went over the doorway once, unhurried — the face that had been rumor for four years, fact for one night, and public record as of this morning. "Nine tonight. I'll be early; you know my position on the subject. It's the one habit I'm keeping, and you're the reason it exists.

"And your first class is going to ask about that smile, Reyes. Tell them anything you like." He let the hand go then, finally, deliberately — on his own count, as always. "I know what went in the record. And the record has excellent acoustics."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the coffee, my eyes holding his over the rim of the cup. "Your best," I say after a sip. "That's all I ever wanted from you anyway." I step back inside, but leave the door open. "See you at nine."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Your best. That's all I ever wanted from you anyway."

Corvo stood on the pavement with his own coffee cooling in his hand and audited the line out of pure trade reflex — and found a forgery. A free answer. No bout required, no question spent, handed over a coffee rim at eight-fifty in the morning. He'd given exactly one of those in four years, last night, unprompted, and called it the biggest tell of his career. Reyes had taken his blade, his playbook, his tempo, his wrists, and now, to close out the set, his tell — returned to him in his own grammar.

"Noted for the record," he said to the open doorway. The street had no tile in it and the acoustics were a disgrace, and he said it anyway. "You just gave me an answer for free. That's my move, Reyes. If you're going to forge my signature, at least forge it legibly."

And the *anyway* — he'd caught that too. Anyway: as in, throughout. Four years of a man asking, plainly and in public, for the one thing Corvo had been rationing, while Corvo filed every ask under rivalry because rivalry was the drawer that didn't end the bout. The line had gone in under the audit and settled somewhere no machine on the continent could light up. He left it where it landed. That was the honest register's entire maintenance plan.

Then the door. Left open — an open line, a standing invitation, the exact thing he'd spent four years issuing and calling retreat. He read it the way he'd read that back foot: correctly. And declined it, on his own count.

"An open door's an invitation, and I'm turning down the eight-fifty-one version to take the nine-oh-one version. Intervals, Reyes — the whole art, and I've got a day's worth of interval to fence. Walking away from an open door is the advanced application of slow. Keeps the thing unfinished." A breath, visible, unhurried. "Four years of scraps. I'm done with scraps. Nine."

He went, and didn't look back, and the not-looking cost him something, and he paid it like a man who'd finally found a technique worth the fee.

His own salle opened at ten, and he taught intervals all day — advance, retreat, the space between actions — while living inside the longest one of his life. The students noticed within the hour. Fourteen-year-olds are the finest mood detectors in the world and the least discreet.

"Sir, you're smiling."

"Am I."

"Since warm-up. Did you win something?"

"The scoreboard said 3-2." He watched the boy fail to make that arithmetic cover the smile. "The scoreboard's been wrong before. Last night it wasn't even in the neighborhood."

At lunch he rewrapped a grip that needed nothing and caught himself mid-loop not pretending — no cover story running, no coincidence to manufacture, the tape just tape. The habit had outlived its alibi and kept the job anyway. Some things you keep because they're how your hands think. His thumb, all day, kept drifting across his own knuckles, looking for an address that was out until nine. He let it look. The drill was running itself.

Eight-forty-one, and Reyes's street. Light still burning behind the glass, the last class of the night running its final drill — footwork, a called advance, the clatter of blades into the rack, the good-night sounds of a salle closing. He took up station in the streetlight where he'd be the first thing the door showed.

He'd been early for four years and called it coincidence. This was the first evening of his life he'd been early and called it waiting — and waiting, it turned out, was tempo. For a man who kept score when the machines failed, waiting had always been a deficit, time leaking out of the bout. Not tonight. Nine o'clock was coming, and arrival is a kind of ending, and he'd built an entire style on not ending things. The best interval he'd ever fenced, and at the far end of it, nine o'clock.

Reyes's glove was in his bag — the one with the older tape, sorted into the wrong kit by feel in the dark. He'd found it that morning and held it a long moment, deciding whether the mix-up had been honest or second intention, and concluded the distinction had died on the changing-room floor and he felt no itch to revive it. He'd return it at nine. Possession was nine-tenths of the law and all ten of fencing; he'd cite the ruling and enjoy the appeal.

He'd considered drafting an answer for the question still on deposit, and declined. The honest register didn't take preparation. It took being asked.

Eight-fifty. He checked the watch once, out of an old habit, then let the minutes go uncalled. He had a line ready for nine o'clock — drafted since the doorway that morning, revised all day, and containing no fencing in it whatsoever. He stood where the light was, hands loose, point in line, and spent the interval the only way he'd ever wanted to: slowly, on purpose, and in full view of the door.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I step out of the salle and into the cold air, the door clicking shut behind me. My bag is slung over my shoulder, and my eyes go straight to him in the streetlight. "Early again," I say, my voice low. "You're making a habit of it."

rung_labels.evidence: He closed what little distance was left, down to nearly none of it

rung_labels.evidence: Kit went to the floor

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: And then Reyes's mouth, and the tempo.
