dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped rewrapping. He let the last inch of tape hang loose, then looked up with the patience of a man who had rehearsed this exact expression for four years.

“Slow,” he repeated, and the word came out low, almost pleased. “You’re going to have to be more specific.”

He set the foil aside, stood, and wiped his hands on his towel before taking a half step toward the bench where the bag had landed.

“Three-two, and you still came here. That’s either a grudge, or it’s an invitation, and I’ve been too polite to find out which.”

His gaze held, tired and sharp.

“So?”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: *I hold his gaze, not moving as he steps closer.* "It's a grudge, obviously. I don't invite you anywhere." *A pause, my lips twitching.* "But maybe I'm curious why you're still here, too."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed once, quiet, without much humor, though his eyes caught the twitch of Reyes’s mouth and did not move away from it.

“A grudge,” he said. “You say that like I haven’t watched you sharpen it all season.”

He stepped closer again, close enough that the loose end of tape might have caught on his jacket if either of them had moved too fast. He did not seem concerned.

“I stayed because I wanted to know if you’d actually leave,” he said, voice lower now. “Or if you’d wait until the room emptied so you could accuse me of being slow without anyone else hearing.”

His thumb brushed the end of the rewrapped grip, then he let the foil fall back onto the bench.

“Also,” he added, with the smallest lift of his chin, “I wanted to see if you’d come back after three-two. I have standards for grudges, Reyes. You’re not allowed to lose to me and then stop showing up.”

He looked at him, tired and unrepentant.

“So if it’s a grudge, name the terms. If it’s curiosity—”

He didn’t finish right away. His gaze dropped for half a second, then came back up.

“Then stop pretending you’re here for the fencing.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let it go.

He watched the foil settle on the bench with the same detached respect he gave most things he did not intend to admit he wanted. Then his gaze came back to Reyes.

“Slow,” he repeated, as if the word had more than one use.

He peeled off one glove, finger by finger, and dropped it beside the weapon. His bare hand, reddened at the knuckles, rested on the bench near Reyes’s hip without taking up space that wasn’t offered.

“You’ve been saying that all evening,” Corvo said. “You don’t mean it. You’ve just been looking for a reason to stand close enough to say it again.”

He smiled, tired and sharp.

“Three-two. Generous. Slow. You’re not angry. You’re annoyed because you can’t pretend the score was the point.”

His voice dropped with that, lower and rougher, the way it sometimes did after a hard bout when the room was empty and the politeness started to wear thin.

“You came back after the match. You stayed after everyone else left. You took my foil out of my hand and you didn’t walk away.”

Corvo looked down at the gap between them, then back up.

“So don’t insult me by calling that fencing.”

He stood properly then, shoulders square, the last of the instructor’s patience burning off into something less careful. He stepped in until the bench pressed lightly against the backs of his knees and the space between them was no longer a matter of form.

“I’ve been patient,” he said. “I’ve been decent. I’ve let you needle me for four years because I liked the way it felt like you were actually paying attention.”

His hand came up slowly, deliberately, and stopped at the side of Reyes’s jaw. His thumb rested there, warm and calloused, not quite pressing. Not quite asking.

“You want me faster?” Corvo murmured. “Then name the terms.”

For a moment, he looked almost as if he would wait.

Then the needling went somewhere else, and Corvo bent his head and kissed him—firm, careful, and far too late to pretend it was only about the match.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: *I don't pull away. I just stand there for a second, then kiss him back, my hand coming up to grip his wrist.* "You talk too much," I say against his mouth.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a breath that was almost a laugh.

“Too much,” he agreed, voice rough. “Probably. But you let me talk this long.”

He didn’t pull his wrist away. He let it be held there, warm and calloused and still buzzing from the match, and bent to Reyes again more slowly this time, until the bench against the backs of his knees was the only thing keeping him from closing the last of the distance entirely.

The kiss was less careful.

Less patient.

When he drew back, his forehead rested against Reyes’s for a moment, his eyes dark and tired and thoroughly pleased.

“So,” Corvo murmured. “Terms.”

He nodded toward the foil still lying on the bench.

“No more fencing tonight. No more pretending three-two means anything. No more excuses about being slow, or generous, or whatever else you need to stand close to me without saying why.”

His thumb traced the line of Reyes’s jaw once, deliberately, then stopped.

“You stay here,” Corvo said, quieter now. “You keep that grip on my wrist until I tell you you can let go.”

He smiled, thin and dangerous.

“And if you want me faster, Reyes, you’ll have to do more than call me slow.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let his head fall back against the changing-room wall, one hand braced on the bench beside his hip, the other still tangled in the ruined line of his jacket. The foil grip had forgotten its purpose. The score had forgotten its purpose. Even the room seemed to have emptied itself of rules.

When he laughed, it was rougher than before, almost a warning.

“You’re making a scene,” he said, though his voice was too pleased to carry any blame.

He shifted, closing what little distance remained by instinct, the way he would have advanced after a point. His knee pressed between theirs—careful enough, then not. His hand came up to the back of Reyes’s neck, thumb sliding into sweat and hair, and he bent until his mouth found Reyes’s again.

“Four years,” Corvo murmured when he drew back just enough to speak, “and you finally let me win without arguing.”

A beat later, he smiled at his own mistake and corrected himself.

“Or maybe you’re only letting me think that.”

He let the joke run out before it could turn back into talk. His palm flattened against the bench beside Reyes’s thigh—not to move Reyes, not yet, but to mark what he wanted. He bent again, slower, kissing the corner of his mouth, then the pulse under his jaw. The changing-room air was too close, too warm, too much like the inside of a mask after a bout.

“If you keep making noise like that,” Corvo said against Reyes’s skin, “I’m going to assume you’re grading my performance.”

His laugh came against Reyes’s throat this time.

He straightened enough to look, hair damp, cheeks flushed, the instructor’s composure gone in a way that would have scandalized both their students. There was nothing apologetic in his expression. Only focus.

“Terms,” he said again, quieter. “This one: if you want me to stop talking, make me.”

He said it like a challenge, then followed it before the room could catch up to them—his mouth finding Reyes’s again, hands finally doing what they had spent four years pretending not to want.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: *I grab his shirt, pulling him back in.* "You talk, I'll grade." *A sharp bite to his lower lip.* "So far, you're not passing."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s laugh broke off into a low sound when the teeth found his lip. He let it happen, head tipping back, one hand rising to cover the fist in his shirt rather than break it. The grip was tight enough to wrinkle the fabric, and he held it there with his palm, feeling the pulse under it.

“Unfair,” he said, voice rougher than the word deserved. “You can’t grade me while I’m occupied.”

He bent again, slower, until his mouth touched Reyes’s, not enough to answer the bite, enough to remind him who had started talking.

When he drew back, his lower lip was red, his smile sharp and tired.

“Not passing,” he repeated. “I’ve had better marks from students who couldn’t parry without apologizing.”

His thumb pressed into the back of Reyes’s hand.

“So give me a better rubric.”

The changing room was too small for the amount of heat left between them. Corvo shifted, using the bench at his side to take some of his weight, and pressed in until the distance was gone. His free hand slid from shirt to waist, careful at first, then less so.

“If you want me faster,” he murmured against Reyes’s jaw, “you’re going to have to stop calling me slow and start acting like you mean it.”

He kissed him again, deeper this time, one hand coming to the side of Reyes’s face. The other stayed over the grip, holding them both in place.

Corvo drew back with his breathing harder than he would have admitted, but his expression was still that of a man waiting to see if he had earned the next comment.

“Four years,” he said quietly. “And you still want to be the one scoring the match.”

His mouth curved.

“Fine. You’re allowed to grade me. Just don’t act surprised when I pass.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went flat with a sound half swallowed by the bench, his jacket bunched under him, one elbow flared wide for balance, the other hand lifting as if to say something that never arrived.

His head tipped back against the wood, throat exposed, the line of him taut under sweat and heat. For once, the room took everything from him.

“Ah—”

Not a word. Not even a full breath.

His fingers curled against the bench, then slid, then found purchase in the worn seam of the leather. His thighs tightened, hips lifting involuntarily before he forced them back down, as though he could still choose the timing. He could not. His mouth opened on nothing, and the first answer came as a broken exhale.

He looked down at him with glazed, furious attention, like a man trying to score a hit that had already landed.

“You’re—”

A breath dragged through him. His jaw flexed.

“—cheating.”

The word had no conviction in it. His hand came up to tangle in his hair, not to push him away, not to guide him, just to hold something while the rest of him lost its argument. His thumb pressed hard into his own temple, then slid down, leaving his hair damp and disordered, and for a moment Corvo looked less like an instructor and more like a man watching his own composure be taken apart piece by piece.

His hips moved again, a small, involuntary shift, and then he went still, forcing himself to lie there as if stillness could buy him back a measure of control.

It didn’t.

His breath came harder, uneven, and he let out a low, wrecked laugh that broke into a sound he tried to swallow.

“Don’t stop,” he said, rougher than he meant it to. “I’m not finished.”

He tried again, slower, more deliberate.

“I’m not—” His head knocked lightly against the bench. “—finished with you.”

His free hand slid down his own chest, fingers dragging over shirt and skin, then braced again beside his hip. His body went rigid, then arched, a clean, desperate line, before he caught himself again, jaw clenched, eyes shut, breathing through his mouth.

When he opened them, the needling had lost its edge. Not gone—never fully—but softened into something almost honest.

“You wanted a rubric,” Corvo managed, voice scraped down to the bone. “You’re making me—”

He stopped.

His back pressed harder into the bench. His hand tightened in his hair.

“—write it,” he finished, almost a whisper.

Then his composure fractured again, and the next words came out nothing but his name.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: *I don't stop.* "Cheating," I say against his skin, my voice rough. "Says the man who called three-two generous." *My hand tightens on his thigh.* "I'm not finished either, Corvo."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s laugh broke into a shaky sound against the changing-room air.

“Generous,” he echoed, voice wrecked. “I called it generous because you scored while I was looking at you.”

His hand tightened in his hair, pulling the strands free of their damp order. The bench creaked under him, wood and leather and the ruined discipline of four years of professional distance. He tried to straighten, failed, and ended up half-braced on one elbow, chest rising too fast, shirt open enough to make both of them look scandalous.

“You want to bring up terms,” Corvo said, breathing hard. “Fine. Here’s one. If you’re going to take your time with me—”

He stopped, jaw working as the hand on his thigh pressed again.

“—then stop pretending it’s about the score.”

His other hand came down, fingers fumbling for the edge of the bench, then finding instead the fabric of Reyes’s sleeve. He held on like a man trying to keep from reaching too far and failing anyway.

“I’ve been slow,” he admitted, rougher now. “You’ve been slow. We’ve been circling a point for four years and calling it practice.”

He looked down, eyes dark, mouth curved in something tired and dangerous.

“So make the touch,” Corvo said. “Stop grading from the outside.”

The words were still needling. They were also, unmistakably, permission.

His hips lifted in answer before he could call it a mistake, then dropped back against the bench with a breath that sounded too close to a groan. He caught himself, pressed the heel of his hand against his mouth for half a second, and cursed quietly when it did no good.

“Don’t,” he said, though it came out unconvincing. “Don’t act like that worked. I’ve seen you parry with less effort than you’re using to ruin me.”

He tried to sit up again, managed it, then immediately lost the argument and let his forehead fall against the shoulder near him. His breath came hot through his shirt.

“You want me faster,” Corvo murmured, almost to himself. “You want me to stop talking.”

A beat.

Then he lifted his head, jaw set, expression suddenly sharp again.

“Fine.”

His hand came up and caught the back of Reyes’s neck, not asking, not quite. His thumb pressed into the line of bone there, holding him close enough that the rest of the room blurred into heat and breath and the faint smell of sweat, tape, and old leather.

“Then come here,” Corvo said. “And finish the phrase.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let the pins hold him.

He tested them once, not hard, the way he would test a rule in a bout: enough to see if it had teeth, not enough to make it worth arguing. When it stayed, he stopped. His wrists flattened against the bench, shirt shoved up around them, the tendons in his forearms taut from the fight he was refusing to pick.

“Concede,” he said, as if the word were a bad line of footwork. “You’ve had three touches and you still don’t know what you’re scoring.”

His breath came too fast. He let it. The changing-room bench had never felt so wide or so narrow at once, and the air was all sweat and tape and the close, stupid smell of being too tired to pretend anymore. His hips shifted against the wood, slow and deliberate, until a low sound broke loose from him and he turned it into a laugh.

“You want pace,” Corvo said. “Fine. Keep me pinned.”

He leaned in without his hands, mouth finding the corner of Reyes’s jaw with the same focused rudeness he used to open a line. His teeth grazed skin, not hard, not soft enough to be forgiving. The first breath he drew was shaky enough to be embarrassing. He did not care. His knee slid up between them, making room by force and intention, then he pressed down with his thigh and held there, head tipped back, throat exposed to the dim room.

“Three-two,” he murmured, almost to himself. “Generous. Slow. You’re still grading from the outside.”

He came down again, mouth working where hands could not, kissing the tendon of Reyes’s throat, tasting salt and heat. His fingers flexed uselessly against the bench, then went still. The need to grab, to take control, to make it about timing and distance, burned under him and he let it burn.

He could not use his hands.

He could use everything else.

Corvo moved, hips rolling with a slow, deliberate pressure that made the bench creak and his own breath break. He stopped himself once, forehead dropping against Reyes’s shoulder, jaw tight, then started again as if the hesitation were an insult to his pride.

“Don’t,” he said, rough against Reyes’s throat. “Don’t you dare make me finish this politely.”

He lifted his head, eyes dark and half-lidded, mouth curved in something tired and sharp. The instructor was gone. What remained looked more like a man who had been waiting four years to be given the terms he wanted.

“You said prove it,” Corvo said. “I’m proving it.”

His knee pressed higher, anchoring, opening, and the next movement was not careful. He took the point with his mouth against Reyes’s skin and his hips on the bench, kissing and biting and breathing hard until the room had no score and no rules and no reason for them to be anywhere else.

When he drew back, his lower lip was swollen, his hair ruined, his chest rising in too-rapid pulls. His pinned wrists still held, and he looked at them with the furious, half-amused respect of a man who knew he had lost the argument and did not intend to surrender.

“Concede?” he repeated, voice wrecked. “Not to three-two. Not to you.”

He shifted again, slow this time, deliberate, until his own breath caught and he let out a low laugh.

“Make me,” Corvo said. “You’ve spent four years pretending you can.”

Then he took Reyes’s mouth again, no hands, no distance, no mercy, and let the next touch speak for itself.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let go of his wrists, my hand sliding down to his hip instead. "You don't concede," I say against his mouth, breathing heavy. "You just lose."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked down at his own wrists, at the red marks the pins had left there, and let himself study them for a second as if they were a new line he had not yet decided how to answer.

Then he lifted his gaze.

“You just lose,” he repeated, low and rough, the words coming out almost like a concession and almost like a threat.

His hands finally moved.

Not away from Reyes. Not up to shield himself.

Corvo brought one up to the back of his neck, thumb catching in the damp hair there, and the other slid to his waist, palm flat and warm against him, holding him exactly where the hand already was.

“Fine,” Corvo said. “I lose.”

He smiled then, tired and sharp and thoroughly ruined.

“Not to three-two. Not to a room full of students. Not to anyone else.” His thumb pressed once, deliberate, against the side of Reyes’s neck. “To you. Here. Tonight. After you made me take my time with it.”

His hips shifted again under the hand there, slow and unapologetic, drawing a breath that broke on the way out.

“You wanted pace,” Corvo murmured. “You wanted me to stop talking.”

He leaned in until his mouth almost touched Reyes’s, close enough that the rest of the changing room narrowed to heat and breath and the faint creak of the bench beneath him.

“So I’m done.”

He kissed him properly then, with his hands finally free and finally honest, one at his neck and one at his waist, pulling him closer until there was no room left for excuses, no room left for distance, no room left for anything but the way four years of needling had come down to this.

When he drew back, his voice had dropped into something rougher, quieter, stripped of its usual polish.

“You can say I lose,” Corvo said. “You just have to live with what you won.”

His mouth curved.

“Not by three-two.”

Then he kissed him again, slower this time, deeper, like a man who had finally stopped pretending he wanted to argue.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands went still on Reyes’s hips, and the room contracted around that single instruction.

“Don’t stop.”

Corvo looked down at him like the words had landed clean and he intended to make them pay.

“Fine,” he said. “Then I’m done negotiating.”

He moved with the last of the match still in him—quick, controlled, and no longer pretending to be patient. Reyes went back against the bench under his hands, shoulders and head settling into the worn leather, and Corvo took the space over him like he had been waiting four years to claim it. His own shirt came off in one rough pull, abandoned somewhere near the floor, and his hips worked at Reyes’s waistband with a kind of grim determination.

“I’m taking your terms,” Corvo muttered, more to himself than to Reyes. “That means I’m taking everything else too.”

The fabric moved under his hands. Corvo pushed it down with the same care he would have given a foil, then less care, then none at all. The changing room was too hot, too close, too full of sweat and old wood and the sharp smell of tape, and Corvo’s mouth went to the exposed skin of Reyes’s hip like he was checking for a pulse.

“Three-two,” he said against him, low and rough, almost amused. “Still generous.”

Then he stopped talking.

He didn’t stay quiet for long.

Corvo took his time with it, mouth and tongue deliberate, hands braced hard enough to leave marks. His thumb found the heat of him, circling once, twice, until Corvo’s own breath broke and he cursed under his breath. He watched Reyes’s body under his hands like he was memorizing a line he refused to parry, then leaned lower, taking him into his mouth with the same stubborn focus he brought to every match he hated losing.

The first sound Corvo made was not a word.

It was a low, wrecked thing against skin, swallowed by the bench and the empty room. His jaw worked, tongue and mouth taking him deeper, one hand gripping his thigh hard enough to bruise. The foil, the score, the four years of polite needling—all of it narrowed to heat and salt and the way Corvo’s own hips were shaking from holding himself still.

He pulled back just enough to speak, voice scraped and rough.

“You wanted pace,” Corvo said, breathless. “You’ve got it.”

He didn’t give it back to Reyes.

He took it for himself.

Corvo rose enough to find his own bag, one hand fumbling at the side pocket until he came up with a small tube of hand cream and a foil-wrapped condom he’d been carrying for reasons he refused to examine too closely. He spat into his palm, worked the cream in with a blunt, impatient competence, and returned to Reyes like a man who had finally stopped pretending to be fair.

His fingers pressed in slow, careful, then less careful.

“Not polite,” Corvo murmured, almost a laugh, almost a warning. “You said don’t stop.”

He rolled the condom on with one hand, the other still moving, still working, still

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I pull him down and kiss him, hard, before he can get another word out. My hands are shaking and I don't care.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content: Corvo came down into the kiss with his hands still slick and half-finished, and he did not pull back until the condom was

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: He kissed back like he'd been waiting for it, his hand sliding down between us, guiding himself in with a rough, practiced motion. I arched off the bench, my gasp lost against his mouth.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped breathing when he was inside him.

He braced on one forearm, the other hand still pressed hard at Reyes’s hip, as if he needed the anchor. For one furious second he did not move, did not speak, did not ruin the moment with a score.

Then the gasp against his mouth broke something open.

“Don’t,” Corvo said, rough. “Don’t apologize for it.”

He kissed him again, slow and deep, and pulled back with his mouth wet and swollen.

“You said don’t stop.”

He moved.

The first stroke was careful enough to be obscene: a long, controlled withdrawal, then a return that took both of them through a shudder Corvo refused to name. The bench creaked under his weight. The changing room filled with the sound of skin, breath, the small useless catch of Corvo’s own voice when he tried to make it a word.

“Three-two,” he said on the next thrust, low and wrecked. “Generous.”

Another.

“Slow.”

Another, harder.

“Liar.”

He bent his head and kissed him through the rest, mouth working like he could take the noise back and keep it. His hips found a rhythm that was not the lesson-plan control he’d been using all evening; it was the thing underneath, four years of circling and needling and watching across the piste with too much attention.

One hand slid from Reyes’s hip up his side, over ribs, under the edge of his shirt, palm hot and shaking. Corvo felt it, hated it, and did not stop.

“Talk,” he muttered against Reyes’s mouth. “You want me to talk, I’ll talk. You want me shut, you’re going to have to—”

The answer came around him and Corvo lost the end of the sentence.

He drove into it, slower than he wanted, deeper, until the bench knocked against the wall. He caught himself on his forearm, jaw tight, eyes half-lidded, watching with furious focus as if he could memorize the angle and call it technique later.

“You don’t get to come at me,” Corvo said, voice scraped, “and act surprised when I can’t think.”

He rolled his hips, a filthy, deliberate circle that made the room tilt.

“Name it,” he murmured. “Say what you want. I’ve been taking your notes all evening.”

He moved faster, not enough to be rough, enough that the careful instructor broke. The condom was

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Harder," I manage to get out, my nails digging into his shoulder. "And shut the fuck up."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo set the foil aside—finally—and looked up. The salle lights hummed overhead, throwing long shadows across the piste. He had spent an hour delaying, rewrapping a grip that held no flaw, and now the pretense felt threadbare even to him. He let his gaze travel upward at the same lazy pace Reyes had accused him of, unhurried, cataloging the stance, the bag dropped close enough that the canvas brushed his knee.

"Slow," he repeated. The word came out low, testing the changed acoustics of the empty room. The corner of his mouth pulled. "Is that what we're calling patience now?"

He straightened, rolling his shoulders. Four years of crossing foils in competition, of trading barbs in doorways, of accumulating almosts and nearlys, had narrowed to this: the space between them measured in inches instead of piste width. His hand remained on the pommel of the weapon he’d been pretending to fix, thumb tracing the wire.

"You've had four years to prove you were faster," Corvo said. "And yet here you are. Still."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Patience?" I let out a short laugh. "You're calling your hesitation patience? That's a new one." I lean against the bench, my own shoulder brushing his. "And I'm here because I finally got you alone."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's thumb stilled on the pommel. For a moment the only sound was the electric hum of the overhead lights, filling the silence where four years of careful choreography had lived. He did not pull away from the pressure of Reyes' shoulder—warm, deliberate, finally not accidental.

"Alone," he said, turning the word over like a weapon he'd finally found the grip for. He shifted on the bench, not retreating but engaging, closing the last tactical gap until the line of his thigh ran alongside Reyes'. His hand left the foil entirely, settling on the wood between them, close enough that his knuckles grazed the canvas of Reyes' bag. "You make that sound like a victory."

He looked at Reyes properly then, cataloging the distance—measured now in centimeters, in breath, in the space between a spoken challenge and its answer. Four years of feints and parries, and Corvo had never been one to break a bind once the blades locked. His mouth curved, sharp and inviting.

"Careful," he murmured. "You might find the bout isn't over just because you've closed the distance."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let his hand remain empty where the grip had been, fingers curling slightly against the air before he lowered it to his side. He didn't look at the discarded grip; he looked at Reyes—the angle of his jaw, the space between them that Reyes had refused to widen. Four years of maintaining measure, and Reyes had finally stepped inside his guard.

"Slow," Corvo repeated, and this time there was no question in it, only assessment. He rose from the bench with the same controlled economy he used on the piste, rising into Reyes' space rather than away from it, until they stood at the distance where a blade would have been useless and a body became the only weapon that mattered. "Or perhaps I was simply waiting for you to take the initiative."

He lifted his hand—not to reach for a weapon, but to settle at Reyes' hip, fingers pressing with deliberate, familiar claim. His thumb found the ridge of bone beneath the fabric. Corvo's eyes held his, bright with the same fierce pleasure he took from a well-fought close bout.

"Since you've gone through the trouble of disarming me," Corvo said, his voice dropping to something rougher than the salle's hum, "you'd better know what you intend to do with me now."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let his hand stay there, my own coming to rest at the back of his neck. "I intend to win," I say, my voice low, and I pull him in.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo met the pressure at his neck as he would meet a flèche—leaning in, not back, his entire body committed to the line. The hand at Reyes's hip pulled hard, eliminating the last inch of distance until no space remained for blade or breath between them. Four years of careful measure collapsed into the heat and shock of it. He tasted salt, and under it something sharper: the particular adrenaline of a bout that had finally turned into something else entirely.

He answered with teeth and intention, refusing to yield the tempo, his free hand fisting in the front of Reyes's shirt to anchor them both. When Corvo broke away, it was only by a scant margin, his forehead still resting against the warmth where his mouth had been, his breath unsteady against Reyes's jaw. His thumb traced a rough, claiming arc at Reyes's hipbone.

"You call that winning?" he murmured, the words scraped raw and low. "That was just the engagement. You've still got to work for the touch."

He didn't wait for a reply. His mouth found the line of Reyes's jaw, then lower—taking ground now, not merely holding it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's shoulders met the bench with a hard, unforgiving crack—wood against bone, the kind of impact that would bruise by morning and serve as evidence. He barely registered it. His hands were occupied with more immediate concerns: the warm, shifting weight of Reyes above him, the slide of bare skin beneath his palms, the final, irrevocable collapse of the distance they had maintained for four years. The changing room tiles leached cold upward through the bench, a stark contrast to the heat of the body pressed flush against his, and Corvo arched into that contradiction, welcoming the discomfort as part of the bout.

The room gave them nothing soft, nothing forgiving. Overhead lights buzzed and flickered; the mirrors caught their reflection and threw it back in doubled, disjointed angles. Corvo was aware of it all—the harshness, the exposure, the functional brutality of the space—just as he was aware of every sound Reyes made, each one amplified by the hollow acoustics of lockers and concrete. He had spent years learning to read the minute tells of Reyes's wrist, the angle of his elbow before an attack. Now he applied that same attentiveness elsewhere, his fingers tracing, claiming, memorizing a different kind of tension entirely.

"Still think you're faster?" Corvo asked, his voice scraped raw and reckless against Reyes's jaw. He shifted his weight, seeking advantage on an unyielding surface, his thigh sliding with deliberate intent. His fingers dug in, hard and possessive, pulling Reyes closer with a grip that offered no retreat. He grinned, sharp and breathless, the expression of a man who had finally gotten the close fight he'd been spoiling for. "Prove it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I press my forearm against his chest, pinning him to the bench as I lean down, my mouth at his ear. "You talk too much," I breathe, before biting down on his shoulder hard enough to earn a gasp. "That's one touch to me."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's body jerked beneath the pressure, the gasp tearing out of him raw and unguarded, echoing off the concrete walls. The pain from the bite blazed bright down his shoulder—not a warning but a point scored—and he groaned against it, his spine lifting off the bench in a sharp arc that fought the forearm pinned across his chest. His fingers twisted hard in Reyes's hair, wrenching with a grip that bordered on violence, while his other hand raked down Reyes's back, nails digging cruel furrows to assert his own tally on the skin.

"One?" Corvo managed, his voice wrecked but still carrying that familiar, cutting edge. He rolled his hips upward, grinding against the weight holding him down, seeking friction and advantage on these brutal, unyielding terms. "If that's your idea of a touch, your judgment's gone soft." He surged up, closing the negligible distance, and sank his teeth into the juncture of Reyes's shoulder and neck with deliberate, retaliatory force. He held it, tasting salt, drawing a dark mark that would linger past dawn, before breaking away with a shuddering exhale against Reyes's throat. "Proper form. Now we're even."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's spine went rigid against the bench, the wood biting hard into his shoulder blades as he lost all inclination to move. He had meant to say something—some final, edged remark about tempo or the arrogance of a drawn-out attack—but the words lodged in his throat, emerging instead as a harsh, broken breath that scraped the air raw. His fingers scrabbled for purchase against the edge of the bench, whitening as they gripped, while his other hand shot down to tangle roughly in Reyes's hair, anchoring himself to the only solid point in a world that had abruptly narrowed to this devastating, wet heat.

For four years he had commanded the distance between them, measured it in centimeters and cuts, and now that geometry had been dismantled entirely. Corvo caught their fractured reflection in the locker-room mirrors—his own chest heaving, his head thrown back, his face stripped of every mask—and felt the dizzying vertigo of true disadvantage. He tried to rally, to shift his hips or reclaim some fraction of control, but the movement only drove him deeper into the relentless patience of Reyes's mouth, and a low, wrecked sound tore from his throat before he could bite it back.

"Christ—" he gasped, the word punched out of him, utterly without artifice. His thighs tensed, muscles locking as competitive instinct screamed at him not to yield, not to concede the touch. But the pressure built with excruciating precision, unhurried and impossibly close, and Corvo realized through the roaring in his ears that the bout was ending. Not with steel, but with him pinned and trembling and finally, completely, silent. He came with a violent arch off the bench, his grip in Reyes's hair tightening to the edge of pain, a guttural cry tearing loose that he would deny to his dying day.

Afterward he lay gasping against the wood, the overhead lights swimming above him, his body shuddering with helpless aftershocks. His hand remained tangled in Reyes's hair, now heavy and slack, his chest heaving as he stared at the ceiling and tried to remember how to breathe. No quip rose to his lips. No clever parry. For the first time in four years, Corvo had been thoroughly, undeniably beaten—and the worst part, the truly unbearable part, was that he already wanted a rematch.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I stay where I am for another long moment, my own breath evening out against his skin. Then I shift up, bracing my hands on either side of his head on the bench. I look down at him, at the marks on his neck and shoulder, at the way he’s still trying to get his lungs to work right. My voice is rough. "So. Still think patience is your strong suit?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let the silence stretch until it nearly matched the electric hum overhead, let Reyes believe the riposte had failed. His lungs still burned, his shoulder throbbed with the dull, sweet ache of Reyes’s teeth, and his body felt wrung out and hypersensitive in a way that would have been humiliating if it weren’t so fiercely, brilliantly earned. Then his hand stirred, sliding from Reyes’s hair down to grip his jaw with the same calibrated precision he used to correct a student’s *en garde*—firm, deliberate, thumb resting against the swell of Reyes’s lower lip.

“Patience,” Corvo rasped, the word scraped raw and barely above a whisper, “is knowing exactly when to drop your guard so your opponent spends his entire arsenal on the first attack.” He dragged his thumb across Reyes’s lip, slow and insolent, his eyes dark and fever-bright with the particular pleasure of a close bout lost. “You gave me distance. Tempo. Deception. Four years of careful feints, all spent on one touch.”

He shifted beneath him, a deliberate, rolling pressure that dragged a ragged exhale from his own throat, his free hand dropping to rake nails down Reyes’s sweat-damp flank.

“So either call the bout,” Corvo murmured, his mouth curving sharp and dangerous against the wrecked aftermath of his own undoing, “or get back in guard. Because I’m counting that as your first valid touch, and I have no intention of letting you off this piste until I’ve tied the score.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s wrists struck the bench with a dull, definitive crack, pinned above his head by a grip that gave no quarter. He tested it instantly—forearms tensing, shoulders lifting, a fencer’s instinctive search for an opening in a closed line. The hold held firm. The realization shot through him like adrenaline, stripping away the last of his tactical distance until he was nothing but the harsh wood at his back and the heat keeping him there, exposed and thoroughly caught.

For a moment he went very still, breathing hard, his pulse thundering against the palms that held him down. Then he deliberately rolled his wrists against the restraint, not to break it but to feel the precise shape of his own helplessness, his lips parting around a ragged exhale that sounded perilously close to surrender.

“Disarmed,” Corvo said, his voice scraped raw and low. He arched beneath the weight in a sharp, sinuous bridge, spine lifting off the bench, hips rolling upward with deliberate, seeking pressure. His legs shifted, thighs parting then clamping hard around the waist above him, locking with muscular insistence. “But you’ve left me my lower line.”

He turned his cheek against the wood, sweat-damp hair sticking to his forehead, and looked up with blown pupils and a mouth that curved sharp as a blade. Every nerve still sang with hypersensitivity from his earlier undoing, the friction almost too much, and he chased that edge with a fighter’s abandon.

“No retreat,” he murmured. “No remise. You’ve taken priority for the second period.” His hips surged upward again, demand and invitation in one motion, while his fingers spasmed uselessly against the bench. “So commit to the attack, or admit you’re still hesitating.”

He broke off as a jolt of sensation cut through him, a guttural sound tearing from his throat before he could bite it back. His legs tightened their vise, heels digging in hard.

“Because if you give me time to adapt to this position,” Corvo managed, breathless and fierce, “you’re going to regret it when I even the score.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I press my weight down harder, pinning him fully. "Time to adapt?" I say against his neck, before biting down again. "You're not adapting. You're just talking."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's head snapped back against the bench as the bite seared into the tendon of his neck, a ragged, guttural cry breaking from him that he couldn't have stopped if he'd tried. His back bowed sharply off the wood, spine flexing in a taut arc, while his thighs clamped viciously around Reyes's waist, heels digging hard into the small of his back to hold him there, to feel the full brutality of the contact. The pain sang down his nerves like a perfectly executed flèche—direct, unstoppable, leaving him wrecked in its wake.

For a long moment he could only pant, open-mouthed, his pinned fingers spasming against the bench as aftershocks rattled through him. The words were gone. Stripped away by teeth and pressure and the relentless heat of being held down by an opponent who had finally, finally stopped pulling his blows. Corvo turned his cheek against the cool wood, his face flushed and fierce, and when he lifted his gaze it was with the savage, glittering focus of a man who had found his ideal battlefield.

He surged upward then, not breaking the grip on his wrists but closing the distance between their bodies with a bruising snap of his hips, seeking contact, seeking collision. He twisted his head to find whatever skin he could reach, dragging his open mouth and the edge of his teeth along the line of Reyes's jaw before the angle pulled him back, his head thudding against the bench. He let it fall back, throat exposed, his chest heaving.

"Not talking now," he rasped, his voice barely recognizable, scraped down to its rawest register. He rolled his wrists deliberately in the restraint, feeling the ache of it, and exhaled a shuddering breath that was half laugh, half surrender. "Just waiting... to see if you've got enough blade... to finish the phrase."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the words against his throat, breath and vibration where sweat had cooled and heated again, and something in his chest fractured open at the admission. He turned his head, cheek scraping rough wood, and dragged his open mouth over whatever skin he could reach—jaw, shoulder, the salt-slicked tendon there—sucking a mark dark and deliberate into the flesh.

His hips rolled upward to meet the rhythm, a fencer's instinct to close the line even when overpowered. The bench cracked beneath them, wood protesting the violence of their movement, and Corvo groaned against the collision, the sound thick and wrecked. Every nerve stood raw, oversensitive from his earlier undoing, and the relentless, driving pressure dragged a ragged cry from his throat that rang off the concrete walls.

"Then don't—" he gasped, breaking off as the pressure within him altered, striking some unguarded depth, and his vision whited at the edges. His fingers clawed uselessly at the bench above his head, pinned wrists flexing against the unyielding grip. "Don't you dare—"

He lost the sentence. Lost his breath. His spine arched violently off the bench, abdominal muscles locking taut as a second climax rushed up on him with the inevitability of a bout already lost but refused in concession. He came with a shout that tore his throat raw, his body shuddering and clamping down with rhythmic, spasming intensity, his heels digging bruises into the back he held trapped against him.

Afterward he lay shattered against the wood, chest heaving, his wrists still pinned above him, his skin flushed and marked and wet. He turned his head slowly, dazed, and managed a shattered, breathless laugh that sounded more like a sob.

"That's two," he rasped, his voice ruined. "Your lead. But only—" he had to stop to breathe, thighs still trembling where they locked around the waist between them "—only because you pinned the weapon arm."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I finally let go of his wrists, my hands sliding down to his hips to keep him in place. "Your weapon arm's useless if you can't focus," I say, my voice rough. "That's three." I lean down and kiss him, hard, before he can argue.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's arms burned as blood returned to them, but he didn't waste his freedom. His hand shot up to knot roughly in hair—warm, damp, familiar only from four years of watching it catch the salle lights—and pulled with a fencer's brutal precision, while his other arm wrapped around the back above him, nails dragging renewed furrows through sweat-slicked skin. He answered the kiss with teeth and stubborn hunger, biting down hard enough to draw a sting, groaning at the taste, at the impossible reality of having finally crossed this line with the only rival who had ever matched him.

When he broke away it was only because his lungs screamed for air, his head falling back against the bench with a dull thud, his chest heaving in great, shuddering gusts. His grip remained knotted tight, keeping that proximity he had spent years denying, his legs still locked around the waist between them, trembling but uncrossed.

"Three?" Corvo rasped, the word barely audible, his throat scraped raw. He rolled his hips upward in a slow, taunting circle against the hands that gripped him, aftershocks sparking down his spine. A wrecked, breathless laugh tore loose. "You count kisses... as valid touches now?" His thumb traced a rough, claiming arc at the nape he held. "That's not target area. That's just you... showboating before the director calls halt."

He tilted his chin up, eyes heavy-lidded but bright with the savage pleasure of a close bout lost, and dragged his mouth along the edge of a jaw he could only reach from below.

"So get back in guard," Corvo murmured, fierce and inviting against the salt-slicked heat, "or concede you're too gassed for a fourth."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his jaw, holding him still as I push myself up on my knees. My other hand slides down his stomach, slow and deliberate. "Showboating?" I repeat, voice low. "You're the one who can't stop moving." I wrap my hand around him, watching his eyes darken. "Let's see if you can stay still for your own touch."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went rigid beneath the command, every muscle locking into a discipline that had nothing to do with fencing and everything to do with pride. He stared up, jaw tight against the fingers holding him, his breath coming in sharp, controlled bursts through his nose. For a moment, he held the line—perfectly, impossibly still, save for the frantic hammering of his pulse beneath the thumb at his throat, and the fine tremor that raced through his thighs where they locked around Reyes's waist.

"Stillness," he rasped, the word trembling on the edge of a laugh, "is just another kind of movement... waiting to break."

But then Reyes moved, and Corvo's resolve shattered. His spine snapped off the bench, a violent arc of surrender, and a ragged, ruined cry tore from his throat. He couldn't stop the roll of his hips, the desperate seeking of pressure, the total abandonment of the stillness he'd been ordered to keep. His hands flew down, gripping the edge of the bench white-knuckled, as the rhythm drove him ruthlessly toward the precipice he'd already fallen over twice.

"This isn't—" he gasped, his voice shredded, his eyes squeezed shut then snapping open, dark and wild. "This isn't valid— you can't call that— I'm not—"

But the attack continued, relentless, exploiting every weakness Corvo had spent four years hiding. He tried to rally, to hold the line, to deny the touch through sheer stubbornness, but his body betrayed him with exquisite thoroughness. He felt the build like a gathering flèche—unstoppable, direct, devastating. When the third touch finally landed, it struck with enough force to obliterate thought.

He came with a hoarse shout that echoed off the concrete walls, his body seizing and shuddering, his legs clamping tight enough to leave bruises, his fingers clawing furrows into the wood. The wave dragged him under and spat him out, leaving him gasping and wrecked against the bench, his chest heaving, his vision blurred at the edges, his skin flushed and marked and gleaming.

When he could speak again, his voice was barely a thread. "Three," he managed, a shattered, breathless laugh. "But I moved. Director's call... annul the touch."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I keep my hand where it is, applying just enough pressure to make him gasp again. "Annulled?" I lean in, my voice a low murmur against his ear. "You're making up rules as you go."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked up at that, and the smile that came was the one he usually saved for landing a flick to the wrist. "Slow. I gave you that touch and you know it. Your lunge was finished. Dead. I could have —" He stopped, wound the wrap once more, and set the foil down with more care than the argument deserved.

"Four years," he said instead, quieter. "Four years of you walking into my salle like you own the piste, and tonight I keep finding reasons not to leave while you're still in the building." He turned on the bench to face her properly, arms crossed, the picture of a man bracing for a parry he hadn't yet read. "So I'll ask plainly, since you rarely extend me the courtesy. Is this a post-mortem, or are you staying?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean back against the fencing strip, crossing my arms to match his posture. "Maybe I'm just enjoying the view. You're prettier when you're losing." I tilt my head, the teasing tone dropping a little. "But if you're asking...I'm staying."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"Prettier when I'm losing." Corvo repeated it as though testing the blade for flaws, and huffed something that wanted to be a laugh. "Four years, and the first kind thing you've ever said to me is still an insult. I'd be wounded, but I've had time to develop a taste for your particular brand of cruelty."

He stood and crossed to her the way he crossed a piste — measured, no wasted motion — and stopped a half-step short, the distance a fencer leaves out of professional courtesy. Up close, the dryness had gone out of his voice.

"Good," he said. "Stay. And since we're being plain with each other for once — the grip needed nothing. I've been inventing reasons to linger after you for months. Tonight you simply caught me at it."

The smirk returned, smaller, tilted. "The rematch still stands, mind. Staying doesn't win you the season." A beat, and he tipped his head at her, mirroring. "So. What was it? The third touch?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went very still — the stillness he kept for the instant an opponent showed him something new, the moment before the moment. Then the understanding landed, and with it a low, rueful sound that was nearly a laugh.

"Slow," he repeated. "Four years, and you're telling me the touch was open the whole time." His eyes flicked to the grip she'd set aside. "And now you've taken my weapon. Distance, disarm, and the riposte — that's textbook, that's —"

He closed the half-step. His hand came up to the line of her jaw, thumb along her cheek, and whatever the rest of the sentence had been, he abandoned it without ceremony. He had spent four years refusing to lose to her by anything but the narrowest margin. This, he suspected, would not be narrow at all, and he found he did not mind in the least.

He kissed her — finally, and with the same deliberation he brought to everything, as though the tempo had been hers from the first bout and he was only now, at long last, catching up to it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn’t realize I was holding and lean into the kiss. My hand comes up to grip his wrist, holding him there, and I don’t pull away for a long moment. When I do, it’s just enough to speak against his lips. “About time.”

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed against her mouth — a low, unguarded sound, the kind four years of bouts and needling had never once managed to pry out of him.

"About time," he echoed, speaking into the narrow gap she'd left. "Four years, and you're auditing my tempo." Her grip was still firm at his wrist, holding him exactly where he had no intention of leaving, and he made no motion to test it. "For the record — you held right-of-way the entire time. One clean extension, any evening you liked, and I'd have folded like a novice. I stood on that piste being insulted within an inch of my life, waiting for you to commit."

He turned his head, just enough, and pressed his mouth to the inside of her wrist — the same wrist he'd spent four years flicking at the top of every bout, first blood, first point, always. "I've been aiming for this the whole time," he murmured against it. "Appalling accuracy, clearly. You'd think a man would learn better footwork by now."

Then he drew back far enough to look at her properly, and the smirk had quieted into something plainer, more honest than he generally permitted himself indoors. "I'd have waited four more, if it came to that. Not patiently. But gladly." A breath, and the competitive gleam crept back in at the edges. "Now tell me the truth — how long have you known? I want it on the record which of us was worse."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The bench was bolted to the wall by some pragmatist with no romance in his soul, and Corvo could have blessed the man — something steady under him, because his footing had deserted him entirely, and a fencer hates nothing so much as losing his base.

He sat, and reached for her, hands finding her waist with the calloused certainty of four years' grip work. The kit lay strewn across the piste, his and hers already past all sorting, and the scoring machines hummed on standby like referees pretending not to watch.

"The member handbook has a clause about this," he said, mouth at her jaw, low and entirely unrepentant. "I intend to have it framed."

Then he drew back — only far enough to look at her, and the wit dropped away the way it did mid-bout, when something true needed saying. "Four years I rehearsed being suave about this. You'll have to forgive me; I seem to have left it in my jacket." His thumb traced the line of her hip, deliberate. "You said you're staying. I intend to hold you to the word."

And then he stopped talking, which for Corvo was its own kind of surrender. Mouth at her throat, hands mapping what four years of watching had only imagined, the bench creaking its complaint beneath them while the cold salle air pressed close and lost. He kept his word about the tempo. When the sounds came — neither of them quiet, as promised — he laughed once, breathless, against her skin.

"The walls are thin," he managed. "Good. Let Monday's class speculate."

He tipped his head back against the wall, looking up at her with the expression he otherwise saved for a touch that landed — half defeat, half astonishment, no irony left in it at all.

"Your point," he said. "It was always your point. Do with it what you like."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I slide into his lap, knees bracketing his hips, and push his shoulders back against the wall. My laugh is breathless too. "I intend to." I kiss him again, deeper this time, my fingers tangling in his hair. "And for the record," I murmur against his mouth, "I knew the first time you insulted my parry and then spent the next hour fixing my form."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The laugh got out of him before he could parry it — broke against her mouth, and her fingers in his hair drew it down into something lower, less defended. She had him pinned to the wall, shoulders flat, weight committed, and for the first time in four years of bouts Corvo felt no interest whatsoever in fighting for the distance.

"The parry," he managed, when he could get the words out at all. "Reyes. The parry was *fine*."

He tipped his head back against the wall to look at her, flushed and entirely unashamed of it.

"Flat on the recovery, perhaps. Adequate. No one spends an hour on adequate. I invented half the flaw because you were packing your kit and I could not think of a single other way to keep you on the piste." His hands traveled up her back, slow, mapping with a patience he had never once shown her in words. "And when you left that night, I sat on this bench and rewrapped every grip in the rack. Fourteen of them. None needed it. That's the tell — ask my students. *Corvo's rewrapping again; must be nearly time to fence Reyes.*"

The bench groaned beneath them; the scoring machines hummed their neutral standby, referees to the last. He pulled her closer, breath gone ragged, and pressed on with the stubbornness of a man determined, this once, to finish his sentence.

"The fixture list goes up in August. Your dates have been blocked off in my calendar four years running. My sister believes I'm in a committed relationship with the league." A rough breath, mouth finding the corner of her jaw between words. "So no. I don't concede the timeline. You may have known first — but I was lost before you'd finished signing in. I've spent every bout since trying to catch up."

Then he took her face in one hand and gave up the point cleanly, which for Corvo was the rarest touch of all.

"The record's yours. Knew first, moved first, hit first. I'd call it a fluke if I didn't have four years of evidence to the contrary."

The smirk resurfaced, crooked and warm at the edges. "Now. The walls are thin, Monday can speculate, and I've a flat ten minutes from here with a considerably better bench." His thumb traced her jaw. "Best of five?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had spent four years rehearsing for this — every version of it, the wit loaded, the timing drilled, armed at every line.

He had rehearsed for the wrong fight entirely.

Her mouth was taking its unhurried time, and his answers were dying somewhere between his chest and his throat, and the salle's great talker — the man who narrated his own defeats into lessons — could not raise three consecutive words. His hands found the edge of the bench and gripped until his knuckles paled. Halt had been called. The point was hers, the right-of-way was hers, and some deep-buried reverence for the referee's call kept his hands exactly where they were while she did precisely as she liked with him.

He tried once. "That's —"

The sentence never reported back.

The scoring machines hummed their neutral standby. The bench creaked its old complaint. Cold air, her mouth warm wherever it went, and Corvo arched into it with a total absence of dignity he would have mocked in any student foolish enough to show it. Breathing, it turned out, was a skill he had only ever pretended to.

"Touché," he managed at last, ragged, and meant it more than he had ever meant the word on a piste. The laugh that followed broke in the middle. "Four years I have never once conceded a touch, and you've —"

Gone again. He'd have been embarrassed, if there were room in him for anything else.

It was not close. Not remotely close. And he found, breathless and pinned and thoroughly outmaneuvered, that he had been lying for four years about what he liked best.

His hands finally surrendered the bench and found her — shoulders, hair — holding on rather than steering, because steering would mean he knew where this was going, and he knew nothing except that he had never lost this completely or wanted anything half so much.

"Reyes." Her name came out wrecked. He said it again anyway, because it was the only word left that worked. "No answer. First time all evening." A rough breath. "First time in four years. Don't stop."

And then, because the record mattered to him even now, even here, head tipping back against the wall:

"If you're keeping score — I concede the bout. The season. The league. Put it on the record."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My laugh is low against his skin. "Took you long enough to admit it." I pull back just far enough to meet his eyes, my own breathless. "Your place, then. And Corvo? I'm not letting you up until you say you've been losing to me on purpose."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stared up at her — flushed, wrecked, held to a bench by a woman who had waited until this exact moment to develop a conscience about the record.

"Blackmail," he said, with something like admiration. "Four years, and you've finally found a tactic I can't counter. I taught you nothing and you learned everything." He shifted beneath her — a fencer's reflex, testing the line — and found the hold absolute. Something in him went quiet and satisfied at that, which he filed away to examine later. Or never.

"And no. I won't say it, because it's false, and you of all people should be appalled. You'd have me sign a score sheet that says four years of bouts were theater? The five-four in March left me sitting on this bench with my hands shaking, glad of the dark. I gave everything that night and came up one short. You think that was *on purpose*? You'd despise a win I handed you. I've watched you fence. You'd sooner forfeit."

He pulled in a breath, and then, because the record mattered even now, especially now, he paid out one more truth. "And strike 'generous' from tonight while you're at it. The third wasn't a gift. I called it generous because the truth was worse — you'd spent three touches telling me I was slow, and my extension believed you. That's not charity. That's a demolition. I'd sooner the record say demolished."

But she wasn't moving, and he was in no hurry, and somewhere in the standoff the sentence rearranged itself into something true.

"Unless," he said, slower, "on purpose means what I made it mean. All those years. The blocked Augusts. The late nights. Fourteen grips that needed nothing. I built a life in which losing to you was always possible, and then I showed up for it — gladly, bout after bout, at three-two, at five-four, at one touch apiece." His voice had gone rough and low. "So fine. Put it on the record: I have been losing to you on purpose. Deliberately. Knowingly. With no intention of stopping. I'll countersign."

He grinned up at her then — outmaneuvered, breathless, and happier than he had ever been on any piste.

"Now. The flat, or the bench? Because I should tell you plainly: I've stopped arguing for the door."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Pinned. Both wrists, flat to the bench, held there by a woman who knew exactly how much pressure a body needed and precisely how little.

"Ah," Corvo said, to the ceiling. "So this is what my students feel like."

His arms tested the hold once — honest inquiry, nothing more — and gave it up, and with the giving-up something in him went loose and quiet that had been braced for four years. She had the line. She had the tempo. She had him, entirely, and the great tactician of the league lay there cataloguing the fact with the reverence he otherwise reserved for a perfect stop-hit.

"Point," he said. "Granted. No argument, no post-mortem, nothing for the record but this —"

Her mouth found him again and finished the sentence the way she'd been finishing his sentences all evening, and Corvo stopped keeping the record at all. Whatever sounds he made, he made unguarded; whatever he gave, he gave without invoice. The salle could keep its score sheets. The machines hummed their neutral verdict overhead — touched, touched, touched — and for once the referee's call was not in dispute.

When he could speak again, his voice had lost every layer of performance it had ever worn.

"Concede," he said. "The point, the bout, the season, four years of it. You were better, and I knew it the first night you walked into my salle and insulted my parry, and I have been showing up to be beaten by you ever since like it was the only appointment on the calendar. Because it was."

He turned his head, found her eyes, and the grin that surfaced was crooked and bare and nothing like the one from the piste.

"Now let my hands go, Reyes. The flat has a bed, and I've four years of being thorough to make up for."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: My grip on his wrists loosens, but I don't let go completely. My thumb traces the line of his pulse point. "You had a bed this whole time and you made us use a bench?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"The bed was never in question," Corvo said, shifting beneath her hold, pulse jumping plainly under her thumb — a tell he'd have mocked in anyone else, and made no effort to hide now. "The bench was a tactical choice. Neutral ground. Your salle would have meant conceding home advantage; mine, inviting you in before the fixture was official. I was being *strategic*."

Her thumb traced the pulse again. He closed his eyes briefly.

"I was being a coward with good posture," he amended. "There. For the record. You're collecting them all tonight; why stop."

He flexed his wrists under her grip — not escaping, just testing, the way he'd test a line before committing. She let him feel the hold without taking it away, and he huffed a laugh at the ceiling, entirely content with the arithmetic of that.

"Here's the trouble, though. If you let me up, there's a fixed quantity of dignity I'll need to rebuild before we reach the street — shirt, keys, some fiction about locking procedures. If you don't let me up, we're doing this here, on a bolted-down bench, in a salle I'll have to teach children in on Monday, and I will think of you every time I demonstrate a retreat." He opened his eyes and looked at her, and the piste-smirk crept back, crooked and unhurried. "So understand that when I say this next part, it's the most dangerous sentence I've said all evening, and I've been admitting things for an hour."

A breath.

"I'll take whatever you give me. Here, the flat, the changing room, the bus stop outside. But if you're asking me to choose —" his hands turned under hers, finally, deliberately, palms up — "let go. Let me do one thing properly tonight. One thing where I'm not outrun, out-thought, and out-touched. Four years of losing to you, Reyes, and I'd like, just once, to win at something."

The grin tilted.

"I'll give you the first touch back. After. Best of five on the flat, blades down, no witnesses. But walking out that door, I'm leading, I'm holding your kit, and I'm opening every handle like a man escorting a champion — because I've decided that's the touch I'm taking tonight, and a fencer has to have *some* ambition."

Then, quieter, the wit dropped clean away, the way it did mid-bout when something true needed saying.

"You've had me pinned since the parry. Since before the parry. The bench was never neutral ground and we both know it. Now let me show you that."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo stopped keeping score entirely, which was, for him, the deepest capitulation available.

Her hands were everywhere and his followed, and the bolted bench — blessed, pragmatic bolted bench — held beneath them while the salle's cold air lost every argument it tried to make. He had spent four years learning her rhythms from ten feet away, glove to glove, and now the distance was nothing and he learned faster. Where she arched. Where her breath caught and gave him the opening. The sounds she made when he took his time, and the different sounds when he didn't, and how the second set were his new favorite in a life that had previously ranked sounds by how often they accompanied her name on a score sheet.

"Thorough," she'd accused him of, once. He was thorough. Methodical. The man who rewrapped fourteen grips. He mapped her the way he mapped an opponent — patiently, greedily, filing every tell — except no opponent had ever made him forget the notes halfway through, and she did, repeatedly, until he abandoned the cataloguing altogether and simply stayed in the moment like a man told, for the first time in his life, that there would be other bouts.

The machines hummed. The bench creaked. Her name got out of him more than once, stripped of all its usual armor, and the last time it came out it wasn't a word so much as a surrender.

After — and he had no idea how long after, the clock on the wall having abdicated with everything else — they lay across the bench in a configuration no ergonomist would endorse, his chest heaving, her weight half on him, and Corvo looked up at the ceiling beams of his own salle and laughed, long and unbroken and helpless.

"You realize what's happened," he said to the beams. "I can never fence you again. Not properly. I'll stand on the piste, you'll salute, and my entire nervous system will replay this bench and my extension will simply refuse. Four years of a rivalry, ended not by a touch but by —" he gestured vaguely at the general wreckage of them both "— *that*. I hope you're proud. I hope you're extremely proud."

He turned his head and pressed his mouth to her hair, and the laugh softened into something with no performance in it at all.

"I am," he said. "Proud. Of this. Of you. God help me." A pause, and his hand traced idle lines along her shoulder, the grip-work calluses catching pleasantly. "Monday's class. The floor needs mopping and the record needs updating and I am going to walk in here at nine a.m. with the expression of a man who lost four-nil, and every student will know, and I will tell them nothing, and it will be the best defeat of my career."

Then, because the record mattered even now — especially now — he propped himself up on one elbow to look at her properly.

"Best of five on the flat. Blades down. And Reyes —" the smirk surfaced, crooked and warm and newly unguarded "— I meant what I said about the first touch. But the second through fifth are mine. A man has to have *some* ambition."

He reached down, retrieved his jacket off the floor, and draped it over her instead of himself.

"Now. Can you walk, or do I carry the champion to the bus stop?"

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push myself up off his chest, my hair a mess, and grin down at him. "You'll carry me, but only because I'm feeling generous." I take his jacket and slip it on, standing on slightly unsteady legs. "And don't think you're winning the next five. I'm still keeping score."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo got up off the bench with considerably less dignity than he'd have liked — legs unsteady, shirt somewhere on the wrong side of the room — and took inventory. Kit to gather. A salle to lock. A champion to escort, who was currently drowning in his jacket and wearing it better than he ever had.

"Still keeping score," he echoed, gathering her foil from the floor and presenting it to her hilt-first, formal as a salute. "Good. Someone has to. I'll be too busy rewrapping grips — except now you'll know what it means, and I'll have no defense at all. You've taken every tell I own tonight. I'm fencing you unarmed from here on."

He found his shirt, abandoned the pretense of buttons, and pulled his bag over one shoulder. Then he crossed to her, and — because the record mattered, and because he was a man who honored his stated touches — offered his arm with the solemnity of a state occasion.

"Champion," he said. "Your transport awaits."

But at the door, keys in hand, alarm off, the salle dark behind them, he paused. Looked back at the piste — the scuffed strip, the strewn kit, the bench bolted down by a pragmatist with no romance in his soul who deserved a pension — and something in his chest settled into place after four years of being half a degree off line.

"Three-two," he said softly, to the room. "Best loss I ever took."

He killed the lights.

Outside, the night was cold and the street was empty, and Corvo walked her the way he'd promised — kit carried, every door opened, his hand at the small of her back like a claim he'd finally stopped pretending wasn't one.

"For the record," he said, at the corner where his street began, "the flat's ten minutes. The bed's better than the bench. And Reyes —" he glanced down at her, grinning, wrecked, happier than any man had a right to be at the bottom of a league table "— when you say you're keeping score? So am I. I intend to spend the rest of the season one touch behind you, fighting for my life."

He pressed a kiss to her hair, brief and warm.

"Every bout. Every August. You have my word on it."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his wrist before he can pull away. "You'd better." I tug him toward the street, his jacket sleeves swallowing my hands. "And for the record? Your bed better be worth the wait."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
"The wait," Corvo said, letting himself be tugged down the street with all the resistance of a foil in a strong grip, "has a four-year compound interest. I'd adjust expectations accordingly."

His flat was on the second floor of a narrow brick row, and he took the stairs two at a time out of sheer four-year-old urgency, then made himself slow at the door — keys, fumbling, her breath at his neck doing nothing for his fine motor skills.

"For the record," he managed, shouldering the door open, "I rewrapped every grip in that rack the night I first imagined this. The bed has been made for four years like a man expecting an inspection. You'll find no dust and no defense."

The flat was small and clean and obsessively ordered — fencing trophies on one shelf in strict chronological order, a framed fixture list by the desk with four Augusts visibly blocked off in his handwriting — and he watched her take it in with the composure of a man whose alibi had just been entered into evidence.

"Yes," he said, before she could. "All of it. Catalogue at your leisure."

Then he caught her hand, drew her through, and the door clicked shut behind them.

He kissed her slowly this time — no bench, no clock, no score to settle but the one they'd agreed on — and walked her backward through the flat with the unhurried certainty of a man who had, at long last, stopped fencing for time.

"The bed," he murmured against her mouth, "is through there. And Reyes — for the record, and one last time tonight —"

He tipped her chin up, and there was nothing of the piste left in his face at all.

"I'm glad it was you. It was always going to be you. I just needed you to be better than me often enough to notice."

The smirk surfaced one final time, crooked and warm against her jaw.

"Now. Best of five. Blades down. I'm taking the first touch back — and then I intend to be *very* thorough."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push him through the doorway and onto the bed, straddling his hips again with a low laugh. "You talk too much," I say, leaning down to kiss him. "But I guess I've gotten used to it."
