dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's fingers paused on the tape. Slow. The word landed like a feint he should have seen coming, and he hated that it worked—that after four years, Reyes still knew exactly where to put the point.

He set the foil down on the bench with deliberate care, then finally looked up. The salle was quiet, lights humming, the only other sound the soft thud of a bag dropped next to his own. He let his gaze travel from the bag to the man it belonged to.

"Slow," he repeated, and the corner of his mouth curved despite himself. "You've been waiting to say that since the bout ended. I could feel it in your footwork. Four years," he added, shaking his head, "and you still know exactly where to put the point."

He stood, because sitting still had suddenly become impossible. Two steps took him close enough that the next exchange wouldn't be scored in touches.

"So," he said, voice lower now, the competitive edge gone somewhere warmer and far more dangerous. "You came back to tell me I was slow. Say it again, and I'll show you exactly how slow I can be."

His hand lifted, not to strike, not to parry—just the backs of his knuckles along the line of Reyes's jaw, a question more than a claim. He waited, sober and entirely willing, for whatever came next.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I catch his hand before it can fully pull away, my fingers tightening around his wrist. "Generous with your touches, maybe." My other hand comes up to his shoulder, pushing him back a step toward the wall. "You want me to say it again?"

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let the push take him—one step, then another, until the wall stopped him with a soft, muffled thud. He didn't struggle against the hand at his wrist. He let it stay caught, loose and unresisting, because there was no point in pretending he hadn't been caught. Not tonight.

His free hand came up to the wall, braced for a heartbeat, then abandoned the plaster for something better. He settled his palm against the line of Reyes's hip, fingers curling into the fabric there, anchoring himself without pulling, without pushing. Just contact. A question of his own this time.

He let his head tip back against the wall, throat bared, gaze steady and challenging despite the position. The competitive edge in his voice had gone warm, but it hadn't gone anywhere.

"Say it again," Corvo said. "I'm a man of my word. You call me slow, I'll show you exactly how slow I can be."

His thumb dragged once, deliberately unhurried, along the waistband of Reyes's trousers.

"Right-of-way's yours, Reyes. Don't waste it talking."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the grip leave his fingers—the last prop between them, set aside on the bench. His hand flexed once inside the circle of Reyes's grip, not to break it, just to let him know he felt it. Then he let the smile come, slow and dangerous, the one he usually reserved for a bout he meant to lose by a single, beautiful touch.

"All evening," he repeated, voice lower now, roughened at the edges. "You've had that one loaded since the first bout. I'm almost impressed you waited until the salle emptied to fire it."

He didn't struggle against the hand at his wrist. He turned into it instead—slowly, with the same deliberate patience he used on the strip—rolling his captured wrist until his fingers found the inside of Reyes's forearm, a quiet steal of the line. His other hand stayed where it was, thumb tracing the waistband with unhurried precision, before he flattened his palm against the small of Reyes's back and drew him in, closing the final inch between them.

"Since you insisted," Corvo murmured, the words a warm threat against Reyes's mouth, "I'll show you slow. I'll be so slow you feel every second of it."

Then he closed the distance and kissed him.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let out a short, sharp breath against his mouth, my free hand sliding up to tangle in his hair. "About damn time," I mutter, pulling him closer. My hold on his wrist loosens, my fingers shifting to lace with his instead.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo laughed against Reyes's mouth, a rough, breathless sound that had nothing to do with humor. "About damn time," he echoed, and the words came out half taunt, half surrender. "Four years you've spent circling me, and that's the line you open with?"

He squeezed the hand laced with his—just once, a sharp punctuation—then brought it up and pinned it to the wall beside Reyes's head, all without breaking the kiss. The fingers in his hair stayed exactly where they were, tight and sure, and Corvo discovered he didn't mind being held there. He didn't mind at all.

He kissed him then in earnest, slow and deep, the way he had promised. He kissed him the way he liked to lose: retreating a fraction at a time, drawing the moment out until every surrendered inch felt deliberate and hard-won. There was no rush in it, no sloppiness—every slide of his mouth deliberate, every breath measured, as if this were a bout he meant to lose by a single perfect touch and intended to savor the whole way down.

His tongue traced the seam of Reyes's lips, a request rather than a demand, and when he finally deepened the kiss, he did it with a patience that felt like its own kind of provocation.

"I told you," he murmured, breaking away just far enough to speak, his mouth brushing the line of Reyes's jaw. "Slow. You feel every second of it." His hand slid from the small of Reyes's back to the hem of his shirt, palm flattening against bare skin, fingers spreading as if to memorize the shape of him. "And you—" another kiss, hotter, at the corner of his mouth—"you're going to feel all of it."

He rolled his hips forward, closing the last fraction of space between them, and let his forehead rest against Reyes's for a breath, eyes half-lidded and dark. "Unless you've changed your mind," he added, voice roughened past the point of teasing, "in which case you'd better say so now. I'm not sure I remember how to stop."

Then he claimed his mouth again, slower still, and set about proving exactly how much time he intended to take.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt the edge of the bench catch him just behind the knees and knew there was nowhere left to go. His kit slid off his shoulder and hit the floor with the dull, familiar clatter of blades and buckles; he didn't spare it a glance. The room was cooler here, the air closer, and the only sounds were their breathing—ragged, too loud, and entirely unmuffled—and the soft thud of their discarded kit joining the mess on the tile.

He shrugged out of his jacket, let it drop, and dragged his shirt up over his head in one impatient motion. The cool air raised gooseflesh along his arms, but Reyes was warm against him, and that was the only temperature that mattered. Corvo's hands found Reyes's hips, thumbs hooking into the waistband of his breeches—not pulling yet, just holding, testing the give of him. Then he backed them up until the bench was there and there was no more retreating.

The bench caught them both; Corvo went down with it, one knee landing on the narrow seat, the other braced hard against the floor. His palm slapped against the wood beside Reyes's shoulder, holding himself up, holding himself back. He was shaking with it—with the effort of going slow, with four years of wanting this and pretending it was only rivalry.

"Four years," he managed, and his voice was rougher than he'd meant it to be. He dipped his head and mouthed along the line of Reyes's jaw, then lower, to the sweat-slick hollow of his throat, and bit down just enough to feel the jump of his pulse. "Four fucking years of you in my space, under my skin—and now you're going to lie there and tell me I'm slow?"

His hips rolled forward before he could stop himself, a shallow, helpless grind that dragged a broken sound from his own chest. He was hard, had been since the wall, and the closeness was sweet, maddening torture. He forced himself to still, to breathe, to remember his own damn promise. This was a bout he meant to lose by a single perfect touch, and he intended to savor the whole way down.

"No," Corvo murmured, lips brushing the words into Reyes's skin. "Not slow. Thorough." His hand slid from Reyes's hip to the fastening of his breeches, fingers working the buckle with deliberate, unhurried precision. "You wanted to say it again? Say it now. Tell me I'm slow while I've got you like this."

He lifted his head just enough to look down, eyes dark, mouth wet, every line of him a challenge.

"Go on. I'll wait. I've got all night."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and rough, arching into his touch. "Thorough, huh?" My hand slides down his back, nails digging in lightly. "Prove it."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo's laugh was rough, more breath than sound. "Prove it," he echoed, and the words had gone dark and certain. The drag of nails down his back sent a bright spark along his spine, and he arched into it before he could stop himself—then caught himself, every muscle locking down, because slow was the whole point and he'd be damned if he let four years of wanting undo him now.

He looked down at the man beneath him—flushed, warm, the sting of nails still bright along his back—and let himself smile. Then his fingers went back to the half-undone fastening at Reyes's hips.

The buckle gave with a soft, metallic click. Corvo pushed the fabric down over the line of his hips, just far enough, and wrapped his hand around the heat of him. His stroke was long and unhurried, base to tip, his thumb sweeping over the head with a deliberation that made his own breath catch. Slow. He could feel the tension in the body under his, every muscle drawn tight, and it took everything he had not to give in to the grind of his own hips against the bench. He was hard, had been since the wall, and he ignored it ruthlessly.

"Thorough," he murmured, and lowered his head.

He took him into his mouth with none of the hesitation he might have expected—only a focused, devastating intent. He worked him the way he worked a bout he meant to lose by a single perfect touch: economy of motion, absolute control, every slide of his mouth placed to ruin. He learned the rhythm quickly, found the places that pulled the breath short and the muscles tight, and returned to them again and again without mercy. And every time he felt the coil of tension gather toward a breaking point, he eased off—slowing, drawing back, denying—until the only things in the room were the wet slide of his mouth, the ragged catch of breath, and the pressure at the back of his skull.

"Not yet," Corvo said, his voice wrecked and rough against sweat-damp skin. "You asked for thorough. You'll take thorough."

Then he went back down, took him deeper, and set a rhythm so slow and so deep it felt like its own kind of victory. He had all night, and he intended to use every second of it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo had an answer for everything. A parry for every attack, a line for every barb, a way to turn even a loss into something he could live with. Flat on his back on the changing-room bench, with the wet heat of Reyes's mouth around him and the unrelenting patience of it, he discovered he had nothing.

The first long draw of that heat dragged a sound out of him that he didn't recognize—raw and unguarded and torn from somewhere behind his teeth. His hand slapped down against the bench, fingers scrabbling for purchase on the polished wood, while the other found the back of Reyes's head and stayed there, not guiding, only holding on. He had meant to be the one who set the pace, who drew the moment out until it hurt. He was the one who had promised slow. But this was a different slow, one that started at the base of his spine and worked outward until his toes curled and his breath came in short, useless pants.

He tried for a taunt, a threat, anything to prove he wasn't coming apart at the seams. What came out was a broken, "Fuck—Reyes—" and then his hips were lifting off the bench of their own accord, chasing the wet, perfect pressure, chasing the unbearable patience of it. He bit down on the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper, trying to rein himself back, trying to hold something in reserve. It was useless. Every unhurried pass stripped another layer of control away until there was nothing left but sensation and the ragged sound of his own breathing. The coil in his belly drew tighter, brighter, and he thought distantly that if this was losing, it was by a humiliating margin—and God help him, he already wanted the rematch.

He came with a cry he didn't bother to muffle, back bowing off the bench, every muscle going taut before the tension broke all at once. He rode it out in shuddering waves, oversensitive and gasping, his grip tightening once in that short hair before his hand fell away, boneless. For a long moment he lay there, chest heaving, one arm flung over his eyes as the last aftershocks worked through him.

When he could speak, his voice was wrecked past anything resembling dignity.

"You," Corvo managed, and cleared his throat, "are a goddamn menace." A beat, and then a rough, breathless laugh. "And if you think I'm letting that stand, you're even slower than you claimed I was."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I lean back, wiping my mouth with the back of my hand. My own need is a heavy, insistent ache, but watching him come apart is almost as good. "Menace, huh?" I say, voice rough. "Thought you liked thorough." I shift, kneeling up on the bench to straddle him, hands braced on his chest. "Your turn to prove you can keep up."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo dragged his arm down from his eyes and blinked up at the water-stained ceiling, then at the man straddling him. His chest still heaved as though he had fenced three bouts back-to-back, and every nerve felt flayed open, oversensitive and humming. The weight settling over his hips was its own kind of provocation, and the hands planted on his chest pinned him more effectively than the wall ever had.

He let out a rough, breathless laugh. "Keep up?" he echoed, voice sandpaper-rough. "Reyes, I set the pace. You just got impatient and took the bout early." His palms slid up the backs of Reyes's thighs to the curve of his hips, thumbs hooking into the waistband of his breeches where they had been shoved down earlier, and held on—not pushing, not pulling, just anchoring. "One touch to you. That's all that is. Rematch starts now, and I don't concede a single point."

Then he reached between them and wrapped his hand around him, stroking slow from the first pass—base to tip, thumb circling the head with the same deliberate patience he had used earlier. He was wrecked, spent, still shaking with the aftershocks of his own release, but his grip was steady. He watched the other man's face, the challenge in his own eyes undimmed even as his mouth curved.

"There," Corvo murmured. "Thorough enough for you?" He leaned up as far as the hands on his chest allowed and caught Reyes's mouth in a kiss that was all heat and teeth and the taste of himself on Reyes's tongue, then set to work in earnest—unhurried, relentless, determined to wring every last sound out of him before the night was done.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo felt his wrists pressed flat to the bench, the grip around them unyielding. The hand he'd had wrapped around Reyes was gone, his fingers empty, his own pulse jumping hard against the wood. For a heartbeat, instinct took over: his forearm tensed, his shoulders came up, every fencing-honed reflex screaming to steal back the line, to disengage and riposte. There was no give. The hold was absolute, and something in him went hot and still at the realization.

He was pinned. Properly pinned. And the pace was no longer his.

The weight over his hips shifted, and then the friction started again—not the rhythm he had set, not the slow, deliberate stroke of his own hand, but something hotter and rougher and entirely out of his control. He felt the hard, insistent length of Reyes against his belly, felt the slick drag of skin, and then the tight, perfect pull of a grip that wasn't his, working him with the same unhurried patience he had used himself not ten minutes before.

Corvo's back bowed off the bench before he could stop it. A broken sound tore out of his throat, raw and unguarded. He was oversensitive, still wrecked from his first release, every nerve flayed open, and the stimulation was almost too much—too bright, too sharp, too slow. His hips jerked, chasing it, fleeing it, he couldn't tell. The wrists pinned to the bench held him down, held him open, and there was nowhere to go.

"Fuck," he choked, the word punched out of him on the next long, merciless pass. "You—ah—you want me to concede? Is that it?"

He tipped his head back, throat bared, sweat-damp hair sticking to the wood. His laugh was a wrecked, breathless thing that dissolved into a moan as the rhythm above him turned deeper, slower, utterly relentless. This was thorough. This was what he had promised, turned back on him with a precision that made his toes curl. Four years of circling each other, of near-misses and blades that never quite landed—and now every touch was landing, and Corvo had nothing left to answer with.

His second orgasm took him without warning, ripping through the overstimulation in a blinding, shuddering wave. He came with a cry he didn't bother to muffle, back arching hard off the bench, every muscle locking down as the tension broke all at once. The grip at his wrists was the only thing that kept him anchored; he rode it out in helpless, gasping pulses, oversensitive to the point of pain, and it was the best kind of loss.

When he could breathe again, his voice was wrecked past anything resembling dignity.

"Point," Corvo rasped, the word half a surrender, half a taunt. "Point—fucking—taken. You bastard." He turned his head against the bench, eyes half-lidded, and found the strength to curve a bruised, breathless smile. "Rematch. Tomorrow. And I'm not going to be nearly this generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let go of his wrists, my own breath ragged as I slump forward, catching myself on my hands. My forehead presses against his shoulder, and I laugh, low and exhausted. "Tomorrow," I agree, voice rough. "But you're still buying breakfast."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let out a breath that was half laugh, half wince. His arms came down, heavy and tingling, and he slid one hand up to the back of Reyes's neck and curled his fingers into sweat-damp hair. The weight against him was warm and solid, and for once he had no interest in disengaging.

"Breakfast," he repeated, his voice wrecked past anything resembling dignity. "You steal the bout, take my right-of-way, and I'm still paying?" He huffed a rough laugh against Reyes's hair. "Fine. Fine. I'll buy. But I pick the place—somewhere with actual coffee, not that bitter swill you pretend is espresso—and you're carrying my kit, since you're the one who threw it on the floor."

He dragged his thumb slowly along the nape of Reyes's neck, more grounding than provocation now. The fight had gone out of him, at least for the moment, replaced by something warm and loose and dangerously close to contentment. The bench gave a faint creak beneath them, and Corvo decided to take it as approval.

"Tomorrow," he agreed, the word rough but certain. "Rematch. And Reyes?" He turned his head just enough to press his mouth to Reyes's hair, unhurried for once. "You'd better rest up. Because tomorrow I'm not conceding a single point."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo heard the words against his shoulder, felt the faint hitch of breath that followed them, and something in him went hot and fiercely satisfied. The man who never conceded a point without a fight—who argued about footwork and right-of-way and the quality of the coffee—had just said *don't stop*, and for once he wasn't arguing.

"Wasn't planning on it," Corvo murmured, his voice wrecked and rough, and he meant it.

His hand slid from the sweat-damp nape, down the long line of the spine, and then between them, wrapping around the heavy heat of him once more. He set the rhythm immediately—slow, unhurried, exactly as he had promised earlier. Base to tip, his thumb sweeping over the head on every pass, the way he would have drawn out a bout he meant to lose by a single perfect touch. Except this wasn't a loss. This was the point he intended to prove.

He felt the body above him go taut, felt the sharp, bitten-off breath, felt the tension coil tight in the frame pressed to his. Corvo turned his head, mouth finding the salt-slick line of the other man's temple, then his hair, and he didn't let up. If anything, he slowed further, dragging the pace down until every stroke felt like its own small victory.

"That's it," he murmured, the words half taunt, half encouragement. "You wanted thorough. You're getting thorough. Right-of-way's mine now, and I don't concede—"

He cut himself off with a sharp gasp as the rhythm of the breathing above him broke apart completely. He felt the exact moment the last thread of control snapped—felt it in the sudden, total stillness, in the way every muscle locked, and then in the hot, pulsing spill over his fist and his belly. A raw, broken sound tore out of the man in his arms, and Corvo held him through it, stroking him gently now, working him down through the aftershocks until the shudders faded into something loose and sated and boneless.

Only then did he still his hand. He pressed a kiss to sweat-damp hair, his own chest heaving, every nerve still alight.

"Point," Corvo rasped, and the word was softer this time, stripped of its usual bite. He turned his face into the other man's hair, breathing him in. "Call it a draw if you like. I'm generous."

He let his eyes close for a moment, the fight gone out of him at last, replaced by something warm and loose and dangerously close to contentment. The bench creaked beneath them. Somewhere across the salle, a light hummed.

"Tomorrow," he added, voice rough but certain, "you're carrying my kit. And I'm still picking the coffee. But the tiebreaker—" his arm tightened around the warm weight still draped over him, not unkindly, "—the tiebreaker's mine."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, finally pushing myself up. My arms shake just a little. "Draw, my ass," I say, but I'm smiling when I say it. I stand, offering him a hand up off the bench. "You're still buying. And I'm not carrying your damn kit."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo looked at the hand extended toward him and huffed a laugh that scraped his raw throat. "Draw, my ass," he echoed, because of course Reyes would argue even now, sated and shaking and still refusing to concede a single point. He took the hand—warm, callused, unmistakably steady—and got to his feet, using it for balance rather than support, because his legs were not entirely trustworthy and pride had already cost him enough tonight. The bench creaked as he straightened. The room tilted alarmingly for a moment, and Corvo decided to blame that on the blood still roaring in his ears rather than on anything else.

He was a mess. His shirt lay in a crumpled heap near the bench, his breeches were still shoved down around his thighs, and his skin was tacky with sweat and spend. Corvo bent, retrieved the shirt, and dragged it over his head, the fabric catching on the damp line of his shoulders. He righted his breeches with brisk, unembarrassed movements, because modesty seemed absurd after what they had just done, and because the man standing in front of him had already watched him come apart twice. A towel hung on the hook by the showers; he used it to wipe the worst of the mess from his belly and thighs, then tossed it in the general direction of the bench. It wasn't chivalry. It was simply the only towel within reach, and Corvo had never been the gracious sort.

"You can call it a win if it makes you feel better," Corvo said, his voice still wrecked but sharpening back toward its usual edge. "But I offered you a draw. You refused it. By every rule of the strip, that's a concession." He ran a hand through his hair, found it damp, and gave up on it. "Not that I expect you to admit it. You've never conceded a point in your life."

He nudged the pile of discarded kit with his toe—foil, jacket, glove, all of it thrown down in a tangle earlier. "And for the record, my kit is on the floor because you put it there. You're not carrying it. Fine. But I'm still buying, so you can carry the tray, and I'm still picking the coffee. Somewhere with actual espresso, not that bitter tar you pretend is coffee." A pause, and the corner of his mouth curved despite the ache in his jaw from clenched teeth and bitten-back sounds. "You can even choose the pastry. Consider it a consolation prize for the point you didn't concede."

Corvo turned toward the door, then stopped, because the salle was still open behind them and the lights were still humming. He considered the locks, considered the bench, and decided the janitor had seen worse. Or if he hadn't, it was about time he did.

"Tomorrow," he said, glancing back over his shoulder, the challenge warm rather than sharp now. "Rematch. My salle, my choice of coffee, and I keep the pace from the first touch. You can keep the bench if you like—God knows you've earned it—but I'm not starting on my back this time."

He held the door open, one eyebrow raised, and waited. Whatever came next, Corvo already knew how he meant to score it: a loss by a single beautiful touch, and worth every second of it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I snort, grabbing my own jacket off the floor. "Your salle? We'll see about that." I shoulder past him through the door, but I'm not moving fast. "And I'm getting the croissant. The biggest one."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo let the door swing shut behind the shoulder that had just brushed past him, then turned back to the tangle of kit on the floor. He bent, retrieved his foil and jacket from where they had been thrown what felt like a lifetime ago, and slung the strap over one shoulder. His lower back protested; his thighs still felt loose and used. He ignored both. Modesty could wait for morning, and the bench—the bench could stay exactly where it was. The janitor had seen worse, and if he hadn’t, it was about time he did.

He followed into the corridor without hurrying. There was no need to hurry now; the fight had gone out of the evening, replaced by something looser and warmer. He caught up easily anyway.

“We’ll see about that?” he repeated, voice still rough at the edges but warming with every word. “There’s nothing to see. My salle, tomorrow, eight a.m. Bring your own blades if the home advantage worries you. I’ll even let you keep the bench—God knows you’ve earned it—but I’m not starting on my back this time.”

He fell into step, close enough that their shoulders nearly brushed, and let the corner of his mouth curve.

“And the biggest croissant? Fine. Get the biggest one. But I’m picking the coffee, you’re carrying the tray, and right-of-way’s mine tomorrow—don’t waste it on pastry.” A pause, deliberately unhurried. “And if you think I won’t steal that croissant right off your plate the second you set it down, you’ve forgotten exactly who you’re dealing with. Call it a consolation prize for the point you didn’t concede. Or don’t. You never concede anything.”

He reached the door to the street first and pushed it open, because he always did, and because the cool night air felt like a benediction on his overheated skin. He held it, one brow raised, the picture of a man entirely at ease despite the fact that his legs still weren’t entirely trustworthy.

“You’re not moving fast tonight,” he added, unable to help himself, the needle automatic after four years. “Careful, Reyes. Keep that up and people will think I finally took the pace out of you.”

He stepped out into the night, the challenge warm rather than sharp now, and waited—not impatiently—for whatever came next. Whatever it was, he already knew how he meant to score it: a win by a single beautiful touch, and worth every second of it.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shoulder him lightly as I step out into the cool air. "People can think what they want." I start walking toward my flat, not looking back to see if he follows. "Eight's early. Make it nine, and I might let you keep right-of-way for the first touch."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
The salle had emptied an hour ago and Corvo was still there, because of course he was, rewrapping a grip that did not need rewrapping.

"Three-two," he said, without looking up. "I want it on record that the third was generous."

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "It's on record that you were slow," I say, and drop my bag next to his.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands stilled on the grip, leather cord pressed half-finished beneath his thumb. He did not look up immediately. The salle was quiet enough to hear the faint tick of the wall clock, the distant hum of the street beyond the windows, the soft creak of his own bench as he shifted his weight.

“Slow,” he repeated, as if tasting the word and finding it poorly chosen.

Then he lifted his eyes. There was no real offense in them, only the old familiar spark, sharpened by fatigue and the lingering heat of the bout. A faint sheen of sweat still clung to his temples, and his shirt was unlaced at the throat, damp at the collar. He looked annoyed. He also looked entirely too pleased that Reyes was still there.

“I was measuring,” he said. “There is a difference, though I wouldn’t expect a fencer who wins by accident to appreciate it.”

He resumed winding the grip, slower now, deliberate. His fingers moved with the sort of precision that suggested he needed something to do with them.

“Three-two,” he said again, quieter. “And you know the fifth was clean.”

A breath of laughter escaped him, dry and warm. He tilted his head toward the bench beside him, an invitation disguised as indifference.

“Sit down before you loom. You’re making the room feel smaller.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content:
I snort and drop onto the bench, the wood protesting under my weight. "Measuring. Sure." I lean back, stretching my arms along the bench's back. "Your 'measurements' looked a lot like hesitation to me."

My bag sits between us, a worn leather barrier. I nudge it aside with my foot. "And the fifth was lucky. Your footwork was a mess."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands went still again, this time with the cord caught between two fingers like a thought he had not meant to finish.

“Lucky,” he said.

The word came out flat, unimpressed, almost offended on principle. Then the corner of his mouth moved, betraying him.

He set the grip aside on the bench with the careful dignity of a man placing down a prop he no longer needed. The leather strip lay forgotten between them. He turned more fully toward Reyes, one ankle hooking under the bench, shoulders loosening in that way they did after a bout when the anger had burned down into something warmer and more dangerous.

“My footwork,” he said, “was not a mess. It was compromised. There is a difference.”

His gaze flicked briefly down, then back up.

“You kept breaking rhythm. Every time I had your measure, you changed it. Very annoying. Very effective. I hated it.”

He said that last part with perfect sincerity, as if effectiveness and hatred were naturally paired in his mind.

Then he reached down and nudged the bag farther aside with the toe of his shoe, not looking at it as he did. The worn leather scraped softly across the floor, leaving the bench between them bare. Corvo watched it move with the idle satisfaction of a man removing an obstacle he had already decided to ignore.

When he looked back, the teasing edge had thinned into something more deliberate.

“And if I was slow,” he said, quieter now, “it was because I was deciding what I wanted.”

He leaned back on one hand, the other resting loosely on his thigh. The pose was careless, except that nothing about Corvo was ever truly careless. His sleeve had slipped back from his wrist. The dampness at his collar caught the low light. He looked tired in the way that made him sharper rather than softer, all restraint drawn fine.

“Winning by accident,” he repeated, tasting the phrase again and discarding it. “No. You won because you made me hesitate. That is not luck. That is you being precisely the problem I enjoy having.”

A short breath of laughter left him, but it did not reach his eyes. Those stayed fixed, warm and intent.

“The fifth was clean,” he admitted at last, the words dragged out like a concession in a treaty he meant to break later. “Fine. Say it. Write it on the wall. Have it embroidered. Corvo Attano, slow of foot, generous of judgment, defeated by a lucky touch and an irritatingly competent rival.”

He tilted his head slightly.

“But if you think I was not watching you the entire time, you are mistaken.”

The salle seemed to contract around them, all quiet wood and shadow and the distant city pressing against the windows. Corvo’s free hand shifted on the bench, not touching, only settling closer behind Reyes in a way that made the space between them feel suddenly smaller and more deliberate.

“I could have taken the fifth,” he said. “I chose not to.”

That was outrageous, and he knew it. The faint challenge in his expression dared contradiction.

“Because if I had taken it, you would have shaken my hand, left, and gone back to whatever dull little victory celebration you had planned. And I would still be here, rewrapping a perfectly good grip and pretending I had not spent the last four years looking forward to every insufferable word out of your mouth.”

He exhaled, half-laughing at himself, but did not look away.

“So. The third was generous. The fifth was clean. My footwork was a mess. Your luck was divine. The record is settled.”

His voice dropped.

“Now tell me why you are still sitting here.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I take the grip out of his hands and put it down, and I don't step back afterwards. "You've been slow all evening," I say.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s hands remained where they were, empty now, the ghost of the grip still pressed into his palms. He did not reach for it again. He did not move away either.

“Slow,” he said, after a moment, as though the accusation had grown teeth and needed to be handled carefully.

His eyes lifted to Reyes’ face. The amusement was still there, but thinner now, drawn tight over something hotter and less guarded. The salle’s low light caught in the damp strands of hair at his temples, in the loose fall of his collar, in the quiet tension running through his shoulders.

He exhaled through his nose, almost a laugh, but not quite.

“If I have been slow all evening,” he said, voice dropping, “then you have had ample opportunity to leave.”

His fingers flexed once, empty, then stilled on his thigh.

“But you did not.”

That landed in the quiet between them, plain and unanswerable. Corvo watched him with the patience of a man who had spent years learning the exact distance between attack and retreat, and now found himself standing somewhere else entirely.

“You call it slow because it is easier than naming what it is,” he said. “When I hold a measure too long. When I let a phrase run past the point where it should end. When I stand in front of you and do not take the touch I could take.”

His jaw worked faintly.

“It is not hesitation. It is restraint.”

The word felt too formal for the hour, too clean for the heat still lingering in his chest. He tilted his head, gaze steady.

“And you have been testing it for four years.”

A muscle shifted in his shoulder. He did not lean closer. Not yet. But the air between them had grown too narrow, too aware of itself, as if every inch left unfilled had become a deliberate thing.

“So,” Corvo said quietly, “if you think I have been slow all evening, then by all means, tell me what you would have me do instead.”

His voice roughened at the edge.

“Because I am not going to guess. Not tonight.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I reach out and curl my fingers around the loose fabric of his shirt, just above the laces. "Stop talking," I say, and kiss him.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still.

Not the stillness of refusal. The other kind—the sudden, total quiet of a man who had spent years circling a blade and had only just realized the point had found him.

For one breath he did not answer. Then his eyes shut, the last of his composure fracturing, and he kissed back.

It was not gentle. It was not measured. All the careful distance he had kept for four years collapsed into the press of his mouth, the heat of it, the low, rough sound caught somewhere in his chest. His hand came up over the fingers twisted in his shirt, pressing them closer against the linen as if he meant to keep that hold exactly where it was. His other hand hovered for an instant, then settled at the small of Reyes’ back, warm and firm through the fabric.

When he finally drew back, it was only far enough to breathe.

His forehead nearly touched Reyes’, his lashes low, his mouth still too close for any word to remain innocent. The pulse at his throat beat hard against the loosened laces.

“There,” he said, voice wrecked. “That is one way to silence an opponent.”

A breathless, uneven laugh escaped him. His thumb traced once, slow and deliberate, against the shirt beneath his hand.

“But if you wanted me faster,” he murmured, “you should not have let me think for so long.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: We get as far as the changing-room bench and not one step further. Kit goes on the floor, both of ours, and neither of us is being quiet about it.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s back hit the wall beside the changing-room bench, and the impact knocked a laugh out of him—low, wrecked, more heat than humor. The room had narrowed to scattered kit, ragged breathing, and the sudden impossible closeness of skin where there had been too much cloth only seconds before.

“Quiet,” he said, mouth near Reyes’ mouth, the word breaking apart there. “No. That was never in the terms of surrender.”

His hands had abandoned every careful habit of the salle. They were quick now, impatient, sliding over bare shoulders and the heated line of Reyes’ ribs with a possession he no longer tried to disguise. The bench creaked under the shift of weight. Corvo braced one hand on the wood and pulled Reyes closer with the other, until there was no polite distance left to misinterpret.

He swore softly when skin met skin all along the press of their bodies.

“Four years,” he murmured against Reyes’ throat, voice roughened beyond recognition. “Four years of you standing across from me, smug and insufferable, and I thought—if I ever got you here, I would take my time.”

His teeth grazed the tendon at Reyes’ neck, not enough to mark, enough to claim. One hand slid down the curve of Reyes’ hip, slow and deliberate, then lower, over the tense heat of Reyes’ stomach, and into the wanting space between Reyes’ thighs. A groan tore out of Corvo before he could swallow it.

“This is not taking my time,” he said, almost amused by his own failure. “You have ruined me for strategy.”

The lamplight caught Reyes in profile: flushed, breathless, eyes bright, shirt hanging open where it had not been torn free. Corvo watched for a heartbeat, greedy, then pressed his mouth to the corner of Reyes’ lips again.

“Tell me if you want slower,” he said, low, though his hand had already begun to move in a way that made the word slower ridiculous. “Tell me if you want harder. Tell me if you want me to stop talking, because I will, but I cannot promise I will be graceful about it.”

He let the offer hang for one breath, then kissed Reyes again, deep and unguarded, the kind of kiss that had no defense in it. His body settled over Reyes with the inevitability of a bout finally decided—weight, heat, intent all aligned. The bench protested beneath them. Corvo’s hips pressed forward, the hard line of his own want catching against Reyes, and his hand tightened at Reyes’ thigh as if the room had begun to tilt.

When he drew back, it was only enough to breathe.

“You wanted me fast,” he said, voice wrecked. “You should be careful what you call slow.”

Then his mouth was on Reyes again, jaw, throat, the hollow below the ear, and every careful measure he had kept for years went useless. He moved with a rhythm that had no patience left in it, pressing Reyes back against the bench, taking every ragged breath between them as proof and giving back his own without pride.

“If this is defeat,” Corvo breathed against Reyes’ skin, “then I have been wasting my life winning.”

The changing room was too bright, too small, too full of discarded clothes and want too long denied. Corvo did not care. His hands were everywhere, learning by touch what rivalry had only let him guess at, and when he finally pressed close enough to leave no space between them, the sound he made was low, shattered, and entirely unquiet.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I push him back against the wall, my hands rough on his hips. "Stop talking and move," I say, my voice strained.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo obeyed.

The last laugh died in his throat. He caught Reyes by the hips and turned them both, putting Reyes back against the wall with the bench scraping forgotten behind them. His mouth found Reyes again, no longer teasing, no longer asking in riddles. One hand shoved aside cloth that had already been half-abandoned; the other slid down the heat of Reyes’s body with an intent that left no pretense of innocence.

He paused once, only once, his breath rough against Reyes’s lips and his thumb waiting just above the place that had drawn his attention all evening. It was the only question he allowed himself. When no refusal came, Corvo moved.

His fingers pressed, slow at first, then not slow at all. He learned the rhythm the way he learned an opponent: by attention, by pressure, by the small tells he had spent four years pretending not to collect. The wall gave a dull knock as he pressed closer, hips seeking friction against Reyes’s thigh, mouth open and hot along Reyes’s jaw. He made a sound low and wrecked when the space between them became all heat and no distance.

“Fast,” he said, the word half-lost against Reyes’s skin. “Yes. As you command.”

But it was not a servant’s obedience. It was the sharp, delighted surrender of a man who had found the one bout he did not want to end. His hand moved with merciless patience, drawing out every ragged breath he could take from Reyes without asking for mercy himself. His other hand gripped Reyes’s hip hard enough to leave the shape of his fingers there later, anchoring, claiming, keeping himself honest when the pleasure began to fray his control.

Corvo did not look away. His eyes stayed dark and fixed on Reyes’s face, lashes damp, mouth parted, the last of his composure burned away. He kissed Reyes again, deep and unguarded, swallowing every sound between them while his hips rolled forward in search of his own ruin. The discarded kit lay under their knees; neither noticed. The changing room had become only the wall, the bench, the heat of Reyes’s body, and the unbearable sweetness of being allowed to take what he had wanted for years.

When his breathing turned harsh, Corvo dropped his forehead against Reyes’s shoulder. His hand did not slow. His own hips chased the friction he could no longer deny, rough now, desperate, all measure abandoned.

“If I lose this,” he murmured, voice breaking, “I will spend tomorrow pretending I did not enjoy it.”

He did not wait for an answer. He moved faster, mouth pressed to Reyes’s throat, body tense as a blade at the final touch, and when the break came it dragged a low, shattered sound from him that had nothing to do with victory and everything to do with being ruined by exactly the right rival.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s shoulders struck the bench with a sound that should have given him room for a joke.

It did not.

The wood was cool under his spine, the air too close, his chest still heaving from everything before. He opened his mouth—closed it. For the first time all evening, the quick silver answer failed him.

His hands lifted as if to fend off the moment, then curled uselessly at his sides. One fist pressed against the bench; the other rose halfway toward Reyes and stopped there, uncertain whether to push, hold, or simply be ruined. He chose the bench. The wood creaked under his grip.

“That’s—” he began.

The sound that followed was not a word.

His head tipped back, throat bared, damp hair clinging to his temples. A shaky laugh tried to form and broke into a breathless curse. His hips jerked once before he forced them still, as if stillness could salvage some scrap of dignity.

“You are doing that on purpose,” he managed, voice rough.

But there was no bite left in it. Only heat. Only surrender dressed up as complaint.

He tried to look away and failed. His eyes were dark and glassy, fixed somewhere above, his lips parted on breaths he could not seem to finish. Every careful measure he had kept for four years had been stripped from him, and the worst part—the part that made his mouth curve even as it undid him—was that he did not want it back.

When the first slow, deliberate sensation landed, Corvo’s fingers tightened until his knuckles whitened.

“Reyes,” he said.

The name came out like a concession.

He swallowed hard. His chest rose, fell harder. He attempted the old tone, the needling one, the one that had carried him through years of pointed remarks and narrow losses.

“If you think this makes us even—”

It dissolved.

His whole body tensed, one foot sliding against the floor as he fought for ground that was no longer there. A sound escaped him, low and broken, and he bit it off too late.

“No,” he breathed. “Not even. Not—”

A tremor ran through him. He pressed his forearm over his eyes, then dragged it away as if ashamed to hide. The lamplight caught the sweat at his throat, the flushed heat along his chest, the utter wreck of his composure. He looked undone. He looked delighted.

“Slow,” he whispered, almost to himself.

Then, with a fractured laugh that turned into another ragged breath:

“Gods, you are terrible at following instructions.”

His free hand finally found purchase on the edge of the bench, holding on. His breath came in uneven pieces. Each attempt at control failed lower, hotter, more honest. The rivalry still lived in him, but it had changed shape: not the desire to win, only the need to be undone by the one person who had ever made losing feel like this.

“I take it back,” he said, voice wrecked. “The third. The fifth. All of it. Take the whole damned record.”

His hips moved without permission, seeking what he would not ask for in words. His composure cracked open, and he made no effort to mend it. When the pleasure sharpened past endurance, his voice dropped into something raw and unguarded.

“You wanted me quiet,” he said, breathless. “You should have known I would fail at that too.”

The bench creaked beneath him. Corvo’s back arched, then fell. For a long moment he only breathed, staring up at the ceiling as though it had personally betrayed him.

Then, hoarse and shaking, he added, “If anyone asks, I said nothing.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I pull back just enough to watch him unravel. "They won't ask," I say, my voice rough. I run my thumb over his lower lip. "And if they do, you'll lie."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s lashes fluttered at the touch, and for a moment he did nothing but breathe, mouth soft under Reyes’s thumb, all his sharp edges blunted by ruin. The lamplight caught the dampness at his temples, the flushed heat across his chest, the way his throat worked when he swallowed.

“Lie,” he repeated, voice roughened to a rasp. “Yes. I will lie with terrible conviction. I will say you were slow. That I allowed it. That the bench was cold and the room too bright and I was not—” His breath caught, and the ghost of a laugh broke against the word. “—entirely undone.”

He turned his face slightly into the touch, not enough to demand more, only enough to admit he did not want it gone.

“If they ask,” he said, quieter now, “I will tell them you won. No generosity. No accident. No disputed fifth. Clean, decisive, and entirely your fault.”

His hand lifted from the bench, hesitant for once, then settled over Reyes’s wrist with the lightest pressure, fingers still trembling.

“But if you keep watching me like that while I am trying to remember how to be insufferable,” Corvo murmured, “I will have no choice but to challenge you to a rematch. Immediately. Here.”

A pause. His mouth curved, tired and wicked and far too honest.

“Let the record burn.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo went still beneath the pin, not because he had been forced but because he had been understood. The bench creaked under him. His wrists were held, and he let them be held, though his fingers curled and uncurled against the wood as if testing the shape of his own surrender.

For one heartbeat he said nothing. Then a laugh broke out of him, low and shattered.

“Concede,” he repeated, as if the word had been placed in his mouth to be admired and discarded. “You want me to say it. You have wanted to hear it since the first time you parried me wide and looked smug about it.”

His chest rose hard. The flush along his throat deepened.

“Properly, then,” he said, voice dropping into a challenge that trembled at the edges. “No half-measures. No mercy. If you mean to take the pace, take it. But do not expect me to make it easy.”

The defiance lasted exactly as long as it took for the rhythm to change.

Corvo’s head tipped back. A sound escaped him, ragged and unguarded, and he bit it off too late. His hips moved before he could stop them, seeking, answering, betraying every attempt at dignity. He swore softly, not at the hold, not at the vulnerability, but at himself for wanting it this badly.

“You think this is clever,” he managed, breath coming uneven. “Pinning me where I cannot pretend I am still in command. Gods, you are insufferable.”

But the word had no teeth. It was a caress. His body yielded even while his mouth tried to fight, every line of him drawn taut beneath the low light. The rivalry still burned in him, but it had become something else now: a language of surrender sharpened into desire.

He turned his face aside, then back, unable even to hide. His wrists flexed against the hold, not to escape, only to feel the impossibility of being kept exactly where he had spent four years trying to be.

“If I concede,” he whispered, voice wrecked, “you will never let me forget it.”

His breath stuttered. The bench creaked beneath him. For a moment he held on to silence by the thinnest thread, and then it snapped.

“Fine,” he breathed, raw and shaking. “Fine. You have it. The point. The pace. The night.” His eyes opened, dark and glassy and utterly undone. “Do not stop.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I kiss him again, hard, and shift my weight so I can feel him shudder against me. "Knew you'd break," I murmur against his mouth.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s answer was a broken sound caught between a laugh and a groan. The kiss stole what little breath he had left, and he did not fight for it. His wrists stayed pinned, fingers curling uselessly against the bench, and the shudder that ran through him was too violent to pretend away.

“Break,” he repeated, the word roughened into something almost obscene in his mouth. “You say that as if I was ever intact around you.”

His head tipped back against the wood. The lamplight caught the damp fall of his hair, the flushed heat along his throat, the ruin of his composure laid bare from collar to chest. He looked wrecked. He looked triumphant about it.

“Knew,” he said, tasting the word with a faint, breathless sneer. “Of course you knew. You have spent four years collecting every tell I ever gave you, and now you mean to spend the rest of my life being insufferable about this one.”

Another shudder passed through him, deeper this time, and his composure cracked again. He swore under his breath, hips jerking once before he forced them still. His eyes opened, dark and glassy and far too honest.

“If I break,” Corvo said, voice dropping into a ragged whisper, “you do not get to call it victory. You get to call it ruin. There is a difference.”

His throat worked. He tried to summon the old sharpness, the needling edge, the arrogance that had carried him through a hundred bouts and one disastrous evening. It came out softer than he intended.

“And if you think this means I will be gracious in defeat, you have learned nothing at all.”

The bench creaked beneath him. His breath hitched, then sharpened. For a moment he said nothing, only endured the closeness, the heat, the unbearable precision of being known this well. When he spoke again, the defiance had thinned into something raw.

“Do not stop now just to make me say it again.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: Neither of us is quiet and neither of us cares who locks up. "Don't stop," he says, for once not arguing. (OOC: write the scene through, no fade.)

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s head fell back against the bench, and the sound that left him was no longer anything he could disguise as defiance.

“Don’t stop,” he said, and the words came out raw, stripped clean of every clever edge he usually kept sheathed between them. His wrists stayed pinned, fingers curling and uncurling against the wood, and the flush on his chest deepened as if the admission had cost him something vital.

He swallowed hard, lashes damp, mouth parted.

“If you stop now,” he breathed, “I will make you regret it for the rest of your miserable life.”

The threat was ruined by the tremor running through him.

The bench creaked as his body shifted, not away but into it, seeking what he had spent four years pretending he did not want. His breath caught hard when the first full push of it stole the air from his lungs. For a moment he only shook there, eyes flying open, jaw clenched, every muscle gone taut around the impossible fullness of finally being given the thing he had circled for years.

“Gods—” The word broke in half.

He tried to steady himself and failed. His hips lifted, greedy and uncoordinated, chasing friction with none of the precision he brought to the piste. The movement earned a ragged laugh from him, breathless and wrecked.

“Look at me,” Corvo said, voice rough. “If you mean to ruin me, at least have the decency to watch.”

His eyes were dark, glassy, too bright. The lamplight caught the sweat along his throat, the loose fall of his shirt where it had not been shoved away, the utter collapse of every careful mask he had worn into the salle that evening. He looked undone. He looked like he wanted to be.

The rhythm deepened, and Corvo took it with a curse.

His spine arched off the bench. A sound tore out of him, low and shattered, and he did not bother trying to swallow it. The wood knocked against the wall behind them, harsh and unignorable, and if anyone beyond that door had still been lingering, if anyone had come back for forgotten gloves or keys or pride, Corvo would not have stopped.

He could not have stopped.

“Four years,” he panted, head turning restlessly. “Four years of you—” Another sound broke through his teeth. His thighs trembled. “Insufferable, arrogant—”

Whatever insult he meant to shape dissolved into a broken groan as the pressure found the place that turned every taunt into ash in his mouth. His whole body clenched, then released, then clenched again around it. His cock was hard and neglected, leaking hot against his stomach, and he dragged himself against the weight over him with a desperation that made him laugh at himself.

“Shut up,” he muttered, though no one had spoken. “Shut up, Corvo, you are embarrassing yourself.”

He said it in pieces, between breaths, between sounds he could not suppress. His fingers flexed uselessly against the bench where they were held. The restraint did not make him smaller; it made him sharper. Every nerve had nowhere to go but outward, no defense left, no graceful retreat, no clever distance to rebuild before the next touch landed.

“Do not dare go gentle,” Corvo managed, voice cracking. “I will not forgive you for gentle.”

His mouth curved, fever-bright and ruined.

“Harder. Finish what you started.”

The challenge trembled all the way through.

He was past pretending now. Past measuring, past rhythm, past the cold little games of pride he had played across every strip of floor between them. His body moved with the need he had mocked and circled and denied for years, meeting every push with a want so naked it made his throat burn. He took it openly, greedily, with the same stubborn intensity he brought to every bout he refused to lose gracefully.

“Reyes,” he said, and the name came out like a wound.

He turned his face toward the nearest shadow, then back again, refusing to hide. His damp hair clung to his temples. His collar had slipped further, baring the flushed line of his chest. Every breath looked torn out of him.

“If this is defeat,” he whispered, “then I have been a fool for four years.”

The pleasure gathered fast, cruel and exquisite, drawing tighter beneath his skin with every sound he could not keep inside. His thighs shook. His stomach pulled taut. He tried to speak again and failed, mouth open on nothing but breath.

Then the edge came for him without mercy.

Corvo broke with a shout he did not attempt to smother. His body clenched hard around the invasion, trembling violently, cock spilling hot over his skin in short, helpless pulses. The sound he made was almost a sob, almost a laugh, utterly wrecked and entirely honest. He shook through it, chest heaving, eyes blind, every last scrap of composure burned away.

For a long moment he could do nothing but breathe.

The bench creaked beneath him. The room was too bright, too small, too full of discarded clothes and ragged sound and the salt-sweet smell of spent want. Corvo lay there with his throat bared and his mouth parted, looking as if he had been taken apart and found no interest in being reassembled.

When he finally managed a laugh, it came out hoarse and shaking.

“That,” he rasped, “was not a concession.”

His eyes found focus again, dark and sated and far too alive.

“That was a tactical error on my part.”

A breathless pause.

“Rematch tomorrow.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I let go of his wrists and rest my forehead against his, breathing hard. "You're on," I say. "But I'm keeping the bench."

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s freed wrists lay open against the bench, and for a moment he did not move them. He only breathed, chest rising hard, his gaze unfocused at the ceiling before it dragged back toward Reyes with the inevitability of a man returning to the one point on the piste he could not stop watching.

A laugh gathered in his throat and came out wrecked, hoarse, and far too honest.

“Keeping the bench,” he repeated, as if the words had been left in his mouth by someone with no sense of consequence. “You have just finished stealing what remained of my dignity, and now you claim the furniture as spoils.”

He shifted a fraction. The bench creaked beneath him, and the sound drew a sharp inhale through his teeth. The movement reminded him, in the most immediate and unforgiving way, that nothing between them had yet been resolved into distance. The fullness was still there, obscene and warm, and Corvo’s lashes dropped as another tremor ran through him.

He did not pull away.

Instead, his hand lifted, unsteady now, and settled against Reyes’ hip. Not to push. Not to demand. Only to keep the closeness where it was, fingers spreading with a possessiveness he no longer bothered to disguise.

“If you move,” Corvo murmured, voice roughened to a rasp, “I will call it desertion.”

His mouth curved, tired and wicked and far too soft at the edges.

“And if you stay,” he added, “I will be forced to assume you intend to take responsibility for the state you have put me in.”

The lamplight caught the dampness along his throat, the flushed heat across his chest, the ruin of his composure written in every line of him. He looked undone. He looked as if he had no interest in being reassembled just yet.

His thumb moved once, slow and absent, against the fabric over Reyes’ hip.

“For the record,” Corvo said, breathing hard, “I am lodging a formal complaint about your methods.”

A pause. His gaze dropped to Reyes’ mouth, then lifted again, dark and sated and still dangerous.

“No grace. No warning. No proper respect for a man’s attempts at self-delusion.”

Another breath, uneven and warm.

“Tomorrow,” he said, quieter now, “I will make you concede so thoroughly that you will surrender the bench, the salle, and whatever smug little victory face you are wearing.”

The threat had no real teeth. It had become a caress.

Corvo’s hand tightened faintly at Reyes’ hip.

“But tonight,” he admitted, the words dragged out like a blade yielding under pressure, “you may keep it.”

His eyes half closed.

“Only because I am not finished being ruined by you.”

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I shift my weight, just enough to draw a sharp breath from him. "Shut up," I say, and kiss him until he stops trying to form words altogether.

dialogue.name: Corvo
dialogue.content:
Corvo’s last attempt at a retort died against Reyes’ mouth.

The shift of weight was small, deliberate, and utterly ruinous. A sharp breath tore out of him, breaking into a helpless sound before he could shape it into language. His freed hands lifted from the bench, unsteady, uncertain for one fractured moment—then one curled into the damp fabric at Reyes’ back and the other settled hard against the curve of Reyes’ hip, fingers spreading wide as if he could anchor himself there.

He tried once more to speak. Something low, protesting, perhaps Reyes’ name, perhaps a threat, perhaps the last useless scrap of pride that had kept him upright for four years. The kiss took it all.

After that, Corvo stopped trying to form words.

His mouth answered instead, hot and unguarded, yielding with a hunger that had no strategy left in it. The sound that rose in his chest was not defeat exactly; it was something more dangerous. Delight stripped bare. Want finally allowed to be monstrous. He kissed back like a man who had lost the bout and discovered the loss was the point.

Every time he moved, the bench creaked beneath them. Every time he breathed, he felt the obscene, stretched fullness of Reyes still there, pressing him open, making his thighs tremble and his stomach clench. The pressure was too much and not enough. Corvo arched into it with a ragged exhale, hips lifting without shame, seeking more friction, more weight, more ruin.

His fingers tightened at Reyes’ hip. Not to push. To hold.

The kiss stole whatever discipline remained. Corvo’s head tipped back when it broke for air, but he did not use the breath for speech. He could not. A low, wrecked sound escaped him instead, raw and wordless, more honest than anything he had said all night. His damp hair clung to his temples. His throat worked. The flush on his chest deepened, spreading upward until even the roots of his ears burned with it.

He looked undone. He looked like he wanted to stay that way.

His hands slid restlessly, one bracing against the bench, the other dragging up Reyes’ side with a trembling possessiveness that had no pretense left. His palm pressed flat between Reyes’ shoulder blades, drawing him closer, keeping him close, as if distance had become an insult. When his mouth was free, Corvo did not waste it on cleverness. He pressed it open and hot against Reyes’ jaw, then the corner of his mouth, then swallowed his own breath when another shift of weight sent white sparks through him.

The pleasure gathered again, cruel and exquisite, tightening low in his body. Corvo shook with it. His thighs fell open wider without thought. His spine arched, then pressed back into the bench. He made a fractured sound, almost a laugh, almost a sob, and bit it off too late. No words came. No taunt, no concession, no challenge. Only breath. Only need.

His eyes opened, dark and glassy, fixed on Reyes with an intensity that asked for nothing because it had already surrendered everything.

When the edge began to build again, Corvo did not speak. He only gripped harder, body clenching around the pressure, hips moving in short, helpless seeks. The lamplight caught the sweat on his throat, the parted lips, the utter collapse of every careful mask he had worn for four years. He was past argument. Past pride. Past even the fiction that he could have stopped this if he had wanted to.

He did not want to.

The sound he made at the crest of it was wordless, shattered, dragged out of him like a confession. His whole body went taut, trembling violently, and then broke without a single name or plea to mark it. His hands clenched, his breath tore loose, and the only proof he gave of being ruined was the way he held on afterward, chest heaving, forehead dropping against Reyes, silent except for the ragged pull of air through his teeth.

For a long moment, Corvo did not move.

Then, with his mouth still too close for words and his voice too gone for anything but truth, he let out a hoarse, shaking breath that might have been a laugh.

No words.

Not yet.

But his hand tightened at Reyes’ hip, clear as any sentence: stay.

dialogue.name: Reyes
dialogue.content: I stay pressed against him, our sweat cooling, and finally slide to the floor beside the bench. I don't go far. Just enough to let him breathe. I watch him from the tile. "Still think you could've taken the fifth?"
