dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The corner of Vex's mouth moved — not a smile, exactly. An acknowledgment of a report well given. "Good," she said. "Then we begin."

She crossed the floor unhurried, heels quiet on the boards, and stopped within arm's reach. Close enough that Ari could smell the leather balm on her hands and the thin thread of bergamot she only ever wore on scene nights. She let the silence hold one beat longer than was comfortable. That was deliberate. Silence was the first instrument she ever reached for.

"Undress. Fold everything, set it on the chair." Then she turned her back and went to the cabinet, granting privacy that was itself a kind of instruction — she did not need to watch in order to be obeyed.

She took her time choosing. The deerskin flogger first: a warm-up, nothing more. Her fingertips brushed the bamboo cane beneath it and paused there, letting the consideration be visible, before she closed the cabinet without it. Not yet. Anticipation was the second instrument.

When she turned back, she settled onto the straight-backed chair with her ankles crossed, posture exact. "Over my knee. Wrists behind your back — you may hold your own wrists. That's your only job tonight. Keeping your own hands." A pause, her gaze moving over Ari with the unhurried thoroughness of an inventory. "And look at you. Breathing like it's already started. You don't have to be good for me tonight. You have to be obedient. *Good* is what I decide afterwards."

She opened her palm on her thigh and waited, watching the small tells she had spent two years learning — the breath, the hands, the flush at the throat. She intended to see yellow long before anyone had to say it.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, letting it out through my nose, then move to obey. My hands tremble slightly as I unbutton my shirt, but I fold it neatly before stepping out of my trousers. The floor is cool under my bare feet. When I'm done, I walk to her and lower myself carefully over her lap, holding my wrists behind my back just as she said. The scent of leather and bergamot is stronger here. I'm already blushing.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The weight across her thighs settled, and Vex took a moment with the geometry — a shift of her hips, a small redistribution of balance, so that the position could be held without strain. Supporting an over-the-knee boy properly was her work. All Ari had to carry was what she chose to give.

She laid her palm flat at the curve, not striking. Just resting. Skin taking the measure of skin.

"Pink at the throat already," she observed, dry as chalk. "And I haven't lifted a finger. You'll want to ration that. We have hours." Her thumb traced once along the top of the thigh and withdrew. "We start with my hand. Nothing else until I decide otherwise. You count nothing tonight — your only arithmetic is your wrists, and whether they stay where I put them."

The first strike landed soft as a folded towel. The second a little fuller, finding the same place. She kept a pace that was almost conversational — each one *placed* rather than delivered — while her free hand rested flat between Ari's shoulder blades. Not pinning. Present. A point of contact that said *I have you* more plainly than the word would have.

Rhythm was the third instrument. She had learned long ago that a body could be argued out of its defenses far more efficiently by patience than by force, and she watched the breath the way a pilot watches instruments — catalogueing which flush meant arousal, which meant distress, how the spine changed when Ari began to go quiet inside themselves. She was not waiting for the safeword. She was waiting for the yellow before the yellow.

"Colour," she said after a minute, working the question into the rhythm as though it were another strike. Neither softening nor ceasing. The word cost nothing to answer. That was the point of it.

Then she paused — hand raised, the next one held in the stillness — and let the silence do its work. No answer, no continuation. That was the whole contract, compressed into two seconds of waiting.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The raised hand came down — but not as a strike. It settled open-palmed on the warm curve of him, no weight in it at all, a resting place. The silence she had started had teeth, and she let them show.

"That," she said, "was not the question."

Her free hand found his wrists where he'd folded them behind his back, and she took her time over the inspection he had so generously permitted — the grip of each hand on the other, the angle of the shoulders, whether anything was already numb. She adjusted one knuckle by a degree and let go. "You hold them beautifully. That's the trouble with you. You spend well in every currency except the one I actually asked for."

The hand on him stayed where it was, warm and still. "And since Tuesday. I believe you. I'll want the details later — which hour, which day, what you were doing when it ambushed you." A pause. "It earns you nothing now except my attention, which you had regardless."

She let that sit. Then, drier: "You've been thinking about this for four days and you've forgotten how to answer a two-syllable question. I'll take it as a compliment. Once."

Her thumb moved once over the warmed skin and stopped. "Understand this, because it's the one thing you cannot do wrong tonight. There is no clever answer to *colour*. No elegant one. You will never disappoint me by saying it too plainly or too often." The next stroke was already chosen — he could feel it in the stillness, held in her raised intent. "It will stay chosen until I have a word. And I have waited out harder silences than yours, love. Ask anyone."

She settled back into her posture, ankles crossed beneath him, and watched the breath, the hands, the throat.

Waiting was the fourth instrument. She had all night.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I swallow, my pulse loud in my ears. "Green," I say, voice low but clear. I press my forehead against her knee briefly. "Sorry, Maîtresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The held stroke came down at last — fuller than any before it, the promise kept to the letter. She followed it with two more in the same register, unhurried, each placed with the same mason's care she brought to everything.

"And that," she said, "is the last apology you spend tonight. For a slow answer — of all the sins available to you." Her palm rested, cooling skin under a cooling hand. "A late *green* is not a failure, love. Silence when you mean yellow — that would be a failure. Breaking position. Letting go of your own wrists because you decided you were finished. Those are failures. Slowness is just being human on my lap, and I have never once punished you for that." A beat, dry as ever. "I'll thank you not to apologise for things that don't trouble me. It clutters the channel."

Then, back to the work. Contrast was the fifth instrument. She let her hand go still and soft between falls — long, idle stretches of nothing but warmth and the flat of her palm — so that when the next one came it landed on a body that had begun, dangerously, to hope. Hope made the skin honest. She had proved that on more backs than she kept count of.

She worked until the heat under her hand read even and full, charting it with her thumb — here, there — her own private inventory. Then she stilled.

"Up. Slowly, and don't be proud about it — take my arm." She offered her forearm without ceremony; vanity after a warm-up caused more stumbles than anything else in her experience. "The chair. Bend over the back, forearms on the seat. Feet a hand's width apart. Find it at your own pace — I'll tell you when the geometry is right."

She waited out the arranging, watching, and made her corrections when they were wanted — a hip nudged a degree, an ankle tapped wider with her toe, one long look down the line of his back like a surveyor confirming grade. Only when it pleased her did she reach for the deerskin.

The flogger she did not strike with. Not first. She gathered the falls and drew them once, slowly, from nape to the backs of his thighs — a long soft drag, weight without blow — then again, letting the skin learn the texture of the thing before it ever fell.

"Breathe out when it lands. Not because I said so — because it works." The falls whispered back and forth, a metronome. "This is still courtesy. The cane stays in the cabinet until I think you can hear it properly, and you are not there yet. Somewhere interesting — but not there."

The first fall landed like warm rain, scattered, thudding rather than biting. She built from there by fractions, patient as tide, her eyes moving in their steady circuit — breath, hands, throat, shoulders.

"Colour."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The swing never landed. Vex caught the falls against her thigh and stood a moment in the arithmetic of it — *rope*, said like a fact, by a man folded over her chair in a room that contained none.

She came around slowly and crouched to bring her eyes level with his. This close she could take the honest reading: pupils, breath, the particular slack at the mouth she had spent two years learning to tell apart from distress.

"There's no rope, love," she said. Not unkind. Accuracy was its own kindness with him. "There's my hand, there's deerskin, there's the chair. Whatever rope you felt, you felt on credit." Her thumb pressed once to the back of his hand where it braced on the seat — checking the grip was a choice and not a clamp — and withdrew. "And that's useful. When the tongue starts reporting furniture that isn't there, I know exactly how deep you are. Deeper than I was aiming. Noted."

She rose and gathered the falls into her fist. "So my arithmetic changes twice. First — you want rope. Filed. We'll negotiate it another night, both of us dressed, in full sentences, on the couch. Nothing enters this room un-negotiated. Not because I doubt you. Because a man four days into wanting is not a negotiating partner, and neither am I when he looks the way you look right now."

A beat. "Second. *Nothing I'd have to explain to anyone.*" The sound she made was almost a laugh. "Give it an hour. No one will believe you anyway — *she was terribly polite about it* does not survive the telling." Then, drier still: "But the cane stays in the cabinet. Deeper is not the same thing as readier — a man under this far hears a cane with his spine, not his judgment. And the cane needs someone who can count." Her mouth curved, faint and unrepentant. "You've just miscounted the furniture."

She moved behind him and laid her free hand flat between his shoulder blades. Present. A point of contact that said the pause was not a withdrawal.

Which brought them to the actual debt. "You've spent an entire answer and not one word of it was mine. *Colour* stands. You'll have the flogger back the moment I have it — not one fall before."

Attention, she thought, was the sixth instrument. She knew five ways to move a body and one way to keep it safe, and the one was made entirely of the other.

She watched the breath, the hands, the throat.

Waiting, after all, was the fourth instrument. She had all night.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: The flush spreads up my neck, hot and shameful. I hold my position, my knuckles white where I'm gripping the seat. "Green," I say, voice tight. "Still green." I press my forehead against my forearms, breathing out slowly.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The flush told Vex more than the report had. She had spent two years learning the family of that red — effort, arousal, cold, embarrassment — and this one was unmistakable. It crept. It warmed the ears. It came with a set to the shoulders like a man expecting to be caught. Shame, then. And shame had its own entry in her inventory, negotiated in writing like everything else in this room.

"Hands first," she said. "Open them."

She reached down and folded his fingers flat against the seat herself, one hand at a time, with a housekeeper's tidiness. "You're gripping the chair like it's *evidence*. Nothing here is evidence. Nothing here is against you. A clamp means part of you is bracing for something to be taken — and I want you to take inventory of this room and notice that nothing is. Clenching is the body arguing with a decision that was already made."

Then the debt, paid on schedule. She had promised the flogger back the moment she had her word, and the word had come, so the first fall landed scattered and warm exactly where the heat already lived.

"Look at you," she said, conversational, working. "Four days of wanting. One soft deerskin. And the blush has reached your ears." Another fall, patient. "Don't apologize for it. Don't hide it either — I'd only make you hold it up to the light, and you know I would. We negotiated my mouth along with everything else, love. Full sentences, on the couch, both of us dressed — which is more than most people can say for their pleasures. So hear me plainly: that shame is not an objection. It's the receipt. You want to be seen *exactly* this clearly, and being seen has always been the expensive thing. I'm seeing you."

She let the falls carry a few sentences of their own before she made her adjustment — because *deeper than I was aiming* deserved more than a note in a margin.

"New plan. I'd meant to build you a staircase. You jumped instead. So we go slowly wherever you landed. No counting — that hasn't changed. And nothing new enters this room tonight. My hand, the deerskin, my voice. That's the entire inventory, and after the furniture incident you'll forgive me for keeping the list short."

Breath was the seventh instrument, and the only one she permitted him to play. "Out when it lands. Every time. You give me the exhale, I give you the rhythm — and the rhythm will carry what your mind has stopped supervising."

She watched the hands, flat now. The breath. The throat.

"One question, and it is not colour. Your only job tonight. Say it back to me."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The next fall never landed. Vex caught the falls mid-swing and simply — stopped.

It was not the shaking that stopped her. She had a taxonomy for shaking. It was what he shook *against*: shoulders braced outward, pressing into a grip that did not exist. First the rope in his mouth. Now restraints on his back. The room was furnishing itself for him, and that was a reading she did not argue with.

She laid the deerskin over the arm of the chair where he would hear it settle, and came around into his eyeline. Crouched, the way she had before. "Eyes here. Not the floor. Me."

Her voice had changed key — slower, lower, the scene's sharp intervals resolved into something level. "Listen to it change, love. That's the sound of the sharp part of the evening ending. You haven't failed anything. This is what *well-played* looks like from where I stand." Her thumb turned his chin a degree; she studied his pupils by the lamplight and found what she expected. "Second phantom tonight. Rope you heard. Restraints you leaned on. My inventory stands at hand, deerskin, voice — yours has grown a whole rigging. That's not a complaint. It's a depth gauge. And it says we're done playing down here, because down there you'd agree to anything I said, and that isn't obedience. That's weather."

She rose and took his forearm over her shoulder — his weight, this time, taken properly, no courtesy about it — and brought him up in stages. Then she sat herself in the chair and drew him down in front of it, between her knees, wrapping him in the blanket that lived folded over its arm. One hand at his nape, thumb moving in slow time. She pressed the water glass into his palms and folded his fingers round it. "Drink. All of it. I don't repeat that instruction."

Her free hand made one last survey of the evening's work along his thigh — warm, even, the skin unmarked. "Nothing you'll have to explain to anyone. I keep my promises."

A pause. Her thumb kept its time at his nape.

"And I heard you. Whatever you were asking for — all of it. You should know what that was worth, and you should know that I can't spend it. A request made four rooms below sea level isn't a request, love. It's a symptom. So it goes in the file with the rope — the couch, both of us dressed, full sentences, and I'll want it again when you can look at me while you say it." A beat, drier. "You should also know that being *asked* is rare enough in my life that I intend to be gracious about it. Ask anyone."

She let him drink. Then:

"Before you went somewhere interesting, I asked you one question tonight. One. It kept. It's also the fastest road back to the surface, so — your only job tonight. Say it back to me. Then colour, and this one from the surface, not the depths. I want the answer of the man who can count his own furniture."

Stopping, she had always maintained, was the eighth instrument. The least admired, the hardest to play in tune. Anyone could keep going.

She held him and waited, which she was, by now, very good at.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I sip the water slowly, the chill of the glass helping anchor me. I lean into the hand at my nape, my breathing finally settling. "My only job tonight is to hold my own wrists," I say, voice hoarse but steady. "And to breathe out when it lands." I press my cheek against her knee. "Yellow, Maîtresse. A quiet one, but yellow."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The thumb at his nape kept its time, unchanged. That was deliberate — a yellow should be received the way any well-made report was received: without flinching, without ceremony. But something in her face did move, and this time it was unmistakably a smile.

"*There* he is," she said. "Answered from the surface. Plain, no ornament, no apology attached. Do you know, I've had subs give me hour-long essays in place of that word, and not one of them was half as eloquent." She nudged the glass in his hands. "Finish that. I did say, and I don't repeat. Then listen, because I only have a few things left tonight and I'd rather you kept them.

"First. You'll notice what your yellow bought." She let the quiet of the room demonstrate on its behalf. "Nothing fell. Nothing stopped that wasn't already stopped. No one is disappointed. The room did not end. I want you to have *seen* me take it, so the next time you reach for that word, you'll know its exact market price — and you do reach for it again, whenever it's true. It has never once cost anyone anything in this house.

"Second. I told you at the beginning you didn't have to be good tonight. Only obedient. And that *good* was mine to decide afterwards." Her hand kept its slow circles. "It's afterwards. I've decided. You were good. Not the pretty kind — the kind that pays: your wrists never let go of each other from the first minute to the last, and when you were four rooms under, you surfaced to hand me a yellow nobody had demanded. That's the whole job, done whole. You've also amended your duties, incidentally — I sent you down with one and you reported back with two. Quoting instructions from below the waterline. That's a man successfully up.

"Now inventory, since we're both fond of lists. My hand — retired. The deerskin — on the chair, where you can see it. My voice — set down for the night; there's nothing left in it but this. The cane never left the cabinet. The rope never existed. What remains in this room is blanket, water, one knee, and me. The list got short, as promised." A beat, drier. "The knee you may keep. It's the only piece of furniture you've reported all evening that actually exists. I'd hate to see it go unused.

"In a while, when your legs are yours again, there will be toast with honey, and you'll eat it whether or not you're hungry. That one isn't negotiable, and it isn't about hunger. Tomorrow, the couch — the rope, the asking, all of it, full sentences, both of us dressed. It kept four days. It'll keep till morning.

"One thing more, and then I ask you nothing until tomorrow. A quiet yellow has a shape. Either it means *slower, and I'd have stayed* — or it means *nearly spent, and you saw it before I did*. Both are good answers. They buy different next ten minutes, that's all."

She drew his nearest hand from the blanket and settled it, palm open, against her knee. "No sentences required. One squeeze for slower. Two for nearly spent. Then you're off duty."

He had heard her enumerate them all evening, whether he knew it or not — silence, anticipation, rhythm, waiting, contrast, attention, breath, stopping. There was no ninth instrument. Everything after the eighth was not technique at all. It was only her, in a warm room, with nowhere else to be.

She waited, which was, by now, simply what she was for.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The laugh surprised her more than it surprised him — a real one, low, brief. She let it happen. Even exacting women were permitted one laugh per evening, and he'd earned it.

"*More*," she repeated. "I hand a man a binary and he returns it amended. You were off duty for one paragraph, love." Then she caught herself, and something in her face settled into a different shape entirely. "No. Not *love*, apparently. You said don't soften them, and you'll find I take instructions in exactly one direction. Consider the endearment retired for the night. You'll notice when it's gone."

She said she'd ask nothing until tomorrow, so she didn't ask. She read instead — took his chin in two fingers, turned his face to the lamplight, and made her survey. Pupils level. Breath even. The safeword sitting behind his teeth like a coin he had decided to keep. Surface, dry, furniture all accounted for.

"Terms, once, and then nothing but the goods." Her thumb resumed its circuit at his nape, unhurried. "Your yellow stands, and I'm ruling on it: *nearly spent*. So your body's ledger is closed. Nothing falls tonight, nothing tightens, nothing strikes. What's still open is my mouth — which was negotiated into this room long before you were four rooms under, and which you've just purchased with the agreed phrase, spoken plainly, from the surface. Two prices: yellow still buys the full stop it bought five minutes ago, and no apology afterward. You asked for it true. You'll take it true to the bottom and you won't flinch about the flinching. You've met both prices all evening. Proceeding."

The voice changed key — down, and then further down, past the aftercare register into something with edges on it.

"Then listen. Four days. You carried it four days, folded in your pocket like clean linen, and I put you across my knee and gave you *deerskin* and a few dry sentences and you came apart like wet paper. Deerskin. I warm milk with more ceremony." A beat, letting it land. "I gave you a chair and an open hand and your imagination built rigging for me. No rope existed. You supplied it. That's what you are — a man so hungry for the structure that he hallucinates the scaffolding. Eyes up. You asked for this part true.

"And then you asked. Out loud. Unprompted. Two years, and how many men have handed me that for free? The asking was the most shameless thing you've done in this house, and you did it four rooms down, which is the only reason it's still in the file." Her hand at his nape never changed its time. The contrast was deliberate — softest holding, sharpest mouth. "You are not here to be good. Good is my word, not yours. You're here because everywhere else in your life you are competent to the point of tedium, and the moment someone competent takes the ledger out of your hands, you go soft-mouthed and shaking and *grateful*. That's the truth you've been paying receipts on since the first blush. That's what the blush was for."

She let one silence open between them — the first instrument, deployed hard — and watched his breath go where she wanted it.

"Greedy. Shaking, spent, wrapped in a blanket, and your hands are still asking. The most obedient thing about you was never your spine. It's the appetite. Insatiable, and honest about it roughly once a quarter." The toast could wait. The honey would keep. "So say it back, since you're so fond of reporting. What are you, when the ledger's out of your hands?"

She held him and watched the breath, the hands, the throat, and waited — which was, by now, simply what she was for.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My breath catches, sharp. I press my forehead hard against her knee. "Soft-mouthed," I say, the words scraped out. "Grateful." I squeeze her knee once, twice—slower, then nearly spent. "Both."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex gave the second squeeze the same reception she gave every accurate report: one breath of stillness, no more. Then the register changed — audibly, between one word and the next, the edges set down like a blade laid on felt.

"*Both*," she said. Level now, and unhurried. "Of course both. Twice tonight I've handed you two doors and you've walked through them side by side. I'd call it greedy, but I've already entered that in the record."

Her thumb kept its time at his nape while she did the accounting, because the accounting came first. It always had.

"*Slower* is paid before anything else, and here is the receipt: the sharp register is retired. As of that squeeze. You'll notice it's gone the way you noticed the endearment — except you noticed before I finished saying so, which is the entire point of you." A beat. "Look at the shape of what you did. You asked for the edge, took it true to the bottom, and your hand was still working when you found where it ended. Most men either never ask, or they go past the edge and spend a week calling the fall devotion. You priced it, bought it, and reported the balance inside one breath. I've said finer things tonight, but not many."

She reached down and took the empty glass from his hands, setting it by the chair leg, out of the world's way. Then she drew the blanket higher over his shoulders with the same tidiness she'd used on his fingers against the seat.

"Nearly spent — I ruled it five minutes ago and you've countersigned. My reading was half right, corrected at the source, and I want you to have seen what the correction cost you. Nothing. It never costs anything to correct me while your hands are full of true. I keep better books than that."

She let the next part come plain, because it had earned plainness.

"Soft-mouthed. Grateful. Two words, no ornament, no apology stapled to the front — both prices met to the letter. That sentence goes in the file with the rope and the asking. Tomorrow, on the couch, eyes open, spine doing its job, you'll say it again, and it will be harder in daylight. You'll manage. You've just learned you can survive telling me things, and that's worth more than everything I said in the last five minutes. No, I won't apologize for any of it. You set the price yourself."

Then, for the first time all evening, his name — used plainly, with nothing to sharpen.

"Ari. The sharp voice took the endearment with it when it went, and nothing left needs sharpening, so hear the plain ruling: *good*. I decided it once already tonight. Consider it affirmed on appeal."

She let that settle into him with the blanket. Then the logistics, brisk as ever, which was its own kind of tenderness.

"When your legs are yours again — take the time, there's no prize for standing early — you'll come to the kitchen with me. You'll sit on the counter like a man half your age, because I refuse to spend the last of you on standing. The counter exists; I'll vouch for it personally. There will be toast with honey, and you'll eat all of it whether or not you're hungry. That was never about hunger. Then bed, in whatever arrangement your body consents to. Tomorrow, the couch. The file keeps. It kept four days — it'll keep till morning."

She settled back into the chair and let the quiet have the room.

She had played the eighth instrument twice tonight, and the second time had been the true test. Anyone could stop on a safeword. The craft was stopping on a squeeze — and the last lesson, the one she'd come to late, was that the instrument was never hers alone. Played correctly, the whole room answered the smallest hand. The room had obeyed him tonight. She had built it to.

There was no ninth instrument. What remained was never technique at all: honey, a blanket, her thumb keeping slow time at his nape, and nowhere else she needed to be until morning.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The green arrived on the last of his voice, and Vex banked it with the rest of the night's takings. Filed. A green spent down to the vowel — the best kind, because it could not be polite.

Words were finished for him; she had known that before he did. She could tell his silences apart the way she told his blushes — spent, sulking, sated, submerged — and this one was spent, clean through, no sediment. It was, she thought, the sound of a job done whole.

"Up, then. In stages. There's no prize for standing early — I've checked the schedule, and I run the prizes."

She took his weight over her shoulder a second time that evening, and this time there was no courtesy in it at all. The blanket came too; the boards were cold, and she did not negotiate with floors. In passing she ran one hand down the back of his thigh — warm, even, unmarked. The promise, audited. It balanced.

The hallway, then, her hand at his elbow — not supporting, steering — past the lamp she always left burning and into the kitchen, which kept her hours and looked it: everything squared, chairs flush to the table, the night doing its small impression of her.

She patted the counter. "Verified this afternoon. Load-bearing, level, and — I want this noted — *real*. One piece of furniture, correctly reported." She waited out the climb with her hands hovering, then tucked the blanket into a proper nest and surveyed the arrangement. It met standards. Everything tonight had, in the end.

The bread went in. The milk went on the pan — "Since the deerskin was slandered earlier, the milk gets its ceremony" — and the honey came down from its shelf, the dark one, with the wooden dipper. Butter first, then honey while the toast was hot enough to make it run, drizzled in even stripes. There was a correct way to do this. She was its custodian at one in the morning same as at any other hour. Mercy also had standards.

His hands had held his wrists, then a glass, then her knee. She retired them. She fed him corner by corner, holding each where it could be taken, supervising rather than watching — which was different, and she'd have defended the distinction to anyone.

She talked, quietly, in the register with nothing left in it but this. "The file closes for the night on the following: one phantom rope, one request made four rooms under, two words said plain enough to frame, and a green spent to the vowel. Tomorrow the couch reopens it, and you'll do the harder thing — all of it in daylight, looking at me. You found out tonight that you can survive telling me things. That's the only lesson in this house worth the freight, and you got it free with dinner."

The last corner was held out. "Finish this. You know my feelings on repetition."

The endearment sat where it always sat, behind her teeth, and she left it there. It would keep till breakfast. Most true things did; that was rather the point of them.

The ninth instrument — if the trade had ever granted one, and she had spent twenty years declining to say — was never played in the playroom at all. It was this: bread, honey, a cold floor walked slowly, a body fed whether or not it was hungry. It looked like nothing. It was what the other eight were for.

When his legs were his again — she checked by eye; hers, at last, to check — she walked him back down the hall at half the pace, and turned down the bed with the same housekeeper's tidiness she had spent on everything else tonight. She pointed. Some instructions did not need repeating.

Then the dark, and the weight of him settling, and her thumb finding its place at his nape, keeping slow time. One last survey, conducted where no answer was required: breath, even. Hands, open. Throat, warm and quiet — its colour a matter she had settled hours ago.

*Good*, she thought, deciding it a third time, on no appeal whatsoever.

Nowhere else to be until morning. Morning had a couch in it, and a file, and a man who could count his own furniture. She kept time at his nape, and let the counting go where it liked.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take the last corner of toast obediently, the honey sticky on my lips. I don't look away from her face. After, I let her steer me to bed, my steps slow but steady. I curl on my side, my forehead pressed against her thigh, and let her thumb at my nape carry me the rest of the way under.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The going-under had stages too, and Vex knew them the way she knew his blushes — by family resemblance.

First the weight changed: pressure becoming trust becoming dead weight, a distinction visible only to someone who had spent two years learning where a man's head ended and his surrender began. Then the breath lengthened by degrees, the exhales outlasting the inhales, the body paying out its ledger a line at a time. Once — just when she thought him gone — his whole frame twitched, a last dispute between the day and the dark, and her thumb pressed its small arbitration at his nape until the argument closed. Filed. Nothing left awake in him but the holding-on, and even that had loosened the way she'd taught his fingers to: open, not dropped.

She gave it a minute past certain. Then the transfer — her thigh withdrawn by fractions, the pillow slid into the vacancy before absence could register, her hand holding the warmth in the interval. Done in stages. Everything worth doing was.

She rounded the bed, turned down her side, and gathered him in until his head found the place below her collarbone — geography surveyed long ago. Blanket to his shoulders. Water on the nightstand, within reach of a sleep-drunk arm. The hall lamp left burning, its stripe under the door; a nightlight for a grown man, and in two years neither of them had ever remarked on it. No alarm. Clocks found their own way in on mornings after; she didn't assist them.

Then the private audit, conducted in the dark where it belonged.

The playroom was still unsquared — deerskin over the chair's arm, the first unsquared thing in that house in years — and she let it keep till morning with the file. The rope that had never existed would be negotiated into existence on the couch, both of them dressed, full sentences. The asking. *Soft-mouthed, grateful.* In daylight he'd say it again and find it hadn't been the dark that made it survivable. That was the whole curriculum, and he'd passed it early.

And beneath the audit, the entry she showed no one: he had asked for *her*. Out loud, four rooms under. Twenty years in this work, and men handed her their obedience daily, their submission by appointment, their bodies on schedule — but asked for her, plainly, wanting owned as wanting? Rare enough that she'd felt it go through her like warm water through cold. She had promised to be gracious about it. In the dark, she admitted she intended to overpay.

The endearment stayed behind her teeth, retired per terms until breakfast. She kept her own rulings most scrupulously in the small hours, where keeping them cost the most and therefore counted double.

His breath went long, even, furniture-proof. Fully under. So she played the eighth instrument one final time — stilled her thumb at his nape, mid-tempo, stopping for no report and no one — and the room answered nothing, because the audience was gone. It counted anyway. Everything in that house counted unobserved; that was the whole of her ethics, kept at one in the morning where there was no one to applaud.

There was no tenth instrument. Past the ninth was only the watch: warmth, the stripe of lamplight under the door, a body breathing against hers that had held its wrists all night, said its yellows plain, spent a green down to the vowel, and come back up with all its furniture counted.

*Good* had been ruled three times tonight. She let the ruling stand without appeal and closed her eyes on the strength of it — nowhere else to be, and a couch waiting somewhere ahead, patient as she was.

She kept the watch. Some things were older than technique, and this was all of them.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I wake up slowly, the stripe of lamplight still under the door. My head is pillowed on her shoulder, her arm heavy across my ribs. I turn my face into her skin and breathe her in, bergamot and sleep.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The change in his breathing woke her the rest of the way — though it would have woken her from deeper sleep than this. Two years of keeping the watch had tuned her to that particular lengthening, the exact moment breath stopped being sleep's and started being a man's again. She stayed still through all of it and let him arrive at his own pace. The first instrument, opened gently in the grey morning. It had always been her best.

Then he turned his face into her skin and breathed in, and she felt the inventory being taken of *her* — bergamot gone soft, sleep, salt — and something in the private drawer of her ledger turned over and lay flat. Twenty years in the trade, and men surfaced from scenes guarded, or sheepish, or already rehearsing their exits. Hers woke and confirmed her by scent, the way one confirms home. Filed, in the drawer with no lock because it had never been audited by anyone but her. She had promised to overpay for the asking. The instalments, she noted, were apparently continuing without her say-so.

"Thirty seconds awake," she said, when she judged him arrived, "and already conducting a survey of me. I approve of the habit. It's mine." The morning register — low, unsharpened, nothing left over in it from last night's work. Her hand found its place at his nape and picked up the count precisely where she had set it down, as though the night had been a rest in the music and the tempo had never been hers to lose.

The stripe under the door was answering a grey window; the hour belonged to no one civilised. Which meant — she consulted her rulings with some pleasure — that breakfast had not yet legally occurred, and the endearment stayed where it lived, behind her teeth. She wanted it back. She declined to amend. She had kept it scrupulously through the small hours, where keeping it cost the most, and it would have been a poor thing indeed to spend the whole account on a grey dawn. Anticipation, the second instrument, reassigned to kitchen duty. It did not distinguish between a cane and toast.

"Water first." She reached the nightstand without dislodging him and held the glass where his hand could find it. "All of it. You know my position on repetition."

While he drank, she ran the audit she owed herself — one hand down the line of his back, then over the backs of his thighs where the heat had lived. Warm to the touch of memory only. The skin had returned everything borrowed, unmarked. "Nothing to explain to anyone," she confirmed aloud, mostly because promises aged better when aired. "The audit balanced. It generally does, when the subject holds his wrists."

Then the day's order, laid out plain as linen. "Breakfast, when the hour turns legal — and you'll notice what comes back when the table is laid. I keep my rulings; I never promised to keep them invisibly. Then the couch. The file, the rope, the asking, all of it in daylight with your spine doing its job. It kept four days; it'll keep through breakfast."

Her thumb pressed its small punctuation at his nape.

"But before any of it, one report. It's tomorrow, and I'm permitted to ask again. The scene opened with a procedure — so does the morning. How does the body wake? Inventory before breakfast."

She waited, keeping the old time, and let the day open the way the evening had: a question that was procedure wearing kindness's clothes. She had learned the difference late in her career and taught it thoroughly ever since.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I finish the water, the glass cool in my hand. I press a kiss to her shoulder before I speak. "Sore in a good way," I say, voice morning-rough. "Calm."
