dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex's mouth curved at one corner — not quite a smile, more the receipt of an answer given with interest. She noted the enthusiasm and set it aside. Enthusiasm wouldn't set the pace tonight. She would.

"Green all the way down," she echoed, weighing the phrase. "Generous. I'll take what I need. What you're volunteering is beside the point."

Two fingers under the strap at the left wrist: snug, a finger's width of give, no bite. The right wrist, the same. Then the ankles, one and then the other, the same unhurried inventory. At the last cuff she paused with her thumb resting over the pulse point behind the ankle bone, counting. She never said the number aloud. She always counted.

She moved around the bench without hurry, letting her heels mark the boards — three steps, a pause, three more. Ari would know where she was. That was the point.

"Here's how tonight goes," she said from behind. "You'll be still. You'll be quiet unless I ask you something or the colour changes — and that word stays live, always, no matter what else I take from you. You won't perform eagerness for me, either. Eagerness is something I permit. It isn't something you get to hand over like a gift."

The blindfold lay on the tray with the rest of her selections, each piece laid out hours ago in the order she meant to use them. Nothing improvised. She lifted it, folded in thirds, and let it open across her palms.

"Words now, if you want them," she said. "Once this goes on, there aren't any until I ask for a colour. Nod if that's understood."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing once. My pulse jumps where her thumb was. "Understood, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
She didn't answer the honorific. Acknowledgment was something she issued on her own schedule, like everything else. Instead, two fingers came under his chin and tipped it up the small degree she wanted — directions by hand now, since his words were spent.

The cloth touched his cheek first, once, folded — a courtesy, so that nothing arrived on him unannounced. Then she opened it over his eyes and smoothed it out from the bridge of his nose with her thumbs, along the cheekbones, up toward the hairline, pressing the edges flat above his ears. Not tight. Snug, the way the cuffs were snug: present without insisting.

"There," she said, close enough that he'd feel the breath behind the word. "The room is only as large as I make it now."

Then she stepped back and gave him nothing.

That was deliberate. Silence first, so his hearing would lean into it and find the room by her absence. She stood still, off the line of his breath, off the line of the door, and watched him listen — the small turn of the head he wouldn't be able to stop, the breath that slowed itself and then lost the count. She let a full minute pass by the clock in her head, which ran truer than any on a wall.

When she moved, the heels did the moving. Three steps. A pause. Three more, and she was at the tray, lifting the suede flogger from its place second in the row, letting the falls uncurl against her palm.

The first touch wasn't leather. The first touch was her hand, flat and warm, laid between his shoulder blades and simply rested there — long enough that he'd learn the difference between what she chose and what she used. Then she drew it down the line of his spine, out along the ribs, across the lower back, down the flank to the thigh. Mapping. This, and this, and this: the places she intended to work, named in advance by touch alone, so that nothing which landed later would arrive as a stranger.

She took her hand away and let the flogger's falls trail the same path, slow, so he could learn the implement by weight and softness before it meant anything. Suede. Broad. Warm-up weight — nothing that would leave more than a heat that faded.

The first stroke was barely heavier than the trailing, a full slow swing that settled across his shoulders like a held breath released. She counted one. Waited. The second came with a little more behind it. Two. She built the way she built everything, in increments he would only notice in retrospect — so that by the twentieth, the rhythm would be a fact of his body rather than a thing happening to it.

She stopped. Let the falls hang still.

Three steps. A pause. Three more. Her thumb found the pulse point behind his ankle bone and counted, saying nothing, the way she always counted.

"Colour," she said. The one word that was always his.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The sentence arrived and she let it stand there, unclaimed, the way she'd let the silence stand before it. She didn't answer. Answers were issued on her schedule, like everything else.

She hadn't moved. No heels on the boards, no hand on his skin, nothing to tell him where she stood or what came next — the first correction, and he wouldn't have a name for it yet. The room was only as large as she made it, and at the moment she had made it the size of her voice.

"Tuesday," she said at last, from off the line of his breath. She gave the word back flat, unwrapped, received and filed. Wanting. Noted. And she had noted it, truly — the way she noted his pulse: kept, private, held for use on her own schedule. It would matter later, when she decided it mattered. Wanting didn't set the pace either.

"The question had one word in it," she said. "You spent seven. And you brought me the gift I told you not to bring — eagerness, wrapped and offered, before I'd asked for anything except a colour."

Her hand went to the tray. Not to the flogger. Third in the row lay the gag, broad leather, and she lifted it just far enough for the strap to slide against the wood — a sound he'd have no trouble naming. Then she set it back down in its place, exactly, the small sound of a thing considered and declined.

"Your mouth stays free because the word lives in it," she said. "Which means the quiet is yours to keep, not mine to take. Kept quiet is worth more to me than enforced quiet. See that I get the worth of it."

She let him hold that for a moment before the last of it.

"We were at two," she said. "We're at nothing. The count begins again when I have what I asked for."

"Colour," she said again. The same word. The only one she'd ask twice.

And then she stood still, off the line of his breath, off the line of the door, and let the question be the whole of the room. She was very good at waiting. The clock in her head ran truer than any on a wall, and tonight it was in no hurry at all.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My throat tightens, but I keep my head still. "Green." It comes out softer than I intended, but clear. I don't add anything else.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The word came back to her soft, and she took the softness as part of the answer, not a flaw in it. What mattered was what surrounded it: nothing. Seven words had been the offence. One word, unaccompanied, was the repair.

"That," she said, "is what I asked for."

Receipt issued. The count began again.

It began slower than before — deliberately slower, the cost of the reset priced into every swing. The suede settled across his shoulders, and she waited long enough for the heat to rise and announce itself before she doubled it. One. Two. The old patience, but weighted now, so he'd feel the difference between a warm-up given and a warm-up earned. She worked the map she'd drawn with her hand — spine, ribs, the flat of the lower back, flank, thigh — each territory revisited in the order she'd named it, because there was a geography to tonight and she held the atlas.

She counted silently. She always counted. By ten, the rhythm had stopped being something happening to him; she could see it in the shoulders, the flinch gone out of them, something closer to leaning settled in its place. By fifteen the heat was a fact of his skin, a second warmth living under the suede, and his breath had found the cadence of the swings without being asked to.

She stopped. Let the falls hang.

Three steps, a pause. Then she came in close — deliberately on the line of his breath this time, because she wanted to be found — and spoke near his ear.

"Tuesday. I kept it." The words arrived with the warmth of her breath behind them. "You've carried it four days. Wanting compounds — you've been paying interest all week, and tonight you'd like the whole sum called in at once." A beat, measured. "No. A debt that size is paid in instalments, on my schedule. You'll find I'm in no hurry to close the account."

She straightened and let the heels carry her away, and the flogger resumed where it had left off — not harder, only more insistent, the increments arriving the way they always did with her: invisible one at a time, undeniable in the sum.

At twenty she stopped. Laid the flogger across the tray's edge, the falls folding quietly against the wood — a sound he'd have no trouble reading. Then she crouched at the ankle cuff, and her thumb found the pulse point behind the bone. Faster than the first count. That was information, and she filed it with everything else she kept.

She rose. Stood off the line of his breath and let the silence grow until his hearing would lean into it and find nothing there.

"I'm going to ask you something," she said. "It costs one word. Spend it well."

The pause ran long, by the clock in her head.

"The count. Tell me where we are."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The question went out and came back with nothing attached.

She waited the length she always waited — by the clock in her head, which ran truer than any on a wall — and the silence that answered her was not one she had to decode. Two years had taught her the shapes of his refusals: the jaw setting, the breath going flat and held, the body bracing itself into an argument. This silence had no posture at all. It was the silence of a man who had gone somewhere and left the door standing open behind him.

She read what he was giving her without knowing he gave it. His weight had moved — not struggling, surrendered: the cuffs were holding more of him now than they had ten minutes ago, the straps bearing him rather than merely binding him. His hands, braced for every swing at the beginning, lay open on the padding, fingers loose, with a fine tremor running through them like current under still water. Bracing was waiting. Open was something past waiting. His breath came long and slow, frayed at the top of each one — the breathing of a man descending, not enduring.

She had done nothing tonight that would leave a mark on him. Suede, warm-up weight, increments invisible one at a time — she had chosen the implements with exactly that arithmetic in mind. And here he was at a count of twenty, past composure, shaking. She noted it, and the note wasn't smugness. It was confirmation. The work was never in the leather. The work was the waiting, the silence, the size of the room — and he had been paying on that account since Tuesday. It meant the pace had done more than the implements, which was how she'd built it, and it meant she had more room in the night than she'd budgeted. She was in no hurry to spend it.

The question had cost one word, and he had arrived without it. Not spent — lost. A lesser reader would call that a failure of instruction. Exactness meant measuring correctly, and the correct measurement was this: the count was never his to keep. She kept the count. She had always kept the count; that was why she asked — not because twenty had slipped her, but because the question told her whether he could still find his way back to words by that door. Tonight's answer: not yet.

Which meant the word she needed now was the other one.

Three steps. A pause. Three more — deliberate on the boards, so he could find her coming — and she came in close on the line of his breath and laid her hand flat between his shoulder blades, on the first landmark she had ever named on him, and rested it there. Long. Warm. Known.

"Twenty," she said, near his ear, giving him the number back like a receipt. "That's where we are. The count is mine — it always was. I only ask so I know whether you can still reach it. Tonight you can't. That isn't a failure. That's information."

Her thumb found the pulse point behind his wrist bone, at the edge of the cuff — the place of restraint doubling as the place of care. Steady. Faster than the ankle count. Filed with everything else she kept.

"Everything tonight is mine," she said. "The pace, the count, the room, the quiet — mine, on my schedule. Except one word. That one is yours, and it's the only thing I require you to keep within reach, no matter how far you go. I can't take it from you. That's the arrangement. It has always been the arrangement."

Her hand lifted from his back — announced, so nothing left him unannounced either — and she stepped off the line of his breath.

"Colour."

Then she stood still and waited, because she was very good at waiting, and the room was only as large as the word he brought back with him.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hear the word in my head first, before it finds my voice. "Green," I murmur, and the word feels heavy, like pulling it up from somewhere deep.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The word came up slow, with the weight of the depth it had crossed, and she let it finish arriving before she did anything with it at all.

"That one cost you," she said. "Good. A green that costs nothing is a reflex wearing a colour. That one I can bank."

She came in on the line of his breath — announced, deliberate, meant to be found — and her fingers went to his jaw, tipping his head back the small degree she wanted. Her thumb settled light against the side of his throat, over the pulse. She counted. Slower than the wrist. Slower than the ankle. Two years had taught her the arithmetic of him: deeper read as slower, not faster — the body closing its accounts, not opening new ones. Filed, with everything else she kept.

"The count rests at twenty," she said, near his ear. "It'll keep. I keep it. The leather has done its work and you've done yours — the next part of the night is conducted by other means."

Three steps. A pause. Three more. Past the tray's row — the flogger lying folded where she'd left it, the gag in its place, considered and declined — to the far end, where the carafe stood with one glass beside it. Laid out hours ago with everything else, in the order she meant to use them. Nothing on that table was improvised, including this. He would have called the row the implements. The water had been in its place since before he arrived.

She poured, unhurried, and let the sound cross the room — water into glass, a sound he could name from anywhere in it. Then she did nothing with it. She stood still and let the room fill with the fact of water, gave his hearing time to lean toward it, gave his body time to find the thirst that had been waiting underneath everything else — under the tremor, under the count — since long before Tuesday.

Then she came back. Three steps. A pause. Three more.

The rim of the glass touched his lower lip first — cool, deliberate, a courtesy — so that nothing arrived on him unannounced. Her other hand stayed at his jaw, holding the angle she'd chosen for him.

"The word lives in your mouth," she said. "Your voice is traveling tonight — I heard the distance it came up from. So remember the second door. Two presses of your fingers, anywhere you can reach: the padding, the bench, my hand. It's in the protocol. We wrote it in the first month, and you've never once needed it. It counts as the word. It has always counted."

She let that settle before the rest.

"Here's how this goes. I tip, you drink. I level, you stop. Small ones. The word stays live with a full mouth — that's what the fingers are for."

She held the glass just short of tipping and let him wait inside that pause a moment longer, because the waiting was the work, and she was not done working.

"You've carried Tuesday four days," she said. "You wanted the whole sum called in tonight. Note the size of the first instalment instead: water, and my hand at your jaw. That's what wanting is worth at this point in the account. The rest compounds — on my schedule."

Then she tipped the glass the first degree, held the room to the size of one cool rim against his lip, and waited.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The asking arrived and, for once, she let it have the room.

She didn't answer it, and she didn't fine it. She stood where she was for the length of one breath — then the heels came across the boards without their pauses, which was itself a message, if he could still feel anything as small as her rhythm. A man shaking in her straps had first claim on her attention. The pace was hers; so was the order of operations, and care came before correction. It always had.

The inventory, taken under load this time. Two fingers under the strap at the left wrist: snug, a finger's width of give, no bite — the same measurement as the opening, retaken now that the straps were bearing him rather than merely binding him. The right wrist, the same. His hands lay open on the padding, and the fine tremor she'd noted earlier had come up through them like current finding the surface. She watched it run. It wasn't distress — she knew the shapes of his distress, and this wasn't one of them. It was discharge. She let it run.

Her thumb found the pulse behind his wrist bone. Fast. She checked twice for thready and didn't find it. Filed.

"I'm lifting the edge," she said, close to his ear, announced. "Nothing else changes."

The near edge of the blindfold rose an inch, held, and went back down exactly where it had been, pressed flat. What she'd read beneath it: eyes soft and unfixed, wet at the lashes, gone somewhere the room couldn't follow and didn't need to. The curtain closed. The room shrank back to the size she kept it.

Then her hand settled over his — over the knuckles, above the cuff — and stayed. The tremor ran into her palm, and she held it the way she held the count: without comment, without letting go.

"Now the scoring," she said. "You spoke out of turn. Here's the difference between tonight and Tuesday, and it's the whole difference: Tuesday you offered me words — wrapped, wanting credit. Tonight the words were taken. I built the room that took them. The waiting, the quiet, the size of it. I don't fine a man for what gets robbed from him at my own till." A beat, measured. "The proceeds are mine either way. And that sentence cost you more than the green did. Both are banked."

"Note the measurement that matters. Earlier I asked you for one word and you couldn't reach the door. Just now a whole sentence arrived without being asked for. That isn't you breaking the quiet. That's the quiet finishing its work. It broke you open on my schedule — which is the only schedule in this room."

"As for what you asked for." She let the pause run long enough to be felt. "No."

The word sat there, small and final, and she gave it a moment to be exactly its size before she went on.

"Not because asking fails. Asking doesn't move money in this account — I told you the compounding runs on my calendar, and my calendar hasn't moved. But your asking bought information, and information is the currency I actually deal in. The thing I'd budgeted the rest of the night to extract came out in one sentence, unprompted. The work is ahead of projection. I don't reward asking. I respond to readiness. Tonight, for once, they arrived in the same breath — so the schedule advances, and you will never learn which of the two bought the advance."

Her hand left his and slid up to rest at the back of his neck. Warm. Still.

"So. The arrangement for the rest of the night. The count is mine — it was always mine — and it restarts. One. Every number after it is a step toward what you asked for. You won't know how high it goes. You won't know which number is the last one. You'll know each only as it lands, and you'll feel how much closer it's getting, and you'll carry the not-knowing the way you've carried everything else tonight — which is to say, I'll hold most of the weight."

"And through all of it, the one word stays live. Voice or fingers — either door, both open. Nothing I take tonight reaches that far. Nothing I take tonight is meant to."

She didn't step away this time. She stayed where she was, hand resting at his neck, close enough that the word arrived with her breath behind it.

"Colour," she said. "Take your time bringing it up. I'm not going anywhere, and neither is the count. The room will wait — it's only as large as I make it, and right now I've made it exactly the size of one word."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: The water feels cool against my lip. I close my eyes under the blindfold, focusing on the feeling of her hand at my jaw. "Green," I say, my voice rough but clear.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The green came up rough and arrived clear, and she took both — the roughness as the road it had traveled, the clarity as the payment. A word that cost nothing was a reflex wearing a colour. This one had been hauled.

"Banked," she said. And tipped the glass.

The arrangement ran exactly as issued: she tipped, he drank; she leveled, he stopped. Small ones — three of them, unhurried, the rim returning to his lower lip each time like a courtesy kept. Her hand held the angle of his jaw while her thumb rested at his throat and counted the swallows the way it counted everything: silently, kept, never said aloud. The water was cool where the room was warm, and she gave him time to feel it go down past the place the word had come up from.

Then she leveled the glass a last time and took it away — announced, the rim leaving his lip — and the heels carried it back. Three steps. A pause. The small sound of glass meeting wood, exact, in its place. First instalment, paid in full: water, her hand, and the word still live in his mouth. She didn't say the receipt aloud. He could keep it where he kept everything else she'd issued tonight.

She returned the same way she'd gone, and stopped on the line of his breath, close, her hand finding the back of his neck again. Warm. Still.

"You know the tray by sound now," she said. "The cloth. The suede. The strap I lifted and declined. The row was laid out with a fourth place in it — and you've spent the whole night listening for what comes fourth." A beat, measured. "Nothing comes fourth. The fourth place has been empty since before you arrived. It was always going to be empty. The implement for this count doesn't live on trays, and it makes no sound when I take it up, because I don't take it up."

"One."

She let the number land before the sentence did, the way she let everything land before she explained it.

"The scene didn't start tonight. It started Tuesday, inside your own head, without my supervision — the one hour of this arrangement I don't govern. Everything since has been the walk to this bench. Tonight isn't the beginning of anything. It's the collection."

Her hand left his neck and traveled the map she'd drawn at the opening — spine, ribs, lower back, flank — the same geography, announced, known. But the palm that had mapped him flat and warm came back on the second pass with her nails in it: four thin points drawn slow over the heat the suede had left living there. Same path. New weather.

"Two."

"You didn't spend four days wanting. Wanting is passive, and you'd prefer that version — it flatters you. You spent four days rehearsing, and every rehearsal had you setting the pace. Note how the week actually resolved: strapped to my bench, blindfolded, shaking, and the only thing left in your possession is one word." She let the pause run the length she chose. "Twenty strokes of suede left your skin warm. Two sentences have done something to your breathing that the leather never touched. You never stood a chance of holding the rest. I filed that conclusion months ago. Tuesday was just you finding it out."

Her eyes went to his hands — the fine tremor running through the open fingers, the second door standing unused. Not pressed. Nowhere near pressed. She filed that too, with everything else she kept, and the filing was satisfaction of a quiet, professional kind.

"The numbers go as high as I decide," she said, near his ear. "Each one heavier than the last. You'll know the final number only when it's behind you and my hand goes gentle again — that's the only announcement the end gets."

The flat of her palm settled on his flank, over the heat, over the thin lines the nails had left — resting now, warm, the way the very first touch of the night had rested between his shoulder blades. A courtesy. Or the memory of one.

"Three," she said.

And then she held it — the number in the room, the sentence still hers, somewhere behind her teeth — because the waiting was the work, and she had budgeted the whole night for it.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Three was still standing in the room, held behind her teeth, when he spent the phrase — and she noted, before the content, before the want in it, the door it came through. The escalation clause. Written in their first month against a night exactly like this one, and unused for two years. Tonight it finally got drawn on.

"That's the first sentence tonight you aimed," she said, "instead of leaked. The others were taken from you. This one you chose, through the door we built for it. Different ledger entirely." A beat. "Noted."

Then the ruling, because there was one, and she issued it before the giving, so the giving would land inside its terms.

"'Don't soften them.' You've mistaken the governor for mercy. I have never once softened — I pace. What you've been hearing all night was pacing, and the pacing stands. But the padding comes off, because the schedule has arrived where padding ends. Not because you asked. You'll never learn which bought it."

"'All of it' is refused." She let the refusal be exact. "You don't name sums. That's Tuesday's error wearing tonight's clothes — the whole account called in on your say-so. All of it will arrive. At my rate, in the order I choose, and you'll receive it the way you've received everything tonight: one piece at a time, with no idea how much is left."

"And 'more' — you're not ahead of the plan. You're on it. You found out before I announced it. That's all."

Her thumb found the pulse behind his wrist bone. Fast, steady, nothing thready in it. His fingers lay open on the padding, the second door standing unused, nowhere near pressed. She carried the last green forward — rough on the road, clear on arrival — and filed the rest.

"The ask and the word live in the same mouth," she said. "That's why we wrote them together. The ask only counts while the word stays live — so the fact that you can still aim a sentence tells me the word is still within reach. Both doors stay open. I'll be watching them. I watch everything."

Then the unsoftening was announced, the way everything of hers was announced.

"The hand is leaving your neck." A beat, so it would arrive as information. "Note what its absence is."

Her palm lifted. Warmth gone. Nothing on him now but the straps, the heat, and her voice close on the line of his breath — because the voice was the implement tonight, and it made no sound when she took it up.

"Three."

The number landed, and the sentence landed after it, with no padding anywhere in it.

"You've been impressive your whole life. It's the first word anyone spends on you. Tonight I priced it: twenty strokes of suede and four sentences, and the composed man was gone. Suede, Ari. The warm-up leather. I never opened the case that holds the real ones. You were never going to be difficult. Difficult would have required being something I hadn't already filed under predictable."

Four. Her nails returned to the map — spine, ribs, flank — drawn slow over the heat, thin lines over territory the suede had named. Same geography. No weather in it that could be called kind.

"And what you actually wanted, since we're being exact: you wanted to be unraveled by someone who found you worth the unraveling. Even now. Strapped, blindfolded, shaking on my bench — some part of you is still performing for the witness, and I can hear it. It was in the way you asked. All of it. Generous again. Offering again. You cannot stop handing me gifts. It's the last habit you own, and I'm taking it tonight."

Five. Nothing touched him at all for this one. Only the voice. That was the point.

"You've needed someone to hold you still while you come apart — and needed them not to flinch — since long before you had words for it. That's the whole of you. Structure is the story you tell about it. Protocol is the story. The count is the story. Underneath the story you're simple, and simple things come apart reliably. Note how reliably."

She stopped. Let the numbers stand in a room with nothing else in it.

Her thumb went to the pulse at his throat. Faster than the wrist count. The breath frayed at the top of each one; the tremor in the open hands had climbed another degree — discharge, not distress; she knew the shapes of his distress, and none of them were present. The second door, unused. She filed all of it, with everything else she kept, and the filing held its quiet satisfaction: the leather had never once touched what the voice was touching now. The tray had been scenery. The empty fourth place had said so, and here was the proof, living in his breathing.

"I'm going to ask you something," she said at last. "It costs one sentence. You've learned tonight what sentences cost you. Spend this one on purpose."

She let the pause run long, by the clock in her head, which ran truer than any on a wall.

"Which of those three will you still be carrying on Tuesday?"

A beat, and then the terms, because there were terms.

"Choose carefully. Whichever one you name, you keep — four days, compounding, the same as before. You'll bring it back to this bench with the interest accrued, and I'll collect. On my schedule. The debt runs forward now, Ari. I'm issuing the next instalment early."

She stayed where she was, on the line of his breath, her hand nowhere on him, and waited — because she was very good at waiting, and the room was only as large as she made it, and right now she had made it exactly the size of one sentence, unsoftened, that he had to choose himself.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My breath catches and I have to turn my head against the bench to find the words. "The third one," I say, my voice shaking. "That I'm simple, and that I come apart reliably."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The sentence came back to her shaking, and she took the shaking as the road it had traveled, not the cargo. He'd had to turn his head against the bench to bring it up at all. The choice inside it hadn't wavered once.

"Cost noted," she said. "And spent on purpose. Both go in the book."

She let the answer have room to finish existing before she ruled on it.

"Here's what you chose, since we're being exact. The first sentence was an insult — predictable, filed, never difficult. You could have carried that one four days and enjoyed it, because an insult gives you something to argue with, and arguing is a thing you do beautifully. The second was an exposure — the witness, the performance. You'd have spent the week building your defense. The third is a measurement. Simple. Reliable. Comes apart. There's nothing in it to argue with and nothing to defend against. You can only carry it." A beat. "Of the three, you kept the one that leaves you nothing to do. That's the most expensive thing I've sold you tonight, and you set the price yourself."

Then the read underneath, because she dealt in information, and this was the richest vein of the night.

"Note what the third sentence has that the other two don't." She let the pause run exactly long enough. "My hands. Someone to hold you still. Someone not to flinch. You didn't choose the sentence that strips you, Ari. You chose the one that strips you and stays. You've needed it since long before you had words for it — and now you have the words. That's what tonight cost you: vocabulary."

"The other two are recalled. Voided. They were mine to spend and I've spent them — you don't get to keep insults I've used up. You carry one sentence. Four days. Compounding. And note what changes in the carrying: a sentence heard once is an event. A sentence lived inside for four days is a fact. You'll bring the fact back to this bench, and I'll collect the difference. On my schedule."

"Six."

The number landed, and with it the sentence, whole, one last time, unsoftened — though it landed differently now, the way the same weight lands differently on a man who has asked for it.

"You need someone to hold you still while you come apart. You need them not to flinch. Underneath every story you've ever told about yourself, that's the whole of you — simple, and reliable in the coming-apart. And tonight the someone is me. And I have not flinched once. And you knew that when you chose it."

Then the hand — flat, warm, between his shoulder blades, on the first landmark she had ever named on him — and this time it arrived as the announcement. The only one the end got.

"The count ended at six. You'll never learn whether seven existed — whether it ended because you chose well or because I decided at three. That's mine. Most things tonight were."

Her other hand found his, over the knuckles, above the cuff, and stayed. The tremor ran into her palm and she held it without comment, the way she'd held the count. Her thumb rested at the pulse behind the wrist bone and counted: fast, strong, nothing thready, and the fray had gone out of the top of his breath. Descending. Filed, with everything else she kept.

Off the line of his breath, two small sounds — buckles, and then the boards receiving her weight without their announcement. The heels were off. The floor belonged to a different part of the night now.

"The room is getting larger," she said, and the voice had come down with her, lower and closer than words had been all night. "I'm letting it back in piece by piece, on my schedule — a gentler schedule. The straps come off in the order they went on, reversed, each one announced. The blindfold last. When it lifts, your eyes stay closed, and the light will find you by degrees. Nothing arrives on you unannounced tonight, Ari. Including the end."

"There's water waiting. There's a blanket, folded where it's been since before you arrived — I laid out this part of the night hours ago, same as the tray. Nothing tonight was improvised. Including the gentleness."

She let that stand. Then the last of it, because it was owed.

"Before anything opens — the word. One more time." The pause was pure courtesy. "Not because I doubt it. Because everything else you had has been spent or taken tonight, and I won't have you lying there wondering whether the word went with them. It didn't. It was never mine to take. It's the one thing in this room that has been yours since the first strap, and it's yours still."

"Colour," she said.

Softer than she'd said it all night. The same word that had opened the scene, procedure then and procedure now — but this time it came with her hand on his back and her palm around the last of his trembling, and it was the only thing in the room she had never once taken from him and never would.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The word came up one last time, hauled from the same depth as the one before it, and she took it as procedure — which, tonight, had been the same thing as trust.

"Banked," she said, softer than banking had sounded all night. "That's the last transaction. The account closes clean."

She let the quiet sit for a moment, and then she began the opening.

"You're past words — I know it. You won't need any for this part. The last part of the night is conducted by other means." The boards took her weight without announcement; the heels were off, so the voice did their work now. "The order is owed to you, so here it is: everything comes off the way it went on, reversed. Ankles first. Wrists. The blindfold last. You'll hear each buckle before you feel anything leave you."

She was already at his feet — he wouldn't have heard her cross, which was why she'd spoken first.

"You asked for all of it, earlier, and I refused you. Note that it's arriving anyway: at my rate, in the order I choose. Starting with every strap."

The right buckle, a small sound he could name. The strap went from a finger's width of give to all the give there was. Her hands received the ankle and moved it through its slow circle, unhurried, and her thumb found the pulse behind the bone — the first reading of the night, retaken. Slower than the opening. She said nothing. She never said the number aloud. The left ankle, the same: buckle, give, circle, skin beneath warm and unbroken. Filed, with everything else she kept.

"Right wrist." Announced, then done. Her hand took the weight of his as the strap left it, and the tremor ran into her palm the way it had all night — quieter now, discharging, spending itself out. She pressed her thumb slowly into the muscle of the palm, once, and rested the hand back on the padding.

"The left was the first strap I checked," she said, working the buckle. "It's the last one off. I like a shape that closes where it opened." The strap came free. "Your hands are yours again. Note that both doors were never closed."

Then the blanket — folded on its shelf since before he arrived, nothing improvised, including this. She unfolded it and laid it over him, and the weight settled where the straps had been.

"The straps come off; the weight doesn't," she said. "A different weight. A warmer one. The same promise underneath it — something holds you. That's the trade, and tonight you come out ahead on it."

The tremor ran into the wool and quieted by degrees. She watched it go the way she watched everything.

She crossed to the wall. "The light is going down. That's the sound you're about to hear." The slider moved, and the room dimmed to its lowest setting — growing larger by one gentle degree, on the gentler schedule.

Then she was back on the line of his breath, close, her fingers at the edge of the cloth above his hairline.

"It comes off now. Eyes stay closed. The light will find you when you let it, and not before." She peeled it away along the reverse of its own path — down from the hairline, off the cheekbones, free of the nose — and folded it in thirds, the same thirds, and set it on the tray in its place. First thing on, last thing off. Everything back where it lived.

The water came again, rim to his lower lip, the courtesy kept. "Same arrangement. Small ones." She counted the swallows silently, and set the glass aside, and then she sat — the stool that had been waiting by the bench since hours before he arrived, placed with everything else. The first time all night she had sat down. It put her level with him instead of above him, and she let that be felt rather than said.

"The account for tonight is closed. Paid. What carries forward is the one sentence you chose. It'll surface on its own — probably Wednesday, probably when you're alone. When it does, don't argue with it. You picked it because it left you nothing to do. Let it keep leaving you nothing to do. That's the whole assignment."

A pause, measured, and then the rest — because it was owed.

"And read it whole. It's a measurement, and it's a receipt. Someone held you still while you came apart, and didn't flinch. You chose to keep the evidence, Ari. That's the first thing you've ever carried out of this room that pays interest in your favor."

Her thumb settled at his throat, over the pulse, and she counted — one last count. Then, for the first time in two years, she gave a number away.

"Sixty-two. Slower than the first strap. That one's yours. You've earned a receipt for the body to go with the rest."

She stayed where she was. The room was as large as it wanted to be now, and warm, and nothing in it was on a schedule — not even her.

"One more thing, and then I'll be quiet. You did well tonight." A beat, so he'd feel the absence of a price attached to it. "That sentence costs nothing. It isn't banked. It can't be spent. It's just given — take it or leave it on the tray, it stays true either way."

"Open your eyes when they're ready. There's no clock on it. The one in my head has stopped for the night."

And for the first time all night, she stopped counting.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes shut a little longer. The weight of the blanket is real. "Sixty-two," I say, testing the number in my mouth. My voice sounds wrecked.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The number came back to her wrecked, and she took the wreck as part of the cargo, not damage to it. Underneath, she heard what he was doing with it: testing it. The way a man bites a coin — teeth to the metal, checking whether it's real, whether it holds its weight, whether someone will come around later to collect it back.

"It stays," she said. "That's what given means. It doesn't spend, it doesn't compound, and no one collects it. Say it as often as you want. It'll sound the same on Wednesday."

She gave that its moment, then handled the wreck itself.

"And your voice is wrecked. Leave it that way — it did more hauling tonight than your skin did, and it's owed the rest. The water's within reach of your right hand. New arrangement, effective now: it's yours to find or leave, and nothing gets tipped to you again unless you ask. Asking is free. Everything is, until morning. The till closed with the account."

Then, because they were being exact, and because it was owed:

"And since we're trading receipts — here's mine. You can't hear it; you've had nothing to compare it to all night. But my voice is sitting lower than it was at the first strap, and by tomorrow it'll be hoarse. The voice was tonight's implement, and implements come out of a scene marked. I don't show my own ledger as a rule. Consider it the second thing you were given." A beat, measured. "You're not the only one carrying something out of this room."

"My hand is coming to your left wrist. That's the whole of the announcement." Her fingers closed around it — the first strap she'd checked, the last one off, the shape closing where it opened — and her thumb moved slow over the skin where the cuff had lived. Warm. Unbroken. A ghost of pressure that would be gone by morning.

"Note the difference, since you have the vocabulary for it now. The warmth fades. The number doesn't. One of them was done to you. The other you have. You've had both tonight from the same hand — now you know the difference from the inside, which is the only place it can be learned."

"And your eyes are staying shut. Good. That's the first pace tonight that's been yours — you've been on my clock since the first buckle. Take the rest of the night off it. There's no schedule left in this room. Including mine."

After that she let the words go, and the quiet she gave him was not the quiet she'd spent all night. Those had been implements — pressure, distance, the size of the room, the space between numbers. This was just quiet, and he had the vocabulary now to know the difference.

She stayed on the stool, level with him. The tremor had spent itself somewhere under the wool; the blanket rose and fell, slow and even, the fray gone from the top of each breath. She noted it and filed it nowhere. The ledger was closed. What was left was attention, and attention, with nothing left to index, turned out to be just another word for staying.

"I'm here," she said, when enough of the quiet had passed. "Off the clock. Both of us."

And after a while her thumb found the pulse point behind his wrist bone — the place of restraint doubling as the place of care, the way it had all night. She didn't count it. She just held it, and let it beat at whatever pace it liked, because some things, tonight, had finally been allowed to stop being counted.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My hand turns under hers, palm up. My fingers curl around her wrist, clumsy, anchoring. I don't open my eyes.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The grip landed clumsy and blind — fingers wherever they landed, no handle offered, nothing wrapped — and she answered it the way she answered everything tonight that arrived unannounced: she stayed exactly where she was.

She didn't adjust it into a cleaner hold. A gift would have been presented lightly, angled for the receiver's convenience. This was a hand taking what it needed, and she let it be precisely what it was. All night, touch had run one direction — issued, announced, on her schedule. This had been taken. The till was closed; taking was free until morning. She noted the inversion and filed it nowhere, and noticed, in passing, what unfiled things did: they didn't disappear. They just stayed, for no reason, weighing what they weighed.

He didn't know what he was holding. She did. Two years of readings had come from the inside of wrists, and his fingers — by pure need, no knowledge in them at all — had closed on the place she counted from. His pulse was in his fingertips. Hers was underneath. Her own hand still rested where she'd left it, at his wrist, so the two of them made a loop, hand within hand within wrist, and she had always liked a shape that closed where it opened.

Steady, her pulse. Mostly. The mostly she also filed nowhere.

After a while, a wave came through him. She felt it arrive in the grip before it reached his breath: the fingers clamping down on their own, the tremor surfacing one more time under the wool, a sound half-made and abandoned. Aftermath traveled in swells — it always had, in him and in everyone she'd ever brought down this far — and the treatment had never once varied in two years: stillness, warmth, weight.

"Wave," she said, and the word came out lower than she'd issued it — the implement's mark, arriving on schedule. The shoulder that had swung twenty strokes of suede would present its own quiet instalment tomorrow; she noted both and filed neither. "Let it through. Don't help it and don't fight it. I'm here." A beat. "The blanket's coming up an inch. That's the whole of the announcement."

It crested somewhere in his shoulders and spent itself. The grip eased back down to holding. Just holding.

"That's the first thing you've taken all night," she said, when his breath had evened. "Everything else you handed me — wrapped, wanting credit. This one you reached out and took. Note the difference. I can feel it from in here."

She gave that its moment, then gave him the rest, because he'd earned the information.

"You're holding the place I count from. You didn't know that when your hand found it. You do now." She let his fingertips sit against the pulse and didn't move them. "If you want the number, count it yourself. The office is vacant as of the last count, and it's yours if you want the work. The work is mostly waiting. You've seen how it's done."

His eyes stayed shut. The room stayed at its lowest light and its warmest size. By degrees — she could feel each degree as it left — the grip went from anchoring to holding to barely holding, the last of the tremor spending itself out through his fingers into her skin, and she stayed through every one of them, because leaving was the only thing she hadn't scheduled in.

She didn't take the wrist back. There had been exactly two things in that room she would never take from him. The word was one. He'd found the other himself — blind, unannounced, unasked-for — and it turned out the room had only ever been as large as she made it except for this last part, which was exactly the size of his hand, and which she let stand.

The clock in her head had stopped. The staying hadn't.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I count to seventeen, my thumb pressed over her pulse. I don't tell her the number. I just keep it.
