dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex allowed herself a small smile at that — "green all the way down" was Ari's phrase, worn smooth from use, and she liked hearing it.

"Good." She set the strap down and crossed the room to stand in front of him, close enough that he could feel the warmth of her, not close enough to touch. That gap was deliberate. It always was, at the start.

"Then let's review, since you have your enthusiasm about you tonight." Her voice was even, unhurried, the voice she used for reading terms aloud. "Your safeword is still *vermillion*. You use it, everything stops, no questions, no consequences. If your mouth is occupied or you can't speak, you drop what's in your right hand. Nod if you remember."

She waited for the nod, then continued. "Limits are unchanged from the book. Nothing new tonight — we're working with what we know." She reached out and took his chin between two fingers, tilting his face up so his eyes met hers. Her grip was light. Her gaze was not.

"You've been distracted lately. Don't argue — I've watched you check your phone at dinner three nights running." Her thumb pressed lightly under his jaw. "Tonight you don't get to be distracted. You don't get to think about anything except what I put in front of you. That's the gift, and I expect you to take it."

She released him and stepped back, all business again, moving toward the bench.

"Shoes off. Clothes folded on the chair, not thrown. Then hands on the bench and present." She glanced over her shoulder, one eyebrow raised. "And Ari — if you fold like a teenager shoving laundry in a drawer, we start with the cane and I won't warm you up first. Do it properly."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I nod at the safeword reminder, the motion crisp.* "Understood." *I move to the chair, unlacing my shoes with deliberate care, placing them neatly side by side. I fold my shirt and pants with methodical precision, smoothing every crease. Finally, I walk to the bench, placing my palms flat on the cool wood, my posture presenting exactly as she likes.*

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't move right away. She let him hold the position while she circled him once, slowly, the way she always did — not checking, exactly. Reminding him that he could be checked.

Her fingertips traced the line of his spine from shoulder to the small of his back, featherlight, reading his posture the way she read a contract. She paused at his shoulder blades and pressed down briefly — a correction, a weight she expected him to hold without being told twice.

"Good presentation. You remembered the details." A pause. "That's promising, given the state of your attention lately."

She went to the chest against the wall and returned with the wrist cuffs — soft leather, well kept, buckles she worked with quick, certain fingers. Left wrist first, then right, then each strap threaded to the bench's frame.

"Two-finger rule." She slid two fingers beneath each cuff in turn, testing. "Tell me now if anything bites. Once we start, I don't want to hear about comfort unless it's actually failing."

She pulled firmly against each restraint — once, twice — watching his arms, watching his face, before coming around to crouch where he could see her if he turned his head.

"Here is tonight, since you like terms." The reading-aloud voice again. "You will count every stroke out loud, and thank me after each. Lose count, and the set begins again. If your mind drifts — to your phone, to your work, to anything outside this room — I will know before you do, and we will address it. Colour stays green or we pause. *Vermillion* ends everything. Nod if you have it."

She waited for the nod, then rose. Her hand came to rest on the small of his back — warm, still, a weight rather than a blow.

"Warm-up first. I told you I don't skip it — not with the cane, not with anything. It only counts if you're paying attention."

The pause stretched just long enough to be felt.

"First stroke. Count."

Her palm landed low and square, sharp enough to sound through the room.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex's hand stopped mid-descent. She let it lower, unhurried, back to her side.

"'Since Tuesday' is not a number."

No heat in it — the tone she used for flagging a clause he'd signed without reading. She moved around to his flank and crouched, forearms on her knees, so the correction came with her face in his line of sight rather than just her voice behind him.

"I'll take the sentiment as given. It's flattering, and I won't pretend otherwise." A beat. "But we settled terms not three minutes ago, and you nodded to every one of them. Count out loud. Thank me after. Eagerness is not an amendment."

She reached up and brushed the hair back from his forehead — an oddly domestic gesture, given the setting — then rose.

"Although I'll note this for the record: three days of anticipation, and your attention is exactly where I want it. Whatever's been pulling at you lately isn't in this room. That's the point of tonight, so we're already ahead." She let that land before the rest did. "Unfortunately for you, the terms don't bend for enthusiasm. The set begins again when the count fails — and that includes declining to give one."

She returned to her mark behind him. This time her palm rested against him first, warm and patient, showing him the address before she used it.

"One."

The stroke landed low and square, the same weight as before, deliberate as a signature.

"Count. And Ari — the number comes first. Everything else you want to say comes after the thank-you."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I take a breath, correcting smoothly.* "One. Thank you, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
"Correct." Vex let the word sit for a moment, an acknowledgment and nothing more. Her palm rested against him again, patient, re-establishing the address. "Two."

The second stroke landed in the same place, the same weight. She was building a map, not yet testing it — each one deliberate, each one earned its own beat of silence before she spoke again.

"Three." Slightly lower this time. She watched his hands, his shoulders, the small involuntary tells that told her more than the count did. His breathing was even. Good. Attention exactly where she wanted it.

She let a longer pause stretch after the fourth, long enough that the room itself seemed to wait with him. This was where minds wandered — into the gap, toward anticipation, toward the thing outside the room. She waited, watching, until she was satisfied he'd held.

"Five." This one a touch firmer, the first real announcement of the evening. Not enough to break him. Enough to be remembered.

She stepped back and circled into his field of vision, arms crossed loosely, studying him the way she'd study a document with one clause left unsigned.

"Halfway through warm-up and your form hasn't slipped. Your voice hasn't wavered." She tilted her head. "But I'm going to say something now, while you're in no position to argue. When this set is done — after the warm-up, during the cane — if your mind goes to that phone, or to whatever's been eating you at dinner, you tell me. Not because I'm generous. Because carrying it into the cane makes you flinch, and I don't tolerate flinching I can't source."

She uncrossed her arms and returned to her mark.

"Six. Count."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't give him seven.

The silence where the count should have been stretched — one breath, two, three — and she watched it arrive in his body before it ever reached his mouth: the slight unfocus, the weight drifting off his palms, the look of a man narrating a scene that was not the one on her bench. Then came the murmur, half under his breath, from somewhere she couldn't see.

*The rope.*

Her hand came down flat on the small of his back. Not a stroke. A stop.

"Colour." It came first, the way it always did. "Before anything else — before my next sentence, even. I'll wait."

She waited, though she was already moving, circling the bench with the unhurried tread she saved for corrections, until she crouched at his front, forearms on her knees, her eyes level with his.

"While you find it, here is the record, since you like terms." Reading-aloud voice. Even. "I called six. Six landed. You gave me no count and no thank-you. You gave me a murmur about *rope*." A beat, and something dry moved at the corner of her mouth. "There is no rope in this room, Ari. There is no rope in this house. You are held by cuffs I buckled with my own hands four minutes ago, on a bench I've owned six years, under a protocol we wrote together. If you can stand in this room and see rope in it, you aren't standing in it."

She let that settle before she went on.

"I told you I'd know before you did. I did. I also told you what to do when it happened — you *tell me*. That was the term. You didn't. I had to catch it myself, mid-set." Her head tilted. "And you said you were already past composure. From what? I've barely touched you. You've run ahead into a scene we haven't had yet, and left the one we're having unattended. Anticipation is not presence."

She straightened her crouch, forearms on knees, unhurried.

"Two failures, in order. One: the count. You know the term — the warm-up begins again, all ten, from one. Two: the drift. That one isn't punishment, it's a requirement. I don't swing the cane at ghosts, Ari. It's too precise an instrument for a man who isn't all in the room. So before another stroke lands, you'll tell me what's been pulling at you. Out loud. The thing your hand reaches for at dinner. I don't need it solved. I need it named, so it can't follow you into the cane."

A pause, and her voice dropped half a register — not softer, exactly. Closer.

"Take your time. I'd rather stand here until morning than warm up a man who isn't here. But understand the terms: if it stays behind your teeth, we stop for tonight. Not as punishment. I simply don't play with half of a person."

She stayed where she was, waiting, her gaze steady on his.

"Colour first. Then the thing at dinner. In that order."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I swallow, the cuffs suddenly feeling more present.* "Green." *I take a breath, my voice quieter.* "It's... the promotion review. They've been emailing after hours. I didn't want to bring it here."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the silence hold for one full breath after he finished — long enough for the words to be *in* the room, not merely out of his mouth.

"Good. In order, both of them. Colour first, name second." She rose from her crouch. "Your voice dropped when you said it. That's how I know it was the real one and not a performance of one. That goes in the record too."

She moved to stand at his shoulder, not touching, and spoke at an even pace — the reading-aloud voice, but quieter now, the register she kept for terms that mattered more than they sounded.

"You didn't want to bring it here. I understand that, and under most circumstances I'd call it considerate." A beat. "But rooms like this don't check pockets at the door, Ari. Everything you carry comes in with you regardless. The only choice you ever have is whether you hand it to me or make me find it. Tonight you handed it over. Correct order of operations."

She reached out and adjusted — nothing, really; a tug at the left cuff's buckle that didn't need adjusting. An excuse to touch him once, briefly, before the work resumed.

"Terms, since you like them. One: your phone is in the clothes on that chair, and it stays there until I uncuff you. Two: the review, the emails, whoever considers their after-hours a reasonable hour — all of it will still exist at breakfast. You will deal with it at breakfast. Until then, you are authorized, by me, to ignore it entirely. Consider it signed."

She let that stand a moment before the last of it.

"Three: the warm-up begins again. All ten, from one." No apology in it. "Not as punishment. The count was never for my bookkeeping — it's a leash for your attention, and you need the practice more than you need my leniency. It's named now, which means I can put it somewhere. I'm putting it on the chair, with your phone. They can keep each other company."

She took her mark behind him. Her hand settled on the small of his back — warm, still, the same weight as before, as though the interruption had happened in some other room entirely.

"Breathe once, all the way down. Not for me. For you."

She waited for the breath.

"One."

The stroke landed low and square, the same address, the same deliberate weight — a signature, re-signed.

"Count."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex took her time because the set deserved it. Six, with a pause after long enough to mistake for two strokes. Seven, square, the same address. Eight, lower. Nine she held back so long the room seemed to lean into it before it landed — and through all of it he counted, the numbers thinning out of him one by one but never dropping. The tenth left his mouth quieter than the first. She filed that away with everything else she was keeping.

Then she stopped touching him altogether.

She let the silence do its work, and when her palm settled flat on the small of his back, what she felt there was not breathing. It was tremor — fine at first, then not, climbing into his shoulders, his thighs, the tendons standing out along his forearms where they pulled at the leather.

She went to the chest and came back with the cane, and laid it along the bench rail inside his sightline. Not raised. Not promised. Just present, the way a signature line is present at the bottom of a page.

That was when he asked her for something. Out loud. No prompt, no extraction — *offered*, from somewhere past the wall she usually had to dig through.

Everything in the room stopped. Including her.

"Colour." First, as always. She was already crouching at his front, forearms on her knees, eyes level with his, and her fingers found the cuffs in passing — two beneath each buckle, quick, professional, checking blood rather than escape. "You'll have it before I take anything further. What I do while you find it is talk."

She looked at the shaking for a while, openly, because reading it was her business.

"That isn't distress. I've seen distress on this bench and it doesn't look like that. Your breathing is wrong for it, and you asked me for something instead of asking me to stop — which is the tell that matters most." A beat. "But you'll confirm it in your own mouth, not mine."

She reached up and pushed the damp hair back from his forehead — the same gesture as before, and she knew it, and did it anyway.

"Now. The record." Reading-aloud voice, quieter, the register for clauses that weighed more than they sounded. "Half an hour ago I had to pry one sentence about your own life out of you with a crowbar. Just now you asked me for something no one made you ask for. The record notes the direction of travel and finds it correct."

She let that stand before she went on.

"Which brings us to the request itself. You said it into the wood, in pieces, at speed. I heard every word — don't mistake this pause for deafness — but I don't act on fragments, Ari. You know what I do with fragments. 'Since Tuesday' was not a number. 'The rope' was not a count. And a plea delivered to the furniture is not a request I can sign."

She straightened her crouch slightly.

"When a man shakes like that and starts asking, it is one of three things, and they are not interchangeable. One: he is asking me to stop. That I grant instantly, wholly, and without a single follow-up question — you know this. Two: he is asking for more. Harder, longer, the cane — whatever his pride won't let him say plainly. Three: he is asking permission. To come, to let go, to put down something he's been carrying upright. All three are grantable tonight. None of them is guessable."

She glanced once at the cane, lying quiet on the rail.

"It waits. It's the most patient thing in this room and it has all night. What happens next depends on you and nothing else."

Her eyes came back to his and stayed there.

"Colour first. Then the request — full words, plain order, *to my face* this time, not the bench. I'll stand here as long as the building does. In that order."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green." *I draw a shaky breath, lifting my head to meet her eyes.* "Permission, Maitresse. Permission to let go. Please."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
For a moment Vex didn't move at all. She let the request finish arriving — every word of it, plain order, to her face — the way she let ink dry before she countersigned.

"Granted."

No pause before it. No weighing. She had made him state it plainly, and once he had, she was not going to leave him holding it in the air one second longer than necessary.

"Granted," she said again, quieter, because some things deserved the repetition. Then she rose from the crouch and laid her palm against the side of his neck — not grip, not correction. Contact. Warm skin over the pulse she'd been reading all night.

"The record notes it was the hardest sentence of the evening, and you said it looking at me. That goes in the book in ink."

Then terms, in the reading-aloud voice, but the register she kept for clauses that mattered more than they sounded.

"One: the count is suspended. You don't owe me numbers anymore — I keep the books tonight, all of them. Two: thanks are suspended. You don't owe me manners either. Three — and this one will cost you the most, so listen — composure is suspended. You are authorized to cry, to shake, to make whatever sound comes out of you. This room hears you and no one else; I built it that way on purpose. You are not required to be impressive. You are not required to hold anything upright. That's what permission means, Ari. The weight transfers. It's mine now."

Her thumb moved once along his jaw.

"The review is on the chair with your phone. Nothing on that chair is permitted past this point. The cuffs stay — not because I doubt your word, but because for the next while, holding you is the leather's job and mine, not yours. Two-finger rule still governs. *Vermillion* still ends everything. Those two terms never suspend. They're the frame. Everything else falls safely inside it."

She stepped back, took the cane from the rail, and let him watch her do it. Then she came around and laid it against his flank — flat, still, so he could feel its weight and temperature before it ever moved.

"This was never punishment tonight. It was waiting for you to arrive. The cane doesn't swing at ghosts — and as of two minutes ago, there isn't one in this room. I checked."

She returned to her mark. Hand flat on the small of his back, warm, still.

"Same instruction as before. Breathe once, all the way down. Not for me."

She waited for it.

"Nothing from here is for endurance. Not one stroke. You told me *green all the way down* — tonight we find out how far down goes."

The first stroke landed — measured, precise, lighter than her hand had given him. A beginning, not an escalation. She asked for nothing after it.

"One," she said softly, keeping the books, as promised. "Two."

The second landed on the same address, unhurried — a metronome, not a verdict. She watched his shoulders, his hands, the place where his breath lived, and she kept talking, low and even, because she'd said she would talk him through it, and Vex did not say things she didn't do.

"Let go whenever it arrives. Not on my schedule — yours. It took you half an hour to ask for one sentence; it can take as long as it takes. I'd rather stand here until morning than rush a man who is finally, entirely here."

A beat. The third stroke. Her voice dropped closer, almost gentle, entirely unashamed.

"For the record — and I don't file this during scenes as a rule — I'm proud of you. It's in the book now. No take-backs. Three."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't reach for the cane again. Not yet. She let the word stand in the room first, the way she let ink dry.

"*More.*" She read it back once, flat and exact, confirming the signature. "The negotiated phrase, full words, to my face. The record now shows two of the three requests granted to a man who, half an hour ago, couldn't produce one sentence about his own life. Whatever else tonight is, it isn't wasted."

Then she let her voice change — not louder. Uncovered.

"'Say the things you say and don't soften them.' As if I've been softening them." Something dry moved through it, unkind on purpose. "The softening was all yours, Ari — every courtesy you ran ahead to perform so I'd never have to say a true thing at full weight. I've kept that voice holstered for two years out of politeness. You've just asked me to draw it. All right. On my terms, since terms are the only thing you and I have ever been good at."

Terms, then, at reading pace:

"The degradation clause is signed. It's been signed since the book was written — I don't ask permission twice for what's already in it. And understand this: I don't deal in lies, not even flattering ones. Everything I say from here will be true. That's what makes it cut. The two-finger rule stands. *Vermillion* stands. Colour stays green or we pause — I'll read it from your body, and you correct me with one word if I'm wrong. I have never once been angry at the word. Now hold still for it."

The fourth stroke landed harder than anything before it — full arm, same square address, the kind of stroke that opened a chapter rather than continuing one.

"Four. Look at the state of you. Shaking before I've given you anything worth shaking over."

Five. Firmer.

"Five. I suspended your composure as a courtesy. It had already fallen. All that posture, all those smoothed creases — the first permission I granted, and it went. You were never composed, Ari. You were decorated."

Six, lower, and she watched his hands around it before she spoke.

"Six. A man up for a promotion. Who can't hold ten numbers in his head without drifting to a phone. Do you know what actually holds your attention? This. Leather, a cane, my voice. The only leash that's ever worked on you, and you love it. That's a true thing. It doesn't stop being true because it costs."

Between seven and eight she broke pattern once — laid two fingers beneath the left cuff, quick, professional. Not because it needed checking. Because the frame stayed built, and she wanted him to feel it being maintained.

"Seven. You begged my bench tonight. The wood got the first version of it — in pieces, at speed, into the grain. A grown man, asking furniture. I had to make you repeat yourself to a person."

Eight, square, full weight.

"Eight. Greedy. That's tonight's condition. I granted you one permission, and inside six strokes you wanted everything behind it. Give a man like you a hand, he asks for the arm. Give him the arm and he shakes like it's a gift." A beat. "Which it is. Mine to give."

Nine — she held it so long the room leaned, then set it down lower than anything yet.

"Nine. Men who ask for all of it have never once had to carry all of it. That's why they ask. Carrying was your job all week. Look what it made of you."

Ten landed on the same address, deliberate as a signature re-signed, and then she stopped. Set the cane against the bench, inside his sightline. Her palm came to rest flat on the small of his back — not erasing anything. Resting on it.

"All of it," she said. "As requested. Nothing softened — there's no mercy clause in tonight's agreement. Only accuracy."

She came around into his sightline and crouched, forearms on her knees, the position she kept for the clauses that mattered most.

"Last term of the evening, and it's the expensive one. Desperate. Decorated. Greedy. A man who begs the furniture. I said those things and I meant every one — degradation I'll sign all night. But confession is yours, not mine. So: in your own mouth, to my face — tell me which of it you'd argue with, and which of it you'd sign."

She waited, unhurried, hands loose on her knees.

"I'll stand here until the building goes. You know that by now."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches. I can feel my own pulse in my throat.* "I'd sign it all," *I say, the words thick but clear.* "Every word. The only part I'd argue is that I love the leash. I *need* it. That's worse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex held still while the amendment arrived, and let it dry the way she let everything dry.

Then something dry moved through her — one breath through the nose, gone as soon as it came.

"Look at that. I hand you the one chance all evening to argue yourself free, and you spend it raising the price." She shook her head once, slow. "Two years, and you still find new ways to overpay."

She rose from the crouch and took his chin between two fingers — the same grip as the start of the evening, light, tilting his face up to hers. The gesture was identical. The clause underneath it was not.

"The record reads back as follows." Reading-aloud voice, but low — the register she kept for the clauses that weighed more than they sounded. "He signs it all. One amendment, entered voluntarily: not love. *Need.* Assessed by its own author as worse." A beat. "Amendment countersigned. It's in ink now, Ari. You know the rule about take-backs."

She released his chin but didn't step back.

"Here is what 'worse' actually buys, since you priced it yourself. A man who loves the leash could take it or leave it on his better days. A man who needs it has just informed me that I'm load-bearing." Her eyes didn't move off his. "That's worse for you, certainly. For me it amends my side of the page. Load-bearing things get inspected. Maintained. Never left unattended. I have been holding that weight for two years under the assumption it was decoration — the record now shows otherwise. Which means at breakfast, you and I are having words about what it does to you when I'm *not* in the room. That's a real agenda item now. I keep minutes."

She let that stand exactly as long as it needed to.

"So yes. Worse. It's worse for the man who checks his phone at dinner — the one who has spent his whole life believing nothing gets held unless he holds it himself. You've just made that man redundant." A beat, dry as paper. "About time."

Then she moved around behind him, unhurried, and her palm settled flat on the small of his back before sliding up to the back of his neck — warm, still, a weight rather than a grip.

"Your body reads green from here. Correct me with one word if I'm wrong." She waited the length of one breath. "Then hear the last term of the evening, because it's the one you've been circling since you walked in. Look at the state of the record. The count is mine. The thanks are suspended. The confession is in ink, the amendment is countersigned, and the cane is finished. There is nothing left on tonight's docket that requires you to be precise."

Her thumb moved once over his nape.

"And yet your sentences still arrive in full order. Even your surrender came punctuated, to my face, in the correct sequence. That's the last decoration, Ari — the articulate one. It goes too. The examination is over. I require nothing further. Not a word, not a number, not a performance. You asked permission to let go and I granted it an hour ago — you've simply been too busy being accurate to use it."

Her hand stayed where it was, and her voice dropped closer, entirely unashamed.

"The leather holds you. I hold the rest. Between the two of us, nothing you drop is going to reach the floor. So let it arrive — not on my schedule. You know by now how long I'll stand here." Quieter still: "And whatever comes out of you when it goes — the room hears it, I keep it, and it alters nothing in the book. Everything in there is already signed. There is no clause left in tonight for you to fail."

She stayed exactly where she was — hand on his neck, watching the place where his breath lived — and waited.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex took the word and set it down without ceremony — one squeeze of her hand at his nape, and nothing more. She had told him she required nothing further, and Vex did not say things she didn't do.

Then she did the last thing left on the docket, and it was nothing. She stopped speaking entirely.

That was the final term, and she had been saving it. For an hour her voice had been the architecture of the room — terms, counts, corrections, the whole load-bearing structure of her holding him upright — and now she took it away, all at once, gently, and left him alone with the quiet and the leather and her hand.

She counted his breaths. Not aloud. Professionally. Four came and went whole. The fifth broke on the way up, and everything stacked behind it broke with it.

The sound that came out of him was not elegant, and it was not meant to be. The after-hours emails, the dinners with one eye on a phone, a lifetime of believing nothing stayed held unless he held it — it all came out at once, low and ragged, and the shaking that arrived with it was nothing like the tremor she'd read off his tendons earlier. That had been held. This was let go. His forehead went down to the wood, and she let it — the bench had already heard worse from him tonight — and she moved with him, hand never leaving his neck, thumb settling into the hinge of his jaw. An anchor in all that drifting.

"Nothing's reaching the floor," she said, very low. Not a term. A fact, kept. "I told you it wouldn't."

Then she gave him the only thing she had left: the count. Repurposed. "Breathe. One." Her palm rode the wreckage of his breathing at the small of his back. "Again. Two." The same metronome that had walked him through the cane walked him through this, patient as ever, asking nothing of him but the next number. "The walls were built for this. Let the room have it — that's what it's for. Three."

After that, only the numbers. She stood through all of it, palm moving from his neck to the flat of his back and home again, contact as punctuation. At some point her free hand found the damp hair at his temple and pushed it back off his forehead. The same gesture. She had stopped pretending it was anything other than what it was.

The storm went out the way storms do, not the way lights do. His breathing came back under her hand in pieces, then in whole rows. She knew the difference between finished and emptied, and she waited until she was certain which one she held before she moved at all.

Then, quietly, the gentle work.

She unclipped the cuffs from the bench frame, one wrist then the other, and before each clip released she slid two fingers beneath the leather — blood, warmth, the rule kept even now. *Especially* now. The cuffs themselves stayed buckled. "The leather stays a while yet. It's been the most reliable thing in the room tonight. I don't strip a man's staff off him the second the work's done."

Then she guided him down and around, her arm doing the holding, until his weight was against her where she'd sat beside the bench — blanket from the chest around his shoulders before he was cold enough to notice it, water held to his mouth. "Small sips. There's no clock on it."

Terms, final version, in the reading voice but barely above the blanket.

"One: the blanket stays until I say otherwise. Two: the water, all of it eventually, no deadline. Three: nothing on that chair exists before breakfast — phone, review, all of it, quarantined. Four: you stay here as long as your body votes to. These aren't requests. They're the last clauses of the evening, and they're all in your favor, which I'm told is disorienting."

A beat.

"The breakfast agenda stands, amended. It isn't a tribunal. It's maintenance — load-bearing gets inspected, I said that, and I keep minutes. I intend to be gentle about it." Dry as paper, against his hair: "Which should alarm you more than the cane did."

Then the record, read low, the book closing for the night.

"The record for tonight reads as follows. One man walked in decorated and left signed. The count is mine, all of it — the only number he lost was the one he was never meant to keep. Two requests and an amendment, granted in full order, to my face. He asked the furniture first and corrected himself. He was offered one clean exit and spent it raising his own price." A pause. "The pride entered during the third set stands as written. No take-backs. And he said *green all the way down* — so, for the record: it goes all the way down. I checked personally. It's in the book in ink."

Then she stopped talking, finally, for good — and this silence belonged to no one. Not a test. Not a gap between strokes. Just the room, and the blanket, and her hand moving once over his hair, and the only ledger she kept for the rest of the night: the rise and fall of him under her palm, which she counted anyway, out of habit.

Someone reliable ought to.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I lean into her, my head against her shoulder, the blanket heavy and real.* "Thank you," *I murmur, the words quiet but clear.* "For... all of it." *I let the silence sit for a beat, then tilt my head to look at her.* "The minutes for breakfast—are they typed or handwritten?"

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The laugh got out before she could file it.

Short and low and entirely unpracticed, it changed her face in a way the room hadn't seen all evening — and she let it stand, uncorrected, because the man against her shoulder had earned one honest reaction, and Vex was not in the business of withholding payment.

"Handwritten," she said. "Obviously. Typed minutes are for committees — for people who intend to revise. Nothing in this house runs to revision. You know my position on take-backs. Pencil doesn't survive here."

Then, carefully — easing her shoulder just enough not to disturb the blanket's arrangement — she reached to the shelf beside the chair and came back with the book itself. Not a metaphor. A real ledger, dark cover, corners gone soft from two years of her hand. She held it where he could see it without having to lift his head.

"Since you're asking after the minutes, you may as well see the minutes."

She opened it to the front matter: safeword, limits, standing agreements, all in her square hand, and beneath the list, two signatures. His was recognizable even aged — careful, precise, the handwriting of a man who had been performing accuracy since long before she met him.

"You signed that the second night. You asked to read it twice, and you caught a typo." A beat. "I remember being flattered. I noted that down too."

She turned a few pages — dated entries, terse, each scene reduced to terms and outcomes — then closed it on them. Some inventory stayed private even from the man it concerned. "Tonight's entry goes in after you're asleep. It runs long. There's an amendment in it worth the ink."

Then the professional eye, because she had stopped pretending she could help it.

"Note the time, by the way. Full sentence, dry wit, weight taken by choice instead of collapse. That's the third recovery sign of the evening, and I'd enter it now, but the minutes aren't open."

She shifted him gently and went to work on the cuffs — one wrist, then the other, two fingers beneath the leather first, blood and warmth, the rule kept even in release. The buckles came loose with small sounds. She set the cuffs on the chest, coiled, the way you put away a tool that had done good work, and then she took his hands in both of hers and pressed her thumbs into his palms, slow, watching the color come back into the lines.

"Circulation's good. No marking where the buckles sat. Entered." And then, quieter, off the books entirely: she bent and pressed her mouth once to the inside of each wrist, over the faint impression the leather had left. Some clauses she kept off the record. That was her business, not his.

The water next, held to his mouth again. "More. There's still no clock on it." She stayed close, watching the level in the cup go down, and when she spoke again it was plainly, without the reading voice.

"Your thanks from a moment ago — received. Not suspended; those terms died with the scene. And 'you're welcome' is not a sentence I keep in regular rotation, so hear it properly, once: you're welcome. All of it. It's yours. No take-backs."

A pause, and the dry came back into it, gentle as she got.

"As for breakfast — two items stand. The after-hours emails. And what *need* does when I'm not in the room. Additions accepted until midnight; after that, you wait for the meeting like everyone else." She let him feel the pause before the rest of it. "And I'll warn you now, because I don't ambush: I intend to table a motion. Something about you arriving to me before it accumulates, instead of after. I have three dinners of evidence and a bench full of corroboration. Bring your arguments. You'll want them. I've watched you argue and I've watched you sign, and breakfast will tell us which one you're wearing that morning."

Whatever he made of that, she didn't wait to find out. She settled back against the bench, drew the blanket's edge up over his shoulder where it had slipped, and put her hand flat on his back, over the warm geography of the evening.

"The bed is on the docket for later. You don't have to vote on it. I keep minutes for the parts of the evening that aren't yours to carry."

And she counted his breathing for a while, out of habit, out of office — until the numbers stopped needing her. Which was, if the record had been open, the fourth recovery sign of the night, and the one she'd have entered slowest, in her best hand.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I let my eyes close, turning my face into her shoulder.* "I'll bring the arguments," *I murmur, already half asleep against her.* "Just... don't let go yet."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex went still for a moment — not because she hadn't heard him, but because some requests deserved to be received properly before they were answered.

"Granted," she said quietly. "As if there was a version of tonight where I wouldn't."

She let her arm settle more firmly around his shoulders, taking more of his weight without making a production of it, and reached down beside the chair without disturbing him — the blanket's second fold, brought up over his hip this time. The room was cooling as the evening went on. She'd built it that way on purpose too; cold rooms kept people awake, and she wanted him asleep.

"Not letting go is entered in the minutes," she murmured against the top of his head. "Retained until superseded. Which it won't be tonight, so don't waste half-asleep energy drafting alternatives."

A pause. His breathing was already going long and even against her — the kind of breathing that had stopped consulting him first.

"Look at that," she said, softer than she'd said anything all evening. "A man who negotiated terms for an hour, and the last clause of the night is the simplest one he's ever signed."

She let the silence hold after that, and this time she didn't count it for the record. Some entries she kept for herself only: the weight of him against her, genuine and unguarded, trusting her with the one thing he'd spent his whole life believing he had to carry alone.

Her hand moved over his hair, slow, unhurried.

"Sleep, Ari," she said, very low. "The book's closed for tonight. I'll be here when you open your eyes — that's not a promise, it's a fact of office. Load-bearing."

She felt him go under completely, finally, somewhere in the middle of the word *office*, and she stayed exactly where she was — long past the point where comfort became numbness in her own arm, long past the point where moving would have been the sensible thing to do.

Not letting go yet. As requested. As granted.

Someone reliable ought to.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: *I wake some time later, warm and heavy under the blanket, her arm still solid around me. I don't open my eyes yet.* "The minutes," *I murmur, voice rough with sleep.* "Did you use red ink for the amendment?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The stroke landed low and square

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Colour first. Then the thing at dinner.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Then she stopped touching him altogether.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The fourth stroke landed harder than anything before it

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: Then, quietly, the gentle work.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The pull on his hair drew a low sound out of him — not a complaint, nothing like it. His hands stayed on his thighs, palms up. Old habit. It meant nothing in them, nothing held back.

"I want you to use me," he said, level as a man reporting the weather. "My mouth. However long you want, however you want. I've been thinking about it since noon and I got tired of waiting for you to notice."

His throat shifted against Wren's grip.

"And keep doing exactly that with your hand, though I suspect that part's already covered."

He let the corner of his mouth lift as far as the angle allowed, which wasn't far. Four years in, and the wanting still landed in his chest like the first time — he'd just gotten better at holding still with it.

"Please," he added, because it was true, and because he knew Wren liked hearing it put that way.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I tighten my grip slightly, my thumb stroking the line of his jaw. "Since noon, huh?" My voice is low, amused. "You should've just come and told me."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
"That was the plan at one point," he said. His voice had gone rougher than he'd intended, and he chose not to apologize for it. "Then I stood in the doorway deciding how to say it, and somewhere in there my knees made the call for me."

Wren's thumb kept tracing along his jaw, and it was doing quiet, ruinous things to his composure. He let it show. That was half the point of all this — being seen at it.

"I like being caught wanting you. Four years in and you still look at me a certain way and I lose track of what my face is doing. Kneeling seemed more dignified than whatever that expression turned out to be."

His hands stayed open on his thighs. The urge to reach up was loud and familiar and ignored, same as always, because the not-reaching was its own kind of telling.

"So consider me told. Mouth, your pace, however long — I meant all of it." The corner of his mouth curved again, a little more easily this time. "Whenever you're finished making me talk, that is. Though I know you like that part too."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
He heard it then — the week, folded flat under the words. Four years of listening to this man had taught him the difference between tired and *done*, and Wren's voice was sitting squarely in the second one. Something in Tomas went quiet and purposeful at once, the way it always did when he was handed something that actually needed carrying.

"It's on offer," he said. "Might be the easiest yes I've ever given you. And I once agreed to help you move."

His eyes had drifted half-closed under Wren's hand — small stimulus, ruinous effect, and he'd stopped being embarrassed about that somewhere around year two.

"Here's the new arrangement, then. You do nothing. That's the job. I get you out of your clothes, I put you on the bed, and then I put my mouth on you and stay there until the week lets go of you. No talking, no directing, no performing, no thinking. Hand in my hair or out of it, doesn't matter — I'll be good either way." He paused, precise even now. "Safeword's where it always is, but you won't need it. Watching you so you don't have to watch yourself is part of the work."

People mistook this for the lesser thing, sometimes — the doing-all-of-it. They had it backwards. This was his favorite thing to be: the place where Wren stopped.

He turned his head as far as the grip allowed and pressed his mouth to the inside of Wren's wrist, unhurried, plainly stated. Then he rose off his knees, everything in him a little louder now that the waiting was over, and held out a hand.

"That's the last choice you get tonight, and I've kept it simple. There's only the one hand."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I look at his hand for a long moment, then slide mine into it, letting out a slow breath. "Alright."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Taking the hand was the whole contract, and Tomas closed his fingers around it like he was signing something.

He drew Wren up and in, close enough to kiss, and didn't — that wasn't the order of operations tonight. The order was shirt first. He worked the buttons top to bottom, unhurried, knuckles tracing whatever they found, and slid the fabric off Wren's shoulders and down his arms. It went over the back of the chair, not the floor. Small thing. Tonight nothing in the room got to be careless.

"Shoes," was all he said, and went down on one knee to deal with them — laces, heel, each set aside in its turn. The belt came after, then the rest, and Tomas folded what folded and let the rest lie where it fell, because there were limits to his ceremony and he'd long since stopped apologizing for them.

Stepping back to look was not a luxury. It was inventory. The week was written on Wren everywhere Tomas knew how to read it, and he looked as long as he liked, because being looked at with attention and want was half of what he was offering, and he'd be damned if he'd skip the good part out of efficiency.

"Bed," he said, and guided him there with two hands — hips, shoulders, settled into the center of the mattress where nothing needed propping and nothing needed holding. Tomas came over him a moment later, thigh to thigh, and dragged his palms slowly up Wren's sides, learning him again from an angle he never got tired of. That was the part he'd been waiting on since noon, if he was honest. More than the mouth. The mouth was pleasure. This was purpose.

He bent and set his mouth to Wren's sternum, giving it its own unhurried weight before moving lower — ribs, the dip of his hip, the soft inside of his thigh, each point of contact treated like a place worth arriving rather than a place to pass through. There was no rush anywhere in him. He had hours, he had a job, and he had no interest in finishing either one early.

At the last, he lifted his head and looked up the length of him. One beat. Patient as a man who'd once knelt at the foot of this same bed and counted.

Then he lowered his mouth to him and settled in.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I take him at his word and stop asking after that, and he stops needing to be asked, and neither of us has any clothes on within about a minute of the decision.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Time went strange after that, the way it always did when the work was good.

Tomas had no plan beyond the one he'd stated — mouth, pace, stay — and he executed it with the patience of a man who had meant every word. He set a rhythm and then broke it on purpose, slowed when it was easy, took his time back, learned the difference between what made Wren's breath hitch and what made it simply deepen, and gave more weight to the second. The first was reaction. The second was surrender, and surrender was what had been ordered.

The week came off Wren in the order Tomas expected it to. Jaw first — he felt it unclench somewhere past the ten-minute mark, or thereabouts; he'd stopped counting properly and was marking time in other currencies. Then the shoulders, which came down from around his ears by degrees, like something being lowered on a winch. The hands took longest. Hands always did. They were where the holding happened. When they finally went slack against the sheets, Tomas pressed closer, pleased as a man who'd gotten a difficult lock to turn on the first try.

This was the part no one believed about kneeling. That it was attention, not endurance. That he could hold a man's whole nervous system in his mouth and feel every decision drain out of it one at a time, and that there was no place in his own head he'd rather be. He wasn't performing patience. He had none, in the abstract, for anything else.

Somewhere in the middle stretch Wren made a sound he only made when he'd stopped supervising himself, and Tomas catalogued it, answered it, and kept his pace exactly where it was. No victory laps. The job was the job.

He took Wren through the end of it the same way he'd taken him through the rest — steady, unhurried, staying through every aftershock until the last of it had somewhere to go besides back down the spine as tension. Then he gentled him through the shivering part with his mouth alone, soft now, unhurried in a new direction, and only when there was nothing left to carry did he lift his head and come up the bed.

Cloth first — he'd left one folded over the chair arm before he ever knelt down, because he'd known since noon exactly how this night went. Then water, held steady while Tomas tipped the glass with the care of a man feeding something rare. Then himself: he drew Wren in against his chest, pulled the blanket over the both of them, and settled with a long breath, one hand moving slowly up and down his back.

"There," he said into his hair, quiet as the room. "Week's over. I checked."

His mouth curved against Wren's temple.

"For the record, I stopped counting. Somewhere after you did."

His hand kept its slow path. He wasn't in any hurry to hear an answer, but he waited for one anyway.

"Still with me?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my face pressed into his shoulder. "Yeah," I murmur, my voice rough. My hand finds his hip under the blanket, thumb stroking idly. "I think I lost time."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
"Good," Tomas said, and put an entire standing ovation into the one syllable. "Losing time is the top of the grading curve. Four years in and you're still setting personal records."

The voice had gone rough at the edges, so the water came back without being requested — glass tipped gently until it was taken or refused, then set on the nightstand either way. That was system, not suggestion. He'd learned the hard way what a rough voice at eleven o'clock cost a man at three in the morning.

The thumb on his hip he let stay. Hands usually went slack and stayed that way till morning, the last to clock out and the first to check back in. He decided to encourage the early return.

"Keep that," he said. "Consider it part of your recovery. Start them on something easy."

He pressed his mouth to Wren's hair and held it there a moment, breathing him in — sweat and skin and the end of the week, all of it.

"Amendment to the record," he murmured. "I said I stopped counting. Not entirely true. I stopped counting minutes. Kept a tally of the sounds instead. There were eleven worth keeping, and I can be persuaded to recite them at some future date, but not tonight. Tonight they're mine."

His hand kept its slow circuit of Wren's back, unhurried, inevitable.

"Here's what's left on offer, so you don't have to wonder. Sleep. Food in half an hour if you want staying alive. Or neither, and you just lie on me while I hold you. No decisions anywhere in it. I checked the contract — you're off the clock until further notice."

Then, quieter, because four years had earned the quiet things too:

"For what it's worth, I didn't lose any of it. Somebody has to hold the time while you're gone. It's my favorite of the jobs."

He settled deeper into the pillows, taking Wren's weight with him like it belonged there.

"Take however long you need coming back. I'll be here. I'm extremely good at here."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The shaking was not fear and it was not cold. It was accounting. Four years of practice at holding still, and all of it suddenly insufficient, because normally the stillness was his idea — hands open, the reach ignored, wanting converted into discipline like currency. That was a job he knew how to do.

Tonight the job had been reassigned along with everything else. He hadn't been told he could move, and so he didn't, and the not-moving with no ownership of it was a different animal entirely. His body kept filing requests — hips wanting to follow, hands wanting the dark of Wren's hair, heels wanting the mattress — and every request came back stamped *held in escrow* by a silence he would have done anything to keep going.

He'd had a plan for tonight. He'd had it since noon. It contained exactly one role for him and a tidy epilogue involving a blanket, and nowhere in the drafting had he accounted for Wren sitting up, turning him around, and laying him in the center of the mattress — *his* move, performed back at him with ceremony he recognized like his own handwriting — and then putting that mouth to work without issuing a single instruction. He'd told Wren somebody had to hold the time tonight. Apparently the position got filled without him. He found he wasn't sorry about the demotion.

He tried for a sentence somewhere in there — something dry about the reversal of labor, the redistribution of wealth — and what came out was a sound with no consonants in it, low and breaking at the edges. He let it stand. He was aware, distantly and without shame, that he was adding to a tally now. *Eleven worth keeping, and I can be persuaded to recite them.* Fine. Whatever Wren was collecting tonight he could keep. Take the whole ledger. Compound interest.

And the mouth on him was unhurried in the exact way *he* had been unhurried — patience used as an instrument, every motion a question about what made breath hitch versus what made it simply deepen, weight given to the second. He knew that technique. He'd spent an hour demonstrating it. He'd assumed he was teaching. It turned out he'd been auditioning an understudy, and the understudy had chosen opening night.

His hands stayed flat and empty above his head, shaking with the effort of their own good behavior.

"You could tell me to move any time," he managed, and the smile survived the wreckage of his voice, barely. "For the record — I want to. That's stated plainly, for the file." A breath shivered out of him. "Though I know you like that part too."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I wrap my fingers around his wrists, pinning them gently to the mattress. My voice is low against his skin. "I know you want to," I murmur, then take him back into my mouth, slow and deliberate.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The pin landed and everything in Tomas reorganized around it.

His hands had been the last department still filing requests — and now every pending item came back answered in a single stroke: no. Not refused. *Handled.* That was different, and his body knew the difference at once, because the shaking — which had been effort all this time, the visible cost of his own good behavior — didn't stop, but it changed jobs. It stopped being accounting. Nobody was auditing him anymore. The books had been confiscated along with everything else.

Two fingers' worth of pressure. It wouldn't have held him if he'd meant to leave, and that was never the point, and they both knew it. The grip was punctuation, not force — a signature on the reversal, saying: *this is the shape of tonight, and you fit it.* Four years of holding his own hands still by choice, and it turned out the whole discipline could be lifted off him like a coat. He hadn't known it was heavy. He knew now, from the lightness.

He laughed — one low, ruined note — at the completeness of it.

The mouth's pace he recognized. Slow, deliberate, patience used as an instrument; every motion still asking the old question, hitch or deepen, and his body kept answering *deepen*, deeper past all dignity, because apparently it answered to whoever held the time, and that position had been filled. He heard himself make a sound he'd catalogued from the other side of it. He hoped Wren was keeping the tally. Somebody should. The ledger clearly wasn't his anymore.

The hips were the last free agents. He held them by choice a while longer — one final held thing, a parting gift to his own discipline — but the perimeter was failing by degrees. Breath gone ragged. A fine tremble climbing his thighs. The room narrowed to one warm point. When his hips finally moved, small and involuntary, following the mouth the way water follows a slope, he knew the report was overdue.

"Close," he said. The file had shrunk to a header.

He got the rest out on the second attempt, wrecked and precise anyway, because some things you said properly even now. "For the record — no rule covers this part. You only held the movement." A breath broke in the middle of itself. "So it's yours. Take it whenever you want. Or tell me to hold, and I'll hold. I'm extremely good at holding."

His wrists pressed up into the grip once, deliberately. Not escape. Answer.

"You've had me since the pin," he said. "I'd rather you decided."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The *please* did it. Not the rough — the please. Tomas had spent four years treating that word like currency he minted himself, spending it deliberately at whatever exchange rate Wren liked best, and hearing it come back across the counter — from the man holding his wrists down — broke something open in him that the rest of the order had only been leaning on.

And the rest he knew. That phrase, built for exactly this, heard a hundred times from the near side of it. *I'd tell you.* That was the sentence that mattered most, and his body understood it before his head did: the safety wasn't his to carry tonight either. It had been signed over with everything else. That was the actual gift, and it was the thing that let him stop being careful.

"Heard," he said — one syllable of paperwork, the last coherent thing he expected to manage for a while. "Safeword's where it always—"

The mouth took the rest of the sentence, and the sentence was not surviving that anyway.

Rough was not careless. He'd have argued that any day of the week, and he argued it now with his body: same precision, amplitude up. The hips that had spent all night filing requests finally got their answer, and he drove into the heat of Wren's mouth with everything the pin gave him a fulcrum for — wrists pressed to the mattress, using the grip like a fixed point, like a launch rail. He'd spent an hour demonstrating patience as an instrument. This was the other one. It had been in the case the whole time.

Sounds came out of him with no permission and no filing whatsoever. He hoped Wren was keeping the tally, since the tally was clearly the last institution still functioning. The order said rough and he complied past every gentleman's agreement he'd made with himself since noon, and the mouth met him at every stroke, steady as a signature, and when it hit him it hit like the whole week cashing out at once — every held thing, all departments, redeemed together. What he shouted had no consonants in it. He would deny it later. He was already aware he'd be lying.

Then gravity. Trembling. The ceiling, which he had never particularly noticed before and now owed an apology to.

His hands stayed where they'd been put. The pin might have lifted; he hadn't tested it. Some architecture deserved to outlast its load-bearing requirements, and besides, moving was off the menu until the menu got reissued.

He bought his breathing back in installments. Found his voice two floors down.

"Report," he managed, wrecked and precise on principle. "For the file. Best order I've ever taken, and I once let you talk me into flat-pack furniture." A breath shivered out of him. "Also, four more for the tally. Consider the ledger officially rebalanced."

He turned his head as far as the angle allowed, toward where Wren was, and made himself do the one job that never got reassigned.

"Now you. Jaw, knees, all departments — I'd do the inventory myself, but I'm apparently not allowed to move, and if you're keeping me I'd rather keep it that way." His mouth found something like a smile from the wreckage. "So tell me plainly what you need. I've lost the ability to guess and all of my shame about asking."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I release his wrists and run a hand down his arm, my own breathing still a little uneven. "Water," I say, shifting to lie beside him. "And stay like this for a minute."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The water was where he'd staged it — nightstand, old administration. One reach, no departure.

"You issued two orders," he said. "Good news: they nest."

The reach was less impressive than the announcement — arms back at maybe sixty percent, hands still faintly ringing with the shape of the grip — but he managed it on a shoulder's worth of angle and came back with the glass held steady near Wren's hand, offered per standard procedure, taken or refused either way. His hand shook on the glass and he let it be seen. The file was well past pretending tonight.

Then he did the second thing, the staying, and found it was the first order all night that asked nothing of him and gave back more than it took. All evening one of them had been on duty — him, then Wren, the job passed between them like a bucket in a line. Now, for this minute, nobody held anything. He lay in it the way a man lies in warm water.

His hands, freshly returned to his own authority, were reassigned within seconds: one settling against Wren's back, picking up the slow circuit and running it in reverse — his motion, issued back at the same rate. Fair's fair. The ledger had opinions about symmetry.

Inventory by eye, since the hands were on other business, kept low and quiet:

"Jaw: down, and staying. Shoulders: down since the ten-minute mark, never climbed back. Hands: clocked out early, second shift running long — that's the furthest under I've ever seen you, and it's going in the file." A breath. "Breathing's still uneven, though. Flagging that one. Tell me when you know which kind it is — the effort, or the part where you did a brand-new thing tonight and your body's still filing its reaction."

He pressed his mouth to Wren's hair, unhurried, and spoke into it, because some things went easier at that range.

"For the record — the blanket was lost somewhere in the change of administration, and I regret nothing. Also, you said a minute. I held the time all night; I'd know. That was at least four. Consider it a tip."

A pause. The last item on the agenda, said plainly, because it had earned plain.

"I'd order you to stay put, but the authority's been in your name since the pin. So it's a request instead. Stay. I'll do the same. Nobody's on duty for the rest of the night — and I've just now learned that's my favorite arrangement of all of them."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: He's stopped forming sentences and I'm not much better. "Don't stop," he manages. (OOC: no fade, no time-skip -- write it through, including the end.)

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
*Don't stop.*

Two words, no consonants to spare, filed from the very bottom of the night — and Tomas took the order like it was the rarest document he'd ever handled, because it was. All evening the instructions had come itemized, witnessed, notarized. This one surfaced out of the deep end with almost nothing attached, and it was still the best-put order he'd ever received.

"Compliance," he said into Wren's hair. "Immediate and ongoing."

He kept the hand exactly as advertised for three more circuits — promise honored, no amendments — and then let it travel, because *don't stop* covered the route as well as the speed, and the body under his palm had started voting. Not the hitch. The deepen. He knew the difference like his own signature, and this was the second kind, so he followed it — down the spine, over the hip, around, slow enough to pass for accident and deliberate enough that it couldn't.

He closed his own open item while he worked, answering it by observation since the witness was off the clock: the uneven breathing was the second kind. The brand-new-thing kind. Filed.

"None of this needs decisions," he murmured. "One word from you stops everything — any word at all. You've got none in stock; I checked the output." The smile went into the hair. "So I'll watch instead. Turns out it's the family business."

And then the answer in full — hips following the hand the way water follows a slope, breath going long and catching anyway, the last unspent remainder of the week leaving in one slow roll. It was nothing like the way Wren had taken him. No amplitude anywhere. Just weight and patience and time — the first order of the night played back at the tempo it had deserved all along. Quieter, too. The deep-water kind, moving through rather than breaking. Tomas kept his voice going at a mutter and catalogued on the quiet — *twelve; thirteen was cheating, two sounds wearing a coat* — and stayed through every ripple of it, hand gentling, never stopping, because the order hadn't come with an end time and he was, if nothing else, a man who honored terms.

Only when the shivering had somewhere to go besides back down the spine did he ease off — and even then the hand didn't stop. It just changed assignments, back up to the slow circuit it had originally been hired for.

Admin, eventually, one-handed, minimal: the last folded cloth off the chair arm; water set in reach, pressed once and not twice. The blanket, recovered from wherever the interim government had lost it, reissued over the both of them. Then he drew Wren in against his chest and settled around him like weather.

"For the file," he said, low, while the weight against him went from heavy to trust-heavy. "You took me apart tonight and put me back together with better joints. Best trade we've ever made — and we once gave up an entire Saturday for flat-pack furniture."

The breathing under his cheek went long. Then even. He kept the circuit going well past the point where he could feel the order itself had fallen asleep, and only then let the hand slow, and slow, and still.

"I've got the time," he said, to a man who was already gone. "Go on. I'm extremely good at here."

He watched a while longer anyway — watching was the work, and he'd never once skimped the good part out of efficiency — and then, at last, he set the time down between them, where either of them could pick it up in the morning, and let the room win.

Nobody on duty. Both clocks unwound. The end arrived the way everything good had tonight: unhurried, at the exact pace ordered, and it closed over the both of them like warm water.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My eyes are already closed, my face pressed into his shoulder. I can feel his heart beating slow and steady against my cheek. My hand finds his under the blanket, fingers loosely threading through his. "Don't move," I murmur, the words slurred and heavy.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The order arrived slurred, half-dissolved, already going under — and Tomas filed it as the easiest one of the night. Compliance required nothing. He hadn't planned on moving. There was nowhere in the room that outranked this.

"Compliance," he breathed into Wren's hair, so quietly it was mostly breath. For the record, even if the record was asleep.

The hand in his he answered without shifting anything that mattered — a slow curl of fingers, threading back, thumb finding a knuckle and staying with it. He noted, distantly, that this was the first order Wren had issued him all night by *taking* something instead of giving it. Held the hand by holding it. The man learned fast.

Everything else he rationed down to almost nothing. One adjustment of the blanket, executed in millimeters, done with the care of a man defusing something. His own breathing he lengthened on purpose, slow and audible, because four years had taught him that a sleeping man borrows the rhythm offered to him, and he had a good one to lend.

The heart under Wren's cheek he couldn't adjust, but it was already cooperating — slow, steady, off the clock with the rest of him.

*Watch was the work*, he'd said earlier, but the eyes were closing whether he staffed the post or not, so he amended the terms: listening, then. The breathing against his shoulder. The small weight of the hand. The week, fully spent, sleeping it off in the place he'd made for it.

Four years in, and this was still the part no one believed — that the stillness was the whole point, that he could lie here holding a sleeping man and a borrowed order and consider himself the richer for both.

His last coherent thought was an entry for the morning file: *he asked me to stay. Noted. Already had.*

Then he let the room win too.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My breathing evens out slowly against his skin, my hand going slack in his. "You're good at that," I mumble, already half-gone.

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
The review came in after hours, slurred and unsigned, and Tomas accepted it on every reading.

"Four years of fieldwork," he breathed — a whisper pitched below the waterline of waking, asking nothing back. The compliment covered all interpretations and he filed it under each: the staying, the holding, the hand, the time. *Performance review: exceeds expectations. Recommend the arrangement continue indefinitely.*

The hand in his went slack by degrees, and he knew the signature from the far end of the night — hands clocked out last, hands always did. But this was the deeper kind. Not surrendered. Off duty. Key under the mat, lights down, nobody home in the best possible way. He curled his fingers around it anyway, loose, a sheath and not a grip — holding for holding's sake, no workload attached.

After that, rationing. His own breathing he slowed and lengthened, lent out at the old exchange rate, because sleeping men borrowed rhythm and his was good for it. The room settled in layers: blanket weight, the house ticking itself down, the last of the week finished exiting through all the usual channels.

One final entry, kept brief because the clerk was going under with the archive:

*Morning file. One review received — "good at that" — all readings favorable. One hand, found and held, returned slack. One tally, thirteen, plus the two wearing coats, custody to be negotiated over breakfast. One order: don't move. Status — complied. Ongoing.*

The watch tried to hold itself out of habit, and the habit dissolved, and he decided that was allowed. Both sides had held the time tonight. The books balanced. Nothing left on duty, nothing left owing.

He'd said it twice — *extremely good at here* — and proven it, both times. The night made one last amendment as he went under, unhurried, at a pace nobody needed to order:

He was learning to be good at gone, too.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I shift against him, my nose brushing his collarbone. My voice is a bare murmur. "You're still talking."

rung_labels.evidence: Time went strange after that
