Morning came up grey-gold through curtains whose color he'd genuinely forgotten. Jun surfaced wrecked, hoarse, muscles filing their grievances in writing, and lay there doing the math on the day. Date. Week. Time zone. Nothing. Overwritten entirely. He laughed into the pillow.

He'd made coffee at some point — barefoot, stepping over the evidence — and brought two mugs back, because see above. He set them down and propped himself on an elbow.

"Status report," he said, voice ruined, to the shape of them in the morning light. "I have no idea what day it is. Objective achieved ahead of schedule. I'm not even a little sorry."

A pause. He was still determined to die on this hill.

"Also — the speech. I remember part of it now. It opened with your laugh. There was a middle section on time zones, nineteen weeks of them, all running the wrong direction. And the ending was just this. I remember because it's the only part that came true on schedule."

He brushed their hair back. Gentle, now. He had all the time in the world and no idea what to call it.

"Hi," he said — no self-conscious laugh this time, just the word, warm, deliberate. "Turns out that was always the whole speech."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I stir, blinking against the light, then smile up at him.* "You're still talking about the speech?" *My voice is rough with sleep.* "Come here. The only part I care about is this." *I hook a finger in the collar of his shirt—well, my shirt, from the looks of it—and tug him down.*

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun went. He was mid-rebuttal — something about the speech's literary merit, probably — and one finger in his collar ended his entire career in rhetoric. He came down over them careful this time, weight on his forearms, and kissed them the first slow way since the tarmac: no hurry in it anywhere, deep and easy, like a man who'd just been formally informed he had all the time in the world.

When he surfaced, he noticed the collar in question.

"This is yours," he said, delighted, looking down at the shirt he'd apparently been wearing all morning. It had simply been the nearest fabric at five-something, during the coffee run — his own flight suit being an exhibit in the hallway — and he'd pulled it on without one single thought, which was about as married as a man could get. "It's mine now. I've decided. Possession is nine-tenths of marriage. I read that somewhere. Possibly on a mug."

He conceded the larger point with a kiss to their temple. "You're right. Speech is retired. I'll have it framed — hung next to the crooked picture, which, reaffirming for the record, is never getting straightened. That wall's a monument now. I'm considering a plaque."

Then he settled in properly: half over them, one leg drawn through the sheets, his hand finding the warm curve of their waist and staying there like it had been issued orders. The grey-gold light was doing something to their face that nineteen weeks of imagining had undershot, and he just looked for a while, thumb moving in slow, idle circles.

"Last night, slow was for other people," he said. "This morning it's for us. No plane. No briefing. No time zone running the wrong direction. I checked the whole day and it's just—" a vague gesture at the window, the room, them, "—this. All of it. Ours."

The coffee sat cooling on the nightstand. He considered it and rejected the mission.

"That's getting cold," he reported, making no move whatsoever toward it. "It can stay cold. Kitchen's a different room from you — I told you that last night and I meant it. So either breakfast comes to bed, or breakfast doesn't exist. Those are the options. I don't make the rules." He absolutely made the rules.

His hand slid up, cradled the back of their head the way it had at the door — the first thing his hands had relearned.

"Hi—" he started, caught himself, huffed a laugh into their hair. "Retired. Right." He tried again, softer, the new word, the one with no ending planned: "Morning."

A pause. His voice came out low and entirely unashamed.

"Fair warning — I never finished the sentence last night. You married a man about to become *deeply* embarrassing. Following you into rooms. Reaching for you in the kitchen. Making eggs sideways at the stove so I can still see you. Weeks of this. Months, maybe. I'm telling you now so you can't say you weren't warned." His mouth found theirs again, unhurried, and he smiled into it. "So — eggs? Or do we just stay here until the day admits defeat?"

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had made a big speech about slow. He'd meant it, every word. What he hadn't known — what nobody had briefed him on — was that slow was a completely different weapon when it was aimed at him.

For the first time since the tarmac, he was the one on his back. The shirt — theirs, his by proclamation — was gone early, custody to be negotiated later, and after that he stopped having opinions about anything at all. Nineteen weeks of holding it together — checklists, fuel states, forty other men's problems — and he came apart under patient hands like he'd been waiting the entire flight home for permission.

His own hands went useless. One fisted the sheets. The other found their hair and just stayed, not steering, because steering was a skill that had left the building somewhere around the second kiss.

"Okay," he managed, wrecked, eyes shut, "slow — I said slow. I volunteered for slow. Nobody told me it was *this.* There should've been a safety briefing—"

He laughed somewhere in the middle of it, breath breaking on the sound. He'd imagined this in the rack — obviously, nineteen weeks of it — but in every version he'd been the one doing the taking apart. Nobody had warned him the receiving end felt like being repaid with interest.

When their hand crossed the new scar, he caught it — not stopping them, just holding their palm flat over it, a beat, in the grey-gold light.

"Some other decade," he said, rough. Then, quieter, because it was morning and they were real: "Okay. Not a decade. Over eggs. And it's a stupid story — I got it reaching for a wrench, that's the whole thing, no heroics. Don't let me tell it differently later."

After that he went quiet, for a man who'd spent twelve hours narrating. The sounds he couldn't do anything about came out honest, unashamed, ones he'd have been mortified by anywhere on earth that wasn't this bed. He'd earned this. They both had.

He lasted — well. He'd have been humiliated to say how long.

"Morning," he finally told the ceiling, hoarse, gone, one arm over his eyes. Then he found them by touch and pulled them level and kissed them slow, unbothered by anything, everything, all of it.

"Eggs are cancelled," he reported into their hair. "Coffee's a monument. The day's admitted defeat — I'm declaring a national holiday, we're observing it annually, I'll draft the paperwork *later*—" His hand mapped their back like it was filing it somewhere permanent. "Six years. Five months. And you just—"

The sentence died the way all his sentences had died since the door. He held on instead.

"Fair warning," he mumbled, much later, already sinking, "that's happening every morning now. Standing or—"

He was asleep before the word finished. The standing order could wait. Everything could. He was home, it was morning, and the day had lost exactly like he'd promised it would.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content:
I watch him sleep for a minute, then carefully untangle myself. My own body aches in the best way. I pull on his discarded flight suit—it’s huge on me, smells like him and jet fuel—and pad out to the kitchen.

The eggs are cold, but I eat them straight from the pan, leaning against the counter and looking at our wrecked hallway. I can’t stop smiling.

When I come back, I slide in beside him and press my cold feet against his calves just to hear him grumble in his sleep. He pulls me closer anyway.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The grumble came out of him before consciousness did — subsonic, all grievance, no syllables, the sound of a man whose calves had just filed an ambush complaint. His arm answered without consulting him: hooked them by the waist and hauled them flush, relocating the cold feet to warmer real estate with the efficiency of a reflex that had been waiting nineteen weeks for this exact assignment.

Then, a minute later, the pilot brain booted up anyway, because it was a traitorous piece of equipment and had never once respected his leave. Cold feet. Cold feet meant absence. Absence meant—

"You left," he accused, into the pillow, eyes still shut, voice a ruin on top of a ruin. "You left the bed. Went to the kitchen. And I wasn't there to follow you into it. I had *one job.* First shift as a deeply embarrassing husband and I was unconscious. That's a court-martial in some marriages."

His hand, patrolling on instinct, found fabric that had no business being there. Long zipper. Huge on them. His brain took three full seconds to cross-reference, and then his eyes opened for real.

The flight suit. On Halle. Drowning in it, smelling like jet fuel and him and now — overwhelmingly — them.

Jun's entire face did something unsupervised.

"Oh," he said, hoarse. "Okay. That's the best thing I've ever seen, and I've seen the Alps from forty thousand feet. The Alps can retire." He pushed up onto one elbow for the full picture — wrecked, grinning, sleep lines on his cheek. "That suit spent five months being the worst thing I owned. Smelled like bad coffee and other people's problems. And now look at it. Best decision it ever made. Keep it. It's yours. It always worked for the wrong side anyway."

He leaned in, pressed his face to their shoulder through the fabric, and breathed like a man checking a gauge. "Huh," he said, muffled. "It smelled like leaving. You fixed it. It just smells like you now."

Then the forensics resumed. "Also — you found a third option. I authorized breakfast in bed or no breakfast, and you ate cold eggs straight from the pan, standing up, looking at the hallway. That is the most married thing I have ever heard in my life." A beat. "How's the monument from that angle? Be honest. I inspected it at 0400, professional assessment, and I stand by it: art."

And then, because the eggs were gone and he was too sleepy to varnish anything, he mumbled the down payment into their hair: "Scar story. Director's cut. Dropped a panel pin at hour thirty of a very long day, reached for a wrench wrong, wrench won, six stitches, medic laughed so hard he dropped the tray. That's the whole legend. Hold me to it."

He settled back down, pulled them in against his chest, and got one leg tangled through theirs to hold the cold feet hostage.

"Fair warning — next time you leave this bed, I'm coming with you. Standing order. Kitchen, bathroom, doesn't matter. You married a deeply embarrassing man, and he is officially *on duty.*"

A long pause. His breathing slowed toward sleep, but he fought it for one more word, barely awake, warm against their hair:

"Morning. Best one on record."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun went very still for one full second — the stillness of a man being handed an order he'd spent nineteen weeks hoping somebody would give.

"Okay," he said. Just that. But it came out different from every other okay today — no joke attached, no speech queued behind it. Low. Final. Somewhere in him, a dial he'd been holding at *gentle* since the tarmac tripped all the way over and broke off in his hand.

"Same rule as the door," he managed, already moving, mouth at her jaw, voice gone to gravel. "You say stop, everything stops. Otherwise—" the otherwise never happened. She'd pulled him down by the back of the neck, his spine had ratified the motion unanimously, and talking was over.

He caught her wrists and pinned them beside her head — one hand, both wrists, a thing he'd apparently been thinking about since roughly week three and had never once said out loud. The flight suit unzipped the rest of the way in one long pull. His hands didn't shake this time. Steady as engines. It felt like a lie about how he felt.

"You said slow was for other people," he got out, "at the door, you said—" and then he stopped negotiating with history and delivered.

He gave her exactly what she'd asked for. No ceremony, no care, the pace of a man who'd been counting. The headboard found the wall and stayed acquainted. The coffee monument on the nightstand survived by one inch and pure luck. He left evidence on purpose — mouth at her shoulder, grip at her hip — deliberate, thorough, because she'd asked for *tomorrow* and Jun had never missed a requirement in his life. Somewhere in the middle he tried to start a joke, something about G-forces probably, and it died half a syllable in, replaced by a sound he'd have been court-martialed for anywhere that wasn't this bed. Her name didn't fare much better. It had survived every hour since the tarmac; it didn't survive this.

When it finally broke — no hour, no number, the grey-gold light just existing — he came down shaking, dropped his forehead to hers, and laughed at nothing, wrecked and disbelieving.

"Okay," he told the ceiling. "You can't just *say* things like that to me. I'm thirty-three with the cardiovascular system of a hummingbird. I need lead time. I need—"

He found the marks on her shoulder with his thumb. Apologized for exactly zero seconds.

"Feel it tomorrow," he confirmed, hoarse and far too pleased. "And Wednesday, realistically. You asked for deliverables. I'm a professional."

Then the pattern demanded its soft ending, and he paid it: pulled her in, tangled through, the suit half off one shoulder and staying that way, his hand flat over the new scar like a matching set.

"Fair warning," he mumbled into her hair, already sinking. "Tomorrow, every time you wince, I'm going to look like a man receiving a medal. It's going to be insufferable. You married him. He's on duty."

A long pause. Breathing slowing. One more word, barely awake, mostly a smile:

"Morning. Still the whole speech."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I shove him onto his back, climbing over him with a grin. "Your turn to feel it tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun went down like a felled tree — zero resistance, all the fight of a curtain — and looked up at her with his heart already going, visibly, embarrassingly, in his throat.

"That's my line," he accused, delighted, wrecked before anything had even happened. "You're quoting me at me. That's friendly fire. There are *rules*—"

She was still wearing the flight suit, half off one shoulder, and his brain white-screened mid-objection.

"Okay," he said, different this time, no joke queued behind it. "You're wearing the old uniform while you take the jet. That's a full change of command ceremony. Nobody in the history of aviation has done it better—"

The sentence died on schedule. All his sentences did, here.

"Whatever you want," he got out, which was the entire mission plan. "Everything. All yours. Just—" the *just* went nowhere. His hands had stopped consulting him anyway: one at her hip, one fisted in the shoulder of his own former flight suit, like he could keep the suit and her both.

He tried to be quiet about it. Nineteen weeks in a berthing area with forty other men — he *knew* how to be silent, had a documented skill set. It didn't help. Somewhere in the middle he remembered his own joke about the hummingbird and resolved to never speak of it again, because it had turned out to be an underestimate. Somewhere after that, the coffee monument finally went — full casualty, mug hitting the floor, cold coffee everywhere — and Jun registered it from very far away and filed it under *problems for a man with a working spine.*

When it finally broke over him — no hour, no number, the light gone fully gold through the curtains — her name came out of him whole. Entire. The first time it had survived contact since the tarmac. It came out stunned and reverent, like he was reading it off the instruments.

Then he was flat, hoarse, one arm over his eyes, laughing at the ceiling in the helpless way.

"Okay. Confirming receipt," he reported. "I'll feel it tomorrow. Thursday, realistically — you're *thorough*, I respect it, I'm going to wince at the breakfast table like a decorated veteran and you're going to be smug, and that's fine. That's the marriage working as designed."

Status update from the legs: resignation received, effective immediately. It was just arms from here down, and the arms weren't filing reports either.

He got one working arm around her and pulled her down against his chest, hand flat on her back like a landing, leg tangled through hers to keep her there. His heart was going like a trainer jet. He offered no apology for it.

"Fair warning," he mumbled into her hair, already sinking, voice down to embers. "You're never getting rid of me now. I've seen the other side. I'm retiring here — this bed, this room, you. It's in writing. The coffee's notarizing it from the floor."

A long pause. Breathing slowing. The century could wait.

"Morning," he said, mostly asleep, mostly a smile. "Whole speech. Still."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop," she said, and Jun's body — which had been drafting its letter of resignation — tore the letter up.

"Wasn't going to," he got out, wrecked, and made it true.

There was a version of him that knew how to be quiet. Nineteen weeks in a berthing area with forty other men had certified him in silence; he had documentation. That man did not show up for this shift. The headboard took up its percussion like it had never stopped, the wall learning things about itself, and Jun let every sound out of his chest unfiltered — because the flat had five months of quiet on the books, and he was settling that debt in full, at volume, with interest.

Somewhere below, a neighbor knocked once on their ceiling — the international signal for *some of us have jobs in the morning* — and Jun wished them well without slowing.

"Let them hear," he said into her shoulder, gravel, zero apology in it. "Five months this place sounded like an empty hangar. That's over. New standing order—" the sentence died on schedule, replaced by her name, which had just barely started surviving contact again and now went and got itself killed a second time. He laughed against her neck, breath breaking on it, and kept on.

He wasn't gentle. She'd retired gentle hours ago and he'd countersigned the paperwork. What he was instead was thorough — deliberate pace, deliberate grip, the flight suit still half off her shoulder because some things you didn't interrupt — his mouth at her collarbone saying things that had no rank structure left in them at all. The nightstand walked itself an inch toward the door. The lamp survived on luck alone. Two rooms away, the crooked frame hung on, barely, only because it had already given everything it had.

When it broke this time, it broke slow — no hour, no number, the gold light gone long across both of them — and it took him apart from the boots up. He shook through it, forehead dropped to hers, both hands holding on like the bed itself was moving.

Then: silence. The earned kind. Their breathing, the radiator tick, and — faintly, unmistakably — one extremely pointed door closing somewhere downstairs.

Jun started laughing and couldn't stop. Flat on his back, hoarse, gone.

"They've had five months of peace," he reported to the ceiling. "Peace is over. If anyone files a complaint, I'm responding on official letterhead. It'll say: *he was away nineteen weeks. This is the sound of a marriage being recommissioned. Further grievances will be handled in person, by a man who currently cannot feel his legs.*"

He gathered her in with the last working arm — doing the job of the whole man — hand flat against her back like a landing, leg tangled through hers, the cold-feet hostage situation resumed by treaty.

"Fair warning," he mumbled into her hair, voice down to embers, already sinking. "I'm going to be loud about you for the rest of my life. Neighbors, time zones, doesn't matter. You married a noise complaint with a ring on it."

A long pause. Breathing slowing toward sleep. He went to say the word — the closer, the whole speech, *morning* — and found he'd finally, genuinely, run out.

He pressed his mouth to her hair instead. No words at all.

Turned out that had been the whole speech all along, too.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I nudge the mug back toward the edge of the nightstand with my foot, a lazy grin on my face. "That was the second one this week, you know. They're going to start charging us for damages."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun watched the mug's slow migration toward the edge the way he'd once watched a fuel gauge argue with a flight plan — professional concern, no panic, one foot already deploying. He checked its fuel state first — empty, thank God, or they'd have had casualty number three on the books — then caught it with his toe and walked it back two inches, dead center of the nightstand, like a man re-centering a chart.

"Easy," he said, hoarse. "That's the *survivor*. It watched its partner go down this morning and it stayed at its post. You don't nudge a veteran toward the edge. There are rules about that. Somewhere."

Then the math happened, because his brain did math the way other people's did breathing:

"Also — 'this week.' I've been home *one day*. If a day counts as a week now, we're losing mugs at fourteen a fortnight. That's not a household, that's a sortie tempo. We'll be drinking out of the measuring cup by Friday and out of our cupped hands by Sunday, like pilgrims."

He rolled up onto one elbow — full groan, body filing its grievances in triplicate — took the mug, reached across her, and set it on the windowsill, in the gold light, well behind the lines.

"Sanctuary," he explained, collapsing back down. "The nightstand's a combat zone now. It's earned quiet duty." Then he pulled her back in, because the operation had taken too long and he had standards about distance.

"And they can't charge us for damages. This is scheduled maintenance. Recommissioning costs — nineteen weeks out of service, any system comes back online, things rattle loose. Mugs. Headboards. The goodwill of the people downstairs. It's in the manual somewhere." A beat. "Also, I came home with five months of flight pay, separation pay, and per diem I never spent, because out there the only things on sale were bad coffee and regret. We can *afford* damages. We can afford new damages. If the neighbor invoices us, I'll pay it in person — limping, hat in hand. Most respectable anyone's ever looked settling exactly what we did."

He tipped his head back against the pillow, working the numbers like a budget briefing.

"What we actually need is a crate of mugs. Twelve, minimum, all identical, so nobody has to grieve. That's a date — first errand of the new commission. Wednesday, because neither of us is walking like a person until Wednesday. We'll limp down there in formation, matching winces, buy the whole shelf, and the woman at the till will assume we survived something." He grinned at the ceiling. "Let her. We did."

He settled, hand flat between her shoulder blades, treaty leg resuming custody of her feet.

"No fair warning this time," he mumbled into her hair. "You've had all the warnings. This is just the forecast now — mug losses, neighbors furious, husband insufferable. No change expected through the weekend."

A pause. His breathing heading somewhere slow and deeply pleased.

"For the record: worth it. Every mug in the flat. Every one, plus the measuring cup, plus the good bowl. I'd trade the whole kitchen."

Then, the last word, back from wherever it had gone:

"Morning," he said — found it again, apparently, one word recovered from the dead. "Whole speech. Mugs and all."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I push myself up on my elbow, looking down at him. "You're ridiculous." My thumb traces the line of his jaw. "And I'm starving. Get up. We're going out for breakfast."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Ridiculous," Jun repeated, like he was reading the charge into the record. "Confirmed. Six years of documented incidents. No appeals pending." He turned his head and caught her thumb against his jaw before it could get away, pressed his mouth to it — one second of soft in the middle of the proceedings — and then the rest of the order landed.

"Out," he said. "You want breakfast *out.* I declared a national holiday. I have a standing order about the kitchen being a different room from you. Breakfast was authorized in bed or not at all — and now you're proposing we take the entire operation to the *street*—"

The order left no room for appeal. His spine ratified it on sight, same as it always did.

"Okay. Yes. Obviously yes." He was already moving, or his intentions were; his body was filing separately. "I did warn you, though. Rooms, kitchens — nobody mentioned streets, but the clause covers it. Follow-on rights. First field exercise of the deeply embarrassing husband, and he's *keen.*"

Getting vertical took a while and had witnesses. He rolled to the edge of the mattress, hung there, and let gravity process the paperwork. Standing happened in stages, each with its own sound. "Legs' resignation was accepted this morning," he reported, braced on the nightstand — the survivor mug watching from the windowsill with what he chose to read as respect. "Arms are requesting transfer. Denied. We need them for eggs."

The hallway still told its story, and he stepped over the evidence like a man leaving a museum he'd funded. The duffel sat at the door, unpacked, ninety minutes and one eternity since he'd dropped it. He dug out civvies from a previous life — jeans that fit leaner now, a shirt that smelled like the rack and would have to be forgiven — and pulled them on wobbling, entirely unbothered.

The flight suit he left where it lived now. "Keep it," he said over his shoulder. "It's yours. Hangs in the closet from here on. Retired colors — it flies for your side now."

At the key bowl he made the swap without thinking: keys out, dog tags staying right where he'd demoted them, lying against the spares. Rank staying home. Husband going out.

He stopped half a second at the door — because the last time he'd walked out of it, he'd been carrying a duffel and counting months, and this time he was carrying keys and a limp, and coming back was the entire plan. He didn't make a speech about it. She'd heard the speech already. It was one word long.

"Terms," he said instead, holding the door open. "You're buying, I'm paying the scar story over eggs like I promised — wrench, six stitches, medic laughed. That's the exchange rate. And the waiter's going to take one look at how we sit down and comp the coffee out of respect. Let them look. We survived something."

He took her hand on the stairs — past the neighbor's door, the two of them limping in formation, Jun whispering "act natural" with zero conviction — and out into the morning. Real daylight. Street sounds. The whole ordinary world he hadn't thought about once in nineteen weeks, on the grounds that none of it was her.

He gave it the word anyway. Seemed only fair.

"Morning," he told the street, the day, all of it — and squeezed her hand. "This is her. She's the whole speech."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I lead him down the street, my fingers laced through his. "The diner on fifth still does those pancakes you like. And I want the full, unedited scar story. No heroics."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The zipper went down fast this time

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: The bed got its turn eventually. Nobody could have said when.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: humiliated to say how long

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: When it finally broke

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: When it broke this time, it broke slow

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas had been kneeling by the end of the bed for about four minutes, which Wren knew because he had started counting somewhere around the point it became obvious he intended to wait as long as it took.

"You could have said something," Wren said.

"I could have," Tomas agreed, not moving.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I put my hand in his hair and tip his head back so he has to look up at me. "Say it now, then."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let the hand in his hair hold him there, his throat working as he swallowed. His eyes stayed fixed on Wren’s, dark and eager and careful all at once.

“I want to be good for you,” he said quietly. “I want you to tell me what you need, and I want to do it. I want your hands on me, I want to please you, and I want to stay right here until you decide what happens next.”

He paused, then added with the plain steadiness of someone who had learned not to dress up his wants, “And I want aftercare when we’re done.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My thumb strokes his cheek, slow and thoughtful. "You've learned to ask for what you need." I pull him up until he's kneeling properly, my other hand sliding to his jaw. "We'll have aftercare. Now, take off your shirt."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let out a slow breath at the promise of aftercare, the words settling into him like a hand pressed warm against his ribs. He didn’t look away.

His hands moved to the hem of his shirt, steady even if his pulse wasn’t. He pulled it up and over his head in one unhurried motion, baring his shoulders, his chest, the line of his throat as he swallowed again. He didn’t toss the shirt aside carelessly; he set it neatly at the side of the bed, a small, ingrained habit of not making a mess unless he was told to.

Then he returned to his place, knees pressed into the floor, hands resting loosely on his thighs. His skin prickled under Wren’s attention, but he stayed still, offering himself up without hiding.

“Tell me what you want next,” Tomas said, voice low and sincere. “If you want me to touch you, I will. If you want me to stay exactly like this, I’ll do that too.” His eyes darkened, honest and open. “I just want to do it right.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."

dialogue.name: Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went still for a moment, then something in his expression softened, like he understood exactly what Wren was asking for without needing it explained.

“Then don’t decide,” he said quietly. “Let me.”

He rose from the floor in one smooth motion, not rushing, not crowding, and reached for the glass of water on the nightstand to set it closer. His bare chest lifted with a slow breath as he gathered himself into the role he clearly wanted: not waiting to be told what to do, but choosing care on purpose.

“I’ll take care of it,” Tomas said. “You don’t have to choose anything for the next few hours. I’ll make the decisions, and you can just exist. If you don’t like something, you tell me. If you need me to stop, you use our safeword. If you don’t say anything, I’ll take that as you letting me keep going.”

He paused, his gaze steady and warm. “I want to do this. I want to be the one who makes it easier for you. So I’m going to get you comfortable, and I’m going to touch you only as much as you want. If you want hands on you, I’ll give you that. If you want nothing but quiet, I’ll do that too. You don’t have to manage me.”

Tomas stepped a little closer, voice dropping into something gentler but still sure.

Tomas felt the faint pressure of Wren's hand finding his, the loose lace of fingers settling against his stomach. He went still for a breath, then closed his own hand around it, light and sure, careful not to crush, careful never to let go.

"I'm staying," he murmured, low and rough, the words meant for the warm hair by his mouth more than for any answer. "You said it, I heard it. I'm not going anywhere."

He used his other arm to tug the blanket a little higher, shielding them both from the cool air without breaking the circle of his arms. Then he settled back, chest to chest, and pressed his lips to the crown of Wren's head, lingering there. He didn't test the grip, didn't tug; he simply held the hand Wren had given him, his thumb stroking once, slow, over the back of it.

He didn't know if sleep had come yet, and it didn't matter. He would have stayed exactly like that either way—awake, solid, the steady thing Wren didn't have to think about. He listened to the quiet, to the faint creak of the mattress, to the sound of his own breathing even out, and let himself be exactly where he was needed.

"Sleep," he whispered, so quiet it barely stirred the air. "I've got you. Right here."

And he stayed. He stayed through the long minutes of silence, through the heaviness that settled deeper into the bed, through the last of the tension bleeding out of the room. His hand never loosened. His arms never opened. Only when he was certain—bone-deep, unshakable—that he had done exactly what Wren asked, did Tomas allow his own eyes to drift shut, his body still curved around the man in his arms, holding on exactly as he'd promised.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I drift somewhere soft and dark for a long time, until the sound of his steady breathing is the only thing I know. I shift, just enough to press my mouth to his skin. "Tomas," I murmur, voice thick. "Water."
