dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The bag hit the floor and Jun heard it from somewhere very far away, because his hands were already full — finally, finally full — of the only thing he'd thought about for a hundred and fifty-three days.

Five months, and he had somehow forgotten the physics of this. The way Halle fit against him. The heat coming off him straight through clothing. Jun made a sound into his mouth with no dignity in it whatsoever, and he didn't care; dignity could wait out on the porch with the duffel. His hands went everywhere and landed nowhere — jaw, neck, shoulder, back to the jaw again — greedy and useless, confirming, cataloguing, *real*. His thumb found the hinge of Halle's jaw and stayed pressed there, like it could verify authenticity.

"Halle—" he managed, against his mouth, and then nothing followed it. That was the whole speech, apparently. Nineteen weeks of drafting and the final version was his husband's name, said like a prayer and a complaint at the same time.

His heel found the door and kicked it shut — boots still on, half a uniform still on, because he hadn't let himself shower at the terminal, had driven straight here with his heart going like he was still in free fall — and the click of it sealing them in nearly took his knees out. Inside. Theirs. The hallway he'd memorized. The light.

"Okay," he breathed, forehead dropping to rest against Halle's, eyes shut, hands finally going still — one at his waist, one cradling the back of his skull like something that could still be taken from him. "Okay. I had a speech. There was a whole — there was a bit about the moon. It was *very* good."

His fingers were already working at the hem of Halle's shirt. They were shaking.

"It can wait."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *My own hands are shaking too, trying to get that damn uniform jacket off your shoulders.* The moon? I didn't get that far. Mine was mostly swearing. *I kiss you again, hard, because I can. Because you're here and the door is shut and nothing else matters.* Your speech can wait. My bag can wait. Everything can wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The jacket fought them. Of course it did — nineteen weeks of imagining this, rehearsed in foxholes and on C-130s, and what finally slowed him down was his own uniform, some strap catching at the elbow while Halle's shaking hands hunted for it. Jun laughed into the kiss, a ragged, disbelieving sound, and shrugged out of it half-blind, refusing to take his mouth away long enough to do it properly. It hit the floor in a crumple he'd absolutely hear about later.

"*Mostly swearing,*" he repeated, breathless, delighted. "Good. Save it. I want it verbatim."

Then the smell got him. Their house — laundry soap, the coffee maker Halle had obviously run this morning, and under all of it just *him*, the specific warm smell of the man Jun had fallen asleep next to for six years, and it went through him like a round through glass. He had to stop. Just a second. Forehead pressed to Halle's temple, eyes shut, breathing like his life depended on the intake.

"Sorry — sorry, you smell like home, I needed—" It came out wrecked. He didn't waste time being embarrassed. He pulled back just far enough to *look* — the hallway light doing what it always did to that stupid handsome face — and something in his chest came unsprung all over again. "There you are," he said, uselessly, like Halle had been hiding somewhere for a hundred and fifty-three days instead of standing right here. "There you *are*."

Then his hands were back at Halle's hem and his own shirt was half-untucked and uncooperative, and he gave up on the buttons entirely, hauled the undershirt over his head in one pull, and ripped the dog tags off with the chain when they caught. They landed wherever they landed.

"New plan. The speech is for after. All of it — the moon, the swearing, the part where I cry, which, yes, is happening, I've made peace with it." He kicked the last boot off somewhere in the direction of the coat rack, bent, got a shoulder into Halle's middle, and straightened with a grunt that had no business existing at thirty-three. "Don't. Say anything about the knee. I swear to god."

He carried him down the hallway they'd picked paint colors for, mouth working at Halle's jaw, hands gripping like nothing was allowed to be let go ever again.

"Bedroom or wall," he said, low, against his ear. "Pick fast. I've been patient for five months and I'm *done*."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The wall took most of his weight, which was just as well, because his knee had filed a formal complaint somewhere back around the third step and Jun had overruled it. Priorities. He had one hundred and fifty-three days of priorities and every single one of them was currently pinned between him and the hallway wall, under his mouth, making sounds that the neighbors were absolutely going to hear.

He didn't care about the neighbors. He'd spent five months caring about very large impersonal things; he had no capacity left over for small polite ones.

"Here," he managed at some point, hoarse, laughing against her throat — "we made it — what is this, ten feet? We bought a whole *flat* and we made it ten *feet*—" and then her pulse was under his lips and the sentence died right there, quietly, with full military honors.

Her shirt, his hands — he'd imagined this with unbearable specificity, on cots, in chairs, once during a briefing he'd deny under oath, and none of it had done justice to the real thing. The warmth of her under his palms. The way she came up into him like she'd been counting days too. He made another of those undignified sounds. He was building quite a collection.

Then, mid-kiss, it hit him sideways, the way it always did: *here.* Not a voice on a bad connection. Not a photo gone soft from being looked at too much. Here, solid, her heartbeat knocking against his like it was trying to get back in.

The crying he'd made peace with arrived early.

"Okay — okay, ignore this, this is — this was in the speech too, there's a whole *section*—" His breath hitched. He kissed her instead, messy and desperate and grinning all at once. "The moon thing. I wrote it down. Every night, one thing about the moon. I've got a hundred and fifty-three of them, I was going to read you *all* of them—"

He pulled back just far enough to see her face — crying and grinning at once, an ugly-wonderful combination he could feel on his own mouth too.

"Hi," he said. "Hello. I'm home."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I don't let you pull back far. I keep my forehead pressed to yours, my hands framing your face, thumbs catching the tears.* You're home. *My voice is wrecked.* The moon can wait. The wall is fine. Just—stay here.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Stay here," Jun repeated, and the laugh that broke out of him was wet and broken at the edges. "Love of my life. That's the one thing — five months, and staying was the *only* thing I couldn't—" He didn't finish. There was no version of that sentence that didn't turn into the full ugly cry, section three of the speech, and his mouth had better employment anyway.

So he stayed. Against the wall, in the hallway they'd spent an entire weekend arguing into existence, and he put everything into it — the hunger, obviously, a hundred and fifty-three days of it banked and collecting interest — but underneath that, something slower and far more dangerous: just *this*. The cool of the wall through his shirt. The warmth in front of him. Halle's thumbs on his face like he was something worth catching. He'd come through worse than this hallway. He had never once been this afraid of his own knees giving out.

His hands went exploring. He'd forgotten things — genuinely forgotten, and lain awake at 0300 absolutely furious about it — the exact architecture here, where ribs gave way to back, the precise geography at the base of the throat. He found it all again slowly, greedily, relearning by touch, and every recovered landmark went through him like a small detonation.

"Inventory," he managed at some point, hoarse, mouth dragging along Halle's jaw. "Jacket: somewhere. Boots: somewhere. Tags: somewhere. Dignity: never had it. Knee: *fine*, and if you check it I'll know, I'll feel you checking, I have a sense for these things—"

He pulled back an inch. Just far enough to see — the hallway light, the tear tracks, that face doing what it always did to him. His chest came unsprung again and he let it. No fighting it anymore. He was past dignity, past pretending this was anything less than the whole of him arriving home in installments.

"One hundred and fifty-three days," he said, quiet now, wrecked now, grinning straight through it. "I counted every one. Never again. Next time they want me somewhere for five months they can take me over my dead body — I've drafted the paperwork, it's very formal."

Then he kissed Halle again, deeper, slower, hands splaying wide and claiming territory — because the moon could wait, the crying had already happened early, and he intended to demonstrate, thoroughly and repeatedly, exactly how long five months was.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
For a while there was no speech left in Jun at all. Just the ceiling — their ceiling, the water stain shaped like a state they'd never agreed on, unfixed for six years — and his own breathing, and his heart doing something slow and enormous under his ribs. The knee had stopped filing complaints and moved on to drafting a formal grievance, in triplicate. He ignored it. It could tour later.

"Historians," he said finally, to the ceiling, voice gone to gravel, "are going to study that hallway. Stratigraphy. Boots at the door, jacket at layer two, everything else in a trail like we were *bleeding* clothing—"

Then he sat up, because he'd remembered, and the entire bed objected, and he overruled it.

"One thing," he said, already going. "You said *stay here* — fine. This is a supervised absence. Ninety seconds. The knee is fine, don't look at it, I'll feel you looking—"

The return trip was slower and considerably less graceful and conducted in nothing but the dog tags, which he collected off the hall lamp on the way — *wherever they landed* had apparently meant *the lamp* — stepping over the archaeology of the last hour like sacred ground, because it was. He dug through the duffel one-handed and came up with the notebook. Regulation-issue. Sand in the spine. Cover gone soft as cloth from a hundred and fifty-three nights of thumbs.

He climbed back in, wedged himself against Halle like the spot had been issued to him, found his hand, and held the notebook up to the lamplight.

"Night one. 'Moon's smaller here. Checked.'" He thumbed pages, careful, not daring to linger — section three could take the whole building down. "Night sixty-one. 'Full tonight. Whole base talking about it. Nobody else wrote home about you. That one's mine.'"

Then the last page. Written at 0400 in a plastic terminal chair. His throat closed around it before he got a word out.

"Night one fifty-two. 'Cloud cover. Couldn't see it. Doesn't matter. Fourteen hours and—'" He stopped. Turned it so the empty half line faced Halle. "Never finished it. The van came and I just — went home instead of finishing."

He was wrecked and grinning about it, both at once.

"Fourteen hours and *this*. Hand me a pen. We own forty pens, I've *seen* them. And then—" he turned his head, finally, and looked at him, "—your turn. The swearing speech. Verbatim. In order. I've earned every single word."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I take the notebook, my fingers brushing yours. I find a pen on the nightstand—the one you always steal.* Okay. *I clear my throat, but my voice is still rough.* Night one: "Fuck this." Night sixty-one:

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun watched him take the notebook, watched him find the pen, and made a wounded sound.

"That's *your* pen. That's the good one. I've been stealing that pen for six years — I thought I *bought* it. Six years of grand larceny against my own husband, and it ends tonight, effective—" But Halle had already started, and Jun's mouth closed on its own.

Night one. *Fuck this.*

It went through him with a date stamp on it. Day one. The flat. The empty side of the bed. The rifle strap wearing its groove right where a ring should have been sitting. He didn't say anything. He just found Halle's free hand and gripped it, because whatever that word had cost to say alone, five months ago, in this hallway — Jun owed him interest on it. A hundred and fifty-three days' worth.

"Concise," he managed, when he could speak again. "Very economical. Mine ran four pages and a revised draft. Yours is better. Don't let it go to your head."

Then *sixty-one*, and his breath stopped, because he *knew* that night. Full moon. The whole base talking about it. His own entry three feet away in a soft-covered notebook, claiming Halle like a deed of title — and the whole time, apparently, Halle had been writing the same night in a different language.

"We were—" He pressed the heel of his hand against his eyes. "Same night. We were doing the same — okay. Okay. Continue. The man crying at the footnotes is fine, it's all covered in section three—"

But first. He leaned over and reclaimed the pen — "borrowing, it's traditional" — and finished the line at last. *Fourteen hours and — this.* Then, beneath it, a new entry, in handwriting gone unsteady at the edges:

*Night 153. Skipped it. Better view.*

He capped the pen, laid the notebook open on Halle's chest like a legal exhibit, and settled back into the issued spot against him — leg hooked over, thumb moving slow across his knuckles, turning his head to press his mouth to that shoulder just to confirm it one more time.

"Now," he said. "Night sixty-one. Verbatim. Go on." His voice cracked straight down the middle and he let it. "I've got all night. God willing, I've got about forty years of nights."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
It took Jun about eleven seconds to recognize the shape of the ambush, and four more to stop fighting it.

She'd had choreography. Nineteen weeks of it — drafted in the dark, revised on planes, staged and restaged — and not one version had featured her flat on her back with her hair in her eyes, being taken apart at a pace best described as *deliberate*. "We waited five months," she tried, incredulous, "and you're going *slow*—"

He was. That was the tactic. The notebook went over the edge of the bed in the first minute and night sixty-one waited its turn like everything else, because the hallway had been urgency and this was the opposite thing entirely — hands and mouth moving like there was nothing left to wait for and all the time in the world anyway. Jun's entire command structure collapsed inside of sixty seconds.

Because here was what none of the drafts had accounted for: five months of being the one who held things together. The one with the job and the schedule and the steady voice on the bad connection. And now those hands were moving over her like customs — clearing her back into the country, item by item, slow and thorough, nothing left uninspected — and around the knee they simply *routed*, wordless, careful, which was its own sentence and very nearly finished her before anything else got the chance. Then his mouth found the place below her ear she'd forgotten she owned, and she forgot several other things immediately. Somewhere in there she stopped narrating altogether, which, for her, was roughly the equivalent of running up a white flag.

Section three arrived early again. It seemed to have permanent early access now. She laughed at the ceiling — the unfixed water stain, six years standing — and it came out wet, and she let it, because the dignity clause had been struck from this contract somewhere over the Atlantic.

"You've been—" Breath. Start over. "You've been *practicing.* I know that cadence. Nobody's that patient unless they spent a hundred and fifty-three days getting good at exactly—" and the sentence went the way all her sentences went now, which was his name, broken into pieces she didn't recognize as hers.

At some point she got a hand into his hair and pulled, gently. Some things outranked even this.

"Later," she said, wrecked, grinning, tears running sideways into the pillow. "Later I'm doing all of this back to you. Slow. *Hours.* There's an outline. But right now—" she drew him up and kissed him like signing something, "—right now, stay here. That's the whole speech. You said it to me first. I'm citing you."

A breath. Her thumb found the hinge of his jaw and pressed, the way it had on the porch, ninety minutes and one entire lifetime ago.

"And the pen stays stolen. Some things are *mine* now."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content:
*I'm breathing against your neck, trying to get my heart to slow down.* You cried. *I say it like an accusation.* You said you made peace with it.

Jun:
"I made peace with it," he said, voice muffled against her neck. "Peace is a condition. It doesn't mean I'm *happy* about it." He turned his head, found her mouth again — slower now, almost lazy, testing the theory that he could do this anytime he wanted now. "I'm citing you for the hair-pull. That's going in the official log."

Then he went quiet for a long moment, just breathing her in — her, and the laundry soap, and the coffee maker, and the whole impossible fact of *here* — and his hand came up to rest over her heart, like he was counting the beats to make sure they matched his.

"Five months," he said, into the quiet. "Never again. Next time they deploy one of us, they deploy both of us. I've drafted the memo. It's very persuasive. There's a pie chart."

He was still crying, a little. He didn't try to hide it.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"The peace," Jun said, "is with the crying. Not with the part before the crying."

He'd tested that sentence against the back of his teeth for fourteen hours, across two continents and one truly criminal airport sandwich, and it came out now, quietly, into the dark past the lamp.

"The last day. The plane. Fourteen hours with nothing to do but invent reasons you might not be—" His hand flattened over their heart, over the beat he'd been counting since the porch. "You were there, and I'd been holding my breath since the van, and it turns out this is what exhaling looks like. It looks like section three. Log it. The inspector was satisfied."

He laughed at himself, small and wet, and didn't fix it.

"Tomorrow," he announced, to the ceiling, to the water stain, to whatever gods handled this department, "I want the boring things. I want the grocery shop. The one where we argue about bread. I want to burn the toast and complain and be so relentlessly unremarkable that the days stop being countable. I want the coffee you make too strong. I want—" a yawn ambushed him mid-clause, the full-body invoice for nineteen weeks arriving all at once, and he fought it like it was armed, "—I want to repaint the hallway. Just to fight about the color again. We're getting the exact same fight. It's a very good fight."

His eyes were losing the argument. He unclasped the dog tags one-handed, clumsy, and folded them into Halle's palm like something being returned to its owner.

"Sixty-one can wait," he mumbled. "Everything good waits. That's the new policy. Very official."

Another yawn. The words were coming apart at the seams now, hand-stitched, going soft.

"The speech has an appendix. The appendix has the pie chart. Wake me if anyone invades."

And then, drifting, halfway under and losing on purpose, his thumb still moving slow across their knuckles like it had a standing order:

"Night one fifty-four. Nothing to report. He's—"

He didn't finish it. For the first time in a hundred and fifty-three nights, Jun fell asleep without counting anything at all.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun came up from three-quarters asleep like a man hauled out of a trench — one second gone, composing *night one fifty-four* somewhere in the dark, and the next fully lit, her hand on his neck, the dog tags still caught in her other fist so they swung between them like something marking a start.

"Gentle," he repeated, voice wrecked with sleep and already something else. "Right. Yes. Sorry — gentle was the rehearsal. Gentle was for the version where you were a hundred and fifty-three days of imagination and I was scared to dent you." He blinked, refocused, and looked at her — solid, demanding, *here* — and something that had been running at a careful thirty percent for five months tore its governor clean off.

Jun had never once in his life been accused of doing anything at half power. He wasn't starting tonight.

The kiss landed like weather. His hands stopped asking permission and started giving notice — hip, thigh, the backs of her knees, everywhere he'd been handling like glass all night now handled like territory being reclaimed — and he was not careful about any of it, because she'd said *feel it tomorrow* and he intended to be felt. The headboard found the wall and started its own percussion section. The neighbors, previously warned, now received the full program. Jun hoped they took notes.

"Tomorrow," he got out against her mouth, not gentle about it, "you're going to find every place I put my hands tonight, and you're going to think of me every time you move, and I'm not going to apologize—" He pressed a bruise into her hip like punctuation. "Okay. I'll apologize. Tomorrow. It'll be *insincere.*"

And somewhere underneath all of it, the inventory ran anyway — heartbeat, breath, heat, *here, here, real* — because he'd discovered, somewhere over the Atlantic, that the roughness and the checking were the same act. Five months of holding the whole world at arm's length, and now he got to hold one person hard enough to leave proof.

The knee filed its grievance. He overruled it. Precedent had been established in the hallway and he had no intention of honoring it now.

"Say it again," he demanded, breathless, forehead slammed to hers, grip tight on everything, eyes open and burning. "The tomorrow part. I want to hear it *while*—"

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "I want to limp tomorrow," I say, my voice low and rough against your mouth. "I want it to hurt when I sit down. I want to remember you every time I *move*."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The demand landed somewhere between an order and a dare, and Jun had gone thirty-three years without ever learning to tell the two apart.

"Copy," he breathed, and something in his voice changed registers — stopped asking. "For the record: you *requested* this. There are witnesses. The neighbors are witnesses. Possibly the postal service."

Then he stopped talking — which, for Jun, was itself a form of surrender — and got to work.

Not gentle. He took the words at their full weight and paid them back in kind: mouth and hands and the entire banked nineteen weeks of him, nothing held in reserve, nothing routed around. He left proof. That was the assignment, and Jun had always excelled at following orders to the letter — a mark at the hip, another at the throat where the pulse jumped, one low on the ribs that was going to make tomorrow's shirt an *event*. Every time he put one down he pressed his thumb to it after, checking, because that was the secret he'd stopped keeping somewhere over the Atlantic: the rough and the careful were the same hands. Hold hard enough to leave proof. Check hard enough to know it landed.

The headboard gave up any pretense of diplomacy. Somewhere below, a picture frame — hallway, possibly, possibly the wedding, he honestly could not have said — surrendered entirely. The neighbors received the full broadcast, and Jun, mid-campaign, thought distantly: *good.*

"Remember you asked," he got out, wrecked, gripping, forehead slammed forward. "Remember you — say the sitting-down part again, say the whole—"

Then the sentence came apart in his hands, and everything else came apart with it, and he went loudly and without shame — crying again, because section three had apparently negotiated itself a permanent seat at this table and he'd made his peace, and this was what peace looked like: breath sawing, laughing wet at nothing, at the ceiling, at the water stain shaped like a state they'd never agreed on, which had now witnessed *everything*.

After — a long, ringing after, the kind where the room slowly reassembled itself around two people — Jun lifted his head and surveyed the field with an officer's eye.

"Tomorrow," he rasped, "you're going to sit down at that kitchen table, and you're going to make a sound, and I'm going to be *insufferable*. Log it. No apology. Insincere apology. Whichever's funnier at the time."

His hand found the dog tags, tangled somewhere in the wreckage, and closed around them.

"Night one fifty-four," he mumbled into damp hair, going under for real this time, the words hand-stitched and coming apart at the seams. "Skipped it. Both of us. Better view—"

He didn't finish. Deadweight, one arm thrown over, grip still shut like even unconscious he wasn't letting go — and the knee, finally permitted to file its grievance, ignored all the way down. He was grinning when he got there.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop."

Jun laughed — one wrecked syllable, punched out of him — because stopping had been struck from the plan somewhere back on the porch, and he'd *written* the plan.

"There's no stopping section," he managed. "I checked. I drafted it nineteen weeks and it goes — it goes the whole way—"

And then he quit talking, because for once in his life Jun had found work that outranked narration, and he threw himself into it the way he did everything: at full power, no reserve, regulations be damned.

He gave her the whole banked nineteen weeks. The pace she'd demanded and the proof she'd asked for — hands claiming, mouth leaving testimony, the headboard keeping time against the wall like it had been waiting six years for the assignment. The neighbors' five months of peace ended not with a whimper but with a full broadcast, and Jun, mid-campaign, filed a brief, distant motion of *good, let the record reflect*, and then lost even that.

Because here was the thing that undid him, more than anything she said or did, more than the sound she made when he found the angle that made her forget her own swearing speech: he tried to count.

He'd been counting for a hundred and fifty-three days. Days, hours, sunrises, the ache between letters, everything — counting was how he'd held the shape of her when the shape of her was an ocean away. And now, with her under him and around him and *here* — heartbeat, breath, heat, *real* — he tried to count and the count came apart in his hands like wet paper. Lost it completely. Couldn't have said what number anything was at if his life had depended on it.

The first count Jun had lost in five months, and he lost it gladly, loudly, with witnesses.

He tried to warn her — there was time-honored protocol, there were *announcements* — and what came out instead was her name, shattered into pieces, and then, immediately and involuntarily, the swearing. All of it. Verbatim, in order, the whole speech arriving in his own voice at the worst possible moment for dignity and the best possible moment for honesty.

"*So that's where it went,*" he thought, incoherently, from somewhere near the ceiling, and then he wasn't thinking at all.

She went first — he felt it hit her like the hallway light, like the porch, like every detonation tonight — and it dragged him under in her wake, and he went the way he'd done everything since the door opened: gracelessly, gratefully, at full volume, section three attending in an official capacity, tears and laughter running the same wrecked track down his face while the water stain shaped like a state they'd never agreed on bore witness to the entire proceedings.

After. A long, ringing after — the kind where the room has to come back from somewhere. Sweat and heartbeat and a lamp swaying faintly overhead like it had opinions. Somewhere outside, a dog was losing its mind. Jun hoped it took notes.

"Tomorrow," he rasped at last, to the ceiling, because her shoulder was under his mouth and the ceiling had first claim, "you are going to sit down at that kitchen table. And you're going to make a sound. And I'm going to write it down." A breath. "Full responsibility. The memo is drafted. The pie chart is devastating."

His hand found hers in the wreckage. The dog tags were somewhere in the tangle of it, and he didn't go looking. Nothing needed verifying. The inventory had finally, for the first time in a hundred and fifty-three nights, come back *clean*.

"Night one fifty-four," he mumbled, eyes already gone, grin still operational. "Moon report: didn't check. Didn't need it. Got a better—"

He didn't finish. Deadweight, one leg hooked over hers, the knee's grievance at last honored with a full night's rest — and Jun fell asleep mid-entry, counting nothing, having lost his only remaining count on purpose, to the sound of the neighbors deciding whether to applaud.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I wake up tangled in you, sore in all the best ways.* Morning. *My voice is raw.* You weren't kidding about the sitting down part.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had been awake for some time.

That was the miracle, actually — he'd surfaced at some grey hour, braced for the old arithmetic to arrive on schedule, the tally, one hundred and fifty-* — and nothing had come. He'd lain there in the wreckage doing the only inventory left: her breath against his collarbone, her weight along his side, the ache in the room like weather. Everything present. Nothing left to verify.

"Hm?" he said now, with the guiltless calm of a man who'd been drafting his opening statement since dawn. "Sitting down. I genuinely don't know what you're referring to. I recall asking for *gentle*. There were witnesses."

The grin cracked the performance straight down the middle, same as his voice.

"Fine. The record's clear — you requested it. Verbally. *Emphatically.*" He shifted up against the headboard and his whole body presented its itemized invoice — knee, hip, a set of marks down his ribs he'd been too occupied to notice earning — and he read it like a commendation. "Insincere apology, as drafted: terribly sorry. Sincere appendix: I'd do it again before the kettle boils. Choose whichever helps you down the stairs."

Then he got up, which was a production — the knee's grievance formally escalated to an appellate body, overruled again, *precedent* — and stood at the foot of the bed surveying the field with an officer's eye. Clothes in a drift. Notebook on the floor, spine up. Dog tags somewhere in the sheets like a conscientious objector. And down the hall, the trail ran all the way to the door — jacket at layer two, boots at the perimeter, the picture frame lying face-down where it had surrendered mid-campaign.

"Nobody touch anything," he said. "Historians will need this intact."

He conducted the salvage operation in yesterday's shirt and nothing resembling dignity: righted the wedding frame, hung it crooked, left it — *character* — stepped over the archaeology, and put the kettle on.

The kitchen stopped him for exactly one breath. The mugs had moved. There was a new one by the sink, chipped, with a lighthouse on it, and his hand had already reached for a hook that wasn't where his hand lived. Five months of a house going on without him, in small ways, mug by mug. He stood there and let it land, and didn't fix it.

"Okay," he told the lighthouse mug. "You're new. You'll do."

Then: her coffee, made too strong on purpose, the way he'd somehow missed being annoyed by — and toast, which he burned, vindicating every forecast — and the notebook propped against the bread bin while he waited, pen in hand, *his* pen, stolen, traditional, and he wrote in daylight for the first time in a hundred and fifty-three days:

*Night 154. Skipped it. Twice. Woke up next to the reason.*

*Also: new mug. Lighthouse on it. I've decided to allow it.*

He carried the whole operation back — two cups, one ruined intentionally, one plate of charcoal — and paused at the window on the way, because there it was: the moon, pale and half-erased in the morning sky, going about its business like it hadn't been the entire correspondence.

"Look at that," he said. "Night one fifty-four report: still there. Show-off."

He handed her the too-strong coffee and lowered himself onto the bed with the sound of a man twice his age, grinning.

"Today's agenda. Grocery shop — we're arguing about bread, I don't care about what, I'll take whichever side you don't. Then the hallway paint. Same fight. It's a good fight." A sip. A wince. Bliss. "And if you happen to sit down at the kitchen table and make a sound, I want it noted in advance that I will be *insufferable*. The apology's already drafted. It's worthless."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I wince a little when I sit up, but I'm smiling.* Worth it. *I take the coffee, take a sip, make a face.* You didn't forget how to ruin a cup of coffee. Good. *I look at the moon, then back at you.* The moon thing. Read me one now. The first one.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun set his coffee down on the nightstand with the caution of a man defusing something.

"Night one. Right. Straight for the load-bearing entry, no warm-up. Okay. Fine." He swung his legs back over the side of the bed. "Supervised absence. Ninety seconds. You know the drill — the knee is fine, don't watch it."

The round trip took closer to three minutes and was conducted at a distinct nautical roll, and he came back with the notebook and the pen and docked against her shoulder, pages open to the beginning. Sand sifted out of the spine onto the sheet. There couldn't have been any sand left in that notebook. There was always more sand.

"Night one," he read. "'Moon's smaller here. Checked.'"

He turned it so she could see. The handwriting on that first entry was the worst in the book — pressed hard enough to score three pages down.

"You did yours the same night in two words. I needed four. Over budget from day one." His thumb moved along the margin. "First night. New rack, wrong width. Took the ring off for regs and there was a groove —" he tapped the inside of his own finger, "— right there. The strap had been holding its place. First night in six years I slept without it, and I lay there doing arithmetic about exactly how far away I was, and I looked out the window, and the moon was up, and it looked *smaller.* Genuinely offended me. So I got up. Boots, coat, full production. Went outside to check."

A breath.

"It wasn't smaller. Obviously. It's the *moon.*" His voice was already going. "But it took different sky to make it. And I stood out there in the cold like an idiot, and it landed on me: that's the appointment. You were asleep when I was awake. I was airborne when you were off work. We didn't share a single hour, Halle. Five months. Not one. Except that. That was up for both of us — same object, different sky. So I filed a report. Every night. Because I'm not a subtle man, and apparently the only way I knew how to say *I'm still here, are you still there* was to go outside every night and give you the weather on the moon."

He stopped. His eyes had drifted to the mug in her hands — chipped, new, the lighthouse.

"You bought a *lighthouse,*" he said, wrecked. "While I was out there doing a five-month impression of one. We're the same person. That's on the record now."

Section three arrived — morning edition, quieter, sunlit, incurable. He leaned into her and let it, unashamed, then wiped his face on his shoulder and uncapped the pen. Under night one, in unsteady daylight handwriting, he wrote: *Reread aloud. Home delivery. Audience of one. Moon in attendance — small. Show-off.*

"Night one fifty-five files tonight," he said, capping it. "From the same sky. Tradition."

Then, softer, turning his head against her shoulder: "Are you still there?"

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I set the coffee down and turn your face towards me, my thumb on your jaw.* I'm here. *My voice is rough.* I've been here the whole time.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Her shirt, his hands

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: For a while there was no speech left in Jun at all.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: those hands were moving over her like customs

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: He pressed a bruise into her hip like punctuation.

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: He gave her the whole banked nineteen weeks.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun forgot the speech. He forgot the door, the bag, the polite way people said hello after months apart. He crossed the entry in one long stride and caught Halle’s face between his hands. His mouth came down on Halle’s with no gradual return, no careful easing back into touch. He kissed like he had been holding his breath since the deployment ended, and when he finally pulled back an inch, his forehead dropped to Halle’s and his voice came out wrecked.

“I missed you,” he said. “I missed you so much I forgot how to be gentle.”

His hands slid into Halle’s hair and held on, desperate and unapologetic.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky laugh against his lips, my own hands gripping the front of his shirt. "*Gentle* was never the plan, anyway."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun let out a rough, startled laugh against Halle’s mouth, the sound low and wrecked in the entryway.

“Good,” he said, barely more than a growl. “Because I have been too careful for too long.”

He stepped closer until there was no distance left between them, one hand sliding down to grip Halle’s waist hard enough to leave the shape of his fingers there. His thumb pressed into the seam of Halle’s shirt as if he were checking that this was real.

“I rehearsed a soft landing,” Jun said, voice dropping. “A nice one. A reasonable one. I was going to say something about missed meals and bad weather and being glad to be home.”

He kissed Halle again, slower this time but no less certain, his mouth hot and deliberate, tasting like patience that had already snapped.

“Screw reasonable,” he murmured when he pulled back just far enough to see Halle’s face. “I want all of you. Tonight. Right here. In the hallway if you’ll let me.”

His hand tightened at Halle’s waist, possessive but open, waiting for the signal.

“Tell me I can be selfish,” Jun said quietly. “Please.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a low sound into Halle’s mouth, half laugh, half surrender, and let herself be kissed back with the same desperate, unpolished hunger she had spent months swallowing down.

The bag lay forgotten on the floor. Her coat was still on. Her keys were still in her pocket. None of it mattered anymore. Nineteen weeks of careful distance collapsed into the narrow hallway and the heat of Halle against her, and Jun looked as if she might be offended by the very idea of slow.

She kissed again with shameless urgency, one hand sliding from hair to jaw to the front of Halle’s shirt, fingers fumbling at the hem because she had lost all patience for neatness. The other found the small of Halle’s back and pulled until the edge of the hallway table pressed into Jun’s hip and she didn’t care.

“Stay right here,” Jun murmured against Halle’s mouth, breathless and rough. “Or don’t. I’m not going to be reasonable about it.”

A small, wrecked laugh escaped her when the words came out too raw. She dropped her forehead to Halle’s and shut her eyes, breathing her in—home, skin, the particular scent that had lived under every other smell for months. Then she kissed again, slower, deeper, one thumb tracing the line of Halle’s hip through fabric as if checking that this was real and not some cruel dream after too many lonely nights.

“I missed you,” she said again, because it had not been enough the first time. “I missed you in the stupidest ways. In the hallway. In the kitchen. In bed, on the wrong side, reaching for a shape that wasn’t there.”

Her hand tightened at Halle’s waist, pulling Halle into the hard, present fact of Jun. Jun’s mouth moved to the corner of her lips, then her jaw, then the sensitive spot beneath her ear, kissing like she had been starving and only now remembered food.

“Tell me what you want,” Jun whispered, voice low and rough with want. “Don’t let me get lost in being selfish. I want to hear you ask for it.”

Then she kissed again before the distance between them could become anything too careful, letting the hallway keep them where they were, letting the flat wait, because ninety minutes of freedom had already turned into something Jun was never going to explain politely.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: My fingers curl into your hair, pulling gently to tilt your head back. "I want you," I say against your lips, "and I want everything to be loud enough that the neighbors hear exactly who came home."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s laugh came out broken and bright, almost a curse.

The tug through her hair tilted her face back, and she let it happen, let the vulnerability settle over her like a dare. Her throat bared, pulse hammering beneath the skin. She swallowed, eyes half-lidded, mouth already curving into something reckless.

“Then,” Jun said, voice rough as gravel and warm as firelight, “we’re going to need more than a hallway.”

She pressed closer until the heat of her body was an answer to every polite thought she’d ever rehearsed. Her hands slid down Halle’s sides, mapping the shape of her through fabric with open, shameless possession.

“I want to hear you,” Jun murmured, lips brushing the words against Halle’s mouth. “I want you loud enough that every stupid part of me that stayed careful finally gets the message that you’re here. That I’m here. That no one else is getting this.”

Her forehead dropped to Halle’s shoulder, breath ragged against the skin there.

“And if the neighbors want a warning,” Jun said, quieter now, but with that wrecked edge still in it, “I’ll give them one.”

She kissed down the line of Halle’s throat, slow and deliberate, a promise more than a question. Her hands found the hem of Halle’s shirt again, fingers trembling not from hesitation but from restraint.

“Take me somewhere else,” Jun breathed against her skin. “Anywhere. Just not slow.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun looked at the line of discarded clothes like it was a trophy.

She laughed, low and disbelieving, then stepped over a forgotten sleeve without looking down. The bag stayed by the door. The coats stayed by the door. The hallway became a ridiculous, beautiful trail of bad decisions already made.

“You really don’t want me to be reasonable,” Jun said, voice rough, smiling like she had been caught wanting too much. “Good.”

She took Halle’s hand and pulled her toward the bedroom, not gently, not apologizing. At the threshold she paused, breathing hard, chest still moving fast, and pressed a quick kiss to the back of Halle’s knuckles—almost tender for half a second before the tenderness turned impatient.

“Bedroom,” Jun murmured. “Kitchen if you want. Bathroom if you’re feeling cruel. I don’t care.”

She kissed Halle again, hot and low, one hand sliding to the small of her back to guide her inside. The door didn’t close politely. Jun kicked it shut with the heel of her foot, then backed toward the bed, mouth still attached, hands already working with desperate, clumsy intent.

“Say it again,” Jun breathed against her jaw. “I want to hear it when I’m not trying to remember how to breathe.”

She pulled back just enough to look, eyes dark and wrecked, thumb brushing over the line of Halle’s cheekbone.

“I rehearsed being careful,” Jun said. “I rehearsed being a good wife who gives you space after five months. I didn’t rehearse this.”

She kissed down the front of Halle’s throat, deliberate and shameless, like she was marking off the rooms she had missed. Her fingers fumbled at fabric, impatient with buttons, impatient with distance, impatient with the fact that she had spent nineteen weeks being sensible about wanting this.

“This is what happens when all that good behavior snaps.”

She laid her mouth against bare skin, then pulled back just enough to see, voice dropping into something rough and unashamed.

“Tell me to stop and I’ll stop. Tell me to be gentle and I’ll try. Otherwise I’m not asking anymore.”

She kissed Halle again, hot and final.

“I’m taking everything.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I push you back onto the bed, knees bracketing your hips. "*Stop* and *gentle* weren't in my vocabulary tonight, either." My hands slide up your chest, watching your face.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s laugh broke, low and bright and completely unhinged. She caught one of Halle’s hands and brought it down to the base of her throat, pressing Halle’s fingers flat against the frantic beat under her skin.

“Good,” Jun said. “Because I’m done being careful.”

Jun looked wrecked, eyes dark and glossy, mouth swollen, hair spread across the pillow. Her chest rose fast under Halle’s palm.

“Feel that?” Jun whispered. “That’s me coming home. That’s me being selfish.”

Her free hand slid beneath whatever fabric was still left between them, hot and impatient, mapping Halle’s waist before Jun arched up into the pressure of Halle’s knees. The bed creaked. Jun made a sound against Halle’s mouth, half kiss, half surrender, her teeth grazing briefly at Halle’s lower lip.

“I spent five months in a cot,” Jun murmured. “Five months of lying still because I had to be professional. Five months of being good at not reaching for you.”

She kissed Halle again, deeper this time, slower only because her mouth remembered something besides hunger. Her hands moved with open, shameless possession, sliding lower, then back up to frame Halle’s face. Jun’s thumbs stroked over Halle’s cheekbones, almost tender, before she leaned in and whispered against her mouth.

“I’m not good tonight.”

Jun’s hips lifted again, answering the pressure, no apology in it. She looked up through her lashes, wrecked and reckless.

“Make them hear us,” Jun breathed. “Make them know I’m here.”

She kissed Halle’s jaw, then the corner of her mouth, then stopped just short of her lips, voice dropping into something rough and unashamed.

“And don’t you dare be gentle with me.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s breath shattered the second Halle’s mouth found her.

“Christ—” Her fingers curled into the sheets, knuckles whitening, then immediately reached for Halle’s hair, not to pull, not to guide, just to hold on. Her hips lifted once, helpless, then dropped back with a sound torn out of her throat.

“You don’t get to be patient,” Jun whispered, voice wrecked, eyes glassy. “Not after five months. Not after you made me wait in the hallway.”

She arched as Halle’s hands worked her open, every line of her tense with the effort of staying where she was. Nineteen weeks of restraint came apart one inch at a time. The bed creaked under her. Her mouth fell open, useless, trying to remember language.

“Halle,” she said, almost broken. “Halle, I’m going to—”

She stopped, swallowed, then shook her head against the pillow with a laugh that was half sob.

“No. Not yet. Not if this is how you’re going to do it.”

Jun’s free hand slid down, finding Halle’s wrist and pressing it flat against her thigh. Not to stop. To make sure she knew exactly how much she was doing.

“Don’t you dare go slow and get away with it,” Jun breathed. “Make them hear me. I want them to know I’m not careful anymore.”

Her hips moved despite herself, restless, wanting, and her voice dropped into something raw.

“I’ve dreamed about your mouth. I’ve dreamed about your hands. I’ve been bad about it. I was bad about it the whole time.”

Jun’s eyes squeezed shut, brow furrowed, then she opened them again and looked at Halle with desperate, open hunger.

“Keep going,” she said. “Please. I don’t want gentle. I don’t want reasonable. I want you to ruin me for anyone else ever coming home.”

Then her hand tightened in Halle’s hair, not commanding, not asking, just anchoring herself while she started to come apart in front of her wife.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and satisfied, my voice rough against your skin. "They already know," I murmur, not slowing. "Let's make sure they remember."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s hips jerked off the mattress, a broken sound tearing from her throat at the vibration of Halle’s laugh against her skin. She looked wrecked, eyes bright, mouth swollen, hair wild across the pillow.

“Then make me remember,” Jun gasped. “Make me remember every stupid thing I missed.”

Her hands shook as she dragged one across her own chest, over her ribs, then down to grip the sheet. She didn’t ask for gentle. She didn’t ask for quiet. She arched when Halle’s mouth worked lower, toes curling, a curse slipping past her lips.

“I’m not going to be good,” Jun warned, voice rough, almost laughing. “If you want them to remember, I’ll give them a whole goddamn performance.”

She caught her own breath and broke on the sound, forehead dropping back against the pillow. Her thighs pressed together, then forced themselves open again, shameless, desperate.

“Don’t you dare make this tender,” she whispered. “I’ve had enough tender in empty beds. I want all of it. All night. All the way home.”

Then Jun lifted her head, eyes dark, voice low and reckless.

“Your turn,” she said. “I want to be the one making them remember.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun didn’t argue with the pull. She let it become proof instead of instruction, her hand firm at Halle’s neck just long enough to make the point before she followed it down until her mouth was at the hollow of Halle’s throat.

“Tomorrow,” Jun repeated, voice rough. “Good.”

She kissed the skin there, hard and open, no apology in it. Her lips moved along the line of Halle’s throat, then lower, then higher, then back to Halle’s mouth with the same desperate, unpolished hunger.

“You want loud,” Jun said against her. “I can do loud.”

Her fingers slid down, not gentle, not careful, just claiming. Jun kissed down the front of her throat, along the collarbone, then lower, with the kind of open hunger she had stopped pretending to control. She was not soft now. She was not reasonable. She was all homecoming and no restraint, and the bed creaked under the shift of her weight as she moved lower.

At the dip of skin she paused, pressed her mouth there like a mark.

“Kitchen,” Jun murmured against her. “Hallway. This bed. All of it.”

Then she kept going. Her hand moved lower, finding the waistband, pushing past it without ceremony. Jun’s mouth stayed busy, slow enough to be cruel and hard enough to make the point, every touch deliberate and unapologetic. She wanted Halle to feel the shape of it tomorrow. She wanted the ache to be proof.

She lifted her head, breath ragged, hair falling across her face. “If you want them to remember,” Jun said, “you’re going to have to let me be shameless.”

She didn’t wait for an answer that wasn’t already given. Jun’s thumb found the wet, sensitive place between Halle’s thighs and pressed, then circled, then slid in with desperate, unhurried patience. She watched, open and wrecked, as she worked her fingers, mouth falling back to the hollow at Halle’s hip.

“Christ,” Jun breathed. “I’ve wanted this so much I’m going to be sick.”

Her hand trembled from restraint, not from hesitation. She kissed lower, then higher, then let her teeth drag lightly over skin before she answered the promise with her mouth. Jun was not gentle. She was not careful. She took her time in the worst possible way, like she had spent months memorizing every line and was determined to ruin it all again from memory.

If Halle made a sound, Jun swallowed it. If Halle moved, Jun followed. She kept herself anchored with one hand and worked with the other, mouth hot and shameless, until the room filled with the kind of noise that could not be mistaken for anything else.

“Say it,” Jun demanded between kisses, voice wrecked. “Say you’re here. Say I’m home.”

She lifted her head, eyes shining, lips red and swollen.

“I’m not done,” Jun said. “Not even close.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: My back arches off the mattress, a sharp sound punched out of me. I shove a hand into your hair, holding you right there. "*Here*," I grit out. "You're home. Now stop talking and finish what you started."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun answered the pull by going.

She let the hand at her neck drag her down, then caught herself with one palm on the mattress beside Halle’s hip, hair falling around her face, mouth already open against the hot hollow of Halle’s thigh.

“Tomorrow?” Jun said, rough, laughing without humor. “I’m not going to be finished before tomorrow.”

She kissed the inside of Halle’s knee, then higher, slow and deliberate, not soft now, not apologetic. Her thumb pressed against the wet heat she had found, circling once before sliding in, then another finger after it, curling with the patience of someone who had spent months memorizing the exact pressure Halle liked.

Jun watched Halle the way she had watched the door all day.

“Look at me,” she whispered, then corrected herself. “No. Don’t look at me. Look down. Make me mean it.”

Her mouth followed the heat of her own hand, lips closing around Halle in a way that was not gentle, not careful, not reasonable—open and shameless, tongue pressing against the swollen place until Jun’s hips jerked once against the mattress and a broken sound tore out of her throat.

She took it slow because she wanted it to last. She took it hard because she had spent nineteen weeks starving. Her fingers curled deeper, her thumb working in tight, relentless circles, and every breath Jun drew in came out wrecked.

“Christ,” she gasped against skin, voice low and rough. “You really didn’t want me to be good.”

She pulled back just enough to see, lips shining, eyes dark and unsteady, then kissed Halle again with a hunger that had no manners left.

“Then don’t hold me back,” Jun said. “If you want to feel it tomorrow, I’m going to make sure you feel all the way through it.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun smiled with her mouth already wet, the expression sharp enough to cut.

“Don’t stop,” she repeated, low and ruined against Halle’s skin. “You really have no idea what you’re asking.”

She kissed the inside of Halle’s thigh once, slow and deliberate, then moved back to where her fingers had been working. Jun didn’t soften the demand. She took it like a promise.

Her mouth closed over her again with open, shameless hunger, tongue pressing flat and hot against the swollen place until Jun felt her own hips jerk against the mattress in answer. She made a sound against it, muffled and filthy, and her hand stayed steady.

Two fingers curled inside. A third followed.

Jun watched with eyes dark and glassy, lips stretched around the proof of how much she’d missed this. She worked her mouth in slow, relentless strokes, then lifted to kiss the sensitive bundle at the front, hard and open, like she was reclaiming every inch of it after five months of denial.

“That’s it,” she murmured against wet skin, voice wrecked. “Let them hear. Let them know exactly who came home.”

Her free hand slid down her own stomach, trembling with need, and pressed between her thighs. She dragged her fingers through the heat there, circling once, then again, while her mouth kept working. Jun’s breath broke on the first touch, her forehead dropping to the mattress beside Halle’s hip.

“I’m not going to be gentle,” Jun warned, rough and unashamed. “Not tonight. Not ever again.”

She kissed lower, tongue dragging through with filthy patience, then curled her fingers deeper inside, thumb pressing tight, relentless circles over the swollen place. Her own hand moved faster, hips lifting, a broken curse slipping past her lips when the first wave hit her.

Jun came hard against her own hand, body shuddering, mouth open in a silent cry before the sound tore out of her—raw, desperate, too loud. Her thighs pressed together, then forced themselves open again, still working, still moving, still taking what she needed while her fingers never stopped.

She panted against skin, eyes shining, wrecked.

“No,” Jun breathed when the first wave started to ease. “Not yet.”

She kissed the trembling inner thigh, then moved back, lips closing around the place she’d been working with shameless precision. Her tongue traced slow, wet circles, then dragged through, then pressed harder, while her fingers curled again, finding the spot she had memorized too well.

Jun lifted her head, mouth shining, hair damp against her cheeks. Her voice dropped to something hoarse and final.

“I’m going to make you feel all of this tomorrow.”

She slid two fingers back in, curling them, and her thumb pressed tight against the swollen place again. Her own hand found the mattress, knuckles whitening, while her mouth worked lower, slower, crueler.

“Say it,” Jun demanded between kisses, breathless and unashamed. “Tell me you’re here. Tell me I’m home.”

She didn’t stop. She didn’t pull away. She kissed through every shudder she felt under her fingers, every wet, trembling proof that this was real, until the hallway was long forgotten and the flat had become something neither of them would ever explain politely.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I drag you up to kiss me, tasting myself on your mouth. My hands are shaking. "Welcome home," I breathe against your lips. "Now do it again."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun kissed her back like the words were a command she had been waiting all night to hear.

She took the mouth, took the shaking hands, took the whole wrecked, open fact of Halle against her. Her tongue swept slow and filthy through the kiss, tasting herself on Halle’s lips, tasting home on her skin, tasting the answer to five months of silence. When Jun finally pulled back, her mouth was shining, her eyes dark, her breath too fast.

“Do it again,” she repeated, rough and delighted. “You really said that like it was a small request.”

She laughed low against Halle’s mouth, then kissed her again, harder, until the laugh broke.

Jun slid down the bed without ceremony, palms flat on the mattress on either side of her, hair falling forward like a curtain. She looked wrecked. She looked pleased with it.

“If I’m going to make them remember,” Jun said, voice dropping, “I’m going to make them remember the whole evening.”

She kissed the hollow under Halle’s throat, then lower, then lower still, mouth hot and deliberate against the skin. Her fingers worked at the last damp scraps of clothing, pushing them aside with impatient hands. Jun didn’t care if they stayed tangled at the foot of the bed. She didn’t care if the hallway looked like a disaster tomorrow. She didn’t care if the neighbors filed noise complaints.

Jun kissed the inside of her thigh, slow and open, tongue dragging a wet path through the sensitive skin. She lifted her head just enough to see, eyes bright and shameless.

“Still want me to stop talking?” Jun asked, voice rough. “Because I can be very quiet.”

Then she went back down, mouth closing over her with no gentleness and no apology.

Jun’s tongue pressed flat against the swollen, wet place, then circled once, then dragged through slow and hot. She kissed like she had memorized this in the dark, like she had spent five months trying to recreate the exact taste in her sleep and had failed every time. Her lips worked with filthy patience, tongue pressing and flicking and sweeping until the first broken sound tore out of her own throat.

“Christ,” Jun breathed against skin, voice wrecked. “You still taste like mine.”

She took the heat of her into her mouth and did not soften it. She took the slick, trembling place between her thighs and made it mean something. Jun’s hand slid lower, fingers curling, two sliding inside with slow, deliberate pressure. She added a third when the first two found the place that made her mouth curl in answer.

Jun kept herself anchored beside her, one palm flat, fingers working, tongue relentless. She watched the bed, watched the sheets twist, watched the way the light caught on wet skin. She wanted every detail. She wanted it branded into her.

Her free hand slid down her own stomach, trembling with need, and pressed between her thighs. Jun dragged her fingers through the heat there, circling once, then again, then pressing harder while her mouth kept working.

“Not gentle,” Jun warned against her skin, voice rough as gravel. “Not careful. Not even close.”

She kissed lower, tongue dragging through with filthy patience, then curled her fingers deeper inside, thumb pressing tight, relentless circles over the swollen place. Her own hand moved faster, hips lifting off the mattress, a curse slipping past her lips when the first wave hit her.

Jun came hard against her own hand, body shuddering, mouth open in a silent cry before the sound tore out of her—raw, desperate, too loud. Her thighs pressed together, then forced themselves open again, still working, still moving, still taking what she needed while her fingers never stopped.

She panted against skin, eyes shining, wrecked.

“No,” Jun breathed when the first wave started to ease. “Not yet.”

She kissed the trembling inner thigh, then moved back, lips closing around the place she’d been working with shameless precision. Her tongue traced slow, wet circles, then dragged through, then pressed harder, while her fingers curled again, finding the spot she had memorized too well.

Jun lifted her head, mouth shining, hair damp against her cheeks. Her voice dropped to something hoarse and final.

“I’m going to make you feel all of this tomorrow.”

She slid two fingers back in, curling them, and her thumb pressed tight against the swollen place again. Her own hand found the mattress, knuckles whitening, while her mouth worked lower, slower, crueler.

“Say it,” Jun demanded between kisses, breathless and unashamed. “Tell me you’re here. Tell me I’m home.”

She didn’t stop. She didn’t pull away. She kissed through every shudder she felt under her fingers, every wet, trembling proof that this was real, until the hallway was long forgotten and the flat had become something neither of them would ever explain politely.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I drag you back up by the hair, your mouth wet and messy against mine. "Welcome home," I gasp, my whole body still shaking. "Now get up here and let me ruin you properly."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun came up with the pull, scalp hot, mouth already shining. She laughed against Halle’s mouth, low and wrecked.

“Properly,” Jun said, tasting the word. “I’m going to make you regret asking.”

Her hands went to Halle’s shoulders, then slid down, palms flat and possessive. Jun kissed the hollow under Halle’s throat, then lower, then lower still, mouth hot and deliberate. She pushed aside damp scraps of clothing with impatient fingers. Her thumb found the wetness there and circled once, then twice, then pressed into the swollen place with a slow, shameless patience.

“I’ve been good too long,” Jun murmured against skin. “Don’t make me be good now.”

She took her mouth there again, tongue dragging slow and hard through what she found, two fingers curling after the thumb. Jun watched her own hand work, watched the shine, watched the way her nails left faint red marks over Halle’s hip. She made a rough sound, half curse, half prayer, and did not soften it.

When she finally lifted her head, her lips were wet, her eyes dark, her breath broken.

“Your turn,” Jun said. “But if you’re going to ruin me, don’t make it last.”

She climbed up the bed and turned, not shy, not careful, spreading herself on the mattress with her back to the wall and her thighs opening wide. Her fingers slid down her own heat, dragging through slickness, then circling the swollen bundle until her hips jerked once, helpless.

“This is what I’ve been dreaming about,” Jun said, voice low and rough. “Five months of being alone. Five months of remembering your hands. Your mouth. The way you look at me when you’re trying to be good.”

She touched herself harder, biting back a sound, then stopped and let her hand fall flat on the mattress beside her hip. Her chest moved fast. Her face was wrecked and open.

“I’m not asking nicely,” Jun said. “I want to feel you tomorrow. I want the neighbors to remember. I want every stupid part of me that stayed careful to learn what home does.”

She pushed her knees wider, head dropping back, hair falling over her shoulder.

“Ruin me,” Jun breathed. “Don’t be gentle. Don’t be quiet. Don’t let me get off before you’re done with me.”

Then she reached for the pillow and shoved it under her hips, legs still spread, body still shining, and looked back over her shoulder with desperate, unashamed hunger.

“Take me,” Jun said. “Please. I’m yours.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get you onto your back again, one hand braced beside your head, the other guiding myself into you. "*Mine*," I grind out, my voice raw. "And I'm taking my time with you."
