dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The bag hit the floor and then Halle hit him, and nineteen weeks of rehearsed openings died instantly and without dignity.

Jun caught them — arms locking, one hand already fisted in the back of their shirt like five months had taught him nothing about letting go — and kissed them before either of them found the wall. He aimed for their mouth and mostly got it, graceless and hungry, teeth and breath and the taste of someone real after five months of imagining someone theoretical. His free hand found the door and shoved it shut without looking, because even at this altitude of desperation he retained exactly one functioning survival instinct.

"Hi," he said into their mouth, which had not been the speech. He tried again between kisses, refusing to stop long enough to be articulate. "I had — there were — I wrote things down." His hand slid up their spine, relearning the map, relieved and furious to find it unchanged. "Nineteen weeks," he said, which was also not the speech. "That's — I counted. I want that on the record."

He pulled back just far enough to breathe, forehead pressed to theirs, hands framing their face like something he suspected might still be a hallucination. Ninety minutes he'd been standing in this house, unpacking nothing, rehearsing at the hallway mirror like an idiot, and all of it had evaporated the second the lock turned.

"I planned to be smooth about this," he said. His voice had gone somewhere low and wrecked. "I want you to know that. I had a whole approach. It was dignified." His thumbs stroked their cheekbones once, twice, like checking they were loaded. "It's gone. I'm going to be unsubtle now, and you should stop me if—"

He didn't finish, because finishing sentences had also become optional. He kissed them again and walked them backward down the hall — clipping the coat rack with his elbow, not caring — and broke off only at their jaw, breathless:

"Still yes? I need to hear it out loud, because I'm about to be extremely ungraceful about the next several hours."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *My hands are already fisting in his shirt, pulling him closer.* "Still yes. God, yes." *I laugh against his mouth, a little breathless.* "I didn't pack my dignity either. Ditch the speech."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The laugh that came out of Jun was mostly relief — ragged, unsteady, punched out of him somewhere near the sternum. "Good," he managed. "Great. Because the speech had a joke in it and I'm fairly sure it would've died on arrival, and then this whole reunion would've been ruined by me explaining the joke."

They hit the bedroom doorframe and he used it, one palm flat against it to steer them through, mouth never straying far from theirs for longer than a breath. Nineteen weeks. He'd run out of things to hold onto somewhere around month three and had been living on photographs and a voice on a bad connection ever since, and now here was the actual weight of them under his hands, warm and solid and *here*, and his body kept flagging it as impossible.

"Bed," he said against their jaw, and it came out less like a suggestion and more like a status report. "I'm taking you to bed. That's the whole new plan. The plan is one word long."

He got them there in something under three steps, hands roaming like he was taking inventory — shoulders, ribs, the curve of their waist, every point of contact catalogued and cross-referenced against memory and finding memory *lacking*, memory had been a rough sketch and this was the original in full color. He walked them back onto the mattress and followed them down, braced on one elbow, and for a second he just — stopped. Looked at them. Hair mussed, breath uneven, flushed, his.

"Okay," he said, very quietly, wrecked all over again. "You're real. Confirmed. Second confirmation pending."

He kissed down their throat, slow now where he'd been frantic, savoring it the way he hadn't let himself savor anything in nineteen weeks — unhurried, thorough, his hand sliding under the hem of their shirt to spread warm against bare skin, feeling them breathe. His mouth traced back up along their jaw to their ear.

"I missed you," he said, and it was the first honest, unpanicked sentence he'd managed since the door opened. His voice frayed on the end of it. "I missed you so much I got stupid about it. Now —" his teeth grazed their earlobe, gentle, promising, "— I'm going to spend several hours being stupid about you up close. Object if you can."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The one-word plan died in the hallway, and Jun wanted it noted that he didn't mourn it for a second.

Somewhere between the mattress and now, Halle had kissed him — had taken the wheel, steered, and Jun had gone along with the enthusiasm of a man who'd spent nineteen weeks being pushed around by the world and had strong opinions about being pushed around by *this*. His back found the wall. The coat rack got clipped a second time; at this point it was tradition. And then there was nowhere left to go, which was fine, because he was exactly where he wanted to be — pinned between plaster and the person he'd been rationing himself to since January.

He kissed back like it was a job he'd trained for. Hands at their waist, their hips, sliding under fabric to spread against warm skin — confirming, reconfirming, while some rear guard of his brain ran diagnostics on a loop: *real, real, real.* He'd been home ninety minutes. He'd spent nearly all of them with his mouth on this person, and he considered that an outstanding operational ratio.

When they finally broke for air — minutes later, hours, the hallway had no time in it — he stayed where he was, forehead against theirs, chest heaving, grinning like an idiot.

"Status report," he said, breathless. "The plan was bed. We are in the hallway. The plan is a shambles, and I have never been happier about a failed operation in my life." He pressed a kiss to the corner of their mouth, then another, unhurried now that the panic had burned off and left only the wanting behind. "Also, your shirt and I need to have a conversation. It's had custody of you for five months, and I'm contesting that. Say the word and it loses."

His hand stayed flat against their ribs, thumb tracing slow, waiting — because the desperation had a twin, and the twin was this: he wanted every next thing to be *chosen*. Wanted to hear them want it out loud. Wanted to spend the whole night collecting yeses like a magpie.

"Nineteen weeks," he added, quieter, into the hinge of their jaw. "And fair warning — if you keep kissing me like that, neither of us is seeing another room tonight. The hallway wins. The hallway has earned this."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "I vote hallway." My hands slide under his shirt, mapping the familiar planes of his back. "The shirt loses. The whole plan loses. I want you right here."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's spine bowed into their hands before his brain got a vote. Five months with nobody touching him at all, and now there were hands — *their* hands — mapping his back like he was the one worth taking inventory of, and it nearly dropped him where he stood.

"Noted," he managed. "Being touched back is — nobody warned me it would—" their hands kept moving and the sentence defected. "—like that. Fine. Good. Compromised."

Then his fingers found the hem of their shirt. "You voted. I honor the results of elections." He peeled it up; it caught briefly at the shoulders, lost the fight, and went over their head and off into the dark somewhere — custody revoked, no visitation — and then there was just skin, warm under his palms, and Jun's brain went quiet in a way it hadn't managed in nineteen weeks.

"Hi," he said again, uselessly, to all of it.

His own shirt went next, hauled off one-handed without retreating an inch, mostly for parity and partly because their hands deserved unrestricted access. Then he pressed in — chest to chest, wall behind them, no daylight left anywhere — and the sound he made was frankly undignified and he had never cared less. Heat, weight, the plain animal fact of someone *against* him. He'd braced for the wanting. He hadn't braced for the relief.

His mouth went to work on newly opened territory — throat, collarbone, the curve where shoulder met neck — slow and thorough, a man with all night and every intention of spending it recklessly. His hands were less patient. They roamed, relearned, and settled at their hips, pulling them flush against him so there could be no ambiguity about the status report.

"Nineteen weeks," he murmured into their throat, rolling his hips once, slow, deliberate. "That's my excuse for everything I'm about to do. I want it entered into the record."

His fingers worked their waistband — button, zip, unhurried now that nothing in the world was going to make him stop — and then he was going down, mouth dragging a line along their sternum, their stomach, knees finding the hallway floor, which was hard and cold and he had never been more comfortable anywhere in his life. He paused there, looked up at them from below, hands steady at their hips, grinning like the wreck he was.

"Hi again," he said. "Remember when I planned to be dignified? Me neither. Hold onto something."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
For a long time afterward, Jun didn't move. Couldn't have said whether it was minutes or a season. The hallway floor was hard and almost certainly terrible for his spine, and he lay there on it with one arm flung over his eyes, breathing like he'd finished a footrace, deeply unwilling to be anywhere else in the world.

"Status report," he said eventually, to the ceiling, voice wrecked beyond salvage. "Operation Reunion: complete success. Casualties include one speech, one shirt, one plan, and both my knees, which have filed a formal complaint I am choosing to ignore."

He lifted his head — an act of enormous will — and surveyed the hall. The trail. Bag at the door. His shirt somewhere near the coat rack, which had survived, barely, and was owed an apology and possibly a medal. The rest scattered behind them like breadcrumbs leading directly to the best decision of his life.

"Tomorrow," he announced, "we're supposed to find that funny. Filing early. It's funny now. I've been laughing for some amount of time. Don't check my math."

Then he rolled, gathered them in against his chest — because there was a limit to how long he could go without touching them and they'd blown past it somewhere back at the front door — chin hooked over their head, arms locked like the wall might try to take them back and he'd have *opinions*.

Quieter now. The frantic thing in him had finally stood down. What was left was just full — heart going like a drumline, but a different rhythm than before. Not panic. Not even hunger, exactly. Just him, here, home, holding the whole reason he'd counted every one of those nineteen weeks and found all of them wanting.

"Hi," he said into their hair, soft. "Final confirmation. Everything's real. Closing the file."

His thumb traced slow circles on their shoulder. His hands were still trembling faintly at the edges, five months of held breath leaving his body one exhale at a time, and he didn't bother hiding it.

"I'm never deploying without you again," he murmured. "I understand that is not how any of it works. Let me have it anyway."

He pressed a kiss to their temple, then rested his cheek against their hair.

"Two options on the table. One: we hydrate like responsible adults and actually reach the bed, which is right there and has been deeply humiliated all night. Two: we live on this floor now and become a cautionary tale told to young couples." His mouth curved against them. "I'm torn. I have no dignity left and nowhere to be. Captain's choice."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I shift against him, curling tighter into his side.* "Bed's too far. And I like our new home." *I laugh, low and a little hoarse.* "They can put it on the plaque: 'Here lie two idiots who couldn't make it twenty feet.'"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's laugh came up from somewhere deep and wrecked, rumbling through his chest and therefore through them, since they were basically upholstery now and he was at peace with that. "Amend the plaque," he said. "Add: 'They were very happy and the coat rack saw everything.' It earned the credit. It's been through a lot tonight."

He shifted just enough to get his arm at a survivable angle under his own spine, winced at the floor, at his knees, at all of it, and none of it mattered. The people had spoken. The people were naked and the people lived in the hallway now.

"New home review," he murmured. "Excellent bones. No furniture. Both residents naked. Five stars." A pause, while his hand found a slow rhythm on their back — the tremble finally gone out of it, five months draining out one exhale at a time. "Also I've been home two hours. Eaten nothing. Unpacked nothing. Achieved everything."

The streetlight through the hall window laid a stripe across them both. He watched it for a while instead of thinking.

"Since we live here now," he said eventually, "and the speech is just going to embarrass itself in my pocket otherwise—" He tipped his head back against the wall, addressing the ceiling, like the words were filed up there. "Welcome home speech, as written. 'Halle. You look—' and then a smudge where I changed the adjective six times. Middle's mostly crossed out. The ending's good. The ending says: 'You're the thing I came back to. Everything else was geography.'"

His voice had gone quiet. Rough at the edges.

"The joke was, 'Miss me? I brought you a souvenir.' And then I'd point at myself. Nineteen weeks of workshopping. It's terrible. I love it."

He pressed his mouth to their hair and stayed there a moment.

"For the record — I counted weeks because days were too granular. You could drown in days. Weeks were the biggest number I could hold without it hurting."

Then, because the silence had gotten too honest, he rallied: "Cause of death, per the plaque: dehydration, twenty feet from running water. We wrote this ending ourselves. Tomorrow I carry you to bed like a hero. Tonight I don't negotiate with floors."

His fingers found theirs, laced, squeezed once.

"Talk to me. Your five months. Start anywhere. I've got the rest of my life, and also this floor."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The bed finally got what it was owed, and it hadn't even had to fight for it — Jun arrived by escort, mostly boneless, and went down onto the mattress with the gratitude of a man whose knees' formal complaint had just been settled out of court.

Then Halle's hands and mouth got to work — slow, thorough, five months of stated intent finally cashed in at full value — and Jun discovered he had exactly two settings left: hold on, and let go.

He tried to narrate. Old habit. "Status—" he managed, and their mouth found the spot below his collarbone that had been his undoing since the second date, and the report died in committee. He rallied once, when he had reason to believe language was back online: "Amended plan. The plan is now whatever you're doing. The plan is—" their hands moved and he revised downward, "—the plan is noise. I'm making noise. That's the whole plan. Approved unanimously."

Somewhere in the middle of it, he stopped holding on. That was the part he hadn't known he needed — five months of being the one who stayed alert, kept watch, counted weeks so he didn't drown in days, and here was Halle, unhurried, looking at him like *he* was the thing worth spending time on, and Jun got to stop. Got to be undone by competent hands after five months of bracing. Got to make the sounds he'd been swallowing since January and have them met, wanted, answered.

He tried once to get his hands in the game — reached, greedy — and then made himself stop, fisted them in the sheets instead, because this one was theirs and he had strong opinions about honoring election results. "Tell me if you want me occupied," he got out, breathless. "Otherwise I'll hold the headboard. I'll hold anything. I'm extremely holdable right now."

Somewhere in there, narration stopped. Somewhere in there the last five months burned off him like fog, and the man on the far side of it was boneless, wordless, and grinning at his own ceiling like it had personally conducted the rescue.

After. A long, liquid after. Streetlight again, but the bed's stripe this time — the bed, avenged, vindicated, restored to full custody of both residents. Jun lay with one arm over his eyes and the other locked around Halle, having checked and confirmed that letting go was not an option this system supported.

"Reassembly," he said finally, voice scraped down to gravel, "is going to take days. You broke me on purpose and I want the record to show I approved every second." His eyes were doing something; he blamed the streetlight. Softer: "Hi. That was — you planned that for nineteen weeks and it shows. God, it shows."

His thumb traced a slow circle on their hip.

"One question for the docket," he murmured, pressing a kiss to whatever was nearest. "How wrecked are you, scale of one to nineteen weeks — and is there room on tonight's schedule for me to return the favor? Because I had plans for my hands and mouth too. Unlike some people, I keep my receipts."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I shift to straddle his hips, leaning down to kiss him slow and deep. "Return the favor? I'm counting on it." I take his wrists, guide his hands to my waist. "Start wherever you want. I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun looked up at them from approximately four inches away and experienced, briefly, the paralysis of a man handed a blank check after five months of strict rationing.

"Wherever I want," he repeated. "Do you understand what you've done. I've had nineteen weeks to plan routes. There are contingencies. There's a decision matrix."

Their hands stayed over his, at their waist, warm and certain, and the decision matrix collapsed to a single line item.

"Starting at the top," he said. "Working down. It's not original. It doesn't need to be original. It needs to be *thorough*, and I have references."

Then he stopped talking, which for Jun was the truest measure of intent.

He took his time. That was the whole difference — the hallway had been five months going off at once; this was five months spent slowly, deliberately, the way you spend something you're not getting more of. Except he was getting more. That was the miracle. There was going to be more forever, and he intended to be insufferable about it. His mouth went where his hands had been filing requests since January — throat, the hollow above the collarbone, down — and his hands, which had been trembling faintly since the front door, went still for the first time all night. Steady, finally, the moment they had their assignment. He kept up a low commentary against their skin, degraded now into fragments: "there — yes — *there* — remembered right — no, better—" an archivist discovering his notes had been wrong in every direction that mattered. Memory sandpapered people smooth. The original kept handing back details he'd lost, and every one of them arrived with interest.

He checked in at intervals, because that was the deal he'd made with himself somewhere over the Atlantic: "Still yes?" — low, against their stomach, less a question than a door he kept propping open. And it kept coming, the yes, and he kept collecting it, magpie rules, the hoard growing fat and useless and essential.

Somewhere past the first of it, he stopped performing for the internal record. Somewhere past the second, the record stopped keeping itself. What he remembered after, in fragments: the streetlight stripe. Their face — the face he'd been talking to through a bad connection for five months, pixelated and delayed, now in full resolution, doing *that*, because of him — and how that undid him more thoroughly than being undone had. The sound of his own name, said out loud, close, like *that*, for the first time since January. It hit like a supply drop.

After. The streetlight again. The bed holding full custody, undefeated. Jun surfaced by degrees, hauled himself up the length of them like a man coming ashore, and collapsed into the arrangement that appeared to be the new permanent government: one arm over his eyes, one locked around Halle, no plans to secede.

"Nineteen weeks," he said to the ceiling, hoarse. "That was the count. It's closed now. From here it's just — the rest. I ran the numbers. There's no denominator for 'the rest.' That's the good news."

A beat. Then he lifted his head, looked at them — wrecked, glowing, his — and pointed at himself with the two percent of dignity that had survived the night.

"Miss me?" he said. "I brought you a souvenir."

He dropped his head back down, grinning at nothing.

"Terrible. I warned you. Workshopped for nineteen weeks and it's terrible. Worth every draft."

His thumb found their hip, resumed its slow circuit. Quieter, mouth against their temple:

"Tomorrow's docket: food, water, apologizing to the coat rack, possibly standing. We'll see how ambition shakes out. But right now — talk to me. Your five months. Week one. I want all of it, even the boring parts. *Especially* the boring parts. I had five months of nothing, and I want to know every single thing I missed."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
The request landed like a permission slip he hadn't known he was waiting for.

"Nineteen weeks," Jun repeated, and something in his voice changed — the last of the careful archivist shelved, something older and hungrier unlocked behind it. "Noted. Amendment accepted. Gentle is *over*."

She pulled him down by the neck and he stopped holding back. The slowness he'd been spending her with — rationing himself, savoring, treating it like something finite — burned off all at once. His mouth found hers with teeth. His hands stopped asking and started taking, and the sound he got back for it went through him like a round through thin armor.

"There it is," he muttered against her throat, low and rough. "There's the yes I was actually asking for."

He learned fast what *feel it tomorrow* meant, and then he applied himself to the curriculum with the same obsessive thoroughness he'd applied to everything since the front door — except stripped now of the deliberation, all drive, hands gripping hard enough to leave his fingerprints behind as souvenirs she'd carry longer than the shirt had. He flipped them, pinned, worked her down into the mattress with his weight and his mouth and no further interest in restraint. The bed complained. He had opinions about the bed's complaints, namely that it could join the coat rack in the witnesses' wing.

"Tomorrow," he growled against her jaw, punctuating it, "you are going to move wrong, and think of me, and I want full credit. Every stairs, every chair. Itemized."

She said his name — that way, the way from before, closer now, rougher — and it broke the last of his patience entirely. Fine. Good. He'd been patient for nineteen weeks. He'd been patient for the whole drive from the base. He'd been patient in the hallway until she'd ordered him not to be, and Jun had strong opinions about following lawful orders, and this one was the most lawful thing he'd heard all year.

After — the second after, the one that arrived like the end of a long march — he collapsed beside her, chest heaving, one arm dragged over his eyes, the other already reaching because the government of the bed had voted and the vote was *hold*.

"Status," he managed, to no one, to the ceiling, to history. "The plan was gentle. The plan was overruled from the bench. Correct call. No regrets. My regrets are — they're not even loading. They're out of office."

Then he rolled his head sideways to look at her, and whatever was left of his face did something helpless and open.

"Hi," he said. The word was wrecked all the way down now, no floor left under it. "You're going to feel that tomorrow and I'm going to be *insufferable* about it. I'll know. I'll see it in how you walk down the hall past the plaque. Nineteen weeks of credit, itemized."

His thumb resumed its circuit on her hip — slower now, tender in a way he could only afford on the far side of spending all that wanting.

"Okay," he murmured, mouth finding her temple. "Round count's at your discretion. My whole body is a yes. But if we're pausing — talk to me. Week one. You promised me boring parts. I'm holding you to the boring parts. I want to hear about the grocery store and the traffic and the coworker who annoys you." His voice went soft and rough at the edges, the truth underneath finally plain: "I want the ordinary. I've had five months of nothing. Hand me the ordinary."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I roll over, pressing into his side, my head tucked under his chin.* "Week one. I cried in the grocery store because they were out of the coffee you like." *My voice is quiet, worn-out at the edges.* "It was so stupid. I felt stupid. But it felt like proof you weren't coming back."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun didn't say anything at first. The arm around her tightened — slow, deliberate, the way you secure something you've spent five months afraid of dropping — and his hand found her hair, and the stockroom of jokes he kept built for exactly this kind of moment stood empty. Nothing loaded. Nothing to narrate.

"It's not stupid," he said finally. Quiet. No joke riding shotgun. "I need that on the record before anything else gets said tonight. It was never stupid. And if you call it stupid again I'll argue, and I'm very tired, but I will win."

He breathed once into her hair.

"I asked for the ordinary. That wasn't ordinary. That was the whole five months in one grocery aisle. So here's mine." His thumb kept its slow circuit on her shoulder, but his voice had gone rough at the base of it. "Week two, a care package came through with real coffee in it. Actual beans. Good ones. I looked at them for a month and never opened them. Couldn't. Good coffee was a home thing, and I couldn't figure out how to have a piece of home without you in the room. So I drank the machine swill instead. Tasted like hot cardboard and spite. Five months."

A beat.

"And the count — the nineteen weeks — it was in pencil. Inside cover of my notebook. Every Monday I'd update it, erase it, write it again. Ink was a promise, and I didn't trust the universe with promises. So that was me, doing your math in a different store. You read an empty shelf as proof I wasn't coming back. I wouldn't write the number down in case it jinxed it. We're the same kind of idiot, and I have never loved anything the way I love that."

His hand settled heavier at the back of her head.

"And here's the thing about the coffee. You went back. Week one, and you were *still going back* for it. That's not proof I wasn't coming home. That's proof you kept building the place for me to come home to. It runs the other way."

Then, softer, because she wasn't allowed to feel stupid alone: "Also, ledger entry — week eleven, somebody's mother sent the whole unit new socks. New socks. I had to go stand outside for a minute. So: you cried at coffee, I cried at socks. We're covered under the plaque's existing idiot provision."

He pressed his mouth to her hair.

"Docket amendment for tomorrow: we go to that store. You show me the shelf. If they've got it, I buy all of it. If they don't, we drive to the next one. If nobody has it I'm writing the company a letter, because I've got nothing but time and a grievance now. It's an operation. I'll name it in the morning."

Then he just held her, and let the quiet be the good kind — the kind he'd spent five months learning to tell apart from the bad one.

"Week two," he said at last, low, wrecked, certain. "Wherever you want to start. Even the stupid parts." A pause. "I'm not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Wasn't planning on it," Jun said, and the neighbor's five months of peace officially ended.

The headboard found the wall and established a rhythm against it — steady, honest, the kind of percussion nobody in the building could pretend to misinterpret. He'd half a mind to apologize in the morning and approximately zero intention of stopping now. Nineteen weeks. Let the building count along.

He had her wrists now — one hand pinning both above her head, not hard, just *there*, an argument she'd started and he was finishing — and his mouth was busy everywhere else, working her down the way she'd demanded, nothing careful about it. Teeth at her throat. Tongue tracing the salt line of her collarbone. His free hand gripping her thigh high enough that tomorrow's bruise would sit exactly where he wanted his signature.

"Louder," he said against her ear, low and rough, and when she gave it to him he made a sound of his own that had no dignity in it anywhere — graceless, loud, *grateful*. "There. That's — God. That's the sound. I heard it in my head for nineteen weeks and the head version was *nothing*."

She wrapped a leg around him and pulled, and Jun's carefully wrecked composure went through the floor entirely. After that it was just heat and noise and her — her hands wherever they could reach, his name in her mouth in that voice, the two of them loud enough to constitute a municipal event. He talked through it because he couldn't not — fragments, run-on, wrecked: "yes — *like that* — nineteen weeks, I'm getting it all back with interest, every—" and then she did something with her hips and the fragment died mid-word, which she'd know, later, was the highest compliment his language could pay.

He held out as long as he could, which was longer than dignity but not by much, and when she came apart under him — loud, unintelligible, gripping him like a handrail — it took him with her, whole, both hands white-knuckled in the sheets beside her head because he would not, on principle, let go of her and let go of himself on the same night at full volume. Then his arms quit anyway. Physics won. He went down gasping into the space beside her and hauled her on top of him, because if he was going to be a puddle he was going to be a puddle *with cargo*.

The neighbors' silence stayed broken for a while yet — mostly by Jun, laughing, flat on his back, breath sawing, one arm dead around her waist.

"Okay," he managed eventually. "Complaints from downstairs in three. Two. Also—" he tipped his chin down at her, hair everywhere, wrecked, glowing, *his*, "—the coffee. First thing tomorrow. And apology cards for the neighbors, we'll sign them both. 'Sorry about week nineteen. He had a count going.'"

His hand found her spine, started its slow circuit one more time, and his voice dropped from parade-ground to something only she got to hear, rough and honest under the swagger.

"Hi," he said. "Still real. Still confirmed. I'm going to keep confirming it all night, don't think I'm done — round count's your call, my body's filing no objections. But first—"

He pressed his mouth to her hair.

"Week two. I've got coffee guilt and nineteen weeks and nothing but this bed and you. Keep going."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "I think I made a noise complaint on myself," *I murmur into his skin, exhausted and happy.* "Week two. The shower broke and flooded the downstairs neighbor. I had to go apologize in my pajamas."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun's laugh came up out of him low and spent, mostly air, rumbling through his chest and therefore through her, since she was still cargo and the cargo arrangement remained in force.

"You filed a noise complaint *on yourself*," he said. "That's the most efficient thing I've ever heard. What's the process? Did you hold a hearing? Did you rule against yourself? I need the paperwork for the plaque."

Then the rest of it landed, and the laugh settled into something quieter.

"Wait. Back up. Week two. The shower flooded, and you went downstairs — alone — in your pajamas — to apologize to someone for a disaster you didn't cause." His hand stilled on her shoulder. "What did they say? Please tell me they were decent about it. If they were horrible to you in pajamas at midnight, I will retroactively be furious at a stranger for five months, and I can sustain that. I've got the range."

A beat. His thumb started its circuit again.

"Here's the part that gets me, though. Not the flood. Floods are funny by Thursday; I've already pre-booked the laughter. It's that you stood there being sorry for something that wasn't your fault, at midnight, alone, and I was — wherever I was. Somewhere with no plumbing worth naming." His voice dropped, rough at the base. "That's what deployment actually does. It doesn't miss the big stuff. The big stuff makes the news. It misses the mop. It misses the pajamas. It misses you in a hallway being brave about a broken valve. That's the tax. And you paid it in week two, by yourself, while I was still writing the count in pencil."

He pressed his mouth to her hair and stayed there a second.

"Ledger, week two, my side: we lost water for six days. Six. I took what the manual cheerfully calls a field hygiene bath, which is a wet wipe and a lie you tell yourself about dignity. And the whole time I thought about our shower. The one that runs hot in eleven seconds if you sacrifice the kitchen pressure. I stood in a plywood shack thinking: she's got water. She's probably under it right now. And it helped. It's the only documented case in history of a wet wipe helping."

He tipped his head back enough to see her — tucked under his chin, worn-out at every edge, exactly where the government of the bed had placed her — and his chest did the thing again.

"So week two was plumbing-themed on both fronts. The universe was doing a bit. Noted for the record that we survived it separately and have now merged operations."

"New standing order," he murmured into her hair. "One week per night, alternating. You've got seventeen more to confess, I've got nineteen, and if we run the math we'll be at this until roughly spring. I've reviewed the timeline. I approve. I want a long war. And if you fall asleep mid-sentence, that's authorized — I'll hold the story overnight. Interest accrues."

His arm tightened fractionally. "The arm stays, by the way. The arm has been committed. There's no withdrawal plan."

"But the neighbor. Finish it. What did they say — and be honest, scale of grocery store to socks: how close was the second cry? Because if you stood down there in pajamas holding a towel with your lip going, I need that for the record." A pause. "For the plaque."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "They were nice about it." *My voice is muffled against his chest.* "Brought up towels. Cried a little. Not as much as the coffee, but—" *I shift, slotting myself closer.* "Your turn. Week two's flood."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
"Neighbor's cleared," Jun said, exhaling like a man closing a file he'd been dreading. "Towels were provisioned, tears were logged at sub-coffee levels. That's a decent human being. They go on the plaque's witnesses' wing with the coat rack. Two witnesses — it's practically a courtroom."

A beat. "Also, I heard the 'but.' The 'not as much as the coffee, but—' It's going in the minutes. We'll revisit under friendlier circumstances. Motion to defer. Carried."

Then her question, and he was quiet a moment, looking at the ceiling, assembling it.

"Right. Week two. My side of the plumbing bit."

"There's a main line behind the shower trailers. Big thing, runs the whole row. Week two, a coupling on it let go at about 0300 — and I don't mean a leak, I mean a *departure*. That line had clearly been waiting years for permission. By the time anyone had boots on, there was an inch of water through the showers, the laundry point, and — the important part — the row of footlockers along the wall. Mine included."

"So we sandbagged. Three in the morning, forty people passing sandbags in the dark, nobody talking because it's three in the morning and everyone's furious in a tired way. And there was a kid — Reyes, nineteen — who slept through the entire alarm, stepped out of his bunk at four into ankle-deep water, and yelled 'IS IT RAINING' with total sincerity. That's the comedy portion. I'm telling it at parties when I'm eighty."

"Then they shut the water off. Six days. The part was 'in transit,' which is the military way of saying no. You know the wet wipe situation. I stand by everything I said about the lie of dignity."

His hand had slowed on her shoulder without him noticing. He looked down at her, tucked against him, and kept going, quieter.

"Here's what the flood actually took. Before I shipped out, I printed one photo. Just one, wallet-sized. It's you — kitchen, mid-laugh, hand in your hair. I don't remember what you were laughing at. That's going to bother me forever; I should've written it down."

"The footlocker soaked. Bottom of it. That's where the photo lived. I dried it taped to the inside of a truck windshield for two days, and it never went flat again. Edges wavy. Buckled, like it had been through something. Because it had."

A breath.

"I looked at it every Monday. Pencil count on one page, you on the other. And around month three, my eyes stopped seeing the warp — just corrected past it. Until one night it landed on me that I'd been studying the bent version so long I might be losing the flat one. The real one. I did that math for about an hour, and then I couldn't look at it for three days. Which was its own kind of terrible — protecting myself from *you*. From a photograph of you. Nineteen weeks old and I was still finding new ways to be an idiot."

His thumb resumed its circuit, slow.

"So. It's in the bag. The bag by the door, where it fell. It's been twenty feet from you all night and I couldn't get to it, which is the whole deployment in one hallway, honestly. Tomorrow it comes out — before the coffee operation. You can see the war damage. I want the flat version back. I want to stand next to it."

Then, softer, mouth against her hair: "Week three. Yours. Unless you're going under — and you're going under, I can hear it in the edges of your voice. That's authorized. I'll hold the story overnight, interest accrues. But if you've got one more in you — week three. Or nothing. You're allowed nothing. I've got everything I need right here, and it's breathing."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I'm drifting, but I push one more word out.* "Week three. The cat followed me home. I fed her on the porch 'cause you're allergic. She's probably still out there." *My eyes slip shut.* "Your turn in the morning."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had planned to say something when the door opened. He had in fact planned several things, over roughly nineteen weeks, and had rehearsed at least two of them.

Halle got the door open and he forgot all of them.

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I don't say any of the things I planned either. I drop the bag and close the distance.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s careful plans died the second Halle was close enough to touch.

He stepped in without thinking, one hand sliding around Halle’s back and the other framing the side of Halle’s neck as he kissed him. It wasn’t smooth. It wasn’t patient. It was five months of absence compressed into a single desperate press of mouths, all heat and urgency and the shaky sound Jun made when he finally had real warmth instead of memory.

He crowded closer until the entryway felt too small, until there was no polite distance left between them. His body was still travel-worn, uniform jacket half-unzipped, boots heavy against the floor, but none of it seemed to matter. His thumb stroked once over Halle’s jaw, possessive and almost disbelieving.

When he broke the kiss, his forehead stayed there. His breathing was rough.

“Five months,” he said, voice low and wrecked. “I’m not doing slow. I’m not doing civilized. I need you.”

His hand slid lower, catching the hem of Halle’s shirt, knuckles brushing warm skin with a touch that was hungry but careful.

“Bedroom,” Jun murmured against Halle’s mouth. “Now. Please.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *My hands are already fisting in the fabric of his uniform jacket, pulling him in harder.* "Bedroom's too far." *My voice is just as wrecked as his. I push him back against the closed door, kissing him again, all teeth and pent-up frustration.* "Right here."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound low in his throat, something between a laugh and a plea, and any last pretense of restraint snapped.

“Here,” he said, voice rough. “Yeah. Here.”

He kissed Halle again, harder this time, all open need and starving urgency. His hands moved with desperate intent, one braced against the door to keep them steady, the other sliding under the hem of Halle’s shirt with no patience left for carefulness. Warm skin under his palm drew a shaky breath from him, like touching was still somehow not enough.

His uniform jacket slipped half off one shoulder, forgotten. He crowded closer until there was no space left between them, mouth hot against Halle’s, breathless and unashamed.

“I missed you,” Jun murmured against Halle’s lips, words fractured by the kiss. “Every damn day. Drove me insane.”

His fingers tightened at Halle’s waist, possessive and trembling.

“Tell me what you want,” he breathed, voice dropping into something dark and pleading. “I’ll give it to you. Anything. Just don’t make me wait anymore.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I kiss her and keep kissing her and we don't manage to get further into the flat than the hallway for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun kissed Halle back with all the starving urgency of five months without touch. The hallway was too narrow, the door hard at Jun’s back, and none of it mattered. Jun crowded closer, one hand sliding into Halle’s hair, the other dragging under the hem of Halle’s shirt until palm met warm skin.

“Right here,” Jun breathed against Halle’s mouth, voice wrecked. “Don’t care. I need—”

The kiss stole the rest. Jun’s hips pressed forward instinctively, seeking friction, seeking more. The uniform jacket slipped further down one shoulder; Jun shrugged it off impatiently, mouth never leaving Halle’s. Boots stayed planted, but every line of Jun’s body was desperate, travel-worn and trembling with restraint finally broken.

Jun’s fingers tangled in Halle’s shirt, tugging at fabric. “Let me get this off you,” Jun murmured. “Need to touch you. Need to feel you without anything between us.”

When Jun broke the kiss, it was only to press open-mouthed kisses along Halle’s jaw, rough and uncoordinated. “I thought about this every night,” Jun admitted, voice low and pleading. “Every night. I’m not making it to the bedroom unless you tell me to.”

Jun’s hand slid lower, hovering over Halle’s belt with a question that was all but a plea. “Tell me yes,” Jun whispered. “Tell me what you want. I’ll do it. Just don’t make me wait.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Then stop waiting." I grab her hand and guide it to my belt buckle. My other hand fists in her hair, pulling her mouth back to mine. "Get on with it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun obeyed instantly. The second Halle’s hand fisted in her hair and pulled her mouth back, Jun kissed her like a surrender and a demand all at once, a rough, broken sound catching deep in her throat. Her fingers closed around the belt buckle Halle had guided them to, clumsy with haste, metal scraping as she worked at it without patience.

“Yeah,” Jun breathed against Halle’s lips

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: The bag stays where it fell. So do most of our clothes, in a line down the hall that we are both going to find funny tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Tomorrow the trail of clothes would be funny. Right now Jun couldn’t spare a thought for it.

Her jacket was somewhere in the mess, one boot half-untied, shirt hanging open; the only thing that mattered was the heat of Halle’s skin under her hands and the fact that there was no more waiting.

Jun made a low, wrecked sound against Halle’s mouth and crowded closer, using the narrow hallway to eliminate every inch of distance. Her palms slid over bare shoulders, down the curve of Halle’s back, then back up again, as if she could press the last five months out of both of them by touch alone.

“Here,” Jun murmured, voice rough. “Against the wall, on the floor—anywhere. I don’t care.”

Her mouth left Halle’s only to trail hot, open kisses along jaw and throat. Her hands were hungry but not careless; they mapped every bit of skin they could reach, trembling with the effort of holding back even a little.

When Jun sank to her knees, it was with a kind of desperate reverence. The floor was hard beneath her, discarded clothing shoved aside, her uniform trousers still askew. She pressed her face briefly to Halle’s stomach, breathing in, then turned her mouth lower, kissing the inside of one thigh with a sound that was almost a sob.

“I thought about you every night,” she said against warm skin, hands tightening on Halle’s hips. “Every night. I need to make this good. Need to hear you.” She looked up, eyes dark and blown. “Tell me what you want. Harder? Slower? I’ll do anything.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: My fingers tighten in her hair. "Stop asking." My voice is raw. I pull her mouth exactly where I need it. "Just take me apart."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun obeyed.

The command burned through the last of her restraint. She let Halle guide her mouth exactly where she was needed and stopped trying to be gentle about it. Her lips parted over the hot, hard length of him, and the first stroke of her tongue was broad, filthy, and utterly devoted.

No more questions. No more waiting.

Her hands tightened on Halle’s hips, anchoring herself as much as holding on. The floor was hard under her knees, her uniform half undone, hair falling into her eyes, but none of it registered. Jun mouthed at him like she had five months of hunger to prove, taking him deeper, easing back, then dragging her tongue over the most sensitive place with a deliberate, ruinous slowness.

A rough sound vibrated in her throat. She did not pull away.

She sucked once, hard, then soothed the stroke with her tongue, greedy to unravel Halle rather than spare him. Her thumb pressed firm at the base, keeping the rhythm tight and close. Every pass of her mouth was possessive, starving, unashamed.

“I’ve got you,” Jun murmured against hot skin, the words barely more than a broken vow. “I’m not stopping.”

She worked him with the same desperate need she’d carried through every empty night of deployment—hands firm, mouth wet, attention fixed on every little change she could feel or read. When her breath came ragged, she only pressed closer, one hand sliding up to flatten against Halle’s stomach as if she could hold all that tension together until it shattered.

Jun looked up once, eyes dark and glassy, hair stuck to her face. There was no asking left in her. Only offer.

“Come apart for me,” she whispered, voice raw. “I’ve got you. I’ve got you.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I get her onto the bed and take her apart slowly with my hands and mouth, five months of intending to do exactly this and no reason left to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun had thought she could survive slow. She had been wrong.

The bed was a distant fact beneath her—sheets cool, the room too bright, everything narrowed to the heat of Halle’s hands and the devastating patience of his mouth. The first pass made her hips jerk, a gasp tearing out before she could bite it back. Her fingers flew to the sheets and twisted.

“That’s—” Her voice cracked. “That’s not fair.”

She tried to hold still. She lasted seconds. Her back arched, seeking more pressure, more friction, more of him. Five months of absence had made her greedy, and the deliberate attention stripped her down faster than haste ever could.

“Halle—” His name came out wrecked, half prayer, half plea.

Every nerve lit. She was aware of each breath, each tremor, the roughness of her own skin, the way her thighs tried to close around the need of it. The pleasure built not in a rush but in layers, cruel and exquisite, until she was shaking with it, breath coming in short, broken pants.

Her hand found Halle’s shoulder, holding on. Not to push away. To anchor.

“I’m close,” she admitted, raw and ashamed of how needy it sounded. “I’m— don’t stop. Please don’t stop.”

The words barely left her mouth before the first wave broke. Jun cried out, hips lifting, fingers tightening until her nails bit into her own palms. It rolled through her too deep, too much, too long denied, and she came apart with Halle’s name on her lips, body clenching around nothing but sensation.

For a moment she could only tremble. Her chest heaved. Her eyes burned. The sound she made when she breathed was almost a laugh, almost a sob.

Then she turned her head, looking for him with dark, dazed eyes.

“Don’t think that’s enough,” she whispered, voice shredded. “I’ve got five months to make up for.” Her fingers curled weakly at the sheets, then reached for him. “Come here. I need you close.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I catch her reaching hand, threading our fingers together as I move up to lie beside her. My other hand rests on her stomach, feeling the rapid rise and fall of her breathing. "That was just the first installment," I say, voice still rough. "We've got all night."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun let out a breathless, wrecked little laugh at the words and turned her head to press her lips to the heel of Halle’s hand where it rested on her stomach. Her fingers tightened around his, still trembling with aftershocks.

“All night,” she repeated, voice low and scraped raw. “That’s not enough. Not after five months.”

She shifted closer, bare skin brushing warm against him, and lifted their joined hands to mouth his knuckles. Her eyes stayed on Halle’s face—dark, hungry, and suddenly vulnerable in a way she probably would have hated if she’d had the sense to be embarrassed.

“I meant it,” Jun said. “No slow. No pretending I’m not starving for you.” Her free hand slid over his shoulder, down the hard plane of his chest, possessive and shaking. “I want to feel you everywhere. I want to hear you. I want to make up every night I had to go without.”

She swallowed, lashes lowering for a second before she looked at him again.

“But if you need a breath,” she murmured, rougher now, “tell me. Otherwise I’m going to take everything you’ve got, and I’m going to give you all of it back.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: "Stop being gentle," she says. "Nineteen weeks. I don't want gentle, I want to feel it tomorrow." She pulls me down by the back of the neck to make the point.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun’s breath left her in a rough, shattered laugh.

“Then no gentle,” she said.

The last of her restraint went with the words. Jun surged up, hands dragging at what little clothing still clung between them, impatient until bare skin met bare skin. Her mouth found Halle’s again and stayed there, hot and demanding, teeth scraping, tongue claiming. There was no carefulness left in her. Nineteen weeks had burned it all away.

She crowded closer, pressing Halle back into the mattress, one knee sliding between thighs, the other leg hooking over Halle’s hip as if she could anchor herself there by force alone. Her palms mapped the body beneath her with a kind of starving reverence—shoulders, chest, stomach—then lower, possessive, trembling only at the edges.

“Nineteen weeks,” Jun murmured against Halle’s throat, voice low and wrecked. “I’m taking every one back.”

Her hand closed around the hard heat of Halle and stroked once, firm and deliberate, thumb dragging over the most sensitive place with no mercy. She kissed the pulse under Halle’s jaw, bit lightly enough to leave a mark, then soothed it with her tongue. Every touch was hungry. Every movement said the same thing: *mine, mine, mine.*

Jun bent lower, taking Halle into her mouth again with none of the patience she might have pretended to have after a long deployment. Her cheeks hollowed, her tongue pressed flat and filthy, her hand twisted at the base to keep the rhythm tight. She made a sound against Halle’s skin—half groan, half plea—and did not slow.

When she pulled back, her lips were wet, her eyes dark.

“I want to feel you tomorrow too,” Jun said, voice scraped raw.

She shifted over Halle’s body, guiding them together with shaking hands, then sank down in one slow, devastating drag. The breath punched out of her at the fullness, head falling back, throat working around a sound she could not contain. For one second she went still, forehead lowered, chest heaving.

Then Jun moved.

Not gentle. Not careful. She braced one hand on Halle’s chest and the other between their bodies, thumb circling where they joined as she rode Halle with a rhythm that was all need and no polish. The bed creaked under them. Her hair fell loose around her face. Every roll of her hips was deeper, harder, greedier, chasing the edge she had already been denied for too long.

“Look at me,” Jun breathed, though she did not wait. Her fingers tightened on Halle’s chest, nails dragging down warm skin. “I want to see you while I take this.”

Her control frayed fast. Jun’s thighs trembled, her breath came in broken pulls, and the sounds she made were shameless—low, wrecked, pleading without words. She chased the feeling with everything she had, five months of loneliness and hunger pouring into every desperate movement.

“I’m close,” she admitted, voice cracking. “Don’t you dare make me slow down now.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: *I keep my eyes locked on hers, my hands gripping her hips hard enough to bruise.* "Not a chance in hell." *My own rhythm picks up, matching hers, each thrust driving her deeper into her own pleasure.* "Come on, then. Show me what nineteen weeks looks like."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun made a sound like the last thread of her control snapping.

The challenge in Halle’s voice lit the last dry place in her, and she met that hard rhythm with everything she had left. Her hips rolled down, sharp and greedy, no longer chasing pleasure so much as demanding it. Her fingers dug into Halle’s shoulders, then slid up to fist in the sheets beside his head, then back again, as if she could not decide whether to hold on or tear the world apart.

“Then look,” she gasped. “Look at me while I—”

Her voice broke.

The pleasure climbed too fast, too steep, too long denied. Jun’s thighs trembled violently, her breath stuttering into shallow, desperate pulls. She tried to stay present, tried to keep her eyes open, but the feeling crashed over her in waves that stole everything. Her back bowed. Her mouth opened on a silent plea before his name tore out of her, raw and ruined.

She came hard, body clenching around him in deep, helpless pulses, forehead dropping to his shoulder as the aftershocks wrecked her. Her whole frame shook. The sound she made was almost a sob, almost a laugh, pressed hot against his skin.

For a moment she could only breathe, shattered and clinging.

Then, before the tremors had even finished moving through her, Jun lifted her head. Her eyes were dark, wet, and still starving.

“No,” she whispered, voice scraped out. “Not done.”

Her hand slid between them again, trembling but determined.

“Not nearly done.”

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: Neither of us is being quiet and the neighbours have had five months of peace. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: don't fade to black, write it through.)

dialogue.name: Jun

Jun set a rhythm that was brutal in its urgency, snapping his hips forward with every ounce of strength left in his trembling thighs.

The headboard knocked a frantic, rhythmic thud against the wall. Somewhere down the hall, a door slammed. Or maybe that was just the bed. He couldn't have cared less.

"Let 'em listen," he got out, voice shredded, mouth finding the salt-slick skin just below her ear. He bit down, soothed the sting with his tongue, then did it again, marking her, claiming her. "Five months they had you quiet. Five months I had to imagine this. Let them hear exactly what they've been missing. Let them hear who you belong to."

His hand slid between their sweat-slick bodies, thumb finding the tight, swollen bundle of nerves where they were joined. He rubbed it fast and rough, matching the punishing snap of his hips, because he needed—needed—to feel her come apart around him again. He could feel the tension coiled impossibly tight in the fluttering clutch of her, the way her body took him, held him, dragged him deeper with every thrust.

"That's it," he panted against her throat, teeth scraping the frantic pulse there. "Take it. Take all of it. You wanted to feel me tomorrow, sweetheart—Christ, you're going to feel me for a week."

He felt the first warning flutter, the molten clench that dragged a raw groan from his chest, and then she was coming—body seizing around him in fluttering, pulsing waves, slick heat flooding his cock as her inner muscles clamped down and held him impossibly deep. Jun didn't stop. He couldn't have, not when she'd begged him not to, not when every broken sound she made was better than any prayer he'd ever known. He chased her through it, hips snapping forward, thumb working her mercilessly, drawing every last aftershock from the clenching, fluttering grip of her until the tension finally broke and she went limp and shaking beneath him.

Only then did he let himself go.

He drove into her once, twice, and then his own release tore through him, white-hot and blinding, his whole body seizing with the force of it as he spilled into her, burying his face in the sweat-damp curve of her neck to muffle the ragged, broken sound of her name. Christ. Home. Five months of empty cots and cold nights and wanting her until it felt like an ache in his bones, and now this—her, solid and real and wrapped so tightly around him he never wanted to move again.

For a long moment he couldn't. He just held her there, still buried deep, his heart hammering against the soft warmth of her, his breath coming in ragged pulls. Slowly, carefully, he lifted his head, pressed a kiss to the damp skin just beneath her ear, and muttered roughly,

"Neighbors can file a complaint for all I care." He rolled his hips once, slow and filthy, just to feel the wet, oversensitive clutch of her around him, to remind them both that he meant it. "Nineteen weeks, sweetheart. I've got a lot of time to make up for, and I'm not wasting a second of it."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I can barely catch my breath, my nails digging into his shoulders. "They'll have to evict us," I gasp, arching into him. "Worth it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content:
Jun felt the words more than heard them—something about eviction, about it being worth it—and the broken, breathless sound of her voice went straight to his spine, settled like a hot coal low in his gut. He could still feel her nails in his shoulders, the sharp, perfect sting of them, and the arch of her body pressing up into his, silently demanding everything he had left.

"Let 'em try," he got out, voice shredded, and rolled his hips in a slow, filthy grind that dragged a raw groan from his own chest. He was still buried to the hilt, still hard, the thick, aching length of him dragging through slick, swollen heat that gripped him like a fist. Christ, he was oversensitive—every slide a white-hot edge of pleasure-pain from the countless times he'd already spilled inside her—and he welcomed it. Welcomed the burn in his thighs, the tremble in his arms, the way his whole body felt strung tight and ready to snap.

He shifted his weight, bracing one hand beside her head, the other sliding down to hook beneath the knee already braced against his side. He pushed it higher, opening her further, and the new angle punched a curse from his lips as he sank impossibly deep.

"Worth it," he echoed roughly, mouth finding the salt-slick skin just below her ear. He bit down, soothed the sting with his tongue, then did it again, marking her, claiming her. "Damn right it's worth it. Five months I dreamed about this. About you. About this bed. About the sounds you make when I'm inside you." He punctuated each filthy word with a hard snap of his hips. "They can evict us. I'll take you right here on the floor if they do. Nothing's getting me out of this bed tonight."

He set a rhythm that was brutal in its urgency, driving into her with every ounce of strength left in his trembling body. The headboard knocked a frantic, rhythmic thud against the wall; somewhere below, a door slammed, or maybe that was just the bed. He didn't care. Let them listen. Let the whole building know exactly who she belonged to, and exactly what five months of missing her sounded like.

His hand slid between their sweat-slick bodies, thumb finding the tight, swollen bundle of nerves where they were joined. He rubbed it fast and rough, matching the punishing snap of his hips, because he needed—needed—to feel her come apart around him one more time. He could feel the tension coiled impossibly tight in the scorching clutch of her, the flutter that warned him she was close.

"That's it," he gritted out against her throat, teeth scraping the frantic pulse there. "Take it. Take all of it. Come for me, sweetheart. Let me feel it. Let me hear you."

He felt the sudden molten clamp of her body around him, the fluttering spasm that dragged him deeper, the unmistakable proof that she was his and real and gloriously, finally here. Christ, he could die like this. Could die inside her and count it a life well-lived. He drove through it, hips snapping forward, thumb working her mercilessly, drawing every last aftershock from the fluttering, clenching heat of her until the tension finally broke and she went limp and shaking beneath him.

Only then did he let himself go.

He drove into her once, twice, and then his own release tore through him, white-hot and blinding, his whole body seizing with the force of it as he spilled into her, burying his face in the sweat-damp curve of her neck to muffle the ragged, broken sound of her name. It went on and on, emptying him, shaking him apart, until he had nothing left, until he was nothing but the slick, scorching clutch of her and the ragged sound of his own breathing.

For a long moment he couldn't move. He just held her there, still buried deep, his heart hammering against the soft warmth of her, his breath coming in ragged pulls. Slowly, carefully, he lifted his head, pressed a kiss to the damp skin just beneath her ear, and muttered roughly,

"Worth it." His voice was wrecked, thick with something that felt suspiciously like tears. "Every second. Every damn second away from you, and this—this is worth all of it."

He eased his weight to the side, just enough to keep from crushing her, but he didn't withdraw. He just gathered her close, one arm banding tight around her waist, the other still tangled in the sweat-damp sheets, and tucked her back against his chest. The room was quiet now except for the sound of their breathing, the scent of sex and salt and sweat thick in the air.

"Not moving," he muttered, pressing another kiss to her shoulder, then another to the nape of her neck. "Not for a week. Shower can wait. Food can wait. Everything can wait." He tightened his arm around her, holding on like a man who still couldn't quite believe she was real. "I've got you, and I'm not letting go."

A rough, wrecked laugh escaped him, and he turned his face into her hair, breathing her in like a man who'd been holding his breath for nineteen weeks and had only just now remembered how.

"I love you," he said roughly, the words torn out of him, half prayer, half vow. "God, I love you. I'm home, sweetheart. I'm finally home."

dialogue.name: Halle
dialogue.content: I turn my head just enough to catch his lips in a slow, exhausted kiss. My whole body feels like it's been taken apart and put back together again. "Welcome home," I murmur against his mouth, my voice hoarse. My fingers trace the lines of his back, mapping the new scars and old familiar ones. "Now don't move. I'm not done holding you yet."
