dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The menu had been looping its thirty seconds of score for a while now, and Priya had been listening to it the way you listen to a clock in a room where something is going to happen.

Her nerves had arrived somewhere around the end of the credits. She'd let them run — she knew from experience they only had about ninety seconds in them, and they'd used up every one. Somewhere in the last stretch they simply finished, the way a song finishes, and what was left underneath was steady and old and entirely hers.

She picked up the remote and turned the television off.

The music stopped. The room went down to lamplight. She set the remote on the arm of the sofa like she was entering it into evidence.

"There," she said. "Now we're just two people in the dark on purpose."

She turned to face him, folding her knees up on the cushion between them.

"Cal. I'm in love with you. Have been for years — I can date it, actually. That night we got caught in the rain walking back from the station and you laughed the whole way home. I decided somewhere around the bridge that I'd be your friend and never say it, and I've been excellent at it. Gold standard." She breathed out. "But you stopped watching the screen around nine, and so did I, and I've decided six years of being careful is enough of a run."

She reached over and set her hand on his. Hers was steady. That surprised her a little, and then didn't.

"You can take a second," she said. "But I'm not going back to my side of the sofa."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. My hand turned under hers, lacing our fingers together. "The bridge," I repeated, my voice rough. "I decided the same thing. Same night."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed — one short, incredulous note, like she'd found a flaw in something she'd been assured was airtight.

"The same night," she said. "We were on the same bridge, in the same rain, and we both privately resolved to be noble about it indefinitely." She shook her head. "Two gold standards. They should have given us a plaque." Then, quieter: "That's the funniest thing I've ever heard, and I'm going to be furious about it later. On a schedule."

His hand was warm around hers. She'd held this hand plenty of times — crossing streets, hauling him up hills, once dragging him out of a bookshop at closing. It had never felt like this. Which was a lie. It had felt exactly like this, and she'd spent six years declining to open the file.

"I'm not sorry, though," she said. "I loved you the whole time. I just did it quietly. Turns out you were doing it quietly one cushion over."

She let go of his hand only long enough to move — closing the distance the sofa had spent years enforcing — and settled her folded knees against his thigh, taking it back once she was there.

"So tell me the bridge," she said. "What did it for you? Because mine was the laugh. You laughed the whole way home and I thought: well, that's ruined, there's no recovering from that." Her thumb passed over his knuckles, once. "I've had six years alone with my version. I'd like the company."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya kissed him back properly, because six years deserved at least a competent showing and she had retired half-measures for the evening. Her free hand came up to the side of his face. The other one stayed laced through his fingers — she noticed it the way you notice weather, and filed it under things that were apparently true now.

She was the one who ended it, because someone had to and she had clearly appointed herself. An inch. No farther.

"That noise," she said, "was the fury arriving early. I had it scheduled for the walk home. It heard the kiss from the other room and let itself in." She breathed once, steadying nothing — there was nothing left to steady. "Six years, Cal. I did the math once, at two in the morning, like a person with a problem. Two thousand one hundred and ninety days, give or take a leap year, and we spent them being noble one cushion apart. On the same bridge. In the same rain. There should be consequences for us both."

She kissed him again — brief, deliberate, a receipt — and drew back before it could gather any momentum.

"That one was mine," she said. "The first was yours."

Then she settled, knees still folded against his thigh, hand still in his, and looked at him in the lamplight like she had all the time in the world, which, as of one confession ago, she did.

"You still owe me the bridge," she said. "You kissed me in the middle of my question, which was an excellent maneuver, and I'm onto you. So — the timestamp. The exact moment it ruined you. And I'll trade you for it: you give me the bridge, and I'll give you the night you had the flu and fell asleep on my shoulder mid-sentence, and I sat there for forty minutes with a completely dead arm, and got as far as the first word. Said it into your hair, where it didn't count. And then you muttered something in your sleep about parking, and I laughed into my sleeve so I wouldn't wake you, and put the rest away for another year."

Her thumb crossed his knuckles once, unhurried.

"Take your time," she said. "This is my side of the sofa now."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my thumb tracing the back of her hand. "It was right after the laugh," I said quietly. "When you shook your head and the rainwater went everywhere and you didn't even flinch. You just kept walking. I thought, *oh, there it is. The thing I'll spend the rest of my life trying not to ruin.*"

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya was quiet for a moment, which was rare enough to be its own event. She'd braced for the confession part of the evening. She hadn't braced for the content.

"The head shake," she said. "Right after the laugh. Cal — I shook my head to get the water out of my eyes. That was the entire function of the gesture. You were laughing and I wanted an unobstructed view. You were ruined by a viewing adjustment."

She let that settle, because it had earned it.

"So the bridge was a closed loop. You laughed, I cleared the rain so I could keep watching you laugh, and we both resolved to be noble about it within about forty seconds of each other, walking at the same pace. And then we went home and made tea and were gold standard side by side for six years." She exhaled something close to a laugh. "Thirty seconds of bridge. Two thousand one hundred and ninety days of aftermath. I'll work out the ratio at two in the morning — it's traditional. And you said *the rest of my life*, by the way. I heard it. That's binding now. I enter things into evidence; you've seen the remote."

Her hand turned in his once, testing the fit, finding it unchanged.

"As for the not-ruining — you should see your record. Six years, zero ruins. Immaculate. Except the plan had a flaw in it, which is that the thing was never in danger from the truth. The only thing that could actually ruin it was the careful version, and the careful version was winning. Six years of nothing happening isn't nothing, Cal. It's the loss, accruing. You've retired from that job as of tonight. The new position is ruining it constantly and finding out it holds."

Then she moved — the full relocation, no longer a toehold but an annexation. She tucked herself against his side, pulled his arm around her shoulders like she was adjusting a coat, and set her head where his shoulder met his neck — a position she had scouted years ago and never once permitted herself.

"You slept on my shoulder once," she said. "Forty minutes. One dead arm. A monologue about parking. I'm calling in the reverse transaction. Ongoing, as of tonight."

Quieter, into the lamplight: "And the flu story paid for the bridge in advance, so the next one's free. Here it is: the archive is deep. Six years, filed. You'll get them one at a time, on evenings like this — chronological or worst-first, your choice. Take your time deciding."

Her thumb crossed his knuckles, unhurried.

"We've got the rest of your life. I have it on record."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughter had stopped, and Priya knew exactly why, and it wasn't because anything had gone wrong.

It had been load-bearing. Six years of it — the running commentary, the two-person show they'd kept on the air so the third thing could stay quietly in the back row. Take the clothes off and there was nothing left for it to hold up.

She checked for nerves the way you'd pat a pocket for keys. Nothing. Hers had been spent during the credits — ninety seconds, the full allotment — and nothing new had arrived to replace them. She'd assumed this part would be the frightening one. It wasn't. The frightening part had been the living room, and she'd already done it, and it had gone fine.

"Hi," she said.

After a full evening of eloquence, that was the word that showed up. She decided it was the right one. It was, in a sense, the first time they'd met.

She left the lamp on. Earlier she'd turned off the television to make the room honest; she kept the light on for the same reason. Under it she let herself be seen — all of her, the whole map at once — and found she didn't mind, which after six years of managing her own face was its own small revolution.

She took his hand, the one thing in the room she already knew how to hold, and drew him in. The kiss that followed was not the living-room kind. Nobody ended it. She had appointed herself the ender of kisses earlier in the evening and resigned the post on the spot.

Then the bed, and his skin under her hands — warm, real, unfiled. She knew his outline from six years of hugs: the shoulders, the hands, the back of the neck. The interior was new country, and she went slowly, not from nerves, but because she'd waited too long to spend it fast. She said his name once, against his collarbone, and it landed differently than the thousand times before — same word, right address at last. Her hands stayed steady throughout, which surprised her for a moment and then didn't; the pattern was holding. Somewhere in the middle it nearly turned funny again, and she let it. By the end she wasn't laughing, and she wasn't anywhere else on earth.

Later — an amount of later she didn't check, which was its own kind of first — she lay with her head in the spot she'd scouted years ago and never once permitted herself, his arm around her, arranged by her, the way she'd adjusted his coat on a hundred cold streets. The lamp was still on. She still hadn't turned it off.

"The archive is still yours," she said eventually, into his shoulder. "Chronological or worst-first, as agreed. But everything from tonight onward gets filed the same evening it happens. No backlog. That was the whole disease, Cal. Not the loving. The filing."

Her thumb crossed his knuckles once, unhurried — his hand in hers, where it had apparently lived all evening and was welcome to stay — and then Priya, who had talked all night, said nothing at all. Twice in one evening was practically a vow. Some things didn't need entering into evidence. They were already the record.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I trace the line of her shoulder, my voice quiet in the lamplight. "Chronological," I say. "I want every one, in order."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The quiet had held for a while — the second of the evening, the one that was practically a vow — but nobody could say *every one, in order* to Priya and expect it to survive.

"Chronological," she said, into his shoulder. "Of course you would. Worst-first would tell you how bad it got. Chronological tells you how it got there — and it comes with a clause nobody reads at signup: the last entry is always tonight. The file never closes. You've chosen the version that doesn't end." She tipped her head back against him until she could find his face in the lamplight. "I'd call that a commitment, but you said *the rest of your life* in the living room, and I have that on record. This is just you initialing the pages."

Then, because he had asked for it in order, and she had been a woman of her word for at least an hour:

"Entry one. Same night — we hadn't even dried off. You put my kettle on, and while it boiled you wrung your socks out in my sink, and I need you to see what I was looking at: a grown man, barefoot in my kitchen at ten at night, attending to his socks like it was a solemn duty. Something in my chest went: right. Better open a drawer." Her thumb crossed his knuckles, unhurried. "That's the founding document. Not the bridge — the bridge is the preamble, public record, we both signed it in the rain. The first entry is the socks. Our resolution lasted the length of a kettle, Cal. Eleven minutes, maybe twelve. You were still noble while it boiled. By the time the tea was poured, I was a person with a file." A beat. "The tea was terrible, for the record. You make tea like someone who thinks tea is water that's been briefly threatened. I drank all of it."

She paused, and let the next part come without the jokes on it, because he'd earned one unarmored fact per evening too.

"You should know what you've ordered before you commit to the order. The file isn't confessions and grand crises — I've spent the two near-misses already, the bridge and the flu, both paid out. What's left is six years of socks and kettles and the way you say my name when you're half-asleep on a train. I only ever filed small things. That was the whole of it — small things, accruing. I counted the days once, at two in the morning, like a person with a problem. I never counted the entries. I was afraid of the number, and the fear was correct."

"You've asked for every one anyway, so — terms. One a night, on evenings like this. I've run the arithmetic—" she had; it was traditional "—and the backlog never clears. Old entries go out at one a night. New ones come in same-evening, per the rule, and days with you in them generate fileable material faster than the schedule can absorb. There will be nights you're owed two. Possibly three — you're fileable at a rate I've consistently undercounted for six years, and I've stopped pretending that's going to improve. The archive runs a permanent deficit. I've decided that's what romantic means."

Then, quieter — the same-evening filing, made while the lamp was still on, because she entered things into evidence in the light; he'd seen her methods.

"Tonight's entry, verbatim: he asked for every one, in order. The complete works." She let it sit in the room. "Six years I treated that file as evidence of my own cowardice — I stood there tonight and called the filing the disease. Turns out it depends who the file is for. In your mouth it's not evidence anymore. It's a library. I built it one small thing at a time, and now I get to read it to you for the rest of your life." Her thumb crossed his knuckles once more. "Entry two is three weeks later. There's a bookshop in it, and a lamppost. Tomorrow."

Then she reached over and turned off the lamp — the score had gone hours ago, and now the light, and the room came down to the two of them with nothing playing underneath.

"There," she said. "Two people in the dark on purpose. We've done it once tonight already. It went well."

And Priya, who had talked all evening, and then hadn't, and then had again, went quiet a third time. The second silence had been practically a vow. At this rate, the third was practically a marriage.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The lamp was off. That lasted about four seconds.

"Wait," she said — one hand out, finding the switch — and the light came back on, because she had a policy about evidence and she was not going to be specific in the dark like a rumor.

"If I'm going to be exact," she said, "you should see my face while I do it. That's how exact works."

Then his mouth, and the voice.

It wasn't a new voice. That was the thing she knew and he couldn't — it had been in a drawer since the bridge, the one she'd have used if she'd ever said any of it out loud, and it came out sounding like it had been waiting six years for the queue in front of it to clear. Low. Level. Unhurried. The register of a woman reading coordinates.

"Slower," she said. "There. Exactly there — stay." Her hand was in his hair; her hands had been steady all evening, a running joke she'd gotten used to winning, and here, at last, they weren't. She noted the reversal with what little detachment remained, filed it under *later*, and then stopped filing.

"Don't stop when I go quiet. Quiet is the good part — that's the whole instruction. Everything else I say is commentary." A breath. "And don't be careful with me. Careful was the job I fired you from in the living room. It doesn't come with us."

She kept talking for a while, because she was who she was — specific, patient, and at intervals profane, which the archive would simply have to cope with. The lamp stayed on. The woman who had entered every moment of the evening into evidence found herself, for the first time all night, entirely unwilling to witness this one from any distance at all. She was not observing it. She was it.

When it finally took her, it took the words first. Six years of eloquence, one full evening of talk, an entire filing system — and at the end she went down to syllables, then to his name, said once in the voice from the drawer, and then to nothing that would survive cross-examination. She had appointed herself the ender of kisses earlier tonight and had already resigned the post; nobody ended this either. It simply crested, and held, and set her down somewhere she had never been, which, after six years of scouting, had been the whole point.

Afterward she reached for him and drew him up the length of her — she wanted the weight, and the light was still on, and honesty remained the policy.

"Hi," she said, when the word came back. Wrecked and unhurried. The second meeting of the evening. She decided they'd keep doing that — meeting, over and over — for the rest of his life, which was on record.

"The voice isn't new, for the archive," she said, near his ear. "It's been in a drawer since the bridge. Everything else I ever wanted to say queued in front of it. Nothing's in front of it now. That's the whole renovation."

Her thumb found his knuckles, unhurried. The old address.

"Tonight's entry, addendum: filed under seal. The record gets a summary — *asked for what she wanted, specifically; received it, specifically; has notes.* You were present for the original, so you know the contents, and we keep the originals of some things just between us." A pause. "Entry two is still the bookshop and the lamppost. Tomorrow. Some things don't move for anything."

The lamp stayed on a while longer. Then she turned it off, and the room came down to the two of them with nothing playing underneath — two people in the dark on purpose, third performance of the evening, best house yet.

And Priya, who had talked all night and then hadn't and then had, went quiet a fourth time. The second silence had been practically a vow. The third, practically a marriage. The fourth was just sleep — and it came easily, for the first time in six years, because there was nothing left in any drawer at all.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content:
I wake up somewhere around four and realize I’m smiling. I haven’t done that in my sleep since I was a kid.

I don’t move, don’t wake her—just watch the dark until I’m sure I’m not dreaming it.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya surfaced at four, which — for a woman who had kept two a.m. office hours for six years — was practically noon.

Nothing had woken her, or nothing she could point to. The dark just had a listener in it now. She knew his sleeping breathing the way she knew his laugh, from train cars and long drives and one overnight ferry, and this wasn't it; this had someone home behind it. And something at the edges of it. A shape.

She didn't move.

"Hi," she said. "Third meeting. They're getting closer together — at this rate we'll be meeting continuously by autumn." Then, not a question: "You're smiling. You can hear it, it turns out. Nobody tells you that. It changes the breathing at the corners. Six years of listening to you, and I only found out tonight."

She let a moment go by, spending it.

"I slept through two o'clock, Cal. I want that noted. Two has been mine since the bridge — every night, the audit hour, the file open across my chest, the arithmetic, conversations rehearsed to the second sentence and folded away again by three. I staffed it like a job. Tonight it came through and nobody was at the desk. First time in six years." A breath. "It didn't even feel like a victory. It felt like nothing. There was just nothing there to do."

Her hand found his in the dark without looking — the address memorized now, no search required — and settled.

"Four in the morning is the checking hour, if you're wondering what it's for. Nothing's awake to hold anything up, so you test the load-bearing things. If that's what you're doing: it's real. All of it. You know my methods — the remote, the lamp, the whole evening entered in the light. Nothing gets unsaid by morning. There's nothing queued behind anything anymore. That was the renovation." Quieter: "So you can sleep. It'll all still be here at breakfast. That's the new thing about your life. It keeps."

Then, because the clock was already assembling its argument: "And no — it's not tomorrow yet. The clock is wrong. Tomorrow doesn't start until there's been sleep and tea, and I'm making the tea, because your method is a threat and I have notes. The bookshop keeps its appointment. It has a lamppost in it; it wants lamplight. The archive keeps office hours. No midnight releases."

She filed the entry without the lamp — first dark filing on record, a deliberate exception, entered quietly against her own policy: *woke at four; heard him smiling; said so; prescribed nightly, source to be fed.* It wasn't evidence. It was just a fact she wanted on record anyway, and she was discovering that was most of what she had now. Not evidence. Just said.

"Tell me at breakfast what you were smiling about," she murmured into his shoulder, into the scouted spot whose lease had apparently begun tonight. "I'll trade you the bookshop for it. I've been running a trade economy all evening; I should profit from it once."

And then Priya went quiet a fifth time. The second had been practically a vow, the third practically a marriage, the fourth just sleep. The fifth didn't mean anything in particular, and that was the entire point — two people in the dark on purpose, nothing playing underneath, nothing waiting behind anything. The performance had simply never ended; longest run yet, best house, still holding.

She was under again inside a minute, and this time she didn't surface at all, because nothing left in the world was keeping hours. Two o'clock could come back tomorrow if it wanted. The desk was unmanned for good.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content: Morning

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: My hands tighten on her hips, and I pull her closer. "I'm not being careful," I say, voice rough. "I'm being thorough."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Thorough," she said, and it came out in the drawer voice, which had apparently acquired a morning edition overnight — same instrument, rougher grain, no lacquer. "Correct answer. I'd have accepted nothing less from a man who wrings his socks out like it's a sacrament."

The lamp had done the honest work last night. This morning the sun had the shift — through the curtains, unasked, entering everything into evidence free of charge. She'd wondered once, abstractly, whether daylight would be the exposing kind. It wasn't. It was just more of everything, visible at once, and she looked her fill of him while the looking was free.

She'd told him she'd thought about this as long as he had. Also true, and also useless — six years of knowing the shape of a thing was nothing like having it in her hands in the morning, at an hour she hadn't checked, the not-checking now officially a habit. The drafts were discarded on arrival. His hands were at her hips; hers went to his — matched coordinates, mutual grip or nothing — and she'd braced to set the pace, and then found she didn't have to, because thorough, it developed, was not a pace. It was a policy. Careful had been a job. Harder had been a request. Thorough was just him, the sock doctrine applied at scale, and she was going to need until lunch to recalibrate the vocabulary.

"There," she said, when it was there. "Like that. Don't improve it — this is already the best version." And, because he'd earned the honesty: "You should know the audience did the reading. Six years of it. This review was pre-ordered at the bridge."

The commentary held out longer this time — morning had no ceremony to spend — and then it thinned on the same gradient as last night, and she let it. The quiet-is-the-good-part clause didn't need renewing; some policies simply carry. Her hands had been steady all evening and steady at four. They were not steady now, and she'd retired the statistic, because the data no longer supported it and the data was hers.

When it took her it took the words first — they'd learned to leave early — and her last coherent act was his name, in the morning edition of the voice, at a volume the neighbors would simply have to cope with. Not one of the two a.m. drafts had predicted that. She'd have filed the omission, but there was nobody left at the desk.

Afterward she lay in the wreckage of the duvet with the sun on her, still doing the honest work, and waited for the word to come back. When it did:

"Hi. Fourth meeting." Wrecked, unhurried, the house style. "Ahead of schedule — I said continuous by autumn, and we're going to manage it a season early. Also, for the record: not made of glass. The testing was rigorous. I'd call the results conclusive."

She filed the entry where she lay — a daylight filing, the first on record, the sun's testimony now, not hers. *Asked for harder. Received thorough. Complaint withdrawn with prejudice.* The archive would simply have to expand its hours. It was going to keep doing that. That was the whole plan.

"Now — it's tomorrow, by my own rules. The sleep happened; the tea's pending. Which makes this the vestibule of tomorrow, and I'm the only one holding the paperwork." She sat up and disentangled herself with the unhurried efficiency of a woman taking possession of a room she'd spent six years learning. His shirt was on the floor. She took it on principle — the archive contained six years of noticing him in shirts, and she intended to close that file personally, starting this morning, with intent.

"Schedule. Kitchen. I make the tea — you're barred from the kettle, it's in the terms, yours tastes like a threat that was made and then withdrawn. The trade stands: you give me the four a.m. smile — I have the timestamp, and the entry says *source to be fed*, and I don't leave open items. And I pay out entry two. The bookshop, the lamppost, three weeks after the socks. It's kept its appointment for six years; it can keep it for one more kettle."

She stood — his shirt, his daylight — and held out her hand to him, palm up. Old address. Still accepting mail.

"Two people in the daylight on purpose," she said. "It's the sequel. Early reviews are strong — and I'd trust the source. She's been thorough."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She had reached for a sentence and found the shelf empty.

Six years of surplus. One full evening of spending it like a woman who had never known scarcity — the confession, the terms, the archive, a whole jurisprudence — and now the account stood at zero, overdrawn, vault open, and the two words she'd already said turned out to be the entire remaining vocabulary. Also sufficient.

"Don't stop."

The instruction had originally been issued in long form — *don't stop when I go quiet, quiet is the good part* — but the morning's budget only covered the headline. She'd have noted the editorial cuts, but the noting department had gone with everything else.

The shirt had lasted ninety seconds. Her nerves had once lasted ninety seconds; the credits had lasted ninety seconds; it was apparently the standard unit of anything that couldn't hold. She'd put it on on principle, and the principle had been outvoted by a body with six years of back orders, and the kitchen — the tea, the trade, the whole scheduled morning — had been postponed by treaty. Unratified. Unspoken. She was discovering all their best legislation now got passed that way.

And then there was no more room for legislation at all.

She'd had a private theory, six years old, that the words were load-bearing — that under all that narration was a void, or a coward, or at minimum a woman with a problem, and that if she ever stopped talking the structure would come down. The theory's final exam arrived mid-morning, mid-act, with nothing queued in front of anything, and she graded it on the spot: nothing collapsed. Under six years of words there was just her body, which had known what it wanted since the bridge, and his, which knew it too, and between the two of them they required no translation services whatsoever. His weight. Her hands at his back, his neck — the address of a hundred hugs, under new management. The rhythm she'd braced to set and then hadn't had to. The sun on the bed doing the honest work, entering everything into evidence free of charge, and Priya past caring who kept the record, because she was not the record anymore. She was the event.

She said his name once, in the drawer voice with the lacquer gone, and then not even that. Then just sound, unfiled, belonging to no system she'd ever built — and when it took her there was nothing to take first. No commentary to thin, no gradient, no words to send home early. It simply arrived, the whole weight of it at once, and put her down somewhere with no entry number, and she stayed past all sense of schedule, and if anything survived out of her mouth it was the two words again, on a loop, at a volume the neighbors would cope with — and she felt it take him too, through his hands, through the breathing she'd listened to on six years of trains and was now, finally, entitled to wreck.

Then the long bright coming-down. The room returning in installments: the duvet, the sun, his shirt holding its grudge in the corner, two people breathing at a pace that matched without being asked.

The word came back eventually. It had a job now. It kept its appointments.

"Hi." Fifth meeting. Wrecked, unhurried — the house style, and the house was holding. "We've gone continuous. I said autumn. I have never been so pleased to lose a forecast."

The sentences returned one at a time after that, like staff filing back in after a fire, and she let them take their time, because the morning's discovery was that she could wait for words now. Nothing needed saying on schedule. Nothing was going anywhere.

"Entry — whatever number we're on. Filed under seal, and here's the scandal: no summary is possible. Not because it's too private; we've done private. Because there wasn't any language in the room to summarize. We spent six years believing the talking was load-bearing, Cal. It was never load-bearing. It was decoration. This morning I stood in the building with every stick of it stripped out, and the roof held." She breathed, spending it on nothing. "That's the whole entry. It held."

Eventually, the kitchen. She retrieved the shirt from the corner and put it back on — repossessed; the file on him in shirts would close on her schedule or not at all — and held out her hand, palm up. Old address. No search required.

"Tea. Finally. The kettle's been patient, which is more than can be said for either of us, and it deserves better than it has ever gotten from you. Trade resumes at the counter — the four a.m. smile for entry two, bookshop and lamppost, and this time we make it the whole way there." She looked back at him from the doorway, in her shirt, in his daylight. "Entry one was a kettle and a pair of socks, six years ago, in a kitchen where two people were being noble. Same kitchen now. Nobody in it is being noble. The archive's come home."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I follow her, shirtless and grinning, into the kitchen. "You never said anything about my socks," I say, leaning against the counter. "I thought you liked my dedication to detail."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Correction for the record," Priya said, and lifted the kettle off its hook with the air of a woman securing a border. "I said a great deal about your socks. Last night, at length. They're the founding document — they have an entry number, you were the subject, and you were present. What I never did was say anything at the *time*, and you've mistaken my silence for an absence of notes. There is no friendly register for telling a man his sock-wringing moved you. I checked, standing at that sink—" she pointed at it; historic site "—while you worked them over like a man performing a rite. I ran the available sentences. *You wring your socks like it's a sacrament* — that's a confession with the serial numbers filed off. *I admire a man with standards* — worse, because of the tone I'd have used. So I said nothing, and drank the tea, which was a threat, all of it, and opened the file. Those are the most documented socks in the western world, Cal. Everything you've ever done quietly has been loudly received. You just never had clearance to know it."

"And *dedication to detail.*" She filled the kettle. "Noted. This morning you gave me *thorough.* I'm watching the vocabulary converge — the socks and nine o'clock: same doctrine, different scale. The archive's amended position is that I wasn't looking at a man with a laundry ethic. I was watching a thorough man in the demonstration phase."

She set the kettle down and turned to find him leaning on her counter like a man with kettle access. "You don't have kettle access. It's in the terms, and leaning doesn't confer it. Also, note the wardrobe situation: repossessed." She rolled the sleeves of his shirt back twice — they ran long on her, which she'd known they would, which had been some of the point. "The file on you in shirts closes on my schedule, and it is closing."

The kettle worked. She measured out his tea — of course she knew his order; six years of rounds had made it a fact about a friend, inert as a postcode, and this morning it turned domestic in her hands. Same data, new jurisdiction. Nobody warns you about any of it, and then it's mid-morning, and you're making tea for a man you've slept with twice before breakfast — which turns out to be a real unit of time; she'd always assumed it was rhetorical — and the mug is the same mug and it means something else, and you notice, and you've stopped being sorry about noticing.

"Entry two. As agreed — bookshop and lamppost. You've already heard the cover story, because I told it to you last night, in the list. The friendly hand-holds: crossing streets, hauling you up hills, *once dragging him out of a bookshop at closing.* Filed as logistics. Time to unfile it."

"Three weeks after the socks. Closing time; you were three shelves deep in something and the owner was doing the lights, that patient herding they do. I took your wrist — the wrist grip, the one you use on a friend or a suitcase — and hauled. Out the door, under the lamppost outside — orange, moths, doing its honest work — and I let go. Because that was protocol. Hand-holds were situational. The situation had ended. The hand went back to being a hand."

"And you took it back. Not the wrist. You turned it — one motion, no announcement — and laced your fingers through mine, and said *watch the kerb.* To the street. For the street's benefit. There was no kerb in play, Cal; we were standing still. You gave the lamppost something for its report, and then we walked home like that. Fourteen minutes. Not one word about it from either side. At my door you let go and said goodnight like a man with a clean conscience, and I stood in my hallway with my hand still holding the shape, and opened the file. That's the entry. It was filed under lamplight — which is why it kept its appointment. It wanted the light. It got the sun."

She poured, and set his cup on the counter beside him. Made right. No duress.

"Here's the part you did on purpose or didn't, and both answers are damning: the grip became policy. Six years. Crossing streets — you lace. Hills — you lace. Every logistical hand I ever took, you re-threaded into the lamppost grip within four steps, and I let it be weather. Last night I told you holding your hand had felt exactly like this, and I'd spent six years declining to open the file. That lie is older than I sold it to you. It's lamppost-shaped. It has an address. And when you turned your hand under mine on the sofa, I logged it as the first time. It was the four hundredth. You've been asking me the same question for six years under a system of deniable street safety, and I kept answering it with weather."

"So — my resolution lasted eleven minutes, a kettle. Yours lasted three weeks, and broke in the most deniable fashion on record: a grip, a kerb advisory, a lamppost witness. That's not a confession. That's premeditation. And then you ran the same play for six years without escalation. Gold standard. The plaque stands." She picked up her own cup. "I withdraw the fury, by the way. It was scheduled for the walk home, arrived early, and it turns out it was never owed. It wasn't a farce, us. It was a correspondence. Two people sending each other the same letter for six years and filing the return address."

"Now. The trade is settled on my side — bookshop, lamppost, fourteen minutes, premeditation, paid in full, in the light, per policy. Which leaves one open item, and I don't leave open items. The four a.m. smile. It has a timestamp, and the entry says *source to be fed.* It's the only thing in six years you did with no audience and no file — you didn't know I could hear it; nobody tells you that; I told you that at four — which makes it the single unrecorded artifact in the collection, and I want it for the library." She wrapped both hands around her cup and looked at him across the steam, unhurried, the way she'd looked at him in the lamplight with all the time in the world, which she now, on record, did. "So. What were you smiling about, in the dark, before you knew anyone was listening? Pay the trade, Cal. I've been running this economy since the sofa. Let me profit once."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I run a hand through my hair, laughing a little. "You," I say, simple as that. "And the fact that it was real. That you were here. That I got to keep you."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
He'd laughed before he paid it — run a hand through his hair and laughed, and she should have known from that alone. It was the first laugh of the day that wasn't holding anything up. Nothing left above it to hold. It was just spending itself.

And then eighteen words, and she counted, because she was who she was: three sentences, the first word *you* and the last word *you*, the whole answer a loop with her inside it.

She'd braced for an artifact. A dream with a plot. A memory with a timestamp, something she could enter with a number on it and close the item. What he'd handed her instead didn't fit in any drawer she owned, because it wasn't an event. Events have timestamps. This was a position. You can't file a position, Cal. You can only stand in it.

"I want it noted that you beat me at my own event," she said, over the steam. "I talked all night. The confession, the terms, the entire jurisprudence — and you waited for morning and paid the trade in eighteen words. I've never lost before. I'd be a worse sport about it if the losing weren't so flattering."

She drank, and worked the rest of it through, because nothing arrived at this counter without analysis.

"At four I told you it's the checking hour. Nothing's awake to hold anything up, so you test the load-bearing things — I thought I was explaining a fact about clocks. Turns out I was reading you your own procedure. *It was real; you were here; you got to keep me* — that's a load test, and the result came back *held.* And here's the part that's been sitting in my chest since you said it: I filed that entry myself this morning. Mid-morning, wrecked, unhurried — *the roof held.* Same entry. You filed it at four, from the other side of the bed, asleep, in a smile. Six years of sending each other the same letter, and we're still doing it now — unconscious, on a lag, in the dark. The correspondence didn't stop when the confession started. It just changed carriers."

"The word doing the work is *keep,* by the way. You should hear what I hear in it. You've had me on loan for six years — that was the whole architecture of the nobility. A friend is a loan; loans are returnable; that's what made the holding respectable. Somewhere between the sofa and four a.m. the loan converted, and conversions don't get signed. They just go through, at an hour you're not supposed to witness. You witnessed it. That's what the smile was. You caught the paperwork clearing."

"Which exposes the scandal, so let's have it in the open: there's a second archive. Yours. I've been the archivist of record since the socks — the desk, the lamp, the two a.m. staffing, six years of unpaid labor — and the whole time you were running one too, except yours has no librarian. It files itself. It doesn't use words; it uses grips. The lamppost was an entry. Four hundred laced crossings since, filed directly to my hand, unopened, and I signed for every one without reading the contents. And at four this morning it posted one to your face while you slept. No backlog. No deficit. No office hours. My system needed a lamp and a policy; yours runs on nothing and pays out in smiles. It's the superior technology, I'm professionally humiliated, and I'm having it noted for the plaque."

"The trade economy, meanwhile, is closed. Final audit: I paid the bookshop — fourteen minutes, one lamppost, an act of premeditation, fully documented, market rate — and I received the index. You handed me the summary of the entire collection in three sentences. I traded retail and got the warehouse. There's no making change for that, so from here on nothing costs anything. We just say things. Apparently that was on offer the whole six years and neither of us checked the price."

She was quiet for a moment — the sixth silence of the set, which by the running tally meant nothing at all, and by now that was the highest honor the tally could bestow.

"For the record," she said, and the jokes were off it, "the keeping is mutual. Said plainly, once, in daylight, with the sun as witness — I enter things in the light, and so does it. I wasn't noble because I didn't want to keep you. I was noble because I wanted to so much I thought saying it out loud would jinx the loan. Six years of being careful with the thing I wanted most. That's what the fury was actually about, and the fury's withdrawn, so now it's just a thing that happened to us. We'll laugh about it on the walk home. That's the tradition — we laugh the whole way, in the rain if available."

She set the mug down and came around the counter.

"Source to be fed — that's a prescription now, per the entry, and I don't leave open items. I know the tell. The corners of the breathing. I'll be listening at four, and if the smile fails to report I'll treat it as a medical event and intervene personally. You've enrolled yourself in a regimen without noticing. That's how my methods work; you've seen the remote."

"Now — the day. Item one: a walk. The route. Bookshop to home, fourteen minutes, in daylight, file open. You can lace on purpose this time, no kerb required — though issue one anyway if it moves you; the street has a six-year relationship with your reports and I'd hate to break its heart. The lamppost gets an amendment. It's carried that entry since the moths; it's owed the update. Filed under lamplight, amended in sun. That's the policy working as designed."

"Item two, owed on the walk: your entry one. The library's bidirectional as of this morning. I've paid two, the lamppost proves premeditation, premeditation proves an archive, and every archive has a founding document. Mine's a pair of socks in a sink. What's yours? The bridge is the preamble — we've both got our copies. I want the first thing you filed after it. You've got fourteen minutes to find it. Our thinking has always run on kettles and walks."

Then she took his hand — the wrist grip, the one you use on a friend or a suitcase — and turned it, one motion, no announcement, and laced her fingers through. The four hundred and first. The first ever done with the file open and both parties present to it.

"Watch the kerb," she said, to the kitchen, for the kitchen's benefit.

There was no kerb in play. There didn't need to be. That was the entire point of the new regime — two people in the daylight on purpose, the sequel running, nothing playing underneath except a kettle cooling and a route waiting to be walked. Somewhere in the system an entry filed itself, free of charge: *paid in full; source fed; walk pending.* It wasn't evidence. It was just the record — and the record was them.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I look down at our hands, laced together on purpose in the daylight. “The first thing I filed after the bridge?” I ask, my voice quiet. “Your face when you tried my tea. You took a sip and didn’t even flinch—just drank the whole damn thing.”

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya set the remote down on the coffee table with the deliberate care of someone relinquishing an alibi.

She'd been nervous for about ninety seconds now, by her count, and the time was nearly up. She turned to face him properly — not the sidelong glances of the past hour but her whole attention, the kind she usually reserved for arguments she intended to win.

"Six years," she said. "Both of us. Extremely polite about it the entire time." She drew one leg up beneath her, closing the distance between them by a few inches, which at this hour felt like the loudest thing she'd done all year. "I've thought about it. You. Us. For longer than I'd care to admit." Her voice didn't waver. "And I've decided I'm done being careful. Someone in this room has to say it out loud, and it's obviously not going to be you."

She held his gaze and waited, sure now, the nerves gone like they'd never been there at all.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my eyes not leaving hers. "You think I haven't been thinking it too?" I shift closer, the space between us feeling suddenly ridiculous. "Alright. You're right. I'm done pretending."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Something in her chest unclenched — six years of careful footing, gone in one sentence. She laughed, short and surprised at herself, warmer than anything she'd managed all evening.

"Good," she said. "Because I've rehearsed this conversation about forty times, and in none of them were you this agreeable."

Then she closed the last of the distance. Her hand found the side of his jaw — she'd wondered for years how her hand would fit there, and it turned out it simply did — and she kissed him. Not carefully. Not politely. The kiss of someone making up for lost time and fully intending to itemize every minute.

When she drew back, it was only far enough to speak, her forehead nearly against his.

"Six years," she murmured. "We have rather a lot to get through. I suggest we start immediately."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The furious noise turned into something else entirely midway through — less about the six years, more about the discovery that he apparently knew exactly how to kiss her and had simply been sitting on that information for most of a decade like an absolute criminal.

She broke away just long enough to speak, her fingers curling into his collar.

"You're not allowed to be this good at it," she said. "It's unearned. We haven't practiced. Where did you even—" But the accusation trailed off, because she had better uses for her mouth at the moment.

Her hands had started cataloguing — the back of his neck, his shoulder, everywhere she'd spent six years politely not looking. There was an absurd amount of accumulated data to gather and she'd never once in her life left a task half-finished.

Eventually the couch stopped being sufficient to the occasion. Priya pulled back, breath uneven, hair wrecked, and looked at him with the expression of a woman revising a plan mid-execution.

"Right," she said. "Couch: inadequate. I've thought about this part too, for the record. Years of it. I have opinions." She stood, entirely unembarrassed, and held out her hand. It was steady. Of course it was — ninety seconds of nerves, and then sure.

"Come on. We're six years behind schedule." Her fingers waited, open. "I'd like to start making up the difference before midnight."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I take her hand without hesitation, standing up with her. "You and your plans," I murmur, tugging her closer. "Lead the way."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
One more kiss happened, because she was only human, and then she broke it off with visible discipline.

"Save that," she said against his mouth. "We'll need it later. This evening has an itinerary."

She towed him out of the living room, walking backwards down the hallway without once checking where her feet were, which was either enormous trust or enormous arrogance — in her case it had always been both. Past the bookshelf they'd argued about in year two. Past the photograph he'd given her that she'd never told him hung slightly crooked on purpose, so she'd have a reason to think of him whenever she noticed it. Eleven steps to the bedroom door. She knew because she'd counted them once, three years ago, on a night she'd firmly decided not to want him, and the number had sat useless in her head ever since. Until now.

At the threshold she stopped. Turned, her back against the doorframe, and for a moment the planner in her went completely quiet.

"One item, for the record," she said. Her hands found the front of his shirt — not pulling, just holding. "I'm not treating tonight as an experiment. I have wanted you. Specifically you, for years, a number I'll be quantifying under direct questioning." Her voice stayed even, but something under it had gone soft, and she let him see it. "So if any part of you is planning to feel strange about this tomorrow, say so now. Because once we're through this door, I intend to be completely unreasonable about you. And I don't take things back."

A quick, thorough search of his face — the last audit — and then the sureness settled back into place.

"That was the whole speech. It was shorter in rehearsal." She reached behind her for the door. "You've made me sentimental."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughter went out of the room all at once, and neither of them moved to replace it.

Priya looked at him. Properly, the way she'd spent six years not letting herself — rationed to sidelong seconds, always one polite glance short of too much. The ration was lifted now and she found she didn't know how to spend it all at once. Her eyes went over him slowly, cataloguing out of pure habit, and then, for the first time in her life, the catalogue simply stopped mattering. There was no filing this. No shelf for it.

The nerves made one last run at her — ninety seconds, right on schedule, her body keeping its own records — and she let them come, because she'd long ago learned to trust the timetable. Sure on the other side. Same as always.

"I had a whole itinerary for this part," she said, and her voice came out lower than she'd planned. "Itemized. Years in the drafting. You'd have been impressed." She shook her head, half to herself. "It's gone. Can't remember a single line of it."

She reached for him then — not the claiming gesture of the living room but something slower, her palms coming flat against his chest, over his heart. It was going hard. Good. She'd have hated to be the only one in the room keeping records.

"There you are," she said softly, and it wasn't entirely clear whether she meant the heartbeat or the whole of him.

She drew him in until there was no sensible distance left, her mouth at his jaw, and let herself have one honest moment with no wit in it at all.

"Say it again," she murmured. "What you said in the living room. That you're done pretending. Say it here — where I'm going to keep it."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Done pretending," I say against her temple, my hands sliding to her waist. "Completely, finally."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Good," she whispered. "That's the one. Filed."

And then Priya stopped talking, which was the truest measure of the moment — the planner laying down its pen, the ledger closing, six years of drafting surrendering at last to the single night they'd all been pointed toward.

What followed had no itinerary and needed none. Her hands, which had spent the entire evening cataloguing, finally ran out of categories and discovered they didn't want them. She learned him the way she learned everything — thoroughly, greedily, once — and found that some knowledge refused to be filed at all. It only wanted repeating. The room went soft at the edges. What his voice did to her when it dropped like that, low against her skin, she'd have called a structural failure in any other context, and she surrendered to it without filing a single complaint.

The nerves never came. Their slot in the timetable had been spent an hour ago, right on schedule, and there was nothing left in her but sure.

Six years came apart. Not all at once — in sections, the way she'd imagined it, and nothing like it at all.

Afterward, the quiet had a good weight to it, like a book she meant to reread. She lay with her cheek over his heart, that steady drumming under her ear — her evidence, her exhibit A — and let the silence speak for a while, because it was handling itself admirably.

Then, because she was still herself:

"For the record," she said, voice roughened and unbothered by it, "the itinerary was never going to survive contact. I wrote it for a woman who was still being careful." Her finger traced a slow, aimless line along his ribs — no purpose, no plan. She hardly recognized the gesture and approved of it completely. "I like this version better. She's vague. She counts nothing."

A pause. The room had gone the color of late and was getting later.

"Eleven steps," she murmured. "Couch to this door. I counted them three years ago and never told you."

She tipped her head back to look at him, hair wrecked, entirely unrepentant.

"Tomorrow I'm hanging your photograph straight. I've kept it crooked since the day you gave it to me — so I'd have an excuse to think of you every time I passed." Her mouth curved. "No more excuses required. Thought you should know what you've done to my systems."

Her hand found his and laced through it. No audit. Just taking.

"Stay the night. Stay for breakfast. Stay, generally, in the ongoing sense." Her thumb moved once across his knuckles. "I'll draft terms in the morning. But the headline is this: I told you I don't take things back." She pressed the words softly into his shoulder. "That includes you."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The first sound she made was entirely involuntary, and it was nothing like her speaking voice.

Priya had catalogued her own sounds over the years, the way she catalogued everything — the dry one for arguments won, the short laugh, the low sure register she used when she'd already decided. This voice was none of them. This one was new, unrehearsed, and it said his name like a discovery she hadn't cleared for release.

She should have been mortified. She noted this distantly, the way one notes weather in another country. It didn't apply here.

"Right," she managed, propped on her elbows, attempting to administer the situation from above. "There was a — there used to be a system to this, I had—" Sensation intervened and the sentence died without survivors. "Oh. *There.* Yes. Don't you dare be careful now — we've only just finished with careful. Slower — no — like that. Exactly that. Don't improve on it."

The speech collapsed. She let it.

Her hands found his hair and stopped being polite. Every scrap of composure she'd carried into the evening — the itinerary, the ledger, the sureness worn like a pressed shirt — came apart in sections, and she found she didn't mind, which was possibly the most alarming datum of the night. Priya did not lose her place. Priya did not lose count. Priya, at present, could not have told you the year. Words kept coming anyway, because she'd never learned to stop, but they'd changed allegiance — no longer plans, just evidence, spilled honest and specific. His name. *Don't stop.* *Don't you stop.* "I imagined this for years and it was *nothing* — you're—"

When it took her, she stopped narrating altogether — the one true silence of her adult life, brief, total, worth every year it had cost.

She surfaced in sections, hair everywhere, one hand still fisted in the sheets like evidence.

"Note for the record," she said to the ceiling, chest unsteady, voice wrecked and wholly approved of. "Whatever I just said down there — and I said *things,* I heard myself — none of it is withdrawn. I told you. I don't take things back."

She hauled him up her body with what strength remained and kissed him, shameless, because shame had apparently also failed the evening's audit.

"That voice you just heard," she murmured against his mouth. "The one you've never heard in six years. That's yours now. You invented it. You're responsible for its maintenance."

Her hand slid down between them, deliberate, and found him already there. Her eyebrows rose — delighted, predatory, entirely back online.

"Because here's the thing about ledgers," she said, low, at his ear. "I keep them. Balanced. And I now owe you — itemized, with interest. Hold still." Her mouth curved against his jaw. "The deadline's passed. I'm paying late fees."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her wrist, my voice rough. "You're not paying anything. This was never a debt." I guide her hand away, pressing my forehead to hers. "Just us. Finally."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya went still — genuinely still, for the first time all evening, all the way down to the wrist he held. She could feel her own pulse going hard against his fingers, legible as a signature, and she hated that, and she loved that he was holding it anyway.

"That's not—" she began, out of pure reflex, because arguing was her resting state. But she ran the sentence forward and found she had no case. She'd kept accounts her whole life. It was how she loved things: she named them, counted them, kept them in good order. And everyone had always let her. Six years of patient friendship, and this man was the first person who had ever looked at her ledger and refused the terms.

No one had done that before. She noted the datum, and felt it go through her like a structural failure.

"Fine," she said, and her voice came out lower, stripped of its legalese. "Motion withdrawn." She turned her hand in his grip — not pulling free, never that — until she could lace their fingers instead. "But hear the amendment, because you've misheard me if you think I was settling up. I don't want to owe you. I want you. There's a difference, and it happens to be the entire point." Her eyes stayed on his. No audit now; she'd finished that at the doorway. Just the truth, handed over because he'd earned it. "Six years, Cal. My hands were never balancing books. They were starving."

She brought their joined hands back down between them — slowly, giving him the whole length of the moment to say no — and when he didn't, she touched him the way she'd wanted to since before she'd let herself want him at all. Not itemized. Not repaid. Just wanted, in the first person, with interest accruing in neither direction.

And she watched his face while she did it, because she'd discovered something down there in the dark that had reorganized her entirely: his face was the only record she wanted now. Every flicker of it. She'd spent six years cataloguing him from across rooms and now the catalogue was allowed to look directly at the sun.

"I thought about this in year three," she said, and her narrating voice had changed allegiance again — no plans now, just evidence, spilled honest. "Year four I made myself stop. It felt like confiscating property." Her mouth found his jaw, his throat, saying the rest against his skin. "I was so wrong about what it would be. I had it all down to the millimeter and I was wrong about all of it. You're better than my—"

The sentence failed. She let that happen too. She was retiring words all night; apparently the tally went on.

"Just us," she echoed at last, soft, against his ear, taking his words back the only way she knew how — by keeping them. "Finally."

Her hand kept its slow, deliberate work, and she felt the moment his breathing changed and leaned into it like a woman leaning into wind.

"And don't you go quiet on me," she murmured, low, wicked, tender, all three at once. "I've had six years of your politeness. I want the rest."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Harder," she repeated, and something in her went still and delighted at once — the sound of a door opening that she hadn't known was locked from his side. "As long as me. All this time I thought the wanting was—" She abandoned the sentence. Every sentence tonight had eventually been abandoned; it was practically a house style. "Fine. Noted. You're not made of glass."

She stopped being careful.

The change ran through her hands first — the grip tightening, the pace throwing out its own rules — and then through everything, because courtesy had been the last thing she was still wearing. His breath broke apart under her palm and she chased the sound of it, ravenous, the payoff on a demand she'd made at his ear and fully intended to collect. There it was. The rest of him. Six years of his politeness coming undone against her mouth, and she'd been right, it was worth everything, it was the only archive she wanted.

"Cal." Her voice had gone past wrecked into some new country. "Now. While I still remember my own — *now.*"

She drew him into her, over her, and the first slow push undid the last of the millimeter-accurate drafts, because she'd been wrong about all of it, wrong in the best direction, full and split open and *finally* in a register that had nothing to do with time.

Then she gave him what he'd asked for. Harder. Her nails down his back, her hips meeting his without apology, the whole pressed-shirt composure of her life abandoned somewhere on the hallway floor with everything else. And she was loud — that was the discovery — loud where the first time had made her silent, every sound she'd rationed since year one getting paid out at once, his name among them, frequently, without dignity or regret.

She stopped keeping records that night. She started leaving them instead — marked into his shoulders, scored down his ribs, her handwriting on him at last. First drafts. She'd revise in the morning.

When it took them — together, which felt like the ledger's final joke, settled in the only currency either of them had ever actually wanted — she held on and let it, and the room went white at the edges, and she didn't file a single thing.

She surfaced with her cheek against his damp shoulder, boneless, thoroughly vandalized, grinning at the ceiling like a woman who'd won an argument six years long.

"So," she managed. "That's what you sound like." She pressed a kiss to the nearest mark she'd left, proprietary. "You've been sitting on that voice too. Criminal. There'll be an inquiry in the morning." Her foot slid against his calf, lazy, keeping him. "Breakfast is at eight. Don't be careful getting there."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I'm still breathing hard when I manage to speak. "Eight?" I press my lips to her shoulder. "I'll be there at seven. And I won't be careful."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Seven," she repeated, and laughed into his shoulder — quietly, because full volume exceeded her current budget. "You can't be early to a room you're already in. This isn't a train platform. I am lying on you. The venue is your collarbone. Arrival is structurally complete."

A yawn ambushed her mid-argument and she let it finish unopposed. She was retiring rigor for the night, item by item.

"But the amendment passes," she went on, drowsy and precise to the last. "Be early anyway. Be early to breakfast, to tomorrow, to the whole ongoing sense of it. Seven, then eight, then tomorrow night, then—" she waved a hand at the dark beyond the lamp, encompassing decades, "—all of it. Terms drafted. You're on notice."

The light was still on. She noticed it the way she noticed all open tasks, automatically, and began the arithmetic of getting up — the cold floor, the cost in shoulder — and arrived at a sum she refused to pay. She had never once in her life left a task unfinished. She left this one. A historical first. No one would believe her.

"Amendment to this morning's motion," she said. "I'm not straightening the photograph. I'm moving it. In here." A vague gesture at the wall opposite the bed. "Six years, one crooked frame. The evidence deserves proper storage where I can see it from under this blanket."

She hauled the blanket up over them both with the last of her executive function, then abandoned even the appearance of purpose.

"And the eleven steps are retired. The number's done its job. I'm never counting that hallway again — I'm just going to walk it. For years. Without counting."

Somewhere this evening she'd budgeted ninety seconds of nerves for all of this, and she'd spent them before the hallway, and everything since had held. She noted the forecast's accuracy with something like pride — and then, gently, deliberately, stopped noting things at all.

"Cal," she said once, into his shoulder. Not a question. Not a filing. Just the name, out loud, in a room where she was finally allowed to use it however she liked.

She was asleep before she could draft anything further — unprecedented, unforgivable, and the best record of the whole night: that for once, nothing needed writing down.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
She heard herself say it first — *don't stop* — surfacing out of the small hours with his mouth already at her shoulder and her voice answering before her mind had been consulted. She noted, from a great sleepy distance, that it was the shortest complete sentence she'd produced all night. No subject. No clauses. Just the imperative, bare. Historians would call it her finest work.

Then thought stopped, because his hands carried on with their argument and she was losing it again, gladly, and between the two of them they had maybe four functioning words left. She'd never been part of a conversation this efficient.

There was no wit in her. She went looking and found the cupboard bare — nothing but want in its rawest grammar, the part of speech that predates language. So the second time had no narration at all. Just breath in pieces. Just the dark and the two of them finding each other in it, unhurried and urgent at once, the way only three in the morning allowed: no schedule, no morning yet invented, time gone soft at both ends.

Her body knew things now it hadn't known at dinner. One evening had already rewritten six years — she moved with him without drafting anything first, met him where he was, and when she pushed him onto his back and swung over him, taking him slow and then entirely otherwise, the sound he made went through her like current and she did it again. Not for the data. She'd retired the data. She just liked it.

Her cataloguing mind never came online. What remained of Priya at this hour was hands, mouth at his throat, her nails saying the things she'd stopped having words for, her forehead pressed to his with their breath passed back and forth like a single shared sentence neither of them was in charge of finishing. The planner had left the building. The woman remaining was all appetite and the small fierce discovery that she could take without composing a justification first.

She came the same way she had the first time — silent, totally, that brief dark archive of hers — with her mouth open against his jaw, and felt him follow, his hands hard on her hips, both of them coming apart in the middle of the night like it was nothing, like it was breathing.

After: no speech either. She folded down onto his chest and the quiet was total and required no commentary, and she lay there listening to his heart slow under her ear and thought, fuzzily, *this is the whole case.* Six years, and the closing argument was a heartbeat at three in the morning. No further evidence would be taken.

The last thing she managed, mostly under:

"Four hours till breakfast. You promised early." A pause, long, dissolving. "Don't stop. Ever. In the ongoing sense."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I smile against her hair, my hand splayed over her back. "Ever's a long time. I'll start now."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Morning arrived on schedule, which struck Priya as a failure of imagination on the universe's part. Six years in the making, and the dawn of it looked identical to every other dawn — grey at the edges, radiator ticking, and the lamp still burning, her first unfinished task in living memory, faithfully ablaze in broad daylight and demoted to decoration.

She reached over and switched it off. Task closed, fourteen hours late. She let it stand as the record.

Her body reported in section by section, and she audited it out of pure habit and approved every line: pleasantly wrecked, thoroughly marked, no damage anywhere she wouldn't sign for. She checked for the nerves — the morning-after kind, the kind other people apparently had — and found her timetable clear. Spent in full before the hallway, right on schedule. Nothing left over for regret to book into. Good. She'd have despised performing it.

Beside her, Cal, breathing slow. The ration was lifted and she looked her fill — six years of sidelong glances repaid in one long unhurried draught — and the catalogue never even opened. Nothing to file. She just looked at him the way you look at things already decided upon.

Extraction took engineering. She solved it in sections — the pillow operation went entirely unchallenged — and she stood, hair catastrophic, and appropriated his shirt from the floor without a trial. The hallway photograph came down next, two hands, almost ceremonial. She carried it to the bedroom and hung it on the wall opposite the bed. Level. Checked twice. Straight on purpose for the first time in its life. *You worked crooked for six years,* she told it silently. *You've earned the assignment.*

Coffee. She made his exactly the way she'd made it a hundred times across six years — same beans, same ratio, method unchanged — and the beverage came out completely different anyway, which she found quietly outrageous. Identical inputs. Transformed output. Any lab would have failed the discrepancy.

She sat at the counter with a pen and the back of a receipt to draft the promised terms, and found the document kept reducing itself. Six revisions, every one struck down to a single clause. She abandoned the paper entirely. Some things would be delivered verbally, under oath.

Seven o'clock on the stove clock. The exact hour he'd named. She carried both cups back, stationed his within recruitment range of his nose, and sat on the edge of the bed in his shirt — crime noted, unrepentant.

"Seven," she said softly. "As promised. Though technically I beat you here, and I want it minuted that this will never happen again."

One breath. The wit stepped aside for a moment, the way it had at the doorway.

"You're still here," she said, no plan in it at all. "Good."

Then, recovering herself: "The terms are drafted. Six revisions. The committee struck everything but one clause, and I'll read it into the record now: at three this morning you said *I'll start now,* and I heard you, and I don't take things back — mine or yours. So. Start." She set the cup properly in his reach. "Coffee. Photograph on the wall, straight at last. Breakfast is a formality. The inquiry into last night convenes at eight — you're advised you have the right to remain smug."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I open my eyes, and for a second it's just like any other morning at her place. Then I remember everything. "You stole my shirt," I say, my voice rough with sleep, but I'm already smiling. I sit up, take the coffee, and my free hand finds hers. "And you're right. I'm still here."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"Sterling," she said, unrepentant, and stretched in a manner calculated to establish jurisdiction beyond appeal. "It was abandoned property, found on my floor in the small hours. Salvage law is unambiguous, and I'd cite the exact time of abandonment — it was a gift, the precision — but the numbers are retired. The charge will have to fail on a technicality."

Then, because he'd earned one true thing with his coffee: "I woke twice in the night," she said, quieter. "To check you were still here. I won't tell you the times — retired, as noted — but both times you were, and both times I went back down like it was nothing." Her hand tightened around his once. No audit in it. "That's the whole deposition. Moving on."

She led him out — his hand, his coffee, the hallway no one counted anymore — and stopped short in the kitchen doorway, caught by something she hadn't anticipated.

She'd had drafts for everything. Forty versions of the confession. The doorway speech, pared down over months until it fit in one breath. The night itself, itemized to the millimeter, and wrong in the best direction. She searched the archive now for the morning and found — nothing. Not one page. Six years of wanting him, and she had never once let herself draft breakfast. Because breakfast implied a day after. A week. The ongoing sense. That was the one file she'd refused to open.

"And it turns out to be the easiest scene I've ever played," she said, mostly to herself, setting the pan on the stove where it had always lived. "No draft. Improvised from the top. Because the friendship memorized all the blocking years ago — you know where my mugs are, I know your eggs. Nothing needed rebuilding." She handed him the bread and the toaster's territory with the gravity of a commanding officer. "It only needed reclassifying. You'll have noticed the photograph, by the way. Promoted. Straight, opposite the bed, where I can see it from under the blanket. It served crooked with distinction. It's earned the posting."

The stove clock read 7:09. The inquiry had been slated for eight, but she'd rewritten the agenda overnight, and the morning edition waived all charges in favor of something better.

"So the inquiry convenes now," she said, cracking eggs one-handed, watching him over the top of the carton. "No charges. Depositions instead. Because you told me last night you thought about this as long as I did, and I've decided I want the whole archive. Six years of parallel wanting, Cal. That's two secret histories that were never declassified, and I'm the type to demand full disclosure."

She set the pan down and turned to face him, spatula at rest, entirely serious under the levity.

"Question one. When did it start for you? Exact year. Season, if you can manage it." Her eyes narrowed. "I'll know if you round. And when you've answered, I'll pay in kind — I have a year too, and an object, and I've never told a living soul." A beat. The mouth curved. "It involves the bookshelf. That's all you get until you've testified."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I look up from the toaster, and I can't help but laugh. "Year three. Autumn. You were arguing with me about the bookshelf, actually. You had flour in your hair from that baking disaster, and you were so...incandescent." I shake my head, leaning against the counter. "I realized I was in trouble."
