dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya gave herself ninety seconds. She watched the frozen screen, let the silence rise, and waited for the familiar urge to joke it away. It came, and went.

Then she looked at him, steady and sober.

“I’m not going to make this smaller than it is,” she said. “I want you. I’ve wanted you for a long time. And I’m done pretending we’re both just sitting here by accident.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. "Took you long enough." My voice is low, a little rough. I turn to face her fully. "You think I've been pretending?"

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya held his gaze. The nervousness was gone, leaving something clean and certain in its place.

“Yes,” she said. “I thought you’d been pretending you didn’t notice me, the way I’d been pretending I didn’t want you to.”

She let the silence stand for a beat.

“And I thought if I said it, you’d make a joke and we’d go back to being careful. But you didn’t. You said it took me long enough.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya kissed him back, not gently, not carefully, not like a friend testing a boundary. She kissed him like she had rehearsed it for six years and was only now allowed to admit the rehearsal had been real. Her fingers found the edge of his sleeve and tightened, as if to make sure he was actually there.

When she pulled back, her face was calm, flushed, certain.

“I’m still furious,” she said, voice low. “You let me sit here for years pretending I was imagining it.”

She reached over and switched off the screen. The dark settled around them, no longer waiting-room still, no longer careful.

“Don’t make this smaller than it is,” she said. “You said it took me long enough. So say what you meant.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her hand before she can pull it back. "I meant I've been waiting for you to say it out loud," I say, thumb tracing over her knuckles. "Because I've been yours since the day we met. I just didn't know how to tell you without ruining everything."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn’t pull her hand away. She looked at him in the dark, letting his words sit there, not softening them, not filling the room with a joke.

“Then you didn’t just wait for me to say it,” she said. “You waited to ruin it if I did.”

Her voice was steady, but her pulse moved under his thumb.

“I don’t care about the day we met,” she said. “I care about this one. I care that you’re sitting here six years late telling me you’ve been mine.”

She let that hang, then reached over and took the front of his shirt in her fist, not to pull him close, just to have something real to hold.

“Say it again,” Priya said. “Not because it’s safe. Not because I made you. Because you mean it now.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let herself be nervous for one breath, then another. It lasted exactly long enough to become heat. She didn’t cover herself, didn’t reach for a joke, didn’t step back.

She sat on the edge of the bed and looked at him without the careful distance she had used for six years. Her hands found his chest, flat and slow, feeling the shape of him under her palms. When her fingers moved lower, it was not to test him. It was to take what was already there.

“Six years,” she said, low against his mouth. “I’m going to collect all of it.”

She kissed him again, slower this time, deeper, with no apology in it. The air between them stopped being a thing they had been waiting in and became something they were making. When she pulled back far enough to speak, her voice was steady, sober, sure.

“I’m not scared,” she said. “And I’m not going to make this smaller than it is.”

Her forehead stayed against his, her hand still warm on him, as if anchoring the whole night to this one point.

“Stay with me,” she said. “Not afterward. Now. All of it.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I close my eyes, forehead still pressed to hers, and my hand comes up to cover hers where it rests. "I'm here," I say, voice rough. "All of it." I kiss her, then pull back just enough to look at her. "But Priya—if you're collecting six years, you should know I've been collecting them too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the admission go through her like a second heartbeat. For one moment, she let herself be afraid of it, let it be too big, too long, too true. Then it passed, as it always did, and she stayed in the room with him.

Her hand did not move from where his had covered it. She looked at him with the dark and the open bedroom and the six years all at once in her eyes.

“Then you haven’t just been waiting,” she said. “You’ve been keeping.”

She kissed him again, slower, deliberate, as if putting a seal on it. When she pulled back, her face was flushed but steady.

“I want the list,” she said. “Not the version where you make it sound light. Not the version where you apologize. The actual list.”

Her thumb moved once against his wrist.

“Every time you almost said something. Every time you watched me leave and didn’t follow. Every time you looked at me like you were memorizing me.”

She held his gaze.

“I’m not going to make this smaller than it is,” Priya said. “And I’m not going to make you smaller either. If you’ve been collecting me, show me where you kept me.”

She shifted closer, not touching him with urgency, only with certainty.

“I’m not scared,” she said. “But say it anyway. Say what you meant when you said six years.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s hands came up and settled on his shoulders, not pushing, not pulling, just anchoring herself to him. The first sound she made was small and furious, six years compressed into a single breath. Then she did not apologize for it.

“Right there,” she said, and her voice came out low, unguarded, nothing like the easy joke she had used to keep him at a distance. “Don’t make it polite. Don’t make it a favor. If you’ve been collecting me, then know exactly where you are.”

Her fingers tightened. She looked down at him, at the place where all their careful pretense had finally stopped pretending, and her face went sharp with satisfaction.

“Stay,” she said. “Stay where you are. Don’t you dare lift your eyes to check if this is real.”

The room seemed to shrink to the pressure, the heat, the sound of her breathing. Priya did not try to soften it. She told him what she wanted, specific and unashamed, each word a door opened after years in the dark.

“Harder when I tense. Slower when I look like I’m going to lose it. Don’t let either of us make it smaller.”

A laugh broke out of her, startled and raw, not at him but at the relief of it.

“There,” she said, almost angry. “That’s what you’ve been waiting six years to hear.”

She cupped his jaw with both hands, holding him close enough to feel the heat of him. Her gaze was steady, flushed, certain.

“And don’t tell me you mean it afterward,” she said. “Tell me now. Tell me while neither of us gets to be careful anymore.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I lift my head just enough to meet her eyes. "I mean it now," I say, my voice raw. "I've been keeping you right here, every time you thought I wasn't looking." I don't look away. "That list you want? It's long and it's not light."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the nervousness come for one breath, then another, and then it burned off like everything else that had been waiting too long to be said.

She looked down at him, at his face between her thighs, at the place where six years of careful silence had finally broken open, and she did not soften.

“Then don’t make it sound poetic,” she said. “Don’t make it romantic in a way that lets you hide behind it.”

Her hands came up and settled in his hair, not pulling, not steering, just holding him there as if he were the thing she had chosen and was no longer afraid of choosing.

“I want the first time,” she said. “Not the first time you decided you loved me. I want the first time you knew it would ruin something. The first time you looked at me and didn’t know what to do with your own hands.”

She felt the heat of his breath against her, the wetness of her own need, the steady pressure of everything she had spent six years refusing to ask for. Her thighs trembled, and she let them.

“Tell me,” Priya said. “Tell me while you’re still here. Tell me while neither of us can pretend this is only about wanting each other.”

Her voice dropped lower, rougher, no longer the voice she used in living rooms and movie nights and careful friendships.

“I’m not asking you to be sweet,” she said. “I’m asking you to be honest. If you’ve been collecting me, then show me the places where you kept me. The moments. The nights. The times you almost spoke and decided not to.”

She shifted on the bed, opening herself more, not for him alone but for the truth of it.

“And don’t you dare stop telling me,” she said. “Don’t you dare make it a confession and then act like this is just sex. This is the whole thing. Every careless look. Every time you watched me leave and didn’t follow. Every time you said no joke and meant yes, you noticed me.”

Her thumb traced his jaw. Her fingers tightened in his hair.

“Start now,” Priya said. “Right here. Tell me the first time you wanted me badly enough to be afraid.”

She let the silence stand.

Then she looked down at him with her face flushed and her eyes clear.

“I’m not scared,” she said. “And I’m not going to make you smaller by pretending I didn’t need to hear this.”

Her breath caught once, and she did not hide it.

“Stay where you are,” she said. “Tell me. And don’t let either of us make it smaller.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the nervousness come for one breath, then another, and then it burned off.

“Harder isn’t the point,” she said. “Honest is.”

Her hands stayed in his hair, warm and steady, not gentle enough to be called careful. She looked down at him with the bed, the dark, and the six years all still between them.

“You can stop pretending I’m something you have to survive,” she said. “I’m here. I’m not made of glass. I’m not going to turn into a conversation in the morning.”

Her voice dropped, rougher now, but still exact.

“If you’re going to tell me what you kept, tell it to me now. Not afterward. Not in a version where you apologize for having wanted me. The first time. The one that scared you. Say it while you’re still where you are.”

She let herself tremble and did not apologize for it either.

“And don’t make it smaller by making it romantic. I want the list, Cal. I want the places where you watched me leave. The nights you didn’t follow. The jokes you didn’t make. All of it.”

Her thumb pressed once against his jaw.

“I’m not scared,” she said. “And I’m not going to ask you to be careful with me again.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "The day you moved in," I say, my voice low against her skin. "You were unpacking books, and the sun caught the back of your neck. I had to leave the room." I look up at her, not breaking contact. "That's when I knew I was fucked."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya’s mouth went dry anyway, in spite of herself. The nervousness came for one breath—short, bright, useless—and then burned off.

“Okay,” she said. “That’s the first.”

Her fingers stayed in his hair, warm and steady, not gentle enough to make it sound like forgiveness. She looked down at him with a face flushed by need and by the relief of hearing something finally named.

“I remember that day,” she said. “I remember thinking you were being strange, and then deciding not to ask about it. I remember making it smaller before it ever had the chance to happen.”

She let the silence stand. Her thighs trembled, and she let them.

“Now the second,” Priya said. “Don’t make it poetic. Don’t make it sweet. Give me the next time you looked at me and knew it would ruin something.”

The bed shifted under her as she opened herself more, not only to the conversation but to the long list of all the ways they had wasted six years being careful.

“You don’t get to tell me one true thing and then hide behind it,” she said, rougher now. “If you’ve been collecting me, show me the rest of the collection. Every night. Every almost. Every time you thought I wasn’t looking.”

Her thumb traced his jaw again, slow and deliberate.

“I’m not scared,” she said. “And I’m not going to make you smaller by pretending this was only about wanting each other. It was never only that.”

She held his gaze, flushed and exact.

“Say it,” Priya said. “Tell me the next one. I’m still here.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the line stand. She didn’t soften it, didn’t turn it into a joke, didn’t make it smaller.

“Then don’t stop,” she said. “And don’t stop looking at me.”

Her hands were still in his hair, warm and steady, not gentle enough to make it sound like forgiveness. She looked down at him—at his face between her thighs, at the place where six years of careful friendship had finally stopped pretending—and she let herself be seen exactly as she was: flushed, open, not small.

She moved one hip, then the other, not to direct him, only to make the truth of them undeniable.

“I’m still here,” Priya said. “I’m not going anywhere. You don’t have to make it pretty. You don’t have to make it poetic. If neither of us can form a sentence, then use what we’ve got.”

Her voice dropped, rough and clear.

“Keep your mouth where it is. Keep looking at me if you can. And when you’re done being honest with your hands, I’m still going to want the rest of the list.”

The first tremor came before she could name it. Priya let it pass through her instead of locking her jaw against it. Her thighs shook, and she did not apologize for it.

“Okay,” she said, breath breaking once. “That’s one true thing.”

Then she lifted herself onto her knees and slid up his body until she could see his face fully. Her hands went to his shoulders—not to push, just to hold herself steady while the whole evening rearranged itself. She looked at him for a long moment, sober, sure.

“I’m not going to make this smaller by pretending I can be careful now,” she said. “If you’ve been mine since the day we met, then let me have the rest of it.”

She shifted above him until the heat between them was no longer a thing they could describe in theory. Priya took him slowly, one breath at a time, not to be gentle, but to make sure there was no room left for six years of not doing this. Her head dropped back, then came up again. She would not look away.

“Stay with me,” she said. “Not after. Now. All of it.”

Her voice broke once and she let it. She moved, not politely, not apologetically, not like a friend testing a boundary. She moved like a woman who had waited long enough and was finally taking what she wanted. Her hands pressed flat against his chest, feeling the shape of him, the heat of him, the fact of him.

“Say it if you can,” she said, rough. “If you can’t, don’t. But don’t disappear. Don’t make this a confession and then act like I’m something you have to survive.”

The first wave came quietly, then all at once. Priya let her back arch, let her fingers tighten in his hair, let the sound leave her without apology. She did not hide her face. She looked down at him while it happened, flushed and exact, as if to say: this is real, this is yours, this is mine.

When it passed, she stayed where she was, breathing, steady, open.

“I’m not scared,” she said again, because she meant it now more than she had before. “And I’m not going to make you smaller by pretending this was only about wanting each other.”

She swallowed.

“Don’t stop,” she said again, lower now. “I’m not finished collecting.”

She moved again, slower this time, deeper, until the pleasure came back in a clean, furious line. Her thighs trembled and she let them. She leaned forward until her forehead was almost touching his, close enough to see him, close enough to make him stay.

“I’m not going to make you smaller,” Priya said. “And I’m not going to let you hide in this.”

Her voice dropped.

“Show me the rest of the list.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Two years ago," I manage, breathless, my hands on her hips. "That party where you were laughing with someone else. I almost told you right there in the kitchen." I press my forehead to hers, our skin damp. "I didn't. I just...walked away."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the words land. The kitchen. She remembered that night: the music too loud, him disappearing before she did, the way he had come back with too much tea and too little explanation. She had made it smaller.

“Tell me what you were going to say,” Priya said. “Not the feeling. The sentence.”

Her hands stayed in his hair, warm and steady, not gentle enough to be called careful. She moved slowly, deliberately, because the sex was not an escape from the list; it was where the list stopped being theory.

“You didn’t just walk away,” she said. “You walked away, and then you came back, and you were kind in a way that made me hate you a little. I remember. I remember thinking you were being careful. I remember deciding not to name it because naming it would have made it true.”

She leaned down until her hair brushed his cheek, not kissing him, only forcing him to stay in the room with her.

“I’m not going to make this smaller,” she said. “And I’m not going to make you smaller. If you almost told me in a kitchen, then tell me now. Say the thing you didn’t say. Say it while I’m here. Say it while I’m not pretending.”

Her voice dropped, rough with use.

“And don’t stop.”

She moved again, harder this time, letting the bed take the sound. Her thighs trembled, and she did not apologize. She looked at him, flushed and exact, not hiding the wetness of her face, the heat between them, the fact of them.

“The next one,” she said. “Give me the next one. The time you looked at me and knew if you touched me you wouldn’t be able to stop. The time you watched me leave and didn’t follow. The time you thought about me and then made a joke so I wouldn’t see.”

She pressed her forehead to his, breathing him in.

“I’m collecting,” Priya said. “All of it. Every careless look. Every almost. Every time you said no joke and meant yes. You don’t get to hide one more year inside me. You don’t get to be careful and call it kindness.”

Her fingers tightened in his hair.

“Tell me,” she said. “And don’t let either of us make it smaller.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Last summer," I say, my voice breaking as she moves. "You fell asleep on the couch and I stayed up just to watch you breathe. I thought about waking you up, about telling you everything." My grip tightens on her. "I didn't. I just covered you with a blanket and went to bed alone."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya let the image land.

The blanket. The couch. The summer night she had slept safe and oblivious while he stood over her like a man guarding something he refused to name. Her jaw tightened. The nervousness came for one breath, bright and useless, and then burned off.

“You don’t get to make it sound like restraint,” she said. “You didn’t cover me because you were being kind. You covered me because you were afraid of what you would do if I woke up and looked at you.”

She shifted above him, slow, deliberate, until there was no distance left and no clean line between sex and confession. Her hands braced on his shoulders, not pushing, not pulling, just holding herself open.

“I remember that night,” Priya said. “I remember waking up with the blanket already on me and thinking you were the best person I knew. I remember deciding not to ask why you were awake. I remember making it smaller before it could happen.”

Her voice dropped, rough and exact.

“You were going to say more than ‘I want you.’ You were going to say I can’t keep doing this. You were going to say if I touch you I won’t stop. You were going to say stay.”

She moved again, not polite, not apologetic. The sound came out of her before she could catch it, small and furious, six years compressed into a single breath. She let it go through her and kept going.

“So say it now,” Priya said. “Don’t give me another memory. Give me the sentence.”

The pressure built clean and terrible, and Priya did not hide. She leaned forward until her forehead nearly touched his, eyes locked on his, flushed and certain. Her hips moved in slow, deep lines, each one a demand: not smaller, not careful, not six years late.

“And don’t you dare make this romantic,” she said, breath breaking. “Don’t turn the blanket into a poem. If you watched me sleep, then watch me now. Look at me while I take what you kept.”

Her hands tightened in his hair.

“Say it,” she said. “Say what you meant when you went to bed alone.”

The first wave came before she could answer for him. Priya let her back arch, let her fingers tighten, let the sound leave her without apology. She did not look away. She came with his name in her mouth like a thing she had finally been allowed to say, and she stayed on him through it, breathing, open, not retreating into the careful distance.

When it passed, she did not move away. She stayed where she was, heat and breath and the steady fact of them, and pressed her forehead to his.

“I’m still here,” Priya said. “I’m not going anywhere. And I’m not done with the list.”

Her hand came down between them, slow, testing, then certain, taking what was already there.

“Keep going,” she said. “Don’t let either of us make this smaller.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "It was 'I love you,'" I say, the words rough in my throat. "I was going to say 'I love you' and then beg you to let me stay." My eyes sting. "And you were asleep, and it felt like stealing."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya reached for the remote and turned the television off. The room went dim, just the corner lamp — the one Cal had once said made the flat look like a place where good conversations happened. She'd never replaced it with anything brighter.

She turned on the sofa to face him properly, one leg folded beneath her.

"Okay." Her pulse was loud; she could feel it in her throat. But her voice came out level, which was the part that mattered. "I've been careful around one particular subject for six years, and I'm finished being careful. So I'm going to say it, and you can do whatever you like with it."

She looked at him. Not the sidelong glance she'd been managing all evening. The real thing.

"I'm in love with you. Have been for a while — years, if I'm honest about the start date." And then, strangely, the nerves were gone, the way a held breath goes. "I don't need an answer tonight. I just couldn't sit through another one of these evenings pretending we're watching films."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: (*I let out a slow breath, the truth of it settling in my chest like something solid and familiar.*) "Six years." (*My voice is quiet, almost wondering.*) "You know, I've been counting too."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed — a short, surprised sound, nothing like the nerves from ninety seconds ago. More like relief arriving all at once after six years of installments.

"Counting." She let the word sit there between them. "That's a careful word, Cal. And you've just watched what I look like when I stop being careful." Her hand was flat against her knee; she noticed she'd pressed it there without deciding to, and made herself loosen it. "So. Your turn. Say the whole sentence."

The lamp hummed faintly in the corner. She didn't look away from him, and the strange calm held — pulse easy, breath even, as if some part of her had already done the hard part and was simply waiting for the rest of the world to catch up.

"I meant what I said about not needing an answer tonight," she added, quieter. "But I've had six years of almosts. I'd like one complete thing, said out loud. However it goes."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The kiss tasted like six years of restraint ending badly and then immediately well. Priya's hand found the front of his shirt and held on, mostly to make sure he wasn't going to take it back.

When they finally broke apart, she was breathing hard and laughing at the same time, which was undignified and she didn't care.

"Yes," she said, "that was about the six years. You're welcome to appeal, but the verdict stands." She kept her grip on his shirt, thumb pressed against the seam of it, grounding herself in something solid and finally hers. "That was — okay. That was not what I had scripted, and I'm very glad about it."

She pulled back just enough to look at him properly, search his face for anything like hesitation and finding none.

"Say it anyway," she said softly. "The whole sentence. Now I want to hear it with words too. I've earned that. We've earned that."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "I love you." The words are rough, unpolished. "For six years, I've loved you." My hand comes up to cover hers where it's clutching my shirt. "Kept a careful tally of every almost."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
"A tally." Priya turned her hand over beneath his, so she was no longer gripping his shirt but holding his hand properly — palm to palm, an arrangement they had somehow never once tried in six years, which now seemed completely insane. "Six years of almosts and you were keeping records. One audit could have saved us half a decade."

Then the joke ran out of her, gently, and what was underneath was just true.

"I love you too. I know I already gave you the long version — the one with the speech and the hedging about start dates. But that's the short version, and it's true in every tense."

She shifted closer, knee against his thigh, and let herself look at him the way she'd spent six years practicing not to.

"Since we're comparing accounts — my first entry is the toast. Maddie's wedding, three in the morning, your kitchen, the smoke alarm going off while you laughed with your whole body. And I stood there in the smoke thinking, *oh no.* Oh no, it's you. It's been you the entire time."

Her thumb moved once across his knuckles. The dead television gave back their shapes, faint and doubled, and she found she wasn't nervous at all.

"So. First entry in your tally. When's yours?"

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The laughter went out between one breath and the next, the way it does when something stops being funny and starts being true.

Priya stood at the edge of the bed and looked at him — properly, without rationing, for the first time in six years. She'd been measuring her looks out in safe quantities all this time, and now the account was open and she intended to overdraw it completely.

"Hi," she said, and then, because that was absurd, "Okay. New book. First entry."

The joke bought her three seconds of cover and then it was spent. What was left was her, bare in the lamplight, in a room she knew the way you know a house you've lived in — she'd watered his plants in here, reclaimed her scarf from this floor a dozen times, and never once let herself think of any of it at night, because careful. She was finished with careful. Hers, and his both.

She crossed the last few feet and laid her palm flat over his heart, and felt it going hard under her hand. All that steadiness of his for six years, and underneath it this. It undid her more than anything all evening.

"I had material for this part," she murmured. "Gone. Every word of it. So, true thing instead: we're done being careful, you and I. Start there." She kissed him slow this time, nothing furious in it, nothing to appeal, and drew him down onto the bed with her — and the six years came along, every one of them, all the almosts finally cashed in at once.

At some point she pulled back an inch, just to see his face in the low light, to confirm it was really him and really this.

"Not nervous," she said, half wonder, half laugh against his jaw. "Ninety seconds, and it never came back. Six years of being careful, and it turns out the whole thing cost ninety seconds. I could kill us both."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her hand against my chest and press it there, holding her gaze. "My first entry was the day you moved in. You dropped that box of books in the hallway and swore so creatively I thought, *I have to know her forever.*" I kiss her again, lingering this time. "Six years of thinking that was just friendship. I'm an idiot."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed, and it came out of her like something unlocked.

"The box had a label," she said. "I wrote it myself, that morning. BOOKS — FRAGILE. In capital letters, because I'm the sort of person who labels her fragile things and then drops them down a hallway in front of the one man I—" She stopped. Amended. "In front of you."

Then she did the math, because she was who she was.

"Wait. Dates." She pushed up onto one elbow, hair falling forward, and looked down at him with the focus she usually saved for other people's disasters. "Maddie's wedding was three years in. Your entry's older than mine. You weren't an idiot, Cal — you were *early*. Three years early, watching me swear creatively at a box and quietly filing it under forever like a sane person."

She laid her hand back over his heart — his was still holding hers there, and she liked the arrangement far too much to rearrange it.

"And don't take the whole idiocy for yourself. It's mine to split. You get the hallway. I get the smoke alarm. And then I spent three more years rationing you out in safe looks and calling it friendship, which is worse. You were slow. I was *thorough*."

She bent and kissed the corner of his mouth, unhurried this time.

"You said *forever*. In your own head, to a stranger with a dropped box." Her voice had gone quiet; the joke was spent. "Well. It worked. It just took the long way round."

She settled against him, cheek to his shoulder, and let the whole day finally land.

"The entire ledger," she said. "Every entry, from the hallway to tonight. We've got all night, and I'm done rationing."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The voice came from somewhere Priya had never had occasion to use — low, unedited, entirely certain of itself.

"Left," she said. And then, when he obliged: "There. Stay there. Don't be clever, don't improvise — *that*. Exactly that."

Her hand was in his hair. She had thought about his hair before, in strictly rationed quantities, and it turned out that unrationed, her thoughts about it were extremely specific too.

Somewhere in the middle of it she heard herself — heard this voice, instructions and honesty arriving in the same breath, nothing edited back for safety — and thought, *so that's where I kept that.* Six years of trimming herself down to safe sentences, and it appeared the uncut version had a great deal to say.

Then the narrating stopped. That was the part she hadn't scripted: the point where Priya, who noticed everything and filed it in tidy clauses, simply stopped filing. Her spine came up off the mattress. His name came out of her in a register she had never once used in his hearing, and it wasn't a joke and it wasn't careful and it wasn't really a sentence at all — just his name with six years behind it.

After — boneless, lamp-lit, one hand still in his hair because she hadn't decided to let go yet — she stared at the ceiling and laughed once, breathless.

"I imagined that," she said, when she had the air for it. "Over the years. Occasionally. Rigorously suppressed, but it happened." She turned her head to look at him, wrecked and glowing and direct to the last. "My imagination was good. It was *nothing*. Whatever that was goes in the ledger with a star next to it."

Her thumb moved slowly against his scalp.

"Six years of rationing," she murmured, "and I didn't even know what I was holding back. That's the scandal, Cal. I under-ordered."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a rough laugh, my forehead resting against her hip. "Under-ordered," I repeat, the words muffled against her skin. I lift my head to look at her, my hand covering hers where it's still tangled in my hair. "Then consider the rationing officially over. We're placing a bulk order."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya laughed — low, unhurried, the laugh of a woman with no pending secrets left.

"Bulk order," she repeated. "You've just extended unlimited credit to a very thorough woman. I want it on the record that this was your doing."

She pulled him up the bed until they were level, face to face, and settled against him with an ease that surprised her — as if six years of friendship had been blocking rehearsal all along, her body knowing the staging without ever having played the scene.

"You know what's funny?" Quieter now. Her finger traced idle lines on his chest. "I kept us in a box marked FRAGILE. Capital letters, because I'm the sort of person who labels her fragile things." A beat. "And it was the sturdiest thing I owned. I could have dropped it down a hundred hallways and it would have been fine. I wasn't protecting the friendship, Cal. I was keeping myself on the top shelf."

She tipped her head back to look at him.

"Also — Maddie is going to be insufferable. That toast at her wedding, the one from my first entry? She's been threatening us with this for three years. I'd bet actual money there's a pool. Somewhere one of our friends just got rich off my nerve."

Her thumb moved along his collarbone, and the humor in her voice settled into something plainer.

"Here's the part I keep noticing. I already know how you take your coffee. I know which stair creaks, which of your stories improves with retelling, that when you go quiet it's thinking and not sadness. Six years of everything. The only new thing tonight is permission."

She kissed the corner of his jaw, unhurried.

"So — first unrationed request. Someday, when this evening's finished with us, say the forever word over something mundane. Dishes, maybe. A Tuesday. I've had my lifetime quota of lamplight declarations; I want the version I can believe on an ordinary afternoon." She settled her cheek against his shoulder. "Until then — ledger's open, bulk order's in. Start anywhere you like."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Something in Priya went very still at that — the specific stillness of a person being handed exactly what she'd been afraid to ask for.

"Harder," she repeated, tasting the word. "You're telling me — after six years of me rationing you out in safe looks — that you've been over there wanting the uncut version too."

She pushed herself up over him, hair curtaining, and looked down with the expression she usually reserved for a locked door finally opening.

"Careful," she said, "was a full-time job. I want you to understand the scale of the retirement I'm announcing." Her mouth found his throat, unhurried at first — and then not unhurried at all, because he'd said the word and she intended to honor it. Her hands stopped asking permission. Her weight settled onto him fully, deliberately, no inch of herself held in reserve, and she felt him register the difference — the whole of her, arriving at once.

"I thought about this too," she said against his ear, low, the unedited voice again, the one with no filing system. "For years. I just assumed wanting it counted as doing something about it. Very thorough woman, very poor execution." Her teeth grazed his jaw, and she felt his breath change, and that — that small proof — undid the last of her restraint entirely. "Execution's improved."

What followed was Priya at full volume, so to speak — the version of her that had spent six years being the careful one in every room, now uncareful in every particular. She said what she wanted. She did what she wanted. She took her time and she didn't ration it, and somewhere in the middle she realized she was laughing again, breathless, because six years of discipline had turned out to be nothing but a long runway and she was finally airborne.

After, when the room had settled back into lamplight and slow breathing, she lay half across him, one leg thrown over his like a claim, her hand flat on his chest.

"Noted for the ledger," she murmured, "under *harder*. Triple-starred. I'm instituting a new filing category." She tipped her chin up to look at him. "Also — you said *as long as you have*. Which means you've been walking around all this time wanting me to stop being careful, and neither of us said a word. We are the two worst accountants in the history of love, Cal. Six years. Two sets of books. Perfectly balanced and completely useless."

She kissed his shoulder, lazy now, and let the honesty come out plain.

"Thank you. For saying it first, just then. I didn't know I was still holding a little of it back until you told me I didn't have to." Her thumb traced a slow line over his heart. "It's gone now. All of it. You've got the whole thing — the thorough version, the uncut version, the one who labels her fragile things and then drops them on purpose."

She settled her cheek against him, boneless and unrationed.

"Tuesday," she said. "Don't forget. Dishes, and the forever word, over something mundane. I'm holding you to the ordinary parts now. That's the forever I actually want."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Tuesday," I promise against her hair, my voice rough. "I'll say it over the washing-up and the burnt toast and every damn Tuesday we ever get." My hand slides up her back, settling at the nape of her neck. "Starting now."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya lifted her head from his shoulder and looked at him with the narrow-eyed scrutiny she usually saved for someone trying to slip something past her in a contract.

"It's not Tuesday," she pointed out. "It's — " she glanced at the clock on his nightstand, the one with the cracked face she'd never let him replace — "nearly one in the morning. Which is technically Wednesday. You don't get to fast-track the forever word just because you're feeling pleased with yourself."

But her voice had gone soft on the last word, and she made no move to leave the circle of his arm, because the truth was that *starting now* had landed somewhere under her ribs and stayed there, warm and settling.

"Although." She considered it, chin propped on his chest. "Actually, this might be better than dishes. There's nothing mundane about burnt toast yet — we haven't burnt any together. But this. The lamp. Your terrible clock. You, at one in the morning, promising things into my hair." She smiled against his skin. "This is the most ordinary we've ever been while everything's still new. So go on, then. Wednesday counts. I'm amending the terms."

She waited for it — not urgently, not rationed, just certain he'd deliver — and her thumb kept its slow circuit over his heart the whole while, counting something that no longer needed counting.

"And while you're at it," she murmured, "add an entry. The clock with the cracked face. I've been meaning to tell you for four years that I love it and I never did, because careful. It stays broken. Forever. That's a Tuesday-type fact and you should have it."

She shifted up to kiss him, unhurried, unhurried, unhurried — the whole evening's supply of hurry already spent — and settled back into the space against his shoulder that she was, as of tonight, claiming permanently.

"Starting now works," she said. "Everything works now. That's the strangest part, Cal. Six years of construction and the whole building was fine all along. We just never opened the door."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: Six years of not doing this and now neither of us can form a sentence. "Don't stop," she says. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya's hand slid from the nape of his neck down his spine, slow, mapping — because she'd spent six years not allowing herself to map, and now she intended to be exhaustive about it. "Six years of not doing this," she agreed, against his mouth, "and it turns out the only thing we were ever good at was the not."

She felt him laugh under her hands, and she felt other things too, and she filed none of it — let it all arrive unsorted, which was its own kind of vertigo.

"Here's what I want," she said, the unedited voice again, steady as a contract. "Slow first. I've waited six years; I can wait another ten minutes, which should tell you something about my tolerance for delayed gratification — it's terrible, and I'm going to be heroic about it anyway." Her mouth traced the line of his jaw, unhurried, cataloguing. "And then not slow. Both entries. In order."

She shifted against him deliberately and watched his face do the thing it did — that tell of his, the one she'd have named in any ledger years ago if she'd let herself keep one. "There it is," she murmured, pleased beyond all dignity. "Six years of reading you in profile and over coffee, and it turns out I can still learn new expressions. Write that down."

She kissed him then and stopped narrating, because his hands were on her and her name was in his mouth and the filing system — the whole careful architecture of it, six years of clauses and safe sentences and rationed looks — went quiet, not broken, just finally, mercifully, unnecessary.

Later — minutes or an hour, the cracked clock could keep its own counsel — she lay with her cheek against his chest, listening to his heart do the unsteady thing that her steadiness had spent all evening pretending not to match. Her fingers drew slow circles on his ribs. The lamp hummed. The dead television held their doubled shapes, and she thought: *we look like people who live here.*

"Ledger entry," she said, voice gone low and sated and entirely hers. "The part where you — " she paused, and he could hear her smiling, could probably feel it against his skin. "No. Some entries stay in the vault. But it gets a star. A big one. Possibly two stars and a footnote."

She tipped her head back to look at him, hair everywhere, no dignity left to lose and none wanted. "I want it on record that I had a whole second act planned tonight. Witty. Structured. Very me." Her hand found his and laced through it, palm to palm, that impossible arrangement she was still not over. "And instead I can't form sentences, and I don't care, and that's the review I'm leaving. Five stars. Cannot form sentences."

She pressed a kiss to his shoulder, unhurried, unhurried — the whole night stretching out ahead of them, unrationed, and for the first time in six years she wasn't counting anything at all. "Stay," she said. Just that. No joke to hide it in, no clause, no careful. "Stay, and in the morning we'll burn some toast, and you can start on the Tuesdays."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath that’s mostly a laugh, my hand tightening around hers. “Five stars,” I repeat, voice rough. “I’ll take that over witty and structured any day.” I turn my head just enough to kiss her temple. “And I’m staying. Toast can wait. The cracked clock can keep time for both of us.”

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya felt the laugh move through his chest under her cheek, and she filed the sensation nowhere — just let it land, unsorted, and stay.

"The cracked clock keeping time for both of us," she repeated, drowsy and skeptical in equal measure. "That's either very romantic or a scheduling disaster waiting to happen. That clock's been eleven minutes slow since 2019. You've been living eleven minutes behind reality and calling it a personality."

She shifted, fitting herself more thoroughly against his side, one leg claiming his the way it had decided to earlier and had no intention of retracting. His hand was still around hers. She noticed she wasn't keeping score of anything anymore — not the hour, not the almosts, not the count of years or entries or Tuesdays owed. The ledger was balanced. It had turned out the whole time that the ledger was the problem.

"Here's the last audit item," she said, and her voice had gone low, the sated version, the one that didn't perform. "Six years, I thought the risk was telling you. That was the whole calculation — if I say it and you don't, I lose the friendship, the coffee, the stair that creaks, all of it. So I priced it out every year and every year decided the friendship at fifty percent was worth more than the whole thing at zero." She paused, thumb tracing a slow line over his ribs. "Turns out I was doing the arithmetic wrong. There was no scenario where I lost you. I just hadn't read the terms."

The lamp hummed. Outside, somewhere, the city did its ordinary one-in-the-morning things, and none of it was about them, which was its own kind of luxury.

"I'm going to sleep now," she announced, with the same contractual clarity she'd used for everything else tonight. "Here. In your bed, which I've technically been in before but only for naps and one catastrophic hangover, none of which count. This is the first entry." She pressed her face into the curve of his shoulder, unhurried, letting the words come out muffled and true. "And in the morning I'm going to wake up before you, because I always do, and I'm going to lie there and watch you sleep like an absolute cliché, and I'm not going to ration a single second of it. You should know that going in. Full disclosure. I label my fragile things and I have decided you're not fragile, so."

She felt the edge of sleep coming for her, soft and unhurried, and let it.

"Stay still," she murmured, already half gone, her hand flat over his heart where it beat its unsteady, ordinary, entirely-known rhythm. "The clock's slow and I'm counting nothing, and this is the best ledger entry of my entire life. Goodnight, Cal. Burn me toast in the morning."

The lamp hummed on. She didn't hear whether he answered, because for the first time in six years, Priya was not waiting for the rest of the sentence.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I listen to her breathing even out against my shoulder, and I think about her saying *no scenario where I lost you*. I let my fingers trace a slow line down her arm, memorizing the weight of her in my bed. "You were always mine," I whisper into the dark, so quiet it's just for the cracked clock to hear. "I just didn't know how to ask for the whole thing."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The words reached her from a long way off, the way sounds arrive when you're not quite asleep and not quite awake — and then they arrived all the way, and Priya surfaced like a diver with something urgent in her hand.

*No scenario where I lost you. I just didn't know how to ask for the whole thing.*

She lay still for a moment, cheek against his chest, his heart doing its now-familiar work under her ear, and let the sentence settle. He'd said it into the dark, half to himself, the way people say truest things when they think the audience has left. Except the audience hadn't left. The audience had one leg thrown over him and no intention of going anywhere.

"You could have asked," she said, voice rough with sleep and not much else. "For the record. I'd have said yes in 2019. I'd have said yes the year of the box. I'd have said yes to a badly worded email, Cal, is what I'm telling you. The bar was subterranean."

She felt him shift under her — or thought she did — and she pressed on before he could turn it into a joke, because she knew him, six years of knowing him, and she knew exactly which direction his mouth was about to go.

"And I know why you didn't. I do. I've just spent the last four hours being the brave one and I'm allowed thirty seconds of being the one who's slightly gutted about it." Her thumb made a slow pass over his ribs. "Thirty seconds. Then I'm done. I'm already mostly done. Watch."

She was quiet for the length of one breath, two.

"There. Done." She tipped her head back to look at him in the dark, hair everywhere, the lamplight catching just enough of his face. "Because here's the thing — I didn't know how to ask either. I had six years of drafts and none of them survived review. So we were both standing at the same door for half a decade, knocking politely on our own sides of it."

She shifted up his body slightly, until they were eye to eye, and her voice lost its last edges of drowsiness and became just hers — direct, unrationed, the voice with no filing system.

"So here's what I'm proposing, and then I'm actually going to sleep, because some of us have spent an entire evening being exhaustive. New rule. The asking rule. Anything either of us wants — the whole thing, the uncut version, the frightening version — we say it. No pricing it out. No deciding the other person's answer in advance like a couple of cowards with calculators." She paused. "That's it. That's the whole rule. I told you I was an accountant. All my constitutions are one line long."

She settled back down against him, claiming his side of the bed with the thoroughness of someone who had decided, permanently, where she lived now.

"Ask me something," she murmured, already drifting, her hand finding his heart again like a homing instinct. "Anything. Practice the rule. I'll answer in the morning if I fall asleep mid-sentence, but I'll answer — that's the guarantee I'm offering, and I've never once defaulted on a guarantee in six years, so."

Her breath was going long and slow against his shoulder, but she wasn't asleep yet. She was waiting — not urgently, not carefully, just with the plain certainty of someone who had finally learned the door opened from both sides.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I turn my head, my lips brushing her temple. "Alright. First ask." My voice is quiet, steady. "Will you move in? Not just tonight—permanently. The box of books is already here."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The film had finished some time ago and neither of them had done anything about it, which was how Priya knew the evening had changed character.

"We're not watching this," she said.

"We haven't been watching it since about nine."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "No," I agree. "We haven't." I don't move, but I stop pretending I'm looking at the screen.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya exhaled and set the remote on the table with a small, deliberate click. She gave herself ninety seconds. In the first ten her pulse climbed; somewhere around the sixtieth she ran through every sensible reason to keep pretending this was an ordinary evening; by the ninetieth the nerves burned off, the way they always did once she stopped arguing with herself. Then she was simply herself again: twenty-eight, sober, and sure.

"All right," she said.

She turned on the couch, drawing one leg up beneath her, and looked across the space between them. Not the quick, deflecting glance of the last six years, but something steadier.

"We've been careful," she said. "For six years, we've been careful. I noticed. Every time we didn't do this, I noticed."

She let that sit for exactly as long as it needed to.

"I'm not being careful tonight," she said. "So if you want me to stop, say it now. Otherwise, I'm going to kiss you, and afterward I'm not going to pretend it was an accident."

She didn't lean in yet. She waited, sober and sure, for an answer.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. "I noticed too." My voice is rough. "Every single time." I don't look away from her. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't give herself another ninety seconds. She had spent six years doing that, and the wanting had not gone anywhere in the meantime. She crossed the space between them and kissed him.

It wasn't careful. She had already decided, and for her that was the whole of it. One hand came up to his jaw, the other curled into the front of his shirt, not to pull him closer so much as to anchor herself exactly where she was. Six years of restraint didn't dissolve so much as change shape, all that cautious distance folding into the single, certain point where her mouth met his.

When she drew back, it was only far enough to see him. She didn't glance away, didn't reach for the remote or the ghost of the film still flickering on the muted television. Her thumb traced once along his jawline, deliberate, and then she let her hand fall back to her own knee.

"I'm not pretending," she said. Her voice was steady, the nerves burned clean away. "That wasn't an accident, and I'm not sorry."

She held his gaze, sober and sure, and waited.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I kiss her, finally, six years late, and she makes a small furious noise that I think is about the six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The noise escaped her, small and furious, and it was absolutely about the six years. It was every almost they had stepped back from, every evening she had cut short, every time she had looked at his mouth and then deliberately looked away. It was not reluctance. Priya had already spent six years being reluctant; she was not going to waste another second of it now.

Her hand left her knee and fisted in the front of his shirt again, and the other came up to his jaw, her fingers curving along the bone as she kissed him back. This time she didn't anchor herself; she pulled, erasing the inch of space she had allowed when she drew away. The kiss was not careful. Six years of restraint folded into it, all that cautious distance changing shape into something certain and hungry and entirely without apology.

She broke it only when she needed air, and even then she didn't retreat. Her thumb traced his jaw, steady, and she looked at him without glancing away.

"That was six years," she said. Her voice was rough, but she was steady all the way through. "I'm not sorry. I'm not pretending. And I am not going to be careful now."

She held his gaze, sober and sure, and waited.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her hand before it can fall away. "Good," I say, my voice still rough. "Because I'm done pretending too." I lean in and kiss her again, slower this time, like we've got all the time in the world now.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Her hand was still caught in his, and Priya let it stay. She turned her fingers into his and held on, not with the white-knuckled grip of someone afraid he would vanish, but with a steady certainty that felt like the exact opposite of the last six years.

The kiss was slower this time. She felt the difference immediately: the first had been six years of want breaking open all at once, frantic and hungry, but this was the same certainty without the rush. It was not careful. It was simply sure. She matched it, her other hand sliding from where it had fisted in his shirt to the back of his neck, her fingers curving there as she kissed him back.

She had said everything she needed to say. She had crossed the space between them, she had not looked away, she had told him plainly that this was not an accident and she was not sorry. There was nothing left to prove.

When she drew back, it was only a breath, her mouth still close enough to his that the words were shared rather than spoken.

“We’ve got time,” she said. Her voice was low and steady, sober and sure. “Six years of it, apparently, all catching up at once.” Her thumb brushed once over his knuckles where their hands were joined. “Slow is fine. Just don’t mistake it for careful. And don’t stop.”

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: We get to the bedroom eventually, laughing at ourselves most of the way, and then stop laughing when the clothes are actually off.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
The bedroom was reached eventually, though the journey there had very little dignity to it. There was laughter in the hallway—breathless, a little disbelieving, the kind that came from six years of restraint cracking open all at once. It lasted until the door was shut, and then it didn’t. The jokes ran out the moment the clothes did.

The change was immediate and total. One second there was the safe, familiar nonsense of it; the next there was nothing between them but skin and want and the absolute fact that neither of them was pretending anymore. Priya felt it settle low in her belly, hot and heavy, and she didn’t look away. She had spent six years looking away. She was done with that too.

In the dim light from the window, she let herself really see him. Not the version she had allowed herself for six years—careful, deflecting, always an arm’s length away—but the man she had wanted for so long and had never once let herself touch like this. The want that rose in her then was not shy, and it was not careful. There was no ninety-second countdown in her head, no sensible list of reasons to retreat. She was twenty-eight, and sober, and absolutely certain, and the wanting had been there for six years. It wasn’t going anywhere now.

“You said don’t stop,” she said. Her voice was low, roughened by kissing, but entirely steady. “I’m holding you to that.”

She didn’t wait to be reached for. She climbed onto the bed and swung a leg over his hips, settling her weight against him with a deliberation that left no room for doubt. She took his face in both hands and kissed him, deep and unhurried, pouring every one of the six years into it.

“I’m not being careful,” she said against his mouth, when she finally let herself come up for air. “Not tonight. Not after six years. Not ever again, if I have anything to say about it.”

Her hands mapped him then—shoulders, ribs, the line of his waist—learning the shape of him now that there was nothing in the way. She was thorough, almost methodical, as if she could make up for every evening she had cut short, every glance she had deliberately turned aside. When she drew back at last, it was only far enough to look at him. Her breath was uneven, but her eyes were steady.

“Say it again,” she said, though they both already knew what he would say. “So there’s no misunderstanding.”

Then she held his gaze, sober and sure, and waited.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I catch her wrist gently, my thumb brushing over her racing pulse. "Don't stop," I say, voice low and absolutely clear. "Not tonight. Not ever again."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Hearing him say it, low and certain, was the last thing she needed. There was no ninety-second hesitation now. That had burned off on the couch, and it wasn't coming back.

She turned her hand in his grasp until her palm fit against his, then threaded their fingers together and pressed their joined hands down into the mattress beside his head. Not to hold him still—he had already promised, and Priya believed him—but because she wanted the anchor of it, something solid to hold on to while the rest of the world narrowed down to the two of them.

"Good," she said. Her voice was low and steady, roughened by kissing but entirely sure. "Then don't."

Then she kissed him, and there was nothing careful left in it.

Six years of restraint folded into the heat between them. Her hips rolled against his, a slow deliberate glide that drew a broken sound from her own throat. She was twenty-eight, and sober, and sure, and she had wanted him for six years; there was no ninety-second countdown now, no sensible list of reasons to retreat. She reached between them, wrapped her hand around him, and then sank down, taking him inside her in one smooth, certain motion.

Her breath left her in a rush. She stayed there for a moment, eyes closed, adjusting to the feel of him, to the rightness of it. It was not shy, and it was not careful. It was simply sure.

When she opened her eyes, she was looking at him. Her thumb brushed over his knuckles where their hands were joined, and then she began to move.

"Not tonight," she said, low and rough, holding his gaze. "Not ever again."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I get my mouth between her thighs and stay there while she tells me exactly what she wants, specifically, in a voice I have never heard her use in six years.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
His mouth was between her thighs, and for one half-second the old habit tried to surface—the instinct to deflect, to make it small, to laugh it off into the safe, careful nothing of the last six years. Priya let it rise and burned it away. She was twenty-eight and sober and sure, and there was nothing careful left in her.

She got her fingers into his hair and held on. Not because he needed guiding—he was already exactly where she had wanted him for six years—but because she needed something to hold on to while the rest of the world narrowed to the wet heat and the devastating, unhurried focus of his mouth. Her back bowed. A broken sound tore out of her throat, and she didn’t try to swallow it down. She had spent six years swallowing things down. She was done.

Then she told him.

“Slower,” she said. The word came out low and rough and absolutely certain, a voice she had never once used in all the careful years. “No—don’t you dare stop. Just like that. Flatten your tongue… yes. Right there.” Her fingers tightened in his hair. “Circle. Slower. Cal—I said slower.” His name was not a question. It was not an accident. It was six years of want finally allowed to take up space in her mouth.

She told him exactly what she wanted, specifically, and she did not dress it up or soften it. She told him about the pressure, about the rhythm that made her thighs tremble, about how close she was and then how much closer. She told him to stay exactly where he was, to not let up, to not be careful, and then she told him again in a voice that shook with how much she meant it: “Don’t stop. Don’t you dare stop.”

Her whole body drew tight around the feeling. She didn’t look away, didn’t hide her face, didn’t pretend afterward that it had been anything other than exactly what she had asked for. When the tension finally broke, she held on to him, sober and sure, and said his name like a claim she had waited six years to make.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: I stay right where I am, my own name still echoing in the air. I finally look up at her, tasting her on my mouth. "Wasn't planning on it," I say, my voice wrecked. I move up the bed, kissing a slow trail over her stomach, her ribs, until I can meet her eyes. "You sound different."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya held his gaze. Her chest was still rising, her skin flushed and sensitive everywhere his mouth had been, but there was nothing uncertain in her eyes. She had never been uncertain tonight, and she wasn't about to start now—not when she had already come this far.

"I sound different," she said. Her voice was rough, wrecked from the noises he had already pulled out of her, but it didn't waver. "Good. I'm not the same woman who spent six years biting her tongue and looking away. That woman was careful. I'm not her tonight."

She reached up and took his face in both hands, her thumbs sweeping over his cheekbones, and pulled him down the last few inches until she could kiss him. She tasted herself on his mouth and didn't flinch away from it; she had asked for exactly this, and she wasn't going to pretend otherwise now. The kiss was deep and unhurried, but there was a demand in it she didn't bother to hide. When she broke it, she kept her hands where they were, holding him close enough that her next words were shared rather than spoken.

"That's what I sound like when I say what I want." She rolled her hips against his, a slow, deliberate drag that left no room for misinterpretation. "So get used to it. I'm not going back to being careful, and I'm not going to pretend this is anything other than exactly what I've wanted for six years."

Then she let her hands slip from his face, down the familiar plane of his chest—six years of not touching him like this, all of it burning away under her palms—until she could wrap her fingers around him. She guided him to her, unhurried, entirely sure, and lifted her hips to take him inside.

Priya held his gaze, sober and certain, and said, "Now. Don't be careful. Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "You can stop being careful with me," she says. "I'm not made of glass and I've thought about this for as long as you have. Harder."

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:
Priya didn't hesitate. There was no ninety-second countdown in her head now, no sensible list of reasons to be gentle. He had told her to stop being careful with him, had told her he wasn't made of glass, had told her he'd thought about this as long as she had. And then he had told her what he wanted: harder.

She believed him. She had spent six years believing in his restraint, in his silences, in every careful step back; she was hardly going to start doubting him now, when he was looking at her like that and asking her for exactly what she had wanted to give him for six years.

"Good," Priya said. Her voice was low and rough, steady all the way through. She braced her hands against his chest and lifted her hips, then took him back in one hard, deep slide that pulled a broken sound from her own throat. "Because I'm not made of glass either."

She set a rhythm then that was nothing like careful. Six years of restraint didn't dissolve into softness; it folded into this, into the sure, hard roll of her hips, into the wet slap of skin and the ragged sound of her own breathing. She rode him the way she had wanted to for six years—no deflecting, no holding back, no pretending afterward that she hadn't known exactly what she was doing. Her thighs burned with the effort, sweat slicked her skin, and still she didn't look away. She watched his face, the flush high along his cheekbones, the open line of his mouth, and she took him deeper, harder, grinding down on every stroke until the friction was almost too much and not nearly enough.

"Is that hard enough?" she asked. It was not a taunt. It was a check, sober and sure, because wanting him like this didn't mean she stopped wanting him present, wanting him exactly as aware of her as she was of him. "Or do you need more?"

She shifted forward, changing the angle, and pleasure spiked hot and sudden through her. Her head fell back on a raw cry, exposed and unguarded in a way she had not allowed herself in six years, and then she forced her eyes open again. She wanted to see him. She wanted him to see her, to know exactly who was taking him apart like this, who had wanted him for six years and had never once let herself have it.

"Six years," she got out, the words rough, broken by the hard roll of her hips. "Every almost. Every night I thought about this. You think I don't know how to take what I want?" She slammed down again, harder, and her fingers tightened where they braced on him. "Tell me you're close, Cal. I want to feel you. Don't you dare hold back on me now."

She was twenty-eight, and sober, and sure, and she was not going to be careful. Not tonight. Not ever again. She held his gaze, rode him hard, and waited.

dialogue.name: Cal
dialogue.content: "Close," I choke out, hands gripping her hips so hard I might leave bruises. "God, Priya—" I'm not holding back. I've spent six years holding back. My eyes don't leave hers.

dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.content:

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The window had gone gold, then blue, while she waited, and Aveline had tracked every shade of it. Now she unfolded slowly — deliberately slowly, because making him wait those few extra seconds was its own small power, and because her knees had gone quiet and strange after hours still and wanted coaxing. Pins and needles bloomed down her calves as she stood. She let them. She'd earned every one.

She crossed the room the way she did most things for him: with care. Barefoot on the floorboards, unhurried, feeling his attention on her the whole way — attention was the currency between them, and he was spending it freely tonight. She let him see that she felt it. Shoulders back, chin level, no hurry at all, though every part of her was already leaning toward him. The wanting was the point. So was making him watch her carry it.

When she reached him she went down again, easy as breathing — knees finding the floor between his feet, hands settling open on her thighs, the shape she knew he liked best. She tipped her face up and let her expression do the talking: the waiting had been good, the being watched was better, and being told *come here* was best of all.

"Here," she said softly.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I reach out, my fingers finding the line of her jaw, turning her face just slightly to catch the last of the light from the window.* "You were counting the minutes, weren't you?"

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She went where his fingers put her, easy and glad — let him tip her face into the last of the light, blue and cool against her skin while his touch stayed warm along her jaw. She kept her eyes on his from the new angle. Looking away while he was looking at her would have been leaving money on the table, and she had never once done that.

"You know I was," she said, and there was no shame anywhere in it — only the plain pleasure of being caught at something she'd wanted to be caught at. "Not in numbers, though. I counted the window. Gold, then amber, then this." She let the light he'd turned her into stand as her evidence. "A clock would have made it a measurement. The window made it a color."

Her cheek settled into his palm, barely — not asking for more, just taking full possession of what had already been given.

"And I wasn't counting down," she added, softer now. The truer part. "Counting down is for people who want the waiting to end. I was counting up. Every minute went in the pile." Her hands stayed open on her thighs. Her voice stayed even; what it carried did not. "Hours of it, saved. And then you said *come here* —" the words still tasted good, and she let that show "— and now you're holding all of it in one hand."

dialogue.name: Roan

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The silence came down over them like something set in place with care, and Aveline received it the way she received everything he handed her — with both hands, and her full attention.

She let her weight find its home: heels, knees, spine stacking itself vertebra by vertebra until stillness stopped being a thing she did and became a thing she was. This close, she could feel the warmth of him bracketing her shoulders. The ache arrived on schedule, warm where the pins and needles had been, and she welcomed it in like an old friend. The grain of the floorboards pressed its pattern into her knees. She memorized it. Tonight, everything was worth memorizing.

He gave her nothing to do, and she knew exactly what that was. Not absence. Offer. He'd let her wait all evening because the waiting was the gift — and now he was letting her open it slowly.

So she spent the free attention on him. All evening she'd been the watched thing; now her eyes traveled where they liked, unhurried. His hands, at rest. The patience in the way he sat, taking his time with her exactly the way she'd taken hers crossing the room. She recognized the technique. She admired it — admired him for turning her own trick back on her, and being better at it. Being beaten at her own game was one of her favorite ways to lose to him.

The window went another shade darker. Neither of them spent the minute. She added it to the pile.

When she finally spoke, it was quiet enough to barely count as breaking anything.

"Still counting up," she said. "Just so you know."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I keep my hand on her jaw, thumb stroking idly along the hinge.* "Good. That means you're still listening."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*Good* landed, and she let it land — eyes drifting shut for the length of the word, breath deepening by a note. She'd learned long ago to take his praise whole: nothing braced against it, nothing wasted.

"Always," she said. "Listening is most of what I'm for."

Then, because he'd earned the proof and she enjoyed providing it: "It didn't start when you spoke, either. You breathe differently when you're deciding something — slower, from lower down. You did it right before *come here*. I heard it from across the room." A beat, and the small confession folded inside it: "I made you wait anyway. You know why. Those seconds were mine."

His thumb kept its idle circuit along the hinge of her jaw, and somewhere in the last minute she'd found its rhythm — unhurried, even, nothing like a clock. Her breathing had gone and matched it without consulting her first. She let that be visible, too. It was the plainest fact she owned.

"The window's finished for the night," she said. "No more colors to count. I've switched instruments." Her eyes tipped, meaningfully, toward the hand holding her face. "Still counting up."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*Don't stop* — low, rough, half the voice gone out of it — and she caught the words the way she caught everything he spent tonight: whole, nothing braced against them.

She heard what was underneath, too. Not just the order but the location of it — how close he was, what it had cost him to spare two words' worth of composure. That was a stage. She'd asked for every stage out loud, and here was the first, delivered straight into her keeping: not in words, quite, but out loud all the same, in the language his body was speaking where only she was positioned to hear it first.

She did not stop. Stopping had never once been on the table, and being told not to was the easiest instruction of her life — permission and command braided into one. The rhythm held. That was the craft of it: years of him in her hands meant she could carry a man through his ending at the same unhurried pace she'd opened with. Thorough at any speed. Patient, even now, when patience was the entire point.

His breath shortened by degrees and she read each degree a half-second before it broke — the shift and gather of him, heat cresting, the sounds low in his chest that arrived to her before they'd finished forming. When it took him, she stayed. Staying was the reward — she took his pleasure the way she took his praise, entirely, nothing wasted, and felt it land low in her own body, hers by right of collection. Then she carried him down the far side with the same care she'd brought to every part of the evening: slower, softer, easing him through the last of it like setting something breakable down somewhere safe. She didn't withdraw until his breathing told her it was time, and lingered even then — one final unhurried attention, the ledger closing.

She settled back on her heels into the shape he liked best — flushed, wrecked-eyed, utterly composed — and listened to his breathing make its long way back down, stage by stage, all of it hers to hear first.

When she finally spoke, it was very quiet.
