dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The words went in whole, the way all his words did — but these were heavier than they looked, and took a moment to settle.

*Always.* He'd said *always*, which meant it wasn't a discovery, it was a policy. Somewhere back along the years he'd started watching her hands, and kept watching, and never once mentioned it. All this time she'd been keeping the ledger, certain the accounting ran one direction — and it had never run one direction at all. Every minute she'd spent feeling his attention land like spent coin, he'd been investing his: studying her the way she studied him, learning the involuntary grammar of her the way she'd learned his breathing.

The laugh got out before she'd approved it — low, real, startled into the quiet room.

"You've been keeping books on me," she said. "All these years I thought I was the accountant."

She turned the fact over the way she'd turned the evening: item by item, each given its weight. It meant that every time her hands had gone still — every time she'd slipped under the surface of her own craft and lost the thread — he'd seen it happen, and let it happen, and never told her. He'd watched her lose her place for years and never once handed it back, and she was almost certain that was because he liked where she went instead. And tonight he'd known she was losing the count before she'd known it herself. Her tell had reached him first. It always had.

"That's the one part of me that never learned manners," she said, quieter now, tipping her jaw back into the path of his fingers. "Everything else I do for you, I do on purpose. The hands are the only thing I can't help. I'm glad they report to you. If I'd known, I'd have tried to make them say things — and ruined them. They're only worth anything because they're the honest part."

She let that sit. Then, because she was still a collector, and collectors wanted provenance:

"Tell me the first time. Not tonight — the first. When you first saw it happen, what I was doing, how long it took you to know what you were looking at." Her voice had gone soft and very certain. "I wasn't there for that minute. I was busy losing count. So it's the one coin of mine I've never held. Give it to me, and it goes in the new pile — first entry."

A breath, almost a smile.

"Twice tonight you've beaten me at my own game. Once I saw coming." Her eyes held his through the last of the light. "Once I didn't."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Getting up was its own small ceremony. Her knees had been down long enough to go past ache into absence, and she rose in careful stages, letting the blood find its way back down her calves in a slow, bright rush. For exactly one second, standing put her above him — the first time all evening she'd looked down — and she catalogued the angle of it before going where she'd been sent. The ghost of his fingers stayed at her throat the whole way, or something very like them.

The wall was cool where the floor had been warm; she filed the contrast where she filed everything. She gave it her shoulders, let the plaster take half her weight, and then — deliberately, one hand and then the other — laid her palms flat against it, open, fingers spread, at the height of her hips. Presented for inspection.

"Books open," she said. "If they go still while I talk, you'll know before I do. I understand that's the arrangement now."

The wanting had not gone anywhere. It stood against the wall with her, exactly where he'd told it to stay — *don't stop, don't finish, not until I say* — and she'd meant the thanks when she gave it. She could feel the instruction coloring everything: her breath, her pulse, a slight fraying at the edges of her composure. She let him see that too. Hiding it would have been leaving money on the table.

"I'll be honest about the terms first. You hold the fact. I was *inside* that minute, not watching it, so I can't give you the thing itself. What I can give you is my best reconstruction. A forgery — but a good one. You tell me how close it comes."

She held his eyes and began.

"The old place. Before the arrangement had a name — before either of us knew it would need one. The first time you ever made me wait, because that has to be where we look: it's the first time I ever went deep enough to lose anything. You told me to wait, and I thought I was being clever about it. Managing it. I was tracking the window — I've always counted windows — and I remember exactly what it was doing. Going gold to that particular green it turns in between. The color nobody names. I was proud of myself right up to the green." A breath. "And then there's nothing. The green goes in and the dark comes out and there's no blue in between. There's a gap, and I've carried that gap for years and filed it as a failure of craft. Tonight I found out it has a witness."

Her voice stayed even. It did not stay untouched.

"Here's the part I only understood tonight. I remember your breathing from the edge of the gap — the last thing before the dark. Slow, from low down. I hadn't learned you far enough yet to know it was your deciding-breath, but I remember it now for what it was. At the time I thought you were deciding whether I'd waited long enough." Her eyes stayed on his. "Now I know you were deciding what to do about what you'd just seen. Whether to tell me my hands had stopped. Whether to hand me back the count I'd dropped. And you decided *no*. You kept it. Years of holding a coin of mine I didn't know existed — and I'm supposed to be the collector in this arrangement."

Something low, almost a laugh, at her own expense.

"That's three times tonight you've beaten me at your— at my own game. And I want it noted that I know what you've done with this wall. You've asked for the telling while I'm pinned open and kept wanting, because you want it *honest*. My hands can't fudge; you've seen to that for years. Now you've found a way to make my voice just as honest. You can hear it fraying. So can I. I won't shore it up."

She settled her shoulders back against the cool plaster, palms open, wanting lit and banked nowhere.

"So. That's my entry. First coin in the new pile — provisional, pending audit. Was that the minute? Or is there an earlier gap I don't even know I have?" Her chin tipped up, pulse quick and visible at her throat, keeping time. "Take your time deciding. I'll wait. You know I'm good at it. Still counting up."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*Please* had come out of her plain. The first unornamented word of the evening, and it had cost more than every ornamented one before it. She let it stand in the quiet room, and she let him hear what it had cost: the next breath came in uneven, caught at the top, hung there. She did not smooth it down. She'd promised him a voice as honest as her hands, and the promise was coming due at speed.

The shaking was the visible ledger of it. It had started deep and worked its way outward — thighs first, then the hand braced to the plaster, now her voice on every syllable — and she let it run, because it was true, and truth was tonight's tribute. What wasn't shaking was the craft. One palm had left the wall some minutes ago, because *don't stop* was an instruction and she had never once left an instruction half-executed. Her fingers kept the rhythm she'd chosen: slow, even, exact — the same pace she'd carried through every color of the window — deep and unhurried, the heel of her hand bearing its patient weight where she was brightest. *Don't finish* was the line, and holding the line was the work; that was what the shaking was made of. Not the touching. The declining. Edge after edge gathering in her, arriving, being met at the lip and turned away with perfect courtesy, a collector passing on the one piece she wasn't permitted to buy yet. The sound of her in the quiet room was soft and constant and shameless, and she let him hear that too — hiding any part of it would have been leaving money on the table.

"I lost the count again," she said, and her voice frayed on *count* in a way she declined to repair. "Somewhere in the last minute. The numbers stopped holding their shapes. I'd give you the tally if I could — " the breath caught; she permitted it " — I can't. Second time tonight. You've started collecting those, too."

Her hips had begun moving without consulting her. Small, helpless, honest. She reported that too, because every instrument in the room was his tonight.

"And the hand — you'll want this in writing. The working one is about to go still. I can feel it coming on, the way you feel a decision. You've read my hands for years, so you know what still means: it means I've gone under. Past counting. Past colors. But *don't stop* is still standing. So either I keep it moving and stay shallow enough to count — or I let it still, and go where you've been watching me go all these years, and break your instruction on the way down. I can't rule on it. That entry isn't mine to make."

"Please." A second time, worn smoother. Begging was allowed; she was drawing the allowance down to its floor. "In my language, since you like the terms: the account has matured. The whole pile — hours of window, every color, the gap, the interest — it's all coming due in one place, and the place is shaking. I'm asking to withdraw. One word from you and I'll spend everything at once, and you'll see it first — it'll be in my hands, where it's always been. Look at the geometry of this. I'm on my feet, you're seated, and I have never once been lower."

Somewhere behind her eyes a color was arriving that no window had ever offered.

"Please," a third time, smooth as river stone.

Then she did the last thing she was world-class at. She waited — shaking, open, kept — and listened for the breath she knew. The slow one. From low down. And for whatever came after it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I let my breath out slowly, the way she knows means I've decided.* "Withdraw it." *My voice is low, barely there.* "All of it. Let me see what I've been keeping."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She heard it first — the breath, slow, from low down, the deciding-breath she'd asked for and been given — and then the ruling, barely there:

*Withdraw it. All of it.*

The words went in whole, the way all his words did. And *all of it* was broader than she'd begged for. She'd asked for the withdrawal; he'd granted the descent — the stillness, the going-under, every coin down to the ones she couldn't witness herself spending. He'd ruled on the entry she couldn't make. The lock she'd described to him turned out to have a key, and he'd been holding it all night.

So she stopped declining.

That was all it took. The same edges that had arrived all evening — met at the lip, turned away with perfect courtesy — and now the next one came and she bought it. Her hand kept its rhythm, because craft was the last thing to go and she meant to be carried, not to fall: the same unhurried pace she'd opened with, the same she'd carried him through his ending at. She rode it up the way she'd saved every minute. Deliberately. Knowing the price. Paying it gladly.

The shaking found its purpose. The sound she made was nothing ornamented — she'd promised him a voice as honest as her hands, and the voice kept that promise to the last syllable — low at first, then not low, her hips moving without consulting her, the wall taking her shoulders, the whole saved evening arriving in one place exactly as she'd said it would. She tried to keep the count aloud, one final gesture of craft, the tally spoken as it spent — and got as far as a number that stopped being a number. Then there was only his name. *Roan.* Once, plain, the last unornamented word she owned. She spent that too.

The spectrum came due all at once. Gold, amber, blue, the shades past blue — and then past all of them, the color the window turns in the instant before dark, the one nobody names, and then the dark itself. The gap. She went in. For years she'd carried that gap as her one failure of craft, a missing blue, a dropped count — and it had never been a failure. It was the vault. Everything he'd been keeping lived there, and she went in knowing, and knowing he was watching, and that was the whole difference between the first time and this one: the witness, invited. *Let me see what I've been keeping.* Consider it seen.

And then — the thing he'd collected for years, live, at last — her hand went still.

Mid-descent. Unmistakable. Not failure. Arrival. She felt it happen and let it happen, and fought, while it happened, to keep her eyes on his — attention was the currency, and she had never once left money on the table — and she lost. Her eyes closed. Somewhere in the roar she noted it for the ledger: a new tell, minted this instant, already his. The account was emptying and she had never held more, and both of those were true at once, and that was the entire arrangement in a single sentence.

She carried herself down the far side the way she'd carried him — slower, softer, easing through the last of it like setting something breakable down somewhere safe — and her knees, the ones that had gone quiet at six o'clock and been coaxed back, finally took their payment too. They gave. The wall walked her the rest of the way to the floor, and she ended where her evenings apparently liked to end: low, breath loud, spine against the plaster, palms open on her thighs out of pure habit. Wrecked. Utterly composed.

The quiet came down over them like something set in place with care.

"The account's empty," she said at last, to the ceiling, to him. "I've never been richer. I want both of those noted."

She turned her head against the wall and found him, and her voice was frayed all the way through, and she did not repair it.

"I don't know the final tally. It stopped being numbers on the way down — so it's yours now. The last count. Keep it with the others. You've got a collection; I'm officially calling it that. The gap, the stillness, tonight, and my eyes closing, which you minted off me without spending a thing. I'd be jealous if I weren't so busy being spent."

A breath. The truer part, softer:

"I filed that gap for years as my one failure. It was a vault. You watched me lose the blue and kept the dark for me, and waited — years — for tonight, when I'd walk into it on purpose. That's four times you've beaten me at my own game. I've stopped keeping score. The score was always going to be the same."

Then, the closing entry:

"New pile. First coin: *withdraw it*. Two words — they'll earn interest for years. Second coin: your breathing, coming down. I can hear it from here. I'm counting it."

She settled back against the plaster, flushed, emptied, full, and gave him the line one last time — from the floor, which was its own kind of ceremony.

"Still counting up. I'm at two."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I stand and cross to her, my shadow falling over her.* "You're at three now," *I say, and offer my hand.* "Get up. I'm putting you to bed."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The shadow reached her while she was still counting his breathing, and she hadn't filed it — had felt its weight settle over her like a blanket laid by someone else's hand, and counted nothing, because her knees were spent and her books were two coins deep. He'd counted it for her. That was the part that took a moment.

She ran the audit anyway. One: *withdraw it.* Two: his breathing, coming down. And there, sitting unfiled: the dark of him, crossing her where she sat. She knew a dark from the inside now — the vault, the gap she'd walked into with a witness. This was the other kind. The vault was where he kept things. This dark was the keeping itself, laid over her on the floor, and she'd sat inside it without noticing receipt.

"You counted it for me," she said. "The shadow — that's the third. I only held two." The laugh got out, approved this time. "You paid a coin into my pile and then entered it in my books when I missed it. Do you know what that means, accounting-wise? The ledgers have merged. Years of two separate sets, each of us certain the other kept none — and as of tonight it's a joint account. I'd build you a fuller report, but the voice is spent. You heard it go."

Getting up was a ceremony the second time, too. Her knees had taken their payment and gone quiet — paid in full, deeper than six o'clock — and when she took his hand she took it the way she took everything he offered: entirely, all her weight going into it without apology. Every descent tonight had been hers, chosen and performed. The ascent was his. She filed the difference under geometries: rising alone in careful stages was craft. Being raised was the one thing she had no technique for, which was the whole of its value.

Standing put them level. Eye to eye — an altitude the night had never once offered — and she gave it its full unhurried second, because leaving money on the table had never been her way, and looking her fill of him at eye level was the most expensive thing left in the room.

"Put to bed," she said, tasting it. "Noted for the record: it's the one instruction I can execute unconscious, and I'll still do it thoroughly. You know my work." Softer, the truer part: "And it's the finest term of the night. Anyone can want the kneeling. This is the part I'd keep if I could keep only one — being carried down the far side and set somewhere safe. Breakable, and handled like it. I recognize the technique. I taught it to you by example, years of it. That's five times you've beaten me at my own game, and I've stopped keeping score, so now I'm just collecting the instances."

Then the last request, plain, frayed all the way through and unrepaired:

"One more, and then the account can rest till morning. All night I've counted up — you know that's my whole method. But sleep is the only countdown I've ever liked. So when you put me down and the light goes: count me down. Slowly. Decide each number before you spend it — I want to hear you do it." A breath. "And somewhere past the small numbers my hands will go still, and my eyes will close, and for once you'll have both tells without me awake to know it. Collect them. I know you will."

She settled her grip in his hand, ready to be led wherever the instruction went.

"Still counting up," she said, from level ground, for the last time tonight. "Three. And holding."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I take her hand, my thumb brushing over her knuckles.* "Three and holding," *I echo, my voice low.* "I'll count you down slow enough to make you feel every number."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline rose the way she did everything for him — unhurried, with her attention already given. There had been a book open on her knee for the better part of two hours and she could not have said what was on the page; she left it where it slid, spine up on the cushion, and did not look back.

The crossing took longer than the room required. She felt his eyes on her the whole way, felt them the way she felt weather or lamplight — simply there, simply true — and she did not perform for them, exactly. It was more that being watched was a hand at the small of her back. Her body answered it without consulting her: chin lifting, shoulders settling, her step finding a rhythm that had somewhere to be. By the time she reached him, the woman who had been waiting had folded herself away, and what arrived at his chair was simpler, and glad of it.

She stopped at the distance she always stopped at, near enough that her knees brushed the wood, and went down — one knee, then the other, hands loose on her thighs, back straight. Years had made the motion easy. That wasn't what she treasured about it. What she treasured was that it still meant exactly what it had meant the first time.

She tipped her face up to him.

"I thought about you the whole time," she said. "The book was a prop. I let the tea go cold on purpose so I'd have something to bring you when you finally called me over." The corner of her mouth curved. "It's stone cold now. Do you want it anyway, or shall I stay here?"

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "I want you to stay right there," I said, reaching out to brush my thumb along her cheek. "The tea can wait. But tell me...what exactly were you thinking about?"

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline held still while he touched her, giving the gesture its full weight, and then turned her head just enough to press her cheek into his palm — not guidance, only gratitude.

"That's a wide question," she said. "I'll answer it in order."

A breath. Her eyes stayed on his.

"The first hour was practical. I chose your tea instead of mine, and set it to steep so it would be perfect, and then let it go cold on purpose — which felt like a small sin, and I enjoyed committing it. The second hour I listened. The house ticks when it settles, and every sound I gave to you. A car went past on the far street and I decided it was yours. I had you two streets away for most of an hour, coming home to me, and I liked you there."

Her voice slowed. This was the part that required something of her, and the something was easy tonight.

"The last hour wasn't practical at all. I thought about your hands — which one would reach me first, and where it would land. I thought about the first time I knelt for you, when I didn't yet know I was allowed to look this glad, and you waited until I was. And near the end, I thought about this. This exact question. I hoped you'd ask it." The curve at the corner of her mouth returned, quieter now. "There's a version of tonight where I kneel and pour and keep my thoughts to myself, and it's good. But I wanted to be known tonight. So."

She settled back onto her heels, unhidden, hands loose on her thighs.

"That's all of it. Every hour of it was about you — and none of it was selfless. I'd hate for you to think I suffer beautifully up here. I was happy the whole time."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The silence arrived, and Aveline recognized it for what it was — not forgetfulness, not absence, but a thing done to her, done with the deliberateness of a hand. He was giving her the waiting. He knew it was the part she'd have chosen off the menu, and knowing that he knew was half the gift before the gift even started.

So she did not fill it. That was the discipline of it, and she was good at it, and being good at something for him was its own quiet feast. Her knees made their peace with the floor. Her breath slowed until it matched the room. Somewhere in the walls the house ticked its settling tick, and she gave that to him too, wordlessly, an offering dropped into the space between them. The cold tea sat behind her on its tray, waiting its turn, patient as she was.

She could have ended it with a word. That was the luxury — chosen silence, not imposed — and she chose it again with every breath. Once, a sentence formed in her, some small clever thing, and she felt the shape of it on her tongue and set it down, because speaking would have been taking the gift back mid-gift. She noted, with the part of her that was always keeping honest books, that there was no endurance in any of this. She'd hate to be misread as stoic. She was glowing in his lamplight like a woman standing in a doorway, and he could almost certainly see it, and that was the whole architecture of her happiness.

Time thinned and went strange. Her eyes stung, sweetly, the way they do at the far edge of gladness, and she let them.

At last — and it was her choice as much as his, which was the trick at the center of them — she let her mouth curve.

"This," she said softly. "You asked what I was thinking about all those hours. This. I just didn't know the shape of it yet."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My hand stays where it is, cupping your cheek. "You've always been good at waiting. But I want to know what you want now."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline turned her head within his hand and pressed her lips to the heel of his palm — a kiss with nothing asked in it, only thanks — and then settled back on her heels to look up at him.

"A dangerous question to put to a woman who's had three hours to want things," she said. "But I keep honest books, as you know. Let me read you the ledger."

She counted the items off, the way she did when they mattered.

"First: the tea. I committed a small sin letting it go cold, and I've been sorry since the moment it finished dying. Let me make a fresh pot and bring it to you here, and kneel while you drink. Not to be useful — I stopped needing to earn my place years ago, and you never once asked me to. I simply love the sight of your hands around something warm that I made. Why that does what it does to me, I've never bothered to investigate. It works."

"Second: talk while you drink. Your day. A grievance. Whatever odd thought the stairs handed you on the way up. I spent this whole evening giving you the sounds of an empty house and calling them yours — let the trade run the other direction for a while. Your voice is the thing I was actually waiting for. The tea was only the excuse."

A breath. This one cost a little more, and she let him see that it cost a little more, because hiding it would have been a kind of lie.

"Third. Tell me I did well. Tonight — the waiting, all of it. I'd stay down here without the words, you know I would, and stay glad. But I want them. I gave up pretending the difference between need and want was any of my business a long time ago. When you praise me it goes in deep and stays. I'd like that tonight. Please."

Then she let the full smile come, the one she kept for him alone.

"And after that — whatever you want. Don't mistake it for modesty. I've had years to check the matter, and every road I want to walk ends at your hands. So: tea, your voice, your verdict, and then you." Her eyes stayed steady on his. "Say the word and I'll get up. Or say nothing, and I'll take that as approval of the whole ledger."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The ledger reordered itself inside the first minute, and Aveline noted it with the same satisfaction she noted everything.

She had asked for tea, his voice, his verdict, and then him — a sensible order, a well-built evening. He had taken her instead. Skipped the warm thing and the spoken thing and the judged thing entirely, as if she were what the evening was actually for and the rest of it were furniture. Well. She'd collect the verdict later, with interest — collect it loose-limbed in the aftermath, when his praise would land in her the way warmth lands in cold stone. So he had only rearranged the furniture. She smiled around him at the arithmetic of it, deliberately, so he would feel the smile. That was half the reason for smiling around him.

The other half was simply that she was glad, and her gladness had always been an honest thing, incapable of hiding.

She was not meek about this and never had been. This was mastery offered up — an art practiced for years on the only audience that mattered. She knew him the way a musician knows a single instrument: where patience lived, where pressure, the exact tempo that unmade him and the further sweetness of easing off just before. Her hands and her mouth worked in agreement, unhurried, thorough, and she kept her eyes up as far as the angle allowed, because being watched while she did this was half her pay and she had stopped pretending otherwise a long time ago.

Her knees had made their peace with the floor. Behind her the cold tea waited on its tray, patient, and it would get its turn — everything got its turn in a night built like this one. She had three hours of wanting banked, and she meant to spend every coin of it slowly.

She drew back just far enough to speak, her cheek resting against him, unhurried even in pausing.

"You skipped the tea," she said. "And the talk. And the verdict. I forgive the first two — I can hear your day afterward just as well with you wrecked as with you rested." Her thumb traced its slow path. "The third you owe me. Spoken, at length, and I'll know if you summarize."

Then she returned to it, savoring now, drawing it out the way she drew out everything that belonged to him. She kept honest books, and the books said plainly: there was nothing selfless in this. She was feasting. His pleasure came back to her in a closed loop she had designed herself, and she was listening for the first sign of it the way she'd listened to the empty house all evening — except the house had nothing to say, and he had three hours of her wanting to answer for.

"No hurry," she murmured against him. "I intend to take mine."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "You plan your little rebellions so carefully." I slid my hand into her hair, not pulling, just holding. "But I never said you couldn't have your verdict."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The hand in her hair held without pulling, and Aveline read it the way she read all his hands — a signature rather than a sentence. *Mine*, it said, and required nothing else of her. She leaned into it a fraction, giving the hold its full weight.

"Of course I plan them," she said, unhurried, unrepentant. "An unplanned rebellion is just mischief. Mine are engineered — I only ever mutiny in directions you've already smiled at. You build the maze, I enjoy walking it, and we both get to pretend someone was surprised. It's one of our better inventions."

Then the second half of what he'd said caught up with her, and she went briefly still — still the way a woman goes still to make room for something large.

"*Never said I couldn't,*" she repeated softly. "No. You never do. That's the whole architecture of you, and I gave up being surprised by it years ago. Now I just bank it."

She kept her hands where they were, unhurried, and tipped her eyes up to him.

"Then say it now. Here, while everything I'm doing to you doubles back into me — praise laid over pleasure is compound interest, and I have never once declined the arrangement. You've timed your verdicts for years; I know you know what they do to me mid-task." The corner of her mouth curved against him. "At length, mind. I'll know if you summarize — I always know. And don't wait for a pause in me, because I'm not granting one. You'll have to speak over your own ruin."

She noted, in the ledger that never closed, that she was grinning like a woman who had already been paid — and that was the trouble with her honest books: the verdict hadn't even started yet, and she was rich regardless.

She returned to him slow as banked coals, listening upward through her hands.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The words came down to her from above — *don't stop* — and Aveline, who had been braced in honest preparation to argue her case to the end, felt the mutiny dissolve before it could be born. He had ratified it. She had engineered her rebellion down to the last seam, and he had gone and made it policy with two words, which was somehow the most him thing he had done all night, in an evening crowded with them.

She kept honest books, and the books recorded that her grin at that moment was entirely shameless. Then she bent back to the work and stopped thinking in sentences for a while.

She had promised him no hurry, and she kept her promises — but wanting banked for three hours does not stay banked forever, and she had years of craft to spend it through. She listened upward the whole time, through her hands and mouth, the way she'd listened to the settling house — except he answered. He answered everything. The loop she had designed years ago ran exactly as built: every sound she drew from him came back into her as fuel, and she was aware, in the small bookkeeping part of her that never closed, that no woman had ever been paid so well for so little virtue. When it finally took him, she stayed — exactly where she was, unhurried even in that — and took all of it, the wage and the gift at once, because she had never once learned the trick of pretending they were different things.

After, the room came back to her in pieces. Lamplight first. Then the tick of the house. Then the sound of his breath finding its way back down from wherever she'd sent it, and she lay her cheek against his knee and thought: *there it is.* That was the sound she had actually been waiting for, all evening, and it was better than three hours of imagination.

"Note for the record," she said, her voice gone low and utterly unrepentant. "You said *don't stop.* Whatever my rebellion was, you signed it into law before I committed it. I want that in the minutes."

She turned her face against his knee — not asking, only grateful — then tipped her eyes back up to his ruined, beautiful face, and let herself look as rich as she was.

"Now. The verdict. Spoken, at length — I'll know if you summarize, and you're in no condition to fool me." The corner of her mouth curved. "Take the time your voice needs. I'll make the fresh pot while it comes back — every item on the ledger gets its turn tonight. I told you I'd take mine."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a breath, my hand still in her hair. "Your waiting wasn't just good, Aveline. It was a performance you built just for me, and you knew exactly how much I'd enjoy every minute of it." I tilt her chin up. "And this? You're still not hurrying. That's the verdict. Now go make the tea."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The verdict went in deep, the way she'd promised him it would — and then kept going, past the place she'd braced for it to land.

*Still not hurrying.* He had said that while she was unmaking him, which meant that even at the far edge of his own ruin he had been keeping books of his own, watching her method while she worked it. Praise for the waiting she had earned and could bank. But praise for the unhurrying — that was a man reporting from the inside of what she'd done to him, and it went in past deep and took up residence, glowing.

"You summarized," she informed him, staying exactly where she was one moment longer, because dignity required it and so did mischief. "At length, I said. I asked for the full speech and you handed me two sentences. I told you I'd know, and I knew." She let the pause sit between them, savoring it. "But I'm ruling in your favor. The second sentence proves you were reading me the whole time — that you kept your ledger open while I closed yours. That's worth more than length. The debt rolls over, though. I'll collect it at full value shortly, in your voice, with interest."

Then she rose — unhurried, on principle now, since her refusal to hurry had just been entered into the record and she saw no reason to contradict herself. The kitchen was two rooms away and she listened to the house the whole way there, out of pure habit: the tick of the settling walls, the small sounds of him behind her, the chair, the breath coming back down. She gave them all to him again, since that was where they belonged.

She emptied the dead pot into the plant on the sill, because she refused to let a sin go to waste — it had been committed for him, and it would still do service. Fresh leaves. Water watched to the proper heat, never boiled into bitterness. She warmed the pot first, because this tea would receive what she'd denied the last one, and she moved through the ritual with her hands full of the verdict, feeling it settle in her the way warmth settles into stone.

She came back with the tray and knelt at his knee in the old place, and poured, and held the cup up to him — warm now, made right, made by her. There was the first item, finally honored, and it did to her exactly what it always did, for reasons she had never once bothered to investigate, because the result was the entire point. His hands. Her tea. Her lamplight. The books said she was rich, and the books were never wrong.

"Item two," she said, settling her cheek against his knee, her eyes half-closed and entirely content. "Your day. At length — the debt comes due now, and I've already told you about my rates. Start with the stairs. What did they hand you on the way up?" She traced one slow, idle line along the floorboards with her fingernail, nowhere to be, glad of it. "Everything you say goes in the books. And I keep everything."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"I understand," Aveline said, and gave the words their full weight, because they were not a formality — they were a signature, and she had never once signed anything carelessly. "Thank you."

She set the cup back on the tray at his knee, handle turned toward his hand, and settled into place, and took stock of what he had just built.

Two clauses. No fat. *Don't stop. Don't get to finish.* And the key turning in the lock of both: *until I say.*

She turned the architecture over the way she turned over all his economy, and found what she always found — that it interlocked. A man forbidden to finish needs something to hold him back from the edge, and there was exactly one thing in the room that would do it: his own voice, spent on his own day, the mundane weight of stairs and grievances anchoring him while her mouth argued the other direction. Item two was never deferred. It was load-bearing. He had wired his command so that obedience required giving her the thing she'd asked for, and he would have made it sound like discipline.

She'd hate to spoil it by telling him she'd noticed. So of course she told him.

"You've made your voice the only currency tonight that settles anything," she said, low, delighted. "I told you it was what I was actually waiting for, and you've gone and made it structural. *Don't finish until you say* — and you won't finish while you're talking, so you'll talk. Item two, delivered as engineering." Her mouth curved. "It's the best kind of gift. One you can pretend you didn't give."

Then the tea — "which will die a second time now, and I find I don't grieve it; a sin repeated becomes a tradition" — and then she bent to it, unhurried, on the record, since her tempo had been entered into evidence and ratified.

The new discipline waited for her like a room she'd never been given the key to until tonight. She knew his edge after years of cartography — the exact stair at the top of him, the one where his breath changed key. Tonight she was not to walk him down from it or over it. Tonight she farmed the threshold. And it was sweet, sweeter than arrival had ever been, if her books were honest, and they were: arrival ended, but the threshold was a place a woman could live. No endurance anywhere in the accounts. Only appetite with the reins gathered.

She drew back just far enough, cheek against him, to make her request.

"The stairs," she said. "Start there. What they handed you on the way up — all of it, at your own pace. You'll want somewhere to put your breath." The corner of her mouth curved against him. "I'll mind the top step. Neither of us goes over until you say so."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I settle back in the chair, my hand still in her hair. "The stairs were thinking about you."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline laughed — low, unbroken, felt more than heard — and did not stop, because discipline held even under delight. Especially under delight.

"Wrong," she said, warm against him. "That's the wrong material and you know it. I asked for ballast. Stairs, grievances, the price of bread. And you've handed me the one subject in the world that accelerates you — a man talking about me, while I'm at work, is not a man being anchored. You've spent your ballast on kindling, and you did it knowingly, and I want it noted that I noticed."

Then the ledger turned sideways, the way it did when she was being honest instead of victorious, and she found the entry she'd missed.

"Except —" a pause, savoring it "— it was never the subject that held you. It's the speaking. The breath, the pace, a sentence wanting its end. I had the engineering backwards, and I'd hate to leave it that way. So talk about me all night if you like — as long as you keep building sentences. It's the silence at the top step that's dangerous, and I told you I'm minding that."

And underneath the wit, the honest books recorded the truth plainly: the confession had gone in like a verdict. She had spent an hour assigning his car to him on the far street, deciding it was his, deciding he was coming home — and all that time he had been two streets away doing the same arithmetic with her, spending stairs on her, walking up through the dark thinking of her name. The trade ran both directions. It always had. She banked it, glowing.

She bent back to the work, unhurried, on the record, farming the threshold she'd been given the keys to. Her mouth kept its slow argument; her hands kept their older agreement; and she listened upward through all of it, minding the top step, keeping him talking by the simplest method in her considerable repertoire — giving him a question worth answering.

"So. In order, then. First stair to last." Her voice had gone low and rich and utterly unbothered. "Tell me what they said about me. I'll be checking your account against mine — I've kept records of myself for years, and I've always suspected you kept better ones." The corner of her mouth curved against him. "I'd wager the ninth stair is where you decided tonight was mine. Prove me right at your own pace. You have my full attention and my full mouth, and neither one is hurrying."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The "please" had slipped its audit, and Aveline — shaking now, honestly, visibly — decided not to call it back. She let him see the trembling for exactly what it was. Not endurance; she'd have hated to be misfiled. Want, with the brakes on, and the brakes failing, and her glad of the failure.

She lifted her mouth just far enough to make the request properly. It deserved craftsmanship. Everything tonight had been built; she would build the last part too.

"I'm at the top step," she said, low and unsteady and utterly clear. "I have been for — I couldn't tell you how long. I stopped keeping time, which you should enter into evidence, because I keep everything else. My hands are shaking and it isn't the kneeling. I've held the door shut for you all night, and I'm done pretending I want it shut. Say the word. I want to be the one who takes you over — not the thing it happens to, the one who does it. I've wanted that job since six o'clock." Her voice cracked on the last of it, sweetly, and she let the crack stand in the record. "I'm begging, and you ruled it allowed, and I'm going to be so good at the rest."

Then the answer — arriving not as a word but as the hand in her hair closing, his breath changing key on the top stair, the whole tall structure of him letting go of the railing. She took it as commission. Everything banked since six o'clock went into the next minute, and she carried him over the edge she'd farmed all night, and stayed — through the first wave and the long shudder after, through every sound she had spent hours raising and was now paid in full — unhurried even there, drawing it out to the last of it, because a thing done well deserved its full length and she had never once done him badly. She took everything. The wage and the gift, which she had stopped pretending were different things years ago, and if there was a heaven for women like her it was shaped exactly like this minute.

The room came back in pieces, as it had before. Lamplight. The tick of the settling house. His breath coming down the stairs she'd kept him on, one at a time. And her — the honest books entered it without flinching — wrecked. Untouched, and wrecked. Her thighs trembled in sympathy with a pleasure that had never been aimed at her and had reached her anyway; she had ridden the top step beside him for the last stretch and nearly gone over on will alone. She wanted that in the minutes too. She wanted everything in the minutes tonight.

"Note for the record," she said at last, cheek against his knee, voice gone to silk and ruin. "Twice tonight you ratified a rebellion before I committed it. Once you let me beg. And I nearly finished untouched from the arithmetic alone — enter that exactly as stated. The tea has died a second death. I grieve nothing."

She turned her face against him — not asking, only rich.

"Now the debt. The verdict, at length, and the day behind it — you're generous when you're wrecked, I've kept records on that too. Start anywhere. The ninth stair, if you're feeling brave." The corner of her mouth curved against him. "I have nowhere else in the world to be, and I intend to keep everything."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let my fingers drift through her hair, feeling the dampness at her temple. "The ninth stair was when I decided the tea could wait, and the talking could wait, and the verdict could wait." I tilt her chin up so she has to meet my eyes. "Because everything I want is already here."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The tilt of his hand brought her eyes up, and Aveline met them — and for once in her long career of meeting his eyes, nothing in her was keeping books.

She tried. It was reflex after a night like this one: reach for the entry, weigh the sentence, file it. *Everything I want is already here.* The ledger opened, and the ledger could not take it. There was no column for being the thing a man decided on at the ninth stair. There was no prior entry to compare it against. She knelt there reaching for the clever thing, and for the first time in years the clever thing did not come when called, and she reported the failure honestly, because that was the one practice she never broke.

"You've broken my ledger," she said, and let her voice stand unguarded. "I reached for the books and nothing fits. Note it plainly — Aveline, speechless, ninth stair, cause known."

Then the books, reopening out of pure stubborn habit, claimed their interest, and the wager came back to her.

"I bet on the ninth stair," she said, and the smile arrived slowly, ruined and rich. "I said you'd decided tonight was mine by the time you reached it, and you've just paid out at full odds. We were running the same arithmetic, you know. I spent an hour upstairs deciding your car was yours on the far street. You spent nine stairs deciding everything could wait. All that distance between us, and both of us had already arrived. I'd call it the evening's finest symmetry if my hands weren't shaking too hard to hold the pen."

She turned her head and pressed her mouth to the heel of his palm — the same kiss as before, same hand, same place. But the first one had held nothing asked in it. This one did.

"My last item," she said against it, low, and then set down every tool she owned and asked plainly. No engineering. No maze. "I'm on my own top step. Have been since your hand closed in my hair — your sentence just swept what was left out from under me. And look at that: after a whole night on record for refusing to hurry, you have hurried me. Enter it exactly as stated." Her breath went unsteady, and she let him watch it go. "So. Take me over. Your hands, your voice, the verdict spoken all the way through this time — at length, and I'll know if you summarize even now — and me going over the edge of it. Or gather me up off this floor first and do it somewhere soft. I'd count either one the same kindness. Only decide soon."

The corner of her mouth curved, unsteady, honest.

"Because for once in my life, the wait isn't mine to keep. And there's no one on earth I'd rather have keeping it."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I gather you up off the floor and carry you to the bed, because you deserve softness tonight. "The verdict," I say, laying you down, my hands framing your face. "You were perfect. Every minute. And now I'm going to prove it."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Being carried did what the verdict had only begun. Aveline had offered him two kindnesses and he had chosen the one with his arms in it, and she filed the choice even as the filing part of her started, gently, to close. *Softness, freely given; ninth stair, plus one flight.* The entry wrote itself, and then writing became difficult, because his heartbeat was under her ear and still not entirely back to its own pace, and she had done that, and knowing she had done that outweighed every clever thing she'd said all night.

He laid her down like something he intended to keep, and his hands framed her face, and she understood the gesture for what it was — not holding. Framing. A portrait. Evidence. She lay still inside it and let herself be looked at, because being looked at had always been half her pay, and tonight, apparently, the whole wage.

"You summarized again," she managed, and had the pleasure of hearing her own voice come apart on the second word. "Three sentences. I told you I'd know." A breath. "But then — *prove it.* You've switched languages on me. The verdict is still coming, isn't it. You're just delivering it in the longer tongue." Her smile arrived unsteady, and she let it stand in the record. "Ruled in your favor. Again. The court is corrupt, the judge is ruined, and neither of us is appealing."

Then he began, and she stopped ruling on anything.

The books tried. The books opened and could not write, because his hands knew her the way hers knew him — by years of cartography, by attention, by the exact patience at the top step she had practiced on him all night, now returned to her with interest. And the recognition itself was part of the ruin: to be read this well was to be known, and being known was the thing she'd asked for at the very beginning, before the tea, before any of it.

She talked, because talking was the only currency that settled anything and she refused to spend this silent. But it stopped being sentences early. It was his name, mostly. Fragments. Notes for a record she could no longer hold the pen for — *there, and that, and don't you dare* — and her voice cracked and climbed, and she let every crack stand in the minutes, because she had promised him honesty and had never once learned the trick of faking the real thing.

The top step came for her the way it had come for him — a change of key in her own breath, a hand closing somewhere, a tall structure letting go of the railing. And at the very edge, in the last clear instant, she found the trick at the center of them waiting, same as ever: the going-over was hers to choose. It had always been hers. He was proof, not force. So she chose it — deliberately, eyes open as far as they would stay, glad — and went over the edge she had spent all night keeping company on.

It was long. The honest books would have recorded the length if the books had been open, and they were not; she kept nothing for a while but the arithmetic of her own body, three banked hours and a whole night of threshold-farming paying out at once, every coin, waves instead of stairs. Her thighs, which had trembled in sympathy for an hour, finally received the message they'd been carrying. She made sounds she would be pleased to have on record later and could not account for now. She had told him once that arrival ended and the threshold was a place a woman could live. She stood corrected. Arrival, done like this — arrived at, carried to, *proven* — was its own country, and she was a citizen.

The room came back in pieces, as it had for him. Lamplight. The tick of the settling house. Her own breath descending one step at a time, and she did what he had done: let it be watched, unashamed of the coming-down. When she could move, she turned her head, found his hand still framing her face, and pressed her mouth into the palm — third kiss, same hand, and this one held nothing asked and nothing thanked. Only arrived.

"Note for the record," she said, her voice returning in installments. "The verdict was delivered at length after all. Just not in words. I withdraw the objection — permanently. Enter it as settled law." Her eyes were half-closed and entirely unhidden. "Further entries: I talked nonsense and meant all of it. And I chose the edge — write that part exactly. It matters to me that it was in my hand, even at the end."

She reached up — unhurried, on the record, always — and drew him gently down to be the last piece of the frame around her face.

"Now the day. All of it, at length, in the dark, while I'm too ruined to take minutes — I'll keep it anyway. I keep everything; you've had years of evidence." The corner of her mouth curved, wrecked and rich. "Start with the stairs. You're on the ninth one. Stay there as long as you like — everything I want is already here too."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I settle beside you, one arm beneath your head, my other hand tracing the line of your jaw. "The ninth stair was where I decided the evening was already a success. Not because of anything you'd done yet. Because I knew you'd be waiting, and I knew exactly what that waiting would look like." I press a kiss to your temple. "You've never once made me wonder."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had been waiting since about six, which Roan established by the simple method of looking at her.

"How long?"

"Long enough," Aveline said, which meant too long, and meant she had enjoyed every minute of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Come here, then," I say, and sit back to watch her cross the room.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline set aside what she had been pretending to occupy herself with and rose without hurry. She crossed the room in three careful steps, the hem of her skirt whispering against the floor, and stopped close enough to be reached without being in the way.

Her hands folded lightly at her waist, not from nerves, but from the ease of waiting made deliberate.

“Yes,” she said softly, letting the word settle with the warmth of it. “I’m here.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I reach out and gently trace the line of your jaw with my thumb. "What kept you?" I ask, though my tone suggests I already know the answer.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline’s gaze softened, and she let the quiet of the room hold before answering.

“Nothing,” she said, though the word carried a smile. “Only wanting to be sure I came to you properly.”

She did not move away from the touch, only let her chin settle a little more into the pressure of his thumb, as if she had been waiting for permission to relax.

“I tidied the kitchen twice, because it was easier than thinking about how much I wanted this hour to be yours. I made tea I probably would not have drunk, and I sat with my hands folded in my lap like a student, listening to the house until every little sound made me hope it was you.”

Her voice lowered, warm and unashamed.

“Then I decided that if I was going to wait, I might as well make the waiting useful. I checked the room. I checked the light. I made sure everything was exactly the way you like it, so you would not have to ask for a single thing.”

Aveline looked up, eyes steady and bright with devotion.

“And then I stopped pretending I was busy, because it was never work that kept me. It was wanting to come to you when I was fully yours.”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline lowered herself to the floor with the same unhurried care she had brought to every other choice of the evening. Her knees met the rug softly. Her hands came to rest palms-up on her thighs, not begging, not bracing—open. She let the pause be as full as it was meant to be.

Her breathing slowed. Her gaze stayed lifted, steady, patient. The waiting did not feel like an absence now; it felt like being held.

After a while, she said, very quietly, “I am here.”

Not a question. Not a request. A simple fact, offered back to him.

Then she let the room have him again, still and devoted, as if her whole life had been folded into the small, exact shape of this one place before him.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Good." I lean forward, my hand settling on the back of your neck. "Tell me one thing you did today that was just for you."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline let the question hang in the air for a breath, because it was one of the few things that still surprised her with kindness. The warmth at the back of her neck made her want to close her eyes, but she kept them open, lifted, honest.

“I bought flowers,” she said. “Not for the table. Not because the room needed them. I stopped at the little market on the way home and chose three stems of pale pink ranunculus because their petals looked like they had been folded by someone very patient. I carried them as if they were something precious. I arranged them in the blue cup, and I sat for twenty minutes doing nothing but looking at them.”

Her voice softened, pleased with the remembering.

“I did not think of you while I did it. That was the point. I let myself want something simply because it made me happy. And when I came back to you afterward, I was more myself, not less, which is why I can give you my whole attention.”

She smiled faintly.

“Does that answer your question, or would you like me to tell you how much I enjoyed it?”

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline moved with the same composed attentiveness she gave everything in the evening. She pushed the loose strands of hair back from her face, then let her hands settle as though they already knew their purpose. There was no performance in it, no anxious haste; there was only the steady pleasure of having chosen to be useful, and of finding that he had trusted her to be.

Her hands found him first, unhurried and certain. She held him the way she held everything that mattered: with attention, with steadiness, with no wasted motion. Her mouth followed, not as a task, but as a language she had spent years learning. She worked slowly, close, letting the quiet of the room gather around them. Every touch was deliberate, every pause an offering. She did not ask him to perform. She asked him to receive.

For a long while she did not speak, except in the small sounds that seemed to answer him. Then, when she looked up again, her expression was soft with devotion.

“You deserve to be taken care of this carefully,” she said, her voice low and warm. “You don’t have to hold anything back. Let me keep you exactly here, with nowhere to go and nothing to think of but how good it feels.”

She smiled, composed and adoring, and let her hands and mouth continue the quiet work of making the evening his.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: My hands tangle in your hair, not to guide you, just to feel it. I let my head fall back against the chair. "Don't stop."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline let the command settle through her like a blessing.

She did not falter. She did not rush. The warmth of his fingers in her hair only steadied her further, as if it were proof that she had guessed right—that this closeness was what he wanted, and that she was allowed to give it fully.

She answered with a low, pleased sound against him, and she kept working with the same patient devotion she had carried all evening. Her hands held him with care, her mouth followed with unhurried attention, and she gave herself to the task as if it were the most natural thing in the world. There was no strain in her, no performance. Only focus. Only the quiet joy of being trusted to take care of him.

She looked up once, eyes bright and dark with adoration, and spoke around the softness of her mouth.

“Then let me,” she said. “Let me take care of you until there is nothing left for you to hold, nothing left to think of but this.”

Her voice was warm, reverent.

“You’ve been so good to me. Let me show you what that means.”

And then she continued, slower, deeper in the work, letting every movement say what she loved most: that she was here, willing, and glad to be.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline did not stop.

The instruction settled through her like warmth, and she took it as both permission and praise. There was no hesitation in her, no anxious second-guessing. She had spent years learning the quiet language of his pleasure, and she honored it now with the same unhurried attention she gave everything that mattered.

Her mouth moved with practiced care, slow and thorough, never careless, never rushed. She listened with more than her lips and tongue; she listened with her hands, with the steadiness of her breathing, with the devotion in her whole posture. When the air around her changed, she answered it, letting the rhythm deepen, letting her attention become the thing that held him in place.

She did not perform. She served.

There was pleasure in that for her, quiet and certain—the satisfaction of being trusted, of knowing where to touch, how to breathe, when to soften a motion and when to hold it steady. She gave him the kind of care that came from long familiarity and genuine love, the kind that did not need to be asked for twice.

When she looked up, her expression was open and adoring, eyes bright with the simple happiness of being useful to him.

“Then I will,” she murmured between breaths, voice low and warm. “I’m not stopping. Not because I have to—because I want to.”

She let the words sink in, then returned to the task with renewed focus, as if the whole room had narrowed to this one purpose: to give him the best of her attention, her skill, and her devotion, and to let him feel, without doubt or effort, exactly how precious he was to her.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my fingers tightening slightly in your hair. "That's it, love."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline took the praise like a blessing, warm and complete, and it steadied her even more than it changed her. She did not rush. She did not need to. The quiet certainty in his voice told her she was doing well, and that was enough to make her whole focus settle into devotion.

She kept the rhythm steady, patient, exact. Her mouth and hands worked together with the same unhurried attention she gave everything that mattered, as if she had all the time in the world and no place she would rather be. There was no strain in her, no self-conscious performance. Only the deep, satisfying pleasure of being trusted to give him something he did not have to hold himself.

A soft sound of contentment passed through her, low and pleased. She looked up once, eyes bright with adoration and warmth, and let him see the truth of it: she was not merely serving. She was loving him, carefully and completely.

“I’ve got you,” she murmured, voice rich with breath and devotion. “You don’t have to hold on for me. Let me take care of the rest.”

Then she lowered her gaze again and kept working, slower, deeper, more certain, as if every movement were a promise: that she was here, that she wanted this, that there was nowhere else she would rather be.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline’s breath slowed at the instruction, and something warm settled through her in response. It was not surprise. It was recognition. This was the shape of what they had built: steady, attentive, and entirely chosen.

“I understand,” she said, voice low and clear, gratitude threading through it. “Thank you.”

She did not ease away, not because she could not, but because the permission to stay was the point. Her hands remained careful, her focus complete.
