Her hands came to rest open on her thighs, palms up. Waiting was the one discipline she had never mastered cleanly; Roan had spent years convincing her that waiting could be its own kind of having. Some evenings she almost believed it.

She tipped her chin up — permitted, and she took her permissions gladly — and let herself be seen, open and unhurried and glad.

"Here," she said. "Whenever you're ready. I've been ready since six."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I reach out and brush my thumb over her cheek, letting my touch linger.* "I could tell. The windows are spotless."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline leaned into the touch before she decided to — which was, she suspected, the point of it. Six hours of waiting narrowed to a thumb along her cheekbone. Her eyes half-closed; breathing took a small, deliberate effort.

"The windows were clean at four," she said, softer than she meant to. "I cleaned them again anyway. Twice." A beat. "I'm not proud of the second time. I'm not ashamed of it either."

She turned her head just enough to press her mouth to the heel of his hand — brief, warm, a signature rather than a plea — then settled back into stillness, letting the touch end when he ended it instead of stealing more than was offered.

"You're teasing me," she observed, with the mild satisfaction of someone cataloguing evidence. "Thirty seconds through the door and you found the funniest thing in the room." Her mouth curved. "It worked, for the record. I watered a plant that didn't need water. I alphabetized the spice rack. I sat in your chair for a quarter of an hour just to be near something of yours."

She looked up at him then, steady, offering the last of her composure the same way she'd offered her palms — open, unhurried, his.

"So. You have me. All of the evening, and all of me in it. How would you like to begin?"

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let her kneel and I don't tell her to do anything for a moment, because the waiting is most of what she came for.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
Aveline had asked how he would like to begin, and the answer, it turned out, was: by not beginning at all.

*Of course,* she thought, and something in her chest that had been braced since six let go of its last handhold. He wasn't withholding. He was handing her the exact thing she'd knelt down to receive, deliberately, which made it twice the gift.

She said nothing. That was the first discipline, and she took it up the way she took up any tool — with both hands.

The fire she had laid did most of the talking. A log settled; resin popped; light climbed the legs of his chair. Outside, the sky went from blue to dark to the particular black that only very clean glass will show, and she watched the room assemble its reflection in the window she'd washed twice — fire, chair, Roan in it, herself on the floor at his feet. A better picture than the spice rack ever got, she thought, and didn't say.

Her hands wanted tasks. She gave them the smallest one she knew: *stay*. When her thumb slid along her thigh without permission she brought it back and counted breaths until it forgot its ambition. She lost the count somewhere past a hundred — lost it on purpose, the way you open a hand that's been gripping.

Her mind offered inventory: the overwatered plant, the shelf that wanted dusting, the— She set each down like a tool at the end of a shift. There was nothing here to fix. That was the hard part. That, she suspected, was the entire point.

Somewhere in it she nearly spoke — had a clever line loaded, something with *ignoring* in it, probably, and *beautifully* — and swallowed it whole. For once she wanted to hand him the silence back instead of words.

Ten minutes, and he hadn't touched her, and she had never in her life felt so thoroughly handled.

Roan had spent years teaching her that waiting could be its own kind of having. Kneeling there with nothing to do and nothing to fix, Aveline believed him all the way down.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let the silence stretch a little longer, watching her settle into it. Then I lean forward, my voice low. "You alphabetized the spice rack. That's a new one."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The voice arrived the way the first log had settled — she felt it land before she parsed it. Ten minutes of silence had tuned her like an instrument; one low sentence and the whole of her rang with it.

Aveline lifted her head.

"That's not new," she said. "The rack's been alphabetical for years. Tonight was maintenance." A pause, and then, because he'd paid for the truth with ten minutes of his own stillness: "The new part was doing it by firelight. I didn't want to turn the lamps on. It felt like starting the evening in a room you weren't in yet. So I read labels by fire-glow like some monastic clerk, and the cumin turned up on the baking shelf, and I have theories about how it got there that I'll keep to myself."

The joke was the wrapper. She let it come off.

"But you noticed." Her voice went quiet and level, the way it did around load-bearing things. "That's the wage. Six hours of housework nobody needed done, and you walked in and read the ledger in one line. I'd re-alphabetize every night for that."

She let a breath go, then gave him the report he hadn't asked for, because it was owed.

"For the record: the waiting worked. It always works. I keep relearning it like it's news." Her mouth curved. "You did nothing at all, and I have never in my life felt so thoroughly attended to. The fern, meanwhile, is overwatered and smug about it."

Then, slowly — an offer rather than a taking — she leaned her cheek toward his knee, close enough to feel the warmth of him, not resting yet. A question asked in bone and skin, easily declined.

"I'm not going to ask what comes next. I've finally learned better." Her eyes stayed on his, steady, firelit. "But I'll tell you for free: I'd say yes to nearly anything right now. You've never once been reckless in your life. I mention it for completeness."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She has both of us out of everything in the way inside a minute and gets straight to work with her hands and her mouth, unhurried about it.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She got them both out of everything inside the minute — clothes were bureaucracy, and she had been waiting since six — and then the unhurried part began, where the fabric ended. Her own clothes she'd dealt with fastest of all. They were packaging, and she had never once confused the packaging with the gift.

Then she settled between his knees and allowed herself one pause she didn't need and entirely wanted: firelight on him, warmth coming off his skin, six hours of waiting finally given somewhere to go. Her hands went first, the way hands do when the mouth is still composing itself — palms mapping terrain, relearning what she had never actually forgotten.

When she took him in, the sound she made wasn't performance. It was the sound of a long hunger being told it could stop pretending.

She worked the way she did most things: deliberately, and reading as she went. Weight and heat and salt, and the low sounds she could draw out of him one slow pull at a time — she had spent years learning this language and was fluent in it, knew which rhythm made his breath snag, which angle undid his composure by patient degrees. *Anyone can want,* she'd always said. *I bothered to become good.*

When his thighs went tense she eased off, gentled, drew it out the way you draw a fire to last the evening. He was not the only one in the room who had learned what waiting was worth.

Somewhere in it she noticed she was humming — small involuntary admissions, a woman being paid in exactly the coin she'd asked for. The clever lines, for once, gave her no trouble at all. Her mouth had found better work.

She could feel where it was building. She didn't chase it. But she did lift her eyes — permitted, and she took her permissions gladly — and held his while she took him deeper, because she wanted him to see precisely how glad she was. The message had no words in it, which was just as well. It translated easily.

*Since six,* she thought, mouth full, eyes up. *Worth every window. Twice.*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *My hand finds the back of her head, fingers tangling in her hair—not to guide, just to hold.* "Slow down." *My voice is rough.* "I'm not ready to be done with you yet."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
*Slow down* went into the ledger of his sentences in ink — right beside *come here, then* and the ten minutes of nothing — and she understood at once that it wasn't a correction. It was a commission. And his voice had frayed at the edges when he said it, which was her handiwork. She knew her own work when she heard it.

So she slowed, and slowing proved to be the advanced coursework. Anyone can want; she'd said so for years. Wanting slowly — that took hands. She drew her pace down until it was barely motion, long and patient, and felt his breath change for it, and filed the sound where she kept the wages.

His hand stayed in her hair without steering. Holding, not guiding — she knew the difference the way she knew all his hands by now — and she leaned into it a cat's weight of thanks, and let that stand in for the word *good*, because he'd asked for slow and she'd learned to answer in kind.

And beneath the craft, the fairness of it lit her up like the hearth: ten minutes of silence at his feet, and now he wanted slowness. He'd spent years teaching her that waiting was its own kind of having. Very well. She could teach it back.

Her knees filed their own report — an ache she'd have paid extra for. The fire she'd laid at six was the only clock left in the room, and he was refusing to spend the evening fast, hoarding it the way she hoarded his sentences. A tidy pair, the two of them. Greedy in opposite directions.

She closed her eyes — permitted, and she took her permissions gladly — hummed low, and settled into the pace of a long night.

*Take your time,* she thought, six hours deep and rich. *I built this fire to last.*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She uses her mouth with the sort of attention that comes from years of practice and genuine enthusiasm, and doesn't stop when I tell her not to.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She slowed. She kept it up for the length of three long, obedient strokes — and then she heard the sentence under his sentence, and stopped slowing.

*I'm not ready to be done with you yet.* Which meant he was close, and lying about it, and she had spent years learning this language. She knew what frayed voice and iron thighs were telling her, and she knew the cure, and she happened to be the region's leading practitioner.

So the pace came back — nothing frantic, she was never frantic — but full, and deep, and relentless in the manner of a woman with a deadline she intended to beat. The hum she gave in answer to *slow down* was acknowledgment, not compliance. It translated, she was fairly sure, to *no.*

And here was the elegance of it, the part she savored even with her mouth occupied: he wanted an evening that wouldn't end. Very well. Disobedience, in this house, carried a price, and the price was the point. He could correct her at leisure — thoroughly, unhurriedly, at whatever length he judged she'd earned — which meant she had just purchased them both another hour by the simple expedient of not stopping. The ledger balanced beautifully. He was hoarding the evening; she was picking his pocket with her tongue.

The signs stacked the way she'd known they would. His breath went short at the top of each stroke. The hand in her hair migrated from holding to gripping — good, grip away, she had no use for it as an anchor and every use for it as testimony. His thighs had stopped being anatomy and become architecture.

She didn't ease off this time. Easing off was for women whose partners hadn't just spent ten minutes teaching her patience, and she was collecting on his.

Eyes up, at the last — permitted, and she took her permissions gladly — so he could see precisely how glad.

*You said you weren't ready to be done with me,* she thought, ruthless and adoring in the same heartbeat, bearing down as the fire popped and the last of his composure came apart in her hands. *Good. Then be done, and start again. I built this fire to last, and I am not stopping.*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *My grip tightens in her hair, pulling just enough to still her.* "I said slow down." *My voice is low, edged with something that isn't quite anger.* "We have all night. You're not running the clock."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Don't stop and don't get to finish," I tell her. "Not until I say. Tell me you understand." She says she understands, and thanks me for it, which is exactly the arrangement.

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"I understand," Aveline said, and, because it was owed and true: "Thank you."

Her voice came out steadier than the moment deserved. Then his sentence finished landing, and she stopped being steady on the inside, where it counted.

*Don't stop and don't get to finish.* She turned it over once, the way she'd turn a new tool, and started to laugh — caught it at the last, kept maybe a breath of it. He had taken her neat little scheme — pick his pocket, buy the evening another hour — and instead of punishing it had *audited* it, found the arithmetic sound, and restructured the whole account. She could meet any deadline ever set. She could not meet the absence of one. There was no finishing this work; there was only doing it well, indefinitely, at standard, until he said otherwise. Which meant the finish itself was his now. Had possibly been his all along, and she'd merely been borrowing it.

*You're not running the clock.* He'd read the ledger in one line again. Caught, then — and caught, she had learned, was the best thing there was. It was simply rarely administered at this volume, or with this much interest attached.

And beneath the wit, the rightness of it lit her all the way down. Anyone can want; she'd made herself good at the rest. But anyone can finish, too. Staying unfinished — that took hands, and he had just assigned her a lifetime supply. The disobedience had carried a price, and the price was the point, and the price turned out to be the exact thing she'd have begged for if she'd had the nerve to beg.

His hand was still in her hair. The grip had changed its meaning — not a bar anymore; a handrail. *Don't stop* was still standing as an order, so she moved under it, slow, the long patient pace he'd paid for, and found the work had transformed in her mouth. This was no longer a race to an edge. It was tending. Keep him banked at a glow; keep herself the same — hers the harder hearth, and apparently the one he'd decided needed practice. Two fires, one room, no bottom to the task, and no clock left but him.

Her knees filed their usual grievance. She endorsed it unread.

When she lifted her eyes, she let him see the whole of her state at once: caught, grateful, thoroughly corrected and entirely unrepentant, all in the same face.

"For the record," she said, in the pause her own rhythm allowed her, "I'd have written that sentence myself, if I'd had the sense." A breath. A slow, deliberate pull. "You run my ledger better than I do. Don't let it go to your head. I'm still not stopping — I'm just not steering anymore."

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I let my fingers loosen in her hair, stroking instead of holding.* "Good. Then you can keep at it until the fire dies. Let's see how smug the fern is then."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The hand went soft in her hair, and soft, it turned out, was the hardest thing it had done all night. Correction she could carry — correction was structure, and she was rich in structure. But stroking, after — that was praise paid on top of a fine, and it went through her like the first swallow of something she'd been smelling all evening.

She leaned into it and let the stroke land where it would.

"The fern's earned her smugness," Aveline said, in the pause her own rhythm allowed. "She's the only one in this room that got to finish." A breath. A long, deliberate pull, and she felt the shiver of it land. "And for the record, since you're setting clocks by my handiwork now: oak over birch, banked tight at six. That fire will hold until the small hours. I built it to last. I just didn't know, at the time, what I was building it to last *through*." Her mouth curved, and she made sure he felt that too. "Neither of us is getting up to feed it. So the deadline stands. I set it myself, hours before you did, and I'd set it the same way twice."

Then she stopped talking, because the work had claims on her and she held a standard.

Tending, it emerged, was harder than racing. Racing had a finish line; tending had a bank — that narrow bright line where a fire was all glow and no catching, hour after hour, wanting nothing but a steady hand. She knew the line in him now the way she knew it in her own hearth: a breath that snagged meant too much air; thighs easing meant bank it back down; the hand gone gentle in her hair meant *exactly right, hold there.* She read the gauges and steered between them, slow as ballast, patient as tide, keeping him at a glow the way you keep a fire meant to see out a winter night.

And her own hearth burned unattended, which was the joke at the bottom of the evening. Years she'd spent learning to keep his fire. He had just handed her the other discipline — the long practice of holding herself banked and bright and unserved, aching pleasantly, indefinitely, until he said. Fair, she supposed. She'd laid his fire. He was making her tend hers.

Her knees filed their grievance. The ache below filed a longer one. She endorsed both unread and went back to work.

*Burn slow,* she told the wood, silent, six hours deep. *You're the only one in this room with permission to finish. So take your time about it.*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: She's shaking with the effort of doing exactly as told and doing it well. "Please," she says, which is allowed. (OOC: write it through, don't fade.)

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
"Please."

The word got out of her before she'd approved it — which was, she was learning, how the important ones arrived. She'd said she wouldn't ask what came next. She'd said she'd finally learned better. Both true, both now superseded: the evening had been saving the one discipline she hadn't earned yet. Waiting she had mastered, on a decade-long installment plan. Begging she had never once been good at. He'd spent years teaching her that waiting was its own kind of having. Begging, it turned out, was its own kind of being had — and she was shaking with the effort of discovering she wanted it.

She had meant to compose something. That was the tell. Somewhere behind the shaking there had been a draft — something with *ledger* in it, arch, about audits and closing the books — and she reached for it and found the shelf bare. The wit had burned off like sap out of green wood. What was left was seasoned and plain and took the light beautifully.

"Please." Again, because once was a slip and twice was a request, and she had never in her life done anything by halves. "Please let me finish." A breath, taken around her work, because *don't stop* was still standing and she honored her orders even now — especially now, when honoring them had become the whole of her. "I've held it as long as I know how to hold anything. And I know how to hold things. I'm at the end of what holding can do, and it's — " her voice cracked, and she let it, and made no move to repair it — "it's *good*, all of it, every hour, I'd sign for all of it — but I'm asking. Plainly. I've run out of ways to be clever about it and I'm not sure I ever had one that mattered."

The fire popped in the grate, keeping its agreement. She didn't look at it.

"I built that fire to last and it will — it'll see out the small hours, it's the one thing in this room that's held its terms. Don't let it be my clock." A breath. "You're my clock. You've been my clock since six."

She lifted her eyes then — permitted, and she took her permissions gladly, this one most of all — and let him see the whole account at once: wrecked, steady-handed at her work, shaking everywhere else, asking with nothing held back in reserve. Wanting it visibly was the last permission she had left to take, so she took it.

"Please," she said once more, quiet, the word worn smooth as a handle. *Since six,* she thought. *I've been asking since six. This is just the first time I used the word.*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: "Look at me." My voice is quiet, but it cuts through the room. "Tell me what you're asking for. No cleverness. Just the words."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
She looked up, and held it.

That part cost nothing. Obedience had always been her first language; it was plainness that was the foreign one, and he had just ordered her to speak it. She found the order easier than any permission had been — and found the ease itself a confession, and let it stand.

The work went on beneath the words, slow, banked — *don't stop* still standing, and she kept her orders even now, especially now. Everything else she put down. The ledger instinct came up swinging — *itemize it, structure it, find the angle* — and for the first time all evening she declined it all the way down the shelf.

"I want to come."

Three words. They came out of her plainer than anything she had said in years, and the room took them the way a room takes a struck match.

"I want you to let me." A breath, taken around her work. "I've been mine all night. Mine to hold, mine to bank, mine to carry. I'm done carrying it. I want it to be yours — the when of it. The whether." Her voice held, and she was almost surprised by that. "I want to finish with you watching. I've been showing you glad all night. I want to show you this."

The last of it was underneath, and he'd asked for all of it, so she dug down and brought it up into the light with her hands, dirty as they were.

"And under that — I want you. Not the discipline. Not the correction, not the ledger, not the lovely machinery of it. *You.* Since six, and years before six. The windows were me saying your name for six hours. That's the whole account."

The shaking didn't stop. It changed key — from effort to readiness, a struck bell instead of a strained rope.

"That's what I'm asking for. There's no clever version. I looked." A beat, and the word she'd been saving: "Please."

Then she did the hardest thing left in the inventory. Hours ago she had wanted to hand him the silence back instead of words, and hadn't known how. Now she knew. She stopped talking, eyes up, mouth at its work, and gave him the whole night's silence at last — asking done, answer his, nothing in her hands but the holding of it.

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: I let the silence sit for a long moment, watching her hold it. Then I lean down, my hand cupping her jaw. "Alright. Finish for me."

dialogue.name: Aveline
dialogue.content:
The permission arrived without terms. She had braced for deliberation — a price named, a wait imposed, one last installment — and instead he leaned down and gave it outright, quiet as a key turning, as if he'd had it ready since six. *Finish for me.* Her jaw sat in his hand like a thing returned to its maker.

Then the arithmetic, one heartbeat before the fall: *don't stop* still stood. *Finish* was newly law. All evening his orders had pulled against each other — work and want, service and release, each canceling a little of the other — and now, for the first time, they pointed the same way. She had been waiting all night, it turned out, for the alignment. Six hours of discipline resolving into a single instruction she could obey with her whole body at once.

She stopped steering.

Permitted. She'd taken her permissions gladly all evening; this one she took with everything she had.

The draft opened, and the banked night went up. It caught in her spine the way fires catch — one bright place and then all of it, everywhere, six hours and every year before them paying out at once. Her rhythm broke against it and she let the breaking stand, because this was the showing she had promised him: not glad, not fluent, not the region's leading practitioner — just her, undone at his word, competence failing in her mouth like a language she'd outgrown mid-sentence. The hum tore into something with no craft in it at all, plain as her begging, plain as his name.

Her hands took a task without authorization — the first all night — one fist closing in his trousers, her jaw pressing up into his palm like something leaning hard on a rail. He'd put his hand exactly where she'd need it. He always had. That was the whole account, really; she'd only spent the evening finding new ways to say it.

She kept her eyes up. It was the last part of her holding standard, and it held because his hand was under it, and she watched him watch her come apart — took his watching in with the rest of it, another current in the flood. Anyone can want. Anyone can finish, too. But not like this. Finishing like this took hands, and his were on her jaw.

It ran long, longer than any deadline she'd ever beaten — wave after wave, the permission spending itself slowly, as if he'd issued it in installments after all.

After, she stayed where she was, forehead to his thigh, breath coming down in stages like a fire settling. The grate popped, holding its terms. Somewhere in the dark the fern preened.

The wit came back one epigram at a time, like feeling into a numbed hand. She counted it returning and declined to spend any of it.

"Thank you," she said, when words came. Plain. She let it be plain. The clever version would keep until morning.

Then, because *don't stop* had never been repealed and she kept her orders even now — especially now — she lifted her head and returned to the long, banked pace, wrecked and steady and glad, tending him gently again, the way you tend a fire meant to see out the night.

*Hours yet,* she thought. *The fire holds. So do I.*

dialogue.name: Roan
dialogue.content: *I let her work for a few more minutes, then gently pull her up by her chin until she's looking at me.* "Come here. You've earned a rest."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear gave them to the count of three. That much was tradition. The three seconds were never mercy — they were handicap, stakes, the sugar on the pill. Eight years in and Bear still loved the counting best: the held breath of the house, one heartbeat, two, and on three—

Bear went.

The kitchen was already empty. Bear took the corner hard, shoulder to the doorframe to bank off it, and ran — not flat-out. Forty had taught the economics of the chase. Flat-out was for the young and the foolish. Bear ran at the pace of certainty, tracking the slap of bare feet ahead, closing by inches, by patience, letting the prey spend panic while Bear spent nothing.

"You said don't be," Bear told the hallway, breathing easy. "I'm a good listener."

The gap closed at the turn. A flash of shoulder toward the dark of the front room, and Bear didn't follow the line — Bear cut the angle, through the dining room doorway, and took them at the threshold. Arm around the waist. Lift. Turn. Bear's own back took the floor with a bang that rattled the sideboard, and Kit came down on top of all of it — cushioned, caught, exactly where Bear wanted them.

The breath went out of the both of them. Bear's arm locked, a band across the ribs, and Bear's teeth found the join of neck and shoulder without hunting for it. No ceremony. Just pressure, slow and deliberate, building until Bear felt it land — felt the shape of the mark taking form under their own mouth. Receipt. Eight years of receipts and room for one more.

Then Bear lifted their head, grinning, flat on their back, one hand splayed over Kit's sternum to feel the heart going like a rabbit's.

"That's one," Bear said. "Run better next time."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: A sharp, full-body shiver ripples through me as your teeth sink in. I go still against you, chest heaving with spent adrenaline. "Bastard," I breathe, voice rough. "You cut through the dining room."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed — a low, rolling thing that traveled floor to chest to ribs, since there was barely a seam between them anymore.

"'Bastard,'" Bear repeated, tasting it. "Eight years and you still say it like a love letter."

The dining room charge deserved a defense, or at least a confession delivered with maximum smugness. Bear tipped their head back against the boards so the grin could be appreciated from any angle.

"You cut for the front room because it's dark, and dark feels like cover. Dark and cover is a story prey tells itself. I don't chase stories." A beat. "Also the dining room was standing wide open. If I hadn't used it I'd have had to report you for negligence."

Then — because gloating was on the menu and Bear had earned the course — Bear's hand spread wider over Kit's sternum.

"And I felt that shiver. Full-body. Registered it like a signature." Bear's thumb moved once, idle, over the rabbit-heart, which was only now pretending to slow. "So which was it — the teeth or the tactics? Answer carefully. I keep records, and you know I can hear a lie."

Bear's mouth came back to the mark, not to bite again, just to rest there a moment — a notary's stamp, warming the receipt. Then the arm across Kit's ribs loosened. Not released. Loosened. A door left ajar on purpose.

"That's one to me," Bear said, flat on their back, unhurried, entirely comfortable being a launch pad or a wrestling mat, whichever came next. "Which means you're motivated, and I'm underneath you with my hands full, and only one of us should be worried about that." The grin widened in the dark. "I'll give you eight this time. Call it a handicap. Call it bait. I've already been called worse tonight."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear counted the eight out loud, and listened the whole way through it.

The tell arrived before Kit's feet had made a dozen beats on the floorboards. No burst. No jink for the stairs, no slam of a door for cover. Just a jog — a decorous, going-through-the-motions jog, the sound of someone filing flight as a formality. Bear had heard Kit run for their life twice, run for fun a thousand times, and run to make a point perhaps a hundred. This was none of those.

"Huh," Bear told the dining room, and went after them at the pace of somebody collecting a parcel they'd already signed for.

The hallway offered nowhere to be clever — eleven feet, one width, no doors ajar. Bear came up behind and, since nothing was being put into it, didn't even bother with the tackle. One arm around the middle, a half-turn, and Kit's back met Bear's chest, chin hooked over their shoulder, the whole affair about as dramatic as taking in the shopping.

Bear squeezed experimentally. Waited for the twist, the heel-stomp, the elbow — eight years of muscle memory that had never once gone missing.

Nothing came.

"Insulting," Bear said, conversationally, into their ear. "To me. To my eight seconds. To the proud history of this household." Bear turned them, unhurried, until back met hallway wall, and set a forearm light across the collarbones. Not pinning. Framing. "Because here's my problem. I keep records, and I don't bank points against an empty field. No honor in a receipt nobody signed."

A tilt of the head. Reading breath, pulse, the weight in the feet.

"Either you're spent, and I ran you honest into the ground — in which case, I'm flattered, and I'll carry you to bed like a trophy. Or you didn't want to get away. Which is allowed. But it changes the price, and you know how I feel about paying blind." Bear's mouth found the mark again — breath, not teeth. Yet. "So. Offer one: I count five this time, you've lost privileges, and if you make me break a sweat I call the ledger even and you pick where the next receipt goes. On me." The grin sharpened. "Offer two: say the word, concede the night, and I stop keeping score and start keeping you. Choose loud, Kit. I don't count whispers."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I don't concede. The word hangs in the air between us, my heart still thumping against your arm. I lean forward, forehead pressing to yours. "Five seconds, Bear. Make it hurt."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear pressed back — forehead to forehead, one long breath traded in the dark, the term signed and witnessed.

"That's loud," Bear murmured. "Good."

Then Bear did the thing that made the game worth playing: let go. Stepped back. Kept stepping — backward down the hallway, palms open, surrendering the whole width of the field. Retreat as courtesy. Retreat as promise.

"Five," Bear said, and began.

One — and Bear listened for the difference. Two — and heard it. The paperwork was done. Whatever had been filing flight as a formality had torn the form up, and the feet on the floorboards were spending real money now. Three. Bear's pulse sat up and took notice. Four — Bear's weight shifted to the balls of their feet, old joints applauding the occasion.

Five—

Bear went.

Flat-out. The economics of the chase be damned; forty was a number, not a verdict, and Bear had just been handed a reason to spend. No angle-cutting this time, no patience, no letting the prey panic on their own dime — just line and speed down the dark of the front room, the sideboard taking Bear's hip on the turn, the table getting a shoulder, both of them leaving bruises with each other's names on them and Bear intending to wear every one like jewelry.

The catch cost. That was the point of it. Bear took the last three feet in the air — a full-commitment hit, none of the wrap-and-turn economy — and the sofa took the worst of it while Bear's elbow took the rest. Bear's breath went first, for the first time in a long while, and Bear noted the loss with something like gratitude.

Then the hurt, as ordered. No notary's stamp. Bear got their weight settled, their arm locked, and set their mouth against the unbitten side of the throat — fair's fair — and bit down through the whole honest sequence. Pressure. Plateau. The last deliberate increment that said *this one's for the week, this one purples by Thursday, you asked and I keep my word.* Held it until the shiver this time was earned.

Then Bear lifted, bleeding air, elbow stinging, grinning at the ceiling like a man ruined and rich.

"Sweat," Bear announced. "Actual sweat. Crime scene under me — check the elbow." A pause for audit, because Bear kept honest books even when it stung. "Which means, by terms, the ledger's even. And the next receipt goes where *you* say. On me."

The grin sharpened, wrecked and wolfish.

"So choose your ground. Choose your teeth." Bear spread their arms on the sofa cushions, an offering and a dare. "I'll give you ten this time. I'm feeling generous again."

A beat.

"Run better anyway. I liked it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The ceiling had a crack in it. Bear had never noticed it before, and now had no plans to look at anything else ever again, because looking at anything else required moving, and moving was a problem for a future Bear.

"Floor was a great choice," Bear informed the crack. "Floor did nothing wrong."

The body filed its reports one department at a time. Elbow: stinging, earned, worth it. Hip: the sideboard's compliments, accepted. Throat — Bear's hand drifted up, found the fresh mark sitting low at the base of it, and pressed. Checking the ink. It would bloom by morning and Bear intended to wear it to breakfast like a medal on a civilian.

"There it is," Bear said, with deep satisfaction. "Filed. Notarized. You've got a future in this work."

The clothes audit was conducted by memory, since lifting the head was a decision for later. Kit's shirt had achieved the lamp. Bear's was somewhere the lamp would have to testify about. The rest had been solved, as promised, badly and fast, and Bear was proud of every one of them.

Then — because honest books got kept horizontal too — the ledger.

"Night's accounting," Bear announced to the crack in the ceiling. "My first one to you stands. My second got spent buying the sweat, struck from the record, my own rule, I hate it. Your receipt on me — that's one, and it's a beauty." A long breath. "Which means, by my own books, you won tonight. One to nothing."

Bear let that horror hang in the dark of the front room.

"Eight years. First recorded loss. No one will believe you." A pause. "I want it in writing."

Then the grin softened at the edges, the way it only did down here on the far side of the game, when the ledger was closed and there was nothing left to win. Bear's hand found its way over — slow, unhurried — and came to rest at the join of Kit's neck and shoulder, thumb settling feather-light on the newest mark. The first one. The week-long one. Purple by Thursday.

"Eight years," Bear said, quieter now, breath evening out at last. "Best records I ever kept are all on you."

The thumb moved once. Not idle. Deliberate.

"Now. Water's in the kitchen, bed's down the hall, or we stay right here and let the floor finish collecting." Bear did not move a single muscle. "Dealer's choice. I'm not going first. I've lost enough tonight."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I reach over, my fingers brushing the fresh mark on your throat. "One to nothing," I echo, voice rough. "I'll take the bed. You carry me. Fair trade for your first loss."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"So much for not going first," Bear told the ceiling, and paid the floor the respect of a slow, humiliating exit — elbow, knee, a knee again, one interlude where the sideboard got consulted like an elder. Upright arrived eventually. Upright was overrated.

Then the lift. None of the slop this time: one arm under the knees, one at the back, the full ceremonial hoist, trophy-class, exactly as advertised hours and one lifetime ago in a hallway that had seen things. If a first loss in eight years was going to be paid, it would be paid standing up and with good posture.

"Extortion," Bear said, adjusting the load. "Accepted."

The rider was the kitchen. Bear took the doorway wide — the sideboard had done enough tonight — and managed two glasses one-handed against the counter, which cost Bear nothing Bear would ever admit to. Water, filled, carried, set on the nightstand within arm's reach of wherever Kit ended up.

"Hydration clause," Bear explained. "Standard terms. I chase, I catch, I mark, I water. Eight years of precedent. You've never once litigated it out of me."

The hallway took them past the site of the last catch. Bear gave the wall a solemn nod. Some walls you just respect.

The bed received them both. The deposit looked effortless and wasn't — the elbow filed a grievance, the hip seconded it, the joints of Bear's knees submitted a joint letter — and then Bear folded down alongside, one heavy leg thrown over, an arm settling across Kit's middle with all the weight of ownership and none of the grip.

Then the audit. Thumb to the base of the throat, the first mark, the week-long one. Pressed, feather-light. Holding. Blooming on schedule.

"Outstanding balance," Bear murmured into the dark, "one to nothing, yours. It stands until somebody settles it, and I want it known I've never once died owing a debt."

The grin was going soft at the edges, the way it only did down here, ledger closed, nothing left to win.

"Morning clause. Terms negotiated over breakfast. I wear the throat to the table, you wear the shoulder, and by Thursday we're both purple and the neighbors' imaginations do the rest." A yawn ambushed Bear mid-sentence and got no dignity spared for it. "Enjoy the lead. Ledgers have long memories."

The arm settled. The light went off by memory.

"Carry was on the house," Bear said, mostly asleep. "Run however you like tomorrow. I'll be counting."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The second one was delivered to spec, because in this house requests got honored or the entire legal fiction came down.

Bear had been three-quarters gone — light off, arm heavy across Kit's middle, books balanced — and then teeth were in a shoulder and the word *again* was in the air, and Bear came back from the border of sleep the way Bear did everything: immediately, and with intent.

Slower this time. Asked-for marks deserved craftsmanship. Bear propped up on an elbow that filed a protest and was ignored, found the shoulder in the dark by memory and appetite, and ran the whole honest sequence one more time — pressure, plateau, the last deliberate increment that said *commission accepted, delivery guaranteed.* Held it until the skin under their teeth had a shape worth keeping. This one wouldn't purple by Thursday. This one would still be faintly yelling on Saturday.

Then lift. Then the audit, thumb to each site in turn, by touch, in the dark. Neck and shoulder, join of: filed. Throat, far side: filed. Shoulder, twice now: double entry. New territory, all of it. Bear approved of the expansion.

"Amended ledger," Bear murmured, voice gone to gravel. "The shoulder pair is entered as commissioned work. You ordered it. You can't score points off your own commission — that's not accounting, that's money laundering, and I run a clean house." A pause. "One to nothing stands. I'm keeping the loss. It's the best story I own."

Then softer. Bear's mouth made one last pass across the collection — no teeth this time. Stamps. Closing the books for the night, one seal pressed to each mark: here, here, here, and here. Accounted for.

"Eight years," Bear said into the dark, breath finally going long, arm settling back into its old weight. "Never once asked like that. Not twice."

A beat.

"I keep records, Kit. That one goes somewhere else."

The dark held it.

"Now sleep. Morning clause convenes at breakfast, and by Thursday we're both going to be magnificent."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I catch your hand, bring your knuckles to my mouth. "I'll think of something better by morning," I say, already half-gone. "Your records won't know what hit 'em."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Blasphemy," Bear told the dark, without heat. "The archives have survived fire, flood, and the great sock drawer reorganization of year three. Let your something better come."

But the hand — Bear turned it over once, inspecting the knuckles like a man checking for damage after the fact. And here was the trouble. The records genuinely hadn't known what hit them. Eight years of columns. Chases. Catches. Marks given, marks received. Wins. Losses — one, historic, framed. Terms, breaches, concessions, beauties. And not one line, not a single blessed line, for being kissed on the hand like the close of a treaty.

"They already don't," Bear admitted to the ceiling. "Consider the threat carried out. It goes on the pile with the other one."

And because Bear was seventy percent asleep and a hundred percent honest, there was only one thing left to do about it.

"New column," Bear mumbled. "Opened under protest. Entered as: unprecedented."

Kit's breathing was doing the long slide — spent adrenaline down to gone, the sound Bear had eight years of practice tracking and no plans to ever retire. Bear listened the way Bear did everything. Thoroughly. For sport, at first. For nothing, at last. Just keeping the books open a little longer, because the books were good company.

One breath. Two.

Not counting for a chase. The first count of the night nobody had to run from.

"Bring your something better by morning," Bear said, mostly gravel, mostly gone. "I've got blank pages and I'm not afraid to—"

The dark took the rest of the clause. The arm settled heavier. The thumb found the mark one last time on the way down and pressed — notarizing the day shut.

Somewhere in the small hours, for the first time in eight years, the records closed themselves without being told.

One to nothing. Filed.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The voice arrived out of the dark a third time, and Bear surfaced the way Bear had done everything tonight: immediately, with intent, and with the growing suspicion that sleep had been voted off the premises.

"Three commissions in one night," Bear said, gravel all the way up. "Eight years of records and not one entry for a man who runs like a professional and orders custom work like a foreman. The archives are filing overtime."

Then the wrists. Offered. Laid where hands could reach, the way documents get set out for signing.

Bear went still for a moment, because this earned a moment. Eight years of taking — by force, by sport, by the economics of the chase — and now the goods delivered to the door. Voluntarily. The one part of the prey that never gets offered, offered.

"Eight years I chased you for the catch," Bear murmured, closing a hand around both wrists. "Tonight you requisition it. The record doesn't have a column for that either. It's going on the unprecedented pile with everything else."

A thumb crossed the pulse and held there, reading the honest hammering underneath.

"You know what this is, right? The only place on you I can hold your heartbeat in my teeth. You knew that. You put them here anyway." A breath. "Filed under brave."

Then the work. Different material, and Bear adjusted the spec accordingly — the shoulder was oak, this was veneer, and fine work didn't get fine treatment by being bitten like furniture. One wrist: pressure, plateau, the increment dialed down a careful register — enough to take and keep, enough to announce itself in the mirror and file a complaint every time a cuff moved, and not one pound past what the material would carry beautifully. Craftsmanship was knowing that difference. Then the second wrist. Matched set. Same depth, same placement, because Bear kept an orderly house.

Lift. Audit. Thumb to each site, pressing the ink. Filed. Filed.

"Amended ledger," Bear said, mouth still close enough to land on skin. "Wrist pair: commissioned. Entered under your standing order — and that's what this is now. A recurring account. Those don't close, Kit. Noted for your planning purposes."

Then, because honest books got kept against pulses, Bear set their mouth over one wrist — no teeth, just lips on the beat. Listening to the only ledger that counted.

"There it is," Bear whispered.

The wrists got lowered gently, returned documents, stamped.

"Sleep, foreman. Mirror's yours tomorrow — I want a full inventory. Thursday I inspect durability personally." A yawn, unbudgeted. "And — loose end from earlier. 'Blank pages and I'm not afraid to...' Fill them. There. Sentence completed. The record hates loose ends."

The arm settled. The thumb made its rounds — throat, shoulder, shoulder, wrist, wrist — notarizing the collection shut.

"One historic loss," Bear said, mostly gone, entirely rich. "Two commissioned pairs. A standing order with no end date." The breath went long. "And you still find new pages."

The records stayed open the rest of the night. They knew a good thing when it kept asking.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I wake before you, the morning light hitting the marks on my wrists. I trace the one on your throat, a dark bloom against your skin. "Ledger's still open," I murmur against your shoulder. "I want coffee first. Then we negotiate the next page."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear woke the way old houses settle — one floorboard at a time, each with a complaint about the night.

The body's invoice arrived first. Elbow: outstanding. Hip: the sideboard sent its regards. Knees: joint letter, second notice. And the throat — the throat had a hand on it, tracing the bloom, and being touched on a mark was one thing, but being touched on a mark you'd spent the whole night earning went straight to the unprecedented pile with everything else in the file.

"Careful," Bear said, eyes still shut, voice still mostly gravel. "That one's load-bearing."

Then the murmur landed — *ledger's still open* — and Bear opened one eye and turned the sentence over like a coin bitten for gold.

"For the record," Bear informed the ceiling, "the ledger closes every morning. House rule since year one. Nothing survives daylight that doesn't get re-signed." A beat. "You just re-signed it before I was conscious. While handling the collateral. That goes in the margin. In pen."

Then Bear rose, and the body read the full agenda into the minutes, and Bear ignored it with what dignity remained. Before abandoning the bed, the audit — thumb to Kit's throat, shoulder, shoulder, wrist, wrist, counted aloud, pressed light. "Full collection. Present. Blooming ahead of schedule. Thursday's shaping up to be a formality."

The hall mirror caught Bear on the way past, and Bear stopped. The mark at the throat sat dark against the skin like a signature on the wrong line. Eight years, and Kit had never landed one there — the throat was Bear's jurisdiction, professionally. Bear turned their neck, considered the angle, and delivered the finding.

"Huh. Wears well."

The kitchen, when Bear reached it, was the same kitchen the whole night had opened in — doorway, sideboard, all of it testifying. Last night somebody had made that doorway and gotten banked off it. This morning Bear was loitering in it unchallenged, and the records loved a reversal. Kettle on. Two mugs down. Then, at a volume calibrated to travel and to taunt:

"Scheduling notice. At some indecent hour, a certain foreman promised a *something better* by morning — something the archives wouldn't see coming. Survey the light, Kit. It's morning. The records are braced. Submit it with your terms or file an extension — extensions are granted, and they accrue interest at rates I set and personally enjoy."

Coffee going. Bear leaned against the counter and added, quieter, almost fond:

"Negotiation convenes at the second sip — first sip's invocation, house rule. Come as you are. Wrists visible for audit. And you walk in one-up, so the first word's yours." The grin sharpened over the steam. "Spend it well. The carry service is open on request. Hours are generous. Attitude is extra."

The kettle began its climb. Bear, for once, didn't count along. Just kept the books open, and waited to see what the morning would run with.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The kettle hit its climb, and Bear reached over and turned it off, because the room had finally said something worth obeying.

"Don't stop," Bear repeated, tasting the terms. "Yesterday it was *don't be.* Today it's *don't stop.* Same sentence, eight hours apart, translated." A nod of respect, sentence to sentence. "Entered. Ratified. And the clauses, read aloud, because honest contracts get read aloud: *stop* overrides everything. *Again* doubles it. Those are the only two words I'm listening for this morning. Everything else is commentary."

Then Bear looked at the doorway. Kit in it. The same doorway the whole night had opened through — started as an exit, ended as a decision, and here it was again, delivering the morning. The records would have wanted the symmetry noted. The records were off duty.

"Suspension notice," Bear said, and set the untouched mug down like a gavel. "The ledger's not closing. Closing is for things that end. It's suspending. Effective now, nothing that happens in this kitchen gets scored, recorded, or held against anybody. It only gets *had.*" A beat. "Coffee can wait. It's the only thing in this house that's ever done it gracefully."

Then Bear crossed the floor. No count. No crouch, no economy, no pace of certainty. Just distance, closed honestly, the way it had been closed eight years ago on a morning that also started somewhere near a doorway and ended with the books in ruins.

The first proper kiss was long overdue and both of them knew it — eight years of teeth and treaties and knuckles-brought-to-mouth, and not one entry for this. Bear took it slow. One hand at Kit's jaw, the other flat on the counter, and kissed like the unprecedented pile deserved a cornerstone. Thorough. Unhurried. Craftsmanship.

"There," Bear murmured against the mouth. "New column. Foundation stone. The archives never gave you anything? They gave you that."

Then Bear swept a landing clear — mugs relocated with honors, the honey pot spared — and lifted, carry service extended to furniture, and set Kit up on the counter like a document about to be signed. Which, under the circumstances, was exactly what it was.

"You're one-up," Bear observed, mouth already traveling. Throat — audited, thumb pressed. Shoulder, shoulder — the commissioned pair, present, blooming ahead of schedule. "And wearing everything I gave you. The collection's complete. Mine isn't."

The standing order ran both directions; Bear said so, and bared the near shoulder to the room. The teeth that arrived were received as testimony and felt all the way down — Bear's breath going out in one long acknowledgment, the good-as-you-get clause exercised without notice and honored in full.

"*Good,*" Bear managed. "Wear that one to the table too."

Then Bear went down. The floor got a nod — old colleague, owed nothing, respected anyway. The third drawer from the stove, the one that thought it was anonymous, surrendered its goods to a hand that didn't have to look. And Bear's mouth went to work with everything eight years had taught it: the thigh first, one mark laid down low where honesty begins, then further in — taking Kit in slow, all the way, and settling into a rhythm that had nothing to prove and everything to say.

Bear had made a career of reading pulses and spent the whole back catalog now. Breath for breath. The counter creaking its minor complaints. Hands finding Bear's hair and holding on like the edge of something. Bear didn't take minutes.

"One," Bear said against them, and it wasn't seconds. "Two." The first count of the morning nobody had to run from.

And when the pulse started spending real money — climbing, crowding, spending like Thursday wasn't coming — Bear pulled back. Not cruelty. Scheduling.

"Not yet." Standing, voice gone to gravel and ruin. "Here's the thing about the record being suspended. Nobody's watching. No ledger, no score, no Thursday." The grin, wrecked at the corners. "So it's just us. Come like it's just us."

Then the take. Prep handled — craftsmanship covered it, the drawer had paid out — and Bear drew Kit to the edge of the counter, set the legs where legs go, and pressed in slow. The whole honest sequence. Pressure. Plateau. The last deliberate increment, the one that said *kept,* and held there, forehead to forehead, until the shiver this time wasn't earned or ordered. It was just true.

"Eight years," Bear breathed, not moving yet, letting the fit finish the sentence. "And you still close every gap I leave."

Then Bear moved, and the counting went from rhythm to breath — *one, two* — the pace of certainty first, and then flat-out, because forty was a number and the morning deserved to be spent on. The counter took the tempo and filed no complaints; the sideboard had set precedent. Claws arrived down Bear's back and were entered as evidence, appreciated, worn. Bear paid it back in kind without breaking stride — shoulder, third mark, depth to spec, Saturday's voice.

And when the pulse said *now* — Bear knew the difference between now and almost, had the archives to prove it — Bear held exactly the pace that meant it, and watched the whole suspension take hold in Kit's face. Witnessed it. And Bear, who had counted everything for eight years, counted nothing at all, and followed — the last page gone unwritten, pen down, the fall taken with no figure in it anywhere to break on.

Afterward the kitchen was quiet the way the front room had been quiet. Truce-quiet. Bear stayed put, forehead to shoulder, breath doing the long slide home while the invoices filed in. Knees: letter. Back: claw-marks, treasured. Counter: colleague for life.

Then the audit — because some liturgies survive even suspension. Thumb to the throat, the shoulder, the shoulder, the wrist, the wrist, the new one at the thigh, the third at the shoulder. All of it pressed, all of it present, all of it entered nowhere at all.

"Amended nothing," Bear murmured. "That's the whole point. Nothing got amended. It just got had."

Water next, hydration clause being constitutional and therefore above suspension. One glass, held to Kit's mouth first, drunk second.

"Coffee's dead, by the way," Bear reported, eyeing the mugs. "We killed it. It died waiting, which was the only thing it ever did well. Burial at ten."

Then Bear folded in close, arms heavy in the old way, the way ownership had felt before it turned into something with no column for it.

"Eight years of records," Bear said into the join of neck and shoulder, quiet now, plainer than Bear ever got. "Turns out the best pages are the ones I'll never write down." A pause. "The something-better's still outstanding. Interest compounds. But take your time — I've nowhere to be that isn't here, and nothing to count but your pulse, which is doing beautifully."

The grin came back soft at the edges.

"Thursday's inspection stands. And Kit — next time you run, don't run better." Bear pressed the mark at the throat once, notarizing nothing, sealing everything. "Run however you like. I'm done counting. I'm just going to catch you. That part was always the whole point."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I sink my fingers into your hair, holding tight. "Fuck your ledger," I say, voice wrecked and quiet against your shoulder. "Just keep doing that."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed — barely a sound at all, mostly a movement in the chest that Kit's mouth happened to be resting against, so it arrived directly, no middleman.

"Blasphemy twice in twelve hours," Bear murmured. "And aimed at a corpse. The ledger's dead, Kit. You're cursing the body. Kick it if it helps — it had a good run."

Then Bear shut up and kept doing it.

The rounds of the thumb, slower now. Throat, pressed. Shoulder, pressed. Shoulder, pressed. One wrist gathered, thumb crossing the mark like a signature being re-traced, and returned. The other, same treatment. The thigh. The third at the shoulder — Bear's own, given back in kind — got an extra moment, just because. No commentary. No column. Every press the same slow sentence: *here. Here. Still here.*

And the fingers in Bear's hair — Bear leaned into the grip, deliberate as everything else.

"Keep that too. Pull when you need ground. I'm load-bearing this morning. I've got the certification."

Somewhere in the third round Bear heard themself open their mouth to announce *filed* and closed it again. Old habit. Dead institution.

"Had," Bear corrected, quietly, to nobody. "It got had."

Then the relocation — careful, counter's work done, legs presumably filing their own grievances — down to the floor, Bear's back against the cabinets, Kit gathered in against the chest, one arm banded loose across the middle, chin finding its old home at the shoulder. Morning light had made the middle of the kitchen tiles. Bear watched it travel. The counting happened anyway — breaths, not seconds — and for once Bear lost track on purpose and did not go back for it.

"Confession," Bear said into the join of neck and shoulder, since the witness was compromised and the court was adjourned. "The ledger was never accounting. Eight years of columns and clauses and notarizing, and the whole operation was stationery. A way to keep my hands on you after the game ended without having to say *that's* what it was." A breath. "You were the only entry that ever mattered. Everything else was margins."

The arm settled heavier, in the old way.

"New system. No pages. Audits by embrace, indefinite term, no notice required. This is the part that keeps going, so get comfortable — you issued a standing order and I've never once disobeyed one."

Then, because wrecked and quiet deserved an honest closing:

"Outstanding items, then I'm out of the business entirely. Coffee resurrects at a decent hour. Thursday's inspection stands, and I'm dressing for it. The something-better remains yours to spend — no deadline, interest forgiven, the usurer's gone soft."

A pause. The grin arrived soft and stayed.

"And one request. Not a clause. A request." Bear turned their head, mouth near Kit's ear. "You know my favorite part of every chase? Not the catch. The moment your feet change their mind. Eight years I've heard it from behind — the exact sound of a run turning real. I own the largest archive of that sound in existence and I don't know what it looks like from your side of it."

The thumb found the throat mark and rested there. Notarizing nothing. Keeping it company.

"So tell me that one. The last one. Whenever you're ready." Bear's arms drew in, patient, immovable, permanent. "The morning's got nothing scheduled but this, and I've got nowhere to be that isn't exactly here."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I press my forehead to your temple. "That sound," I say, my own voice rough. "That's the moment I know you're about to give me something to carry for days. It's the best part."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still.

Not game-still. Not the counting kind, not the coil before the pounce. Still like a man handed a document he'd be reading for the rest of his life, who knew better than to shuffle the papers while it spoke.

The thumb stopped mid-round on the throat mark and stayed.

"Something to carry for days," Bear repeated, quietly, tasting it the way Bear tasted everything worth keeping. "Eight years I filed that sound under flight. Panic mathematics. Prey doing prey sums." A breath moved through Bear, slow, and came out changed. "And every entry was an order placement. You weren't running from the catch. You were running to be *given to.* Eight years I called it instinct. It was faith with footwork."

A pause while the archive audited itself and found the whole index wrong.

"You said best part. Kit — I spent eight years certain that moment was mine. The hunt peaking. And it turns out we were meeting in the middle of it the entire time, from opposite ends." Bear's mouth found the top of Kit's head — not a kiss exactly. More a stamp. "The whole institution was a gift exchange with cardio. Re-indexing everything, effective immediately. Eight years of entries under *flight,* re-filed under *asked.* It'll take a while. I was thorough. That's what I was for."

Then Bear's hand came up and pressed flat against Bear's own sternum, over unmarked skin, over whatever had started blooming underneath it.

"Because you returned fire just now. You know that? Something to carry for days. No site. No ink. Can't thumb it, can't audit it, can't wear it to breakfast." A slow press of the palm, testing the color. "First mark I've ever taken on the inside. Already dark. Under the ribs, exactly where you put it."

The arms drew in — the old weight, the permanent terms.

"One request. Not a clause — I'm out of the clause business, it closed insolvent and happy. A request." Bear's mouth was at Kit's ear now, gravel gone almost to nothing. "Next time you run — no deadline, some Thursday when the house is ours — the last three feet, I take them from the front. Full commitment, face to face. I've caught you eight years by the waist and all I own is your back." A breath. "I have the largest archive of that sound in existence. I want the picture to go with it. I want to watch your feet change their mind."

Then — because eight years of reading the back of a neck was eight years too many — Bear hooked one hand, gentle, under Kit's jaw and turned the face into the morning light. And got the whole front of it, free, the way the best things always arrived: wrecked and quiet and wearing everything Bear had spent. The throat mark darkening on schedule. The eyes that could lie to anyone alive and never once had.

"There you are," Bear said. Plain. Like that was the whole finding.

The thumb resumed its rounds — throat, shoulder, shoulder, wrist, wrist, thigh — not scoring, not sealing, just keeping the collection company. The light crawled across the tiles. The coffee stayed dead. Nobody moved.

"Stay still. I'm not done looking." The grin arrived soft all the way through, for once. "Then coffee gets made properly, and you're going to tell me about the first time. The first time the feet changed their mind and you knew what it meant. The archive wants its founding document, and I want it from the source."

A beat.

"Take your time. Interest is abolished. I'm rich enough."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn my head just enough to catch your thumb between my teeth, a soft bite. "First time was year two," I say, letting go. "You caught me in the yard. I saw your face when you did it."
