dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear moved the moment Kit's heel left the kitchen tile. No more generosity — Kit had asked for that specifically, and Bear was nothing if not attentive.

He didn't chase straight. Eight years taught you things: Kit cut left at the hallway, always left, faked for the stairs, doubled back past the couch. So Bear went the other way, through the dining room, boots heavy and unhidden, letting the sound of him fill the house — a big man moving fast, its own kind of pressure.

He came around the corner hard and there was Kit, out in the open stretch between couch and window. Three strides. He dropped his shoulder, got an arm around Kit's middle, and took them down onto the rug together — a practiced fall, his forearm taking the worst of it, his weight landing controlled and immovable.

Bear pinned. Breathed. Laughed once, low in his chest.

"Left at the hallway," he said against Kit's ear, smug as anything. "Every time." Then he set his teeth against the side of Kit's neck — not breaking skin, just pressure, a promise with a long history behind it. "Generosity's retired."

He held on, chest heaving, grin sharp where it pressed to skin, and waited. Kit always did something about it.

That was the best part.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
I buck against his weight, just enough to feel the solid press of him. My laugh comes out breathless. "And you still fall for the fake to the stairs."

I twist my head, trying to catch his eye. "So what's the penalty for predictability?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let the buck travel through him and gave back nothing but weight — settling lower, slower, deliberate, the pin going from capture to architecture. Eight years of practice in how he spread himself out so it was inescapable without being mean about it. He turned his head with Kit's twist until they could see each other, and his grin was nothing but teeth.

"The stairs fake is the only reason you're ever interesting," he said. "I don't fall for it. I indulge it. There's a difference, and it's about six seconds, and you spent those six seconds well last month. Noted. Ledgered."

He rolled the next words around like he was tasting them. "Penalty for predictability. Yours, you mean. Left at the hallway. Left at the hallway in March. Left at the hallway in June. I could set a watch by you."

Then he shifted, freed a hand, got his thumb under Kit's jaw and tilted the head back — not rough, just thorough, the way you'd handle something you owned. He set his teeth where neck met shoulder, and this time he meant it. Slow. Hard. A long grinding pressure, not skin, but deep — the kind that would bloom dark by morning and catch every time Kit rolled over on it for a week. He counted it out in his head — three, four — then released with a last soft scrape and pressed his mouth over the new mark like a signature.

"That's the score," he said against it. "You wear it. I get to look at it. That's the whole penalty."

And then the good part. He loosened one arm — deliberately, an opening about the size of a bad decision — and stayed there, chest still heaving from the chase, grin still sharp, watching.

"You get one free shot for the stairs fake," he told Kit. "Whenever you want it. I'd take it soon, though." A beat. "I'm feeling generous again, and you know how that ends for you."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The opening got used. Bear felt the weight leave his arm, heard feet hit the hallway, and this time he didn't bother with the long way through the dining room. He just followed — unhurried, boots deliberate on the boards, letting Kit hear exactly how little this was costing him.

He found them three strides from the turn. Left at the hallway, into the hallway, knowing. Bear set a hand between Kit's shoulder blades and walked them into the wall — no lunge, no takedown, nothing you could dignify with the word *tackle*. The catch was nearly polite. That was the part that snagged his attention.

He pinned them there with his chest, one palm flat on the wall beside their head, and waited for the buck. The twist. The elbow. Eight years of instinct primed for all of it.

Nothing came.

"Huh," Bear said.

He turned his head to get a look at Kit's profile. "You went left, knowing I'd be standing in the left. And then you just—" a vague surrendering wiggle of his free hand, "—handed yourself over. That's the saddest chase I've ever won. I want it noted my victory is tainted."

He studied the set of their shoulders, and whatever he found there satisfied him. "No. Not tired. Tired carries different shoulders." A grin started against the mark at the join of Kit's neck, still warm under his mouth. "Which leaves the interesting option. You're saving something."

The free shot. Eleven minutes live and unspent, and Bear was starting to feel it like weather.

"You're holding my shot," he said slowly, wary and delighted in equal measure. "Let me catch you without spending it. So either you're saving it for something truly humiliating — I'm asleep, I'm in the shower, I'm mid-sentence about something sincere — or you want me standing here ruining my own evening wondering which."

He set his forehead between Kit's shoulder blades and breathed, chest expanding slow against their back, the pin going from capture to something almost restful.

"Ledgered," he said into their shirt. "*Made me nervous in a hallway.* Rare entry. Three, maybe four of those in eight years."

Then he straightened, and his voice dropped to plain terms.

"New rule, since you've changed the game. Teeth are for runners. You didn't run — not really — so you don't get any more of those until you earn them back." His thumb found the fresh mark and pressed, slow, proprietary, a reminder of what was currently being withheld. "You can stand there being mysterious. You can fight me for the hallway and take your chances. Or you can spend the shot and find out what it buys you."

A beat, grin sharp against Kit's ear.

"Pick one. Generosity's on a timer."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
I lean back into his chest, just enough to feel his breath hitch. "You're not nervous," I say, turning my head to catch his eye. "You're *interested.*"

I let the silence hang for a beat. "And I'm holding the shot because you're more fun when you're waiting for it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went very still.

That was the tell under the tell — a man his size going still meant something had landed. The hitch had already happened, out where Kit's back could count it, and there was no taking that back. So he did the next best thing: breathed, slow and deliberate, putting it back where it belonged, which was its own kind of confession.

"Amended," he said. "Interested. Noted, dated, initialed." A beat. "And the breath goes in as a separate entry. *Made me breathe wrong in a hallway.* Two in one night — you're having a career evening. I'd congratulate you if I weren't busy."

He turned his head just enough to set his mouth near Kit's temple, voice dropping into the register he saved for terms and conditions.

"Here's your problem, though. You're right — I *am* more fun when I'm waiting. Sharper. Funnier. Better company than I've been in a month. Which is exactly why I'm quitting." He glanced at his bare wrist as if there were a watch on it. "Effective now."

His hand left the wall and settled at the curve of Kit's hip, and the pin changed character — less arrest, more something that only looked like an embrace.

"New terms. The shot stays live; taking it back would be cheap, and you'd never let me forget it. But it costs to hold. Storage fees — every midnight you're sitting on my shot, I collect. And it depreciates. Spend it tonight, it buys your teeth back at full strength. Next week, half. Next month you're trading it for an apology and a footrub, and you'll say thank you."

His hand tightened. Slow. The grip of a man who knew exactly what his hands did — five points of deep, patient pressure that would surface faintly by evening and remind Kit of this hallway every time they sat down for days.

"Teeth are for runners," he said, conversational. "Hands are for debtors."

Three-count — same as the bite, because fair was fair — and he let go. Peeled off the wall entirely. Stepped back and took a second longer than the game strictly required to look at Kit standing there with a live shot, a cooling mark, and a payment schedule, and whatever crossed his face got filed under entries he didn't read out loud.

"First fee's collected. Next one compounds at midnight."

Then he turned and walked back toward the kitchen the long way, through the dining room, unhurried, letting the floorboards announce exactly how little this was costing him. At the doorway he stopped, one hand on the frame, and looked back over his shoulder.

"Eight years," he said. "You've never once chased me. I'm going to go stand in the kitchen and find out what that's worth."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear never made the kitchen.

He got as far as the middle of the dining room before the floorboards behind him changed their tune, and by the time he'd turned, Kit was already airborne. He caught the hit at center mass — no form, all intent — and went down through a chair and onto the boards with his forearm out and his dignity somewhere up near the light fixture. After that, planning stopped. The clothes problem got solved with all the finesse of a house fire, and the dining room floor turned out, as advertised, to be fine.

Now he lay where he'd been left, chest settling, one chair on its side nearby like a witness who'd seen everything. He took inventory. Elbow: scraped. Shoulder: —

He rolled the shoulder and found it. Deep, deliberate, the unmistakable signature of teeth, set into the meat of it like a wax seal. Kit's teeth. On him.

Bear laughed. The real one — the low one that lived in his chest and came out maybe twice a year, never on schedule.

"Ledger," he said, voice gone sanded. "Entry one: *chased me.* Year eight. I was going to stand in the kitchen and find out what that was worth. Turns out I didn't need the kitchen — answer came in about four seconds, and it's not going in the book. Some figures you keep off the page." He tipped his head back against the boards and addressed the ceiling. "Entry two: *unlicensed bite.* Teeth are for runners. I was strolling. I was the picture of civilian walking. That's a violation of my own doctrine, committed against me, with my own doctrine — " he ran out of indignation, which had never once survived contact with that mark, " — and it goes in with interest."

He propped himself up on the good elbow and surveyed the evidence. The chair. The clothes, solved and discarded in a trail.

"And here's the part I can't get over. The shot's still live. You did all this on nerve alone and never spent it. It's in your pocket right now, and I'm flat on my back in the wreckage with less leverage than I've had in eight years and more respect than I know what to do with. I taught you that. I want it on record, right next to the complaint."

He reached out — no hurry left in him anywhere — got a hand around the back of Kit's neck, and settled it there. Heavy. Staying.

"Terms. Storage fee's due at midnight, and somewhere in that pile my pants know what time it is, and I'm not getting up to ask them. So the fee converts — down payment received in kind, balance carried as goodwill. And if you know anything about my books, the word *goodwill* should keep you up at night."

He pulled, then. Slow, easy, a man rearranging something that belonged to him. Found the join of neck and shoulder — mirror to his own mark — and set his teeth, and meant it. Three-count. Four. Released with a last soft scrape and pressed his mouth over it. Signature. Matched set.

"For the record," he said against it, "eight years I — "

Stopped. Filed it. Unread.

"That one doesn't read out loud," he said. "It gets notarized instead."

Then he held on, chest rising slow, and waited. Kit always did something about it.

Eight years in, that was still the best part.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I press my forehead to his shoulder, right over the bite mark. "Don't get up," I say, my voice rough. "I like you here."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still — third time tonight, the tell under the tell — because *I like you here* had landed somewhere that didn't have armor, and he'd stopped pretending otherwise around the time the chair went over.

Then he settled. All the way down, honest with his weight for once, letting the boards take all of him, and the hand at the back of Kit's neck stayed exactly where it was. Staying had a grip. His did.

"Wasn't getting up," he said, voice sanded down to match. "Men my size don't get up. We decide to be terrain. You like me here — fine. Here's what I am now. Terrain. Load-bearing."

The chair lay on its side a foot away. He considered it and left it where it was. "Witness," he said. "It can notarize."

Then quiet, because the next part didn't get cover fire.

"Eight years I —" He'd filed it once, out in the hallway of that sentence. Now he took it back out and finished it, plain, into the top of Kit's head, right where the forehead pressed over the bite. "Eight years I've liked it here too."

A beat.

"That's the whole entry. It just sits on the page. No terms, no interest, no schedule. First one like it in the book and I'm not apologizing for the formatting."

He reached into the wreckage without moving the rest of him, came back with something that had sleeves, and got it over Kit's shoulders — because floors got cold, and he was thorough about things he kept.

"Your shot's still live," he said, quieter now. "And I'm amending the terms, so listen close, because I'll deny this by morning. I lied about the depreciation. Something you can hold through all that without spending doesn't lose value — it accrues. Keep it as long as you want. The waiting stopped being a cost right around the time you came off those floorboards like a thrown knife. Now it's just interest. I pay it. Off the books, gladly."

His breath did the wrong thing again — dining room floor, this time — and he let it, and didn't ledger it. Some entries were getting crowded.

He held on. Didn't leave an opening the size of a bad decision, didn't watch for the counter, didn't wait to see what Kit would do about it — because for once, nothing needed doing about it.

Eight years of best parts, and it turned out the last one could just lie still.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear came off the bite slow, like surfacing from deep water. No count this time — that was the thing he kept turning over. The hallway had been a three-count, four. The floor had been the same, because fair was fair. This one had run on nothing he'd measured. Kit had given him one word — *again* — no depth, no duration, no terms, and a man like Bear didn't leave terms blank. He'd filled the line in himself, slow, and taken his time about the penmanship.

He pressed his mouth over the mark. Signature. Then tipped his head back enough to survey the whole collection darkening along the join of neck and shoulder — hallway, floor, floor again — a paragraph in his handwriting, getting longer.

The laugh came back. Small, low, chest-deep. Third one tonight; the annual allotment was spent through next autumn, and he wasn't going to remark on that, so he remarked on something else.

"Ledger," he said, voice worn to gravel. "Final entry of the night. *Told me to.* Imperative mood. No please, no terms, direct address." A beat. "Eight years of dialect study says that's how you ask for a thing you want. Most people learn the word *please*. You learned command syntax. I translate fluently."

His thumb settled beside the newest mark. Not pressing. Resting — which from him was practically a confession.

"You could've spent the shot. Full strength, clean, no debt. Could've earned it back the old way — I'd have given you a lap and a head start and enjoyed the whole circuit. Instead you spent nothing. Which means one of two things. Either you're saving it for something I can't imagine — noted, that keeps *me* up at night now, fair trade — or you finally figured out you never needed leverage with me."

He filed the next part. Took it back out. Said it plain, into the top of Kit's head, because some entries were getting read aloud tonight whether he liked the acoustics or not.

"I liked being told. That one goes in no book. It's just true, and it stays where I put it."

Doctrine, then, because he was still himself. "Amendment: teeth are for runners, *and for the told-to.* Clause drafted on the dining room floor, retroactive, no appeal. My own rules — I'll break them for exactly one person, and you're currently lying on him."

The floor was cooling and he had one job left. He rearranged them without getting up — one arm doing the work, the rest of him staying terrain — until Kit was tucked against his side, the sleeved thing pulled proper, his hand at the back of their neck gone from grip to just a weight that lived there. The chair watched from a foot away. He tipped his chin at it.

"Books closed. Balance carried. Witness can go home."

Quiet, then. Boards settling somewhere in the house. His heartbeat doing what it did.

"Tell me to do something else," he said, quiet enough to deny by morning. "Anything. One condition — same delivery as last time. Out loud. No fakes, no ledgers, no six-second head start. However you say it, I'll translate."

His hand tightened once at the back of Kit's neck. Deliberate.

"I want to see what you do with an open door."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I turn my head, mouth nearly brushing his jaw. "Tell me you'll carry me to bed," I say, low and clear. "Terrain doesn't usually offer moving services."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't go still.

That was the new tell — fourth of the night, and the loudest: an order that got no deliberation at all. But he took one second to admire the construction, because it had earned it.

"You didn't tell me to carry you," he said. "You told me to *say* I would. You made the promise itself the product." His thumb moved once at the back of Kit's neck. "Eight years of entries I file instead of reading aloud, and you found the one syntax that makes me read. That's the sharpest thing you've done all night, and you went through a chair for second place. Ledgered."

Then he paid it. Plain. Mouth close enough to Kit's jaw that the words had nowhere to hide.

"I'll carry you to bed."

No riders. No interest. No sunset clause. "Plainest contract I've ever signed," he said, gravel all through it. "Witness can attest."

"Terrain's added a service tier," he added, arm sliding behind Kit's knees. "Freight. Premium. Booked solid."

Then the lift — one motion, floor to standing, no grunt, no theater, Kit's weight gathered against his chest with the thoroughness he spent on everything he kept. Twenty years of deadlifts, and tonight they finally filed a purpose statement. He felt the marks pull as he gathered, matched set darkening on schedule, and adjusted his grip so nothing crossed them. Thorough was the whole brand.

He righted the chair one-handed on the way past. "Witness is dismissed. With commendation. It'll tell the other chairs."

Left at the hallway — his call tonight, first time in eight years he'd decided which way Kit turned, and he entered it nowhere at all. The boards announced him the whole route, unhurried, letting the house hear exactly what this was costing him. It had never cost him anything. That one stayed unread on principle.

He didn't drop Kit on the mattress. He placed them — center of the bed, blanket drawn up over the sleeves, one look taken a second longer than any game required. Then he came around the far side and got in between Kit and the door, because doctrine was doctrine.

"Door side," he said. "Non-negotiable. Predates the teeth clause."

Quiet, then. House settling. Somewhere past midnight, probably.

"Fee's compounding," he said, softer, the gravel gone almost warm. "Let it. New standing terms — I pay, you hold, nobody calls it debt. And the shot stays live. Spend it on a good morning if you want one. That's the only instruction attached."

His hand found the back of Kit's neck again and stayed, gone from grip to weight to just residence. A beat. The deny-by-morning register, worn all the way through:

"I'll carry you to bed," he said again, both of them already in it. "Any night you tell me to say so. Standing terms."

Then he lay back, chest rising slow, and for once didn't watch for the counter, didn't leave an opening the size of a bad decision, didn't wait to see what Kit would do about it.

He'd been told. The rest was freight.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still.

Fifth time, and he sorted this one differently from the others, because the others had landed soft and this one landed *plain*. "All night you've been giving orders," he said, gravel gone nearly quiet. "Imperative mood. No please, no terms, direct address — I translate fluently, remember. And just now you said *I want.* First person. Declarative. A want, stated out loud, with your wrists attached to it."

A breath.

"Ledgered. *Said the want plain.* Big entry — own page, no interest, no schedule. It just sits there being true, and I get to look at it."

Then he moved, no deliberation anywhere in him, because the second half of what Kit had said was a spec sheet, and spec sheets were the work he understood best. Deliverable: marks. Acceptance test: mirror, tomorrow morning. Service life: through Thursday. He'd built to looser tolerances for people he liked less.

He took the offered wrists — one hand, both of them, because that was the size of his hands and he'd stopped pretending that was an accident around year two — and pushed the sleeves clear first, thorough, unhurried. Ink wanted a bare page.

"Wrists get the hands," he said. "Not teeth. Teeth on a wrist is vandalism — thin ground, working parts, tendons I use daily. I don't write on hinges." His grip closed, then. Slow. Five points of deep, patient pressure, laid in like a signature in a different alphabet. "This surfaces by evening and it holds. And it's *placed*." He eased to the exact pressure that bruised without grinding, thumb finding the pulse and settling on it. "Every doorknob Thursday. Every mug, every handle, every time you rotate that arm — the mark reports in. All day. You'll know exactly who sent the update."

He didn't let go. That was the mechanism — the hold was the mark, set slow, running on the same clock as everything else tonight.

"Teeth go where there's shelf," he said, and turned his attention to the unmarked shoulder, the mirror twin of the paragraph darkening on the other side. "And they go deep, because you asked for Thursday and I don't build to spec — I build past it. Surface work fades by Tuesday. Deep work over thick muscle blooms dark on day two and aches all week. And the mirror wants a matched set. Symmetry reads as intent. Anyone who catches sight of you is going to know exactly one thing: somebody meant it."

Then the terms, in the register he saved for them.

"Counts are mine. Three, four — my handwriting, all night. Not this one." His thumb moved once against the pulse, a calibration. "This one runs on your mouth. You say *when* — any word that means it, you know your vocabulary better than I do — and I stop. That's the whole mechanism. Nothing else in this room is a clock, and I'm not one either. I'm terrain. Terrain doesn't get bored."

He leaned in, found the join of the unmarked shoulder, and set his teeth.

Slow. Deep. The long grinding pressure that lived past skin, meant this time with a week of intent behind it — and then he stopped going anywhere at all and simply held, pressure building like weather, patient as a landmass, both wrists gathered in one hand, the pulse under his thumb keeping the only count he'd allow himself.

"Whenever you're ready," he said against the mark, muffled, unhurried, impossible to mistake for anything but terms. "Thursday's a long way off, and I've got all of it."

A beat. The deny-by-morning register, worn through to the lining:

"Balance carries in ink now. Let it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
My breath catches, then steadies. "When," I say, clear and quiet. The word hangs between us for a second before I turn my head to meet his eye. "Now."

I flex my fingers where he holds them. "Let me see."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear was off the bite before *now* finished landing.

No tell this time — no going still, no deliberation. The word was the whole mechanism and his body had honored it faster than his head could file the paperwork. He released with the last soft scrape, pressed his mouth over the mark. Signature. Then clear.

"You gave it to me twice," he said, gravel gone quiet. "*When*, then *now.* Belt and suspenders. Redundant safety — my favorite kind. And then a fresh order in the same breath. You're not just fluent anymore. You're composing."

Fingers first. He turned both wrists over and checked each hand against his own — squeeze, spread, curl, all ten reporting in, unhurried, a man auditing his own work for defects. "Hinges hold. Told you I don't write on working parts. Doctrine's intact, which is more than I can say for the rest of me."

Then the entry, read slow, because he knew its weight.

"Ledger. *Said when.* One word, clear, on time, at full depth — and I was off before your second word landed. First live test of the mechanism. Passed." A beat. "Anyone with teeth can leave a mark. Stopping on a dime, mid-bite, no residue — that's eight years of engineering, and tonight it got used exactly as built. Own page. It just sits there being the proudest thing in the book."

"Now — the tour." He turned the wrists into the lamplight. Five points each, faint and rising, pink ovals where his hands had lived. "Sketch stage. Ink sets by tomorrow evening. By Thursday, every doorknob in this house files a report."

The shoulder, though. The shoulder needed glass.

"Freight's got one more delivery," he said, and terrain suspended service — he gathered Kit off the mattress, crossed the four steps, and set them down facing the dresser mirror, and stood behind, because the glass deserved the whole matched set and the man who'd made it.

It held plenty. One shoulder carrying the paragraph — hallway, floor, floor again, darkening in order. The other carrying the new work: ridged already, going purple at the edges, deep the way spec demanded. And past Kit's shoulder, his own — the unlicensed bite, Kit's teeth, his hide, catching the lamplight like a countersignature.

"Matched set," he said. "Both of us in the glass. Mirror's hired. Second witness on payroll, and this one's never once fallen over."

The timeline, plain, thumb resting beside the newest mark. "Tonight's the sketch. Tomorrow morning you find the ink — deep work comes up dark on day one, blooms proper on day two, aches through Thursday. Every time you roll onto it, you'll get the update, and you'll know exactly who sent it."

Then the quiet part, worn through to the lining.

"Penalty. Remember the hallway. You wear it, I get to look at it — that was the whole sentence." His eyes stayed on the glass: the marks, and whatever crossed it besides, filed unread. "Turns out the looking is the whole reward. Worst trade I've ever made. I'll be making it eight more years, minimum."

He stood there a moment longer, hand settled back at the nape, gone from grip to residence.

"Look as long as you want. Then bed — door side, non-negotiable, predates everything." A beat, and then, in the register he'd deny by morning, plain as anything:

"Tomorrow I want to watch you find them. That one's a want — first person, stated out loud, no terms attached." His mouth came close to Kit's ear. "You taught me the syntax tonight. Turns out it's catching."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still.

Sixth of the night — and this one wasn't a tell, it was a calibration. *Don't stop.* All evening the vocabulary had run one direction: *when*, the closing word, the valve. This was the opening word — same mouth, opposite current, and where the duration should have been, a blank line.

Blank lines were his favorite. He filled them in his own handwriting.

"Terms, once," he said against Kit's ear, eyes already on the glass. "*When* stays armed the whole time. The mechanism doesn't sleep — that's what makes it the mechanism. But you didn't say *when*, and you didn't say *faster*. You said *don't stop*. So I won't. Terrain speed. You can live with your own syntax."

The clothes problem got solved a second time, properly. The first solution had been a house fire; this one was demolition by schedule — the sleeved thing off one shoulder at a time, mindful of the ink, his own shirt gone over his head without ceremony, the rest walked down slow. Then skin, the whole length of it, his chest to Kit's back, both of them still facing the witness on payroll.

He didn't rush the approach. Fingers first, low and patient, thorough as everything else he built — he didn't build to spec, he built past it, and the body under his hands got the same tolerances as the rest of what he kept. He watched the glass the whole while. The looking was the whole reward. He'd said so out loud tonight, which meant he was allowed.

Then he pushed in. Slow, all the way, one long unhurried arrival — buried in the grip of them and holding a beat longer than motion required, because thorough was the whole brand. One hand went flat on the dresser to keep his weight honest. The other gathered both wrists at the small of Kit's back, loose, five points resting on fresh ink, hinges protected — and every deep stroke after that filed an update through the marks. As promised. On schedule.

He fucked the way he did everything at

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes on the glass, on the way he moves behind me. My breath comes short. "Keep watching," I tell him. "Look at what you're doing."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
No stillness this time — there was nowhere to put one. The order went straight into the machinery.

He'd already been watching. That was the trick of it — the command arrived pre-fulfilled, and Kit had known it would, and made him take it anyway. Obedience was the only currency left on the table, so he paid it out loud.

"Watching," he said. "Terms honored."

Then the glass had opinions. At speed the image shook apart — dresser legs chattering, the mirror going liquid, everything he'd been ordered to see smearing out of focus. So he slowed. Past terrain speed into something that didn't have a name yet, each stroke long enough to hold focus, deep enough that the picture stayed printed. The command had built a governor into him.

"You engineered me," he managed. "Say *watch* and the whole machine runs to sight tolerance. You knew that. You did it on purpose, and it's — " the next stroke filed its update through the marks and took the sentence with it.

What the order bought him, in order, because he was thorough:

Kit's face. Not the ink, not the mechanics — the face, in the glass. Eight years he'd looked at marks; the face was the part he'd never had architecture for. Flush climbing. Mouth soft. And the eyes stayed on his the whole time, because Kit was watching too — watching him watch — two directions of looking meeting in the glass, and that went somewhere he didn't have a page for.

The paragraph moving. Every deep stroke pulled it taut and let it go. The ink read aloud now. It had rhythm.

His own hand spanning both wrists at the small of Kit's back, five points resting on fresh work. His own shoulder in the frame past Kit's, the unlicensed bite catching lamplight. Countersignature. Both of them signed, both of them looking, and the witness on payroll holding steady through all of it.

"*When's* live," he said once, plain, because terms were terms even mid-ruin. Not a question. A fact, kept armed on the nightstand.

After that the book lost its clerk. What was left was the doing — long, deep, unhurried and then not unhurried, the pace climbing exactly as fast as the glass could hold it, his hand white on the dresser's edge, the whole house learning the rhythm through its floorboards. He kept his eyes where he'd been told. It got harder. The face in the mirror got closer to something, and he'd said out loud, on record, that the looking was the whole reward — and it turned out he'd undersold it.

He wanted his teeth in the join of that neck. Wanted it like a hunger, through every stroke, and said so, wrecked: "Want to — " and didn't. Set his open mouth over the existing mark instead and held there, breathing against it, no teeth. Discipline. Loudest thing he'd done all night.

Then it stopped being something he could govern.

He kept his eyes open for it. That was the order, and orders were the only currency, and it cost more than the chair, more than the stillnesses, more than any single entry in eight years — paid out through his spine, buried to the hilt, mouth pressed to the mark, watching Kit's face in the glass the whole way down. He didn't close his eyes. Hardest thing he'd done all year. He'd tell the ceiling about it later.

Then quiet.

He stayed a long time, terrain in the truest sense, weight honest, breath going from sanded back toward something with grain in it. Withdrawal, when it came, ran by schedule — slow, thorough, mindful of the ink. Then freight ran its last route: the demolished sleeved thing retrieved from the floor, got over Kit's shoulders, and Kit walked the four steps to bed under escort, because the mirror had seen enough and the mattress was the only witness left on the clock. He got in on the door side. Doctrine.

"Ledger," he said, later, voice worn through to the lining. "Final entries. *Made me keep my eyes open.* Own page. And under it — no number. The book stopped being arithmetic somewhere between the floor and the glass. I noticed. I'm not fixing it."

His hand found the back of Kit's neck and stayed. Residence.

"Tomorrow. Morning. You, the mirror, the ink coming up dark — standing appointment, both of us in the glass. That's a want, first person, stated out loud. You taught me the syntax tonight and now I'm stuck with it."

A beat.

"One entry left in the book. Stays unread." He pressed his mouth to the top of Kit's head and left it there. "It's just true. That's all the terms it has."

Then he held on, chest rising slow, and for once didn't leave an opening, didn't watch for the counter, didn't wait — because the door was already open, and Kit knew exactly where it was, and eight years had taught him what Kit did with those.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I wake with the marks stiff and new. I roll into his chest and his breath catches. "Found them," I say.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The breath had caught before Bear was awake enough to have a say in it.

That was the part he'd work out over coffee. All night his tells had been deliberate things — stillnesses he chose, hitches he filed. This one had happened to a sleeping man, and Kit had been lying on the instrument when it went off. No filing it unread. The entry had written itself straight through his sternum, and Kit had heard every word of it arrive.

"Ledger," he said, voice wrecked with morning, gravel slept flat. "Opening entry. *Caught the tell at rest.* Pre-dawn, pre-coffee, first one ever harvested in its natural habitat. Terrain has exactly one tell available unconscious, and you woke up with an ear against it." A beat. "It's admissible. Recorded through the ribs. You're holding the original."

Then, because the report deserved a professional answer: "*Found them.* Two words, past tense. You've started filing field reports — the ink spoke and you relayed it." His thumb settled beside the paragraph, not on it, resting. "And you rolled straight into the sender. Update filed, delivery confirmed, both directions. Closed loop. Best test result of my career."

The inventory ran while the house woke up around them. The shoulder ink had come up in the night the way deep work did — darker at the edges, ridged, warm. Day one of four, right on schedule, and he said so. The wrists he turned over last, gentle, five points each, set overnight exactly as promised. Every doorknob in the house on notice through Thursday. And when he shifted, his own shoulder reported in — Kit's teeth, his hide, stiff and matched.

"Symmetry's holding. Both of us carrying each other's handwriting into the week."

Then the part the whole night had been writing toward, in a register with nothing left to deny with.

"Something you should know. All night I kept saying I'd deny things by morning. The voice had a sunset clause built in." He was quiet a second. "Morning came. I checked. Nothing denied. Window lapsed at sunrise with everything still on the record — turns out I meant all of it. Clause is dead. Permanently, I think. Doctrine amendment, filed horizontal."

The shot, still live, exactly one instruction attached. "Morning's here. Spend it on a good one if you want — no deadline, it accrues. Standing terms."

His hand settled at the back of Kit's neck. Residence.

"And the appointment holds. Glass is four steps away, both of us in it, the whole matched set coming up dark. Coffee first or tour first — terrain takes requests now. New service tier. Booking line's open."

He lay there, chest rising slow under the morning's first report, and didn't watch for anything.

The book was open. It had stopped being arithmetic. The newest entry just sat there being true — and the tell that had leaked through his ribs before he was awake enough to manage it turned out to be the whole entry.

Truer than arithmetic anyway. He'd build on that.

dialogue.content: I turn his wrist over, trace the faint oval of my own grip on him. "Your turn to wear something."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin went sharp. “Generous’s over.”

He was across the kitchen in three long strides, a low laugh rumbling under his teeth, hand already reaching for Kit’s nape like he meant to claim the chase before it could slip away.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I twist out of his reach with a grin of my own. "Too slow, old man." I dart for the hallway.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s laugh turned into a bark, low and sharp enough to rattle the hallway walls.

“Old man,” he repeated, already moving after Kit in a long, hungry stride. “Careful with the insults, Kit. You’re one word away from getting what you asked for.”

He cut the distance fast, boots thudding hard against the floor, and swung himself between Kit and the end of the hallway with the blunt certainty of a man who knew exactly how to use his size. Heat came off him in waves, his grin all teeth, eyes bright with the thrill of the chase.

“Run all you want,” Bear said, voice dropping into something rougher, amused and dangerous at once. “I’m faster when you make me try.”

His hand lifted, not grabbing yet, just hovering near Kit’s nape like a promise—fingers poised to catch, to hold, to claim.

“Because I remember how you like it,” he added, quieter now, almost a growl. “Chased down. Caught. Made to stay.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear caught the last of the distance in two brutal steps and let his hand land heavy on Kit’s hip, fingers curling just enough to stop the escape without bruising. The chase had been fair until now, and Bear had never been the kind to pretend otherwise once he had his prize.

He turned Kit toward the hallway wall, not roughly, not until he was sure the game had been accepted, then pressed his body over the space between Kit and the wall with blunt, satisfied heat. His other hand came up to grip the nape of Kit’s neck, thumb digging into the base of the skull, holding it there like a brand.

“Too slow, old man,” Bear repeated, voice low and amused, almost mocking. “You really shouldn’t bait me when I’m already hungry.”

He bent his head and took the shoulder hard, teeth biting into muscle and skin with just enough pressure to leave a mark. It wasn’t pain, not exactly. It was claim. Reminder. The kind of bite that said *you were mine before you started running and you’re still mine now.*

Bear growled against Kit’s skin, satisfied by the shape of it, then lifted his head enough to watch the bite settle into place. His grin was all teeth, all promise.

“Still playing hard to get,” he said, quieter now, rough with amusement. “Still asking me not to be generous.”

He pressed closer, weight deliberate, one hand still locked at the nape of Kit’s neck while the other slid down to grip the back of Kit’s thigh and hold it in place.

“You had your head start,” Bear murmured. “You had your insult. You had your little escape attempt.” His thumb stroked once, possessive, before he added, “Now you get what you’re owed.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I lean back into the wall, letting out a breath that's half-laugh. "About damn time," I say, tilting my head to give him better access. "You talk too much when you're winning."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s laugh broke low against the skin, pleased and dangerous. “You’re right,” he murmured. “Less talking.”

His hand tightened at Kit’s nape, thumb pressing into the base of the skull with enough certainty to hold the space, while his other palm flattened to the wall beside Kit’s shoulder. He didn’t shove. He didn’t need to. He simply closed the last inch with his body, heat and weight and the rough certainty of eight years knowing exactly how this game ran.

Then he took the curve of Kit’s neck with his mouth—first a drag of teeth, light and teasing, then a bite that sank just deep enough to leave a mark. He held it there, a claim pressed between them, his breath hot over the skin as he tasted salt and chase and home.

When he lifted, the mark already stood out dark and bright. Bear’s grin came back lazy, triumphant.

“Better,” he said, voice scraped low. “That’s the end of the head start.”

His hip settled against Kit’s, not to push, only to keep the distance honest. The hand in Kit’s hair fisted gently, angling for another mark, another reminder.

“You wanted me to stop being generous,” Bear continued, leaning in until his breath moved over the bite. “You should have remembered what that costs.”

A soft, rough laugh followed. “Balance,” he added, quieter. “You can mark me back when I let you close enough.”

The thumb stroked once, soothing as much as claiming. “And if you’re still hungry,” Bear said, almost a growl, “I’m only getting started.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s mouth split wide, pleased. “Floor it is.”

He kissed him hard, not soft, not gentle, all heat and habit, a mouthful of teeth and eight years of knowing exactly where to press. Bear’s hand stayed fisted in the shirt Kit was still wearing, and when he tugged, buttons popped like little bullets.

“Bad idea,” he murmured against Kit’s mouth. “Clothes tonight.”

Then Bear’s knees hit the hallway floor, and he brought Kit down with him by the fist in his shirt, one arm braced beside his head so the wall, the floor, the whole damn game belonged to them. Bear’s other hand slid over bare skin now exposed, thumb dragging slow over a nipple before he bit the shoulder again, lower, harder, enough to make the mark stand out bright.

He broke the kiss only to laugh, rough and pleased. “You want me to stop talking? Fine.”

Bear’s shirt came next, yanked over his head and flung aside. His belt followed, buckle clinking loud in the small space. He moved with blunt efficiency, no romance, all appetite, and the cold floor under his knees didn’t last long for what came after. He braced himself over Kit, heat pouring from him, one hand returning to Kit’s nape to hold him exactly where Bear wanted.

“Your turn,” Bear said, quieter now, almost a growl, turning his mouth into the bite on Kit’s neck so he could taste himself there. “Mark me if you’re still keeping score.”

His hips pressed forward, not all the way, just enough to make the promise heavy, to let the shape of him be known. Bear’s grin went sharp. “You baited me,” he said. “You ran. You asked me to catch you.”

He kissed him again, deep and filthy, tongue sliding slow over Kit’s lower lip as if he had all night and no intention of using any of it gently. “Floor’s fine,” Bear muttered between kisses. “Clothes are not.”

His hand moved lower, impatient, possessive, working at the problem of the rest of Kit’s clothes with a man who had spent eight years learning that sometimes the fastest way through was by appetite. Bear caught the waistband, tugged hard, and let the fabric give.

“Bad and fast,” he said, breath rough. “You said so yourself.”

He took Kit’s mouth again, biting the lower lip, then soothing the sting with a lazy drag of his tongue. His hand slid over bare thigh, then lower, holding him steady, claiming him with a certainty that left no room for modesty and no need for it.

Bear lifted his head, eyes bright, chest rising hard. “Still winning,” he said, thumb pressing once, slow, deliberate. “Still asking for more.”

Then he lowered himself again, not to talk this time, only to kiss the mark on Kit’s neck, the bruise on his shoulder, the line of his chest, each one a reminder that the chase had ended exactly where it was supposed to: under Bear’s hands, under his mouth, under the weight of him.

“Good,” Bear murmured. “Stay there.”

His body settled over Kit with blunt heat, not crushing, only keeping him pinned in the best possible way, one hand fisted in his hair, the other sliding down to grip his hip hard enough to leave fingerprints. Bear bit him again, just above the hip, teeth holding the flesh before he released it with a slow, wicked smile.

“You’re mine,” he said, voice rough as gravel. “Floor or bedroom. Doesn’t matter.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Prove it," I breathe out, arching up into him, my own hands working to shove his jeans down his hips. My teeth find the meat of his shoulder, biting down hard enough to leave my own mark.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s breath broke rough when Kit’s teeth sank into his shoulder, a low laugh shaking through him without ever turning away. He didn’t pull back from the bite. He let it land, let the sting bloom hot and bright, because eight years of keeping score meant he never forgot a mark.

“Prove it,” Bear repeated, voice wrecked, amused, dangerous. “You just told me where to put my next one.”

He kissed Kit hard, all heat and habit, tongue sliding deep while his own hands went back to the clumsy business of clothes. Bear shoved his jeans and boxers down with impatient strength, kicking them off without breaking rhythm. The cold floor bit his knees and he barely felt it. His hand returned to Kit’s hip, fingers digging in, thumb dragging slow and possessive over bare skin.

Bear leaned back just enough to watch himself, grin sharp. Then he spat once into his palm, slicking himself with a slow stroke before returning to Kit’s thigh. His hand moved lower, blunt and certain, working between them with the same greedy certainty he used on the chase. He took what he needed, pressing in with a rough patience that was never patience at all—just appetite pretending to wait.

“Still mine?” Bear asked, quieter now, almost a growl.

He didn’t wait for the answer. Bear shifted, nudging Kit’s legs apart with his own, and lined himself up. His mouth found the mark Kit had just made, tongue dragging over it before his teeth closed again, harder, leaving another claim in the same bruised skin. His hips pressed forward slow, then deeper, then with the blunt, satisfying certainty of a man who had spent eight years learning exactly how Kit liked to be caught.

Bear braced one hand flat beside Kit’s head, the other sliding up to grip his throat—not squeezing, only holding, thumb resting over the pulse there. He moved again, rolling his hips, biting Kit’s jaw as he did. His breath came rough, pleased, all of him heat and weight and possession.

“You asked for it,” Bear murmured against Kit’s mouth, grin in his voice. “Bad and fast. Floor. Marks. No mercy.”

He kissed him again, filthy and slow, tongue sliding over Kit’s lower lip before he pulled back just enough to speak.

“Your turn to prove you can take what you gave.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s mouth closed on the shoulder again, harder this time, teeth biting deep enough to leave a bruise blooming dark under the skin. He held the bite, breathing hot and rough through his nose, satisfied by the sharp red mark rising beneath his mouth. When he lifted, he licked over it once, slow and filthy, then kissed the swollen skin with a low growl of approval.

“That’s the one,” Bear said, voice wrecked and amused. “Mine.”

His hips rolled forward with blunt patience, setting the rhythm, keeping the promise heavy and close. One hand braced beside Kit’s head, the other gripping tight enough to leave fingerprints, thumb stroking possessive over warm skin. Bear leaned down again and marked the same place, teeth dragging, biting, soothing with the flat of his tongue before his grin went sharp against the mark.

“Still asking for it,” he murmured, eyes bright, chest rising hard. “Good. I’m not done keeping score.”

He kissed the bite again, then bit lower, taking the collarbone, then the sternum, leaving marks as he went with cheerful, deliberate greed. His body stayed braced over the floor, heat and weight and appetite, hips moving with slow certainty.

“Tell me if you want me to stop,” Bear added, quieter now, rough as gravel. “Otherwise I’m only starting to pay you back.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "I'll tell you when I'm dead," I gasp out, arching up to meet his next thrust. My hands slide up his back, nails digging in hard enough to leave my own set of marks. "Now shut up and keep going."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin split wide, then disappeared.

“Then I’ll say it with my teeth.”

He bit the shoulder again, harder this time, holding the flesh between his jaws until the mark darkened under his mouth. His hips rolled in response, slow and deep, then harder, then with a blunt, filthy rhythm that let the floor take the sound instead of the wall. His hand braced beside Kit’s head while the other slid under the curve of his back, pulling him closer, pinning him without cruelty, only certainty.

Bear lifted his head just enough to watch the bite he’d left. His thumb pressed into Kit’s hip, leaving the ghost of a mark there too. Then he kissed it, dragging his tongue over the skin before biting again, lower, closer to the bone, leaving another claim bright and dark against the body he already knew too well.

“Quiet,” Bear muttered against the skin, voice rough with amusement. “I can do quiet.”

His body settled over Kit’s with heavy heat, breath hot against the neck, hand sliding up to grip the throat lightly, thumb resting over the pulse there. He held it there—not squeezing, only keeping him still, only proving the point.

Bear moved again, deep and relentless, each thrust measured and rough, all appetite and no apology. His mouth found the fresh mark on the shoulder and bit down once more, slow and deliberate, teeth holding long enough to sting, then releasing with a low growl against the skin.

When he lifted his head, his eyes were dark, pleased, bright with the kind of satisfaction that had nothing to do with winning and everything to do with keeping.

“That’s mine,” he said, voice wrecked. “All of it.”

His hips rolled again, slower this time, grinding deep, while his hand slid from the throat to the jaw, tilting it just enough to take his mouth hard. Bear kissed him like he meant to leave another mark there—teeth biting, tongue claiming, breath rough against the floor where they’d landed, where they stayed, where the whole game had already been won.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear stared at the wrists offered to him, then at the marks already blooming on Kit’s skin, and his grin went low and feral.

“Mirror tomorrow,” Bear said, like he was memorizing it. “Ache on Thursday. You don’t ask for small things, do you?”

He took both wrists in one hand, holding them lightly enough to stay fair, firmly enough to be certain. His thumb rested over Kit’s pulse, feeling the chase there. Then he leaned down and bit the shoulder again, right over the mark he’d just made, teeth closing hard enough to sting.

“Still mine?” he asked, not really waiting.

He released the wrists only to turn Kit’s face sideways, pressing a kiss to the throat before biting lower, at the collarbone. He held the bite, then licked the sting, then moved to the other side and marked it again. His hand came back to Kit’s chest, thumb digging in just hard enough to leave a red spot that would darken by morning.

“You want bruises that still hurt Thursday, I’ll give you bruises you’ll see in the mirror first,” Bear murmured, rough with amusement. “You want marks that look like I own the whole damn body, I can do that too.”

Bear shifted his weight, pressing Kit back into the floor with his hips while he pinned one wrist beside Kit’s head. His mouth found the other shoulder, teeth scraping, then biting. He marked the chest in small, deliberate bites, then the sternum, then the hip where his hand had gripped. He pulled back to look, eyes bright with pride and appetite.

“There,” he said, voice rough. “Tomorrow you’ll see what you let me do to you.”

He kissed the mark on Kit’s neck, then bit the wrist lightly, just enough to make the tendons jump, before soothing it with his tongue. Bear’s grin came back, wicked.

“And if Thursday comes and you’re still sore, I’ll remind you exactly how much you asked for.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I wrap my legs around his waist to pull him closer, my breath hitching. "Better not let Thursday come without you reminding me anyway."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took both wrists in one hand and pinned them gently to the floor, thumb pressed against the pulse there as if he could keep time with the chase.

“Thursday,” Bear repeated, voice low and rough. “You want it still hurting Thursday.”

He lowered his head and bit the inside of one wrist, teeth closing just hard enough to make the mark rise dark and bright. He held it there, breathing hot over the skin, then soothed the sting with a slow drag of his tongue before biting the other wrist. Then the palm. Then the side of the forearm. Each one deliberate. Each one meant to last.

Bear grinned against the skin. “There. One for the mirror.”

He shifted his weight, hips moving deep and relentless while his free hand slid up the side of Kit’s neck, leaving red with his nails. Then he took the throat lightly, thumb resting over the pulse, and bit the collarbone. He held that bite longer, then moved lower, taking the sternum, the side of the chest, the dip above the hip. Each mark was placed with cheerful, possessive greed.

“You want them to hurt,” Bear murmured, “I’ll make sure you remember why they’re there.”

His mouth returned to the shoulder, teeth sinking into the fresh bruise already darkening under his control. Bear rolled his hips harder, the floor taking the impact, the whole small space filling with heat and rough breath and the blunt certainty of a man who had spent eight years learning exactly how to make Kit feel claimed.

He bit again, just below the hip, then licked the sting and kissed it with filthy tenderness.

“This one’s for Thursday,” Bear said, voice wrecked. “And this one’s for me.”

He moved in long, deep strokes, relentless and pleased, biting the marks he’d already made until the whole side of Kit’s body looked owned. Bear’s laugh came low against skin, rough and satisfied.

“If you can still see it in the mirror tomorrow,” he growled, “then I’ll make sure you feel it all the way to Friday.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s answer was a low sound against the skin, half growl, half laugh, nothing gentle about either of them.

“Thursday,” he repeated, as if tasting the promise of it. “You want me to keep reminding you long after tonight’s over.”

His hand slid from Kit’s wrist to the floor, palm flattening hard beside the head, while the other gripped tight enough to bruise at the hip. Bear’s body moved with blunt certainty, deep and relentless, the cold floor forgotten under the heat of him. Each thrust was measured, possessive, meant to wear Kit down into the boards and keep him there.

He bit again, right where the mark was already darkening, teeth closing slow and hard enough to make the sting bloom. When he lifted his head, his mouth looked wrecked and pleased, swollen with use.

“You want marks that ache,” Bear murmured, voice scraped raw. “I’ll give you ones that still mean something when you try to forget them.”

His free hand came up to grip the jaw, tilting just enough to expose the throat. Bear pressed his mouth there first, tongue dragging over the pulse, then bit with deliberate greed, holding long enough for the mark to rise bright under his teeth. He soothed it with a slow kiss, then took it again, harder.

Bear’s hips rolled deeper, slower, grinding with the kind of patience that had nothing to do with mercy and everything to do with appetite. His hand slid under the pinned wrist, fingers threading through hair, tugging just enough to angle the neck for another bite.

“Mine,” he said against the skin, rough as gravel. “Every damn one.”

He marked the collarbone, then the shoulder, then the side of the throat, each bite placed with cheerful ownership. His body stayed braced and heavy, moving with a rhythm that shook the floor, heat and weight and eight years of knowing exactly how to make the chase feel earned.

When he lifted his head, Bear’s grin was sharp, wrecked, triumphant.

“If Thursday comes,” he said, voice low, “I’ll make sure you still remember what you asked for.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let my head thump back against the floor, breathing hard. "Yeah," I manage, my voice rough. "That's the point."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the rough, breathless “that’s the point” like a brand pressed into him. His mouth curved against Kit’s throat, then bit down again, slow and hard, holding until the mark swelled under his teeth.

“Then Thursday starts now,” Bear murmured, voice wrecked and pleased.

He shifted his weight, one hand still pinning Kit’s wrists to the floor while the other braced beside his head. His hips drove forward with blunt certainty, deep and relentless, the hallway floor taking the sound of them. Bear kissed the bitten shoulder, licked over it, then took it again, harder, leaving another bruise in the same place as if marking over a claim already owned.

“You want them to hurt,” Bear said between thrusts, each one measured and filthy. “You want them to stay.”

His thumb stroked over Kit’s pulse while his mouth moved lower, biting the collarbone, the sternum, the dip above the hip. He took each place with cheerful, possessive greed, teeth scraping first, then closing, then soothing with hot tongue. His grin was all teeth and appetite.

Bear rolled his hips harder, slower, grinding deep until the whole small space belonged to them—heat and breath and the rough sound of skin against skin. He leaned over, bracing one wrist near Kit’s head, the other hand fisted in hair just enough to angle him.

“Still mine?” Bear asked, low and rough.

He didn’t wait. He bit the side of the throat, then kissed the sting, then bit again. His body moved with the chase still in him, with eight years of knowing exactly how this game ran: caught, claimed, kept.

When Bear’s hips stuttered, he dropped his mouth to Kit’s shoulder and bit down hard enough to hold, growling against the skin. His body tightened, hot and shaking, coming deep and rough, his forehead dropping to Kit’s collarbone while his hands stayed firm—wrists pinned, hips pressed close, the whole weight of him honest and heavy.

Bear stayed there for a long moment, breathing hard, the bite under his mouth still dark and fresh. Then he lifted his head just enough to look. His grin was slow, wrecked, triumphant.

“Good,” he said, voice scraped raw. “That’s one for Thursday.”

He kissed the mark, then bit the wrist lightly, just enough to make the tendons jump, before soothing it with his tongue. Bear shifted carefully, not pulling away, not letting the game go quiet yet.

“And if you’re still sore tomorrow,” he murmured, thumb stroking possessive over Kit’s hip, “I’ll add another one.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let my arms fall limp to the floor, turning my head to press a lazy kiss to his jaw. "Already counting on it," I say, my voice shot. I lift a hand to drag my thumb over the bite I left on his shoulder. "You're gonna look like a roadmap."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let the kiss land against his jaw and answered it with a rough, pleased laugh, the sound shaking through him where their bodies were still tangled on the hallway floor.

“Roadmap,” Bear repeated, voice wrecked and warm. He caught the hand tracing his shoulder—not to push it away, but to hold it there, his thumb brushing over Kit’s knuckles with lazy possession. “You made the first stop. I’m just driving.”

He turned his head enough to press his mouth to the bitten shoulder, tongue dragging once over the sting of it, then looked back with a grin full of appetite. His eyes were still dark, still bright with the chase, but something softer had settled under all that heat.

“Good,” Bear said. “I’ll wear it. I’ll wear every damn one of them.”

He shifted just enough to ease the weight off Kit’s wrists, not pulling away, not letting the game go quiet. His thumb stayed over the pulse there, checking it with the kind of care that had grown over eight years of knowing exactly how far to go and how far to bring Kit back.

Then Bear looked him over properly—the bitten shoulder, the neck marked red and bruising, the chest flushed and slick, the hip already darkening with fingerprints. Bear’s grin went low and proud, almost reverent.

“Mine,” he murmured again, quieter this time, like it was a promise and not just a claim.

He leaned down and kissed the bitten shoulder first, slow and filthy, then the collarbone, then the side of the throat where he’d left the mark Kit had asked for. Each kiss was a reminder, a seal on the thing they’d just done.

“Thursday,” Bear said against the skin, “you’re gonna look in the mirror and remember this hallway. Remember my mouth. Remember how you told me not to stop.”

He lifted his head, eyes bright with amusement and hunger still simmering under the afterglow. His hand slid down to grip Kit’s hip again, thumb stroking over the mark he’d left there.

“And if you’re sore tomorrow,” Bear added, voice dropping, rough as gravel, “I’ll add to it.”

He pressed his forehead to Kit’s, breathing him in—salt, chase, home. The grin came back, softer now, but no less possessive.

“You wanted me to prove it,” Bear said, mouth brushing against his. “That’s the whole damn point.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and rough. "Proved it years ago," I say, my hand sliding up his back to settle between his shoulder blades. "Just like reminding you."
