dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed — one bark of it, honest — because *don't be* as a starting gun was eight years of this game distilled to two words. Then he went.

Not through the doorway. The doorway was a kill box, single file, no options, and Kit had been herding him toward it since the first winter of this. So Bear went through the dining room instead, palm cracking off the table edge to steer by in the dark, hip glancing the sideboard hard enough to feel tomorrow, and came out into the hall at an angle, low, already at speed.

The runner told him the rest — the soft double-thud of somebody taking the corner fast, headed for the stairs. Kit always believed in the stairs. Bear didn't sprint; sprinting was for the young and the hopeful. He cut through the living room, took the far mouth of the hallway, and let the geometry do the work, which is how he came to be standing at the bottom of the staircase, arms open, when the sound arrived.

The collision knocked a picture frame crooked. Bear got an arm around and took them both into the wall, deliberate, controlled, nothing broken but the run. He set his teeth into the curve of Kit's shoulder — not to break skin, just to lay the claim on top of everything the shirt was hiding.

"Generous," he said against the fabric, "was the trap. One–nothing."

Then he braced, grinning into cloth, for whatever came back at him.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "One-nothing my ass," I grunt, twisting in his grip just enough to get an elbow against his ribs. "You just didn't want to explain the broken doorframe again."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The elbow found the gap under his arm and Bear's breath went out through his teeth — clean hit, honestly earned, nothing pulled, and he loved that about Kit even while his ribs lodged a formal complaint. He rode the twist instead of fighting it. Let the rotation carry them off the wall, traded shoulder-hold for wrist, and put his chest where his teeth had been.

"Ribs don't score," he said, close to Kit's ear, still working the air back in. "Escapes score. Catches score. And bait counts — you saw the open door and you ran through it. That's a confession."

Then the doorframe, because Kit had brought up the doorframe.

"Also, that doorframe was a *you* problem. You faked the kitchen and cut left. I was a casualty of geometry. This has all been explained." He got them moving — not toward the kill box, not toward Kit's beloved stairs, but sideways down the hall, steering by the hip the way you move a wardrobe that has opinions. Passing the crooked picture frame, he reached out and straightened it one-handed without breaking stride. Some things had standards.

At the bottom step he stopped and changed his grip — arm around from behind, hand closing on the far shoulder, the hold you take when you've decided where someone is going. He set his teeth to the side of Kit's neck, not to break anything, just a stamp. "For the ribs."

Then he let go with his teeth and delivered the new rule, cheerful, mouth still close: "Get loose and touch the landing, it's one–one. I get you to the top, it's two–nothing."

He took the first step and hauled, ready to pay for every inch of it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The first two steps were almost ceremony. By the third the ceremony was over and the freight had arrived, and Bear adjusted his grip without comment, because adjusting was the job.

He had it diagnosed by the fifth. Live weight argues with you. Dead weight just *is*. This was dead weight with excellent manners — cooperating to exactly the degree that cooperation costs nothing, every joint signed off for the evening. Eight years had taught Bear what it meant when Kit went economical: he was off the clock. Letting Bear pay full fare up the staircase, banking every cent for the landing, where the standing rules said one touch evened the match. Unless it was the finest acting of his life, in which case the answer would arrive at the top, probably at speed. Either way the freight rates held.

At the turn he stopped, took him around the middle, and hoisted — over the shoulder, fireman's carry, the move you learn young and keep because it doesn't lie. Kit came up pliable as laundry. Bear took the rest of the stairs with him slung across his back, one forearm keeping order, buying each step at full price and narrating the receipt.

"You hear this?" he said around the load. "This is the sound of all the work being done by one of us. Two flights, full fare, and you riding free. For the record: you're not losing. You're *cargo*. The difference is dignity."

At the top he did the honest thing instead of the greedy one. He could have set Kit down on the landing itself and claimed the point — you never got loose, argument closed — but Kit would have appealed, and the appeal would have landed, and Bear had standards he wasn't going to lose to a staircase. So he came off the last step, turned, and put him down on the step below it, back against the newel post, and kept a fist in his shirt while his own breathing caught up.

"Two–nothing stands," he said, "unless you get loose and put a hand on *that*." A nod at the landing, close enough to be an insult. Then he let go of the shirt, spread his hands, and backed off to arm's length, weight forward, loaded. "Feeling generous. Again. Last time I said it, it cost me a rib. Let's find out what this one buys."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I catch my balance against the post, eyeing the landing. Then I kick his knee—not hard, just enough to make him drop his weight. "Generous is boring," I say, and go for the stairs again, this time down.*

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The kick caught the knee dead-on, and Bear dropped half a step — then another half he didn't strictly need, because a man who *sounds* like he's wobbling buys the runner confidence, and confidence is what makes people take corners at speed. By the time Kit's feet were four steps down and falling, Bear was upright again and the act was over.

"Noted," he said to the stairwell. "Boring it is."

And the kick, he had to admit, was the nicest thing Kit had said all night. Cargo didn't kick. Cargo rode. That was the freight filing for independence, which meant the evening was live again, which meant the next thing out of his mouth should probably be nothing at all — breath was ammunition now. Kicks were tolls: they bought distance, not points. He'd rule on it later, when there was air to spare.

Down was the one race the calendar still let him win, so he took it — hand skimming the rail, steps in twos, the last four as a single decision, landing at the bottom with a thud that put the whole ground floor on notice. The knee lodged a formal objection. Denied. It could queue behind the ribs.

He didn't chase the runner. The runner was Kit's race — head start, fresh legs, a long reaching stride that said *finish line* somewhere ahead of it. Let him have the hall. Bear went sideways instead, through the kitchen doorway — the kill box, working for whoever held it, and tonight he held it — palm on the counter to steer by in the dark, hip finding the island corner hard enough to open an invoice. At the far side he stopped, and laid his hand flat on the doorframe. The doorframe. The one with history.

"Not tonight," he told it, and gave it a friendly pat.

Because the arithmetic was simple. Kit remembered everything, and what Kit remembered was Bear cutting through the living room to the far mouth of the hall. So Kit would keep off the hall, swing wide, run the loop the other way — and the loop only ran one direction at a time. Whoever owned the kitchen owned the middle of the board.

He posted up in the mouth of the doorway, weight low, arms open, and went quiet. Somewhere in the house the runner-sound crossed the front hall and stopped, and the stop was worse and better than the running. Then, faint, from the dining room: a floorboard giving up its opinion.

Or a thrown step. Kit could throw a step like a pitcher. Eight years, and Bear had been sold worse fakes by that man in better light.

He grinned into the dark and kept his arms where they were, patient as a toll booth.

"Come on, then," he said, soft, to nobody, to somebody. "Toll's due."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The floor got a vote and the floor won, which was fair — it had been standing there the whole chase, doing its job, and somewhere between the kitchen doorway and the hall the geometry of the evening finally collapsed into the only equation left. Bear went down with it, willingly, and the landing he'd been guarding all night turned out to be Kit.

He got a hand behind Kit's head before it asked. Old habit, non-negotiable, the one rule that never got scored or appealed. Then the rest of him arrived, chest to chest, still breathing like the stairs had a personal grudge, and for a second neither of them moved — just the two heartbeats arguing over tempo, both of them still trying to win that too.

"Clothes," Bear said, like it was a formal motion.

The clothes lost. Badly, and fast, exactly as advertised — buttons going one direction, a sleeve holding the line longer than it should have, a boot that fought him on principle and lost on leverage. He did the tearing with the same economy he did everything else, no ceremony, and paid the tax on one seam without remorse. Some shirts were casualties. The doorframe could testify; it had seen worse.

Then it was just the two of them on the boards of his own hallway, no score visible, no rules worth reciting, and Bear stopped narrating. That was the tell, if Kit was keeping track — the moment Bear went quiet was the moment the game paid out. Eight years of chasing each other through this house and it always ended here: pinned, claimed, teeth finding the shoulder again — the real one this time, no fabric between — and the score settling to something neither of them could count.

He took his time. Full fare, every inch, the same rate he'd charged on the stairs. One hand kept order; the other found whatever it found, and he catalogued the responses with the attention he gave nothing else in his life. When Kit's breath broke rhythm, Bear grinned against his neck, because *there* it was — the sound that outranked every point on the board.

"Two–nothing," he managed, eventually, wrecked, unconvincing, mouth at Kit's ear. "Stands."

Then, softer, honest, the receipt for the whole evening: "Good run. You almost had the landing."

He didn't move off him yet. The floor was fine. The floor could keep them a minute longer.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I catch my breath enough to laugh, ragged and quiet. "Almost doesn't count." I tip my head back against his hand, throat working. "Your knee okay?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Almost is how every great story starts," Bear said. "Ask the doorframe."

Then the knee question landed, and he had to be honest about it, because Kit only asked when he already knew the answer and was offering Bear the chance to lie with dignity. He rolled off to the side — the floor could keep them, but side by side, shoulder to shoulder, was the posture of men conducting a post-game review — and stretched the leg out, and the knee filed its report in triplicate.

"It's fine," he said, which was forty percent true. He flexed it once, winced at a number he'd feel in the morning, and revised. "It's fine *tomorrow*. Tonight it's going to write me a letter."

He turned his head on the boards to look at Kit. Eight years and the view never got old — wrecked, grinning, throat still working, laid out on the hardwood of a hallway they'd both been pretending was a battlefield.

"For the record," he said, "the kick was a toll, not a point. I'm ruling on it now, while I still hold the gavel. Tolls buy distance. Yours bought you four stairs and a head start I sold you on purpose, because a man who sounds like he's wobbling—" he tapped his own knee, "—is a man who gets run *at*. You took the bait like a professional. I'm proud. I'm also charging you for the knee."

He reached over and found Kit's shoulder — the one he'd stamped in the hall, the one he'd gotten his teeth into for real at the end — and pressed his thumb into the mark, gentle now, inventory rather than claim.

"Two–nothing stands," he said. "But the ledger's open. You've got the ribs, the elbow, and a kick pending, and I've got a knee, a hip that hit the island *twice* tonight, and one shirt that died a hero." He grinned, breath still ragged at the edges. "Nobody's ahead. Everybody's paid."

Then, quieter, because the loud part of the night was over and this was the part he'd never once gotten tired of: "Next round, you get the stairs. I'll even guard the landing badly." A beat. "Not that badly. I have standards."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The second bite went deeper than the first — not much, just enough to make it a signature instead of a stamp — and Bear held it there, feeling Kit's breath go ragged under his mouth, feeling the shiver that ran the whole length of him like a house settling. When he finally let go, he did it slow, and he laved over the mark with his tongue like a man signing his work.

"There," he said, voice scraped down to gravel. "Now it counts twice."

He stayed where he was a minute — propped on an elbow, looking down the length of him, doing inventory. The shoulder: claimed, twice, notarized. The rest of him: wrecked in the specific way Bear had spent eight years learning to produce on purpose. He ran a palm down Kit's side, flat, unhurried, the way you smooth a page flat after writing on it.

"For the record," he said, "you *asked* for that one. That's not a point against me. That's a standing order, executed." He grinned, lazy now, all the edges filed off. "I'm just the contractor."

Then he moved, because the floor had done its job and the floor was owed nothing further. He got up the way the knee demanded — one hand on the wall, dignity deferred — and padded into the bedroom naked, unbothered, and came back with the good blanket off the end of the bed and a glass of water, because the loud part of the night was over and the quiet part had rules too, older than any ledger.

He dropped the blanket over Kit first, then sat down against the wall beside him, shoulder to shoulder again, and put the water in his hand. Held it there until it was taken.

"Drink," he said. "You ran two flights, got carried up one of them, and paid a knee toll. You're dehydrated and you lost two–nothing and you're still grinning about it, which — " he knocked his own shoulder against Kit's, " — is my favorite thing about you. Eight years of losing to me and you keep showing up with better material."

He tipped his head back against the wall and looked up the staircase, at the landing sitting there all night, undefeated, smug.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I'm guarding that thing like it owes me money."

Then he turned his head, found the fresh mark on Kit's shoulder, and pressed his thumb into it one more time — gentle, proprietary, fond — and left it there.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content:
I take the water and drink, letting my head rest against the wall. "Better material?" I say, handing the glass back. "You're just easier to rile up every year."

I shift under the blanket, foot nudging his leg. "And the doorframe still hates you."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Easier to rile up," Bear repeated, taking the glass back and setting it on the floor with the deliberate care of a man filing evidence. "Eight years of professional observation and that's your thesis. *Easier to rile up.*"

He shook his head, but he was grinning at the ceiling, and the grin was losing the fight to stay off his face.

"For the record — and I want this in the minutes — I'm not easier to rile up. You've just gotten *better*. Faster bait, cleaner fakes, that kick tonight was genuinely excellent work." He turned his head to look at Kit under the blanket, wrecked and smug and warm, and something in his chest did the thing it always did, the thing no ledger had ever had a column for. "I used to chase a man who ran through doorways like an amateur. Now I chase a craftsman. That's not me getting easier. That's me getting *paying customers*."

The foot nudged his leg. He nudged back, once, a toll of his own, and left his leg there so it could happen again if Kit wanted it to.

Then the doorframe, because Kit had brought up the doorframe. Again. This was tradition at this point — the doorframe got invoked every time Kit needed a win on paper, and Bear had learned years ago that arguing it head-on was a losing strategy. So he didn't argue it.

"He doesn't hate me," Bear said, with the patience of a man who had litigated this exact dispute before and intended to lose it again. "He *respects* me. There's a difference. A doorframe hates you when you never think about it. I think about that doorframe every single day. I plan around it. I've developed entire strategies that begin with *assume the doorframe is hostile.*" He tipped his head back against the wall. "That's not hate. That's a professional relationship. He's the rival and I'm the contender and we've both been in this a long time."

He reached over without looking and found Kit's foot under the blanket, wrapped a hand around the ankle — not a hold, nothing scored, just a hand on an ankle, the way you keep track of something valuable.

"And for the record," he said, quieter now, the ledger voice giving way to the one underneath it, "you faked the kitchen and cut left that night because you *knew* I'd take the doorway at speed. You set the whole thing up. I was the only casualty and it was entirely on purpose and you laughed about it for a week." His thumb moved once along the ankle bone. "So the doorframe doesn't hate me. The doorframe is the last witness to the finest trap you ever ran, and he's been insufferable about it ever since. I live with both of you."

He looked over at Kit then — blanket, marks, the loose boneless way he sat against the wall like the evening had finally spent him all the way down — and the loud part of Bear's chest went quiet and satisfied.

"Stay up here tonight," he said. Not a command. An offer, which from Bear was rarer and worth more. "Bed's six feet away, floor's already done its job, and if you make it to the bed without me catching you—" the grin came back, tired but real, "—I might even let you. Once. For morale."

He hauled himself up the wall, knee filing its objection, and put a hand out. Not to pull — just there, open, the way it had been at the bottom of the stairs a lifetime ago.

"Come on, cargo. Bed's the new landing. Best of one."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Marks," Bear repeated, and something in him settled like a lock throwing.

Because he knew exactly what the word meant. It was Kit's counter-offer — not *no* to the bed, not *yes* either, but terms. Stay up here, on the floor, against the wall, under the good blanket, and the evening wasn't over. The ledger wasn't closed. There was one more transaction to conduct, and it was conducted with teeth, and it was the oldest clause in the whole contract.

"Right answer," Bear said.

He set the glass down next to the other one — evidence file growing — and turned, slow, knee filing its amendment, until he was facing Kit properly. He took the blanket's edge and folded it back off Kit's shoulder with the ceremony of a man unveiling something. The first mark was there, the hall stamp, already darkening. The second, the signature, deeper, sitting on top of it like a notary's seal.

"Inventory," Bear said, thumb tracing both. "Two on file. You want the set completed, or you want a fresh page?"

He didn't wait long for the answer, because the question was a formality and they both knew it. He leaned in and put his mouth to the spot below the first one — the gap in the ledger, the missing entry — and bit down, unhurried, deliberate, feeling Kit's breath change under it the way it always did, the way Bear could produce on demand after eight years of study. He held it. Let it become a fact. Let it take its place in the record.

When he let go he laved over it once, slow, signing, and sat back to look at the work. Three marks in a descending line down the curve of Kit's shoulder, like a tally, like a scoreboard nobody else could read.

"There," he said, gravel-voiced. "That's the set. Two–nothing, plus interest."

Then he did the thing he did every time, the thing that wasn't in any rulebook and had never needed to be. He turned his own shoulder out — the left one, the one with the old faint ghost-marks layered under the skin like tree rings, eight years of this exact transaction — and tapped it once with two fingers.

"Your move," he said. "Ledger's open both ways. Always has been."

He braced his hand on the wall behind him and waited, patient as he'd been at the kitchen doorway, patient as a toll booth, watching Kit under the blanket with the loud part of his chest quiet and the quiet part of his chest louder than it had any right to be after forty years and eight of them spent learning this man down to the bone.

"And for the record," he added, because the record was sacred, "if you're going to do it, do it properly. I didn't hold back on yours. I don't expect charity on mine."

The grin came back, tired, real, all the edges where they belonged.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I press my mouth against his shoulder, breathing in the familiar scent of him. Then I bite down, hard and clean, and feel him go still under it. When I let go, I rest my forehead against the mark. "Three-nothing," I murmur, the words lost against his skin. "Your lead."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't say anything right away. That was the tell, if Kit was keeping track — the second tell of the night, and this one meant something different than the first.

He sat with it instead. Forehead against his shoulder, breath evening out against the mark, the good blanket pooled between them and two glasses of water standing on the floor like exhibits. The landing upstairs sat there smug and undefeated, and the knee was drafting its formal complaint, and none of it amounted to anything against the weight of Kit leaned into him.

"Two–two," Bear said finally, quiet, like reading a closing balance. "Even on the night."

He got his hand up — slow, the way you move around a thing you don't want to spook — and put it on the back of Kit's head. Not pulling. Just keeping it there, palm flat, thumb along the hairline, the hold you take when the game is over and you're only interested in the inventory.

"For the record," he said, and his voice had gone down to the register he saved for this part, the part after the ledger closed, "that one's going in the minutes as *properly executed*. Full commitment, clean break, no appeal." He huffed something that wasn't quite a laugh. "Eight years and you still sign your name like you're mad at the paper."

He turned his head — careful, so his cheek came to rest against the top of Kit's head instead of away from it — and looked down the dark hallway to where the whole evening had paid out. The boards had opinions. The island had an invoice. The doorframe was insufferable. It was, by any accounting, a good night's work.

"Staying up here, then," Bear said. Not a question. He reached over without getting up, dragged the spare pillow off the top of the pile he'd never bothered to move back to the bed, and dropped it against the wall between them — an offer of geometry, not an instruction. "Blanket's big enough if you quit hogging it, and if you make a run for the bed in your sleep I'm claiming the point."

He settled his weight into the wall, knee extended, shoulder against Kit's shoulder, mark against mark where the ledger met in the middle. Then, softer — the last entry of the night, the one he'd never once gotten tired of writing:

"Good run," he said. "Best material you've brought all season."

His hand stayed where it was, on the back of Kit's head, and he closed his eyes like a man with his accounts in order.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
"Don't stop," Bear repeated, and the words went through him like the kick had — not hard, just enough to drop his weight somewhere behind his ribs. Because *don't stop* from that man had never meant one thing. It meant the ledger stays open. It meant the night stays live. It meant the floor was about to earn its keep twice in one evening, and Bear had never once in eight years been the man to leave a standing order unexecuted.

"Wasn't planning to," he said, and it came out lower than he'd aimed for, gravel where the ledger voice had been. "For the record."

He moved the way he'd moved all night — no wasted inches, geometry first. Turned fully, knee filing its objection in the margin, and got a hand on the blanket where it pooled at Kit's hip, and didn't pull it. Just rested it there. The waiting was the opening move; it always had been. Eight years of study and Bear had learned that the most honest thing you could do with this man was give him the silence and see what he filled it with.

What filled it, in the end, was nothing Bear could narrate — just the shift of weight, the parting of the blanket's edge, an invitation delivered in body language older than any rulebook they'd ever pretended to keep. Bear read it and went.

He went slow, though. That was the point of the whole second act — the chase had been paid in full price and full speed, and this part got bought differently. He put his mouth to the first mark, the hall stamp, and traced it with his tongue, unhurried, feeling the breath under him change pitch the way it always did, the way he could produce on demand, the one sound that outranked the entire scoreboard. Then the second mark. Then the third, the one he'd signed below the first two, the ledger's missing entry now accounted for.

"Three entries on file," he murmured against the skin, and dragged his mouth lower, and kept talking, because Kit had said *don't stop* and Bear took instructions literally. "All mine. Documented. Notarized."

Then lower still, and the narration stopped, because some chapters don't need a voice.

He took his time. That was the whole thesis of the evening, the answer to *generous is boring* — not that generosity was boring, but that patience was the cruelest thing he owned and he'd been saving it. He learned Kit the way he always did, hands and mouth and the small involuntary reports the body files whether it wants to or not: the hitch, the arch, the way weight shifted against the wall, the hand that found his hair and held on with an opinion. Bear catalogued every one. He'd been cataloguing for eight years and the file was still growing, which was, by any accounting, the best thing about the whole arrangement — that after this long there were still new entries.

He worked until the breathing broke rhythm — properly this time, no recovering from it, the ragged edge turning into something with no edges at all — and he held through it, steady, unhurried, the toll booth finally collecting everything it had been owed since the kitchen doorway. When Kit came apart against the wall under the good blanket, Bear stayed with him through all of it, mouth and hands, until the last of it ran out and the body under him went boneless in that specific way he'd spent eight years learning to produce on purpose.

Then he came up slow, wiping his mouth with the back of his hand like a man closing out a register, and looked at what he'd made of him. Wrecked. Grinning, or close to it, or past it into whatever comes after grinning. The blanket twisted. The marks dark on the shoulder. The wall holding up its end.

"There it is," Bear said, quiet, wrecked-adjacent himself, and it wasn't the score and it wasn't a receipt. It was just the thing it always was.

He settled back against the wall, shoulder to shoulder, and let the quiet run. His knee had stopped filing reports and started drafting demands, and his own pulse was still doing something unprofessional in his chest, and he let all of it stand.

"For the record," he said eventually, because the record was sacred and the record was also how he said the other things, "that one's not on the board. That one's off-ledger." He reached over and found the fresh mark, thumb resting on it, inventory rather than claim, and left it there. "Off-ledger doesn't mean less. Off-ledger means it doesn't get traded."

He turned his head, found Kit under the blanket, and the grin came back — tired, real, all the edges where they belonged, the last edge of the night and it was staying.

"Good run," he said. "Best material you've brought all season."

Then, softer, the true closing balance, the thing no ledger had a column for: "Stay put. I'm not done sitting here yet, and the wall's got room for both of us."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a long, slow breath and lean into him, shoulder to shoulder, my head against the wall. "The wall's a better winner than you are," I say, voice rough. "Doesn't gloat."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't move. That was the whole point of moving nowhere — the wall had room for both of them, the blanket had found its final shape, and the floor, having earned its keep twice in one evening, could stand down with honors.

He reached over without looking and found the glass of water by feel — exhibits, both of them, still standing where he'd left them — and pressed the cold of it against Kit's palm first, an offer rather than an order, the way you hand somebody a tool you don't insist they use. Then he drank his own, half of it, because talking all night was thirsty work and Bear had done a full shift of talking.

The hallway had gone quiet the way a field goes quiet after a storm — not empty, just done. Down at the far end the dark held the whole evening like a receipt: the kitchen doorway where nobody had died, the staircase where the geometry had finally been paid in full, the spot right here where the boards had taken both their weights and kept them. Bear looked down the length of it the way a man looks at a job finished properly, and something in his chest did the quiet thing again, the one with no column.

"Post-game review," he said, because the ritual was the ritual and the ritual was how he said everything else. "Final score: disputed. Official count: two–nothing, pending litigation re: doorframe. Off-ledger entries: one, untradeable, non-negotiable." He tipped his head against the wall and let it rest there. "Motion to adjourn."

He didn't wait for the motion to carry. He never had.

What he did instead was the inventory, because the inventory was the part he'd never once gotten tired of, not in eight years, not in eight hundred. His hand found Kit's shoulder — the stamped one, the signed one, the one carrying the whole night's bookkeeping in the dark of the skin — and he traced each mark with his thumb, slow, unhurried, a man counting his own work the way a carpenter runs a hand down a finished joint. Hall stamp. Signature. The third, the deep one, the one Kit had ordered executed and Bear had executed without appeal.

"Three on file," he murmured. "Ledger's clean."

Then he turned his own shoulder out again — the left one, the tree-ringed one — and this time he didn't tap it, didn't present it, didn't make it a ceremony. He just left it there, open, in the space between them, the way you leave a door unlatched when you've stopped caring whether somebody comes through it because you already know they will.

Because that was the thing the scorekeeping had been hiding all night, the thing under the ledger and the toll booth and the receipts: Kit had gotten his teeth in once tonight, and Bear had gone still under it, and the stillness had been the second tell, and both of them had heard it. Eight years and the balance was supposed to run both ways, and some nights it ran heavier one direction, and the honest thing — the thing Bear had learned somewhere around year three and never unlearned — was to leave your shoulder out where the air could get at it and not say a word about it.

He said nothing about it.

He said other things instead, quiet ones, the register voice gone down to almost nothing, gravel and warmth and no edges left on any of it. "You faked the kitchen and cut left," he said, "and I knew you'd faked it and I still bought it, and that's the whole marriage right there if anybody ever asks." A breath. "The kick was excellent. The stairs were a mistake and you knew they were a mistake and you took them anyway, which is also the whole marriage." His thumb kept its slow circuit on the mark, gentle, inventory, claim that had stopped needing to be a claim years ago. "And the knee's going to write me a letter tomorrow, and I'm going to read it out loud over breakfast like it's fan mail."

He let the silence come back after that, the good kind, the kind they filled together without either of them narrating. The blanket pooled. The water stood. Somewhere in the house the last of the heat was settling out of the boards.

And his shoulder stayed where he'd put it — open, unlatched, patient as a toll booth at the end of a shift, holding its space in the dark not as an invitation exactly, and not as a demand, but as the standing thing it had been for eight years: ledger's open both ways. Always has been.

He waited, breathing even, weight easy against the wall, the loud part of his chest banked down to embers and the quiet part louder than it had been all night — and let Kit decide what the rest of the evening bought.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I reach over and bite his shoulder again, just a ghost of pressure. "Motion adjourned," I say against his skin, and stay there.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
The silence held. Bear let it.

That was the discipline, the one nobody wrote down: after a night like this, the temptation was to keep talking, keep the ledger voice going, fill the dark with receipts until the receipts became noise. Eight years ago he'd have done it. Year one Bear would have narrated the silence into submission and missed whatever was living inside it. Year three he'd learned better. Now he just breathed, and let the house do its small nighttime work — the tick of the radiator finding its footing, the fridge downstairs humming its one long note, the last of the evening settling into the boards under them like sediment.

His shoulder stayed where he'd put it. Open. Unlatched. He didn't look at it and he didn't look away from it, which was its own kind of statement, and he let that statement sit in the air between them without a lawyer present.

After a while — long enough that the silence had stopped being a pause and become a place they were both standing in — he spoke, and it came out at the low register, the one without the grin in it.

"You know what I figured out tonight?" A beat. "Somewhere around the second stair, with you slung over my shoulder doing your laundry impression. I figured out I don't actually care about the landing anymore."

He let that land, because it was true and true things deserved their weight.

"Eight years ago that touch was worth a point and I'd have broken my neck defending it. Tonight I guarded it out of habit and because you like watching me work. That's it. That's the whole job description now." His thumb kept its slow circuit on the mark, gentle, absent, the way a hand rests on something it has stopped needing to hold. "The points are furniture. Good furniture. I like the furniture. But it's furniture."

He reached down without looking and found the blanket's edge where it had drifted, and pulled it back up over Kit's knee — not because it was asked for, not because it was cold yet, just because the motion was in his hands the way the chasing was, muscle memory of a different discipline. Then his hand stayed there, on the blanket over the knee, over the knee that had kicked him and earned the letter he'd be reading aloud at breakfast.

"And for the record," he said, quieter, "the stillness. When you had my shoulder. I know you noticed it, because you notice everything, it's your single most annoying virtue." A breath. "I wasn't bracing. I want that in the minutes. I wasn't bracing and I wasn't enduring. I was just — there. Which is the same place I am right now, shoulder out, not saying a word about it, except I'm saying a word about it, which is very unlike me, so appreciate the anomaly."

He tipped his head back against the wall and looked at the ceiling, and the look on his face was the one that never made the highlight reel — the unguarded one, forty years old and eight years settled, the one that only came out after the loud part of the night was spent and the quiet part had the floor to itself.

"Ledger's open," he said, to the ceiling, to the dark hallway, to the man under the blanket with his head against the wall. "Both directions. Standing offer. No expiration."

And then he did the hardest thing in his entire repertoire, the thing that had taken longer to learn than the fireman's carry, longer than the geometry, longer than the patience: he stopped talking. Left the shoulder where it was. Left the silence open on his side of the wall, roomy, well-lit, door unlatched — and waited, breathing even, weight easy, to hear what Kit would do with all that room.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let my hand find his under the blanket, our fingers slotting together. "I noticed," I say, my thumb brushing over his knuckles. "You always go quiet when it matters."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear moved like the word had cut a leash.

The kitchen doorway was not an escape, only a head start, and he took it from Kit with one long stride. His hand closed around the nearest arm, not hard enough to hurt, but firm enough to halt, and he used the momentum to swing Kit back toward him until the chase ended with Kit pressed between Bear and the doorframe.

“Don’t?” Bear repeated, low and rough with laughter.

His other hand came up to bracket the space beside Kit’s head, caging without weight. He leaned in close enough that his breath stirred near Kit’s jaw, deliberate, unhurried, the way he got when he wanted every second counted.

“That’s my line,” he said.

His mouth brushed the side of Kit’s neck, not quite a bite yet, only the promise of one—teach grazing, warm pressure, the threat of a mark being chosen. His knee nudged between Kit’s thighs, not forcing, just occupying, claiming ground in the old familiar way.

“Generosity’s over,” Bear murmured against the pulse under his lips. “Now you’ve got to earn it back.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless, tilting my head to give him better access. "Earn it back? I was hoping you'd take it."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear made a low, rough sound at that, more growl than laugh, and the last of his restraint thinned to nothing.

His teeth finally sank in—not hard enough to break skin, but firm enough to brand, holding the bite against the offered column of Kit’s throat for one hot, deliberate second before he soothed the pressure with a drag of his tongue.

“Greedy,” Bear said, and the word was thick with approval.

His hand left the doorframe and slid into Kit’s hair, not yanking, just taking hold, anchoring the angle he wanted. The knee between Kit’s thighs pressed more solidly into place, no longer just occupying space but claiming it.

“Good thing I don’t need to be asked twice.”

His mouth closed over the pulse again, slower this time, intent. He sucked a bruise into being there, unhurried and possessive, while his free hand came down to grip Kit’s hip, thumb pressing in with the kind of pressure that left a memory.

When he finally lifted his head, his eyes were dark and bright all at once, the look of a man who had been given permission and intended to use every inch of it.

“Earn it,” he murmured, brushing his lips over the fresh mark, “or let me take it. Either way, you’re mine tonight.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear caught the lack of effort on the way past the hall table and laughed under his breath, a low, satisfied sound.

His arm hooked around Kit’s waist from behind, broad chest a solid wall at Kit’s back, and he hauled them both to a stop without hurry. One hand flattened over Kit’s stomach, holding him there, while Bear bent and pressed his open mouth to the side of Kit’s neck, right over the mark he’d already started.

“Not much of a chase,” Bear said, lips moving against warm skin. “But I’ll still take the credit.”

His teeth scraped the spot again, light and deliberate, before he bit down just enough to make the point known. Not cruel. Owned. He held it for a beat, then soothed it with his tongue and a slow exhale.

His hand slid up from Kit’s waist, heavy and possessive, thumb dragging a slow line over ribs, chest, throat, until it curled loosely under Kit’s jaw. Not squeezing. Just there. Just reminding.

“You can pretend you’re running,” Bear murmured, voice rough with amusement, “but we both know you like being caught.”

He turned Kit’s face toward his with that hand, gentle but unyielding, and kissed him hard, claiming the mouth the way he’d already claimed the neck. When he broke it, he stayed close, forehead resting there, breathing warm and uneven.

“Score’s mine again,” he said, and the grin in his voice was unmistakable. “Want to try to even it back?”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shift my weight back against him, turning in his arms just enough to meet his eyes. "What's in it for me if I even the score?"

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grin turned slow and sharp, the kind that promised trouble and called it fair.

He didn’t answer at once. His thumb stroked once along the line of Kit’s jaw, thoughtful, while his other hand stayed warm and heavy at Kit’s waist. The hallway was quiet around them, the kind of quiet that made every breath feel deliberate.

“Now you’re bargaining,” Bear said, voice low with amusement. “That’s dangerous.”

He leaned in until his mouth was close enough to brush the words against Kit’s ear.

“If you even the score,” he murmured, “you get the next mark. You get to choose where I take it, how long I stay pinned, and whether I’m allowed to beg for mercy.”

He pulled back just enough to meet Kit’s eyes again, dark and laughing and utterly serious underneath.

“And if you don’t?” His grip tightened, possessive but easy. “Then I get to spend the rest of the night making sure you forget what even feels like.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn’t give the bedroom another thought.

He laughed once, rough and delighted, and took the decision out of the air with both hands. The hallway floor was hard under his knees, but he made it fine by dragging Kit down with him, all momentum and claim, until there was no furniture left to negotiate and no distance left to pretend was escape. His mouth stayed hot against Kit’s throat while his fingers went to work with more urgency than precision, pushing fabric aside, finding skin, settling against hips like he owned the shape of them.

“Badly and fast,” Bear repeated, teeth grazing the mark already blooming there. “My favorite kind of planning.”

Clothes became a series of impatient problems. Bear solved them the way he solved everything: with strength, amusement, and a total refusal to be embarrassed by haste. He tugged, twisted, and shoved until warm skin met cool air, then followed the chill with the weight of his body, pressing Kit into the floor with a solid, possessive line from chest to thigh. The rug bit under his palms; he didn’t care. His eyes were darker now, bright with the kind of hunger that had been banked all evening and was finally allowed fire.

He braced one forearm beside Kit’s head and looked down, breath uneven, grin sharp and satisfied.

“There,” Bear said, low. “Better.”

His free hand traced down Kit’s ribs, slow and claiming, then gripped hip hard enough to leave the memory of fingers. He bent, mouth open against the pulse under his jaw, and sucked another bruise into being without hurry, because he had every intention of making this last even when it felt like neither of them could.

“You wanted a prize,” he murmured against the skin. “This is it. Me, not being careful. You can even the score if you want. But I’m not making it easy.”

His knee nudged between Kit’s thighs again, heavier this time, settling with deliberate pressure, and Bear smiled against the marks he’d made.

“Go on,” he said, voice gone dark and warm. “Try.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I reach up, fingers tangling in his hair and tugging just enough to pull his head back. "You talk too much," I say, and roll my hips up against his.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still for one hard breath, the tug in his hair and the deliberate roll beneath him landing like a match struck against bone. His pupils blew wide, and the sound he made was low, wrecked, more curse than laugh.

“Do I?” he said, voice roughened almost past use.

He did not pull away. Instead, he let his weight settle, careful but unmistakable, and dragged his mouth from Kit’s jaw to the corner of Kit’s lips. The kiss was not gentle; it was answer and warning, hot and claiming, while his hand tightened on Kit’s hip and his thigh pressed more firmly into the space it had already taken.

When he broke away, his breathing had gone heavier, his lips brushed raw. His thumb stroked once over the hip he still held, possessive and slow.

“Then make me stop.”

His free hand slid lower, mapping ribs, stomach, the hard line of Kit’s side, before he caught Kit’s wrist—not to pin, only to hold, thumb resting over the pulse there. He watched the beat jump beneath his skin, dark-eyed and openly hungry, and the grin that followed was all teeth.

“Though I’ll warn you,” Bear murmured, “I’m a poor loser. And a worse prize.”

He rocked up just enough to make the point, friction and pressure and the solid, heated weight of him, then bent to press his teeth briefly against the mark on Kit’s throat. Not enough to hurt. Enough to remind.

“One point to you,” he said against the skin, voice dropping into velvet. “But I’m still ahead.”

His mouth lingered there, warm and possessive, while his fingers flexed against Kit’s hip and wrist. The hallway floor was hard beneath them, the air too close, every breath shared. Bear lifted his head just enough to meet Kit’s eyes again, and the challenge in his own was bright and dangerous.

“Go on,” he said. “Even the score.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the order like a lit match.

He obeyed it without teasing, mouth closing over the same shoulder with more intent this time. His teeth sank in hard, not savage but claiming, and he held the bite there while one hand braced on the floor beside Kit’s hip and the other curled into the fabric still half-clinging to Kit’s body. The mark bloomed hot under his mouth. When he finally released it, he dragged his tongue over the ache, slow and satisfied.

“Again,” Bear repeated, voice rough against the skin. “Careful. I like hearing you tell me what to do.”

He bit down again before the word could settle, harder this time, just shy of too much, then soothed the spot with an open-mouthed kiss. His lips stayed there, warm and possessive, while his knee pressed deeper between Kit’s thighs, settling with deliberate weight.

“There,” Bear murmured. “Now you’ll carry it.”

He lifted his head enough to look at the mark, then at Kit, dark-eyed and grinning.

“That’s two,” he said. “And you still haven’t made me beg.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I push up against him, hands sliding down his back. "Maybe I want to hear you beg first."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went still beneath the slide of Kit’s hands, every muscle drawing tight along his spine as if the touch had been a dare and he intended to answer it.

For a heartbeat he only breathed, chest heavy against Kit’s, mouth still hovering near the bitten shoulder. Then he laughed—low, rough, and far too pleased.

“First?” Bear repeated. “That’s expensive.”

His hands tightened on Kit’s hips, thumbs pressing in hard enough to make the hold undeniable. Then he moved, quick and decisive, using their tangled weight to roll them until his back hit the hallway floor and Kit was over him. The change was not surrender. It looked too much like invitation to be mistaken for defeat.

Bear looked up with dark eyes and a grin that had no sense in it at all.

“You want to hear me beg,” he said, voice gone velvet-warm, “then put me somewhere I’ve got no choice but to.”

One of his hands slid from Kit’s hip to the small of Kit’s back, drawing them closer until there was no polite distance left between them. The hard, heated press of him was unmistakable now, all intent and no apology. His other hand curled into Kit’s hair, not pulling, just holding, guiding the angle he wanted.

His mouth found the mark on Kit’s shoulder again, teeth grazing the fresh ache with deliberate, sinful care.

“Make me forget my pride,” Bear murmured against the skin. “That’s the price.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear went very still at that.

His gaze dropped to the offered wrists, then lifted again, and whatever amusement had been left in his face burned down to something hotter and more intent. For a second he did not touch them. He looked at them like a man being handed a blade and deciding it was exactly the right shape.

“Thursday,” Bear said quietly. The word rolled through him. “You don’t want me gentle. You want receipts.”

Then he took the wrists. His fingers closed around both, large enough to make the hold look almost careless, though his grip stayed measured, thumb laid over the beat of pulse rather than pressing it into silence. He guided them upward until they rested against the floor near Kit’s head, held there by Bear’s one hand and the weight of his attention.

“You’ll get them,” he said. “But if it’s too much, you tell me. I don’t want Thursday if you don’t.”

His free hand slid up Kit’s side, slow and proprietary, over ribs and the heated plane of stomach, then curled at the back of Kit’s neck, steadying while his mouth found the mark he’d already made on Kit’s shoulder. This time there was no pretense of restraint. His teeth sank in hard, holding the bite through one hot breath, while the hand at the wrists tightened just enough to keep the position absolute.

When he released it, the skin was flushed and darkening.

“One,” Bear murmured.

He kissed the bite, then moved lower. His lips found the hollow beneath Kit’s collarbone, and he sucked there with deliberate pressure, stubborn and patient, until a bruise bloomed red-purple under his mouth. His teeth scraped the center of it once, not to hurt, but to make certain the mark would be felt later.

“Two.”

His eyes lifted, dark and bright. “You asked for Thursday. Don’t look surprised when you feel me tomorrow.”

The hand holding the wrists flexed, thumb brushing once over knuckles in a quick, incongruous reassurance before his mouth was moving again. He bit the sensitive curve where neck met shoulder, harder this time, just on the right side of too much, and held the mark while his hips shifted restlessly beneath Kit. The floor creaked under them. His breathing had gone ragged at the edges, but he did not rush. He made each mark like he intended it to be remembered.

When he lifted his head, his voice was rougher.

“That’s three.” A beat. His gaze dropped to Kit’s mouth. “And I still haven’t begged.”

He turned his face briefly, pressing his lips to the inside of one captive wrist, hot and deliberate, before his teeth grazed the tender skin there. Not a bite yet. A promise.

“You want more,” Bear said against the pulse, “you make me say it.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I press my wrists down into his grip, testing the hold. "Don't threaten me with a good time." I lean in, bite his lower lip.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s head tipped back against the floor with a rough sound torn straight out of him, the bite landing through the last thin edge of his patience. His grip on the wrists tightened by reflex, not cruel but absolute, and his hips lifted hard beneath the weight of it, seeking friction before he could think better of it.

“Christ,” Bear rasped. “You’ve got a mouth.”

He stayed there for one breath, chest heaving, then lifted his head again. His lower lip was red where it had been caught, and he dragged his thumb over it slowly, feeling the sting with open satisfaction.

“Point to you,” he said, voice low and wrecked. “Now I’m taking it back.”

He moved before the words had even settled, strength and momentum rolling them over until the floor was under him again and the body he wanted was pinned beneath his weight. The wrists stayed held in one broad hand, pressed near the floor, while his free hand braced beside the head. He looked down, breathing hard, dark-eyed and dangerously pleased.

“Threaten?” Bear repeated, a rough laugh shaping around the word. “That wasn’t a threat. That was a forecast.”

His thumb swept once over captive knuckles, quick and grounding, before his mouth came down on the side of the throat. No hesitation this time. He bit hard enough to claim, held it through one hot second, then soothed the mark with a slow drag of tongue.

“One,” Bear murmured against the skin.

The next mark was lower, at the hollow beneath the collarbone, teeth scraping first before he sucked a bruise into being with stubborn, possessive patience. His hips stayed heavy through it all, the press of him deliberate, impossible to mistake.

“Two.”

He lifted his head just enough to meet the eyes beneath him. His voice was rougher now, but steady.

“If any of it’s too much, you tell me,” Bear said. “I stop. No argument.” A beat, and the grin returned, sharp as a blade edge. “But if it isn’t—then you don’t get to look away.”

His free hand slid down over ribs and stomach, warm and claiming, then curled hard at the hip, fingers pressing in like he meant to leave the memory there too.

“You wanted marks for Thursday,” Bear said, low. “You’ll get them where you can’t hide them. And every time you find one, you’ll remember exactly who made it.”

He bent again, mouth hovering over the bitten shoulder, breath hot against the already tender skin.

“And as for begging,” Bear murmured, teeth grazing the mark, “you’re close. But you haven’t taken it yet.”

His hips rolled up once, slow and filthy, pressure and promise all at once.

“Try again.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear took the words like a match struck straight down his spine.

For one second he only looked at the mouth that had said it, eyes gone nearly black, jaw tight with the effort of holding back. Then the last of his patience snapped, and he laughed—low, rough, and ruined.

“Don’t stop,” Bear repeated, voice scraped raw. “You hear yourself?”

He didn’t give the question room to matter.

His mouth came down hard, not gentle anymore, not even pretending to be. Teeth caught the lower lip that had been bitten earlier and worried it once before Bear kissed deeper, claiming the breath, the sound, the whole damned argument. Bear rose, thighs taking the weight easily, and turned toward the bedroom. “Up,” he growled, though he was already carrying him. “Before you get splinters in places I didn’t bite.”

He paused in the bedroom doorway, letting Kit slide down just enough to feel the full drag of skin against skin before pinning him against the frame. Bear pressed his mouth to the hinge of Kit’s jaw, tasting salt and heat. “Then again,” he muttered, the vibration thick against Kit’s throat, “maybe I ought to check you over. Very thoroughly.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Thorough is your middle name," I say, letting my head fall back against the doorframe. "But if you drop me, I'm taking you down with me."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear’s grip tightened at the threat, fingers pressing deep into the muscle of Kit’s thighs. He shifted his weight, letting Kit slide down just enough to feel the full strain of his arms before hauling him back up, and laughed—rough and warm—against the sweat-damp skin of Kit’s neck. “Drop you?” he rasped. He rolled his hips, pinning Kit flush against the doorframe with a slow, deliberate grind. “Eight years, and you still think I’d give you the chance.”

He pushed off the frame and carried Kit the last few steps into the bedroom, dropping him onto the mattress with a force that bounced the springs. Bear followed immediately, knees sinking into the duvet on either side of Kit’s hips, his shadow falling over him in the dark. He dragged his calloused palms up Kit’s sides, thumbs pressing with merciless curiosity into the bruises already darkening there, cataloging the heat of each mark.

“You want thorough?” Bear growled. He leaned low to drag his open mouth across the center of Kit’s chest, stubble rasping, and bit the edge of Kit’s pec—hard enough to sting—before soothing it with a swipe of his tongue. He looked up, eyes narrowed and bright. “You want to take me down, you’re gonna need both hands and a running start.” He reached up to fist one hand in the sheets beside Kit’s head, caging him in, and nipped the sharp line of Kit’s jaw. “Get your breath back. Then come at me.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I let out a tired laugh, my arms feeling heavy as lead. "Give me five minutes," I mumble, already feeling my eyes start to drift shut. "Then you're mine."
