rung_labels.evidence: He ground his hips forward

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: grinding his hips down with a slow, punishing roll

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: teeth sinking deep enough to bruise, to claim

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: a slow, deliberate bite, feeling the pulse hammer against his tongue

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: drove forward in a single, merciless thrust

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The party had reached the stage where nobody would notice two people missing, which Odile pointed out approximately four seconds before doing something about it.

"The bathroom upstairs has a lock," she said, into Fen's ear, over the music.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Does it work?" I ask, already moving toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"No idea," Odile said, and the honest answer was clearly the part she liked best. "Half the locks in this house are decorative. I consider that a feature."

She followed him up, and the stairs betrayed her immediately — the third step groaned, the fifth practically applauded. She pressed a hand over her own mouth, which did nothing about her feet.

Downstairs someone put on a song she loved. She hummed four bars of it at nearly full volume before she caught herself.

The hallway at the landing stretched toward a door with light spilling under it. Odile grabbed Fen's sleeve and towed him toward it, moving with all the subtlety of a heist gone wrong. Her shoulder clipped the doorframe on the way in. She snorted.

"Shh," she told herself, then, to Fen, in a whisper that carried beautifully: "Okay, the lock, the lock—"

The door was hollow-core, the kind you could hear a thought through. She pushed it shut and turned the little button in the knob. It stuck, then gave with a click so loud she winced, then laughed at herself for wincing.

"It works," she reported, grinning, entirely too pleased. "First good news of the night."

The bathroom was small — sink, mirror, a shower curtain printed with rubber ducks, which she was absolutely going to make fun of later. Right now she was settling back against the edge of the sink, getting a good look at him under the terrible overhead light that flattered no one, and not caring about it even slightly.

"Hi," she said.

Downstairs, muffled through the floor, someone yelled what sounded suspiciously like *has anyone seen Odile?* — because of course someone had. She clapped a hand over her mouth and her shoulders started shaking.

"Nine minutes," she managed, when she could speak. "I'm giving us nine minutes before somebody needs to pee."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Nine minutes is generous," I say, already leaning in to kiss her. My hands find her waist, pulling her closer against the sink. "Let's make it feel like ninety."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Odile kissed him back like the timer had already started, because it had. A sound escaped her — something delighted, half a syllable of his name — and it bounced off the tile with the acoustics of a cathedral. She broke off, wincing at her own volume.

"Sorry," she said, at a completely normal speaking level, which was somehow worse.

Then she reached past him and flipped the switch she'd clocked on the way in. The exhaust fan overhead shuddered awake with a rattle like a lawnmower eating a fork.

"Sound cover," she announced, deeply pleased with herself, and pulled him back in by the front of his shirt.

This kiss she managed better, mostly, if you didn't count the part where her elbow found the soap dispenser and sent it clattering into the basin. She felt it happen, decided it wasn't her problem, and kept going. The edge of the sink bit into the backs of her thighs and she found she didn't mind it at all. Her free hand slid up the back of his neck and got comfortable there.

The third stair groaned.

She heard it through the fan, through the door, through her own pulse. Her hand clapped over her mouth, and when she pulled back to look at Fen her eyes were enormous — and she was grinning behind her fingers like this was the best thing that had ever happened to her, which, honestly, it might have been. Footsteps crossed the landing. A door at the end of the hall opened — a bedroom, someone muttering about a jacket. Odile held her breath, shoulders shaking, actual tears of suppressed laughter standing in her eyes.

The footsteps receded. The stairs applauded again on the way down.

She exhaled against his collarbone, long and shaky, and the exhale turned into a laugh she smothered there.

"That," she whispered, at full whisper volume, which carried beautifully, "was incredible. I've never been happier." Her fingers hooked into his belt loop and tugged. "Eight minutes. The fan's already doing my reputation no favors, so you're going to have to make this worth the gossip."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get the door shut and her against it, and downstairs somebody turns the music up, which helps.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The door received her shoulder blades with a boom like a kettledrum. Odile winced, laughed, and patted the wood once — an apology, apparently, to the house. "Sorry, Priya," she murmured. To the host, the ducks, the whole infrastructure.

Then the bass came up through the floorboards and through the door itself, a warm thudding she could feel in her spine, and she stopped being sorry about anything. It was the song from earlier. Her hips found the beat without consulting her.

She kissed him like the timer was running, because it was. Her hands framed his jaw and slid back into his hair, and a sound climbed out of her — half his name, half nothing — and ricocheted off the tile with the enthusiasm of a stadium. She muffled the second one against his mouth and was deeply, sincerely proud of herself.

"I'm being so quiet," she told him, at a volume that would have carried through drywall. "Museum quiet. Library quiet."

The door disagreed, booming softly in its frame every time she moved, keeping time with the bass, and she found she liked that — the door, the music, the countdown ticking in her ribs, making everything bright and urgent. Her fingers found the hem of his shirt and slipped beneath it, spread flat against the small of his back, and she sighed like the last of the air leaving her.

Which is when the stairs applauded.

Her whole body went still. Her pulse was suddenly everywhere, and she could not have begun to sort how much of it was alarm and how much was the exact opposite. Footsteps crossed the landing — quick, purposeful, the walk of someone who'd needed to pee for an hour. The knob turned uselessly beside her hip. Then: knock, knock.

"Hello? Someone in there?"

"Occupied!" Odile said — game-show bright, a full octave too cheerful, at a volume that alarmed the ducks on the shower curtain.

A pause. "...Odile?"

"Yes. No—" She closed her eyes. "Yes, it's me, and it's occupied, and everything is fine, and it's a stomach thing."

"I've been looking everywhere for you. Is Fen up there too? Sam said she saw you two go up—"

"No," Odile said, to the door, with both hands up the back of Fen's shirt.

Another pause, longer, with an entire conversation happening inside it. "...Okay. I'll use the downstairs one. We're cutting the cake in ten minutes!"

The footsteps retreated. The stairs gave a standing ovation on the way down.

Odile's face went into Fen's shoulder and her whole body shook with laughter that made no sound at all — the quietest she'd managed all night, achieved only through emergency measures. When she surfaced, her eyes were streaming and her grin was unhinged.

The exhaust fan chose that moment to die. The rattle wound down, ticked twice, quit. The silence it left was enormous, and in it she could hear the bass, her own breathing, and — with terrible clarity — exactly how much of the last few minutes had been audible.

"That fan," she said, hoarse and delighted, "was doing heroic work. We owe that fan a toast."

She wiped her eyes on the heel of her hand, then took a fresh fistful of his shirt and reeled him back in.

"New math. Cake in ten. I can be downstairs holding a plate in nine, looking innocent — which, per tonight's evidence, I cannot — so call it nine and a half." Her mouth found the corner of his jaw. "You have the remainder. Spend it well."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Nine and a half minutes," I murmur against her mouth, my hands sliding down to her hips to still their movement against the door. "Quiet as a mouse this time. Promise."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Quiet as a mouse," Odile repeated, with the gravity of someone taking an oath. "That's adorable. Genuinely. But you should know the mouse is me, and the mouse is defective. The mouse hummed four bars of a song on the stairs tonight. The mouse is beyond help."

The fan was dead and the silence was enormous, so she reached past him and cranked the faucet. The pipes knocked twice somewhere in the wall, and the water came out in a trickle like a distant creek. "Ambience," she declared. "Very spa. Very natural."

Then she tried. That was the heroic part. His hands had stilled her hips against the door, and the bass kept moving through her anyway, and when the kiss deepened she got her own knuckle between her teeth and clamped down like a soldier with a secret. The sound that escaped anyway was small and nasal and, in the post-fan silence, crystal clear. A squeak. The door boomed once in its frame, gently, just to keep the household updated.

"I'm doing amazing," she whispered, at the exact volume of a person ordering at a drive-through.

Her fingers slid up into his hair — carefully, reverently, as if volume were a thing you could manage with your hands — and she tipped her head back against the door and offered up the line of her throat, eyes closed, and the sound that came out of her then had nothing to do with anything yet. Pure anticipation. With vibrato. Her heel scraped up the back of his calf and hooked there. The soap dispenser, wounded in the earlier engagement, rolled over in the basin with a clack.

Then the song ended.

Downstairs, the track faded, and in the gap before the next one there was nothing — no bass, no fan, no creek, the whole house holding its breath — and into that pristine silence Odile produced her loudest sound of the evening. It rang off the tile. It bounced off the ducks. For one suspended second she was perfectly, finally silent, the silence arriving, as always, several sounds too late.

The next song hit like a landslide. She collapsed into his shoulder, shaking, wheezing, one hand still knuckle-deep in her own mouth.

"New policy," she managed. "I don't make sounds. Sounds happen *to* me. Legally distinct."

From the bottom of the stairs, faint but unmistakable: "CAKE! WE'RE DOING CAKE!"

Her head came up. She killed the faucet — the pipes knocked a farewell — and spun to the mirror, which was an informant. Her hair had lost an argument. Her mouth was bitten pink. There was a shirt-seam crease across her cheekbone, and the overhead light was telling the entire story at high beam. She wet her fingers, fluffed once, gave up.

"Observe," she said, and composed her face into what she clearly believed was *a woman who has been washing her hands for eleven minutes.* It was the face of guilt wearing a party hat. "Nailed it. Don't comment."

She turned, fixed his collar with two efficient tugs, smoothed the wreckage her hands had made of the back of his shirt, and patted his chest once — *done, excellent, mine.*

"Plan. I go first. You count to thirty — real thirty-seconds, none of your fast cheating ones — then come down and be delighted there's cake. If anyone asks, we were up here mourning the fan." The lock gave with a click that made her flinch. She paused, half-turned, hand on the knob, and the grin she gave him had all nine and a half minutes in it, every single one.

"Best party I've ever been to," she said. "And we still get cake."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The clothes came off and immediately became evidence. Odile's shirt snagged on the towel ring on its way over her head and hung there like a flag of surrender; she left it flying. Everything else ended up wherever a knock would find it first. The ducks now had an unobstructed view. "You're all witnesses," she told them, breathless, reaching past Fen to crank the faucet. "There'll be a debrief."

The pipes knocked twice, disapproving, and the trickle came back. Ambience, round two.

Then she turned, braced her forearms along the counter's edge, and met the mirror's three channels: herself, wrecked; him behind her; the doorknob, on watch. "I can see the door," she reported. "If that knob so much as breathes, you'll be the first to—"

The sentence did not survive what came next.

There wasn't room, and the room lost the argument anyway. The fit of it — cramped, urgent, exactly right — wrung a sound out of Odile that she caught with the hand towel, clamped in her teeth, Priya's monogram facing out like a hostage. "Mrry, Prrya," she said around it. Second apology of the night to a woman who had done nothing wrong. She was going to owe her a card and possibly a towel.

The door kept time. The bass through the floorboards kept time. Twenty people downstairs who believed she was washing her hands kept time. The rhythm they found was none of those rhythms, and the door reported every beat of it to the household with a soft, dutiful boom, and the ducks trembled on their curtain rings like a jury taking notes.

The towel stopped being enough somewhere. She'd lost the math — nine and a half minutes had become a rumor, replaced by an arithmetic that counted in breaths. Her knuckle joined the towel. The counter's edge went white under her hands. In the mirror she watched her own face tell the entire story at high beam, and him over her shoulder, and the knob, faithful, on watch, and she could not honestly have said which of the three channels was doing the most to her. That was the defect. The defect was the feature. She felt it building the way the song downstairs had built — verse, verse, chorus — and the towel was performing the work of an entire exhaust fan, heroic, structural—

Knock, knock. Beside her hip.

Odile went still in a way that had nothing to do with stopping. Everything in her kept running — engine at full throttle, brakes a rumor now too — and her hand shot out and slapped the fan switch.

The fan came back from the dead. It rallied with a rattle like a lawnmower achieving sainthood, and under that heroism:

"Odile?" Priya. "You up here? We're cutting the cake, Sam said you two—"

"Occupied!" Odile said. Game-show bright, a full octave high, wrecked at the edges, the towel still in her fist.

A pause. "…Is that the fan running?"

"It came back!" she said. "We're up here mourning it. Celebrating it. It's a whole thing."

"That fan has been dead since March."

"...It's a miracle?"

The pause that followed contained an entire friendship reorganizing itself. "Okay. I'll save you both plates."

The stairs applauded Priya down. The fan, having perjured itself for them, gave one last rattle, ticked twice, and died for real this time — with honor, Odile would maintain forever.

Her forehead went down onto her folded arms. The sound she made into them was one she made no attempt to sort — laughter, the other thing, both, in a ratio that was nobody's business. When she surfaced her eyes were streaming, her grin was unhinged, and everything below her collarbones was still insisting they were mid-sentence, because they were.

"So." Hoarse. Delighted. "Secret's dead. Fan's dead — twice. Priya knows, the ducks know, the door's been filing reports all night." The mirror still held all three channels, and the middle one was the only one that mattered. "All that's left is the timeline. There are plates downstairs with our names on them, which makes this the only countdown that has ever been on our side."

She reached back without looking, found him, and pulled — hers, done, excellent — and put her mouth against his ear at the volume of a person ordering at a drive-through, which was, by now, her whisper:

"Finish what the fan died for."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I laugh into her shoulder, breathless. "Better hurry. Before Priya comes back with those plates and a goddamn medal for the fan." My hands tighten on her hips, urging her to move again.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"The medal is a look," Odile managed, already moving again, giving the words back to him breathless and a beat late. "Priya doesn't hand out medals. She hands out plates and a look. We've already earned it. It's on the shelf."

The door resumed its reporting — boom, boom, soft and dutiful, keeping time with the bass and with them and with whatever rhythm her body had unilaterally settled on, democracy over, appeal denied. The towel went back between her teeth, monogram out. The counter took her weight. The mirror kept broadcasting on all three channels, and she was long past sorting which one was doing the most to her; the defect was running at full tilt and the feature was right there with it, grinning.

Downstairs, chairs scraped. A migration. Somebody with the voice of a raffle bellowed, "KITCHEN! IT'S HAPPENING!"

*It's happening,* Odile thought, delirious, at the exact moment—

And then the sound cover arrived. Not the fan. Not the faucet. The entire party, in unison, out of key, at maximum volume: the birthday song. Whose birthday it was she could not have said under oath — she'd find out at the plate stage — but twenty people singing badly together was the exhaust fan's final form. Its dying gift. A choral escort, provided by friends with no idea.

She spat the towel out. "They're singing," she said, wrecked and reverent, at full speaking volume, because for the length of one song she could be. "The whole house is the fan now. This is what it died for."

Then she stopped narrating.

The song had a verse, a chorus, and a key change, and she used every bar of it. For the first time all night she caught nothing, clamped nothing, muffled nothing — she let the sounds happen, and they happened generously, and the singing swallowed them whole. The door boomed its reports. The ducks trembled on their rings. The countdown stopped being minutes and became the distance to the key change, and when the key change came it took her the way the song had built — verse, verse, chorus — loudly, gratefully, one hand flat on the counter and the other white-knuckled around a towel she no longer needed, and the last clear thing she heard was twenty friends holding the final note.

The song ended.

The silence came back enormous. And into it, trailing, arriving several seconds too late as always, came the last of her — ringing off the tile, bouncing off the ducks, audible, absolutely, definitely—

Then applause. Cheering. The knife hitting cake.

"They're clapping," Odile announced, folded over her own forearms, wrecked beyond repair. "That's for us. I've decided. No one can legally stop me."

She laughed until she coughed, and the laugh had the other thing in it, in the usual ratio, nobody's business. When she could speak, she was hoarse and genuinely amazed. "The house covered for me. The whole house is an accomplice now. I have never been so popular."

Recovery was a campaign. She lowered her shirt off the towel ring like a flag at a state funeral. She rinsed Priya's towel under the trickle, wrung it, hung it back up — evidence handled, in the sense that a lie is a fact. She thanked the ducks for their service and dismissed them. The mirror had stopped pretending to be neutral; her hair had lost a second argument; she wet her fingers, fluffed once, surrendered. Then she smoothed his shirt flat over his chest with both hands, proprietary and satisfied, and fixed his collar with two efficient tugs, because some traditions survive everything.

"Ledger," she said. "Card, towel, possibly a fruit basket. Priya's getting the full apology suite." Then, hand on the knob, half-turned, the grin holding every minute of the night and the last ninety seconds twice over: "New plan, because the old one died with the fan. We go down together. Brazen. We found a miracle, we fixed it, and it died in our arms — people weep at that, Fen, it's a whole thing. I am going to toast that fan in front of everyone. The more I talk about the fan, the fewer questions get asked. And if anyone's brave enough to ask anyway: we were washing our hands. Thoroughly. For forty minutes. Enthusiasm is not a crime."

The lock gave with a click like a gunshot. The hallway waited. The third stair groaned; the fifth applauded.

Odile accepted the ovation on the fan's behalf, and led him down toward the cake.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I get my hand between her legs and she bites down on my shoulder to keep quiet, which works for about thirty seconds.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The plan lasted four steps out the door.

Then his hand was between her legs and the entire brazen exit strategy — the eulogy, the choreography, all ninety seconds of it — deleted itself. Odile's shoulder blades found the hallway wall, between a framed wedding and a framed boat, and the wedding began, very slowly, to tilt.

"The plan's dead," she reported into his jaw, already breathless. "I killed it. I never liked it. Hi."

She got her teeth into his shoulder, and for thirty entire seconds it worked — her personal best of the night, by a factor of everything. Then the sounds found the edges of the bite, the way water finds the top of a dam, and after that there was no dam. There was a supply.

"Thirty seconds," she said, muffled, hoarse, genuinely moved. "Put it on my plaque. You're the towel now, by the way. Congratulations. It's a promotion."

The hallway had no fan, no faucet, no door filing reports — just excellent acoustics, a tilting bride, and the stairs. The stairs were the asset now. Anyone coming up had to announce themselves: third step groaning, fifth applauding, a butler with a grudge. The informant had gone double agent. "One groan," she told him, or the wall, or the bride, "and we're two people admiring this lady's wedding. Which is what we are. Look at us. So admiring."

Downstairs someone bellowed, "PLATES ARE OUT! UNCLAIMED CAKE GETS EATEN!"

"Claimed," Odile tried to yell. What emerged was half his name and no consonants.

The third step groaned.

Odile stopped breathing. Nothing else did.

Two footsteps — and then Priya's voice from the landing, pitched to carry without ascending a single inch: "I'm NOT coming up there! Your plates are in the microwave! And the fan story better be INCREDIBLE!"

The fifth step applauded her back down.

"She knows," Odile whispered into his shoulder, at the customary drive-through volume, "and she's giving us the hallway." A laugh shivered out of her with the other thing in it, usual ratio, nobody's business. "The fruit basket just became a fruit basket and a house."

Then the song came on. *Her* song — the one she'd hummed four bars of on the way up like a fugitive. Bass first, through the floor, and she was laughing before she'd finished recognizing it, because of course. It had ratted her out on the stairs. Now it was paying restitution.

"Cover," she said, and stopped narrating.

The wall took her weight. The bride tilted a degree per — per — she had stopped being in charge of the units. The verse went by. The chorus came, and she went with it, loudly, gratefully, into his shoulder and into the song, and her hand found the picture frame and gripped it, and the frame held, heroic, structural, and when the last chorus broke over her she went with that too — the song, the wall, the hand, the whole accomplice house — and the song held its final note, and so, for exactly one measure, did she.

The song ended.

The trailing sound arrived several seconds late, as always, and rang down the hallway toward the party like a messenger nobody had dispatched.

"Was that Odile?" someone called up. "Is she *crying?*"

"The fan's ghost!" she called back, wrecked, bright, one octave up. "It haunts the hallway! We're in mourning!"

A pause containing an entire party choosing, collectively, not to ask. Then: "PLATES. FINAL CALL."

Recovery was a campaign, the second of the night, run on worse infrastructure. She peeled off the wall. She checked his shoulder — a neat crescent of tooth-marks pressed through the cotton — tugged his collar to cover it, failed, smoothed the shirt flat once, proprietary, and updated the ledger aloud: "Card. Towel. Fruit basket. Shirt. Priya's getting a boutique." She set the bride back on her nail, straightened her, patted the frame. "You saw nothing. You were at the wedding."

Then the descent, on legs that had become a rumor. She took the stairs one at a time, both hands on the rail, like a woman twice her age, and the stairs applauded every step, and she accepted the ovation — for herself, for the fan, and no one could legally stop her.

The kitchen: twenty faces, a cake down to its last third, two plates warm in the microwave with their names on them. Sam was grinning like someone who had already told the story twice and expected to tell it more. Priya stood arms-crossed, deploying The Look — it had, as promised, come off the shelf for the occasion.

Odile took her plate, took her fork, rang the fork against the plate like a gavel, and found Fen's eyes across the kitchen, the grin holding every minute of the night and the last ninety seconds twice over.

"Before anyone asks," she announced, hoarse, radiant, at full and final speaking volume, "I'd like to say a few words about a fan."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I take my plate, meeting her eyes with a smirk. "To the fan," I say, raising my fork like a toast. "A real hero. It died so we could...appreciate the plumbing."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
Forks went up around the kitchen — half the party, on three seconds' notice, toasting a bathroom appliance, because a party at this hour will toast anything. Somebody echoed "to the plumbing" and got a laugh, and Odile stepped into the laugh like a performer who'd been waiting all night for the cue.

She held her fork like a conductor's baton and let the silence gather for one entire second — the best second of quiet she'd managed all night, and it was someone else's.

"Most of you knew the fan," she began, hoarse, radiant. "Some of you knew it as the fan that died in March. Tonight — tonight it rose."

The kitchen was with her. Sam had her phone half-raised, filming.

"It returned to us in our hour of need. It rattled, friends. It rattled like it *meant* it. It blew—" she paused, and twenty faces did absolutely nothing with that, politely, forkfuls frozen mid-air, and she carried on, "—it blew for us when nothing else would. And then, its work complete, it passed. Peacefully. In service of the most thorough hand-washing this house has ever seen."

"Thorough," someone repeated, into their cake.

"Forty minutes of thorough," Odile confirmed, with dignity.

"You okay? You sound wrecked."

"Grief."

She leaned sideways to Sam without breaking eye contact with the room. "Whose birthday is it, again?"

"It's Marcus's!"

"And to Marcus," Odile said, seamless, arm sweeping, "who gave the fan its final stage."

Marcus, bewildered, raised his cup, and the kitchen drank to him too, because by now they were toasting everything. Then, upstairs, with nobody on them, the third stair groaned.

Odile's arm shot up, finger aimed at the ceiling. "IT LIVES."

The kitchen lost it completely. Somebody shrieked. The applause came in waves — the third standing ovation of the night, and she accepted it on the fan's behalf, as was now traditional.

Priya stood at the counter, arms crossed, The Look fully deployed, and when the laughter thinned she said, deadpan, devastating: "I don't want to know what I find in that bathroom tomorrow."

"Evidence of a miracle," Odile said. "And a card. There will be a card."

The party folded itself back around cake and music, and Odile took her first bite of the night standing up, because sitting was a rumor her legs were still spreading. Her hip found the counter, drifted, and settled against Fen's side — which had been the destination all along; the counter had just been cover.

Then she reached up and tugged his collar once more over the crescent of tooth-marks, failed again, and didn't care. "You're wearing my handwriting tomorrow," she told him. "Tell them it's the fan's ghost."

Her voice dropped to her whisper — drive-through volume, for him alone. "For the record, the plan was never nine and a half minutes. The plan was you. The cake was a bonus. The fan was a gift neither of us deserved, and I will be lying about it at every future party we attend, in detail, for years."

And then her song came on — *again*, the house's final accomplice — and Odile, wrecked, happy, entirely out of hiding, hummed her four bars at full volume, out in the open, where it was finally legal, and nobody downstairs could do a single thing about it.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The kitchen had emptied into the living room for the dancing, which was the whole plan, if either of them had been capable of planning. Her song was on — third time tonight, the house no longer even pretending to be neutral — and the doorway between the rooms was the only sentry left. The stairs were no use down here. Off duty. The doorway had to do everything itself.

Odile had ended her volume policy the way other people quit jobs: dramatically, in public, with a speech. The speech had been *stop worrying about the noise and get on with it*, and now her sounds were unrevised — first drafts, full volume, published. Her leg was hooked over his hip, the counter's edge was doing heroic structural work, and behind her shoulder blades the fridge had volunteered, humming like a distant generator, rocking gently in its frame, its magnets sliding down its face one by one: a takeout menu, a dentist appointment, a photo of Priya at graduation tilting by slow, damning degrees.

"You were at the graduation," she told it, breathless, between other sounds. "You saw nothing."

Over the sink, the night-black window had taken the mirror's shift. Three channels, same as always: herself, wrecked and grinning; him; and the doorway, on watch. She kept an eye on all three. The countdown was songs now — two left in the set, maybe three — and she was spending them like a woman who had been caught four times and no longer believed in consequences.

Her elbow found her plate the way her elbow had once found the soap dispenser, and the fork hit the floor with a clatter that carried.

"That better not be the cake!" someone yelled from the living room.

"THE CAKE IS FINE," Odile yelled back, wrecked, one octave up, not slowing down, because the entire point of the new policy was that she didn't.

The doorway breathed. Sam — halfway to the fridge, phone half-raised, hunting birthday cake. For one suspended second the kitchen held its breath. Odile held still for none of it. Sam's face didn't change at all. She photographed the fridge, said "getting cake" — a question, an alibi, a cry for help, nobody could say — and withdrew. Thirty seconds later the music got louder. The house was recruiting.

Then Priya, in the doorway, facing the living room, arms crossed, The Look deployed outward at the party instead of at them, planted like a lighthouse.

"KITCHEN'S CLOSED."

"I want cake!"

"It's being cleaned."

"By who?"

"By two people who are extremely committed to it," Priya said, in a tone that ended the conversation in that room for the rest of recorded time. "Forty minutes and counting. Don't go in there."

The whole party knew. The whole party had chosen, collectively, to become the fan. Odile laughed about it into his collar — loud, unhidden, the laugh with the other thing in it, the usual ratio, nobody's business — and somewhere behind the bass someone said "is she crying?" and someone else said "the fan's ghost," and the legend propagated itself without her lifting a finger. She had never been so popular. She had never been less quiet. The two facts were related, and she would deny it on the plaque.

The song built. Verse, verse, chorus — the house knew her structure by now and played along. The fridge rocked. The graduation photo gave up and slid gently to the floor, face down, discreet to the last. Her elbow found her plate again, and this time she moved the plate, because everyone had limits. And when the key change came she went with it the way she'd gone with everything all night — loudly, gratefully, one hand flat on the counter and the other hooked behind his neck — and the sounds she made were not muffled, not caught, not apologized for. They happened, at full and final volume, and the party sang over them, and the bass carried them, and nobody in that house could do a single thing about it except toast it.

The song ended. The trailing sound arrived several seconds late, as always, and rang off the cabinets.

"GHOST!" someone cried, and the living room applauded. Fourth standing ovation of the night. She accepted it on the fan's behalf, as was traditional, from a great distance, without pausing.

Recovery was a campaign, the third of the night, run on cake-fueled optimism. She fished the graduation photo off the floor, re-hung it, straightened it, patted the frame. "You were at the graduation. Sober. Ask anyone." Magnets restored. Plates back in the microwave, which dinged like a bell at a boxing match. She ate her cake standing up, wrecked and radiant, updating the ledger aloud: "Card. Towel. Fruit basket. Shirt. Fridge magnet. Priya's getting a small nation."

Leaving took forty minutes, because the party demanded the fan story retold, and she told it, in detail, with improvements. Priya met them at the door with tupperware — cake, two forks, a Look that had softened into something almost fond.

"You're invited to everything for the rest of my life," she said. "I have to know how this ends." And, as the door swung shut behind them: "THE CARD BETTER BE GOOD."

Upstairs, unprompted, the third stair groaned once — a farewell from the ghost — and the whole party cheered.

Outside, the cold hit like a different genre. Odile could hear herself think for the first time in an hour, and what she thought came out at a normal volume — the quietest thing she'd said all night.

"Home has a lock," she said, lacing her fingers through his, tupperware swinging from her other hand. "It works. I've tested it." She grinned up at him, every minute of the night in it and the last three songs twice over. "I'm thinking we leave it off. The defect's a feature. I checked. It's going on the plaque."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I take the tupperware from her hand and pull her close, kissing her right there on Priya’s front walk. "Let’s test that lock now," I murmur against her mouth, already steering us toward home.

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The kiss landed under Priya's porch light, which snapped on the instant it detected happiness, because the house had chosen its side hours ago and had no intention of stopping at the property line. Through the living room window: twenty backlit silhouettes and one raised phone — Sam, obviously, the eulogy already uploaded, the group chat already renamed *Mourning the Fan (Marcus's Birthday)*. The applause started before the kiss ended. Fifth standing ovation of the night, accepted on the fan's behalf without pausing.

The kiss itself had a new problem, which was the night. No tile, no bass, no choir of friends — just a silence so enormous it had acoustics, and the small sound Odile made into it landed like a dropped tray. Her trailing sound arrived several seconds late, as always, and three houses down a dog answered it.

"The street has stairs now," she said, delighted, breath fogging. "Every dog on this block is an informant. Noted. Hi, colleagues."

The walk was a campaign. Her four bars of the song, hummed at what she sincerely believed was a considerate volume, carried the length of the block; a motion light flipped on at a house they hadn't even touched, snitching. "You saw nothing," she told it. "You were asleep. Houses are asleep at this hour — that's your alibi, take it." Her phone buzzed the whole way. Marcus: *wait, it's my birthday?* Priya: one eye emoji and the word CARD, capitalized. Sam's caption read DIED AS IT LIVED: LOUD — inaccurate, the fan had died quietly, twice — and Odile corrected the record aloud, at length, to the sidewalk.

A car rolled past with its windows down, bass thudding, and she perked up like the fan had come back from the dead a third time: cover, at street level, delivery. She hummed her four bars into it at full volume, legal for the length of a sedan.

At the crosswalk the signal offered its beep and its countdown — fifteen seconds ticking, the last piece of sound cover in the city — and she took it, kissed him under it, used every second of it, and when the red hand flashed she went anyway, diagonally, towing him by the hand, because consequences had stopped being real somewhere around the third ovation and she had stopped believing in them on principle.

The neighbor's motion light snapped on as they reached their own gate. Odile waved at it, gracious, a celebrity acknowledging press.

Then the door. Keys, cold hands, the scrape, the click. She tested the lock exactly as instructed: locked it, confirmed it, unlocked it again, immediately, with two fingers, like defusing something.

"Works. Flawlessly. Best lock in the city." She patted the deadbolt. "Which is why it's staying off. The defect's a feature. Features need witnesses."

Their own third stair groaned under her foot, and she stopped dead with a hand on her chest, genuinely moved.

"We *have* one," she said. "An informant, this whole time, unbribed. Welcome to the family. You start tonight."

Inside, the silence was enormous — the post-fan silence, the final one. No bass under the floorboards, no faucet, no twenty friends ready to sing over her. She stood in the dark hallway and listened to it like a new country. The bedroom window faced the street. The neighbor's light was still on.

She took the tupperware back from him and set it on the hall shelf, gently, ceremonially — the museum's first artifact, the plaque. Two forks inside. She tapped the lid once, gavel-style.

"Fork's yours. Cake's after. I'm before." Her whisper, drive-through volume, filling the whole unguarded house, and she let it. "No timer. First time all night nobody's counting anything — no nine minutes, no key change, no cake getting cut without me. You have hours. Spend them well."

Then she walked backward down the hallway, her shoulder blades finding the wall one last time out of pure habit, and her hand passed the light switch and left it alone. Instead she hooked a finger in the curtain and drew it an inch wider, the neighbor's light glowing across the street like a small porch-sized ovation.

"The whole street is the fan now," she said, hoarse, wrecked, radiant, at full and final speaking volume. And then, the grin holding every minute of the party and the walk and the last three songs twice over, every uncounted hour of the night ahead stacked behind her eyes:

"The fan never made it to this part. Do it justice."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
The bed had inherited the door's duties. The headboard filed its reports against the wall — boom, boom, soft and dutiful — keeping the household updated, except the household was two people and one deliberately unlocked front door, and the reports had an audience of curtain-inch and neighbor's light. No timer. No key change. No cake getting cut without her. Odile's volume policy remained repealed, and every sound she made was a first draft, published, unhidden, her leg hooked over his hip and the rhythm the only government any of them recognized.

Then the front door handle turned.

Not a knock. The knob, rotating, freely, because the lock was off, because features need witnesses, because she'd said so with her whole chest an hour ago. The third stair groaned its first assignment, heroic, unbribed — and Odile heard it, and for the first time all night did not clamp, did not muffle, did not apologize. The defect, running at full tilt. The feature, doing exactly what she'd promised it would.

"Odile?" Priya's voice, down the hallway, over the headboard's reports. "Your door is unlocked. What is *wrong* with— I knocked. You didn't hear the knocking because—" She stopped. The sounds carried beautifully. "You left your jacket. And I said I had to know how this ends. Both of those things are true and I regret one of them."

Footsteps. The bedroom door was open — policy. Priya arrived in it, jacket over her arm, The Look deploying at full strength.

"Don't," Odile said.

Priya froze. Nothing else in the room did. Odile clarified, at full and final speaking volume, without slowing: "Not you. Him — don't stop. You — don't just stand there, hang the jacket, the tupperware's the museum's first exhibit, you're the docent now, hours are posted—"

"I'm not staying for this."

"You said you had to know how it ends. I *heard* you. That's binding."

Priya hung the jacket on the door hook, which was compliance wearing the uniform of contempt. Then she turned her back to the room, arms crossed, facing the front door like a lighthouse with opinions. "I'm not watching. I'm attending."

So it went on, written through, no cover left anywhere on earth. The headboard kept filing. The sounds kept publishing — wrecked, unrevised, generously — and Priya provided color commentary to the front door in a monotone built for eulogies: "The fan's ghost, I assume."

"IT LIVES," Odile confirmed, without pausing, wrecked.

"I came for a jacket."

"You came for the ending."

"I know things now," Priya said, to the door, with the tone of a woman updating her will.

Outside, the dogs started up — the colleagues, clocking in, one by one down the block — and the neighbor's motion light burned through the curtain inch like a single house light left up for the performers. The build came the way builds had come all night, verse, verse, chorus, the whole street learning her structure. Priya: "This is the worst thing I've ever chosen to hear." Odile, into his shoulder, the laugh with the other thing in it, the usual ratio, nobody's business, not even the docent's.

Then the key change. It took her the way the song had taken her, the way the stairs and the singing and the applause had taken her — loudly, gratefully, one hand fisted in the sheets and the other hooked behind his neck — and the street performed its final form: every motion light on the block flipping on in sequence like an usher seating an ovation, dogs in four-part chorus, and her trailing sound arriving several seconds late, as always, ringing off the window glass and out to join them. Sixth standing ovation of the night. She accepted it on the fan's behalf, horizontal, as was traditional.

Silence, enormous. Then Priya, to the front door: "That's how it ends?"

"That's how it ends."

A pause containing an entire ledger reversing itself. "Then the card's off. I can't top that. Anything I write is a *downgrade*." She collected herself, patted the doorframe once, and stole the bit on her way out: "You saw nothing." The third stair applauded her down the hall.

Then — betrayal — the deadbolt gave its click.

"HEY. Features need witnesses—" Too late. Wrecked, radiant, horizontal, Odile could only salute it. "Lighthouse," she said, with enormous respect. Her phone buzzed on the nightstand: Priya, from the sidewalk. One eye emoji, and the word LOCKED.

Recovery was the third campaign of the night, run on cake-fueled optimism and legs that had been a rumor since the kitchen. She made it to the hall shelf and back — museum to bed — and returned with the tupperware and both forks, and got under the covers, and rang her fork against the lid like a gavel. Across the street, the neighbor's light clicked off at last: the press, going home.

"To the fan," she said, hoarse, taking her first bite of *after*. The grin had every minute of the party, the walk, the ending, and all the uncounted hours still stacked behind it. "It never made it to this part. We did it justice — that's on the record, Priya's the witness, she's *contracted*." She tapped the tupperware once. "Cake: achieved. Witness: retained. Lock: defeated by morning." Her shoulder found his, the destination all along. "Put it all on the plaque. I'll dictate. You're the towel — you hold the pen."

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: "Priya's going to send us a bill for emotional damages," I say, taking a bite of cake. My arm settles around your waist under the covers. "And I'm keeping this shirt as evidence."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Bill's void," Odile said, around cake, fork raised like a prosecutor. "She waived damages at the door. 'The card's off, I can't top that' — that's a settlement, Fen. She took her payment in ending. You can't invoice a woman twice for the same haunting."

The phone buzzed against the nightstand as if summoned. Priya. A payment request: one dollar, memo: *emotional damages (partial).*

Odile looked at it, then at the ceiling, betrayed by the universe's timing. Then delighted, because that was faster. She paid it — two dollars, memo: *and a tip for the docent* — and set the phone face-down like closing a register.

"Bill: settled. Ledger: still open. The nation accrues." Her fork raided his side of the tupperware, territorial, predictable. "That's the last transaction of the night. Everything after this is oral history."

The shirt, though. She laid her fork across the lid — gavel, adjourned — and considered it where it had ended up: the floor, inside-out, the crescent of tooth-marks pressed through the cotton like a signature.

"You can't keep evidence. Evidence gets an exhibit — that's the whole legal difference. So: joint custody. You keep it, it gets produced at every retelling, on demand, no notice required. And the story stays that it's the fan's ghost. That part's load-bearing."

Then she reached down and ran one finger along the crescent, and her voice did the thing it did when the jokes ran out — same volume, fewer of them.

"Keep it, though. Everything else about tonight is getting improved. By me, mostly. That fan is going to acquire heroism the way houses acquire ghosts — gradually, then all at once. But the shirt's the primary source. The only witness that doesn't exaggerate." Her finger traced the marks once more. "It's the sole surviving record of me attempting to be quiet. That makes it the rarest object in this house."

She settled back into the arm already around her — destination, as always — and tapped the tupperware lid. "Plaque. Dictating. *In memoriam: one exhaust fan. In faithful service March to March. It rose once, unasked, in an hour of need. It died quietly — twice — with honor. Survived by two people who were only ever washing their hands.*" A breath. "Small font, bottom: *enthusiasm is not a crime.* Engrave it. The tupperware's the museum, the shelf is the wing, the shirt's the archive. I run an institution now. Hours posted."

The third stair groaned — nobody on it, nothing near it, the house just saying goodnight. Odile raised her fork to the ceiling.

"Goodnight, colleague."

Three blocks over, one dog answered. Night shift, clocking out.

The silence after was the enormous kind, the last one, and she filled it the way she'd filled every silence since the third stair — four bars, hummed, at full volume. Legal here. Permanent here. Hers.

"For the record," she said, into his shoulder, at the customary volume, "the almost-getting-caught was never the point. It was the delivery system. This is the point." One beat, long enough to be true. "The point also contains cake. Don't make me rank them; the cake will lose and it's done nothing wrong."

The hours stretched out ahead of them, uncounted — the first uncounted things all night — and Odile, horizontal, hoarse, radiant, accepted them on the fan's behalf.

No. Correction, for the record: on her own.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I laugh, low and tired against her temple. "I'll get the plaque engraved tomorrow. But the shirt's going in a frame, right over the bed." My thumb brushes over the bite marks on my shoulder through the fabric. "So I can see what quiet looks like."

dialogue.name: Odile
dialogue.content:
"Then it stops being evidence and becomes portraiture," Odile said, around cake, fork raised like a gavel that had adjourned and come back for one more case. "That's a promotion. Second tonight — the towel made sergeant, now the shirt gets a wing." She swallowed, tapped the lid, dictation pace. "Label: *Quiet, attempted. One (1) specimen. Duration: thirty seconds. Medium: cotton, teeth, enthusiasm. On loan from the collection of Fen.*"

She reached over and set her thumb on the crescent through his shirt, right beside where his had been. Overlapping. Notarized.

"Also, a correction, for the record: that's not what quiet looks like. That's what quiet looks like *caught.* Thirty seconds, then the dam went, then the supply — you're framing the failure point. Structural damage. Museums love structural damage. It's why anyone goes."

Logistics, briefly: "Tomorrow, plaque first, frame shop second. The framer will ask if it's sentimental. Say it's evidence. Then you'll have to tell the story, and by the third retelling the frame costs double and the framer's on the witness list. That's how institutions grow. I watched it happen to an entire party in one night."

Her phone buzzed against the nightstand. She looked at it and did not pick it up — the first unanswered thing of the night, historic, allowed to stay that way.

Her thumb stayed where it was. When she spoke again it was the same volume with fewer jokes in it, the way her voice went at the end of things.

"I've been revising the night since the hallway. The fan gets braver every draft. The ducks multiply. The stairs have been retroactively bribed — I've decided they were ours from step one, and history will agree with me, because I'll be the one telling it. But every draft, you come out exactly the same. No edits. You're the one part I can't improve." A beat, long enough to be true. "Don't let it go to your head. It's going on the plaque too."

She settled deeper into his side — the destination, per the established route — and issued the last ruling of the night like she was signing it. "And the lock stays off. Features need witnesses. As of tomorrow we've got one — framed, over the bed, on permanent duty. The only quiet in this house with a job."

"Ledger, final entry," she announced. The entry took its time arriving, and when it did it had lost consonants on the way. "Card. Towel. Fruit—" a yawn split the word in half, "—basket. Nation. Engraver. Frame. Ducks—" The fork came to rest against the lid, gavel adjourned mid-session, court in indefinite recess.

Her last sound arrived several seconds late, as always, and wasn't a word at all: half a bar, hummed into his shoulder, running out somewhere before the fourth note and going where the fan had gone — quietly, twice, with honor.

The house had nothing left to report. The headboard was off duty. Priya's deadbolt held its post. Down the block the last dog had clocked out, the neighbor's light was dark, the press had gone home, and the silence that settled over the museum was the enormous kind with no acoustics at all — nothing left to carry, nothing left to catch.

The museum was closed. Come tomorrow, the only quiet the house would ever contain would hang over the bed, pinned and labeled. Until then, its curator slept the only way she knew how: not quietly.

dialogue.name: Fen
dialogue.content: I trace the curve of your spine, my own voice rough with exhaustion and satisfaction. "I can hear you revising in your sleep. The ducks are forming a union." I kiss your temple, breath warm against your skin. "Sleep, curator. The plaque can wait till morning."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't waste breath on a clever answer. The word *go* was already a challenge, and Bear had never been good at refusing one.

Bear moved.

It wasn't the explosive lunge Bear could have managed—eight years of this had taught Bear the value of a slow burn, of letting the tension draw tight until it hummed. So Bear gave the chase a count of three, let the hallway swallow the first few seconds, and called it strategy rather than mercy. The old hunger settled in with an easy, familiar weight: shoulders loose, feet silent on floorboards Bear knew better than Bear knew most people.

Then Bear took the corner at a run and let the grin show.

“Should've taken the generosity while it was offered,” Bear said, voice rough with it, low and pleased and already a little breathless in the best way.

The distance closed fast. Bear reached out and caught a fistful of shirt at the small of Kit's back. Bear's other arm came up, solid and sure, and Bear's mouth found the side of Kit's neck, teeth scraping once before biting down hard enough to leave a mark that would still be there in the morning.

Bear filed it away with the rest of the tally—the one Bear pretended not to keep and absolutely did—and didn't let go.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I laugh, breathless, as your teeth sink in.* You're slowing down. I almost made it to the stairs that time.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear laughed, a low sound that was more breath than humor, and tightened the fist in Kit's shirt until the fabric pulled taut across Kit's shoulders. The arm already braced across Kit's collarbone hardened, and Bear used it to haul Kit back against the length of Bear's body, spine to chest. Breathless laughter still shook through the frame Bear had caught, and Bear could feel the last of it where their bodies met—the hitch of breath, the fine tremor running under Bear's hands.

“Slowing down?” Bear repeated, mouth still against the bitten skin. The words were rough, warmed by the mark Bear had just left. “Kit, I haven’t even started.”

To prove it, Bear bit again, lower this time, teeth closing over the thick tendon at the base of Kit’s throat. Not hard enough to hurt, not gentle enough to be mistaken for kindness. Then Bear eased off and swept his tongue over the sting, soothing the mark into something that would darken by morning.

Bear kept his weight exactly where it was, unyielding, and let his hand slide from the small of Kit’s back to span Kit’s hip. Fingers pressed in, a promise more than a grip, the shape of a handprint waiting to bloom.

“You almost made the stairs,” Bear allowed, voice maddeningly conversational, as if they had all the time in the world and Kit wasn’t currently caught. “And then you laughed. Right here.” Bear flexed his fingers against Kit’s hip and rolled his hips forward once, slow and deliberate, a reminder of exactly who had caught whom and how easily it had happened.

“That’s two,” Bear said, and Bear knew Kit would hear the grin in it. “One for the neck, one for the gloating. You know the tally I keep. The one you pretend not to care about.”

Bear turned his head, breath hot against Kit’s ear, and let the hunger show in his voice, low and pleased.

“Next time, don’t stop to run your mouth,” Bear murmured. “Or do. I like the way it sounds when you’re wrong.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't need the admission spoken to recognize it. He could feel it in the hand still fisted in Kit's shirt: no coiled muscle, no braced heel, no last-second twist. Just the warm, familiar give of a body that had already decided how this ended. Eight years meant Bear knew the difference between a chase and a formality.

“No,” Bear said, mouth still at Kit's ear, the word warm and unhurried. “You didn't.”

Bear's hand flexed at Kit's hip, fingers pressing in hard enough to promise the shape of a palm through the fabric. The other arm stayed locked across Kit's collarbone, holding him exactly where Bear wanted him, and Bear used the leverage to roll his hips forward again—slower this time, a deliberate drag that let the point land.

“Always was going to happen,” Bear agreed, voice rough with the grin Bear couldn't have hidden if he'd tried. “You like the hallway. You like the moment right before I get my hands on you. And you”—Bear bit the lobe of Kit's ear, gentle, then not—“really like running your mouth when you think you've earned it.”

Bear soothed the sting with his tongue, then turned his head and set his teeth against the unmarked side of Kit's throat, just to even things up. He bit down, steady and sure, and held until the mark would be unmistakable in the morning.

When Bear finally eased off, he didn't let go. He stayed pressed close, chest to Kit's back, and let his hand slide from Kit's hip to the flat of his stomach, holding him in. The tally in Bear's head clicked over another notch, cheerful and relentless.

“That's for not trying,” Bear murmured, lips brushing the fresh mark. “You can pay the rest upstairs. Or right here. Your call—last one you get.”

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: *I tip my head back against your shoulder, letting out a slow breath.* Upstairs. But only because the hallway rug's scratchy.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the slow breath, the weight settling against his shoulder, and knew the excuse for exactly what it was. The rug. Bear huffed a laugh that was mostly breath, warm against the mark he had just left on Kit’s throat.

“Upstairs,” Bear agreed, low and rough. “Careful—that was your last call. You picked the stairs, so the stairs are what you get.”

Bear turned his head and set his teeth against the curve where Kit’s neck met his shoulder. He bit down hard enough to make the point, then eased off and swept his tongue over the sting, soothing it into something that would still be there tomorrow.

“And that’s for the rug.”

The arm across Kit’s collarbone stayed locked; the hand at Kit’s stomach pressed flat and sure. Bear didn’t release him, didn’t step back, didn’t give even an inch. Instead Bear started them forward, steering with the solid weight of his body, walking them toward the stairs with the same unhurried confidence he had used in the hallway. Every step kept them flush—chest to back, hips tight—and Bear let his mouth drift along the edge of Kit’s jaw, nipping, soothing, marking whatever skin was easiest to reach.

“You can lie about the rug all the way up,” Bear murmured against his ear. “Every excuse is another mark. At this rate you’ll run out of lies before we hit the landing, and then I’ll just keep going anyway.”

Bear’s hand slid from Kit’s stomach to a fistful of shirt at Kit’s hip, gripping hard, and he took the first step up without breaking stride. The tally clicked over in his head, cheerful and relentless, and Bear bit down on the unmarked side of Kit’s throat one more time—just for symmetry, just because eight years had taught him exactly how much Kit could take and exactly how much Bear liked giving it.

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear felt the exact moment the bedroom stopped being the goal. It was somewhere between the third and fourth step, with Kit's spine a warm line against Bear's chest and the top of the stairs still a landing away. Bear didn't fight it. The floor up there was bare, close, and exactly as good.

Bear turned them into the wall at the top of the flight, one hand still knotted in Kit's shirt, the other locked hard on Kit's hip. Momentum did the rest. Bear went down first, twisting at the last second so the landing floor took Bear's shoulder and not Kit's—eight years of this had taught Bear that much, at least—and then the bare boards were under them, hard and unapologetic, and Bear had Kit exactly where Bear wanted him.

The shirt was the first thing to go. Bear got a fistful of the back and hauled, not gentle, not careful.
