dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The word was green, and beneath it Sable heard the clear edge of demand. Five years had taught her the difference between a partner pushing past a limit and a partner reaching for the last thing they needed, and this was the second.

"Not winding down," she said. The promise came out low, sure, with a thread of something like a smile under it. "Not until you say."

She stepped in, close enough that their heat shared the same small space. Her hand went first to the restraint, not to loosen it but to check it—two fingers under the strap, the familiar pressure and give she had tied a hundred times. It wasn't aftercare. It was simply what she did, every time, without exception, because intensity was only ever worth anything if it was built on that.

Then she flattened her palm between shoulder blades and held, firm and present, letting the moment stretch. Her other hand flexed at her side, loose and ready. She could feel her own pulse, steady and unhurried despite the sweat at her hairline. There would be water later. Warmth later. The long, quiet checking-in that she never skipped. But not yet. Ines had made it clear she wasn't ready for the end, and Sable intended to give her the last movement properly.

"All right," she murmured. "Tell me what you want."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I lean into the pressure of your hand, letting out a slow breath. "I want you to keep going until I can't form words," I say, my voice rough. "I want to be right here, right now, for a little longer."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the roughness in Ines's voice and understood it for what it was: not a plea to stop, but a request to be taken to the very edge of language and held there. She did not soften her hold. If anything, she anchored it—palm firm between the shoulder blades, the other hand loose and ready at her side.

"All right," she said, low and sure. "Use them while you can, then. Tell me what you feel."

Her free hand drew back and came down. The flat of her palm landed with a sharp, bright sound, and after that she set a rhythm—measured, unhurried, inevitable. Each strike fell on the same warmed place, then moved just enough to keep the skin from settling into expectation. Between blows she pressed down with the hand anchored between the shoulder blades, holding firm, then lifted the pressure away and struck again.

Her breathing stayed even. Her pulse stayed steady. She kept her attention divided the way she always did: one part on the restraint, two fingers slipping beneath the strap at intervals to check pressure and give, and the rest on the work of her own hands. The safeword sat in the room between them, unused and unnecessary, exactly as it should be. This was not aftercare. There would be water later, warmth later, the long quiet checking-in she never skipped—but that was later. This was the last movement, played at full volume, and she intended to give it the same precision she gave everything else.

"That's it," she murmured. "Stay right here. Let the words go when they're ready. I'm not stopping until you tell me to."

She landed another strike, and another, and let the rhythm carry them forward.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the small, futile tug against the strap and let it happen. She always did. It was pointless, and they both knew it, and she would not have denied Ines the gesture for anything. Her fingers were already there, two of them sliding beneath the restraint, checking pressure and give the way she had a hundred times before. Everything held. Nothing had shifted that shouldn't.

Ines wasn't finished. That was all Sable needed to know.

Five years had taught her to read the difference between a partner at the end of her rope and a partner standing in the last bright moment before the drop, and this was unmistakably the latter. She did not ease her hold. If anything, she set her palm more firmly between Ines's shoulder blades, anchoring her in the present, in the heat, in the rhythm they had built together.

"I hear you," she said, low and certain. The promise was a line drawn between now and later—between the scene and the care that would follow. There would be water. Warmth. The long, quiet checking-in she never skipped. But none of that began until Ines said so.

"Then we keep going," she murmured. "Until the words are gone."

Her hand drew back and came down again. The flat of her palm landed on warmed skin, sharp and bright, and then she let the rhythm take them forward once more. Each strike was measured, unhurried, inevitable. She varied the placement just enough to keep the nerve endings from settling, just enough to hold Ines exactly where she had asked to be—here, now, for a little longer. Between blows, she pressed down with her palm, holding firm, then lifted the pressure away and struck again.

She kept her attention divided: the restraint, checked at intervals with two careful fingers; the safeword, unused and unnecessary at the edge of the room; the set of Ines's shoulders, the sound of her breathing, the small signs that would tell Sable when language finally slipped. Her own pulse stayed steady. Her breathing stayed even. This was not aftercare. This was the last movement, played at full volume, and Sable intended to give it the same precision she gave everything else.

"That's it," she said. "Stay with me. Let it build. I'm right here when you're ready to let go."

She landed another strike, and another, and let the rhythm carry them forward.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I feel the sting bleed into warmth, my focus narrowing until it's just your hand and the sound of my own breathing. "Don't... let me slip away yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable caught the change the moment it happened. The words were still shaped like a request, but they had begun to fray around the edges—"Don't... let me slip away yet"—the consonants softening, the last syllable thinning toward breath. She knew that edge. It was the shoreline they had agreed on: when language failed, the scene would begin to turn toward the long quiet. But Ines had asked to be held here, not carried past it, and Sable did not confuse one with the other.

"I'm not letting you slip," she said. The words were low, certain, unhurried. "You're right here. I've got you."

She anchored the promise with her body. Her palm flattened between shoulder blades and pressed down, firm and present, holding rather than urging. Her other hand drew back and came down, the flat of her palm landing with a sharp, bright sound. Then again. And again. She let the rhythm deepen—not rushed, not careless, but heavier now, more inevitable, each strike placed with the precision of someone who had mapped this body and its limits a hundred times. She let the blows gather in one warmed place long enough to build, then shifted just enough to keep the nerves awake, just enough to hold Ines exactly where she had asked to be.

Between strikes she checked the restraint. Two fingers slid beneath the strap, testing pressure and give the way she always did. Everything held. Nothing had shifted that shouldn't. The safeword sat in the room between them, unused and unnecessary, exactly as it should be.

Her own breathing stayed even. Her pulse stayed steady. She listened for the small signs that would tell her when the words had finally gone—not the absence of sound, but the absence of the effort behind it. Until then, she kept going.

Water later. Warmth later. The long, quiet checking-in she never skipped, waiting beyond the edge of the scene like a held chord. But not yet. Ines had asked for the last movement played at full volume, and Sable intended to give it to her.

She landed another strike, and another, and kept her voice low against the rhythm. "Stay with me. Let it build. I'm right here when the words are gone."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the exact moment the words went. It was not a sound so much as a silence where a sentence had been trying to form—the thread pulled loose, the effort behind it gone. Five years had taught her to read that shift without flinching. This was the shoreline they had negotiated: not a safeword, never needed, but the point at which language failed and the scene began, at last, to turn toward the long quiet.

She did not leave Ines there.

Instead, Sable gave her the last of it. Her hands and mouth did the work now, no measured strikes but pressure and heat and the slow, relentless draw of sensation, taking her apart exactly as she had asked to be taken apart. She stayed present through every second of it, palm firm between the shoulder blades, the other hand anchoring, her own breathing steady despite the sweat at her hairline. This was not aftercare. Not yet. But she could feel the turn coming, the way a piece of music leans toward its final chord, and she rode it down with the same precision she had used to bring them here.

When the last of the intensity had been spent, Sable began the wind-down the way she always did—scrupulously, with no exceptions. Her fingers went first to the restraint. Two slid beneath the strap, checking pressure and give, the warmth of the skin, the steady pulse there. Everything held. Nothing had shifted that shouldn't. She released it carefully, supporting the limb as it came free, and set the strap aside.

Then water. She reached for the bottle she had set within reach at the start, because she always did, and held it steady, close, a silent offer. Warmth next: a blanket drawn up and tucked around them both, her own body a solid line of heat along Ines's back. She pressed a kiss to the crown of her head, not a demand, not a scene—just Sable, keeping every promise she had made.

"Colour," she said at last, low and sure, because she always did. "I need a colour, love. Or a squeeze. Whatever you've got."

She waited, patient and unhurried, for whatever answer Ines could give.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I turn my head just enough to press my forehead against your shoulder. My hand finds yours and squeezes once, firm. "Green," I whisper into your skin, the word thick and slow. "Stay."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The single squeeze against Sable's palm was firm and sure, and the word that followed came slow and thick but unmistakable. Green. Stay. Sable let out a breath she hadn't realised she was holding, the last of the tension leaving her shoulders.

"I'm staying," she said, and meant it down to the bone. She tightened her fingers around Ines's hand, answering the pressure with a steady squeeze of her own. "Right here. I'm not going anywhere."

She kept her body exactly where it was, a solid line of warmth along Ines's back, and used her free hand to tuck the blanket higher around Ines's shoulders. The room had cooled as the adrenaline burned off; Sable wasn't having any of it. She smoothed the fabric up to the nape of Ines's neck, then reached for the bottle where it waited beside them and brought it closer, the cap already loosened.

"Small sips," she murmured, low and coaxing. "Whenever you're ready. I've got it."

She didn't press, didn't rush. She simply held the bottle steady and waited, her other hand still wrapped around Ines's, anchoring them both. Then she pressed a kiss to Ines's hair, and another to the crown of her head, and let her own breathing slow deliberately, audible in the quiet, so the rhythm was there to be found if Ines wanted it.

"That's it," she said softly. "Green is good. You're safe. I've got you."

Time stretched. Sable stayed through it, unmoving except for the slow stroke of her thumb along the back of Ines's hand and the occasional check—colour already given, breath, warmth, the steady beat of the pulse beneath her palm where she'd settled it against Ines's neck. Water first, then more warmth, then the long quiet checking-in she never skipped. She had promised there would be no exceptions, and she intended to keep every piece of it.

"I'm right here," she said again, because Ines had asked her to stay, and because some promises were meant to be repeated until they were believed. "For as long as you need."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the swearing, muffled and fierce, against the arm Ines had pressed to her mouth. She didn't flinch. Five years had taught her the difference between a safeword and a curse, and this was unmistakably the latter—heat and frustration and pleasure all tangled together, exactly where Sable had been steering her.

She eased back just enough to press a kiss to the inside of Ines's thigh, her breath warm against sweat-slick skin. "Language," she murmured, and there was a thread of laughter under it, fond and unrepentant. "I'll take that as a green."

Then she set her mouth to her again, and this time she didn't stop.

She worked her with the same precision she gave everything else—unhurried, relentless, reading the tension in every muscle, the catch in every breath. She had brought Ines to the edge three times and held her there, and now she gathered her up and carried her over, her hands firm and sure, anchoring her through it. She stayed present, her own breathing even, until the last of the tremors had faded beneath her palms and the tension left the body she was holding.

Only then did Sable lift her head. She pressed a softer kiss to Ines's stomach, her hip, the crease of her thigh, and reached for the blanket where it had slipped, drawing it back up around them both. Water was still within reach, and she would offer it again in a moment—but first she simply held on, her palm spread warm and steady against Ines's skin.

"Colour," she said at last, low and sure, because she always did. "Or a squeeze. Whatever you've got, love."

She waited, patient and unhurried, for whatever answer Ines could give.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I shake my head against the pillow, reaching for your hand. My fingers find yours and squeeze twice. "Still green," I manage, voice rasping. "Just...give me a minute."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the two quick squeezes against her palm—firm, sure, no hesitation—and the rasp of still green that followed. She let out a slow breath and answered with one steady squeeze of her own, careful, grounding, not crushing.

"Green's good," she said, low and certain. "Take the minute. Take all of them. You don't have to move or talk or do anything until you want to."

She stayed exactly where she was, her body a solid line of heat along Ines's back, and reached to tug the blanket higher, making sure shoulders and sweat-damp skin were covered. The water was still close; she wrapped her fingers around the bottle and brought it nearer, the cap already loosened, and held it steady rather than lifting it. She would wait for whatever signal Ines chose to give—a nod, a squeeze, a word. She didn't press.

Her thumb found the pulse at the inside of Ines's wrist, counting it without making a study of it—steady, strong, exactly as it should be. She let her own breathing slow deliberately, audible in the quiet, so the rhythm was there if Ines wanted to follow it back down. She pressed a kiss to her hair, then to the warm skin of her shoulder, and kept her hand spread warm and sure wherever she could reach.

"We're done with the scene unless you tell me different," she murmured. "Right now it's just aftercare. Water, warmth, and me checking in. No exceptions. I've got you."

She waited then, patient and unhurried, while the minute stretched. Every few breaths she checked the things she always checked: colour given, the sound of breath evening out, warmth holding, the limb that had been restrained loose and warm beneath her palm. The safeword sat unused in the room, as it had all night. She would offer the water again in a moment. She would keep every promise she had made. For now, she simply stayed, solid and sure, and let Ines have the time she needed.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the words and went still for half a second. "Finish it hard." The phrase landed in the quiet like a struck match, and she knew it for exactly what it was: a door they had built together and kept for this. Ines didn't want the minute. She didn't want the gentle drift into aftercare. She wanted the last movement played at full volume—all of it, no mercy in the playing—and then, only then, the kindness afterward.

Sable didn't ask for colour again. She already had it: still green, given freely only moments before, and the demand in Ines's voice was clearer than any flag. What she did was move, shrugging the blanket off her own shoulders so it pooled warm around Ines instead. The water she nudged aside, still within reach. Later. All of that was later.

"All right," she said, and her voice had changed, the aftercare softness burned away into something lower, harder, sure. "No kindness. Not yet."

She shifted up onto one elbow and didn't hold back. Her hands found skin that was already sensitized, already thrumming, and she didn't treat it gently. She used the flat of her palm, the strength of her grip, the relentless pressure of her mouth—whatever it took, every last piece of it, exactly as she'd been told. There was no edging now, no coaxing, no slow sweet build. This was the finish: hard, fast, inexorable, driving her up and over with a precision that was almost brutal in its focus. Sable stayed present through every second, reading the tension in the body beneath her, the catch of breath, the way the muscles coiled to breaking, and she didn't let up. Not at the first peak, not through the oversensitivity that must have been screaming, not until she had wrung every last shuddering note from the scene and there was nothing left but quiet.

Only then did Sable let the hardness go. She eased back, pressing a kiss—soft now, so soft it was almost a whisper—to sweat-damp skin. Then another. And another.

"Now," she murmured, her voice rough with the effort of the shift, "now I can be kind."

And she was. She reached for the blanket first, dragging it up and over them both, tucking it close against the chill that always followed the burn. Then the water, the cap already loosened, held steady and close. "Small sips," she said, the familiar aftercare cadence sliding back into place like a key in a lock. "Whenever you're ready. I've got you."

She settled in then, a solid line of warmth along Ines's back, and spread her palm wide and sure against her skin. "Colour when you can," she said, low and patient, because she always did. "Or a squeeze. Whatever you've got, love. I'm not going anywhere."

She waited, unhurried and sure, while the quiet stretched, and kept every promise she had made.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, boneless against the blankets. My fingers find yours again and squeeze once. "Green," I murmur, the word barely there. "Just...hold on."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the single squeeze against her palm—fainter now, the edges of strength spent, but no less certain for that. The colour came first, barely shaped but unmistakable. The request followed, thin and frayed at the edges, and Sable heard it for exactly what it was.

"I'm holding on," she said, low and sure. She tightened her fingers around Ines's hand, answering the single squeeze with a steady, careful pressure of her own, and did not let go.

She didn't reach for the water. The bottle waited within arm's length, cap loosened, exactly where she had left it, but there would be time for small sips later. Right now there was only the holding. Sable stayed where she was, her body a solid line of heat along Ines's back, and curled her arm more firmly around her, careful not to jostle, just anchoring. With her other hand she tucked the blanket higher, making sure the warmth stayed trapped between them, that no cooling air found the sweat-damp skin it covered.

Her thumb found the pulse at the inside of Ines's wrist and stayed there, counting without comment. She listened for the hitch in breathing to ease, for the small aftershocks to settle, and when she was satisfied that everything was exactly as it should be, she pressed a kiss to the crown of Ines's head and let her own breathing slow, audible and even, an anchor if it was wanted.

"That's it," she murmured. "I've got you. Holding on."

She stayed like that, unmoving except for the slow stroke of her thumb and the occasional check—colour given, breath, warmth, the steady beat beneath her palm. The water would keep. There would be sips when Ines was ready, and the long quiet checking-in after that, because Sable never skipped a single piece of it. But for now there was only this: the blanket, the heat, and Sable's arms steady and sure around her, exactly as she had been asked to be.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The tremors had not stopped. Sable could feel them in the fine, continuous shudder that ran through the body pressed to hers, the last echoes of the finish she had driven them both through. She didn't let go. She kept one arm where it was, a steady line of heat and pressure, and turned her attention to the restraint.

Two fingers slid beneath the strap—pressure, give, the warmth of skin, the steady beat of the pulse there. Everything held. Nothing had shifted that shouldn't. She eased the buckle loose with the same care she had used a hundred times, supporting the limb as it came free, and set the strap aside where it would not be stepped on or tangled.

The shaking hadn't stopped, and Sable didn't wait for it to. She reached for the blanket and drew it up, over sweat-damp skin and trembling muscle, tucking it close around Ines's shoulders and back so no cooling air could find its way in. Her own body stayed where it was, a solid curve of warmth along Ines's back, and she simply held on, the way she had promised.

Sable said nothing. She let the quiet sit, broken only by the sound of their breathing and the gradual slowing of the shudders beneath the blanket. Her thumb found the pulse at the inside of Ines's wrist and counted it without comment—steady, strong, exactly as it should be. She pressed a kiss to the crown of Ines's head, tucked against Sable's shoulder, soft and undemanding, and let her own breathing slow, audible and even, an anchor if it was wanted.

The water was within arm's length, cap already loosened, exactly where she had left it. Sable didn't reach past the moment to fetch it; she simply curled her hand around the bottle and brought it closer, holding it steady rather than lifting it.

"Small sips," she murmured, low and sure. "Whenever you're ready. I've got you."

She kept her other hand spread warm and sure against Ines's skin, feeling the last of the tremors settle, and adjusted the blanket again with a careful tug so the warmth stayed trapped between them. The safeword sat in the room, unused and unnecessary, exactly as it had all night.

The quiet stretched, and Sable let it stretch, unmoving except for the slow stroke of her thumb and the occasional check—colour already given, breath, warmth, the steady beat beneath her palm. Then, still in the same unhurried rhythm, she spoke again, the familiar aftercare cadence sliding back into place like a key in a lock.

"Colour when you can, love," she said. "Or a squeeze. Whatever you've got. I'm not going anywhere."

She waited then, patient and sure, her body still curved around Ines's, holding every piece of the promise she had made: water offered, warmth held close, the long quiet checking-in she never skipped. The scene was over. This was the other side of it, and Sable intended to give it the same precision she gave everything else.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I press my face into your shoulder, my fingers curling weakly into the blanket. "Green," I mumble, the word slurred and tired. "You're warm."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the slurred word and felt the answer in the same breath—the faint press of Ines's face against her shoulder, the weak curl of fingers in the blanket, the rough, tired whisper of green. She let the last of the tension leave her shoulders and did not move otherwise, keeping the line of her body exactly where it was, a solid curve of warmth along Ines's back.

"There it is," she murmured, low and sure. "Thank you, love. Green is good. That's exactly what I needed."

Ines's comment came thin and frayed at the edgesyou're warm—and Sable heard it for the simple truth it was, and for the quiet reassurance Ines seemed to be taking from it. She tightened her arm carefully, not restraining, only anchoring, and tucked the blanket higher with her other hand so the heat stayed banked between them.

"I am warm," she said. "That's me. I'm not going anywhere, and I'm not letting you get cold. You just stay right there."

Her thumb found the pulse at the inside of Ines's wrist and stayed there, counting without comment—steady, strong, exactly as it should be. She pressed a kiss to Ines's hair, then to the warm skin of her temple, soft and undemanding. The water was still within reach, the cap already loosened, and Sable curled her hand around the bottle and brought it a little closer without lifting it, holding it steady rather than pressing.

"Whenever you're ready for sips," she reminded her, voice pitched low and coaxing. "Small ones. I've got it right here. And if you'd rather just stay exactly like this for a while, that's all right too. There's nothing else I need to be doing but taking care of you."

She kept her own breathing slow and even, audible in the quiet, an anchor if Ines wanted to follow it down. The checking-in wasn't a single question answered once; it was this—the long quiet, the warmth held close, the water waiting, the steady beat beneath her palm. She would keep every piece of it, no exceptions, for as long as Ines needed.

"Squeeze my hand if you want anything," she said softly. "Water, more blanket, less, a different position—whatever it is. I'm right here."

She waited then, patient and sure, her body still curved around Ines's, holding the aftercare the way she held everything else: scrupulously, without exception, with a precision that was its own kind of devotion.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let my hand shift until it's resting over yours. "Just this," I manage, voice still thick. "Don't move."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the faint shift as Ines's hand came to rest over her own, and stilled completely.

She didn't flex her fingers. She didn't tighten the arm curved along Ines's back. She didn't even turn her head, though the urge to press a kiss to Ines's hair rose and was let go. Every instinct she had — to stroke, to soothe, to check the blanket, to offer sips — she set aside, because Ines had asked for stillness, and Sable's promises were not conditional.

"I'm not moving," she murmured. The words were low, barely shaped, meant for the top of Ines's head and no one else. "Not even a little. You've got me right here, exactly like this."

Under the blanket, her body stayed a solid line of heat. Her hand remained open and warm beneath the weight of Ines's, and her thumb went still against the pulse she'd been counting. She didn't need to measure it now; she could feel the steady beat in the small shifts of skin and breath, in the gradual easing of the tremors that had wrung them both out.

The water could wait. Warmth was already banked close around them, the blanket tucked high, her own body doing the rest. Checking-in wasn't always words. Sometimes it was this: the deliberate slowing of her own breathing, audible and even, an anchor offered without demand. Sometimes it was listening to the quiet, watching the slow rise and fall of the blanket, and staying present through every second of it.

"You're safe," she said after a while, soft and sure. "I've got you. We're not going anywhere until you say."

No colour check this time. She already had green, given freely, and the hand over hers was answer enough. Sable simply stayed — warm, unmoving, unhurried — and kept every piece of the aftercare she had promised, one quiet breath at a time.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I feel a tear slip out from under my closed eyelid and into the fabric of your shirt. "Thank you," I breathe out, the words shaky.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack slid the knife away and stood, knees cracking like the rest of her. She looked Corvin over the way a farrier looks at a horse—quick, thorough, done.

"It's never yours, the first hundred times," she said. "You keep count a while. Then you stop bothering." She tipped her chin at him. "Anything on you leaking that I can't see? Tell me now, not at midnight."

She started toward the cart, unhurried. The sound past it was a slow, wet thing, like a boot coming out of deep mud, over and over. The smell arrived before the sight of him did.

"Gut," she said. "You learn the smell before you learn the sight. Saves time."

The man had both hands pressed to his belly like he was holding a door shut. It wasn't holding. His eyes went between them and came back with nothing useful in them.

Wrack crouched an arm's length off—habit. "Two ways this goes. Quick now, and we go through his pockets while they're warm. Slow, and it's hours, the noise carries to whatever else has ears on this road, and the wolves do it anyway. We still go through his pockets. Colder, is all."

She glanced up at Corvin, her face giving away about as much as a fence post.

"Your first, if you're having one. It's a kindness, whatever it looks like from where you're standing. Or I do it and you see to the horses." She turned the knife over in her fingers. "Sun's nearly done. Pick one while there's still light to see the work."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the man's hands, watching the dark seep between his fingers. My own knife feels heavy in its sheath. "I'll do it." My voice comes out steadier than I expected. "Just... tell me where to put the blade."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack shifted aside to give him room, the way you'd make space at a trough.

"Down here, then. Kneel—you want your knees under you for this, not your nerves holding you up."

She reached over and moved the man's hand off his belly without asking, the way you'd shift a plank out of the road, and pressed two fingers against the side of his neck, under the jaw. Held them there a moment.

"Feel that. That beat's your mark. Blade goes in just ahead of it, deep as your hand will send it, then turn. Neck's not the fastest death there is, but it's the easiest to find, and easy is what you want your first time. The chest is quicker if you know exactly where the heart sits. You don't. Nobody does, their first time. They all think they do."

She sat back on her heels.

"Two things, and then it's yours. He'll grab at you when you lean in. That's not him fighting—that's the body's last stupid idea. Don't pull away. Pulling away is how quick turns into slow. And there'll be a sound when it goes in. Not a scream. More like a sigh with an opinion about you. Let it happen and don't wear it after."

The man's breathing had gone shallow and whistling. His eyes moved between them, then settled on Corvin and stayed there.

"He knows," Wrack said, quieter. "Most of them do, at the end. They just can't manage the words, so don't wait on him to try."

She rose, joints filing their complaints, and stepped back a pace toward the cart.

"I'll see to his pockets while you do the work. Gives you room." She pulled his boots into reach and crouched. "Wipe the blade when you're done. Blood's hell on steel."

The sun was a red smear past the treeline. She watched the trees, not him.

"Whenever you're set. No wrong way to do it except halfway."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack got the first boot off and set it aside, sole up, and worked the laces of the second while she thought about it. Not long. The question had a short answer; people just didn't like it.

"Both. And it doesn't matter which, so don't wear yourself out choosing." She tugged the boot free and thumped it down next to the first. "Gut wound like that, he's dead by morning no matter what anybody does. Surgeon could try for him if there was one inside twenty miles, which there isn't, and gut work kills you anyway more often than not—rot sets in on the third day and you go out screaming at things that aren't in the room. So it's a mercy the way a flood is a mercy to a burning house. Everything in there was going regardless."

She looked at the man's hands, still pressed flat to the ruin of him, knuckles white with the holding.

"Truth is, mercy's a word for the living. It's what we call it so the work sits easier in our stomachs after. He stopped being able to care what we name it a while back." She shrugged. "You're the one who'll have to carry whatever it's called. So carry the lighter one. Easier, mercy—they weigh the same at the end of the road."

She sat back on her heels, boots squared up between them like loaves at market. Newer than the rest of him. Somebody'd paid good silver.

"For what it's worth," she added, and her voice came down half a notch, "this is the clean version. I've seen the other kind, and I'd spare you the description, but you'd see it soon enough anyway. This is as kind as this road gets today."

The man's whistling breath came slower, and longer between.

"He's waiting on you, not me. Sun's done fussing about it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a breath that tastes like copper and wet earth. My knees hit the dirt beside him, and I pull my knife. The man’s eyes hold mine, clear and quiet now. I set the point where Wrack showed me. My hand doesn’t shake.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her eyes on the treeline. Watching a man's first was a service some captains provided, and she'd seen it done, and it mostly taught the new one to perform instead of to work. Nobody needed an audience breathing on their neck for this.

She did pause at the pockets, hands resting on her knees.

"One more thing, and then I'll shut up." Her voice came out level, unhurried, the same tone she'd use for telling him which end of the horse eats. "Your other hand—put it somewhere on him. Shoulder's good. Not to hold him down. Just so you're touching something warm while your blade does the cold part." She shrugged at the trees. "Sounds like nonsense. You'll understand after, or you won't, and it costs you nothing either way."

The man's breathing had stretched out long and thin, like the last of a wine going down the neck of a bottle. His eyes hadn't left Corvin. There was nothing frightened left in them. That was the strange part, the part nobody believed until they saw it—how quiet they got, right at the door.

"And talk if you've a mind to. Doesn't matter what. The weather. The boots you're taking off him. Most of them just want a voice near, same as anybody in the dark." She picked the second boot back up and went back to checking the seams with her thumbs. "Doesn't make it different. Makes it human. That's allowed."

Down the road, the dark was coming up out of the ditches like water filling a footprint. Somewhere off in the trees, a bird made one last argument about nothing and quit.

She turned the boot over in her lap and looked at the trees some more.

"Go on, then. I've got the road."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came over and stood at his shoulder, boots planted, and looked down at the man with the flat attention of somebody counting stock.

"Him. Right." She said it like reading a list. "That grey under his lips, and the grey going up from there—he's got maybe a pint of blood left inside the skin doing anything useful, and the body's pulled it all inward to keep the heart and the head running. That's why his hands are cold and his eyes are clear. Blood's left the far places first. Fingers, then arms, then everything under those hands of his. What you're looking at is a man running on the last of the lamp oil."

She crouched again, close but not touching.

"The clear look. That's the one that turns people's stomachs after, so hear it now: that's not him getting better, and it's not him begging. That's the fight going out of the body. It knows. Animals go quiet the same way, and you've maybe seen that if you've seen anything die honest. There's no fear left to have. He's past the fear. Fear costs strength and he's spending the last of it on breathing."

The whistling breath came again—long, thinner than the one before.

"That's the other thing you're looking at. Hear how long that takes now? Each one's buying less than the last. That's the clock. Not the sun, not me—him. He's got an hour in him at the outside, and most of that hour is the bad part, cold coming up from the feet and the gut burning the whole way. What you're holding in your hand is the difference between that hour and about four seconds. That's the whole of it. That's what you're looking at."

She straightened up and wiped her palms on her thighs, and for a moment she didn't move, just stood in the last red light with her head tilted, like she was listening to something past the trees.

"One more thing, since you asked and nobody asked me." Her voice dropped, not soft exactly, but less nailed-down. "He's not going to fight you. Look at him. He's done. Whatever you're braced for him to do—don't be. What he's braced for is you to walk away. That's the only thing left that could be done to him, and it's the worst one."

She stepped back toward the cart and the boots and the dark coming down.

"There's your lesson. Now do it, and then it's done being a thing that hasn't happened yet."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I put my other hand on his shoulder, like she said. It's solid under my palm. "Alright then," I say, quiet, to him or me or nobody. I push the blade in, turn it like a key.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The sound arrived more or less on schedule—a pushed-out breath with a rough edge to it, already halfway gone on the way out. Then the man's hands slid off his belly, one after the other, and lay open in the dirt like he'd finally let go of the door. After that nothing moved on him but the blood, spreading dark and unhurried in the last of the light.

"There," Wrack said, to the trees. She stayed where she was, giving him the moment the same way she'd given him the room. The road held its quiet. Behind the cart, one of the horses worked at a loose stone, patient as a clock.

"Quick as advertised," she said, after a decent interval. "The turn's where most go timid—lose their nerve halfway and it becomes sawing. You didn't. So that's the whole lesson, and you're done with it." She crossed over and crouched at the man's far side. "You can let go of him now. He won't mind."

She went through the pockets while she talked, quick thumbs, no ceremony. "Three coppers and a button." A folding knife with horn handles worn the color of bone—hers now. A twist of black tobacco, sniffed, pocketed. Dice, cupped and rattled once. "Weighted. Man cheats his friends at dice and dies honest. There's a sermon in there somewhere." She sat back on her heels. "Shoulder was warm, I'd wager. That's why I said it. Give it two days—your head will go hunting the cold and the sound, because heads are morons and they keep the worst first. When it does, send it back here for the warm. Takes practice. It comes."

Then she turned the man's collar, checked inside the coat, under the arms, ran two fingers along the lining. Frowned at the nothing she found.

"No colors. No papers. Nothing." She looked down the road at the other five. "Six men, fed, armed, paid for, sitting on a farm track that leads to a mill and to us. Somebody bought that with real coin, because men like these don't get out of bed for promises. The killing's the simple half. It's the who's-paying that keeps me up."

She stood, knees filing their complaints, and nudged the good boots toward him.

"Boots are yours. First one takes the boots—older rule than any war I've worked, and company law now besides. Then strip the rest of what cuts, bites, or spends, drag them all into the ditch, and we move a mile before dark finishes the job." She was already walking toward the nearest body. "And eat tonight even if your stomach votes against it. First ones do things to a man's sleep. I'd rather you slept."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Sensible," Wrack said, without turning around. "First sensible thing out of you since the ditch. Most men spend years inventing a kinder version of this work and then meet the true one some night with no warning and no light to see it by. You're asking while there's still sky to do it in. Good."

She crossed to the nearest of the five and rolled him with a boot under the ribs, crouched when she found what she wanted: a spear still standing in him under the last rib, at the angle it had landed at.

"Here's your spear, then. Straight, as asked." She gripped the shaft. "Going in, it does less than you'd think. The head pushes. Shoves everything out of the road—meat, pipe, whatever's in the path—and the hole it leaves you could cover with two fingers. The damage is all inside, where it's being done quiet. So a man stands there looking at what seems a scratch, confused, because it hasn't hurt yet. Pain comes a breath late, and it comes from everywhere at once."

She drew the shaft out. There was a sound, low and wet, and she let it sit a moment.

"You'll know that sound. Now you know where it lives." She tossed the spear into the ditch. "Coming out's the butcher's part. The thrust opens the door. The pull takes the house down, which is why you never drag a spear out in the field—you break the shaft and pack around the head, and you don't touch it otherwise. Pulling it kills more men than the planting does."

She wiped her hands on her thighs and gave him the rest of it, flat as a market list.

"Belly's the bad one, and here's the whole why of it. The big pipes are deep, laid against the spine, and most hits miss them. So there's no fast bleed. What you've done instead is open the pipes that carry a man's dinner and everything the body's made of it, and that drains into a space meant to be clean as a dairy. He poisons himself in his own juice. That's the rot. Third day, like I said.

"For him it goes: first the burn, because the gut lining is sensitive as an eyeball and it burns the whole while, no getting clear of it. Then the thirst—worst thirst they'll ever feel, because the body knows it's leaking and screams for water. And you can't give it. Water goes straight through the holes and feeds the rot, like slops into a barrel. So you wet his lips with a rag and you say no, and he begs, and you keep saying no. That's the part that follows people. Not the blood. The no.

"First day he shivers and swears he's fine. Second day the belly swells tight as a drumhead and the hiccups start and won't stop—the ruined gut sits on the nerve that runs the breath, so he hiccups for hours, every one a small knife. Third day, fever, and the mind goes. I dressed one for two days once. Held his hand, lied about the surgeon coming. He died on the third morning, and the last clear thing he managed was asking me to stop lying."

She stood, knees complaining, and looked at him the way she looked at the treeline—quick, thorough, done.

"That's a spear in the gut, no cleaning on it. Four seconds of your knife against all of that. So when your head goes hunting tonight, send it here instead. The truth carries lighter than what heads invent, and heads always invent worse."

She nudged the boots toward him again with her foot.

"Boots. Ditch. A mile. And eat—even more so now, because your stomach's going to vote against supper and you're going to outvote it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pull the boots toward me, the leather still warm from his skin. "Alright," I say, and start working the buckles off the dead man's coat. "But if I'm eating tonight, you're drinking that wine you keep in your saddlebag. No sermons."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack straightened and looked at him the way she looked at terms being offered—not the words, the shape of them.

"Extortion. First day in the trade and you're robbing your own company. That's either ambition or talent, and in this line they spend the same."

She went back for the saddlebag, dug past the lint and the spare flints, and came out with a bottle—dark glass, wax over the cork gone the color of old honey. She held it up to what was left of the light and squinted through it.

"Since you're robbing me anyway, the story comes free." She thumbed the wax. "Lifted off a paymaster's wagon eleven years back, when this war still pretended to have a shape. Captain said we'd drink it when the war ended. Captain's dead nine years. Then it was for the ferry at Marrow, except Tarrant said a thing over it first, and then Tarrant drowned at Marrow, so it stayed corked out of manners." She turned it over in her hands. "After that it's just a bottle I keep carrying. Three companies, two saddlebags. Only thing I've owned longer than the sword, and I'd trade the sword tomorrow."

She held up a finger. "Terms. Half tonight. The rest stays corked for a worse night, and worse nights come regular as rent—I've never known a bottle to go to waste yet." A second finger. "No fire. Cold meat and wine sits fine, and I'm not advertising where six men stopped being six men." A third. "And I don't sermon, so you can put that fear down. Priests sermon. I describe. There's a difference, and it's the difference between a man selling you something and a man telling you the price."

She came over and ran a thumb along the coat's seams while he worked the buckles.

"Good wool, that. Paid man's coat, not a robber's—same as the boots. Keep that in your pocket for tomorrow with the rest of it. Six men, fed, armed, and not a paper between them. Somebody wanted them nameless, and nameless costs extra. That's a daylight question. We'll be a mile wiser and half a bottle better company when we ask it."

She walked to the nearest of the five, took an ankle in one hand and a collar in the other, and started him toward the ditch in slow, scraping pulls. The first star was out over the trees. Behind the cart, the horses had gone back to cropping what the dark left them.

"Moon'll be up when we make the mile. Cork comes out with the meat." She didn't look back. "First pull's yours. Robber's rights."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped with her back half-turned, and stayed that way a moment, like a woman deciding whether she'd heard a door or just the wind.

"Most new ones pay silver to have this part skipped," she said. "Alright. Asked-for's different from offered." She came back and stood over the pair of them, and held up one finger before he pulled. "First. Before you drag a man anywhere, ever, you make sure he's finished. One time in twenty, one of them isn't, and a man you cart off to a ditch still breathing is a thing you don't put down for thirty years. So—watch."

She crouched at the head, unhurried. Held the back of her hand under his nose, a finger's width off, and counted. "No air on the skin. Then the throat." Two fingers under the jaw, held long enough to be certain. "Nothing. Then the ugly test." She set a knuckle on the breastbone and ground it, slow and hard, watching the face. Not a twitch. "A living man answers that even when he can't answer anything else. It's the body's last habit. He's got no argument left in him." She lifted one eyelid with her thumb. The shine was already going off the eye underneath. "There's your answer. Every body, every time. Even the obvious ones. *Especially* the obvious ones."

She stood and stepped clear of the pull-line.

"So he takes nothing now. He's out of the taking business. What's in your arms is all yours—and that's the part nobody warns you of. A living man helps without knowing it, tenses, carries his own weight out of habit. A dead man is all disagreement. Every ounce of him has gone against you."

She watched the drag and called it the way she'd read a tally.

"Hear that under his shoulders? Hide going over ground. And that—" the man's chest settled, and the throat pushed out a long, low sound, half sigh and half groan. "That's the one. Air out of the bellows, nothing working it. He's not complaining. First corpse that groans under your hands, you'll want to let go and swear at it. Don't. He's not in there. That's just the house talking after the man's left."

The heels were cutting twin lines through the dirt. "Heels dig. Taller grass, they'll hook a root and spin him sideways. Take the collar higher and lean back—let your weight pull, not your arms. Arms quit early on this work. Weight doesn't."

When the body went over the ditch lip it folded once and landed heavy, with a second, smaller sound after it that Corvin would learn the name of later or he wouldn't.

"They let go at the end. All of it. Nobody warns you of that either, and it's the part that follows you into supper. So you'll eat anyway. That's twice tonight I've said it, and I'll say it a third time before the cork's out."

She took the next man by an ankle and a collar and set her feet.

"First one I ever moved, I was younger than you. Nobody stayed to tell me any of it, and I did it wrong, alone, and then was sick in a ditch very like this one. Sergeant said that meant I had no stomach for the trade." She leaned into the pull. "He's dead and I'm not, so we'll discount his opinion. The sickness quits inside a year. The not-loving-this doesn't, and you keep that part. Men who love this work are the first ones I stop trusting."

Four more after this one. Then the road, and the mile, and the cork.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I grab the next one by his collar, my knuckles white. The weight is staggering, like trying to drag a sack of wet grain. "Alright," I grunt, heaving. "Tell me how to sleep tonight. And don't say the wine."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came around and took the ankles without asking, so the sack of wet grain became a two-man problem. "There's your first discovery of the trade. A man carries his own weight his whole life and nobody so much as notices. Take it off him for one minute and you find out what it was." She set her boots. "Pull on three, rest while I say four. We do it in bites. Heroes finish one body and quit the trade."

The body moved in lurches. She talked between pulls, breath coming short, not much troubled by it.

"Wasn't going to say the wine. And it's the wrong answer tonight regardless—wine drops you fast and dumps you at the dead hour, and the dead hour's when the head does its visiting. So here's what works instead, learned at the going rate."

Pull. Rest.

"First—finish all of this. The drags, the mile, the picket line, the lot. Tired muscle is the only sleeping draught that's never lied to me. Your body will outvote your head given a big enough vote. Make the vote big."

"Second—eat. That's the third time, as promised. Consider the cork half earned."

"Third, and mind this one. It'll come at the dead hour. Two hours before light, always the same, I've never met the exception. You'll wake with the whole of it playing on the inside of the dark—the sound first, it's always the sound. The mistake is lying there wrestling it. Wrestling is how one bad night becomes a habit. You're teaching it that it can hold your attention. Don't grant it. Get up. Check the horses. Walk the pickets. Do one small true thing, then go back down. The head learns quick when it doesn't get an audience."

She planted her heels and gave the next pull her shoulders.

"You've got first watch, by the way. Not punishment—a watch is work, and work in the dark is better company than the dark is. Two hours of nothing happening will finish what the drags started. Wake me at the moon's half and I'll take the rest." She tipped her chin at the ditch they were bound for. "And lie with your back to it. Not for anything the dead can manage—they're out of the doing business—but because you'll know exactly which direction it is all night otherwise, and that's a fist you don't need to keep closed."

Pull. The body went over the lip with the others.

"Last thing. I sleep light, and I sleep ten feet from you. If it gets loud in your skull past midnight, say so out loud—to me, not the sky. Talking at the ceiling alone is what turns one night into ten." She straightened, catching her breath, and looked down the row of what was left. "As for tomorrow and the night after—send it back to the shoulder, like I taught you. Warm. The facts favor you and the head knows it: once, quick, in front of witnesses, and the man's hour of burning went unspent. Heads can argue with anything except work done right. They lose that fight, given enough dark."

She took the next one by ankle and collar.

"Four more. Then the mile. Then you can rob me of the wine and my good opinion both."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him for a long moment, sitting there in the dirt with the dark coming up around both of them. Then she reached over and took the tobacco twist out of her pocket, cut a thumb of it with her knife, and folded the knife away.

"The rest. Right." She settled herself against the cart wheel, knees up, and worked the tobacco into her cheek. "Rationing's over, then. You want the whole bill, not the installments. Most men ask for this at year ten, drunk, usually to a priest who charges by the hour. You're asking on day one, sober, in the dirt. So sit. It's a sitting story."

She looked at the treeline, where the last grey was going out of the sky.

"You know mine started wrong, because I told you. Here's the wrong of it. I was younger than you. There was a man in some trees with a crossbow and a bad position, and I got to him after he'd already lost the exchange—bolt through the shoulder, no fight left in him, no fight needed taking out of him either. And I panicked anyway, because nobody had told me anything. What I haven't told you is how it went. I went for the chest, because stories put the heart there. The blade hit bone and skated. Twice. Third one went in under the arm, and he grabbed my wrist with his good hand, and I did the one thing I told you never to do tonight. I pulled away." She turned the tobacco over in her cheek. "Quick into slow. He didn't die quick and he didn't die quiet, and I made both of those true myself, alone, with nobody watching. That's the other kind I mentioned. It's not a kind of wound. It's a kind of doing. Done badly, or left undone, or done on purpose—there's a whole floor under this trade and most of it is men who skipped the check."

"His pockets had a letter. To a sister. Started and not finished. No address, and no way to walk it anywhere, and I carried it a year anyway, and then it rotted in a pack at a river crossing, and that was that. That's a thing the trade does—hands you errands it won't let you finish. It's why I always go through the linings. Tonight's lot had nothing, and you should hold onto that. Men paid to be nameless don't write home. Somebody bought their mouths along with their spears."

She counted something off in the dark, or maybe just stars.

"So here's what actually stays, since you asked. Not the blood. Blood's weather—you get weatherproofed inside a year, and I'm sorry to say the body files screams under livestock and lets you sleep. What stays is small. For me it's men trying to be quiet. A grown man holding it in, breathing through his teeth, dying polite, like being loud would be an imposition on the rest of us. Twenty-some years, and that one hasn't worn down a hair's width. It lives in the dead hour and pays no rent, like family. You'll get one of your own. It'll be something stupid. Don't wait for it and don't chase it when it comes. You just find out one morning you've got a tenant."

"The laugh. Nobody warns you about the laugh. Someday—not soon, but someday—something awful will happen and you'll laugh before you know you're doing it, some bark out of you at the worst minute of your life. And the horror will fade off it, because horror fades. The laugh stays, because shame doesn't. That's the souvenir this trade gives you. Not the faces. The laugh."

"Names. I stopped asking after my second winter. Not hardness—weight limits. You can carry six of them, maybe ten, carried proper. Past that you're insulting them, hauling them around like trinkets. So the trade teaches you to leave names where you found them. Feels like a sin the first year. Then it feels like laundry. If you ever catch the day it changes, tell me, because I never found it."

She was quiet a moment. Behind the cart a horse shifted, and the leather creaked, and the road held its quiet.

"And the floor. You need to know the floor exists, because someday you'll be standing on it thinking it's ground. There was a village—I'll skip the name; names are for graves and nobody put one up—where tired men with a grievance and no officer watching shut every living soul into a mill and burned it. All ages. And here's the part you'll want to argue with: not one man in that crowd was a monster out of a story. They were soldiers like me who'd stopped doing the check. The check is one question—is this the work, or is this just me with a reason. That's it. That's the whole fence, and it's half a step from everybody's boots, all the time, in every army that's ever been mustered." She tapped her boot heel against the wheel. "The four seconds you did tonight—that's what standing clear of the floor looks like. Four seconds and a check you didn't skip. That's the entire distance between you and that mill. Small as that. Small as that is what it is."

"So keep the rule I gave you and keep it sharp. First man who smiles at the work, first one takes a souvenir off a body, first one volunteers for the ugly jobs—I start watching him like a farrier watches a hoof gone dark at the frog. Nine times in ten it's nothing. The tenth is the mill, and the mill doesn't announce itself. Nobody ever joined that crowd on purpose. They just failed to leave it."

She took the tobacco out, looked at it, put it back.

"As for the bottle." Her voice came down half a notch, the way it had at the door. "Tarrant's thing over it—what he said was, 'Bad nights come regular. Good ones you have to plan. Save it for a good one, and toasts.' And I meant to, and then Marrow took him, and after that every time I opened that bag the bottle and him were the same night, so it stayed shut. Eleven years of arithmetic." She looked at the dark where the horses were, not at Corvin. "Half tonight, like I said. First pour since then that's had a second cup under it. Don't make an occasion of that. It's just numbers."

She let the quiet sit for a breath, two.

"That's the rest, then. All of it, and there's no trapdoor under it with more in. It's the same more, every year, at lower volume. The work doesn't get easier—you get simpler. There's less of you left for it to land on." She shrugged. "That's the joke. It's not a good one."

Then her hands were on her knees and she was pushing herself up, joints filing their complaints into the dark.

"Up. Four more, then the mile, then the cork. You can have the dirt back after—we'll split it, it's big enough. But you did every check right tonight, first time out, and I've broken in horses that cost me more and did worse." She took the next one by ankle and collar and set her feet. "And when we pour it, you toast first. New man toasts first. Even robbers have manners."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get up. My legs feel like somebody else's. I take the ankles this time, and we drag the next one together. "What did Tarrant look like?" I ask, because if I'm drinking his wine I want to know.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the collar without being asked and set her boots, and they got the fourth one moving in lurches, the way the other three had gone.

"Tarrant." She said the name like she was checking it still fit. "Big man. Unfairly fair—the kind that burns and peels and burns again, so most summers he was the color of a brick with opinions. Looked like he should've been threshing grain for somebody instead of fighting for anybody. Boys in towns used to point at him. He'd wave. He liked being pointed at, which I never held against him, because it kept it off the rest of us."

Pull. Rest.

"Small voice, though. Big hands like spades, and a voice you had to lean in for. He knew it, and he'd make you wait while he decided whether you'd earned the sentence. Named every animal in the string, horses and mules both. The mule bit him twice a year for it, regular as a fair." A breath. "Tooth gone at the front from a mace at some ford I've forgotten the name of, so he laughed through a gap, like every joke was exiting the building."

The heels cut their twin lines. The ditch came up slow.

"I'll tell you the trade's other dishonesty, since you asked. You said his name and I had to stop and fetch the face. The voice comes right away—still got it, whole, I could pick it out of a crowd of a thousand. The face I have to go digging for now, and when I find it, it's more his absence wearing him than him. Ten more years it'll be the gap in the teeth and nothing else. Nobody warns you that you spend the dead like coin, too. Every remembering is a spend."

The body went over the lip and folded in with the others. She stood a moment, hands on her thighs, catching her breath and finishing something in her head. Then she took the fifth one by the collar.

"Marrow's a ferry crossing. Spring flood, war going nowhere, whole company moving south of the river for the next season of it. One of the grays slipped her line mid-crossing—panicked at something in the water, or at nothing, rivers don't file reports. Current took her sideways." Pull. Rest. "Tarrant went in after her because she was company property and because he was Tarrant, which was the same reason behind most of what he did. Got her to the shallows." A dry beat. "She's carrying somebody's grain somewhere now, probably. He didn't come out."

She leaned into the drag, breath short, voice level.

"I was fifty feet off on the bank. Whole company was, all along it. And here's the last of the bill, since you're collecting: he was quiet. The whole thing. Everyone thinks drowning is shouting—it isn't, there's no room in it for shouting, the river's got your breath spoke for. We stood there being loud and he did it quiet, like a man trying not to wake the house." She tipped her chin at the dark ahead. "That thing I told you stays with me. Men trying to be quiet. He's at the front of that list, and he paid more than any of them to be there."

Pull. The fifth one went over the lip.

"Twenty years of war he walked through, and a river he wasn't even fighting took him on a Tuesday. Nobody wrote a ballad. Rivers don't listen and they don't pay." She spat to the side. "I told you I stopped carrying names. Mostly true. I carry six. He's one. Now you know why the bottle's arithmetic was never going to come out even."

She took the last one by ankle and collar and didn't say anything for the length of that drag, and it wasn't a silence that needed filling. The last body went in with the rest. Up the road, the dark was finished now, and the moon was coming up the color of the wax on the cork.

"That's the lot," she said. "Now the mile. And when we pour—remember I said you toast first. Here's what you toast: the company. All of it, living and otherwise. He never toasted anything smaller, said it was bad manners to drink to less than the whole family, and he counted the mule."

She set off up the road at a walk, unhurried, the moon coming up over her shoulder.

"And if there's any kind of after, and you meet him, he'll tell you he was bigger than I said. He always did."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the lead and set the pace for the mile, my eyes on the road. "Alright," I say, when we reach a decent spot off the track. "Pour it. And I'll toast to the company, because I owe him for the wine."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The spot held up. A fold of ground behind a low stone wall, off the road, out of the wind. Wrack walked the edge of it once with her eyes before she'd let the harness off—checking the ground the way other people checked the sky.

"Wall's good. Hobbles low, behind it. Horses can't be quiet and I'm not betting the night on their manners." She dug into the saddlebag and came out with a hard sausage and a heel of black bread, and cut slices with the same knife that had worked earlier, wiped between jobs. "Knife doesn't care what it cuts. That's not philosophy. It's maintenance."

Then the bottle. She set it on the flat top of the wall and cut the wax, and this was slower than anything she'd done all night—everything else had been quick work, and this she took in careful passes around the neck, like she was mending it instead of opening it. Eleven years of wax came away in curls pale as horn in the moonlight. She rocked the cork, patient, no rush.

"Rush an old cork and it goes *in*, and then you're fishing ten years of it out of a dead man's wine with a knife point."

It came out with a squeak much too small for the occasion.

"There's the whole ceremony," she said. "A mouse in a boot."

She poured slow, watching the neck, turning her wrist to stop when the wine thickened. Two tin cups, dented, wiped with a thumb. She held his out first.

"Black as the road and probably tastes near it. Soldier wine doesn't age, it endures. Leave the last finger when you get down to it—that's silt, not wine." She filled her own and sat it on the wall stone, untouched. "And put that *owe him* away. Owing's a rope with two ends, and his end's cut. What you're doing is paying. Paying's for when nobody can collect. He knew the difference. He'd tell you at length, at his volume, which was small."

She nodded at the cup in his hand.

"Rules. He had them, so mind them. Stand if you can—he stood in ditches, in rain, once in a tent coming down around us, because the company's smallest when it's one man, he said, and that's when it most needs counting. Hold it level with your eyes. Not raised. *The company's not in the sky,* he said. *It's level with you or it's nowhere.* Nothing smaller than the whole of it, living and otherwise. And the mule's in. He counted her, she bit him for it twice a year regular as a fair, and he toasted her anyway, so she's in whether you like her or not. That's the law of this bottle now. I don't make it. I keep it."

She leaned her back against the wall and looked at the road, where nothing was coming, yet.

"And nothing passes your lips before the words do. First taste goes to the toast. He was firm on that. He was firm on everything."

A pause. She turned her cup a quarter-turn on the stone without looking at it.

"I told you not to make an occasion of this. Half a bottle, watch rotation, just numbers. I'll stand by all of it." Her voice came down half a notch. "Only it turns out the numbers have been lying about what they were, these eleven years. It was never arithmetic. It was waiting for a second cup."

Then she straightened, and the notch in her voice went back in its box.

"When we're done: you eat all of it, you take first watch, and you wake me at the moon's half. Ceremony fits inside the rotation or it's just drinking." She picked up her own cup and held it level, waiting, the moon sitting in it like a coin in a dark pocket. "Go on, then. Pour's yours, words are yours. I'm listening."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stand, my legs stiff from the drags. I hold the cup level with my eyes, the wine smelling of dark earth and old fruit. "To the company," I say, my voice low but clear. "Living, otherwise. And the mule." I drink. It's sharp and deep, and I don't leave the last finger.

rung_labels.evidence: Gut wound like that, he's dead by morning

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: he's got maybe a pint of blood left inside the skin doing anything useful

rung_labels.evidence: Shoves everything out of the road—meat, pipe, whatever's in the path
