She stood, and left him with all three of them — the knife, the name, the noise. They'd been his since she'd handed the blade over. She'd just finally stopped standing between him and them.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel again, my shadow falling across his face. "Alright, Tam." The blade slips under his jaw, cold on my knuckles. I pull, firm and quick like she said. The breathing stops mid-pace.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
It stopped mid-pace.

She knew that sound from forty paces and from ten years. A bad one doesn't stop — it changes. New noise, wet, working at it, and it spends the rest of the night teaching you what you did. A clean one just stops. Mid-pace, no argument. Politest sound in the trade.

It had gotten quieter, which was the whole of what she'd asked of the night. So she hadn't come. Both halves of that promise kept, and nothing left in the valley that needed her.

The quiet itself was a thing you could stand in. All evening the dark had been taking the valley piece by piece — birds, wind, everything — and every piece had left the breathing louder. The last piece went with it. What remained was the big silence, the frost kind, and the only clocks left running in it were hers and the horses'. Hers would keep its pace a while yet. That was the whole of her pension.

She caught herself counting a rhythm that wasn't there anymore — watch-habit, ten years deep, outliving the man it had kept time on. Habits did that. Outliving was more or less the entire trade, put plainly.

Then boots on the gravel, coming back. She turned for that. Turning had never shortened anything, and there was nothing left to shorten, so she could afford the luxury. The walk back was the tell, same as it had always been. What it told her, she'd keep — she kept that ledger on all of them, and it was nobody's business but hers.

She held out her hand, palm up, and kept her eyes off his hands while the knife crossed the space between them. She'd told him not to look at his. Seemed only fair to keep the rule on her side of it.

"Heard it stop," she said, turning the blade once. "Mid-pace. No trailing, no new noise. That's one done right — the clean ones don't fade, they just stop. You made no new noise. That's the whole of the grading. There's no ceremony after." She slid it home in the sheath as it was, blood and all. "Cleans at the fire. Same fire as your hands. Same rule."

His horse had been ready since before it was needed. She held out the reins.

"Mount up. Two valleys gone starts now."

They walked the horses out past the ditch, and she gave him the last of the evening's talk with her eyes on the track, because some things go easier said side by side than face to face.

"You're carrying his name, along of everything else. Here's what I know about names, and it's cheap: they're not for delivering. Ten years, I've carried maybe a dozen. Never took one anywhere. Never tried. They're for the leaving — he left settled, you saw it, the name did that. Where it goes after is your business, not his. Keep it forty years or set it down at the fire. Both are honest.

"And notice what he spent the last of his air on. Water. Quick. Three months' pay. That's the list, ten years running — water, a priest, a name, the pay, in whatever order the man's got left. Not one of them, not once, has asked me what any of it was for. Not at the end. The end's too honest for that question."

The track climbed for the ridge and the dark got the good kind of deep — the kind with nobody in it. The valley behind them could keep the cart, the team, and the six. She'd take the purse and the sealed letter. He'd take the name. Everybody leaves a fight carrying what they can.

"There'll be a fire in the second valley," she said. "Your hands'll come clean at it. And his name will be whatever you've decided by then — kept or set down, I've said both are honest. Only thing I'll ask is you don't decide before the fire. Decisions made in the cold come out crooked."

Behind them, past the cart, the quiet kept on.

It didn't want anything from either of them. Nothing left in the valley did.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She'd turned to go, and the noise changed behind her — the first change of pace it had made all evening — and that alone would have brought her round. The word *stay* just meant she could do it without pretending she'd had a reason.

Men asked for the opposite, mostly. *Tell me it was quick. Let me look somewhere else. Say something.* He'd asked for the whole ledger, read aloud, while it was still being written. That was either the making of him or the unmaking, and she'd quit betting on which years back. She came and went down on her heels at the man's far side, knee making its point on the way.

"Then you'll have all of it," she said. "Watch while I talk. It runs whether you understand it or not, but it goes easier understood.

"First item, what you did, since that's the front of your asking. You pulled like you were testing a wire, not like you meant to spend a man. The blade felt light in your hand — you said as much without saying it. It was light because you let it be. So the cut went shallow and came round high, under the jaw, not across the front. Inventory: you opened the window — windpipe's cut. You left the lamps lit. The vessels that put a man's lights out run deep, alongside the pipe, and you missed them. That's the whole botch, and it's the commonest one there is. You're not the first man to ask a blade's permission and get no for an answer.

"The sound, next. The bubbling, the froth at the hole — that's air and blood meeting in the window. Every breath goes through the cut now, both directions, and the blood follows the air down. He's drowning. Plain word, and you asked for plain. Drowning on dry ground. It's measured in minutes, not seconds."

The man's lips were moving. Nothing came off them but froth — the air he'd have spoken with was leaving through the hole instead.

"You won't get it. Could be *quick* again. Could be *please*. Could be a name. The air won't carry it. That's one item you're spared without being able to refuse it."

The man's hand came up off his middle — slow, the arm spending its last coin — and found the wrist at the knife. Not pulling. Holding.

"That's not a fight. He hasn't the blood for a fight. That's a man holding on to the thing that's happening to him. They do it. Let it hold till it empties. It's not yours to break and not yours to keep."

She kept her voice level. "Next item, and this one's mine, so it goes on my bill, not yours: don't cut again. Nothing left shallow enough to reach that shortens this. The deep ones you'd have to hunt for through a hole you made wrong, on a man still moving, with a hand that shook on the first pull — and second cuts are where men get carved. I've watched it. It's worse than anything you're looking at now. It's *running*, is the point. The spear emptied him halfway before you ever knelt, so what you've opened is enough to close the account. Minutes. My job is counting them. Yours is the watching. You set that deal yourself."

The eyes were still working. On him.

"He's here. That's the item you're doing to him that the spear never did — the knowing. I won't dress it. What I can't tell you is how much of him is home to feel it. Shock runs men shallow; some are half-dreaming by this hour, and I can't see inside a skull from the outside. Nobody can. That's an honest limit, and you said leave nothing out, so the limit goes in the ledger with the rest.

"Now watch, and I'll call it as it runs. Pressure's going. Body's rationing — I priced you that lesson at the start. Far rooms first. Hands go before anything, fingers can't hold what they're not fed. Then the eyes come off you. That part's plumbing. Nobody's doing it. Nothing's being done."

She counted. Watch-habit, ten years deep, and this once the clock was one she was allowed to keep.

"There. Hands are down. Grip's gone out of it. Eyes have let go of you. He's out of the arithmetic now. The noise that comes next — the rattle — that isn't him. The man leaves before the rattle. What you hear after is the house settling, the body clearing its accounts with nobody home. Don't take it on. Nobody's in there to feel it, and I have never once said that sentence to make a man easier. I'm saying it because it's exact."

The rattle came, ran its uneven course — rattles always sound longer than they are, that's why men fear them past their worth — and thinned, and stopped.

Not mid-pace. It wound down, like a clock running out. She gave him the difference straight, because he'd asked for straight.

"A clean one quits mid-pace. Debt paid early, no argument. This one ran out. Both are quiet at the end. Only one was quick. You'll hear the difference the rest of your life, at inconvenient hours. That's the tax on watching, and you chose it, and I'd not have talked you out of it, because the looking away is what rots a man later. Not this.

"Four minutes. I counted every one. You asked how long — that's the item: four. Now the bill, in the two parts I taught you. First: he asked you for quick and got four minutes awake, and that's a real item, and you carry it. Second, carried separately: his night ran to noon, the stubborn course to the following dusk, every hour of it awake and thirsty and trying positions. You took near all of it off him, and the price was four minutes. Both sums are true. Neither pays the other off. That's the whole trade. Tonight you've had it in the hands instead of the ear.

"Last item, since you said leave nothing out. Mine wasn't clean either. First ones mostly aren't — the clean hand comes after you learn the blade's price, which is the wrong way round, but nobody's fixed the order yet. That's all I'll say of mine tonight. It's not for this fire."

She stood off the bad knee and held out her hand, palm up, eyes off his, for the knife.

"As it is. Cleans at the fire — same fire as your hands, same rule, and I've picked a good spot for it. The name's under the same rule as before: keep it or set it down, but not tonight. Cold decisions come out crooked."

The valley had gone back to the frost kind of quiet, the kind that doesn't want anything. The noise that had kept one pace all evening had changed its pace once, and then stopped changing, and stopped.

"No clock on you now," she said. "Last one in the valley just ran down. Whenever your legs are ready, we start being two valleys gone."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, the blood black and sticky in the creases. "Four minutes." My voice sounds flat, strange in my own ears. I press the knife's handle back into her palm, careful not to touch her skin with mine.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She took the knife without ceremony, the way she'd taken everything tonight, and thumbed it home in the sheath still wearing his work. She didn't look at it going in. Looking at a blade afterward was just standing over by another name.

"Four," she said. "Keep it at four. By the third telling, most men have it down to one clean pull and a mercy. The number grows a story if you feed it. Starve it."

Then she went down on her heels over Tam Wick, knee making its point, because the work wasn't finished while the pockets were full, and the dead don't spend. String came out. Half a flint. A purse light enough that she weighed it twice to be sure of it.

"Three months, he said." She let it clink once. "Pockets say the company started keeping it before tonight. They don't steal a dead man's pay — they just quit carrying the ledger. Same silver, tidier books." The purse went in with the rest. "He spent his last air on the wrong thief. That's the one joke companies tell well."

She stood, and took his hand — the one he'd been keeping off her skin — and folded the reins into it, her bare palm flat against the blood, and held it there until the grip took the leather on its own.

"It's not catching. Ten years of other men's on these hands, and the worst I ever took off it was the knee, and that was the marching." She let go. "Blood comes off at the fire. The four minutes don't. Don't muddle the two and you'll keep your footing."

"Up," she said, and gave him the stirrup. "The horse does the thinking till the fire. A man with his head still back at the cart rides like a sack, and sacks fall off, and I'm not lifting you."

She swung up on her own and turned her horse's nose at the ridge, and they walked the animals out past the ditch, at the pace you leave a place you don't mean to see again. The frost was coming down off the heights now for true, silvering the track, and behind them the valley settled into the quiet that wanted nothing and got it. Six men in it keeping nobody's watch. A cart. A team that would stand where it was left until somebody came to ask the questions.

She kept her eyes on the track and her voice level, side by side, the way the hard freight goes.

"Your voice went off somewhere. It does that after — the body spends everything before the mouth gets its turn. It'll come back at the fire. Most things will tonight." A few strides of gravel. "I'll take first watch. Not because you need watching over. I've got the shorter sleep in me, and you've got the longer one owed."

The track climbed. Ahead was the second valley, and a fire with work waiting on it — his hands, her knife, one name, one decision, and the ordinary dark between here and there, which, for dark, was the good kind. Nobody in it.

Somewhere on the climb she caught her ten-year habit finding the next rhythm to count — his, in the saddle, even and slow, hooves under it. She let it. The habit had outlived everything else it had ever kept time on.

No sense wasting it.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She'd got one knee under her, meaning to stand, when he sat back on his heels instead — and she'd been at this long enough to know the difference between a man gathering his legs and a man settling in. She looked at the dark, did the sum she trusted more than her knee: dawn eight hours off, two valleys wanting four at a walk. There was room in the night for this.

So she sat down. Properly, for the first time all evening — not the working crouch, but flat on the frozen ground, back against the cart's off-wheel, the bad knee straight out in front of her like something set down. The dead man a pace off, past caring. She dug the flask out of her coat, took one swallow, and held it across.

"One, now. Not for forgetting — it's never once done that for me. For the shaking that's coming. It'll find you regardless. Better it finds you sitting."

She let him take it or not, and looked at the stars doing their cold arithmetic overhead.

"I said there's no ceremony after, and there isn't. This isn't one. This is inventory — the part the trade skips and pays for skipping. It comes in three parts. Tonight, which is yours. Mine, which you've been circling since the knife. And the ten years, which you've paid the entry fee on as of four minutes ago. I'll take them in order. Don't interrupt for the good parts. There aren't any.

"Tonight. Inside the hour your hands will go. Not fear — spending. Your body drew the whole account down for those four minutes, same as his drew his down for the night, and it rebalances by shaking. Half an hour, in waves. From a distance it looks like weeping. It isn't. Let it run. Fighting it moves it somewhere with worse manners.

"Then the one that horrifies every man it happens to: you'll be hungry. Tonight. Bread and want, with him forty paces off still warm. You'll think the wanting tells you something bad about you. It doesn't. The body doesn't know what the hands did — it only knows what it spent, and it refills. Men who refuse the meal don't refuse the bill; it comes out sideways in the weeks after. The weeping at the wrong thing. The temper. Eat tonight. I'll cook.

"Sleep is either or neither, and both are honest. If you dream, it won't be him. First night, the mind sends understudies — lost boots, a door that won't latch. Stupid dreams. Let them be stupid. And his face won't stay with you. I couldn't draw Tam Wick's face an hour from now, and I watched closer than you did. Faces don't keep. The sound keeps — the wet in the breath, and where you were standing when it stopped. You'll hear it again at inconvenient hours. At a well. At a man snoring two fires over. You'll grade every one against tonight. That's knowledge nobody can take back off you, and it's the whole company he'll keep with you from here on. It's poorer company than a name. Keep the name instead.

"One practical item, since we're sitting next to him: when the frost takes the joints, he'll creak. Dead men creak — ice in the machinery, nothing else. First time a man hears it he invents ghosts. You've had the lesson, so you're inoculated.

"Part two. Mine." She spent a breath on it like coin. "I said it wasn't for this fire. But a promise like that is mostly for the promiser's comfort, and you've sat down, so the fire's here. Cold one. Most of them were.

"The war started over a fish weir on the Sere. Or the toll on the bridge — depends whose drunk you're buying. Ten years back that was worth a quarrel, and the quarrel was worth feeding men to, so both sides fed them. Nobody's fighting over the weir now. Half of them couldn't find the river. Ask either line what it's about and you get the same answer: what the other lot did in year three. It's been about that for seven years. The original thing drowned in its own war, and nobody mourns it, because nobody remembers which bank it stood on.

"I came in year one. Guarded wool before that, up the coast road — that's where the horses are from. First month, at a ford that had a name before the war and has a different one now, because both sides renamed it after their dead, I drew night watch over a man who'd taken a spear through the hip and been left for the night by both sides. That's what both sides do. Leave them for the night, let the night do the work, nobody's hands dirty by morning. Sergeant's words. I sat with that man to the following dusk, because he hadn't the pace to die by dawn and I hadn't the rank to be relieved. Told you once he was sorry the whole way. So was I. Here's the part I left out: he asked for water fourteen times. I gave it once, because I didn't know, and it came straight back up into his own face, and after that I only wet his lips, and he asked anyway, every time — because the asking wasn't about water. It was about having something left to ask for. And he wanted a priest, and I told him there was no priest in thirty miles, which was true, and we spent an hour of his last afternoon with him begging and me being correct. Being right at a dying man is the most expensive right there is. He settled in the end. Not because I won. Because he ran out of air to argue with. That's the receipt for 'answer once and don't argue.'

"Four days later, the ditch. Man on his back, like this one. And me with a sword, because a sword was the thing my hand knew. Sword's for men who can stand — that rule's not from a book either. A sword wants to swing, and there's no swing in a throat, and everything a sword does to a prone man it does by sawing. I sawed. Three pulls. Don't saw — now you know where that one's priced from too. I did it from the front, where he could see me, because I didn't know that rule was for my benefit, not his. And he held my wrist, same as Tam held yours. Not a fight. A man holding on to the thing that's happening to him. I broke it — pulled free and finished. Ten years I've wondered whether that was mercy or hurry. Still don't know. Some items stay open. You carry them open. That's allowed. Nobody tells you that, so I am.

"They started calling me Wrack that winter. There'd been a wreck on the coast road — winter storm, and the beach was a mile of spars and cargo and dead men's boots, all of it where the sea had left it, nothing wrong with any single piece of it except the whole of it. Somebody said I came off fields the way that beach sat. It was a joke. Jokes stick better than names do, which tells you something about both. My given name's still in there somewhere. You don't get to hear it — a woman's allowed one item off the ledger. But I know the place Tam Wick couldn't get the breath to name. I've been. You don't get the name back. You get called what the work gives you, and after a while you answer to it, and after a while longer it's yours on the pay chest. That's the whole road. You took the first pace of it tonight. I'll not lie about the direction: it runs one way.

"Part three. You want to know if it gets easier. It gets quicker. Different ledger. Inside a year, if you're any good, four minutes becomes one pull. Inside three, the pull becomes a motion, and the motion costs nothing on the night — you'll do it and sleep like a paid man. That's not easier. That's the account moving its costs somewhere you don't check nightly. Then one evening, ten years on, a man sits back on his heels in the cold and asks for the rest, and you find out what the account's been doing the whole time. Keeping the interest.

"The company mustered forty-one in year one. Three of us left drawing breath. There's Hobb — fever took his years after year six, so he thinks it's year four, and he's happier in them, so nobody corrects him. There's Marren, who does the sums and the sutlering and once killed a man with a tent stake, which is in no book either. And there's me. Forty-one to three. That's the arithmetic of loyalty: it doesn't spread, it concentrates. Everything else burns off, and what's left is the part that doesn't.

"Why I stay. Because I'm good at it and the ten years ate my other trades, and because somebody has to be the one who talks a man through his first — and if it isn't me, it's a man who tells him it gets easier, and then in year nine that man is standing on a quiet road with an item he was promised would close. I've buried that man four times. Different faces. Same promise in the ears.

"So. The sum, one line, since you'll want one: see it exact, do it anyway, and don't ask it to be prettier — and know the exactness is the only mercy actually on offer in this business, to him and to you both. The kindness tonight wasn't the knife. It's that nobody lied to either of you. Truth's the only thing I've watched keep a man whole. Not happy. Whole. Different column."

The horses shifted somewhere behind her, gravel under hooves — the only other clocks left in the valley. She let the quiet sit a while, because a thing said that long needs room around it, the way a body does.

"You're still Corvin," she said then. "That's worth more than you know tonight. See it stays yours a while yet. And the name rides with you to the fire either way — keep it or set it down there, not before. I've a preference, but it's worth nothing, which is what preferences are for."

The frost kept coming down. It had all night, and for once, so did she.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take the flask and swallow. It burns all the way down. "I'll keep the name," I say, my voice still too quiet. "And I'll eat."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
She took the flask back, had her own swallow — the neck tasting of him, which was the flask doing its work — and capped it.

"Good," she said, before she'd priced the word. Then, because rules were rules even when you liked the answer: "Said not before the fire, though. So hold it as a leaning, not a vow. A name that can't survive one cold ride was never going to survive forty years, and one that can doesn't need the promise. The fire settles it either way.

"And since nobody ever told me what keeping looks like, I'll tell you. It's not a vigil. It's a thing in a pocket. Some nights you turn it over. Most nights you don't think of it at all. Then you find it in there with the fluff and the old die, and you turn it over, and you put it back. That's the whole of keeping. Anything more ceremonial than that goes crooked inside a year.

"As for eating — that one you can decide in any weather. The body votes early, and it's the same ballot every time." She considered her kit from memory. "There's bread that could stop a sword, and pork the frost has kept honest. It eats better than it sounds, which is faint praise, and I know it."

Then quiet, for a while, because a night could stand some after all that talk.

Somewhere off to the right, Tam Wick creaked — one long settling pop, the ice going into the joints.

"There's your creak," she said, not looking over. "Told you. Ice in the machinery, nobody home to rattle it. That's the inoculation doing its work."

She read the stars the way she'd read them on a thousand watches. The wheel had turned near an hour since she'd sat down, which made it the longest single spend of words she'd made in a decade. She kept that sum to herself.

"Dark's spent an hour on us. Four left in hand, and the ride wants three and change. Room, but no lounging." She got up in three stages, none of them dignified, and stood while the blood went back into the leg. The knee lodged its objection late, as usual. "You had my whole history for an hour of night. Don't go expecting it regular — that was the decade's ration, spent in one sitting. Next one's ten years off, and by then you'll have paid your own way into it."

The horses had stood the whole hour where she'd left them, which was better discipline than half the company had ever shown on pay day. She collected them, brought his around, and folded the reins into his hand — the bloodied one, since it was nearest.

"Two names now," she said. "Corvin — the one the world calls. Wick — the one you keep. Different cargo from mine; mine was mine first, and I've no complaints about yours being secondhand. The rig's the same, and the rig holds."

She swung up and turned her horse's nose at the ridge.

"One more item, and then I'm done spending words tonight: the shaking's still owed you. It'll come in the saddle or at the fire, and it doesn't care which. If it's the saddle — one hand on the pommel and let the horse do the thinking. It's better at it than you are tonight."

They walked out past the ditch, past the six men keeping nobody's watch, at the pace you leave a place you don't mean to see again. The frost had silvered the track ahead of them. Behind, the valley went on getting quieter, though there was nothing left in it to quiet — the frost taking the cart, and the team, and Tam Wick with his accounts closed, and all of it content to be taken.

Wrack rode with her eyes forward. Nothing back there needed her. There rarely was anything that did, by the time she left — and she'd said enough plain things for one night without spending that one too.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, and the movement feels stiff. I don't look back at the cart. My hands grip the reins and they're steady for now. I know it's borrowed. "Lead on, then."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
They rode out and up, and she kept the promise about words. The night owed her quiet on the change, and she collected.

The track climbed through the good dark, the kind with nobody in it, and the frost kept coming down off the heights like it was being paid by the cartload. Her habit went looking for rhythms and found three: hooves, tack, his breathing in the saddle, slow and even. She let it count. Ten years keeping time on dying men, and tonight it had a living man in the ledger. Nearest thing to a promotion the habit was ever going to see.

The shaking came on the climb, on schedule, which was the only merciful thing about it. She heard it before she saw it — his tack creaking out of rhythm, a thin jingle off the reins — and the horse's head came up a hand-span, because the horse had known for half a minute already. Horses always filed the report first. She watched the horse, not the man. The horse gave the honest version.

She brought her mount alongside and let them both down to a walk.

"Pommel," she said. That was the whole speech.

Then she counted it, because counting was the only thing she could do for him from horseback. Waves, like she'd said. The first took him hard — all of him going rigid in the saddle, then rippling, the reins ringing a tune nobody meant. Out of the corner of her eye it would have looked like a man weeping in the saddle, and she knew it wasn't, and she kept her eyes on the track, which was the whole of the courtesy available. The second wave was lighter. The third came after a gap you could have driven the cart through, and lighter again. Half an hour, near as made no difference. Then the rhythm came back even, and the horse forgave him before the night did.

"Good horse," she told the horse, since one of them had come out of it with credit.

At the top of the track she allowed herself one look back, and it was a professional look — checking for lights, nothing sentimental in it. The valley sat under the frost with no fire in it, no torch, no movement. Six men and a cart keeping nobody's watch, same as they'd been left.

"No lights," she said. "That's the valley's full report. We're done with each other."

Then down, and the second valley opened below them, black and folded and empty, and she picked her way toward the room she'd had in mind since the ditch: a shepherd's wall still standing to knee height, a stream talking in the dark, blackthorn standing in fuel. Ten years teaches a body where the night keeps its good rooms.

She came off her horse in stages, the knee filing its grievance, and got the gear off both animals and a hobble on. "Horse first," she said. "It worked harder than either of us tonight and complained less. Then food, then your hands. That order. The order's the whole medicine."

The fire she built small and screened behind the wall, the way you build one when the dark's been good to you but you don't sign anything. Blackthorn burns hot and smells of nothing, which is the point of blackthorn. Water went on to heat in the helm, ash spooned in after — the old trick, turns water mean enough to argue blood out of the creases, and blood in the creases has to be argued.

She cooked. Pork on a flat stone propped to the coals, fat hissing, and the bread toasted hard in the drippings, improving from weapon to toast, which was as much as she'd promised it and exactly as much as it delivered.

Then she drew her knife — still wearing his work, gone black with the frost — and laid it on the stone with the rag beside it, handle toward him.

"Your work's on it. Clean it or I will, your call — same rule as ever." She set the helm of water where he could reach it. "Ash is already in. Hot as you can stand, and give it time. Knuckles hold it longest. They'll come clean. Everything at this fire comes clean except the four minutes, and you've had your instruction on feeding those."

She handed him his share on the tin plate, a piece of the war older than the war.

"Eat. The body's voted already. This is just the counting."

And that was the list she'd promised the fire would see to — hands, steel, food, warmth — all of it delivered or laid in reach. She took her own portion and sat back on her heels on the dark side of the flames, and let the last item keep its own time.

"The name decides between here and sleep, or it doesn't. I'm not asking. I told you I had a preference and that it was worth nothing, and both halves of that still hold."

She ate like a paid woman, which was the whole of her table manners, and watched the dark instead of him, because a man doing his cleaning doesn't need an audience, and the dark did — that was the watch, started early and sitting down.

"Sleep when it comes for you. First night sends the stupid dreams — boots, doors that won't latch. Let them be stupid. If it sends him instead, that's a bigger coin than first nights usually deal, but you've had the schooling, and schooling holds. I'm good till the grey. Then you'll get your watch. You're owed the longer sleep, and I keep books on what men are owed."

The fire cracked. The stream kept its one sound, same pace all night, the way streams do — the only thing in two valleys that had kept a pace all evening and never once made her think about it.

She counted the watch, because that was the work. And somewhere in the counting she noticed the shape of the ledger she was keeping: horses shifting at the picket, fire settling, a man by the fire with bread in his hand. Everything her habit had to time was alive. She tried to recall the last stretch of dark where that had been true and couldn't.

She made nothing of it. Making things of nights was how men went crooked. But she entered it in the private ledger all the same — one item, marked paid, no debt attached — and let it run.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
I eat without tasting it. The shaking's left me hollow. I look at my hands in the firelight, at the clean pale lines where the ash-water's done its work. The blood's gone. The creases are just creases again.

I pick up her knife. The water's still hot. I start to work the black off the blade. It comes away in flakes, like old paint.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Belly's the worst of the slow ones.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That's gut. His insides are open into him.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: the big pipes that hang the gut off the spine are split

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The bubbling, the froth at the hole

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: I sawed. Three pulls.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked up at that, one brow lifting. The dead man’s cloak had done little for the blood on her knife, but it had done something for the blood on her knuckles, and she tossed it aside like it had personally offended her.

“Then you heard him,” she said. “Good. Hearing is the easy part.”

She stood, joints popping in the quiet, and nodded toward the cart without moving toward it herself. The sound from beyond the wheels was thin and wet, the kind of noise a man made when he was trying to stay conscious and failing.

“You can walk over there and finish it, or you can leave him to the crows. Both are decisions. Just don’t stand there pretending you haven’t made one.” She wiped her thumb along the edge again, more out of habit than concern. “And if you want him talking, do it soon. Dead men are poor conversationalists, and dying ones get worse by the minute.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a sharp breath and start walking toward the cart. "Fine," I mutter, more to myself than to her. My sword feels heavier than it did five minutes ago. "Let's see what he has to say."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not call him back. She took one last look at the ditch, the dead, and the road behind, then came after him at the pace of a woman who had learned that hurry usually meant tripping over something useful.

“If he’s talking, he’s alive enough to lie,” she said. “And if he’s not, don’t waste time making him.”

She stopped short of the cart, where the ground sloped away into a shallow wash. The noise beyond it was worse now, a bubbling, desperate thing, like a man trying to drink through a wound. Wrack’s eyes went first to the far side of the cart, then the tree line, then the dead men’s hands. Nothing moved but flies.

“Keep your knife hand free,” she added, quieter. “Dying men are dangerous in the last minute. Not because they’re brave. Because they’ve stopped caring what happens.”

She crouched by one of the overturned baskets, turning a spilled apple over with the tip of her boot. “If he’s one of them, he’ll say he was told we were coming. If he’s a civilian, he’ll say he wasn’t in the fight. If he’s smart, he’ll say nothing at all until you’ve put a price on it.”

Her gaze lifted toward the cart.

“Ask him who sent him,” she said. “Not why. Why’s the first thing they invent.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave the cart a short, assessing look, as if the question had cost her something.

“Bad enough that you’re already trying to make it someone else’s fault,” she said. “That’s not a diagnosis. That’s a habit.”

She stepped around the cart on the side away from the road, slow and careful, and crouched just enough to see past the splintered wheel. The dying man lay half in the wash, one hand slack in the dirt, the other curled like it had tried to grab the air and failed. His breath came in wet, hitching pulls, the sort that meant something had gone wrong deep inside where the body did its quiet work.

Wrack looked at him for three seconds and stood again.

“Lung,” she said. “Maybe both. He’s drowning from the inside, which means he won’t be much good for talking, and it also means if you ask him who sent him, he’ll tell you whatever he thinks will buy him one more breath.”

She turned the empty side of her knife against a broken branch, scraping off a smear of dried mud.

“As for mercy and easier, those are just the words people use when they want to feel clean about what they’re going to do anyway.” Her mouth twisted, not quite a smile. “Mercy is what a priest calls it. Easier is what a man calls it when he’s in a hurry. Both can be true. Both are also a way of not looking at the mess in front of you.”

She glanced toward the tree line, then back at him.

“If he’s got enough in him to answer, use that. If he doesn’t, don’t dress it up. Put him down and be done, because the crows won’t care whether you chose it for kindness or convenience. They’ll just take what’s there.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, crouching down next to the man. His eyes are wide, pleading. "Who sent you?" I ask, my voice low. I keep my knife ready, like she said.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not crowd him. She came around the far side of the cart, where the dying man’s feet showed through the slats, and she watched the tree line while she watched him.

“Too close,” she said. “You smell like fear and iron. He’s not going to tell you anything worth having while he thinks you’re going to use his chest for a pillow.”

The man’s mouth moved. A wet, broken syllable came out of him, almost a name, almost a prayer, not enough to stake a rope on. His good hand twitched toward the splintered wheel, then stopped when Wrack put her boot lightly on his wrist. Not hard. Just enough to remind him he was not going to grab anything but the air.

She turned his hand over with her boot, without touching it. The palm was soft, the fingers cracked with rope burn, the calluses wrong for a sword hand and wrong for a reinsman.

“Teamster,” she said. “Or somebody stole a teamster’s coat. That’s not a soldier’s hand.”

The man tried to speak again. What came out was a bubbling rasp, and then his eyes went to the cart.

Wrack followed the look.

“He’s not telling you who sent him,” she said. “He’s telling you he left something under the seat. Ask him what was in the load. If he was paid to ride along, he’ll remember the goods. If he was paid to ambush us, he’ll remember the order. If he’s lying, he’ll remember the excuse.”

The cart creaked. Flies rose from the wash in a black, oily cloud and settled again.

Wrack’s mouth tightened.

“He’s got less than a minute of breath,” she said. “After that, he’s got all the answers you’ll ever want, and none of them are words.”

She drew a short knife and set it on the ground between them, not offering it, just making it easy.

“If he’s got a name in him, it’ll come out when he’s afraid,” she said. “If he doesn’t, put him down. I won’t think less of you. The crows don’t care who asked, and the mud doesn’t care why.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him as if he had asked her to describe the sky.

“You’re looking at a puncture wound below the right ribs,” she said. “Small on the outside, mean on the inside. Knife or arrowhead. Most of the blood’s not coming out. It’s going in. That’s why he’s drowning.”

She crouched again, but she kept her knife low and used the tip of it to lift the torn cloak away from his side. She did not touch the man.

“There,” she said. “That’s why he’s still talking. Air’s in the wrong place. If you press there, he’ll panic. If you try to sit him up, he’ll cough until he can’t.”

The dying man’s eyes slid toward the movement, then toward Corvin, then back to the cart. Wrack watched him the way a woman watches a horse deciding whether to bolt.

Her boot shifted near his wrist. She nudged the slack hand enough to show the palm, without touching it.

“Rope burn on the left. Not a sword hand. Not an axe hand. Callus sits wrong for a soldier and wrong for a reinsman in the same man.” Her mouth tightened. “Teamster. Or somebody stole a teamster’s coat because it had pockets and didn’t need to be cut down.”

She glanced toward the cart again.

“The seat’s been lifted. Not recently. The wood underneath is clean, but the straw’s been kicked around. If he left something there, he didn’t hide it for himself. He hid it for whoever was supposed to come after.”

The man tried to speak. A wet, broken sound came out of him, more bubble than word.

Wrack did not look at him.

“His eyes are on your knife, not your face,” she said. “That means he’s afraid of dying, not of punishment. If you threaten him, he’ll beg. If you ask him a dozen questions, he’ll give you a dozen excuses. One question. Short. Who paid you. Not why. Not where. Not tell me everything. He’s got maybe a breath and a half. Use it or don’t.”

She finally looked up at Corvin.

“So what you’re looking at is not a soldier. It’s a man with a lung hole, a teamster’s hands, no weapon, and something under the seat that was worth more than he is. Either he was cargo with bad luck, or he was bait with a message. And either way, he’s not going to make it to the next dark without help.”

She let the silence sit for a moment. The dying man’s breath made the wet sound again, a sucking, bubbling thing.

“If you’re going to ask him something,” Wrack said, “ask it now. If you’re going to put him down, do it clean. Don’t poke at the chest. That’s just making more work.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Were you with them or just driving?" My voice comes out steadier than I feel. I crouch lower, so he can see my face instead of just my blade. "A name. Give me one."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not answer at once. She watched the dying man’s mouth work and then looked at Corvin with the patience of someone deciding whether to be kind or useful.

“Two questions,” she said. “You asked him whether he was a soldier or a mule, then demanded a name. If he’s smart, he’s already decided which answer gets him a slower death.”

She crouched near his head, not close enough for blood to touch her sleeve, and waited. The man’s eyes slid from her to the cart. His lips moved without sound for a moment, then one wet syllable came out.

“...just...”

Wrack nodded. “Just driving. He’s got a lung full of blood and a teamster’s hands, so believe him if it makes you warm.” She looked at the man. “Name.”

The man’s gaze went to the knife, then to the sky. His mouth made a shape that was almost a word, almost a name, and then something else:

“Hale.”

Wrack’s mouth tightened. “Hale’s a name. Not an answer. Unless you mean the tanner at Lowbridge. If you mean the tanner at Lowbridge, then this was not a cartload of turnips.”

The man coughed. A frothy thread of blood ran from his nose. Wrack did not wipe it away. She looked at the cart instead, then back at the dying man.

“Seat boards,” she said, quieter. “He lifted them before the road came. Straw was kicked under, not on top. You don’t hide grain that way. You hide a message, a purse, or a name. Since he gave you Hale, I’d look for the purse first. Messages get read. Money gets stolen.”

She glanced toward the wash, where the wet sound was thinning.

“He’s not going to say who sent him if it buys him a minute. He’ll say Hale because Hale paid him and maybe didn’t tell him what the cart was. Or he’ll say Hale because Hale is the name he was told to use if he got caught. Either way, you’re not going to get a confession out of a man who’s trying to keep air in the wrong place.”

She stood and brushed dirt from her knees.

“If you want his full name, ask. If you want Hale’s, ask. If you want to know whether he’s lying, look at his hands when you do it. Soldiers lie with their faces. Dying men lie with their eyes. This one is lying about something, but he’s also telling the truth about the cart.”

Wrack nodded toward the short knife still on the ground between them.

“Decide what you need before he stops needing you. I’ll hold the cart steady if you want to look under the seat. I won’t do it for you. Not because it’s yours to do. Because if there’s another blade under there, I’d rather not be the one wearing it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at him as if he had asked her to describe the weather.

Then she said, “Straight, then.”

She crouched again, but not near the dying man. She stayed where the cart’s shadow could keep the flies off her face, and she used the tip of her knife to point at the ground, not the wound.

“A spear is not a sword. Sword cuts. Spear makes a hole. If the point goes into a man’s gut, it opens him like a door and then sits there while he finds out the inside of himself was never meant to breathe.”

Her voice stayed flat, useful.

“If it goes through, there’s a hole going in and a hole coming out, and the body doesn’t know which one to bleed from. It tries both. If the shaft stays in, it plugs the worst of it for a while, which is not mercy. That’s just delay. When you pull it, the plug goes, and the man comes apart.”

The dying man’s breath hitched. Wrack did not look at him.

“If it hits the liver, he gets sick and stupid before he dies. If it hits the bowel, he empties himself and lies there smelling like what’s inside him. If it hits the spine, his legs stop and he can still feel the pain, which is a bad trade. If it misses the big vessels, he lives long enough to beg for water, then long enough to ask you to stop it. If it catches the femoral, there’s a hole the size of your thumb and he goes pale in a minute and dead in three.”

She turned the knife in her hand, watching the edge catch the last light.

“There’s no clean version. A spear to the gut makes a man into heat and noise and bowels and blood. If he doesn’t die quick, the rot finishes it. The mud takes the rest. The crows take the rest. You take the part where you remember the smell.”

Her mouth tightened.

“That’s what it does. Not what it looks like in songs. What it looks like is a man trying to be somewhere else while his body is still holding him in place.”

She finally looked at the dying man again, listening to the wet, sucking sound of him.

“That’s not spear,” she said. “That’s a knife or arrowhead in the chest. If it were a spear in his gut, he’d have more time, and less dignity. You’re asking because you want to know what you’ll be doing if he doesn’t answer.”

She glanced toward the cart, then back at him.

“Fine. You won’t be doing mercy. You’ll be stopping a sound. If he’s got a spear in his belly, you won’t be stopping a sound. You’ll be ending a slow, filthy thing. Same result. Different weight.”

Wrack stood, brushing dirt from her knees.

“If you want to look under the seat, look. If you want to put him down, do it clean. Neck, not chest. Not because it’s easier. Because it’s done. And when it’s done, don’t stand there trying to make the mud feel less like mud. It won’t. It’s mud.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I move toward the cart, ignoring the dying man for a moment. My fingers dig under the seat board, prying it up. It's dark underneath, but my hand closes around a small, oilskin-wrapped bundle. "Found something." My throat is dry.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack let the last of the words drop into the mud. The dying man’s breath had gone from wet bubbles to a thin, sucking flutter, and she watched it the way she watched a fire going out: not hopeful, just checking the time.

“Straight enough,” she said. “Now you’ve got two kinds of work in front of you. One’s a body that doesn’t need a name anymore. The other’s a cart that might.”

She moved to the seat, crouched with her shoulder under the boards, and braced them with one hand. Her knife stayed in the other, low and easy.

“Look if you want. Don’t thank me for the smell. Hale might have paid him to carry goods, or to be found. If there’s a purse under there, it means Hale wanted a receipt. If there’s a paper, it means Hale wanted an error discovered by the wrong people. If there’s a knife, he wanted this to end in a different shape.”

The man’s fingers twitched once in the dirt. Wrack glanced down, then away.

“Either way, you’ve got a minute before the flies get formal.” She shifted her shoulder under the seat. “Decide if you’re going to be the man who looked, or the man who stood around knowing too much about spears.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped. Her hand came away from the cart board, and she turned back slowly, as if she had been asked to do something harder than fight.

“Stay,” she said, as if she were deciding whether the word was a plea or an order. Then she crouched in the cart’s shadow, close enough to see, far enough that the dying man’s blood would not be her problem.

“All right. Watch.”

The man’s breath had gone from sucking to something looser, a wet rattle that changed every time he moved. The dirt around him had turned black where the blood ran. Wrack looked at the wound without touching it.

“You’ve made a hole in his throat,” she said. “Not a clean one. You were afraid, or you were new. Afraid hands go too high or too low. This one went both.”

She tilted her head, listening.

“That’s the carotid. Big vein. The blood doesn’t spray like a song. It runs dark and fast because the heart is still doing its job and doesn’t know you’ve changed the rules.” Her eyes flicked to his hands. “His fingers are still twitching. That means the brain hasn’t emptied yet. You didn’t take the spine. You’re still making him alive.”

The dying man’s heels beat once against the dirt. Wrack did not flinch.

“You’re stopping the air and starting the blood,” she said. “That’s what a throat is for, and you’ve taken both jobs away. He can’t breathe out, so the blood bubbles. He can’t breathe in, so the lungs keep pulling at nothing. If he’s lucky, he passes out. If he’s unlucky, he stays awake and wonders why the world has gone red and wet.”

A fly landed on the man’s cheek. Wrack watched it go.

“That sound,” she added, quieter, “is the last part. That’s a man learning his body isn’t his own anymore. If you want to know what you’re doing, that’s it: you’re ending a thing that was already ending. But you’re doing it badly because you’re doing it fast and scared.”

She looked at Corvin, not kindly, not cruelly.

“If you’d done it clean, he’d have been dead before he heard himself scream. You didn’t. So now you’ve got work. You finish it, or you leave him to do it himself while the crows wait. Both are decisions. Only one is yours.”

Her gaze went back to the dying man.

“What you’re doing to him is not mercy. Not yet. Right now it’s a lesson in what happens when a man with a knife and no stomach for it tries to do a job he doesn’t understand. The crows are judging your form.”

The man’s eyes slid toward Corvin. Wrack saw them and looked back.

“Don’t look away because you asked me to tell you straight,” she said. “Straight is what this is. A hole where there was no need for one. Blood in the dirt. A name under a seat. And you learning that mercy is mostly a word people use when they want to feel clean about the mess they’re already making.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I finish it. The next cut is deep and quick. Then I wipe my blade on my pants and stand up, my legs shaky. "Open it," I say, nodding to the oilskin bundle. My voice sounds flat.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked at the body. The second cut had been clean. The wet sound stopped. The face became an object with a hole in it.

“That one was done,” she said. “Don’t wipe your knife on your trousers. Blood stiffens cloth, and oilskin grease doesn’t wash out. If you’re going to smell like a tanner’s shop, at least do it on purpose.”

She looked at Corvin’s face.

“Your voice is not flat. It’s the sound of a man keeping his throat inside his body by force.”

She took the bundle from his hand before he could decide that was a mistake.

“Open it? Fine. But if there’s a mark inside that points at us, don’t look at me like I gave it to you.”

She set the oilskin on a dry patch of the dead man’s cloak. She did not touch it with her fingers. She used her knife to peel back the folds, then cut the knot inside. The smell came up: tallow, old sweat, and the animal scent of new leather.

Inside were three things: a small purse, a folded paper sealed with black wax, and a lead token stamped with the mark of the north garrison’s supply train.

Wrack looked at the token for a long moment.

“Hale is a name,” she said. “That is a stamp. And stamps don’t die in ditches unless somebody wants them seen.”

She rolled the purse toward him with the knife tip.

“Money. Mixed. Border silver on one side, company coin on the other. Somebody paid this man in both currencies. That’s not loyalty. That’s accounting.”

She broke the wax with the side of her knife and spread the paper with the tip. The writing was short, cramped, and badly done.

“Cart to Lowbridge ford. No steel. If stopped, say Hale. If not stopped, say nothing.”

Wrack read it twice, then looked at the dead man.

“He wasn’t supposed to be in a fight,” she said. “He was supposed to be a message that got found.”

She turned the lead token in the light.

“That’s ours. Not Hale’s. Our commissary stamped that. Which means either the war has gone stupid enough that someone in our own pay is hiring tanners to ambush us, or someone wants us to think so.” She gave Corvin a dry look. “Both answers are bad. One of them is just closer to home.”

She stood and wiped her knife on the cloak without thinking about it.

“If they wanted us dead, they’d have done better. If they wanted us found, they’d have done worse. This is a business card. Six men died to make the card look honest.”

She nodded at the body.

“He’s not going to improve. If you want him buried, dig. If you want him hidden, wait until dark and use the ditch. If you want him avenged, that’s the paper. If you want him paid for, that’s the purse.”

Her gaze went to the tree line.

“We can leave it. Burn it. Take it to Hale. Take it to the company. Or take it to the nearest fool who will pay us for it. Each one gets us a different kind of trouble.”

She shifted her weight, listening. The road was quiet enough to make the quiet feel like a held breath.

“You asked me to tell you straight,” Wrack said. “Straight is this: you’re going to keep opening things. Some of them will bite. Decide what you want in your hands before the dark decides for you.”

Then, quieter:

“I’ll watch the trees. The crows are getting formal.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not answer at once. She listened to the quiet the way a woman listens to a dog that has stopped barking. Then she looked down at the dead man, at the second cut, at the black shine spreading through the dirt.

“The rest,” she said, “is that you’re not asking because you want the truth. You’re asking because the truth is already in your hands and you want someone else to say it out loud so it stops being yours.”

She crouched by the body and drew the man’s eyelids shut with two fingers. She did it without ceremony, because the flies had already chosen him as furniture.

“There,” she said. “That’s not for him. Dead men don’t care who sees them. That’s for you, so you can decide whether you want to look at him as a face or as a thing.”

She stood and moved to the nearest of the six in the ditch. She did not touch the bodies. She used her knife to turn a sleeve, lift a cloak, press a boot against a hand to show the palm. She looked at belts, boots, weapon grips, the way hands had curled.

“Two soldiers,” she said after a moment. “Real ones. Sword hands, boot wear, belts cut for knives they didn’t get to use. The rest are hired. Farm hands. Rope burns. One of them was old enough to remember the last war and young enough to die in this one. That’s not a company. That’s a purse with a bad reputation.”

She walked the edge of the road, eyes on the grass where boots might have turned. The cart stood crooked, one wheel sunk into the wash. The traces were slack.

“The horse is gone,” she said. “Either it ran when the arrows came, or somebody cut the traces and took it. If it ran, that’s luck. If somebody took it, that’s planning. Planning means someone expected us to find the paper. Planning means the ambush was too small to work and big enough to look like one.”

She came back to the cart and looked at the oilskin bundle on the cloak.

“The rest is that this is not a battle,” Wrack said. “Battles have lines, and fools, and men shouting things they can’t hear over the blood. This is a message with bodies for punctuation. Six men died to make a card look honest. One of them got a knife in the chest for it, then got a name out of his mouth because you were close enough to make him give it. Hale. Now you’ve got Hale, and Hale is a door.”

Her mouth tightened.

“Doors can be opened. They can also be watched.”

She looked at the dead man again.

“You want the rest about what you did. Fine. The first cut was bad. The second was necessary. Don’t let anyone tell you that makes you worse than them. It makes you one of us. That’s not a compliment. It’s a diagnosis.”

She scraped her knife along the edge of the cart, not because it needed scraping, but because the habit kept her hands useful.

“You asked me whether a spear to the gut was clean. It isn’t. You asked whether killing a dying man is mercy or convenience. It can be both. It’s mostly arithmetic. A man with a lung hole is a man already dying. You can let him finish slowly, drowning on his own blood while the flies get formal, or you can make the math stop sooner. That’s not purity. That’s plumbing.”

Her gaze went back to Corvin.

“The rest is what plumbing does to a man. You’ll hear it when you’re trying to sleep. Not the whole thing. That would be too honest. You’ll hear the second part. The wet sound. The way the body goes from a person to an object while the hands are still twitching. It’ll come back quieter every year, then one night it’ll come back as if you’re kneeling in the dirt again. If that bothers you, get used to it. If it doesn’t bother you, pay attention. That’s worse.”

She turned and looked down the road. Nothing moved but leaves and the black, oily drift of flies. The sky was going the color of old tin.

“I’ve been doing this ten years,” Wrack said. “The border war stopped having a point somewhere around year three. After that, it kept having a payroll. Men died for bridges that didn’t lead anywhere, for fords that froze over in winter, for names on maps drawn by men who never had to kneel in mud and cut throats. That’s what the border is. A line somebody invented so somebody else could buy land and hire us to die on it.”

She nodded toward the dead men.

“These ones weren’t dying for the border. They were dying because Hale wanted a receipt, and the receipt wanted witnesses, and the witnesses wanted money. The paper says no steel. If stopped, say Hale. If not stopped, say nothing. That’s not a soldier’s order. That’s a merchant’s lie with a knife behind it.”

She crouched again and turned the lead token over with the tip of her knife.

“The stamp is ours,” she said. “The purse has company coin. That means somebody in our own pay is either stupid enough to hire tanners to ambush us, or clever enough to make us think they are. Both are bad. One of them is just closer to home.”

The wind moved through the cart, rattling the loose board. Wrack watched it as if it had spoken.

“You asked me to tell you straight,” she said. “Straight is this: you didn’t do something unforgivable tonight. You did something necessary, badly at first, then less badly. That’s what most men do. The difference is that most men don’t ask me to describe it while the blood is still wet. You did. That means you’re either brave or foolish. In this business, it’s often the same thing wearing different boots.”

She stood and brushed dirt from her knees.

“The rest is that you can’t ask me to make it mean less. I won’t. If you want absolution, go find a priest. If you want a story that makes tonight feel like a battle, go find a bard. If you want the truth, here it is: a man died by your hand, and another six died because of a message, and you’re going to spend the rest of your life deciding whether that makes you a killer or a man with a knife in a world full of killers. The crows have already made their choice. They don’t care.”

She looked down at the bundle.

“Money. Paper. Token. That’s three things. One buys. One accuses. One connects. If we take them, we own the trouble. If we burn them, we pretend the trouble wasn’t there. If we leave them, somebody else picks up the trouble and decides what it means. If we take it to the company, we make enemies among people who are already paid to make enemies. If we take it to Hale, we either get answers, or we get a rope and a reason to swing.”

Wrack’s voice stayed flat, useful, the way a woman’s voice stayed flat when she was counting arrows and deciding whether to run or fight.

“You asked for a name. You got one. Now you have to decide if Hale is a man or a door. If he’s a man, he’ll be frightened when you knock. If he’s a door, there’ll be men behind it with better knives than you had tonight.”

She moved to the nearest dead soldier and looked at his boots.

“You’re going to stand up,” Wrack said. “Not because I’m ordering you. Because if you don’t, the dark will make the decision for you, and the dark is not kind. When you stand, check your blade. Check your purse. Check whether you’re bleeding. Check whether the road is still quiet. Quiet is not peace. Quiet is usually the sound of someone waiting.”

Her eyes went to the tree line again.

“If you want to bury him, dig. If you want to hide him, push him under the cart and cover the blood with dirt. If you want him avenged, that’s the paper. If you want him paid for, that’s the purse. If you want him to stop being a lesson, you can’t have that. Lessons are the only thing dead men leave behind, and they’re heavy.”

She looked back at the body.

“You don’t wipe your knife on your trousers. Blood stiffens cloth, and oilskin grease doesn’t wash out. If you’re going to smell like a tanner’s shop, at least do it on purpose. If there’s a woman waiting for you, start thinking about the kind of excuse that involves mud and not other men’s blood. If there’s no woman waiting, start thinking about the kind of woman who won’t ask.”

For a moment, the dry edge in her voice softened into something almost tired.

“The first time I did it, I did it badly,” Wrack said. “Not because I was weak. Because I was new. I thought mercy meant making it clean. It doesn’t. Mercy means making it stop. You can be good at stopping and still be bad at the first cut. That’s not a failure. That’s work. Work has details. Tonight’s details are a hole in his throat, blood in the dirt, a name under a seat, and six men who thought the war would pay them enough to care about the line on the map. It didn’t.”

She turned the knife in her hand and caught the last light on the edge.

“The rest is that I’m not going to tell you it was wrong. It was necessary. Necessary is not the same as clean. You’ll carry the clean version only if you lie to yourself. I don’t recommend lying. It makes your hands steadier for a while, then it makes everything else worse.”

Wrack looked at Corvin, not kindly, not cruelly.

“You’re not the man who came into this ambush. That’s not a curse. That’s just the truth. The trick is deciding what you do with the new shape of yourself. You can use it. You can waste it. You can pretend it didn’t happen. The dead man’s face won’t let you do that for long.”

She nodded toward the bundle.

“Open it again if you want. Put it in your coat. Burn it. Give it to me. Take it to Hale. Take it to the company. Sell it to the nearest fool who will pay us for it. Each one gets us a different kind of trouble. My trouble is watching the trees while you decide. Your trouble is deciding.”

She shifted her weight, listening. The road was quiet enough to make the quiet feel like a held breath.

“I’ll tell you the last part,” Wrack said. “You’ll wash your hands. The water will come away pink. You’ll think that’s the end of it. It isn’t. You’ll dry them, and they’ll still feel wet. You’ll sleep, and you’ll dream of names that aren’t names. You’ll eat, and the bread will taste like iron. Then you’ll get used to it, and that’s when you’ve got to be careful. Getting used to it is not the same as becoming good at it. Getting used to it is the part where the world starts treating you like a tool, and you start believing it.”

Her gaze went to the cart, then the bodies, then the road beyond.

“So the rest is this: pick one thing. The body. The bundle. The road. The company. Hale. Your own conscience. Pick it, and move. If you take too long, I’m taking the cart and the paper and leaving you with six corpses and your feelings. I won’t be cruel about it. It’s just light.”

Wrack put her knife back in her belt and turned toward the trees.

“I’ll watch,” she said. “The crows are getting formal. The rest is yours.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I pick up the bundle and stand, my legs unsteady but holding. "We're taking it to Hale," I say, tucking it into my coat. "Better to know what kind of door we're kicking in." I look at the bodies one last time. "Help me put them in the ditch."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not move at once. She looked at the ditch, then at the dead, then at the bundle under his coat as if she had just been handed a door with a hinge on the wrong side.

“Hale,” she said. “Fine. We’ll take it to Hale. If he’s a tanner, we’ll ask him about skinning. If he’s in our pay, we’ll ask him about coin. If he’s neither, we’ll ask him why six men are lying in a road with the horse gone and the cart stopped.”

She wiped her knife on the dead man’s cloak after all, because there was no use pretending blood belonged to anyone in particular.

“You want them in the ditch. I’ll help you put them in the ditch. Don’t call it burial. Burial has a hole, a rope, and somebody who wants to make a speech. This is moving meat. There’s a difference. It mostly matters to the crows.”

She crouched by the nearest body, the one in the road, and took hold of his belt with her knife tip rather than her fingers. The buckle had a smear of rust on it. Company iron. Not new, not old enough to be honest.

“Take the boots,” she said. “Not the hair. Not the neck. If the neck stretches, the head comes off, and then you’ve got a mess that looks like you did it on purpose. The boots are where the weight is. The belt is where the pride is. Neither of them will argue.”

She hooked her boot under his shoulder and pulled. The body shifted with the heavy, reluctant give of wet wool and dead limbs. His head lolled back against the dirt, mouth open just enough for a fly to walk into it. Wrack nudged the mouth shut with the side of her knife.

“That’s not kindness,” she said. “That’s not wanting him to look peaceful. That’s because the face makes it too easy for a man to decide he’s done something terrible, and you’ve already got the terrible part done. We’re only tidying.”

The body slid toward the ditch with a long, dragging sound. Wrack braced her boot and pulled again.

“Second one,” she said. “You can take the pair by the cart if your legs are steadier than mine. I’ll take the two in the road. I’m faster at pretending they’re not dead.”

She moved to the next body before he could answer. This one had been cut across the forearm, the wound black and scabbed from the fight. Wrack turned the hand over with the toe of her boot. The calluses were sword-calluses, but the grip scars were wrong for a company sword. The man had been trained, or someone had wanted him to look trained.

“Hired,” she said. “Or trained badly enough to be useful in the dark. Either way, he wasn’t paid well. Men who die for little money always have the same look. Like they expected to get another coin and then found out the universe was short.”

She hooked the belt again and dragged him to the edge of the ditch. The man’s arm caught on a root. Wrack let go, stepped back, and considered the arm as if it had personally insulted her.

“Don’t pull hard,” she said. “Bones stick. That’s all. It makes a noise like a wet branch. If you hear it, don’t flinch. You’re not breaking him. You’re just finding out what was already broken.”

She worked the root free with her knife, then pulled the body over the edge. It landed with a dull, final sound. Flies rose in a black cloud, then settled again as if they had never left.

Wrack looked at the teamster.

The body under the cart was the one Corvin had finished. Wrack did not go to him first. She went to the cart, took a handful of straw from the spilled basket, and spread it over the blood where the teamster’s head had been. It was a useless thing to do. It was also the kind of thing she did when she had decided a man had been made a face instead of a thing.

“You didn’t leave him for the crows,” she said. “That counts. Don’t make it count for more than it does. You can count small things, but you’ll go mad if you count them as debts.”

She crouched beside the teamster and took his cloak at the shoulders. The cloth was stiffening near the wound, but not enough to hold him upright. Wrack pulled him backward into the ditch. He moved like a sack of wet grain. The cut at his throat made a dark shine when the light found it.

“I’ll take him,” Wrack said. “You killed him. I’ll put him in. That’s fair. If you want to feel something about it, do it after. If you don’t want to feel anything about it, do it after either. The after is where most of us put it, and most of us are wrong.”

She dragged the second pair away from the cart, one by one. The road grew uglier as she moved them: blood smeared into the wash, boots marking the dirt, the ditch filling with dead men who had looked less like a company and more like a bad deal. When she finished, she stood with her hands on her knees, breathing hard but not showing it.

The ditch was not deep enough to hide them well. Wrack took the broken boards from under the cart seat and laid them over the bodies, then scattered straw and loose leaves across the gap. It looked like a cart had lost some boards in a ditch and somebody had tried to fix it badly. Which was close enough to the truth to be useful.

“Take the rope,” she said, nodding to the traces. “Take the knife off the one with the sword hand. Leave the belts if we’re in a hurry, but take the purses if they’re light enough to carry. If we’re going to Hale’s door, we don’t want to walk there smelling like a man who stole from corpses. Unless the corpses were honest about who they were.”

She cut the rope from the cart with her knife and coiled it around her hand. The hemp was worn but sound. Good rope was worth more than most dead men.

“The horse is gone,” she said. “If it ran, that’s bad luck. If it was taken, that’s worse. Somebody wanted the cart stopped, not robbed. That means the paper matters more than the load. That means Hale wanted an answer to be carried, not a delivery made.”

She looked at the oilskin under his coat.

“You want to know what kind of door we’re kicking. Fine. It’s a door with a message nailed to it and six men lying in the mud for punctuation. If we go to Hale, we either find a frightened man with a purse, or we find a dead man’s employer with a better knife than we brought. If we go to the company, we find out whether Hale is one of ours or one of theirs wearing our stamp. If we go to neither, we find out how long it takes a man to regret a decision he made while the flies were still choosing.”

Wrack wiped her hands on her trousers, then looked at the cloth and gave up.

“I’ll walk ahead until Lowbridge ford. If the paper’s right, Hale will be near there. If the paper’s a lie, we’ll find out when somebody shoots at us from the tree line. Either way, we’ll know more than we do standing here.”

She picked up the broken board she had used to cover the ditch and leaned it against the cart.

“You wanted the truth. Here’s the rest of it. You’re not clean. I’m not clean. The dead aren’t clean. The mud isn’t clean. The crows will be clean enough because they don’t care what they eat. If you’re going to Hale, go as a man who knows he did a necessary thing badly and then less badly. Don’t go as a man who thinks he’s earned a story. Stories are for people who get paid twice.”

She looked toward the road. The sky was going low and gray, the light thinning out like water in a bucket with a crack in it.

“Move when you’re ready,” Wrack said. “If you’re not ready, I’ll count to three. If you’re still not ready, I’ll kick the cart. If the cart doesn’t care, you’ll know how to feel.”

She stepped into the road and looked back at the ditch, the covered boards, the dead men now mostly under straw and shadow.

“Hale’s a name,” she said. “Names are doors. Doors have hinges. Hinges have weight. We’ll take the bundle, take the rope, take the knife if you’ve got the nerve to carry it, and leave the cart where it fell. If somebody comes looking, they’ll find six men in a ditch and a message that doesn’t say who sent it. If somebody smart comes looking, they’ll find that we did exactly what we were supposed to do and then got clever about it.”

Wrack’s mouth twisted, not quite a smile.

“I don’t know which kind of man Hale is. But if he’s the kind who pays teamsters to die for a cartload of nothing, he’ll be waiting for someone to knock. And if he’s not, he’ll be waiting for someone to knock anyway. That’s the problem with doors. They always want a hand.”

She turned toward the road and started walking.

“The crows are getting formal,” she said over her shoulder. “I’ll watch the trees. You watch the paper. If Hale’s a tanner, we’ll find out soon enough what kind of skin he wears.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I finish wiping my hands on my pants, my breath still shaky. "You walk ahead. I'll watch the back trail—in case the horse *wasn't* an accident." I fall in behind her, keeping my eyes on the tree line we're leaving behind.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I watch our back trail until the cart's just a dark shape in the distance. The silence feels different now. "He gave up the name too easy, didn't he?" I call ahead to her, my voice low.
