dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack drew the knife slowly through the dead man’s cloak, leaving a dark smear on the wool, then checked the edge again in the failing light.

“Then you heard him,” she said.

She stood with the unhurried economy of someone who had learned not to waste motion on pain. Her knees gave a faint crack. Past the cart, the sound came thin and wet, more breath than voice, stopping and starting like a pump losing its prime.

“If he’s calling to friends, he’ll keep at it until he can’t,” she said. “If it’s just lungs filling, he’ll do it slower.” She slid the knife into its sheath. “I can quiet him. You can. Or we can leave him and see if he’s still making noise at first light.”

Her eyes stayed on Corvin, flat and patient, not unkind.

“Either way, don’t stand there listening to him decide for you.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "I'll do it." I start walking toward the cart, my hand going to my own knife. "Just... don't watch."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a short nod. “I wasn’t going to,” she said. “Watching doesn’t make it cleaner.”

She turned her back and moved to the nearest body, nudging a dropped sword out of easy reach with the toe of her boot. The wet sound beyond the cart hitched, stopped, started again.

“I’ll check the harness,” she said, low and practical. “You’ve got until I’ve counted the buckles.”

A pause. The wind moved through the ditch grass, thin and cold.

“Don’t apologize to him,” Wrack added. “It only makes them hope.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack’s hands kept moving over the harness, counting buckles the way she’d said she would. One, two. The leather was good, better than the dead men had any right to carry. Three.

“Bad enough,” she said. “From the sound of him, lung or gut. Maybe both. If it’s mercy, it’s mercy. If it’s easier, it’s that too.”

She set a cracked strap down without anger, as if the damage were merely information.

“Don’t make a rite of it,” she added, voice low and level. “Don’t ask him his name. Don’t tell him it’s all right. Just put steel where it ends quick, and be sure you’ve done it when you walk away.”

Four buckles. Five.

The wet breathing past the cart stopped for a long moment, then came back thinner, like water trying to run through a choked pipe.

“Six,” Wrack said. “I’m done counting.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
My boots crunch over the gravel as I round the cart. He's propped against the wheel, one hand pressed against the dark stain on his tunic. He's young, maybe my age.

I don't say anything. My knife is out before I think too hard about it. I kneel, and my free hand finds his shoulder to hold him still.

*I look away when I do it. That's the coward's way, I know.*

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her back to the cart.

She did not watch, and she did not pretend to be listening for anything but the end of it. Her hands went on working, sorting what was worth keeping from what was only weight: a good strap, a cracked buckle, a knife with a loose tang that might serve someone else better than it had served its owner.

The sound beyond the cart changed. Brief, ugly, then gone into a silence that had shape to it.

She let the silence sit for a breath longer than comfort required, then said, without turning, “Wipe the blade before it dries. Grass, dirt, your sleeve if you have to. Blood’s hard on an edge.”

Only then did she straighten and come around the cart, slow, boots finding the uneven ground with old habit. Her gaze went first to the still shape by the wheel, then to Corvin’s face. Not pitying. Assessing.

She crouched with a faint crack of knees and pressed two fingers briefly to the young man’s throat, more custom than doubt. Nothing answered. She wiped her fingers on her cuff and stood again.

“Dead,” she said, as though reporting weather.

Her eyes stayed on Corvin for a moment.

“If you looked away, that’s your business,” she said. “The dead don’t grade you for it. Neither do I. What matters is you didn’t leave him breathing.”

She glanced down at the body once, practical again.

“Search him if you can. Boots, belt, anything in his pockets. If you can’t, say so and I’ll do it. No shame in that. Only work left over.”

The wind moved through the ditch grass again, colder now. Somewhere far off, a bird gave one thin call and stopped.

“And don’t start making a story out of it,” Wrack added, quieter. “Not tonight. Tonight it’s just one more thing we did so we could keep moving.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not answer at once. She crouched again beside the body, close enough to be useful, not close enough to make a ceremony of it.

“You’re looking at a man after the use has gone out of him,” she said. “Not a monster. Not a warning. A dead enemy with good boots and maybe a belt purse.”

She nodded toward the body without touching it.

“See the wet at his mouth? That’s lung. He’d have drowned in it if you hadn’t ended it. Your knife went in here.” She indicated the dark stain with a brief movement of her thumb, not pointing like a child teaching letters. “Don’t expect much bleeding now. The heart’s stopped pushing. If he’s twitched or fouled himself, that’s normal. Corpses do what living men can’t control and then get blamed for it.”

Her eyes lifted to Corvin’s face, flat and steady.

“If you’re asking how to look, don’t start with his face. Start with his hands. Rings, knife, coin sewn into a cuff if he had sense. Then belt, pouch, pockets. Boots last, unless they’re better than yours and you’re not squeamish about taking them.”

The wind moved through the ditch grass again, thin and cold.

“If you’re asking what it means,” Wrack said, quieter now, “it means he isn’t going to ambush anyone else. That’s all the meaning this field gives. You can feel sick after. You can dream. But not while we’re standing over him. Right now he’s inventory.”

She straightened with another faint crack of knees.

“And if you need to retch, step away from the gear. Good steel doesn’t need your supper on it.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down, my hands moving to his belt first like she said. My fingers fumble on the buckle. "Got a pouch," I say, my voice sounding too loud in the quiet.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack’s gaze flicked toward the darkening road before settling back on Corvin’s hands.

“Lower,” she said. “Dead men don’t need announcements, and living ones might.”

She moved a half-step closer, not to hover, but to put herself between the pouch and the last gray light. Her shadow fell long over the body.

“Don’t yank it. If the drawstring’s knotted, work it loose or cut the leather beside it. A purse torn open spills coin into muck, and then you’re kneeling in a stranger’s blood for coppers.”

Her tone stayed flat, instructional, the same voice she might have used for sharpening a blade or stitching a boot.

“Empty it into your palm, not the ground. Count later. If there’s paper, keep it dry. If there’s a seal, a unit mark, or a captain’s sign, that matters. If it’s a love token or a saint, leave it unless it’s silver. Sentiment is heavy and pays poorly.”

The wind moved through the ditch grass again. Somewhere behind them, one of the harness straps creaked faintly where it hung loose.

Wrack listened for a breath, not just to the pouch but to the field beyond it, the road, the trees. Then she looked down again.

“And if your fingers go clumsy, stop, breathe, and start again. Fumbling’s how you cut yourself on someone else’s knife.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack’s jaw worked once, not in disgust but in decision.

“Straight,” she said. “A spear in the gut is a hole in a bag of shit and supper.”

She said it as plainly as if she were naming tools in a shed. Her eyes did not leave Corvin’s face, but they did not press either.

“If it opens the bowel, what was inside him leaks into the belly. It doesn’t stay where it ought. The flesh goes hot, then swollen, then bad. He’ll fever. His belly will tighten like a drum. He may vomit what he ate, then bile, then brown water. If it’s high enough and bad enough, he’ll smell like shit on his breath before the end, because the rot’s already started while he’s still alive.”

The wind moved through the ditch grass again. Wrack did not glance toward it this time.

“If it tears the liver, he bleeds inside and goes cold. If it catches the spleen, same, maybe faster. If it’s low and opens the bladder, he poisons himself with his own piss from the inside. Some die in hours. Some last days, begging for water they can’t keep down. Some stay clear-headed long enough to know what’s happening, which is the worst part.”

Her voice stayed level, but not cruel.

“If the head’s barbed, pulling it out tears more meat. If it’s left in, it plugs the wound until someone moves him and it opens again. There’s no clean part about the middle of a man. Chest wounds can drown him quick. Throat wounds can end it faster. Gut wounds make him pay for every breath left in him.”

She gave the smallest shrug, the kind that belonged to weather and bad roads.

“So if you wanted the truth because you think it’ll make you steadier, here’s the use of it: when you see a man gut-hit, don’t poke at it and don’t promise him he’ll walk. If he can be saved, it’s a surgeon’s work and clean hands and time we usually don’t have. If he can’t, your knife is kinder than waiting.”

Her gaze flicked briefly to the body by the cart, then back.

“This one had lungs filling. Ugly, but quicker than gut-rot. You didn’t give him the slow version. That’s the only grace this kind of work has.”

She shifted her weight, listening for a moment to the darkening road, then became practical again.

“Now finish the search. Boots, belt, pockets. If you need to be sick, do it past the harness and not on the steel.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I cut the pouch free, my hands steadier now. "Just coins," I say, pouring them into my palm. "No papers." I shove them into my own pocket and reach for his boots.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack’s eyes went to the boots, then to the last gray smear of light along the road.

“Good leather,” she said. “Better than his company deserved. If they fit, take them. If they don’t, strip the laces and cut what you can use.”

She crouched again, not to take over, but to point with the blunt practicality of someone explaining how to mend a saddle girth.

“Don’t haul on them. Loosen the laces all the way, work the tongue free, and roll the heel down. Dead feet go stiff fast, and if you yank, you’ll tear the leather or put your hand somewhere you’ll regret later.”

Her gaze flicked once to the dead man’s hands.

“If there’s a ring, twist it toward the palm, not away. Skin catches less. If it won’t come, leave it unless you’ve got a knife you don’t mind using on fingers. I’ve seen men lose their appetite over less.”

She stood again, knees protesting in that small, familiar way, and scanned the ditch, the cart, the darker shapes of the other dead.

“Check the tongues while you’re at it. Men hide coin there, or folded paper, or some cheap saint’s medal they think will keep their bowels in their belly. If it’s silver, it’s ours. If it’s paper, keep it dry. If it’s sentiment, leave it unless it can buy bread.”

The wind stirred the grass again. The road was getting harder to read.

“Count the coins later,” she added. “Not here. If there’s a captain’s mark or a mint sign, that changes things. If it’s just field silver and copper, we split it once we’re clear.”

She moved a few steps away and began dragging the nearest dropped sword toward the ditch by its blade, careful with the edge, unhurried.

“When you’re done with the boots, help me pull these clear of the track. Dead men can lie where they fell, but a cart and bodies in the road invite questions. Questions invite patrols, and patrols invite more work than we’ve got night for.”

She paused, the sword half-lifted, and looked back once.

“And if you find yourself thinking about how he looked when he was still breathing, don’t. Look at the boot. Look at the lace. Look at the work. Thinking can wait until there’s a fire and something to eat.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped.

She did not turn away again at once. The sword she had been dragging stayed where it was, its point resting in the dirt, and her hands settled on her hips as if she were deciding whether the request was stupidity or need. Maybe it was both. She had seen both often enough in the same face.

“No,” she said at last. Not sharp, but final. “I’ll stay. I’ll watch, if watching is what keeps your hand from shaking. But I won’t stand here and tally his dying for you like it’s a job of work to be graded.”

She came back a few steps and crouched near the body again, close enough that Corvin would not have to feel alone in it, far enough not to crowd the blade. Her eyes went briefly to the young man’s face, then away.

“You want it plain, then hear it plain,” she said. “You’re not giving him something new. You’re finishing what the ambush started. The sound will be worse than the act. Air through blood makes a wet, broken noise. He may hitch. He may shake. He may make a sound like he’s trying to speak, and it won’t be speech. That’s the body running out of road.”

Her voice stayed low and even.

“If you put the steel where it belongs, it will be quick. Seconds. Sometimes less. If you don’t, it will take longer, and you’ll know because he’ll still be fighting for air instead of leaving it. Then you correct the mistake. Don’t saw. Don’t pull it out to look. Don’t ask the dead for permission.”

She looked up then, steady and unflinching.

“I’ll tell you if it’s done. I’ll tell you if it isn’t. That’s the part you need me for. The rest you keep for yourself, because once you start wanting someone else to narrate killing, you’re either making a story of it or trying to hand it off. Neither one helps the dead, and neither one helps you.”

The wind passed through the ditch grass again, colder now, carrying the smell of iron and turned earth.

“So do it,” Wrack said. “I’ll stay. But I won’t make it easier by pretending it’s anything but what it is.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content:
My hands are shaking. I press the heel of my palm against the hilt to steady it. "All right," I say, and then I don't say anything else. I find the spot she'd pointed to earlier, under the ribs, angled up. I look at it, not at his face. I push.

The sound is wet. He jerks once, his heels scraping against the gravel. Then he goes still, and the silence after is a different kind of quiet. I don't pull the knife out yet. "Well?" I ask her.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack looked from the knife to the still shape by the cart wheel, and her face did not change.

“Well enough,” she said. “Except he was already dead.”

She crouched again, close enough to see the wound, but she did not touch the blade. Her eyes tracked the dark soak in the tunic, the slack mouth, the nothing in the chest.

“That jerk was meat remembering motion,” she said. “Air and sinew. Nothing more. The sound was blood shifting where it had no business being. It wasn’t breath. It wasn’t him.”

Her gaze lifted, steady and unflinching.

“I told you he was dead because he was. I don’t say it twice for comfort. What you’ve done is open a corpse, not kill a man twice. If that feels worse, it’s because your hands are still catching up to what your eyes already know.”

The wind moved low through the ditch grass. One of the loose harness straps creaked again behind them.

“You asked me to watch,” Wrack said. “I watched. There was no moment where he left you. He’d already gone. You didn’t steal anything from him. You didn’t botch a mercy. You put steel into something that had already stopped being a threat and was on its way to being a smell.”

Her voice stayed flat, practical, but not cruel.

“If you want the whole truth, here it is: sometimes the body gives you one last ugly show and makes you think you’ve done something new. You haven’t. Corpses twitch. They settle. They make noises that sound like meaning because living folk are desperate to find meaning in them. Don’t let it fool you.”

She nodded once toward the knife.

“You can draw it now, if your hand’s steady. Draw it back along the way it went. Don’t twist it, don’t yank it, and don’t look surprised if it comes out slicker than you expect. Blood doesn’t behave politely once it’s had time to cool.”

Wrack did not reach for the body. She left that to Corvin, but she stayed crouched, present, not looking away.

“Wipe it on his cloak,” she said. “Then grass if there’s any green left in it. After that, check the boot laces and see if they’re worth the trouble. If they are, take them. If they’re not, cut what’s useful and leave the rest.”

Her eyes flicked briefly toward the darkening road, then back.

“You asked me not to leave anything out. So here’s the last of it: there was no second death here. Only work done after the work was done. You can carry that, or you can set it down with the rest, but don’t stand over him pretending it makes you monstrous. It doesn’t.”

She straightened slowly, knees cracking again.

“Finish the search. Then we drag what’s left clear of the track. Night’s coming, and dead men don’t need our company any longer than we need theirs.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not answer at once.

She stood with her hands loose at her sides, looking down at the dead man, then out toward the road where the last light had gone thin and gray. The wind touched the ditch grass again and left it colder than before. Somewhere behind her, the loose harness strap gave another faint creak.

“The rest,” she said at last.

She crouched again, slower this time, as if the night had settled into her joints. Her face was hard to read in the dimness, but her voice stayed level.

“The rest is that I watched you more than I watched him. He was already past most of what matters. You weren’t. Your hand was shaking, but it didn’t matter that it shook. It mattered that it finished. I saw you look for the place. I saw you choose it. I saw you push. There was a catch when the blade went in—not bone, probably cartilage, maybe the edge of rib. Then a give. The body always gives once it realizes it’s been opened. Not like cloth. More like fruit gone soft.”

She glanced briefly at the body, then away.

“The sound was wet and small. Less than you’d think. More breath than voice, like someone trying to speak through a mouthful of water. His heels scraped because the legs remember what the mind’s done with. His fingers may have opened. His face may have changed. None of that was him choosing. The meat was spending what was left in it, and then it was spent.”

Her eyes came back to the place where Corvin sat. She did not soften.

“It took three breaths, maybe four. From the moment you pushed to the moment he was still, less time than it takes to count coins. But you’ll stretch it later. You’ll make it last as long as you need to. That’s what the living do. The dead don’t keep time. We do.”

She shifted slightly, crouching lower, elbows resting near her knees.

“You want the exactness of it, so here it is. When a man’s dying, he doesn’t always look like a man leaving. Sometimes he looks like a man fighting sleep. Sometimes his eyes stay half-open because eyes don’t close themselves neatly unless someone closes them. Sometimes the mouth hangs slack and there’s blood on the teeth, or froth, or nothing. Sometimes the body fouls itself because the muscles let go at the end. Bladder, bowels, whatever was held out of habit or fear. It stinks, and it means nothing except that he was an animal once and now he isn’t even that.”

Her voice stayed flat, but not careless.

“If you leave the knife in, it plugs the wound and keeps the worst of the mess from following the blade out. If you draw it, it comes slick and warm because blood has no manners after death. It may smell like iron and opened earth. It may smell like shit too. That doesn’t make you worse. It makes you close.”

She looked down at her own hands for a moment, then back.

“After, the body begins to change faster than people like. The warmth goes out of it first. Then the face loses whatever you thought was still there. The skin cools. The joints stiffen. If you try to move him too late, he’ll feel like wood dressed in cloth. If you roll him, air may move in his throat and make a sound. A groan, maybe. A sigh. It won’t be pain. It won’t be memory. It will be gas looking for somewhere to go.”

The wind stirred again. Wrack did not look toward it.

“If we leave him here, crows will find him by morning. They start at the eyes and the mouth because those are soft. Foxes and dogs come after. If we bury him shallow, something will dig him up when the smell gets honest. If we burn him, the smoke may bring questions. So we take what can be used, move what can be moved, and leave the rest to the world. The world is not gentle with dead men. It never has been.”

She paused, and when she spoke again her voice was quieter, but no less direct.

“Now the other rest. The part you’ll carry.”

Her gaze stayed steady.

“You’ll smell blood later when there’s none near. You’ll wash your hands and feel like the water’s lying. You’ll eat and taste copper under the bread. You’ll close your eyes and see the exact moment your hand moved, except it will be slower in your head than it was in truth. You’ll hear that wet sound again and wonder if it was louder than I said. You’ll wonder if he felt it. You’ll wonder if he knew. You’ll make up a face for him, a name, a mother, a sweetheart, a life he never had, because the mind hates a blank space and fills it with whatever hurts most.”

One corner of her mouth moved, not in humor.

“If you dream, don’t be surprised. If you don’t dream, don’t be proud. If you wake sick, step away from the fire. If you wake angry, don’t spend it on me or yourself. If you feel nothing, that’s not proof you’re made of stone. It’s proof you’re tired, or frightened, or still too close to it to know what it cost.”

She straightened a little, though she did not rise.

“I won’t tell you he forgave you. He didn’t know you. I won’t tell you it was nothing. It wasn’t nothing. I won’t tell you it was holy. It wasn’t that either. It was a man at the end of a bad road, and you shortened the last step. Maybe that’s mercy. Maybe it’s only easier. Most things in war are both, and trying to sort them clean is work for people who weren’t there.”

Her eyes narrowed slightly, not with suspicion, but with thought.

“You asked me not to leave anything out, so hear this too: I have seen men die clean and men die filthy, and I have killed in ways I’d rather not remember. Sometimes it’s quick. Sometimes it’s ugly. Sometimes you do the right thing and it still feels like a stain. Sometimes you do the necessary thing and it doesn’t feel like anything at all until days later, when you’re safe enough to afford it. The feeling doesn’t make the act evil. The act doesn’t make you innocent. You can carry both.”

She looked once toward the other bodies scattered near the ditch.

“They had names. We’ll never know most of them. You’ll invent one for him if you’re not careful. Don’t. Names make ghosts where there should only be dead. He was a soldier, or a boy with a spear, or someone’s fool brother, or all of those at once. Now he’s weight under a cloak. We’ll take his boots if they fit. We’ll take his purse because we need bread more than he needs it. We’ll move him out of the road so the next patrol doesn’t stop to ask questions. That’s not disrespect. That’s the only respect the dead get from people still living: we use what they don’t need, and we keep moving.”

Her voice dropped, but each word stayed plain.

“You may hate me for making you do it. You may hate yourself. You may hate him for being there, for being wounded, for making the choice real. That’s allowed. Hate is cheap and doesn’t keep you warm. Don’t build a house out of it. Don’t tell yourself you’re monstrous because you did what the ditch required. If you start believing that, you’ll either get soft or cruel, and neither one helps anyone.”

She drew a breath through her nose.

“And if you want me to say it was easy, I won’t. It wasn’t. If you want me to say it will get easier, I won’t say that either. It gets quieter. You learn where to put the memory so it doesn’t sit at the fire with you every night. You learn not to look for meaning in the sound a body makes when it stops. You learn to clean the blade, eat what’s cold, sleep where you can, and count the living before you count the dead.”

Wrack’s eyes went briefly to the knife still in the body, then back.

“The last thing, since you asked for all of it. When we move him, he may bleed a little more. Not much. The heart’s stopped, but blood settles and shifts. If we turn him, it may come out of the wound darker than you expect. If we drag him, his head may loll like a drunk’s. His eyes may open wider. His mouth may make a shape that looks like a word. None of it is speech. None of it is blame. It’s only the body finishing what the body does when the man’s gone.”

She rose then, knees cracking in the cold.

“You can sit with that as long as you need. But don’t sit so long you make a shrine of him. He isn’t a lesson. He isn’t a punishment. He isn’t your confession. He’s one dead man among six, and the night’s getting darker.”

She looked down once more, practical again, though not unkind.

“Wipe your blade when you can. Finish the search if your hands will work. If they won’t, say so and I’ll do it. Either way, we move the bodies clear of the track before full dark. Dead men don’t need our grief. They need us to stop standing over them.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the knife on his cloak, slow. "I'm done," I say, and my voice doesn't shake. I reach for his boots again, my fingers working the laces loose. "They'll fit."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack gave a single nod, as if the steadiness in Corvin’s voice were a tool that had passed inspection.

“Then take them,” she said. “Don’t sit asking the leather.”

She moved to the dead man’s feet and crouched there, knife loose in her hand but not raised. The last light had gone thin enough that she was reading more by shape than color: the angle of the boot, the pull of the laces, the dark soak of blood where it had settled in the cloth.

“Good boots on a dead man are a gift with a rude face,” she said. “Laces first, all the way. If they’re knotted with blood or mud, cut beside them, not through the eyelets. Eyelets are hard to replace and grudges are harder.”

She tilted her head toward the boot Corvin was working.

“Get the tongue free. If it sticks, don’t peel it. Slide your thumb or the flat of your blade along the inside and break the suction. Dead feet swell and stiffen quicker than living ones, and the leather remembers the shape it died in.”

Her voice stayed practical, stripped of ceremony.

“Heel down, toe up. If the ankle fights, press it once, firm. It may crack. It may feel like something giving that shouldn’t. That’s not you hurting him. That’s the body being what it is now. If you yank, you’ll tear the boot or your own knuckles.”

She glanced toward the darkening road, then back.

“Check the inside once they’re off. Some men hide coin under the tongue, some in the sole, some in a rag wrapped around the ankle. If the stocking’s wet, don’t put your fingers in blind. Cut it open where you can see. If there’s a ring on a toe or a mark cut into the skin, leave it unless it’s silver. We’re scavengers, not ghouls. There’s a line, even here.”

Wrack reached down and touched the dead man’s cloak near the shoulder, testing how much of it could be used. The wool was damp and heavy, darkened in places where blood had spread and begun to cool into a stiff sheen.

“If the boots come clean, put them aside sole to sole. Don’t wear them yet. Dead men’s boots fit strange, and if they’ve got blood inside they’ll make your feet slick. Stuff them with grass for now.”

She straightened slightly, knees creaking, and looked over the body as one looks over a load that must be shifted before rain.

“When you’re done, we’ll move him. Not by the feet. Feet dig furrows and make a trail a blind man could follow. Under the arms, or by the cloak if it holds. If his head knocks, let it. If his heels bump, let them. We’re not carrying him gently; we’re carrying him out of the road.”

Her eyes went briefly to Corvin’s face, then away.

“You said you’re done. Good. Done doesn’t mean clean. It means the work’s behind us instead of in front. Keep saying it if it helps, but say it while your hands are moving.”

She took hold of one of the other bodies by the collar and began dragging it toward the ditch, boots scraping a shallow line in the dirt. The dead man’s head turned with the motion, mouth slack, eyes half-open to the gray sky. Wrack did not pause to arrange him.

“Boots first,” she said. “Then him. Then we count what we’ve got and leave what we can’t carry. Night’s not going to wait for our manners.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get the boots off. There's a little silver coin tucked under the tongue. I pocket it and shove the boots into my pack. "Help me roll him," I say, and my hands are already under his shoulders.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came back at once, leaving the other body where she had dragged it, half in the ditch grass and half in the shadow of the cart wheel.

“Under the shoulders is right,” she said. “Don’t get tender with him now. He won’t feel the difference, and your back will.”

She crouched on the far side of the dead man, knees cracking in the cold, and gathered the cloak at the shoulders where the wool was still sound enough to bear weight. Her eyes flicked once to the place where Corvin’s hands had gone beneath him, then to the dark stain spreading stiff and glossy across the tunic.

“If the cloak tears, take the belt,” she said. “If the belt fails, take the ankles and drag him low. Don’t try to carry him like a man asleep. He isn’t asleep, and he isn’t light.”

She tested the dead man’s weight with a small pull, enough to know how he would settle.

“He’ll feel heavier than he looks. Dead weight isn’t a saying for nothing. The body stops helping. It hangs where it’s put and then slides where it isn’t.”

The wind moved through the ditch grass again, colder now, carrying the iron smell of the field and the faint sourness of opened earth.

“Roll him away from the cart wheel,” Wrack said. “Not over it. If he catches, don’t fight it. Lower him, shift him, and start again. No point tearing him or yourself.”

She glanced toward the road, where the last gray light had begun to thin into true dark, then looked back.

“That coin under the tongue,” she added, “spend it where no one knows his face. Silver doesn’t care where it’s been, but people do.”

Her hands tightened in the cloak.

“On me. Not because it helps him. Because it helps us keep from dropping him on our own feet.”

She waited only long enough for the weight to begin moving.

“Now.”

Wrack lifted. The body came up with the dull, sagging insistence of grain sacks wet through. It did not resist. It did not help. The head lolled sideways, mouth slack, hair falling across the face in a way that looked careless rather than peaceful. One arm slid loose and brushed the gravel, fingers curling faintly as the joints shifted.

Wrack did not flinch.

“Let his head go where it wants,” she said. “You don’t owe him a straight neck.”

The dead man made a sound as they moved him: a thin, wet creak from the throat, not breath, not speech, only air forced through what was left of him by the change of posture. It was small and ugly and over quickly. Wrack’s expression did not change.

“That’s all,” she said. “Gas and blood. Nothing following it.”

The body shifted heavily between them, boots gone, cloak dragging in the dirt. Blood had begun to settle in the lower folds of his clothing, darker now, less bright, more like stain than wound. Where the knife had been drawn, the opening in the tunic gaped slightly, showing the wet black beneath.

Wrack tucked the loose arm against the chest with one hand, not gently, not roughly, simply to keep it from catching.

“Watch the wheel,” she said. “If he snags, don’t yank. Lift past it.”

The cart’s shadow fell over them as they moved him, the wood dark and splintered where the ambush had knocked it askew. One of the horses had gone quiet in the traces, shifting its weight from foot to foot with the nervous patience of an animal that had learned to wait out men’s work.

“Past the wheel,” Wrack said. “Toward the ditch. Not far. Just far enough that a patrol doesn’t trip over him and start asking questions.”

The ground was uneven there, cut by hooves and boot marks and the shallow furrows made by dragged steel. The dead man’s heels left short lines in the dirt as they moved him. His body settled lower with every step, growing harder to hold in a way that had nothing to do with strength and everything to do with the fact that there was no longer any shape inside it meant for carrying.

Wrack’s breath came even through her nose.

“If you need to stop, say so,” she said. “Don’t be proud. Dead men are poor dancers and worse partners.”

The ditch grass brushed against the body as they brought him near the edge, where the other shapes lay waiting in the half-dark. Wrack looked down at the ground, choosing the flattest place, not for kindness but for ease.

“Here,” she said. “Down easy. Not because he deserves it. Because noise carries.”

She lowered her side as the weight went down. The body settled with a soft, final sound, cloak folding around it like a ragged shroud. One eye remained half-open, showing a pale line of white beneath the lid. Wrack reached down and drew the cloak edge over the face without ceremony.

“No need to leave him staring at the sky,” she said. “It won’t answer.”

She straightened slowly, pressing the heel of one hand against the small of her back for a moment before letting it fall again. Her gaze went over the body once, checking not for life but for what had been missed: a strap, a pouch, a knife, anything that might still be useful or dangerous.

“Blood on your sleeves,” she said. “Wipe it now while it’s wet. Later it’ll be a chore.”

She looked toward the road, listening. The field had gone quiet in the way fields did after violence, not peaceful so much as emptied. The bird that had called earlier did not call again.

“He’ll bleed a little more if we move him again,” Wrack said. “Not enough to matter. Enough to make your hands slick. If we have to drag the others past him, keep him on the low side. Dead men roll downhill faster than you’d think.”

She turned back to the cart, where the remaining bodies lay in the deepening gray.

“One more with boots worth taking,” she said. “Then we count what we’ve got, wash the worst off our hands, and decide whether we risk a fire or eat cold.”

Her eyes came back to the body by the ditch, then away.

“You did the work,” she said. “Now finish it. Not for him. For us.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my hands on the grass and the stains don't come out. "I'm not hungry," I say. I start walking toward the other body she pointed out.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack finished with the dead man’s cloak, folded the blade closed, and slid it home. She followed the sound a moment—wet, methodical, like a boot stuck in mud—and then looked at Corvin’s wrist, still shining in the cold air.

“He’s not asking for anything,” she said. “Just leaking out loud. But sound carries farther than you’d think, and we’ve still got ground to cover before camp.”

She stood, her knees cracking, and wiped her hands down her thighs, leaving dark smears on the worn leather. “If you’re going to do it, do it before full dark. I once spent twenty minutes searching a ditch for a man I’d already killed, just because I waited too long and couldn’t find him after. Don’t recommend it.” She shrugged, the motion barely visible beneath her padded jack. “Up to you. But the dark doesn’t care either way.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath and start walking toward the cart. "Alright." My voice comes out steadier than I feel. When I get close, I see him—just a kid, really. His breath's making little clouds in the air.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn’t follow. She’d seen enough boys in enemy colors to know the shape of what came next, and Corvin hadn’t asked for company. She went back to the ditch instead, rolling the nearest body with her boot to check for a coin purse or anything that rattled. The light was bleeding out fast across the treeline in that particular grey that made distances lie.

“Fifteen, maybe sixteen,” she called out, not loud, just enough to carry. She didn’t look up from her work. “Old enough to hold a pike, old enough to die in a ditch. The math’s simple.” She pulled a belt knife from a sheath and wiped it on her own thigh, adding to the stains. “Don’t let him talk to you. They get religious sometimes, or they want their mother, and it doesn’t help anyone. Throat or heart, your choice, but make it clean. Messy work draws scavengers.”

She stood, scanning the tree line, her hand resting loose on her sword pommel. “And Corvin—if he’s got a rabbit or a hard cheese on him, bring it. We’re behind on rations.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack scraped mud from her boot against the dead man’s leg. She didn’t look toward the cart.

“He’s bad enough that the distinction won’t matter to him,” she said. “Only to you, afterward.” She stood, leather creaking, and wiped her hands down her thighs, leaving fresh smears. “Mercy, convenience—call it what you need to. I’ve called it both, and the blade weighs the same either way.” She tilted her head, listening to the wet rasping from beyond the cart. “What he is, is unfinished. The ambush doesn’t end when they fall down. It ends when they stop making noise. Everything else is just bookkeeping for your own head.” She shrugged, the motion barely visible. “So decide which word lets you sleep, if you sleep, and finish it. Dark’s coming.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare down at the kid. His eyes are open, glassy. "Alright," I say again, more to myself this time. I slide my dagger out. "Close your eyes."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't watch. She'd seen enough of Corvin's face to know this was one of those moments that either hardened a person or hollowed them out, and either way, looking on didn't help. She crouched by the nearest body and set to work on the man's boots, prying at the frozen leather with short, efficient movements.

"Words are free," she said, not loud, but carrying in the stillness. She didn't look up. "But don't let him answer you. Last thing you need is a conversation." The boot came loose with a wet sound, and she tossed it into the weeds. "And Corvin—blade goes in at the base of the skull if he's lying down. Up through the mouth if he's sitting. Less bone, faster stop."

She sat back on her heels, scanning the darkening treeline, her own knife already back in its sheath. "Messy is just more laundry."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped prying at the second boot and listened to the wet sound carrying across the ditch. She didn’t look over.

“You’re looking at a body that’s finished the business of living but hasn’t stopped moving yet,” she said. “Glassy eyes mean the blood’s stopped delivering to the brain in useful amounts. Shallow breath means the chest cavity’s either filling with fluid or the belly’s bleeding out underneath him. Both feel the same from the inside—cold, then heavy, then nothing.”

She tossed the boot aside and wiped her hands on her thighs, leaving fresh smears on the leather.

“If he’s grey at the gums and his fingernails are blue, that’s peripheral shutdown. Heart’s keeping the important organs fed and letting the extremities rot in place. He’s got minutes, maybe a quarter hour, before the lights go out on their own. Longer if it’s gut—then he just keeps leaking until he’s empty.”

She stood, scanning the tree line, her silhouette going grey against the grey.

“Practical part: his muscles might still jerk when you stick him. Bowels might let go. That’s just nerves and gravity, not a commentary. The part that would care about the indignity is already gone, or too far under to register.”

She adjusted the sword at her hip, settling it comfortable.

“So you’re not looking at a person. You’re looking at a death that’s been slow to arrive. Your hand on the blade is the reminder that it doesn’t have to be.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: My hands are cold. I can see the blue in his nails from here. I nod once, though she's not looking. "Right." I kneel in the mud beside him.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack abandoned the second boot to the ditch. The cold was settling into her knuckles, turning her fingers clumsy, and the first corpse had yielded enough coin for a warm bowl at the next garrison town. She stood, her knees cracking like green wood, and did not look toward the cart. Instead she watched the tree line, where the dark was climbing up from the valley in slow, grey increments.

"Don't wipe the blade on his clothes after," she said. "Wool snags an edge. Use the grass, or the mud if you're in a hurry." She shifted her weight, testing the lip of the ditch with one boot. "And don't kneel too long. Hard to run with a cramped calf, and we're still on their side of the river."

The wet rasping beyond the cart hitched, then stopped. Or perhaps it was only the wind moving through the dead weeds. The silence that followed had a heavier quality, as if the air itself had settled.

"Check his pockets if you're already down there," she said. "Then we walk. I don't fancy making camp in a killing ground."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack did not turn. She kept her eyes on the treeline, where the dark had begun to pool between the trunks like ink on blotting paper, and rolled her shoulders once to settle her jack against the cold.

“A spear in the gut doesn’t kill clean unless it nicks the aorta or splits the liver wide,” she said. Her voice carried no more weight than if she’d been describing a loose horseshoe. “Most times it punches through the abdominal wall, tears the intestines. Stomach acid, bile, the shit from the bowels—all of it spills into the cavity. The body doesn’t tolerate foreign matter in the chamber. It starts to cook itself from the inside. Peritonitis. Fever, swelling, pressure building behind the ribs like a fist.”

She shifted her weight, leather creaking, and loosened her sword in its scabbard to check the draw.

“He feels cold because the blood retreats from the skin to keep the organs fed. But the belly goes tight as a drumhead. If the blade twisted on entry, the lacerations run up and down the tract like a ragged seam. He can’t draw a full breath because the diaphragm’s fighting the swelling, and every inhale pulls fluid where air ought to be. That wet sound you hear—like boot soles in thick mud—that’s his chest cavity filling with what his guts are leaking.”

She exhaled, a short cloud that vanished in the grey air.

“He won’t scream much. Not enough air for it. He’ll shiver, maybe retch blood if the stomach’s perforated. If the spear went low, urine and feces seep into the wound along with everything else. Smells sweet. Wrong. The nerves in the belly stay awake longer than you’d think, so he feels the tearing every time he moves, every time he coughs. Shock might take him early, if he’s lucky. If not, he drowns in his own soup over an hour or two, conscious most of the way. Hearing goes tinny. Vision tunnels. But the pressure stays.”

She finally glanced down at the body by her boots, then away.

“The hole in front is neat. The hole in back, if it went through, is ragged and sucks air. But the real damage is all inside, turning his plumbing to sludge. There’s no fixing it. Not here. Not anywhere. So when you stick him, you’re not adding to that mess. You’re stopping the clock before the interest compounds. That’s all.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. My hand tightens on the dagger. "Okay." I put one hand on the kid's forehead, press the tip of the blade just below his ear. It's a strange, soft resistance, then a sudden give. He lets out a wet sigh and goes still. I wipe the blade on the frozen grass like she said, my fingers numb.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack listened to the wet sigh cut short, and the silence that followed had a different weight than the silence before. She let it hold for three slow breaths, watching the treeline for movement that didn't come, then turned from the ditch.

She picked her way across the churned ground to the cart, her boots squelching in the frozen mud. She didn't look at the boy's face. Instead she crouched by his hip and ran her hands over his belt and pockets with the same detached efficiency she'd used on the corpses in the ditch.

"Grass was a good choice," she said. "Wool would've cost you an hour with a whetstone tonight." Her fingers found a half-empty pouch of dried peas and a flint striker. She left the peas and tucked the striker into her jerkin. "No cheese. Shame. They never carry anything good."

She stood, her knees cracking, and looked at Corvin's hands rather than his face, reading the tremor there, or the lack of it.

"Dark's got the valley now," she said. "We'll follow the creek bed down. Harder to track, and the water sound covers most sins." She turned and started walking, not waiting to see if Corvin followed. "You did the math. Don't keep running the figures. The answer stays the same."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked back, her face empty of anything except the same tired attention she’d give a loose strap on a saddle, and folded her arms.

“Fine,” she said. “I’ll watch.”

She did not look at Corvin’s face. She looked at the boy’s throat, and at the blade, and listened.

“You’re low and shallow,” she said, her voice carrying no more emotion than a carpenter noting a split board. “Below the ear, but you’ve skated across the muscle instead of punching up through the base of the skull. So you’ve got the carotid, maybe the jugular, but the spine’s intact. Hear that?”

She tilted her head.

“That’s not a sigh. That’s blood filling the back of the throat faster than he can cough it. The airway’s compromised but the brain’s still lit. That’s why his heels are drumming against the frozen dirt. Spinal discharge. The fingers too—opening and closing. He can’t feel it. It’s just wiring.”

She watched the boy’s chest hitch.

“Heart’s beating faster now, trying to keep pressure up. The blood coming out of him is bright. Arterial. If you watch, it’s timed to his pulse. A fountain, slow but steady. If you’d hit the vein instead, it would just ooze. This is cleaner to look at, messier to finish.”

She counted under her breath, her lips barely moving.

“Twenty seconds. The pupils are fixed and different sizes. Brain’s losing perfusion. The jaw slackens—there. The mouth drops open because the muscles went limp. That twitch in the shoulder is the diaphragm spasming. He thinks he’s breathing, but he’s only moving blood.”

She shifted her weight, leather creaking.

“Forty seconds. The drumming stops. Now it’s just the chest, hitching every few seconds. Agonal breathing. The body’s last inventory. Sounds like snoring through a wet cloth. Then a pause. Then another hitch. Each one shorter.”

She glanced at the treeline, then back down.

“Ninety seconds, maybe two minutes. The hitch stops. What comes out now is just air from the lungs, passing through the hole you made. Sounds like a sodden rag being wrung out. Then nothing. The eyes might stay open. Usually do. The color’s already going grey at the gums. By morning he’ll be stiff as a board if the cold doesn’t freeze him first.”

She looked at Corvin’s hand, not his face.

“That’s what a ragged blade does. You opened the plumbing and let him drain conscious. Not crueler than the gut wound, just faster. But not fast enough to be kind. The difference between a clean stop and a hard one is about three inches of steel and the angle you drive it. You missed by half an inch, so he got twenty extra seconds of drowning in his own blood. That’s the math.”

She stepped back, her boots crunching in the frozen mud.

“Wipe your blade. We need to walk.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe the blade again, slower this time, watching the blood turn the grass black. My hands aren't shaking anymore. "Half an inch," I repeat, my voice flat. I slide the dagger away and stand. "Which way's the creek?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack jerked her head toward the dark fold in the land where the alders grew black against the last of the grey.

“East,” she said. “Where the water sounds loud enough to cover a lie.”

She set off without waiting, her boots finding the frozen ruts with the unconscious certainty of a woman who’d spent two decades walking away from places she’d rather not remember. She didn’t look back. She knew the sound of Corvin’s stride, and she’d hear if it broke.

“Angle up next time,” she called back, not loud, just enough to carry over the wind. “Up through the base of the skull, toward the roof of the mouth. Bone’s thin there. Like punching through an eggshell. You went level, so you cut the pipes but missed the wires. Throat’s easier if you’re shaking, but the spray goes everywhere. Up is cleaner. Less laundry.”

She reached the creek bed and descended the gravel slope without breaking stride. The water ran black and quick over the stones, swallowing the smaller sounds of their passage. She stopped once in the shallows, scanning the ridge behind them. No lanterns. No voices.

“Stay in the current,” she said. “Washes the mud off your boots, and the dogs can’t sort the scent. Cold’ll numb your feet by the second mile, but numb still walks.” She started moving again, downstream into the dark, her silhouette going grey against the grey. “And Corvin—don’t mistake still hands for steady ones. The shakes come later, or they don’t. Both mean the same thing. Just don’t let them cost you another half inch when it matters.”

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stood in the creek, the current tugging cold at her ankles, and looked back at Corvin sitting in the mud with the dead boy between them. She did not come closer. She let the distance hold, and when she spoke her voice carried no more warmth than the frozen stones around her.

"You want the rest," she said. "Fine."

She looked down at the water, then up at the ridge, then back to the body.

"The rest is that he's still pissing himself. The bladder goes when the sphincter relaxes, which it already has. By now it's soaked through his breeches and steaming in the cold. In an hour it'll freeze against his thighs. The blood you let out is pooling under his left shoulder because you had him turned that way, and it's thickening. Already turning to jelly at the edges. By morning it'll be black and crusted, and if we were staying to watch, you'd see his skin go the color of old tallow—waxy, grey-yellow. The lips will draw back from the teeth. Not a snarl. Just the muscles shrinking as they cool."

She shifted her weight. The water moved around her boots.

"The rest is the smell. Right now it's copper and shit and the sourness of a body that's stopped digesting. But the gut bacteria keep working even after the heart stops. They'll start breaking down the intestinal walls from the inside. Gas builds. The belly bloats. In three days, if the foxes don't get to him first, he'll swell like a wineskin. The tongue will push out between those drawn-back teeth. The eyes, which you left open, will cloud over milky white, then sink as the fluid drains behind them. Crows go for the soft parts first. Eyes, lips, the wound you made. They'll tug the tendons in the neck and his head will move like he's nodding. He won't be. It's just mechanics."

She paused, listening to the creek.

"But you didn't ask about the body. You asked about the rest. The rest is that you sat there and listened to him drown in his own blood for ninety seconds because you didn't angle the blade right. You felt the give when you hit the muscle, and you felt the softer give when you punched through the artery, and you didn't push through to finish it. You stopped at enough. Enough is the enemy. Enough means he got to feel every heartbeat pushing blood out the hole you made. Enough means his brain lit up with panic while his body refused to answer. That last minute wasn't pain-free. It was just too full of blood to make noise."

She looked at Corvin's hands, then away.

"The rest is that you'll carry the exact pitch of that wet breathing. Not today. Today you're numb. Tomorrow you'll wash your hands and swear you still smell copper under the nails. Next week you'll wake up at the exact moment the light hits the tent wall a certain way, and you'll hear that hitching breath again, clear as if he were lying beside you. It won't come as a nightmare. Nightmares have the decency to scare you. This will just be there, like a splinter you can't dig out. You'll be eating hardtack or fucking or pissing by a tree, and suddenly you'll remember the way his heel drummed once against the frozen dirt. You'll count the seconds again. You'll wonder if he knew it was you. You'll wonder if he hated you, or forgave you, or if he was already too far gone to think in words. The wondering is the tax. It compounds."

She folded her arms.

"The rest is that there is no story here. You didn't save him from a worse death. You didn't become a harder man or a wiser one. You just killed a boy in a ditch because the war put him there and you were the one holding the blade when his luck ran out. Half an inch truer and faster and you'd be the same person you were yesterday. You aren't. You're the person who did this specific thing, in this specific mud, and the detail matters because it's the only truth you've got. Everything else is just stitching you make up after to close the wound in your own head."

She looked at the treeline one last time.

"The rest is that you'll do it again. Maybe better, maybe worse, but the next time someone is leaking in the dirt and the sergeant says finish it, or the enemy is coming and you need the silence, you'll do it again. And the time after that. And eventually you won't ask for the rest because you'll already know the weight to the ounce. You'll just wipe the blade and check the pockets and hope for cheese."

She turned back toward the creek, the current black around her legs.

"So get up, or don't. The water's cold, the dark is here, and that boy is done whether you sit there all night or not. The rest doesn't change the answer. It just makes you carry the work home."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I get up. My knees are stiff, my boots heavy with mud. I follow her into the creek, the cold water shocking the numbness out of my legs. "Lead on," I say, my voice quiet against the rush of water. I don't look back.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't answer. She turned downstream and set a pace that ate the miles, her boots finding purchase on the submerged stones with the rote memory of a woman who'd waded more rivers than she could name. The cold climbed through the leather, biting at the bone, but numb feet were honest feet—they told you when the ground shifted, and they didn't daydream.

She kept to the deepest part of the channel where the current ran black and swift, erasing the mud from their passage. Twice she stopped, one hand raised, and listened to the dark behind them. Only the wind. Only the water.

After the second stop, she glanced back without turning her head.

"Eyes forward," she said. "The ridge behind us is empty, and the ditch is full of dead boys who spent their last seconds looking back. Save your vision for what comes next. There's a ford two miles down where we cross, and the eastern bank's thick with briar. You'll want your hands free and your mind empty."

She moved on, her silhouette dissolving into the alders ahead, her voice coming back hollow against the rush.

"And if you're going to vomit, do it in the water. The sound carries less, and the current takes the evidence."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes on her back, the rhythm of her steps. My stomach's a hard knot. "I'm fine," I say, but it comes out thin. The cold water's a steady shock, keeping me here, now. I focus on that.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't break stride. The alders closed in ahead, their bare branches knitting a tunnel against the last of the grey. She heard the thinness in Corvin's voice—that particular reedy quality that came after a first close killing—but she didn't comment on it. Comments didn't help.

"Fine's a word for quartermasters and priests," she said. The current tugged at her calves, numbing the old scar tissue above her boot. "Out here it's just noise. Let your stomach twist if it wants. The cold water does the same work as a slap to the face, slower and without the indignity."

She waded around a half-submerged log, one hand brushing the bark to steady herself, and checked the eastern bank. The briar line showed black against the snow-dusted stones.

"Two miles to the ford. Then uphill through thorn until we hit the ridgeline trail. Camp's four miles past that, if the pickets haven't frozen to death and deserted." She adjusted the sword at her hip, making sure the belt hadn't shifted in the wet. "Focus on the briars. They demand attention. Every snag's a problem to solve—lift the branch, step through, don't catch the cloak. Give your hands something to do besides remember the weight of the blade."

She glanced back once, not at Corvin's face but at his footing, watching how he placed his boots in the current.

"And if you're going to fall behind, tell me now. I'll set a slower pace and blame it on my knees. Otherwise we keep this speed until the ford. The water stops numbing after twenty minutes, and then it's just misery. I'd rather reach the briars before that particular truth sets in."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes on her back, matching her pace step for step. The water's so cold it's starting to feel like a burn. "I'll keep up," I say, and I mean it. I focus on the briars she mentioned, on the next mile, on the next step. Anything but the quiet.
