dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack sheathed the knife and stood up in stages, knees cracking like green wood in a fire. She glanced at the wet stripe across Corvin's face, then away.

"Not yours, by the look of it. Comes off the same either way." She crouched by the nearest body and went through its coat with two fingers, unhurried, a woman taking inventory. "Him past the cart — that's a belly, by the sound. Belly gives you an hour, sometimes two, and it gets louder before it stops. Sound carries at dusk. Carries a long way out here."

She found a purse, weighed it in her palm, grunted, and put it away.

"Six men, and this wouldn't buy the rope to hang us with. Some war." She looked up at Corvin then, level, nothing in it you could call a judgment. "So. Three ways this goes. You go finish it. We sit in the dark and let him do it himself. Or I do it for you, and you owe me — and I collect."

She went back to the pockets.

"Nobody picks wrong, for what it's worth. You just pick."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, tasting grit and salt in my throat. "I'll do it." I push off the ground, my legs shaky, and head toward the cart without looking at Wrack.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't watch him go. She worked the second boot off the nearest body instead, rocking it loose at the heel, and set it down beside the first.

"Behind the ear, if you can turn him," she said, to the boot. "If he's flat on his back, under the jaw and push up. Hand flat on his shoulder so he doesn't jump into it. One push, all the way in, then leave it a breath before you draw — comes out cleaner that way. Less of him on you."

She moved to the next body and started on its laces. "Don't stand square over him. A gut man can't rise, but he can hold an ankle, and a dying man's grip will surprise you. Kick, don't pull."

A pause, the length of a knot coming undone.

"And if you start and your stomach turns, just say so. I'll come finish it. Costs you the same either way — I don't charge extra for rescues." She got the boot free. "You can tell him it'll be quick, if you like. Only lie I'd allow. Don't say sorry, though. Sorry's for you, and he's past buying."

Then it was quiet work for a while — pockets, a knife worth keeping, a coat with good seams. She stopped at something on a cord: a square of lead, stamped with a device worn near to nothing. A tower, maybe. A hand. She turned it over twice and put it away.

"These weren't ditch-robbers. The boots alone cost more than the purse." One brief glance toward the cart, gone again. "Somebody dressed them for work. We'll want to be elsewhere by morning."

She went back to the pockets, eyes down, and said the last part quietly, like it wasn't meant to carry.

"First one's the only one that costs anything. After that it's just weather."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped working. She'd been wrist-deep in the third coat's pockets; she came out of it and sat back on her heels, and that was all the ceremony the question got.

"Both," she said. "It's always both. You're wanting me to make it one or the other so it only weighs the once. Doesn't split. Never has." She tipped her head toward the cart without looking at it. "You do both tonight, and after, you don't get to pick which one you did."

She counted the rest off like inventory.

"I haven't laid eyes on him. Belly, by the sound — low, and he's still spending air on words, so nothing up top's gone yet. Belly's a coin toss. Some men go in a day. Some take three or four, going hot by inches, calling for water the whole way. Flies find them the second day. Out here, with a ditch and what's in our packs, nobody's stitching him. He's dead. All that's left is the timetable and who hears it."

"And easier — yes. It's easier. A quiet man doesn't bring whoever paid for those boots down on us in the dark. You want the easier part not to be true so the mercy part comes clean. It won't. They came bundled together tonight. That's rare. Most days you get one without the other, and then you find out what you're made of. Take them while they're bundled."

She went back into the coat.

"He'll ask for water. Belly men always do. It won't save him and it won't kill him — that one's between you and your own head, and I'd keep it private." A knot came free. "Now. You've been nearer him than me. Tell me what you've got — words or just noise, where he's holding himself, the color of him. I can give you the timetable off that, near enough. Same knife either way. But you'll know what you're shortening. Worth the asking."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: (He’s mostly noise.) I flex my fingers, then make a fist. "He's saying 'water' and 'mother'—but I think the mother one is done." I glance toward the cart, shadows stretching long now. "His hands keep coming off his gut like he can’t believe it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack nodded slowly, like Corvin had read her a list of goods and the count was short.

"Hands coming off it. That's the tell." She spat into the ditch, thoughtfully. "A man who knows he's dead holds himself shut with both hands and doesn't spend them. This one's still arguing with his belly. Thinks if he looks away it'll have mended by the time he looks back." She shook her head once. "That's not a three-day man after all. But it's not an hour man either. He's got fight left in him, which means he's got time left in him, which means the water thing's real. He'll keep at it."

She got up off her heels, joints filing their complaints, and walked a slow half-circle, checking the tree line out of habit more than hope.

"Mother's done, you said. That's the one to mind. Mother means he's young, or he's far from her, and either way he's not talking to you when he says it. Don't answer it. Answering a man's mother when you've got a knife for him — that sticks to you. Water you can give or not, your call. The mother you leave alone."

She came back and stood a few feet off, arms crossed, looking at Corvin properly for the first time since the ambush ended. Taking stock, the way she'd take stock of a blade before buying it.

"Hands like that, he might grab at you when you come close. Not to fight. To be held, or to hold — same thing at that point. You'll want to have decided before it happens whether you let him. Either answer's fine. Being surprised by it is what ruins men."

A pause. Dusk was coming down out of the hills behind them, filling the ditch first.

"Go on, then. While there's still light enough to see what you're doing. Nothing worse than your first one done blind." She turned back toward the bodies, then added, not turning around: "I'll be listening. Not for trouble. In case."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack came over at an amble, the way she did everything that wasn't killing. She stopped an arm's length from the cart and crouched, head tipped, reading the man like a ledger in the last of the light.

"Huh. That one's mine." She said it the way she'd claim a dropped glove. "Low left, the cut. He came off the cart at me in the press and I gave it back, and I thought the fall had finished what I started. I was wrong." No apology in it, and none offered. "I do tidy work. It's the last inch I left loose."

Then the read, flat and quiet, item by item.

"Twenty, maybe. Soft hands — the sword's newer than the boots. Cut's a slice, not a hole, which is why he's slow about it. Cold sweat — you can feel it off him from here. Lips graying from the corners in. Hands cold, belly hot. Eyes still tracking, which is the bad news. I said coin toss before. Seen him now: it's landing. Two hours, less if he keeps spending breath on shouting."

She didn't reach for him. "I'm not touching him. He's yours tonight. I'll say what I see, that's all."

The man had gone quiet. That was the worst of it, and Wrack said so.

"See that? He's stopped because you came close. Thinks you're the water." She let that sit exactly as long as it needed to. "Water," the man said then. Just that. Looking at Corvin.

And his hand came up off his gut and closed on Corvin's sleeve, weak as a child's but not letting go.

"There's the part you were to decide about," Wrack said, not moving. "He's not fighting you. Couldn't. He's holding the last warm thing in reach. Stay or step free — both are fine. They let go when they're done. They always do."

She rose, joints grinding, and stepped back a pace.

"He's propped on the wheel. Behind the ear, from his left — you'll be beside him, not over him. Kinder for both of you." She turned half toward the tree line, hands loose. "Light's going. I'm right here, minding the dark. Take whatever time you need. Not a minute more."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I look at his face, younger than I thought. His hand's on my sleeve, not pulling—just holding, like a drowning man. I put my free hand on his shoulder like she said. My mouth's dry as dust. "You won't feel it," I lie.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack kept her back to it, as promised, and gave the tree line her attention. Nothing moved under the trees. She checked twice anyway; checking was work, and work kept a body from listening too hard.

She listened anyway. Everyone does, the first time. The grip went out of the sleeve — she heard the cloth fall slack — and then a long breath, all at once, like something set down. Then the small sound after. Then nothing.

The quiet was the same quiet as after the fight. It just sat lower in the ditch.

She gave it a ten-count and came back at the same amble. She crouched by the wheel, looked at the man's face — eyes open, done tracking now — and put two fingers to his throat out of habit, not doubt.

"Clean," she said. "Quick. That's the whole eulogy, and he got better than most." She nodded at the freed sleeve. "There's the letting go. Told you. They always do." A pause. "You spent the one lie I allow, and it came true by the end. He died believing you. That's more than most men get from anyone."

She stood, knees registering their usual objection, and started giving orders in the tone of a woman discussing supper.

"Knife out — a breath's long past — wipe it on the cloak. Don't study your hands while you do it. Studying comes later whether you schedule it or not." She unhooked the waterskin and held it out, eyes on the ridge while she waited. "Drink. That one's for you, not him. And I'm not asking about the water. Told you it was private."

She walked the ditch's edge as she talked, counting bodies like cordwood.

"Five get stripped and laid in. Not him. He keeps the boots, the coat, all of it. Don't ask why — I'll invent a reason and we'll both know it's invented. Cart goes to the ford and the ford keeps it. You wash at the water, downstream. Not over him. Scrubbing your hands in the ditch you laid a man in — that's a picture that outlasts the doing."

She shouldered her pack, and said the last of it to the road rather than to Corvin.

"I told you after this it's weather. It will be. Tomorrow, maybe the day after. Tonight it's allowed to weigh — one night won't ruin you. Making a relic of it would." She jerked her chin at the nearest body. "Come, then. Ankles. Dead men lie about their weight, so lift with your legs, and we'll be at the water before the moon clears the ridge."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped with a boot in her hand and looked at him over the body between them.

"Spear," she said. "That's a different lesson, and it isn't the one you got. That was my knife, low left, and since it's mine, I'll account for it. Spears another night, if you still want it. Short version: a spear makes holes, holes bleed inside where nobody sees it stop, and the man looks better than he is for the first hour. There. Spears done."

She set the boot down and went back to work while she talked, because this was easier said to her hands than to his face.

"Here's what your eyes took in and your head skipped. The belly's not a bag of blood. It's layers. Skin, fat, then muscle in sheets, then a slippery skin holds the whole works in, then the works. My knife went through the wall of him like through a belt, and every layer stopped the blade a half-heartbeat before it gave. Fat first — yellow, like wet suet. Twenty years old and there's still fat in there. Then muscle, which grabs. Then the give. That give is the sound you'll hear again at bad moments. It's quieter than you'd think."

"The smell comes before the sight, and it outlasts both. Blood's nothing — iron and a butcher's shop, you're used to it inside a season. An opened gut smells like a privy and a slaughterhouse together, and sweet under that. Your head keeps that one."

She worked the laces free, not hurrying.

"What came out first was the fat apron — omentum, if you want the word. It comes to the door when you knock, like it means to argue. Then the bowel itself. Gray-pink, slick, and moving on its own, slow, like worms in a puddle. That's the part nobody expects. It doesn't lie still. It's working while the man's dying. Still doing its job. There's something in that I've never decided what to do with."

"And here's what killed him, because it wasn't the blood — there wasn't blood enough to matter. A slice opens him along a seam. The spill is slow. What kills is the leak — the bowel's contents going into a place that has to stay clean. His own supper, poisoning the cavity of him. That was the fever. That's why his belly was hot and his hands cold: the heat was the fight, the cold was everything leaving his edges to guard the middle. And that's the water, too. His gut was burning from inside and drinking can't reach it. He wasn't asking you for a drink. He was asking the fire to stop."

She looked up then, and gave him the whole of it straight, no dressing.

"That's everything. Every detail, none of it cleaned. You asked straight, and it was the right ask — a man who knows what the work does can decide honestly whether to do it. A man who doesn't know finds out in the middle of doing, and that's the man who breaks." She stood, wiped her hands on her thighs. "But hear the line under it. You get to know it once, tonight, in words. You don't get to run it every night behind your eyes in pictures. Words you can put down. Pictures put you down. When they come — and they come — you say: I know. I was told. I did it anyway. Then sleep."

She toed the nearest body, businesslike again.

"And you're going to do it again, so the knowing's not wasted. That's not prophecy, it's arithmetic — you're with me, there's a war, and neither of us is lucky." She bent and took her grip on the dead man's ankles. "Moon's clearing the ridge. Light enough to work, dark enough to leave by. Take the other end, lift with your legs, and mind the ditch edge — it's slicker than it looks."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I nod, slow and grim, and don't look away from her. My hands are steadier than they were. I move to the other body's ankles, the leather of its boots cold under my palms. "Tell me if I'm doing it wrong."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"Already wrong," Wrack said, without heat. "You're gripping the boots. Leather stretches. Ten feet of that and you'll be holding two boots while the rest of him stays where he started." She took her own grip on the first body — ankle bones, one in each fist, thumbs locked over. "Bone, not leather. The boots come along if they feel like it."

She hauled backward and the body came out of the grass in a long, grudging slide, heels furrowing, arms trailing like a man late for his own hanging.

"Don't lift the whole way. Nobody lifts a grown man the whole way, not twice. Drag him to the lip, then swing. Dead men travel best in an arc — you build the swing and let it do the work." She swung twice, shoulder and hip together, and let go on the rise. The body dropped into the ditch with a sound like a rolled carpet, one hand slapping stone.

"Mind his head on the lip. Not for him — he's past noticing. Skulls knock loud, and sound carries at dusk. You remember." She was already walking back. "And if he lets go of his water on the swing, that's not spite. Dead men lose their doors, all of them at once, sometimes. Plumbing, not character. The ford forgives boots."

"Two in," she said, taking her grip on the third. "Three to go, and one of them yours. Match my pace and we're done before the moon's fully up."

Halfway down the ditch she stopped and looked at him properly.

"Your hands have stopped shaking. Noticed that. Don't trust it. That's not courage — that's the body deciding the fight ended an hour ago. It comes back at stupid times. Three days from now, mid-meal, most likely. When it does, let it happen. Fighting the shake costs more than the shake."

She nodded back toward the cart, where the young man lay as they'd left him.

"You didn't ask why he keeps his boots, so here's the invented reason, as promised. Soldiers get buried. Looters get ditches. Five stripped men in a hole reads as robbery gone well. One man by his own cart, dressed, face up — that reads as a man whose company moved on and couldn't dig. Whoever finds this tomorrow will read it like a letter, and I'd rather they read the second." A beat. "That one turned out true, as it happens. Don't get used to it."

Two more went in, hers, while she laid out the rest of the night like kit on a blanket: the ford, wash downstream and not over him, food he wouldn't want eaten anyway, because the body keeps its own ledger and it collects.

Then she fished the lead token from her pocket and held it up to the moonlight — the worn stamp, tower or hand, still undecided.

"Last thing tonight. Look at this and tell me honest: have you seen the device before? A tower, a hand, anything near it — a banner, a seal, ink on some paymaster's arm. Say it now, in the light, where knowing is cheap." She turned it over once more and held it out. "Tomorrow it may be expensive."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She'd had the token in her fist and the last body in her eye, and what held her was a hand — one of the ditch men's, moving on the stones. Slow. A spider in cold weather.

"Huh," she said, and came back, and stood over the pair of them, and looked her mistake full in the face. "That's twice tonight I've signed off on a dead man ahead of his time." No apology, and none dressed up as one. "This one I went through coat and all while he held still for me. Cold takes their breath down to nothing — you can put your ear on a chest like that and lose the count. I'll blame the cold. It's the only one of us without a reputation to protect."

She crouched at Corvin's shoulder, where she could see all of it, and stayed.

"You asked me not to leave anything out. Good. Most men can't ask — the throat shuts and the pictures take the job uninvited. Words are cheaper. So. Words, as it happens."

"That scrape you just made — that's bone. The ridge of the skull. The blade will skate on it all night; there's no arguing with it. Stop a breath. Come down a thumb's width and forward, behind the corner of the jaw, where the meat's soft. Find the give with the point before you spend the push. There. That address."

The man stirred when the pain found him — a sound out of him like a saw pulled through wet wood, no words in it. His eyes came open to slits and didn't track.

"Eyes open. Look at them anyway — not for him, for you. Nobody's home. Lamps lit, house empty. He'll not know you were ever here, and that mercy only runs one way. All the knowing in this is yours." His hand crawled, found Corvin's wrist, and closed. "There's the grip. You decided about this already, so it's just weather now."

Then the push went home, and she named it as it landed. "There's the give. Quieter than you'd think — told you. A thumb through the skin of a plum." His back arched off the stones, heels drumming twice. "Not him. That's the wires firing with nobody home to answer. Chickens do it headless. Don't take it for a fight."

"Count with me now. He'll take longer than the young one — cold bodies are slow at everything, including leaving." The grip on Corvin's wrist eased by degrees. "Little finger's gone. Ring finger. Thumb pays last. They always do." A long, uneven pull of breath, then a gap. "That's not him deciding anything. That's a bellows with a split seam, running on habit. One more, likely." There was one more. Then the grip was gone entirely and the cloth fell slack, and Wrack counted ten under her breath and put two fingers to his throat, then to the spot behind the ear where the work was done.

"Done. Call it a minute, first touch to last breath, and half of it was you finding the address. The young one went quicker. Not because you failed — this one started poorer and colder." She nodded at the ear, where a dark thread was making its slow way down. "That's the whole blood budget. The head's a good bucket; most of it stays home. Wipe on the cloak. Don't study your hands — studying's scheduled for later whether you like it or not."

She took one of the dead man's hands first, turned it over in the moonlight: rope calluses, old ones, a laborer's hand in a soldier's boot.

"Now the amendment, since you'll be keeping books. I told you the first one's the only one that costs. That stands. This one didn't cost — this one taught, and you paid in mess instead of coin, which is the better price. But look at that hand. Somebody's dressing plowmen and pointing them at travelers, and I'd very much like to know who's holding the purse."

She fished out the lead token and held it up between them, turning it so the worn face caught the moon.

"Which brings cheap knowledge back to the table. You skipped it once. Tower, hand, anything near it — a banner, a seal, ink on a paymaster's arm. Say it now."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I squint at the token, but the stamp's too worn. "Looks like a hand holding a tower, maybe. Or just... a bad drawing." I wipe my knife clean on my own trouser leg, ignoring the cloak. My hand isn't shaking.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
"A maybe," Wrack said. "Maybes are cheap. I'll take it."

She turned the token under the moon once more before pocketing it. "Hand holding a tower, or a bad drawing — every badge in this war is a bad drawing somebody died for, so that part tells me nothing. Here's what does. I've marched under eight sets of colors and deserted one, and a real device gets defended. Argued over, polished, sewn on straight. This was struck soft so it never took clean. Or rubbed clean after." She flipped it. "Back's blank. Never finished. Somebody didn't want these read, and went to the trouble of making sure."

"Hand and tower. There's a siegemasters' brotherhood down the coast keeps a tower on theirs. The hand's new to me. Blank's the likelier story either way. Men who wear no colors are doing work their paymaster wants to be able to deny. Blank men, blank work. Blank work pays better than honest and hangs faster than either."

She went through the last bodies with a new question and got the same answer twice: same lead, same worn stamp — one flat in a boot sole, one stitched under a collar, where a man keeps what he's been told to keep. She collected both. "Robbers take everything. That's what makes them robbers." At the cart she searched the young man for that one thing and nothing else, found the same stamp, and left it where it lay. "His stays. The finders should know what regiment of nobody he belonged to."

"Same stamp, all six. That's not keepsakes, that's an issue. Somebody struck a bagful and dealt them out with the boots — which means there's a bag, and a hand that deals from it, and more men where these came from. Six is a file. Files have sisters."

The last of them went into the ditch without ceremony. She built the swings and let the arcs do the work, and the ditch took them the way ditches do — grudging, then done, then just a ditch again.

Then she gave his trouser leg and his hand each their due.

"You wiped my knife-work onto your own leg instead of his cloak. Don't know what that means yet. I'll know by the third time you do it. Meanwhile that cloth's done till it sees water — gut-stink doesn't come out with wishing. Strip it at the ford."

"And your hand's not shaking. I noticed you noticing. It won't tonight — I gave you the timetable. Three days, mid-meal. Stop checking it. A man who checks his hands is rehearsing the shake, and rehearsing is how you send invitations."

On her way past the cart she stopped long enough to square the young man's coat and turn his face to the sky. Not for him. For the letter — dressed, face up, by his own cart, a soldier his company couldn't stop to dig for. She stood over him a breath longer than the work needed. Then the work took her back.

"One more thing for the books," she said, shouldering her pack. "You asked me to stay and watch, and to leave nothing out. Most ask the opposite — walk off, give them their privacy. I've buried the ones who asked for privacy." She said it without weight, a line in a ledger. "So. You'll do."

She set off along the ditch top, away from the road, laying out the night as she went: ford a mile south, wash downstream, cold food, no fire, first eyes hers, wake her at moonset. Then, without turning:

"Now the expensive question, since cheap just left the table. Dressed men in a ditch are a posted ambush, and posted ambushes wait for something. Six is a lot of men to spend on chance traffic — roads don't pay that well. So they were waiting for the road, or for someone on it. The few of mine left don't know my steps this week, and nobody's paid me the compliment of a price yet." One glance back at the ditch, then not again. "So it's you, or it's luck, and you've heard my opinion of luck. Who knew you'd be on this road today?"

"Take your time. But take it walking."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the dead man's hand, still curled like it was holding something. "He was waiting," I say, finally. "For the toll-taker. Me." I look up at her. "They knew I'd be here, didn't they?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped on the ditch top, five steps gone with the moon on her back, and stood a moment while the answer settled. Then she came back and sat down in the wet grass beside him, which was more ceremony than she'd given any dead man that night.

"Yes," she said. "They knew."

She let it sit while the ford argued with its stones below.

"Told you it wasn't luck. Luck's never this organized." She broke a grass stem for something to do with her hands. "An ambush isn't a guess. Six men is wages, rations, a bagful of struck lead, and somebody to deal from the bag. Nobody spends that hoping a toll-taker happens past. Somebody had your road, your day, your hour — well enough to dress the file for it. So here's the rest, since you asked for the rest." She put up three fingers. "What you know, what you guard, or what you are. A man at a crossing sees everything that passes — who moves by night, what they carry, whose faces don't match their papers. You keep a ledger at your post, I take it. Toll men always do. Correct me if I'm wrong — it's cheap now. Because if you do, your ledger is somebody's secrets with dates on them. Or it's the crossing itself. Crossings outlive their wars. Someone wants yours shut, or open, or unwatched for a week while something heavy goes over quiet. Or it's you, and six dressed men is a strange price for one man with soft hands."

She folded the fingers down.

"So before anything else: what do you carry? Ledger, seal, keys, letters — anything that isn't a spoon. If they were sent to take a thing off you, the thing's still in your pack, and the men who want it know only that their file stopped answering. When that silence reaches them, they send the question again. Dearer."

She looked at him then, sidelong, and put the last of it in before the dark could put it in crooked.

"And put this in your books. Nothing tonight changes what you did by the cart. A dying man asked. You answered. That he'd have opened your throat an hour sooner doesn't make the mercy smaller. It makes it stranger. You can carry strange. Small, I'd have to argue."

She turned the lead token over in her pocket, lead clicking on knuckle.

"Now my books, since we're keeping them. Last week you were a stray walking my road, and I let you, for company, because company's been thin. Tonight you're a purse with men following it, and that changes my price — I won't lie and say it doesn't. But somebody dressed six men on my road and never priced me. The ambush I can respect. The arithmetic insults me. And there's a bag out there, and a hand that deals from it, and I'd like a word with the hand. So I'm still walking your road. For now. Priced."

She stood, joints filing their complaints, and told him up with a jerk of her chin.

"Tonight runs as planned — ford, wash, cold food, no fire. It's tomorrow that split. You can't go back to your post. Your post is the first place they'll look, and your relief is bought, or blind, or next in a ditch." She shouldered the pack and set off, speaking to the road. "One more thing before the names. Give it a day before you swear you've told me everything. A man who learns he's worth six dressed men usually finds he knew more than he thought — ledgers he signed, friendly questions he answered without thinking them questions. It surfaces. Let it."

She waited until his boots were moving, then:

"Who knew your road? Not who paid — you don't know that, and if you hand me a name I'll know it's a guess. Who *knew*. Your relief. A clerk. The woman who sells you bread. A stranger who asked after schedules and bought you a drink doing it. All the names, in any order. I'll do the sorting."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "The ledger's back at the post," I admit, my voice too steady for the words. "And the woman at the baker's keeps it when I'm off-shift." I stand, my legs stiff now. "My relief is a man named Halder. He asked last week when I'd be collecting the southern tolls."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack took the names the way she'd taken the purse — weighed once, pocketed. She kept walking and gave the road the worst of it.

"Halder first. There's the map, whether or not there's the leak. Relief men need schedules — that's what makes the question invisible. The job hides it. If I wanted a toll-taker's road, I wouldn't ask him and I wouldn't search his house. I'd buy his relief a drink." A few steps went by. "And you told him. Don't trouble denying it — men tell their relief the day and the hour, that's what relief is for. Not a sin. It's the job working as designed, which is why it's the cheapest theft there is. Maybe he asked for coin from the start. Maybe he asked honest and got squeezed after. Weighs the same, either way. Innocent and used — same weight, same ditch. Halder's a door now, and somebody holds a key."

She let him absorb that at his own pace, which was the pace of the road.

"Now the part I didn't say before, because I didn't have the shape of it. Six dressed men for one soft-handed toll-taker — I kept calling it a strange price for a killing. It's not a killing's price. It's a taking's price. Dead men don't open ledgers. They were sent to lift you quiet and ask you questions somewhere with a table in it. What they got instead was me, and their questions died in the ditch with them." She glanced over, once. "Which means the sender still wants the answers. And a sender who's lost six doesn't send six again — that gets noticed. He sends one friendly stranger with good boots and a drink. So from tomorrow, every kind soul on a road is a price on two legs. Put that in your books."

"The bread woman next. She keeps your ledger, so she's the leak or she's next — next being whoever calls at the post once the silence lands. And it lands. Think the shape through: six men go quiet. The sender doesn't know if that's success or failure. Silence reads both ways. Done quiet — someone comes to collect what the file was sent for. Gone wrong — the question comes again, dearer. Either way, the next move touches your post. You're out here being dead to them. The post is the stage, and two people you like are standing on it." A beat. "And no, you can't send them word. A letter from a dead toll-taker is a flare. It tells the watchers where you are and that their file failed, and it spends the bread woman's life to buy your conscience an hour. Warned in person or not at all. You don't have to like it. You do have to carry it."

She held out a hand, flat, without stopping.

"Were you collecting today? Is there southern toll coin riding in that pack? Because if there is, the senders paid for a collection they didn't get, and unpaid men are loud men. You'll turn everything out at the ford — all of it on a coat, and we'll read it like the tokens. Walking's for sorting names. Water's for sorting property. And give the bread woman a name while it's cheap. Names tell me which people you'll do stupid things for, and I plan around stupid."

The ford's argument was audible now under the frogs.

"There's your day, by the way. I said give it a day before you swear you've told me everything — Halder's question surfaced inside a minute. The rest comes slower. Let it come." She turned the lead token over in her pocket, once. "And one thing I did tonight may have mailed a letter already — I left the boy his token face-up for the finders. If the finders are theirs, our clock just got shorter. If they're honest, it did somebody good. Both can be true. Keep both."

Then she laid out the night's last piece, flat as kit.

"Clock, since you keep books. How loud the silence is depends on what the file promised. Word by dawn — a lamp, a rider, a token in a crack — then tonight's already loud. Report in two days — then we've bought two. You don't know which. Neither do I. So we plan for the short clock and hope for the long. That's how you plan with strangers' timetables."

She stopped at the lip of the ford path and looked at him, moon behind her, nothing in it you could call a judgment.

"Three ways this goes. Same as by the cart, same rules — nobody picks wrong. You just pick." She put up fingers. "One: run. South of the ford there's nothing of yours for two hundred miles. Cheapest in blood. Costs the post, the ledger, the bread woman, Halder, and your name — and running only works if you were never worth six men, which we've settled. Two: go back. Not heroes — thieves stealing their own lives. Night, no lantern, in and out. The ledger, one look at Halder — you'll know bought from blind in a look, you've watched him for years — and the truth in the bread woman's ear or nothing, whichever you can carry. Dearest in risk. Buys the most back. Three: the hand. We follow the lead. Tokens are struck somewhere and dealt from somewhere, and the man who deals them knows why you were worth six. Doesn't buy the ledger back. Might not buy you tomorrow. But the arithmetic insulted me, and I meant it."

She folded the fingers down.

"You can't have all three. Two can be had together if you're greedy — the post and the hand are cousins, maybe. But pick one to mean. Men who pick two mean neither." She started down toward the water. "Pick out loud. Cheap now."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stare at the black water of the ford, my face still streaked with blood that isn't mine. "The hand," I say, and it feels like throwing a key into a river. "But first the post. I need to know if Halder's still breathing."
