dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"No, you're not," Sedge said, not looking up. "Doesn't matter. Nobody ever is. Hands stay where you put them."

The lamp got shifted twice and guttered at her both times, so she set it on the crate at the head of the table, where at least her own hands wouldn't throw shadow into the wound. The light it gave was yellow and bad. She'd worked in worse.

The man's eyes were still open. That was the good news; she'd quit trusting the quiet ones with their eyes shut years ago. She took his wrist, counted, let it go. Fast, but knocking steady. There was fight left in him.

"You," she said. "The wall won't tell you when he moves. He will. Eyes on him."

She opened the trouser leg with the shears. The entry hole was small and clean; everything below it was swollen, hot, stiffening. She talked while she finished the row — probe, forceps, scalpel, gut thread and the curved needle for after, the ligature she hoped she wouldn't need.

"Fragment's deep, sitting against the big vessel in your thigh. It comes out tonight or the leg comes off by morning. You'll feel me go in after it. I won't pretend otherwise."

His eyes had crawled over to the row of steel and stuck there.

"Nobody enjoys this part," she said. "It just has to be done."

She rolled a bandage tight and set it between his teeth. "Bite. Screaming's fine. Moving's what kills you." Then, to the weight on his shoulders: "Hips are mine — I'll lean on them. Everything above the waist is yours."

She set the scalpel where the track ran deepest. "Here we go, son."

The first stroke opened the channel, and the man came up off the table with all that spent voice finding one more — a sound with no words in it — his back arching, his shoulders driving upward hard enough to skid the table legs in the mud. Sedge got her forearm across his hips and bore down, leaning her whole forty-four years into it.

"Hold," she said.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: (His shoulders wrench under my hands, muscles bunching like rock. I grunt, driving him back down, my boots slipping in the mud.) "I've got him," I grit out, my voice tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Then keep him," Sedge said. "He's spent most of what he had on that first push. Half a minute, he'll be down to shaking."

Her forearm stayed across his hips and she went in with the probe.

The channel filled faster than she liked — dark blood welling up in the bad yellow light, closing over the floor of the wound before she could read it. She swabbed, laid a strip of gauze in, counted ten, drew it out hot and soaked through. Twice more. The third time the floor came clear enough to work.

"There's the vessel," she said, because saying it was part of doing it. "Right under the track. You can see it move. That's the neighbor we don't wake."

The probe rode the torn channel down, a centimeter at a time, her wrist loose, her eyes on his face as much as the wound — the face told her when she was getting warm. He went rigid under them both and the sound through the bandage climbed into something with no breath left under it.

"Close. I know." Flat, not unkind. "Out is the only direction, son. None of this is for my enjoyment."

Then the probe touched it, and she felt it before she heard it — a small hard click, steel finding steel, running up the shank into her fingers.

"There it is." No triumph in it. Just a job with edges now. "Flat, edge down, lying on the artery like a slate. I can feel his pulse through the metal. That's how close we are."

She drew back and traded probe for forceps, and gave them the whole of it, because people held better when they knew. "I don't pull. Pulling drags the edge through the vessel and he's dead on this table inside two minutes — I've watched it, it's quick and it isn't clean. I go under the far edge and tip it up, like lifting a slate. That's the whole move. When it comes, he'll find whatever he's got left, and everything above the waist is still yours. All of it."

The forceps went in. She got the point seated under the far edge, and the man came up once more — shorter, weaker, heels drumming the end of the table — and she leaned her weight in and said, "Now," and tipped it.

The fragment came free with a wet give, and she had it out and dropped in the tin cup — a bright little ring, absurdly small — before she registered the wound had stopped welling and started spurting. Brighter blood, timed to the pulse. The edge had rocked off and taken a branch with it. Her fingers were in it before the next beat, and the spurt stopped against her thumb.

"He's finished — look at him, shaking is all he's got left." Sweat ran off her jaw and she let it fall. "I need your right hand more than I need his shoulders. There's a pad coming down on this wound and your palm goes on it, straight down, all your weight, and it does not lift until I say. Left hand stays where it is."

Her free hand was already folding gauze into a tight pad.

"Ten minutes of this and I tie off what's torn, and if the ankle still beats after, he keeps the leg." She set the pad against her fingers, ready to trade. "Press like it's his leg. Because it is."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Neither," Sedge said. "It's a branch, not the trunk. If it were the trunk he'd have gone grey and stopped caring by now — men who bleed out from the big ones go quiet long before they go. He came off this table twice tonight with enough left to skid it through the mud. That's a man with blood to spare. Now your hand."

She took his wrist and set the palm down on the pad, over her own fingers, and came out from under it slow — one finger, then the rest, her hand hovering a breath above his knuckles.

"Straight down. No sideways. Sideways shears the clot off and we start from nothing. If you feel warmth spreading through that pad, you say so. You don't lift to look. Warm means I come back in."

She went down the table and took the ankle, two fingers behind the inner bone, counting against her own pulse. The lamp gave its bad yellow light and she let it.

"Faint," she said. "Could be your pressure leaning on the line, could be the leak still stealing from it. We'll know when the knot's in. That's the honest answer — the leg lives or dies on one tie, ten minutes from now, and I've done a hundred of them. If the ankle's still beating when it's set, he keeps the leg, limps a month, and lies about ever limping."

She straightened and looked at Wick properly for the first time since the table legs had skidded.

"The kind part looks different from this. When it's that, there's nothing under my hands worth pressing on, and I take them off and hold his instead. There's plenty under yours. So press."

She cut gut thread to length and threaded the curved needle mostly by feel — the light was for the wound, not for her. The man had gone from shaking to a long low tremor, eyes still open, fixed on the tent ridge.

"You're keeping the leg so far, son," she told him. "Flat and patient. That's the whole job now — it's ours."

Then, back to the shoulder and the palm: "Ten minutes. Your arm goes numb around the fourth. Numb's fine. Numb is the job."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press down, the warmth of the wound seeping up through the gauze. My arm's already starting to ache. "He's still looking at the ridge," I say, my voice low. "That's something, right?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"It's something," Sedge said. "The ones who are going stop looking at things in the tent. They find something past the wall to watch — four years, and I've never once seen what it is. A man glaring at a rafter is a man who's still here and hates it, and hate keeps the pressure up. Let him glare."

She worked the wait like everything else, in pieces. At what her own pulse told her was halfway, she took the ankle again — still faint, still ambiguous, and she said so, because a holder lied to is a holder who relaxes. She laid two fingers briefly on the back of the pressing hand, checking for soak without asking; the hand had enough to do without talking. Warm, but not spreading. The clot was doing more of the holding now than either of them.

"When the arm starts shaking, don't fight it," she said. "A shaking arm is still an arm that's holding. Fighting it is how it lets go. You're in the easy half — the last five minutes belong to the blood, not to you."

The man's tremor had run itself down to breathing. Long, ragged, even. The lamp guttered once and steadied. The table sat crooked in the mud where he'd skidded it, and she left it that way; straightening could wait its turn like everything else.

"Time." She came up beside the pad with fresh gauze and the threaded needle laid ready. "Here's the trade. On three, straight up — up, not sideways, not off at an angle — and then the hand goes to your knee and stays there. I'm in before the wound knows it's open. One. Two. Three."

The pad came away and she was into the space it left, swabbing, lifting the dark clot off in one piece like a scab that hadn't been earned yet. Under it the torn branch showed — a small ragged point, welling dark at each beat instead of spurting. The ten minutes of pressure had bought her that: a bleeder she could see instead of one she had to chase.

"There you are," she said to it. To the table: "Branch only. The trunk's still sleeping, and it stays that way."

The needle went under, around, and back — a small loop of thread with the artery inside it. The man flinched, a small spent thing, all he had left, and she reached up and drew the rolled bandage from between his teeth so he could breathe around the end of it.

"Done shouting, son. Breathe instead."

She tied — first knot doubled so it couldn't slip, then two more, snug, her fingertips reading his pulse through the thread as the loop closed. Then the welling stopped. Just stopped. She watched the floor of the wound through three of his heartbeats and it stayed dry.

She went down the table, put two fingers behind the inner bone of his ankle, and counted. And counted.

"There." She held it a moment longer. "Again. There it is — faint, slow, and his. Nobody's pushing that. He keeps the leg."

His eyes came down off the ridge at last, found her, and shut. She leaned over and checked them anyway — old habit — and what she found was a wrung-out man the right color for one, breathing like a laborer at noon. An hour ago she wouldn't have trusted a closed eye on this table. Now it was just a tired man.

She tipped the tin cup so he could see it before he went under: the little bright ring of metal, absurd against all the noise it had cost. "That's what all the argument was about." She set the cup down by his hand. "For later, when you're lying about ever limping."

Then she straightened and wiped her hands down her apron — blood to both elbows, more of it his than hers, none of it meaning anything now.

"You can stop pressing. Take the arm slowly — it'll come back wrong for a minute, all pins, and holders always knock something over right then. The lamp, usually. Let it hang at your side and be stupid a while. It's earned it." She nodded toward the brazier. "Kettle. I need it hot. The wound stays open tonight — a sewn-shut wound is a grave for pus, and this one wants to drain. Three days clean, then I put skin on it. The leg's won. The man's got a fever to get through before I'll call him anything, but he'll have the leg to have the fever in."

She looked at Wick properly for the second time that night.

"What do they call you? I don't learn names until the bleeding's stopped. Cheaper that way."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Still not a name," Sedge said. "But I'll take the trade. Come round this side — where my hands were, by his knee. And don't lean on the table. It's done all the moving it's owed tonight."

She took the lamp off the crate and held it low, so the light pooled in the wound instead of skidding across it. Then she picked up the probe, because she pointed with steel, not fingers — fingers carried dirt, and this wound was going to stay clean if it took all night to keep it so.

"Top to bottom, the way I went in. The little round hole, high on the leg — that's where it went in. Shell steel makes small doors. Everything wrong with this leg is behind the door, not at it. The long cut is mine. I opened the track to reach the bottom of it. It looks worse because it is worse — but it's the honest one. The hole is the liar."

"Yellow layer under the skin — fat. Everyone's surprised by the yellow. Below that, the dark red. Muscle. Meat; not a figure of speech, the same stuff, and it's his. Muscle hates being cut. It pulls back from the knife and springs apart, which is why the wound gapes — the body making itself a bigger mouth to complain through. Stupid, but it's all it knows."

She lowered the probe into the deep of it and touched nothing, only indicated.

"There. The cord, thick as your little finger, running with the leg. Pale. Watch it a moment." She held the lamp still and let the pulse show itself — a small patient jump, over and over. "That's the artery. The trunk. Every one of those jumps is his heart, seen from the wrong end. That's what I worked beside for half an hour with a piece of edged steel lying on it like a slate on a roof. Now you know why I don't pull. The edge was sitting on that."

"Off to the side — the pale knot. Mine. Gut thread, doubled so it can't slip. Under that knot is a branch the size of a matchstick, torn when the fragment tipped up and out. It was spurting to his pulse when your hand came down on it. Now it's tied like a bootlace, and the blood behind it has found other roads. A leg is all roads. That's the whole reason he keeps it — the tie didn't cut him off. It just sent the traffic around."

"The leg itself — swollen, hot, tight as a drumhead. That's not the wound. That's the body's answer to the wound. It crowds its own soldiers in, and soldiers crowd. That crowding is why he'll hurt worse tonight than he did on my table, and why fever's still coming for him. The mess has to have a way out or the crowd turns to poison."

She laid a strip of gauze along the wound's edge, ready for when the water came.

"So it stays open, and this goes down to the floor of it as a wick. Whatever builds up climbs out along it. Wounds close from the bottom — floor, then walls, then skin last, like filling a trench. Roof over a trench that's still full of men and you've made a grave. I said that before. I meant the shape of it."

She nodded at the tin cup by his slack hand. "And that. Steel off a shell casing, by the burr on it. Every pulse moved the leg, the leg moved the metal, and the metal worried the vessel like a stone in a boot. Give it one more day and it wears through — deep, where no hand can press. Small ring. Big argument."

She set the lamp back on the crate.

"You'd rather know than imagine. That's the right way round — imagination's a liar in a tent. It only ever shows you prettier or worse, never the thing itself. And knowing keeps the hands steady, and there'll be a next time for your hands. This war has run out of everything except work."

"Now the kettle. Bring it hot, and bring your name with it. I ask twice. I never ask three times — past that you're just 'holder' until spring."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I walk stiffly over to the brazier, my arm prickling back to life. "Wick," I say, grabbing the kettle's handle with a still-numb hand. "My name's Wick." I carry it over, careful not to slosh. "You want me to pour?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Wick," she said, and took it with a nod. "Before I had to ask twice. Last easy thing either of us gets tonight." She tipped her chin at the strip of gauze laid along the wound's edge. "It'll stick, too — that's the same word as what goes in him next. I remember names by the job the man was doing when I learned them. You're the one who held a leg on with his hand. That's yours now."

She hooked a dented tin basin out from under the table with her boot and shoved it under the low corner.

"Not onto him yet — kettle's at a boil and his flesh has had all the cooking it wants. Pour half into the basin first." She dipped the inside of her wrist into it when it was half full and held it there, counting. "Blood-warm. Good. Now him — slow, from the high end. The table's crooked. First useful thing it's done since sundown. The tilt gives the water a road, and everything that shouldn't stay in him rides out on it."

When the water came, it ran down the channel she'd opened and off the low corner wrong-colored — dark first, then pink, threads of spent clot and small dark slivers going with it. She swabbed behind the flow, following it down. The knot sat where she'd left it, dark and dry. The artery jumped its small patient jump.

"There. Floor, walls, tie, and the trunk still sleeping. Clean as this tent gets."

She took the strip with the forceps and fed it down to the floor of the wound, tail laid over the lip of the cut. "To the bottom, one end out. Whatever builds in there climbs out along this for three days. Wet it down — once more, straight down the strip." Then gauze over the top, laid and taped loose. "Not a bandage. It's not holding anything in. It's keeping the dirt off the door."

She slid a rolled blanket under the calf. "Uphill, slight. Swelling hates it, and he'll hate it, and that's tomorrow's argument." A second blanket went over him. "Shock settles its bills in cold. He'll shake again tonight and it'll mean nothing — just the body counting up what it's owed."

She opened the medicine tin and counted out loud, because a count nobody hears isn't a count. "Morphine, four doses. He takes one." She got an arm under his shoulders, just enough. "Son. Drink." He swallowed on half a reflex and went back down. "He's earned a night without the ache. The other three stay in the tin for whoever's next. There's always a next."

Pencil stub from the apron pocket, writing on the tape at his ankle: *L. thigh. Steel out. Branch tied. Day 1.* "The tape keeps the arithmetic. Day three, if it's clean, he gets skin. If it isn't clean, it's a different job and a longer one, and I'd rather not meet it."

Then she straightened and looked at Wick across the table.

"You're on him till morning. You're the holder, so you're the watcher — the war's run out of everyone else. Four things fetch me. Bright blood soaking that dressing. Red climbing up the leg, hot and hard. Smell — pus smells sweet and thick, like a room where something's been left too long; smell gets me fastest. And quiet. Everything else — the fever, the sweat, the complaining when he wakes — that's the honest work. Let it happen. Loud and hot is a man fighting. Quiet and hot is a man losing."

She took what the kettle had left, tempered it through her wrist, and washed her forearms over the basin, working the blood out of her knuckle-creases with her thumbnail while the lamp guttered and steadied and guttered again.

"Now sit somewhere that isn't the table. Holders crash — ten minutes, cold sweat, the shakes, and it looks like fear and it isn't. Your arm held a man's leg on for ten minutes. The body keeps books too, and it collects. Hardtack in the crate by the lamp. It's terrible. Eat it anyway."

She wrung the water from her hands.

"Questions — ask now, while I'm still upright. By the time that lamp dies I'll be stupid with tired, and you'll be shaking, and neither of us will keep the answers."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge hooked the crate out from the head of the table with her boot and sat down on it — first time all night her weight had gone anywhere but into a man. She broke a corner off the hardtack and ate it, because the body kept books and hers was owed.

"All right. Straight. First thing, throw out the picture you've got, because it's wrong. You're imagining a knife. A knife goes in sharp and leaves a wound like a sentence — written, finished. This is a torn piece of casing." She tipped the fragment from the tin cup into her palm and held it near the lamp. "See the burr. Torn, not ground. It didn't arrive sharp. It arrived mean. Jagged, tumbling, and slower than you'd think by the time it's crossed the ground to him — which is why the door is small and the room behind it is ruined. And it's cold. Men tell each other the steel comes in red-hot and sears the track clean behind it. Four years, I've never pulled a hot one. They arrive cold as a coin, and whatever's riding on them stays riding."

She let that word sit, then fed it.

"Riding. That's the part nobody imagines. This didn't fall out of the sky into a clean man. It crossed the ground first — trench ground, the same mud that's under this tent. It went through trouser cloth that hadn't been washed since spring, through everything that cloth had been lying in, and it swept all of it along, into him. The hole is small because the steel is small. The corridor behind it is a pocket of the battlefield buried in the man. That's what a shrapnel wound is. Not a cut. A burial."

She finished the hardtack and dusted her hands on her apron.

"So it does three things. One — it tears. One-time cost, over before he hits the ground, and the body's good at tears; it's been mending them since before there were wars. Tearing is the honest part of the whole business. Two — it imports. The mud is alive. That's not poetry, that's the trouble with it. It has tenants, and they ride the steel in and find a warm room with everything to eat. Three — and this is the one that matters — it stays. A bullet mostly passes through and takes its argument with it. This stops. And stopping isn't resting. Every pulse shifts the leg a hair. Every step the man ever takes again works it around. The piece walks. Our man's sat down on the trunk artery and worried it like a stone in a boot, and I've pulled them out of places a long way from where they entered. Slow, but they've got nothing else to do with their time."

She leaned over and took the ankle — habit now, not need. Two fingers behind the inner bone. Still beating, still his. She let it go and went on.

"Where it lands matters more than what it's made of. Meat forgives — drains, heals, complains the whole way and mends anyway. Our man is mostly meat. That's his luck. Bone is worse. Bone holds the dirt for years, drains on its own schedule, and I've men on my books three winters deep from one chip. A joint is a sealed room — once it fills, the joint's finished, and the man learns to walk without it. The belly is the one I dread, and I'll say why plainly. Steel through the gut and the man walks in talking — that's the trick of it. Filth loose in a clean room doesn't hurt at first. Then the room poisons him over three days, and there's nothing a tent does about a fouled belly. I can tie a leg. I can't tie a man's middle. Those men get the other version of me, the one that says *we'll see*. I usually know by the smell within the hour. He gets to not know a day longer. That's the whole medicine I have for it."

"The quick ones — trunk vessel, heart, the right part of the head — I nearly count as kind, and I mean that as arithmetic, not sentiment. I watched a man bleed out from the femoral in under two minutes. He was mid-sentence when it let go. He never found out the worst of it. The slow ones find out the worst of it every hour of every day it takes them."

"And most men don't get one piece. A shell throws its steel in a fan, and a man caught in the fan wears the map. I counted thirty in one man's back once and pulled two — the one on a vessel, the one in a joint. The rest stay and do nothing. That's the truth nobody says out loud: most shrapnel just sits there. He'll ache when it rains, call it rheumatism, and the rain will be right."

She stood, because the last part wanted her on her feet, and pointed at the sleeping man's leg with the forceps — steel, not fingers.

"But the mud's worst trick is the thing I'm actually watching for in him, and you asked for it straight, so. It isn't pus. Pus is sweet, thick — a room where something sat too long. This is different. The leg goes mottled, brown and yellow at the edges, and when you put your hand on it, it crackles. Gas in the flesh, bubbles under the skin, like half-thawed snow under a boot. It moves in hours. A leg that was only angry at midnight is dead by morning, and the man's whole blood goes sour behind it — fastest of the slow deaths. Your stomach will know the smell before your nose has named it. So we amend the list. I told you four things fetch me. Make it five. If his leg crackles under your hand, you don't press around finding out how much of it does. You fetch me at a run and you put the kettle on, because if it's that, I take the leg off on this table before the morning's old."

She looked at the wound — the loose gauze, the wick's tail laid over the lip of the cut — and set the cup back down by his slack hand.

"So there's your answer. Everything I did to him tonight after the cup rang — the water, the wick, leaving it open, the three days — none of it was about steel. The steel took me half an hour and it's sitting in a tin cup. The mud gets the next ten days, and the mud is what kills most of the men this war kills. Not the shell. Not the steel. The ground it crossed getting into him."

She sat back down on the crate, slower this time.

"You asked to know instead of imagine. Now you know what you're holding the door against. It was never the steel, Wick. It was always the mud."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my eyes tracking from the wound back to her face. "Christ." I pick up a piece of hardtack, turn it over in my hand. "So we're not just soldiers. We're...groundkeepers for the mud?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Groundkeepers," Sedge said, taking the word the way she'd taken his name — flat, once, for weight. "No. Groundkeepers work *for* the ground. Nobody in this tent works for the mud. Turn the picture the right way round and it gets simpler, and at this hour simpler's the only thing on offer."

She nodded at the hardtack. "And you're turning that over like it's going to explain itself. It won't. It's payment. Eat it."

She let him get a bite into it before she went on, because the body kept books and a man chewing was a man listening.

"A man's a warm room. Blood at body heat, lights on, everything in him the mud wants to eat, and the mud is always hungry. A wound is a door left open in that room. Everything I did tonight was doors. I cut his wider, on purpose — a door open on my terms drains, and a door open on the mud's terms floods. Three days, if the room's clean, I shut it. Skin last. And you — you put your hand flat on a door and held it shut for ten minutes with nothing under you but your arm and your stubbornness. So no. Not groundkeeping. Doorkeeping. That's the trade, and you're in it now whether you meant to be or not."

She stood, slower than she'd sat down.

"You want the whole war in one line, since you're asking philosophy on no sleep: two lines of men dug themselves into the ground, and now they spend every daylight hour throwing the ground at each other. I'm the return service. Four years, that's my entire commission. After tonight it's some of yours."

"Now the last of it, because I'm about done talking. The crash is due — I told you ten minutes, and it's been ten. Sit before it finds you, and put your hands around something that isn't a door. Canteen's in the crate. When he wakes he'll want water like it's owed him — blood loss does that. A mouthful at a time and he keeps it down. Pour it and he wears it. Lamp's got two hours. Candle's in the crate, and don't sit in the dark. The dark is where imagination does its work, and you know what I think of imagination in a tent."

"I'm on the cot behind the screen, boots on. I'll be up twice before morning to take his ankle and smell that wound whether you hear me or not. You fetch me for the five things and nothing else. Not his shaking, not his fever, not his complaining, and not yours. And the steel gets boiled at dawn — first job, before tea, before anything. Dirty steel is just mud with a handle on it, and I've had my fill of mud tonight."

She looked at him properly for the third time that night, and this one stayed a while.

"His bleeding stopped an hour ago. By my own rule, I'm allowed his name now. I'm not taking it off the tag — tags are how you learn a man's name after it's stopped mattering whose it was. He can tell me himself in the morning. That's tomorrow's first job, and it's a good one. Days that start with a name in them tend to end the right way round."

She went behind the screen. The cot complained; she didn't. Her voice came back out of the dark, already fraying at the edges with tired.

"Goodnight, holder. And Wick — if it crackles, you don't knock. You run."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge came around the screen at a run, apron half on, and the first thing she did at the foot of the table was stand still and listen — which looked like nothing and was the whole triage.

"Breath," she said. "Hear it under the noise? A scream with breath in it is a man fighting. The scream I run for has no breath under it — that one belongs to a man already leaving. He's not leaving. Ease him — not off, *ease*. He's not fighting you, he's fighting the leg, and a man who's crushed fights twice as hard as a man who's held."

Her eyes went down her own list while he arched and the table skidded its crooked legs deeper into the mud.

"Dressing's pink where the wick sits — that's the wick working, and I'll show you the difference before I'm done. Face is flushed, not grey; grey means the trunk, and the trunk's asleep where I left it. No smell." She leaned her face down over the wound and breathed in slow and deep, which no one ever did, which was why she was the one paid to. "Nothing sweet. Nothing sour. Good." Her palm went flat on the thigh above the cut, light, listening through her hand. "Hot. Hard as it was, no harder. No crackle — that I'd feel like frost heave under a boot. This is the honest hot."

"So it's the pain, and part of it's mine. I dosed a man on half a reflex — half that morphine went down his throat and the rest went down his beard. He slept till the first half wore thin, then woke up *inside* the leg. I told you hours ago he'd hurt worse tonight than he ever did on my table. Being right about it is worth nothing to me."

His eyes were open but wrong — rolled toward the ridge, looking at something the tent didn't contain.

"He's surfaced in the wrong room. Men come up out of morphine wherever the pain keeps them, and some of those rooms have shells in them. We don't argue with the room. We give him a better one. Son. Son. Here. Name and number, like the ledger wants."

He fought it, and then the training won where the will couldn't. "Cole." A rasp. "Private. Cole." A number in pieces, which she caught and said back to him whole, because a thing said back whole is a thing a man can stand on.

"Cole. You're in a tent. The shell's finished — I've the steel to prove it." She took the tin cup off the blanket and folded his fingers over the little bright ring. "There. Something in your fist heavier than what's in your leg. Hold that."

The medicine tin. "Now the dosing, and you asked for all of it, so here's the arithmetic. He gets *half* of one dose. Not whole. A man who's bled off a third of his blood gets drunk on half the spoon — dose him full and I put his breathing to sleep, and then I've spent the night saving a leg for a corpse. Half." She broke the tablet along its score, dropped it in a mouthful of canteen water, swirled, got an arm under his shoulders — the same lift as before, gentler. "Drink. All of it down the throat this time. None on the beard."

While it landed, she lifted the gauze — "I lift, you don't; my hands are clean and yours are full of man" — and went still. A thread of red ran down the wick's tail.

"For one breath I didn't like that. Now I've read it. Old blood — dark, keeping no time with anything, riding out on the wick because that's the wick's whole job. New blood is bright and it keeps time with his pulse — every beat, a beat. This keeps no time. Say the difference to yourself until it's boring. Boring is what saved looks like." Under the gauze the knot sat dark and dry, the artery jumped its small patient jump, the floor was clean. She tempered water through her wrist, wet the strip down, laid the gauze back. "Nothing's moved. He screamed the tent crooked and didn't scream anything loose. That's not luck. That's your arms."

She sat on the crate, because standing had become a negotiation.

"You asked how much longer. Four answers, and you'll have all of them, because you asked while holding a man down, which is the right way to ask. One — this round: ten minutes, five once the half lands, and it's landing now. Watch him go from screaming to shaking and don't mourn the change; shaking is the honest work. Two — the night: he'll surface twice more, once before the candle's half gone, once near dawn. Same three things every time — water a mouthful at a time, his name, and a voice. The dose doesn't repeat. From here to daylight the whole pharmacy is water, warmth, and talk. Three — the wound: day three, if it's clean, he gets skin. Four — the mud: ten days to its verdict, and the mud's verdict is the only one that counts. Past all four: a month of limping, a lifetime of lying about it. That's the ledger. Most men ask me to leave the worst out. You asked for the lot. You'll do for this work."

Sweat stood on him now. "Fever's arriving on schedule. Let it. Loud and hot is a man fighting — I said that once tonight and it's still true. He's loud, he's hot, he's Cole, and he's fighting. One in the morning, in this war, that's a good picture. And when he surfaces he may call for his mother, or a brother, or a dog. Answer to whatever he calls you. The room he wakes in is gentler than this one, and there's no harm being borrowed for it."

Pencil stub, the tape at his ankle: *M ½*. And above the rest of it, *COLE*. "The tape keeps the arithmetic. Now it keeps the name. He was meant to tell me in the morning — he told me at one o'clock instead, in the middle of his own noise. I'll take that trade. Days that start with a name end the right way round, and this one started early."

She stood. Her hands had an hour of stupid left in them before they turned dangerous; she meant to spend it lying down. "The five things still fetch me — blood, red streaks, smell, crackle, or quiet. Quiet's the liar of the five, and he's the loudest man in this army right now, so you've got margin. I'll be up before dawn for the ankle and the smell whether you hear me or not. And Wick — your voice is the last item in the pharmacy. Use it. He doesn't need words. He needs a voice in the room that isn't pain, and yours will do."

She went behind the screen. The cot complained; this time she did too. Her voice came back out of the dark, frayed and low.

"Goodnight, Cole. Goodnight, holder. One of you will be asleep in five minutes. The other one should eat the rest of the hardtack."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I wipe the sweat off my face with my sleeve, then turn the piece of hardtack over again before finally taking a bite. It tastes like dirt and salt. I watch Cole’s face as the morphine pulls him back under. “You hear that, Cole? Your leg’s still yours.” My voice sounds rough, but I keep talking. “That’s something.”

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Her voice came back through the screen one last time, worn down to the threads.

"He didn't hear a word of that." A pause, long enough for sleep to have a go at her between sentences. "Doesn't matter. The ear keeps its door open after the man's left the room. Same words, over again — they don't need to be new, they need to be *there*. A rope doesn't get clever the longer you hold it. It just needs to stay a rope."

"That's the last of me. One of us gets to be stupid tonight. I've claimed it."

Then nothing, and the tent's small sounds had the dark to themselves — Cole's breathing, long and ragged and even, the brazier ticking, the basin under the low corner giving up its last drip into the mud.

She went under the way the bone-tired do, no choosing in it, just a slope. What woke her, two hours gone by the pulse in her wrist, was nothing at all — no sound, no hand on her shoulder. Her own clock, keeping the promise her mouth had made: up twice before morning, heard or not.

She came around the screen without noise. The lamp had spent itself down to a coal, so she struck a match on the crate and gave the candle the job, and stood a moment while the tent assembled out of the dark — the table still crooked in the mud where Cole had skidded it, the hardtack mostly gone to crumbs, one ledger settled, and Wick in the chair, on watch, with the whole night's work on him. Cole under the blanket, flushed and damp, one fist still closed around its small bright argument.

"Don't get up," she said, low. "And don't report. Reports get tidied. I'd rather read him myself."

Her hands had come back from stupid somewhere in the two hours; they were hers again, and she spent them the way she always spent them — out loud, because saying it was part of doing it.

Ankle first. Two fingers behind the inner bone, counting against her own pulse. "Still his. Faint, slow, and his." Then she bent over the wound and breathed in slow and deep, the way nobody ever did, which was the whole reason it was her job and not anyone's. Nothing sweet. Nothing sour. Nothing that introduced itself to the back of her throat. "No smell. Best smell in the army."

Palm flat above the cut, light, listening through her hand. Hot, hard, the honest hot. No frost-heave under the skin. "Still just angry. Angry's allowed." She lifted the gauze's edge and read the wick's tail — soaked, but thin and pink, keeping no time with anything. "Serum, riding out on the strip. That's the drain earning its pay. Old blood would be dark. New blood would keep time with his pulse — every beat, a beat. This does neither." She laid it back. "Boring. I told you what boring looks like. It still looks like that."

Back of her hand to his sternum, and a count. "Fever's landed. Properly, now. On schedule — I'd have trusted him less if it hadn't come. He's quiet-hot, but that's the half dose sitting on him, not the liar-quiet. The heat's the fight, working under the blanket. Let it work."

Pencil stub out. Pencil stub back in the pocket. "Nothing to write. Best entry a tape ever gets."

She nodded at the brazier. "Feed that before it dies all the way. Dawn wants the kettle hot — the steel boils first, before tea, before anything, and I'll hold me to it. I'll be up once more before light for this same round. Between now and then the pharmacy's water, warmth, and talk, and you're the whole apothecary."

It was while she was still on her feet that his breathing changed — the long evenness breaking into something shallow and quick at the top. His head turned on the blanket. The spent tremor came back into his hands, and his eyes moved under the lids like a man walking behind a curtain, and then they were open, fixed on the ridge, in the wrong room.

"Surfacing," she said. "Early. Men keep their appointments coming out of morphine better than they ever kept them going in."

She didn't go to him. She went the other way — back to the crate at the head of the table, sat, hands flat on her knees, as far out of the work as a woman could be and still be in the tent.

"Three things, and they're yours. Water — canteen, a mouthful at a time; he'll want it like it's owed him, and it is, but pour it and he wears it. Then his name — Cole; he answered to it once tonight, it'll hold. Then whatever name he hands you, and he's about to hand you one that isn't yours. Take it anyway. In the room he's in, it's yours, and there's no harm being borrowed for it. I told you that once already. It's about to be useful."

His free hand came off the blanket and opened. Palm up. The oldest asking there is.

"Tommy," Cole said, to the ridge. Then, with asking in it: "Tommy."

Sedge stayed on the crate, hands on her knees.

"Well," she said, quietly. "Go on, holder. Be Tommy."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
It ended the way she'd said it would. The half dose took Cole down between one breath and the next, mid-asking, his hand folding back under the blanket with the ring still shut in the fist. She took the ankle on her way past — two fingers behind the inner bone, a count against her own pulse — still his. She left him to his sleep.

Then she came and stood over the floor, because that was where the next patient was.

"There it is," she said. "The crash. Two hours late — you held it off all the way through the Tommy business, and the body can be made to wait, but it doesn't forget. Don't get up. Men get up right about now, and then I've two patients and one table, and the paperwork alone would finish me."

She crouched and took the wrist, counting. Fast, then slowing as she held it — the books settling. Grey around the mouth and coming back. The shakes had arrived on schedule; forecasts never softened anything. She fetched the canteen and held it to his mouth herself, because a man in the crash can no more pour than a man on morphine can, and counted his swallows the way she counted everything. Then she went behind the screen and came back with her own blanket and dropped it over his shoulders. The cot could keep the greatcoat.

"You're not the patient. Your body doesn't know that. It kept books tonight same as his, and it's collecting in the coin it uses — sweat, shakes, and the floor. The floor's part of the treatment. Nobody tells holders that. Ten minutes of it, and after ten the floor stops being medicine and starts being an address."

Then she did the thing she almost never did. She sat down in the mud beside him, her knees taking the receipt for all forty-four years on the way.

"Four years telling the mud where it's allowed to go, and look at me. Sitting in it. There's a sermon in that if either of us had the strength, and neither of us does." She fed the brazier from the woodpile and set the kettle on it, because dawn's first job had been promised and she meant to keep it half-awake if she had to. "Say the rest. All right. You've bought the back pages tonight — you held a leg on with your hand and you were somebody's brother for half an hour, and you paid for the back pages without ever being told there was a price, which is the only honest way anybody pays anything in this war. So. All of it, top to bottom, the way I showed you the wound."

"First — what just happened to you, since you'll be imagining it otherwise, and imagination lies worst of all about the inside of your own head. You went into the room with him. The gentle one. The mother, the dog, whoever it held. That part's not on any list I gave you, because there's no fetch-me for it and no forceps for it either. He handed you a name and you put it on, and it fit, and that's the danger — borrowed names always fit, that's why they get handed out. Then he went down and you walked out of that room alone, and nobody walks out of a room like that carrying nothing. You're carrying a name that isn't yours and half an hour that was. The floor is where you set it down for a minute. That's all it's for. And you don't give the name back — he doesn't know he lent it. You keep it. It goes in the pocket with the rest of the weight, and the pockets get heavy, and that's why people in this trade sit down sometimes. It isn't only holders. I'm getting to me."

"Second — the names. I told you I don't learn them until the bleeding's stopped, and I said cheaper that way, and you didn't ask why, and I noticed you not asking. So. First winter, I learned them early. Both hands, eager, the way you're learning them. There was a man with a leg like Cole's. I knew his name before I knew whether he'd keep it, and his village, and his mother's, and his dog's. The leg lived. He didn't — fever turned on day six, and by day eight I was reading his tag, and I already knew everything written on it and a fair amount that wasn't. Eleven more tags that month. That's where the rule comes from. The tag-ones rest. The named ones come back — between rounds, at the foot of the cot, not accusing, just known. There's no fetch-me for that either. So: names after the bleeding. It isn't coldness, it's bookkeeping. Inside a year you'll do it the same way, and you'll feel like a bastard the first time you catch yourself at it, and you'll keep doing it, because it's the difference between four years in this tent and one."

"Third — why it's just me in here, since you've noticed and not asked that either. This tent has had seven of me in it, counting me. The mud took two — fevers, the same sweet smell I put my face down over Cole's leg for. A shell took one between tents; quick, the kind I told you I nearly count as kind. Two went home whole in every way you could point at and no way you could see — too many doors held, the fare adding up, no floor big enough. One's still at it down the line; we write when there's paper. And me. I don't know why me. Four years and I don't know, and the honest answer is the one I give the belly men: we'll see."

"So when the shelling hands me a man with good hands who'd rather know than imagine — I keep him. That's what tonight was, and I'll say it flat, because you'd rather know. Cole's leg, yes. And this: I'm making the next of me out of you, one night at a time, slow, the way the mud works. Because a table is coming someday with nobody standing at the head of it, and somebody in that room has to know you don't pull. You tip."

"Last of the rest is me, top to bottom. Four years does this: I sleep two hours at a stretch and wake on my own pulse — no clock in this tent keeps time, so I've become one. My hands go stupid every night and come back every morning; they've worn the trip smooth. I can smell pus through canvas. When a man goes quiet — the quiet with no breath under it — I feel it asleep, like a step missing from a stair, and I'm up before I've finished deciding to be. And twice this month I've held a hand instead of pressing on a wound, because there was nothing under my hands worth pressing on. I know both those names. The rule doesn't cover them. The rule can't. Those you learn by heart, because there's nothing else to put in the space where they were. That's the tax on the kind work. Nobody warns you about the tax. Consider yourself warned."

"Now look at the shape you're in. On the floor. Under a blanket. Water by mouthfuls. A voice in the room, and dawn coming. That's the pharmacy — I told you: water, warmth, and talk till daylight, and I told you you were the apothecary. The rest is that the apothecary takes his own medicine. Same shelves. No exceptions. That's why I'm down here in the mud instead of being kind to you from a standing position. It's not kindness. It's rounds."

The candle was down to a thumb of itself. The kettle had started its low argument with the brazier. Cole breathed his long ragged even breath under the blanket, one fist full of steel, one ledger written as far as dawn.

"In an hour the sky comes up the grey it always does. Steel boils first, before tea, then his ankle, then my face over that wound, and if there's nothing to write, we write nothing — and nothing is the best word that tape will ever hold. Day two of ten. His ledger's written as far as dawn." She looked at the floor. "So's yours, as it happens. You're on my books now, Wick. I told you I learn names after the bleeding stops. Yours stopped tonight. Just not anywhere I could put a pad on it."

She stayed for the ten minutes. Sat in the cold mud with her back against the crooked table leg and let the candle spend itself, because the books said somebody should sit with him while the floor did its work, and tonight the somebody was her.

"Days that start with a name end the right way round — I said that, and it's held all night. This one started with two names in it and the sun isn't even up. That's as good a start as this war has ever handed anybody. I'll take it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I rest my head back against the table leg, the blanket scratchy on my shoulders. "So I'm on your books." My voice is hoarse. "What's the going rate for sitting in mud?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Nothing," Sedge said. "Mud's the only thing in this war that doesn't charge. You've got the picture wrong way round again — third time tonight, so I'm narrowing it down from the tired to the temperament. Nobody pays a man for sitting in the mud. Sitting in the mud is what the man pays *with*."

She counted the wage out anyway, because a wage deserved itemizing like everything else.

"Look at what the installment bought. A man keeps his leg. A man had a brother for half an hour, and the brother was good enough that nobody caught the substitution. And you know now — know, not imagine — what you're holding the door against. Three items. I've watched men pay more mud than that for less, and I've watched men pay everything and carry nothing home. You paid one floor's worth of sitting and a borrowed name, and the ledger balances. That's the going rate. It isn't posted anywhere, and it never comes down. Nobody believes that last part until the second year."

The candle's thumb of itself spent out while she talked, and she let it go — the canvas overhead was already doing better work, going from black to the flat grey that passed for morning within a mile of the guns. The shakes ran their ten minutes and thinned. The breathing beside her lengthened out. Grey came back where it had gone from the mouth. She stayed put until the floor stopped being medicine, then got up, knees filing their complaint on the way, and let the complaint stand.

"And what I pay out — hardtack, a blanket, tea when there's tea, and the back pages, which you got tonight unbudgeted. That's the whole wage in this tent. The army pays less and lies about it, which is why I never struggle to keep help. Only to keep it." She looked down at the mud she was leaving on the seat of her apron. "For the record, I sat in it too, and I'm not on the books — I'm the books. What I got paid tonight is a man with good hands who'd rather know than imagine, going cheap because nobody else bid. Four years, that's the only wage I've ever turned a profit on."

The kettle had finished its argument with the brazier and won. She took it off with the rag, and the first job of the day went the way she'd promised it would — steel before tea, before anything, and the first person she kept promises to in the morning was herself.

"Boiling doesn't clean," she said, dropping the instruments in one at a time, named as they went, because a count nobody heard wasn't a count. "Probe. Forceps. Scalpel. Needle. Shears. It evicts. The mud's tenants hold their lease at any temperature a man can stand — a hundred degrees and they're out on the street, and the street is the steam, and good riddance to them." Five minutes at a rolling boil, the water making its small angry sounds, the steam climbing into the cold. Then out with the forceps and onto the clean cloth, laid in a row — the same row as last night. The row would fill again. It always filled again.

She emptied the basin out the back of the tent while the steel worked, wrong-colored water going back into the mud it had come from, and didn't say anything about it, because there was nothing to say that the mud didn't already know.

Then the round, in the order she'd posted. Ankle first — two fingers behind the inner bone, counting against her own pulse. "Still his. Fainter than I'd like, steadier than I feared, and both of those are day-two words." Face down over the wound, the slow deep breath nobody ever took. Nothing sweet, nothing sour, nothing introducing itself to the back of her throat. Palm flat above the cut: hot, hard, the honest hot, no frost-heave under the skin. Pencil stub, the tape at his ankle: *Day 2.* Nothing after it.

"Day two with nothing to report. In this tent that's a love letter."

It was the grey coming all the way up that surfaced him, near enough to dawn to keep his appointment. But he came up in the right room this time — you could tell, because the first thing he did was wince, and the second thing he did was find the tent roof and look betrayed by it.

"Water," Cole said, and she gave it the way she'd told Wick to give it — a mouthful at a time, because pour it and he wears it. Between the second mouthful and the third, his fist remembered what it was holding. He opened it and stared at the small bright ring like a man finding someone else's key in his pocket.

"What's this, then?"

"Yours. You argued with it for the best part of an hour and won. It sat on the main artery of that leg like a slate on a roof, and every heartbeat knocked it a hair. Keep it — when your leg aches in the rain and you tell them it's rheumatism, it'll be the truth. That'll be the piece reminding you it's still your leg to ache."

"Did I shout?"

"The table's still crooked. You skidded it half a foot through the mud. That's yours too."

Cole considered this with the gravity of a man running on half a morphine tablet and two-thirds of his blood. "Sergeant'll want my hide for lying on a table."

"Sergeant can join the queue. The mud's ahead of him, the fever's behind him, and I'm at the front of it. Drink."

He drank, and went back down the way the wrung-out do — no choosing in it. She left the ring in his open hand where he could find it again.

Then tea, which wasn't tea — burnt barley with ambitions — two mugs of it, one set down on the floor within reach of the blanket, because the apothecary took his own medicine and she'd written herself into that rule the day she wrote it.

Outside, the war clocked back in. First the far guns, working their way along the line like men shaking out a hose. Then the nearer ones. Then boots somewhere down the communication trench, the day shift taking over from the dark. It had stayed out of the tent all night — not mercy. It simply hadn't been invited, and nobody here had been fool enough to post it an invitation.

"Now the shape of your day," she said, standing over the floor with her mug. "You sleep till noon — behind the screen, on the cot; I'll take the crate, I've learned to sleep sitting, which is a trick that can't be taught, only worn into you, and you haven't got the wear. Noon, you eat. Then you find me, and by then there'll be a lamp wanting holding, because there always is, and this war has run out of everyone except us."

She crouched again — knees, complaint, standing ruling — for the last thing, because it wanted to be done at floor level.

"First lesson, before you sleep. Small one — that's why it's first." She dipped the inside of her own wrist into the tempered basin water and held it there, counting. "Inside of the wrist, never the back. The back is weathered and flatters. The inside keeps honest time. Three seconds and you know blood-warm before your eyes do. Every wash, every dose, every dressing starts there. Practice on the tea — too hot now, right in about ten minutes. A medic who can't find blood-warm by wrist is a man starting fires in flesh, and I've met him, and I've treated what he did, and I'd rather never meet him in you."

She stood. The row of steel lay clean on its cloth, steam gone off it, waiting the way steel waits — no opinion in it either way. Cole breathed his long ragged even breath, fist open around the ring, tape reading *Day 2* and nothing else.

"Lesson two's the pulse — you count a man's against your own, because no clock in this tent keeps time and I've become the clock, a promotion I never asked for. That's tomorrow's. One lesson a day. Any faster and you start knowing things your hands haven't earned, and a man who knows faster than his hands is a man who pulls when he means to tip."

She drank off the last of the not-tea and made the face it always earned.

"So there's your rate, holder, since you asked it in the mud and earned the answer standing up. The man you sat with keeps his leg. You get up in the grey and boil steel. The war owes you nothing — it never will, it's the one honest debtor in that direction — and you're rich anyway. Best exchange on offer in four years, and I'd know; I've been shopping the whole time." She set the mug down on the crate. "Take the trade before the mud reconsiders. It reconsiders hourly."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take a slow sip of the tea — still too hot. "Alright," I say, my voice rough. "Where's the cot?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Behind the screen," Sedge said. "Ten feet from where you've been all night. Everything in this tent is ten feet from everything else — on a night like this one, that's the only distance there is."

She went around first and did the handover the way she did everything, out loud, because a cot handed over in silence was a cot somebody woke up in wrong.

"Greatcoat's on it. Mine — smells of lamp oil and the not-tea, nothing you can catch. Keep the blanket over the top of it; the cot's own blankets went to better causes, and by better causes I mean him." She pulled the coat straight along the pallet. "It'll complain when you get on. You've heard it twice tonight, so you know it's nothing personal — it does it to everyone. Only thing in here that treats us all alike."

She nodded at his boots. "Off. Mine stay on — I'm the one who runs today, if anything runs. Yours have got nowhere to be till noon."

Then the shift change, and she said it standing still, so it would land as procedure and not kindness.

"The five things are mine till noon. Blood, streaks, smell, crackle, quiet — mine. I wake on my own pulse, and it hasn't been late once in four years. Cole's mine — water, name, voice, and I've been the voice in this tent so long the canvas answers to it. If he surfaces and asks for Tommy, I'm Tommy. Borrowed names get handed round. You know that better than anyone I've ever taught it to."

She pinched out the candle stub with her thumb and forefinger. The canvas overhead had the job now — doing it in grey, but doing it. The lamp had died sometime during the Tommy business and nobody had mourned it.

"You'll come up once, midmorning, feeling like the table skidded you instead of him. Arm dead, mouth like the inside of a boot. That's the books settling the last of the night — let them. Water's on the crate, a mouthful at a time, same rules as him. Then back down. Nobody needs you till noon, and I mean that as the cleanest arithmetic this war ever handed anybody."

She took her mug of cold not-tea back to the crate and sat, boots flat in the mud, hands around the tin for whatever warmth was left in it.

"Sleep, Wick. You're paid up."

From behind the screen, the cot complained a third time. She counted that as the shift properly changed, and settled in to hold it — the day's watch, hers now, the way the night's had been his. Outside, the guns worked their slow way along the line. Cole breathed his long ragged even breath under the blanket, fist around its small bright argument, the tape at his ankle reading *Day 2* and nothing after it.

She went down the way Cole had — no choosing in it, just a slope — except sitting up, boots on, which was the only way she'd ever learned to arrive anywhere.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I listen to the cot groan under me, the greatcoat scratching my neck. "Sarge said I was a waste of a set of hands," I mutter to the dark. "Maybe he was right."
