dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Ready's a thing that happens to other people," Sedge said. "Hold anyway."

She turned the bad lamp a quarter-circle, squinted at what the light did, and turned it back, then stepped so her own shadow fell across the near shoulder. Using herself as a lampshade. Four years of that.

"Eyes on his chest, not the wall," she said. "The wall can't stop breathing. If his breathing goes wrong, you tell me before you feel it in the arms."

She ran her thumb along the right shoulder — the worse one, she'd already decided — and found the head of the bone sitting up proud under the skin where it had no business being, with a hollow below it like a bite out of a loaf.

"Out the front. Good news, that. Forward usually means the socket's still a socket."

She took hold of the forearm, wrist and elbow both, and set her boot against the man's ribs under the armpit. Flat of the sole, never the edge — the edge breaks ribs on a man too tired to complain about it.

"Pulling now. No jerking. Jerking is how a shoulder turns into a snapped arm. I lean, I turn the arm out slow, like turning a key. The bone remembers where it lives. It just needs someone to walk it home." She leaned. "He'll buck on three or four breaths. Don't count for him. Counting gives him something to fight."

The man bucked. She kept her weight exactly where it was and kept talking, low, the same sentence more or less, the way you'd talk a mule past fire. Then the joint went home with a thud she knew Wick would feel down both arms before he heard it.

"That's it seated. That grinding is the sound of a thing going back where it belongs, and no, I don't enjoy it. I want that said plain, so you're not wondering later. Anyone who enjoys that sound doesn't get to hold the tools."

She was already moving to the left arm.

"Second one. He's got less scream left, so he'll do this one quiet, which is worse for you and no worse for him." She set her boot, took her grip, leaned out over him slow. "Don't let quiet get into your hands. Quiet is just the last shoulder wearing out."

It took longer. The man wept instead of shouting, and then the left shoulder went in with a sound like a boot in wet clay, and the whole tent seemed to sag half an inch.

"Sling him when I tell you," she said, wiping her hands. "Both arms crossed over. He'll need feeding for a month and swearing at for two. Then you can go back to looking at the wall all you like."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my hands still pressing down on the man's shoulders. My palms are sweating. "Right," I say, my voice tight. "Feeding and swearing."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Off slow," Sedge said. "Hands don't leave a man straight up. They trail off, like taking your half of a blanket without waking him."

But first she went to the wrists, two fingers on each, and counted against the pulse in her own throat.

"Both full. Even with each other. If the joint's seated and the wrist is full, the pipe isn't kinked." She took the man's hand and pressed each thumbnail in turn, watching the color. "White, pink. White, pink. Blood's going out and coming back. His fingers will tingle tonight like he slept on them. That's honest. Numb and staying numb is when you come get me."

Then she stepped back. "Now off. Ease your weight out of it like setting down something you don't want to wake."

The man turned his head and said something into the canvas that wasn't words, and wept a little more, quieter, the way rain lets up.

Sedge poured water into a tin — not the bottle, the bottle spills — and held it where he could reach without lifting anything. "Sips. He'll want to gulp and gulping comes back up, and what comes back up on a man with two fresh shoulders is a whole new problem." Then, to the man himself, flat and almost kind: "Drink. You'll live to be sore."

While he drank she pulled a folded cloth from the shelf. She kept them folded. That was the whole trick — folding things when there was still light and nobody bleeding.

"Arms crossed over the chest, hands toward the opposite elbows. Wipe your palms on your trousers first. Sweat slips, and a slipped sling is a shoulder looking for an excuse." She passed him the cloth. "Wrap once around the arms and the chest together, snug, and put the knot in front, over the breastbone. That's the one bone in the neighborhood that can take a knot. Knot on the spine is how a sore back becomes a bedsore."

She watched his hands do it, correcting nothing yet.

"You held when he bucked," she said, after a moment, the way she might note a pulse reading. "Most don't, the first time. It's rarer than it should be, so I say it when I see it. Once. It won't be said again."

She began laying the tools in the boil pan, not looking over.

"When he can talk, find out what did it. Shoulders come out in pairs for reasons. A fall with a strap across the chest. Hauling rope. Or men." The pan lid rang as she set it. "I like to know which, because the ones done by men tend to come back through this tent in pairs too."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Right question," Sedge said, not looking up from the boil pan. "Most of them ask 'will he be all right,' which is a question with no answer in it. Yours has an answer, so you get one."

She set the lid on the pan and turned the lamp wick down a half-turn, now that she could afford to admit the light was bad.

"It's the kind one. He keeps both arms. Shoulders out the front, both back in, both wrists full, nails pink. On my ledger that's the best thing I'll fix this week, and I'm not saying it to warm up your palms. I'm saying it because it's the count."

She wiped the table in one long stroke, elbow to elbow, and slung the rag over the bucket rim.

"Losing a leg is a different ledger. When it's the leg, I do the shortening myself or mark him for the tent at the end of the row, whichever way the bone votes. Tonight nothing voted. Tonight the treatment and the mercy were the same act. That's rarer than a shoulder going back in, so don't get used to it."

She came back to the table and bent over the man, not touching yet. "Now the part of the bill nobody reads. A shoulder is a ball sitting in a saucer, held there with rope. First time out is the hard one — that's the one we just did. Every time after is easier, and easier is not a favor. He'll feel weather in that joint. He won't throw overhand again worth a damn. He'll feed himself in a month and haul in six if he does the exercises, and he won't, because nobody does, which is why I write them on his arm in charcoal instead of on paper. Paper gets left in tents. Arms walk around."

She put two fingers outside the sling, over the joint, then on his fingertips. Warm. She counted his breathing against the pulse in her own throat — sixteen, even, the number she liked.

"And he's coming up to the surface with about a minute of words in him before sleep takes the rest. Sleep is medicine. I'll allow it. But I want the answer first, because the answer decides whether I burn boot leather to the captain's tent tonight or sleep instead." She straightened and stepped back out of the man's eyeline, putting Wick in front of him.

"So you ask, not me. I ask, and men answer like I'm their mother. You ask, and he might answer like it's a story he gets to tell. Rope, beam, fall, a wagon, men. Listen for which word he takes the longest to get past. That's the true one."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean closer, my voice dropping. "Hey. Can you tell us what happened? Was it a rope, a fall... men?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The man's eyes came around to Wick slow, like they had to be carried there.

"Hauling," he said. "We was hauling the gun out of the mud, and the rope went, and I—"

He stopped.

Sedge, at the shelf with the charcoal, did not turn around. But her hand stopped. The pause went on long enough to hold a whole other word inside it.

"Men," he said, mostly to the canvas. "Two. They'd been round the bake ovens a few days. Had a rope over the door-beam before I'd said a word. Hung me up by the wrists to go through my coat. Took the pay. Took the boots." A small, terrible laugh, the kind that costs more than it spends. "Told them where the pay was straight off. No hero in it. There wasn't a version of tonight where I was a hero."

"If you see a big one and a lame one—" he began, and his minute ran out, and sleep took the rest of the sentence the way it takes everything, without asking.

Sedge came back to the table. She turned his wrists over, one and then the other, and tilted them into the lamplight for Wick to see.

"Rope burns, high on both, above where a cuff sits. The body testifies better than the man does. Remember that order of witnesses." She let the wrists down gentle. "And you heard the swerve. He set out with hauling because hauling is respectable. He got past rope easy, because rope was the lie. The long road was into 'men.' That's the one I told you to listen for. You heard it."

She took up the charcoal and wrote on his forearm, small and square, the letters that would walk around camp for a week: FINGERS. WRIST. SQUEEZE. HOURLY.

"For what it's worth to him, telling them where the pay was quick was the correct answer. Shoulders heal. Dead men stay broke." She capped the charcoal. "They brought rope to a bake oven they'd been loitering at, and they knew he drew pay. That's neighbors, not strangers. So the answer decides it: I'm going to the captain, and then the provost, and if either asks who reported it, it's me alone. A medic reporting is weather. Two names reporting is a feud, and he's got a month of feeding ahead without adding that."

She put the water tin where his hand would find it without hunting, and stood.

"Your watch now. If he wakes, sips, same rules. If he comes up fighting in his sleep, don't hold him — those shoulders aren't ready to be held. Talk instead. Talk him down the same way I talked the joint in." She picked the lamp wick down another half-turn. "And if his fingers go numb and stay numb, you run. Not walk. Run."

At the tent flap she stopped, half into the dark.

"He told it to you like a story. That's what I said would happen, so I get no credit for it. But it means you cost him nothing, asking." A breath. "Find him boots by morning if you can. Bare feet in this camp is an invitation, and he's had his fill of those."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge came back from the flap and turned the wick up the half-turn she'd paid out. Light was cheaper than ignorance. She'd stopped keeping track of how many times a night she proved it.

"Then look with your eyes and I'll put words under them. That's the whole method. Seen first, told second."

She took the near wrist and tilted it into the lamp, turning it slow, her thumbnail riding just above the mark.

"Half a finger wide, and it goes around — deepest at the back of the wrist where the weight sat, shallower in front where the rope only crossed. Skin off the top layer only. It'll weep clear by morning — clear is honest — scab in two days, itch in four. Bruising in the margins, purple, where the rope crushed what it didn't rub. And the twist of the strands is printed in it. A rope signs its work same as anything else."

She let the turn carry the wrist back the other way.

"Now the reading. High above the cuff means his arms were overhead when it bit. Around the whole way means his weight never came off it — a man tied standing gets a shallow front and a clean back, because then the rope's a bracelet. On a hung man it's a scale. And it's rubbed raw, not just pressed. A patient man leaves a white line. Raw means he fought. Twisted, dropped onto it, hauled his own weight up on his own arms." She set the wrist down gentle. "That's the machine for taking both shoulders out the front at once. Hauling a gun takes one shoulder, if it takes any, and usually the one that pulls. Two, clean, both sides — the shoulders said 'men' before he worked his way to the word. That's why I trust the order of witnesses. The body goes first and it doesn't know how to lie."

She turned the hand over, palm up.

"And there's his honest morning. One blister at the root of the fingers, rim dried yellow — real rope work, before the rope broke. Two different hours written on one man. Old damage dries at the edges. New damage weeps in the middle. Learn that and a body will hand you a timeline no witness will."

She straightened. "And now you know why I took the wrists and counted, and it wasn't all the shoulders' business. The rope rode exactly where I pressed. Hung by the wrists crushes the same pipes a porter's load does — the pulse flattens, and the nerve runs through the middle of the crush and takes its share. Full pulse, pipe's open. White-pink nails, the small pipes at the end are open. Tingling is the nerve complaining. Numb and staying numb is the nerve losing. Same tripwires I gave you. I just hadn't said yet what they were tripping over."

She took up the charcoal and added a line to the forearm, square letters under square letters: ITCH IS HEALING. DO NOT SCRATCH.

"He claws these open in this dirt and they rot, and then I'm doing a wrist instead of a shoulder, and a wrist has less to give. Yellow weeping, or red lines climbing the forearm — red lines are rot in transit — you run. Same word as before."

At the flap she paid the light back down.

"Seen and then told. That's the order that holds. What you've looked at stays on the table where you left it. What you only imagine follows you out of the tent and works all night where nobody can correct it. Keep asking. The sweat dries up around the fourth of these, and the asking is what makes it the fourth instead of the fortieth. Boots by morning — and no agonizing over whose feet wore them last. This far into a war every pair has a past and none of the pasts are fit for church."

She held the flap off the ground with one hand, half into the dark.

"He'll sleep till near dawn. Sips if he wakes. And you can go back to staring at your wall — his chest can be trusted to keep moving an hour without your opinion."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch the tent flap settle behind her. I look back at the sleeping man, then at the rope burns on his wrists. "Boots," I say to the quiet tent. I sit on an empty crate, my own boots suddenly feeling too new, too clean.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The flap stirred before the tent had finished settling. Sedge came back in the way she'd left — no apology, no explanation until the reason was already in her hands.

She paid the wick up the half-turn again. Third time tonight the light had been argued back and forth; it was becoming a conversation.

"Canvas is thin. I heard 'boots' from outside, and I heard how you said it." She went to the shelf. "Three things before I walk to the captain's. Then I'm gone for true."

She took a heel of bread from her coat and put it in Wick's hand without asking.

"Eat that. The shaking isn't nerves, it's fuel — you held a grown man against his own weight on an empty stomach, and the bill comes due about now. Eat it while it's still bread and not a relic."

She counted the sleeping man's pulse against her own throat, got the count she wanted, and moved the charcoal within reach of the crate.

"Thing one. Feeding, because he'll wake starving and you'll be the hands. Three rules. Cut everything small enough to go in one bite — a man biting a piece off a spoon held in the air feels like a horse being fed, and he won't tell you, he'll just stop eating. You own the tilt, he owns the swallow: bring the tin to his lips and tip, never pour. And this is the one men get wrong." She tapped the crate. "Let him do everything he can still do. If he can hold the cloth, let him hold the cloth. Doing for a man the thing he can manage himself is how you rob him without touching his pockets, and he's been robbed enough tonight to last the month. Feed him off your ration and I'll square it. I keep a slate."

"Thing two. Boots are in the dead-box, third crate behind supply, the lid that doesn't sit square. Take a size big and two pair of socks — big boots shrink to fit a man; tight boots only ever get tighter. Scrub the insides with vinegar, air them overnight. Boots keep a man's feet longer than his name. And don't stand there weighing whose feet wore them last. You were told once."

"Thing three is the one you can't prepare for, so I'll say it plain and you'll believe me at dawn instead of now. He'll wake twice. First waking is soon, for water — easy, he'll drink and go under. The second is nearer morning, and that one is shame coming up with him. The body sleeps through what was done to it. The standing doesn't. A nightmare you fight. Shame you lie still inside of."

"Don't argue him out of it. Don't say it wasn't his fault — he'll hear charity, and charity closes a man like a fist. Hand him the tin. Let him get to the word the way he got to it before. You already know how to wait for the long road, and he found it once tonight with your ears on him. Men find it twice, more often than you'd think, if it's the same ears both times."

She took the rag off the bucket rim, folded it, set it back folded. The whole trick, still working with nobody bleeding.

"Captain's tent, then the provost. If I'm back before the lamp's burned a thumb's width, all that happened out there is talk. If I'm not back by dawn, the rules don't change with the light. Sips. Pulses. Pink nails. Run if it's numb."

At the flap she stopped, half into the dark, the same as before.

"And Wick." First time she'd spent the name all night. "You asked to see it rather than imagine it. That question will keep a person standing at this work longer than any stomach for blood ever kept anybody. The stomach is nothing. The question is the whole spine of it."

A breath.

"That's the last nice thing I'll say tonight, and it isn't even nice. It's inventory."

Then the flap, and the dark, and this time the quiet held.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The flap came back a third time, and this time Sedge didn't pretend it hadn't.

"That's the canvas beaten three for nothing tonight," she said, paying the wick up its half-turn again — fourth argument with the lamp, and the lamp winning on points. "But you've asked the right question at the cheap hour, and the cheap hour is the only one worth teaching in. Ask that over a stretcher and it costs double. The captain can have four minutes. He's had worse waits from me."

She stood a moment with her hand still on the wick.

"First correction, and it's not a dodge. Straight and tidy aren't the same thing. Tidy is when I leave out the losing and the luck and hand you a story with a shape to it. You get none of that. But it goes in a body's order, because a heap of horrors is its own kind of tidying — a mess standing exactly where a map should be."

She went to the shelf, down on one knee at the bottom of it, and came up with a tin, rust at the corners. She set it on the table clear of the sling and tipped four or five pieces of iron into her palm. They made less noise than buttons.

"Teaching stock. Not trophies — a trophy is kept for pride, and these are kept because a thing in the hand beats a thing in the head. I'm not spending my whole life as the only one here who's held one."

She picked the flattest, the size of a thumbnail, and put it in Wick's palm and closed his fingers over it with hers.

"There's the famous iron. First lie to fall out of is size. Men imagine cannonballs. It's gravel and broken pot at speed, and speed is the entire crime. The big pieces are honest — they hit like a hammer and the man goes down where everyone can see the trouble. It's the little fast ones that come in at midnight and keep me up. Feel the edges. A knife you could follow with a probe. That's a torn thing that tears. And it doesn't travel clean — it shoves a wad of cloth, dirt, a button, whatever was in its road, ahead of it or drags it behind. Every shrapnel wound is a delivery. Nobody is just wounded. Somebody has posted something to them."

The sleeper murmured. She waited it out, watching his chest, and went on at the volume you'd use talking a mule past a fire.

"Second. The hole is the door, not the room. It shoves air and flesh aside going in, and the ruin runs wider than the opening by as much as a hand. You will never see most of what a shell does. The wound is a keyhole. Entry tells you the direction. Exit tells you the pace it had left. No exit means it stayed and spent itself inside, moving what would move and breaking what wouldn't. My whole trade is standing at the keyhole making an educated guess about the room."

"By neighborhood, then. A limb: hit a bone and the bone changes sides. Goes to gravel, and gravel cuts everything it meets, and gravel can't be set. A clean break I pull together same as tonight. That's the vote I mentioned — now you know what the vote is, and that when it goes against, the trade is length for life."

"A belly. Gut is full of what gut is full of, and opened inside a man it seeds a fire there's no putting out. I can wash a leg in a bucket. There is no bucket for a belly. So a gut wound is a clock. Day one he complains. Day three the pulse climbs and the belly goes board-stiff. Day four, five, seven, the clock rings. There are tents full of arithmetic like that, and now you know what the arithmetic is."

"A chest is a bellows with the fire still inside it. Punch the bellows and it either sucks where it shouldn't or fills the man with his own blood. Men have drowned on dry canvas six feet from a medic's hands. Sometimes the whole six feet is a thumb."

"And the plainest killer isn't any single hole. It's the adding. A man carries so much blood and not a drop more. Lose a pint, he swears at me — healthy. Lose three, he goes quiet and gray and starts apologizing. Apologizing. The dying are courteous, near the end. It's the ones with blood to spare who complain. Any man goes suddenly sweet-tempered on my table, I count twice and put a hand underneath him looking for wet."

She turned one of the jagged pieces over with her thumbnail, then left it in the tin.

"Day three is when the metal's real work shows, because nothing traveled clean. That's why I open wounds that look closed and cut flesh that looks like it might live. Ruined flesh left in place is a lodging house for rot, and rot kills surer than iron. Half my trade is finishing what the shell started — carrying off what it ruined and didn't trouble to take. And when it takes anyway, there's a smell. Sweet. Wrong sweet. You'll wish I hadn't said that one, and you asked."

"Now the untidiest fact of all, since untidy is the order of the evening: against shrapnel I mostly lose. Not every bed. But the shell's only honest weapon is chance — the same burst that kills the man on your left puts the man on your right in my tent for a week and home by autumn. No merit in the first, no fault in the second, no reason for either. Men will stand in front of you begging for a reason and the truth is weather. Meet that idea tonight, because the first time you watch me do everything right and lose anyway, I'd rather you'd already been introduced."

"Last. We leave most of the metal where it landed. Lead sits quiet in a man for forty years. I dig for blood and gut and gravel, not souvenirs. So the iron mostly stays in there. What we fight is everything it did on the way."

She nodded at the flat piece in Wick's hand.

"Yours. It's retired — spent its pace in the outside of a hip in spring, and the man who owned the hip walked out of this camp in June. First time you're at a table when one comes in and your hands go stupid, put your hand in your pocket. It'll be there. It will tell you it's only iron, and iron I can beat. It's the minute spent standing back worshipping it that loses men."

The tin went back on the shelf, bottom row, where it lived.

"And put all of it in its place before I'm gone: none of it is in that man. Rope did him, and men behind the rope. He itches in four days and swears in six weeks and there's no shell in his story anywhere. The war keeps both ledgers open on the same desk. Tonight's page is the good one. Read it twice before the other one opens."

She turned the wick down its half-turn, took the rag off the bucket rim, folded it, set it back folded.

"Eat the bread or I report you to myself. That's logistics, not kindness." At the flap she stopped, half into the dark. "Captain, then provost. Thumb's width on the lamp, sips if he wakes, run if it's numb. You know the whole catechism now."

The flap fell. This time the steps kept going, quick on the packed dirt, and the quiet held.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I turn the piece of iron over in my fingers, then slip it into my pocket. My stomach growls, reminding me. I tear off a piece of bread and eat it, watching the man sleep. His chest rises, falls. I listen for the steps outside, but they’re gone. Just the quiet, and the lamp burning down.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The steps came back with the lamp still a thumb's width from the mark — near enough that she'd call it beaten, and nobody awake could prove otherwise. She came in with the cold still on her coat and nothing in her hands, which was itself the report. Nothing had needed carrying back.

"Captain first," she said, at sleeping-man volume. "He gave me four minutes and spent two of them on his insides. I got the rest, which is better than last spring, so we'll call it a good season. There'll be a man walking the ovens road at night now. Whether that's a patrol or a man with a lantern depends on the week."

"Provost next. He wrote it down, and he knew the description before I'd finished giving it — big one and a lame one, working the bake line. Third coat off the ovens in a fortnight. I was news to the captain and arithmetic to the provost, and arithmetic is better, if you're wondering. Known is half-caught." She worked the cold out of her fingers. "He said he'd walk past the ovens. I asked when. He looked at me the way men look at rain. So: recorded, half-measured, worth the walk. That's the army's whole arithmetic — a crime goes in, a form comes out, and the form takes its time. It's the only machine we have, so I feed it."

"Nobody spent the man's name. A double shoulder out the front is a signature. The provost's people will know who's wearing it without me pointing." A pause, short. "And the provost knew the lame one by description and hadn't gathered him. Knew him and let him lie. That's a fact I'm putting in my pocket next to your iron. It'll come in handier than it should."

Her eyes went to the crate, to the bread heel with a piece gone out of it. "Fuel's in. Good."

She took the sleeper's wrist, two fingers, counted against her own throat. Sixteen, even. The count she liked.

The first waking kept its appointment inside the half hour. His eyes opened to slits, and Sedge was there before he'd worked out what he wanted.

"Tin." She had it herself — brought it to his lips, tilted, never poured. "Sips." He drank with his whole attention, and she took the tilt away before his throat could ask for more than it could carry. He went under again in the middle of whatever he'd meant to say.

"That's the whole art, and now you've seen it. He owns the swallow, you own the tilt, nobody wins anything." She set the tin back where his hand would find it. "He won't remember that one. Water drunk that close to sleep doesn't get filed."

Then she sat down. Second crate, first time all night, no announcement. She looked at the lamp instead of at Wick.

"One correction to my own instructions, since I'm the only one who'll catch it. I told you shame comes near morning. He's ahead of schedule. Robbery teaches a man that nothing keeps hours. So don't relax because dawn is far off, and don't relax because I'm sitting. Sitting is fuel too."

She turned the wick down a half-turn, then back up a quarter, which was not logic but was what the lamp wanted.

"When it comes, I'm going to do nothing. Notice that the nothing is on purpose. Everything I haven't said tonight is also instructions."

She heard it before she saw it. Sleep has a rhythm, and his changed gear — too quick for depth, too flat for dreaming. Then his whole body went rigid under the sling, and he fought the cot, and got nothing from his arms but the news of them, and lay back down. Turned his face to the canvas.

"My boots," he said, to nobody. "Pay was in the left one. I told them. I told them where—"

And then the whole of it arrived again, fresh as the first time. His shoulders shook inside the cloth. No sound at all. Even now he was spending something to keep the tent from knowing.

Sedge rose and moved around the foot of the table, out of the man's eyeline, and put Wick between herself and him — same geometry as before, and both of them old enough in this tent to know it.

"Don't fill the quiet," she said, at the volume for one person. "He'll apologize. Let it stand. 'Not your fault' is charity, and charity closes a fist — you were told. What he gets from you is the tin and the fact that you haven't gone anywhere. You own the tilt."

She took up the boil-pan lid and polished what was already clean, eyes down, furniture.

"Same ears," she said.

And then nothing, which was the last instruction, and the loudest.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"All of it, then," Sedge said, and her voice went to the flat fast register she saved for seconds that were being spent. "You've asked for the whole method by accident. Narration isn't for you. A medic who's talking is a medic who's breathing, and a medic who holds her breath makes her mistake in the last ten seconds. So I talk. Listen while I do."

"But first — your hands. Where are they? On the shoulders. And where did the rope sit? Wrists, and the shoulders carried the weight. So keep the hands and drop the grip. Hands that rest are company. Hands that clamp are two more men at a bake oven, and in the dark he can't tell the difference. If you've got fingers digging into tonight's whole invoice, ease them to dead weight — ride him, don't pin him. If he truly throws himself at the edge of the table, take the hips. Hips have no history with rope."

She was already at the head of the table, out of his eyeline no longer — this time she put herself in it, and paid the lamp a quarter-turn up.

"First question with any scream. The body or the sleep. A pain-scream has an address — a man guards the hurt place, goes small around it. A dream-scream fills the tent. This one fills the tent." Her eyes went down him without touching. "Sling's holding. Knots front, over the breastbone, neither slipped. Both shoulders sitting even under the cloth — no new hollow, no proud bone. One palm, flat, outside the sling." She laid it on, light as the rag. "Head of the bone's home. Seated, both sides. So it's the sleep, and the danger isn't the noise. The danger is the pulling. Fresh caps. A second time out is easier, and easier is not a favor — his shoulders could learn that lesson in one bad night, and I'd spend months unteaching it."

The man shouted again and swallowed air with it.

"And he's drinking wind with every yell. What comes back up on two fresh shoulders — you already know the size of that problem. So we bring the bellows down. You want the number. A scream like this runs about a slow hundred of my pulse if nobody feeds it. Every hand that fights it buys it another hundred. Your clamp bought it one. So we stop paying."

Then she bent into the man's finding-range and began, low, the same sentence more or less, mule and fire.

"Medic tent. Middle of the night. Lamp's on. Your arms are crossed on your chest in a sling and both shoulders went back in. The rope's done. It's in a corner somewhere, doing nothing. Medic tent. Lamp's on. Your arms are crossed."

She kept her eyes on his chest and counted his breathing against her own throat and did not stop, and did not hurry, and did not fill the sentence with anything new, because new words are a thing to fight.

At ninety-some the scream thinned to tearing air, and his eyes came open — not awake, but aimed — and found the lamp, and then her face.

"Don't let them—" he said. "I told them where—"

"They're got," Sedge said, level. "You told them where the pay was and that bought your arms and the rest of you. That's not comfort, it's the accounts, and the accounts don't care how it felt." The tin was already in her hand. "Sip. He owns the swallow. I own the tilt."

He took two, and went under — a different gear this time, slow and deep, the kind that files things.

She stood over him and did the whole catechism anyway. Wrists. Two fingers, her own throat. Sixteen, even. Thumbnails pressed, white, pink; white, pink. Fingertips warm. Shoulders even under the cloth.

"There. Now the bill, since you asked for all of it and the cheap hour's over. One: I told you not to hold him and gave you nothing to do with your hands instead. A rule with no substitute is only a wish. The substitute is what you've just heard — weight without grip, hips not shoulders, and the voice louder than the hands. Two: he'll keep some of this. Not the scream. The lamp, maybe. That's not a cost — a man who remembers the tent twice remembers his way back to it, and that's how the tent wins."

She turned the wick down, then thought better and gave it back a quarter. The lamp wanted what it wanted.

"Your number. The scream: spent. Tonight: maybe one more waking, near dawn, and it'll likely be the quiet kind — shame you lie still inside of. The arms: a month of feeding, six weeks to haul, if he does the exercises, which he won't. The sleep—" she paused, and gave it straight. "Sleep sets its own terms and won't show me its ledger. Most men are sleeping through by the time the sling comes off. Most. That's the entire honest size of my promise, and you'll notice it isn't small."

She took the rag off the bucket rim, folded it, set it back folded.

"You've held a man twice tonight — once against his weight, once against his sleep. That's two nights' fuel spent in one, and I won't have you feeding him cold rations on an empty tank. Lie down on the second crate. I'll take the watch — waking people is the easy part, and I've had four years' practice at it. Boots at first light, and the catechism holds: sips, pulses, pink nails. Run if it's numb."

She sat where the lamp could see her and the man could see the lamp, and counted his breathing against her own throat until she got the count she liked.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lie down on the crate, but I don't close my eyes. "What happens to the rope?" I ask, staring at the tent ceiling. "After."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge let the question sit while she took the sleeper's wrist again — two fingers, her own throat — and got sixteen, even, for the third time running. Only then did she answer, at the volume that kept.

"Which rope. There are three of them in that question, so you get three answers, and after tonight you do the sorting yourself."

"The hauling rope broke and broke well. That's the whole employment of hauling rope — to fail before the arms do. Somebody spliced it within the hour, because you don't waste a fathom of good rope in a war, and by now it's pulling a gun through the same mud it failed in. It doesn't know. That's the thing about rope after: nothing happens to it, because rope is the only honest worker in this army. It does what the hand at its end tells it and keeps no ledger of its own. Men could stand to be more like rope. They mostly manage the opposite."

"The second rope is over the door-beam at the ovens. I walked under it twice tonight, going and coming to the captain. Still there. Still loaded — you'll remember I said a rope signs its work. There's skin and blood seated in the lay of it, high up where his wrists rode, and it's the one witness in this business that can't be coached. I hand that to the provost with the rest, and then it's his rope, not mine. If it's still over the beam at dawn, it's evidence. If it's gone, somebody took it down in the night, and that's a confession that walks. Either way it answers. That's rarer than it should be. Most evidence just rots."

"The third rope is the one you're actually asking after, because it's the one that came home. It's seated in the backs of his shoulders now, and it'll be hanging over every door-beam in this camp for a season, whether there's rope on them or not. He'll duck coming through my flap next week. That rope doesn't get gathered by provosts. It wears out the way the burn does — you saw the rule tonight on his palm. Old damage dries at the edges. New damage weeps in the middle. I'd be lying if I claimed fear works different, and it's near tidy when I put it that way, so take it at discount. The edges dry. The middle weeps last. What hurries it is months of feeding and swearing and hauling, all of it dull. Rope comes out of a man the way it went in: slowly, and while he's busy with something else."

She turned the spare cloth on the shelf so its fold faced out. Nobody bleeding, still the whole trick.

"And since a rope is only ever the middle of the story: the men. If the provost gathers them — and a lame thief is a thief with a short market, I'd give it a week — don't go looking for justice in what follows. The army won't stamp on them for his shoulders. It'll stamp on them because a camp where drawing pay gets you hung up at the bake ovens stops being a camp where men draw pay. Hygiene, not virtue. Post and lash if the captain's feeling lawful. And if the war is hungry that week, they'll be marched to the line instead and put in front of whatever's there, which is the sentence I'd choose for them anyway, if anyone asked me, and no one will. The war keeps both ledgers open. I said it about iron. It's slower about men, but it balances."

She looked at the man a moment — breathing gone deep, the gear that files things — and gave one last piece of accounts.

"You'll have noticed I promised him, in his sleep, that the rope was in a corner somewhere doing nothing. There was no rope in this tent. He came in cut down at the ovens and carried. It's the one lie I keep in stock, and I keep it because a rope in a corner, doing nothing, is a thing a man can lie next to. The true rope never sits still long enough for that."

The lamp was down near the mark and holding.

"Eyes open is allowed. I ordered a crate, not sleep." She settled back where the lamp could see her and the man could see the lamp. "Breakfast, you practice the feeding rules on him, and I square the slate. Now the tent and I have a watch to keep, and the catechism hasn't changed since sundown: sips, pulses, pink nails. Run if it's numb."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him on the floor for a while, and didn't tell him to get up.

"Crate was the order. Floor's what the night paid out. I won't quarrel with the difference." She fetched the jug and poured the second tin — she kept two of everything, that was the other half of the trick — and put it in his reach. "Sips. The rules apply to you too. The body lends a man speed for a night and collects at first light, with interest."

She took the sleeper's wrist, two fingers against her own throat. Sixteen, even. Thumbnails pressed, white, pink; white, pink. Fingertips warm. Shoulders sitting even under the cloth, knots forward where she'd set them.

"Night's closed. Nothing else is coming — I've had four years of learning what the back half of a night keeps in stock, and past this hour it keeps nothing but gray. The near-dawn waking came and went while the lamp was at the mark. Quiet kind, like the forecast. He surfaced into the shame and lay inside it, and the tent let it be, and after a while he worked himself down the long road and got most of the way to a word. Most is what first tellings manage. So that's all three accounts: shoulders seated, wrists full, and the shame came up with him and he stayed breathing inside of it. Ledger's shut."

Then she sat down on the floor across from him, back against the table leg, which she had not done in front of anyone in some time.

"The rest, then. You've had the trade all night — the hands part, the counting part, everything a bad lamp can teach. What you're asking for is the bill for the trade. I pay it out about once a year, whether or not anyone asks. You're asking, so it gets said in front of a witness for once. Don't interrupt, and don't be sorry for me. Pity's the same closed fist, aimed the other way."

She took the rag off the bucket rim and held it in her lap, folding as she talked.

"Item one. Every rule I gave you tonight has a name written on the back of it. You thought you were learning a catechism. It's a graveyard in working order. I'll read you one grave, so you have the shape of the thing.

"Two summers back a man named Petrie lay in that cot. Not rope — a crate of shot came off a wagon wrong and rode his wrists into the ground. Same pipes crushed, same rules. I did everything I liked and everything I liked was correct: pulses full, nails pink, fingers warm. What I didn't know was that the nerve was dying under the crush, quiet, the way nerves die. No pain to report. Only a hand going to sleep and not waking up. And Petrie was the no-trouble kind — the kind that won't bother the medic at a bad hour over a thing he's ashamed he hasn't shaken off. Three days on, the hand was a glove. A week after, the arm was a cost, and the arm voted, and you know now what the vote means.

"So the sentence I've served since is *run if it's numb*, and I press the thumbnails myself, hourly, and no man's modesty gets to be the witness of his own body. You've heard me say that rule forty times tonight. You've been listening to a dead man's name said small, and didn't know it. And *sips* has a name on its back, and *knot on the breastbone* has one, and I'm not reading you the whole yard. You have the shape. The catechism doesn't change because every change is already paid for. Rules that change are opinions. That one's a grave."

Her hands had stopped on the rag. She looked down at them, finished the fold, and set it on the shelf, fold out.

"There. You saw that. Half a breath where the hands went somewhere else. Don't gloss it — seen first, told second. That's what a slipped payment looks like. One pause, and it files back under wages. I could tell you which Tuesday it comes from and lose an hour I want for something else. But there's the honest size of the damage, since you asked for things straight all night: it isn't what the ballads do with it. It's small, and frequent, and it compounds.

"Item two. Me.

"First year of this war there were seven of us with bags marked for the forward tents. Census this morning: me, and a boy two rows over who can close a wound but can't stay in the room for what the wound costs after, so he closes and runs. Half a medic. One and a half, for a whole section, and the war has been spending the one and a half at both ends for three years.

"You asked what happens to the rope and I told you. Here's what happens to the lamp. A lamp gives light by burning down, and the only part you get to argue with is the wick — you've watched me argue with mine all night. Four years ago there was a row of us burning. Tonight the section's down to a thumb's width.

"The ones who felt all of it and kept no books went through like straw fires — a season apiece. I put two of them on wagons to the rear myself. You have my sign already for a man running out of blood: quiet, gray, apologetic. It's the same sign in medics. I stood at a tailboard and watched a friend apologize to me for it, and I knew the reading exactly, and the treatment is one I can't pour.

"The ones who never felt anything lasted fine, and I wouldn't leave a man on my table with one of them awake in the room. There was one, second year, who liked the sound. I told you whoever enjoys that sound doesn't hold the tools — that wasn't a principle, it was a Tuesday. I took the pan off the table with the work half done, finished one-handed, and walked him to the captain myself. The army thanked me by making him a forward stretcher-bearer, which is the army's arithmetic to the digit. I don't know which ledger he's in now. I know which one I'd put money on.

"And me, I'm the middle way. I feel it and bill it later. The ledger lets me work the night and pushes the payment into a Tuesday that never quite arrives. But the bill sits, and it folds into ordinary days. Three smells I can't stand near since a spring two years back. Pork is off my table. I take my bread from the far oven and walk the long road to it, and as of tonight that road has two reasons and only needed the one. That's what a deferred bill looks like at four years. Not dramatic. Folded into a Tuesday."

The sleeper stirred, gears changing, the deep kind. She waited, counted him through it, went on.

"Item three is the one with an apology attached, so I'll say it while I'm still flat enough to say it properly.

"I've been teaching you all night. Not kindly, and not for your improvement — for the tent. I measured you from the first hold. You held when he bucked, which I told you was rare. You asked to see instead of imagine. You asked the right question about the leg. And somewhere in the shrapnel tin I stopped talking to a helper and started pricing a pair of hands, and I never asked your leave. Taking a man's night and spending it on your own need without his mark on the page — that's the medic's first theft. I robbed you tonight, with bread on the side.

"So here's the accounts, both sides, and then I shut the book. The cost side you've heard — Petrie through the lamp. The wage side is this: most nights, somebody walks out. Tonight's man feeds himself in a month and hauls in six and swears at me on the road every time we pass, and that's the entire pay, and I've found it buys bread. There's no other wage. If you came in wanting the kind they put in paintings, the tent will cure you inside a month.

"You cost him nothing, asking. I said that at the flap and I'll stand by it — it's the rarest thing in this tent and the one thing I can't teach. Everything in the catechism can be learned by anyone with two hands and a bad stomach. The asking can't. That's why you got measured, and I'd do it again tonight, which is why the apology is owed rather than felt.

"Don't answer. Nobody signs a ledger on an empty tank. Say no at noon and nothing in this tent changes except my arithmetic, which is my problem, not a debt on you."

The gray was in the canvas now, thin, along the seam. She got up, taking the table's weight on one hand.

"Four years and it's the knees go first. Everyone warns you about the sleep. Nobody warns you about the knees." She took the rag off the shelf once more. "You were told that was the last nice thing I'd say tonight. The night turned over. New day, new budget.

"And the last item — the actual whole trick, which I've been doing in front of you with the door standing open. The rag. I fold it every hour, bleeding or not, mostly not, in here, between. Folding is a thing that can still be done properly. When the ledger's full of lines you'd rather not read, you keep one motion in your hands that comes out right every time, and you do it hourly, wanted or not. That's the trick. Small. Compounds the right way. Now it's yours, and I didn't even charge you for this one."

She set the rag down, fold out.

"Breakfast when he wakes — feeding rules, off my ration, slate squared. Boots: dead-box, third crate, crooked lid, size big, two pair of socks, vinegar, air them today. If the provost's man walks the ovens road at first light and the rope's still on the beam, we'll know what kind of night his was." She turned the wick all the way down — first time all night — and the lamp stood down, and the gray did the rest of the work.

"Catechism holds. Sips. Pulses. Pink nails. Run if it's numb — and now you know what's written on the back of it." She looked at him on the floor a last moment. "Now get up off my floor. The floor is where this trade stores people. You're not inventory."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get up. My knees ache. "The tin," I say, my voice rough. I take it from her and drink. "I'll get the boots."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Then you've answered like a sensible man — errand, not vow," Sedge said. "Keep those two separate. Noon still stands, and nothing you carry back from the dead-box signs anything but the boots."

She put out a hand for the tin.

"Dead-box particulars, once, while the light's still cheap. Corporal Vinney keeps it. Old, slow, counts everything twice. If he starts telling you about whichever man wore the pair you're taking, he isn't after a listener — he's after a name to say, and the dead won't hold still for it. Give him mine. I keep a shelf for that kind of thing."

"Third crate, crooked lid. Size big. Two pair of socks under the boots, left side. They'll be folded. Keep the fold — Vinney worked the trick out alone, same as I did, and two men finding it separately is the whole proof it's true."

"Vinegar's the waxed bottle, third shelf. Borrow it, don't drain it, bring it back. The cook already thinks I steal, and I've spent three years earning exactly half of that."

She dropped the remaining heel of bread into the water tin to soak. By the time boots came back it would be spoon food, and the feeding rules would have their first pupil.

"He'll wake while you're out — starving, unlucky, and loud about neither. I'll be here, and breakfast is now ahead of you instead of behind, so don't come back at a run with the scrubbing half done. A helper who arrives breathless twice in one day gets mistaken for a habit, and habits get issued duties."

"You'll pass the ovens going to supply. Don't stop, don't touch, walking pace, eyes only. If the rope's still on the beam, that's one story. If there's a clean band on the wood where rope sat all night, that's another. And look at feet. A stolen coat hides under a blanket. Boots get worn, because feet are urgent — they're the one theft that has to be worn in public. His pair went somewhere, and somewhere is a place with feet in it."

She checked the sleeper between instructions — two fingers on the wrist, count against her own throat. Sixteen, even. Thumbnails pressed, white, pink; white, pink. The count held through the gray coming up the seam of the canvas.

"And if the rope's gone, remember what I pocketed at the provost's: he knew that description a fortnight old and hadn't gathered the man. Rope gone plus provost slow equals somebody warned somebody. Then it's not a theft anymore. It's a habit with friends, and habits with friends come through my flap in pairs, same as shoulders. So look, and don't stand there being a witness longer than a breath."

She took up the rag, folded it, set it back — fold out, the first fold of the new day, paid in on schedule.

"The dead man's boots onto the robbed man," she said, mostly to the shelf. "The army will file it as redistribution. I'll call it one line balancing, signature blank. Don't read further into it than the leather. You were told about pasts fit for church."

At the flap she did the morning version of the night's sign-off — held it open to the gray instead of half into the dark.

"Catechism holds from both sides of it now. Sips, pulses, pink nails, run if it's numb. Scrub, air, size big, two pair. Look at the beam, look at the feet."

A beat.

"And bring the vinegar back."

Then she turned to the table and began laying out the morning's tools in a row, because the war's first customers came an hour behind the light and in four years had never once been late.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I head out into the gray dawn. The air's sharp. When I reach the ovens, I slow. The beam's bare — a pale stripe where the rope hung. I keep walking, eyes on the ground. Boot prints everywhere, but none fresh enough to read.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge came up the ovens road at the pace of a woman collecting bread, because that was what she was doing, and bread gave a medic leave to be anywhere before the light without it meaning anything.

"Walking pace was the order," she said, drawing up beside him. "And here you are at a dead stop. I'll allow it — I've stopped too. The difference is I'm on the books for it. Bread buys me this road. You're supposed to be buying boots."

She turned to the beam and looked at it the way she'd looked at the wrists.

"Seen first, words under. The beam's black — soot, and soot is the camp's recording wax. One take only. A rope sitting a fortnight bakes a rim of grime into the edges of its band, a tar line where soot met hemp. The rim on that one is bright. The band widened last night, and there's the smear under the edge, dragged toward the yard side. Someone hauled it off slow enough to leave a signature and not slow enough for the signature to cost them."

She measured the height with her eye, hand over her own crown.

"And the machine was built to size. That beam, plus rope, plus a man's wrists hauled taut, puts his heels a finger off the dirt — hung, not dropped. Weather doesn't measure a man. My table is built to my trade's dimensions and so is this. Machines built to size are built by men who mean to use them again."

She moved to the fire-mouth, crouched over the raked ash — paid for it in the knees, got even — and read the ground with one finger hovering, touching nothing.

"Cook rakes before first bake. Always has. So everything printed on top of the rake marks happened inside the last two hours, in the working dark, in front of men paid to be awake. Two sets. One walks even and heavy in the toe. The other—" her finger stopped over a shorter print, shallow on one side, a drag at the heel "—is lame on the left, and he stood here a while, feet together, facing the beam. The lame one came back for his signature. Men leave signatures lying about when no one's ever made them sign for anything." She straightened. "And the fire's been fed something that wasn't wood. There's a smell under the smoke, sweetish, like hemp's cousin burning. Or I'm tired and tired smells everything twice. Tired gets the discount. Either way, the provost's evidence is now arithmetic: a fortnight-old description, my report, and a burn."

She went to the serving hatch. The cook had flour to the elbow and a face that kept its own counsel.

"Two loaves."

He passed them through. "Busy night?" she asked.

"Fires at three. Bread at five." A silence with a shape to it. Then, as she turned, to the oven rather than to her: "Third coat off my line this fortnight. I sell bread. I don't sell watchmen."

"There's the camp's whole treaty with its ovens," Sedge said, walking back to Wick with the loaves. "The one road that's worked in the dark is the road nobody watches. The thieves knew it. The baker knows it and said it out loud, which for a cook is a deposition. That's not a blind spot. It's a lease, and they hold it."

She put the second loaf in his hands.

"Breakfast, off my slate, and now the bill for the hour. One: this was housekeeping between neighbors, not panic. They came back in working hours, took their rope, burned it, and the men awake at the ovens kept their side of the lease. Habit with friends — I pocketed that at the provost's and it's spent already.

"Two: what it changes for him. Nothing medical. Everything else. A marked man convalescing in the same camp as his robbers, both entries still open in the ledger, is a calendar with a date on it. I can't arrest — I've never arrested anything and I don't mean to start at my age on these knees. What I have is paper. The day he can sit a wagon, I write him unfit for this camp, and the army moves him at its own expense to a camp where nobody knows his wrists. That's my whole constabulary: a transfer form. Moves slower than a rope. It's the only lever in my kit that lifts a man clear.

"Three: what it changes for you. You were never here. Medics walk to bread, helpers walk to supply. You'll have seen a bare beam because every man in camp sees it by noon, and that's the entire size of your testimony. Any testifying with a name in it, I do alone, as agreed."

She checked the gray coming up behind the ovens' smoke and got her bearings.

"He's in the deep gear and the deep gear holds an hour, so nobody's dying of my loaf. Boots, socks, vinegar, back — walking pace, and don't run anywhere twice in one day, you were told about habits. And when you're back: he doesn't sit alone after dark. Not because tonight's coming for him. Because men who come back for rope also come back for witnesses, and a witness on two good legs makes a harder paragraph than one on a crate."

She turned back up the road at the pace of a woman with bread, which covered everything.

"The fresh loaf's his," she said, not turning. "You get the heel. The tent's rules travel."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the loaf, still warm. My eyes go back to the pale band on the beam. "I'll be quick," I say, and start toward supply, the bread tucked under my arm. The vinegar bottle feels heavy in my pocket already.
