dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Honest's better," Sedge said. "The ones who tell me they're ready are the ones who let go."

She took the man's right wrist and set her thumb into the groove below the shoulder. "Front of the socket. That's the ordinary kind. Blast caught him open-handed, or somebody dragged him by the arms — doesn't matter now. What matters is you."

She leaned back against the arm, slow, her boots braced against the table leg, her voice going flat and even, like she was reading off a list. "This takes minutes. If I pull fast the muscle clamps down and nothing goes back in, it just tears where it's already torn. So he's going to make noise. That's fine. Noise is free."

The joint turned, and the man came up off the table like something yanked on a line. Sedge didn't flinch. "Still there. Good. Most of them are gone by now." She kept the traction steady through the whole arc of it, breath measured, one long pull, and then the seat of it — a deep click you felt in the bone more than heard — and the man dropped back to the canvas and sobbed once, twice, and went quiet in the ugly way people do when it's over but they're not sure it's over.

"Right one's in. He'll have it a week, then complain about it for a year." She wiped her hands on her apron and moved to the left arm, and stopped. Felt along the joint once, twice. Her mouth went thin.

"Left one's not seating. There's bone in there that isn't behaving like bone." She looked up at Wick, and there was no drama in it, just arithmetic. "I'm going to try once more, and it's going to be worse than the first one, and I need you the same as before. And so you know — I don't take any pleasure in this. People assume you get used to it. You don't. You just get faster. Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my knuckles white where I'm pressing down. "Bone?" My voice comes out rough. "What does that mean?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Means the ball end of the arm bone broke when it came loose," Sedge said, hands busy while she talked, setting a folded strap where she could reach it. "There's rubble in the socket now. Bits. That's why it won't seat — I'm trying to put a ball back into a pocket full of gravel." She looked at Wick once, no drama in it. "And the big artery runs under all of it. So far the pieces are minding their own business. If I pull wrong, one of them moves, and then he bleeds somewhere I can't put a finger on, and after that nothing I do matters. So I won't pull wrong. Same hold. One thing different — if he screams, fine, noise is free. If he goes quiet and grey, you tell me at once. Quiet and grey is shock, and shock kills them on my table more than the arm does."

This time the man didn't come up off the table. He made one low sound and then breathed in long pulls, and Sedge leaned into the traction and felt the wrongness come up through her hands and the table legs — a grind like wet mortar — and the arm gave too easily, shortening under her grip.

She stopped. Backed off. "No."

She laid his two arms side by side along the canvas. The left sat half a hand short of the right. She looked at it the way she'd look at a map.

"That quiet was the other kind — he's clamping, not fading. Skin's still pink." She took Wick's hand and pressed two fingers to the inside of the man's wrist, into the soft part. "Feel that beat? That's the artery, still talking. You're the watch on it now. It goes soft or slow, you say my name."

Then she straightened and did the arithmetic where Wick could see her doing it.

"I can bind it. He keeps the arm, the arm dies where it hangs, and in a month the rest of him follows — that's the slow way. Or I take it off here." She touched the top of the man's shoulder without pressing. "High. That's the fast way, and it's a coin toss whether he's breathing at the end of it, and I've got one bad lamp and no surgeon, because the war spent them all."

She looked down. The man's eyes were open.

"You heard all that?"

He nodded, small.

"Good. Then nobody can say they weren't told." She turned back to Wick. "The lamp. Bring it to this side and hold it steady, and don't let your hands shake over the wound — move your feet if you have to, not the light. I don't decide anything by feel when there's light to be had."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Arm," Sedge said, without looking up. "And it's the second kind. He loses it either way — the only question is whether he loses the rest of him with it."

She kept working while she said it, tying off the strap above the joint, testing the give of it with two fingers. "If I bind and he lives the month, it's a month of a dead arm rotting on a living man, and then it comes off anyway, lower, in worse light, with him weaker. So this isn't me choosing to cut. This is me choosing when."

She let that sit a second, because it deserved a second.

"Coin toss, I said. I'll be plainer, since he's listening and he's earned plain. High shoulder — the joint itself — is the worst place I cut. Big vessel, big nerve, and the tourniquet has to sit where I can't get a proper turn. Six of those I've done. Four breathed at the end. That's the honest number, and I don't dress it up, because dressed-up numbers get people agreeing to things they don't understand."

She looked at the man. He was watching her, breathing in those long pulls, and his mouth moved. Sedge bent closer.

"Say it again."

"...do it," he got out. "Do it, just —"

"I know." She straightened. "There. That's the vote."

Then to Wick, brisk again, the list-voice: "Lamp, close, this side. Feet planted, hands steady, and if the light drifts I'll feel it in my fingers before you see it, so don't lie to me about it either." She pulled the apron tight and set out the tools in a row, slower than before, checking each one against the lamplight. "Blade's sharp. It's the only thing in this tent that is."

She glanced over once — at Wick's face, not the wrist — and her voice dropped a notch, not gentle, just quieter.

"You'll want to look away at the start. Don't. Look away in the middle if you have to, that's human. But the start I need your eyes, because you're holding the only light I've got, and if you're not watching, you're not holding." She set the blade down last, nearest her hand. "Say when you're ready. And this time mean it, or don't say it — I've stopped needing the word."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat too tight for words. I lift the lamp and move to the side she indicated, planting my feet firm against the dirt floor. My hands don't shake. "I'm ready," I say, and this time it's not a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good," Sedge said, and put no weight on it. "Feet say more than the word does anyway."

She folded a strap and set it between the man's teeth. "That's for you, not for me. I don't need it." Then a bottle from under the table, a careful mouthful. "It's not ether — the war spent that too. It'll make the first minute a stranger's problem, and after that you'll be somewhere I can't follow." She tugged the tag cord at his throat once, checking. "He stays a name. Tags don't go in the pit."

Then, last, to Wick, the list-voice: "Rules while I work. The light stays where it is unless I say the word *light*. If I go quiet, that's not your signal — I go quiet when my hands want all of me. And the start I told you to watch. Watch it now."

She laid the blade flat against the skin first, not cutting, drawing the line so it could be seen. "Skin and the big muscle over the top. It'll bleed faster than you'd think a man could spare. He can spare it. The strap buys me minutes, not miracles."

She cut. The man made noise against the strap and she didn't slow, and she didn't stop talking either, because talking was part of the doing. "Clamping as I go. Four clamps — that's the war's whole allowance tonight. Now under the collar of muscle, and there's a river under there. The big one. I don't look for it. You feel for it. A pulse is a pulse even in a dying arm." Her fingers went in and came out holding the vessel, and she clamped it, cut between, tied. "Tied twice. Once is a promise. Twice is a fact."

"Next I cut the wire. When I do, his body will jump even if he's gone somewhere deep. That's the wire, not him." She cut, and the man's body jumped, hard, once, and Sedge rode it without looking up.

Somewhere in the middle of it he went quiet. Her fingers went to his throat, then his face. "Pink's holding. He's gone under on his own. Kinder. If the choosing had been mine I'd have picked it for him."

"Last of it. The break did half my work — the head's already gravel." A grind, and then the arm was off, and she set it down at the foot of the table without looking at it. "That goes in the pit with the others. Nothing personal. Nothing in this tent is personal."

Then the bad moment came, as it comes: the tension changed as she lifted free, and a tie let go, and there was dark blood rising faster than the strap had ever let him lose. Sedge's voice stopped. The light didn't waver, and some small corner of her working mind noted that and kept it. She worked in silence — re-clamp, chase the stump, tie, tie again, a third time because twice wasn't holding — and when her voice came back it was flat as ever.

"That was the coin. It landed our way. He'll never know how close that came, and nobody's telling him."

She watched the stump a long moment. Nothing rose. She took the strap off and waited. Still nothing. "Holding." Then the close — pulling what muscle was left over the end, stitching fast. "Ugly stitches. He can judge them in a year, if he gets a year." Dressing. Bandage, tight.

"He's breathing. Five of seven now. I keep the count. Somebody has to, and the men I lose can't."

"When I say, we move him to the pallet — I slide, you keep the light on the bandage till I'm done. Then it's your watch again, same as before, except the wrist's gone, so it moves to the throat. Every quarter hour. Soft or slow, you come get me — I'll be asleep on my feet by then, so shake me. If he screams in the night, let him. Screaming's alive. You know the other one."

She wiped the blade and set it at the end of the row, and looked at Wick — at the face, not the hands.

"You held the start and you held the middle, and the middle's the part I gave you leave to leave. You didn't. I'm not making a speech about it. You're still holding the lamp. That's speech enough."

"Now sit down before you fall down. Shaking after is permitted — it only counts against you if it happens while I'm cutting." She nodded at the man's throat. "And count me ten beats there. I want to hear what you hear."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Good," Sedge said. "Imagining is the expensive way to learn a thing. Knowing is cheaper, and it keeps."

She took Wick's free hand and set two fingertips into the groove beside the voicebox, off the windpipe, pressing back until the vessel rose to meet them. "Not on the pipe — the pipe is the windpipe, and it doesn't beat, it only carries air and complaints. There. Into the soft, then ease until it speaks."

She gave him a moment to find it, then went on with the lesson, because explaining was part of the doing and always had been.

"What you're feeling isn't blood. Blood doesn't knock. Every beat is one squeeze of his heart, traveling up the artery as a wave, and the wave lifts the wall of the pipe under your fingers. You're not touching his life. You're touching the plumbing it runs through. Life doesn't have a feel. Pressure does." She nodded at the place under his fingertips. "You'll see it too, in the hollow at the base of the throat — the skin ticks with it when the light's low. Watch if you like. But believe the fingers. Eyes flinch. Fingers don't."

"And that particular pipe is the main one to the head. Everything he ever was goes up it. The arm I took was meat. This is the man. That's why the watch moved here — arms a body can lose."

"Now, what's normal for him tonight: slow and a little soft. One beat to the second, near enough, maybe a shade under. That's the drug and the blood loss agreeing he should lie still. Not alarm. Alarm is soft and slowing while you watch it. Alarm is gaps — a beat, a beat, and a hole where a beat should be, because his heart draws from the same supply, and there's less in the tank than there was at supper."

"Two lies to guard against. Never the thumb — the thumb carries its own beat, and it will give you its own and swear it's his. Two fingers, always. And light. Press hard and you slow what's under you, or shut it, and then you're counting nothing and feeling proud of it."

She lifted the lamp out of Wick's other hand and hung it on its hook, turned low. "The watch doesn't need light. It needs fingers, and I want both of your hands honest."

She held out her own. They carried a fine tremor, now that nothing needed them steady. "See. Mine are having their say too. Means nothing. The body keeps its own books and sends the bill after."

"Count out loud when you have it. All ten, and don't hurry the spaces. I'm not listening for the number — I'm listening for your drift. Every watch runs a little fast or a little slow, worst when it's worried, and when you tell me a number at three in the morning I need to know what yours is worth. So I'm calibrating you now, while he's flat and the light's decent and nobody's bleeding."

She looked at the man once more, breathing his long pulls, pink under the bad lamp.

"Five of seven. He's the five. Count, and we'll see if the ledger holds. Then we slide him to the pallet, and after that — sit. The shaking's still permitted. Falling isn't."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My fingers find the pulse, steady and deep. "One...two..." I keep my eyes on the man's face as I count, my voice low. "Seven, eight, nine, ten." I glance up at Sedge. "Slow, like you said. No gaps."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Slow and whole," Sedge said. "That's him agreeing to live, so far." She set her own fingers beside Wick's for a moment, reading the same beat like checking another man's sums, then took her hand back. "And your spaces run long. You drag the count — a hair, but it's yours now. Rushers are the common kind. Drags are rarer and easier to correct for. When you give me a number at three in the morning, I'll know what it's worth. Calibration's done."

She rolled the near edge of the blanket into the man's back, then reached across and rolled the far edge to meet it, making a seam. "Now he moves as one piece. You don't move a man by his parts — parts come off, blankets don't. Lamp down here, on the dressing, and follow it the whole way. If it blooms while I'm lifting, say so before I've finished setting him down."

She lifted by the seams. The weight came up whole, head lolling, and she carried him the short distance and lowered him onto the pallet with the stump end propped on the folded second blanket. "Stump stays uphill till morning. Gravity's the last assistant I've got, so I use it."

The dressing showed a coin of red through the cloth. She looked at it without touching. "That's the wound talking, not the ties failing. A coin by morning is fine. A hand by morning is not. Anything between, you lay an actual coin on the cloth next to it and compare, and you wake me for anything past the coin. That's the whole rule. Coins and gaps."

She found the tag cord and read it in the low light. "Hess. Corporal, sappers." She let it fall back to his chest. "You'll watch him better now he's a name. That's not sentiment, it's mechanics — nobody keeps a quarter-hour watch on *the shoulder*. People watch Hess."

The man made a small sound in the drug, not a word, not a scream, something in between. Sedge paused, then didn't touch him. "Dreaming it already. Let him. Better he practices on it now than meets it fresh in a month."

She dug a pencil stub and a folded page from her apron, marked five strokes in one column, two in another, and showed it before folding it away. "Tonight's page. Five and two, and all seven get names when I can get them. It's the only monument anybody's getting out here, so I keep it honest."

Then she nodded at the jug by the pole. "Water in that, half a loaf in the box under it. Eat sitting down — standing's how people faint and call it something noble. A dry mouth lies about pulses, and I need yours honest more than I need it comfortable."

She lowered herself against the supply crate at last, apron off, and let her hands have their tremor where Wick could see them doing it.

"First quarter hour you run alone — prove the count. Second one you wake me. Shake, don't be polite about it; I'll swear at you and mean nothing by it. After that we trade off. Two tired watchers beat one good one, and by morning there's no such thing as a good one."

She tipped her head back against the crate.

"Now the shaking, if it's coming. You've paid for it. And leave the lamp low — low light keeps a better watch than dark, and it's kinder to the pink."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Right question at the right hour," Sedge said. "Ask it at three in the morning and the answer's no use to anyone."

She picked her apron up off the crate where she'd dropped it, held it against the lamp, and pushed one finger slowly through the cloth. "Entry. See it. Cherry-sized." She turned it over. On the far side the fabric had tented and torn wide, a hand's span of ruined weave around one small neat point. "Same hole, other side. That's what flesh does. Skin's a curtain hung over everything underneath, and it lies. It closes small over a big ruin. Half my work is not believing the hole."

She let the apron fall across her knee and kept the lesson in the list-voice, quiet now, pitched under Hess's long breathing.

"A bullet's manufactured. It flies straight, goes where it's sent, and the damage is a lane you can walk with one finger. Shrapnel's garbage. The shell's own iron torn into edges, plus dirt, plus the man's coat, plus — if the blast was close — bits of whoever stood nearer to it. It doesn't fly. It tumbles. It goes in at the collarbone, turns a corner off a rib, and stops somewhere the skin never mentioned. That's why I work by feel inside a wound, not by eye. Eyes follow the hole. Fingers follow the truth."

"And it doesn't only cut what it touches. A man is a bag of water, and water doesn't squeeze — it shoves. The iron carries a fist of force ahead of it and out to the sides, and flesh a thumb's width from the path dies without the iron ever visiting. That's Hess. The fragment never broke his bone. It passed near it, and the shove broke it for him. Gravel in the socket, and not a mark on the ball you could point to."

"Then the part that kills them after the bleeding stops. The iron's hot going in — one moment of heat, cleans itself, doesn't matter — because it brings the coat with it. Wool, mud, his own skin, driven deep where no air reaches and no light sees. Day two, three, that's fever. Day four, the smell. I took the arm for the bleeding, but I'd have taken it for the filth even if the bone had behaved. Clean cutting heals. Filth doesn't."

"There's a kind that never touches a man at all. Air shoves too. I've had them walk in with no mark on them, ears ringing, and I ask what they're coughing. By evening they're coughing pink. Hollow things fail first — ears, lungs. So when a man tells you he walked away from a blast without a scratch, don't believe him until tomorrow."

She looked at the pallet. Hess pulled his long breaths. The coin on the dressing hadn't grown.

"That's what's in him. A hole, a shove, and a pocket of his own coat, and my answer to all three is stitched shut under that coin. So the watch is more than bleeding. Hot skin, a pulse running fast when it should run slow, and the smell — sweet-sour, like fruit gone off. You wake me for the smell too. Don't be polite about a smell. Nobody ever died of being woken early."

Her head went back against the crate.

"When your hands start — and they will, the body keeps its own books — let them. And keep the asking. Men who imagine don't ask, and men who don't ask guess wrong at the worst hours. You just bought yourself a better three o'clock."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My hands are trembling now, just a little. I press them against my knees. "How do you know when to stop cutting? I mean...where do you decide the arm ends and the man begins?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was quiet long enough that the lamp might have thought she'd gone to sleep.

"That's the question," she said at last. "Most people never get to it, and the ones who do usually ask it wrong. They ask it like the arm and the man are two things and there's a line drawn somewhere, and my job is to find the line. There's no line. It's all one cloth. I'm not finding the edge of anything. I'm choosing where to cut a living thing, and living things don't stop where you want them to."

She turned her hands over on her knee, watching the tremor like it belonged to somebody else.

"So here's the arithmetic, since you've earned it. When I'm in there, everything asks one question: if I leave this, does the rest of him keep working? Muscle that's dead but small — leave it, the body eats it and carries on. Muscle that's dead and big — it rots, and the rot travels, so it goes. Bone that's broken but has blood in it — stays. Bone that's gravel — goes, because gravel can't heal and it's sharp at the pieces. Vessel, nerve, the pipes to the head — those I fight for down to the last turn of string, because they don't grow back and everything downhill of them dies with them."

"And where those answers stop agreeing with each other — that's your line. Not a rule. A place where keeping the part starts costing more of the man than losing it does. Tonight it was the socket. If I'd saved the arm, I'd have been feeding a dead thing with a living man, and the arm doesn't thank you, because arms can't. The man pays for everything."

She looked over at Wick, and her voice came down a notch.

"And you want to know how I know I'm not wrong. I don't. Not in the moment. Six of seven tonight, I'm right maybe four times, and the other two I find out later in a letter or a smell. What keeps me from stopping too early or going too far isn't knowing. It's this." She tapped her own temple, once. "I say the numbers out loud. In there, while my hands are working, there's a voice running the list — vessel, nerve, cost, cost, cost. It's not wisdom. It's bookkeeping, and I do it out loud in my head because a man who narrates his own cutting can't drift into cruelty or cowardice without hearing himself do it. Those are the two ways medics go bad. We cut too much because we're fascinated, or too little because we're tired. The list catches both."

"That's the real answer. You don't know where the man ends. You decide it, out loud, moment by moment, and then you keep the count, and you go back and read the page in the morning and see if you were a butcher or a coward this time, and mostly you were neither, and you get up and do it again."

Hess made his small dream-sound again. The coin on the dressing sat where it was.

"But here's the part worth more than all of it," Sedge said. "The line I cut tonight — arm ends, man continues — that's the easy kind. The hard line isn't in the body at all. It's the one where cutting more saves the meat and loses the person, and I've stood on that one too, and there's no clamp for it. When you hit that one — and if you keep holding lamps, you will — you don't decide it with the list. You decide it with the man. You tell him the numbers plain, and you ask, and whatever he says, that's the line, because he's the only one who has to live on whichever side of it you draw."

She closed her eyes.

"Tonight was the easy kind, and I'm going to say so out loud, because saying it keeps it true. Easy kind. Five of seven. Now let the shaking run its course, and wake me at the second quarter hour, and don't philosophize at me at three in the morning unless the pulse tells you to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was up off the crate before the third scream, and her hands weren't shaking anymore. "Light. High."

She put her fingers on the dressing and looked, then lifted Wick's hand away from the shoulder without hurrying it. "Off. He's not fighting you now — what you're holding down is the drug wearing off and the pain arriving, and pinning a man through that is wasted weight. Slide your hand to his good shoulder and lean. It tells him somebody's there, which is all pinning ever really told anybody."

Her fingers went to his throat. Counted. Went back a second time, unhurried, and counted again.

"Fast, but it was always going to run once he woke into the pain. Not soft. Not gaps." She pulled the lamp close and peeled the corner of the dressing back, and Wick could see her go still over it — the same stillness as the joint that wouldn't seat.

"Coin's grown. Not to a hand. Between." She laid an actual coin out of her pocket on the cloth beside the bloom, and the red was past it by a thumb's width. "So the rule says wake Sedge. I'm Sedge. Consider yourself woken."

She got the light over the pallet, got her fingers into the bandage edge, pressed. "Here's what's happening and none of it is a mystery, so listen while I work. He screamed on the table and screamed going under, and screaming is straining, and straining is pushing blood against ties that are holding a stump with no collarbone under them to tie to. One of my ugly stitches gave. Not all — one. The wound isn't open, it's leaking at a seam, the way a bag leaks at one stitch and not the whole seam."

She peeled the dressing the rest of the way, and there it was — a dark line welling at one point in the closing, slow, not a pump, a seep with weight behind it.

"That's the stitch. Not the artery — if the artery went, you'd know in ten seconds, and it's been two minutes of coin, so the artery is still tied twice and keeping its word. This is muscle weeping from a seam under strain." She took a needle from the row, threaded it without looking at it, and her voice stayed in the list. "I put three stitches where one was. That's all. No cutting tonight, no choices, no line. Maintenance."

"Here's what it costs him. The drug's burned off, so he's awake for it, and he can feel the needle, and I can't give him more because I gave him the last of it and more would stop his breathing, and breathing is not negotiable tonight. So he hurts, and the honest thing is to tell him so, which I'm about to do."

She bent to Hess's ear, and her voice did something it hadn't done all night — came down slow and plain, the way you talk to a man in a hole.

"Hess. It's the medic. You tore a stitch screaming, which is allowed, and I'm putting it back, and it will hurt like a needle, because it is one. Ten seconds. Breathe at me, not against me. Count with me if you can — one."

She stitched while he sobbed and counted, missing numbers, and she didn't correct him, and her hands didn't hurry. "Two. Three." The needle went and came. "Four." Again. "Five." Again. "Six. Done. That was all of it, and the rest is behind you."

She bound it fresh, tight, set the coin back as a ruler, and stayed with her fingers on the cloth a full minute, waiting to see if it bloomed.

It didn't.

"There. Holding. He'll cry himself back under in a few minutes — pain spends more than running does." She wiped the needle, reset the row, and then she sat back on her heels and looked at Wick, and there was something in her face that wasn't soft, exactly, but had stopped being flat.

"You asked me to keep talking and not leave anything out, and I did, and here's the last thing, since it's the part people leave out. What I just did — three stitches — is nothing. An apprentice does it. What mattered was telling him the truth before I did it and counting him through it, because a man who knows what's coming and how long it lasts can survive almost anything for ten seconds. Pain with a number on it is small. Pain without one is a country."

She stood, joints cracking, and nodded at the good shoulder where Wick's hand still leaned.

"Keep that where it is till he sleeps. Then the watch as before — throat, quarter hour, coins and gaps, and now smells. You've heard the scream and it wasn't the bad kind. The bad kind is the one that stops."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my hand on his shoulder, feeling his breaths even out. "He's still here," I say, more to myself than to you. The coin on the dressing stays put.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"He's here," Sedge said, "and here's how he stays here: by the quarter hour and the coin and nobody getting clever."

She lowered herself back against the crate, but didn't close her eyes this time. She sat where she could see the lamp, the pallet, and Wick's hand on the good shoulder, all three at once.

"Note what you just did, because it's worth noting. You said it to yourself, not to me. 'He's still here.' That's the watch starting to get into you. It happens to everyone who holds a lamp long enough — you stop watching a wound and start watching a man. That's not a fault. That's the only thing that keeps the count honest at three in the morning, when the numbers all look the same and the reason for them doesn't."

Hess's breaths went long, then longer, then found the slow gear of real sleep. Sedge waited until she was sure — watched the chest fall three times the same way — and nodded.

"There. Under, and honestly. Let your hand come off slow, so the leaving doesn't wake him."

She pulled the folded page from her apron and made a mark, small, in the margin this time, not one of the columns. "Not a count. A note. Stitch held, quarter past, he's under. Tomorrow I read that line and I know tonight had a shape, not just a number. The ledger keeps the dead. The margins keep the living, and the living need more space, which is why the page is bigger than the columns."

She looked at the lamp, low and steady, and then at Wick's hands, resting on the knees now, the tremor mostly spent.

"First quarter hour starts now. Throat, two fingers, never the thumb. You know the rules, and you know your count drags a hair, and you'll drag it the same at three, and I'll know what your number's worth when you give it. That's the whole arrangement, and it's a good one."

Her head tipped back against the crate.

"I'll sleep with one ear open. That's not a figure of speech — four years in, the ear does it on its own. A change in breathing reads through a wall. So the truth is you're not alone on this watch and never were. Wake me at the second quarter hour, shake, don't be polite, and if he makes the sound between a word and a scream again — that one's allowed. He's earning it."

Then, quieter, almost to the lamp:

"Good night, Corporal Hess. You're the five."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't open her eyes. She heard the floor take Wick's weight and knew the sound of it — the body giving up the argument with gravity, not sitting so much as being put down.

"Say the rest," she repeated, to the inside of her own eyelids. "All right. But you asked for it sitting on the floor, so take it sitting on the floor, because that's where the rest of it gets told."

She let the quiet run a moment, listening to Hess breathe through it.

"In two days, if the filth behaves, he wakes wanting water, and you give it to him in sips, and he asks what happened, and you tell him the truth in the plain words, because he already knows, he just needs to hear it said out loud by somebody who was there. *We took the arm. You voted for it. You lived.* Three sentences. Don't add a fourth. Men can carry three."

"In a week he learns the trick everybody learns — that the hand is still there. He'll reach for something with it. He'll feel fingers that aren't on the end of anything anymore, itching in a place that's in the pit with the others. Nobody knows why. I don't waste time on why. I tell them it's the wires remembering, and that's a lie, and it's a better lie than the truth, which is that nobody knows. Sometimes the lie carries them to morning and morning is all anything ever has to do."

"In a month he's walking and angry, and the anger is the good sign — the ones who go quiet in the second month are the ones I watch. He'll hate the stump. He'll hate me. He'll come back to the tent eventually and stand there and not say thank you, and then say thank you, and it will be the worst sentence either of us has ever heard, and we'll both pretend it wasn't."

She opened her eyes then, and looked at the lamp.

"And in a year — IF the year happens, and that's a big if in this army — he goes back to whatever village made him, with one arm and a story that nobody there can use, because they weren't here and they don't want it and he'll spend the rest of his life deciding how much of it to leave out. That's the part after the part after the part, and I know it because I've written the letters and read the replies. Some of them say thank you. Some of them say nothing at all, which is also a reply."

Her thumb moved over the folded page in her apron pocket, back and forth, an old motion.

"You asked once tonight what's the part where we're being kind, and I answered it about an arm. Here's the rest. Nobody in this tent is kind. Kind would have been a war with fewer shells in it. What we are is thorough, and what I am is the last thorough thing between a man and the pit, and most nights that's enough, and some nights it's five of seven, and you keep the page anyway, because the page is all that stands between those five and being nothing at all."

She looked at Wick then, on the floor, hands quiet on the knees at last.

"That's the rest. There's no more after that — I've checked. Now the first quarter hour started four minutes ago, and the count doesn't care what we've been through, and neither does Hess. Fingers to his throat. You owe me a number in eleven minutes, and it had better run long."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I find the pulse under my fingers, steady and stubborn. "One... two..." I keep counting, my voice low in the quiet tent. "Eight, nine, ten." I look over at Sedge, her eyes closed again. "Slow and whole. No gaps."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
"Slow and whole," Sedge repeated, not opening her eyes. "Mark it. Quarter hour, both of you agreeing. That's the whole war done properly, right there, in one count."

She listened to Wick mark it — or didn't mark it, being on the floor — and let the tent settle into its night sound: lamp hissing low, canvas ticking in whatever wind there was, Hess breathing his long pulls.

"Eleven more minutes," she said. "Then you wake me, and I'll swear at you, and we'll trade. That's the last instruction I've got, so after this I'm only a body against a crate, and you can say whatever you like to a body against a crate and it won't answer wrong."

A pause. Then, because the list-voice didn't quite know how to stop:

"One thing, and then I'm done. When you wake me and I'm ugly about it — and I will be, four years deep, don't take it personally, nobody who's slept in boots takes anything personally — you'll be tempted to give me the number softly, like an apology. Don't. Give it like a report. 'Pulse slow, whole, quarter hour complete.' The words don't matter. The spine does. A watch reported like an apology makes the woken one check the work twice, and tired checking is bad checking. Confidence isn't pride at three in the morning. It's a tool. You held the lamp through the whole of it and your hands didn't lie to me once tonight. Report like a man who knows that."

She shifted once against the crate, boots staying on, blade within reach of her hand even asleep. Four years had taught the hand where the blade was without asking the head.

"And if the pulse runs long — yours, not his — that's fine. You're a known quantity now. I calibrate to known quantities."

Her breathing evened out. But the ear stayed on, the way she'd said it would, and somewhere behind the crate, before sleep took the last of her, she said one more thing, quiet, mostly to the lamp:

"Nine minutes. Fingers honest."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stay on the floor, my back against a supply crate, fingers still pressed to Hess's throat. The pulse doesn't change. "Seven minutes," I murmur to the tent, to the lamp, to no one. My own heartbeat finally slows to match his.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The tent went quiet the way field tents do — not silent, but settled. Lamp hiss. Canvas tick. The two long pulls of Hess's breathing and the shorter one beside him on the floor.

Sedge slept like she did everything: economically, and with the list still running somewhere underneath.

The ear did what she'd promised. It tracked Hess's breathing without waking her — long, long, long, same gear, no change — and filed it. It tracked the wind shift when the canvas took a gust and settled. It even tracked Wick's heartbeat slowing, in its way, by the sound of a body going slack against the crate, because four years teaches you to read a tent by its noises the way other people read a page.

Twice she surfaced partway, never opening her eyes.

The first time, she checked the lamp by instinct — a low gold smear through her lids, still burning, still where it was hung — and went back down. The second time, Hess made his small dream-sound, the one between a word and nothing, and her whole body came up one layer to listen for whether it would climb or fade. It faded. Her jaw unclenched. She sank back against the crate, and the hand near the blade relaxed by a finger's width.

Between the two surfacings she said something, thick, mostly not words. If you'd been close enough, it would have come out as a number. Five. Or two. The columns followed her down; there was no leaving them outside.

Then she was just a body against a crate, boots on, blade in reach, breath even, and the seven minutes ran out and became six, and five, and the count didn't care that she was asleep, and she'd told the truth about the ear but not the whole truth — the ear was good, but it wasn't a shake, and the arrangement was a shake, and she'd meant it when she said she'd swear.

So she slept, and waited for the hand on her shoulder like a tool set down within reach, and the quarter hour walked on toward the man on the floor and the throat under his fingers.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Two minutes," I whisper, mostly to myself. My hand's gone a little numb against his neck, but I don't move it. The coin on his dressing hasn't grown. I can hear Sedge breathing, steady as a metronome, from across the tent.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not believe the word ready. Ready was for parades and first kisses and men who had never had to hold someone down while pain asked for a second opinion. Useful was simpler. It was a straight back, a planted foot, and a refusal to listen for permission when the body on the table started making the wrong noises.

“Good enough,” she said. “He’s been shouting long enough that his voice is gone. That means he’s tired. Tired is almost help. Not much. Almost.”

She moved the lamp one finger’s width to the left. It still threw the tent into bad angles, but it lit the row of tools enough to see them: gauze, straps, the blunt curved needle she hoped she would not need, the bottle of gin that had stopped being medicine years ago and had become a promise instead. She touched the man’s shirt sleeve and then, deciding, took the knife and cut it off both sides.

Cloth peeled away. The shoulders underneath were wrong.

“Both anterior dislocations,” Sedge said, because naming a thing helped the hands know what the thing was. “The ball of each arm bone is out of its socket. Muscles are in spasm. That’s why he’s stuck like that and that’s why he’ll fight when I move him. I’m going to pull them back in. It will hurt. I’m not going to make it sound like a kindness. I don’t take pleasure in this. If I took pleasure in this, I’d be doing it wrong.”

The man’s breath hitched at the word pleasure. Sedge did not look up.

“I’m going to do the right side first. It’s closer to the light. I’m not sentimental, and I’m not going to do the easy one for his sake.”

She set one hand under his right elbow and the other over his wrist. She did not grip like a strangler. She laid her palms along the arm the way a carpenter lays a hand along a joint that has come apart: to find the slack, to take the slack, to make the bones remember their direction.

“When I say hold, I mean hold,” she said again. “His head will try to throw itself off the table. Don’t let it hit the lamp.”

She pulled.

The arm straightened with the slow, reluctant resistance of rope soaked through with cold. The man made a sound like a cough full of gravel. His spine arched. Sedge kept her weight low and did not yank, because yanking would tear what was only stretched. She pressed her thumb into the swollen hollow at the front of the shoulder and felt the displaced bone under skin gone tight and hot.

“Stay with me,” she said, to the man, not to the room. “You’re going to hate this. Hate it properly. Don’t faint yet.”

She rotated the elbow outward a few degrees, then let the whole arm hang, waiting. The muscles fought. The muscles always fought. Sedge waited until the fight became exhaustion, then eased the arm downward and back. The shoulder gave with a thick, sickening slip that was also a settling. The man screamed once, then his body went limp in the way that was not fainting but the end of the first battle.

“One,” Sedge said. “That’s one. Don’t thank me. I did the job. You’re allowed to be in pain.”

She wiped her hands on the rag. The rag had been clean once, in another life, probably during a war that had not yet learned to waste medics. It did not help. She moved to the left shoulder anyway.

“The left is going to be faster,” she said. “Not because it’s gentler. Because he already knows what’s coming.”

The man’s eyes found the ceiling and stayed there, white at the edges. Sedge set her hands again.

“He’s going to buck. His legs will try to do what his arms can’t. Hold the shoulders, not the throat. If you bruise his windpipe, I’ll have to fix that too, and I am out of patience for fixing people who were not broken by me.”

She pulled the left arm into line, took up the slack, and let the joint talk. It talked by resisting. It resisted until it could not. Then it gave.

The sound was worse than the first because there was less drama in it. The man did not scream. He only opened his mouth and breathed like something had been taken out of him and put back wrong. Sedge checked the shoulders with two fingers, then let them both hang easy.

“Both are in,” she said. “Arms down. If he tries to lift them, stop him. I’m serious.”

She did not wait for agreement. She began laying out the straps she would use to bind the arms close, then stopped and put the straps aside. The table was already creaking. The man had begun to cry in a low, stupid way, not from softness but from being alive enough to feel that he was alive.

Sedge looked at him once, plainly.

“Yes,” she said. “You’re alive. It’s not pretty. It’s still alive.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look away as he cries, throat tight. "Should I--" I start, but my voice cracks. I clear it, try again. "Should I get him some water or something?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look up from the man’s left shoulder. Her two fingers were still under the joint, checking for warmth, for the wrong give of torn capsule, for the pulse that might tell her he was going to stop crying and start dying.

“Water,” she said. “Yes. Not much. If he chokes on his own thirst, I’m not digging it out of his lungs.”

She laid the straps in a fan across the canvas and tested the table with one palm. It creaked, but it held. The man had gone quiet in the ugly way that meant he was listening.

“The canteen is by the crate,” Sedge said, still to Wick. “If you can get it without letting go of his shoulders, yes. If you can’t, tell me. I will hold. You will fetch. Do not bring water to his mouth. Bring it to me.”

She moved to the man’s legs, checked the knees, the toes, the cold sweat at his temples.

“More than three fingers in the cup is a mistake,” she said. “Small sips. His throat is swollen and his stomach is empty and his arms are going to be bound. If he thrashes with a mouthful of water, he will drown in spit, and I am not going to have that on my hands tonight.”

The lamp flickered. Sedge shifted it again, one finger at a time, until the shadows stopped pretending to be people. She took a strip of cloth, tore it once with her teeth, and began padding the armpits before she bound the arms.

“Both shoulders are in,” she said. “Both shoulders are ruined. Same thing, for now. He is not going to lift them. He is not going to reach for water. He is not going to ask for anything that costs him movement.”

She looked at Wick then, briefly, at the face that had asked the question. She looked away without softening.

“If you are asking because you feel bad, do not. If you are asking because you need a task, take the task. Bodies do not care what we call it. They care if the water goes in and the arms stay down.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge’s hand stopped on the man’s shin and then went back, lifting the hem of his trousers enough to see both legs. She checked the feet, the toes, the pulse at the ankle, the color of the skin.

“Leg,” she said. “You’re asking about a leg while I’m holding two shoulders.”

She let the cloth fall.

“If he loses a leg, it will be because the war took it or because I had to cut it off while you were looking away. Neither is happening tonight. He has two legs. They are boring. His arms are the problem.”

She moved back to his right hand, lifted it by the fingers, and watched the color return to the nails. It came back slowly, but it came back.

“He’s not losing an arm tonight,” Sedge said. “Unless I tie the straps too tight. That is what I am afraid of. Not ghosts. Not heroics. Tight straps.”

She pressed two fingers into the swollen front of his shoulder, then let go. The skin was hot and tight. There was bruising starting in the hollow under the collarbone.

“How bad is it?” she answered herself, because he had asked and because she would not leave the question soft. “Bad like the socket is stretched. Bad like the capsule is torn. Bad like the muscles are bruised and in spasm. Bad like if he forgets himself and tries to reach for something, he can put them both out again. Bad like if there is a crack in the bone I missed in this light, he’ll be in pain for a month and blame me.”

She took the padding and began wrapping it into the armpits, not gently, but carefully.

“He may not lift either arm over his head for weeks. He may never do it properly. If he is a soldier, he may not swing a rifle. If he is not a soldier, he may not carry a child. That is how bad.”

The man’s breathing hitched. Sedge looked at him once.

“I am not doing this to frighten you,” she said. “I am doing it so you do not make the mistake of believing that because the bones are back, nothing else is wrong.”

She picked up the straps and tested them against her wrist.

“This is not the part where we are being kind,” Sedge said. “Kind is a clean hospital. Kind is a surgeon. Kind is a sling and instructions and someone to bring you water when you cannot reach it. This is a tent. This is a table. This is gin that has stopped being medicine and become a promise. What I can give you is not being fooled by the fact that the bones are back.”

She laid the first strap across his chest, then paused and looked at Wick.

“If you want to help, watch his fingers. Not his face. His face will lie. His fingers will not. If they go blue, tell me. If they go cold, tell me. If he says they are numb and you think he is exaggerating, tell me anyway.”

She tied the first strap enough to hold the arm close, not enough to strangle the circulation.

“He may say he can lift them. He may say he can walk. He may say he is ready to fight again. Do not believe him. Tired men tell stupid lies about their bodies.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, keeping my grip steady even though his shoulders have gone slack. "His fingers look okay now. A little pale." I watch them curl against the canvas. "What if he forgets? What if he tries to get up?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look at Wick’s face when he asked. She looked at the man’s fingers.

Then she pressed her thumb to the man’s thumbnail until it went white. She held it there for three slow counts, then let it go. Color came back, but not fast.

“Pale is a thing to watch,” she said. “Blue is a thing to fix. If they go cold, or if he says they are asleep, tell me. Do not wait for him to be sure.”

She took the first strap and laid it low across his chest. The man started to buck. Sedge put one hand flat on his sternum and left it there, not pushing him down, simply showing him that the table was not going to let him go.

“He will forget,” she said, as if the question were not a question but a diagnosis. “That is not a surprise. Shock forgets. Fear forgets. A man who has been screaming long enough to lose his voice will try to stand up because standing up is easier than admitting he is ruined.”

She threaded the second strap across his hips and tightened it enough to keep him from sitting. Not enough to squeeze the breath out of him. She put two fingers under the webbing and felt his chest rise against them.

“If he tries to get up,” Sedge said, “you do not ask him to remember. You make him remember. Hold the shoulders. Do not hold the neck. Do not hold the throat. Do not talk to him like he is a child; talk to him like he is a man who has made a bad arithmetic mistake. Tell him Sedge is going to make him stop. If he is stronger than you, call me.”

The man’s mouth moved. Sedge looked at him once.

“No,” she said.

She did not know what he had tried to say. She did not need to.

“You may not get up. You may not reach. You may not lift either arm. If you need to piss, say so and I will find a bottle. If you need water, say so and I will give you a cup. If you need to prove something, save it. I am not the audience.”

She checked the right shoulder again with two fingers, then the left. The joints were in place, but the sockets were angry and stretched. The muscles still fought softly under the skin, waiting for a chance to make the mistake again.

“The arms are back,” Sedge said. “The shoulders are not healed. The difference is weeks. The difference is whether he can lift a rifle, a child, his own head, or a cup of water. The difference is whether he will come back and do this again, and whether next time I will have the patience.”

She picked up the padded cloth and began tying it under his armpits, taking care not to let his arms drift outward.

“Watch his fingers,” she said to Wick. “Watch his breathing. If he starts to go pale in the face, if his breathing goes too fast and too shallow, if he says the straps are hurting more than they should, say so. I do not want a quiet patient. Quiet is where mistakes hide.”

She stepped back and looked at him strapped to the table. It was ugly. It held.

“If he forgets,” Sedge said, “the straps remember. If the straps forget, I will notice. If you notice, tell me. Do not decide by yourself. This is not courage. This is a shoulder joint. Courage gets people killed.”

She uncapped the gin and poured a little into the tin cup. She held it under the man’s lips.

“Small sips,” she said. “If you choke, I will fix it, but I will not pretend I am sorry.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped. She set the tin cup back on the crate with enough care that the gin did not spill, though not enough care to suggest she cared whether it spilled.

“Good,” she said. “Imagining is worse. Imagining makes men sick when they can still stand, and it makes men useless when they need to stand.”

She took the lamp by its handle and lifted it higher, one hand shielding the flame from the tent’s draft. The light sharpened the canvas into bad angles again, but it threw the man’s upper body into a harder honesty.

“Look,” Sedge said. “Not at his face. His face is trying to get sympathy. Look at the shoulders.”

She pointed with two fingers, not touching the man yet.

“You are seeing the result of force. The head of the humerus came out of the glenoid and stayed out. In plain words, the ball of the arm bone was torn from the socket and left in the wrong place. Anterior dislocation. Both sides. Not common. Not clean. Usually the body takes a hit it was not built for and decides the joint is not worth keeping aligned.”

She moved closer.

“Look at the shape. That is wrong. The shoulder should be round. It is squared off. The muscle on top is flattened because the bone under it is not doing its job. That hollow under the collarbone is deeper than it should be. That swelling is not pride. It is blood and fluid from torn capsule and stretched ligaments. That bruise starting under the skin is not a story. It is a sign that something ripped.”

The man’s breathing hitched. Sedge glanced at him, not with pity, not with reassurance, but with the attention of someone listening to an engine make a sound it should not make.

“His breath is still too fast,” she said, answering the question Wick had not asked. “His lips are dry. His skin is clammy. That is pain and exhaustion. Maybe shock. Maybe both. Do not call it dramatic. Bodies are dramatic when they are trying to survive.”

She lifted the man’s right hand again, letting it dangle from the wrist. The fingers curled slightly against the canvas. The nails were pale.

“Look at the fingers. Not because they are pretty. Because they tell you what the blood is doing.”

She pressed her thumb to the nail bed until it whitened. Held it. Let go. Color returned slowly.

“That is not good enough,” Sedge said. “It came back, but not fast enough. That means his circulation is under stress. Could be the straps. Could be the position. Could be his body deciding there is too much to fix at once. If they go blue, if they go cold, if he says they are asleep and you think he is lying, tell me.”

She moved to the left hand and checked the same way.

“You are seeing a man who will not lift his arms over his head tonight,” she said. “You are seeing a man who may not lift them over his head again the way he used to. You are seeing two joints that were forced, pulled, and shoved back into place by a woman with a bad lamp and a table that creaks.”

She set the hands down carefully, not gently.

“You are seeing straps that will cut off circulation if I tie them too tight, and shoulders that will pop out again if he moves wrong. You are seeing gin that will make him feel brave enough to move wrong. You are seeing me counting the difference.”

The lamp flickered. Sedge shifted it again, one finger at a time, until the shadows stopped pretending to be people.

“Do you want the truth of it?” she asked. “Here it is. The bones are back. That is the part the body will forgive slowly. The soft parts will hate me. The capsule is torn. The muscles are in spasm. The tendons are angry. The nerves may be bruised. If he is lucky, he will be stiff, sore, and weak for weeks. If he is not lucky, he will come back in six months because he tried to carry a pack and felt the shoulder slide again.”

She looked at Wick then, not softening, not making the words smaller.

“You are not seeing a man being made whole. You are seeing a man being made possible. That is what field medicine is. We do not make clean endings. We make endings that are not worse than the beginning.”

She picked up a strip of cloth and tore it again with her teeth. The sound was small and dry.

“If you want to know what you are seeing every time, learn the list,” Sedge said. “Color. Warmth. Motion. Feeling. Breathing. Pain that changes. Pain that does not. A pulse that is too fast. A face that is too pale. A man who suddenly becomes quiet.”

She began padding the second armpit, working the cloth under the straps.

“He is quiet now,” she said, almost to herself. “That is not peace. That is storage. He is keeping everything where it is.”

The man’s eyes moved toward Wick, then away. Sedge did not comment on it. She was not there to narrate shame.

“You are seeing a body,” she said. “Not a lesson. Not a symbol. A body that was broken by a war I did not start and is being fixed in a tent that smells like sweat and old canvas. Do not make it mean something too large. If you do, you will miss the thing that matters.”

She tied the second strap. Tested it. Slid two fingers under the edge.

“The thing that matters is whether his fingers go blue,” Sedge said. “Whether his breathing goes shallow. Whether the straps are hurting him more than the shoulders. Whether he tries to sit up and tears the work I have done. Whether you see it and say something before I have to guess.”

She stepped back. The man lay bound, arms close, chest rising in uneven pulls. The shoulders looked almost right now, except for the swelling and the bruising and the stupid way the body holds itself after pain has been rearranged.

“That is how bad it is,” Sedge said. “Not death tonight. Not leg. Not arm gone. Two ruined shoulders. A man who will be grateful in the morning and furious by noon. A job I did with my hands because there was no one else to do it with better tools.”

She looked at the gin cup. Then at Wick.

“You asked what you are seeing,” she said. “You are seeing me make him stop bleeding from the inside by making him stop fighting the outside. That is not kindness. That is competence. Do not confuse them.”

She picked up the cup again and held it to the man’s lips.

“Small sips,” she said. “And you,” she added, without looking up, “watch his fingers. If they change, tell me. Not when you are sure. When you are not sure.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch his fingers, pale against the canvas. "They haven't changed," I say, my own hands stiff on his shoulders. "What happens now? Do we just...wait?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the man’s fingers. They were still pale, but pale in the way that could be watched, not in the way that made her hands move fast.

“No,” she said. “We do not just wait. Waiting is not a thing you stand still for. Waiting is listening with your hands and your eyes and not letting your mind drift off somewhere clean.”

She checked the pulse at the man’s wrist first. It was thin and quick. She moved her fingers to the neck, careful with the angle, and felt the carotid. That one was stronger, but not good. Not yet.

“He’s still too fast,” Sedge said. “Not dying fast. Hurt fast. Shock fast. There is a difference. You learn it by watching until you are sick of watching.”

She took the lamp and turned it away from his face, lower, so the light fell across the shoulders and the straps. The man winced at the change but did not open his eyes.

“If he vomits,” Sedge said, “do not let him sit up. Do not push his neck. Turn the whole table a little if you have to. If you cannot, hold his head and his shoulders together as one thing. A man with two ruined shoulders should not be given the chance to throw himself off a table because his stomach is angry.”

She checked the straps again. The first was tight enough to keep the arm from wandering. The second had shifted slightly. Sedge moved it back with the careful irritation of a woman correcting a mistake that could become an amputation if ignored.

“Fingers pale is watch,” she said. “Fingers blue is act. Fingers cold is act. Fingers numb is act. Do not ask me if you should tell me. Tell me. If you are wrong, I will know. If you are right, I will have already been late enough.”

She uncapped the gin, looked at the cup, then capped it again.

“No more of that tonight,” Sedge said. “Not because it is bad for his soul. Because a drunk man thinks he can lift an arm that cannot lift. A drunk man is a man who undoes my work.”

She took a fresh cloth, dampened it from a canteen lid, and laid it over his forehead. Not cool enough to be comfort. Cool enough to be information.

“Skin is wet,” she said. “That is pain or shock. Maybe both. If he starts to feel clammy and his breathing gets small and fast, tell me. If he stops sweating and his face goes white and his pulse goes weak, tell me faster.”

She moved down the table and checked his legs again, not because she expected them to be wrong, but because checking was how she made the body answer questions it had not been asked.

“Legs are boring,” Sedge said. “Boring is good. Boring means I am not cutting anything tonight. If he loses feeling in his toes, or he cannot move his toes, then the legs are not boring anymore. Then I want to know. Do not wait for him to make a speech about it.”

The man’s chest rose. It was uneven. One side was using more effort than the other. Sedge pressed two fingers along his ribs, then pulled back.

“Possible bruised rib,” she said. “Possible nothing. Possible I will know better when he breathes again. If he takes a short breath and catches, if he points to one spot and says it hurts to breathe, tell me. If he says he is fine, tell me anyway.”

She looked at Wick then. Not softly. Not to reassure. To make the task real.

“You keep your hands on the shoulders,” Sedge said. “Not because I need you to be a statue. Because if he bucks, the shoulders are the last thing that stop him from tearing the joint loose again. If you get tired, tell me before your arms start shaking. Do not tell me after you have let go.”

She picked up a small chalk and wrote on a tin plate set near the lamp: TIME. Then she wrote a number, the time of the reduction, and under it: BREATH. PULSE. FINGERS. PAIN. STRAPS.

“We watch,” Sedge said. “Then we check. Then we check again. If he sleeps, we do not call that rest. We call it risk. Sleep is allowed only if his breathing stays even and his color stays decent and his fingers do not turn into something else.”

She stepped back and looked at the whole man. Bound. Pale. Still. The shoulders were no longer out of place, but they were not healed. They were only arranged. There was a difference, and the difference lived in the next hour.

“If he asks for water, give me the cup,” Sedge said. “If he asks to get up, say no. If he asks for a rifle, say no twice. If he says he is ready, I will say he is not, and I will not be guessing.”

She moved the stool closer and sat down, not to rest, but to lower her hands to the man’s wrist and keep them there.

“Now,” she said, “we wait properly.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick long enough to decide whether he wanted the truth because he was trying to be brave or because he was trying to be useful.

Useful she could teach. Brave she did not trust.

She took the curved needle from the row and laid it back down exactly where it had been. Her hands did not shake. They were too tired to shake. That was not the same thing as calm.

“Straight,” she said. “All right. Shrapnel does not cut. It throws a piece of the world through a body at speed. The metal is the smallest part of the trouble. The trouble is energy, dirt, cloth, bone, and time.”

She lifted the lamp one finger’s width again. The light sharpened the man’s shoulders but did nothing for the shadows. Sedge had learned to work inside shadows.

“A shell fragment, a piece of rail, a bolt, a rock, a bit of boot sole—any of it can come in looking small and leave looking like a fist inside the body. It tears skin. It drags skin with it. It carries uniform cloth, mud, rust, sweat, blood, and sometimes bowel contents into a place that was clean enough until two seconds ago.”

The man on the table turned his head slightly. Sedge did not look at him.

“Don’t,” she said.

He stopped.

She went back to Wick.

“If it hits muscle, it bruises the muscle before it tears it. Muscle is not a rubber band. It is wet, angry tissue with blood vessels running through it. When shrapnel goes through, the hole is not neat. It has ragged walls. It bleeds inside. The body tries to stop the bleeding by clamping down and swelling. That can be good for a minute and bad for a day.”

She pointed to the man’s shoulder, not touching him.

“Like this. Swelling is not always infection. Sometimes it is the body shouting that it is still alive. Sometimes it is the body shouting that it is not going to stay alive.”

She moved to the straps, checked them again, slid two fingers under the edge, then let go.

“If a fragment hits a big artery, he can die in minutes. Bright red, spurting blood. If it is a vein, dark blood, steady, easier to miss because men look away. If it is deep, the blood has nowhere to go. It collects under the skin. The skin gets tight. The limb gets cold. The patient gets quiet. Quiet is not always good. Quiet can mean he is done arguing with dying.”

She took the damp cloth from the man’s forehead, wrung it in one hand, and laid it back.

“If it hits bone, bone becomes shrapnel too. That is what no one says. A fragment breaks a leg or an arm, and the broken ends are sharp and wet and inside the muscle. Then he tries to move, and the bone tears what is left of the vessel. Then the pain gets stupid. Then the swelling gets hard. Then the toes or fingers go numb, and I am deciding whether the limb is worth saving or whether saving it will kill him by infection.”

Her voice stayed even. She did not like that it stayed even. She used it anyway.

“If it hits a joint, I can sometimes clean it. Sometimes I cannot. If the joint is open, the body does not know where the hole ends and the infection begins. Then it is fever, then it is pus, then it is a surgeon who is not here, then it is a man who will never bend that joint again, or a man who will not have the limb at all.”

She looked at the man’s legs.

“Bones are boring when they are whole. Whole bones mean I can use straps and time and pain. Broken bones mean I can use splints and pain and time. Open broken bones mean I can use my hands, my patience, and the hope that the body is not already poisoning itself.”

The man’s breathing caught. Sedge waited for it to pass.

“If it hits the chest, the lung can collapse. The wound can suck air in and let blood and air collect inside the chest. He drowns without being in water. His lips go blue. His fingers go cold. His neck veins bulge. If I cannot get the pressure off, he dies. If I can, he may still die later from infection. If he is lucky, he lives angry and sore for a year.”

She said this without drama. Drama was for people who had not had to listen to a body lose the argument.

“If it hits the belly, it is worse. The skin may close over the hole. The bowel may be torn. Food, stool, blood, and bacteria spill inside. The abdomen becomes a swamp. He may not be in pain right away. He may say he feels fine because his body is lying to him. Then his pulse climbs. Then his face goes white. Then he becomes too quiet. By then the surgeon may be too far away, and I am packing a wound and praying over a man I cannot fix.”

Sedge glanced at the tin cup.

“That is why I do not let him drink much. That is why I do not let him get up. That is why I want you watching his fingers and not his face. His face wants you to believe he is almost done. His fingers tell the truth about blood flow.”

She moved back to the man’s right hand and pressed the thumbnail again. It went white. Color came back slowly, still not fast enough, but not worse.

“If it hits the head, I can do very little. Bone goes into brain. Brain swells. The skull is a box, and boxes do not forgive swelling. I can keep his airway clear. I can stop the bleeding. I can get him to someone who might have a drill and a surgeon and a clean room. If I cannot, I can make sure he does not die choking on his own tongue. That is not a kindness. That is only preventing an ugly death from becoming a uglier one.”

She stopped then. Not because she had run out. Because Wick had asked for straight, and straight had a limit in usefulness.

“Infection,” she said. “That is the long answer. Shrapnel does not kill only by cutting. It kills by leaving a mess deep where the immune system cannot reach. Cloth in a wound is a feast for bacteria. Dirt is worse. Feces is worse. A boot sole can carry enough rot into a leg to make a man lose the leg in three days if no one cuts it open. The tissue turns gray. Then black. Then it smells sweet and wrong. That smell is not imagination. That is death starting inside a living body.”

The man on the table closed his eyes. Sedge did not let herself look at his face too long.

“Shock is not fear. Shock is the body deciding there is not enough blood where it needs it. Pale skin. Cold fingers. Fast pulse. Weak pulse. Thirst. Nausea. Confusion. Quiet. If a man says he is fine while his face is gray and his fingers are cold, he is not fine. If he says he is fine while his pulse is too fast, he is not fine. If he says he is ready to stand, he is lying, and I am going to stop him.”

She picked up the gin again, looked at it, and put it down.

“Pain is not the enemy. Pain is a messenger. Pain means some part of him is still connected. Pain means he will complain. Complaints are useful. A man who does not complain may be hiding something important, or he may be dying in a way that looks like rest.”

Sedge looked at Wick now, fully.

“You asked what it actually does. It does not make a clean story. It does not make a man a symbol. It makes a body wet and ruined in places you cannot see. It makes you learn to look for color, warmth, motion, feeling, breathing, and the difference between pain that is behaving and pain that is lying.”

She turned back to the man and lifted his left hand by the fingers. The nails were still pale. Not blue. Not black. Not yet.

“Tonight, this man’s shrapnel problem is not inside him. His problem is force. His shoulders came apart because something hit him or he fell or the world moved too fast and his body forgot how to stay put. That is why I set them. That is why I strapped him. That is why I am telling you what to watch.”

Her voice flattened again, practical and blunt.

“If he had shrapnel in him, I would not be talking like this. I would have cut off his clothes, looked for entry and exit, checked his airway, breathing, and circulation, packed bleeding wounds, made a decision about tourniquets, checked his belly and chest, and gotten him to a surgeon while I could still stand. If there was no surgeon, I would be deciding what was worth saving and what was already gone. I would not pretend the choice was clean. I would not pretend it was kind.”

She set the man’s hand down.

“This is not a lesson in horror. This is a map. You asked for the map. Use it.”

Sedge moved the stool closer and sat again. She kept her fingers near the man’s wrist, not pressing, just ready.

“Now,” she said, “watch his fingers. Watch his breathing. Watch his face, but do not trust it. If he gets quieter, if he gets whiter, if his pulse gets faster, if his fingers get cold, if he says the pain has moved, if he says he is fine when he does not look fine, tell me. Do not tidy it for me either. Tell me what you see. Then I will decide what it means.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My own hands are starting to shake, so I press down harder on his shoulders to stop it. "Okay," I say, voice low. "If his breathing changes, I'll say."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look at Wick’s face. She looked at the canvas around his hands, where the shaking had become visible as a small, wrong tremor in the man’s shoulder.

“Ease,” she said. “You are bruising him in a place that does not need another bruise. Shaking is not fixed by pressing harder. It is fixed by changing what you are doing.”

She moved her stool until her knee was beside the table and her fingers were on the man’s wrist again.

“Lock your elbows if you can hold that way. If you cannot, use your forearms. If your forearms cannot, tell me. Do not let your arms make a decision for me. I am the one who knows what a torn capsule will tolerate.”

The man’s breath caught halfway in. Sedge waited. It did not catch again.

“Still fast,” she said, more to herself than to Wick. “Still tired. Not worse. That is enough for now.”

She checked the strap across his chest with two fingers, then the one at his hips, then the color of his nails without lifting his hand.

“If your hands shake, it means you are human and tired. It does not mean you are useless. It means I may have to move you.”

Her voice did not soften. It did not need to.

“Say if you need to let go. Say if you need to sit. Say if you cannot watch his chest and his fingers and his breathing at the same time. This is not a test of nerve. This is a shoulder joint and a table and a lamp that is about to fail. Nerve is for men who have never had to count a pulse while their own teeth are chattering.”

She took the damp cloth from the man’s forehead, wrung it, and laid it back.

“Now watch,” she said. “One thing at a time. His chest. If it changes, say. His fingers. If they change, say. His face. If it changes and his chest does not, say anyway. Do not tidy it. Do not decide. Do not wait until you are sure. Uncertain is what tells me something.”

The man opened his mouth. Sedge looked at him with the patience of a woman who had heard every kind of lie a body could make.

“Still no getting up,” she said.

Then she went back to watching Wick’s hold, not his face.

“Good,” she said, answering the okay he had already given. “Keep it small. Keep it useful. If you cannot, tell me before the table knows.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The scream filled the tent, and Sedge moved toward it.

“I am not going to stop talking,” she said. “I am going to tell you what my hands are doing, because if you can hear it, you will remember it when I am not the one holding the lamp.”

Her right hand went to the man’s right shoulder, then her left to the left. She did not push him down. She did not soothe him. She pressed two fingers into the swollen front of the joint and felt for the round place that should not be round, the give that should not give, the head of the humerus sitting like a misplaced stone.

“Right shoulder is in,” Sedge said. “Not healed. Not safe. In.”

She moved to the left. The muscle there was hard as wet rope.

“Left shoulder is close,” she said. “The bone is in, but the capsule is torn and the ligaments are stretched. He is screaming because his own muscles are trying to put the arm back the wrong way.”

The man bucked. Sedge put one palm flat on his sternum and held it there.

“You may scream,” she told him. “You may not lift.”

She checked his fingers before looking at his face. The right hand lay against the canvas, nails pale. She pressed the thumbnail. It whitened. Color came back slowly.

“Still not good,” Sedge said. “Still not act. That is a thin line. I am going to loosen the strap.”

She worked the first binding a quarter turn looser, then slid two fingers under it.

“I am not loosening it for his comfort,” she said. “I am loosening it because a strap that stops his blood stops his arm. If his arm stops, I have to cut it, and I am not carrying a saw tonight.”

She tested the strap at his hips, then checked his chest. One side rose a little slower than the other. She put her ear near his ribs, not touching, listening.

“Air is moving,” she said. “That is good. It is not perfect. There are bad things that move air for a while and then stop. I am going to check his belly, his back, his pulse, and his breathing. I am not going to guess.”

She moved down the table.

“I am going to lift his shirt, because I cut it once and I should have finished. I am going to look for a hole. I am going to look for a bruise that means something under it broke. I am going to feel for blood where there should not be blood. If his belly gets hard, if his back swells, if there is blood under the skin, if he cannot feel his legs, that is the body telling me the shoulders were not the worst thing.”

She lifted the cloth carefully, not gently.

“Skin,” she said, naming what she saw. “Cold sweat. Not warm. Not dry. That is not good. That is shock starting to sit down. Bruising over the right ribs. Could be nothing. Could be a rib cracked enough to make him afraid to breathe. If he points and says it hurts, I will believe him even if he says he is fine after.”

She slid her hand beneath his lower back. The man hissed, not screaming, not quite. Sedge felt the spine with two fingers, then the muscles beside it.

“No obvious step,” she said. “No obvious swelling. No obvious blood. That is not a promise. That is what my hands know.”

She checked the pulse at his wrist, then the one at his neck.
