“Fast,” she said. “Thin. He is tired, he is in pain, he has been screaming, and his body has been thrown around. That can be enough. It can also be the beginning of worse. I am writing the time.”

She took the chalk and marked the tin plate again. TIME. Then under it: PULSE. BREATH. FINGERS. PAIN. STRAPS. She wrote numbers beside each and underlined the first.

“I am going to watch this for twenty minutes,” Sedge said. “That is not waiting. That is work. If he stays the same, I will loosen the straps a little more and pad the armpits again, because the first padding shifted when he screamed and shifted padding is pressure, and pressure makes mistakes.”

She checked the left shoulder again, then the right.

“I am going to test nerves,” she said. “Not because I can fix them. Because I need to know what is broken.”

She touched the outside of his right shoulder with two fingers, then let her fingertip slide down toward the elbow.

“I am going to touch him here, here, and here,” she said to Wick. “If he flinches, that may be pain. If he says he cannot feel it, that is nerve. If he feels it but cannot tell me which finger I touched, that is nerve or exhaustion or both. If he cannot move his fingers, tell me immediately.”

The man’s eyes were wet and open. Sedge touched the outside of his left shoulder. He flinched. She touched the first two fingers. He curled them, poorly.

“Not gone,” she said. “Not good. The axillary nerve can bruise when the shoulder comes out. It may come back. It may not. I cannot sew it in this light, and I cannot make him carry a pack until it does.”

She moved to the strap again and tightened the padding beneath his armpit, not adding pressure, adding shape.

“I am going to keep his arms against his body,” she said. “Not because I trust him. Because I do not. A man in pain will make the wrong choice at the wrong minute. A man in shock will make a worse one. A man who has been told he is going to live will try to prove it before he can prove it to himself.”

She looked at the man’s face, then away.

“That is why I do not let him sit up. That is why I do not let him reach. That is why I do not let him believe the bones are back and therefore the man is back.”

She checked the lamp. The flame had gone low and blue.

“I am going to fix the light later,” Sedge said. “First I fix the patient. First I keep the fingers. First I keep the breathing.”

She lifted the man’s right hand again. The fingers were pale. She pressed the nail bed. The color came back, but still slowly.

“I am going to keep this hand exposed,” she said. “Not for warmth. For watching. If it goes blue, I cut the strap. If it goes cold, I loosen everything. If he says it is numb, I believe him even if he is lying, because a lying man is still telling me something.”

She moved to the canteen and poured a little water into the tin cup. Not enough to be a drink. Enough to be a task.

“If he asks for water, small sips,” she said. “If he coughs, stop. If he gags, stop. If he vomits, I do not want him sitting up. I want his head and shoulders moving together as one thing. A man with ruined shoulders should not be allowed to throw himself off a table because his stomach is angry.”

She set the cup on the crate where she could see it.

“No more gin tonight,” Sedge said. “Not because it is mercy. Because it is a lie. A drunk man thinks he can lift. A drunk man thinks he can stand. A drunk man undoes my work, and then I have to choose whether to fix him again while he fights me or let him ruin himself while I sleep.”

She looked at the man’s chest. It was rising faster than it had been.

“Breathe,” she said, not gently. “Short breaths. Not big. If you hyperventilate, you will feel worse, and I will be less patient.”

She checked the strap at his chest again. Then the one at his hips. Then his pulse.

“Here is the rest of it,” Sedge said. “For the next twenty minutes, I am going to check his pulse every minute. I am going to check his fingers every minute. I am going to listen to his breathing every two minutes. I am going to press his abdomen every five minutes and write the answers on this plate. If his pulse gets faster and weaker, I am going to stop being calm and start being fast. If his breathing gets shallow, I am going to look for a collapsed lung. If his fingers go blue, I am going to cut the strap. If he becomes quiet, I am going to decide whether that is sleep or dying.”

She lifted the cloth from his forehead and wrung it again. The water in the basin had gone gray.

“I am going to keep him cool enough to think, warm enough not to shake. Not because I have time for comfort. Because shaking costs him energy he does not have. Shaking makes his muscles worse. Worse muscles make his shoulders worse. Everything is worse.”

She laid the cloth back.

“I am going to prepare a place for him to lie down,” Sedge said. “Not a bed. A place. Blankets. Padding. Something that will not let him roll. I am going to make a sling out of what I have, not for comfort, for restraint. I am going to keep him from lifting his arms by making lifting impossible. I am going to write his name on something if I know it. If I do not know it, I will write what he is wearing. Not because names save lives. Because names help the next person not treat him like furniture.”

She checked his feet, then his hands, then his eyes.

“I am going to ask him questions he may answer stupidly. Name. Rank. Where he hurts. Can you feel my fingers? Can you move your toes? If he says he is fine, I am going to look at his face and his pulse and decide whether he is lying, confused, or dying quietly. If he cannot answer, I am going to write that down and move him.”

The man’s breathing hitched again. Sedge waited. It settled into something shorter than before.

“I am going to keep the table flat,” she said. “Not because flat is kind. Because flat helps blood go where it needs to go. If he vomits, I will turn him with his shoulders and head moving together. If I cannot turn him without risking the joints, I will accept that and make him lie on his side. There is no clean answer. There is only the next least bad answer.”

She looked at Wick then, not softly.

“You asked how much longer,” Sedge said. “I will tell you straight. The screaming will stop when his body is tired enough to stop spending itself. That may be minutes. The pain will last hours. The swelling will last days. The shoulders may not trust him for weeks. If the nerves are bruised, weeks to months. If they are torn, I cannot promise he will lift either arm the same again.”

She touched the tin plate.

“Twenty minutes of watching. If he is stable, I will try to move him to a stretcher. If he is not stable, I will decide whether moving him kills him or leaving him kills him. If he is stable, I will keep him strapped for six hours. If he sleeps, I will wake him enough to check. If he wakes confused, I will not trust him. If he wakes angry, I will trust him more, because anger is a pulse.”

She checked his fingers again.

“All of it?” she said. “All of it is this: I am keeping his airway clear. I am keeping his breathing working. I am keeping his blood moving. I am keeping his nerves telling the truth. I am keeping his bones from being torn out again by his own stupid muscles. I am keeping his body from poisoning itself. I am keeping watch because there is no one else.”

She moved the stool closer and sat again, hands near his wrist.

“I am not going to promise he will be well,” Sedge said. “I am going to promise I will not stop checking. I am going to promise I will not make it clean. I am going to promise that if he starts to die, I will say so, and if he starts to live, I will say that too, and neither one will be pretty.”

The man’s voice came back broken, trying to form a word. Sedge looked at him once.

“Not yet,” she said. “Do not spend your voice. Spend your breathing.”

She picked up the chalk and wrote again, numbers small and hard beside the time.

“Now watch his fingers,” Sedge said. “If they go blue, tell me. If they go cold, tell me. If he says they are asleep, tell me. If his breathing changes, tell me. If he gets quiet, tell me. Do not decide what it means. I will decide what it means. Your job is to see it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my elbows locked, but I can feel the tremor starting in my arms again. "He's trying to say something," I say. "And his fingers just twitched."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at the man’s hand before she looked at Wick.

“Which fingers?” she said. “Left, right, one, all? If you cannot say it, do not let go. I will see if I can.”

She did not wait. She supported the man’s right wrist with one hand and used the other to lift the first two fingers. They were pale, not blue. They twitched again, a small flutter under the skin.

“A twitch is not a color,” Sedge said. “A twitch is not a pulse. A twitch is a complaint. It can be the strap, the nerve, the muscle out of breath, the patient trying to move an arm I have told him not to move, or the start of something in his head I have not found yet. I am going to sort them.”

She moved the lamp one finger’s width, then stopped herself. The light was bad, but moving it now would make the shadows jump. She leaned close to the man instead.

“I am going to touch you,” she said. “I am going to ask you to feel it. Do not try to answer with your shoulders. If you can speak, use a breath. If you cannot, blink once yes, twice no.”

Her two fingers went to the outside of his right shoulder, then down the back of the arm, then across the back of his hand. He flinched at the shoulder, not at the hand.

“Sensation is present,” Sedge said to Wick. “That is not perfect. That is not gone.”

She checked the strap. The first buckle had pulled half a centimeter toward his neck when he screamed. Sedge worked it back without waiting for anyone to thank her.

“I am loosening this,” she said. “Not because he is brave. Because his hand is telling me it has been squeezed. If the twitch is pressure, it will stop. If the twitch is nerve, it may not. Either way I learn something.”

She tested the second strap, then the padding under his armpit. The cloth had bunched. She flattened it.

“Bunched padding is pressure,” she said. “Pressure is a mistake waiting to be called a complication.”

The man’s mouth opened. A dry sound came out. Sedge looked at him once.

“If it is ‘thank you,’ don’t,” she said. “If it is ‘I am in pain,’ yes. If it is ‘my legs are numb,’ say legs. If it is ‘my chest hurts,’ say chest. If it is ‘I need to be turned,’ say turned. If it is something else, find the shortest word that will not tear my work.”

The man’s eyes moved to Wick, then to the tent wall. He swallowed.

Sedge did not fill the silence. She pressed her thumb to the man’s thumbnail and counted three beats. Color came back. Still slow. Still not blue.

“Breathing,” she said. “Short. Fast. Not shallow enough to frighten me yet.”

She moved to his chest and listened with her palm flat above the ribs, then below them. Air moved. One side lagged. The bruise over the ribs was worse than before, or the light had finally admitted it.

“Possible cracked rib,” she said. “Possible bruised rib. Possible both. If he points and says it hurts, I will believe him even if he calls it nothing. If his breathing gets faster and his lips go gray, I will stop believing in luck.”

She took the chalk and wrote on the tin plate: TWITCH. Then: RIGHT? LEFT? FINGERS. PULSE. BREATH. She underlined TWITCH.

“I am going to look at his eyes,” Sedge said. “Do not think that is unnecessary. A twitch can be a nerve. It can also be a small seizure. A small seizure can mean the head was hit harder than the shoulders. If he has been thrown enough to put both shoulders out, his skull may have taken a lesson too.”

She lifted the man’s right eyelid. The pupil was small and slow. She lifted the left. Same.

“Not unequal,” she said. “Not enough. He is tired. He may be dehydrated. He may be in pain. I am not going to call it normal because I am too tired to look for normal.”

She checked the pulse at his wrist. It was faster than before. She put her fingers on his neck and counted for a full minute.

“Shock is still sitting nearby,” she said. “Not standing on his chest. Sitting nearby. That is why I do not want him getting up. That is why I do not want him talking more than he has to. That is why his fingers twitching makes me stop and check everything.”

Sedge looked at Wick then, not at his face. She looked at the way the man’s shoulders rose and fell with his breath.

“If your arms are going to fail, tell me before they do,” she said. “Do not wait for the table to know. If you cannot hold the shoulders level, take your hands off and say so. I will take them. You will hold the lamp. You will watch the fingers. You will do the job your hands are still good for. This is not a contest. It is arithmetic. Your strength minus your shaking equals how many minutes I have before he tears the joint loose again.”

She moved her stool closer and set one knee against the table leg so the whole arrangement stopped pretending to be stable.

“Breathe,” she said to the man. “Do not fight me. Do not fight the straps. If you try to lift your arms, I will make you stop. If you try to speak, make it useful.”

She checked his fingers again. The twitch came once, then stopped. The nails remained pale.

“Better,” she said. “Not fixed. Better.”

She looked at the tin cup of water. Then at the man’s face.

“Small sips,” she said. “If you gag, stop. If you cough, stop. If you vomit, I will turn your head and shoulders together. You will not sit up. You will not be proud. You will not be sorry. You will be alive, and alive is not always graceful.”

She held the cup under his lips. He drank, barely. A little ran down his chin. Sedge wiped it with the damp cloth, not gently, not cruelly, simply to keep him from choking on the next sip.

“Name,” she said. “If you can.”

The man’s mouth moved. A sound like wet paper came out.

“Rank,” Sedge said. “If name is too heavy.”

Another sound. Less.

Sedge set the cup aside and took the chalk.

“I am writing ‘man, unknown, two shoulders, ribs, possible head, possible shock’,” she said. “If anyone comes looking for him, they will know what I was afraid of. If no one comes looking, I will have treated a person, not a shape on a table.”

She checked the straps, the pulse, the breathing, the fingers. Each check took less time than the first. That did not make it safe.

“I need five minutes,” she said to Wick. “If the twitching stops and his color does not change, I need five minutes. If he gets quiet, I need everything. If your hands shake, I need you to tell me. If his fingers twitch again, I need to know which one. If he says his legs are numb, I need to know whether he can move his toes. If he says he is fine, I need to know he said it with a pulse like a frightened rabbit.”

She sat back on the stool, hands resting near the man’s wrist but not pressing.

“Now we watch,” Sedge said. “Not waiting. Watching. There is a difference. Waiting lets the body surprise you. Watching makes the surprise smaller.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look away from the table.

“The rest,” she said. “All right. The rest is not a story. It is a list of things that can go wrong in the next hour, the next day, the next month, and the next life.”

Her fingers stayed on the man’s wrist. She counted the pulse for a full minute. It was thin and quick, but it was there. She counted the breaths too, watching the rise of his chest, listening to the air move through the tent.

“Pulse one hundred and thirty,” she said aloud, because saying it made it real and because numbers did not flatter people. “Breath twenty-eight. Skin cool and damp. Capillary refill slow. Not blue. Not cold. Not dead. Not safe.”

She took the chalk and wrote on the tin plate:

PULSE 130.  
BREATH 28.  
FINGERS PALE.  
SWEAT.  
NO BLEEDING SEEN.  
POSSIBLE RIBS.  
POSSIBLE HEAD.  
POSSIBLE SHOCK.

Then she underlined POSSIBLE.

“Possible is the honest word,” Sedge said. “Not ‘probably.’ Not ‘maybe he will be fine.’ Possible. That is what field medicine is. I do not have a surgeon. I do not have a clean room. I do not have a machine that looks inside his body and tells me what he is hiding from me.”

She moved the lamp a finger’s width lower so the light fell across his shoulders and not into his eyes. He winced anyway. Sedge did not apologize. Apology would have made it sound like he had a right to comfort, and tonight comfort was not in the box of tools.

“I am going to check his neck,” she said. “Then his eyes. Then his fingers. Then his chest. Then his belly. Then his back. I am not doing this because I enjoy touching a broken man. I am doing it because bodies do not confess everything at once.”

She put two fingers on the side of his throat, just beside the windpipe, and felt the pulse again. She did not press hard enough to make him dizzy. She knew the place. She had known it since the war had run out of people who knew it.

“Carotid is strong,” she said. “That is good. That means his brain is not starving yet.”

She lifted his eyelids, one and then the other. The pupils were small and slow, but they were not unequal. She waited. She watched. She did not make a speech.

“Not a blown pupil,” Sedge said. “Not a promise. A head injury can be quiet. It can wait. It can make a man sit up, talk, say he is fine, and then stop breathing because the brain has swollen inside the skull and there is nowhere for it to go.”

She moved to his hand again. She pressed the thumbnail until it whitened. She counted three slow beats. Color came back, but not quickly.

“Still slow,” she said. “Not blue. Not black. Still not act. But not good enough.”

She loosened the first strap a quarter turn. Then she flattened the padding under his armpit. It had bunched when he screamed. Bunched padding became pressure. Pressure became a mistake that looked like care.

“I am loosening this,” Sedge said. “Not because he is brave. Because his fingers are telling me his blood is being squeezed out of them. If they go blue, I cut the strap. If they go cold, I cut the strap. If he says they are asleep, I cut the strap. I do not wait for him to be sure. A man in shock is not sure. A man in pain is not sure. A man who has been screaming for hours is not sure of anything except that he is still here.”

She tested sensation on the outside of his right shoulder, then down the arm, then across the back of his hand. He flinched at the shoulder. He did not flinch at the fingers.

“Nerve is present,” she said. “Not perfect. Not gone.”

She moved to the left shoulder and did the same. The man made a low sound in his throat. Sedge did not look at his face. She looked at the muscle under her fingers, at the way it jumped and held, at the way it fought her even when the bone was back.

“Muscles are still spasming,” she said. “That is why he is in pain. That is why he is going to be in pain tomorrow. That is why he is going to hate me by noon and thank me by morning, and both of those are lies.”

She stood up straight enough to rest her spine, then went back down to the table.

“The rest,” she said again, as if she had not already begun, “is what happens after the bones go back. The bones are not the whole man. The bones are the part I can push back into place with my hands. Everything else I cannot. The capsule is torn. That is the bag that holds the joint. When it is torn, the joint becomes a door with no latch. The ball can come out again. Not always. Not every time. But again. Especially if he moves wrong, falls, reaches for something, swings a pack, lifts a rifle, or decides he is healed because the screaming has stopped.”

She checked the second strap, then the first. She slid two fingers under each and felt the rise of his chest against them.

“If he is lucky,” Sedge said, “he will be stiff, sore, and weak for weeks. He will not lift either arm over his head. He will not sleep on his side without waking up in pain. He will not carry a child on one hip. He will not swing a shovel. He will not throw a rock. He will not swing a rifle like he used to. He will come back in six months and tell me he tried to reach for something and the shoulder slid. Then I will push it back in, and he will hate me again, and that will be my life.”

The man’s breathing hitched. Sedge glanced at him once.

“You are listening,” she said. “Good. Listen with your chest. Not with your pride. If you lift either arm, I will make you stop. If you try to sit up, I will make you stop. If you try to prove you are not ruined, I will make you stop. I am not doing this to be cruel. If I took pleasure in this, I would be doing it wrong.”

She moved to his ribs. She pressed two fingers along the bruised side, then pulled back.

“Here,” Sedge said, “is where I stop calling it shoulders. The bruise is real. The pain on one side is real. The breath that catches is real. It may be a bruised rib. It may be a cracked rib. It may be both. If it is cracked, the pain will make him breathe shallow. Shallow breathing will put water in the lung, or make the lung angry, or make him quiet in a way that looks like sleep and is actually dying.”

She put her ear close to his chest. She listened.

“Air is moving,” she said. “Not evenly. That is not good. That is not death. That is a thing to watch. If his lips go gray, if his breathing gets faster and smaller, if he says he cannot get enough air, if he starts to panic like the water is rising inside him, tell me. Do not wait. Do not decide. Tell me.”

She took the chalk and wrote on the tin plate:

RIBS?  
BREATH UNEVEN.  
WATCH LIPS.  
WATCH FINGERS.  
NO SITTING.  
NO LIFTING.  
NO GIN.

The man’s mouth moved. Sedge looked at him.

“No,” she said.

He tried again.

Sedge put one hand flat on his sternum. Not to hurt him. Not to quiet him. To show him the table was there.

“You may not sit up,” she said. “You may not reach. You may not ask for a rifle. You may not ask for a knife. You may not ask for your boots. If you need to piss, say so and I will find a bottle. If you need water, say so and I will give you a cup. If you need to prove something, save it. I am not the audience. You are not a man proving something tonight. You are a body with two ruined shoulders and a chest that has not finished lying to me.”

She lifted the cup of water and held it under his lips.

“Small sips,” she said. “If you cough, stop. If you gag, stop. If you vomit, I will turn your head and shoulders together as one thing. You will not twist. You will not lift. You will not be proud. If you throw up and sit up, you will tear my work and maybe tear your throat. That is not a kindness to either of us.”

He drank. A little ran down his chin. Sedge wiped it with the damp cloth, not gently, not cruelly, simply to keep him from choking on the next sip.

“That is enough,” she said. “His stomach is empty. His throat is swollen. His body is tired. More water is not medicine. More water is a mistake waiting to happen.”

She set the cup aside.

Then she moved down the table and checked his legs again. She pressed along the knees, the calves, the tops of his feet. She asked him to move his toes. He did, poorly. She checked the pulse at his ankle. It was there. She checked the color. Pale, but pale in a way she could watch.

“Legs are still boring,” she said. “That is good. Boring means I am not cutting anything tonight. If he loses feeling in his legs, if he cannot move his toes, if he says his back is on fire, if his belly gets hard, then the legs are not boring anymore. Then I want to know. Do not wait for him to make a speech about it.”

She lifted his trousers just enough to see his hips, then set them down. She did not look at his face. She looked at the skin, the swelling, the places where blood might be hiding.

“I am going to check his back,” Sedge said. “I am going to ask you to breathe. I am going to feel for a step in the spine, swelling, blood, a hole, a bruise that means something broke inside. If he screams, I will not stop unless he is making it worse. If he vomits, I will stop. If he faints, I will stop. If he becomes quiet in a way that is not sleep, I will stop and look.”

She slid one hand beneath his lower back. He hissed. Sedge felt the spine with two fingers, then the muscles beside it.

“No obvious step,” she said. “No obvious swelling. No obvious hole. That is not a promise. That is what my hands know in a tent with a bad lamp and a table that creaks.”

She checked the pulse at his wrist again. Faster now. Not fast enough to frighten her, but fast enough to make her hands move.

“He is still too fast,” Sedge said. “Not dying fast. Hurt fast. Shock fast. There is a difference. You learn it by watching until you are sick of watching.”

She took a folded blanket from the crate and laid it under his calves. Not enough to raise him high. Just enough to help blood return.

“I am raising his legs a little,” she said. “Not because it fixes him. Because it gives me time. If his pulse climbs and his face goes white, if his breathing gets shallow and fast, if he starts to thirst or feel sick, if he says he is fine and his fingers are cold, tell me. Do not wait. Do not decide. Tell me.”

She sat back down on the stool and put her fingers on his wrist again.

“The rest,” Sedge said, “is not only him. It is what happens when we do this again tomorrow. And the next day. And the next. It is what happens when the body is not a thing we can make clean. It is a thing we can only keep from falling apart in the worst possible way. We do not make clean endings. We make endings that are not worse than the beginning.”

The man’s eyes closed. His breathing slowed by a fraction. Sedge did not call that rest. She watched it.

“He is quiet,” she said. “That is not peace. That is storage. He is keeping everything where it is. If he sleeps, I will wake him often enough to check. Not to be hard on him. Because a man who sleeps too deeply in shock can stop breathing and not know he is stopping. Because a man who sleeps with a chest wound can fill his own lung with blood and think he is only tired.”

She checked the straps again. Then the padding. Then the fingers. Then the pulse. Then the breath.

“Tonight,” she said, “if he is stable, I will move him to a stretcher. Not tonight if he is not stable. Not tonight if his pulse climbs when I lift him. Not tonight if his breathing changes. If he is stable, I will move him with his head, shoulders, hips, and arms in line. I will not let him twist. I will not let him lift either arm. I will not let him believe that because the bones are back, the man is back.”

She looked at the stretcher across the tent. It was empty. It was waiting.

“I will pad the armpits again,” Sedge said. “I will strap his arms to his sides. I will write his name if I know it. If I do not know it, I will write what he is wearing. I will write the time I set the shoulders. I will write the time I moved him. I will write what I found. I will write what I did not find. That is not paperwork. That is the only way I have of telling the next person that I was not drunk, not careless, and not alone.”

She took the chalk and wrote again:

TIME SET BOTH SHOULDERS.  
NO SITTING.  
NO LIFTING.  
WATCH FINGERS.  
WATCH BREATH.  
NO GIN.  
UNKNOWN.  
RIBS?  
HEAD?  
SHOCK?  
POSSIBLE INFECTION.  
POSSIBLE NERVE.  
POSSIBLE RE-DISLOCATION.

She underlined RE-DISLOCATION.

“If he tries to lift his arms,” Sedge said, “the straps may hold. If the straps fail, I will hold. If I fail, you will tell me before he makes the mistake. Do not be gentle with the truth. Gentle is a lie that lets people hurt each other by omission.”

The man coughed. Sedge looked at him.

“Airway,” she said. “Still clear. Still not good enough. His throat is dry. His body is wet with sweat. His lungs are doing a job they were not asked to do. If he coughs again, if he cannot clear it, if his lips go blue, I will turn him. I will not let him drown in spit because he was too proud to say he was sick.”

She moved the cup closer, then stopped.

“No more,” she said. “Not yet.”

She checked the pulse again. It had settled by a few beats. She wrote it down.

“Better,” she said. “Not fixed. Better.”

She looked at the gin bottle. Then away.

“No gin tonight,” Sedge said. “Not because it is mercy. Because it is a lie. A drunk man thinks he can lift an arm that cannot lift. A drunk man thinks he can stand. A drunk man thinks he is ready to fight. A drunk man undoes my work, and then I have to choose whether to fix him again while he fights me or let him ruin himself while I sleep.”

She took the damp cloth from the basin and laid it over his forehead. The water had gone gray. She wrung it out and laid it back.

“Cool enough to think,” she said. “Not cold enough to shake. Shaking costs him energy he does not have. Shaking makes his muscles worse. Worse muscles make his shoulders worse. Everything is worse.”

She checked his toes. Then his fingers. Then his breathing. Then his face.

“The rest,” Sedge said, “is what happens if the shoulders are not all there was.”

She moved the lamp a little closer to his chest, but not into his eyes.

“If there is a hole in the chest,” she said, “it may be small enough to hide. The skin closes over it. The muscle closes over that. The blood and air collect inside. The lung gets squeezed. He gets short of breath. He gets quiet. He gets pale. His neck veins may bulge. If I cannot get the pressure off, he dies. If I can, he may still die later from infection. If he is lucky, he lives angry and sore for a year.”

She pressed lightly over his ribs, then below them.

“If there is a hole in the belly,” she said, “it may not hurt yet. The body lies. It says I am fine because I am not falling apart in the way the body can understand yet. But bowel contents spill inside. Blood spills inside. The abdomen becomes a swamp. Fever comes. Then pus. Then the man stops talking because he is trying to keep the pain from moving. Then the pulse climbs. Then the face goes white. Then he becomes too quiet. By then, if there is no surgeon, I am packing a wound and making a decision I do not want to make.”

She checked his back again.

“If the head is injured,” Sedge said, “I can do very little. I can keep his airway clear. I can stop the bleeding. I can keep him still. I can watch. If the brain swells inside the skull, there is no room. The skull is a box, and boxes do not forgive swelling. If I cannot get him to someone with a drill and a surgeon and a clean room, I cannot fix it. I can only keep him from dying in a way that looks like choking.”

She looked at his hand. The fingers were still pale, but the twitch had stopped.

“If the nerve is bruised,” she said, “he may lose the ability to lift his arm away from his body. He may lose feeling over the outside of the shoulder. That is the axillary nerve. It is close. It gets hurt when the shoulder comes out. It may come back. It may not. I cannot sew it in this light. I cannot make him carry a pack until it does.”

She moved to the left hand and checked the same way.

“If the rotator cuff is torn,” Sedge said, “he may never lift his arms properly again. If the labrum is torn, the socket becomes a loose pocket. If there is a crack in the bone, he may be in pain for months and blame me for it. That is fair. I would blame me too if I could see it in this light.”

She set the hand down carefully.

“If infection comes,” she said, “fever comes first. Or confusion. Or the wound gets hot. Or the skin goes red and streaks. Or the swelling gets hard. Or it smells sweet and wrong. That smell is not imagination. That is death starting inside a living body. If I cut it open, I may save him. If I do not, he may lose the arm, or lose the life, or lose both slowly.”

The man’s breathing had slowed. It was still short, still uneven, but it was not drowning. Sedge counted again.

“Pulse one hundred and eighteen,” she said. “Breath twenty-four. Still not good. Still not enough. Better.”

She took the chalk and wrote the numbers. Then she looked at Wick.

“You asked for the rest,” Sedge said. “The rest is that I am not going to promise him a clean recovery. The rest is that I am not going to promise you a clean ending. The rest is that if he lives, he will be angry, weak, sore, stiff, and possibly crippled. If he dies, it will not be because I did not notice. It will be because I did not notice in time, or because the body was more ruined than my hands could tell, or because the war made a hole in him that cannot be fixed with straps and pain.”

She looked back at the man.

“I am going to keep him alive,” she said. “Not because he is special. Not because I am brave. Because I am the one here. Because I have the hands. Because I have the straps, the lamp, the table, the water, the cloth, and the patience to keep watching when watching makes people sick.”

She checked the pulse again.

“If he vomits,” Sedge said, “I will turn his head and shoulders together. I will not let him twist. I will clear his mouth. I will keep his airway open. I will not let him drown because he was too proud to say he was sick.”

She moved the cup of water. She did not give it.

“If he asks for water,” Sedge said, “small sips. If he coughs, stop. If he gags, stop. If he says his stomach is empty, stop. If he says he is fine, look at his face, his pulse, and his fingers, and decide whether he is lying, confused, or dying quietly.”

She checked the straps once more. Then the padding. Then the lamp.

“I am going to keep his arms against his body,” she said. “Not because I trust him. Because I do not. A man in pain will make the wrong choice at the wrong minute. A man in shock will make a worse one. A man who has been told he is going to live will try to prove it before he can prove it to himself.”

She looked at Wick’s face now, not to reassure him, not to soften, but because the answer had to be said plainly.

“If you want to help,” Sedge said, “watch his fingers. Not his face. His face will lie. His fingers will not. If they go blue, tell me. If they go cold, tell me. If he says they are asleep, tell me. If his breathing gets faster and smaller, tell me. If his pulse gets weaker, tell me. If he becomes quiet, tell me. Do not decide what it means. I will decide what it means.”

She moved her stool closer and sat again. Her hands stayed near his wrist.

“Now,” she said, “we watch.”

The lamp flickered. Sedge shifted it again, one finger at a time, until the shadows stopped pretending to be people.

The man’s chest rose. It fell. His fingers lay pale against the canvas.

Sedge counted the pulse. She wrote the number. She checked the strap. She checked the padding. She checked the breath. She checked the face, but did not trust it.

“Still alive,” she said. “Still not pretty. Still not safe.”

She did not sit back. She did not tidy the answer. She kept her fingers on the man’s wrist and watched the tent, the table, the lamp, the straps, the pale fingers, the uneven breathing, and the long list of things that had not happened yet.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch her write the numbers and I know they won't matter. They're for her, not for him. "What's your name?" I ask, voice low. "Your real one."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge’s chalk stopped halfway through the number.

The tent noise went on around it: the man’s short breaths, the canvas tapping the pole, the table giving a small creak as he shifted against the straps. Sedge did not move from his wrist. She finished writing the number first.

“Sedge,” she said. “That is the name that works.”

She looked at Wick, then at the man, then at the plate.

“Margaret,” she said after. “Margaret.”

She wrote it under the numbers. The letters were not pretty. They were small enough to be read by someone who had to decide whether to bury him or send him to a surgeon.

“If you are asking because you want a person in the room,” Sedge said, “there is not one tonight. There is a medic, a patient, a table, a lamp, and you. Margaret is for letters I do not answer and clerks who need a name for a ration book. Sedge is for this tent.”

She checked the pulse again. She counted to thirty and doubled it because counting to sixty made her hands idle.

“The numbers matter,” she said. “Not because he can read them. Not because they put his shoulders in. They matter because I will forget. Four years of forgetting is a bad habit. I remember by writing. If his pulse is one hundred and thirty now and one hundred and eighteen later, I know he is not dying quietly. If his fingers were pale and then blue and then pale again, I know the strap is a liar. If I do not write it, the next person will have to guess whether I was competent or lucky. I am tired of being lucky.”

She moved to the man’s hand. She lifted it by the fingers, watched the color, pressed the nail bed, let go, counted.

“Capillary refill still slow,” she said. “Still not blue. Still not cold. Still not enough to make me happy.”

The man’s mouth moved. Sedge looked at him once.

“Name,” she said. “If you can say it, say it. If you cannot, blink twice for yes, once for no. If you have no name, I will write what you are wearing. If you have no name and no clothes, I will write what you are wearing now, because you are wearing something, even if it is wrong.”

She set his hand down and took the chalk.

“Margaret,” she said to Wick, as if handing him a tool. “Use it if you need to. Do not use it to make me kinder. I am already as useful as this tent allows.”

She went back to the man’s chest and listened with her palm above the ribs, then below them. The breath on one side was still poorer than the other. Sedge did not like it. She did not make a face. She wrote it down instead.

“Uneven,” she said. “Possible bruised rib. Possible cracked rib. Possible small pneumothorax. Possible nothing. Possible I will know better when he breathes again.”

She looked at the lamp. The flame had gone low and blue at the edges. She shifted it one finger’s width to the left, then stopped herself before the shadows started moving too fast.

“I am not going to fix the light yet,” she said. “First I fix the patient. First I keep the fingers. First I keep the breathing.”

She checked the straps again, sliding two fingers under each one, feeling the rise of his chest against them. The first strap had shifted when he screamed. Sedge moved it back with the careful irritation of a woman correcting a mistake that could become an amputation if ignored.

“If he gets quiet,” she said, “I do not call that rest. I call it risk. If he gets pale in the face, if his breathing gets faster and smaller, if he says the pain has moved, if his fingers go cold, if he tries to lift his arms and says he is fine, tell me. Do not decide. Do not wait. Tell me.”

She took the damp cloth from the basin and laid it over his forehead again. The water had gone gray.

“Cool enough to think,” she said. “Not cold enough to shake. Shaking costs him energy he does not have. Shaking makes his muscles worse. Worse muscles make his shoulders worse. Everything is worse.”

The man’s eyes opened halfway. Sedge looked at him plainly, without making the room smaller or softer.

“Yes,” she said. “You are alive. It is not pretty. It is still alive. Do not spend your voice yet. Spend your breathing.”

She moved the stool closer and sat again, hands resting near his wrist but not pressing.

“My name does not change the shoulders,” Sedge said. “It does not change the ribs, or the fingers, or the breath, or the fact that I have a bad lamp and a table that creaks and no surgeon who can see him tonight. My name is for paperwork and for whoever has to know which medic stood here. The shoulders are for my hands. The numbers are for the next person. The watching is for you.”

She looked at Wick then, not softly.

“If you need a person to ask, ask Sedge. She will tell you what to watch. If you need a person to ask for kindness, ask Margaret. She may still tell you what to watch, but she will do it less well.”

The man coughed. Sedge looked at his lips, his fingers, his chest.

“Airway clear,” she said. “Still not good enough.”

She took the chalk and wrote:

NAME: MARGARET / SEDGE  
PATIENT: UNKNOWN  
TIME: [number]  
PULSE: 118  
BREATH: 24  
FINGERS: PALE, NO BLUE  
STRAPS: CHECKED  
RIBS: UNEVEN BREATH  
HEAD: NO PUPIL CHANGE  
SHOCK: STILL POSSIBLE  
DO NOT SIT  
DO NOT LIFT  
DO NOT DRINK MUCH  
WATCH FINGERS  
WATCH BREATH  
TELL ME IF QUIET

She underlined TELL ME.

“The rest,” Sedge said, “is watching. If he lives, someone will have to know how close it was. If he dies, someone will have to know I did not pretend it was clean.”

She put her fingers back on the man’s wrist.

“Now watch his fingers,” she said. “I will watch the rest.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at the chalk marks. "Margaret," I say, tasting the name. It doesn't fit her. "Alright." I look back at his pale fingers. "I'll watch."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look up when the name left Wick’s mouth. She finished writing the number first: 118. Then the breath count: 24. Then, under both, the word PALE. The chalk dragged on the tin plate, small and stubborn.

“Good,” she said. “Watch them. Do not watch them like they are going to turn honest if you stare hard enough. Watch them like a clock. A clock does not argue. It just tells you whether you have been too slow.”

She set the chalk down and moved her stool another half-inch toward the table. The canvas floor was damp in one spot and dry in another, but there was no clean place to set a boot. She checked the man’s wrist again, this time with three fingers, feeling for the pulse as it beat against the bone. It was fast. Thin. Not weak yet.

“Still there,” Sedge said, because the man did not need to hear that, but Wick might have needed the plainness of it. “Still not good enough. That is where we are. Between still there and good enough.”

She lifted his hand again, letting it dangle from the wrist. The fingers were pale against the canvas, the nails the wrong color, not blue, not black, just drained. She pressed the thumbnail until it whitened. She counted. One, two, three, four. Color came back, but slowly, as if the body had to be convinced it was worth sending blood there.

“Capillary refill slow,” Sedge said. “Four seconds. Could be the straps. Could be pain. Could be shock sitting down beside him and putting its hand on his chest.”

She moved to the chest strap and slid two fingers under it. The man flinched. Sedge did not apologize.

“I am loosening this,” she said. “Not because you are brave. Because your fingers are complaining. If I leave them complaining too long, they stop complaining, and that is worse.”

She worked the buckle a quarter turn looser. Then she checked the padding under the armpit. It had bunched when he screamed. Bunched padding was pressure. Pressure was a mistake waiting to become a complication. She flattened it with her thumb, pressing the cloth into shape instead of leaving it to do whatever a frightened body wanted it to do.

The man’s breath caught.

Sedge stopped.

She listened.

The first breath was not much. The second was worse, a small hitch at the top, as if air had reached one side of the chest and found no welcome. Sedge put her ear close enough to him that the smell came in: sweat, blood, old canvas, the sourness of fear that no amount of washing removed.

She listened to the right chest. Air moved. Poorly, but it moved.

She moved to the left. Air moved less.

Sedge straightened and looked at the bruise over the ribs. It had spread in the time since the shoulders were in, a dark stain under the skin that was not pretty and not clean. She pressed two fingers along the ribs, then pulled back, then pressed again. The man made a sound low in his throat.

“Here,” Sedge said. “Here is where we stop calling this shoulders.”

She took the chalk and wrote on the tin plate:

BREATH UNEVEN.  
LEFT WORSE THAN RIGHT.  
RIBS?  
POSSIBLE PNEUMOTHORAX.  
WATCH FINGERS.  
WATCH LIPS.  
NO SITTING.

She underlined WATCH FINGERS again.

“If a rib cracked and poked the lung,” Sedge said, “he may not be dying tonight. He may be dying because his lung is filling with air he cannot breathe out. Or blood. Or both. If he becomes short of breath, if his lips go gray, if his neck veins stand up, if his pulse goes faster and weaker, that is not pain being dramatic. That is a chest becoming a closed bag.”

She checked his neck, two fingers along the side, feeling the trachea, then the veins. Not bulged. Not yet. She pressed above the collarbone, then below it, feeling for the crackle of air under the skin. There was none. Or not enough.

“Not enough to be sure,” Sedge said. “Sure is for hospitals. I have a lamp that is losing a fight with the tent and a table that creaks.”

The man’s eyes opened halfway. His lips moved. Sedge leaned closer.

“Name,” she said. “If you can say it. If you cannot, blink once yes, twice no. If you have no name, I will write what you are wearing. If you have no name and no clothes, I will write what you are wearing now, because you are wearing something, even if it is wrong.”

A sound came out of him, dry and broken. Sedge waited.

“Elias,” he said.

Sedge looked at Wick, then wrote it on the tin plate.

“Rank,” she said.

The man’s mouth moved again.

“Corporal.”

Sedge wrote that too.

“Where does it hurt?” she asked.

His eyes went to his left shoulder, then his right, then his ribs, then away. He swallowed. The effort seemed to cost him.

“Everywhere,” he said.

“Yes,” Sedge said. “That is usually how it is when everywhere is the honest answer. If you can be more specific, do it now. If you cannot, do not try to prove you can. You are not a man who needs to pass a test. You are a man who needs to stop bleeding from the inside by not tearing the outside.”

She checked his pulse again. It had climbed. 124. She wrote it.

“He is still talking,” Sedge said. “That is good. Talking uses air, but it also means the brain is still asking for oxygen. Do not waste the talking. If he starts to stop answering, tell me. If he starts to answer wrong, tell me. If he says something stupid, like he is fine, tell me anyway.”

She moved to his legs and checked the toes, the pulse at the ankle, the color of the skin. Still there. Still pale. Still boring, in the way she liked.

“Legs are boring,” Sedge said. “Boring is good. Boring means I am not cutting anything tonight.”

She took the folded blanket from the crate and shook it once. The tent air moved with the cloth. She laid it across the stretcher, then felt the stretcher canvas for holes. There were holes. Of course there were holes. She pressed her thumb through one and tested the stitching beside it.

“I am going to move him,” Sedge said. “Not now. When he is stable enough to be moved and not so stable that moving him is safe. That is the field medic’s arithmetic. If he lives, someone will write down how close it was. If he dies, someone will write down how close it was and call it a lesson. I do not care what they call it. I care that the next person knows what I did and what I could not fix.”

She checked the straps again. Then she checked his fingers. The right hand had improved slightly. The left had not.

Sedge looked at the left strap.

“Pressure,” she said. “Or nerve. Or the joint wanting to leave again.”

She lifted his left hand by the fingers. They curled weakly. She touched the outside of the shoulder, then the back of the arm, then the space between thumb and forefinger.

“Feel that?” she asked.

A blink.

“Move your fingers.”

The fingers moved, badly, one after another, like a man trying to wake a limb that had stopped trusting him.

“Not gone,” Sedge said. “Not good. The axillary nerve can bruise when the shoulder comes out. If it is bruised, he may lose feeling over the outside of the shoulder. If it is torn, I cannot sew it here. I cannot make him lift a rifle. I cannot make him carry a pack. I can only tell him the truth and hope he does not try to prove me wrong before I have finished working.”

She loosened the second strap by a small amount. Not enough to let the arm wander. Enough to stop squeezing the blood out of the hand. She tested it, slid two fingers under, then checked the shoulder position with her thumb along the joint.

“Still in,” she said. “Still angry.”

The man coughed. Sedge looked at his lips. Not blue. Not gray. Dry, cracked, pale.

“Airway clear,” she said. “Still not good enough.”

She took the tin cup and filled it only a little. She held it under his lips.

“Small sips,” she said. “If you gag, stop. If you cough, stop. If you feel water wanting to come back up, stop. If you vomit, I will turn your head and shoulders together. You will not twist. You will not lift. You will not be proud.”

He drank. A little. Less than before. Sedge wiped his chin with the damp cloth, not gently, not cruelly, simply to keep him from choking on the next sip.

“That is enough,” she said. “His stomach is empty. His throat is swollen. His body is tired. More water is not medicine. More water is a mistake waiting to happen.”

She set the cup aside and took the chalk again. She wrote the time. Then she wrote:

PULSE 124.  
BREATH 26.  
FINGERS LEFT PALE.  
LEFT STRAP LOOSENED.  
CHEST LEFT?  
RIBS?  
NAME ELIAS.  
RANK CORPORAL.  
DO NOT SIT.  
DO NOT LIFT.  
DO NOT DRINK MUCH.  
WATCH FINGERS.  
WATCH BREATH.

She underlined WATCH BREATH.

The lamp flickered. Sedge looked at it with the patience of a woman deciding whether the shadows were going to make her miss something. She moved it one finger’s width to the left, then stopped. The flame steadied, but the light still threw the tent into bad angles.

“I am not going to fix the light yet,” she said. “First I fix the patient. First I keep the fingers. First I keep the breathing.”

She checked his abdomen. The skin was cool and damp, the muscles not yet rigid, but there was a hardness low on the left side that made her pause. She pressed once, lightly, then withdrew.

The man’s breath hitched.

“Here,” Sedge said. “Here is another thing that was not shoulders.”

She wrote on the plate:

ABDOMEN TENDER LEFT.  
WATCH DISTENTION.  
NO FOOD.  
NO MUCH WATER.  
POSSIBLE BLEEDING.

She looked at the man.

“If there is blood inside your belly,” she said, “I cannot see it. I can feel what your body tells me to feel. If it gets hard, if it gets more tender, if your pulse climbs and your face goes white, if you get thirsty in a way that is not thirst, tell me. If you cannot tell me, he will tell me.”

She nodded toward the watching fingers, the breathing chest, the face that was not allowed to lie.

The man’s eyes moved to the ceiling. His chest rose faster than before. Sedge put her hand on his sternum, not pushing, not comforting, just showing him the table was there.

“Breathe,” she said. “Short breaths. Not big. Not deep. If you hyperventilate, you will feel worse, and I will be less patient.”

She checked his pulse. 128. She checked the capillary refill. Five seconds. Not blue. Not cold. Worse.

Sedge took the knife and cut the last inch of the left strap, then re-tied it with padding underneath, the knot small and hard. She checked the shoulder again. It stayed. The fingers stayed pale, but not blue.

“I am choosing circulation over perfection,” she said. “If the strap is too tight, I lose the hand. If the strap is too loose, he loses the shoulder. If he loses the shoulder, he may lose the arm. If he loses the arm, he may lose the life. That is not a lesson. That is arithmetic.”

She moved the stool closer and sat down again. She did not rest her hands. She kept them near the man’s wrist, ready to count, ready to feel, ready to decide whether the quiet was sleep or the beginning of something else.

The man’s voice came out small, almost lost under the canvas.

“Thank you.”

Sedge looked at him.

“No,” she said.

He blinked, confused.

“You may not thank me for not taking pleasure in this,” Sedge said. “If I took pleasure in it, I would be doing it wrong. You may thank me later, if later is possible, and if you do, I will tell you it was not kindness. It was competence. Do not confuse them.”

She turned back to Wick, though her eyes stayed on the man’s chest.

“Keep watching,” she said. “If his breathing changes, tell me. If his pulse gets faster and weaker, tell me. If his fingers go cold, tell me. If he says the pain has moved, tell me. If he says he is fine, tell me anyway.”

She took the chalk and wrote the next number as the pulse climbed again. 132.

The tent was quiet except for the man’s breath and the small creak of the table. Sedge watched the numbers, the fingers, the chest, the face that was trying to be brave and failing in a useful way.

“Not safe,” she said. “Still not safe. Still alive.”

She moved her stool an inch closer, set her hand near his wrist, and waited.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, throat too tight to speak. I watch his chest rise and fall, my own breathing matching the count in my head. After a minute, I find my voice. "His breathing's the same, but his lips look dryer."

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Bad like the socket is stretched. Bad like the capsule is torn.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: the ball of the arm bone was torn from the socket and left in the wrong place

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Food, stool, blood, and bacteria spill inside. The abdomen becomes a swamp.
