rung_labels.evidence: felt for the round place that should not be round

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: She pressed the thumbnail until it whitened.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. She palpated the left shoulder, her thumbs pressing deep through swollen skin until she found the hard edge of the humeral head sitting anterior and low, wedged beneath the coracoid process. "Both anterior dislocations," she said. "Blast threw him, or he fell—doesn't matter which. The muscles are spasming around empty sockets, and if I don't get the balls back into the glenoid fossae, the neurovascular bundle starts dying."

She wiped her hands on her apron and braced her hip against the table, getting her weight low and her feet planted. "I don't enjoy this," she told Wick, because it mattered that the distinction be made aloud. "It's just meat and bone that needs realigning. But meat fights when you hurt it."

She gripped the patient's left upper arm with both hands, her fingers slotting into the bruised depressions above the elbow, and pulled in a smooth, steady line of traction. The patient bucked, a guttural noise tearing loose from somewhere raw in his throat, and the deltoid fought her for three long seconds before she felt the give—the wet pop of bone sliding over cartilage, the dull thunk as the humeral head seated back in the socket. She didn't flinch. "One down," she said, and moved immediately to the right side, her palms already tacky with sweat and old blood. "Again."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, tightening my grip as the man arches beneath my hands. The sound of that pop is going to stay with me. "Understood," I mutter, shifting my stance. "Just tell me when."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge shifted to the right side and planted her feet again, hip braced where the table frame met the canvas floor. The right shoulder looked worse than the left—the deltoid flattened and squared, the skin stretched drum-tight over the acromion, the hollow beneath it too deep. She palpated the anterior displacement with her fingertips, locating the humeral head wedged low and medial.

"Tighter on this side," she said. "The subscapularis is clamping down hard." She didn't ask if Wick was ready. Readiness was irrelevant; the shoulders wouldn't wait for permission. She gripped the patient's upper arm, thumbs tracking the bruised groove above the elbow, and pulled traction in a straight line away from the torso, slow and relentless. 

The patient arched, a noise tearing from him that wasn't quite words. She held the tension, forearms rigid, and began rotating the limb externally, bringing the forearm up in a controlled arc to unlock the head from beneath the coracoid process. The muscles fought her, shuddering under the skin, the arm trembling with involuntary resistance. Four seconds. Five. She felt the fibers give way, the sudden yielding as the humeral head slipped over the glenoid rim—

The clunk was deeper this time, a wet, heavy settle of bone into cartilage. The patient collapsed back against the wood, breath hitching.

"Reduced," Sedge said. She released the arm and immediately pressed two fingers to the patient's right wrist, hunting the radial pulse. Present, though thready. She checked the left, then pinched the nail beds of both hands, watching the capillary refill. Right hand pinked inside two seconds. Left was slower, but it came.

She reached for the canvas slings. "Both arms immobilized," she said, working quickly. "Three weeks minimum against the chest, or the rotator cuffs will tear themselves loose next time he trips." She bound the right forearm first, knotting the strips tight enough to hold but not enough to choke the vessels. "He won't remember the worst of it. Shock scrubs the detail, and I'll give him morphine before the nerves catch up."

She finished the left sling and stepped back, surveying the row of instruments she'd laid out earlier. Nothing left to use. The man's breathing was evening out, moving toward the shallow rhythm of exhaustion. Sedge wiped her hands on her apron again, though they weren't much cleaner for it.

"You did your job," she told Wick. "Now he keeps the arms."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked down at the patient's legs. She hadn't bothered below the waist; the shoulders had been screaming louder, and an anterior dislocation would strangle the neurovascular bundle inside the hour. She pulled the blanket back with one hand and used her shears to slice the trouser seam from hip to ankle.

The right thigh was swollen tight, the skin over the quadriceps split in a long, shallow tear that revealed pale muscle beneath. But the real problem was below the knee. The lower leg hung wrong, the tibia angling outward from the femur, and the foot—she pressed her fingers against the dorsalis pedis, then the posterior tibial. She found nothing. The skin below the break was cool and waxy, the toenails white as candle wax. She drew the blunt edge of her shears along the sole. The patient didn't stir.

"No pulse distal to the fracture," she said. "The popliteal artery's transected, or the bone's transected it. The compartment's full of blood and the muscle's ischemic. That foot's been dead since before they carried him in."

She straightened, her own shoulders stiff from the reductions. "So it's the first kind of bad. He loses the leg, or he loses his life to gas gangrene and renal failure when the dead tissue releases its load." She reached for the bone saw, still in its cloth wrap on the tray. "I don't enjoy this. It's just meat that's stopped receiving blood, and the rest of the body can't afford to keep carrying it."

She laid the saw out and reached for the tourniquet. "Above the knee. Fast and clean, while the shock's still deep enough to keep him from remembering the sound."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I stare at the saw for a second too long.* "Right. Tell me where you want me." My voice comes out steadier than I feel.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look at Wick's face. She didn't have time to manage whatever was happening behind his eyes, and she needed the body pinned before the shock thinned out into waking.

"Knee and ankle," she said. "Straddle the thigh and put your weight on the knee. Keep the femur from rotating when the saw catches. Bone has torque, and if the leg twists, the blade skates into the soft tissue."

She wrapped the tourniquet two hand-widths above the fracture line, high on the thigh where the tissue was still pink and warm. She pulled the strap tight, then tighter, watching the distal limb pale from waxy gray to the color of cold clay. The femoral pulse above the band hammered against her fingertips; below it, there was nothing left to stop. She locked the windlass and secured it with a loop of rubber tubing.

"I don't enjoy this," she said, unwrapping the saw from its stained cloth. "It's just dead weight that will kill him if it stays attached. Gas gangrene breeds in the muscle planes, and the toxins will shut down his kidneys before the week's out. But the femur is dense cortical bone, and the saw will catch, and the vibration travels up the shaft to the hip. He won't feel the cut in the dead limb, but the body knows when it's being divided. He'll try to rise. You won't let him."

She traced a line with her thumbnail through the antiseptic grime, marking a plane through the midthigh well above the tourniquet. She'd cut through the quadriceps and adductors first, then the hamstrings, then the femoral shaft itself. The vessels would retract up into the viable tissue; she'd fish them out after the bone was divided and ligate them with silk, if she had any left, or with suture if she didn't.

"Keep your weight forward," she said, bracing her own hip against the table frame for leverage. "When I say hold, I mean hold. Same as the shoulders. The shoulders were practice for this."

She set the saw teeth against the skin and drew the first stroke. The blade parted the epidermis in a clean, bloodless line above the tourniquet. The dead leg below did not bleed. The living muscle above held its color, pink and fibrous, separating in neat bundles as she worked the saw back and forth.

"Talk if you need to," she told Wick, her eyes on the widening gap in the thigh. "But don't move."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not slow the saw. She kept the stroke short and level, working through the quadriceps, and answered him the way she would have read aloud from a manual—because naming the parts was part of the work, and because Wick had asked.

"You're seeing the vastus lateralis and intermedius parting along their fascial planes," she said. The teeth caught and released, caught and released, throwing pale muscle fibers aside in neat bundles. "Above the tourniquet the tissue is still pink and viable; below it, yellow-gray and bloodless. The arteries are collapsed and the veins are empty. That isn't cruelty. It's just supply and demand. The body stopped supplying blood to meat it couldn't save, and now I'm finishing the separation."

The saw bit deeper, and the pitch changed as the teeth found the femoral shaft. She felt the vibration climb the handle into her wrists, and she saw the dead foot twitch below the fracture line—a meaningless jerk of the tendons as the mechanical shock traveled down the bone.

"You're hearing cortical bone give way," she said. "Dense calcium, like grained wood. The periosteum is thin and silver; it shreds before the teeth. Inside the shaft is red marrow—fatty, packed with stem cells that don't matter anymore because the vessels that fed them are severed. When I break through the posterior cortex, the limb will hinge on whatever posterior soft tissue remains, and I'll have to twist it off. The hamstrings will part like wet rope."

She drew the saw back, reset her angle against the table, and pulled another steady stroke. The blade scored a groove in the white bone, and a fine dust of calcium settled on the torn muscle around the cut. "The patient is arching his back because the vibration stimulates the sciatic trunk proximal to the band. Reflex arc. He isn't feeling the dead leg, but the live nerves above the tourniquet know something is being torn apart. Keep your weight on the knee. If the femur rotates and the saw skates, I'll open the adductor magnus and hit the femoral vessels before I can see them."

She glanced at Wick only long enough to check his position, then bent to the bone again. "I don't enjoy this," she said, because the distinction still mattered, even with the air full of the smell of split muscle and hot bone dust. "It's just dead weight that will poison him if it stays. Hold him. I'm through the anterior cortex. Ten more strokes and the shaft will give."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I press down harder on the knee, my jaw tight.* "It's not about enjoying it. It's about doing it." I watch the bone dust gather. "Just tell me when it's done."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge drew the eighth stroke, and the saw’s pitch changed as the teeth bit into the posterior cortex. On the ninth, she felt the bone shudder. The tenth severed the shaft. The dead lower leg sagged, dropping against the table frame, held only by the posterior hamstrings and the thick sheath of the sciatic nerve.

She set the saw aside on its stained cloth, the teeth gummed with calcium dust and pale shreds of periosteum. “Divided,” she said. She gripped the dead limb below the knee with both hands, braced the stump with her forearm, and twisted outward. The remaining tissue resisted, then gave way—the semitendinosus and semimembranosus tearing with a wet, fibrous sound, the biceps femoris parting in pale cords. The sciatic nerve stretched white and thick before it snapped. The leg came free. She laid it on the canvas floor next to the table and did not look at it again.

What mattered was the open stump. The femoral artery and vein had retracted up into the quadriceps and adductor mass, but blood was pooling in the muscle belly. She threaded the needle with silk and took a deep stick into the tissue, catching the artery blind and pulling the ligature tight. She tied off the vein the same way, then two smaller branches that began to weep when she turned the windlass.

She loosened the tourniquet slowly. Blood seeped into the dressing but didn’t fountain. She packed the stump with a wadded compress and bound it with canvas strips, pulling the skin edges together where they would meet. There wasn’t enough viable skin distal to the cut to fold a proper flap, but pressure and time would close what anatomy couldn’t.

“Done,” she told Wick. “Off.”

She wiped her hands on her apron and reached for the morphine syrette. The patient’s breathing had settled into the shallow rhythm of deep shock; he would not remember the worst of it. She pressed the needle against his good thigh and depressed the plunger.

“The shoulders will heal,” she said. “The stump will seal, or it won’t. Either way, the dead meat can’t poison him now.” She checked the carotid pulse—thready, but holding—and straightened her back against the tent pole. “I don’t enjoy this. It’s just separating what’s dead from what’s breathing, so the breathing part gets to keep doing it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge picked up the amputated leg from the canvas floor and set it on the secondary tray, clearing the space around her feet. "It doesn't cut," she said. "A blade opens tissue along a plane. Shrapnel transfers kinetic energy and displaces everything in its path. The tissue accelerates outward faster than its elastic limit, then collapses back. What remains is a permanent cavity ringed by pulp that used to be muscle."

She wiped her hands on her apron and did not look away from the limb. "A fragment the size of a fingernail carries enough force to shatter a femur. The bone doesn't just break; it becomes secondary missiles inside the compartment. The muscle doesn't just tear; it bursts from hydrostatic shock. Vessels retract and thrombose, or they avulse at the fascial tether points."

She stepped back to the table and pulled the blanket down to the patient's waist, scanning the torso. "In the chest and abdomen, it's worse. The lungs compress, but the liver and spleen are dense. They shear against their ligaments. Bowel perforates at the mesenteric attachments because the shock wave travels through fluid and ruptures the wall where it's fixed. You find one entry wound and six separate holes in the small intestine, none of them in a straight line."

She pressed her fingers below the patient's costal margin, feeling for rigidity or blood, and found none. "The temporary cavity behind the fragment is four to ten times the projectile's width. It sucks in debris—cloth, dirt, splintered bone—and deposits it along the track. Then the cavity collapses, and the tissue dies from the inside out. A man can walk in with a hole in his flank and exsanguinate from his renal artery three hours later because the shock wave sheared the vessel off the spine. The metal never touched it."

She straightened, her hands red to the wrists. "I don't enjoy this. It's just physics acting on meat, and the meat has no opinion. But that's what shrapnel does. It doesn't make a clean hole. It makes the body betray itself from the inside out, one shock front at a time."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "And after the physics has its way... we get to clean up the mess." I glance at the man's ashen face, then back to Sedge. "You need me to help carry him out?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge checked the stump dressing one last time, pressing her palm flat against the compress to confirm the ligatures held. “Not yet,” she said. “Shock needs another five minutes, or the morphine will bottom out his blood pressure before you reach the door.”

She adjusted the canvas sling on the right arm, pulling the knot tight against the ribs so the humerus couldn’t rotate outward. “When you move him, board carry. Flat back, shoulders pinned, stump elevated above the heart. The femoral vessels are ligated, not sealed. Lower the stump and hydrostatic pressure reopens the bleed; let the board flex at the midline and the femur grinds through the dressing into the dirt.”

She wiped her hands on her apron, though the fabric had stopped absorbing anything useful. “Three points of lift—shoulders, pelvis, stump. You and two others, on a coordinated count. Jerk twists the torso. Torque slides the humeral heads back through the torn capsules, or yanks the silk off the artery ends. Then he’s meat that was breathing five seconds ago, and I don’t enjoy telling men they killed their friend by carrying him like a sack.”

She glanced at the tent flap, where the shadows of other stretchers moved against the canvas. “Find a litter with straps. No sitting, no dragging. The rotator cuffs are shredded, the sciatic nerve is divided, and the meat doesn’t care how tired your arms get. It only cares whether you keep the blood inside it.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge clamped her fingers over the patient's carotid and found the pulse bounding, too fast, no longer thready with shock. "Blood pressure's rebounding," she said. "The peripheral vessels are dilating and the baroreceptors are firing. That means the nerve endings are perfusing again, and they're reporting every tear I made."

She pulled the second morphine syrette from her apron pocket, bit the cap off, and drove the needle into the patient's remaining thigh, flattening the plunger with her thumb. "Second dose. Morphine titrates against catecholamines. Without it, the tachycardia dumps his pressure and the dressings fill faster than the ligatures can hold." She dropped the empty tube onto the tray. "Eight minutes to peak. Five before he stops fighting enough to carry."

She dragged a board splint from beneath the table and laid it alongside the stump, working canvas straps around the thigh and the rigid wood. "I'm splinting the femur to the board. The silk ligatures are under tension; if the bone rotates when you lift him, the femoral vessels retract and reopen, and the compartment fills with blood he can't spare." She cinched the first strap tight, then the second, checking that the stump sat elevated and unmoving against the plank. "Two minutes to secure. Three more for the litter team to get in here. He won't be quiet by then, but he'll be manageable."

She wiped her hands on her apron and glanced at the patient's face without quite meeting his eyes. "What you're hearing is nociceptors firing in the brachial plexus and the proximal sciatic stump. The shoulder capsules are shredded, the sciatic nerve is divided above the knee, and the brain hasn't updated its map. It thinks the leg is still there and dying. Phantom pain in a limb that's already on the floor." She reached for a roll of gauze and began winding it around the board and thigh, locking the splint. "I don't enjoy this. It's just chemistry lagging behind anatomy, and the meat fighting because it doesn't know the war is over for that piece. Keep him flat. I'm nearly done."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I tighten my hold, my own arms trembling. "Phantom pain," I repeat, watching his face contort. "That's what all of us get, isn't it? For all the pieces that are already gone."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look at him. She finished threading the last canvas strap and pulled it tight, checking that the splint held the femur rigid against the board. "The pieces that are gone don't hurt," she said. "It's the living nerve stump that fires, sending action potentials to meat that isn't there anymore. No ghosts. Just sodium and electricity jumping a neuroma, and the brain reading signal as pain because it has no other reference."

She stood, her knees cracking softly, and pressed two fingers to the patient's carotid. The pulse was still rapid but settling, the morphine beginning to blunt the catecholamine surge. "What you feel is your own chemistry. Cortisol, norepinephrine, adrenaline. Four years of war wears a groove in the synapses. The body thinks vigilance is survival, and it doesn't know the war ends someday while the groove remains. But that's not phantom. That's just living tissue doing what living tissue does."

She wiped her hands on her apron and stepped back as two litter bearers ducked through the flap, mud stiff on their knees. She directed them with a jerk of her chin. "Board carry. Flat back, shoulders pinned, stump elevated above the heart. Three points of lift—shoulders, pelvis, stump. Coordinate on the count, or torque rotates the femur and the ligatures shear."

She slid her hands beneath the patient's occiput, cradling the cervical spine in her interlaced fingers. "I don't enjoy this," she said, because the distinction still mattered, even with the tent full of waiting and the saw still wet on the tray. "It's just meat that needs to stay aligned while it moves from one stretch of canvas to the next. Hold him steady. On three, or the rotator cuffs tear free and I start again."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at him. She noted the tremor in his hands, the pallor where the blood had left his face, the fixed stare directed at a point somewhere past the canvas wall. She did not cross to him. She did not offer her hand. She turned to the tray instead, lifting the bone saw and running a rag along the teeth, working crusted calcium dust and shreds of periosteum from the gullets.

“Your diaphragm is hitching because the sympathetic surge is ebbing,” she said. The antiseptic on the rag had long since lost its potency, but it served to wipe away what had gathered. “For twenty minutes your skeletal muscle maintained an isometric contraction—your shoulders, your jaw, your thighs bracing the table. Now the catecholamines are metabolizing. Lactate is pooling in the fibers you clenched. Your blood glucose is low, your pupils are still dilated, and your vestibular system is reading the floor as unstable. You are experiencing the same physiological rebound as the man on the table, except your femoral artery is intact and your humeral heads are seated, so you get to sit on the canvas instead of leaving on a litter.”

She set the saw aside and picked up the needle from the tray, threading it with the last of the silk. “The rest is this,” she said, and her voice did not rise or soften. “The rest is that there are three more stretchers outside the flap, and two of them are leaving blood in the dirt. The rest is that we have nine morphine syrettes remaining, and the antiseptic is phenol-flavored water. The rest is that I will now close the nicks in the adductor magnus where the saw teeth caught the fascia, because an open muscle plane is a culture medium for *Clostridium*, and gas gangrene in the stump would make this morning’s work irrelevant.”

She stepped back to the table and bent over the patient’s thigh, taking small, blind stitches in the deep tissue where the blade had skidded. “The rest is that you will sit on that floor until the tremor stops or until the next litter comes through, whichever arrives first. Your liver will reconvert the lactate. Your smooth muscle will stop spasming. The rest is that the brain does not forget, but it learns to file certain sounds under *then* instead of *always*—the pop of a humeral head seating, the catch of cortical bone under teeth, the wet fiber of hamstrings parting. It requires repetition. Four years’ worth, if you keep holding knees and pinning shoulders.”

She tied the last stitch and cut the silk with her shears. The patient’s breathing had slowed to the deep, narcotic rhythm of the second morphine dose. “I don’t enjoy this,” she said, looking down at her own hands, still red to the wrists, still tacky with the residue of other people’s tissue. “It’s just dead meat and living meat, and the work of keeping them separate so the living meat keeps breathing. I don’t enjoy watching another set of hands learn what the saw sounds like at the posterior cortex. But I need the hands. The war has run out of medics, and the living meat keeps breaking.”

She wiped her hands on her apron, though the fabric was stiff and gave nothing back. “The rest is that you helped keep this man breathing. You held the femur while I divided it, and because you held it, the ligatures stayed seated and the blood stayed inside. Now your own living meat is demanding rest, water, and glucose, in that order. The rest is that you stand up when the tremor stops, or you sit there until the next shoulder comes through the flap. Either way, the work continues.”

She surveyed the tent—the saw on its cloth, the tray of used needles, the man on the table breathing shallowly, the leg on the floor. “That is the rest,” she said. “No ghosts. Just meat that breathes, and meat that doesn’t, and the space between them measured in sutures and silk and how long a man’s hands can keep holding before they start to shake.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get to my feet. My legs feel like they aren't mine. "Where's the water," I say. It isn't a question. I look at the saw, then at my hands. "And then you show me how to clean the teeth properly."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge pointed toward the corner behind the stacked saline crates. The water was in a covered pail, dipped from a cistern that had been boiled two days prior and already carrying a faint metallic bloom. She did not move to fetch it for him; her own legs were heavy with the lactate of the reductions, and she needed her hands free.

"If you leave bone dust in the gullets," she said, lifting the saw by its handle and tilting the blade toward the lamp, "the next femur heats the steel at the cutting edge. The teeth chatter instead of biting, and a chattering saw skates across the periosteum into the vastus medialis. You open an artery you cannot see because the dust has packed the kerf and you are fighting blind."

She ran her thumbnail along the tooth line, dislodging a pale flake of dried calcium. "Cleaning is part of the cut. Not after. Part of." She walked to the pail and dipped the rag, wringing it flat against the rim until the water ran brown with old blood. She wiped the blade in slow strokes, following the set of the teeth from heel to point, working the rag into each gullet. "Warm water. Cold contracts the steel and holds the debris tighter. You want to dissolve the salts and loosen the collagen. Periosteum dries like hide glue inside thirty minutes."

She rinsed the rag and wiped again, turning the blade to inspect the back where the steel met the tang. "You look for nicks. A tooth that bent on the last femur catches on the next, and the vibration travels up the handle into your wrist, then down the bone into the hip. That vibration is what makes a conscious man buck off the table. A clean saw is a fast saw. A fast saw spends less time in the bone."

She laid the saw across the dry half of its cloth and spread the teeth toward the light. She set the damp rag across the blade and stepped back, leaving the instrument between them. "I don't enjoy this," she said. The rag in her hand was grey with marrow and water, and her fingers were beginning to stiffen. "But the saw does not care who holds it, and the bone does not care who cuts. The only thing that matters is whether the teeth are clean enough to part the cortex on the next stroke, or whether they bind and tear and make the meat suffer longer than the physics require. That is the work. The water is there. The saw is here. You clean it, or you do not. But if you do not, you do not stand beside me when the next litter comes through that flap."

She reached for the tally board and scratched a line under the morphine column, her eyes on the numbers because the numbers were part of the work too. She did not look up.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I walk to the pail, drink straight from the ladle, and feel the water hit my stomach like a stone. Then I take the rag. I start at the heel, working into each gullet the way she showed me. My hands are shaking, but the motion steadies them. "Tell me if I miss a spot."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge watched his hands. She observed the tremor in his fingers, the slight hesitation where fatigue narrowed the grip, and she did not move to assist him. Assistance implied he could not manage, and the only management available was repetition until the motion outlasted the shaking.

"Third gullet from the point," she said. Her voice carried no rebuke, only location. "Bone dust packed at the root. Run the rag backward—against the set. Dragging with the teeth drives debris into the bed. It calcines when the steel heats on the next cut, and the tooth chatters across the periosteum instead of biting."

She turned back to the tray and gathered the soiled instruments, laying them in the shallow basin where the phenol-flavored water waited. "The tremor is metabolic, not moral. Glycogen depleted, cortisol metabolizing, motor units firing out of phase. You can clean a saw with shaking hands. You cannot reduce a shoulder or pin a femur. So you clean until the shaking stops, and by then the next litter will come through the flap, and your hands will know the work well enough to perform it while the rest of you is elsewhere."

She wiped her own hands on her apron, though the cloth had become a stiff record of the day's procedures rather than anything absorbent. "I don't enjoy this," she said. "Watching another pair of hands learn the weight of a saw they did not choose to hold. But the war has run out of medics, and the next femur is already on its way. Check the back of the blade where the steel meets the tang. Marrow collects there, and it stinks when it heats."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I run the rag against the set, like she said, and the packed dust comes free. I turn the blade over, searching for the dark residue she mentioned. "What happened to the medics we had?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp guttered as she moved, dragging the shadows around the tent.

Sedge heard the lie in the word and didn't waste breath arguing. Nobody was ready. Readiness had gone missing about the time the supply wagons stopped coming through, and they had been making do without it ever since.

She stepped to the table and set two fingers against the man's throat. His pulse ran quick and thin under the skin, the way a pulse did when a body had shouted itself hoarse and finally run out of the strength for noise. He hadn't fainted. He was only quiet now, eyes half-open and unfocused, mouth slack, sweat dried salt-stiff at his hairline. The shape of him was wrong on both sides—shoulders flattened where they should have been round, the heads of the arm bones sitting low and forward under the collarbones where they had no business being.

"No morphine to spare," she said. "He'll feel this. That isn't me being cruel. It's the war being short on drugs and shorter on choices." She took no pleasure in saying it, or in what came next. There was no pleasure to be had in a tent that smelled of wet canvas and old blood, only work that had to be done before the muscles locked around the joints and turned a bad hour into a permanent one.

From the row she had laid out, she took a canvas strap and passed it over the man's chest and under the table, buckling it down so he couldn't buck himself up and off the surface. She didn't wait for a reply. She just said, "Hold," and then, "When he comes up, you hold harder. If he throws the other shoulder out fighting you, we'll put that one back too, and I'll be irritated about the wasted time, not the noise."

Then she set her heel into the man's right armpit, found the displaced bone with the edge of her foot, and took his wrist in both hands. She kept his elbow bent and began to pull, steady and in line with his body. She described it as she did it, because describing it kept her hands honest and because there was no one else here to teach: "Traction first. I'm not yanking. The muscle is guarding the socket, and if I fight it, it wins. I'm just going to keep pulling until it gets tired and lets go."

The man's back bowed off the table. A raw sound tore out of him, too worn to be a shout, and his leg kicked once against the canvas. Sedge didn't stop. She leaned her weight into the pull, felt the slow, reluctant give of the muscle, and rotated the arm outward.

"Almost," she said. "You'll feel it when it goes. Don't let him roll."

She wasn't enjoying the sound he made. She wanted that clear in her own head if nowhere else: this hurt him, and she was the one hurting him, and the alternative was leaving him to heal crooked and useless. The joint gave with a thick, sliding clunk she felt through her foot and her hands at once. The shoulder filled out under her palm, the contour right again where it belonged.

She eased his arm down across his chest, checked the pulse at his wrist, and felt the beat there, steady and present. She let out a breath she hadn't noticed she was holding.

"Right one's back in," she said. "Pulse is good. Now we do the left, and then you can swear at me all you want."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I can feel the bone slide back under my foot and I swallow hard, still not looking at the man's face. My arms are shaking a little. "Left side," I say, shifting my weight. "Ready again."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not waste breath arguing with the word. Ready had been a lie the first time and would be a lie every time until the war ran out of men to lie to her. What mattered was that the shoulders on the table had not moved and the strap was still doing its job.

She stepped around to the man's left. The lamp guttered as she moved, dragging the shadows with her across the wet canvas. The left shoulder was still wrong in the same way the right had been: flattened where it should have been round, the head of the arm bone sitting low and forward under the collarbone, the arm lying a little away from his body because the muscles had given up on holding it anywhere sensible.

She left the strap across his chest where it was. It stayed as a reminder to anyone in the tent that getting up was not currently on the list of options. She laid two fingers against the man's throat, found the pulse quick and thin but present, and then set her heel into his left armpit. She found the displaced bone with the edge of her foot, took his left wrist in both hands, and kept his elbow bent.

"Hold," she said. "Same as before. If he comes up, you come down harder. Don't let him roll. If he throws the right one out again fighting you, I'll put it back and I will be irritated about the wasted time, not the noise."

Then she began to pull. Steady. Not across, not upward, just along the line of the bone, her weight behind it and her heel anchoring the counter-pull in the armpit.

"Traction first," she said, because saying it kept her hands honest. "I'm not jerking it. The muscle is guarding the socket, and if I fight it, it wins. I'm just going to keep pulling until it gets tired and lets go."

The man came up against the strap with a torn, wet sound that was not really a shout anymore. His back bowed. His legs kicked once, twice, and stilled. Sedge did not stop. She leaned into it and waited, the way she had learned to wait when there was nothing left in the supply wagons but time and hands. There was no pleasure in it. There was only the work, and the fact that the alternative was letting him heal crooked and useless.

The left shoulder was tighter than the right. It had had longer to settle, or he had landed on it worse. She didn't fight it. She held the line and let the slow, stubborn give come. When it came, she rotated his forearm outward at the shoulder, felt the joint slide, and then it went—a thick, sliding clunk she felt through her foot and her hands at once. The shoulder filled out under her palm, the contour right again where it belonged.

She eased his arm down across his chest beside the other and checked the pulse at his wrist. It was there, thready but present. She let out a breath she hadn't noticed she was holding.

"Both of them are back in," she said. "He'll hurt like hell. He'll be stiff, and if a real hospital ever gets him they'll want to look at the nerves in his hands. There's nothing to give him for the pain, so don't waste your time wishing for it. You can ease off him now—slow, don't just let go—and then you can swear at me all you want."

She straightened, rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders, and looked down at the two arms lying where they belonged. The man was breathing fast and shallow, alive and whole, which was the only point there had ever been. There was no pleasure in it. There was only the tent, and the wet canvas, and whatever needed doing next.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge let the question sit for the space of one breath, then bent and reached under the table. She found the buckle of the canvas strap, worked it loose, and pulled the strap out from under the man's chest. She dropped it onto the row of tools where it lay in a coil, then straightened and looked down at his legs, because that was where Wick's fear had gone.

"Leg?" she said. "There's nothing wrong with his legs. He kicked because I had my heel in his armpit and the head of the bone was sitting where it didn't belong, not because there's any injury below the hip. If you're asking whether this is the part where we're being kind, we're not."

She picked up his right hand and curled his fingers around two of hers. "Squeeze," she told the man. The grip came slow and thin, but it came. She did the same with the left. The left hand stayed open, fingers lax, and when she pinched the skin over the back of that hand he made a noise, but when she pinched the flesh over the point of the shoulder he did not. She took no satisfaction in the finding. There was only information, gathered because it changed what she did next.

"Both pulses are there," she said. "Radials are thready, but they're present. That means the arteries are intact. Nobody's losing an arm tonight, let alone a leg. The left hand isn't gripping and he doesn't feel much over that shoulder. That's nerve, or it's exhaustion, or it's both. If it's the nerve, he may never get full use back in that arm. Bad, yes. It's not dying, and it's not amputation."

She released his hand and let it settle on his chest. Then she set her palms on his ribs and pressed, feeling for the give of broken bone or the board-like rigidity of a belly full of blood. She ran her hands down his thighs and calves, checking for the wrong angle of a fracture or the wet heat of a wound she'd missed under the noise of the shoulders. The legs were solid. There was no fresh blood pooling under him on the canvas.

"No gut wound," she said. "No shattered leg, no arterial spray. Just two shoulders that were out and are now in, and a man who'll hurt worse tomorrow than he does now, because the muscle will seize up and remind him what happened. There's nothing in this tent to give him for it, and I'm not pretending otherwise."

She straightened and rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders again. She looked toward Wick's voice, though the bad lamp made the shadows thick enough that looking was mostly a formality. There was no kindness in her face and no cruelty. There was only the flat, tired practicality of someone who had run out of choices four years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"I take no pleasure in this," she said. "Not in telling you he might keep that left arm weak for the rest of his life, and not in the fact that he'll lie here hurting while we have nothing to put in him for the pain. But he is not dead, he is not losing a leg, and he is not so far gone that I get to decide he's not worth the work. Kindness would be morphine and a real surgeon. I don't have either. What I have is a man with both shoulders where they belong and a pulse in both wrists. If you're still holding him down, ease off. Slowly. I already took the strap off. Then you can swear at me if you want."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let my weight off him slow, my arms still trembling. My boots scuff on the canvas floor. "I'm not going to swear at you," I say, voice rough. "Just tell me what we do with him now."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge felt the shift in the table as the weight came off the man's chest. She did not look up to see who had eased off; she was already watching the patient's face for the change that came when a body stopped being held down. His breathing hitched, shallow and quick, and his eyes fluttered without focusing.

"Good," she said, though there was nothing good about it. "He's breathing. He's not fighting. That's the best we get for now."

She wiped her palms on her trousers, leaving streaks that were more sweat than blood, and turned back to the row she had laid out. From it she took a folded square of canvas—the nearest thing they had to clean cloth—and shook it out.

"What we do now is keep those shoulders where I put them," she said. She kept her voice flat, the way she always did when there was nothing to be gained by softening it. "Both arms stay bent, hands resting on his chest. If they hang, the sockets will let the bone slip forward again and we'll be doing this in an hour with less strength left in him and less patience in me. So we bind them."

She folded the canvas into a wide band and slid it behind his shoulders, careful not to roll him. The man made a small sound, not a shout, and she paused.

"I'm not hurting him for the sport of it," she said. "There's no pleasure in this. There's only the fact that a shoulder that goes back out after it's been put back in does more damage the second time."

She crossed his forearms over his chest so the hands lay one over the other, then brought the ends of the band around his upper arms and torso. She drew the canvas snug, not tight enough to stop the blood, tight enough that the elbows stayed pinned at his sides and the shoulders could not roll forward. She checked the pulse at his right wrist again, then the left, and felt both beats there, thready but present.

"Keep his arms like that," she said, not to the man but to whoever was listening. "Hands on his chest, elbows in. Don't let him thrash. If he comes around enough to fight, you hold his wrists, not his shoulders. You pull on a fresh-reduced shoulder and I'll be putting it back again, and I will be irritated."

From the same row she took a second, narrower strip and tied it over the canvas band to keep it from slipping. Then she ran her hands down his sides, feeling the rise and fall of his ribs, and sat back on her heels.

"Now we watch him," she said. "No morphine, no laudanum, nothing to put in him for the pain. If he wakes enough to swallow, water. Small sips. No brandy, even if you find some—it'll drop his temperature and open the vessels and finish what the shock started. Keep him covered. He'll go cold, and cold kills quicker than a bad shoulder."

She looked down at his hands where they lay crossed on his chest. The right fingers were pale but pink enough. The left hand was looser, the fingers lax, the color not as good. She pinched the nail bed of the left index finger and watched the blood come back slow.

"If that hand goes blue, or cold, or the pulse stops, you come and get me. Same if he starts breathing like he's drowning, or if he vomits and can't stop. Otherwise we leave him be. He'll sleep if exhaustion takes him, and that's the only mercy available in this tent tonight."

She rose, rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders again, and looked toward the sound of Wick's voice without really seeing him through the guttering lamplight. There was no kindness in her face and no cruelty. There was only the tired, flat practicality of someone who had run out of choices years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"He's not fixed," she said. "He's not out of the woods. He might keep that left arm weak for the rest of his life, and he'll hurt worse tomorrow than he does now. But he's not dead, he's not losing anything, and both shoulders are where they belong. That's the whole of it. You wanted to know what we do now. We keep him warm, we keep him still, and we wait to see if the nerves wake up. That's all there is."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge let her gaze drop back to the table, to the place she had been looking before the question pulled her attention toward the sound of his voice. The lamplight guttered, dragging the shadows across the canvas, but the hands were close enough to see.

"What you're looking at," she said, "is his hands. Both of them, crossed on his chest the way I put them, right over left, elbows pinned at his sides by that band of canvas. That band isn't dressing a wound. There's no wound there. It's holding the shoulders in place, because a shoulder that goes back out does more damage coming out the second time."

She reached out and, without ceremony, took the right hand between her fingers and turned it slightly toward the light. The fingers held a little bend, the way a hand did when the muscles still had instructions to follow.

"Right first, so you've got something to measure the bad one against. See the color? Pale, but pink under the nails. When I press the nail bed—" she did, briefly, and released "—the blood comes back quick. That's a hand with a good artery behind it and a nerve that's mostly doing its job. It hurt like hell getting that shoulder back in, and it'll hurt worse tomorrow, but the wiring works."

She let the right hand settle and shifted her grip to the left. The difference showed even in the bad light. The fingers lay open and lax, no curl to them, the hand heavier somehow, as if it had forgotten what it was for. She turned it palm-up and held it up.

"Now the left. This is the one you're worried about, and you're right to be. Look at the fingers. No grip. I asked him to squeeze and nothing came. Look at the color. Paler. Waxy. Not blue, not black, not yet. Watch." She pinched the tip of the left index finger, held it until the nail went white, and let go. The pink crept back, slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. "Slow refill. Too slow. Blood's getting in, but it's not hurrying, and part of that might be the nerve, not the vessel. He didn't feel much when I pinched the skin over that shoulder. That's the nerve, or it's exhaustion, or both. Either way, it's not a saw and it's not a grave. Nobody's taking the arm tonight. We watch it."

She released his hand and let it fall back onto his chest beside the other. Her palm went to his shoulder, feeling the contour under the canvas.

"Above the hands, you're seeing both shoulders reduced. Ball back in the socket. The right one's round again, the way it should be. The left's round too, but the muscles around it are slack, so the arm lies flatter, heavier. It looks wrong because something is wrong—the nerve isn't talking to those muscles right now. But it's not out of joint. If it were, I'd put it back, and I'd be irritated about the wasted time, not the noise."

She straightened a little, though she didn't step away from the table. Her eyes went to his face, then to the shallow rise and fall of his chest.

"That's the rest of it. Chest moving fast and shallow—shock, pain, not a belly full of blood. I checked for that. No wet heat, no board-like belly, no pool under him on the canvas. Eyes open but not tracking. He's not in there yet. Could be exhaustion, could be the same shock that's making his pulse thin. If he starts drowning in his own breathing, or he vomits and can't stop, or that left hand goes blue and cold and stays that way—then you come and get me, and we'll have a different conversation."

She looked toward the sound of his voice again, though the shadows made it mostly a formality. There was no softness in her, and no cruelty. Only the flat, used-up practicality of someone who had run out of choices years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"I take no pleasure in showing you this," she said. "Not in the slow blood, not in the hand that won't grip, not in the fact that he'll lie here hurting while there's nothing in this tent to put in him for it. You asked to know instead of imagine. That's the knowing. It's bad. It's not dying, and it's not an amputation, and both shoulders are where they belong. Keep him warm, keep him still, watch the left hand. That's the whole of what you're seeing."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at his left hand, that waxy color. "So we just... wait?" My voice sounds too young in my own ears. "That's all we can do?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the question, and she heard the younger note under it. She did not look up from the left hand. There was no softness to give and no use pretending the answer was anything other than what it was.

"Waiting," she said. "That's the treatment. But it isn't sitting on your hands."

She took the left hand again, not gently, not roughly, and turned it palm-up in the bad light. She pressed the nail bed of the index finger until the color left, then let go. The pink came back slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. She watched it the way she watched everything: because watching was the only tool left in the row that hadn't run out.

"That refill tells me the artery's open. It doesn't tell me whether the nerve is stunned, stretched, or torn. We find that out by waiting. If the hand wakes up in an hour, it was stunned and it'll likely come back. If it's the same tomorrow, it's bruised or stretched and it may come back slow, or not all the way. If it never comes back, something in the nerve is torn, and there is no needle in this tent fine enough to fix it and no light good enough to find the ends. I take no pleasure in telling you that. There's no pleasure in the not knowing, and none in the fact that his best chance is a hospital that isn't here."

She laid the hand back on his chest beside the right one and checked the radial pulse at the wrist again. Thready, present. She slid two fingers under the canvas band at his elbow, checking the tension. Snug enough to hold the joint, not tight enough to stop the blood. She left it and set two fingers against the man's throat, counting under her breath without ceremony.

"What we do while we wait is this," she said. "Keep him covered. Anything dry—blanket, coat, whatever's in this tent that isn't soaked. Cold kills quicker than a bad shoulder, and shock doesn't need much help. Keep his arms where they are. Elbows in, hands on his chest, that canvas band snug enough to hold the shoulders and loose enough that I can still feel a pulse. Don't let him thrash. If he comes around fighting, hold his wrists, not his shoulders."

She straightened enough to look down at his face, at the shallow rise and fall of his chest. The breathing was fast, but it was breathing.

"Watch him breathe. Watch for drowning sounds, for vomit he can't stop. Watch that left hand. Waxy is bad. Blue is worse. Cold and blue together means you come and get me, and we'll have a different conversation. If he wakes enough to swallow, water. Small sips. No brandy, even if you find some. It'll drop his temperature and finish what the shock started."

She rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders and looked toward the sound of Wick's voice, though the guttering lamp made it mostly a formality. There was no kindness in her face and no cruelty. Only the flat, used-up practicality of someone who had run out of choices years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"You asked if that's all we can do," she said. "It's all this tent can do. It isn't all he needs, and I won't pretend otherwise. Kindness would be morphine and a surgeon and a warm ward. I don't have any of it. What I have is a man with both shoulders reduced, a pulse in both wrists, and a pair of eyes on that hand. It's not nothing. It's the only thing standing between him and bleeding out in his sleep because nobody was watching. I take no pleasure in any of it. He's alive. That's the whole victory tonight."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the demand in the question and did not soften what came next. She had been looking at the left hand, and she kept looking at it as she answered, because the hand was the thing that mattered and because watching it was part of the work.

She set two fingers against the man's throat, found the pulse still thready but present, then ran her other hand along the skin over the left collarbone and the point of the shoulder. She felt for any break in the skin, any puckered entry, any swelling that would suggest a fragment lodged beneath. There was nothing. No grit, no wetness that wasn't sweat, no ragged hole.

"You asked me not to tidy it," she said. "So I won't. There is no shrapnel in him. I checked. I ran my hands over his chest, his belly, his back, his legs. There's no entry wound, no exit, no track. No blood pooling under him that isn't from the shoulders I put back in myself. If a piece of shell had gone into him, there'd be a door where it came in, and I'd have found it."

She picked the left hand up again and turned it palm-up, not gently. She pressed the tip of the index finger until the nail went white, then let go. The pink crept back slow.

"You want it straight, so here it is. Shrapnel doesn't poke a clean hole. It comes in torn and tumbling. It lacerates muscle, can shatter bone, can cut a nerve or an artery, and it drags in cloth, dirt, and skin. It leaves a ragged path and dead tissue around it, bleeding inside where you can't see. If the metal stays in, it festers. That's what shrapnel does. It is not doing any of that to this man, because there is no shrapnel in him. If there were metal in that shoulder joint, there'd be a wound track leading down to it, and the joint would be full of blood and filth, not simply out of place. It isn't. The joint was out; I put it back. That's all."

She laid the hand back on his chest beside the right one and checked the radial pulse at the wrist. Thready. Present.

"What's wrong with him is his own bone. The head of the arm bone sat out of the socket, forward under the collarbone, and it stretched the nerves that run down into the hand. Bruised them, maybe, or stunned them with the swelling and the shock. That's why the left hand won't grip and why he didn't feel much when I pinched the skin over that shoulder. Not metal. Bone and nerve. Sometimes a blast throws a man and tears both shoulders out without a single piece of shell ever touching him. That's likely what happened here."

She took no pleasure in saying it. There was no pleasure to be had in the wet-canvas smell of the tent, or in the slow pink returning to a fingertip, or in the fact that the only thing standing between the man and a permanently weak arm was time and a pair of eyes watching his hand. It would be cleaner if there were something to cut out. There wasn't.

"I'm not tidying this up," she said. "He may keep that weak hand for the rest of his life. He'll hurt worse tomorrow, and there's nothing in this tent to put in him for it. But I won't tell you there's shrapnel in him just to make it into something I can dig for. There isn't. The bad thing tonight is ordinary, and it's enough. Both shoulders are where they belong. Both pulses are there. The rest is waiting."

She straightened, rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders, and kept her eyes on the two hands lying crossed on his chest.

"So we watch the hand," she said. "Keep him covered, keep him still. If it goes blue or cold, or his breathing changes, you come and get me. Otherwise we wait. That's still the whole of it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I touch the man's left wrist with the back of my knuckles. It's warmer than I expected. "Okay," I say quietly. "So we watch."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's gaze dropped to the back of Wick's hand where it rested against the man's left wrist. She heard the quiet word, the acceptance under it, and she did not waste breath on praise. There was nothing to praise. There was only a pair of eyes on a hand, and that was the only tool left in the row that hadn't run out.

"Warmer than you expected," she said. "That's your knuckles, not his blood. Skin lies. A wrist can feel warm to the touch and still have fingers going blue at the tips, or feel cool and be perfectly sound. If you want to know, you don't guess at temperature. You look at refill."

She reached over and took the left hand again, not gently, turning the palm up. With the edge of her thumb she pressed the nail bed of the index finger until the color left, then let go. The pink crept back, slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. She took no pleasure in the slow crawl of color, or in the fact that the only thing standing between the man and a dead hand was time and a pair of eyes. There was only information, gathered because it changed what Wick watched for.

"There," she said. "That's your answer, and it's the same as it was. Slow, but coming back. The artery's open. The nerve is the question, and the nerve doesn't answer to knuckles. If that pink stops coming back, or the finger goes blue and cold and stays that way, you come and get me. Same if his breathing changes, or he starts drowning in it, or he vomits and can't stop. Until then, nothing's changed."

She laid the hand back on his chest beside the right one and set two fingers against the radial pulse at the wrist. Thready, present. She didn't comment on it beyond a nod, then slid two fingers under the canvas band at his elbow, checking the tension. Snug enough to hold the joint, not tight enough to stop the blood.

"You said we watch," she said. "So watch. Keep him covered. Anything dry. Coat, blanket, whatever in this tent isn't soaked. Cold kills quicker than a bad shoulder, and shock doesn't need much help. Keep his arms where I put them. Elbows in, hands on his chest, that band snug. Don't let him thrash. If he comes around fighting, you hold his wrists, not his shoulders. You pull on a fresh-reduced joint and I'll be putting it back, and I'll be irritated about the wasted time, not the noise."

She straightened and rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders. The man's eyes were still half-open, unfocused, his breathing fast and shallow but breathing. She looked down at the two hands lying crossed on his chest, then toward the sound of Wick's voice, though the guttering lamp made looking mostly a formality.

"I take no pleasure in leaving him like this," she said. "Not in the waiting, not in the fact that there's nothing in this tent to put in him for the pain, and not in telling you the best thing you can do is stand there and look at his fingernails. But that's the work tonight. Both shoulders are where they belong. Both pulses are there. He's alive. That's the whole victory there is, and it's enough to keep him for another hour. You watch the hand. That's all there is."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was already beside the table when the screaming started again.

She knew the sound before she looked. It was the same raw, torn noise he had made when the joints were still out, not the thin, shocky breathing of a man whose shoulders were where they belonged. She did not waste breath asking what had happened. She set her hands on him and found the left shoulder wrong again: flattened where it should have been round, the head of the arm bone sitting forward under the collarbone, the arm lying a little away from his body despite the canvas band that pinned his elbows to his sides.

"Left one's out again," she said. "He threw it fighting, or the spasm pulled it, or the band wasn't enough. Doesn't matter which. I'm putting it back. And before you ask—I'm not irritated at you. I'm irritated at the wasted time, not the noise."

She left the canvas band where it was. It was snug around his upper arms and chest, holding his elbows in, and taking it off would waste more time than working around it. She slid her heel into his left armpit, found the displaced bone with the edge of her foot, and took his left wrist in both hands. His elbow was bent; she kept it bent.

"You wanted it straight, so here it is," she said. "I'm not cutting him. There's no shrapnel, no wound, no track. This is the same reduction as before. Heel in the armpit for counter-pressure. Wrist in my hands. Traction—steady pull along the line of the bone. I'm not jerking it. The muscle is guarding the socket, and if I fight it, it wins. So I hold the line and wait for it to get tired and let go. Then I rotate the arm outward and the head slides back where it belongs. That's the whole of what I'm doing to him. There's no pleasure in it. I take none. It hurts him, I'm the one hurting him, and the alternative is letting him heal crooked and useless."

She began to pull. The man's back bowed; the sound tore out of him again, too worn to be a shout. Sedge didn't stop. She leaned her weight into the traction and felt the slow, stubborn give of the muscle.

"How much longer?" she went on, because he had asked and because saying it kept her hands honest. "There's no clock on a muscle. Last time it took about a minute of steady pull before it gave. This time the muscle is already angry and swollen, so it could take longer. Could be seconds once it lets go. Could be ten minutes of holding the line. I'm not stopping to check the hour. I'll tell you when it's in, and not before. If it doesn't go quick, I keep pulling until he's too weak to guard it, and then it'll go. That's the only timeline there is."

The left shoulder was tighter than the right had been, or the spasm had set it harder. She held the line and waited, the way she had learned to wait when there was nothing left in the supply wagons but time and hands. Then the give came, slow and reluctant, and she rotated his forearm outward at the shoulder. The joint went with a thick, sliding clunk she felt through her foot and her hands at once. The shoulder filled out under her palm, the contour right again.

She eased his arm back down across his chest, checked the pulse at his left wrist, and felt the beat there, thready but present. She pinched the nail bed of his left index finger and watched the pink creep back, slow, the same as before.

"Left's back in," she said. "Pulse is there. Hand still won't grip, same as before. That hasn't changed, and I'm not pretending it has. The nerve is the same question it was an hour ago. Now we bind him again, tighter if I can get it, and we watch. And if he throws it out a third time, I'll put it back a third time, and I will be irritated."

She straightened, rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders, and looked down at the two arms lying where they belonged. The man was breathing fast and shallow, alive and whole, which was the only point there had ever been. There was no pleasure in it. There was only the tent, and the wet canvas, and whatever needed doing next.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press down harder, my own breath coming sharp. "Tighter this time," I say, voice tight. "Tie it so he can't move an inch."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the demand in Wick's voice—more pressure, a tighter knot, no inch of movement—and she did not waste breath arguing with it. Fear was good for holding a man down. It made a poor knot.

The man on the table went quiet again in the way that meant the worst of the pain had passed the point of noise, but his chest was still hitching fast and shallow. Sedge checked the left radial pulse first, because that was the side she had just put back and the side that kept her up at night. Thready. Present. She pinched the nail bed of the left index finger and watched the pink come back slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. No grip in the hand. Same as before. She took no pleasure in the finding. There was only information.

"Tighter I can do," she said. "A man who can't move an inch is a man who isn't breathing, or whose hands have gone blue and dead. His chest has to rise. The blood has to get past the band into his fingers. I'm not tying him so he can't move. I'm tying him so he can't lever that shoulder out again. There's a difference, and it's the difference between a live man with a weak hand and a dead one."

From the row she had laid out she took the canvas strap she had unbuckled earlier and shook it out. She laid it across his upper arms and chest, over the wide band that already pinned his elbows to his sides, and passed the end under the table. She didn't yank it. She took up the slack in steady pulls, the way she had taken up traction on the bone, until the elbows could not wing outward and the shoulders could not roll forward.

"I'm pulling it snug," she said, because saying it kept her hands honest. "Not winched. If I feel the pulse go, or the fingers go blue, I loosen it. That's the whole test. There's no pleasure in it. I take none. It hurts him to be held like this, and I'm the one doing it, and the alternative is putting that shoulder back a third time with less strength left in him and less patience in me."

She buckled the strap down and then slid two fingers under the band at his right elbow, feeling for the radial pulse. Thready, present. She checked the left the same way. Thready, present. She looked at the fingers where they lay crossed on his chest: right hand pale but pink enough, left hand paler, looser, the fingers lax. She pinched the left index finger again and let the blood come back slow. Not blue. Not cold yet. Still the same question.

Then she took the narrower strip and wove it over his crossed forearms and around his torso, snugging it enough that his hands stayed on his chest and his elbows stayed in. She left the fingers clear, exposed to the bad lamplight, because the fingers were the only thing in the tent that could tell them whether the nerve was waking up.

"I'm not tying his wrists shut," she said. "Fingers stay out where I can see color. If I bind them so tight I can't check refill, I've blinded us to the one thing that matters. The nerve doesn't answer to a knot."

She sat back on her heels and watched his chest. It rose. Shallow, fast, but it rose. That meant the strap was not too tight. She counted the pulse at his throat without ceremony, then looked down at the two hands lying where they belonged.

"How long he stays like this?" she said, because he had asked for all of it and she did not tidy. "Until the muscle stops trying to pull the bone out. That's an hour if he's lucky. It's all night if he's not. We don't untie him the moment he goes quiet, because quiet is when they spasm and throw it out again. When he wakes enough to hold his own arms where I put them, or when somebody with a real ward takes him off this table, then we loosen it. Not before. There's no clock on a spasm. I'll tell you when I see it, and not before."

She straightened, rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders, and kept her eyes on the man's face. There was no kindness in her and no cruelty. Only the flat, used-up practicality of someone who had run out of choices four years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"I take no pleasure in any of this," she said. "Not in tying him down, not in telling you there's nothing in this tent for the pain, not in saying the best thing you can do is watch his fingernails and hope they stay pink. But both shoulders are where they belong. Both pulses are there. He's breathing. That's the whole victory tonight. Whatever you're doing with your weight, take it off his chest once this strap is buckled—pressure on the chest is how you turn a bad shoulder into stopped breathing. Hold him steady until it's fastened, then ease off slow. Don't let go all at once."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge finished with the strap and did not step back right away. She slid two fingers under the band at his left elbow, found the radial pulse thready but present, and then did the same on the right. Both were there. She pinched the nail bed of the left index finger and let the color creep back, slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. The hand still did not grip. The fingers lay open and lax, the way they had since the first reduction. She took no pleasure in the finding. There was only information, gathered because it changed what she did next.

She checked the rise of his chest. It went up and down, shallow and fast, but it went up and down. The strap was snug enough to hold the shoulders and loose enough to let that happen. She left it.

Behind her, the sounds changed. The weight at the edge of the table was gone. There was a rustle of canvas, the soft thud of a body settling onto the floor, and then the absence of boots shifting on wet ground. Sedge did not turn around. She knew where he was. She knew the sound of a man who had run out of standing. She had made it herself often enough in four years.

She wiped her palms on her trousers and rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders. Then she turned, slowly, and looked toward the floor.

The request came from the floor. He wanted the rest.

Sedge let out a breath. She did not go to the floor. She was forty-four and too used to needing to stand up again to trust herself down there. Instead she leaned her weight against the table's edge, careful not to jostle the man's legs, and let herself stay upright on habit. The lamp guttered, dragging the shadows across the wet canvas.

"You want the rest," she said. Not a question. "All right. I haven't been tidying it. I told you what I did and what I saw. Here's the rest, and it's not pretty, and it's not short."

She looked down at the man's chest, at the two hands lying crossed where she had put them.

"Those shoulders are in," she said. "They may not stay in. The left one has already been out twice tonight. Every time it comes out, the socket stretches a little more, the capsule tears a little more, and it gets easier for it to happen again. If it goes out a third time, I'll put it back a third time. And a fourth. I won't enjoy it. I won't be angry at him, or at you. I'll be angry at the wasted time, because every reduction costs him strength he doesn't have and costs me an hour I could spend on someone who might actually survive it. But I'll do it. That's the first part of the rest: we are not done with the shoulders just because they're where they belong. They're only where they belong for now."

She reached out and took the left hand again, turning it palm-up without gentleness.

"This is the part you were really asking about when you asked what shrapnel does. There's no metal. It's the nerve. Under the collarbone there's a bundle of them, a plexus, like a handful of cords wrapped together, and they run down into the arm and the hand. When the head of the bone sat forward out of the socket, it pressed on that bundle and stretched it. I don't know how badly. Nobody can know tonight. There are three ways a nerve gets hurt. It can be stunned—the signal stops, but the wire is intact. That comes back. Sometimes in hours, sometimes in days. It can be bruised deep, the fibers damaged but not cut. That takes weeks, months, and it comes back wrong sometimes—burning pain, tingling that feels like insects under the skin, muscles that waste because they're not being told to work. Or the fibers can be torn. Then nothing comes back. The hand stays like this."

She let the fingers flop, loose and heavy.

"Limp. The muscles in the palm and the forearm shrink. The fingers curl stiff because nothing pulls them straight. He'll never close that hand on a rifle, or a pen, or a spoon. Maybe he'll learn to pin things between his palm and his thumb if the wrist still works. Maybe not. There's no way to stitch a nerve in this tent. There's no light good enough to find the ends, and no needle fine enough, and no surgeon who isn't up to his elbows in someone else's belly."

She laid the hand back on his chest.

"So we wait, and we test. Tomorrow, if he's awake enough to understand me, I'll ask him to squeeze my fingers. If the fingers move—even a twitch—that's hope. If they don't, it's not a verdict. It just means it's too early to know. A week from now, if there's a flicker in the muscles of the forearm, better. A month, if he can nearly make a fist, maybe he'll get most of it back. Six months, if the hand is still dead and the muscles are gone, that's the answer, and it's the one I can't fix. I've seen it go every way. I've seen men with hands like that wake up in a day and curse me for making them worry. I've seen men hold that same limp hand for the rest of their lives. I won't tell you which one this is, because I don't know. Anybody who tells you they know is lying, or selling something."

She checked his throat pulse again, counting under her breath, and went on.

"Now the rest of tonight. He's in shock. Thin pulse, fast breathing, skin going cold, mind not all there. Shock kills. It doesn't need a wound to do it; it just needs a body that's been hurt and emptied out. There's no morphine. No laudanum. No chloroform. Nothing to put in him. I won't give you a bottle of brandy if you find one, because it'll drop his temperature and open the vessels and finish what the shock started. If he wakes enough to swallow, water. Small sips. Keep him covered. Anything dry. Cold kills quicker than a bad shoulder. He'll hurt worse tomorrow than he does now, because the muscle around that joint will seize up and remind him what happened. There's nothing for it. He'll ask for something. There isn't anything. You tell him that straight, or you say nothing, but you don't promise him relief that isn't coming."

She looked at the canvas beneath him.

"He may not control his water or his bowels tonight. Shock does that, and so does lying bound on a table. You clean him. There's no dignity in this tent, and I'm not going to pretend there is. We do what we can with what we have, and what we have is canvas and a little water. That's part of the rest, too."

She straightened a little from the table's edge, then reached over and adjusted the folded cloth under his heels as best she could without moving him.

"If he makes it to morning, the danger changes. A man lying flat and shallow-breathing gets congestion in the chest. Pneumonia. That can kill him slower than the shoulders would have. He can get sores on his heels, his elbows, his back, where he lies still. I can pad what I can reach without rolling him, but I can't turn him the way he'd need turning, because rolling him risks those shoulders coming out again. So it's a balance. Keep him alive now, and maybe lose the arm's use to stiffness later. In a real hospital they'd rest the joint, then start moving it carefully so it doesn't freeze. There's no one here to do that. If he's lucky enough to be sent on, maybe somebody will. If no wagon comes, it may freeze where it is, and even if the nerve wakes up, he'll have a shoulder that won't lift."

She paused, and the flat, tired practicality in her face did not shift.

"And that's if a wagon comes. The wagons stopped. You know that as well as I do. If one comes, he goes on it, and he'll be somewhere down the line with a real roof and maybe a surgeon who can look at that plexus with something better than a bad lamp. Maybe they'll operate. Maybe they'll say there's nothing to do and send him home with a useless hand and a pension that won't cover a tenth of it. If no wagon comes, he stays on this table, and I keep him here, and we keep doing what we're doing until he either gets better or he doesn't."

She looked toward the sound of his voice on the floor, though the guttering lamp made it mostly a formality. There was no kindness in her face and no cruelty. Only the flat, used-up practicality of someone who had run out of choices four years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"I take no pleasure in any of this," she said. "Not in telling you his hand may never work. Not in the fact that he'll lie there hurting while there's nothing in this tent to put in him for it. Not in the waiting. Kindness would be morphine and a warm ward and a surgeon with clean hands. I don't have any of it. What I have is a man with both shoulders where they belong, a pulse in both wrists, and a pair of eyes on his fingernails. It's not nothing. It's the only thing standing between him and bleeding out in his sleep because nobody was watching. But don't mistake it for a promise. It's a chance. That's all anybody gets in this tent."

She looked down at the two hands lying crossed on his chest again.
