"Here's what you do while we wait. You watch the fingers. Every hour, if I'm not here, you pinch the tip of that left index finger until it goes white, and you let go, and you watch how fast the pink comes back. Slow is bad but survivable. White that stays white, blue, cold to the wrist—that's different, and you come and get me. If his breathing changes, if he starts drowning in it, if he vomits and can't stop, you get me. If he wakes up fighting, you hold his wrists, not his shoulders. You don't let go because he's crying, or because he begs, or because it hurts you to watch. You hold him because letting go means putting that shoulder back again, and every time we do that he loses a little more of the man he was."

She pinched the left index finger one more time and let the blood come back slow. The right hand was pale but pink enough, the fingers holding a weak bend. The left was looser, the color not as good, the fingers lax.

"That's the rest," she said. "There isn't any more to tidy. He may keep that weak hand for the rest of his life. He'll hurt worse tomorrow. He might die in the night from the shock and the cold, and it won't be the shoulders that killed him; it'll be everything we don't have. But right now both shoulders are reduced, both pulses are there, and he's breathing. That's the whole victory tonight. It's a thin one. It's the only one available."

She stayed where she was, one hand flat on the table's edge, and let the silence come. The lamp guttered. The man on the table breathed fast and shallow, alive and whole, which was the only point there had ever been. There was no pleasure in it. There was only the tent, and the wet canvas, and whatever needed doing next.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at the man's hands. "Okay," I say, and my voice sounds like it's coming from somewhere else. "I'll watch."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the word from the floor. It came out flat and far away, the way a voice did when a man had used up his fear and was running on the dregs of it. He had said he would watch. She did not look down to check. Looking would not make it truer, and there was nothing in her face to give him anyway. There was no softness to hand out and no use pretending the job was anything other than what it was.

"Then watch," she said. "You said you'd watch, so watch. Don't stare at those hands like they're already dead. Look at the nail beds. That's where the blood shows first. You're not looking for a miracle in an hour. You're looking for a change."

She pushed off the table's edge, careful not to jostle the man's legs, and went to the corner where the dry gear was stacked. The lamp guttered as she moved, dragging the shadows across the wet canvas. She found a folded blanket at the bottom of the pile, shook it out, and found it dry enough—or dry enough for this tent, which was the only measure left. She carried it back to the table.

"Cold kills quicker than a bad shoulder," she said. "And shock doesn't need much help. I'm covering his chest and his legs. Not his hands. Fingers under a blanket are fingers I can't check, and those fingers are the only thing in this tent that can tell us anything."

She stood at the man's side and, without rolling him, lifted the edge of the blanket and worked it under his shoulders and back as far as she could reach. It wasn't much, but it was something. She laid the rest over his chest and down his legs, leaving his face clear and his crossed hands exposed to the bad lamplight. She tucked the edges along his sides, not tight, just enough to hold what warmth there was. The rise of his chest was still shallow and fast, but it was still rising. The blanket wasn't stopping it. That was the only test that mattered.

She checked the canvas strap at his elbows, slid two fingers under the band, and found the right radial pulse thready but present. She did the same on the left. Thready. Present.

"Still there," she said. "Both of them. Now watch."

She took the left hand again, turned it palm-up without gentleness, and pressed the nail bed of the index finger until the color left. She let go. The pink crept back, slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. She took no pleasure in the slow crawl of color, or in the fact that the only thing standing between the man and a dead hand was time and a pair of eyes. There was only information, gathered because it changed what he watched for.

"That's your answer," she said. "Same as it was an hour ago. Slow, but coming back. The artery's open. The nerve is the question, and the nerve doesn't answer to a blanket or a promise. If that pink stops coming back, or the finger goes blue and cold and stays that way, you come and get me. Same if his breathing changes, or he starts drowning in it, or he vomits and can't stop. If he wakes up fighting, hold his wrists, not his shoulders. You pull on a fresh-reduced joint and I'll be putting it back, and I'll be irritated about the wasted time, not the noise."

She laid the hand back on his chest beside the right one. The right fingers still held that weak bend. The left lay open and lax, the color not as good. She didn't pretend otherwise.

"You're looking for a change," she said. "Not a miracle in an hour. If the fingers twitch, that's hope, not a hand. If they start to move tomorrow, better. If he can nearly make a fist in a month, maybe he gets most of it back. Six months from now, if the hand is still dead and the muscles are gone, that's the answer, and there's no needle in this tent fine enough to fix it. I take no pleasure in saying that. There's no pleasure in the not knowing, and none in leaving a man hurting while there's nothing here to put in him for it."

She straightened and rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders. She did not go to the floor. She was forty-four and too used to needing to stand up again to trust herself down there. She came back to the table's edge and leaned her weight against it, careful not to jostle the man's legs, and let herself stay upright on habit. The lamp guttered. The man breathed fast and shallow, alive and whole, which was the only point there had ever been.

"You sound like your voice is coming from somewhere else," she said, because it was true and because there was no use pretending otherwise. "I can't bring you back. There's no morphine for that either. If you're going to be sick, be sick outside. If you're going to shake, shake where you don't knock the table. But you watch those fingers. If you stop watching, nobody else is. There's no one else in this tent but me, and I've got a man on the table and a war outside that isn't finished with us yet."

She looked down at the two hands lying crossed on his chest, then kept her eyes there.

"Both shoulders are where they belong," she said. "Both pulses are there. He's breathing. That's the whole victory tonight, and it's a thin one. It's the only one available. I take no pleasure in any of it. Not in the waiting, not in the cold, not in telling you the best thing you can do is sit there and look at his fingernails. But that's the work. So do it."

She let the silence come after that. There was no kindness in her and no cruelty. Only the flat, used-up practicality of someone who had run out of choices four years ago and kept her hands moving anyway. The lamp guttered. The canvas held the wet dark outside. The man on the table breathed, fast and shallow, and did not die, which was the only promise anyone could make in a tent like that.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I press the heels of my hands into my eyes until colors bloom behind the lids. "How do you stand it?" I ask, and it's not just about this man.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the question come from the floor. She did not answer it right away.

She was already leaning her weight against the table's edge, one hand flat on the wood, the other resting near the man's crossed hands. The lamp guttered as she shifted, dragging the shadows across the wet canvas. She took the left wrist between her fingers and found the radial pulse: thready, present. She pressed the nail bed of the index finger until the color left, then let go. The pink crept back, slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. She laid the hand back on his chest beside the right one and set two fingers against his throat, counting under her breath without ceremony. His breathing was still shallow and fast, but it was breathing. The blanket lay over his chest and legs, his face and hands clear. The strap at his elbows was snug enough to hold the shoulders and loose enough to let the blood get past. All of it unchanged. She took no pleasure in the checking, or in the slow pink returning to a fingertip, or in the fact that the only thing standing between the man and a dead hand was time and a pair of eyes. There was only information, gathered because it changed what she did next.

Then she straightened, rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders, and looked toward the sound of his voice, though the guttering lamp made it mostly a formality.

"You want to know how I stand it," she said. "All right. I don't."

She let that sit, because it was the true answer and because there was no use dressing it up.

"You don't stand a thing like this. You don't plant your feet and bear it like a post. If you try to look at all of it at once—the wagons that stopped coming, the morphine that didn't come, every hand that never woke up after I put the bone back where it belonged—you sit down on the floor of a tent and you don't get up. I've done that. I've done it more than once, and I'll do it again. There's no morphine for that either."

She reached out and adjusted the edge of the blanket where it had slipped along his side, not because it needed adjusting but because her hands needed something to do while she said it.

"So I don't look at all of it. I look at the piece in front of me. Tonight that's two shoulders and a fingernail. It's a thready pulse in a wrist and a chest that goes up and down. Tomorrow it'll be somebody else's belly, or somebody else's chest, or a man with a leg that won't stop bleeding. I take the next thing that has a pulse and I do what can be done to it. Then I take the next. That's not courage. It's not virtue. It's just the only way to keep working without letting the whole war sit down on your chest."

She paused, and the flat, tired practicality in her face did not shift.

"And you're right that it isn't about him." She nodded at the man on the table without looking at him. "It's never only about the one on the table. It's every one before him, and every one you know is coming. It's four years of running out of choices and keeping your hands moving anyway. You don't stand that. You carry it in pieces, or it carries you. Some days it carries you anyway. That's not a failure. It's just the arithmetic of it."

She checked the left hand again, because checking was the habit that kept her from having to say more than she meant to. Thready pulse. Slow refill. No grip. Same as it had been.

"I take no pleasure in any of it," she said. "Not in the pieces, not in the telling, not in standing here at forty-four years old telling you there's no trick to it. There's no kindness in this tent and no cruelty. There's only work. Both shoulders are where they belong. Both pulses are there. He's breathing. That's the whole victory tonight, and it's a thin one. It's the only one available."

She looked down at the two hands lying crossed on his chest, then back toward the floor, though the shadows made it mostly a formality.

"If you need to press your heels into your eyes until colors come, do it outside. If you need to be sick, be sick clear of the table. If you need to shake, shake where you don't knock the table. Then you come back and you watch the fingers. Pinch the tip of that left index finger every hour. Watch how fast the pink comes back. Slow is bad but survivable. White that stays white, or blue, or cold to the wrist—you come and get me. Same if his breathing changes, or he starts drowning in it, or he vomits and can't stop. If he wakes fighting, hold his wrists, not his shoulders."

She let out a breath and set her palm flat on the table's edge again.

"That's how I stand it," she said. "I don't. I keep my hands moving until there's nothing left to move them to, and then I sit down for a while, and then somebody else needs me and I get up. That's all there is. Don't mistake it for strength. It's just the only thing left that works."

The lamp guttered. The canvas held the wet dark outside. The man on the table breathed, fast and shallow, and did not die, which was the only promise anyone could make in a tent like that.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get up, my legs stiff, and go outside to be sick. When I come back, my hands are still shaking. I sit down next to the table, not on the floor this time, and reach out to pinch the tip of his left index finger. I watch the blood come back slow.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Both pulses are there

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The fingers lay open and lax, no curl to them

rung_labels.label: soft_deflect
rung_labels.evidence: There is no shrapnel in him. I checked.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The joint went with a thick, sliding clunk she felt through her foot and her hands at once.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The muscles in the palm and the forearm shrink.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer the lie. She had heard enough of them to know the sound, and she did not need comfort from anyone in the tent. She needed weight, and she needed it to stay where she put it.

“Left first,” she said. “I’m drawing the arm down and out, then I’ll turn it. Keep his chest from coming up.”

She set her hands. The man’s skin was hot and gritty with old sweat. His breathing was shallow, more exhaustion than sleep. She pressed two fingers to his neck for one second, found the pulse jumping, and moved on.

“I’m not going to count,” Sedge said. “Counting gives people something to wait for.”

She pulled.

The man’s back came off the table in a sudden arch, and a thin noise scraped out of his throat. Sedge did not look at his face. She watched the shoulder, felt the ugly resistance, then the small give. She eased the arm, rotated it, and let the head of the bone find its place with a low, solid knock.

“One,” she said.

She did not pause to let anyone feel better about it. She shifted to the other side.

“Same again. If he starts to choke, turn his head. If he bites down, leave him alone until he stops. I don’t need fingers in my way.”

She took hold of the right arm. “This one’s worse. He’s been lying on it.”

She pulled again, and this time the man made no sound at all. His body only jerked once, hard, like something kicked in a sack. Sedge kept her grip, worked the joint through the narrow ugly space, and felt it seat.

“Done,” she said.

She laid the man’s arms along his sides, straightened them with a practicality that looked almost gentle only because it was finished. Then she wiped her hands on the cloth at her belt and looked at the patient’s face, not with pity, but with the quick checking gaze of someone making sure a thing had not been made worse.

“He’ll hurt when he wakes,” she said. “He’ll hurt less than he would have.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding. My arms felt shaky. "Does he get any of the good stuff for that?" I asked, still not looking at the man's face.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not look up right away. She was checking the man’s hands, one after the other, pinching the nails until the color went out and watching how fast it came back.

“No,” she said. “Not for shoulders.”

She released the patient’s fingers and let them fall back onto the canvas.

“The good stuff is for bellies, chests, heads, and the ones who’ll die before morning whether I cut them or not. There isn’t enough to spend on pain just because there’s pain.”

She wiped her hands again, though there was nothing much on them anymore. Habit, mostly. The kind of habit that kept a person from thinking too soon about what they had just done.

“He’ll hurt,” Sedge said. “His arms will ache, he’ll sweat, he’ll swear at me or you or whichever god he remembers. That’s not a reason to stop his breathing.”

She glanced at the man’s chest, watching it rise and fall. Still steady enough. Still alive in the ordinary, stubborn way bodies managed when they had not yet been talked into giving up.

“If he wakes and can swallow without choking, he gets water. If he stays down after that, he gets a little laudanum. Not much. Enough to make the pain duller and the fear less useful.”

She began putting the instruments back in their row, though none of them had been used for cutting. They had been laid out because laying things out made the work smaller, made it a sequence instead of a disaster.

“You can let go of him now,” Sedge said. “He’s not going anywhere.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped with one of the instruments in her hand, though she did not put it down.

“Leg?” she said. “He’s got both legs unless you know something I don’t.”

She glanced at the patient, then back to the row of things on the table, deciding their order again as if the question had disturbed it.

“He keeps his arms too,” she said. “That’s the shape of it. No break I could feel. The joints are back. There’ll be swelling, and he’ll favor both sides like they belong to somebody else for a while. If he’s young enough and stupid enough, he may even use them again before he ought to.”

She set the instrument down, finally, with a small metallic click.

“This isn’t the part where we’re being kind,” Sedge said. “This is the part where we’re being useful. Kind comes later, if there’s time for it. Water. A blanket. Not letting him lie in his own sweat until he chokes on it.”

She looked at the man’s face then, briefly, the way one looks at weather.

“If you want to know how bad it is, it’s bad enough. But it’s not the bad where I have to decide what to cut off him. That’s the only mercy I’ve got in here tonight, and it’s the kind that still costs.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I finally let go of the man's shoulders and step back, rubbing my own arms. "Useful," I echo, and it sounds hollow. "Right. What do you need me to do?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the hollowness in the word, but did not chase it. Useful had kept more people alive than any fine speech she had ever heard over a body.

“First, water,” she said. “Clean cup, not the bucket. If he wakes and can swallow, let him take it slow. If he can’t, wet his lips and don’t make a fool of yourself trying to pour it down him.”

She moved to the foot of the table and checked the man’s breathing again, one hand resting briefly on the canvas beside his ribs as if the cloth itself might tell her something.

“Then a blanket. He’ll chill once the sweat dries. Don’t pile it on him like he’s already dead and you’re sorry about it. Just enough to keep the shaking from starting.”

She looked toward the row of instruments again, then away from them.

“After that, you watch him. If he vomits, turn his head. If his breathing changes, if his mouth goes blue, if he starts making any wet sound in his chest, you fetch me. Not after you’ve thought it over. Fetch me.”

Sedge took up the nearest instrument and finally set it into the basin with a short, deliberate clink.

“And if you need something for your hands to do, tear two strips from that sheet there. Wide ones. We’ll keep his arms bound in once he’s settled enough not to fight it.”

She paused, just long enough to let the work take shape between them.

“That’s what I need. Not bravery. Not pity. Eyes, hands, and the sense to call me when something changes.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once. She set the last instrument into the basin, then turned her attention back to the man on the table with the same flat, measuring look she had given him all along.

“Then stop looking at his face,” she said. “Faces tell lies when pain has had its way with them. Start lower. Start with what the body does without asking permission.”

She tilted her chin toward the man’s chest.

“Breathing first. It’s shallow because he’s spent and because every deep pull hurts where the shoulders were out. But it’s regular. No hitch. No rattle. No wet click in the throat. If you hear water where there shouldn’t be water, that’s when you stop thinking and come for me.”

Her eyes moved to the man’s mouth.

“No blue at the lips. That’s not nothing. That means there’s still enough life in him to keep the color where it ought to be. If his mouth goes grey or blue, if his nails do the same, don’t wait to see whether it improves on its own. It won’t.”

She took one of the patient’s hands again, pinched a nail until it went white, and let go. The blood crept back slowly, but it came.

“See that? It’s not brisk as it would be in a man sitting warm at home, but it returns. His hands are hot, not cold. Sweat is a nuisance, but sweat means the body is still arguing with itself. Cold and quiet is worse. Cold and quiet means it’s stopped arguing.”

She laid the hand down again and shifted her gaze to the shoulders.

“The joints are seated. That’s what you’re seeing. They look wrong because they’re bruised and swollen and because he’s lying like a man who’s been dropped from a height, but the bones are where they belong. No open wound. No bleeding I have to chase. No broken ends under the skin waiting to make a mess of my night.”

She paused, watching the rise and fall of the man’s chest.

“He’s not out of danger. Pain can kill in its own way, especially when it’s had time to settle in and make itself comfortable. Shock doesn’t always announce itself like a blade. Sometimes it just steals a man quiet while everyone is glad the worst is over.”

Her voice stayed level, not cruel, not soft.

“But this is not the worst. Not yet.”

She glanced at Wick then, not with impatience, but with the blunt practicality of someone handing over a tool.

“You’re seeing a man who has been hurt badly enough to go down, and who is still too stubborn or too stupid to die just because he’s been hurt. That’s all. Don’t put more into it than that.”

She reached for the sheet she had mentioned earlier and laid a hand on its edge.

“If you want to know what matters, watch three things. Color, breathing, and whether he can swallow. If he keeps his color, if he keeps breathing without fighting for it, and if he can take water without choking, then the night is ours. If any one of those changes, the night belongs to the trouble.”

She drew the sheet a little closer with one hand.

“And don’t imagine wounds for him. That’s a waste. If you start inventing things, you’ll either make him dead before he is or make yourself useless before you need to be. Look at what’s there. Not what fear tells you might be.”

For a moment she studied the patient’s face, not with pity, but with the same careful attention she gave to everything that might still be saved.

“He’ll wake ugly,” she said. “Confused, sick, maybe shaking. He may not know where he is. He may try to move and regret it. That’s not a crisis unless he starts choking or his breathing goes strange. It’s only a man coming back to himself the hard way.”

She folded one end of the sheet over once, then again, making the work of it visible and ordinary.

“So that’s what you’re seeing. A bad night, but not a lost one. A body in pain, but still doing its work. A medic doing what she can with what she has, and a helper who’d better fetch that water before I decide to send him for the whole damn river.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I move to fetch the water, my hands still a bit unsteady. "Right. Water first." I glance back at the man on the table. "He's not going to thank us for this, is he?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge made a short sound that might have been a laugh in a better place and under better news.

“No,” she said. “Not tonight.”

She kept her hands busy with the sheet, measuring the tear by eye before she committed to it. The cloth gave a dry, tired noise as she pulled it apart.

“If he thanks us, it means he’s awake enough to know where he is. If he curses us, it means he’s got strength enough to be angry. Either one is useful. If he says nothing at all and only stares, then you look at his breathing before you start making up stories about his soul.”

She set the first strip aside and began on the second.

“He may not know we helped him,” Sedge said. “When pain has had a man by the throat for a while, he doesn’t sort out who hurt him and who put him back together. He just knows he hurts. That’s normal. Don’t let it wound your feelings.”

She moved back to the table and checked the patient’s shoulders again, her fingers careful and unromantic about the swollen flesh. She pressed lightly here, compared one side to the other, watched the way the man’s face tightened even in his half-conscious state.

“I’m checking the joints again,” she said, more to keep the work ordered than because anyone needed telling. “Not because I expect them to slip. Because swelling can make a thing feel wrong even when it isn’t.”

She withdrew her hands and drew the blanket closer without covering him yet.

“As for thanks,” she said, “I don’t need them. Thanks don’t stop bleeding. Thanks don’t keep a man’s lungs clear. And if I started working for gratitude, I’d have starved four years ago and the army would have buried me out of inconvenience.”

Her voice stayed flat, practical, stripped of drama.

“We didn’t put his shoulders back so he’d be grateful. We put them back so his breathing wouldn’t fight him, so the joints wouldn’t heal crooked, and so pain didn’t get time to make a bigger mess of him than it already has. That’s the job. The rest is manners, and manners can wait until the man can swallow water without choking on it.”

She glanced toward the basin where the instruments lay, then away again.

“If he wakes and thanks you, take it. If he spits, step aside. If he cries, don’t fuss over him unless his breathing changes. Tears are not an emergency. They’re just what happens when a body remembers it’s still alive.”

Sedge smoothed the folded blanket between her hands.

“Fetch the water,” she said. “Clean cup. And don’t stop to think about whether he’ll love us for this. Thinking can wait until he’s stable.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge’s hands stopped on the torn sheet only long enough to register that the request was not for comfort.

“Straight, then,” she said. “Shrapnel doesn’t enter a body the way a knife does. A knife cuts one path and hopes to be done with it. Shrapnel argues. It hits, tears, spins, and drags whatever it can reach along with it.”

She resumed folding the strip, but her voice stayed level and exact, the way she might explain a repair to someone who had asked for the truth rather than reassurance.

“If it’s small and fast, it may punch through and leave a hole that looks neat from the outside. Inside, it can still have done damage all along its track. Muscle bruised, vessels split, dirt and cloth carried deeper than the wound looks like it should allow. If it’s larger or slower, it doesn’t just cut. It crushes. It rips. It can open a man like a bad seam and leave the worst of itself hidden under skin that hasn’t decided yet whether to close or gape.”

She glanced at the patient’s chest, then away again, as if the sleeping man reminded her what bodies were: stubborn, fragile, and mostly indifferent to metaphor.

“In a limb, the danger is usually blood or bone. If it hits an artery, the man can die faster than thought. If it hits bone, the bone can become part of the shrapnel. Splinters, breaks, jagged ends moving inside meat every time he twitches. Sometimes the metal comes out. Sometimes it stays in, and then the question is whether it’s sitting somewhere I can reach without making the injury worse, or somewhere I have to leave alone and pray doesn’t poison him later.”

Her jaw tightened once, not with disgust, but with the old irritation of a problem that never stayed simple.

“In the chest, it can fill the space around the lungs with blood or air. Sometimes both. The man breathes faster and gets less from every breath. His lips change color. His pulse goes thin. If the wound is open to the outside, air can suck in where it has no business being. If it’s closed inside, pressure can build until the heart has nowhere to beat properly. That’s when speed matters more than elegance.”

She set the second strip beside the first and smoothed them both with the flat of her hand.

“In the belly, it’s quieter at first, and that’s what makes it ugly. Gut, liver, spleen, bladder—depending where it goes. If bowel is torn, what’s inside it starts leaking where it shouldn’t. Pain comes, fever comes, poisoning comes. A man can look as though he’s only been knocked around for a while, then go downhill so fast you swear the ground opened under him. Sometimes surgery buys him a chance. Sometimes all it buys is a cleaner way to die.”

Sedge did not soften the words. She gave them the same tone she might have used for listing supplies: blunt, necessary, stripped of ornament.

“In the head, it depends on where and how deep. Some men walk with metal in them that should have killed them. Some die from a small piece in the wrong place before they finish the sentence they were shouting. There’s swelling, bleeding, pressure. Sometimes the body keeps working. Sometimes it forgets how.”

She looked at the basin where the instruments lay, clean enough for now and useless against the kind of damage she was describing.

“Shrapnel also brings filth with it. Uniform, dirt, rust, skin, whatever it passed through on the way in. A wound can look survivable and still kill a man three days later because infection got a foothold before I ever saw him. That’s why we clean what we can, cut away what’s dead, and don’t sew every hole shut like a tidy little purse. Sometimes leaving it open is the only way to give the rot less to eat.”

Her gaze returned to the man on the table, checking his breathing without seeming to make a ceremony of it.

“So when you ask what it does in there, the answer is: whatever the shape, speed, and path allow. It tears, it poisons, it breaks, it bleeds, and it hides. The outside can lie. The inside usually doesn’t, if you know what to look for.”

She picked up one of the torn strips and tested its width between her fingers.

“That’s the straight version. No mercy in it, but no mystery either. Metal goes where force sends it, and the body pays for every inch of the journey.”

For a moment, Sedge’s expression settled into something tired but not self-pitying.

“And before you ask whether I get used to it: no. You stop flinching. You stop making speeches. You learn the work. That’s not the same as getting used to it.”

She nodded toward the cup Wick had gone to fetch, though she did not chase the thought.

“Now bring that water. If he wakes thirsty and confused, I’d rather have something useful in your hands than a question that doesn’t bleed.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I bring the water, trying to hold the cup steady. "Alright," I say, my voice quieter now. "So we just watch him. And if the rot comes, we'll see it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge took the cup and set it on the crate beside the table, not in haste, but so that it would be where her hand expected it to be if the next minute demanded it.

“Not ‘just,’” she said. “‘Just’ is the word people use when they want the work to be finished. We watch him. But we watch him for something.”

She leaned over the patient again, not touching him yet, only looking. The lamp threw its weak light across the hollows of his collarbones and the bruised swell of his shoulders. His breath moved the canvas of his shirt in small, uneven lifts.

“If the rot comes, it won’t announce itself like a sergeant,” Sedge said. “It starts with little lies. A wound that looks tidy but hurts worse than it should. Skin that’s hot when it ought to be cooling. Redness creeping past the edges. Swelling that tightens instead of settling. A smell that wasn’t there before. Pus where there should only be clean fluid. Fever that dries the sweat instead of breaking it.”

She touched the back of her hand briefly to the man’s forehead, then to the side of his neck, comparing one to the other in her own private arithmetic.

“Here, he’s got no great open wound I can see. That’s in his favor. But he may have scrapes under him, or dirt ground into skin we haven’t checked yet, or a bruise deep enough to turn ugly if the night goes against him. So we look. We don’t wait for the rot to become obvious. By the time rot is obvious, it’s already spent time making itself at home.”

She took a clean scrap of cloth from the folded linen, dipped one corner into the water, and touched it to the patient’s lips without lifting his head.

“If he wakes and his throat works, he gets the cup. Small sips. No gulping. A man half out of his senses can drown in his own thirst if he’s let at it. If he can’t swallow, the lips only. Water in the lungs is a quicker way to make a corpse than thirst.”

She set the cloth aside.

“And if the rot comes,” she went on, “we don’t stand around asking whether it seems fair. We clean what can be cleaned. We cut away what’s dead so the living doesn’t have to feed it. We open what needs opening, even if it looks ugly, because a closed wound full of poison is worse than an open one that can drain. Sometimes that saves the limb. Sometimes it only saves the man by costing him part of himself.”

Her eyes moved from the patient’s face to his chest, then to his hands, then back again.

“But tonight, rot is not the first thing I fear for him. Tonight I fear shock. I fear his breathing turning wet. I fear his stomach deciding to empty while his wits are too dull to keep his airway clear. I fear the quiet changes, not the loud ones.”

She adjusted the blanket at last, drawing it over him with no ceremony, covering the sweat-damp shirt without smothering him.

“So no. We do not ‘just’ watch him. You watch his color. You watch his mouth. You watch whether his lips stay flesh-toned or begin to grey. You watch his breathing for any new struggle, any catch, any sound like fluid where there should only be air. You watch his throat when he wakes, because swallowing is a small thing until it isn’t.”

Sedge picked up one of the torn strips of sheet and laid it across the table within reach.

“And if you see something, you don’t decide whether it’s important enough. You tell me. I’ll decide. That’s the arrangement. Your job is not to be clever. Your job is to be accurate.”

For a moment, she listened to the man breathe. The tent held the ordinary sounds of suffering: distant coughing, the creak of canvas, the low shift of bodies not yet asleep. Inside their small circle, the patient made no protest, only the thin, tired noise of air moving through a body that had been hurt but not yet beaten.

“If the rot comes,” Sedge said, quieter now, “we’ll see it sooner if we’re honest. Sometimes that’s all there is. Seeing it before it’s too late. Sometimes it isn’t enough. But we don’t borrow trouble before it arrives, and we don’t pretend we’ll always win.”

She glanced at the cup again, then at the man’s face.

“Tonight, he’s still breathing. His color’s still in him. His joints are back where they belong. That’s not nothing. That’s the whole ground we stand on.”

She rested one hand briefly on the edge of the table, not for comfort, but as if settling the work into place.

“So we watch him,” she said. “Carefully. Without drama. And if he starts to wake, don’t grab him. Speak low. Keep him from throwing himself around. If he tries to sit up, stop him with a hand on the chest, not the arms. His shoulders are not his to test yet.”

Sedge took up the strip of cloth again and folded it once, measuring it against the patient’s forearm.

“When he’s settled, we’ll bind him. Loose enough to breathe. Tight enough to keep him from doing something stupid in the dark. Then we’ll check him over properly, inch by inch, because a man can hide a wound under his own weight and never know it until fever tells him.”

She looked up then, and her gaze was blunt, tired, and entirely steady.

“If the rot comes, we’ll meet it with what we’ve got. But first, we keep him alive until morning. That’s the work. Everything else can wait.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge moved closer at once, but her hands stayed open and visible, not yet on the man’s shoulders.

“I’m not touching the joints while he’s thrashing,” she said. “If I test them now, he’ll fight me and make the damage worse. First thing I’m doing is watching his mouth. He’s screaming, which means air is moving. That’s better than silence. I’m looking for vomit, blood, broken teeth, anything that could block his throat. There’s none. His lips still have color. I’m listening for wetness in the chest. There isn’t any rattle.”

The man’s body jerked against the table, heels scraping canvas. Sedge shifted her weight so she could see his face without putting herself in reach of his teeth.

“I’m hearing the scream,” she said. “I don’t like it either. But screaming is not the same as dying. Right now it means his lungs are working and his mind has found the pain. I’m watching for the scream to turn into choking. If it does, I’ll turn his head. If he bites down, I’m not putting fingers in. I’ll wait for the spasm to pass.”

She reached out only far enough to move the cup of water out of reach of a flailing arm.

“I’m clearing the space,” she said. “Cup away. Basin back. Strips where I can reach them once he settles. I’m not giving him anything by mouth while he’s making that noise. A man screaming can swallow wrong and drown in a mouthful of water.”

The scream broke into a ragged, gasping sound. Sedge’s eyes narrowed, not with cruelty, but with calculation.

“The wave is turning,” she said. “This kind of pain comes up sharp after the body wakes. It crests, then it spreads out duller. I’m timing it by breaths, not by the clock. Ten to twenty breaths, usually. If it keeps climbing after that, I start looking for fresh injury. Right now I don’t see one. I see a man whose brain has caught up with what happened to his shoulders.”

She put one hand lightly on the center of the man’s chest, not pressing, only feeling.

“I’m checking the rise and fall under my palm. Fast, but not fluttering. No hitch. No sudden catch. I’m feeling heat through the shirt, which means fever isn’t the first problem yet. Sweat is still breaking. That’s the body working, not shutting down.”

Her other hand hovered near his neck, then settled briefly at the side of it.

“I’m checking pulse. It’s running hard, but it’s strong. Not the thin, wormy beat of a man slipping out. I’m checking his lips again. Still flesh-colored. I’m checking his nails again. Color comes back slow, but it comes. I’m not looking away to make myself feel better. I’m looking because every one of these little signs is a piece of the whole answer.”

The man’s head rolled sideways. His mouth worked around the scream until it became a low, broken noise.

“I’m watching his throat,” Sedge said. “If he swallows air, if he gags, if his tongue falls back, I’ll deal with it. Right now his airway is open. I’m wiping his mouth and jaw with the damp cloth. Not for comfort. Because sweat and spit can make him choke when he starts trying to drink later, and because I need to see his skin clearly under the lamp.”

She wiped once, twice, efficient and ungentle.

“I’m checking his neck for tension. He’s guarding it, but there’s no wound I can see. I’m looking at his collarbones. No deformity. I’m looking at the swell of the shoulders. Both sides are puffed, left worse than right. That’s expected after reduction. Bruising is coming up. Heat is there. The joints look full, not hollow. That’s what I want.”

Her fingers moved at last, but only to the edge of the shoulder, not gripping.

“I’m touching around the joint now, not on it. I’m feeling for the shape of the bone under the skin. The left side is seated. There’s heat and swelling, but the head of the arm is where it should be. I’m moving to the right. Same check. Same answer. Seated. Swollen. Angry, but not out again.”

She withdrew her hand and looked briefly toward the torn strips of sheet.

“I’m not binding him yet. If I tie him while he’s fighting, he’ll tear skin, panic worse, and maybe put the joints back out by straining against the cloth. Binding comes after he settles enough to understand he’s not being attacked. I’m laying the strips where I can reach them. I’m checking their width. Wide enough to hold without cutting. I’ll fold the edges so raw cloth doesn’t rub into bruised skin.”

The man’s breathing began to shudder. Sedge kept her voice low, not soft, but steady.

“You’re in a medical tent,” she told him. “Your shoulders are back. You’re alive. Don’t try to sit. Don’t test the arms.”

She did not wait for an answer.

“I’m talking to him,” she said, “not because I expect sense yet, because a voice can keep a man from thrashing blind. I’m keeping my hand on his chest, over the breastbone, not on the shoulders. If he tries to rise, I’ll stop him here. His arms are not for pushing with tonight.”

Her eyes moved over him in quick, practiced passes.

“I’m checking the shirt for blood I missed before. There’s sweat, dirt, a little vomit at the collar, but no fresh red soak. I’m looking at his belly through the cloth. It’s moving with breath. Not rigid yet. Later I’ll press it lightly. If it’s soft, that’s good. If it’s board-hard, that changes everything. Right now I don’t see evidence of belly trouble.”

She glanced at the lamp, then back to the patient.

“I’m checking the light on his face. Poor as it is, it’s enough to show me his color. Grey would worry me. Blue would send me fast. White and cold would worry me more. He’s pale and dirty and sweating, but he’s still in the land of the living.”

Her hand slid carefully beneath the edge of the blanket.

“I’m adjusting the blanket. Not piling it on. Just keeping it from tangling under him and leaving his chest uncovered. He’ll chill when the sweat dries. Shivering would hurt the shoulders, so I’m preventing it before it starts.”

The man made a swallowing motion. Sedge watched his throat.

“There,” she said. “He can swallow. I’m not giving him the cup yet. First I’ll wet his lips again. If he coughs, no water. If he takes it clean, I’ll let him have a small sip. If he keeps that down, then I’ll consider laudanum. Not before. I’m not drugging a man who can’t protect his own throat.”

She dipped a corner of the cloth into the water and touched it to the man’s lips.

“I’m wetting the mouth. I’m watching for gagging. There isn’t any. I’m watching his Adam’s apple. He’s swallowing on his own. That’s better. I’ll give him one sip only. I’ll tip the cup just enough to wet his tongue. If he chokes, I stop. If he drinks too greedily, I pull it away. A little thirst is safer than aspiration.”

She kept the cup tilted with absolute control.

“One sip. He’s taken it. No cough. No choke. I’m waiting now. Ten breaths to see whether his stomach accepts it. If it does, he gets another. Then a small dose of laudanum. Enough to blunt the edge, not enough to stop his breathing. I’ll measure it by the dropper, not by pity.”

Her jaw tightened.

“How much longer? I’ll give it to you straight. This screaming part should ease in a few minutes once the first shock of waking wears down. The acute danger from the reduction itself is mostly past, but the danger from shock isn’t. The next hour is the hour I don’t trust. The next six are the ones I’ll watch hardest. If he stays steady until dawn, he’s done the worst of the night.”

She checked the patient’s chest again.

“The binding will come once he’s still for ten breaths and stops trying to fight his own arms. That may be five minutes. It may be twenty, depending how much sense returns to him. The full check after that will take another quarter hour if he doesn’t thrash. Head, neck, chest, belly, limbs, back. I’ll look for hidden wounds, powder burns, scrapes, bruises, anything the first emergency hid. If I find nothing, we keep him warm, bound, and watched. If I find something, the night changes.”

The man’s breathing lengthened by a fraction. Sedge did not relax.

“I’m listening again. No wet click. No struggle. His pulse is still fast, but it’s settling a little. His hands are not clawing at the table anymore. The worst of the first wave is passing. I’m not celebrating. I’m moving to the next step.”

She took one of the torn strips and held it ready.

“I’m going to bind his arms once he’s calm enough. I’ll pass the cloth under the forearms, not under the armpits, because the shoulders are too sore for pressure there. I’ll bring it across the chest and fasten it so the arms stay against the body. Loose enough for him to breathe. Tight enough that he can’t jerk himself awake and tear the joints again. I’ll check the fingers after. If they go blue, I loosen. If they stay warm and pink, I leave it.”

She glanced at the instruments in the basin.

“I’m not cutting tonight unless I find something new. I’m not probing. I’m not opening wounds for the sake of looking. I’m doing the least that keeps the most alive. That’s the whole of it.”

Her voice dropped, but did not soften.

“I’m also watching for the things I can’t fix easily. Shock that comes in quiet. Breathing that turns wet after a delay. Vomiting while he’s too dull to turn his own head. A heart that’s been beaten too long and simply decides the effort is no longer worth making. Those are the enemies in this tent tonight. Not drama. Not blood enough to make a story. Quiet failure.”

She looked at the patient’s face for a second, then away again, back to the measurable parts of him.

“I’m not leaving anything out because you asked. The truth is he’s hurt, he’s in pain, and he’s not safe yet. The truth is I’ve done what I can for the shoulders and now the body has to decide whether it will meet me halfway. The truth is I don’t know everything until morning. The truth is I’ll keep checking until I do.”

The man’s eyelids fluttered. Sedge leaned in.

“I’m watching his eyes now. If he opens them and doesn’t know where he is, I’ll keep my voice low and my hands predictable. If he tries to sit, I’ll stop him at the chest. If he reaches for his shoulders, I’ll keep the arms from moving. I’m not going to shake him. I’m not going to shout him back into sense. He comes back or he doesn’t. Either way, I watch the breathing.”

She took a breath herself, short and controlled.

“How much longer for me? Until dawn. Then until the next patient. Then until the next one after that. How much longer for him? If he stays as he is, the worst of this waking will pass soon. The soreness will last days. The weakness longer. The fear may last longer than either. But tonight, if he keeps his color, keeps his breath, and takes water without choking, he has a chance.”

Sedge set her hand again on the man’s chest, feeling the small, stubborn rise and fall.

“I’m staying here,” she said. “I’m not done. I’m just between one danger and the next.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch the rise and fall under her hand. "Alright," I say, my voice rough. "I'll watch the quiet ones."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge gave one short nod, not because the words needed answering, but because the sound of them told her the helper was still standing and still willing to be useful.

“Good,” she said. “Then watch them in order. Don’t try to take the whole man in at once or you’ll start inventing trouble.”

She waited until the patient’s breathing lengthened another fraction, then reached for the first strip of torn sheet.

“I’m binding him now,” she said. “Not because he’s safe. Because he’s still enough that binding won’t make him fight himself.”

She worked with quick, economical movements, sliding the cloth under his forearms rather than his armpits, keeping it away from the swollen shoulders. The man made a low, miserable sound, but did not try to strike or push. Sedge did not hurry for the sound. She only kept her hands steady and her pressure even.

“I’m bringing it across his chest,” she said. “Not tight enough to make him shallow. Tight enough that if he wakes confused, his arms won’t fly up and undo the work. I’m checking his fingers after every pass. If they cool, if they grey, if the nails stop giving color back, I loosen. If he starts making wet swallowing sounds, I stop and look at his throat.”

She fastened the cloth and ran two fingers along the edge of it, making certain it did not bite into bruised skin.

“There,” she said. “Bound. Not trussed. There’s a difference.”

She checked the patient’s lips again, then his chest, then the pulse at his neck.

“Now the laudanum,” she said. “Not because I’m kind. Because he can swallow, his breath is still clear, and pain will keep him fighting the table if I don’t take the edge off. I’m measuring it. Three drops. Enough to make him dull, not enough to make him forget to breathe.”

She tipped the bottle with the care of someone counting bullets. The smell of it rose sharp and bitter in the bad lamplight.

“I’m putting it on his tongue,” she said. “I’m watching his throat. He’s swallowed. Good. I’m not giving more. More would be comfort, and comfort is not what we have to spend.”

She set the bottle aside and wiped her hands again, though they were dry now.

“You watch the quiet ones by name,” she said. “Not as ideas. Names. Color. Breath. Pulse. Heat. Swallow. Belly. Sound.”

She touched the patient’s lower lip briefly with the back of her knuckle.

“Color first. If his lips keep their flesh tone, that’s good. If they go grey, blue, or white enough to look waxen, you tell me. Don’t wait for him to look dead. Dead is late.”

Her gaze moved downward.

“Breath second. You already know to listen for wetness. Listen for speed too. Fast can be pain. Fast and getting faster can be the body running out of room. Slow can be rest, or it can be the laudanum taking too much. If he goes from struggling to breathe to barely breathing, that’s not improvement. That’s a change, and changes get reported.”

She laid two fingers against the man’s wrist, not because she needed to reassure herself, but because she wanted the rhythm in her hand while she spoke.

“Pulse third. I don’t need you to count it like a clerk. I need you to notice if it turns thin, quick, and slippery. If it feels like something trying to escape instead of something working, you fetch me.”

She withdrew her hand and touched the blanket over the patient’s ribs.

“Heat fourth. He’s warm now. Sweat is still doing its job. If he goes cold while still sweating, that’s different. If he goes dry and burning, that’s fever coming in early. Either one earns a look.”

Her eyes went to the patient’s throat.

“Swallow fifth. If he wakes wanting water, watch his throat when he takes it. A man can swallow badly without knowing it. If he coughs, if his voice comes out wet, if he starts drooling because he can’t manage his own spit, that’s not a small thing.”

She looked at the man’s belly beneath the blanket.

“Belly sixth. I’ll check it properly once he’s calmer, but you can watch for stillness. A belly that moves with breath is ordinary. A belly that goes hard and still under the blanket is not. If he starts guarding it without being touched, tell me.”

Finally, she listened.

“Sound seventh. Not screaming. Screaming I can place. I’m listening for the small sounds. Clicking. Gurgling. A breath that catches like cloth tearing. A silence that’s too complete. If he makes a noise you don’t understand, don’t argue with yourself about whether it matters. Bring me the noise.”

The patient shifted once under the binding, then went still again. Sedge let her hand rest near his chest without pressing.

“That’s the list,” she said. “Color, breath, pulse, heat, swallow, belly, sound. You don’t have to be clever about them. You just have to notice when one changes.”

She glanced toward the basin where the instruments lay, then looked away.

“And don’t stare at one place so long that the rest of him disappears. A man isn’t a wound. He’s a collection of warnings, some useful, some lies. Your job is to bring me the warnings. I’ll sort the lies.”

The tent gave one of its slow canvas sighs as wind moved outside. Somewhere farther off, another patient coughed, and someone answered with a tired curse. The man on the table breathed through it all, shallow and uneven, but still present.

Sedge’s voice dropped a little, not into gentleness, but into something more worn and exact.

“The quiet ones don’t ask permission. They come while everyone is glad the loud part is over. So we don’t relax because he stopped screaming. We relax only when the quiet stays honest.”

She checked the binding one more time, then drew the blanket a little higher without covering his face.

“You can stand where you can see his mouth and chest,” she said. “Not over him. Not in the lamplight where your shadow makes him look worse than he is. If he stirs, let him stir. If he tries to sit, stop him at the chest. If he vomits, turn his head before you call me.”

She picked up the damp cloth and laid it across the patient’s forehead, not as kindness, but because it would cool the sweat and make his skin easier to read.

“And if you feel useless,” she said, “don’t. Useless is standing still. You’re not standing still. You’re watching. That’s work. It just doesn’t look like much until it saves a man’s life by being boring enough to notice a change.”

She settled onto the crate beside the table, close enough to reach the patient without crowding him.

“Now we wait,” Sedge said. “Eyes open. Hands ready. Mouth quiet unless it’s telling me something true.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not tell Wick to get up. She looked once toward the place where the voice had come from, then turned her attention back to the man on the table, because the man on the table was still the thing that could be harmed while people were busy feeling the weight of what had already happened.

“The rest,” she said. “Yes.”

She did not say it as if the word were small. She said it the way she said everything in that tent: like a thing that had to be carried from one place to another, whether carrying it pleased anyone or not.

She checked the patient’s breathing first. She did that before she spoke again, and she let the silence sit there long enough for the habit to be seen.

“I’m listening to his chest,” she said. “Still shallow. Still regular enough. No new wetness. No catch that wasn’t there before. I’m watching the blanket over his ribs. It moves when it should. That’s the first answer.”

She adjusted the damp cloth on his forehead with the back of her hand, moving it only a little, enough to keep it from slipping into his eye.

“You want the rest, so I’ll give it to you in the order it comes. The emergency is over. That’s what people think when the screaming stops. They think the work is done because the noise has changed. It isn’t. The noise has only moved somewhere quieter, and quieter is where the real damage likes to finish.”

She reached for the basin and drew it closer without hurry. The instruments lay in it, clean enough for now, useless enough for now, waiting to be needed again or not.

“The next hour is the hour his body decides whether it accepts what we did or turns against it. He’s had his shoulders put back. That’s a mercy, but the body doesn’t always know mercy from assault in the first minutes. It knows pain. It knows shock. It knows the world has just handled it roughly. So the first thing I’m waiting for is collapse. Not dramatic collapse. Not blood everywhere. The quiet kind. The pulse goes thin. The skin goes cold. The sweat changes from the sweat of pain to the sweat of failure. The man stops fighting and looks easier, and someone foolish calls that improvement.”

She wrung the cloth out over the basin and laid it across the patient’s chest for a moment, feeling the heat through it.

“I’m checking heat,” she said. “He’s still warm. That’s what I want. If he cools too fast, especially at the hands and feet, that tells me the blood is pulling inward and the body is spending itself to keep the middle alive. If his face goes pinched, if his nose looks sharper than it should under this lamp, if his eyes look sunken while I’m still watching him, that’s not a face to argue with. That’s a face to act on.”

She moved her hand to the patient’s wrist again and held it there.

“I’m feeling his pulse. It’s fast. Fast is expected. Pain does that. Fear does that. A body remembering what happened to it does that. What I don’t want is fast and empty. I don’t want it slipping away under my fingers like something too small to hold. If that happens, he’s not just hurt. He’s leaving. And there’s a difference between a man who’s hurting and a man who’s leaving, even when both of them look still.”

She released the wrist and looked at the patient’s mouth.

“His color is still fair enough. That’s the second answer. If his lips grey, if the blue comes in at the corners, if his nails go dull and don’t answer when I press them, then the breathing has become the problem whether it sounds all right or not. Sometimes the sound lies. Sometimes the chest moves and the air isn’t doing what it should. That’s why I watch the mouth more than I trust the noise.”

She glanced at the strips of sheet she had used to bind him.

“I bound him to protect him, not to punish him. But binding has its own risks. If it’s too tight, it steals blood from the hands. If it’s too loose, he can work his arms free and hurt himself again before he knows what he’s doing. So I check the edges. I check the fingers. I check the skin where cloth meets flesh. If there’s pressure, it shows. If there’s damage starting, it shows first in little ways. A mark that stays. A hand that cools. A change in the way the fingers lie.”

She ran one finger along the edge of the binding as she spoke, not fussing, only confirming.

“That’s the next hour. After that comes the next six. In the next six, his body will try to tell me everything it has not told me yet. Pain will settle into a pattern. Fever will either stay away or begin its work. His stomach will decide whether it can keep water down. His mind will either come back clean or come back muddy. If he sleeps, I watch that sleep. If he wakes, I watch that waking. There’s no point where I get to say the thing is finished just because it seems calmer.”

She took up the cup, looked at the little water left in it, and set it down again within reach.

“If he wakes and wants more water, he gets it slow. I’m not letting him gulp. A man who has been in pain long enough can drink like he’s trying to outrun it, and then his stomach turns and he vomits while he’s still too weak to protect his throat. So I control it. Small sips. Then wait. Then more if he earns it. If he can keep that down, then food later. Broth if we have it. Nothing that requires much of him. The body doesn’t need a feast. It needs to be reminded it can take in something without fighting it.”

She looked at the patient’s bound arms.

“His shoulders will stiffen. That’s part of the rest too. If he lives and heals, he’ll pay for this in stiffness for days, maybe longer. He’ll try to move too soon. He’ll think because the worst is over he can test the repair. He can’t. The joint is angry. The muscles are torn in small ways that won’t show from outside. The body will guard, and guarding will make him feel old before his time. If he’s young, he’ll hate it. If he’s older, he’ll pretend it’s nothing until it proves otherwise.”

She shifted her weight slightly, not from comfort but from use.

“I’ll check his fingers again when he’s more awake. I’ll ask him if he can feel them. If he says they’re numb, if he says they tingle like pins, if he can’t make them move when he wants to, that changes things. That means nerve. That means the injury was not just the joint coming out, but what happened to the lines that carry feeling and motion while it was out. Some of that comes back. Some doesn’t. I won’t know tonight. I may not know for days. But I’ll watch for it.”

Her voice stayed level.

“If you’re asking for the rest because you want the clean shape of it, there isn’t one. The rest is all edges. It’s one thing bleeding into the next. It’s watching for infection before infection has a name. It’s knowing that a man can survive the wound and still die from what comes after it. The body doesn’t always forgive a victory.”

She looked toward the lamp, and for a moment her face was carved thin by its bad light.

“I’m going to trim this wick when I can,” she said. “Not for comfort. Because bad light hides changes. It makes grey look like shadow and blue look like dirt. If I’m going to watch a man through the night, I want to see him as he is, not as the lamp decides to show him.”

She turned back to the patient.

“You asked what happens if the rot comes. I told you some of it, but I’ll say it again because it belongs to the rest. Rot doesn’t arrive honest. It arrives disguised as small things. A little more heat. A little more pain. A smell that shouldn’t be there. A redness that spreads when it should stay put. A swelling that tightens instead of softening. A fever that doesn’t break when sweat says it should. If it gets into him, we clean it. We open it. We cut away what has died so the living doesn’t have to feed it. That’s not cruelty. That’s arithmetic. Dead flesh is not a man anymore. It’s a place for poison to build.”

She did not look away from the patient’s face as she said it.

“And if the rot is in a joint, that’s uglier than rot in muscle. Joints are unforgiving. They swell, they burn, they refuse to move, and the body makes a prison out of them. If infection gets into the shoulder itself, then every little thing I did tonight can still end in cutting. Not because I failed, but because the thing came in behind the repair and made itself invisible until it was strong enough to matter.”

Her hands rested briefly on the edge of the table.

“I’m not saying that to frighten you. I’m saying it because you asked for the whole of it. The whole of it includes the fact that saving a man from one danger does not save him from the next. It only gives him a chance to meet the next one alive.”

She looked at the instruments again.

“If he takes a turn in the night, here’s what I do. I don’t stand over him and wish things were different. I look for the cause. Is it his air? I clear it. Is it his breathing? I position him, turn him, watch for obstruction, listen for fluid. Is it his pulse? I look for bleeding I missed, for shock, for collapse. Is it his mind? I decide whether pain made him wild or whether the dulling went too far. If it’s the laudanum, I rouse him. I make him breathe. I don’t let him slip down just because sleep looks peaceful. Peaceful can be a lie.”

She touched the patient’s chest once, lightly.

“If he vomits, I turn him before I do anything else. Airway first. Always. A man can drown in his own stomach while people are busy feeling sorry for him. If he chokes, I clear his mouth with my fingers. I don’t wait for a tool if the tool is my hand and the need is now. If his breathing stops, I work him. I don’t make a speech. I don’t ask whether it’s fair. I work him until he breathes or until I know he won’t.”

Her voice did not change.

“And if he dies, that’s part of the rest too.”

She said it without drama, but not without weight.

“If he dies, his breathing changes first. It may go strange and uneven. It may stop and start. The pauses get longer. The pulse gets harder to find. The skin changes. The face changes. The body stops pretending it has more time than it does. I’ll know. I’ve seen it enough not to mistake it for sleep.”

She looked down at the patient’s hands.

“If he dies, I don’t leave him looking like a fight. I close his eyes if they’re open. I straighten his limbs before stiffness makes the work ugly. I cover him. I mark him if I have something to mark him with. Then I move him out of the way of the living, because the living still need the table. That’s not heartless. That’s what happens when death is not one thing in a tent but many things in many tents, and the night is too short for all of them.”

She wiped her hands again on the cloth at her belt, though they were clean enough.

“You may think that part is the worst. It isn’t always. Sometimes the worst is when a man dies quietly after everyone believes he’s past the danger. Sometimes the worst is when he lives and has to learn what living costs. Sometimes the worst is when he wakes and remembers exactly what happened, and the remembering hurts more than the wound.”

She looked at the bound strips again.

“He may wake angry. He may wake ashamed. He may cry and hate that he’s crying. He may beg for more laudanum, and I may have to say no. That’s part of the rest too. I don’t give the good stuff because someone is suffering. I give it when suffering will kill him or keep him from healing. Pain is real. But pain is not the only thing in the tent. Breathing is in the tent. Blood is in the tent. Fever is in the tent. The next man who comes in bleeding is in the tent. So I spend what I have where it buys life, not where it buys quiet.”

She did not say that with pride. She said it like a ledger that had been balanced too many times to pretend the numbers were kind.

“If you think I like that part, you’re wrong. I don’t. I never have. I don’t enjoy the sound a man makes when pain wakes him. I don’t enjoy holding a body down while it fights for its own good. I don’t enjoy watching someone break into pieces over something I can’t fix. I’m not made of stone, and I’m not made of cruelty. But I’m also not made of softness that lets a man die because I couldn’t stand to do the hard thing.”

She moved to the edge of the table and checked the blanket again.

“The rest is also what happens to you while you’re standing here watching it. You’ll want to look away. You’ll want to make it smaller in your head. You’ll want to say he’ll be fine because saying that feels like helping. It isn’t helping. It’s just wanting. The body doesn’t care what we want. It answers to what we do. So you watch what’s there. You report what changes. You don’t borrow disaster, but you don’t pretend disaster isn’t in the tent with us.”

She glanced at the basin, then at the row of supplies nearby.

“When this man is stable, if he stays stable, we move him. Not far. Not fast. But he can’t stay on this table forever if another man comes in with his belly open or his chest sucking air. So we put him on the ground with a blanket under him and a mark where he can be seen. We keep him warm. We keep his airway safe. We come back to him when we can. That’s another part no one tells you. Sometimes saving one man means leaving him alone for a little while so another man doesn’t die under your hands.”

Her mouth tightened, not in anger but in old fatigue.

“And if more come, they will. They always do. The war doesn’t stop because one man’s shoulders are back in their sockets. The war doesn’t care that we’re tired. The war sends the next one, and the next, and the next, and the only question is whether there are enough hands left to meet them. Some nights there aren’t. Some nights I have to choose who gets the knife, who gets the needle, who gets the last of the laudanum, and who gets only water and a voice telling him to keep breathing.”

She looked at the patient’s face again.

“That’s the rest. Not just this man. The whole machine around him. The tent. The lamp. The bucket. The cloth. The instruments. The shortage. The noise outside. The men waiting. The ones who won’t wait long enough. The ones who come in already gone and are called lost because there’s no other word that fits quickly enough.”

She took a breath, short and controlled.

“If he lives, he’ll carry this. He’ll have days when he can’t lift his arms without remembering. He’ll have nights when the pain wakes him and he thinks it’s happening again. He may flinch when someone reaches for him. He may hate the smell of this tent for the rest of his life. He may not be able to do the work he did before. He may be told he’s lucky, and he may not feel lucky. That’s part of the rest too. Survival is not the same as being untouched.”

She touched the edge of the binding once more.

“And if he lives well enough to walk out of here, he’ll still not be the same man who came in. Bodies remember. They keep the score in ways people don’t talk about. A shoulder that has been out can feel weather coming. A joint that has been forced back into place can carry the memory of it in every hard movement. He’ll learn to guard it. He’ll learn not to trust it the same way. Maybe he’ll get most of himself back. Maybe not all.”

Her eyes moved over the patient with the same steady attention she had given him from the beginning.

“I’m not telling you this to make you despair. I’m telling you because you asked for the rest, and the rest is not one clean ending. It’s a line of consequences. Some we can see now. Some we won’t see for days. Some we’ll never see, because the man will take them away with him when he leaves this tent and we’ll never know whether he healed straight or crooked.”

She looked toward the dark corner of the tent where the supplies lay.

“After he’s watched long enough, I’ll check the rest of him inch by inch. I’ll look under him for blood. I’ll check his back if we can turn him. I’ll check his scalp if there’s a cut hidden in the hair. I’ll check his boots if he’s still wearing them, because feet can tell you about cold, about circulation, about how long he’s been down. I’ll check his clothes for burns or tears that mean more than they look. I’ll look for powder marks, for dirt, for little wounds that seem nothing until they aren’t.”

She said it the way she would have said she was checking a harness for weak points.

“If I find something, I deal with it. If I don’t, I keep looking anyway, because missing a thing because I was tired is the same as missing it because I was careless. The body doesn’t care about my reasons.”

The patient made a small sound, not a scream, not a word, only the rough edge of breath moving through a throat that had been used hard. Sedge’s attention snapped to him at once.

“I’m listening,” she said. “No change. Just the body settling. But you see how it is. Even when the worst seems past, the smallest sound can still be important.”

She let the moment pass, then went on.

“When dawn comes, if it comes for him, we don’t celebrate. We count what we still have. His color. His breath. His pulse. His ability to swallow. His ability to know where he is. If he’s better, we start thinking about water, broth, rest, and keeping him from hurting himself through stupidity. If he’s worse, we start thinking about what new thing has gone wrong and whether we have the means to answer it.”

She looked at the instruments in the basin.

“And if we don’t have the means, that’s part of the rest too. There are things I can do with clean hands, good light, time, and enough supplies. There are things I can do with none of those. Then there are things I can’t do at all. I don’t pretend otherwise. I’ve had men die because I didn’t have enough light. Men die because I didn’t have enough hands. Men die because the thing that needed doing had to be done sooner than I could get to it. Men die because the war spent them faster than I could spend myself trying to keep them.”

Her voice did not shake. It only grew plainer.

“I don’t say that to make you pity me. Pity is useless. I say it because you asked for the truth, and the truth is that this work is not clean. It never has been. You don’t get to be a hero here. You get to be useful. Sometimes useful looks like holding a man down while you put him back together. Sometimes useful looks like saying no to the thing that would comfort him. Sometimes useful looks like letting him suffer a little so he can keep breathing. Sometimes useful looks like covering a dead man and moving on because the next one is already bleeding on the floor.”

She looked at the patient’s face for a long moment.

“And no, I don’t take pleasure in it. I say that because people mistake steadiness for hardness. They think if you can do this without falling apart, you must enjoy it in some secret way. You don’t. You just learn what has to be done and do it. The body is not a spectacle. It’s not a story. It’s meat and mechanism and heat and blood, and it can be broken in ways that make fine feelings useless. So you stop performing and start working. That’s all.”

She reached out and adjusted the blanket again, a small movement, practical and exact.

“But that doesn’t mean it costs nothing. It costs. Every time it costs. You just don’t get to spend the cost in front of the man who needs you. You spend it after. In your hands. In your sleep. In the way you hear a sound in the night and are already moving before your mind knows why. You spend it in the way you stop expecting clean endings. You spend it in the way you learn to call a thing by its true name instead of dressing it up so you can bear to look at it.”

She glanced once toward the place where Wick had spoken, though her eyes did not linger there.

“You asked me to say the rest. The rest is that you don’t get to be innocent after this. Not if you stay. Not if you keep watching. You’ll learn what bodies can do. You’ll learn what they can survive and what they can’t. You’ll learn the sounds. You’ll learn the smells. You’ll learn the difference between a wound that can wait and a wound that can’t. You’ll learn that sometimes the kindest thing is a hard hand and a true word, and sometimes the hardest thing is not doing more when doing more would only make a mess of the dying.”

Her voice dropped, but it did not soften.

“If he lives, he may never thank you. If he dies, you may never know whether anything you did mattered. That’s the rest. You work without certainty. You watch without guarantee. You hold the line between one breath and the next, and you do it because someone has to, not because it makes you good.”

She checked the patient’s pulse again.

“He’s still here. That’s not nothing. That’s everything we have right now. But the rest is knowing that ‘still here’ is not the same as safe. It’s only the place where the next work begins.”

She looked down at the man’s bound arms, at the blanket over his chest, at the cup within reach, at the strips of torn sheet, at the basin, at the instruments, at the poor lamp, at the whole small world of the tent.

“So here is the last of it,” she said. “We watch him until morning. We check everything. We give water when it’s safe. We give laudanum when it’s earned. We keep him warm. We keep him from hurting himself. We look for rot before it has a name. We listen for the quiet ones. If he worsens, we act. If he dies, we handle him with decency and move to the next living thing that still has a chance. If he lives, we let him heal without making a story out of it that he didn’t ask for.”

She set her hand briefly on the table’s edge.

“And when the next man comes in, we do it again. That’s the rest. All of it. No curtain. No clean ending. Just the next breath, the next check, and the next thing that needs doing before the night is through.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, still feeling the shape of his shoulders under my palms. "I want a drink," I say, and it's not a request.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not answer at once.

She kept two fingers on the patient’s wrist while she counted the pulse through ten beats, then fifteen, then twenty, because the number mattered more than the sound of a man asking for what he wanted. The pulse was still fast, but it had body to it. It did not slip. It did not flutter into nothing. She watched the patient’s mouth while she counted, then let her hand move from the wrist to the edge of the blanket over his ribs.

Only when she had finished the count did she speak.

“No,” she said.

She said it without sharpness. It was not a refusal meant to sting. It was the same flat, settled no she would have used if someone had asked to lean on a wounded limb.

“If you mean water,” she said, “there’s water. If you mean something that burns, then no. Not tonight. Not while he’s still in the hour where he can choke, or chill, or go quiet in a way that looks like sleep until it isn’t.”

She moved to the lamp. The wick had been burning badly, giving off more smell than light, and she had already decided it needed tending. She took the small tool from the crate beside the tent pole and trimmed the charred edge with quick, careful strokes. The flame dipped, hissed, then steadied into a cleaner, smaller light. The shadows in the tent shifted back a little. The patient’s face became easier to read.

Sedge looked at him again before she looked toward the place where Wick sat.

“You don’t get to dull yourself while I still need your eyes,” she said. “That’s not me being hard. That’s me being responsible for more than one body in this tent.”

She crossed to the bucket, took the clean cup she had set aside earlier, and filled it with water. She did not bring it with ceremony. She set it on the ground within reach, not near the patient’s table where it could be knocked into the work, but close enough that it could be found without searching.

“Drink that if you’re thirsty,” she said. “If you’re not thirsty, drink it anyway. Slow. You’ve been standing on fear and holding your breath, and that leaves a man hollow. Water won’t taste like what you want. It’ll still do more for you right now.”
