She wiped her hands on the cloth at her belt, then checked the patient’s forehead with the back of her hand. Still hot, but not the dry, tightening heat she would have hated to feel. The sweat had not turned cold. That was good. She left her hand there only long enough to be sure.

“If I gave you liquor now,” she went on, “you’d feel kinder for twenty minutes. Maybe thirty. Then your hearing would go soft. Your eyes would start to rest too long in one place. You’d miss the little catch in his breathing, or the change in his lips, or the sound that means he’s about to bring up what little water he’s had. And then I’d have to choose between him and you. I don’t want to make that choice. Neither do you.”

She glanced at the basin where the instruments lay.

“There’s a bottle in the chest,” she said. “You know there is. It’s for cleaning, for wounds, for the kind of last-ditch work that makes a man scream through his teeth so I can keep him from dying of rot three days later. It’s not for steadying hands after the worst is past. If we start spending it on that, we’ll have none left when it has to do a real job.”

Her voice stayed level. She was not preaching. She was laying out the shape of things the way she laid out instruments: one beside the other, where they could be seen.

“You want a drink because your hands still remember what they held,” she said. “Because you helped keep a man down while his body fought him, and because you heard him scream, and because now the quiet has come in and your head is looking for a door. I know the want. It’s not weakness. It’s the body asking for some way to put the night down.”

She looked at the patient’s bound arms.

“But you don’t put it down with whiskey while there’s still work on the table. You put it down with the work. You wash your hands. You drink water. You watch his color. You listen to his chest. You let your body come down slow instead of knocking it sideways with something stronger. That’s not a sermon. That’s how you keep from making yourself useless when I need you useful.”

Sedge moved back to the patient’s side and checked the edges of the binding again. She ran one finger along the cloth where it passed near the skin, not to adjust it, but to make sure it had not shifted in the minutes since she had fastened it. The patient’s fingers were still warm enough. The nails still answered when she pressed them. She let her touch linger on the nearest hand for a moment.

“If he takes a turn,” she said, “I need you on your feet and clear-headed. If he vomits, I need you to turn his head before I’m halfway there. If his breathing changes, I need you to hear it and name it, not stare at it while your thoughts swim. If he wakes wild, I need you to keep your hands where they’ll help and not where they’ll hurt him. That’s the arrangement. You asked for the rest, and this is part of it too: after the loud work, you still have to stay sharp enough for the quiet work.”

She straightened the blanket a little, not pulling it higher, only smoothing it where it had bunched near the patient’s side.

“When the night is over,” she said, “if there’s anything left that can be spared, you can have a small measure. Not enough to forget. Enough to taste that you got through. If there’s nothing to spare, then you’ll have water and sleep and the fact that you didn’t fall apart when it mattered. That may not sound like much right now. It’s still what I’ve got.”

Her eyes moved from the patient to the cup she had set on the ground.

“If you need something stronger than water before then, you tell me. You don’t reach for the medicine chest. You tell me, and I’ll decide whether you’re near the edge or just tired enough to think you are. There’s a difference. I’ve seen both.”

She paused, listening to the patient breathe. The sound was thin, but steady. No wetness. No new struggle. The tent held its usual low sounds around them: canvas shifting, distant coughing, the faint creak of someone moving in pain somewhere beyond their small circle of lamplight.

“I’m not going to pretend the want isn’t real,” Sedge said. “It is. You’ve earned it. But earning a thing doesn’t mean you get to take it in the middle of a watch. Sometimes earning means carrying the weight until the work lets you set it down.”

She looked at her own hands for a moment, not with sentiment, but with the same practical attention she gave everything else. They were steady. They were also tired. She closed them once, then opened them again.

“My hands shake too,” she said. “Not now. Later. Sometimes in the night. Sometimes when I’m washing blood off them and there’s no more blood to wash. Sometimes when I’m eating and the food tastes like nothing because the tent still smells like opened bowels and hot iron. That’s part of this. You don’t get to be untouched by it just because you did the right thing.”

She turned back to the patient and checked his lips again. The color was still there. Faint, but present. She let out a breath through her nose, not relief exactly, but acknowledgment.

“So here’s what you get instead of a drink,” she said. “You get the truth. You helped keep him alive long enough for me to put him back. You’re still needed. You’re not useless. You’re not cruel for having held him. You’re not weak for wanting something to take the edge off. And you’re not finished yet.”

She picked up the damp cloth from the patient’s forehead, rinsed it in the basin, wrung it out, and laid it back with the same efficient care.

“Drink the water,” she said. “Then look at his fingers. If they cool, if the color stops coming back when you press them, if his breathing turns wet or his face goes pinched, you tell me. Not after you’ve decided whether it’s important enough. You tell me.”

Sedge settled back onto the crate beside the table, close enough to reach the patient in one movement, far enough not to crowd him. She did not look away from the man on the table as she spoke again.

“And when this watch is done,” she said, “you can want that drink as loud as you like. Until then, you want with your eyes open.”

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I pick up the cup and drain it. It tastes like nothing. "Alright," I say, and the word's heavy. "Tell me what to look at next."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge did not try to lift the word. She let it sit where it had fallen, because some words had to be carried, not decorated.

“His hands,” she said. “We start at the edges and work inward. The edges confess before the center does.”

She leaned over the patient’s bound arms without touching them yet. The lamp gave better light now, but it was still poor enough to make shadows out of harmless folds in the blanket. She noted that, too, and shifted her body so her own shadow did not fall across the man’s chest.

“I’m looking at the fingers first,” she said. “Not to see whether they’re clean. They aren’t. Dirt under the nails is ordinary. What matters is color, warmth, and whether the blood still knows how to come back.”

She bent closer to the patient’s right hand.

“I’m pressing the nail now. One quick press, then let go. See how it goes pale? Now I’m watching the color return. It’s slow, but it returns. That tells me the blood is still reaching the end of the limb. If it doesn’t return, or if it takes so long that I start wondering whether I’m watching a corpse’s hand, then something is wrong. The binding may be too tight, or the body may be pulling back from the hands to keep the middle alive.”

She moved to the next finger, and the next, not with ceremony, but with the same dull thoroughness she would have used to check stitches in a seam.

“I’m doing more than one,” she said. “One finger can lie. A whole hand is harder to lie with. I’m comparing the right to the left. The right is a little cooler. Not cold. A little. That may be because he lay on it, or because the shoulder was worse, or because the binding is sitting differently. I don’t jump from a small difference to a conclusion. I mark it and watch whether it grows.”

Her thumb passed lightly over the patient’s knuckles.

“I’m feeling for sweat. Sweat is still here. That’s useful. Dry, hot skin would tell me one thing. Cold, wet skin would tell me another. This is the skin of a man in pain whose body hasn’t given up arguing. I’m also feeling the weight of the hand. If it lies too loose, like something dropped, I don’t like it. If it curls a little, even without meaning, that’s life in it.”

She checked the edge of the torn sheet where it crossed the forearm.

“I’m looking at the binding now. Not to admire my own work. To make sure it hasn’t become a second injury. Cloth can cut without a blade if it’s pulled wrong or if swelling comes up under it. I’m looking for ridges in the skin. I’m looking for marks that stay after the cloth shifts. I’m looking at the way the hair lies on the arm. If the skin below is puffed and tight, I’ll loosen it whether he likes it or not.”

She slipped one finger beneath the edge of the strip, not enough to disturb it, only enough to test the space.

“There’s room,” she said. “Not enough to make me lazy, but enough to keep it from being a tourniquet. If his fingers begin to swell, if the nails go blue, if the hand below the binding gets colder instead of warmer, I’ll cut it open before I argue with myself about whether it’s too soon.”

She released the arm and moved to the wrist.

“I’m taking his pulse here because it’s closer than the neck and less likely to make him thrash if he’s half awake. I’m not counting for the pleasure of numbers. I’m listening to the shape of it. Fast, yes. But there’s weight to it. It isn’t running away from me. Laudanum will slow him some. That’s part of what it does. If it slows him into a deep, loose quiet where his breathing becomes hard to see, I’ll rouse him. I won’t let him slip down just because he looks easier.”

She counted in silence for a few seconds, her eyes on the patient’s face rather than on her own hand.

“I’m watching his mouth while I count,” she said. “If the pulse changes, the mouth often shows it before the whole body does. His lips are still flesh-colored. There’s a little grey at the corners, but that’s exhaustion and pain, not the blue I fear. If the blue spreads, if it settles into the middle of the lip, if it shows in the tongue when he opens his mouth, that’s not a thing to think over. That’s a thing to shout for me over, even if I’m only six inches away.”

She let go of the wrist and straightened just enough to look down the length of the patient’s body.

“Next, his face,” she said. “Not the expression. The expression will make you sorry. Look at the parts of it that do work.”

She pointed with her chin, not with her finger, because her hands were still near the patient.

“The nostrils first. If they start pulling wide with every breath, that means he’s working harder to draw air than he should. If they stay quiet, that’s better. The mouth next. If it hangs open and the jaw falls back, I worry about the tongue. If the teeth are clenched, I worry about him biting himself or swallowing wrong. If there’s froth at the corners, I look at the chest. If there’s vomit, I turn him before I finish the thought.”

She leaned closer again, watching the patient’s throat as if it were a small, unreliable door.

“I’m watching for swallowing,” she said. “A swallow is a little thing until it isn’t. If he can swallow his own spit, his throat is still answering him. If he can’t, if it starts to gather in his mouth, if his voice comes out wet when he tries to make a sound, then the airway is in danger even if he’s still breathing. I’ll keep his head turned if that starts. I won’t prop him up like he’s sitting at supper. I won’t pour water into him. I’ll keep the path clear.”

She touched the back of her hand to the patient’s cheek, then to his forehead, then to the side of his neck, comparing one place to another.

“I’m checking heat by touch,” she said. “Not by guessing. The face can burn while the hands go cold. The neck can tell a truer story. He’s warm. Still sweating a little. That’s the body working. If he starts to shiver, I’ll add more blanket, but not until I know whether the shiver is chill or fear or pain. If he burns dry and his lips crack, that’s fever coming in too early. If he goes cold and damp in a way that feels spent, that’s shock. I don’t need you to know which is which yet. I need you to notice the change and bring it to me.”

Her gaze moved down to the patient’s chest.

“After the face, the chest,” she said. “But not the whole chest at once. Pick one place. Watch it move.”

She laid her hand flat over the center of his shirt, not pressing, only resting.

“I’m feeling the breastbone rise. I’m watching both sides. They should move together. If one side lags, if one side seems to pull while the other drags, that tells me something inside is not doing its work. I’m not looking for heroism here. I’m looking for symmetry. The body is honest about imbalance if you give it time to show you.”

She kept her hand there while she spoke.

“I’m counting breaths now. Not because the number itself saves him, but because changes in number tell me whether he’s climbing or falling. Fast can be pain. Faster can be fear. Faster still can be the body trying to make up for something it isn’t getting. Slow can be rest, but slow can also be laudanum taking too much. If his breathing becomes so shallow I have to hold my own breath to see whether he’s still taking any, I’ll wake him. If I can’t wake him enough to make him swallow or move, then the trouble has changed shape.”

She leaned closer to the patient’s mouth and listened without touching him.

“I’m listening for sound,” she said. “Not for loudness. For texture. A clean breath can still be weak. A noisy breath can still be strong. I’m listening for wetness. I’m listening for a click. I’m listening for a whistle that wasn’t there before. I’m listening for the little stop at the top of a breath that says the body is bracing against pain. If I hear wetness, I’ll turn him, check his mouth, and listen again. If the wetness stays, I’ll need to know whether it’s in the throat or lower down. The answer changes what I can do.”

She straightened again and moved her hand to the edge of the blanket over the patient’s belly.

“Then the belly,” she said. “People forget the belly because it isn’t where the shoulders are. That’s foolish. The belly can be quiet while it’s turning bad, and it can be loud when there’s nothing wrong at all. I’m watching it move with breath first. If it rises and falls easy, that’s good. If it goes still, if it looks like he’s holding it away from the rest of him, that’s a warning.”

She placed her palm lightly on the blanket, not pressing.

“I’m feeling for hardness,” she said. “Not yet with real pressure. Just enough to know whether the wall under the cloth is soft or board-like. A soft belly can still hide trouble, but a hard belly is trouble announcing itself. If I press and he flinches in one place, I’ll remember the place. If he guards before I touch him, that’s worse. If he starts to sweat more just from my hand lying there, I’ll take that seriously.”

She lifted her hand again.

“I’m not going to dig around in him for the sake of finding something. But I’ll check him properly once he’s calmer. I’ll press in small circles, one place after another, and I’ll watch his face while I do it. Pain that jumps under the hand is different from pain that spreads. Pain that stays in one spot can be a bruise or a torn muscle. Pain that makes the whole body stiffen can be something leaking where it shouldn’t.”

Her eyes moved over the patient’s shirt.

“I’m looking at the cloth now,” she said. “Not because cloth matters more than flesh, but because cloth remembers what flesh sometimes hides. I’m looking for damp patches. I’m looking for blood that’s dried dark and stiff. I’m looking for fresh red showing through old sweat. I’m looking for tears that mean something dragged across him. I’m looking for powder burns, because if there’s a burn I missed, it changes how I clean the skin.”

She reached for the edge of the patient’s collar.

“I’m opening his shirt a little,” she said. “Not to expose him to the cold. To see what’s under the neckline. If he fights it, I’ll stop and steady him first. Right now he’s still enough.”

She drew the fabric back just enough to reveal the hollow of his throat and the upper plane of his chest. The skin there was dirty, streaked with sweat and grime, but there was no bright soak of blood. There was a shallow scrape across one collarbone, raw at the edges and already weeping a little clear fluid.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I watch her hands expose the scrape. "That's new," I say. My voice comes out flat. "Does it need cleaning?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good," Halloway said. "Wrong shape is the honest answer. Names lie. Shapes don't."

She lowered the lamp to knee height and tipped it so the light lay flat along the water. Raking light. Anything that moved under the surface would show itself in rings.

"Here's my read. Man-sized. Folded forward at the waist — not slumped, *folded*, like a penknife closing. Knees straight. Arms longer than arms should stop at. Skin's the wrong colour for a drowning and the wrong texture for anything I've hauled out of water before." A beat. "And it was moving until we came down. Corpses don't have timing. I don't trust anything with timing."

The water lay dead flat. She watched it anyway.

"So nobody touches it yet. Four feet of standing water is the finest instrument in this cellar — nothing breathes down there without the surface telling on it. We stand still and we watch for rings. Small ones. Hair-wide. Anything that has to breathe has to displace."

She glanced at Pike then, brief, and back to the water.

"Now you. Tell me what's wrong with the shape, specifically. Count it out — limbs, joints, proportions. If you can say precisely what's wrong with a thing, you're halfway to knowing what it is." Her mouth twitched, without much humour in it. "And the other half is knowing what kills it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath and stare at the silhouette under the water. "The arms... they bend wrong. Too many joints. And the head's too small for the shoulders."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Two for two," Halloway said. "Both true. Neither one's the worst of it."

She kept the lamp low, the light flat on the water.

"Count the bends in the near arm. I make it four. Could be five, the water's lying to us a little. A man gets two — elbow, wrist. Four bends isn't an arm, it's a *chain*. And a chain doesn't fold the way a limb folds. It folds because folding is what it's for."

A beat.

"Head's small, yes. But refine it: with shoulders that wide, either the skull's undersized or what I'm calling shoulders isn't shoulders. Could be the top of something folded down over where a neck ought to be. I'm not betting either way until I see it out of the water — and I'm in no hurry to see it out of the water."

She straightened up an inch, still watching the surface.

"Here's what your two facts add up to, Pike. That silhouette is a lie. It's not a body, it's a *packing* job. Folded that tight with joints to spare, it's half the size it runs at, and when it opens, those arms reach twice as far as anything that shape has a right to. We're not looking at the thing. We're looking at how it travels."

"And it stopped moving when we came down the stairs. It knows the door. It knows we're here. And it folded itself into the one shape guaranteed to make somebody wade into four feet of cold water — a drowned man, poor devil, somebody ought to go get him." Her voice stayed level. "I've seen this play before. Flooded wheel pit under a mill, twelve years back. Looked like a boy folded in the shallows. My partner went in and came out one arm lighter, with a story. The story was worth less. It took the rest of the night and most of a boat hook to get the thing into pieces."

"Water's still flat, and that's not comfort. Either it's holding whatever passes for its breath, or it doesn't need any. A thing that doesn't breathe can wait down there a week, and I can't. So nobody wades. We do not fight it in its own swimming pool."

"So. Inventory. What did we bring down — and don't say hope. Rope, iron, anything with a long handle and no part of us attached to it. Because I count three plays: drain the cellar and make it come out dry, smoke it out, or stand here being interesting until it decides we're worth unfolding for. I like the first two."

The water moved.

Not at the far end. One ring, thin as a hair, opened by the bottom step — not six feet from Halloway's boot, in water where nothing was. The folded shape at the far end hadn't shifted. She'd have sworn to that.

"There it is," she said, very quietly. She didn't step back. "Lamp stays up. Watch the water by your feet, not the body. The body's the advertisement." Her eyes tracked the ring out to nothing. "And it hasn't moved, which means one of two things. Either it's got a friend down here — or it's longer than it's showing us."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"No," Halloway said. "And I'll give you the whole answer, because it's the right question and it deserves better than a head-shake."

She kept the lamp low, light flat on the water.

"I've pulled eleven drowned men out of rivers, wells, and one decorative pond. You learn the reading. Hours old: skin goes marble-pale, hands wrinkle like a laundress has been at them. A day: the belly swells. Three days: green, floating face-down, arms trailing behind like he's still swimming. The dead *drift*, Pike. They go where the water puts them and they hold nothing."

A beat.

"That thing is holding a pose. Knees straight, spine folded, arms tucked. Dead muscle can't tuck — it hasn't got the opinion. Living muscle folded that tight is muscle *choosing* to be small. So: not a drowned man. Not recently a person. Probably not ever a person — and I say probably, because I once said 'not' in front of a mill wheel and it cost a man his arm."

She let the lamp drift left, along the stair riser. There was a tide mark on the stone, silt-dark, set in at knee height.

"I told you shapes don't lie. I'll amend it: stolen shapes lie badly. It's wearing a drowned man the way a bad actor wears grief — outline's right, every joint gives it away. Four bends in an arm. Head lost in the shoulders. The wrongness you noticed is the truth leaking through the seams."

"And here's the part I like less. That costume was *learned*. Nothing folds itself into a drowned man by accident — it folds into that shape because the shape works. Bait keeps its shape because bait gets taken. Somebody came down here at some point, saw something in the water that needed carrying, and went in after it." She nodded at the tide mark. "Water's stood at this level long enough to stain the stone. Months, not days. And four feet of water that old should stink like a tannery if there's a body under it. Smell anything? Neither do I. Whatever's down there doesn't leave leftovers."

She looked back at the far end, at the folded shape that hadn't moved.

"So. Was that a person? No — it's doing an impression of one. Badly. But well enough to get somebody killed, which is the only standard that matters in this room. Was there a person here recently? If so, they're not what we're looking at. They're the lesson it learned."

Her voice dropped a register.

"And that ring by the step — it opened where a wader's third step lands. Far end's the advertisement. Near end's the mouth. So two jobs while we stand here being boring. Inventory: rope, iron, anything long-handled with no part of us on the end of it. And count the dry steps behind you. If that thing unfolds, the stairs are the one argument we win — and I want to know exactly how many of them are ours."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My heart's pounding. I count the steps behind me without looking away. "Three dry steps. I've got a rope and a pry bar." I swallow. "And you said don't say hope."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Rope and a pry bar," Halloway said. "Correct answer to every question I've ever asked in a cellar. And you didn't say hope — you'll do. Hope never held anything down. Iron does. A pry bar's a boat hook with opinions, and I've done respectable work with worse."

She wound the free end of the rope twice around her fist. Held, not tied. That distinction was the whole game.

"Three dry steps is our country. The waterline's the border, and we don't emigrate. Division of labour: I keep the lamp and the line, you keep the bar and your eyes, and your mouth is the alarm. Call every ring the instant it opens. Wrong and loud beats right and quiet — I can ignore a false alarm. I can't ignore the one you swallowed."

A beat.

"Here's what we don't know: one animal or two. So we ask. I throw past the far body, let the coil sink, and draw the line back across it — slow, like dragging thread over a sleeping dog. Three answers. It twitches: the far end's a hunter. It doesn't twitch and the near water stays flat: dead bait, and the live one's somewhere we haven't looked, and I already hate that answer. It doesn't twitch and the near water rings: one animal, longer than this cellar looks. Watch for which."

She threw flat and low, a stone you wanted to stop mid-water. The coil opened in the air, slapped down past the folded shape, and sank. Rings spread from the splash, ordinary and lazy, and died. Nothing rose to the noise. Patient, then. Patience in a predator means it's never lost an argument down here.

She drew the line in an inch at a time. The rope cut a fine V into the surface. It dragged across the shoulders-that-weren't, across the small drowned head, and the shape did not care. Not a shiver.

*Bait doesn't care about rope.*

She was three feet into the recovery when the line stopped. Not snagged — snagged jerks. This was weight. Steady, live weight, pulling down and toward the stairs. And the V where the rope entered the water had turned around. It was *travelling*. Walking the bottom on whatever it used for feet, coming toward the steps with no more wake than a pike under a float.

No offence.

Halloway opened her hand. The rope ran out through her fingers, hissing over the stone, and the water took all of it — gone in four seconds, swallowed politely.

"Mill rule," she said. "You don't argue with a thing in its own water. It wants the rope, the rope is a tax. My partner argued. Cost him an arm and bought us the rule, so it's expensive and I keep it polished."

The V didn't slow when the rope ended. So the rope wasn't the point. They were.

"Up the steps, Pike. Walking pace — running says prey. Bar in your strong hand. I'm behind you, and that's not chivalry, it's arithmetic: if anything comes up these stairs it comes through me first, and I've been a doorway before. It's survivable."

The V crossed the last stretch of dark water, reached the foot of the steps, and stopped. Settled. Directly below their boots, the surface went still, and stayed interested.

"There it is," she said quietly. "Under the stairs. Of course it's under the stairs. That's where I'd sit."

A beat.

"And think on the climb. We come back with fire or a pump, and at the top I'm going to ask you which, and why. Walking pace. Now."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
For two full seconds Halloway said nothing, which from her was a shout.

"I said the stairs," she said, very quietly. "We'll discuss your hearing somewhere with a door." Then she came down into the water after Pike, walking pace, no wake — because the last man who improvised in water like this was the reason she owned rules, and she'd watched that from dry stone once already. She wasn't doing it twice.

The cold took her past the knee, then the hip. She kept her eyes on the surface behind them. Flat. Flat had stopped being comfort and started being manners.

"It let you pass," she said. "You walked within arm's reach of where it's sitting and the water didn't so much as ripple. That's not luck. A thing that lets you by has already decided where you're allowed to stand. It gave us the deep end and kept the door. I said the stairs were the one argument we win — I think it was listening."

She stopped an arm's length off the folded shape and let the light do the work.

"Plainly, then. You've earned plain — you're standing in it. Skin's not skin. No pores, no hair, no grain. Nothing's ever been warm in it. Colour of something that grew in the dark, texture of something that grew wet. Seams at the joints, like a glove. It was *made*, and whatever made it can sew."

"Near arm. Four bends, and between them, under the skin, segment lines — each segment the length of your forearm. That's not an arm, Pike. It's a *finger*, built to arm size. Drawn by something that only ever had the idea of one. Head's the same story: smooth, one seam where a mouth would be useful. Last knuckle, wearing the notion of a face."

"And here's what answers your question. Left shoulder — real cloth. Shirt collar, sodden." She didn't touch it. She used her knife, tip only, iron between — the knife hadn't got an opinion to lose — and turned the collar. A laundry mark, faded. Initials. "Near arm ends in a boot. Good leather, laced, hanging off the chain-end like a glove off a hand. No foot in it. No leg above it. The chain runs down into the boot and out the other side. It dresses from its meals."

"So. Months back a man came down those steps. Water already standing. He saw what you saw, and did what you just did — only first, and for kinder reasons. It took him under the way it took our rope: politely. Then it kept what worked. Boot, collar, the details that read human at ten feet in bad light to somebody kind. The rest of him it spent — there's no smell in this water, Pike. Months of it, sealed, and it smells like a well. Somewhere there's a household short one man and a shirt in a drawer with this mark on it, and nobody's told them to stop looking."

"You asked what happened to it. Wrong direction. Nothing happens to it. It *happens to people*."

While she said it, the small head turned. No ripple. No bubbles. The water didn't even file a report. It rotated on its seam, unhurried, and stopped with its absence of a face toward the lamp — the first movement it had offered in a quarter of an hour.

"There it is," Halloway said. "The costume's done its work. We're in the water; it doesn't need to look drowned for our benefit any more." A beat. "And note — the far end moved while the near end sits still under the stairs. Two animals, or one, longer than this cellar looks, and we've been standing inside it since the rope. I don't get to know which yet. What I know is the door's its country, and the water by the steps has gone quiet, and a thing that stops showing you where it is has decided where *you* are."

"New arithmetic, and then you talk. Lamp's a pint of oil. Oil floats, oil burns, and this cellar is four feet of the finest fire-spread I've ever stood waist-deep in. There's a coal chute, right wall, above the tide mark — iron flap, I marked it coming in. That's our door if the stairs stay his. And we've maybe ten minutes before this cold takes our fingers off the job."

"I was going to ask you at the top of the stairs — fire or a pump, and why. You've saved me the climb. So answer it here, in its swimming pool. What's directly above us — rooms with sleepers in them, or rafters and rats? Because fire's the right answer in one of those and murder in the other, and I'd rather know which before I tip the lamp."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the coal chute. My teeth are chattering. "Rooms with sleepers," I say. "A family, two floors up. Fire's murder."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Correct," Halloway said. "Fire's murder. So the lamp's demoted back to a lamp, and the answer's the pump — which is a daylight job, because four feet of water standing for months means something *feeds* this cellar, and pumping an inlet is bailing the sea with a hat. We find the source. We drain its country out from under it. Then it's a long wet thing in a dry room, and dry rooms are my country. That's tomorrow's arithmetic."

A beat.

"Tonight's is shorter. Out of the water, up the chute. Along the right wall — there's a coal bay under the chute mouth, brick pen, waist-high. That's our dry ground. Walking pace."

She moved first, hugging the brick, and the small head turned to follow the light — no ripple, unhurried, like a lighthouse that had decided it disliked them specifically.

Then every inch of the water broke into rings at once.

Off the walls. Off the stairs. Around their own knees. Hair-wide circles, ten thousand of them, the way rain hits a pond — and there was no rain, and nothing moved, and the silt-dark tide mark on the stair riser went quietly under. The third dry step drowned.

"There it is," Halloway said. "Displacement doesn't lie. Nothing came into this cellar and the water rose anyway — so something under the silt just took up more room. It's not *in* the cellar, Pike. It's *under* it. The drowned man was one end. The stairs are the other. Everything between — every foot of floor we've stood on since the rope came tight — is coiled middle. I said we'd been standing inside it. I'd hoped I was being colourful."

At the far end, the folded shape was folding further. *Down*. Sinking joint by joint into the silt, the collar going under, then the boot, unhurried — a lure being retrieved. And by the bottom step, the water had stopped being flat and started being busy.

"Mind the direction of the arithmetic. It's not hunting us — we're the entertainment. It's piling itself into the stairwell, and every coil it stacks there lifts the water a finger's width. Three dry steps when we came down. I count two. When that count finds nought, the door's in its country — and above the door, a family that's slept two floors up from a lake since spring and called the noises *settling*."

A beat.

"Coal bay, then the chute, and you're first up. The flap's iron, hinged at the top, opens outward — you'll shoulder it halfway up a black throat with your heels trailing in the dark, and it'll ring like a church bell, and everything in this water will know our address. So you go loud and fast, and you don't stop for anything you hear me say behind you. I'm last up. The last thing up a throat is the part that gets bitten, and I've thirty years of seniority."

"One decision first, and it's yours, because the lamp's in your hands. Take it up, and I hold this water blind with a knife and whatever the dark feels like showing me. Leave it with me, and you find that flap by feel, at speed, with a pint of oil swinging at your hip and a family sleeping over your head if you drop it. I've an opinion. I'm keeping it — I'm not the one in the throat. Choose fast, your teeth are already arguing. And then climb like the water's rising."

It was rising.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Right question," Halloway said. "Wrong hour. You get it anyway — the ones who ask it at the waterline get to ask it again someday. The ones who don't, I write to." She was already moving, hugging the right wall, walking pace, eyes on the stair water, which had gone from busy to *interested*. "And since you never chose, you get my opinion after all: the lamp goes up with you. I carry it to the throat; from the first foothold it's yours. The coal's been drinking cellar water since spring — oil on wet coal smoulders and swears, it doesn't take. I'll gamble a pint of oil against a hinge you can't find by feel. Those are the odds, and they're good ones."

A beat.

"What's under the skin. I know, because of the mill. A night and most of a boat hook got me the anatomy lesson nobody offers twice. No bones. No gut. No heart. Not one animal — a chain of them, sealed segments, forearm-length, and a mouth at every seam. That's the fact I'd underline: it hasn't got *a* mouth. It's got a mouth for every joint, and none of them is ever in a hurry. That's how the rope went down so politely — a seam opened in the dark and the water handed it in."

"And inside the mill one, when I broke the segments: the pond's missing decade. Buttons. A wedding ring worn smooth. Teeth — sorted by size. *Lined up*, Pike, like a tradesman's drawers. Messy is an animal. Sorted is a bookkeeper."

"So. Him. Spring, when the water first stood. He came down with a light, saw what you saw, and did the kind thing — the same thing you did tonight, only first, and alone. Third step. Here's the mechanics, since you asked for exactly: it doesn't grab. It *accepts*. His shin met a seam, the seam closed at his knee, polite as a turnstile. Then he reached for the rail — and that was the arm. It takes what's offered, deepest first. Every move he made to save himself, he paid for in a limb. He got one hand on the rail. It leaned. The water came up to meet him. Inside a minute the cellar was flat again — no fight, no noise, nothing you'd hear from a kitchen two floors up. That's the part I'd want his people told. The whole thing was quieter than we've been tonight."

"Then the bucket line — passed segment to segment, down into the silt, the way buckets go at a fire. Months. What's left of him is what it can't spend: the teeth. A ring, if he wore one. Tomorrow, when its country's drained, I'll break it open on dry stone and count them, and match a laundry mark to a house, and somebody stops looking. I'm the postmistress for that kind of letter. Somebody has to be."

"Under the skin now: chain and nothing else. The skin was never his — it grows its own, dark and wet and seamed. Whether it sews for itself or something sews for it is above my pay and below my interest, and that arrangement is how I've seen fifty. The collar and the boot it kept because they're proven parts. Bait keeps its shape because bait gets taken. His kindness taught it a costume."

"You asked how far it got. Do the arithmetic with me. The mill one was the length of a rowboat. This one is a cellar. I can't prove what it spends them on — growth, I'd guess — but things that grow, grow on what they're fed. Look at the room, Pike. Some of the size of this room *is him*."

The second dry step went under while she said it. No ceremony. The tide mark just stopped being a tide mark.

"There it is. One step left, and that's what the lecture cost. I'd have said it faster; you'd have remembered it worse." She reached the coal bay, brick to her back, and lifted the lamp toward the chute mouth above. "If you meet another one, three rules. Water that's lost things and doesn't stink has an accountant in it — dead water should smell. It stops moving when you arrive — corpses don't have timing, and nothing folds that tight to sleep; folded is travel. And never wade, never reach. Somebody in the water gets a gaff from dry stone, and when your heart argues, remember its entire costume is built out of somebody's heart arguing. Don't teach it anything. Kindness is how it gets dressed."

"And if you must kill one, take its country first — drain it, and a long wet thing in a dry room is rope-work. Then count the pieces. The mill one, in the boat, in nine parts — every part still turned to watch me. You're finished when nothing in the bucket is interested in you."

She held the lamp up to the black throat of the chute.

"Your turn to be loud. Lamp in the off hand, bar in the strong. Shoulder that flap like it owes you money, and don't stop for anything you hear me say behind you — the last thing up a throat is the part that gets bitten, and I've thirty years of seniority." A beat. "You asked the right question at the worst time. That's the whole job. Now climb."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content:
I take the lamp, the iron warm from her grip. My hand shakes. "I'm not going to meet another one," I say. "Because we're going to kill this one."

I get my boots into the brickwork and start climbing. The bar makes a terrible racket against the sides of the chute. I can feel the water rising at my ankles.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Good," Halloway said. "Keep that. Cold hands, warm intent — tomorrow runs on it. But get the sequence right, because wanting a thing dead while standing in its water is precisely how arms get lost. My partner wanted this one's cousin gone, and wanted it from waist-deep. Tonight we leave. Tomorrow we find what feeds this cellar and drain its country out from under it. Then it's rope-work and buckets, and we call the whole ledger killed. You can't kill the thing you're standing in, Pike. You can only leave, and be rude about it later."

A beat.

"And your hand's shaking. Let it. Shaking's honest. Steady, in this water, would be acting. Climb."

The lamp went up the throat and took the light with it, and the dark came down like a lid. She let it. Ears can work a room if you've listened for thirty years, and hers had tenure. Water finding new stone, one stair at a time — the last dry step went under while she stood there, a small swallow, no ceremony. Then the swallowing went on, and it wasn't stairs any more. It was the doorframe. The thing was stacking itself into the doorway, coil on tidy coil, and every coil lifted her water a finger's width.

She waded the coal bay — thigh-deep now, cold with teeth in it — and took the throat the proper way: spine against one wall, boots against the other, palms flat on the brick. Nothing hooked. Nothing offered. *It takes what's offered, deepest first.* The dead man reached for a rail and paid an arm for the reach. She pushed. That difference was the whole of his obituary.

Two body-lengths up, the tax came due.

Her trailing heel dipped at the waterline and something closed on the boot. No pull — that was the ugly part. Nothing pulled. The boot simply stopped being hers, held the way a turnstile holds a coin: already spent, already counted. Every instinct she owned said *kick*, and every one of those instincts was the dead man's. So the knife finally got honest work — two strokes through her own laces — and her foot came out of the leather and up, and below her a seam settled around an empty boot with a sound like a polite cough.

"Up the chute," she called, flat and unhurried, because hurried is what prey sounds like. "That splash was a boot, not me. You'll know the difference if it's ever me — I swear more. Rope, then boot. It's buying us in instalments, and I'm declining the payment plan. Climb."

Inventory, revised: one knife, one sock, thirty years of seniority. She'd carried worse kits into better rooms.

She climbed. Stockinged foot on wet brick — skin was cheaper than leg; she'd invoice herself later. Above her the bar rang off the iron like a bell-ringer with a grudge, and she was glad of every clang: they'd promised this cellar a church bell, and Pike was paying in advance. Better the address shouted than whispered. The water followed her up the throat, an inch at a time, patient as a debt collector.

Then the swallowing stopped.

Mid-ledger, no warning. The water at her ankles stopped rising, and neither of those was mercy, because mercy doesn't do arithmetic. Things stop piling when they're finished being where they were.

Below her, in the drowned bay, the coal began to move. Not a slide — coal slides when the pile's overfull, one rude rush and done. This was *rolling*. Piece over piece, a little at a time, tidy as bookkeeping. The sound of a long thing taking an interest in the delivery route. One animal or two, she still wasn't entitled to know. What she knew was that the audience had started moving house.

"There it is," she said quietly, to nobody, the way she'd said it for thirty years.

Then, up the throat, at the pitch that carries up iron:

"Flap. Now. Shoulder it and ring the whole church — the racket's already given it our address, so spend the noise. And mind the rule: nothing you hear behind you stops you. This isn't behind you, it's under both of us." A beat. "I told you the last thing up a throat is the part that gets bitten. I'm the last thing up this throat, I've thirty years of seniority and one sock, and I'd like that to stay a theory. Be quick."

The coal went on rolling, closer, unhurried. And the water in the chute began to rise again.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Every question you've asked tonight has come at the worst possible hour," Halloway said. "Keep that habit. It's the one that outlives people." She looked up the throat at the lamp Pike held steady above her and didn't argue with the disobedition, because she needed it. "You stopped to be a lamp-stand. Good. I want light on my hands more than I want you gone for the next half-minute. After that I'll want you at the flap more than I've ever wanted anything. Dead steady, that lamp. If it shakes, the knife picks the wrong cloth."

Then the water collected its second tax.

It had been climbing past her braced boots, patient as rent, and when it reached the trailing heel, the seam came up with it. No pull — nothing about this thing had ever pulled. The water simply closed around boot and trouser-cuff together, and both stopped being hers. Entered. Filed.

"There it is," she said quietly. "The second boot. It came back for the pair. Somewhere under that silt is a thing that owns matched boots and no legs to put them on — that's the whole animal in one sentence. Watch, since you won't look away. Lecture with the demonstration included."

The knife went in at the lace — two strokes, and the foot came out of the boot, same trick. But the seam had the cuff as well, and wet cloth grips like a promise. So she laid the blade flat against her own calf, a hair off the skin, and opened the trouser seam from cuff to knee in one long stroke, and stripped her leg out of the cloth the way you strip a bandage off a wound you're sick of looking at. Below her, the seam accepted boot and half a trouser leg together, a two-course meal, and settled with the sound of a slot taking a coin.

"My fault, before you say it. I let the trailing foot dip. Thirty years, and I paid a trouser for the lapse. The dead man paid an arm for the same lesson. I got it cheap." A beat. "And note the mechanics while you're watching. No teeth anywhere. Teeth are for animals that argue with their food. The seam doesn't bite — it *zips*. A purse-string with patience. That's why there's never any noise in this cellar, Pike. Nothing here has ever fought anything."

"Inventory: one knife, one sock, half a pair of trousers, thirty years. The kit's lost every argument tonight and the seniority's the only thing that hasn't shrunk. Now — the rest."

She climbed as she talked, spine to brick, palms flat, offering nothing.

"Open one — I did it at the mill with the boat hook — and the first thing you learn is there's no blood. The skin parts like wet harness-leather and what runs out is pond water. Cold. It's not blood, it's *ballast*. The smell, since you asked: stone and iron and crushed waterweed. A cellar locked a hundred years — the smell of nowhere lived in. That's the tell. Everything that hunts you smells like something that's been alive — musk, rot, blood. This smells like the inside of a flint. And under it, faint, a sweetness with no business being there. Ditch-honey. Dead-smelling water with something moving in it means the smell is a costume too."

"Inside: no gut, no heart. Grey packing like wet felt, and hollows in it. Drawers. The mill one was nine parts and nine drawers, every one sorted — buttons with buttons, teeth in size order, a ring worn smooth on somebody else's decade. Messy is an animal. Sorted is a bookkeeper. There's a mind in it, and it's a clerk's, and the drawers nearest the head hold the newest stock. When we break this one open on dry stone, whatever's left of him will be in the top drawers. I'll find his teeth before I find his name."

"How far it got. With him — teeth and a collar, that's the whole estate. How far the *thing's* gotten is the uglier sum. One man since spring doesn't buy a cellar's worth of chain. The mill one was a rowboat long, and it cost that pond ten years of dogs and drunkards. So this one's fed from the inlet — and ask yourself what travels down a coal chute and a water pipe. Rats, Pike. The family's been rat-free since spring and thought themselves lucky. That's how far it got. It got the whole delivery route. And the coal rolling below us isn't hunting. It's *measuring*. The waterline is its pencil. It's pricing the chute."

The rolling reached the foot of the throat. The water at her ankles rose a finger's width, then another, and stopped being patient.

"That's the bill arriving. Up. Shoulder the flap and spend the noise — I'm out of boots to pay with. Nothing you hear behind you stops you, and I'm the last thing up this throat, and I intend to stay a theory. Ring the church. And when we're out and the door's barred — *then* you can look away. That's what doors are for."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I shove the pry bar into the flap's edge and heave with everything I've got left. The iron groans, then screams open, and cold night air hits my face. I scramble out onto the cobbles, then twist around and thrust the lamp back into the darkness. "Your hands! I can see them--take them!"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Not the hands." It came up the throat flat and fast, before her own reach could get a vote. "Nothing of ours goes down into that dark, Pike — that's been the whole sermon of the night and you're about to fail it out of kindness. The dead man reached for a rail. You're offering two hands into a rising throat, and it takes what's offered, deepest first. Lamp steady. That's your job and you're doing it. I climb."

The last body-length she did the proper way — spine to brick, palms flat, offering nothing — and the water came with her, an inch at a time, unhurried as interest. At the top she took the iron of the flap frame, cold and honest, nothing on it but coal-dust, and pushed.

The trailing foot paid the final instalment, because the trailing foot had been the whole evening's ledger. The seam came up with the water and closed on the sock. No pull — nothing had pulled all night. The sock simply stopped being hers, accepted and filed, matched to the boots. She swore once, flat and heartfelt, as advertised, and gave the foot to the push instead of the kick — kicking is offering — and came over the lip in one rude piece. Below her, the seam settled around an empty sock with a sound like a slot taking a farthing.

The flap fell home and boomed shut, the last note of the service. Gravity on their side for once: iron, hinged at the top, hanging closed. She threaded the bar through the outer hasp and jammed it against the cobbles — not because the thing would push. It had never pushed anything in its life. Because water rises without asking, and enough water floats iron.

Then she stood barefoot on ice-cold cobbles and listened down through the metal.

The coal stopped rolling. Mid-piece, tidy, no ceremony. Under that, faint as a settling house, the stairwell began giving its water back a stair at a time.

"There it is," she said quietly. "It's unstacking. Going home. And by daylight it'll be back at the far end — folded at the waist, knees straight, a drowned man for the next kind person with a lamp. The trap doesn't sulk, Pike. It resets. Bait keeps its shape because bait gets taken."

She looked at Pike then, properly, in lamplight, the first time all night there'd been nothing between them to look at.

"I promised we'd discuss your hearing somewhere with a door. There's the door. So: you stopped in a throat with the water rising and offered your hands into the dark. I know why. So did it — that kindness is the whole of its wardrobe. Every stitch the thing owns, somebody reached out of pity. It doesn't take arms, Pike. It takes *gestures*." She let that sit. "But you held the light dead steady, you never looked away, and you asked for the detail when detail was the last thing a sane person would want. That's the trade, and you'd do for it. Keep the kindness. Spend it on the living. Down there it's just cloth."

Above them the house stood dark, two floors of sleeping arithmetic. No window lit.

"Nobody woke. If somebody asks at breakfast about the bell, tell them rats — nearest true thing I've got, and it's practically the accounts." She took the lamp and turned it down to a thumbnail. "Oil's for breakfast, not midnight. Sit against the wall, bar across your knees, and sleep. I've got the flap till first light. Thirty years of seniority, and it's the only thing left in the kit that hasn't shrunk."

Her hands were shaking now. She held them out, looked at them, and put them away under her arms. "My turn. Fair's fair — shaking's honest, and tonight I'd sooner honest than steady."

A beat.

"Dawn, we find what feeds this room — a pipe, a spring, a drain with its mouth open somewhere — and we close it. Then it's a long wet thing in a dry room, and dry rooms are rope-work and buckets. I still don't know if that was one animal or two. By noon I will. And then one letter gets delivered: a laundry mark, a collar, teeth in the top drawers, and somebody stops looking. Postmistress. Somebody has to be."

She settled against the wall by the flap, knife across her knee, bare feet drawn in out of the cold.

"You wanted it killed. Keep that — cold hands, warm intent, tomorrow runs on it. And Pike — the door's barred." A beat, and this time the humour made it the whole way up. "You can look away now. That's what doors are for."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: D

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the closed flap, breathing hard. "Tomorrow, then." I pull my knees up and rest my forehead on them. My hands won't stop shaking. "I'm not sleeping."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Tomorrow, then," Halloway agreed. "Dawn, we walk the outside of this house until we find what feeds the cellar — a pipe, a spring, a drain with its mouth open where a mouth shouldn't be. Close it, pump the rest, and by noon the thing's a long wet problem in a dry room, and dry rooms are rope-work. Buckets. Counting. One letter." She recited it flat as a chore list, because that's all it was now. Terror kept night hours. This was the day shift clocking in early.

"And you won't sleep. Of course you won't. Nobody sleeps the first one." She settled against the wall beside the flap, knife across her knee, the lamp at her hip breathing its thumbnail of light. "I didn't. Took three days and a barn loft before my body collected what it was owed, and I woke under half a haypile I'd pulled down over myself with no memory of the pulling. The body files its own reports, Pike. That's what the shaking is — not fear arriving late. The ledger balancing. Nothing's wrong with you that breakfast won't argue with."

A beat.

"My partner didn't sleep the night after the mill, either. Sat up till dawn with his one arm cradling the stump like it still had a vote in things. Said staying awake felt like owing the trap something. That's the last trick in an animal like that — it gets a night out of you even when it gets nothing else. It's had my boots, a sock, half a trouser and a rope tonight, and I'm telling you the account is closed. It doesn't get the night as well."

"So. You don't have to sleep — sleep isn't a vote, it's a tax, and it'll collect whether you co-operate. But you can pay it lying down or sitting up, and lying down's the cheaper posture. First, the wet. You waded to the shoulders and there's frost in this air, and wet wool at midnight is a slow knife. I'm not losing you to *weather* after we both declined the monster. Wring everything, twisted hard, put it back on. Damp's survivable. Soaked's a debt."

While she talked she worked the knife into the coal sacking baled against the chute wall and cut two rough squares, wrapped each foot, lashed them with strips off the same bolt. "Not my best cobbling. But the kit stands at one knife, two sack feet and thirty years — worst kit I've ever stood a watch in, and I've stood watches in better rooms with worse odds. Meanwhile the thing below has a matched pair of boots, one sock and half a trouser, and no legs to put any of it on. First animal in thirty years to win the footwear argument outright. I'll want those back, mind. Evidence."

She set two knuckles against the iron and listened down through the metal. Under it, faint: the stairwell giving its water back a stair at a time, unhurried. And under that, far off at the far end, a long soft sound like wet harness settling onto a peg.

"There it is. Dressing again. Folding back into the drowned man, joint by joint, and it'll hold that pose for the next kind soul with a lamp — all the patience in the world and nothing to spend it on but us." She took her knuckles off the iron. "You'll hear it two or three times more before light. Small sounds. Let them be the lullaby. A thing you can hear is a thing you don't have to check. It's silence that costs sleep, and there won't be any."

She tipped her head at the night beyond the chute. "Now listen past the iron. Dog, two streets off. The house ticking as its timbers cool. A cart somewhere that has no idea what it's driving over." A beat. "Ordinary dark. The world didn't hold its breath with you, Pike. First night, that feels like a betrayal. Give it a week and it's the only mercy going."

"Four hours of dark left, near enough. I'll stand the last of it — my feet have stopped complaining and started filing reports, so standing's the only office they've left me. You take the wall. Bar across your knees, hands in your armpits, eyes open or shut as you please. The flap's barred, gravity's on our payroll till morning, and the last thing up the throat got up."

She looked at the sky, then at the iron, and settled in.

"Dawn's coming either way. And it's bringing rope."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I pull my wet sleeves over my hands and stare at the flap. "You said you've seen fifty. Is that what you tell their people? That they're in the top drawer?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Fifty's the years," Halloway said. "How long I've lasted, not what I've counted. If you're counting the things I've killed, I gave up that tally decades back — monsters don't need a postmistress." She worked her shoulders back against the wall, settling in for the last watch. "The letters, though. Those I can give you to the digit. Nine. Eleven, if you count the two I never found enough of to deliver — and I count those two, because somebody's still opening a door for them every night. That's the arithmetic that keeps me rude." A beat. "The honest drownings get letters too, but those write themselves. The water did it, and a parish understands water. It's the other kind where the post office earns its keep."

"And no. Nobody gets told about the drawer."

A beat.

"The first one, I did wrong. Twenty-three, and proud of my precision the way only the young and the armed ever are. Canal town. A lock-keeper, eight months gone. I'd opened the thing that had him, and I brought his widow the tin — teeth, a ring, two buttons — and I laid out the whole mechanics, drawers and all, because I'd decided the entire truth was the respect she was owed. She heard me out. Held the tin. Said, *this isn't a him.* And she was right, and I stood there with nothing, because I'd brought a woman an inventory and called it a funeral."

"Her vicar told me later she didn't sleep a year of nights. Not grief — grief she knew how to do. It was the picture I'd drawn. She took in sewing for the whole street, and after me every button that passed through her hands meant something, because she knew now where buttons go. I'd handed her the one fact in the world that's got no door to put behind it. Sentiment gets people killed in a cellar, I've told you. In a kitchen, it's precision that does the killing, and it does it slower."

"So I rebuilt the trade, and here's the whole method, since you've asked your last question of the night at the worst hour of it — as is your habit. The family gets a death, not an inventory. I knock. I say he drowned — true. I say it was quick and it was quiet, nothing fought, nothing screamed, cold and then gone — true, and it's the one place in this entire business where the whole truth is actually kind. I say he went in after somebody — true; he went in after what he believed was somebody. Then the freight goes into their hands. Teeth, ring, collar. Travels in a brass tin I've had longer than most of my knives — worst tool in the kit, and the one I'd never leave behind. You can't bury a *gone*, Pike. A coffin wants weight in it. The teeth are ballast. The story is the coffin."

"And the words that never leave my book: *it*. The sorting. The boots. That he's being worn. That stays shut in here with the rest of the ledger — not mercy, containment. Same rule as the water. You keep it where it can't reach anybody."

A beat.

"Nor do I soften past true, and not out of tenderness. Missing is worse than dead. I've watched a town keep a lamp lit at night for a man a pond had already filed. They keep looking. And looking means kind people going down stairs with lamps. Its whole wardrobe is stitched out of that — every costume it owns, somebody kept hoping. You remembered the rule from the top of the stairs: don't say hope. In a kitchen it's a virtue. In a cellar it's chum. The letter isn't the gentle ending, Pike. The letter is the last trap you spring. You close the hope, and the next costume starves before it's ever sewn. Half this job is killing things. The other half is paperwork, and the paperwork is what stops there being a next thing to kill."

She looked at the iron flap, then east, where the dark had gone one shade thinner without asking anybody's permission.

"Tomorrow's letter, since you'll stand there and hear it. A knock, a laundry mark, a collar gone soft since spring. He went down to help what he thought was a drowned man. It was quick. It was quiet. The house never heard a thing. Here is what's his. And that first part — that he went in to help — isn't the nearest true thing. It's the truest one in the ledger. The trap spent him as cloth. The helping it couldn't spend, and that's the part they keep. Families can live thirty years on that. I've watched them do it."

Under the iron, faint and on schedule, came the long soft sound of wet harness settling onto its peg. The drowned man, dressing for the morning's trade.

"There it is," Halloway said, without heat. "The lullaby, as advertised. Punctual — the only virtue it has."

She drew the knife back across her knee.

"Nine letters in thirty years. Eleven, counting the undelivered. The whole aim of this trade is to put the post office out of business. Some years I manage. This isn't one of them." A beat. "Now pay your tax lying down if you can manage it. The letter gets written at noon, and you'll want to be awake for it — somebody ought to watch him get delivered. That's the part the job's actually for. The rest is just keeping your boots."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit up and wipe my nose on my wet sleeve. "Will you let me write the letter? I want to get the words right."
