dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Wrong is a feeling," Halloway said. "Good instinct, bad report. Take it apart. Count the limbs. Find the joints. Tell me where you think the head is."

She raised the lamp and did it herself, flat as a list. "Size of a grown man, longer through the middle than it should be. The near arm has two elbows, or the elbow's on backwards — the water's flattening it, hard to swear to. Hide, not fur, whatever it is. No blood spreading under it, which means it doesn't bleed or nothing's opened it yet. Something at the far end that's either a head or a knee."

She crouched on the bottom step, lamp steady, and did not go in.

"And it stopped moving a minute ago. A minute is nothing. I've held still for an hour with a broken wrist waiting for one of these to get curious, and I'm told I'm very convincing dead. So we watch before we wade. Breathing shows on open water — small ripples, slow and steady, easy to mistake for the drips off that ceiling except drips aren't that regular. Ten minutes of standing on this step is cheaper than ten seconds in that water and finding out wrong."

She nodded at the far end without taking her eyes off it.

"Go on. The head. Or the knee. Which, and why."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint at the far end. "If it's a knee, it's pointing the wrong direction. The...the joint's on the side, not the front." I glance at the still water. "No ripples. You said it was moving a minute ago. Did it just...hold its breath?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Joint on the side, not the front," Halloway repeated. "Good. That's a fact, not a feeling. Facts are what you trade on when the lamp dies."

She tilted the light a fraction, following the line of the thing under the water.

"So it's a head shaped like nothing, or a knee on something that folds backwards. Could be either. Stop trying to fit it to a man — that's the mistake that gets people opened up. You'll brace for a lunge from the head-end and it'll come from the middle."

The breath question she answered without looking away.

"Things hold their breath for two reasons. They're hiding, or they're dying. Both are patient. And anything that plays dead has met a hunter before — it survived one, or its mother did. Nothing learns stillness for free."

She wedged the lamp against the rail of the step, dug in her coat, and came out with a coin.

"Watch the water, not the body. That's the trick." She tossed it — flat, underhand, three feet short of the far end. Small splash. "If it's truly done, those rings roll over it and nothing changes. If it's holding still, something slips — a flinch, the rings stuttering where the hide's tense under the surface. Bubbles most of all. It's under four feet of water. Whatever it breathes, it breathes through that."

She went back to stillness, eyes on the spreading rings.

"Count ten for me. Then tell me what the water did."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Person recently," Halloway said. "Likely. Most of them are — nothing's born looking like a dropped glove. Two ways it happens. Either it wore a man, and something wore its way out from inside, or it never wore anything and somebody fed it one."

She didn't look away from the water while she said it.

"You tell them apart at the opening, not before. The teeth give you half the answer. The stomach gives you the rest, and you won't thank me for it. If there's someone in there, we dig them out and send them home to their people. That's part of the work. You'll do it and not enjoy it, and that's correct — enjoying it is how you find out you're in the wrong trade. But it's the part that comes *after* the part where we're still breathing, so put the question away for an hour. Pity in four feet of water is just meat scent."

A beat.

"Also — you stopped counting to ask it. Your attention went to the past tense and the water went unwatched. That's the trade the water always wins."

She tilted her chin a fraction toward the far end.

"For what it's worth, you missed something. Rings rolled out clean across the near half of it. Where they crossed the middle, one broke — stuttered, like the surface flinched. Then a thread of bubbles, small, off the far end."

Her voice stayed flat, which somehow made it worse.

"So it's not dead and it's not drowning-scared. It held still through a coin landing three feet off. Stillness is learned, like I said. This one's been hunted before. Or taught."

She picked the lamp up off the rail.

"And here's where your question earns its keep. If it was a person recently, it remembers stairs. Lamplight. Which end of a cellar a hunter stands on. Animals guess. Old men *know.* Second lamp in your coat — light it, don't raise it, keep it off the water. When I say, we trade which one's lit, and you tell me where the next stutter comes from. Near end or far. Go."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I fumble for the lamp in my coat, fingers clumsy. "You want me to be the second light," I say, striking the match. "It'll watch you, not me."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Half right," Halloway said. "It doesn't watch me. It watches the light, and I've been the light for ten minutes. When the light moves, it has to decide what moved. Things give themselves away deciding."

She stepped up one stair, clear of the water's reach, and turned her shoulder so her lamp threw nothing into the room.

"And a thing that learned stillness learned it from hunters, and hunters arrive with light. To it, a lamp going dark isn't an accident. It's the last thing that happens before the bolt comes. Some animals run on that. The dangerous ones charge it. Either way, three seconds of trading lights buys more than ten minutes of standing. So — your lamp up when I say. Not at the body. Waist height, near wall. Light what's moving, not what's lying still." A beat. "And yes. Tonight the light is you. Try to look expensive."

Her hand found something in her coat and stayed there.

"Steady the match hand on the way up. Nervous light flickers, and flicker reads as movement to a thing waiting for exactly that. On three. One. Two."

She shut her lamp. The cellar went black for the length of one breath.

"Three."

In the small light: nothing at the far end. The head-or-knee never twitched. But the near arm — the two-elbowed one — was sinking, deliberate, folding under, and off it a wake set out slow and broad. Not toward the middle of the cellar. Along the near wall. Toward the steps.

"There," Halloway said, flat as ever. "Far end's a knee or a tail or its idea of a joke. The head's the arm. Two elbows that fold flat isn't an arm, it's a trap — something that eats by closing."

A slow breath out.

"I said people remember stairs. Worse news. It's not remembering them. It's covering them. So — where is it now? Don't look for a shape. Look for where the water's wrong."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The water said it before Pike finished doing it — one slosh, then rings rolling out wide from the steps, ten minutes of careful map wrecked in four seconds.

Halloway didn't shout. Shouting spends air and tells the room where everyone stands.

"Second lamp and the deep end of the room," she said. "Two promotions nobody voted for. And that's twice tonight your attention went backward — first time it cost you a count, this time it cost you the dry half of the cellar. The water wins that trade every time it's offered."

Then the wake stopped.

She watched it stop. The arm's wake had been setting along the near wall, patient, toward the steps — and now the rings thinned, stalled, and the surface went glassy over it. A different stillness than the room's stillness. A held one.

"It heard you better than I did," she said. "And it changed its mind. The stairs were a door it wanted shut. You're better than a door. You're warm, and you're standing in its water, and you gave it your location in slosh."

She came down the steps without lifting a foot — flat foot, slide, weight asking the water before committing to it. "You never step in black water. You ask. Something's always under the step."

At the bottom, off Pike's shoulder and out of the light's edge, her hand came out of her coat. Short thrower. Bolt already seated. She set her stance so the lane past Pike's hip stayed clear.

"Lamp down a foot. Light your own knees, not its face. If it closes, I need the water in front of it, not its eye. There'll be a ridge pushed up ahead of it — that's your half-second's warning."

A breath.

"And plainly, since you've asked twice. It's lying about being dead. It's wearing somebody or ate somebody, and the teeth will say which, and that's the homework. What happened to it is six feet from being what happens to you. So it has to die twice — it's practiced the first one."

The glassy patch held. Waiting.

"It's waiting for your next mistake. Make none, and it has to choose, and choosing is where things get stupid. Your legs are in its water — they'll know before my eyes do. Pressure on the shins, a cold line moving. You say *now*. One word, nothing else. I do the rest."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My knees feel numb from the cold water. I lower the lamp slowly. "Now," I whisper, just as a deep, cold pressure slides against my calf.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway had been sighting down her arm since before the word was out.

"No ridge," she said, conversational, to the water. "That was the answer, not the quiet. No ridge means it's already inside striking distance — the warning stage is behind you."

The water over Pike's calf mounded once, and the trap-limb came up through its own ripple and began to close.

She put the bolt into the second elbow at the waterline.

The crack of it went around the stone room twice. The closing stroke died an inch short of through — teeth or edges scoring trouser, a wet tearing sound, and then the whole limb shuddered and went wrong-jointed, folding sideways the way she'd said it would, hinged now on a hole instead of a joint. It thrashed at the end of the thing's body like a snapped rope, and dark blood came with the thrashing, spreading under the lamplight in a slow black bloom.

The rest of the mass convulsed. The far end — knee, tail, whatever it was — slapped water flat, and the whole animal hauled for deep water, dragging itself in strokes. The ruined arm caught on the cellar floor and anchored it.

It pulled twice more. Then it understood, in whatever way such things understand, that it was caught on its own mouth.

"'Now.' One word, at the correct speed." Halloway didn't move the thrower off it. "Note that you did that. Most people need three syllables and a sob."

She came a half-step down, flat-footed, reading the blood's spread.

"So it bleeds after all. Nothing had opened it before tonight — that's answered. And it's snagged on the same trap it hunts with, which is the oldest joke in this trade. Things that eat by closing always close on something they can't swallow."

A slow beat.

"It has two choices now. Tear the arm off and go — you'll hear that, cartilage goes like a boot pulled from mud — or spend itself thrashing and lie there for study. Don't run if it tears. Step back once. Running people go down in four feet of water, and that water is its home ground, not yours."

The thrower stayed level.

"Lamp up. On the mouth, the open end. And do the homework you asked for twice — the teeth. Plainly, this time. Tell me what you see."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The thing put its weight into one more pull while Pike asked — a real one, water heaving out heavy from the far end — and Halloway's arm didn't move. The pull failed. Something under the surface clicked, the way rope doesn't.

"It's choosing," she said. "Slow about it. Losing your mouth makes a thing honest, but we don't trust honest." A beat. "And you've stopped shifting your weight. Cold's taken your knees or you've turned into furniture. Either way your warning system's down — you can't feel its water now, so it doesn't get to have you standing in it. Back up onto the second step. Flat-footed. Lamp on the mouth from there. Lectures go better with dry feet."

Then she answered, because Pike had asked three times and three was the limit of her pretending not to hear.

"Exact is the one thing nobody can give you tonight. The exact answer is inside it, and it doesn't exist until we open it. The body's the only witness and it hasn't testified. Anyone who tells you what happened to him before that is guessing, and guesses in this trade get buried along with the guesser." A breath. "But the outside testifies. So listen, and I'll give you what's knowable."

Flat, like inventory.

"The way these work — I've opened two, so this isn't guessing — they don't eat a man the way animals do. They keep him. The outside is useful; shape is a tool. What they take is the inside, for material, and they build through what's left of his frame. First thing rebuilt is the limb that holds, because holding is eating, to these. It grows the second joint so it folds flat and closes. That arm was finished. That's why it's the mouth now."

She nodded at the length of it, the middle sitting too long under the water.

"Then the middle. His spine's been re-run — that's your extra length through the torso. The far end was still underway. It wasn't finished. Nothing interrupted the work until tonight. It was partway through a meal that used to walk down those stairs on its own legs."

A beat.

"What it took: the inside. What survives is the skin, some bone it kept as scaffolding, and its own work threaded through. And you'll know him by what it didn't want. A ring. Buckles. Fillings. It takes what's useful — what it leaves is who he was. That's what goes home to his people. The leavings."

The mouth, she noted, was still owed. "A set of human teeth kept somewhere in that arrangement — the way you keep a coat button — means it wore a man. All its own teeth means it never was one, and somebody fed it. The stomach answers whether he was the first."

Then the correction, mild as weather.

"You keep asking me to look. Secondhand facts come with the holes still in them, and someday you'll meet one of these without me standing behind you. So tonight you open it, you read the teeth, and you say it out loud. I'll stand next to you and say nothing unless you're wrong." She almost smiled. "You asked three times. Third time's volunteering."

The thrower came level again, because the thing had gathered itself once more.

"And mind what I told you — the arm tears before it gives up. Boots from mud. That's why you're on the steps. When you hear it, you'll want to run, and running people go down in four feet of water. So: one step back. Keep the lamp on the mouth. It's the only part of him left worth watching."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I move onto the second step, the lamplight trembling. "The teeth," I say, forcing my voice steady. I see the glint of metal in the ruined maw. "Fillings. It wore a man."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Fillings," Halloway said. "Better than teeth. Sit with why."

The thrower never came off the water while she taught. That was its own lesson.

"Teeth can be kept. Anything can — rings, buttons, a lock of hair. Things keep souvenirs same as widows do. But a filling means a chair, and a stranger with a drill, and a bill somebody paid. It means he lived somewhere, among people, long enough to need a dentist. Teeth only say it wore a man. Fillings say there's a name attached, and likely a town, and a dentist who knows their own work the way I know mine. That's the difference between what it was and who he was. Tonight you get to return the second one."

The thing chose then.

It went at the root of the arm — a wrench, not a pull, the whole front of it coiling against its own anchored mouth, and the sound was the one she'd promised: a boot coming out of deep mud, if the boot had bones in it. The arm came away and stayed behind. The body went for the deep end with everything it had left.

She put the second bolt into the middle. The long part.

"Spine's the rope the whole rebuild hangs on," she said, watching it land. "Cut the rope, the rebuild quits."

The animal made six feet and then made none. No thrash at the end. It simply stopped keeping, the water settled over it ring by ring, and as it quit, the far end sighed — one long exhale through plumbing that used to belong to somebody.

"Don't build a ghost out of that. Air moves through a throat. But note where it came from — the unfinished end. Matches the order of the work." A beat. "That's the second dying. The one it hadn't practiced."

Then the coin, out of the coat, tossed underhand over the body the same as the first time. The rings rolled out clean across everything — and where they crossed the severed arm, the arm closed once, hard, on nothing at all.

"See that. Freelance now. Trap-limbs keep working for hours after the rest quits — nerve's local. That's why the teeth come out of it with something longer than your fingers." She glanced up the steps. "And note you didn't run. Rarer than it should be."

Then the knife, out of the coat, offered handle-first.

"You asked three times what happened to him. This is the asking price. He's ready to testify, and you're the examiner. Cut the seam, not the belly — where its work meets his skin there's a line. His skin gives. Its work doesn't. Go where the give changes, or you'll spend the night fighting rope instead of untying knots. The teeth are in the arm, kept like a coat button — those first. They name him, so they go home first. Then the stomach. Everything it took pools there. One man's leavings means he was the first and we stop looking. More than one set, you start counting, and the count goes in the report."

She wedged the lamp so the light fell on the work and on nothing else, and stood where she could see Pike's hands without standing in the way.

"Same rule as before. You read it out loud. I say nothing unless you're wrong."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Done," Halloway said. "New trade. Your hands do the work, my mouth does the map. I'll give you everything under the blade — what's there, what it smells like, how long it took. Everything but the last line. The last line's been yours since you took the knife."

She moved to where she could see past Pike's shoulder into the cut.

"Smell first, since you asked for all of it. There's two arguments in there. Copper and stale water — that's him and the cellar, that's nothing, that's every body in four feet of water. The sweet one underneath, like a melon that's given up — that's its work. Learn that one above everything else tonight. You'll smell it before you ever see one again. It's the smell of a thing being rebuilt. And breathe through your nose. Mouth-breathers gag, gagging people drop lamps, and we've traded enough lamps."

The blade found the change in give, and the arm opened along the line.

"There. Skin's his — it kept the outside because shape is a tool, and the tool still has to pass. Now you're under it. Bones are his. Muscle's mostly gone — taken early, that's the material. What's strung on the bones is its tissue: pale, gristly, and it parts under the blade like candle wax, not like meat. Don't hack. It clenches when you hack, and your fingers are closer to it than mine."

At the second elbow, the blade showed rings.

"Cut through the joint. Layers, paper-thin, one on the next. It isn't born, it's built — every ring is a day. Sixteen of them, near enough. So: somebody in town has had a man missing two weeks and a quiet cellar two weeks, and those are the same fact. That's the first half of your how-far."

At the shoulder end, she nodded. "Anchor point. There's a pocket in its work — seam like the inside pocket of a coat. Open it. Use the pliers, not your fingers. I told you the teeth come out with something longer than your fingers."

When the pocket split, the arm on the floor closed once, hard, on nothing at all.

Halloway set her heel on the wrist without looking down. "Freelance. It doesn't know it's been let go. Nerves are local — it can't be upset, there's nothing left in it to be upset *with*. It'll do that for a few hours and then it's finished. Mind your fingers anyway."

Inside the pocket: crowns, small and pale in the lamplight.

"Just the crowns. It eats the roots, keeps the crowns — hard material, and it hoards hard material the way misers hoard coin. Two molars, lower left, one carrying gold. A canine with amalgam the size of a thumbnail. That's not a keepsake, that's a chart. Any dentist in the county matches that inside a day, and a chart gives you a name, and a name gives you a door to knock on. Tin. Inside pocket. They go home before anything else we do tonight — I mean that in order."

She watched the arm's work a moment, then nodded at the body.

"Now the long seam. Same rule — where the give changes, go. It runs from the collarbone down."

When the middle opened, she named it flat.

"That cord, pale as lamp wick, running the whole length — his spine. Kept, sleeved in its work, run through him like wire through a wall. Everything it built hangs off that. That's the rope. One bolt through it and the rebuild quits — you watched it work. Now the far end. Press with the knife-flat, not a finger. See — goes through like bread. This work is days old. Firm at the front, soft at the back; that's the whole calendar. It was a week from finished. Seven more days and the far end sets, and it walks up those stairs on his legs into streets that have never seen it, and starts the trade over with better tools. You interrupted a job in its last week. Write that down somewhere you'll keep."

A beat.

"Last. Past the hips, at the tail end — its own pouch, not where his stomach sat. It doesn't digest like you digest. It sorts. Useful goes into the build, the rest pools. This is the worst breath of the night. Nose, short ones, and don't stop cutting because it's bad."

When the pouch came open, she read the pool as it emptied into the light.

"Ring first. White metal, worn thin — he was married a long time, and that ring is how she gets told. Belt buckle. Bone-handled penknife. Coin purse, four coppers. One set. Count is one — he was the first, we stop looking, and the report says one. That's a small mercy. This trade deals in them by count, and tonight you got one."

She tipped her chin toward the deep end, where the lamplight just reached the floor.

"And there's his lamp. Where it dropped when his hands stopped being his. Note what he did right — came down slow, brought a light, watched the water. He did everything you did tonight. An hour earlier, and alone. That's the entire difference, and it's the only one that matters."

Then she straightened, and her voice didn't change at all.

"One thing left in the pool. Brass fob, hand-engraved. A dentist gives you a chart. An engraver gives you the man. Pick it up, tip it to the light, and read it out loud. That's the last line, and I told you — the last line's yours. I'll say nothing unless you're wrong."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My hands are shaking. I pick up the fob, hold it close to the lamp. The letters are worn, but they spell out a name. "Alistair Finch." I look at her. "Is that him?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Alistair Finch," Halloway repeated, flat, letting it sit in the lamplight like a weight being set down.

"You weren't wrong. By rights I owe you silence. But that was a question, and questions cost me sentences, so here's yours: that's the *name*. Whether it's him is tomorrow's work. One witness is a story. The fob says the man who wore that pocket was called Finch, and the count is one, so it's his pocket. Tomorrow the crowns are the second witness — chart, name, see if a dentist agrees with an engraver. The ring is the third. Wives know their own white metal to the week. When three witnesses line up, the report says Finch and nobody gets buried under the wrong stone. That's the whole ceremony. Less romantic than certainty. Stays bought."

She crouched, took her heel off the severed wrist, and watched. The arm didn't close.

"Slowing. Two hours of spite in it, maybe three. Good."

She stood and answered the other half of the question, the part Pike hadn't asked correctly.

"And mind your tense. *Is* that him — no. That's what it made of him. Him is the tin, the ring, a chair in a back room with a bill somebody paid, and a woman who married thin white metal a long time ago. You opened what it was. That fob is the first piece of who he was. Different jobs. You did the first one without stopping the knife, which puts you ahead of my first attempt by one entire dinner."

Then the orders, because order was the only thing holding the night together.

"In sequence. Tin in your coat, crowns wrapped dry — that travels first, I meant that. Ring, buckle, knife, purse with the fob — leavings travel together or they get lost separately, and lost leavings are widows who never get told. We don't carry him tonight. The arm's still freelance, my back has opinions, and nothing in this cellar will trouble him now but honest water. First light we come back with a box and two more backs."

She looked at the fob, then held her hand out for it — and didn't take it. Closed her fingers on nothing and left it in Pike's palm.

"Keep that one. You read him out of the water; you carry him to a door. Tomorrow splits two ways. The dentist gets crowns and a name — that's a chart and a signature, he's a tradesman, he wants his afternoon back, give him exactly that and no stories. The wife gets the ring and the rest of her life in about nine words. *Found. Certain. He's coming home.* She'll ask how. Tell her the part of him that could hurt was gone before the work started — that's true, the material went early, I read it in the rings. It's the only mercy this cellar stocked. Spend it. Everything else you saw stays in this room and becomes your wages. Paying her your wages helps nobody."

A beat.

"You'll want to warn her first. Don't. Warnings are for weather. Weather comes back."

She picked her way to the steps, then paused with one hand on the rail.

"And note what your hands did tonight while they shook. Lamp level. Knife on the line. Last line read out loud anyway. Thirty years in, mine still shake on the last line. You're not doing it wrong. You're doing *it*. Those are different things, and only one of them is rare."

"So — dentist or widow. Sleep on it if you can. I want you fed, dry, and deciding by the time the sun's up."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Finish it," Halloway repeated. "That's the first order tonight I'd have given myself."

She looked at the water — the black bloom thinning at its edges, the far end quiet under settled glass, the arm lying finished at last.

"The thing's dead twice. Bodies don't get finished. They get boxed, charted, and carried. So you mean the account. Good. That's the part people leave open, and an open account is what sits on your chest at three in the morning. Closed accounts weigh what paper weighs."

She came down one step and sat, because her back had opinions and the night had stopped requiring her to stand for them.

"Ground rule, then I start. The body testifies to order and to count. It doesn't testify to hours. So some of what follows is fill, and I'll mark the fill every time, because unlabeled fill is how lies get into reports, and reports are the only thing in this trade that outlives us."

She looked at the far end, not at Pike, which was its own kind of consideration.

"Seventeen days ago — fill — there was a man in this town with a chair in a dentist's back room and a bill somebody paid. Two lower-left molars, one carrying gold. A canine with a thumbnail of amalgam. A thin white ring worn down to grooves. And a brass fob, hand-engraved. Mark the fill: engraving is usually a gift. You don't buy that for yourself. Somebody gave it to him, and the ring says the somebody kept giving. Not testimony. Fits the testimony, which is the next best thing."

Then the facts.

"Sixteen days ago, near enough, the work started — the rings are its calendar and the calendar's inside the arm we cut. Which means sixteen days ago it took him too, because these don't build before they've got material, and the material was him. Fact."

"The taking. Fill where I flag it, and I'll flag most of this — but the shape of it isn't guesswork. It's the same shape I watched twice tonight, once on you and once on him. Something sent him down. Smell, sound, a light left on, a bill that didn't add. The cellar asked and he answered alone. *Fill.* He came down slow, brought a lamp, watched the water. His light's at the deep end because he kept it in his hand until his hands stopped being his — that's fact, and it tells you he never set it down to run. He wasn't running. He was doing it right."

A beat.

"He felt the cold line on the calf. He was standing where you stood. And he'd have looked at the water and felt what you felt — something wrong with the shape of it. Wrong is a feeling. It was his last report. There was no one behind him with a bolt seated, so the word *now* died in his mouth or never got born, and the close came, and the first thing it built was the limb that holds, because holding is eating. Fact, on the order. What saved you tonight wasn't nerve and it wasn't youth. It was a second pair of boots on the steps."

"The mercy, dated, read off the same rings: the material went early. First night's work — hours, not days. What made him Finch was spent before the second sunrise. The sixteen days were its days. He wasn't in them. I told you not to build a ghost out of the breath at the end; the same rule runs backward. There's no one in the middle of that story for anything to happen to."

She glanced over once.

"So the middle fortnight has nothing in it to tell. It has work in it. Holding limb, then the spine re-run like wire through a wall, then the far end underway — firm at the front, soft at the back, a week short. Seven more days and it walks up those stairs on his legs in the dark of some morning, and the town gets a quiet man who walks oddly, and the trade starts over with better tools. You interrupted a job in its last week. That's the whole of what happened here, start to end — and you were the end. Say it to yourself that way once, plainly. It isn't morbid. It's accurate, and accuracy is what lets people sleep."

She looked at the coins lying somewhere in the black water and left them.

"Coins stay. The room kept score. The room can keep the stakes."

"The account's finished except the one line that never is. Where it came from. Stillness like that is taught or survived, and neither happens in a cellar. It was put here, or it walked here small. Somebody knows which. That line goes in the report as open, and gets carried until it closes. Carrying open lines is most of the weight of this job. You get used to the weight. You don't get to put it down."

She stood, took the rail, and paused on the bottom step.

"Now the errands, because finished means everything after this is errands. Upstairs. Tin travels first, crowns dry, ring with the leavings, fob in the pocket where you read him out of the water. Food, dry, sleep — in that order — and no deciding dentist or widow before the sun's up, because tired people give bad news badly. By first light even the arm's spite will be spent, so the box men get a quiet morning and so do we."

A beat.

"And that's it. That's the whole thing, ended instead of stopped. Learn the difference. Stopped is when you quit talking. Finished is when there's nothing left that owes being said. You asked for everything and you didn't stop the knife, and now you've heard a thing finished all the way through. Most people never do. They just stop."

She started up the stairs.

"Bring the lamp. Leave the dead their dark — they've earned it, and we haven't."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I put the fob in my pocket. It feels heavier than it is. "I'll carry the leavings." I pick up the lamp, but don't move yet. "Where do you put the rest of it -- the work? After the box."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped three steps up, considered her back, and came down two instead.

"'The work.' Keep that word. Most people say *the body*, and a body is one thing with one grave, and that's how its tissue ends up under his stone. There are two cargoes in this room. They don't travel together and they don't arrive together."

She counted it off, flat as inventory.

"The bones first. Tomorrow, daylight, a table and a good lamp — the yard behind wherever we're sleeping, and I'll choose the sleeping before I choose the table. The two backs belong to a farrier and his boy. They lift and say nothing, which is the whole job description. We strip the work off the frame the same way you stripped it off the arm — where the give changes. The bones are his. It kept them because scaffolding keeps, and it kept them sound, because it doesn't build on rotten timber. Washed, wrapped, and handed to whoever buries people in this town, under his name, lid down the whole way. Nobody views. The face is his face and that's exactly the problem — a lid costs nothing and I've never once regretted one."

"The work goes in the second box. The one with no name on it. Out of town the same morning, unannounced, by cart, to the lime kiln past the north fields. I've used it twice. It draws hot and it doesn't gossip. Fire down to white, then stir it, and mind this part — the arm will grab at the flames. It doesn't know it's on the menu yet. Nerves are local and local nerves die slow. First one I burned, I leaned in to check and nearly paid a glove for it. Now I stand back and let it shake hands with the fire. That's the entire funeral it gets."

"Then lime on the ash and a spade's depth of field over the top. Not the water." A beat. "Don't ask me to defend that one. Four feet of standing water did sixteen days of work in this town while everyone walked over the top of it. The ash doesn't get a bath."

She moved a hand, taking in the cellar, the settled water, the far end gone glassy and final.

"And it burns the same day, and that's not efficiency. Someone put it here or it walked here small, and if it was put here, the putter comes back — to check the work, or collect it. What they find should be worth nothing. A corpse tells them the rebuild failed and *how* — the rings, the bolting, all of it, a free lesson. Ash tells them the rebuild failed. Full stop. Fire is the only arithmetic I know that gets a number like this one to zero."

"The first of these I ever handled, I buried instead. Ground was closer than the kiln and I was younger. Next spring a dog carried a piece of it six miles into town and the piece was *gripping*. Ground keeps. With these, keeping is the danger. So — kiln."

"The knowing goes on paper. Tonight, before sleep, which is why you eat third. Rings and their count. The teeth chart. The pool inventory. One line marked open — *origin*. That report lives out on my shelf, not filed, until the open line closes. Everything I've closed in thirty years is ink somewhere. Paper's the only part of this trade that keeps hunting after we've stopped."

She looked then at the coat pocket where the fob sat, and answered the question Pike had actually asked.

"The rest of it — the part that made the fob weigh what it weighs. That part doesn't go to the kiln and doesn't go on the shelf. I told you at the bottom of the stairs. You get used to the weight. You don't get to put it down. That's not a flaw in the trade. That's the load-bearing part of it."

Then she took the stairs in earnest, one hand on the rail.

"Now up. The tin travels first and nothing sits on it, and I want food in you before you decide anything. Errands don't improve by standing in the dark admiring them — and bring the light. I'm fifty, the stairs are wet, and the county has one of me."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I follow her up, one hand on the damp wall. "You said you had a first one. Did you get it right?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped with her hand on the rail. She looked back down into the dark once — the water keeping its score — and came two steps back instead of going on.

"No," she said. "Flat answer first, because you've earned one. Then the accounting, because a no without an accounting is just weather."

She sat on the third step, which she'd blame on her back, and counted it off the way she counted everything.

"Three ways wrong. Every rule I sold you tonight is a receipt from that first one. You've been handling my failures all evening. I just had the bills torn off."

"One. The knife. I cut where the give *looked* like it changed instead of where it changed. Wrong is a feeling — I cut a feeling, and then I fought rope for two hours because of it. And then I stopped. Set the blade down, went up the stairs, and lost my dinner in the yard. When I told you you're ahead of me by one entire dinner, that wasn't wit. That was arithmetic." A beat. "Here's what the dinner costs. By the time my hands went back in, the lamp was dying and I was stupid with it, and I rushed the reading. I had one witness — a worn band in the leavings — and the town had a missing man, and I made the one into the other. Buried him under that name. The missing man came home the following spring, sober and married. I heard it from the farrier and I never went back to that town." She said the last sentence evenly, which was how you could tell it had been said to herself many times. "Whoever was actually under that stone, I went back in the winter with better eyes and read him properly. Teeth with nothing to match. He's still the only one I never returned. I still know it was a Tuesday. That's not memory, that's inventory — inventory means you counted it more than once. That's the open line on my shelf. Oldest paper I own. Still hunting."

"Two. The ground. I told you the fact earlier — dog, six miles, gripping. Here's the bill. The piece had closed on the dog's jaw. These things don't unlatch, and it turns out farmers with a fence stake can't either. I put the dog down myself, because it was my piece in its mouth and wages run both directions. Then I burned the piece in the farmer's forge and learned what a kiln does, in a stranger's yard, a year late. Every rule I gave you tonight was written once, in worse handwriting."

"Three. The widow. Different case — my third. I had a name by then and I was so pleased to have one that I gave her the whole account. All of it. She asked if he was in there at the end, and I was twenty-two and *precise.*" She let that sit. "It took four widows to get the sentence down to nine words. You'll spend my scar tissue tomorrow. That's what it's for. That's the entire economy of this trade — nothing in it is new, everything in it is paid for."

She looked at Pike then, level.

"As for did I ever get one *right* — you're asking the wrong arithmetic. There's no right in this trade. There's less-wrong, in smaller denominations, compounding down year on year. Tonight you did four things I did wrong at twenty. Didn't stop the knife. Didn't run. Read the last line out loud. Kept the water watched. That's not because you're better. It's because you were standing behind somebody who'd already paid. Someday you'll be the somebody on the steps, and some twenty-year-old will clear every bar you paid for, and it will look to both of you like talent."

She took the rail and stood.

"Now. Up, food, dry, in that order, tin on top of nothing. My first one taught me that too, incidentally — every mistake I've ever made got made hungry and cold, and I've stopped volunteering for the combination." She started climbing. "Bring the light. The dark down there has kept enough of my history."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I follow her up, the fob heavy against my hip. "The report," I say, my voice quiet. "Will you show me the shelf?"
