dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Wrong is a start," Halloway said. "Wrong is also where most people stop. Wrong how? Too long. Too many joints. Bent where nothing should bend. Those are three different animals, and they want three different funerals."

She lowered the lamp until the light lay flat across the water, the way you'd light a page you meant to read.

"Meanwhile, the waterline. Four feet of flood, and it's showing us a back the size of a rowboat. Do the arithmetic. Most of it is below the surface, and most of it is not ahead of us." She didn't look down. "We're not standing near it. We're standing in it."

The lamp held steady in her hand. Thirty years will do that.

"No blood, either. Whatever stopped, it didn't bleed, or it bleeds slow, or it bleeds inward. Dead things leak. Keep that in the ledger."

She turned her head a fraction toward Pike, eyes still on the far end of the cellar.

"Second question, and then we decide whether we're hunters or witnesses tonight. Look at the surface. Not at it — the water around it, and the water behind us, where our ripples went. Something about it will bother you in about ten seconds. Tell me what."

Behind them the stairs ran up six steps, dry from the third. Halloway knew that without checking. She always knew where the dry was.

"And Pike," she added. "I've known three things in my life that go still in water so as to be underestimated. Two of them live around here."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the water's surface, trying to see what she sees. Then I get it. "The ripples...they didn't reach the far wall. They stopped halfway." My voice drops. "Like something's under the water between us and it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Halfway," Halloway said. "Good. Now read it properly, because the line isn't what you think it is."

She kept the lamp low and flat. "Water does one thing with light. Breaks it up — coins, glitter, sparks. You've seen it a thousand times. Now look past the line. No sparks. One dull sheen, like a boot that's been oiled too many years." She let the silence hold a beat. "That line is a waterline, Pike. It's where its back breaks the surface. Everything between here and the far end that you've been calling water is more of it."

She let that sit exactly as long as it needed to.

"So. The thing at the far end isn't the animal. It's the animal's far end. Probably the head. Probably the smallest part of it, which is not a sentence I get to say often." A pause. "And no, I'm not shooting it. A gun wants a side to aim at. That thing is all middle."

Her voice stayed level, ledger-flat.

"Update your entries. No blood meant one of two things, and now we know which. It didn't bleed because nothing's touched it. And dead things leak — I told you that. This one hasn't leaked. So it isn't dead." Her eyes never left the seam where the glitter stopped. "Of my three still things, the two that live around here: one plays dead and waits for you to kneel down and feel sorry for it. But pretenders perform. They twitch. They want you closer. This one hasn't twitched once. This one is still because nothing in its whole life has ever required it to move quickly."

A pause.

"Yet."

"So. Hunters or witnesses — I promised you the question. Witnesses, tonight. We go back up those stairs slow, heels first, no splashing, like leaving a sleeping bear. I watch the line. You watch the far end. The moment anything out there moves before we do, Pike, you don't tell me quietly. You climb."

She began to back, lamp steady, and stopped mid-step.

The line was closer than she'd marked it. A hand's width, and moving.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Wrong tense," Halloway said. She took another step, heel first, and the water folded around her boot without a sound. "Ask me 'is.'"

The lamp stayed low and flat on the far end. "It has a face. I'll grant it that. Jaw, nose, closed eyes, all filed under the right headings. But 'person, recently' comes with a price list, and none of it's been paid. The drowned bloat — lips first, then the eyelids. They shed. Hair lets go. Skin comes off in gloves, and I've bagged enough gloves to know the schedule." A half-step. "That face is dry. Composed. It looks like it's resting, and I don't mean at peace."

"So. Two entries. One: it ate somebody recently and kept the face. I don't love that one, because things that eat people whole don't leave the face mint. Teeth do work. Two: it grew that face itself, which I like even less, because nothing grows a face it doesn't intend to use."

The line of the back slid another hand's width and stopped.

"Third thing. The one that doesn't live around here — I put it down in '89, three counties north. Opened it up after, because I make a rule of knowing what I bury. It had a face." A pause. "It had six. None of them were its own."

She didn't blink. "Now watch the water just past its mouth. Not the face. The water."

A ring of ripples moved out from the far end. Small. Even. Patient.

"Living things breathe. Dead things leak. That's four feet of flood moving on an exhale, Pike. Do the arithmetic on lungs that size."

Then the far end stopped being a face at rest. Both eyes came open. They didn't wander. They found them, found the stairs, and came back.

"I said two of them live around here," Halloway said, already turning, the lamp swinging toward the steps. "Add one. It just moved in."

"I'm amending my rule. When it moves, I won't tell you quietly either. Climb."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My heart is hammering in my throat. "It's looking at the way out," I whisper, already backing up, heel catching on a submerged brick. I can't look away from those eyes.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The splash went out in rings, and at the far end the small even ripples stopped.

"It held its breath," Halloway said. She was already two steps back, lamp high, voice low and quick. "Living things breathe. Things that mean to move hold their breath. Make the entry."

She took the next step heel first and kept the lamp flat on the water behind them.

"And fix your read. It's not watching the way out. It looked at the way out and came back to us. That's not worry, that's pricing. It already knows where the door is. Now it's deciding which of us goes through it first."

Pike was still in the eyes. Halloway didn't spend breath on sympathy.

"It grew that face to be looked at. It's a lure with eyelids. Every second you spend in those eyes is a second not spent on the stairs. Six steps. Rail on the left. Count them out loud — I want to hear your voice working."

Then the water climbed.

Not a wave. A level. Smooth as a tide in a bowl, the waterline walked up the bottom step, then the second, quiet as something keeping a promise.

"Cellars don't flood uphill," Halloway said, and for the first time that night her voice moved — a hair, no more. "That's not water rising. That's it standing up."

The dry on the third step went dark. She was on the fourth.

"Thirty years," she said. "First time in my life I've had to say the dry is leaving."

Behind them the far end of the cellar was closer. Nothing had visibly moved. The wall had simply come to meet them, because the distance between here and there was the animal, and the animal was gathering itself the way you'd gather a sheet.

"Up. Hands on the rail, heels on the treads, and don't touch the water even to steady yourself. You're standing in the animal and the animal has noticed."

She held the fifth step, put her back to the wall, and swung the lamp around, watching the water come up the stairs after them at its own patient pace. The lamp never shook. Thirty years.

"When we're through that door, we don't close it. We board it. Tomorrow it's a pump, two drums of lime, and the sheriff if he's sober, in that order. Things that are all middle can't hide their middle from daylight."

A beat.

"And Pike — when we're out, don't ask me what it is. Ask me why a thing that just moved in chose a cellar under a house with people sleeping over it. Nothing grows a face it doesn't intend to use, and it's had all night."

The water touched the fourth step.

"Now climb. Count loud. And remember the stairs go both ways."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Morning did what mornings do after nights like that — arrived gray, ordinary, and no help whatsoever. They'd taken the boards off the door at first light, and daylight got as far as the third step before the cellar swallowed it. Hence the lamp in Pike's hands, held where Halloway wanted it.

The pump had run two hours for nothing. By dawn the cellar was slick mud and six inches of black, and in the middle of the floor lay the thing.

"Plainly, then." Halloway knelt at it, gloves to the elbow, knife in hand, two canvas bags open at her knee. "But first decide which 'it' you mean — the animal or the boy. The answer's the same sentence either way, and it's worse for that."

She turned the husk with the knife tip. Six feet of it, laid out like a coat off a hook. Same hide as the sheen Pike had named in the dark — oiled leather, too many years.

"Entry one. Nothing happened to it. It isn't dead. Around three this morning the water started down — not draining, leaving. Cellars don't empty themselves either, Pike. By the time we came back with the pump it was gone, and we ran that machine two hours out of spite. It left through the floor. There's a well cap under the stairs, older than the house. The cap was off. Wet rings around it. I told you the stairs go both ways. I meant it all the way down."

"What's left is entry two. Not a body — a glove. I told you skin comes off in gloves; I was talking about the drowned, but the principle travels. Empty inside. No meat, no organs, no seams. It wasn't a mask, it was a growth, and it doesn't leak because it was never alive. It shed the lure and left it here the way you'd leave a coat on a chair. Same make as '89. I'd have said that line died with the one I put down. Ledgers lie."

Then she stopped working and looked at the face a moment.

"You wanted plain. Here's plain. Look at the face. Properly. You've seen him — the ribbon on the gate, the plate laid at supper."

"Daniel Brandt. Seventeen. Went under at the ford in April when the river came up. No body. His mother has been sleeping over this cellar ever since. That's the why I told you to ask. It didn't pick a cellar under a house with people in it. It picked a family, and it came up the river in April to collect the material."

She wiped the knife and folded it shut.

"It's been growing him since April. As of last night, the fit is right. That's what happened to it — nothing. It's finished. And a finished face is a key, and keys get used. Some night soon there's a knock at that door, and a boy on the step, dripping, asking for supper. And she opens it, because mothers open doors."

"So. The husk gets bagged, not buried — my rule is know what you bury, and there's nothing here to bury. The well gets capped, then the cistern, then every well in a half-mile, because things that are all middle don't leave. They redistribute. The sheriff looked at it this morning, said 'that's a big eel,' and went to sit in his truck. I've had worse assessments."

She held out a bag.

"Bag the face. Hands don't touch it. It grew that face to be looked at, and I've no interest in learning what it grows to be touched. Then we go upstairs, and I tell Ellen Brandt her son died in April — and then the part that isn't true, which is that he stayed dead."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My hands shake a little as I take the canvas bag. "That's why it was looking at the door," I say, my voice low. "Not at us. It was looking at how he'd come home."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Amend my entry," Halloway said. She knelt back over the husk, knife already working. "I had it pricing us. Your read is better. It wasn't pricing anything — it was taking measurements. The stairs, the rail, the door, which side the light falls when it opens. You don't measure a door you don't mean to use." A beat. "And it did its measuring through a dead boy's face. Hold that thought."

She cut the face free along the hairline, the way you'd lift a label off whole, and floated it into the bag on the flat of the knife. The canvas took the weight.

"Before it folds — the lids." She raised the left one with the knife tip and brought the lamp close. Nothing. Not removed. Never there. The lid grown over solid, like a doll's.

"Entry. The face has no eyes and never did. What opened last night was the wearer, looking out through the fit." She let the lid down. "In '89 I counted six faces, none of them its own, and it never once occurred to me to ask where the animal kept its own eyes. Thirty years, Pike. The ledger still has blank pages."

Then she went under the stairs and knelt at the well cap, at the wet rings.

"I read these as leavings this morning. Look again. Every ring is on the cap. Not one leads away. Nothing walked out of this cellar and went anywhere." She sat back on her heels. "It went down. And down from the well is the cistern, and the cistern is under the kitchen floor. I told you things that are all middle don't leave — they redistribute. Amendment: it hasn't left the house. It left the room."

She stood and wiped the knife.

"Three months it's been under that floor, listening to a woman set a table for the boy whose face it's been fitting. That's not a cellar under a house. That's a fitting room under a kitchen. So the order changes. The half-mile of wells keeps. The mother doesn't. She's out of this house by dark — her sister's, the church hall, I don't care who's put out. Nothing sleeps over that kitchen tonight."

She started up the stairs, lamp first.

"Briefing, while we climb. You give her April first. A body is an ending, even this one — endings can be grieved, and grief buys you the ten minutes you need. The rest comes after she's sitting down. And the word 'it' stays out of that kitchen. 'It' is for cellars. Upstairs we say 'drowned,' and we lie in the direction of mercy until she can hear the truth without it going all the way through her." A pause. "Your hands can shake. They're honest. Just don't let them vote."

At the top: "The dry came back. Most of it." Then, over her shoulder: "There'll be a plate set for him at that table. There's always a plate. You look at it once, and then you don't. The second look is how she learns you've seen it, and then she'll spend the whole conversation not-looking with you, and I need her looking at me. Also the sheriff's in his truck with the engine running, guarding us from the big eel. Leave him to it."

The kitchen was warm and smelled of bread. A small woman stood at the counter with her back to them, and behind her the table was laid for three.

"Mothers open doors," Halloway said, mostly to herself, and raised her hand to knock —

The tap coughed. A cup of dark water spat into the sink, then the stream ran clear.

Halloway's hand came down. She stood very still, watching the water, and when she spoke her voice was ledger-flat.

"Change of order. The telling waits five minutes. You take the kitchen — ask her, plain, no hunter in it, how long the water's been doing that. I'll stand where I can see the tap and the floor both. And Pike. Watch her hands when you ask, not her face. Faces rehearse. Hands don't."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at her for a moment. Then she turned and went back down two steps, out of earshot of the kitchen, and set the lamp on the rail.

"All right. But understand what you're asking for. This is a fitting, not a corpse. A corpse tells you what killed it. A fitting tells you what's coming."

She held up a hand, counting entries.

"One. It didn't take anything. That's the part your stomach will fight. There's no wound, no bite, no place of entry, because the boy was never opened. In April he went under at the ford, and something was under the ford, and that's the whole of the transaction. It doesn't take a body. It takes a drowning — a body that's stopped arguing. Then it grows around what's there."

She turned her palm flat.

"Two. Under the skin — and you're asking what's under the skin now, so plainly: nothing. No organs, no bone worth the name, no structure a surgeon would own. What's under there is the same hide the outside is made of, all the way through. Oiled leather, all middle, no inside. In '89 I opened one of the six faces and found it went all the way down — the whole animal was a stack of faces with a core like a knot of wet rope between them. Not a stomach. Not a brain, as far as I could tell. A grip. It doesn't digest what it takes. It wears it until the fit is right, and then the question is what wears the fit."

"Three. What it took, then, wasn't meat. It took the shape. The weight of him — you felt the bag, didn't you. Too light for a boy. It grows the outline and leaves out the contents. The voice I can't confirm, but last night it understood doors and stairs and which side of a table the light falls on. That's not a husk learning. That's it reading three months of kitchen through the fit. Everything Daniel was near it, it has. Everything Daniel was, it has the outside of."

She wiped her hands on her thighs, slow.

"Four, and this is the one you'll meet again. The tell. The eyes. A grown face has no eyes of its own — the lids close over solid, like a doll's, and the only time you see eyes in it is when the wearer looks out through the fit. So: drowned boy on a doorstep, dry hair after a river, no bleeding, no leaking, and if you're ever unlucky enough to see it blink — it won't. The lids will move. There'll be nothing behind them doing it. That's your detail, Pike. That's the whole detail. A face that moves and no eyes in it."

A beat.

"And five, the one I keep in the back of the ledger. In '89 there were six. It wore six people at once. So when you ask yourself how many are under a town — the answer is: whatever a town's drownings can supply. Every river, every well, every flooded ford since April. Check the missing-persons files going back years and count the ones that ended 'no body recovered.' That's not a list of the dead. That's a wardrobe."

She picked the lamp back up.

"That's what it did to him: nothing, which is worse than anything. Now go ask the lady about her tap, and watch her hands." A pause at the top of the stairs. "And when you look at that third plate — the first look is already spent. Don't spend the second."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a breath and step into the kitchen, keeping my eyes off the table. "Ma'am," I say, voice steadier than I feel. "I'm sorry to bother you, but has your kitchen tap been doing that? Coughing dark water?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stood where she'd said she'd stand — angle on the tap, angle on the floor, back to the wall. She didn't watch Ellen Brandt. She watched the sink.

Ellen turned from the counter with a dishcloth in her hands and a smile already arranged. "Oh — you're the ones from downstairs. Yes, off and on since spring. Since the flood, the man from the county said. Air in the pipes, he called it. It runs brown a moment and then it's fine."

Her hands said something else. The cloth had been worked into a rope, and her thumbs were still turning it, and she hadn't looked at the tap once — hadn't looked at it, Halloway noted, the way you don't look at a thing you've made a private arrangement with.

"Since the flood," Ellen said, and the smile held. "It's just the pipes."

Halloway let the quiet sit exactly as long as it needed to, then came off the wall.

"Ma'am," she said, "I'm going to tell you about April now, and I need you to sit down before I do. Not because you'll fall over. Because what comes after the sitting-down part needs ten minutes from you, and I'd rather you spent them listening than standing."

She pulled the chair out herself. Didn't touch the woman's elbow. Mothers didn't need handling; they needed warning.

"Your son is dead, Mrs. Brandt. He died in April at the ford, and he didn't suffer long — the river was up and it was over quick. We found him." A beat, level as a spirit gauge. "I won't pretend the finding was gentle. But he's found, and he's home, and he isn't in that river anymore."

She watched the hands. The cloth stopped turning. The rest of Ellen went on arranged and smiling for two full seconds before it came down all at once, like scaffolding, and she sat in the chair Halloway was holding out because her knees decided before she did.

"I'm sorry," Halloway said, and it wasn't soft, because soft would have been a lie in that kitchen. "That's the true part done. Now I have to tell you the part that isn't true, which is that it ended in April, and then a third part, which is that it isn't over — and the third part is the reason you're sleeping at your sister's tonight, and I don't care what's put out, whose bed, or whether it's convenient. It isn't a request and it isn't the sheriff's. It's mine."

She turned her head a fraction.

"Pike. The stove's still warm and there's bread on that counter. Cut her some. And when you do —" the fractional head-turn became, briefly, an actual look — "you'll want a plate. Don't. The third plate stays where it is."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the bread knife out of Pike's reach and set it flat on the counter — not taking over, just making the point that knives in this kitchen had one worker at a time — then steered the description low, under the clatter of cutting, in the voice you'd use for inventory.

"It doesn't smell like a body. Bodies have a schedule and I know every date on it. This has no smell at all, and that's its own entry. Wet rope and boot oil — that's the '89 note, word for word. Underneath, there's no 'how far it got,' because 'it' and 'him' were never two things that met. There's no border, no seam, no point where Daniel stops and the animal starts. You'd cut into that boy and find hide, and cut through the hide and find hide, and at some depth a knot like tarred cordage, and that's the whole architecture. A glove with a grip in it."

She glanced at the table once — the third plate, straight-backed, knife laid parallel — and didn't look again.

"How far it got: the fit is right. That's how far. Height, weight of outline, hairline, the jaw. It hasn't got his voice yet, or I don't think it has. What it's got is his geometry and three months of this kitchen memorized from below — where the light falls, which chair, which plate."

Ellen's head came up at 'plate.' Halloway didn't falter.

"Mrs. Brandt. The bread first. Then the rest."

She waited until Ellen's hands were moving again, however badly, then went on, quieter, not gentler.

"One more entry, and it's the one that matters to you. What's under the skin of the thing wearing your son's face is nothing. No inside. Which means whatever you're imagining — that he's in there, aware, held — he isn't. April took Daniel whole and quick. What grew after is a coat cut to his pattern. There's no boy under there to save, and no boy under there suffering. I need you to hold onto that tonight, because the thing's whole method is making you look for him in it. That's what the face is for. It grew that face to be opened for."

The tap coughed again. One cup of dark, then clear. Halloway watched it the way you watch a hand near a knife.

"And there's the last of it, Pike, since you want everything." She nodded at the sink. "It coughs because it's drinking. The house's water, the well, the cistern — it's been feeding off the pipes since spring, under the kitchen, on the family's water. That's why it's finished early. Fittings run on schedule; fed ones run ahead. So it's not waiting for autumn. It's ready now, it's one floor down, and it's already eaten tonight."

She picked up her bag from the stairs.

"Ellen Brandt — coat, purse, nothing else from this kitchen, and I mean nothing, not his cup, not his jacket by the door. Things that are all middle read a house through its leavings, and we're not leaving it a key. You're at your sister's by seven. Pike walks you to the truck. I'll be in the cellar."

She paused at the cellar door, lamp up.

"Because it moved out of the room, not out of the house. And I want to know what a finished fit does for an encore in an empty kitchen." A beat. "And if the tap coughs a third time while I'm down there — Pike, you don't come after me. You drive. Some entries a person makes alone."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: My hands are sweating on the lamp handle. "Halloway, wait. I'm going with you." I don't move to follow her, but I don't step toward Ellen either. "You said some entries get made alone. But I haven't learned to read them yet if I'm not there to see."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped with one boot on the bottom stair and didn't turn around for a moment.

"First lesson, then, and it's free: that's how it gets people. Not teeth. Not dragging. Someone at the top of the stairs saying 'I'm going with you,' and the other one going 'all right.'" She turned. "It was listening to us all night, Pike. I'd bet the truck it heard that sentence. Hold onto that. Being brave in front of a listener is different from being brave."

She came back up two steps, so they were level, and looked at her the way she'd looked at the waterline.

"But your argument is sound, which is annoying. You can't read waterlines from a truck. And if I go down alone and something goes wrong, the entry gets made by nobody, because you'll do the faithful thing and drive off with a grieving woman, and I'll be a paragraph in the county paper between the parish bake sale and the road repairs." A beat. "Thirty years, that's the whole obituary I've got planned. I'd hate to waste it."

She held up fingers.

"Terms. One: you're cargo, not crew. Lamp stays where I put it, feet stay where I put them, and the second time I say your name without a sentence after it, you're moving before you know why. Two: hands free. Nothing in them but what I hand you. Three —" she nodded toward Ellen, still small at her own table, bread going cold — "she leaves first. She's in the truck with the doors locked and the engine running before we take the second step. That's not negotiation. If it comes up the stairs tonight, it comes up after its own shape, and I want the shape's mother a quarter mile away."

She went and stood over Ellen long enough to hear the terms said out loud, and to take the 'all right' — small, cracked, but said — and then walked them both to the door.

At the threshold she stopped, and for once her voice dropped the ledger.

"Mrs. Brandt. Last thing. Some night soon, maybe, there'll be a knock, and a boy on the step, wet-haired, asking for supper. It won't be him — we settled that, no one's in there. If it ever happens, and I'm not alive to stop it: you don't open the door. Not because you're afraid. Because mothers open doors, and that thing did its whole arithmetic on that fact. Starve it of the one thing it planned around. Can you do that for him?"

Whatever Ellen said, Halloway took it, nodded once, and sent her to the truck.

Then she took the lamp from Pike, checked the oil with a tilt, and handed it back.

"You hold it. I want my hands for the knife." She opened the cellar door. The stairs went down into a dark that the morning light outside had no opinion about. The air coming up was cool and wet and smelled of nothing at all.

"Ledger's open," she said. "Watch the walls more than the floor. Water's down to the boards — which means it's not water down there anymore, it's inventory. And Pike." She took the first step. "Last night it had no eyes of its own and it still found us in the dark. If your lamp swings, swing it slow. Things that are all middle feel light the way you and I feel a hand on our back."

A beat, from the darkness below.

"And count the steps both ways. I meant that too."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the last of the stairs with the knife low and her weight on her heels.

The cellar was down to an inch of black water, and the water had gone still — not calm, the way water goes calm, but held, the way a breath is held. Her boots found the boards and the boards held. Six steps. Rail on the left. She counted.

"Lamp up and level," she said, without turning. "Not at me. At the middle of the room. You're lighting my page, not my back."

The middle of the room was where it stood.

She'd expected it spread — a sheet gathered on the floor, all middle, four feet of flood turned to hide. That was what the ledger said things like this did in the dark: went flat, went wide, waited for weight. What she found was something standing.

Not tall. Assembled. Daniel Brandt's face on a body of oiled hide, six feet of it, joints bending where nothing should bend and holding anyway. The face was dry. Composed. Resting.

"Amendment to the ledger," she said, conversational, because talking was as much for the thing as for the girl on the stairs — let it price the voice, let it learn the voice was steady. "You're upright. Things that are all middle don't stand up. So there's a spine in there somewhere, or there's something standing inside the middle wearing it like boots. Either way, that's new."

The eyes opened. Both of them. They came to her, went past her — up, to the stairs, to the lamp in Pike's hands — and came back.

"There it is," Halloway said. "I wondered how long before you did the arithmetic on the girl. You should know I did the same arithmetic on you. I win, because I did it in daylight."

It moved.

Not fast. That was the thing nobody would ever believe afterward. It moved the way water moves — the level simply being somewhere else now — and it was between her and the stairs, and the face was still resting, and the arms had come off the body like roots leaving soil.

"Two," Halloway said, and that was Pike's name without a sentence after it, exactly as promised.

She heard the girl move. Whether up or down she couldn't know, and had decided not to spend the attention finding out.

Because the arms weren't reaching for her. They reached past her, down, and the hands flattened on the boards, and the boards — the boards began to breathe. The floor lifted a hair and dropped, lifted and dropped, and the inch of black water shivered into rings, small and even and patient.

It was under the floor. It had always been under the floor. The standing thing was a hand.

"Ah," Halloway said quietly. "You're not in the room. You're in the house."

The whole cellar came up an inch. Every board. The stairs too — she felt them go, felt the rail shift against her hand as the entire structure flexed like a chest.

Living things breathe. Houses with things under them do too, apparently. New page.

She didn't fight the floor. Fighting a floor is how you end up in one. She read the water instead — the rings were spreading from the well cap, from the mouth of the hole, and the thing had made one honest mistake. It had shown her where the middle was. Everything on this earth has to keep its grip somewhere, and the grip was down the well.

So she did the unfashionable thing. She didn't cut at the standing boy. She walked — heel first, level, lamp-light swinging slow because Pike had held it steady, she'd known Pike would — to the cap, knelt, and put the point of the knife to the knot of tarred cordage that had come up through the hole like a fist through a sleeve.

"Entry," she said. "In '89 I put one of you down and never learned what the middle wants. Tonight I don't need to. I only need to know what the middle does when the grip's in a knife."

She cut. Wet rope, boot oil, no smell at all — and a sound, low, not a scream, more like a mooring line parting under load, heard from the far side of a bay.

The standing thing sat down all at once, like laundry dropped. The house breathed out. The boards came back. The tap, three floors of pipe away, coughed once — and she chose to believe it was spitting.

The middle had gone. She could feel the absence, the way you feel a hand leave your back. Down the well, down the cistern, down and away and into whatever else in this county had ever drowned. It hadn't been beaten. It had been evicted. Those were different entries and she wrote them both in her head, properly, while she re-capped the well with her boot on it and three turns of chain.

Then she climbed. Counted both ways.

At the top she sat down next to Pike on the steps, took the lamp out of the girl's hands, and looked at the flame for a while.

"Full entry, since you asked and since you held the light steady, which is the whole job and half the people can't even do that." She turned the lamp down to a coin. "It's not one animal. It's weather. It goes where the water goes, and every low place in this county is a door, and I've spent thirty years thinking I was hunting things when I was mostly hunting rooms. Tonight it left a room and I still had to cap it, because things that are all middle don't leave. They redistribute."

She stood, and put her hand briefly — once, and never again to be spoken of — on Pike's shoulder.

"You counted when I told you to. You didn't come down when you wanted to. That's two more than I could do at your age." She picked up her bag. "Now. The well's chained, the mother's at her sister's, and the sheriff's still guarding us from the big eel. So there's one item left on tonight's ledger, and we're going to attend to it."

She looked toward the kitchen door, and the table beyond it, and the third plate.

"Ellen Brandt needs to hear that the house is quiet. And when she asks — and she'll ask, mothers ask — whether her son was under there. You're going to give her the true part. No one was in it. Nothing of him was in it. April took him whole."

A pause, lamp steady.

"And then we're going to throw out that third plate, Pike. Not wash it. Throw it out. The dead don't need plates, and the living shouldn't have to keep setting them for a shape that learned its geometry in this kitchen." She was already walking. "And then I'm having that bread, because I've made an entry tonight and it's made me hungry, and if that bothers you, hold the lamp."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at my hands, still shaking a bit. "I think it was testing the steps," I say quietly. "When it came up the first time. It was learning how he'd walk home."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped with the bread knife half-lifted and set it back down on the counter.

"Say that again."

Pike said it again.

Halloway stood very still, looking at the middle distance, which was where she kept the ledger nobody else got to read.

"Yes," she said. "Yes, that's the entry I fumbled. I had it pricing us — hunter, witness, girl with the lamp, which one goes through the door first. Wrong column, thirty-year habit. It wasn't pricing anyone." She turned and looked back at the cellar door, dark now, chained at the well below. "It was rehearsing. Coming up those stairs slow, patient, in its own time, on the shapes of feet it hadn't grown yet. Not escaping toward us. Practicing toward us. Six steps, rail on the left, and then a kitchen, and then —"

She tapped the table once with one finger. The third plate sat there, straight-backed, knife laid parallel.

" — a doorway, at suppertime, with the light behind it. Wet hair. Asking for supper." She looked at the plate the way you look at an opponent's piece on a board. "It wasn't learning to walk home, Pike. It was learning to come home. Those are different sentences, and the second one is worse, and I'm writing yours in the ledger and crossing out mine."

A pause. Then, dry as lime:

"Congratulations. Three days in the field and you're amending my entries. Took me thirty years to fill that page and you've bled on it already."

She took the plate before she could think better of plates — held it a moment, weighing the ceramic like it might weigh back — then carried it to the door, opened the bin, and set it in facedown. It didn't break. She seemed mildly disappointed.

"No ceremony," she said. "Ceremony's how it would've wanted it. It grew a face for this kitchen; it doesn't get the plate too."

Then she came back, cut two slices of the bread, and put one in front of Pike whether the girl wanted it or not.

"Eat. Hands that shake work better with bread in them; I don't know the mechanism, but I know it's true." She sat, which she almost never did in other people's kitchens, and looked tired the way fifty looks tired — all at once, in the chair, where it could be hidden again in a minute.

"Now the last of it, and then we're done for tonight, and I mean done — sleep, food, and no ledgers before noon." She turned the bread over in her hand without eating it yet. "It's evicted, not dead, and it's gone down into every low wet place in this county. So starting tomorrow we do the unfashionable work. Missing-persons files, back twenty years, every one ending 'no body recovered.' Flooded fords, drowned wells, the pond behind the church — you're going to learn to read coroner's reports the way you learned to read a waterline tonight, and you're going to hate it, and you'll do it anyway."

She finally ate, and it seemed to improve her opinion of the evening.

"Because here's the number I didn't say downstairs, and I'll say it now while there's bread and daylight. In '89 there were six. I told you a wardrobe is whatever a county's drownings can supply." She looked at the sink, the tap, the quiet pipes. "This county flooded in April, Pike. Rivers came up all over it. I've no idea yet how many faces got fitted this spring, and neither does anything else, and that's the entry I like least of all the ones I made tonight."

She pushed her chair back and stood, and the tiredness folded away somewhere, put back in its drawer.

"But it doesn't get tonight. Tonight the house is quiet, the well's chained, the mother's told the true part, and the plate's in the bin. That's a full page." She picked up the lamp and turned it down to nothing. "Sleep. And Pike — if anyone knocks on your door before noon with wet hair, don't open it. Ask me first."

A beat.

"It's a joke. Mostly. Thirty years, that's as close to reassurance as I get."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the bread in my hands. "It's not a joke," I say, quiet. My hands have stopped shaking. "Not with that thing in the county's water." I take a bite, chew slow. "You're teaching me to read waterlines. Tomorrow you teach me to read the coroner's reports."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway chewed, and considered her over the bread.

"No," she said.

She let that sit through one whole swallow.

"Tomorrow you sleep. Then you eat. Then, day after, you start on the files — and not because I've gone soft, but because there's a mechanism to this and I've watched it work for thirty years. Read coroner's reports with shaking hands and you start seeing faces in every 'no body recovered,' and faces make people stupid, and stupid people go to low wet places alone at night to check on things. You'll do it slower and better on the third day." A beat. "That's not reassurance either. That's scheduling."

She turned her bread crust over, then looked up.

"But I'll tell you what tomorrow actually is, since you're staying. We drive the county. Every flooded ford, every drowned well, the pond behind the church, the culvert on Miller's road. I'm going to stand at the edge of each one and do nothing, and you're going to stand next to me and watch the waterline — not the water, the line where the shine breaks. You'll know it when you see it. You saw it in the dark with a lamp in a shaking hand, which is more than most people manage in daylight."

She stood, and the chair scraped, and the kitchen sounded like a kitchen again.

"One more thing, and then the lamp goes out for good tonight." She stopped at the sink, washed her knife, folded it shut. "You said 'not a joke.' You're right, and I'll own the amendment — that's twice tonight you've corrected my ledger, and if it happens a third time I'll start paying you. But here's the difference between a joke and a lie: the joke was mine to make. I've been doing this thirty years, and the way I stay clinical about remains is that every so often I let one thing be a joke, even the ones that aren't. You're not there yet. You'll earn it. The first time you put something in the ground and sleep fine afterward — that's the day you get to make the bad joke, and mean it, and it'll keep you alive same as the knife does."

She picked up the lamp, checked the oil, and left it unlit on the counter.

"Until then you get my jokes and my scheduling, in that order. Six hours, front step of the sheriff's office. Bring bread if there's any left, and don't open your door to wet-haired boys, and count your steps both ways even in daylight."

At the door she paused.

"Waterlines," she said, to the dark outside more than to Pike. "Coroner's reports. And one day, if you're still here, you learn the last lesson, which is when to close the ledger and go home. Thirty years, and I'm still working on that page myself."

The door shut behind her, and the kitchen was just a kitchen.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I pick up the lamp from the counter, my thumb tracing a smudge of oil left from her hand. "Waterlines," I whisper to the empty room. Then I eat the rest of the bread.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway adjusted the lamp so the beam cut flat across the black water, throwing the shape at the far end into sharper relief. "Correct," she said. "The arms have too many joints. Human radius doesn't bend backward like that."

She stayed on the step, four feet of murky cellar water lapping at the stone just below her boots. The thing drifted slightly, nudged by some current Halloway couldn't see, and she tracked it with the light.

"See the torso?" she said. "No rib structure. Just a hollow tube, like a mud wasp's casing. I found three of these in a parish outside Prague in '09. They'd stuffed them full of river weed and dead fish, wore the carcasses like insulation until the flesh ripened."

She glanced back at Pike, her expression flat. "Don't go testing reflexes. If it's the same breed, the epidermis secretes a paralytic for ninety minutes post-mortem. I checked a pulse with bare fingers once. Couldn't hold a knife for a week. Highly inconvenient line of work to lose hand function in."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow and nod, keeping my hands firmly in my pockets. "So... how do we move it, then?" I squint at the torso. "And what do they want with insulation?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway unshouldered her pack and drew out a pair of iron meat hooks, their handles wrapped in scarred leather. "We don't," she said. "Not with bare hands, in any case. Leather buys about thirty seconds of contact if it hasn't split. These buy considerably more." She tested the weight of one hook, then flicked her eyes toward the wall behind Pike without turning her head. "There's a gaff behind you. Rusted through at the shaft, but serviceable enough for rolling. We flip it facedown—the glands run dorsal—and tow it to the steps. After that, we can decide whether the local parish pays bounty by the specimen or by the inconvenience."

She swung the lamp back toward the hollow torso, holding the beam steady on the tube-like midsection. "As for the insulation, they don't feel cold. They feel *wrong*. The carcass is a nursery. A breeding female deposits eggs in the cavity, then packs it with whatever biomass rots slowest in the climate. River weed, fish, once found one stuffed with wet straw and cat bones in Galway. The decomposition generates enough bacterial heat to keep the larvae viable in four feet of standing water, and the outer shell serves as mobile camouflage until they're large enough to require something more substantial."

Halloway considered the corpse with the detached interest of a butcher assessing a disappointing cut. "The one in Prague ripened early while a farmer's wife was beating rugs. Emptied its casing in the courtyard. Very awkward scene for the district coroner. I had to explain that the teeth marks on her clavicle were exit wounds, not entry. Made a hash of his paperwork." She held out one of the hooks, handle first. "So. Shall we fetch your gaff before this one decides to hatch?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway studied the shape through the lamp haze, her expression unchanged. "Not recently," she said. "And not as a whole organism. What you're looking at is larval architecture—chitin, not bone. See the segmentation? Three nodes past what passes for an elbow, no ball-and-socket joint. That limb was never inside human skin."

She tilted the lamp, angling for a better view of the hollow thorax. "What it may be wearing is a separate question. The interior packing could be fish, livestock, or something that walked on two legs and answered to a name. Human hair digests slowly—tends to float free of the weed. We'll know if we see threading."

She shifted her weight on the step, water lapping at the stone. "But the frame was never a person. It was engineered to occupy one. Like a hermit crab with a taste for meat instead of shells."

She held out the meat hook again. "Grab the gaff. If there's someone inside, they're past the point of introductions, and I'd rather not meet what's meant to replace them."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I turn and grab the gaff, the rust flaking under my grip. "Right." I try to keep my voice steady. "So we flip it. Which end is the, uh, dorsal side?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway trained the lamp on the creature’s thorax. “The dorsal side carries two raised glandular ridges, running from the sternal junction to the pelvic socket—like a fused zipper. Pale, slightly iridescent. That’s where the paralytic ducts open. Ventral is the smooth concave band; that’s the seam of the cavity.”

She tested the weight of the hook again. “Come at it from the left. The limbs on that side are folded under, so if it twitches, the right appendages whip toward the wall instead of your thigh. Slide the gaff under the ventral seam, just below the thoracic hollow. Don’t pierce the chitin—if the casing splits, we trade one corpse for a few hundred larvae, and then we’re wading through a nursery instead of a cellar.”

She stepped down one stair, black water lapping over the toe of her boot. “Roll it in one clean motion so the ridges go down into the muck. The joints are arthropodic; they’ll catch and shudder, but they won’t detach unless you force them. Think of flipping a waterlogged mattress, only the mattress secretes neurotoxin and resents you personally.”

She watched the shape drift another inch, tracking it with the light. “Once the dorsal side’s submerged, relocate your gaff to the tow-notch—second ridge from the top, where the chitin thins to a ring. Hook there and pull for the steps. And Pike—if the cavity starts peristalsing, that isn’t post-mortem gas. Drop the gaff and climb.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the gaff in her off-hand and kept the meat hook ready in her right. With Pike holding the lamp, her shadow cut a long, thin shape across the black water. She studied the ventral seam without touching it yet.

"Plainly," she said. "It drowned."

She pointed with the curved hook, indicating a dark ribbon trailing from the split in the creature's underside. "The ventral seam's torn two inches below the thoracic hollow. That effluent is hemolymph mixed with cellar water—it's still leaking out. These things don't have lungs. They run a dorsal spiracle row that needs direct air contact, and a heart-tube that can't pump once the cavity floods. Four feet of standing water in a stone box with no airspace. It couldn't surface. Couldn't ventilate. The gills seized, the tube filled, and it sank."

She shifted her grip on the gaff, testing the weight. "The movement we saw a minute ago was terminal ganglial firing. The nerve cord dies slower than the brain, such as it is. Think of a headless chicken running in circles, except the chicken is a hollow tube full of eggs and the barnyard is a flooded basement."

Halloway slid the rusted gaff carefully under the ventral seam, finding leverage against the chitin. She did not lift yet. "It tried to climb before the end. The left distal limbs are scraped to the second joint—see the pale scoring? Stone abrasion. It beat against the walls until the water won. Bad timing for it; worse timing if anyone had been down here while it was still ambulatory and desperate."

She glanced back at Pike, though her hands remained steady on the shaft. "So it's dead. Not dormant, not playing possum. Just a failed incubator that made poor real estate choices. The paralytic glands will hold another hour or so, but the corpse itself won't get any livelier. Hook the tow-notch on your end. Let's drag it into daylight before the larvae notice their central heating has failed."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I hook the notch, the rusted metal scraping against chitin. "It chose wrong," I say, more to myself than to her. "The cellar's too cold."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway set her weight against the gaff and pulled. The corpse slid through the black water with the low, grinding rasp of chitin on stone, dragged by the tow-notch.

"The cold didn't kill it," she said. "These things thrive in cold. The bacterial bloom in the cavity likes fifty-five to sixty degrees—practically tropical for the larvae. It drowned because it couldn't reach air, not because it needed a warmer postcode."

She shifted her grip on the meat hook, letting the line slacken slightly while she checked that the dorsal ridges stayed submerged. The lamplight caught the glandular strip, dull and iridescent, sliding just below the meniscus of the black water.

"Still, you've hit on the irony. It wanted insulation. It chose a waterlogged stone box with no ventilation and died wearing whatever it could scavenge. There's a lesson in real estate there somewhere."

The thing bumped against the bottom step. Halloway lifted the meat hook, ready to pin the thorax if it rolled against the stone.

"Pull steady," she said. "Keep the ridges under. If that dorsal seam breaks the surface and sprays hemolymph on your boot, you'll spend the next ninety minutes learning to blink one eye and drool symmetrically. Highly undignified way to end a Tuesday."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the gaff rest against the step and kept the meat hook ready. She did not look at Pike. She looked at the half-submerged shape and spoke as if reading from a logbook.

"If there's a man inside this one, he's past the point of complaint," she said. "But the mechanics don't change. Plainly: the creature doesn't eat the host. It evicts him."

She angled the lamp to catch the ventral seam.

"It enters through the soft tissues—mouth, navel, the pelvic floor—and it clears the thoracic cavity. Stomach, liver, the intestinal tract, the lungs if they obstruct the space. The ribcage is cracked along the costal margin and folded flat against the vertebrae to make room. I've pulled them out of occupied hosts where the ribs looked like pleated fan blades. Very tidy, considering the structural violence required."

She shifted her weight against the gaff.

"What's under the skin is chitin bracing and eggsac. The creature anchors to the host's pelvis and scapulae with hooked tarsae. That's how it puppeteers the limbs. The human legs still bear weight because the thing rides the bone from inside, flexing the joints past human tolerance. Knees hyperextend. Elbows invert. That's your first field sign: gait wrong and limbs that bend like a grasshopper's."

The water lapped at the step.

"If the host was taken breathing, the brain goes last. The creature oxygenates the blood through its own spiracles, so the face stays pink and the eyes track for days after thought has stopped. Useful for luring family. The larynx still operates on residual air. I've heard them call for help in a voice that didn't know it was dead yet. Sentiment says run toward the crying. Discipline says check the elbows."

She kept her voice flat.

"How far it got depends on incubation. Under a week, the host passes for human at twenty feet. Past two weeks, the skin thins and the dorsal ridges show through the back like a second spine. This one drowned. If it had a passenger, the water flooded the nursery before the larvae could hatch, so nobody had to explain exit wounds to a coroner. If it didn't—if this cavity is only fish and weed—then some local lost his livestock instead of his brother."

She tested the weight of the gaff again.

"In a live encounter, don't shoot the head. The brain isn't driving. Go for the knees or the dorsal ridges. Sever the internal bracing, and the puppet collapses. If the skin is still on, you'll know you're too late when the teeth marks point outward."

She glanced back at him.

"Plain enough?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I breathe out slowly, my knuckles white on the gaff handle. "Plain enough." I nod toward the corpse. "So we open it here? To be sure?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway measured the distance from the torn ventral seam to the water with her eyes. "Not here," she said. "Breach that cavity in four feet of standing water, and any viable eggs go into suspension. Then we're not cleaning a cellar; we're draining a nursery, and I don't keep waders tall enough for that."

She nudged the carcass with the meat hook, rolling the split underside upward until it cleared the black water by two fingers' breadth. "First dry tread. Pry the seam there, let the packing drain onto stone. Human hair catches in the chitin teeth—if there's a tenant, we'll see threading before the smell announces him. If it's only fish and weed, the rot will say so plainly enough, and we can burn the husk where it lies."

She set the gaff against the step and tested the leverage, finding the balance point in the rust-pitted shaft. "The sternal plate runs three-eighths thick, but the tear gives purchase. I'll hook the seam and pull toward the stairs." She glanced at the lamplight without turning her head. "That beam stays on the opening. No shadows in the thorax until I know whether I'm filing parish paperwork under livestock or missing persons."

She judged the height of the next dry step above the waterline. "If there's a man inside, we note it, close the seam, and hand him to the local priest with a recommendation against an open casket. If the cavity's empty of anything that answered to a name, we douse the carcass with spirits and drop a match from the top step. Either way, dry stone first. I didn't spend thirty years not getting killed by larvae just to drown in a soup of them because we were too impatient to climb three stairs."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway hooked the torn lip of the ventral seam with the meat hook and leaned back, letting her weight do the work. The chitin parted with a low, wet crack, opening the thoracic cavity to the lamp.

The smell rose in layers, and she catalogued them without recoil: anaerobic river mud first, then the copper-sweet note of hemolymph, and beneath both, the particular cloying sourness of human adipose tissue breaking down under bacterial heat. Fish never smelled like that. You learned the difference in locked summer cottages, or you learned it once and filed it correctly forever.

“Under the seam,” she said, “secondary chitin. A rib-replacement lattice, off-white, porous. It’s wet with peritoneal slurry—whatever the host hadn’t finished digesting when the occupant took residence.”

She worked the hook deeper, peeling the cavity wider. The lamplight filled the hollow. The interior walls wore a papery grey membrane, slick with mucus. Black river weed coiled around the bracing struts, but caught in the forward chitin teeth, there was a tangle of finer fiber. Pale. Curly. Still rooted at one end.

“Hair,” Halloway said. “Human. Fair, greying at the root. Male, middle-aged. Shaved within a day or two of occupation; the follicles outlast the scalp by weeks.”

She lifted a sodden mass from the cavity floor. It came in pieces—there was no organ integrity left. “Abdominal cavity cleared and repacked. Liver absent. Stomach deflated against the lumbar bracing, drained flat as a discarded bellows. What fills the space is eggsac. Translucent nodes, each the size of a grain of rice, clustered along the inside of the host’s ribs like frogspawn. They’re inert. The cold water halted metabolism before neurulation.”

She tapped the dorsal wall with the blunt end of the hook. “The creature’s heart-tube overlays the host’s sternum. That corrugated hose, ventral-to-dorsal, with the longitudinal striations. Muscle tissue, not tendon. Contracts sixty times a minute when active. Here, it’s still.”

Halloway’s mouth tightened at one corner, the closest she came to a smile in circumstances like these. “The scent profile is the good news. Fish and weed smell like a dockside market. This smells like a dockside market where someone left a side of pork in the sun. So we’re not filing livestock. We’re filing a name, if anyone’s reported a missing fair-haired man who stopped answering his door.”

She studied the upper reaches of the cavity, where the membrane thinned against the host’s residual tissue. “Cranial bracing not yet installed—no fracture to the skull, no ocular anchors. The thing was still wearing his face, using his larynx, walking his legs. Another week, perhaps ten days, and it would have cracked the mandible to widen the emergence path. He died with his features still in approximate order. Relative mercy, if one keeps score.”

She let the hook fall away. The cavity settled with a wet slap against the water. “That’s the inventory. Chitin lattice, eggsac cluster, and a middle-aged man reduced to insulation and packing material. How far it got: far enough to silence him, not far enough to stop him resembling himself. If you meet another one upright, remember the elbows and the voice. Don’t run toward the crying. Plain enough?”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the pale hair caught in the chitin. "So someone's going to miss him." My voice is quieter than I mean it to be. "We should find out who."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway resettled her grip on the meat hook and let the ventral seam fall closed, the chitin teeth clicking softly against the caught hair. "Someone's already missing him," she said. "The trick is whether they reported it to the parish constable or to the local gossip. One gets us a name. The other gets us a casserole and three theories about elopement."

She nudged the carcass with her boot, rolling the torn seam above the black water. "First we drag this to dry stone and burn the nursery. Then we check what it's wearing. These things don't dress themselves—they keep the host's clothes until the skin splits. If there's a wallet in a back pocket or a watch still ticking against chitin, we take it. If not, we follow the hair. Fair, greying, middle-aged, shaved recent. In a town this size, that description narrows to the butcher, the schoolmaster, or the man who complains about the church bells."

She tested the weight of the gaff, finding the leverage to haul again. "Sentiment says knock on doors until a widow weeps. Discipline says check the dental work once the fire cools. Teeth survive the kind of fire we need. Records survive records. We intersect the two, and someone gets a box to bury instead of a cellar that keeps them awake at night."

Halloway glanced at the lamp flame, checking the oil level with a practiced eye. "And Pike—when we move him, keep the dorsal ridges down. I don't care if Saint Peter himself is waiting at the top of these stairs with the man's baptismal certificate. If you drop this corpse and crack an eggsac on your boot, you'll be the second fair-haired man in this parish who stopped answering his door. Highly inconvenient for the both of us."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway set the meat hook against the step and knelt beside the carcass. Her knees cracked—fifty years, too many of them spent on damp stone—and she ignored the complaint. The host's coat was sodden wool, heavy with cellar water and hemolymph. She ran her gloved hands over the chest, finding the right breast pocket by the sag of the lining. Her fingers closed on a square of sodden pasteboard. She drew it out carefully, watching the ink feather across the surface, and tucked it inside her own oilcloth coat without reading it. The left pocket held nothing. The waistcoat yielded a watch chain, brass, the fob missing. She checked the trousers, working past the broken chitin at the hip: a clasp knife with a cracked bone handle, the blade rusted shut. She laid the objects on the driest step. Nothing named him yet, except what sat in his jaw and what might dry legible on the card.

She stood, retrieved the tin flask from her pack, and unscrewed the cap. The spirit inside was grain alcohol, ninety proof, nearly as expensive as the bounty itself. She poured it in a steady stream into the open ventral seam. It pooled in the thoracic hollow, turning the papery membrane translucent, and ran in thin rivulets down the dorsal ridges. She soaked the joints, the tangled weed, the hair. The chitin wouldn't burn; it would blister and curl like a burnt fingernail. But the eggsacs would cook, and the human fat packed against the sternum would render and feed the flame. That was the engineering.

"Shift up a step," she said. "Unless you want to smell like a tannery for the rest of the week."

She took the vesta case from her belt, struck a match on the stone, and dropped it onto the creature's chest.

The flame caught with a low, blue snap. It raced along the alcohol tracks and bloomed outward, turning hungry yellow as it found the adipose tissue. The hair went up with a sharp, acrid crackle. Then the eggsacs began to burst. Small, wet pops, like fat raindrops hitting a hot stove. One. Two. A cluster of six near the pelvic socket detonated in a minor burst of steam and cooked ichor. The chitin blackened at the edges, peeling away from the heat in thin, horn-like curls. The left distal limb jerked, a tendon-dehydration spasm, and Halloway pinned it with the gaff until it stopped.

The smell rose: hot iron, burned keratin, and beneath it the unmistakable sweet note of roasting pork. Halloway breathed through her mouth. Thirty years had not made that perfume pleasant, but it had made it routine. She watched the ventral seam split wider under the heat, exposing the cooked lattice of the internal bracing. The heart-tube shriveled to a dark, corrugated wire. She turned the carcass with the meat hook, rolling the unburned dorsal side into the flame. The glandular ridges blistered, their iridescence bubbling like old varnish.

Smoke rose in a greasy, black column, heavy and thick, flattening against the cellar ceiling and spreading toward the stairs. She tracked its color. Black meant tissue and river weed. White would have meant viable eggsac, and a white plume would have sent her running for the hatch. It stayed black. She waited until the chitin plates cracked with an audible snap, until the popping stopped and the flame settled into a steady, consuming chew. Then she poured the last finger of spirits over the thoracic cavity, and the fire leapt again, licking out of the hollow as if the thing were trying one final time to reach air.

When the flame sank to embers, she prodded the husk with the hook. It weighed far less now—water driven off, fat consumed, the chitin desiccated. She kicked apart the charred bracing. The jawbone had survived, exposed where the chitin mask had burned away. She hooked the mandible and tilted it toward the lamplight. The teeth were intact. Two molars capped with pewter. An incisor, crooked inward. Someone's dentist had kept impressions. Someone's wife had probably nagged him about that cap.

Halloway let the jaw settle back into the ash.

"Done," she said. She wiped the hook on her trouser leg and considered the sodden pasteboard in her coat. "If the ink dries legible, we knock on one door. If not, we start with the dentists and the men who stopped shaving. Either way, he's ash. The larvae are soup. And you still have the full use of both hands, which makes this a marked improvement over my last Tuesday in Prague."

She recapped the empty flask and shouldered her pack. "Bring the lamp up slow. The smoke's heavy, but it won't climb past the threshold. I'll seal the hatch once the embers cool. Nothing's walking out of that. Not unless it has a grudge and a pair of pewter molars."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the blackened jawbone. "We're giving him to a priest, then." My voice sounds raw. "Not just a box."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at the jawbone resting in the embers. The pewter molars caught the lamplight like dull coins. "A priest gets what a priest can use," she said. She prodded the ash with her boot, spreading the cooled embers to check for any surviving eggsac fragments. All char. Good. "That jaw and whatever name we find goes to the parish. The rest is carbon and chitin. A priest won't thank you for a box of soot and a lecture about thoracic parasites."

She bent and retrieved the sodden pasteboard from her coat, holding it near the lamp. The ink had feathered but the surname held—Kohler, or perhaps Koehler, with an address half-dissolved into a brown blot. She tucked it away again. "We'll knock on the door first. A widow deserves a warning before a stranger walks in with her husband's teeth in a pouch and an explanation that starts with 'there was a creature in the cellar.'"

She wiped her hands on her trouser legs, though the gloves had taken most of the mess. "If there's a priest worth his salt in this parish, he'll bless the jaw and say the words over the ash. That's as close to an open casket as this situation permits. I've seen parishioners get hysterical when the corpus is incomplete. Better to tell them he drowned saving a child from the flood—true enough, in its way—than to detail the elbow joints and the eggsac peristalsis."

Halloway shouldered the gaff and meat hook, securing them with leather straps. "Besides. A priest who knows what he's doing will seal the cellar and the well. Half the job of killing these things is stopping the parish from drinking the water downstream. The funeral's incidental. Useful for closure. But the hydrology matters more."

She looked toward the stairs, her expression flat as slate. "So yes. We give him to a priest. After we give him a name, a story the relatives can repeat without fainting, and a quicklime wash on these stairs. The priest gets the jawbone in a linen wrap. You get the satisfaction of doing right by a fair-haired man with crooked teeth. And I get to file the bounty as 'deceased host recovered and rendered non-viable' rather than 'unidentified biomass, origin unknown.' Everybody's faith is served, give or take the details."

She turned and set her boot on the lowest dry step. "Now climb. The smoke's thinning, but the air down here still tastes like burnt nursery, and I've developed a sentimental attachment to having both lungs functional. The priest can have his sacraments after I've had a mug of something that doesn't smell like a rendering plant."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I follow her up the stairs, the smell of burnt hair clinging to my clothes. "He deserves a story they can tell," I say. "Not just... this." I glance back at the cellar hatch, then at her. "What do we say about the teeth?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped on the step and looked back toward the glow below. "We say teeth endure," she said. "Bone outlasts flesh. Pewter outlasts bone. A flood takes the soft tissue, a fire takes what remains, and the jaw surfaces in the slurry. It's plausible. I've delivered dentures from chimney ash that used to be vicars. Nobody questioned the enamel."

She touched the pocket where the pasteboard rested. "The crooked incisor and the capped molars are the proof. The dentist identifies him. The family gets a partial corpse and a closed casket. We say he went down to check the cellar during the storm, that the water trapped him, that a lantern tipped and burned what the flood left. It's true in sequence. Water killed him. Fire finished him. We simply omit the middle tenant."

She climbed another step, her boots scraping against the wood. "A priest doesn't need theology to bless a jawbone. He needs a name and a mourner. We give him both. The widow gets a grave to visit instead of a cellar to dread. And I avoid an inquest where I must explain to a magistrate that the deceased was wearing an exoskeleton full of rice-sized eggs."

She reached the top of the stairs and set her palm against the hatch. "Accuracy is a luxury for the living, Pike. The dead don't mind a polite edit. Now kill that lamp before the updraft draws the smoke. We've got a surname to decipher and a dentist to bribe."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I kill the lamp, plunging the cellar into near-darkness, the glow of embers below the only light. "Alright," I say, following her out. "But I'm buying the priest a drink first. Might make the story go down easier."

rung_labels.evidence: chitin, not bone

rung_labels.label: engaged

rung_labels.label: engaged

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept the lamp high enough that the cellar’s damp could not claim the wick, but low enough to throw the far end of the water into relief. She did not step any closer.

“Wrong how?” she asked. “Not enough parts? Too many parts? Parts in the wrong order?”

The thing lay half-submerged, pale as old tallow, its outline broken by the tremble of the surface. One limb had curled back under it at a hinge Halloway did not recognize. The head, if it had a head, sat too far forward on the neck, as if the body had tried to look over its own shoulders and failed halfway.

She studied the water for bubbles, for ripples, for the telltale lift of something breathing.

“Right,” she said, grimly. “If it’s wrong, then we’re early.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to see past the water's shimmer. "Too many joints," I say, pointing a hesitant finger. "The arm's got an extra elbow."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not lower the lamp. She let the light run down the limb from shoulder to curled tip, counting as if the thing could hear her arithmetic.

“One elbow,” she said. “A second. A third where a wrist should have been.”

The extra joint had a pale, puckered seam, too smooth to be a wound and too deliberate to be a mistake. The fingers—if they were fingers—ended in flattened points, too long and too numerous, and they lay in the water in the fan-shape of something trying to stand without knees.

“Too many joints,” Halloway repeated, voice dry. “That’s not a man in a bad condition. That’s a man who has been persuaded to grow.”

She watched the surface. No bubbles. No swell beneath the ribs. Only a slow, oily tremble around the thing’s side, as if the water were remembering movement rather than making it.

Halloway shifted her weight to the back foot and kept the lamp between herself and the cellar mouth.

“Don’t step closer to see better,” she said. “If it’s got more hinges than a door, it’s got reach we haven’t mapped. And if you can see every joint clearly enough to count it, that probably means it’s letting you.”

Her gaze slid to the too-far-forward head, then back to the water.

“Right. What else is wrong? The shape? The water? The way it’s stopped moving like it’s thinking about it?”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the question sit for a moment, because it deserved more than a quick yes. She moved the lamp a fraction, just enough to see how the water took the light and where it broke the shape into lies.

“Depends what you mean by *was*,” she said.

The pale thing did not answer. It lay there with its impossible elbow bent beneath it, fingers fanned out in the water like a hand that had learned the idea of fingers but not the limits.

“If you mean, did a person come down these stairs,” Halloway said, “then yes, probably.”

She let the beam run up the too-long neck, over the too-forward head, down the ribs that were not quite ribs.

“If you mean, is that person still in there, then no. Not in any way I’d trust.”

Her voice stayed flat, practical, the way she used it when the dark was trying to make her sentimental.

“Human joints don’t rearrange themselves after death. Human skin doesn’t grow seams like that because a man drowned or bled out. That extra hinge was not an accident. It was improvement.”

She studied the oily tremble around the body’s side. Still no breath. Still no movement. Still the wrong sort of stillness.

“So, yes. Recently enough to have had a name. Recently enough that someone will come looking for it. Recently enough, probably, that the person was still warm when this started.”

She gave the last word a little emphasis, as if it had personally insulted her.

“But no. Not a person anymore. Not if it ever was.”

Halloway shifted the lamp again, keeping it high, keeping it between herself and the cellar mouth.

“If you’re asking because you want to know whether we should be gentle with it, the answer is no. If you’re asking because you want to know whether we should be afraid of it, that answer is yes. If you’re asking because you think we might go closer and see a face we recognize—”

She stopped, then said, dryly:

“Then you’ve already made the mistake. People don’t grow extra elbows to be recognizable.”

A short laugh slipped out of her, joyless and quick.

“The advantage is we can mourn whoever came down here without touching it. The disadvantage is it might still be wearing their boots.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my eyes fixed on the too-long fingers. "I was hoping you'd say it was an animal," I admit, my voice low. "The water's too still. It's not even floating right."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway heard the hope and did not mock it. Hope was one of the few things she could understand without wanting to cut it open.

“Animal would be easier,” she said. “An animal has rules. It gets hungry. It gets angry. It gets shot. This has too many hinges for an animal, and too much patience for a man.”

She moved the lamp a little lower, not toward the water, but along the edge of it, letting the beam catch the line where the body met the surface.

“You’re right about the floating,” she said. “That’s the worse part. A thing that drowned recently should be sinking. A thing that’s been here long enough to start putting on gases should be bobbing, bloating, and stinking enough to keep us company. This one is doing neither. It’s resting there like it’s on a stool.”

The pale shape sat in the water without swaying. The too-long fingers remained spread, the extra elbow curled beneath it, the head forward and still. No little waves ran out from it. No swell moved under the ribs. The water around it looked less like water and more like something holding its breath out of habit.

“Still water,” Halloway said, dryly. “Too still. If it moved a minute ago, there should be ripples. If it sank, there should be disturbed silt. If it’s floating because the body is changing, the surface should be showing signs of it. This looks like a painting of a thing in water that never learned what water does.”

She kept the lamp between herself and the cellar mouth.

“If it’s an animal, it’s an animal that’s been given a tailor’s opinion about limbs. If it’s a person, it’s a person that’s been given a carpenter’s opinion about bones.”

Her mouth tightened, not quite a smile.

“Either way, it’s not leaving us alone to guess.”

She studied the body again, looking past the wrong shape to the way it sat. Not high. Not low. Not rocking. Not sinking. Not floating. Not quite there.
