“That means one of two things,” she said. “Either something is holding it up from under the water—a chain, a stone, a root, a hand, a line running out of this cellar. If that’s it, we may find something we can cut, which would be a mercy. Or it’s not floating wrong because it’s weighted. It’s floating wrong because it’s not finished becoming what it wants to be.”

She paused.

“I don’t like either answer. The first means someone set a trap here. The second means the trap is already awake.”

The lamp trembled in her hand, though not enough to betray her.

“So don’t look for a face yet,” Halloway said. “Faces are how it will try to make you care. Look under it. Look where the water should move and doesn’t. Look for what’s holding it, or what’s under it, or what came down after it and hasn’t left the room.”

Her gaze slid across the cellar mouth, then back to the thing in the water.

“Right,” she said. “Tell me what the water looks like under it. Not the surface. Under.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not step closer to the body. She moved sideways instead, putting herself between Pike and the dark of the cellar mouth, keeping the lampbeam where it was useful and the water where it was not.

“Plainly,” she said, as if the word had teeth in it.

She looked at the thing in the water, then at the ripples fading out from where the wading had disturbed the surface. The ripples did not reach it. They broke short, as if the thing sat in a different pond from the rest of the cellar.

“Plainly: it was alive when this started,” Halloway said. “Not alive now, unless you count being able to hold a room’s attention. That’s not life. That’s a stain.”

Her eyes ran down the pale limb again, to the extra joint, the healed seam, the fingers fanned in the water.

“The elbow was grown in. It’s not a wound. There’s skin over the hinge. That means time. Days, maybe. Someone had this apart and was building it back wrong while it was still warm enough to bleed.”

She said it without flinching, because flinching would have made the sentence sound like something she could not carry.

“Then it was put here. Not drowned. Drowning doesn’t make new joints. It doesn’t pull a head too far forward on the neck. It doesn’t make water go still around a body like the body is a stone and the stone is pretending not to be there.”

Halloway kept her voice level, but her gaze went under the water, searching for the dark smudge of a chain, a line, a root, a hand.

“Plainly, if you want the short version: a person came down here. Something decided the person wasn’t finished yet. It added what it wanted, took away what it didn’t, and then either left it waiting or left it listening.”

A grim little breath passed through her nose.

“If you want the long version, it’s a construction site. Somebody’s been doing carpentry with a man. The nails are wrong, the measurements are worse, and the builder hasn’t come back to finish the job.”

She lifted her chin toward the water, not toward the body.

“That’s what happened to it. What happened *by* it, I don’t know. Don’t ask the water for comfort. It’s not giving any.”

Halloway did not move her hand from the knife at her belt.

“And don’t wade any deeper than you have to. If the water’s too still around it, the stillness may spread.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the seam on the elbow, my stomach turning. "Who does that?" I whisper. "And why?" The water around my boots feels colder than it should.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She let the lamp fall a little lower, not toward the body, but toward the place where the water had stopped behaving like water.

“The wrong question,” she said. “Who does that is somebody with tools. Why does that is somebody who thought he had time.”

The pale thing lay where it had lain, fingers spread, extra hinge curled beneath it like a mistake someone had tried to hide under skin.

“An extra elbow means planning,” Halloway said. “Planning means hands. Hands mean a maker. And a maker means somebody came down here with a bag, a knife, and a very bad idea about what a body is for.”

She studied the seam again. Smooth. Closed. Too deliberate to be injury, too ugly to be healing.

“Not a butcher,” she said. “A butcher has a cut. This is a fit. Someone opened the arm, built in a new joint, closed the skin over it, and expected it to work.”

Her mouth twisted.

“That’s not murder. Murder’s messy. That’s carpentry with a man.”

The cold in the water seemed to sharpen around the edges of the cellar, as though the room had begun thinking about ice.

Halloway shifted her stance, keeping the lamp between herself and the stairs.

“As for why,” she said, “it’s usually fear. A person builds a thing with too many hinges because he wants it to keep moving even when the legs are gone. Or he wants it to reach around corners. Or he thinks God will approve of the measurements. Or he’s a priest with a saw and a book, or a doctor with a theory and no mercy, or a rich man who wants a servant that won’t die on him in the kitchen.”

She glanced at the too-long fingers fanned in the water.

“Sometimes it’s just a man who decided that one person wasn’t enough work for the job.”

The thing did not move. The water did not move around it.

Halloway looked at the stillness, then at the cold spreading from it.

“That,” she said, quieter now, “is why I don’t like standing here asking for comfort. Water doesn’t get colder because you feel sad about a body. Water gets colder because something is taking heat from it.”

She lifted the lamp again, throwing light along the surface, watching for steam, for ice, for the black smudge of a line beneath.

“If the thing were dead, the water would do what water does. If it were alive, it would move. What we have is a room losing its warmth to something that isn’t finished yet.”

A short, dry breath passed through her nose.

“So don’t ask the dark why it built that elbow. It won’t answer, and if it does, you won’t like the grammar.”

She kept her eyes on the cellar mouth, then back on the thing in the water.

“We find out who came down here. We find out what they carried. We find out what they left behind that’s still working.” Her gaze slid to the too-still surface. “And we do not do it while standing in a drain.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway gave a short nod, as if he had finally asked a question worth answering.

“Good,” she said. “Fear with detail is work. Fear without detail is just weather.”

She unhooked a long iron crook from her belt, the kind used for lifting cellar lids and dragging things out of the reach of other things. She did not offer it to him, and she did not step toward the body either. She set the hook into the water a good foot away from the pale shape and drew it back in a shallow arc, parting the surface without disturbing whatever lay beneath.

The water resisted in a way it should not have. It did not splash. It did not ripple outward properly. It simply gave way, then closed again too soon, as if it had been cut by a hand that was tired of the mess.

Halloway watched the surface knit itself back together.

“Right,” she said. “That’s not water behaving like water. That’s water behaving like it’s been taught.”

She angled the lamp lower along the shoulder of the thing, keeping her hand still.

“What’s under the skin,” she said, “starts with what’s missing from it.”

The pale flesh over the extra elbow was smooth, too clean for a corpse and too tight for healing. Under it, the normal bumps of bone did not sit where they should. Something deeper had been bored out. She could see it in the way the skin lay: no bruising, no swelling, no ragged edge of violence. Just a seam, closed and set, like a lid fitted onto a box.

“His arm was opened while he was still warm,” Halloway said. “Not after death. Death doesn’t stretch skin that way. If it had been a corpse, the builder could have taken his time, but the skin would have gone slack and the blood would have pooled wrong. This is tight. This was built while the body was still trying to be a body.”

The beam found the seam again, running from the old joint into the new one.

“Under the skin now, there’s no normal bone left where that extra hinge sits,” she said. “At least not all of it. The original elbow would have been cut back. Cleanly. Then something else was put in. I can’t see it, but I can see its shadow. There’s a dark line under the pale, running along the arm like a rope threaded through a pulley. Not vein. Veins branch. This one goes where it wants to.”

She shifted the lamp to the forearm. The fingers lay fanned in the water, too long, too many-jointed, the tips flattened and white.

“The fingers are grafted,” Halloway said. “Not bone. Something softer. Wood, maybe, or antler, or the kind of thing that grows in wet places where light hasn’t been polite enough to ask permission. The builder took the old bones out of the hands and put new rods in. Then he put skin over the ends and expected them to bend.”

A dry breath passed through her nose.

“He didn’t expect them to work. He expected them to move. That’s worse.”

She moved the lamp to the chest. The ribs did not sit like ribs. They were too far apart, and the skin between them was drawn tight over something underneath that was not breathing.

“The chest was widened,” she said. “Not broken. Widened. Ribs were cut and reset. One or two may have been taken away entirely and used elsewhere.”

Her gaze slid to the neck.

“The head sits too far forward because the neck bones have been moved. Not snapped. Moved. He was opened at the throat and then closed over something else. The water’s too cold around him because something in him is taking heat out of it. Not the body’s heat. The room’s.”

Halloway let the hook rest against the wall and kept the lamp high.

“So. What did it take?” she said. “That depends on whether you mean what it took from him or what it took to make him this.”

The thing lay still. The stillness had texture now, the way a held breath has texture.

“It took his warmth,” Halloway said. “That’s the first thing. Warmth is easy. It leaves a body when you stop paying attention to it. Then it took his breath. Not because he was drowned. Because breath makes movement, and movement makes noise, and a thing under construction isn’t supposed to make noise.”

She looked at the too-still water around the body.

“It took his weight,” she said. “That’s why it isn’t sinking. That’s why it isn’t floating. It’s not obeying the rules for dead things. It’s not obeying the rules for living things either. It’s obeying somebody else’s measurements.”

Her voice stayed flat, practical, as if she were reading a list of missing tools.

“It took the parts that made him stop. The joints that would lock. The bones that would break. The muscles that would tear. The brain would have said no, but the brain is upstairs and the builder doesn’t care what the brain says until the head starts looking over the shoulders.”

A short, joyless breath escaped her.

“The builder is a carpenter, not a doctor. A doctor wants the body to go on living. A carpenter wants the piece to sit flush.”

She glanced down the body again.

“How far did it get?” Halloway said. “Far enough to make a new hinge. Far enough to lengthen the fingers. Far enough to move the neck and widen the chest. That means it got to the arms, hands, throat, and ribs. That’s not a small job. That’s a body being revised.”

Her eyes narrowed at the shoulders.

“If the shoulders are wrong, then the spine is next. If the spine is wrong, then the legs are next. If the legs are next, then it will stand, and standing is not the same as rising.”

She let the hook slide a little farther into the water, testing the edge of the pale shape’s shadow without touching it.

“But it stopped at the face,” she said. “That’s the detail that matters. The head was moved, but not finished. The face is still there, under all that wrongness. That means two things.”

The lamp trembled once in her hand, though her voice did not.

“Either the builder ran out of time, or he wanted him to be seen before he was done.”

Halloway looked at the thing’s too-long fingers, then at the water that had closed too quickly around them.

“If you meet another one,” she said, “don’t look for a body. Look for work. Seams at the elbows, wrists, knees, neck, and spine. Look for skin that’s too smooth over new joints. Look for fingers that bend when they shouldn’t. Look for water that doesn’t ripple right. If the body is warm where it shouldn’t be, then something is still feeding on heat. If the body is cold where it shouldn’t be, then something is keeping the heat inside it. If it’s in the water and the water is still, don’t assume it’s dead. Assume it’s listening.”

She drew the hook back and wiped the water from it with a cloth from her belt, then threw the cloth down beside her and did not look at it again.

“It didn’t take his name,” Halloway said. “It took his hinges.”

The thing in the water did not move.

“And that,” she added, “means it isn’t done with the room.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a step back, the water sloshing around my boots. "If it's listening," I say, my voice too quiet, "then it heard every word."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not look at him. Looking meant taking the lamp off the body, and the body had already learned too many things from their voices.

“Then it heard the part where we decide not to touch it,” she said. “That’s better than a name.”

She kept the iron crook low, its hook resting in the water a foot away from the pale shape. The surface had closed around the metal too neatly, without splashing, without protest, as if it had been folded shut by a tired hand.

“If it’s listening, it isn’t listening for words,” Halloway said. “It’s listening for weight. Heat. Breath. The cold where a person used to be.”

She shifted sideways, moving until the lamp sat between herself and the cellar mouth, and until the beam fell across the body’s shoulder and ribs. The too-long fingers remained fanned in the water. The extra elbow stayed curled beneath the arm. The head sat forward and still, as if it had tried to turn and had been interrupted halfway through the thought.

Then the topmost finger moved.

Not a twitch. Not the loose flutter of a corpse losing a gas pocket. It bent one joint, slow and careful, and tapped the surface once. The sound was small, almost polite. A single pale circle widened from the fingertip, then another, as if the water were answering.

Halloway stopped breathing for the two seconds she allowed herself.

“There,” she said, very flat. “That’s not listening. That’s testing the floor.”

She drew the crook through the water in a wider arc, feeling for chain, rope, root, stone, anything that could be cut. The iron passed through the cold ring around the body without resistance. There was no snag. No weight beneath. No shadow of a line running away into the dark.

“The water isn’t holding it,” Halloway said. “That’s the bad news. Something under it is holding the water.”

She lifted the lamp higher. The beam struck the surface at a sharper angle and pulled the body’s shadow long across the floor. The fingers cast too many shadows. The extra elbow made a knot of darkness that did not match the limb above it. The head’s shadow leaned a little farther forward than the head itself.

Halloway watched the wrongness and filed it away.

“Plainly,” she said, “because you want it plain: the builder didn’t make a monster. He made a mechanism with a meat casing. It stops when the heat gets too low, or when the maker leaves the room, or when it’s waiting for a hand to put back on. It started again because we made noise. That doesn’t mean it’s alive. It means it’s not finished.”

A short laugh escaped her, dry as ash.

“If it heard every word, then it also heard you ask what it did to him. That’s rude of us. We should answer by taking it apart and seeing.”

She kept the hook ready and her eye on the far end of the cellar, where the water turned black and the walls lost their stone.

“Right. Here’s what you do next, plainly. Keep the lamp high. Don’t stand in the cold patch. If that head turns any farther, don’t look for recognition. Look for the seam. If the neck opens, we get out and we burn the stairs. If it stands, we get out and we don’t ask questions about why the stairs are already too warm behind us.”

The thing in the water did not move.

The water did not move around it.

Then, almost too slowly to be trusted, the too-forward head tilted a single degree toward the cellar mouth. Not toward Pike. Toward the stairs. Toward the place where a person might come down.

Halloway’s hand tightened on the lamp.

“Ah,” she said. “Not listening to us.”

She looked at the head, at the seam under its jaw, at the fingers that had tapped once like a man checking whether a door was locked from the inside.

“It’s listening for the next one.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the long knife from her belt and set the crook aside against the wall. The iron rang once on stone, then stopped ringing too soon, as if the cellar had swallowed the sound.

“Everything means everything,” she said. “Then keep the light where it can do some good.”

She did not go to the head. She went to the arm. The extra elbow had a seam running along the inner side, pale and tight, with no scab and no swelling. Halloway laid the knife tip into it, pressed until the skin gave, and drew the blade down.

The sound was not wet enough.

It parted like damp leather pulled from a saddle. The edges of the cut stood open without bleeding, pale flesh folded back from pale flesh. No red. No heat. Only a thin line of something darker than serum, black-brown and oily, moved along the seam and stopped at the water’s edge.

“First thing,” Halloway said. “It’s closed too well. A corpse that’s been cut doesn’t shut like that. The skin remembers it was alive, and this remembers being worked.”

She widened the cut with the flat of the blade. The fat under the skin was gone. Not wasted. Removed. What lay beneath the pale layer was not muscle as she knew it, but long strands braided together and bound in something waxy and white, like candle grease poured into a mold. The strands did not glisten. They held their wetness without wetness, the way a thing looks when it has borrowed the idea of damp.

Beneath that, the old elbow had been sawn back.

The bone ends were clean, capped, and set into a hollowed socket of something not quite bone. It was pale as antler, smooth as old ivory, and ringed with fine dark lines. Halloway pressed the flat of her knife against it. The ringed material gave a little, then not.

“Cartilage,” she said. “Or something pretending to be cartilage. Not enough for a man. Too neat for an animal. The builder bored out the joint and inserted a hinge. He didn’t make it work. He made it hold.”

She cut deeper, toward the forearm. The black-brown line moved a little under the skin, slow, reluctant, as if the body had once been warm enough to carry it and had now decided it would not be bothered. The smell rose then.

Not rot.

That was the first wrong thing. A thing that had been dead a day or two in standing water should have begun to smell like the room had been opened by mistake. This smelled of wet wool, tallow, cellar mold, and something sweet underneath, like milk left too long in a tin. The sweetness was not pleasant. It was the sort of smell that made a person’s mouth water before it made their stomach turn.

“Second thing,” Halloway said. “No rot. No blood. Smells like a chapel pantry after a flood. That means the body was sealed and fed while it was being built. The builder kept it from spoiling so he could finish his work.”

She moved along the forearm. The skin there had been opened and closed more than once. Tiny stitch marks lay under the seam, not thread, not wire, but something like dark hair drawn tight and then cut short. Halloway shaved a little skin away and found the marks gone clean, as if they had been meant to disappear.

“The hands were rebuilt,” she said. “Old bones taken out. New rods put in. The fingers were lengthened and jointed by grafts.”

She cut into the back of the hand.

Under the skin were no nails. The nail beds had been flattened and covered with a thin layer of pale tissue, smooth as the inside of a mussel shell. The ends of the fingers had been packed with something dark and fibrous. When Halloway pulled the edge open, the fibers did not snap. They bent. They looked like wet rush stems, or sinew soaked in oil, or the roots of something that had grown in a place where nobody had thought to ask whether it should.

She cut one finger fully open.

There was no bone.

Instead, a slender rod lay inside, hollow at the center. The dark fluid moved in it, not upward, not downward, but with the slow patience of something that had all the time it was given. Around the rod, the old marrow cavity had been scraped clean and lined with a waxy film.

“Third thing,” Halloway said. “The bones are not just wrong. They are missing where the body should be stiff. It has been taken apart and put back with hinges where a man should not have them.”

The too-long fingers did not twitch. They lay open in her cut and kept lying there, as if they had learned stillness from something worse than death.

Halloway worked up to the shoulder.

The joint was wrong before she cut it. The shoulder sat too high, and the collarbone, under the skin, had been moved. She found the seam at the root of the neck and opened it carefully, because necks were where men kept their last names and their worst faces.

The throat had been cut wide. The skin had been drawn back and closed over something that was not the voice box.

“Fourth thing,” Halloway said. “The larynx is gone.”

She said it flatly, the way she would say a boot was missing from a corpse. The cut lips did not bleed. The cavity beneath was dry, pale, and ridged. Where the voice would have been, there was a folded membrane, whitish and thin, stretched across a dark ring. The ring was not bone. It was not cartilage. It was a circle of something black and lacquered, like a belt buckle left in rain.

“Not for speaking,” she said. “For holding.”

She probed it with the knife, then stopped. The black ring did not change, but the water around the body moved one finger’s width, inward, as if it had leaned closer.

The cold sharpened.

Halloway lifted the knife and cut along the collarbone seam. The flesh opened with that same bad sound, not tearing, but being allowed to part. Beneath, the clavicle had been sawn, reset, and bound with thin dark bands. The ends had been fitted into the shoulder with a socket made of the same ringed material as the elbow. She tapped it once. It made no click. It made a dull, wet answer, like a stone dropped into flour.

“He took the strength out of the arm,” she said. “Not the movement. The strength. A dead arm should not bend. A living arm should not bend like this unless it means to. This one has been made to bend without wanting. That is the work. Not resurrection. Not surgery. A machine with meat wrapped around it.”

She moved the blade to the chest.

The ribs were the first obvious wrong thing from the outside, but under the skin the wrongness was worse. The chest had been widened, not broken. The old seams at the sides had been closed with skin that looked too new, too smooth, like a child’s burn healed over. She cut one of those seams open.

The body did not sigh.

That was the thing. A chest opened should sometimes sigh, or not, depending on the state, but it should do something. This did not.

Inside, the ribs had been cut and reset. Two were gone from the left side. The others had been pulled outward and held in place by thin dark rods threaded through drilled holes. The rods were not metal. They looked like charred bone, or root, or something that had grown through ash.

The lung beneath was not a lung.

It was a folded sheet of pale membrane, dry and layered like the pages of a wet book that had been pressed open and dried again. It did not rise. It did not collapse. It simply sat there, too broad for the chest, too still for anything that breathed.

“Fifth thing,” Halloway said. “No lungs. No breath. No blood where blood should be. The chest was cleared. Something else was put in for shape, and something else was taken for warmth.”

She cut deeper.

The black-brown fluid was thicker inside. It moved along the dark rods as if following a plan. The smell rose stronger now, sweet and metallic, with the cellar’s damp underneath it like a bad cellar trying to apologize for a bad thing it had been asked to hold.

Halloway found the stomach next.

It had been removed.

The cavity where it should have been was empty and lined with the same waxy film, and in the center of that cavity sat a knot of black fibers drawn tight around a small, pale object. She worked the knife around it and lifted the object free.

It was a tooth.

A human tooth, root and all, set into a ring of dark thread. The thread had been knotted through the waxy lining of the cavity, and when Halloway touched it, the body’s too-long fingers tapped once against the water.

Not a twitch.

A tap.

Halloway looked at the fingers. They were still open from her earlier cut, pale flesh hanging, hollow rod showing, dark fluid moving slowly in it. The tap had come from the third finger, the one nearest the wrist, and it had come from a hand she had already cut.

She looked at the head.

The too-forward head remained still.

“Right,” Halloway said. “That is not listening.”

The water around the body went colder. The wick of the lamp drew down a little, though the cellar air had not moved.

Halloway did not step back. She put herself sideways, between the light and the stairs, and kept the knife in the chest seam so the thing’s own opened body held the blade.

“Sixth thing,” she said. “It has begun to answer to cuts. That means the builder left a nerve path, or the meat remembers being made. Either way, it is not finished. It is still learning what the room is for.”

She cut down from the neck seam, past the collarbone, into the upper chest. The dark line under the skin ran from throat to knot to arm. She followed it with the knife until the pale skin peeled back in a long strip.

Underneath were no veins.

There were channels.

They were narrow, blackened, and lined with something that glistened only when the light struck it sideways. The channels ran from the throat into the chest and down the arms, with knots at every new joint. At the elbow, the channel had been looped through the ringed hinge three times, like cord through a pulley. At the shoulder, it was stitched into the waxy membrane with dark thread. At the wrist, it spread into the fingers in thin, useless branches.

“The builder threaded it,” Halloway said. “Not for life. For movement. He wanted the limbs to answer without being asked.”

She cut lower.

The belly had been opened and closed again. The skin there was pale and tight, with a seam that looked almost kind, the kind of seam a mother might make over a torn coat. Halloway cut it open.

The intestines were gone.

The cavity was clean. Not sterile, because nothing in this cellar was clean in a living way, but scrubbed and scraped, the inner walls lined with the same waxy film. In the center, the knot of fibers still held the tooth. Around it, the old fat had been rendered away. The spine showed through, but not as bone.

The spine had been cut open.

Halloway looked down the length of it. The vertebrae were split, widened, and lined with the black rod material. The dark line from the throat ran down between them, tied at intervals with thread, each thread knotted to a rib, each rib pulled outward to make room.

She lifted the body’s head with the crook of her knife.

The neck did not turn.

The head moved because she moved it.

The face was still there.

That was the worst part.

The skin was too pale, the cheeks too full, the mouth too tightly closed, but the face was a face. It had once belonged to someone who had used it to eat, speak, and be mistaken for a person. The eyes were open now, not because Halloway had opened them, but because the lids had given way where the neck was cut. One eye looked at the cellar wall. The other looked at the water.

Neither looked at her.

“Seventh thing,” Halloway said. “The face is unfinished. The builder got to the eyes but not the expression. That means he wanted it to look human enough to be seen, but not human enough to be known.”

The eye that looked at the wall moved a little.

Not toward her.

Toward the stairs.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“Eighth thing,” she said. “It is not finished because the room is not empty.”

She set the knife down inside the chest cavity and wiped the blade on the waxy lining. The body did not protest. The water did not ripple. The black thread around the tooth gave a small, wet sound, as if the knot had tightened by itself.

Then the pale shape moved.

The cut elbow straightened.

It did not jerk. It did not spasm. It straightened with the slow, wrong certainty of a hinge being tested by a hand that knew exactly how much weight a thing could bear. The fingers drew together, the too-long tips closing around the edge of the water. The head lifted from the crook of the knife, not because Halloway raised it, but because the neck muscles that were not there pulled it up.

The body sat.

Not stood.

Sat.

Its shoulders rose. Its ribs spread, opening further along the seams Halloway had made. The black fluid ran down the chest in slow threads. The eye that had looked at the stairs moved fully now, focusing with the dreadful patience of a thing that had been taught to look.

Halloway did not step closer.

She stepped back, keeping the crook low between herself and the body, and kept the light off the face.

“Right,” she said. “It heard us. It heard me. It heard the knife. That is not the same as being alive, but it is worse than being dead.”

The thing sat in the water. Its mouth opened.

No breath came out.

No sound came out.

But the cellar air moved a little toward it, as if the room itself had been told to lean closer.

Halloway looked at the cut shoulder, the new hinge, the threaded spine, the hollow fingers, the empty chest. She looked at the face that was still almost a face.

“How far did it get?” she said, answering herself. “Far enough to make the arms reach. Far enough to make the spine sit up. Far enough to make the head turn. Not far enough to stand. Not far enough to walk. Not yet.”

The thing’s fingers tapped once on the water.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

The taps were not random. They were too even, too patient. They came from the hand nearest the stairs.

Halloway’s gaze went to the water.

The ripples from the taps moved outward in pale rings, but they did not reach the far end of the cellar. They stopped short, turned back, and pressed against the body’s own stillness. The water was not moving away from the thing. It was moving back to it.

Something under the floor had begun to breathe the cold upward.

The lamp wick shrank again.

Halloway looked at the too-forward head, at the open mouth, at the eye that was learning the room.

“Ninth thing,” she said. “The builder did not leave it here to wait.”

The body’s extra elbow bent.

Not to reach.

To rise.

The shoulders lifted. The cut ribs drew apart. The black fluid ran down the waxy cavity, and the knot of fibers around the tooth gave a small sound like a thread pulled through wet cloth.

Halloway took a step back.

“Tenth thing,” she said. “It wants the next person to see it finished.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I shove the lamp into her hand. "Tell me what to break." I'm already moving toward the stairs, my heart hammering. "Before it learns how to follow."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway caught the lamp by the handle before its flame could kiss the water. The wick steadied in her fist, but she did not lower it.

“The throat-ring,” she said. “Break the throat-ring.”

She moved closer, not because the answer required proximity, but because the thing had begun to take the answer seriously.

“The black circle under the jaw,” Halloway said. “Not the neck. Not the head. The ring. It’s not a voice. It’s a latch. If you break it, the head stops watching the stairs.”

The thing’s extra elbow had straightened fully now. Its cut ribs opened like the gills of a fish that had never needed them. The too-long fingers pressed into the water, and for the first time the surface accepted them; it did not ripple outward so much as cling to the joints, wet and deliberate.

“Break the elbow if you want a lesson in reach,” Halloway added, grimly. “Break the spine if you want a lesson in patience. Break the throat-ring if you want the thing to stop learning the room.”

She set the lamp on the dry shelf at the foot of the stairs, where it would burn and not drown. Then she took the crook and the knife.

“Attention first,” she said, mostly to herself. “Then weight. Then memory.”

She hooked the crook under the thing’s jaw and tilted the head back just enough to expose the throat seam. The face moved with the tool, not with the will. That was the mercy of it. A face that moved with will was already a person again. A face that moved because a woman hooked it back was still a corpse with ambitions.

Halloway opened the throat with short, practiced cuts.

The membrane stretched across the black ring had no voice in it. There were no vocal cords, no soft wet folds that might have once shaped a name. The membrane was dry and ridged, like the inside of a bellows left in the sun. The black ring beneath it was set into the tissue with tiny teeth, as if it had been bitten into place.

“Not bone,” Halloway said, leaning close enough to smell the cellar-sweetness of it. “Not metal. Resin. Horn. Something that doesn’t want to rot.”

She worked the crook into the ring and levered the head back.

“If this were a man,” she said, “I’d be looking at a dead voice. If this were a puppet, I’d be looking at the hinge. As it is, I’m looking at a door handle.”

The thing’s fingers tapped once.

Halloway ignored them.

She put the flat of her knife against the black ring and struck the crook’s hooked end once with the heel of her palm.

The ring cracked.

The sound was small and wrong—dry seed, old comb, a knuckle popping in a quiet house. A line ran through the lacquered circle, and the tiny teeth at its edge shivered loose. The black channel beneath it pulsed once, then flattened.

The head did not fall.

The eye that had been looking at the stairs slid sideways, losing focus, and then the whole face seemed to forget which direction it was meant to be human in. The too-forward posture softened by a degree, as if the neck had been told, without words, that the room no longer mattered.

Halloway did not exhale.

“Good,” she said. “That’s one hinge of the mind.”

The extra elbow bent.

Not to reach.

To pull.

The cut ribs spread wider. The black fluid in the chest ran down the dark rods in slow threads, and the knot of fibers around the tooth in the belly tightened. The water around the body shivered inward, all at once, as if the cellar had drawn breath through the thing’s mouth.

Halloway looked down the opened throat.

The broken ring was not falling away. Its fragments were sinking into the membrane, and the membrane was knitting over them with the same patient smoothness that had closed the arm. The black channel had not been cut. It had been redirected.

“Ah,” she said. “Of course.”

She shifted the crook from the jaw to the belly.

“The ring was a latch, not the lock. The lock’s in the meat.”

She hooked the pale edge of the abdominal seam and drew it open enough to see the knot of fibers around the tooth. The tooth gleamed wet and clean, more present than the rest of the cavity. Around it, the dark thread was not tied in a simple knot. It had been threaded through the waxy lining and down toward the floor, through a hole that had not been there a moment before.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“Second target,” she said. “The tooth. Break the tooth, and you break the memory it’s using to wait. Don’t take it. Break it.”

She leaned closer.

“But don’t touch the thread.”

The thread pulsed once, drawing a thin ripple across the surface of the cellar. The body’s shoulders rose another inch. The head, though its eye had lost the stairs, began to turn toward Halloway by degrees, as if the ring had only taught it one direction at a time.

Halloway set her knife against the tooth and struck the handle with her palm.

The tooth did not shatter.

It split with a sound like a child’s milk tooth snapped between two stones. A flake of enamel curled loose. From inside the split came a pale grit, dry and fine, that spilled into the water and did not dissolve. It floated on the surface in a ring, white as bone dust, and the ring closed around the thing’s cut shoulders.

The body went still.

For a heartbeat, stillness almost felt like success.

Then the split tooth opened further, not because Halloway had made it, but because the dark thread pulled. The fibers around it drew tight, and from the bottom of the tooth came a single black strand, thinner than a hair and longer than it should have been. It ran through the hole in the floor and vanished into the drain beneath the cellar.

Halloway watched it.

“Right,” she said. “It isn’t anchored to the body.”

The water began to move.

Not around the thing.

Toward it.

The standing water slid in slow, oily lines, gathering at the body’s edges, climbing along the too-long fingers, filling the hollow rods of the arms from below. The cold in the cellar deepened until the lamp flame seemed smaller and more personal, as if it had been reduced to a single warm thought.

Halloway stepped back, keeping the crook between herself and the rising thing.

“The thread goes down,” she said. “If you want to break it, break it where it leaves the body. The tooth is only the door.”

She looked toward the stairs, then at the thing, then at the black strand threading through the floor.

“But if you go up the stairs while that thing is learning to follow, you’re not escaping. You’re showing it the road.”

The body sat higher.

Its broken mouth opened.

No breath came. No voice came. But from the water, from the black strand, from the split tooth, from the drain below the cellar, came a thin tapping. Tap. Tap. Tap.

Not the thing’s fingers.

Something answering.

Halloway’s face did not change, though the lamplight made her older.

“Third target,” she said, very flat. “The drain. If you can reach it, break the line. If you can’t, burn the floor. If you can’t do either, don’t let it stand up where it can see you walk away.”

The thing’s shoulders rolled back. The extra elbow locked into place. The cut ribs spread until the membrane in its chest tore with a soft, wet sound like a page separating. The broken ring in its throat shifted, resettled, and began to close again.

Halloway drew her long knife and set her foot against the thing’s sternum.

“And stop asking who did this,” she said. “The who is in the room. We just haven’t cut off his hands yet.”

She pushed the blade into the knot around the tooth, not to pull it free, but to sever the black strand where it entered the body.

The strand did not snap.

It tightened.

The cellar water rose an inch.

Halloway looked down at the drain.

“Right,” she said. “He’s holding the other end.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the lamp without spilling the flame. The handle was warm, the wick low, and the cellar made the light look too small for the job.

“The stairs are not the thing to break,” she said, and her voice had the dry, practical tone of someone correcting a man about to set his own coat alight. “If you climb them now, you’re not escaping. You’re teaching it the sound of someone choosing the door.”

She set the lamp on the lowest dry stair, angled so the light ran down the water and stopped short of the body. Then she hooked the crook over the black strand emerging from the hole beneath the split tooth. The strand resisted like wet sinew threaded through a pulley.

“Break the line where it leaves the floor,” Halloway said. “Not the body. The body is only the handle.”

She drew it up an inch.

The thing’s shoulders lifted. The cut ribs spread. The broken throat-ring clicked as it resettled, and the eye that had lost the stairs found Halloway instead.

“Good,” she said, as if noticing a poorly hung door. “Now we know where the attention is.”

She did not bring the lamp closer. She used the crook to keep the strand away from the water, then slashed across it with the long knife.

The strand did not snap cleanly. It frayed, black fibers curling back from the cut like burnt hair. A smell rose with them: lamp oil, wet rope, and that same milk-left-in-a-tin sweetness, now gone sour.

The tap from the drain stopped.

For a moment the water stood still in a way that was almost worse than moving.

Then the strand jerked downward.

The body folded with it—not in pain, not in fear, but as a thing folds when the hand that built it releases a pin. The extra elbow buckled inward. The too-long fingers lost their careful spread and dragged through the water. The head, still too far forward, fell sideways because the throat-ring had no reason left to hold it up.

The black strand drew itself into the hole, leaving a wet line across the floor. The hole narrowed, not because stone was closing, but because the floor remembered it was supposed to be whole and was trying to obey.

Halloway did not celebrate. She put a boot near the water’s edge and watched the surface.

“Still not dead,” she said. “Just unplugged.”

The thing’s mouth opened again. The membrane in the chest tore and did not refill. The broken ring in the throat shifted once and went quiet. The eye nearest the lamp rolled toward the light, but did not focus on it. That was a mercy. A thing that looked at a lamp without wanting to reach it was not finished, not yet. It was only meat with a bad habit.

Halloway lifted the lamp from the stair.

“The tooth is cracked. The line is cut. The drain is still there.” Her mouth twisted. “That means whatever was feeding it heat is still under the floorboards. It does not mean the thing in the water can follow you up the stairs anymore.”

She stepped backward, keeping the light on the body, keeping her knife across the seam of her own sleeve as if it might need to be drawn by the water.

“If you’re going to move, move now. Don’t touch the cold patch. Don’t pick up the tooth. And don’t go back down here without salt, oil, and something you’re willing to lose.”

The thing lay half-submerged in the stilling water, one cut hand open, the other curled beneath it. The pale fingers stopped tapping.

Halloway’s gaze went to the hole in the floor.

“Right,” she said. “That’s not an answer. That’s a pause.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the hole in the floor. "It's still down there," I say, my voice hoarse. "The builder. You said he's holding the other end."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway looked at the hole, but she did not move toward it yet. The black strand lay across the lip like a burned bootlace, frayed at the end, wet with water that had no right to move. The circle in the cellar surface had slowed, but not stopped. It turned with a patient, sucking patience, as if something below were tasting the rhythm of the room.

“Yes,” she said. “It’s still down there.”

She let the words sit for a moment, then added, “But not the way you mean.”

She shifted the lamp high and moved to the edge of the cold patch. Her boots stopped short of it. The stone around the hole was too smooth. There were no chisel marks, no broken grating, no chipped rim where a man might have dragged a bucket or a corpse across it. The edges were worn inward, rounded by movement that had no business being in a cellar.

“That’s not a drain,” Halloway said, as if naming a thing could make it behave. “A drain has a mouth and a purpose. A mouth has no purpose except to be used.”

She hooked the crook under the frayed black strand and drew it up an inch.

The strand moved with her, but not like rope. It moved like a tendon in a dead hand: reluctantly, with a memory of life still clinging to it. As it came, the water in the cellar shivered toward the hole. The pale thing in the far end did not rise, but its too-long fingers opened a little wider, as if the water had been pulled through its own bones.

“Warm,” Halloway said quietly.

She looked at the strand. The end she had cut was blackened, not scorched. The fibers had curled back from themselves, wet and shining, and when the lamp touched them, a thin pulse ran along the length of it. Not a twitch. A pulse.

“Eleventh thing,” she said. “The builder is down there. He may even be alive. But if he is, he is not alive the way a man is alive in a room. He is alive the way a nerve is alive in a thing that has been cut and is still trying to move.”

She worked the crook farther into the hole.

The iron went down easier than it should have. There was no bottom at the length of the crook. The water resisted for a handspan, then gave, then closed around the metal with the same tired neatness as before. Halloway’s jaw tightened. She tried a short sweep left, then right.

Something brushed the hook.

Not the rough drag of stone. Not the soft give of cloth. The hard, jointed knock of a hand.

Halloway drew the crook back.

What came with it was a hand.

It rose from the hole wrapped around the iron hook, fingers closing over the crook with the slow certainty of a thing that had been waiting for something to hold. It was not the pale, fanned, too-long hand from the body in the water. This one was human. Broad-palmed. Callused. The skin was gray-white from wetness, but it had the shape of a working hand. The thumb was short and thick. The index finger ended in a ragged, healed stump. The nails had been cut close, blackened beneath, one of them split and grown out crooked. Around the wrist was a strip of leather, swollen with water, its buckle green with rot.

The hand flexed.

Halloway stepped back half a pace, not in fear, but to get a better angle. She held the crook level and let the hand hang from it, dripping. The fingers tightened once, then loosened. The thumb moved. The split nail caught the lamplight.

“Ah,” she said. “There’s the grammar.”

She looked at the stump, the callus, the leather strap.

“Harness maker,” she said, almost to herself. “Or a tanner. Someone who worked with wet hide, awls, thread, and patience. Someone who knew how to keep a thing from spoiling and how to make it pull without wanting.”

The hand twitched.

Halloway did not let it go. She used the crook to lift it toward the lamp and turned it slowly, clinical as a butcher examining a hook. The palm had no blood. The wrist where it had been severed was not a clean cut. The tendons had been threaded. Each black strand ran back up the forearm and disappeared into the drain, not tied, not broken, but drawn through the meat like stitches through a seam.

“He didn’t hold the other end,” Halloway said. “He was the other end.”

The body in the water gave a single, shallow tap.

Not a finger. The palm. One flat, deliberate sound against the surface.

Halloway looked toward the far end. The cut elbow had not moved. The too-forward head had not turned. But the palm lay open now, fingers spread, as if the hand had remembered a command and sent it to the nearest available limb.

“Don’t answer it,” Halloway said, though the warning was not only for the room. “That’s not speech. That’s a hinge.”

She brought the hand back to the hole and studied the drain. The water around the lip had begun to turn faster. The cold patch spread by a finger’s width, then stopped, then spread again, as if the floor were taking a breath through its mouth. Halloway lowered the crook until its tip touched the opening.

The stone did not ring.

It gave a little.

Not much. A single soft flex, like a lid over a wound.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“The builder started with himself,” she said. “That’s the plain part you asked for. He came down here with tools and a theory and a very bad idea about what a body is for. He made the drain first. He threaded it. He put his own hand into the work to teach the thing what a hand was for, because a builder who trusts only his own hands is the worst kind.”

She looked at the severed hand on the crook.

“Then he used the victim as a model. No. Not a model. A replacement. He cut out what a man should have and put in what a man should not have. The extra elbow was not for the victim. It was for the work. The builder wanted a thing that could reach where a man couldn’t, bend where a man should lock, and keep moving when a man should be wise enough to stop.”

The hand’s fingers curled slowly around the crook.

Halloway struck it once, sharply, with the flat of her knife.

The fingers opened.

“Twelfth thing,” she said. “The builder is still down there, but he is not whole. If he were whole, he would have a body. He has hands. Hands are the part a builder trusts most.”

She wedged the crook under the edge of the hole and leaned her weight into it. The stone did not crack. It slid. Not much. A finger’s width. The lip peeled back like a scab that had decided not to fight. The smell rose then: wet chalk, sour milk, old lamp oil, and beneath it something clean and awful, like a chapel floor washed too often over something that had died under it.

Halloway put the lamp closer.

The drain was not a pipe. It was a shaft, round and wet, narrowing then opening again somewhere below into a larger dark. The black strands ran down it from every edge, threaded through stone, through wood, through something pale and curved that might have been a bone or might have been a rib. At the bottom of the shaft, water moved upward in slow, oily threads, feeding the drain rather than leaving it.

And in that water, something sat.

Not a full body. Halloway could not see a full body. She saw a shape in the dark, shoulders broad, head low, hands buried in the black threads. The left wrist ended in a stump, gray and swollen. The right hand still held the line. The fingers were curled through the strands with the careful grip of a man stitching a seam. The head lifted a little.

A face looked up.

It was not a good face. It had once been the kind of face people trusted because it was weathered and steady: a square jaw, a broad nose, eyes set deep under a working man’s brow. Now the skin was too tight over the cheeks. The eyes were open without breath. The mouth was stuffed with black thread, and the thread moved there, not speaking, not swallowing, only shifting like something that had learned the shape of speech and not the meaning.

Halloway held the lamp steady.

“Right,” she said. “There you are.”

The face did not change.

The body in the cellar water moved.

Not much. The cut shoulder lifted. The extra elbow bent one joint. The too-long fingers tapped once, twice, three times. The pattern matched the movement of the builder’s right hand below. Halloway saw it and filed it away without looking away.

“He’s teaching it,” she said. “Not from the drain. Through it. The victim is the lesson. The builder is the hand.”

The builder’s right hand tightened on the black strand.

The body in the water shuddered. The membrane in its opened chest tore wider. The black fluid in the dark rods ran faster, pulling toward the throat, toward the broken ring, toward the face that was no longer looking at the stairs. It was looking at Halloway now.

The builder’s mouth moved beneath the thread.

No sound came.

But the body in the cellar answered.

A wet, shapeless noise rose from the thing’s opened throat. Not a word. Not a name. A sound like a man trying to speak through a mouthful of wet wool. The too-forward head lifted another degree. The eye that had lost focus found it again.

Halloway did not step closer.

She did not step back.

She set the crook across her forearm and drew the long knife with the other hand.

“If you’re asking for mercy,” she said, flatly, to the builder, “you spent it on him.”

The builder’s head tilted. The face was too still for a man, too patient for a corpse.

Halloway looked at the right hand holding the black line. The knuckles were white. The tendons stood under the skin like ropes. The fingers had been threaded through the strand, not merely gripping it. That was the worst of it. He had made himself a part of the work. He had stitched his own hand into the drain so the thing would remember how to hold.

“Thirteenth thing,” Halloway said. “You don’t ask a builder to stop building. You take the hands off.”

She hooked the crook around the builder’s right wrist.

The metal bit into swollen skin. There was no blood. There was no warmth. The builder’s fingers did not flinch. They tightened around the black strand.

Halloway pulled.

The builder’s arm came up an inch. The water in the shaft moved with it, climbing the sides in slow black threads. The body in the cellar water rose another inch. Its cut ribs spread. The extra elbow locked. The too-long fingers pressed into the surface and for the first time the water accepted them without protest.

Halloway put her boot against the edge of the hole and used the crook as a brace.

“Good,” she said. “Hold there.”

She struck the wrist with the crook once. Not to break it. To open it.

The fingers loosened.

The builder’s face did not change.

Halloway slashed the knife across the black strand at the wrist. The strand did not snap. It frayed, pulling back from the cut, revealing a pale core inside: tendon, hair, and something waxy that caught the lamplight and held it. The smell of sour milk sharpened. The cellar water moved faster toward the hole. The body in the far end began to rise on its own.

Halloway cut again.

The builder’s right hand opened.

The black strand fell from the wrist, slack, and for a heartbeat the cellar was still. The body in the water froze halfway up. The taps stopped. The builder’s face remained lifted, but the mouth did not move. The eye at the bottom of the drain lost focus and became only wet.

Then the hole breathed.

Not air. The cellar air moved down into the drain, hard and sudden, pulling the lamp flame sideways. Halloway’s sleeve snapped toward the opening. The water in the shaft rose without splashing, black and smooth, and the builder’s shape began to climb.

It was not standing. It was being pulled, or pushing, or becoming a thing that no longer cared which. The shoulders rose out of the water. The left stump swayed where the hand had been taken. The right hand, freed but still threaded, scraped against the shaft wall. The face came up until it was level with the hole, mouth full of moving black thread, eyes fixed not on Halloway but on the lamp.

Halloway moved the lamp back.

The builder’s head followed, too fast, too smooth. The neck was wrong. The too-forward angle had traveled down from the victim to him. The face had learned the posture before the body had.

“Fourteenth thing,” Halloway said. “He won’t ask for help. He’ll ask for hands.”

The builder’s mouth opened.

The thread pulled taut between his teeth. From the drain below came a sound like fingers tapping stone. From the cellar body came a matching tap. From the walls came a faint, wet answer, as if the house itself had learned the rhythm and was practicing.

Halloway looked at the thing in the water.

It was sitting higher now. The cut elbow bent. The opened chest widened. The broken throat-ring shifted under the membrane, resettling with a sound like a seed cracking in a quiet room. The face was still unfinished, but the eye was learning the stairs again.

Halloway did not like stairs.

She liked doors, because doors could be held. Stairs were just mouths

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I move to stand between him and the stairs. "The door," I say, and my voice doesn't shake. "We hold the door."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Stairs were just mouths that had been taught to stand up straight. Doors were better. Doors had hinges, and hinges could be broken, barred, burned, or left open on purpose.

Halloway did not look at the place Pike had chosen. Looking meant accepting the arrangement, and she had never accepted an arrangement made by fear.

“We hold the door,” she said, “if the door can be shut. We do not hold the stair. The stair is his if he learns it.”

The builder’s right hand slid toward the first step.

It moved with the patient certainty of a thing that had spent its life reaching for tools. The fingers were broad, the palm thick, the split nail catching the lamplight like a chip of old bone. The leather strap at the wrist had swollen black with cellar water, and the buckle had sunk into the flesh so that the skin had begun to grow over it.

Halloway hooked the crook around the wrist and pulled.

The arm came up without resistance. The shoulder followed. Then half the chest rose out of the hole, wet and gray, the ribs too far apart, the skin pulled tight over something underneath that did not breathe. The builder’s face remained at the lip of the drain, mouth full of black thread, eyes fixed not on Halloway but on the stairs behind her.

“He’s not aiming at you,” Halloway said, though the remark was for the room. “He’s aiming at the exit. Exits are tools. Builders love tools.”

She laid the long knife across the wrist.

The first strand ran under the extensor tendons. She cut it. It parted with a dry pop, not a wet one. No blood followed. A black bead of fluid stood at the cut, then sank back into the hole, as if the body had decided it could not afford the waste.

The builder’s index finger twitched.

“Still taking notes,” Halloway said.

She cut the second strand beside the radial nerve. The middle finger lifted. The third went through the palm; the hand opened. The fourth and fifth she cut together, across the thumb and forefinger. The hand lost its grip on the hole’s lip and hung from the crook.

The builder’s face did not change.

The mouth-thread moved.

From the drain came a sound like a dozen fingers tapping wet wood.

The body in the cellar answered.

Halloway did not turn to it. She lifted the severed hand toward the lamp.

“Sixteenth thing,” she said. “He stitched the line into the hand. That means the hand was still useful. That means it would have kept teaching even after he took it off himself.”

She turned the hand, counting the black strands. Four cut. Two still ran from the palm into the wrist. She cut those with short, clean strokes.

The hand went limp.

The body in the water stopped tapping.

Then it began to rise again.

Halloway looked at the builder.

The stump at his wrist was not bleeding. It was knitting. The black strands from the drain crawled into the wound and began to rethread the tendons, one by one, like a tailor sewing on a button that had been asked to behave.

“Ah,” Halloway said. “He’s not dead. He’s only unemployed.”

She moved the lamp to the shelf where it would burn and not drown, then took the cloth she had thrown down. It was cellar-damp, but the corner had caught lamp oil. She touched it to the flame. It lit with a small, honest blue edge.

“Do not breathe that,” she told the room. “It will make you want to be useful.”

She laid the burning cloth across the builder’s wrist.

The black strands recoiled. They hissed like wet hair held too near a candle. The smell was not human burning. It was tallow, chalk, sour milk, and something under that like a church vestry left shut after a flood. The builder’s mouth opened. The black thread inside it pulled taut, then slack, as if the thing below had flinched through a rope.

The builder’s right hand, already severed, convulsed on the crook. The fingers bent. They tried to close around the iron.

Halloway dropped it into the cellar water.

It went down and did not sink. It floated palm-up, fingers spread, too many shadows under the lamp. The body in the far end turned its unfinished face toward it.

“No,” Halloway said, to the body or to the builder or to the room. “That is not a lesson. That is a receipt.”

The builder’s arm at the hole stopped knitting. The strands pulled back into the drain, dragging the burning cloth with them. The flame went out below the water, but the hole breathed once more, and this time it smelled scorched.

The builder’s head fell back an inch. The mouth-thread went still. The eyes, for the first time, looked at Halloway.

She did not give him the satisfaction of moving.

“Seventeenth thing,” she said. “He still has a face. That’s how he’s going to cheat the room. Builders never trust a thing to be understood by its hands alone. They put a face on the work so the work can apologize.”

The builder’s mouth moved. The thread moved with it.

The body in the water answered, lifting its head.

Halloway saw the pattern and did not like it.

The builder’s eye at the drain was the eye that had lost the stairs in the body. The builder’s mouth was the mouth that had opened without breath. The builder’s head was the head that had sat too far forward because it had learned the victim’s posture from below.

“He’s not teaching it from the drain,” Halloway said. “He’s learning from it.”

She put the crook through the builder’s mouth.

The iron slid between the teeth and through the black thread. The builder’s head snapped back, not from pain, but because the thread had been used as a guide. The crook’s hook caught the knot at the base of the tongue. Halloway twisted.

The mouth-thread tore.

It did not bleed. It unraveled. Long black fibers came out of the builder’s mouth and curled into the air, trying to find the drain, trying to find the body, trying to find the stairs. Halloway struck them with the knife, cutting as much as she could while keeping the crook hooked in the mouth.

The builder’s face lost shape. Not flesh. Shape. The square jaw sagged. The deep eyes slid toward the lamp. The mouth stayed open around the crook, but the thread inside it stopped moving.

The body in the cellar gave one tap.

Then another.

Halloway looked at the hand floating palm-up. The fingers moved. They were not the body’s fingers. They were the builder’s. They tapped against the surface in the rhythm of a man counting.

“Eighteenth thing,” Halloway said. “He’s still teaching from the hand. Of course he is. Hands don’t need faces to be persuasive.”

She hooked the floating hand with the crook and lifted it out of the water. It dripped black fluid and came free with a small sucking sound. The body in the water turned with it, head following the hand like a dog following a thrown stick.

Halloway carried the hand to the stairs.

She did not go near Pike. She did not tell him to move. She set the hand on the lowest dry stair, palm up, fingers open, and laid the flat of her knife across it.

“If he wants the door,” she said, “he can have a hand to hold the handle. He can’t have both.”

The hand’s fingers closed on the knife’s edge.

Halloway struck it once with the heel of her palm.

The fingers loosened.

She struck again.

The split nail flew off. The skin under the palm split along the lifeline and did not bleed. The black strands inside came out in a loose braid. The hand twitched, then lay still.

The builder’s head at the drain jerked forward.

Halloway did not wait. She took the burning cloth’s last corner, touched it to the exposed strands in the severed hand, and let the hand catch.

It burned badly. It burned like a thing that had been told to be useful one last time. The fingers curled. The palm cracked. The black braid inside smoked, shrank, and snapped. The smell was tallow and wet wool and the sweet ruin of milk gone over. The builder’s head pulled back into the hole as if a rope had been cut from his neck.

The body in the cellar went still.

Not the stillness of a thing learning. The stillness of a thing dropped.

The too-long fingers closed. The extra elbow bent and stayed bent. The head fell forward into the water, and this time the water accepted it and made a small, ordinary ripple.

Halloway watched the ripple.

“There,” she said. “That’s better. That’s water.”

The drain gave a long, wet sigh. The hole’s lip closed by an inch, not because the stone had healed, but because the thing below had lost interest in the edge.

Halloway picked up the lamp.

She did not look toward Pike. She looked at the cellar mouth, at the stairs, at the door beyond them, at the space where a person might choose to stand and be foolish.

“Nineteenth thing,” she said, voice dry. “The builder is down there. Not whole. Not finished. Not holding the line anymore. That doesn’t mean he’s gone. It means he’s gone to find another hand.”

She moved to the lowest stair, keeping the light on the water.

“If you’re holding the door, hold it where it can be shut. Don’t let him bring a hand through the gap. Don’t let him bring a voice. If the thread comes up again, cut it at the wrist, not the door. If it comes up wearing a face you know, cut the face anyway. That’s the advantage of doors. They make liars work for it.”

She reached the first step. The wood was dry. It took the lamp’s heat and did not answer.

“I’m coming up,” Halloway said. “If you want to be useful, make the door a door. If you want to be brave, make it a wall.”

The thing in the cellar did not move.

The hole in the floor did not breathe.

Halloway climbed.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the hand burning on the step. "I'll make it a wall," I say, and my voice is steadier than I feel. I step to the cellar door and slam it shut, my back against the wood. "What do we burn it with?"

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: That extra hinge was not an accident.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Somebody’s been doing carpentry with a man.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: Ribs were cut and reset.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The larynx is gone.

rung_labels.label: engaged
rung_labels.evidence: The membrane in the chest tore and did not refill.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway shifted the lamp until the beam lay flat across the water instead of straight down into it. The light rode the surface, caught a slow ripple near the steps, and reached the far end in a dull smear. Something low and compact occupied the shadows there, and the shape of it was indeed wrong—though wrong was an observation, not a conclusion.

"Wrong is a beginning, not a diagnosis," she said. "Things that stop moving after a minute aren't necessarily done. They're dead, dormant, or reconsidering." The corner of her mouth moved, though calling it a smile would have been generous. "So count what you can see. Limbs, if there are any, and whether the joints bend the way they should or the way they shouldn't. Head, or a reasonable impersonation of one. Symmetry, if it has any. Tell me what's where before you tell me what it is. And don't hand me a story yet. Stories get people killed faster than the thing does."

She kept the lamp steady and did not step down. Four feet of standing water hid ankles, holes, and teeth with equal enthusiasm, and none of those were worth guessing about.

"Take your time," she added. "It's not going anywhere. Probably."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I squint, trying to ignore how the water distorts things. "I think... four limbs? But the back two look too high up. And there's no head I can make out, just a... lump where it should be." I swallow. "It's not symmetrical at all."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the lamp drop until the beam lay almost flat again, this time angled up so the light caught the underside of the lump instead of the top. The shadows on the far wall reversed. She held it there.

"You said you didn't know yet," she said, "then gave me four limbs, a hind pair set too high, a lump where the head should be, and no symmetry. That's not ignorance. That's a description with the brakes on. Keep them on."

She watched the lump through two slow breaths. The water over it did not drip. No bubble rose. The limbs stayed where they were.

"High hind limbs mean one of three things," she went on. "It's crouched to spring, it died mid-crouch and rigor took it, or the things it uses for hips are sitting up where a shoulder blade ought to be and it never read the same anatomy as anything else. First means alive. Second means recently dead. Third means we're not looking at a cow, a dog, or a man, and we adjust downward from there."

From her coat she produced a short iron bolt and tossed it underhand. It struck the water a yard short of the thing and sank with a flat plunk. The rings spread, touched the far wall, and came back. The lump did not move. The surface over it did not bulge.

"Didn't react to the splash," she said. "Dead, dormant, or polite. Assume the first two; polite things in cellars are rare. The lump's the part I'd watch. A head can be tucked. A lump can be a head that hasn't unfolded yet. So we treat it as a face until it proves otherwise—no walking up to the front, no reaching over it, and no assuming the teeth are where the limbs say they should be."

Her mouth twitched. "If it's reconsidering, it's doing it quietly. Give it another minute, then I'll put a rope on it and drag it into the light. If it objects, we'll know it wasn't as finished as it looked. Eyes on the lump. Seam, slit, or anything shiny and wet, you say so. If it rises, you say it louder."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway let the question sit for a breath. She did not turn the lamp toward Pike. Her eyes stayed on the lump.

"Was it a person?" she said. "You're asking me to tell you it used to be somebody so you'll know whether to be sorry. I don't trade in sorry. I trade in what's where."

She shifted the beam a fraction, tracing the line where the thing's shoulder—if it had one—met the water. "It's got four limbs, a central mass, and a lump where the head should be. That's the same layout as a man, a pig, and a pile of wet coats. Layout isn't identity. The hind pair is set too high for a human pelvis. A man's hips sit low; they don't ride up under the ribs just because he's facedown in four feet of water. So either it was never human, or it was human and something folded it wrong. There's no bloat, no sloughing, no gas I can see. If it's dead, it's recent—hours, maybe a day. But 'recently a person' and 'is a person' are two different tenses, and only one of them gets a funeral."

The corner of her mouth moved. "The lump's still the part I don't like. If it was a man, that's where his face went. If it wasn't, that's where the face is waiting. Either way, treat it like it can see us."

She slid the coil of rope off her shoulder and kept the lamp trained on the far end.

"Minute's up. I'm putting a loop on it and dragging it into the light. Dragging is undignified if it was somebody. If it wasn't, undignified is the best outcome. Eyes on the lump. Seam, slit, shine, or anything that comes off—say it. If it rises, say it louder."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "There's... a wet shine on the lump. Like it's reflecting the lamplight in patches." I keep my voice low. "No seams, though."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not take her eyes off the lump. She moved the lamp a hand's width to the left, then back. The shine did not slide across the surface with the light; it stayed put, fixed to whatever it was sitting on. That meant it belonged to the thing, not to the water.

"Shine in patches, no seams," she said. "Patchy shine means wet, and wet means it's been in the water, it's leaking, or it has a surface that doesn't dry. No seams means nothing has opened yet. Seams are where the surprises live, so I'll take the lack of them as a small mercy and not a promise."

She shook a loop into the rope and weighted it with a short iron fitting from her belt. The bolt was at the bottom of the cellar with the other secrets; she wasn't going in after it. She swung the loop twice at her side, judged the distance, and threw.

She did not aim at the lump. The loop went over the far end of the central mass, behind where a shoulder should have been, and snagged on something that held. Halloway took the slack, set her boot against the top step, and hauled.

The body rolled a quarter turn in the water. It moved because she moved it; nothing grabbed back. A limb broke the surface as it turned, and Halloway tracked it with the lamp.

The joints were wrong up close. The limb had one bend too many, and the bend that should have been a knee went the wrong way, like a hinge installed backward. Where a hand or a paw ought to have been, there was a cluster of short, pale digits that did not agree on a direction. Nothing human was arranged like that. Nothing that had been assembled correctly, anyway.

The lump came around with it. The patches of shine stayed exactly where they were, fixed to the surface, too evenly spaced and too numerous to be a single eye. There were five, maybe six of them set in a rough crescent, each one a wet gleam about the size of a thumbnail. They did not blink. They did not track the light. Between them the skin—if it was skin—was smooth, pale, and slightly translucent, stretched over the lump like a membrane that hadn't finished deciding what was underneath.

"If that was a man," Halloway said, "somebody put him back together without the instructions. If it wasn't, it never read the same book. Either way, the face end still hasn't got a face, just those shiny bits where one is thinking about showing up."

She kept the rope taut and did not step down into the water.

"Keep your eyes on those patches," she said. "If they open, if anything comes out of them, or if the rest of it decides it has opinions about being dragged, you say so. If it rises, you say it louder. I'd rather be rude than surprised."

She gave the rope a testing tug, ready to haul again or let go, depending on what the cellar decided next.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not look at Pike when the water shifted and the lamp beam lay flat across the body. She kept her eyes on the lump and gave the rope a small, testing tug. The thing rolled another inch, then settled. Nothing grabbed back.

"You're in the water now," she said, "so mind your feet. This cellar hides holes and teeth with the same enthusiasm, and neither one announces itself. If you feel something that isn't the bottom, you say it before you lift the foot."

She let the rope stay taut and used the beam to point rather than her finger, tracing the bad joint on the exposed limb.

"You asked for it plain. Plain is: it quit. It was moving a minute ago, now it isn't. No blood in the water that I can see, no tear on the parts I've got in the light, no bloat, no slough, no gas. If it's dead, it's recent—hours, maybe a day. Nothing here says it was shot, stabbed, or chewed. So either it died quiet, or whatever was animating it let go and the frame locked up."

The beam moved to the hind limb, the one set too high.

"What happened before that is the ugly part. Look at the construction. One bend too many in that limb, and the bend that should be a knee opens backward. The digits don't agree on a direction. The hind pair rides up under the ribs where hips have no business sitting. That's not a wound. That's not a birth defect. That's assembly. Somebody or something put this together out of pieces that didn't come from the same animal, or didn't come from the same plan, and didn't bother matching the joints."

Then the lump again. The patches of shine stayed where they were, fixed, unblinking.

"The head end never got a head. Just that lump, and those shiny patches. Too many to be one eye, too even to be rot, too still to be anything that's tracking us. They could be eyes that haven't opened, or places where eyes were going to go. No seams means nothing has split yet. That's the only mercy on offer, and I'd not spend it."

She gave the rope another small tug, just enough to keep tension, not enough to roll it again.

"Plainest version? It got built wrong, or rebuilt wrong, and then it stopped. If it was a man, somebody took him apart and put him back wrong and didn't finish the face. If it wasn't a man, it was never a whole animal to begin with, and you're looking at the first draft of something that shouldn't have got past the planning stage. Either way, it's a body until it proves otherwise. You can be sorry for it later, when it's not in a position to take advantage."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I keep the light steady on those pale patches. "It's like someone tried to *copy* a man, but never saw one up close." I shiver, and not from the cold water. "Should we drag it out?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
"Tried to copy a man," Halloway repeated. She did not laugh; the sound that came out was a laugh with the edges worn off for safety. "That's generous. A copy means they had an original and botched the details. This thing looks like it was assembled from a rumor. Somebody had the right number of limbs and no working notion of what a man does with them. Hips up under the ribs, knees that bend like a hinge put on backward, fingers that can't agree which direction is out. If that's a man copied badly, the man was described secondhand by something that only got a quick look and wasn't taking notes."

She kept her gaze on the pale patches while she spoke. The crescent of wet gleams stayed fixed, too evenly spaced, too still. No seam had opened. No bubble rose. The face end still hadn't decided to have a face.

"Should we drag it out? Yes." Halloway took a turn of rope around her fist and set her boot against the top step again. The rope was wet and cold and had not slipped yet.
