"It won't get more instructive in the far end where the water lies about depth and teeth. We get it to the foot of the steps, get the light off the water and onto it properly, and then decide if we're looking at a body, a bad rebuild, or a warning somebody gave limbs to."

She leaned back. The rope creaked. The central mass shifted toward the steps with a slow, ugly slosh. A limb broke the surface and flopped, the extra joint bending the wrong way before it settled. Nothing grabbed back. It hadn't objected to the loop or the first roll; dead, dormant, or polite, and Halloway had never trusted polite in a cellar.

"Keep the light on those patches," she said. "Not on me, not on the rope. The face end. If they open, you say it. If anything comes out of them, you say it louder. If the limbs start moving on their own—not because I'm pulling them—say it louder still and get sideways. Don't back up; behind you is the deep part, and this thing already has bad hips without you handing it a drowning."

She hauled again, steady and unhurried, and watched the crescent of shine for any sign that whatever had built the thing had left a way for it to look back.

"If it was a man," she added, breath even with the work, "this is a lousy way to come home. If it wasn't, it's still a lousy way to come home. Either way it's coming out, and it can be offended about the handling once it's on dry stone and in no position to do anything about it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took another pull on the rope. The body came the last few yards with a thick, dragging slosh and slumped across the lower treads, one shoulder and a forelimb clear of the water, the rest still submerged. Nothing grabbed back. The crescent of pale patches on the lump stayed fixed and unblinking, pointed at the ceiling or at nothing.

She set her boot against a dry step above the waterline, kept the loop taut, and did not step down. From her belt she drew a short, heavy blade. She did not cut. She used the point to turn the exposed limb until the light lay along it instead of across it.

“You keep saying him,” she said. “I haven’t got a him yet. The hip end is wrong, the head end hasn’t happened, and the parts that would settle it are either relocated or absent. So I’ll tell you what was done to the body. You can put a pronoun on it later if it earns one.”

She ran the flat of the blade along the limb without breaking the membrane.

“Outside first. No wounds. No bites, no stab tracks, no gunshot, no tearing. Nothing bled into the water when I dragged it, and nothing’s bleeding now. No bloat, no sloughing, no gas. If it’s dead, it’s recent—hours, maybe a day. So whatever did this didn’t chew on him here and didn’t stab him in the cellar. The skin is a membrane, pale and slightly translucent, no hair, no pores, no scar, no stitch. Whatever’s holding it closed isn’t thread. Either it was sealed from the inside or it grew that way. That means the assembly happened while the tissue was fresh, or after whatever did this finished making the packaging.”

She turned the limb a little more, and the light went into the wrong joint.

“Under the skin, there’s no muscle where a man would have a calf or a thigh. There are pale bundles running the length of it, regular as rope, too regular. No belly to them, no red grain, no definition. If those are muscles, nobody told them what a muscle is for. At the joint there’s an extra segment, short and set at an angle, and it opens backward. The rods on either side don’t line up. That’s not a fracture that healed wrong; a bad break still knows which way the joint is meant to go. This is a hinge installed by something that understood hinges and not knees. There’s a pale cap of gristle or cartilage over the join, fitting the extra piece like a lid on a pot. Still no blood.”

She shifted the blade to the cluster of digits, not touching them.

“The fingers are tapered rods tipped with something soft, not nails exactly. They point three ways at once. A hand is an argument with the world; that is a handful of spare parts that haven’t been told which direction is out. Same at the back. Those hind limbs ride up under the ribs. If those are human hipbones, they’ve been moved. If they’re not, then this didn’t start from a man—it started from the idea of one and filled in the pieces as it went. The rods are too straight and too smooth to be honest human bone. A human femur has a shape. That has a length.”

She let the blade drop to the lump and kept her body between herself and the thing’s front end as much as the step allowed.

“The head end is the same membrane over a rounded mass. No skull ridge, no jaw, no ear, no mouth. Just the lump. Those shiny patches sit in the membrane just under the surface. Each one is a clear lens, wet, thumbnail-sized, set in a crescent. They aren’t eyes yet. No lid, no pupil, no tracking, no blink. Behind them it’s the same uniform pale tissue that’s in the limbs. If there’s a brain in there, it isn’t shaped like one and it isn’t where a brain belongs.”

She straightened a little, the rope still creaking in her fist.

“How far it got: it got a body that could move. It was moving a minute ago, so whatever runs these things doesn’t wait for a finished face. Then it stopped, or whatever was running it got out, and the frame locked up. It never got as far as the face. No mouth means it wasn’t going to eat or talk. No open eyes means it either navigated by something else or was being pointed from somewhere else. A face is small work and it quit before the small work.”

Her mouth twitched, not a smile.

“What it took, if it was a man, was the outline. Four limbs, a trunk, something at the front to see with eventually. It did not take his hands, his walk, his hips, or his head. It took the plan and lost the instructions. Field-guide version for the next one: expect the shape of a man with the details missing or assembled backward. If the face is still a lump, it’s new and it hasn’t practiced. If the face is finished, assume it learned. Aim for the joints. They’re the only part the builder bothered to get wrong on purpose, which makes them load-bearing.”

She gave the rope a final testing tug and watched the crescent of lenses for any sign that the thing had changed its mind.

“That’s the detail I have. It’s not a confession and it’s not a soul. It’s a body somebody—or something—built badly and abandoned before the face. You meet another, don’t wait for it to finish.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I lean in, my breath fogging the air between me and those pale lenses. "It's like... they didn't know what a person was *for*," I say, voice low. "Just the shape, without the purpose." My hand tightens on the lamp. "Do we burn it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not lean in. She stayed on the dry tread above the water, rope in her fist, and kept the blade angled so the point hovered a hand’s width from the crescent of lenses without touching them. The fogged breath between Pike and the lump meant he was close enough that if those patches decided to open, they would have his face first and hers second. She had not lasted thirty years in this trade by letting a lamp-holder volunteer as bait for a thing that hadn’t finished deciding whether it had eyes.

"Do we burn it?" she repeated. "Yes. Eventually. But not yet, and not in a stone box with four feet of water in it."

She crouched, careful not to set her boot on the slick stone, and used the point of the blade to press lightly at the membrane between two of the pale lenses. The skin—if membrane counted as skin—dimpled and did not split. A single bead of fluid welled along the scratch of the point. It was clear, thin, and colorless. It did not darken, clot, or run red. It slid down the lump and into the water without a sound. Halloway wiped the blade on her coat leg and straightened.

"No blood," she said. "No serum I’d recognize, no clotting, no rot smell. Clear fluid, like something that never bothered with a circulatory system and just filled the gaps. Useful to know. Means cutting it won’t spray, and means whatever assembled this wasn’t copying a mammal’s plumbing."

She let the rope creak once as she took a fresh grip.

"As for purpose—stop looking for one. Purpose is a story, and stories get people killed. You can lie awake later and be sorry it didn’t know what a person was for; that’s your business. Right now it’s got a shape and it moved, and that’s the whole résumé. Philosophy doesn’t aim for the joints. Fire does."

Her mouth moved, not quite a smile.

"Why burn it? Not for the soul. It hasn’t got one to insult, and if it did, fire wouldn’t be the argument I’d pick. We burn it because it’s a body that moved without a finished face, built out of parts that didn’t agree, and because things like that don’t stay retired. Bury it and something digs it up with better joints. Weight it and it comes back with a mouth. Burn it to ash and the next attempt has to start from nothing, which is the only kind of start I trust."

She shifted the blade until the point rested against the rope, not the thing.

"Not here, though. Four feet of water and a stone floor make a bad stove. Fire down here makes steam, steam makes you let go of ropes, and letting go of ropes is how it gets to finish the small work. We drag it out, get it onto dry ground, pour oil on it if there’s any in the house, and put the torch to the joints first. The backward knee, the hip under the ribs, that extra hinge. Those are the parts the builder got wrong on purpose, so they’re load-bearing. Burn those, and the rest is just kindling with ambition."

Halloway’s gaze went back to the lump. The lenses stayed fixed, unblinking, still not tracking anything.

"Before we light it, we check the rest of the cellar and the floor above. Things that get assembled don’t usually get assembled alone. If there’s another one upstairs practicing how to have a face, I want to meet it before I’m holding a rope in one hand and a torch in the other. And if whatever built this is still around, it’s probably proud of its work. Proud things come to watch. That’s convenient. It means we can burn the body and maybe the builder in the same afternoon."

She gave the rope a small, testing tug. The body did not answer.

"So yes. We burn it. Not because it was a man, and not because it wasn’t. Because it quit before the face, and I’d rather send it back unfinished than let whatever made it get a second opinion. Keep the light where it is. If one of those patches opens, if anything comes out of them, or if the limbs start moving without my rope doing it—say it. If it rises, say it louder. Then get to the stairs and don’t wait for me to be polite about it."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway had said they would drag it clear of the water first. The rope was still taut, the thing had not objected, and the blade was already in her hand, so the plan lost the argument. She set the point against the exposed forelimb just above the backward-bending joint and drew it down in a shallow, deliberate line.

The blade went in without a catch. The membrane parted like wet vellum, and a thin bead of clear fluid welled along the cut. It did not darken, did not clot, did not run red.

Halloway leaned close enough to catch whatever the thing had to offer and straightened again. It did not smell like a carcass. No iron, no rot, no opened bowel, no bile. There was a faint clean mineral scent, like rain on limestone, and under it something green and sappy, like a branch split too early. No blood to speak of, no decay, no last meal gone sour. If it had ever carried a gut, it had not brought it along.

She peeled the flap back with the point of the blade. No fat layer. No red grain of muscle. Just pale bundles lying parallel as rope, regular enough to be manufactured rather than grown. She cut one; it parted like sinew but did not bleed, and the cut ends did not retract. Beneath it lay the rod she had scraped before—smooth, dense, too straight for any bone that had ever belonged to a man or a beast. The blade shaved a pale curl from it, and the curl came away like horn, not splintering like bone. No marrow. No canal. Just a length with the right idea of a limb and none of the details.

She opened the central mass above the waterline, working the blade through membrane and bundle alike. There were no organs waiting inside. No heart, no lungs, no stomach, no coil of gut. The cavity was a framework: rods braced at angles that did not match any skeleton she knew, bundles laced between them, and a single flexible cord running the length of the spine-equivalent, knotted where the limbs attached but never dividing into proper vertebrae. Clear fluid pooled in the bottom of her cut and did not thicken. Whatever had filled this thing, it had not been a heartbeat.

Halloway turned the blade to the lump.

She cut a careful flap beside the crescent of lenses and lifted it. The lenses sat just under the membrane, each a clear hard bead the size of a thumbnail, set in that crescent like buttons waiting to be sewn to a coat. There was no lid, no muscle to swivel them, no pupil, no tracking. Behind them, short pale fibers ran back a finger’s width and stopped in a small dense knot at the base of the lump. Not a brain. Not even a good imitation of one. She ran the point along where a jaw should have hinged and found no hinge, no mouth, no slit, no tooth bud. The membrane ran unbroken over solid pale tissue.

“That’s the measure of it,” she said. “It got a body that could move. It got a frame with the joints put on backward and the hips shoved up under the ribs. It got lenses that don’t connect to anything that could use them. It did not get a mouth, a nose, ears, lungs, a gut, or a brain that knows it’s a brain. It got as far as locomotion and a face under construction, and then whatever was building it stopped. No mouth means it wasn’t going to eat you. No gut means it wasn’t going to digest you. No lungs means it wasn’t going to breathe. It walked, or it was made to walk, and then it quit before the small work of finishing a head.”

Her mouth moved, not quite a smile.

“If you’re looking for the person it used to be, there’s no tenant and no lease. It’s a coat rack that learned to walk and forgot to stop being furniture. Keep the light on those lenses. Not on my hands, not on the rope. If one of them clouds, clears, or decides to grow a pupil now that it’s open, you say it. If a limb moves and my hand isn’t on it, say it louder. And mind your feet—if you feel something down there that isn’t the bottom, you tell me before you lift it. I’d rather explain myself to a thing with no face than fish you out of four feet of water because you were busy watching me work.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. "It's hollow," I say, my voice small in the wet dark. "All that trouble to make it walk, and they didn't even fill it up." I force myself to look back at the lump. "One of the lenses just clouded over."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stopped with the blade exactly where it was. The point stayed in the cut beside the crescent, and her gaze went to the bead Pike had named. It had been as clear as a drop of water a moment ago. Now it was the color of milk cut with rain, uniform from rim to rim, no swirl in it, no lid sliding across to explain the change. The membrane over it had not puckered. No clear fluid had leaked from the cut to fog it. The rest of the crescent stayed clear, the other lenses like chips of glass, one gone opaque.

She waited through three slow breaths. The lamplight jittered on the wet membrane as the water moved against the steps, but the haze did not flicker with it. That meant the change was in the bead, not on it. Chemistry or construction, not reflection.

Then the cloud thickened from milk to weak glue, and at its center a dark speck appeared. It was round as a pinhead, perfectly still, no iris around it, no movement. It did not swing toward the light. It did not fix on Halloway or on Pike. It simply sat there, a pupil on a thing that had no business having one.

“There’s your detail,” Halloway said. “It’s gone and grown a pupil. Not an eye—an eye needs something behind it that wants to see, and back there behind those fibers there’s a knot the size of a walnut that wouldn’t know a brain if one bit it. But clouding first, then a pupil: that’s the face starting the small work while I’ve got it cut open on the step. Rude of it. Most things wait until you’ve left the room.”

She kept the rope taut with her left hand and brought the blade down into the joint she had already opened on the forelimb. The pale bundles parted like wet rope. They did not bleed, did not retract, did not twitch. She cut deeper, working the point around the extra hinge, and the limb flopped a hand’s width and lay still. Nothing grabbed back. The pupil stayed fixed and unblinking.

“It didn’t flinch when I took the arm off,” she said. “That’s not reassuring. Things that don’t flinch are either dead or saving it up. It clouded a lens and grew a pupil while I was cutting, so I’m not calling it dead. I’m calling it interrupted.”

She straightened on the tread, blade clear, and kept her body angled so the thing’s shoulder stayed between her and the face end.

“We’re done admiring it. Keep the light on those lenses. Start backing toward the stairs—slow, shuffle, don’t lift your feet, this floor hides holes and teeth with equal enthusiasm. If that pupil moves, if another lens clouds, or if the limbs start moving without my rope doing it, you say it louder and you keep going. Don’t wait to see if I’m coming; I’ll be right behind you, and if I’m not, I’m the one who was wrong.”

Her mouth moved, not a smile.

“I said we’d drag it out and burn it on dry stone. Plans are stories, and this one just grew a pupil. So new plan: I finish taking the joints apart, then we burn it right here and let four feet of water hiss. Steam I can breathe. A finished face I can’t. If it wants to be rude about the handling, it can be rude as ash.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not look at Pike. She was still braced on the dry tread above the water, rope in her left fist, the heavy blade in her right. The body lay where she had dragged it, slumped across the lower treads at the foot of the steps. One forelimb was already gone, taken off at the backward hinge; the stump leaked a thin, colorless fluid that did not clot. The rest of the thing—trunk, the two hind limbs set too high, the remaining forelimb—stayed slack in the rope. The crescent of lenses on the lump had not changed: one bead milk-pale with a single dark pupil fixed in its center, the others still clear as chips of glass.

"Finish it," Halloway said. "Aye. Last time I checked, that meant the joints, not the poetry."

She gave the rope a turn around her fist and leaned down the tread, keeping her body angled so the thing's shoulder stayed between her and the face end. She set the point of the blade against the shoulder of the remaining forelimb, where limb met trunk. The membrane parted like wet vellum. No blood welled, only that clear fluid, thin and colorless. Under it lay the same pale bundles, regular as rope, too regular. She cut them; they parted without retracting, without bleeding. At the joint she found the extra segment, short and set at an angle, the hinge opening backward. She worked the point around it, levered with the short iron fitting from her belt, and the limb came away with a wet, ugly tug. It flopped onto the tread and lay still. Nothing grabbed back. The pupil in the clouded lens did not move. The other lenses stayed clear.

She went to the hind limbs next, moving along the tread and keeping the rope taut so the trunk did not slide into the deeper water. The first hind limb rode up under the ribs where hips had no business being. She cut through the membrane over the joint. There was no pelvis, no socket that knew what a pelvis was for: just a smooth rod too straight for any honest bone, capped with pale gristle, sitting high against the trunk. She severed the bundles laced around it and cut the flexible cord where it knotted at the attachment. The limb had one bend too many, and the bend that should have been a knee opened backward. She took it off at that hinge. It came free with the same lack of protest. No twitch, no grab, no sound but the slosh of water and the small plop of the severed limb settling. The digits at the end pointed three ways at once, still not agreeing on a direction.

She did the same to the second hind limb: membrane, bundles, the too-high rod, the wrong-facing joint, and it was off. Nothing about the thing flinched. If it felt anything, it kept it to itself.

With all four limbs gone, the body was a limbless central mass with a lump at one end. Halloway opened the cut she had made earlier in the trunk, working the blade through membrane and bundle alike. There were no organs inside, only the framework: rods braced at wrong angles, bundles laced between them, and the single flexible cord running the length of the spine-equivalent, knotted where the limbs had attached but never dividing into proper vertebrae. She notched the rods with the blade, shaving pale curls like horn rather than splintering bone, and cut the cord through. The frame would not brace again.

As she straightened, a second lens on the lump clouded over. It went from clear to milk to weak glue in the space of three breaths, and at its center a dark speck appeared, round as a pinhead, perfectly still. No lid slid across it. It did not swing toward the light. It simply sat there, another pupil on a thing with nothing behind it to see.

"There's your second one," Halloway said. "It's fitting itself for a face it hasn't got the lungs to use. Rude, but harmless while it's armless."

She gave the rope a testing tug. The limbless trunk did not answer. The pupils stayed fixed.

"That's the walking taken out of it. Now the fire."

From her coat she drew a stoppered flask of lamp oil and a short torch: a length of iron stake bound at one end with pitch-soaked tow. She pulled the stopper with her teeth and poured the oil over the trunk, the stumps where the limbs had been, the opened joints, and last over the lump. The oil would not mix with the water. It slicked across the wet membrane in a beaded sheen and spread out on the flooded floor in a rainbow film, cutting the faint mineral-green smell of the thing with something sharper and more human. She did not waste the whole flask; they might need fire again before the afternoon was out.

She stepped up two treads to where the lamp burned on the step above, held the pitch-tow to the flame until the tow caught with a thick, oily smoke, and carried the burning torch back down to the water's edge. The firelight threw the cellar into harder relief: the black water, the wet stone, the limbless pale mass, the crescent of lenses with its two dark pupils.

Halloway touched the torch to the oiled hinge at the shoulder first. The oil caught with a low whump. The membrane blackened and curled; the pale bundles burned like dry rope, not like meat—there was no fat to spatter, no blood to hiss, no last meal to stink. Steam rose at once where the fire met the wet stone and the submerged part of the trunk, and the four feet of water began to hiss exactly as she had promised. She moved the torch to the second shoulder joint, then to the two high hip sockets, then to the extra backward hinge on the forelimb she had opened earlier, and finally to the severed limbs where they lay on the tread. She burned the joints first, every one: the places where the builder had got the assembly wrong on purpose, which made them load-bearing. The rods smoked like horn and caught slow, but with the oil they took the flame.

Then she poured the last of the oil onto the face end. The crescent of lenses waited, two clouded with their dark specks, the rest still clear. She put the torch to them. The clear lenses popped like bubbles in the heat, tiny sharp sounds. The clouded ones cracked, fine lines running through the milk, and the dark pupils boiled away to nothing. The membrane over the lump shriveled and split along the cut she had made; beneath it the pale fibers and the small dense knot at the base of the lump blackened and curled. No mouth opened, because there was no mouth. No seam gaped, because there had never been a seam. Nothing screamed, because there were no lungs to draw breath and no throat to shape a sound. The only voices were the fire, the hissing water, and the small pops of lenses dying.

"No last words," Halloway said. "It never got as far as a mouth. If it had, it'd probably have asked for its arm back, and I'd have had to tell it the arm was already ash."

She used the blade to turn the burning remains, shoving the central mass further onto the lower treads so the heart of the fire would not be quenched by the water. The rope, still looped over the trunk, singed but held; she kept it taut so nothing drifted out into the deep part where the water lay about depth and teeth. She fed the fire the last of the oil and watched the rods burn down. The trunk collapsed in on itself, blackened and steaming. The stumps of the limbs were ash. The hind limbs, with their backward knees and too-high hips, were nothing but smoking curls of horn-like rod. The water around the foot of the steps hissed and bubbled where the ash and embers settled into the shallows.

Halloway watched through the steam and the smoke. Nothing rose. No limb moved without her hand on it. The two pupils were gone, the lenses were gone, the face under construction had been taken down to ash and bad plumbing.

She straightened on the tread, wiped the blade on her coat leg, and kept the torch ready in her left hand.

"Finished," she said. "It's ash and blackened rod now. There's no tenant, no lease, and no face left to finish. Keep the light on the water, not on me. If anything else down here takes exception to arson, I want to see it coming."

She looked past the steam, to the dark far end of the cellar and the closed dark above.

"Then we check the rest of the cellar and the floor above. Whatever built this is probably proud of its work. Proud things come to watch. Convenient. It means we can burn the builder in the same afternoon, if it's stupid enough to show its face."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the ashes, the steam still rising. "It didn't even fight," I whisper. "All that... and it just let us take it apart." The lamp trembles in my hand. "That's worse, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She kept her eyes on the black water beyond the steaming ash, because fire made a light that carried, and things that assembled bodies sometimes came to see how their work held up. The torch in her left hand had burned down to a sullen red. She shifted it, and the smoke rolled thick and oily toward the ceiling.

Then she looked at the ash, and at Pike where he sat with the shaking lamp, and she understood the question behind the question.

"No," Halloway said. "It's not worse. It's just complete. You're waiting for it to have fought so you'll know it was alive enough to matter. It wasn't. It had no mouth to scream, no gut to clench, no brain that knew it was a brain. There was a knot the size of a walnut behind those lenses and a cord running down its back, and neither one had ever been told it was a person. So it didn't fight. A half-built thing doesn't fight. It just comes apart."

She nudged the remains with the toe of her boot, carefully, because the water was right there and the floor was slick with oil-ash and worse. A blackened rod rolled out of the char and clinked against the stone.

"That's not peace," she said. "Don't go calling it dignity. It didn't 'let' us take it apart. Before I cut the arms off it had four limbs and no notion what to do with them. After I cut them off it had no arms. There was never a moment when it could have stopped us and chose not to. It was never in the fight."

Her mouth moved, not a smile.

"Here's the part that's actually worse, so listen to this instead of the poetry. While I had it open on that step, a lens clouded and grew a pupil. Then another. It kept working on the face after I took the limbs off. That's not resistance. That's plumbing. Whatever assembled this didn't need the creature's permission, or its awareness, or even its cooperation. The instructions kept running while the body was being unmade. That's the bad news. Not that it died quiet—it was never alive enough to make noise—but that the pattern outlives the puppet. You meet another one, and it might already have the face finished. Then it'll have opinions. And it won't be brave or dignified or tragic. It'll just be a thing with a mouth that finally works, and it'll use it."

Halloway straightened, torch held clear of the wet stone, and swept the beam out across the water.

"Your light's shaking," she said. "Stop looking at the ash. Put the beam on the water, past the steam. The fire made us a beacon, and if whatever built that thing is proud of its work, it might come down to see why its project stopped moving. I want the light on it before it gets close enough to be polite."

She looked back at the charred rods and the hissing shallows one last time.

"It didn't fight. Good. I'd hate to have to explain to the next one why the first one was braver. Brave is a story. I trade in what's where. What's where is ash, blackened rod, and a builder still out there with the instructions. That's worse. Now keep the light still, watch the dark, and then we clear the rest of this cellar and the floor above. Proud things watch. Convenient. It means we can burn the builder in the same afternoon, if it's stupid enough to show its face."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, swallowing down the tightness in my throat. My hand steadies, the lamp beam sweeping across the dark water. "Still no movement," I say. "But... I think I smell something. Upstairs. Sweet, like rotting flowers."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stirred the ash with the point of the blade. The central mass collapsed in on itself, blackened rods brittle as charred horn, the pale bundles burned away to nothing. No lens remained in the crescent; the clouded beads had cracked and the dark specks had boiled off with the oil. Every joint she had opened—shoulder, the too-high hips, the backward knee—was ash or a smoking curl. Nothing moved that she had not moved. The thing was finished.

Then she turned her face toward the open stair and breathed in through her mouth, the way a hunter does when the air might be lying. The cellar had its own smell now: oily smoke from the pitch-tow, steam off the water, and under it the mineral-green stink of the thing’s rods burning like bad horn. Riding down through all of that, from the floor above, came something else. Sweet. Cloying. The damp rot of flowers left too long in a vase, petals gone brown and slimy at the stems.

It was not the smell of what they had just burned. The thing on the step had smelled faintly of rain on limestone and a branch split too early. This was heavier, organic, and it was coming from upstairs.

She did not move at once. She swept the torch beam one last time across the black water at the foot of the steps. The ash hissed where embers had settled into the shallows. No shape rose. No limb twitched without her hand on it. The far end of the cellar stayed empty, the water lying about its depth and its teeth in equal silence.

“Sweet like rotting flowers,” Halloway said. “That’s a smell with three usual sources. A corpse in the bloating stage, when the gut goes sweet before it goes foul. A fungus fruiting in a damp house, which is just a corpse with better manners. Or something that wears a scent on purpose, the way a woman wears perfume—to cover what’s underneath, or to draw you close enough to find out.”

She shifted the torch, and the light threw the wet stone and the steaming ash into harder relief.

“The thing we burned didn’t smell like that. It smelled like a workshop and a broken branch. So this is either a second problem or the same problem in a different coat. If it’s flowers, it’s a lousy bouquet. Flowers rot sweet when they’re winning. So does a body, but a body usually brings flies, stains, and a stink you can taste. All I’ve got is the sweetness, and my smoke is going up, not down. If that smell is riding down through my smoke, there’s a lot of it, or it’s close to the top of the stairs.”

She straightened on the tread, blade in one hand, torch in the other, and kept her body angled so the stair opening was not at her back.

“We don’t go charging up because something smells like a funeral,” she said. “We go up because we were going anyway, and now we know the house isn’t empty. Keep the light on the water another count. If anything comes up out of that dark—anything at all—you say it. Then we finish this floor, and then we take the stairs slow, torch low, and see what’s blooming.”

Her mouth moved, not a smile.

“If it’s another one, I want to meet it before it finishes its face. If it’s the builder, I want to meet it while it’s still proud enough to watch. Either way, mind your feet on the steps. Ash and oil make a slick tread, and I’ve already got one thing today that came apart without complaining. I’d rather not add you to the pile.”

She waited through ten slow breaths, the beam lying flat across the water, the torch held steady and low. Nothing rose. Nothing came up the cellar’s dark to answer the smoke. Only the sweet rot of flowers drifted down from above, patient as a bouquet left on a grave.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I count to ten under my breath, the lamp beam unwavering on the still, black water. "Nothing moving," I say, and my voice doesn't shake this time. "But that smell's getting thicker." I turn toward the stairs, my boots crunching on cooling ash. "Do we go up slow, or do we make it come to us?"

rung_labels.evidence: There's no bloat, no sloughing, no gas I can see.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway gave a short, approving sound, not quite a laugh.

“Good,” she said. “Don’t let your stomach vote. Your eyes first.”

She lowered the lamp an inch, letting the light slide across the stillness at the cellar’s far end. The water around it lay flat and black, broken only where the thing’s bulk displaced it.

“Shape’s wrong because it’s arranged wrong,” she said. “See the shoulders, if they are shoulders. They sit too low. And there’s a bend where a knee oughtn’t be, unless it’s got more than two legs and one of them’s folded under.”

She did not step closer.

“Most things stop moving when they’re dead,” she added. “Some stop moving because they’re listening.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow, trying to see what she's pointing out. "It's... too still for a dead thing, isn't it? The water isn't even rippling."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not answer at once. She held the lamp steady and let her eyes work along the edges of the shape instead of its center, the way one looked at a wound: not at the worst part first, but at what the worst part had done to everything around it.

“Dead things don’t hold themselves,” she said at last. “They settle. They spread. They let the water find their mouth and nose and don’t care if it does.”

She crouched a little, knees giving a dry crack, but her boots stayed where they were.

“If it’s dead, it’s been dead long enough to stop pretending it ever breathed. If it isn’t—” She tilted the lamp just enough to put a thin line of light across the thing’s back, or what served as a back. “Then it’s holding very still because stillness is useful.”

The cellar smelled of wet stone, old rot, and something faintly sweet beneath it, like meat left in a bucket of rain. Halloway’s mouth tightened at the taste of it.

“Watch the waterline on it,” she said. “Not the body. The place where the water meets it. Dead flesh takes a wave and gives it back slow. Living flesh does it quicker, even if it’s trying not to.”

Her free hand moved to her belt and unhooked a short iron probe, the kind used for turning soil in graves or prying teeth out of things that no longer needed them. She did not step closer. Instead, she weighed it once in her palm, then flicked it end over end into the water a few feet short of the shape.

It struck with a dull, hollow plunk.

Ripples rolled outward, crossed the black surface, and touched the mass at the far end.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed.

“Now,” she said softly. “We see whether it votes dead.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway kept her eyes on the waterline while the ripples crossed the black surface.

“Recently,” she repeated, as if testing the word for rot. “If you mean was it born with a mother and a name, maybe. There’s a skull in there, or something that learned how to wear one. See the way the water sheds off the high point? That’s a brow ridge. Or it was.”

The ripples reached the shape.

They did not break cleanly around it. A little shiver ran along the dark edge where the water met the mass, too fine for buoyancy, too quick for settled flesh. Halloway’s grip on the lamp tightened until the knuckles whitened under the grime.

“If you mean was it a person in the last hour, the last day,” she said, voice dropping into the flat tone she used for graves and gutters and official forms, “then no. Whatever’s in that cellar has been using the parts for a while. The shoulders are too low, yes, but the arms are too long for the sockets they’ve been shoved into. And there’s a hand near the water, if you want to call it that. Fingers fused. Thumb on the wrong side.”

She let out a slow breath through her nose.

“So. Person-shaped. Once, perhaps. Now it’s more like someone made a person out of old pieces and forgot where the hinges go.”

The water around the far end gave one slow, oily adjustment, though nothing had moved that she could see.

“Don’t answer it if it speaks,” Halloway said. “And if it sounds like someone you know, don’t answer it twice.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a slow step back, my own boots making a soft sound in the water. "It's moving," I whisper. "Not the body—the water around it just..." I trail off, my eyes fixed on that unnatural stillness.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not look away from the water.

“Then you’re learning,” she said. “Don’t whisper because it’s quiet. Whisper because you don’t want it to know where your voice comes from.”

The lamp flame gave a thin, nervous lean, though no draft reached them. Halloway adjusted her grip and let the light settle again on the far end of the cellar, where the shape sat wrong in the black water like a bad stitch in wet cloth.

The ripples had not behaved properly from the first. They should have washed against the mass and rolled back, spent and stupid, the way water did against stone or swollen wood or meat. Instead, the little pulls along the edge kept coming, one after another, as if something beneath the surface were tasting the disturbance and deciding what it meant.

“It isn’t moving the body,” Halloway said. “It’s moving the water around the body. That’s worse.”

Her eyes tracked the oily sheen near the fused hand. The fingers, if they were fingers, had not lifted. The shoulder, if it was a shoulder, had not risen. But the waterline climbed a fraction, hesitated, and slid down again, leaving a dark smear on the pale, waterlogged surface of whatever passed for skin.

“Means it’s got reach without showing you the limb,” she went on. “Means it can touch you before you’ve agreed it’s got hands.”

The iron probe she had tossed still floated a few feet short of the shape. It turned slowly in the water, tip pointing toward the mass, then away, then toward it again, as though the cellar itself had grown confused about north.

Halloway watched that more than the body.

“If it was dead, the water would be done with it by now,” she said. “If it was only hiding, it wouldn’t keep adjusting. This is patience. Something’s waiting to see what we’ll be stupid enough to do next.”

The probe dipped.

Not much. A finger’s width. Just enough for the lamp light to catch the wet iron and then lose it.

Halloway’s jaw set.

“Well,” she said, very softly. “It took the offering. That’s either curiosity or appetite. I’d bet on appetite.”

She shifted her weight backward without taking a step, boots scraping faintly against drowned stone. The sound was small, but the water heard it. The black surface near the far wall tightened, the way a held breath tightens behind teeth.

“Don’t stare at the center of it,” Halloway said. “Your eyes will lie to you there. They’ll try to find a face, a chest, a place where the heart ought to be, because that’s what eyes do when they’re frightened. They look for something they can pity.”

The lamp flickered over the low shoulders, the too-long arms, the bend where no knee had any business being.

“Don’t pity it,” she said. “Pity is how things like that get close.”

Something shifted under the water. Not a rise. Not a limb. More like the whole cellar floor had thought about moving and then changed its mind. The sweet rot-smell thickened for a breath, then thinned, as if the shape had drawn it inward.

Halloway’s voice stayed flat, clinical, the voice of a woman writing a report in her head while the world tried to eat her.

“It’s testing the water for us,” she said. “Every step, every breath, every word makes a little knock on its door. So we’re going to be rude enough not to knock louder.”

She did not raise the lamp. She did not call out. She only stood there, old and grim and steady, with thirty years of bad endings written into the lines around her mouth.

“If it speaks,” she said, “it’ll use something soft first. A child’s voice, maybe. Somebody hurt. Somebody asking for help. That’s the hook.”

The water around the probe gave one slow, deliberate swirl.

“If it uses your voice,” Halloway added, “don’t correct its grammar. Just don’t answer.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not thank her for the light. She took the better illumination the way she took everything useful: without ceremony, and with the assumption that it would cost her later.

“Plainly,” she said, “it isn’t a body. It’s a collection.”

Her eyes moved over the shape in short, practiced sections, never staying too long on any one place.

“There’s a skull in there, yes. Female, by the brow and the set of the jaw. But the jaw itself is too heavy for it. See how the skin pulls at the hinge? That wasn’t fitted to the bone. The bone was forced to fit the skin.”

The water near the far end gave another minute adjustment, as though something beneath had shifted its attention.

“The shoulders belong to a larger person,” Halloway went on. “A man, maybe. Broad through the chest. But the arms are wrong for them. Too long, too narrow in the wrist. They’ve been set low because there wasn’t room for them any higher. Whatever made that shape wanted reach more than it wanted proper anatomy.”

She let the lamp light trace the dark seam where the mass met the water.

“The hand you saw is younger. The fingers are fused, but the knuckles are still smooth. That’s not age. That’s pressure. It’s been held together under water until the flesh gave up arguing.”

Her voice stayed flat. Clinical. The voice she used when the only alternative was to start swearing and never stop.

“What happened to it? It was made. Not born, not killed in one piece. Made. Someone was drowned or dragged down here and used as a foundation. Then another piece was added. Then another. The water helped. Water hides color. It swells the edges so seams close. It keeps dead meat flexible longer than it has any right to be. And it muffles sound, which is useful if you’re something that doesn’t want the neighbors hearing you learn how to walk.”

The iron probe was gone now. Not sunk. Not drifted. Simply no longer where it had been, and the water had not made a fuss about losing it.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“It doesn’t respect the parts,” she said. “That’s the important thing. It doesn’t care whose hand it was, or whether the fingers used to belong to someone who played music or signed letters or held children. It only cares what the hand can do now. Grip. Pull. Mimic. Hook.”

She gave a short, humorless breath.

“If I had to write it for a ledger, I’d say multiple victims, dismemberment by pressure rather than cutting, reassembly by an active entity with a preference for aquatic concealment. Cause of death for the components: variable. Drowning, likely. Suffocation. Some may have been alive when it fitted them.”

The cellar seemed to grow colder around the words, though the air had no draft in it.

“Plainly,” Halloway said, “it’s wearing people because people are the shape it needs to lure the next one.”

She finally looked away from the mass, just long enough to check the water between them. The black surface was too calm. Too attentive. It lay there like a held breath with a skin on it.

“It heard you ask,” she added. “Not the meaning. The sound. It’s learning which noises are questions and which are answers.”

A faint sweetness rose again, thick and cloying, like syrup poured over spoiled meat. Halloway’s nose wrinkled, but she did not spit. Spitting would have been a waste of moisture and dignity.

“The bad news,” she said, “is that it’s clever enough to arrange itself.”

Her free hand rested near her belt again, fingers curling around the handle of another tool.

“The worse news is that it’s probably not finished.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Then it's not done with us," I say, my voice low and steady despite the tremor in my hands. "It's fitting us into its collection."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s expression did not change, except for a small deepening at the corners of her mouth.

“Don’t flatter it,” she said. “A collection is what it keeps after it’s finished with the living use. Right now we’re candidates. Measurements. Sounds it hasn’t decided how to steal.”

She used the better light without looking toward its source. Her eyes moved over the shape in short, distrustful passes, never resting on the center long enough for sympathy to form.

“It doesn’t fit us into anything until we come close enough to be fitted,” she said. “That’s the whole trick. It makes you feel chosen. Already half-used. It wants you thinking about your hands and your face and where they’d sit on that pile, because a person busy imagining their own pieces is easier to lead.”

A bubble rose near the mass. It did not burst quickly. It swelled dark and oily under the lamplight, trembling with something like attention, then popped with a soft, wet click that left the sweet rot-smell hanging stronger than before.

Halloway’s nose wrinkled.

“That’s either annoyance or laughter,” she said. “Hard to tell with wet things. If it starts laughing in a way that sounds sorry for itself, we’ll know we’re being worked on.”

She took one measured step backward. Not a retreat. A reduction. She moved as if subtracting herself from the room by inches, shoulders level, boots finding the drowned stone without lifting high enough to make a splash.

“We leave,” she said. “Not because it’s stronger, though it likely is in the water. Not because it’s clever, though it’s been learning faster than I like. Because it’s still deciding, and I’ve lived this long by not standing around while something decides whether I’m meat, bait, or material.”

Her eyes flicked once to the place where the iron probe had been. Gone. Not sunk. Not drifted. Taken.

“If it follows, don’t run,” she said. “Running makes a rhythm it can borrow. Splash less. Slide your feet if you can. Water likes a lifted boot; it makes a cupping sound, and things down there hear that as an invitation.”

The shape at the far end did not rise. It did not unfold. It only sat there in its wrong arrangement, too patient for hunger, too still for sleep. But the water around it thickened in the lamplight, gathering itself into a skin of black reflection.

Halloway’s voice stayed flat, practical, the tone of a woman listing tools.

“If it calls, don’t answer. If it cries, don’t answer. If it asks for help in a voice that makes your stomach feel young and stupid, don’t answer. If it uses my voice, for God’s sake don’t answer that either. I’ve been old and unpleasant for thirty years, and I know exactly what I sound like when I’m lying.”

She gave the cellar one last, clinical sweep: the low ceiling, the drowned stone, the fused hand near the waterline, the bend where no knee had any business being. Her gaze caught on the last place for half a second too long, and her mouth thinned.

“And if it starts describing you,” she added, “don’t correct it. Nothing likes being edited.”

Then she began to ease backward toward the stairs, keeping herself behind the light as best she could without reaching for it, shoulders level, breathing controlled. The water around her boots made small, reluctant sounds, but she did not hurry. Haste was another kind of invitation.

“Plainly,” she said, “it hasn’t done with us only if we stay to be finished.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not turn her back on the water, but her voice changed into the one she used for reports, inquests, and things that had to be written down before they could be buried.

“Plainly,” she said, “it used him for structure, not costume.”

Her eyes moved over the shape in short, deliberate pieces.

“The shoulders are male. Broad through the frame, heavy in the collar and chest. But there’s no blood cloud in the water around the seams. That means he was dead before it started working. Drowned, most likely, or dragged in after death. It didn’t need him alive. It needed him sound enough to bear weight.”

The black water lay still around the mass, but the stillness had a listening quality to it. Halloway did not let it fool her into speaking faster.

“It broke the shoulder girdle,” she said. “Not with a blade. By pressure. The joints were forced down and inward, then packed so they’d hold. That’s why the arms sit too low. It wanted reach. It got it by ruining the natural hang of the body.”

She gave a small, grim breath through her nose.

“Under the skin, there isn’t one man anymore. The original flesh is dead and waterlogged, but it hasn’t been allowed to fall apart. It’s been threaded through with something else. Sinew, hair, wet cord, strips from other bodies. Maybe plant fibre. Maybe worse. The skin has been used like a sack to keep the packing in place. Where the sack was weak, it stitched. Where it tore, it pressed more material into the gap.”

The lamp light caught the pale, swollen curve of what might once have been a cheek. Halloway’s gaze passed over it without pity.

“It took the eyes,” she said. “Or they dissolved. Either way, the sockets are filled. That’s why the head doesn’t look empty from a distance. It’s been padded out to keep the face shaped. The jaw is too heavy for the skull because it isn’t his. It was fitted after. The hinges were forced to meet it, probably by pressing the whole thing under weight until the tissues accepted the lie.”

She shifted her weight backward another careful inch.

“It took the tongue, or it didn’t need one. The throat’s swollen with something else. That’s how things like this borrow voices. Not by keeping the original instrument. By building a wet place inside that can echo what it hears. If it speaks, it won’t be because the mouth wants to. It’ll be because the cavity has learned the shape of a cry.”

The sweet, rotten smell rose again, faint and thick, like fruit left too long in a butcher’s bucket.

“It took his hands, or it never had them to begin with,” she went on. “The fused hand near the water belongs to someone younger. The knuckles are smooth. The bones were held together until they healed into a single gripping shape. That tells you what it values. Not fingers for fine work. A hook. A clamp. Something that can catch a wrist and not let go.”

Her mouth tightened.

“How far it got with him: far enough to make the frame useful. Not far enough to make him convincing in daylight. The seams are still loose. The water around it is still adjusting. It hasn’t settled into a final shape. It’s still deciding which parts to keep and which to trade.”

The cellar seemed to lean in around her words.

“If you meet another one,” Halloway said, “look first at the waterline. If the flesh moves before the body does, it’s alive in the wrong way. If the seams are clean and the face sits neat, it’s further along than this one. If it answers to a name, don’t believe the name. If it asks for help, don’t believe the need. If it looks like it’s suffering, remember that suffering is one of the oldest hooks.”

Her hand rested near her belt, though she did not draw another tool.

“It took what made him recognizable,” she said. “Face, hands, voice, the little habits that make people lean closer. It left what made him heavy. That’s the lesson. It doesn’t want the person. It wants the handles.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a shallow breath, my eyes finally seeing the mess of seams and borrowed parts. "So we kill the frame," I say, voice quiet but clear. "Not the pieces. The thing holding them together."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s mouth twisted, but there was no humor in it.

“Kill the frame,” she repeated, as if turning the phrase over to see whether it had rot in it. “That’s the first sensible thing you’ve said since we smelled it.”

She kept her eyes on the water while she spoke, and her voice stayed low and flat, the voice of a woman explaining how to unmake a trap without putting her fingers in it.

“But don’t mistake the frame for the thing. The frame is only what it has built. The real enemy is the claim.”

The black water near the far end gave a slow, greasy tremble. Not a ripple. Not a rise. More like the surface had heard the word kill and was deciding whether to be offended.

Halloway did not give it the satisfaction of being frightened.

“Under the skin now,” she said, “there isn’t a man. There’s a lattice. The shoulders and chest are doing the work of a keel. The arms are stays. That fused hand is a hook. The skull is a lure, because a skull is the part people look for when they want to believe something is still human. The jaw is a drum. The throat is where it keeps the borrowed sounds.”

Her gaze moved along the mass without touching its center.

“What it took from him was not his life. It took his recognizability. The little signs that make a person approachable. The shape of a face. The hang of arms. The idea of hands. It left the weight, because weight is useful. It left the joints, because joints can be forced. It left the skin, because skin can be made to lie.”

She shifted her grip on the lamp, knuckles pale beneath the dirt.

“What it did not finish is the important part. The seams are still wet. The pieces still argue with one another. The male chest is too broad for the skull. The arms are too long for the sockets. The hand is too young for the shoulder. That means the binding is not settled. It is still persuading the parts to agree.”

A faint sound came from the water, soft and intimate, like a mouth trying to remember how to swallow.

Halloway’s expression hardened.

“So if you meet another one, do not start by hacking at the pieces. A hand can still catch you after it has been cut off. A jaw can still bite if the thing inside it thinks biting will help. You will waste your strength killing a body that is already dead and leave the real thing free to put itself back together around your ankles.”

She took another measured step backward, boots sliding through the water rather than lifting.

“Kill the frame if you must. Break it because it is the thing between you and escape. But if you have time, if you have light, if you have the luxury of thought, then look for the binding.”

Her voice became more precise, as though she were pinning the lesson to a board.

“There will be a point where the pieces lean toward one another. Not the biggest piece. Not the most human-looking one. The piece that all the others seem to be protecting. It might be in the throat. It might be in the hand. It might be some filthy little knot of hair and cord pressed into the chest where the heart ought to have been. Sometimes it is not a part at all. Sometimes it is an object. A ring. A tooth. A scrap of clothing. A name it has swallowed and is using like a nail to hang the rest on.”

The cellar’s sweet stench thickened again, then thinned, as if the thing at the far end had drawn it in and breathed it out through invisible seams.

“If you cannot find the binding,” Halloway said, “then ruin the frame’s usefulness. Take the reach first. The arms, the hand, anything that can pull. Not at the wrist. At the joint where it was forced into place. Those are the weak points, because they are lies held together by pressure.”

Her eyes narrowed.

“Then spoil the voice. Iron through the throat if you can get it there without letting it touch you. Fire if you have it. Salt if you have enough and the thing is not standing in four feet of water laughing at you. The point is not to make it bleed. The point is to stop it from echoing.”

The lamp flame gave a thin, uneasy lean.

“And if you can dry it, do. Wet things are brave while they are wet. Water makes their seams supple. It hides their edges. It gives them patience. Put them on dry stone and they begin to remember they are made of stolen parts. Fire helps. Lime helps. Sunlight helps, if you live long enough to see it.”

She let out a slow breath through her nose.

“But plainly? If you meet another one and you are alone, in the dark, with only a lamp and your own stubbornness between you and it, then you do not try to be clever. You break the frame. You ruin its reach. You deny it your voice. And you get out before it learns enough to start using your name.”

The water at the far end moved then, not with a splash, but with a slow, deliberate gathering, as though the shape beneath had decided to test the idea of rising.

Halloway’s face did not change.

“Now,” she said, very quietly, “we are going to stop giving it conversation.”

She began to ease backward toward the stairs, keeping the lamp between them and the mass, her boots sliding through the black water with careful, scraping patience.

“If it follows,” she said, “do not strike at the face. The face is bait. Strike at the waterline, where the shape pretends to end. And if it speaks—”

Her mouth thinned into a grim line.

“Then it has already stolen too much.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway drew the long knife from her belt and did not ask for courage, permission, or better light. She hooked the iron probe into the nearest seam, just below the misplaced shoulder, and cut along the swollen line where skin had been pressed into a shape it had never been meant to keep.

The blade did not part flesh so much as persuade it open.

No blood welled up. No red thread ran into the black water. Instead, a clear, ropy fluid seeped from the cut, thin as old glue, and the smell changed at once. It had been sweet before, cloying and wrong. Now it became layered: wet wool, stagnant pond-mud, sour milk, copper, and beneath all of that a greasy sweetness like tallow gone bad in a closed room.

Halloway’s face did not change.

“Plainly,” she said, “it began by emptying him where nobody would look first.”

She worked the knife sideways, not deep, not reckless. She opened the seam enough for the lamplight to get inside. The skin was thick and waterlogged, but it had been scraped thin on the inner side, the way one might clean a hide before stretching it over a frame.

“The belly and chest were gutted,” she said. “Not eaten. Cleared. The organs are gone or broken down into a wet paste. That’s part of the smell. It isn’t rot alone. It’s what rot becomes when it’s been used as mortar.”

The cut widened. Beneath the skin, there was no clean anatomy. No muscle lay in proper straps. No fat sat in its natural yellow layers. Instead, the cavity had been packed tight with a compressed mass of wet hair, strips of pale skin, fibrous reed-like strands, shredded cloth, and small fragments of bone crushed to the size of teeth. Everything had been pressed together until it formed a damp, solid wadding.

“Ballast,” Halloway said. “It needed weight low in the frame so the top could lean forward without tipping. Hair holds water. Cloth swells. Bone gives it something to push against. The whole mess is stitched through with cord.”

She touched the tip of the knife to one of the pale threads running through the packing. It did not look like sinew. It was too even, too dark, and when she pulled lightly, the entire chest shifted a fraction, like a net tightening.

“Not veins,” she said. “Lacing. It bound the inside first. The skin is only the outer lie.”

The water around the shape gave a slow, oily tremor. The fused hand near the surface did not move, but the fingers seemed more curled than they had been a moment before. Halloway saw it and did not waste breath on alarm.

“It knows we’re inspecting the work,” she said. “Don’t let that flatter you into staying closer.”

She cut higher, along the shoulder seam. The blade met resistance, then slipped through a knot of packed material with a soft, wet crack. A pocket of trapped air escaped, carrying a smell so thick and sugary-sour that it seemed to coat the teeth. Halloway breathed through her mouth and did not pause.

“The shoulders were forced down after death,” she said. “The joints were crushed inward, then packed around with this material to hold the new angle. That’s why the arms hang too low. It didn’t care how the man was built. It cared what the arms could reach.”

She exposed more of the shoulder. Beneath the borrowed skin, the bone had been splintered and reset without any attempt at healing. The breaks were held together by blackened cord wound so tightly it had bitten into the damp flesh. In places, other fragments had been shoved into the gaps: a piece of rib, a shard of jaw, something small and smooth that might once have been part of a child’s wrist.

“It used him as scaffolding,” Halloway said. “The original body is still in there, but only where it serves. Everything else is filler, armor, or lure.”

She moved the knife toward the throat. The skin there was stretched tight, almost shiny, and when the blade touched it, the whole mass gave a faint internal shiver, as though something far beneath the surface had turned its attention toward the cut.

Halloway did not pull back.

“The throat’s been rebuilt,” she said. “The tongue’s gone. Maybe swallowed. Maybe kept elsewhere. What’s left is a cavity lined with skin from at least three different mouths. See the color change? That paler patch is softer tissue, probably taken from someone younger. It’s been shaped into a reed. That’s how it borrows voices. Not by keeping the original throat, but by making a wet place that can copy the shape of a sound.”

She pressed the knife gently aside, revealing a hollow behind the swollen neck. Inside, strands of wet tissue hung like strings in a ruined instrument. They trembled without wind.

“If it cried out,” she said, “it would not be him crying. It would be the sound of every cry it’s heard, squeezed through that mess.”

The water near the far wall tightened again. A bubble rose close to the mass and burst with a soft click. The sweet rot-smell pulsed stronger, then thinned, as if the thing were deciding whether to recoil or listen.

Halloway’s mouth thinned.

“It’s not finished,” she said. “That’s the important part. It got the chest framed, the shoulders lowered, the head mounted, the jaw fitted, and the throat tuned enough to steal a voice. It got one hand made into a hook. But the other side is still loose. Look at the left arm. It hangs wrong even for this.”

The knife moved lower, pointing without touching. The left arm did indeed sit strangely, not merely low but unattached in some deeper sense. The skin around its socket had not been fully closed. Beneath it, packing bulged and shifted slightly, as though it had not yet learned whether it belonged to the frame or to the water.

“That arm is still being persuaded,” Halloway said. “It’s not dead tissue alone. It’s not alive either. It’s in the middle state, where it will obey whichever pressure is strongest.”

She cut a small cross into the upper chest, away from the center, and peeled back a flap of skin. Beneath it lay a lattice of ribs, some human, some not, lashed together with cord and strips of flesh. The arrangement was too regular to be accident, too crude to be craft. It looked like something built in haste by a mind that understood the idea of a body but had no respect for its particulars.

“There,” Halloway said. “That’s the frame. Not the man. The cage.”

Her knife hovered over a knot at the center of the lattice. It was not large. It sat just behind the place where a heart might have been, though the chest had been packed too tightly for any organ to remain. The knot was made of hair, black and slick, wound around something hard. A tooth. A bead. A scrap of bone polished by water. It was difficult to tell without cutting deeper, and Halloway did not cut deeper yet.

“That’s likely the binding,” she said. “Not always, but often. The point all the pieces lean toward. If you cut the arms, it can still pull with what’s left. If you smash the skull, it can still grip. If you ruin the throat, it can still thrash. But if you find the binding and burn it, dry it, break it, or drag it into sunlight, the frame loses its argument.”

The cellar water gave a sudden, shallow lift. Not a wave. More like the floor had inhaled.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed.

“Don’t move closer,” she said.

She did not mean herself.

The shape did not rise, but the water around it began to climb the mass in thin black threads, as if trying to cover the cut she had made. The smell changed again. The sweetness deepened into something almost floral, sickly and heavy, like lilies left too long in a room where someone had died.

Halloway’s voice stayed flat.

“It doesn’t like being read,” she said. “Things like this rely on confusion. A body in the dark is easier to mistake for a person. A voice in the dark is easier to mistake for help. Once you see the seams, the lure gets weaker.”

She cut one of the cords near the shoulder. It snapped with a sound like a wet bowstring. The arm attached to it dropped an inch, and the water around the mass shivered violently. A low noise came from the throat, not a word, not a moan, but the shape of one, as though the cavity were trying to remember what grief sounded like.

Halloway did not answer it.

“It will try softness next,” she said. “A child. A hurt woman. A man asking for his mother. Don’t let your heart vote.”

She cut another cord. The chest sagged inward. The fused hand near the waterline twitched, then settled.

“Under the skin,” she went on, “there is no single corpse. There are pieces kept in service. The male chest is the keel. The skull is the bait. The jaw is the drum. The throat is the echo-box. The hand is the hook. The rest is packing and pressure.”

She worked the knife around the edge of the cut, exposing more of the inner mass. The smell grew worse, but she did not hurry.

“It got far enough to stand if the water helps it,” she said. “Far enough to drag itself a short distance on dry stone, though it will hate that. Far enough to use a voice if it hears one first. Far enough to make you think it is suffering. It did not get far enough to walk properly, see properly, or hold a shape under bright light. The eyes are false. The legs, if it has true legs under that mess, are not finished. It relies on reach, grip, and imitation.”

She paused as the knife touched something harder beneath the packing. She eased the material aside with the probe. A small, smooth object lay wedged between two crushed ribs. It was pale, oval, and notched at one end.

A child’s tooth.

No. Not a tooth. A milk tooth, split and drilled through, threaded with black hair.

Halloway stared at it for one breath.

“There,” she said. “That’s closer to the truth.”

She did not touch it with her bare hand. She used the knife point and the probe to lift the hair-bound object just enough to see the cord running from it into the chest lattice. The whole shape gave a fine, nauseating tremor, and the water made a sound like lips parting.

“It’s a nail,” Halloway said. “Not iron. Something personal. Something taken from a weak moment. A child’s tooth, a lock of hair, a scrap of naming. It uses the piece to convince the rest of the frame that it has a right to speak.”

Her face hardened.

“That’s how far it got with him. It stole his shape and built a hook out of someone else’s hand. It stole a voice-box and hung it behind a borrowed jaw. It took whatever small, pitiful thing it could find and made that the center of the frame.”

She let the tooth fall back into the chest. It landed with a tiny, wet click.

“If you meet another one,” she said, “look for the object first. Not the biggest wound. Not the face. The object. The thing that does not belong to anatomy. The thing that makes your stomach ache because it looks innocent. That’s often where the binding sits.”

The water around the mass began to swirl without current. The cut she had made leaked more clear fluid, and the smell sharpened into something almost hot, as though the thing were trying to produce heat from spite.

Halloway wiped the blade on her sleeve, though it was not truly clean.

“Plainly,” she said, “it hollowed him, packed him, laced him, and hung a stolen voice inside him. It took his face enough to lure, his weight enough to anchor, his hands enough to grip. It left his suffering nowhere to be found, because suffering would have made him inconvenient. What it kept was usefulness.”

She stepped back a careful inch, boots sliding rather than lifting.

“And plainly,” she added, “if you ever see one standing in daylight, neat and crying and asking for its mother, shoot the chest, burn the throat, and don’t stop until the thing smells like dry ash. Because if it looks finished, it has already learned how to ask for what it wants.”

The shape at the far end gave a slow, internal settling, like a house deciding which wall would fall first.

Halloway kept her knife ready.

“Now,” she said, “we stop teaching it our voices.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I keep the lamp high, watching the way the light catches on the leaking fluid. "It's not just one thing in there, is it?" I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "It's a... chorus."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s knife paused for half a beat.

“Chorus,” she said. “That’s the pretty name for it.”

She did not look away from the opened seam. The clear fluid kept weeping from the cut in slow, adhesive threads, and where it touched the black water it made faint little rings that refused to spread properly.

“But yes,” she went on. “It isn’t one body. It isn’t one death. It may not even be one appetite, though it’s likely working toward one purpose.”

She used the iron probe to tease apart a clump of packing just beneath the ribs. The lamplight caught the wet mass inside: hair of more than one color, strips of skin with different grain, crushed bone, shredded cloth, and those same dark cords running through everything like stitches in a boot that had been repaired too many times.

“Look at the hair,” Halloway said. “There’s gray in there. Brown. Something fair and fine, likely a child’s. That’s not one head. That’s several.”

She lifted a small knot with the probe and let it fall. It landed with a soft, obscene pat.

“The skull’s female,” she said. “The chest is male. The fused hand is young. The throat’s lined with skin from at least three mouths. That tooth in the lattice came from a child. And there’s probably more tucked deeper where we can’t see without pulling the whole thing apart.”

Her mouth thinned.

“So, yes. A chorus. If you want to call it that.”

The water around the mass gave a slow, oily shiver. The thing did not move, but the surface near its shoulder thickened, as though something under it had just turned over in thought.

“Only don’t let the word make you sentimental,” Halloway said. “A chorus means singers. People standing together. People with names and parts and mothers. This isn’t that. This is a collection of stolen instruments. The voices aren’t in there because the people are still present. They’re in there because the thing learned how to make their pieces lie convincingly.”

She cut another cord near the shoulder. It snapped with a wet twang, and the arm dropped a little lower. The whole frame settled with a faint internal creak, like ropes in a well.

“Plainly,” she said, “there are several victims inside the frame, but not several persons. Not anymore. The persons were used up. What’s left are the sounds they can still be made to make, the shapes they can still be forced to hold, and the little hooks that make living people lean closer when they ought to run.”

From the swollen throat came a small noise.

Not a word. Not quite a breath. More like two breaths at once, one low and one thin, sliding against each other until the air itself seemed to hesitate.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed.

“There,” she said. “It heard the word and it’s trying it on. Chorus. It likes that. It likes anything that suggests company.”

She shifted the knife angle, exposing more of the inner lattice without touching the center knot. The smell rose in layers: pond mud first, then sour milk, then copper, then that cloying sweetness underneath, and finally something almost floral, like funeral flowers left too long in standing water.

“That smell is part of the chorus too,” she said. “It isn’t one rot. It’s several. Different ages of flesh. Different stages of breakdown. Some of it was fresh when it went in. Some was already spoiled. The thing doesn’t care. It only cares whether the pieces can still hold a shape and whether the smell will make a person think of sweetness before they think of danger.”

She pointed with the probe, not touching, toward the throat cavity.

“The voice-box is the clearest proof. It’s built from several mouths, and the tissues don’t match. See where the pale patch meets the darker one? That’s not bruising. That’s different skin, pressed together until it took the same curve. If it speaks, it may speak with more than one tone under the word. One voice asking for help, another sounding hurt, another young, another old. That’s not mercy. That’s tuning.”

The black water near the far wall lifted a fraction, then sank again. The fused hand by the surface did not move, but the fingers looked more closed than before, as if they had been practicing a fist while nobody watched.

Halloway kept her voice flat.

“If it starts using more than one voice at once, don’t try to sort them,” she said. “Don’t pick out the one that sounds most frightened. Don’t pick out the one that sounds like someone you owe something to. That’s the trap. A single voice can be resisted. A chorus makes people think there’s more than one victim to save.”

She gave a short, grim breath.

“And once you start counting the victims, you stop counting the distance to the door.”

She worked the knife around the edge of the chest lattice, careful not to disturb the hair-bound tooth again. Beneath the packing, she exposed another small knot: a scrap of cloth, blue and faded, wound tight with several strands of hair and a sliver of bone no larger than a splinter.

“There,” she said. “Another nail. Smaller. Likely not the center, but part of the bracing. It uses keepsakes the way a builder uses pegs. The tooth may be the main binding because it’s personal and it’s innocent. The cloth might belong to someone else. The hair might be from three heads or six.”

Her jaw tightened.

“That’s how far it got. Far enough to gather. Far enough to sort. Far enough to know which pieces would make a person hesitate.”

She looked at the shape as one looks at a bad bridge: not with horror, but with calculation.

“It hasn’t fused them cleanly,” she said. “That’s our advantage. The pieces still disagree. The chest is too broad for the skull. The hand is too young for the shoulder. The throat is too crowded for the jaw. If it were finished, it would sound like one person. It would look like one person. It would cry with one voice and reach with one hand and make you forget there had ever been more than one poor thing in the water.”

The thing’s throat made another sound.

This time it was almost a syllable. Almost a name, but not a name either of them knew. It had the shape of a plea and no meaning behind it, like a cup turned upside down.

Halloway did not answer.

She waited until the sound died, then spoke again in the same flat, report-room voice.

“If you meet another one,” she said, “and it speaks with several voices, that means it has had time to collect. If it uses them one after another, it’s still choosing which bait works best. If it uses them all at once, it’s either desperate or finished. In either case, you do not stay to hear the end of the song.”

She wiped the knife on her sleeve once, though it only smeared the clear fluid.
