“Kill the frame if you have to. But don’t think you’re killing the chorus by cutting the mouths. You’re only breaking the instruments. The song is in the binding. The song is in the thing that convinced all those stolen pieces to lean the same way.”

Her eyes went back to the tooth.

“Find the nail,” she said. “Find the object that doesn’t belong. Find the keepsake that makes your chest ache. That’s likely where the chorus is tied together. Burn that, and the voices fall out of time. Break that, and the frame remembers it’s only meat.”

The water gave a sudden, shallow pull, as though something beneath had sucked at it. The lamp flame leaned again, though the air remained still. Halloway’s face hardened.

“It’s listening too hard,” she said. “We’ve given it enough for now.”

She took one careful backward step, boots sliding through the water rather than lifting.

“Plainly,” she said, “yes. It’s a chorus. But not a fellowship. Not a crowd. A chorus the way a net is a family of knots. Every piece has been caught. Every piece has been pulled tight. And the whole thing only moves because something in the middle knows how to drag.”

The mass at the far end settled lower into the water, or seemed to. The cut in its chest leaked another thread of clear fluid. The sweet, funeral smell thickened until it sat on the tongue.

Halloway’s voice dropped.

“If it starts singing,” she said, “don’t listen for words. Just put fire in the throat and leave.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway turned the word over once, as if checking it for rust.

“Finish it,” she said. “Yes. It’s past lessons.”

She did not look toward the steps for approval. She looked at the water between herself and the thing, and at the way the lamplight lay across it in a long, shaking wedge. The cellar had gone quiet in the wrong way: no drip from the ceiling, no small settling of stone, only that thick, attentive stillness that made the ears invent sounds to fill the gap.

Halloway came back into the black water.

She did not go straight at the frame. She moved around it, a slow half-circle, boots sliding over drowned stone, the iron probe held low in one hand and the long knife in the other. The water resisted her legs, cold and greasy, and the smell rose in layers each time she disturbed it: pond-mud first, then sour milk, then copper, then that cloying sweetness underneath, like fat gone bad in a closed room.

“Plainly,” she said, “we take it apart in the order it would use us.”

Her eyes stayed on the fused hand near the surface.

“Reach first.”

She stopped just short of the hand and used the probe to press down on the water beside it. The surface tightened at once. Not a ripple. A response. Something beneath the frame had felt the pressure and considered it.

Halloway’s mouth thinned.

“Manners,” she said.

From her belt she unhooked a short iron spike, thick as a thumb and blunt at the head. She did not swing it. She set the point against the fused hand just above the knuckles, where the wrong thumb joined the mass, and struck the head once with the heavy pommel of the knife. The spike bit into the hand. The hand closed.

Not around her. Around the spike.

It closed fast, too, with a wet, sucking sound, the fingers drawing together like the jaws of a trap that had been waiting for exactly that shape. Halloway did not give it time to decide whether the iron was prey. She drove the spike downward until it pinned the hand against the cellar floor.

The water around it shivered. The frame’s low shoulder lifted a fraction, then dropped again, as if the arm attached to it had remembered it was not supposed to move yet.

“That’s the first courtesy,” Halloway said.

She cut at the wrist, if wrist was the word for the swollen joint where the young hand had been forced into the older arm. The blade met resistance, not bone but bundled cord and packed tissue, and she sawed through it with short, controlled strokes. Clear fluid wept from the cut, thick and adhesive, and the smell sharpened into something hot and sugary. Beneath the skin, there was no clean separation between hand and arm. There were only laced cords, crushed bone, and strips of flesh pressed together until they had taken the shape of usefulness.

The hand twitched on the spike.

Halloway cut deeper.

“Not yours,” she said, not to it, but in the flat tone of a woman marking inventory. “Not anymore.”

The last cord parted. The fused hand came free with a soft, obscene pull, leaving the arm ending in a ragged, waterlogged stump. Halloway lifted the hand by the spike, not by the flesh. It hung there, fingers still curled, thumb on the wrong side, knuckles smooth and terrible in the light. Water ran from it in slow threads.

She carried it to the nearest dryish stone she could find, a broken lip of wall half above the waterline, and set it down. Then she took a smaller blade from her belt and cut the tendons in the palm, one by one. The fingers loosened. The trap-shape died.

“No more hook,” she said.

The frame at the far end gave a low, internal adjustment. The water climbed its side by a finger’s width and slid back down. From the swollen throat came a small sound, two breaths at once, one thin and one wet, rubbing against each other.

Halloway did not answer it.

She went back for the arms.

The right arm was the longer of the two, the one that had been set too low in the male shoulder to give the frame reach. Halloway did not try to bend it. She cut into the armpit, where the borrowed skin had been folded and stitched. The blade found the crushed shoulder joint and the blackened cord wound around it. She worked the probe into the gap and levered sideways.

The arm lifted.

Not naturally. Not as a limb lifts when muscle chooses it. It lifted like a rope pulled from the other side of a wall.

Halloway’s face did not change.

“There,” she said. “That’s the lie.”

She cut the cord.

It snapped with a wet twang. The arm fell back into the water and immediately tried to rise again, this time reaching toward the sound of her voice. Halloway stepped inside its arc without splashing, hooked the probe behind the elbow, and broke the joint backward. The bone gave with a dull crack. She cut through the remaining straps of flesh and pulled. The arm came away in a tangle of packing and cord, trailing clear fluid.

She did not set it down gently. She dropped it onto the same stone ledge and cut it open from shoulder to wrist.

Inside, there was no proper muscle. There were long strips of pale tissue wound around a core of crushed bone and reed-like fiber, all bound with dark cord. The wrist had been packed with small fragments, teeth-sized bits of shell or bone, to give it weight. The hand attached to it was older than the fused one, the knuckles rougher, the nails gone, but the fingers had been sharpened at the tips by pressure until they came to stiff, curved points.

“Climbing hands,” Halloway said. “Or dragging hands. Not hands for holding.”

She cut the fingers off at the first joint and scattered them into the water where they could not gather. Then she split the forearm and severed the cords that had made it behave like a single limb. The pieces sagged into ordinary dead weight.

The left arm was worse because it was less finished.

It hung from the frame in a way that suggested it had not yet decided whether it belonged to the body or to the water. The skin around the socket was open, and beneath it the packing bulged loosely, wet and unsettled. When Halloway touched it with the probe, the whole arm rippled, not from the shoulder down but from the middle outward, as if something inside it had tried to turn around.

“This one’s still being persuaded,” she said.

She did not cut it cleanly. She drove the iron spike through the forearm and pinned it against the submerged stone before it could coil. Then she opened the shoulder seam and found the lacing. It was looser here, newer, the cords not yet bitten into the flesh. She cut them one by one. With each cut, the arm jerked faintly, not in pain but in confusion, like a draft animal that had lost the rein.

When the last cord parted, the arm slid free and immediately tried to sink away from the frame. Halloway caught it with the probe and hauled it to the ledge.

“None of you get to vote separately,” she said.

She cut it open and found the same packed mixture, but less settled: hair, shredded cloth, strips of skin, a sliver of rib, and something soft and gray that might once have been tongue. There was no object in it, no keepsake, only pressure and intent. She cut it into three pieces and broke the cords in each.

The frame now had no reach worth fearing. Its shoulders sagged inward, the low sockets empty, the chest listing slightly in the water. The head, if it could be called that, remained above the surface, the borrowed jaw too heavy for the skull, the eye sockets padded out and dull.

Halloway looked at the throat.

“Now the voice,” she said.

The cellar answered before she could move.

From the frame’s mouth came a sound so soft it almost disappeared under the water’s own silence. A breath. Then a small, broken note, the kind a child makes when trying not to cry too loudly. It had no words yet. It did not need them. It was shaped to make a person lean closer.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed.

“No,” she said.

The sound changed. It became older, rougher, a man’s voice with water in it.

“Cold,” it said.

Only that one word. Not a name. Not a plea. Just enough to suggest a person who had been in the dark too long.

Halloway waded closer.

“Cold is a weather,” she said. “Not a witness.”

She did not look at the mouth. She looked at the waterline under the jaw. The throat had been rebuilt, and the skin there was stretched too tight, almost shiny, with faint seams where different colors of tissue had been pressed together. She set the knife beneath the jawbone and cut upward, not into the mouth but into the throat cavity below it.

The frame shuddered.

The sound that came out was not one voice. It was several, badly timed: a woman’s gasp, a child’s hiccup, a man’s low groan, and underneath all of them a thin, wet hiss like air escaping a drowned lung. The smell burst upward, sweet and rotten and floral, thick enough to sit on the tongue.

Halloway breathed through her mouth and kept cutting.

“Open,” she said. “Let’s see what you’ve been practicing.”

The throat peeled apart.

Inside, there was no tongue. There was no clean windpipe either. Instead, the cavity had been hollowed and lined with skin from several mouths, pale patches and darker patches pressed together until they formed a wet, uneven tube. Strands of tissue hung across it like strings in a ruined instrument. Behind them, a second chamber had been packed with soft, spongy material that trembled even when nothing touched it.

Halloway used the probe to lift one strand.

It vibrated.

Not with sound. With memory.

“That’s the echo-box,” she said. “It doesn’t keep voices. It keeps the shape of them.”

The frame’s jaw worked. The heavy borrowed jaw dropped a little, then closed, then dropped again. The throat cavity tried to form the movement into speech. What came out was a mangled chord: “Help—” in one voice, “Mam—” in another, and, underneath, a small, precise imitation of Halloway’s own tone saying, Don’t answer it twice.

Halloway’s face hardened.

“That one’s mine,” she said. “And I don’t give it back.”

She cut the throat out.

It came away in a wet cluster, more like a knot of reeds than any human anatomy. She did not let it touch her bare hand. She held it with the probe and knife and carried it to the stone ledge. There she laid it open and found the true work inside: three small rings of gristle, not all from the same size of body, lashed around a sliver of bone and a scrap of soft leather that might once have been part of a shoe. The leather had been chewed by water and time, but it still held the shape of a small foot.

Halloway stared at it for one breath.

“Bait,” she said, but the word came out flatter than usual.

She took a waxed pouch from her belt and shook out a handful of coarse salt. She packed the salt into the opened throat cavity of the frame, pressing it deep into the ruined voice-box with the probe. The flesh hissed faintly, not from fire but from the shock of it, and the water around the frame tightened into black glass.

Then she took a rag from her kit, wrung it as dry as she could, and soaked it with oil from a small blackened flask. She stuffed the oily rag into the throat where the voice had been.

From an inner pocket she drew a short coil of slow-match and a striker. She struck once. The spark caught. The slow-match bloomed into a dull red point, then a thin yellow flame.

The cellar light seemed to lean away from it.

Halloway touched the flame to the rag.

The throat caught with a soft, greasy whoomp. Fire did not burn cleanly there. It burned through oil and salt and wet tissue, making steam and a high, thin screaming sound that might have been air escaping or might have been the last shape of several voices trying at once. The frame’s head jerked back. The water around it rose in a ring, not outward but upward, as if the cellar floor had tried to stand.

Halloway did not step back.

“Spoil the voice,” she said. “That’s the second courtesy.”

The fire ate inward. The throat cavity blackened, the mismatched skin curling, the reed-strands snapping one by one. The smell changed from sweet rot to scorched hair, burnt fat, and something mineral, like hot stones in a dirty river. The frame’s mouth opened, and for a moment it produced no sound at all. Then it produced a silence so complete it felt like pressure in the ears.

Halloway watched the throat burn until the fire slowed.

“Now the frame,” she said.

She went back to the chest.

The earlier cut still wept clear fluid, but the frame had begun to draw inward around itself, the water climbing its sides in thin black threads as if trying to hide the opened seams. Halloway cut the stitches around the first flap of skin and peeled it back farther. The lamplight from the steps reached the wet lattice inside and made the cords shine like black veins.

Under the first layer of packing, there was another layer she had not yet exposed.

This one was finer. Hair, mostly, but not loose. It had been woven into a thin caul with thread made from dried sinew, and the caul had been pressed against the inner ribs like a lining. Beneath it lay a paste of crushed bone, pond-mud, and something gray that looked like powdered shell. The smell coming from it was less sweet and more old: closed rooms, damp wool, graves opened after rain.

“Second skin,” Halloway said. “Keeps the pieces from arguing too loudly.”

She cut through it.

The frame convulsed.

Not a rise. Not a lunge. A full internal shiver, as if every stolen part had tried to move in a different direction at once. The water around it broke into oily ripples. The fused hand pinned on the stone ledge clicked against the rock. The cut arms twitched. The burning throat gave a sudden flare, then sank into smoke.

Halloway’s knife did not hesitate.

“Plainly,” she said, “it doesn’t like being known.”

She worked the probe into the chest lattice and spread the ribs apart. The frame had been built like a bad boat: the male chest served as the keel, the crushed ribs as ribs, the cords as stays. The pieces leaned toward the center, just as she had said. Not toward the skull. Not toward the hand. Toward the knot behind the place where a heart might have been if the thing had ever needed one.

The binding was there.

The child’s tooth hung in its web of black hair, pale and notched, threaded through with cord. Beside it lay the blue scrap of cloth and the sliver of bone she had seen before. But now, with the chest opened wider, she saw more. A small copper ring, green with age, wound through a loop of hair. A fragment of a clay bead. A knot of ribbon so faded it might once have been red. And beneath them, pressed into the packing like a nail driven through wood, a single human finger bone, small enough to belong to a child.

Halloway’s mouth tightened until it looked carved.

“There’s the chorus,” she said.

The frame tried to speak.

Without a throat, it should not have been able to speak. But the chest cavity itself vibrated, the cords humming, the packed material shaping the vibration into something almost like words. It was not language. It was the idea of language, the ghost of several voices at once: young, old, hurt, frightened, gentle, all of them layered into a single wet chord.

It sounded like help.

It sounded like company.

It sounded like someone who had been alone in the dark for a very long time and had learned how to make loneliness into a hook.

Halloway did not answer.

She took a shallow iron dish from her kit, the kind used for melting wax or holding evidence too small to trust to a pocket. She set it on the stone ledge, within the wedge of lamplight. Then she returned to the chest and began removing the binding objects one by one with the knife point and probe.

The child’s tooth first.

The hair around it tightened as she lifted it, as if the frame were trying to keep it. Halloway cut the hair away close to the knot and let the tooth fall into the iron dish with a tiny click.

The blue cloth next. It came away trailing clear fluid and a single strand of fair hair.

The copper ring. The clay bead. The ribbon. The finger bone.

Each time she removed one, the frame shivered. Each time, the sound in the chest changed pitch, losing one layer, becoming less like a voice and more like water moving through broken reeds.

When the last object lay in the dish, Halloway looked down at them.

“Not a person,” she said. “A set of handles.”

She poured oil over the objects. Then she touched the slow-match to the dish.

The hair burned first. It flared with a sharp, animal stink, curling into black sparks. The ribbon caught next, briefly blue beneath the flame. The bead cracked. The copper ring blackened. The finger bone hissed and split. The child’s tooth resisted longest, glowing at the edges before it popped into fragments with a sound like a small knuckle breaking.

The frame screamed.

Not with a mouth. With the whole cellar.

The water lifted around it in a black crown. The stone walls gave back a sound that was not an echo but several echoes arriving late and wrong. The lamp-light shivered. The sweet rot-smell turned suddenly hot, then thin, then empty, as if something had been pulled out of the air by the roots.

Halloway stood over the burning dish and watched until nothing in it moved.

Then she took the probe and ground the burnt remnants into ash.

“No song,” she said.

The frame began to come apart.

Not dramatically. Not all at once. It sagged. The water around it lost its oily skin. The pieces stopped leaning toward one another. The chest cavity collapsed inward where the binding had been, and the packed material began to loosen, hair and cloth and bone drifting apart in the black water like rubbish after a flood.

Halloway did not trust it.

“Frames remember being frames,” she said. “Break the habit.”

She went back into the chest with the knife.

She cut the central lattice where the ribs had been lashed together. The cords snapped one by one, each with a wet twang, and the male chest spread open like a ruined basket. She cut the stays that held the shoulders in their low, wrong angle. The sockets crumbled inward, bone fragments slipping from their places. She cut the packing free and pulled it out in fistfuls, letting it sink or drift, checking each handful for hidden objects.

She found one more thing.

Wedged low in the belly packing, near where the frame’s weight had been concentrated, was a smooth stone wrapped in a scrap of burial linen. The linen had gone brown with age and water, but the knot was tied with a child’s hair. Halloway lifted it with the probe and felt the whole frame give a weak, dragging pull, as if the stone had been an anchor it had not yet admitted to using.

“Sneaky,” she said.

She cut the hair and dropped the stone into the iron dish. The linen burned slowly, smelling of damp and old graves. The stone cracked in the heat but did not explode. When it cooled, Halloway crushed it with the probe and found nothing inside but a smear of gray powder.

“Still sneaky,” she said. “But less.”

She turned back to the frame.

Now she worked without conversation except for the short, practical words she used to mark each stage.

“Shoulders.”

She broke the remaining shoulder joints apart and cut the cords that had held them low.

“Spine.”

There was no true spine, only a bundle of bones lashed around a length of dark wood, perhaps part of a fence post, perhaps part of a coffin. She cut the lashing and pulled the wood free. It came away slick and swollen, and when she split it with the knife, black water ran from the grain.

“Hips.”

The pelvis had been built from two different bodies forced into one shape. She found the seams and cut them apart. One half sank at once. The other floated for a breath, buoyed by trapped gas, before Halloway opened it and let the water in.

“Legs.”

There were legs, after a fashion, but they had not been finished. One ended in a foot too small for the body, the toes fused into a paddle. The other was mostly packing and cord, with a human thigh bone set sideways through it. She cut both free, split them, and broke the joints.

“Skull.”

She saved it for last.

The head floated lower now, the borrowed jaw hanging loose. The eye sockets still held their padding, and from a distance it could still look almost human, almost pitiful, almost like something that had once had a name. Halloway did not give it the chance.

She hooked the probe under the jaw and forced it open. Inside the mouth, there were teeth from at least three different people, some worn flat, some sharp, one still holding a fragment of milk-white root. The tongue-space had been filled with a knot of wet hair and shredded skin. She pulled it out with the knife point and let it fall into the iron dish.

“Bait,” she said again.

She set the blade under the skull’s brow and cut the cords that had fixed the jaw to it. The jaw came away with a soft, sucking sound. She cut the padding from the eye sockets. Beneath it, there were no eyes, only two shallow cups packed with clay and hair. She scooped them out.

Then she placed the skull on the stone ledge and struck it once, twice, three times with the pommel of the knife until it cracked. She did not smash it out of anger. She broke it the way one breaks a lock that has been picked too many times. The skull split into several pieces, and from inside the cranial cavity fell a small folded scrap of paper, soft as cloth from long immersion.

Halloway stared at it.

She did not touch it with her bare hand.

She lifted it with the probe and knife and carried it to the iron dish. The paper was too wet to read, but the ink had bled into the shape of a name, or perhaps several names, layered over one another until no single letter remained legible.

“Naming,” she said. “Of course.”

She burned it.

The paper did not flame easily. It smoked, blackened, and curled, giving off a smell like wet wool and old candles. Halloway held the slow-match to it until the last corner turned to ash. Then she scattered the ash into the water and watched it disappear.

The cellar grew quieter.

Not peaceful. Quiet in the way a room grows quiet after a machine has been stopped.

Halloway returned to the frame and began the last work.

She took the waxed pouch of salt and the larger pouch of quicklime from her belt. She opened the salt first and worked it into every cut she had made: the shoulders, the chest, the belly, the skull fragments, the ruined throat. Salt drew water. It made wet things remember dryness. The frame’s flesh tightened where it touched.

Then she used the lime.

She poured it into the opened chest cavity, into the broken skull, into the throat where the fire had blackened the tissue, and into the joints where the arms and legs had been forced. The lime fell white against the dark water and the wet flesh. For a moment nothing happened. Then the water around the frame began to steam.

It did not boil. It heated in a slow, angry way, the lime biting into the wetness, drawing it out, turning the slick surfaces dull. The smell changed again. The sweetness died under mineral sharpness. The pond-mud smell thinned. The cellar began to smell like a burnt wall after rain.

Halloway stood back and watched.

The pieces of the frame lay separate now, but she did not trust separation alone. She took the last of her oil and poured it over the exposed flesh, the broken chest, the skull fragments, the cut arms, the fused hand on the ledge. Then she touched the slow-match to each place in turn.

The fire caught slowly, because everything had been wet for too long. But oil is patient in its own way. It found the dried edges where salt and lime had done their work. It found the hair in the packing. It found the oily residue in the throat. The flames were not bright and heroic. They were low, blue at the base, yellow at the tips, and they burned with a thick smoke that smelled of char, salt, burnt fat, and old cloth.

Halloway used the probe to turn the pieces.

She opened each burning heap and looked for movement. She looked for the waterline climbing. She looked for the little shiver that meant something was still listening. She found none. The fused hand curled once in the heat, then cracked and lay still. The arms blackened and fell apart at the cords. The chest cavity collapsed inward, the ribs slipping free of their lattice. The skull fragments whitened, split, and crumbled at the edges.

The water around the remains grew sluggish and ordinary. Black still, but no longer attentive.

Halloway waited.

She waited long enough for the fire to burn down to embers on the stone ledge. She waited long enough for the steam to thin. She waited long enough for the cellar to become only a cellar again: wet stone, standing water, burnt smell, and the ordinary dark beyond the lamplight.

Then she took the probe and touched each piece one last time.

The fused hand did not close.

The arms did not reach.

The throat did not echo.

The chest did not lean.

The skull did not turn.

Halloway wiped the knife on a clean rag from her kit, then wiped the probe, then wiped her hands. She did not put the tools away immediately. She stood there, breathing through her mouth, watching the water for any last lie.

At last she spoke.

“Plainly,” she said, “it took several dead and made them into one lure. It hollowed the chest for weight, lowered the shoulders for reach, built a false throat for voices, and used stolen keepsakes as nails. It got far enough to almost pass in the dark, far enough to ask for help, far enough to make a person forget the seams.”

She looked at the ash and broken fragments.

“Now it’s only evidence.”

She crouched, stiff knees cracking, and gathered the burnt remains of the binding objects with the knife and probe: the cracked tooth, the blackened ring, the ash of cloth and hair and paper. She placed them in a clean waxed pouch and tied it shut. Not because they were precious. Because they had been handles, and handles should not be left lying where another pair of hands might find them.

When the pouch was secured, she finally allowed herself one small, grim sound that might have been a laugh in a kinder life.

“If it starts singing after this,” she said, “I’ll be very put out.”

The cellar gave no answer.

Halloway straightened, wiped her blade once more, and looked toward the lamplight on the steps.

“Plainly,” she said, “it’s finished.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I stare at the charred pieces floating in the black water, the smell of salt and burnt bone thick in my throat. "It never tried to run," I say, my voice low. "Even at the end. It just... let you take it apart."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway did not look away from the black water at once.

The charred pieces floated low, nudged by nothing, moved by nothing worth naming. Salt had dulled the surface. Lime had turned some of the water cloudy near the stone ledge. The smell was no longer sweet. It was mineral, scorched, and tired in the way a room smells after a fire has been made to do unpleasant work.

“Don’t say let,” Halloway said at last. “It gives the thing too much grace.”

She used the probe to turn a blackened fragment over. It was mostly bone, or what had been bone before the fire and the water and the pressure had made it into something else. Nothing inside it moved. Nothing leaned toward the light.

“It didn’t run because it had no proper running in it,” she said. “Running needs agreement. Bones have to agree with joints. Joints with muscles. Fear gives the order, and the body takes it. That frame had no agreement. It had cord, pressure, stolen weight, and pieces still learning one another’s lies. The legs were not finished. The hips were two arguments tied together. The spine was a post and a hope. It could reach. It could float. It could make the water do its thinking. It could not turn and flee.”

She wiped the probe on a rag, slow and thorough, though the rag was already ruined.

“And there’s a worse reason than that,” she went on. “It didn’t need to run while it still had a lure.”

Her eyes moved over the remains without softening.

“Lures don’t chase. They sit. They look hurt. They make the living do the traveling. That thing was built to be found, not to hunt in open ground. It relied on stillness, voice, and reach. If we had come closer, if we had answered it, if one of us had leaned in with pity already half-formed in the throat, it would have spent everything it had left on that one moment. It didn’t need speed. It needed a mistake.”

She set the probe against a piece of burnt packing and pressed it apart. Inside, there was only ash and wet fiber. She watched it disperse.

“Don’t mistake patience for surrender,” she said. “It wasn’t submitting. It was waiting. There’s a difference. Submission knows it’s beaten. That thing did not know anything so useful. It was still measuring. Every cut I made, it lost a little of the shape, but it kept listening. It heard my voice. It heard yours. It heard the tools. If it could have taken one of those sounds and made a door out of it, it would have.”

Halloway straightened slowly, knees giving their dry complaint. She kept her gaze on the waterline around the broken remains.

“It didn’t run because running would have wasted what little was left. It had no lungs for flight. No heart for panic. No self worth saving in the ordinary sense. The binding was its self, and the binding was in that dish. Once I burned the tooth, the cloth, the hair, the paper, the rest was only meat remembering instructions.”

A thin curl of steam rose from the lime. She watched it until it vanished.

“If it had run,” she added, “I’d have been more impressed. And significantly more annoyed.”

She began gathering her tools, checking each one before it went back to belt or kit. Knife wiped. Probe wiped. Spike cleaned of black residue. The iron dish scraped free of ash and tucked away. The waxed pouch containing the burnt remains of the binding objects she kept separate, near her hand, not in the depths of the kit where it might be forgotten.

“But don’t comfort yourself with it,” she said. “The fact that it stayed put doesn’t mean it was harmless at the end. It means it had reached the limit of its design. It was still dangerous the way a flooded cellar is dangerous. Not because it wants you dead. Because it can hold you under while you’re busy thinking you’ve won.”

She looked once more toward the far end of the cellar, where the water had begun to settle into a dull, ordinary black.

“It let me take it apart,” she said, correcting the phrase again, harder this time, “because I spoiled the lure. Once the seams were seen, the voice named, the binding found, the frame had lost its best defense. It could no longer make us believe it was a person. It could only be a thing. And things can be broken.”

Her mouth twisted, not with humor, but with something close to exhaustion.

“So no. It didn’t run. It waited for us to be stupid enough to finish the work for it by coming closer. We didn’t. That’s the only victory here.”

She wiped her hands one last time and looked toward the stairs, though she did not move toward them yet.

“If you dream about it singing,” she said, “don’t hum along.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the water, then at her face. "It would have used your voice first," I say quietly. "Because I'd have come for you."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway’s hands paused over the kit. She did not look at Pike at once. She listened to the cellar instead, to the ordinary drip beginning again somewhere beyond the lamplight, to the small settling of stone after fire and salt and lime. When she finally spoke, her voice was flat, but not unkind.

“Then it would have been clever,” she said. “Not kind. Not personal. Clever.”

She tied the waxed pouch shut and pressed the knot flat with her thumb.

“It doesn’t use the voice that’s truest. It uses the voice that spends best. If my voice would make you step closer without counting the water, then my voice is worth more to it than a stranger’s cry. A child’s voice brings pity. Mine would bring habit. Obedience. The stupid little reflex that makes a person move toward someone who has sounded reliable for years.”

She looked up then. Her face was tired, lined, and entirely unsentimental.

“It would not have made me sound brave,” she said. “Brave makes people cautious. It would have made me sound hurt. Or winded. Or just steady enough to make you think I still knew what I was doing. It would not have told you to run. It would have said here. Or help me. Or don’t leave me. It would have found the place where your training ends and your loyalty begins.”

She set the kit down but kept one hand near it, as if the lesson was not finished.

“If you hear my voice in a place I have no business being, do not come for the sound. Look for the body. If there is no body, it is bait. If there is a body, assume it is bait anyway. Check the waterline. Check the seams. If the voice knows things I know but the shape is wrong, that is not me. That is something wearing my habits like a borrowed jaw.”

A faint, grim humor touched her mouth and vanished.

“And if it starts giving orders in my tone,” she said, “be suspicious. The real me would be telling you to get back, keep the light steady, and stop making faces at corpses.”

She let the cellar’s quiet stand for a breath.

“You don’t owe the voice a rescue,” she said. “If it has my voice, it has already taken something from me. The only thing left to do is not let it take you too. You owe me that much: don’t answer, don’t lean in, and burn whatever is doing the talking.”

Then, after a moment, quieter but still practical:

“If I am really in trouble, I will make it unpleasant enough that you won’t mistake it for a song.”

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I look at the water again, then back at her. "Would you have come for me?" I ask, not looking at her face. "If it used my voice."
