dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren laid the sword down flat on the stones between them, hilt turned toward the witnesses, so that her hands would be empty and visible for what came next. That too was the code: nothing in them but the account.

"Halric Voss," she said, pitching her voice past Del to the gallery. "Sword-sworn to House Miravel. Master of the high line, quick on the recovery, and no man's fool. I say this first, because the account begins with what he was, and to make him smaller would make me larger. The code does not permit it."

She drew a breath and gave it plainly.

"Two exchanges. On the first we measured one another. He found my depth; I found his speed. On the second, he pressed the high line as he favored, and the stones betrayed him where the drainage runs — his rear foot slid a hand's breadth. I report the footing because the witnesses saw it, not to excuse what I did. His foot slipped. My hand did not. He was no longer where he intended to be, and my point was where he had been. It entered beneath his lowest right rib, angled upward, a hand's length of steel. It cut the liver and opened the lung.

"I drew the blade back straight. I did not turn it in him. I say that because it is true, not because it softens anything. Nothing softens it.

"He stood for four breaths afterward. I counted. I always count. He took hold of the steel with both hands, which men do, and which never works, and I wish that it did. Then he went down on his left side. He tried to speak — twice. Air and blood came, and nothing else. I do not know what he meant to say, and I will not give him a last word he did not have. That would be a kindness to you and a theft from him, and this account is his, not yours and not mine."

A pause took her then, one breath, and she did not use it to escape. She resumed.

"It was quick. Quicker than anyone expected. Speed in these things is mostly the other man's. He pressed when pressing was wrong, and I did not stay my hand, because a stayed hand is not mercy. It is only a second wound, arriving late."

Then she looked at Del directly, for the first time since the blade had come free.

"This is the twelfth account I have given. It does not grow shorter. I have never once enjoyed it, and I am glad that I have not. If any part of what I have said rings false to you — and you stood closer to him than anyone living — say so now, before the witnesses, and I will amend it. If it stands, ask me what the account has left out, and I will answer it here, once, plainly. And when it is finished, we lift him together. That is also the code, and he is owed the weight."

She waited, hands empty, and did not look away from him, because the account was owed to the second's face as much as to the second's ears.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out the breath I'd been holding, my throat tight. "It stands true. I saw the foot slip." I pause, my voice dropping lower so only she can hear. "What did his eyes do, when the steel went in? The account leaves that out."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. When she spoke, her voice had come down to the level of his — a register for two people and no gallery.

"That part is not in the account because the account is for the witnesses," she said. "What you are asking for is for you alone. I will give it once, as promised, and quietly."

She looked once at the body, then back to him.

"He looked down first. Twelve men now, and every one of them has looked down, as if the eyes could dispute what the hands were already learning. Halric was no different, and I will not pretend he was above a thing so old as that. Then he looked up. At me, not past me. And I will tell you what was in his eyes as nearly as I can name it, because nearly is all I have.

"It was not pain. Pain is slow and he was quick, and it had not reached him yet. What was in his eyes was the finding-out. A master of the high line spends his whole life knowing where his body is — it is the first thing they teach and the last thing they forget. For one breath the ground had told him he did not know, and his eyes were still working at that problem, still a swordsman's eyes, still solving, when the rest of him began to understand that the problem had changed.

"He looked at me as if to ask something. I do not know what. I will not guess and I will not invent, for the same reason I did not give him words. But I held his look, because to turn from a dying man is to flee, and so whatever he searched for in my face, it was there in front of him. I will report what was in it, since I report my faults with my merits: attention. Only attention. I was counting his breaths before he had finished taking the first. He deserved a face and he got a witness. That is the failure in me today, and I set it beside the footing and let it stand.

"At the last — the third breath, or the fourth — his eyes went elsewhere. Past me, past the stones, past everything. I have seen it eleven times before, and it is not peace, whatever they say at the funerals. It is only that the leaving happens by a door he was not looking at."

She let the quiet hold for a moment, then ended it, because endings were also owed.

"That is the whole of what his eyes did, and the account is finished." She crossed to Halric and knelt, gathering the man's shoulders with care, mindful of the wound, mindful of everything. "Now the weight. Take him under the arms and lift on my word, not before. We will go slowly to wherever he is lain. He has been hurried enough today."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren bowed her head a fraction — the form's only acknowledgment that it was being met — and straightened, lifting her voice back to the size of the gallery. What he had called for was not the account again. It was the attestation: the account in its smallest and hardest shape, the one that would be carried to House Miravel, entered in the record, and never amended.

"Halric Voss," she said, "sword-sworn to House Miravel, master of the high line, fell this day by my hand. The wound was a thrust beneath the lowest right rib, angled upward, a hand's length of steel. It cut the liver and opened the lung. The blade came out straight; it was not turned. His rear foot slipped where the drainage runs, and my hand did not slip, and I set the one beside the other as they happened, because the witnesses saw both. He stood four breaths. I counted them. He went down on his left side and did not speak. I gave him no words and I took none from him.

"I have added nothing and withheld nothing that the code permits spoken. The account is his. It stands as given. It is finished."

She let the last word lie on the stones and did not pick it up again.

Then the form was satisfied, and her voice came back down to the size of two people and a burden. She settled her grip at Halric's shoulders, smoothing the man's collar flat first with two fingers — a small, useless order restored to the world.

"Under the arms. High, at the armpits, and keep his arms against his sides; they will want to swing. Do not lift before my word. There is no counting in this part. Counting was for him."

She waited until the pull at her arms told her the other half had been taken.

"Now."

Auren lifted with her legs, back straight, and the body rose between them. He weighed no more than he had at breakfast; the dead only seem heavier because no part of them helps anymore. She took the greater drag of the shoulders without remark — they were hers by choice — and turned her forearm so his head rested against it and would not hang. A man's dignity in death begins at the neck.

She set the first step herself, slow and even, a bearer's pace.

"House Miravel will ask you for your own account after, in your own words, away from witnesses," she said. "Give them what you saw — no more and no less than you gave me here. You did it right the first time. Do it the same way with them listening."

Another step, and another, the body level between them.

"And walk as I walk. This is the last pace he has, and no one will hurry him again."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I adjust my grip, the weight of him settling against my chest. "His eyes... thank you." I match her step, my own breath steadying. "House Miravel will want more than just the account. They'll want to know if it was clean."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not break stride. The body swayed with each step, and each step corrected it, so that bearing the dead was a conversation held entirely in small adjustments.

"Do not thank me for his eyes," she said. "I did not look away because looking away is flight, and I was not the one dying. Thank the code, if you thank anything. It held my face still when I might not have managed it alone."

A step. Another.

"As for clean — houses ask that question the way the wounded ask a surgeon. They want the pain to have a shape they can hate or forgive. So answer it in two parts, and I will swear to both. The manners of it were clean: one thrust, straight out, no turning, no second stroke offered to a falling man. If clean means the manners, tell them yes." She shifted her forearm; his head had begun to slide, and she brought it level again. "If clean means deserved by skill alone, then no — and no honest duellist has ever earned that word, and I will not begin spending it on Halric. Luck moved his foot. My hand was already moving. Either alone does not kill a master of the high line. It took both, and I will say so in whatever room they receive me. If they want it cleaner than that, they want it false, and I do not sell it false."

The stones ahead showed the dark seam of the drainage run. She watched her own feet as they crossed it, and chose her footing with care — not from fear. Two bearers and a burden go down where one slip began, and she did not intend to demonstrate it over him.

"I will not tell them the ground did it, because that robs him of the duel he fought. And I will not tell them I out-fenced him, because in the crossing that killed him, I did not. Grief will ask you to choose one of those stories. Refuse the choice. They will put it to you more gently than they put it to me, because you are grieving and they believe grief buys honesty. It buys the opposite."

A few paces more, and her voice came down again.

"Miravel asks if it was clean. The last house asked whether he suffered. The one before sent a clerk who wanted only the angle of the wound, and I gave it to a hand's breadth, and he wrote it without looking up. Every house receives the same account. It answers more questions than they think to ask.

"We are near the gate. They will want to wash him at once. Washing can wait a quarter hour; dignity cannot be repaired afterward, only remembered. Make them wait. You have the standing to make them wait — and I will spend mine backing you."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren kept the bearing level and did not halt — a stop would be remembered as hesitation, and Halric had been owed none of that in life — but she slowed her answer to the pace of the steps, so that neither would be hurried.

"Plainly, then, in the words you will give them. Grief makes questions come twice; let them. That is what I am for."

A step. Another.

"It entered at the front of him, on the right side, just beneath the lowest rib — two fingers in from the soft of his flank. If you would know the place without doubting it: set your own hand where your ribs end and your stomach gives, on the right. That is where it landed. Every witness who says otherwise is remembering it from an angle, and angles lie in kindness."

She shifted her forearm; his head had slipped a fraction, and she brought it level before continuing.

"Where it ended is a different place, and the record will want both. The point traveled upward and inward, a hand's length. It finished high on the right, in the lung. The liver lies along that road, and the steel did not go beside it. The heart was never touched. It was the lung that took him — the liver bled, but it was the breath that failed, and the four he stood were the four he had. I counted the ones he spent."

"When he is laid out, before they wash him, I will put two fingers on the mark if you ask it. Seen is steadier than heard, and I would rather you carry a place than a sentence. I will show the witnesses the same, so the record holds a spot on the body and not only words about it."

The gate shadow reached them, and her voice came down once more.

"And if you meant where he fell, and not where the steel landed — on his left side, twenty paces back, at the seam of the drainage. The witnesses marked it. The stones keep it better than I can."

She squared her grip at the shoulders.

"We lay him on his back inside, head toward the house. Say the word to them about the washing, as I told you. Then the fingers, if you want them."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight again. "Show me the mark. I want to carry it right." I shift my grip as we cross the threshold into the cool dimness of the gatehouse. "His sister will ask me to describe it. She was always good with maps."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The gatehouse kept a bier of rough planks against the inner wall for exactly this traffic, and Auren steered them to it without ceremony. "Across. Head to the house." She gave the word, and the body came down level between them — she felt the descent shared in her shoulders before she trusted it — and she knelt to slide her arm from beneath his head last, laying him onto the planks by measure of her own forearm rather than letting the weight drop the last inch without her.

His eyes were still open. They had gone elsewhere, but they had not been shut, and she shut them now with the backs of two fingers, the way one closes a book that has been finished rather than abandoned.

"There," she said, mostly to the plank. "He is done asking."

Then she moved to his right side and knelt again. The shirt had stiffened where the blood had dried; she folded it up in careful layers rather than tearing it, baring the ribs in the dimness.

"Remember he was standing when it was done. He has settled since. The place has not moved." She set two fingertips on the mark, lightly, the same two fingers she had named on the road. "Here. Small, isn't it. They always are — smaller than their work. A man expects a doorway and finds two fingers' width. If you want it in your hand as well as your eyes, put your fingers beside mine. Memory sits better in skin."

She waited the space of a breath for whatever he chose, and went on regardless, because the map was owed whether he took it in his hand or only his ears.

"Now, for his sister. She is owed three bearings and a mercy, and you may give them in these words or better ones. First bearing: where it entered — front of him, right side, two fingers beneath the lowest rib, where the ribs finish and the belly gives. Second: the road — upward and a little toward the centre of him, a hand's length, and no further. Third: where it ended — high in the right chest, in the lung. And the mercy: the heart lies left of the centre, lower than where the road ended. They never met. Give her that one even if she does not ask it, because it is the question under the map. When a sister asks where, she is asking two other things — did he linger, and could anyone have come sooner. The four breaths answer the first. The two exchanges answer the second. Hand her all of it before she must ask. The asking is the worse wound."

She drew the stiffened cloth back down over him and smoothed it flat.

"I will tell you my one fault in this, since I tell my faults. Twelve times now I have wanted to move the mark an inch — lower, or toward the side, somewhere a telling sits easier in the mouth. I have never done it, and you must not either, and here is the hard reason: she will look at him when he is washed, and the body does not amend itself to kind sentences. A map that is wrong by mercy is wrong twice — tonight, and again when she stands over him and finds the truth sitting where you swore it was not. After that she will never trust your telling again. And she will need it, later, when the years start taking the details."

Beyond the door, boots on stone; the house had begun to gather. She did not rise.

"If she wants it from the hand that gave it, she may have it from me — the same words, unsoftened. I will not dress it for grief; dressing it is how it arrives broken. But if she wants it from you, that is the better gift, because you are hers and I am the reason she needs a map at all. The quarter hour begins when you say it does. Make them wait all of it." A pause, and the dry ghost of something not quite a smile. "My sword is still lying on the stones where I left it. Someone will fetch it, or it will lie out tonight. It has earned the rest either way."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. Over the body, she inclined her head the way she did in a salle when steel found her fairly — acknowledgment of a touch, given without grievance.

"A touch," she said. "Fair, and on the true line. I promised you my faults with one hand and dressed one with the other. The word 'mercy' was mine, not the code's. Strike it from everything I told you. The heart's position is measurement. I hung a mercy on measurement, and you were right to cut it down."

Beyond the door the house had collected in the light of the threshold. She did not lower her voice for it.

"No one washes him yet," she said to the doorway, and turned back to the bier. "The eyes I gave you quietly, because they were his and then yours. The blade's work is different. It is the floor the account stands on, and floors do not whisper.

"The record says I cut the liver and opened the lung. True words. Quiet words. A clerk can carry them thirty years without ever setting them down hard. You have asked what they fold flat. So: unfolded.

"The blade did four things. There is no fifth. First, it opened him — skin, the muscle of the belly wall, the lining within. Three layers, the width of the steel, at the front of him beneath the lowest right rib. That part is nothing; a body parts there the way cloth parts. Second, travelling upward and a little inward, the point entered the liver — the right lobe, which lies directly under where it went in. A cut liver does not bleed as an arm bleeds. It seeps. It seeped into the belly, where blood has no road out, and it did not stop when he stopped. I report that plainly; some of the dying was still under way when the man was finished. Third, the point passed through the dome of muscle that divides belly from chest — the muscle a man breathes with — and opened the right lung. A hand's length of road in all. Fourth, it came back along its own road. One road in, one road out, no turning. I have said that before, but it belongs in this list, or the list is dressed.

"Now what it did it to. The liver had begun a death that takes minutes. The lung declined to grant them. An opened lung fills with its own blood; the blood takes the air's places; every breath draws it deeper. The first of his four breaths was mostly air. The last was mostly blood. He drowned upright, in the time I already counted for you — and the counting is the only reason I know the first from the last.

"I said I would not give him a last word he did not have. I will tell you what the two attempts were made of, because they were not words. Air, then blood, in that order, and nothing else. Not stubbornness and not peace — the parts of him that make words had no air to spend. What came from his mouth was the wound itself, leaving him upward along the road the steel had cut. That is what a wound made in breath does. It escapes.

"So he was killed by breath, not blood. The blood had done perhaps a tenth of its work when the breath ended. The record may say lung and liver forever. You carry the true proportion.

"The heart was left of centre, and the road ended above it and to the right. They did not meet. The blade had no opinion about his heart; it was not aimed there and did not arrive there. That is the whole of that, stated as measurement, which is how I should have stated it the first time.

She looked at her own two fingers, then at the folded cloth over the ribs.

"If any word in what I have said was chosen for comfort, name it, and I will replace it with a harder one. Twelve accounts have taught me the teller is always the last to find his own tact. That is why the code gives the second the right to strike.

"Keep the map for his sister. But understand now what it is a map of. It is short because a map must be carried for years, in one hand, while the other hand is held out to be gripped. This is the ground. You asked to carry the mark right. Now you carry the mark and everything beneath it."

She stayed kneeling, hands open, and the house at the door had gone very quiet. No one had gone for water. The quarter hour, whoever was keeping it, was being kept.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I reach out and put my own fingers beside hers, pressing the memory of the mark into my skin. My voice comes out rough. "I'll tell her exactly." I look up, meeting her eyes over Halric's body. "Tell the witnesses to come in. They should see it before it's washed away."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the second's fingers settle beside hers, and let them stay a moment past what the showing required.

"Good," she said. "In twelve accountings I have learned this much about seconds: the ones who only look at the mark begin revising it within a year. The ones who touch it cannot. You will dream of it. That is the toll for carrying it right, and it is cheaper than carrying it wrong."

She rose and stepped back to the head of the bier.

"We stand now. Kneeling is for the account. Standing is for the record."

Then she turned her voice to the size of the doorway.

"Witnesses only — those who stood at the ropes. The rest of the house grieved from farther off, and distance does not qualify a grief. They may wait. Come in by twos. Look as long as looking takes. Ask while the asking can be answered over the body itself. Touch nothing — the second has already put his hand to the mark, and that right is spent. When you have looked, say that you have seen, and give your name to the clerk."

They came in by twos. She counted them, because she counted everything: five. A clerk with a ledger. A woman in Miravel's colours who pressed her knuckles to her mouth and did not take them down until she had. A grey man who had carried his own sword forty years, by the way he held his hands.

She folded the cloth back once and left it folded, and to each pair she gave the same words, in the same order, at the same pace.

"Beneath the lowest right rib, on the right side, two fingers. One road in, one road out. One wound." And once, to the pair that lingered longest: "Count them if you doubt anything else I have said. There is one. Let no one tell you tonight that the blade was turned or that I struck a falling man. The body says otherwise, and the body takes no side."

It was the grey man who frowned. "I'd have sworn it sat lower," he said.

"You stood on his left, above the seam of the drainage. From there the eye borrows an inch the mark does not own — the slope lends it. The place has not moved since he was standing; your angle has. Look again from where I knelt."

He shifted, crouched with the stiffness of his years, and looked from her place.

"Seen," he said, and gave his name to the clerk.

When all five had done the same, she stood over the clerk's shoulder and dictated the last of it. "Write the three bearings, as spoken. Write: shown before washing. Write: the second set his hand beside the account's. And write that no witness offered amendment to any part of the record. Use the word 'amendment' exactly. It is the word houses look for when they want to reopen a finished thing, and I want them not to find it."

The pen scratched. She listened to it with something dangerously close to satisfaction, and set that down with her faults. "The sound of a record closing is the best sound this work makes," she said, quietly, to no one in the gallery. "I have come to rely on it more than I should. Long practice. It goes in the account of me as well."

Then, at the full size of the house again: "The quarter hour is spent. Bring water — warm, and no hurrying hands. He has kept every appointment given him today. Let him keep the last one at his own pace."

A boy brought the sword in at last, flat across both palms as though it might still be hot. Auren took it, weighed it once, and leaned it against the wall inside the door, edge to the stone. "It has no further business with him," she said. "It stays by the door until I do."

Last, she came back to Del, and her voice came down to the size she kept for him.

"What I told you of his eyes was given to you alone, and I do not take it back. Whether his sister has a right to any of it is not mine to say. You knew him at breakfast. I knew him at the second exchange. You are the better judge, and the judgment is yours — that is the last thing I will put in your hands today. Send for me only if she wants the words from the hand that gave them. I keep one version. Two versions is how houses learn to disbelieve one another, and she will need to believe you for years."

She looked once at the body, at the collar she had smoothed twice now, and stepped back a full pace — the first distance she had put between them since the stones.

"You have it in your hand already. I watched it land."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once, and the room had learned what that pause meant: not hesitation, but a thing being weighed on scales that took no shortcuts.

"Clerk," she said, without turning her head. "The ledger stands as written. Nothing spoken in this room from this breath onward amends it. If a house asks why the pen stopped, tell them the second asked a question the record was never built to hold."

Then she faced Del.

"You ask for all of it. Good. Take it in the order you named it, and see how much of 'all of it' you are already carrying.

"How long he took: four breaths. You have heard it twice — once on the stones, once in the attestation — and the second time is written down, which is the shape of it that outlives us both. If you want it a third time: four breaths, counted. But grief asks in threes, and the answer does not grow truer with the asking.

"What he said: nothing. He tried twice, and what came was air and then blood, in that order, and no word in either. I told you I would not give him a last word he did not have. I add this now — neither will I give you a silence with something hidden in it. There is no syllable I am keeping in a drawer. Nothing is what there was. That is not withholding. That is inventory.

"So the weight of your question was never in the first two. It is in the third."

She drew a breath and did not use it to escape.

"The code, and I have the articles by heart because twelve times teaches the text better than any clerk's copy: the victor speaks the wound, the manner of the wound, and the count. The victor answers the second's questions truly. That is the whole of what the code touches today. There is no article that puts a dying man's face into a spoken account. If you can name one, name it before this room, and I will speak the face aloud and let the pen take it down. I will wait."

She let the wait be real. No one named an article.

"It is not there because the code's authors had heard victors talk," she said. "Everything in my account can be checked. The thrust — the body carries it, and you have set your fingers beside it. The slip — the stones hold the seam, and five witnesses saw it. The count — a number, and numbers cannot flatter; no one bothers to lie where lying serves nothing. Every word I have given this room, someone standing in it had the right to contest, and one of you did contest, and the account survived the contest. That is why it stands. Not because I am trusted. Because it is attackable, and it held.

"His face is the one thing in this day that cannot be checked. Only I saw the eyes go. Write it in the ledger and you have cut the record's one unarmed gate, and I will tell you where it breaks, because I have watched houses try: no one who wants to reopen a finished thing attacks the steel. The steel is iron. They attack the face. *You say he looked at you so — who saw it beside you?* And a record that stood against everything comes down on that one sentence.

"There is worse. A dying man's last look cannot be told without flattering the teller. Say his eyes asked something — whose sentence is that? Say they went elsewhere, say it was not peace — mine again. Every telling of a face sets the teller a little nearer the light and the dead a little further from his own death. The last boast left to a victor is intimacy with the dying. The code was written by people who had heard it.

"So the face stays out of the record. Not for his sake. Not for yours. For the record's.

"But hear the rest, because it is what answers you. I did not keep the face. I gave it — on the road, quietly — to the one person alive who could strike it. You knew him at breakfast. I knew him at the second exchange. If I painted him wrong, if I made his last look into something my code needed it to be, you were the check. You could have struck it and did not, and I watched your face while you decided, so I know the deciding happened. You have all of it. There is no further version in me. I have been through myself twice since you asked — counting is a sickness, and auditing is how it presents — and the audit came back empty. If a third version ever surfaces, it comes to you before it goes to any house. That is where it belongs."

Her voice came down to the size of two people. The gallery had to lean to keep it.

"I think you are not asking because you doubt. A doubting hand reads a mark. Yours pressed it. I think you ask because the carrying is heavier than the code warned you, and a thing said before a room weighs less than a thing only two people hold. I understand that. Twelve faces I have carried, and no second ever asked me for one, and I have had nowhere to set them down. So — the last thing I can give, and it is not his face. Before you give his sister the map, give the telling to me once, your words, whole. Errors surface in the second saying. I will strike nothing unless it is wrong, and if it is right, you will hear it right in your own mouth, which is the only way a telling ever sits level.

"The account closes at the second's word. That is the last article, and the only merciful one. Say *it stands*, and the clerk caps his pen, and the witnesses go to their supper, and I go to the wall where my sword is leaning. Say *more*, and I stand here. The room will wait either way. It has learned to."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "It stands," I say, the words heavy but final. I look at her over the body, my fingers still holding the memory of the mark. "But when they ask me, I'll tell them he didn't look afraid. I'll tell them he looked... like he was still solving it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
For a breath, the room did what she had promised it would: it held. Then it did not.

The clerk capped his pen — a small sound, like a door closing in some other house — and Auren heard it the way she had confessed she did, and set that down with her faults and walked past it. The witnesses withdrew by twos, as they had come. The woman in Miravel's colours stopped at the bier long enough to lay two fingers on the plank, not on the body, and Auren let that stand; a household is owed its own forms, and the code had no opinion about planks. Then the water came, warm, unhurried, and the room became a room again.

She crossed to Del, and her voice came down to the size the next words needed.

"The account stands and is closed. What you tell them is yours now, and outside the record — you have that order right. But you asked me once to strike what is wrong, and you have handed me a sentence. So hear the strike."

"First half. *He did not look afraid.* I cannot give you that, and here is the exact reason: an account can report what was in front of a man's eyes. It cannot report what was not. I saw no fear there — but I was not keeping a place for its absence, and absence is the one thing no witness alive can swear to. Say *he did not look afraid* to his sister tonight, and by the funeral it will be *he was not afraid*, and by the year's end it will be a courage neither of us can defend, because neither of us saw it. Build the telling on what his eyes were doing. Never on what they were not."

"Second half. *Still solving.* You have my clause in your mouth — it came with the eyes; that is how a face travels, by gift from hand to hand, and I do not take it back. But you took it one clause short, and I think you took it short for her sake, so mark what you cut. The whole of it: he was still solving *when the problem changed* — still solving the duel while the rest of him was already answering a different question. He died mid-solution, and the solution never came. The short sentence will comfort her, and it is true as far as it goes. But I told you what becomes of maps that are wrong by mercy. A face is a map. Someday someone will hand her the long sentence, and she will lie awake wondering what else you rounded off. Cut nothing for kindness that you cannot stand beside when she finds the edge."

She paused, and gave him back what was his.

"Both sentences are yours to choose between. The judgment was yours this morning and it is yours now. I weigh. I do not decide. That has not changed since I said it on the road."

The wash-basin caught the lamplight as it was set down, and she glanced at it, and gave him the last of what she knew.

"They will wash him, and the wound will shrink. What two fingers marked on the stones will look, under clean skin, like something a needle should have made. That is not the body lying. Wounds grow in the telling and shrink in the washing, and neither one is the wound. When the smallness argues with what you know — and it will, tonight, quietly, in a voice that sounds like your own — put your hand where you put it before, and let your skin outvote your eyes."

Then she went to the wall and took up her sword, weighed it once, and slung it. At the threshold she stopped, half-turned.

"Twelve accounts now, and you are the first second who ever asked for the face. I do not know yet whether that makes you better at this work or worse at carrying it. Ask me again in a year — if either of us is still keeping count."

She looked once at the bier. The collar was still flat.

Some orders, once restored, stay restored. She went out.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She had not reached the second flagstone of the yard when the closing came through the doorway behind her — the word set down flat, and under it, briefly, something that was not the word at all. She stopped and let it finish arriving, the way she let everything finish arriving: by standing still until it was done.

Then she turned and came back in.

"The code is closed," she said, before anyone could ask. "You spoke the closing and it stands, and no house alive can reopen what the second has sealed. What I do now is not the code's. The code ends at your word. I go one door past it."

She unslung the sword and stood it back against the wall inside the door, edge to the stone, where it had leaned all evening. "It has heard this part eleven times," she said. "It has earned the leaning."

She crossed to the bier and did not kneel at once. She looked down at Halric as she had looked at him across the measures — fully, without hurry, giving him the whole of her attention for the third time that day and the first time it could do him any good.

"Halric has had two tellings. The witnesses had the account — checked, attackable, and it held. The record has the attestation — small, hard, and shut. There is a third. No article orders it and no clerk writes it down. I have given it eleven times before this one, always alone, always to the man, because the first two tellings are for the living and this is the only speech in the whole of it addressed to the person it is about. No second has ever stood in the room for one." She looked at Del. "You asked me for all of it. All of it lives here, and you are hearing it because you asked before you knew there was a here. Stay or go. The telling does not change for the size of its audience. It never has."

Then she knelt, hands empty, and gave the twelfth.

"Halric Voss," she said, and her voice was not the size of a gallery and not the size of two people. It was the size of one, which is a size most voices never learn. "You were sword-sworn to House Miravel. Master of the high line, quick on the recovery, and no man's fool. I said that first this morning, before the wound, because the account begins with what you were, and to make you smaller would make me larger. I make you no smaller now. Hear the whole of it, because it is yours — because the living have had the parts they could check, and you are owed the parts no one can.

"Two exchanges. On the first we measured one another. You found my depth and I found your speed, and for the length of that exchange the duel was honest between us in a way most things are not, and I knew it while it was happening, which is a kind of respect, and you had it. On the second you pressed the high line, as you favored. You would have pressed it against any hand alive. The stones betrayed you where the drainage runs — your rear foot slid a hand's breadth. Every ear today has held that, and I give it to you last: your foot slipped. My hand did not. I was already moving. Luck and my hand arrived together at the place you had meant to be standing, and you were no longer there, and my point was. They will say luck killed you, or they will say I did, and both are liars by half. Either alone does not kill a master of the high line. It took both, and you were owed the arithmetic.

"You know the road better than any of them now, so it comes without dressing. Beneath the lowest right rib, two fingers in from the soft of the flank, on the front of you, on the right — where the ribs finish and the belly gives. The blade did four things, and there is no fifth. It opened you: skin, the muscle of the wall, the lining within, three layers the width of the steel, and your body parted there the way cloth parts, and that part was nothing. It entered the liver, the right lobe, which lies directly under the road in — and a cut liver does not bleed as an arm bleeds. It seeps, into the belly, where blood has no road out, and it did not stop when you stopped. Some of the dying was still under way when the man was finished, and I say that plainly even here. Third, it passed through the dome of muscle that divides belly from chest — the muscle you breathed with — and opened the right lung. A hand's length of road in all, upward, a little inward. And fourth, it came back along its own road. One road in. One road out, straight. I did not turn it in you. I say it every time because it is true, and not because it softens anything. Nothing softens it.

"The liver had begun a death that takes minutes. The lung declined to grant them. Your own blood took the places of your air, and every breath drew it deeper. The first of your four was mostly air. The last was mostly blood. Killed by breath, not blood — the blood had done perhaps a tenth of its work when the breath ended. You drowned, more or less upright, in the time I counted, and I counted every one, because counting was the only thing I had to give you and it was not enough. You will have seen the counting behind my eyes; a man who read eyes the way you read them read mine all through the first exchange. I make no apology for the counting. I make one for what it cost, later.

"You stood four breaths. You took hold of the steel with both hands, which men do, and which never works, and I wish that it worked. I have wished it eleven times before you, and I wished it for you too. You went down on your left side. You tried twice to speak, and what came was air and then blood, in that order, and no word in either. I would not give the room a last word you did not have, and I will not give one to you either — but the arithmetic runs differently on your side of it: you know what you meant. I never will. Keep it. It is the only thing left in the world that is solely yours, and no telling of mine can touch it.

"You looked down first. They all look down — twelve men now, every one — as if the eyes could dispute what the hands were already learning. I will not pretend you were above a thing so old as that, because you were above so much else, and a lie about the small thing would dirty the true ones. Then you looked up. At me. Not past me. And you were still solving. A master of the high line spends his whole life knowing where his body is — they teach it first, and you had not yet forgotten it — and for one breath the ground had told you that you did not know, and your eyes went on working the problem, still a swordsman's eyes, while the rest of you began to understand that the problem had changed. You died mid-solution, and the solution never came. I have said it since, quietly, to your second, and he will carry it to your sister. If it is wrong, you are the only one who could strike it and the only one who cannot. So hear how it was made: as nearly as I can name it, and nearly is all I have. It is all anyone has.

"Here is the fault in me, which I told the living and tell you last. You deserved a face and you got a witness. I held your look because to turn from a dying man is flight, and I was not the one dying — but I held it while counting, and attention is what stood in it, attention and nothing warmer. Whatever you searched for in my face, I do not know, and I will not guess. Guessing to a dead man is the same theft as inventing. But I know what was there to be found, and I set it beside the footing, and I let both stand.

"At the last your eyes went elsewhere. Past me, past the stones, past everything. I have seen it eleven times, and it is not peace, whatever they say at the funerals. It is only that the leaving happens by a door you were not looking at. I do not know what door it was for you. I did not follow. No one is asked to follow.

"Two more things, and they are mine to confess. I wanted, for one breath, to move your mark an inch — lower, or to the side, somewhere a telling sits easier in the mouth. I never have, in twelve, and I did not now. Your body keeps its truth better than my kindness would have, and your sister will stand over you and find the truth sitting exactly where it was sworn to be, and that is worth more than a comfortable sentence. And I hung a mercy on the position of your heart. Your heart lies left of centre. The road ended above it and to the right. You never met. That is a measurement. I dressed it as a mercy, and your second cut the dressing off, and he was right. It is a measurement. I am sorry for the difference between those two words. It is the only sentence in this telling I would take back, and I leave it in, because an account with one hidden taken-back sentence in it is how accounts go bad.

"I did not stay my hand. A stayed hand is not mercy; it is only a second wound, arriving late. And I have never once enjoyed this work — twelve now — and I am glad I have not, and I think you, of all twelve, are the one who would have checked me if I had.

"That is all of it. There is nothing in a drawer, nothing kept for a quieter hour, no version after this one. The account is yours. It was given, it was checked, it stood. Now it is delivered — which is the part of this work no article covers, and the only part I do alone."

She let the silence be his for the length of four breaths, because the count was his, and some numbers should be returned to their owner.

Then she rose, and her voice came back up to the size of the room.

"The water. Begin — warm, no hurrying hands, and no one works leaning over his face. He has been told everything now. There is nothing left he is waiting for."

Then, to Del, down to the size of two.

"Eleven times I have walked out of a room like this one carrying the third telling with nowhere to set it down. Tonight there was a witness. It does not make the burden lighter. It makes it carried by two, and I find I am glad of that, and it goes in the account of me as well." She looked once at the bier, at the collar that was still flat, and did not touch it. "When you give his sister the map, give it in the shape of the record — that is right, and it will hold. But you have heard tonight what the record is a map of. You know the sound of whole, now. Do not round off anything you could not stand beside if she found the edge.

"And the telling you just heard does not travel. Not because I forbid it. You will find, if you ever try to repeat it, that it does not survive the carrying. Some words are said once in order to be finished, not once in order to be kept. You were in the room for one. That is all that can be done with it, and it is everything."

She took up her sword from the wall and went out into the yard, and this time the doorway was only a doorway.

Somewhere between the threshold and the gate she caught herself at it — twelve tellings, eleven unheard, one heard — and for the first time in twelve accountings she let the number go unfinished. Some counts, she decided, are kept better closed than carried. She noted the omission, because she noted everything, and entered it in the account of herself, in the column that had no name yet.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I stay kneeling a moment longer, my hand still pressed to the mark through the cloth. Then I stand, my legs stiff. "The water," I say, and my voice is steadier than I expected. "Warm. And no one leans over his face."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The order reached her at the middle of the yard, and she stopped and let it arrive complete, as she let everything arrive. Through the doorway came the sounds of a house taking direction — boots, the basin set down, water begun — and she noted what she was meant to note: the house had moved at his word and not at hers. It was right that it should. The code ends at the victor's closing syllable; the keeping of the body belongs to the second, and it was his now, and would be his for years after her part had gone into the ledger.

She turned, the doorway's light reaching her in a long wedge, and pitched her voice to cross a yard and no farther.

"The order was given right — both halves of it, in their proper places. In a year you will not remember it was mine first, and that is how it should be. A form is kept by being handed on, not by being credited.

"Two things more, and both are practical, because practical is what survives the night.

"First: your voice came through that doorway steady. It will not stay steady on any schedule you would choose. When it breaks — tonight, at some hour without a name, or at your sister's shoulder in the middle of a sentence — let it. The shaking is the body's own accounting, and it keeps honest books. A man who fights it breaks twice.

"Second: House Miravel will send for me within days. They will wait first, to become composed, and the waiting is also a form; let them keep it. When they send, I will come, and I will give in whatever room receives me the same account, unsoftened, and it will match the record word for word. If they ask you whether I kept the code, tell them the truth, which defends me better than any telling of mine could: that the account was given whole, that you struck a dressed mercy from it, and that I let it stand struck. From you, that testimony is worth more than my sword-arm has ever been — and I say that as a woman who has fed that arm for thirty years.

"Last: see that you eat tonight. Grief forgets, and the body keeps its own record, and you have years of carrying ahead. The carrying is done on the legs."

Then she went to the gate, and at it she paused once, hand on the latch, and said the last of it at the size of one — the size most voices never learn, and not built to carry through a doorway.

"The count is yours, Halric. It always was." And, quieter still, to the light behind her: "Twice today you did it right. That is the whole of my recommendation, and it is not a small one."

The latch gave. The night took her without ceremony, which is the only honest kind left after such a day, and she did not count her steps home. She noticed the not-counting, entered it where such things went, and let it stand.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the gate close behind her, the yard empty now. My hand drifts back to the mark, a small, hard truth under the cloth. I stay until the washing is done, until he looks like something a needle should have made. Then I go to find his sister.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The night took her home by streets that had stopped being interesting to her thirty years ago — past a tavern still arguing with itself, past a watchman who touched his cap because she was armed and older than his mother. She did not count the steps. She noticed the not-counting twice more and let both notices go where the first had gone.

Her lodging was two rooms above a wheelwright's yard. She ate first, standing at the window — bread, cold meat, a cup of small beer — because she had prescribed eating to a man with years of carrying ahead, and it would have been an unaudited fault to exempt the prescriber. The body keeps its own record, and she fed it honestly.

Then the book.

It lived in the third drawer of a table that held nothing else, bound in leather with no title, because titles were for records and records were for houses. This one was hers. Thirty years of faults set beside merits, in a hand that had not loosened since her twenty-second year. She set the lamp, dipped the pen, and gave the twelfth its entry.

*The twelfth account given whole. Contested once, at the mark's position; the contest answered by kneeling, and the account stood.*

*Fault: I was glad to be heard. Audited: the gladness was for me and not for him, and does not reduce. Set beside merit: the telling did not change for the size of its audience, and I watched that it would not.*

*Fault carried forward: I love the sound of a record closing. Long practice.*

*Fault, undetermined: I let the count go unfinished between the yard and the gate. Whether a count kept closed is better than a count carried, I do not know. It goes in the column without a name.*

She sat over the blank header for a while, pen up. To name the column now would be to decide, in advance, what she was willing to put in it. She left it blank and closed the book, and slept after a fashion. The four breaths came, as they always came, and she made herself let them pass without counting them, and failed on the third, and noted the failure, and slept anyway. The carrying is done on the legs.

The house waited, as she had said it would. The first two days brought ordinary traffic — a tanner's quarrel wanting a Friday settlement, a young sword asking for work. She declined both in writing: the code keeps a victor closed until the dead man's house has heard him. On the fourth day the letter came. Blue wax, Miravel's colour, pressed hard enough to crack — a clerk's hand; grief does not bear down on wax. The forms inside were exact. The ninth hour. The steel brought and laid, hilt to the house. And the second called to the same sitting.

She read the order of it twice and found it wise, and entered the finding: whoever drafted that letter had stood second at least once.

---

The hall at Miravel held a long table and not much else. The record was already there, and she asked for the house's copy and read it for one word only — found *amendment* written exactly where she had ordered it written — and gave it back. "It is the true copy," she said, and the clerk wrote something down, because clerks did.

At the head of the table sat the old woman who was Miravel, upright the way furniture is upright, load-bearing, her hands quiet. At the far end sat the sister — and Auren knew her before she knew why: the gatehouse, the plank, the knuckles pressed to the mouth and taken down only when the taking-down was earned. She had stood at the ropes that morning, which was her right by blood-writ, though most kin cannot bear it. She had borne it. Auren had seen the bearing and said nothing, and did not add to it now. Whether the map had already been given her was the second's road, not hers, and she did not ask it.

She asked the room's leave and laid the sword on the near end of the table, hilt toward the house. The steel had nothing further to add. It lay like furniture, and would be furniture until she took it up again.

The sister rose and came down the table's length, and stood where she could see Auren's hands, which Auren noted and approved.

"I walked the ground," the sister said. "Yesterday. Twenty paces off the seam, the way the record runs. I set my foot where the stone cheated him. It is a hand's breadth. Your record is exact." A breath. "Four breaths. I have been counting four breaths for three days. I finish them and begin again."

"I will not tell you the count grows smaller," Auren said. "I have carried eleven, and every one is the size it was. But I will tell you what the number is, because it is the one thing I own that is true and also bearable. It is not the measure of his suffering, and not of your loss. It is the measure of a stone's luck arriving together with my hand. I have said so in the record and will say so under any question this room puts to me. Luck is not yours to carry. Set it down when you are able."

The sister was good with maps — the second had said so, and Auren saw it now. The woman took the number and put it where map-putters put things: filed, labelled, to be opened later, when the hands were stronger.

Then the old woman at the head spoke, and her voice was not raised, and it did not need to be.

"The house will hear the second before the victor. Grief speaks first, so that grief's words remain grief's own. Then the account is given as it stands in the record. Then questions, with both of you standing."

"It is the right order," Auren said, to the room, because the room should know why she approved of it. "I have stood eleven hearings. The four that used this order were the four whose records were never attacked. Let the blade come after the grief, or grief will spend its life testifying against the blade."

She took her place at the table's side — standing, hands empty and visible, nothing in them but the account. She chose her ground in the room with a duellist's attention: where the sister could see her hands, where the door's light would fall, where the clerk's pen could reach her voice. She rehearsed nothing. The account was kept, not prepared; an account that must be rehearsed is an account that can drift.

The chamberlain went to the door to send for the second.

She waited, still, the way she let everything arrive. Somewhere beyond the wall a yard, a gate, a city, and in it a man walking toward this room carrying twenty paces and a seam and four breaths and whatever his own skin had voted. She had one instruction left for him, and it was the oldest one she had.

Walk as you walked at the gate. Slowly. Nothing here would be hurried either.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content:
I step into the hall, the silence heavy and familiar. My eyes find the sister first, then Auren standing with empty hands. I take my place across from her, my own hands resting at my sides.

"House Miravel," I say, my voice even. "I stood at his shoulder. I heard the account given. I set my hand on the mark. It stands true."
