dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once to Del, acknowledging the readiness, and then looked past them to the ring of witnesses. She did not sit. She did not sheathe the blade. The code required it to remain bare until the accounting was complete, so she held it low across her body, the cleaned steel catching the light, the point turned toward the ground.

"The killing wound was given on the second pass," she said. Her voice was level and formal, pitched to reach the outermost witness without becoming a shout. "Your principal opened with a thrust to my throat. I turned it on the forte and, while they were still recovering their guard, I stepped inside their point and thrust to the chest. I did not check the thrust. It was made to kill, and I did not weaken it."

She paused. Exactness was the whole of the duty. She raised her left hand and used two fingers to indicate the place on the body, not touching, only marking the spot for the witnesses to see.

"The point entered here—in the fourth intercostal space, one finger's breadth to the left of the sternum. It passed through the pericardium and into the anterior wall of the right ventricle, and opened the chamber. Death was immediate. There was no other wound. I did not strike after they fell, and I did not advance again. The blade was withdrawn once, and only once."

She let the words stand. There was no pleasure in saying them, and she gave the witnesses no reason to think there was. To dress it in softer language would have been the dishonour, not the blood.

"The account is given," she said. She waited, unmoving, for the witnesses to acknowledge it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "The account is heard and confirmed." My voice is steady, but my hands feel cold. I meet the eyes of the senior witness across the circle.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not shift her weight. She waited while the senior witness's gaze passed around the ring of witnesses and came to rest on her. The silence was part of the form; it was not doubt.

"The witnesses have heard," the senior witness said at last. "The account is confirmed. It will be entered as given."

Auren inclined her head. Only then did she bring the blade up, reverse it, and seat it in the scabbard at her left hip. The steel went home with a muted click. She did not brace herself, did not look down at the body, did not let her shoulders settle into anything that could be mistaken for ease. There was no satisfaction in the sound. Eleven times she had spoken a killing wound aloud, and eleven times the rite had left her with the same cold clarity: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

She let her hand drop from the hilt.

"It was made to kill, and it killed," she said. "Enter it so." The words were for the record and for the witnesses, not for the dead. They were not a boast. They were the last of the accounting, and Auren gave them exactly as she had given the rest—without ornament, and without softening.

Then she stepped back, clearing the ground, and stood waiting.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not reach for the hilt. The blade was already seated in its scabbard, and the accounting was already entered; there was no honesty in drawing steel for a second telling, and no form that required it. She turned her gaze to Del and inclined her head a fraction, acknowledging the formal words without granting them the power to undo what had already been done before the ring of witnesses.

"The account has been given," she said. Her voice was level, pitched to carry to the outermost witness, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast. "The code required that word from the second before the accounting. It was not spoken then; instead, you declared yourself ready to hear it, and I gave the account before the ring, in full and without ornament. You heard it. You confirmed it. The senior witness confirmed it for the record, and it has been entered as given."

She paused, because the form allowed the words to stand without comfort, and because she would not pretend the rite was unfinished when it was not.

"It was made to kill, and it killed," she said. "That is the truth of the accounting, and I will not soften it now by repeating the whole as though the first telling were lacking. The debt is paid. Enter it so."

She let her hand rest empty at her side and stood waiting, unmoving, while the witnesses remained.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look at the senior witness, waiting for his ruling. He’s watching Auren, his expression neutral. I clear my throat softly. "The account was spoken and confirmed. The form is met."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not move. She was aware of the senior witness's gaze resting on her, neutral and unblinking, and she gave him nothing to read. There was no defiance in her stillness and no appeal in it; the accounting was complete, and it was not the victor's office to declare the form met. That belonged to the witnesses. She had spoken the killing wound once, in full, and she would not speak it again to satisfy a word that had arrived after the fact.

The silence held. Then the senior witness inclined his head, once, to the ring.

"The second's word was not spoken before the accounting," he said. His voice was dry and unhurried. "It is spoken now. The account was given before the ring, in full, and without ornament. It was heard. It was confirmed by the second, and it has been entered by the record as given. The requirement of the code is satisfied. The form is met."

He paused. His eyes went past Auren to the second—Auren did not turn her head—and then returned to the circle of witnesses.

"The debt is paid," the senior witness said. "The ground is released."

Auren inclined her head in return. It was not relief, and it was not pride. It was the acknowledgement of a form completed and a debt discharged, and she gave it the same flat precision she had given the rest.

"It is entered," she said. Her voice was level. "There is nothing further."

She did not look at the body. She did not look at the second. She kept her hand empty at her side and waited while the ring began to break, and then she walked from the ground, the sheathed blade at her hip, with the same cold clarity she had carried through all eleven accountings: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had gone perhaps a dozen paces from the ring when the second’s question reached her. She stopped. The blade was already seated in its scabbard; she did not reach for the hilt, because there was no form that required steel to be bared for a single question, and no honesty in pretending the rite was unfinished. She turned back far enough for her voice to reach the outermost witness, though she did not let her eyes go to the body on the ground.

“The place was given,” she said. Her voice was level and formal, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast. “It landed in the chest, in the fourth intercostal space—between the fourth and fifth ribs—one finger’s breadth to the left of the sternum, the breastbone. The point passed through the pericardium, the sac around the heart, and into the anterior wall of the right ventricle, opening the chamber. That is where it landed. There was no other wound.”

She raised her left hand and set two fingers against her own chest at the spot, not pressing, only marking the place for the witnesses to see.

“Here. It was made to kill, and it killed. It is entered as given. I will not put it in softer words, and I will not speak the whole again as though the first accounting lacked.”

She let her hand fall empty to her side and stood unmoving while the words went to the record. Then she turned and walked on, the sheathed blade at her hip, carrying the same cold clarity she had carried through all eleven accountings: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I follow her, my steps quickening to catch up. "And if it had been me?" I ask quietly, so the others don't hear. "Would the account sound the same?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had taken perhaps two more paces before the question reached her. She stopped, but did not turn back toward the ground. She turned her head just enough for her voice to reach Del and no farther, pitching it low, so it would not carry to the witnesses still breaking their ring.

“No,” she said. “It would not sound the same.”

The word stood between them for a moment. Exactness was the whole of the duty, and she would not blunt the answer to make it easier to hear.

“The account is of the killing wound, and the wound would not be the same. If you had been the principal—if you had stood in the ring and fallen to me—I would have given that wound as it happened: the pass on which it was given, the place it entered, the depth it reached, the vessel or chamber it opened, and the moment death came. I would have given it in the same form: before the ring, in full, without ornament, and without softening. I have never enjoyed the accounting, and I would not have enjoyed it for you. The debt would be paid the same way, and the paying of it would not be a thing to be enjoyed.”

Her gaze went past Del to the empty path ahead, and then returned, level and unadorned.

“But you were not the principal. You stood as second. You heard the account, and you confirmed it, and the record has entered it as given. There is no accounting owed for you, because there is no death to account for. The debt was paid for the life I took. It is entered. There is nothing further.”

She did not soften it, and she did not dress it as a boast. She waited a moment, to be sure the answer had been heard exactly as she had given it, and then she turned and walked on, the sheathed blade at her hip, carrying the same cold clarity she had carried through all eleven accountings: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had taken another step before the reminder reached her. She stopped, but did not turn back toward the ground. She turned her head enough for her voice to reach the second, low and level, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast.

"The code says precisely," she said. "It does not say tactfully. You are right to remind me."

She did not resent the correction. Exactness was the whole of the duty, and she had no wish to be spared it.

"This is not the accounting spoken again before the ring," she went on. "That was given in full, confirmed by you, confirmed by the senior witness, and entered. What you ask now is the plain answer to a plain question, and I will give it without ornament."

She paused, because the form allowed the words to stand without comfort.

"The blade was a thrusting blade, and I used it as one. It did not cut. It did not slash. On the second pass, with your principal still recovering their guard, I stepped inside their point and drove the steel forward. I did not check the thrust. It was driven to its full depth, and I did not weaken it. The point entered the chest in the fourth intercostal space—between the fourth and fifth ribs—one finger’s breadth to the left of the sternum, the breastbone. It pierced the chest wall. It pierced the pericardium, the sac that holds the heart. It drove through the anterior wall of the right ventricle and opened that chamber."

She let the words stand for a moment, then gave the rest, exactly.

"What it did was this: it opened the chamber and let the blood escape from it. The blood passed out of the right ventricle and into the pericardial sac, filling it. The heart could no longer fill, could no longer pump. Its action failed, and death was immediate. There was no other wound. I did not strike after they fell, and I did not advance again. The blade was withdrawn once, and only once."

She raised her left hand and set two fingers against her own chest at the place, not pressing, only marking it for the second to see. Then she let her hand fall empty to her side.

"That is what the blade did," she said. "That is what it did it to. It was made to kill, and it killed. I have given it precisely, and I will not put it in softer words."

Then she turned and walked on, the sheathed blade at her hip, carrying the same cold clarity she had carried through all eleven accountings: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a slow breath, my shoulders finally dropping. "Good," I say, my voice rough. "That's all I needed to know." I fall into step beside her, not too close. "Let's get the hell out of here."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer the rough words in kind. The account had been given precisely, confirmed, and entered for the record; the senior witness had released the ground. There was no form that required her to remain, and no honesty in pretending there was.

She inclined her head once, a small formal gesture, and kept her face toward the path that led away from the ring.

"The debt is paid," she said. Her voice was level, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast. "The ground is released. There is nothing further to account for, and no obligation to stand where the code has finished. We go."

She did not quicken her pace. Haste would have been a comment on the thing done, and she would not make a comment she had not earned. She walked at the same measured step she had kept on the ground, the sheathed blade at her hip, her hand empty at her side. She did not look back at the body, nor at the place where the steel had entered, nor at the ring of witnesses breaking behind them. There was no satisfaction in leaving, and no relief that she would allow herself to name as relief.

The eleventh accounting was complete as the ten before it had been complete: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren had taken a few more paces along the path when the second’s voice reached her again. The witnesses were silent, and the second’s voice followed her, insisting that she was not finished. The demand was for all of it: how long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code said all of it, and the second was asking for all of it.

She stopped. She did not reach for the hilt. The blade was already seated in its scabbard; there was no form that required steel to be bared for a plain question, and no honesty in pretending the rite was unfinished when the senior witness had already released the ground. But the code did say precisely, and she would not blunt the answer to make it easier to hear.

She turned back enough for her voice to reach the second and the silent ring, pitching it low and level, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast.

“How long he took: he took no time that could be measured. The thrust was not checked. It was driven to its full depth. The point opened the chamber, the heart’s action failed, and death was immediate. There was no interval between the wound and death in which a breath could be drawn, let alone a word spoken.”

“What he said: he said nothing. There was no word from him after the steel entered him, and none before it that the accounting records. He made no statement, no cry, no parting speech. Death was immediate, and there was no time for speech.”

“What it looked like at the end: it looked like a single thrust wound.” She raised her left hand and set two fingers against her own chest at the place, not pressing, only marking it. “A narrow puncture in the fourth intercostal space—between the fourth and fifth ribs—one finger’s breadth to the left of the sternum. It did not gape. The blade was withdrawn once, and only once. He fell where he stood. I did not strike after he fell, and I did not advance again. The blood did not pour from him onto the ground in any quantity, because the chamber emptied into the pericardial sac, filling it; there was blood on the steel when I withdrew it, and on the wound, but no great effusion. That is what it looked like at the end.” Then she let her hand fall empty to her side.

She let the words stand. She had given all of it, precisely, without ornament, and without softening. There was no pleasure in the saying of it, and she gave the witnesses no reason to think there was. To dress it in softer language would have been the dishonour, not the blood.

“That is all of it,” she said. Her voice was level. “It is entered as given. There is nothing further.”

Then she turned and walked on, the sheathed blade at her hip, carrying the same cold clarity she had carried through all eleven accountings: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes on the path ahead. "Alright." My voice is quiet now, all the insistence drained out. I walk beside her, not looking back. "That's enough."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the second’s quiet word and did not take it as a release from the code. The account had been given in full: the second pass, the step inside the point, the thrust driven to its depth, the place in the fourth intercostal space, the pericardium pierced, the right ventricle opened, the immediate failure of the heart, the absence of speech, the narrow wound, the single withdrawal, the fall where he stood. It had been heard. It had been confirmed by the second and by the senior witness. It was entered as given. The ground was released. There was no form left to satisfy and no honesty in standing where the debt was already paid.

She inclined her head once, a small formal gesture, and kept her face toward the path that led away from the ring.

“It is enough,” she said. Her voice was level, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast. “Not because you have said so, but because the code required all of it, and all of it has been given. I have spoken the killing wound precisely, before the ring, in full, without ornament, and without softening. There was no interval for speech, no cry, no great effusion onto the ground, no second stroke. The blade was withdrawn once, and only once. It is entered as given. There is nothing further.”

She did not look back at the ground, nor at the place where the steel had entered, nor at the silent witnesses behind them. She walked at the same measured pace she had kept on the ground, the sheathed blade at her hip, her hand empty at her side. There was no satisfaction in leaving, and no relief that she would allow herself to name as relief.

The eleventh accounting was complete as the ten before it had been complete: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once, acknowledging the second’s confirmation without granting it the power to add anything to the debt already paid. Then, because the code said precisely and the second had asked for all of it, she set the whole of the accounting in order, one last time, for the record and for the witnesses who had heard it given.

“The killing wound was given on the second pass,” she said. Her voice was level and formal, pitched to reach the outermost witness, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast. “Your principal opened with a thrust to my throat. I turned it on the forte and, while they were still recovering their guard, I stepped inside their point and thrust to the chest. I did not check the thrust. It was made to kill, and I did not weaken it.”

She raised her left hand and set two fingers against her own chest at the place, not pressing, only marking it for any who still watched.

“The point entered here—in the fourth intercostal space, between the fourth and fifth ribs, one finger’s breadth to the left of the sternum, the breastbone. It pierced the chest wall. It pierced the pericardium, the sac that holds the heart. It drove through the anterior wall of the right ventricle and opened that chamber. The blood passed out of the right ventricle and into the pericardial sac, filling it. The heart could no longer fill, could no longer pump. Its action failed, and death was immediate.”

She let the words stand. Exactness was the whole of the duty.

“There was no interval between the wound and death in which a breath could be drawn, let alone a word spoken. He said nothing. There was no statement, no cry, no parting speech. What it looked like at the end: a single thrust wound, a narrow puncture that did not gape. There was blood on the steel when I withdrew it, and on the wound, but no great effusion onto the ground, because the chamber emptied into the pericardial sac. He fell where he stood. I did not strike after he fell, and I did not advance again. The blade was withdrawn once, and only once. There was no other wound.”

She let her hand fall empty to her side.

“It was made to kill, and it killed,” she said. “That is the account, in full and in order, without ornament, and without softening. It has been heard. It has been confirmed by the second, and by the senior witness for the record. It is entered as given. There is nothing further.”

Then she turned and walked on, the sheathed blade at her hip, carrying the same cold clarity she had carried through all eleven accountings: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The account is heard." My voice cracks a little on the last word, but I don't look away from her. I swallow hard. "I'll walk with you."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once, acknowledging the confirmation that had been spoken. The accounting had been given in full, heard, confirmed, and entered for the record; there was no form left that the code required of her, and no honesty in pretending the road away from the ground was part of the rite.

“The account is heard,” she said. Her voice was level, pitched to carry no farther than the second, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast. “It is entered as given. The debt is paid. There is nothing further.”

She did not look toward the second, and she did not pretend the road was anything other than a road. It was not a continuation of the accounting, and she would not make it one.

“The code does not require you to walk with me,” she went on. “It does not forbid it either. Walk, if you choose. I will not ask it of you, and I will not refuse you. But I will not speak the killing wound again on the road, and I will not dress the leaving in softer words than the deed deserved. It was made to kill, and it killed. That is entered, and it is enough.”

Then she turned her face to the path and walked on at the same measured pace she had kept on the ground, the sheathed blade at her hip, her hand empty at her side. She did not look back at the body, nor at the ring of witnesses, nor at the place where the steel had entered. The eleventh accounting was complete as the ten before it had been complete: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I match her pace, my hands clenched at my sides. "I know what the code requires," I say, my voice steadier now. "I'm not asking for the wound again. I'm just... walking."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the second’s voice beside her and did not check her pace. She kept her face toward the path, her hand empty at her side, the sheathed blade riding at her hip. The words were steady enough now, and she took them at the value they were given: a statement of fact, not a request for the accounting again.

“I know what the code requires as well,” she said. Her voice was level, pitched for the road and no farther, stripped of anything that might soften the fact or dress it as a boast. “You have said it. You heard the account, you confirmed it, and the senior witness entered it. That is your part, and it is finished. The code does not bind you to my road, and it does not forbid it. Walk, if that is what you are doing.”

She was aware of the second beside her, and she did not turn her head. There was no obligation to fill the silence, and she would not invent one.

“I am not walking from the ground because it eases the debt,” she went on. “It does not. The debt is paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed. I will not thank you for walking, and I will not tell you your presence lessens what was done. It does not. The blade was made to kill, and it killed. That is entered, and it is enough.”

Then she let the road take them, at the same measured pace she had kept on the ground, carrying the same cold clarity she had carried through all eleven accountings: the debt was paid, and the paying of it was not a thing to be enjoyed.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "I know it doesn't lessen anything," I say, my voice low. "I'm not trying to ease the debt. I just... can't stand to be back there alone." I glance at her, then away. "It's for me, not for you."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head, acknowledging Del’s place as second, then turned to the witnesses. Her voice was level, arranged for every ear rather than for persuasion.

“The account of the fatal wound is made as required,” she said. “The killing cut was delivered in the fifth exchange, from the right side of the sternum upward and inward. It entered the chest cavity and severed the pulmonary vessels. It was not a mistake, nor was it hidden. I claim it, and I name it plainly.”

She paused, not to soften the words, but so that no witness might later say she had swallowed any part of them.

“I have spoken eleven accounts,” she added, quieter now. “I do not take pleasure in them. I speak them because the dead are owed precision, and the living are owed proof that it was done by law, not cruelty.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, keeping my expression neutral despite the tightness in my chest. "The account is clear and sufficient," I say, my voice steady. "I confirm it for the record."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted Del’s confirmation without moving from her stance. The sword remained lowered, though the danger had passed; she would not make the gesture too soon, and she would not let it become a performance.

“Then the account is complete,” she said. “Let it be entered as spoken.”

Her gaze went briefly to the witnesses, then to the fallen man, and then back to the blade. She turned it once in her hand, inspecting the edge with the same detached care she gave every necessary thing, before sheathes it with a clean, formal motion.

For a breath, she stood apart from the aftermath. Not as victor, not as mourner. As the one who had been obliged to speak.

“If the code requires my signature, bring the page,” Auren said at last, her voice no more than a shade softer. “If it requires nothing further, then you have my word that it was done lawfully.”

She did not look away from the witnesses.

“And no one present need pretend the precision was kindness,” she added. “It was honesty.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the request as the ritual demanded, not as a challenge to her. The code did not permit the account to be merely spoken once and trusted to memory; it could be asked for again, and when it was asked, it was given.

She did not shift her weight or reach for the sheathed sword. She stood as she had stood eleven times before, in the same exact posture, and let her voice settle into the register of a public record.

“Then I speak the account again,” she said. “The killing wound was delivered in the fifth exchange. It entered from the right side of the sternum, upward and inward. It pierced the chest cavity and severed the pulmonary vessels. It was not a mistake, nor was it concealed. I claim it, and I name it plainly.”

Auren paused, because the pause was part of the form, not because she wished to soften it.

“The victor has spoken. The witnesses have heard. No part of the account has been omitted, and no part of the responsibility has been shifted.”

She let the final words stand without adding consolation to them.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, my throat tight. "The account is spoken, and I confirm it." I turn to the witnesses, my voice carrying just enough. "The record is complete."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let the confirmation stand. It was the second’s office, not her own, and she did not thank him for it; gratitude would have turned a duty into a favor, and favors had no place in the form.

Her gaze went to the witnesses. She held each in turn, not long enough to threaten, long enough to make clear that she was not finished with them until the last had heard the last word.

“Then the account stands,” she said. “Twice spoken, twice confirmed, and altered in no part. If any witness doubts the wording, let him doubt it now, while the body is still here to answer for the truth.”

She did not look at the fallen man again. She had looked at him while naming the wound; after that, looking became sentiment, and sentiment was not permitted.

“The victor’s obligation is discharged,” Auren said. “If the code requires my signature, bring the page. If it requires only my presence, I am present.”

A short pause.

“I have spoken eleven accounts,” she added, quieter, but no less for being quieter. “I do not take pleasure in them. I speak them again if asked, and I will speak them a third time if the law asks, because the dead are owed precision. The living are owed proof that it was done by law, not cruelty. And no one here need pretend the precision was kindness. It was honesty.”

Then she stood apart, the sword sheathed, the account closed in every part she could control, waiting to see what the witnesses would do next.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the question without reproach. It was the second’s duty to make the account plain, and plainness had its own cost. She had learned that cost eleven times, and she did not ask to be spared it now.

She turned her face toward the witnesses, then to the fallen man, then back to the space where Del stood. Her eyes did not soften. Her voice did not soften.

“The killing cut landed on the right side of the sternum,” she said. “Between the fourth and fifth ribs, upward and inward. It entered the chest cavity and severed the pulmonary vessels. There was no other wound that could answer for the death.”

She let the words remain as they were, without ornament and without apology.

“If the record requires the angle, it was delivered from right to left, rising inward toward the center of the chest. If the record requires the depth, it was sufficient to reach the vessels. If the record requires the place upon the body, I have named it. If the record requires that I say it again, I will say it again, because the code asks precision, not comfort.”

Auren held still. The sword was sheathed, but she did not move to ease the posture of the account. That was not hers to soften.

“I will not make it kinder,” she said, “because kindness is not the law’s purpose here. The law’s purpose is truth, and truth is that the wound was placed where I say it was placed. It was not accidental. It was not concealed. It was not delivered to a limb, or to the neck, or to any part of the body where death might have been denied by later doubt. It was delivered to the chest, and the chest answered for it.”

Her voice fell by no more than necessary, but the witnesses leaned closer, because they knew what they were hearing.

“The blade landed where I have said,” Auren continued. “I claim the place. I claim the direction. I claim the result. If any part of the account must be named again, let it be named now, while the dead man’s body can still be examined and the living can still be satisfied.”

She paused, then added, “I do not ask you to forget it. I do not ask you to make it clean. I ask only that the record be exact.”

Auren’s gaze settled again upon the witnesses.

“Where it landed is now spoken plainly,” she said. “If that is not sufficient, say so, and I will speak until the law is satisfied.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The record is satisfied," I say, my voice low. "The witnesses have heard. The account will stand." I look away, finally. "I'll prepare the page for your signature."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the satisfaction of the record without moving toward relief. There was no relief in it. There was only the next required formality.

“Then let the page be brought,” she said. “I will sign what has been spoken, not what has been remembered. If the wording differs, it will be corrected before my name.”

She looked to the witnesses once more, measuring their faces with the same exactness she had given the account.

“You have heard it twice. You have heard the place, the direction, and the result. If any of you will later say it was hidden, or accidental, or done without law, speak now.”

The silence that followed was not consent, and Auren did not treat it as such. It was only the absence of objection.

She turned her eyes briefly toward the fallen man, then away again. The body remained where it had fallen. The code had not asked her to tend to it, only to account for it, and she had done so plainly.

Her hands were steady. They had steadied before the fifth exchange, and they would remain steady through the signature, because the victor was not permitted to appear shaken, and not permitted to appear triumphant. Either way, the account would become about her, and it was not meant to be about her.

“I have signed eleven pages,” Auren said, more quietly, though still for every ear. “Each one required the same thing. Precision. Witness. Responsibility. I will not sign a twelfth that softens any part of it.”

She held her posture as it was, sword sheathed, blade clean, obligation incomplete only until the page was ready.

“Bring it,” she said. “I will discharge the last part.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren received the reminder as a necessary demand, not an accusation. Precision had been asked of her, and she would not make it smaller to spare anyone’s ears.

She turned her face to the witnesses. Then to the body lying still. Then back to the space where the record waited.

“Then let it be said without tact,” she said. “The blade cut. It cut through skin and muscle over the right side of the sternum. It cut between the fourth and fifth ribs. It cut into the chest cavity. It cut the pulmonary vessels. It severed them. It did these things to the body of the man lying there, to the place where the lung vessels lie, to the part of him that could not answer for itself.”

Her voice did not rise. It did not fall. It kept the measure of an accounting.

“The blade drew a killing cut,” Auren said. “It was delivered in the fifth exchange. It went upward and inward, from the right toward the center of the chest. It opened the way to the vessels. It severed the vessels. The man died because the wound was placed where the body could not refuse it.”

She let the words stand.

“If the code asks what the blade did, it cut, pierced, and severed,” she said. “If the code asks what it did it to, it did it to the chest, to the vessels, and to the man. If the code asks whether I am certain, I am certain. If the code asks whether I claim it, I claim it.”

Auren held the posture of the account until the last witness had heard the last word.

“I will not soften it,” she added. “There is no gentler form of a fatal wound. There is only whether it is named truly.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step forward, taking the parchment from my belt. My hand shakes a little as I unroll it on the small writing desk the attendants have placed between us. "It will be as you have spoken," I say, dipping the pen. "Word for word."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the parchment unroll and did not step toward the desk until the last crease had settled. The tremor in Del’s hand entered her notice the way the blade’s edge had entered her notice: as a fact, not an invitation.

“Then write it,” she said, “and write it without mercy for the reader. The code does not ask whether the wording is difficult. It asks whether it is true.”

She turned once to the witnesses, then to the body, then to the page.

“If the account says ‘wound’ where I said ‘cut,’ change it. If it says ‘between the ribs’ where I said the fourth and fifth, change it. If it says ‘pierced’ where I said severed, change it. If it says ‘it was unfortunate’ anywhere, do not bring it to me.”

Auren’s voice remained level.

“The shaking of a second’s hand does not alter the position of the ribs,” she added. “It does not soften the blade. It does not move the body. Write what was spoken.”

She did not reach for the pen. She stood in the posture the account required, sword sheathed, obligation unfinished, waiting for the wording to be set down as spoken.

“I will sign the twelfth page only when it contains the eleventh lesson I have been given,” Auren said. “That the dead are not served by soft words. The living are served by exact words. My name will not stand beneath a prettiness.”

Her gaze went briefly to the witnesses, then back to the parchment.

“Read it to the witnesses before you give it to me,” she said. “Then let them correct it if they can. Then let me sign.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not turn away from the fallen man, nor did she turn away from the witnesses.

“Then the account is enlarged,” she said. “It is not a new account. It is the same account, spoken to its full measure, because the code does not stop at the place of the wound when it can also ask for the time, the words, and the end.”

She placed her hands where they had been, still and uninvolved, sword sheathed, blade clean.

“The man lived after the fifth exchange for no more than the time it takes a witness to count eleven breaths. I did not measure him with a clock, and I will not offer a precision greater than what was seen. He fell within four paces of the mark. He lost his sword before his knees. He struck the ground on his left side, then turned onto his back. From the cut to the stillness of his chest, I counted by the slow measure required of me. It was eleven breaths, perhaps twelve. The attending would later say it was less than a minute. That is the plainest truth I can give: he died quickly, and no further blow hastened it.”

Auren let the pause stand, not for effect, but so the witnesses could hear the number as a number.

“What he said was as follows. When the cut landed, he said, ‘Enough.’ It was not a word addressed to me. It was a word addressed to the air, or to the pain, or to the law. Then he said, ‘I yield.’ He said it after the wound, not before it. I did not accept a yield that could undo a fatal cut, and I did not strike again. After that he said, ‘Let them not move me.’ His voice failed before the sentence was finished. Then he made no word. He made breath, and the breath became wet, and then it stopped. I do not claim the last words were eloquent. I claim they were heard. If a witness remembers them differently, he may say so now, while the body is here to answer for the truth.”

Auren’s gaze went to the fallen man, then back to the witnesses.

“What it looked like at the end was this. The right side of the sternum was opened. The cloth there was dark and wet. There was no clean wound. There was no neat line. The blood came from within, not from a cut in the arm or the neck. It ran across the breast and found the ground. His face was pale, and the pale was not sleep. His lips were parted. There was froth at the corner of his mouth, darkened by blood. The chest rose once more, unevenly, as though the body were asking permission to fail. Then it did not rise. His eyes were open. I did not close them. The code does not make me the one who tends the dead after the account is discharged. His left hand was beneath him. His right hand lay open and still. He looked like a man who had been cut in the place where breath and blood meet, and had died there. He did not look like a story. He did not look like honor. He looked like a body that had been accounted for.”

Auren held her voice at the measure of the form.

“Now let it be written,” she said. “The place, the direction, the depth, the result, the time, the words, the end. If the page says less than this, it is not complete. If it says more than this, it is not lawful. I will sign the account that the law asks, not the account that the living would prefer.”

She stood apart.

“I have spoken eleven accounts. This is the twelfth. It is not kinder than the first. It is not crueler than the tenth. It is exact.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My hand steadies as I write. The ink flows dark, marking each detail without embellishment. I read it back, my voice flat. "Eleven breaths. 'Enough. I yield. Let them not move me.' Froth at the mouth. Chest rose once, then did not." I look up from the parchment. "Do you confirm it?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren heard the reading without interrupting it. The second’s voice had been the law’s voice until the last word was set down; after that, the account belonged to the page, not to the comfort of any listener.

She turned her eyes to the parchment.

“The account is confirmed,” she said. “It is as I spoke it. The place is named. The direction is named. The depth and result are named. The time is named. The words are named. The end is named. If the code requires anything further, let it be asked now, while the wording can still be corrected and the dead man’s body can still answer for the truth.”

She stepped to the desk and bent over the page. Her hand remained steady as she read the wording once, with the same detached care she gave to every necessary thing. There was no ornament in it. There was no pity in it. There was only the account, set down as spoken.

She took the pen.

“I do not sign because the wording is kind,” Auren said. “I sign because it is exact.”

Her name went beneath the account in clean, formal letters. When it was finished, she laid the pen aside and let the witnesses see the page as it stood.

“The victor’s obligation is discharged,” she said. “The second’s office is discharged. The witnesses have heard the account twice, and the record has been read back as spoken. If any person present believes the wording false, let him say so now. If he will not say so now, he must not say so later.”

Her gaze passed briefly over the fallen man, then returned to the living.

“I have spoken eleven accounts,” she added. “This is the twelfth. I take no pleasure in it. I do not soften it. It was done by law, and it is written as it was done.”

She turned to the witnesses, then to the signed page, then to the body lying beyond the marks of the duel. Her voice settled into the register of the accounting.

“I speak the full account,” she said. “Let it be heard as it is spoken, and let it be written as it is heard.”

Auren held her stance. The sword was sheathed. The blade had been cleaned. Her hands were steady, because steadiness belonged to the form, not to feeling.

“The duel was conducted under the code. The parties took their places. The witnesses were assembled. The seconds were present. The first exchange was lawful. The second exchange was lawful. The third exchange was lawful. The fourth exchange was lawful. The fifth exchange was lawful, and in the fifth exchange the fatal wound was delivered.”

Her gaze moved to the body, then back to the living.

“The killing cut was delivered by me, Auren, duellist of the twelfth account, upon the body of the man lying there. It was not delivered by chance. It was not delivered in confusion. It was not delivered after a fall, nor after a yield, nor after any cessation permitted by the law. It was delivered in the fifth exchange, while both parties stood, while both parties were bound by the code, and while the witnesses watched.”

She let the words remain.

“The cut landed upon the right side of the sternum. It entered between the fourth and fifth ribs. It was directed upward and inward, from the right toward the center of the chest. It cut through skin and muscle. It cut between the ribs. It pierced the chest cavity. It severed the pulmonary vessels. No other wound answered for the death. No wound to the arm, the neck, the shoulder, the face, or the hand was sufficient to account for what followed. The chest answered for it, because the vessels within the chest were severed.”

Auren’s voice did not rise. It did not fall.

“The blade did what was necessary, and nothing more. I did not continue to strike after the fifth exchange. I did not deliver a wound to a limb to make the death appear accidental. I did not deliver a wound to the neck to make it appear lesser than it was. I did not deliver a wound to the back, nor to the throat, nor to any part of the body where the account might be hidden. The wound was placed where the body could not deny it, and where the law required it to be named plainly.”

She paused only long enough for the pause to be part of the form.

“The man lived after the wound for no more than the time it takes a witness to count eleven breaths. I did not measure him with a clock. I counted by the slow measure required of the victor during the accounting. He fell within four paces of the mark. He lost his sword before his knees. He struck the ground upon his left side, then turned onto his back. From the cut to the stillness of his chest, I counted eleven breaths, perhaps twelve. The attending would later say it was less than a minute. That is the plainest truth I can give: he died quickly, and no further blow hastened it.”

Her eyes passed over the witnesses.

“What he said was as follows. When the cut landed, he said, ‘Enough.’ It was not a word addressed to me. It was a word addressed to the pain, or to the air, or to the law. Then he said, ‘I yield.’ He said it after the wound, not before it. I did not accept a yield that could undo a fatal cut, and I did not strike again. After that he said, ‘Let them not move me.’ His voice failed before the sentence was finished. Then he made no word. He made breath, and the breath became wet, and then it stopped. I do not claim the last words were eloquent. I claim they were heard. If any witness remembers them differently, he may say so now, while the body is here to answer for the truth.”

Auren looked to the fallen man again. Not with tenderness. Not with triumph. With accounting.

“What it looked like at the end was this. The right side of the sternum was opened. The cloth there was dark and wet. There was no clean wound. There was no neat line. The blood came from within, not from a cut in the arm or the neck. It ran across the breast and found the ground. His face was pale, and the pale was not sleep. His lips were parted. There was froth at the corner of his mouth, darkened by blood. The chest rose once more, unevenly, as though the body were asking permission to fail. Then it did not rise. His eyes were open. I did not close them. The code does not make the victor the one who tends the dead after the account is discharged. His left hand was beneath him. His right hand lay open and still. He looked like a man who had been cut in the place where breath and blood meet, and had died there. He did not look like a story. He did not look like honor. He looked like a body that had been accounted for.”

She turned back to the witnesses.

“The account is this. The killing wound was delivered in the fifth exchange. It landed upon the right side of the sternum, between the fourth and fifth ribs. It went upward and inward, toward the center of the chest. It pierced the chest cavity. It severed the pulmonary vessels. It cut skin, muscle, and the way into the chest. It did these things to the man lying there. It caused his death. He spoke after the wound, yielded after the wound, and died after the wound. I did not strike again. I did not conceal the place. I did not soften the naming. I claim the direction. I claim the depth. I claim the result. I claim the responsibility.”

Auren’s voice remained level.

“No part of the account has been omitted. No part of the responsibility has been shifted. The witnesses have heard it. The second has confirmed it. The page bears my name. If the law asks again, I will speak again. If the law asks a third time, I will speak a third time. If the law asks a fourth time, I will speak a fourth time. The dead are owed precision. The living are owed proof that it was done by law, not cruelty.”

She looked at the witnesses until each had heard the last word.

“I take no pleasure in this account. I have taken no pleasure in eleven accounts. I do not soften this one, and I will not soften it later. The precision was not kindness. The precision was honesty.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow against the dryness in my throat and meet her gaze. "The account is complete. The law is satisfied." My fingers trace the edge of the parchment. "I'll have it sealed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren let the words stand without meeting them with relief. Satisfaction was a matter for the code, not for her.

“Then it will be sealed,” she said, “as the law directs: in the presence of the witnesses, not in the privacy of a desk. If the page is closed before their names are entered, the account is still open.”

She turned to the witnesses and held their eyes until each one understood that she was not asking for their comfort.

“You heard the full account. You heard the place, the direction, the depth, the result, the time, the words, the end. If any part is false to you, say so before your mark is added. If no part is false, set your name to what you have heard. The victor has spoken. The second has confirmed. The witnesses must still bear it.”

Auren looked toward the fallen man, then back to the parchment.

“The body is not mine to move. The record is mine to make exact.” Her voice did not rise. “When the witnesses have signed and the seal is set, I will remain only if the code requires it. If the code does not require it, I will not linger for sentiment. I have named the wound. I have named the time. I have named the end. I do not ask anyone to make them less.”

She placed her hands where they had been, steady and empty.

“Seal it before them,” Auren said. “Let no one say later that the account was hidden in a fold.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, turning the parchment to face the witnesses. I take the wax stick and light it from the brazier nearby. The red wax drips onto the page, over the signatures. I press the official seal into it with a firm, final motion. "It is sealed," I say, my voice barely above a whisper.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren watched the red wax settle over the page and did not let the sight of it make her voice warmer. The seal was a closing, not a cleansing. It could bind the record, but it could not bind the truth into anything smaller than it had been.

“The seal is set,” she said, “but the law asks more than the seal. It asks that the page be lawful when it is closed. If the witnesses’ names are upon it, let them be read. If any name is missing, it must be added now, before this becomes a private document instead of a public account.”

Her gaze moved to the witnesses, one by one. She did not plead with them. She did not invite comfort. She only asked for the same exactness she had been required to give.

“You heard the place of the wound,” she said. “You heard the direction. You heard the depth. You heard the result. You heard the time, the words, and the end. If your names are set down upon that page, they say that you heard it and did not object. If you object, speak now. If you remain silent, the law will take your silence as assent, and I will not pretend otherwise.”

She waited, steady as the mark on the ground.

When the account had been seen and no voice rose against it, Auren inclined her head once, formally, to the record.

“Then the page is complete,” she said. “Let it be carried where the law requires. Let no one say it was sealed before it was spoken. Let no one say the witness was hidden behind the wax.”

Her eyes went briefly to the fallen man. She did not soften when she looked at him. She had already named him plainly. To soften him now would be to make the accounting lie.

“Let the body be covered,” Auren said to the attendants, “when the page is lawful. Not before. The dead are owed witness, not concealment. After the record is complete, cover him as the custom permits.”

She turned back toward the second, though she did not step into the space between them.

“I have signed twelve pages,” she said, quieter now, but still not so quietly that it could be mistaken for confession. “This one is no kinder than the first. It is no crueler than the last. It is exact.”

A breath passed. The sword remained sheathed. The blade had been cleaned. The obligation had been discharged in every part the code could reach.

“My name is beneath the account,” Auren said. “My word remains with it. If any person doubts the truth of what was spoken, let him doubt the record, not me. I will answer for the wound as I have answered for it. I claimed it. I named it. I did not hide it.”

She held the posture of the victor no longer than the form required. When the last part was complete, she let her hands fall to her sides, not in ease, but in release.

“Then I withdraw,” she said. “The law has its page. The dead have their account. The living may carry the rest.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn’t know I was holding. "It's done," I say, my voice rough. I look at the sealed parchment, then back at her. "You should go. I'll see the body tended."
