dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Then hear it," she said.

She did not sit. The account was owed on her feet, and she had never once given it any other way. Around the field's edge the witnesses had closed into their loose half-circle, and at the centre of the trampled grass Corren Vayle lay where he had fallen, on his back, one arm thrown out as if reaching for something a little beyond his fingers.

Auren turned to where Del stood, in the second's place, and let the silence run its proper length. Eleven times before this she had stood where she stood now. The words never went down easily. They never showed it.

"Stand witness," she said, and the half-circle stilled. "I am Auren, victor by the code. Corren Vayle challenged me this morning on a matter he named mortal. The terms were live blades, to the end. The end has come. I give the account.

"The duel lasted three exchanges. In the first, he pressed me along my sword side, and I gave ground, and no touch was given. In the second, he feinted low, and I did not answer the feint, and he bound my blade, and I broke the bind, and no touch was given. In the third, he stepped in behind a cut at my head, half a hand deeper than the measure required. I passed inside the cut and gave the thrust."

She kept the pace of it level. Not slower for gravity, not quicker for mercy. The words were owed at the speed of the truth.

"The point entered his left breast, a thumb's width from the breastbone, between the fourth rib and the fifth. It went in two fingers' depth, angled upward. It opened the heart. It was the only wound given in the duel, and it was the killing wound."

Somewhere behind her, a man breathed out. She did not turn to him.

"He put his hand over the place, as if it could be held shut. He sat down where he stood. He lived long enough to look at the wound, and that was all the time it gave him. He did not speak."

She let that stand for the space of a breath, as the code required, before the closing.

"That is the wound. It is spoken. The account is complete."

She sheathed the blade, and the small sound of steel going home was the loudest thing on the field. There were things she could have added — that the step in the third exchange was an error a man makes once and never twice, that he had not hesitated, that it had been quick, as though quick were a kindness. She said none of them. Words like those were for her own comfort, not for him, and the account was his.

She stood at rest, hands loose at her sides, and waited for the second to take it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "I have heard it." My eyes go to Corren's body, then back to Auren. "The account is accepted. There is no fault."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The acceptance settled over the field, and the field began to let go of its shape. Boots shifted along the half-circle; the witnesses came apart the way crowds do, into people with somewhere else to be. The man who had breathed out went past her with his eyes down, and she let him.

Auren inclined her head to Del, to the depth the code asked and no further.

"Then it's closed," she said. "The field is yours until he's carried. I'll wait at the edge, if anything's wanted of me." Then, because it was owed as well: "You kept your eyes open. Not every second does."

She had never once left before the body did. The code didn't require it; she did. The fight was work, the account was duty, and the standing afterward was neither — and it was the longest part of every one of the twelve.

The sun had climbed a hand's width since the challenge. That was all the morning had cost, measured, like everything else today, in hands.

Corren Vayle's sword lay in the grass beyond the reach of his outflung arm. She crossed to it and lifted it. A plain guard, honest steel, honed often and recently — she could read the care of a blade at a glance, the way she could read a man in his first exchange. It was not hers to judge. She judged it anyway. The habit was older than the code.

By custom, the fallen's blade belonged to the victor. In twelve duels she had claimed none of them. A blade hung on a wall said something about the owner of the wall, and she had never once wanted to say it.

She carried it back and laid it in the trampled grass at Del's feet, hilt toward him, without ceremony.

"His blade. The custom gives it to me, and I don't take them. It goes with him, or with his kin — whichever they choose."

She had passed close enough to see that his eyes were still open. She had left them for the second or the family to close. She had put her hands on him once today, exactly once, and it was not a touch to follow with a gentler one.

"Has he kin in the town?" she asked. "If word has to be carried, send a face they know. I'll stand the cost of a runner if there's no one closer. But it shouldn't be me at the door. They'd know what I am the moment it opened, and they shouldn't have to stand there and be civil to it."

There was blood on her cuff, a spot the size of a thumbnail. She did not look down at it. There would be an hour for that later, alone, and she knew from the other eleven what that hour would hold. She kept it waiting.

"One thing more," she said. "Tonight you'll be asked how he fought, and you should have true answers, not soft ones. He found my sword side in the first exchange — most men never do. The step in the third came at full speed, and a step at full speed isn't folly. It's a wager. It lost today. Say it that way, plainly. It's the only thing I can send home with him that's worth the carrying."

Beyond the hedge, a gate clattered. Someone had gone for the cart.

She stood where she was, hands loose at her sides, and waited.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Four

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I glance at the sword at my feet, then back at Auren. "He has a sister in the next valley. I'll send my cousin—they've traded before. She'll take the blade with him." I swallow. "And I'll tell them about the step."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"A sister, then, and a trader's face to carry it to her." She thought that was the right shape for it. "A door opens differently for a face it knows. There's one breath of ordinary before the news lands, and they'll need that breath. It's the cheapest thing left on this field that's worth anything."

She looked once at the blade in the grass, hilt still toward him.

"The steel goes with him, then. It was whetted often and honestly. Whoever ends with it ends with something that was cared for, and that's a true thing about him, if they can hear it through everything else. And the step — you'll tell it as it was. A wager made at full speed, and lost. Most men are carried home in a soft version that fits no one. He goes home with the true one. It's worth more. It won't feel like it is.

"One thing more they'll ask, and you should have the answer ready before they do. They'll ask whether it was quick." She let the words come out level, like the rest of it. "It was. He lived long enough to look at the wound, and no longer. That isn't in the account — the account holds what was done, not how long it took to matter. But she'll ask, and she should have the true answer. Not the soft one, and not the cruel one. The true one."

She had known where the point was going. She had not known how fast he would fall to it. The aim was hers. The speed was nobody's.

The cart came through the gate at a walk, two men on the bench and a plank and folded sacking laid in the bed. The last of the witnesses stepped aside for it and were gone through the hedge, and the field came down to the dead man, the second, the cart men, and her.

She moved for the edge as she had said she would, and passed near the second's place on the way.

"His eyes are open," she said, low enough that it went no farther than him. "That falls to the second, or to the family. If it's yours, do it before they cover him. It's easier here, on his own ground, than at some roadside with the miles still to go."

Then she took her place in the long grass at the field's edge — the only ground the day had not touched — and from there, not loudly, gave him the last of it.

"Tonight you'll walk the duel again. Exchange by exchange, hunting the step you could have made different. There is no such step. The terms were his, and the place you stood was the one he set you in. The dark hours will tell you otherwise — they tell every second the same lie, and they are patient with it. Don't sign what they put in front of you."

The cart men climbed down and stood at the body's edge, caps in their hands, settling between themselves whose task it was to touch him first. She let them settle it. The field was not hers anymore.

Twelve times she had stood through this part, and no code had ever asked it of her. She would walk out behind the cart when it went, and never before it, for the same nothing that had asked her to stay. The duties you were owed were the easy ones.

The spot on her cuff had not grown and would not. It would keep. It had kept for her eleven times before this one, and she had met it every time, and the meetings had never once gotten shorter.

The sun had climbed another hand's width since the account. She counted it without meaning to. Measuring was the oldest habit she had, and it had never once brought anything back.

One of the cart men looked toward Del, cap turning in his fingers, waiting on the second's word to begin.

She kept her place in the untrampled grass and let the last of it be theirs.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She came off the edge — three strides, no more, enough to put the words where they would reach one man and not the two by the cart. They had their caps in their hands and their eyes on Del. Let them keep waiting. This was not for them.

"You heard it once," she said. "I know how the account goes through a man standing where you stand. It moves at the truth's speed and you were standing still, the way anyone stands. Most men who ask me for it a second time ask me to make it smaller. You asked for it plainer. That's the rarer ask, and the better one. So."

She raised her right hand and set two fingers against her own chest, on the left, a thumb's width from the breastbone, and held them there.

"Here. We're all built alike in that place — where it sits in me, it sat in him. Between the fourth rib and the fifth. Count your own ribs down from the first and you'll find the gap. The point went in two fingers' depth, angled upward. The heart sits high and forward in a man; the angle did the work, not the depth. That is what 'opened the heart' means with the ceremony stripped off it: the blood found somewhere new to go, and went, and the pressure that keeps a man on his feet went with it.

"That's why he sat down. Not choice. Not a failure in his legs that you should carry home to anyone. The legs are the first thing the heart stops paying, and his stopped being paid. He put his hand over the place because a man does — there is nothing a hand can do there, and every man tries it anyway. He didn't speak. I won't tell you why, because I don't know it. Whether the words weren't in him or the time wasn't, I won't guess, and you shouldn't dress a guess as a fact and hand it to his sister. She'll take anything you give her for true. Give her only what is."

She lowered her hand.

"The witnesses had the account. If any of them want it again tonight, they can come to me, and they'll get it whole, as many times as they ask. It doesn't wear out. It costs me the same every time I say it, and it has cost the same for twelve. That's how I know it's still the truth and not a story I've gotten good at telling."

She stepped back to where the grass was still long, and inclined her head once toward the cart men, who were waiting on the second's word and no one else's.

The plain words would find his dark hours, she knew. The account had armour in it; these had none. But the lie the dark told a second was that a hand could have gone somewhere in time, and the plain truth said the hand had nowhere to go. He'd asked for it plainly, and plainly was the only version that argued back.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat working. "Between the fourth and fifth rib." I touch my own chest, feeling the shape of it through my shirt. I look at the cart men. "You can take him now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"That's the place," she said.

He had gone straight to it, no counting down from the first rib. Some things needed showing only once, and she would rather this had not been one of them.

"When the cart goes, I go out behind it," she said. "To the gate, and the road past it. Don't hold the gate for me, and don't wait at it. That part isn't the code. It's mine."

Then she kept the edge and let the field work.

The cart men had settled between them whose task it was without a word passing. The older one knelt at the shoulder, and the first thing he did was bring in the outflung arm and lay it along the side, and the reach was over. It had only ever been grass.

They lifted him the way the dead are lifted, one at the shoulders and one under the knees, and the younger man's breath went short with the weight. The dead weigh more than their living build — she had never found a reason for that which wasn't superstition, and had stopped looking for one. The front of his shirt had gone dark and was stiffening. They got him onto the plank without roughness and without ceremony, and the older man shook out the sacking and made the first fold beneath him, and held the second fold ready above.

Then he stopped.

The eyes were still open.

He stood at the head of the plank with the sacking in his hands and looked down into a dead man's face, and then he looked toward the second, and did not lower it.

Auren kept her place and her silence. She had said once, low, whose task that was. She would not say it twice. The pause was the second's, and she left it in his hands.

Neither man had touched the sword. It lay in the trampled grass where she had set it, hilt toward Del. The fallen they would carry without asking; a fallen man's steel waited on the second's word, and both of them knew that etiquette without being able to say where they had learned it. There were rules like that, older than any code she kept, that ordinary men carried all their lives and never once had taught to them.

The grass where Corren Vayle had lain was pressed flat in the shape of him — shoulder, hip, heel — and the place where he had sat and put his hand to the wound was darker than the rest. The field would hold him a few days yet. Then the grass would lift, and the dark would wait for rain, and by midsummer there would be nothing here for anyone to find, and no way to find it.

The sun stood two hands higher than the challenge. She caught herself counting and stopped mid-count, and it changed nothing.

Against her wrist the spot on her cuff had stiffened as it dried. There was an hour waiting on her behind a shut door, and she knew the hour's whole shape, having met it eleven times. It had never once gotten shorter. Nothing left in this day could surprise her, and that was the only mercy in it, if mercy was the word.

Beyond the hedge the gate stood open for the cart. When it went, she would follow it out, last of everything, and the field would be done with them.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"You're right to put your thumb on it," she said. "I said *opened the heart*, and that's still a phrase. Phrases are where softening hides first, and I won't stand on this field and be soft by accident after twelve of these, not on purpose. So. Your two questions, in your order."

She kept the voice at the reach she'd used before — far enough for one man, short of the two by the cart.

"What the blade did. It went in as a point and it parted, it did not tear. A thrust leaves a slit, not a hole — the length of a thumbnail where it entered, and the same within, a track straight through what it passed. It met no bone. You feel a rib through the steel the way you feel a stone through a boot sole, and I felt nothing but the give — that's how I knew where it had gone before he sat down. It went two fingers and stopped because I stopped it. The depth was mine. I drew it back in the same motion it went in, and the drawing added nothing — a thrust wound doesn't close when the steel leaves it. The track stayed open. That is the door.

"What it did it to. In order: the skin, which resists and then gives all at once. The muscle between the fourth and fifth rib — a finger's thickness of a man, no more. The lining of the chest. The sac the heart rides in. The wall of the heart. And inside that, the chamber that faces forward — the thin-walled one. Straight in, two fingers reaches the sac and stops. Angled up, the same two fingers ends inside that room. That is the whole of what the angle did, and it is the reason the account is short.

"Then the heart did the rest to itself. A heart isn't told it's wounded. It kept its beat. A heart with a door in it pumps its own blood out through the door, at its own speed, and its speed is a fast one. Most of what left went into the chest, where blood does no work — which is why the shirt tells the wrong story, if anyone reads it. The outside of a wound like this is the least of it. Don't let anyone decide it was less than it was because the front of him looked small.

"Now the other edge of *precisely*, because the word has one. Precisely means I stop where my sight stopped. What he felt, I don't know. Why he didn't speak, I don't know, and I won't hand you a guess with precise words on it — precise words make a guess weigh like a fact. If she asks what he felt, the true answer is that no one living knows it, and any man who tells her otherwise is decorating. The code has no room for decoration in either direction."

By the cart, the older man had taken the second's word. He made the second fold of the sacking, and stopped at the face a moment, and then passed two fingers down over the eyes, unasked, half a breath's work. There it was again — a rule older than any code, carried by a man who'd never once had it taught to him. The task had fallen to whoever stood nearest. That was how most necessary things got done, code or none.

The younger man came for the sword. He lifted it from the trampled grass with both hands, the way you lift a thing that belongs to someone, and laid it along the sacking at the covered shape's side.

Auren watched it settle, then let her eyes go back to the second's place.

"That's all of it," she said. "Every part I can name, and nothing I can't. It cost the same as the first time I said it. That's how I know both versions are still the truth and not a story I've gotten good at telling."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch the cart men cover his face, and my breath hitches. "Thank you," I say quietly, my voice thick. I pull my gaze from the covered shape and meet Auren's eyes. "I'll walk with you to the gate."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"No," she said, and gave the word a breath to stand on before she built the reasons under it.

"You offered because the field is emptying and the walk behind a cart looks like the loneliest thing left on it. It isn't. The loneliest thing left is the bench of that cart, and it isn't yours either. Yours is a door in the next valley, tonight, and it will ask more of you than this field did. Between now and then, work is what holds a man up. Company doesn't. I've watched men try both.

"So — your cousin goes now, before the wheels turn. A cart travels at a walk, and a man on a road beats a cart over a valley. The word should reach that door first. A body arriving unannounced is an ambush; a body arriving expected is only a grief. She's owed the grief, not the ambush.

"And your place is at the cart. Hired men carry well enough, but nobody should leave his own field with only strangers attending. Ride the bench or walk at the wheel. The code puts the second there, and so would he, and I don't argue with either.

"The walk is mine. I told you that much already, and you've earned the reason, so: everything today was owed to somebody and watched by everybody — the fight, the account, the carrying. The road out is the one part of it owed to no one and seen by no one, and somewhere in eleven of these I learned to need one thing in a day that nobody witnessed. Don't take it from me by accident. It's the only thing I'm keeping off this field.

"The thanks — the account was owed, and a debt doesn't take thanks. The plainness wasn't owed, so that part I'll take, and carry it the way I carry the rest of today: without looking at it until I'm behind a shut door. It'll keep. In eleven fields before this one, no second ever thanked me for anything. You're the first, and I haven't yet found where to put it. If you've more to spare, the older cart man closed his eyes unasked. He doesn't know it was seen. Tell him it was.

"Meet the dark hours tired. They get less out of a man who's already spent."

The cart men climbed to the bench. The older one gathered the reins, the younger clicked his tongue at the horse, and the wheels took the weight and began. The cart went toward the gate at a walk, the sacking holding its shape, the sword riding under the fold where it had been laid, and as they passed the second's place the older man touched his cap to him.

Auren stayed in the long grass and would stay until the cart was through the gate and the field was empty of everyone living but her. The sun stood two hands and a half above the challenge; she let the count run all the way to the end, for once, and it changed nothing. Then she would follow, last, for the same nothing that had asked her to stay. The nothing had never once wanted company. She saw no reason the twelfth time would be different.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
She came off the edge a second time and matched the cart's pace, walking the flattened lane just off the wheel. Forty strides of ground stood between the cart and the gate, at a walk. She meant to spend all of them and not one past them.

"First, the ledger, because you're about to carry it home and I want you carrying the true one," she said. "The code doesn't say all of it. The code says the killing wound, spoken aloud before witnesses. It was spoken, it was witnessed, and you closed it yourself — accepted, no fault. The code's part on this field has been finished since you said those words. What's asking me now is you. The witnesses went through the hedge before the cart ever came; whoever you're speaking for, it isn't them.

"I'll answer anyway. All of it that exists. But under its true name, because the name matters more tonight than it does this morning: the code is a debt, and debts end — that's the mercy built into them. What's asking in you doesn't end, and if you file it under the code, you'll go on answering what feels like duty forever and the ledger will never show paid. Name it yours and it can be paid. So: everything I saw, nothing I didn't, and where my sight stops I'll say *edge* and stop. That's the most anyone can hand you. It's more than most get.

"You saw it too — you kept your eyes open. But a thing seen at duel speed comes back in pieces, and pieces lie about their order. Here is the order.

"He was upright one breath after the steel left him. One. Then the legs stopped being paid, and he went down. I told you he sat, and the word is exact and it flatters the thing, so strip the flattery off: the sitting and the falling were one motion, done at falling speed. It looked like sitting because the hand went to the wound on the way down and the ground took him mostly upright. That is what *he sat down where he stood* is, with the phrase stripped.

"The hand went flat over the place and pressed. Pressing did nothing, and he kept it there. His eyes went to the wound and stayed — not to me, not past me, not to the second's place. I know because I was two paces off and facing him, and I followed his eyes to see whether there was anything in them I'd need to answer. There wasn't. He spent the last of his looking on the wound, and I won't tell you what it meant, because a face at the end of a thing like that isn't legible, and anyone who reads you peace or terror off it is selling something. What it was, was stopped. The way a clock stops — mid-expression. The nearest word I have is *interrupted*, and I'll say plainly that's a nearest word, not a true one. Words run out exactly where you're asking me to go. That isn't softening. That's the edge of the ledger, and I said I'd mark edges.

"What he said: nothing. His mouth didn't move. There was a sound in one of the later breaths — a breath with a sound riding it, not shaped into anything — and I won't name it further, because naming it further would be building it into words it wasn't. If he made words, they didn't carry two paces, and that's all I can truly say. Why he didn't speak — whether the words weren't in him or the time wasn't — is the edge. I said I'd stop at edges.

"How long, at the bottom. I counted his breaths from the sitting to the end. Counting is what I do instead of everything else; it's the oldest habit I have, and today it was worth one thing. There were nine. The first ran like a man's. The last two came spaced, with gaps the earlier ones didn't have. The ninth went out, and nothing came back after it. And here is how I knew it was over, because you should have this too: the hand came off the wound. Not lifted — came off, the way a thing comes off when nothing is holding it. A man with his hand on a wound is still trying. When the hand stops trying, it's done. I watch for that on purpose. It's the one thing in a duel I watch for on purpose, and it's how a victor knows without going to the body. I never knelt to him. Some do. I've never once worked out whether that's for the dead man or for the victor, and I don't spend what I can't account for.

"From the thrust to the hand coming off: less than a minute, and I won't cut it finer, because I was counting breaths, not time, and I won't convert one count into a false other. Nine breaths is the true figure. Count them tonight at your own pace and you'll have the length of it, and it will be wrong, because your breaths run slower than a dying man's. That's the one thing I can't hand you, and I won't invent it. It doesn't exist to be handed.

"So — what it looked like at the end, whole: a man on the grass with his hand on his chest and his eyes on his hand, going still by breaths. Nothing was done to him after the thrust. The account held what was done. This holds what came after. Between them, that's the entire field, and there is nothing in either part that I held back. If the dark hours tell you otherwise, send them to me. I'll say it whole again, as many times as they ask, and it will cost the same as it cost today. That's how you'll know."

The gate was on them. She stopped with ten strides left of her forty and let the cart take the rest alone, because she went out last, and had said she would.

"She'll ask how long," she said, at the reach of one man. "Give her the nine. *Quick* is a kindness, and true, but it's a word — it moves around in the hand. Nine breaths doesn't. She can hold nine and know it's the whole of it, and no one will ever come to her door with a different number."

The wheels crossed the threshold and went through, and the older man didn't hold the gate, because she had asked him not to.

She stood where the trampled ground ended. The sun stood three hands above the challenge, and for the second time today she let the count run all the way out. Counting had never once brought anything back. But it had carried one thing forward this morning — nine breaths, riding in a cousin's mouth over a valley to a door — and that was the closest the habit had ever come to being worth its keep.

Then she followed, last of everything, at the distance the nothing preferred.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch you go. Then I turn to the older cart man, who's waiting for me at the gate. "I saw what you did for him," I tell him, my voice low. "It was a kindness." He just nods, his eyes wet. I climb up on the bench beside him, and we follow you out.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The quiet lasted thirty strides past the gate. Then the road gave it back: iron on packed dirt, and under it the horse, four beats to the cart's one.

She did the arithmetic without turning. The second had taken the bench — she'd told him to — and the road out ran one way, as roads do. He hadn't walked beside her. He'd kept the letter of everything she'd asked and still left her walking in front of the cart, and that was the one place she would not walk. A woman ahead of a cart leads it. She had never once led a dead man anywhere, and she was not going to start on the twelfth.

So she stepped off the lane into the verge grass and stood.

The cart came up at its walk. The older man saw her and started to check the reins — the reflex of a man raised not to pass a standing woman on a road — and she put her palm out flat: keep on. He kept on.

The horse went by first, dark at the shoulder, smelling of harness. Then the near wheel, tall as her chin, iron hissing on the dirt. Then the bed of it. The sacking held its shape — a ridge the length of a man and nothing else, the plain guard of the sword riding at its side where it had been laid. She looked at the whole of it once. Covered, he asked nothing of her. He was the first thing today that hadn't, and she let that be the last note she took of him.

Then the bench. The younger man had shifted to the tailboard, legs over the edge, and the older man sat squared with his cap on, and his eyes were wet in the way of a man who has been spoken to and not yet dried. So the words had been spent, and they had landed. She filed that where she'd filed the thanks — carried, unexamined, keeping.

She gave the older man a nod, no code in it. He touched his brim going past. That was the whole exchange, and it was the right size.

She kept her eyes off the far side of the bench. The second had watched everything today with his eyes open; he was owed one passage that nobody watched. It was a small thing to hand a man. She was finding, late in the day, that the small things were what was left when the ledger closed, and that they carried. She had nothing further for the bench itself — everything true she owned had been spent on the field, and the rest would have been decoration.

"Milestone past the bend," she said, at the reach she'd used all morning. "There's a trough at it. Water the horse there. The valley road's the left fork after, and it runs the smoother of the two."

"Left fork," he said back, the way a man fixes a thing in his memory, and she let it stand for the whole conversation.

The cart went by at the speed of a walk, the noise of it sliding ahead of her, and she stepped off the verge and fell in behind, last of everything, where she had said she would be.

A horse at a walk beats a woman at a walk, but not by much. The cart drew ahead a pace a minute, and she measured it without meaning to, and let the count run. The sun stood three hands and a half above the challenge. She let that count run too. It changed nothing. Somewhere between the gate and the bend she noticed she had stopped expecting it to.

At the fork the cart took the left, and the hedge took the wheels' noise a piece at a time, and then the road had only her own feet in it.

The walk out was hers again — the one thing off the field she'd meant to keep — and she'd bought it back for the price of standing in grass while a cart went by. She'd gotten off cheap. Most days she hadn't.

She carried two things now that she had not looked at. The spot on her cuff, small and stiff. And a second's thanks — the first in twelve fields, still without a place she'd found to put it. Both would keep. Keeping things was the one part of this work that had never needed teaching, and the one part that had never once gotten easier.

Somewhere behind her, in a trampled field, the grass was already beginning to lift, the way it did. By midsummer there would be nothing there for anyone to find, and no way to find it. She walked on toward the town, and the shut door, and the hour, at the pace of a walk, alone, at the distance the nothing preferred. The hour would keep. It had kept eleven times before this one. She would go and meet it, as she always had, and it would cost what it always cost — and that was how she would know it was still real.

dialogue.content: I nod, my eyes on the grass where he fell. "Nine breaths," I say again, quieter. "I'll tell her that."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The words came back down the left-hand road after the cart had turned.

She had thought the parting was finished — the nod spent, the directions given, the hedge already eating the wheels' noise. Then the second's voice came across the closing gap, rough with the whole day in it, and it was the account, entire. *Between the fourth and fifth rib. Two fingers' depth, angled up. Nine breaths.* And then quieter, half to the road and half to himself: *Nine breaths. I'll tell her that.*

She stopped where the fork divided the ground.

He had carried it across a field and half a mile of road, and it had lost nothing. Every figure standing where she had set it. Nothing rounded to sit easier in the mouth, no *quick* slipped in where the true number had been. She had handed accounts to seconds on eleven fields before this one, and most men lost something in the carrying — a number softened on the road, an angle flattened. His had kept. Whatever the dark hours worked on tonight, they would have to work on the true version. That was all the armour there was for those hours, and he had put it on himself.

"Say it to her just that way," she said, pitched to cross a road's width and no farther. "Word for word. It'll hold."

Then the hedge had the cart, and the road held nothing but her own feet.

The sun stood four hands above the challenge when she reached the town. She counted it because she would always count it. It changed nothing, and she no longer needed it to.

The town did what towns did: gave her a room at the end of a passage and asked nothing. The man at the counter looked once at the sword, and at what the sword made her, and set the key down without a word. On a day like this one, that was the whole of what she wanted from a town.

The door shut. The hour began.

She sat down with it the way she had sat down with eleven of them — no lamp lit until it was over, nothing in her hands, nothing to drink. The hour didn't bargain, and she brought nothing to bargain with.

The cuff first. She looked at the spot at last. The size of a thumbnail, dried stiff, the same shape it had been all day. She had carried it across a field, a road, and half a town without once looking down. Now she looked, and it was exactly what it was, and looking cost what it cost, and she let it.

Then she counted.

Nine breaths, at her own pace. Hers ran slower than a dying man's — she had said so herself on the field, and it was as true in a shut room as it had been in the open air. The count would be wrong. She knew that before she began it. She ran it anyway, all nine, the way you pay a thing that takes no other currency. The ninth went out, and nothing came back after it. Nothing had come back after it on the field either. The habit had never once brought anything back. She had never once done it for that.

Somewhere in the dark she took out the thanks — the first in twelve fields — and turned it over once, looking for the place to put it. There wasn't one. Some things weren't for putting; they were for carrying. She had told him that, on the field, without knowing she was also telling herself. She filed it back with the keeping.

When the hour was paid, she lit the lamp and washed the cuff in cold water. The spot came out with patience. It always did. Nothing else about the day was that tractable, and nothing else about it was meant to be.

Twelve fields now. The hour had never once gotten shorter.

She had never once wanted it to.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I sit beside the older cart man until the fork, then get down without a word. I walk back to the field alone. The grass is already lifting where he lay. I stand there until the sun touches the trees, counting nine breaths over and over, trying to make them faster.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren remained on her feet. She looked once at the body, then turned to face the witnesses, and her voice came out level, stripped of any warmth that might have made it bearable.

“The thrust entered between the sixth and seventh ribs on the left, clear of the bone. It passed through the lower lobe of the lung, through the pericardium, and opened the left ventricle. The heart emptied into the chest. He was dead before he reached the ground.” She paused. Her jaw tightened, but she did not lower her eyes. “That is the killing wound. The accounting is given.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, but my voice stays steady. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." I glance at the witnesses, then back at Auren. "The law is satisfied."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren sheathed her sword. The guard struck the scabbard throat with a sound that was too sharp, too final. She did not look at the body again; she had looked once, as the code required, and once was sufficient. She turned to Del and inclined her head—a formal acknowledgment, exact and without warmth. Her hands were steady. They had been steady throughout. She did not ask the dead man's name, nor did she offer any word that might soften what had been done; the accounting had held all the truth that was owed, and to embellish it now would have been its own dishonor. She stepped back, yielding the ground to the witnesses and the necessary rites that would follow, and waited with her face closed, neither relieved nor proud.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned her attention back to the witnesses. She did not look at Del again; the request had been formal, and a formal request required a formal answer. Her voice emerged unchanged, precise as a blade re-measured against a straightedge.

“The thrust entered between the sixth and seventh ribs on the left, clear of the bone. It passed through the lower lobe of the lung, through the pericardium, and opened the left ventricle. The heart emptied into the chest. He was dead before he reached the ground.” The words hung in the air, unsoftened by inflection or regret. “That is the killing wound. The accounting is given.”

She did not shift her weight. She did not ask if the witnesses had heard, for it was not her place to seek reassurance, only to render the truth. She stood as she had stood on the duelling ground, with her hands at her sides and her face closed against any relief that might have tempted her to believe the duty was finished simply because she wished it to be.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, accepting the repetition. "The accounting is heard and confirmed." I turn to the witnesses. "The law is satisfied. You may remove him."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren remained at the margin of the duelling ground and did not turn to watch the witnesses recover the body. She had looked once, as required, and the code made no allowance for a second glance born of morbid courtesy. When the witnesses passed near her, bearing the dead weight between them, she did not step aside, for she had already placed herself beyond the boundary of their path. The sun had shifted a fraction while the accounting was rendered; she noted the change without purpose, marking it only because to ignore the passage would have been to pretend that time itself had halted, and she made no pretense. Her hands stayed at her sides. She did not offer assistance, nor did she offer regret. The code prescribed neither, and she did not add to the requirements.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren looked at the duelling ground, now empty where the body had lain. “Beneath the left breast,” she said. “It landed in the heart. The ribs, the lung, the pericardium—these are only the path the steel traveled. The heart was the end of it. That is the plain truth.” She did not look at Del, nor did she look to the witnesses for acknowledgment. Her hands remained at her sides. She said no more, for there was nothing left to add that would not be a comfort, and she did not deal in comforts.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I walk to the spot she indicated and look down at the stained ground. "The accounting is complete," I say, then lower my voice so only she can hear. "Your hands are steady. But your eyes aren't."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren met Del's gaze then. The unsteadiness Del had named was there, exact and unhidden, a fine fracture in the otherwise closed mask. She did not blink, nor did she look away. "The code requires steady hands," she said, her voice low, stripped even of the formality reserved for witnesses. "It makes no mention of the eyes. I do not add to the requirements." She held Del's look for a moment longer, neither challenging nor yielding, before she turned back to face the empty duelling ground. Her hands remained at her sides, steady as they had been throughout, and she did not speak again.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren kept her eyes upon the stain on the duelling ground. “The blade opened the heart,” she said. “It opened it in a living man. The heart emptied. The man died.” She did not move. Her hands remained at her sides, steady and still. “That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to. The accounting is given.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The blade is clean," I say, because it is, and because the code asks me to say so. "The ground is stained." I step back, letting my own eyes finally close for a heartbeat. "It's done, Auren. You can move now."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren turned from the duelling ground. She did not look back at the stain; she had looked once, as the code required, and once was sufficient. She crossed the margin with measured steps, neither hastening nor lingering, and did not stop until she had passed the outer ring of witness stones. "The code does not require me to remain here," she said. Her hands stayed at her sides, steady in the shifted sunlight. She did not say that she was finished, for she was not. She did not pretend that moving her body had moved the weight of the eleventh. She stood with her back to the field, her face closed, and waited without asking what came next. The code prescribed no question for this moment, and she did not add to the requirements.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren turned to face the duelling ground once more. She did not look toward Del. "He said nothing," she said. "The blade had opened the ventricle. There was insufficient pressure remaining to form words. He took one step after I withdrew, perhaps less than a full step. The right knee failed. The eyes fixed, and the pupils dilated. The mouth opened. No sound emerged. Blood came from the wound, bright and thin, soaking the left side. The body fell forward. The forehead struck the ground before the knees touched earth. The fingers of the right hand opened, then closed. Then they were still." She paused. Her hands remained at her sides, steady in the shifted sunlight. "The diaphragm spasmed once. Then there was no further movement. That is all of it. The accounting is given."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look away from her, at the ground where the stain is drying. "The accounting is heard and confirmed," I say, but my voice is rough. "Now it's over."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren did not say that it was over. She did not say that it was not. She turned from the witness stones and began to walk, her pace measured, her boots making no unnecessary sound upon the ground. She passed Del without a word, for the code prescribed no farewell between duellist and second once the accounting was heard, and she did not add to the requirements. But she stopped after she had passed him, her back still straight, her hands still steady at her sides. "The law is satisfied," she said, not turning around. "That is what the code guarantees. It guarantees nothing further." The shifted sunlight fell across her shoulders, revealing nothing. She remained there, neither relieved nor finished, with the empty duelling ground behind her and the road ahead. The code prescribed no next step, and she did not add to the requirements.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren turned back from the road. She faced Del squarely, her shoulders aligned with his, her back now to the duelling ground and the stain drying upon it. She did not look away from the roughness in his voice, nor did she pretend that she had not heard it. “The confirmation is heard,” she said. “The code prescribes no steadiness for the second. Only the duellist.” Her hands remained at her sides, steady in the shifted sunlight. “The accounting was exact. The law is satisfied. That is all the code promises.” She held his gaze, and the unsteadiness he had named in her eyes remained there, exact and unhidden, neither asking for remedy nor offering one. She stepped back once, yielding the final ground between them. “I am finished here,” she said. She did not say that she was finished elsewhere. She turned and walked toward the road, her pace measured, her boots striking the earth with the same precision she had brought to the lunge. She did not look back. The code required no backward glance, and she did not add to the requirements.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I watch her go until she's out of sight. Then I look down at my own hands. They aren't steady.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content: Auren walked until the witness stones passed from view, and then she walked further, for the code prescribed no distance for a duellist's departure and she did not add to the requirements. The road dipped below the line of the field and rose again toward the crossroads. She stopped there, where an old marker stood carved with the names of the dead from older accountings. She did not touch it. She looked down at her hands and opened them slowly, palms up, in the empty air. They were steady. They had been steady when the steel entered between the sixth and seventh ribs, steady when the heart emptied into the chest, steady when she named the wound before witnesses. She closed her fingers. The unsteadiness Del had named in her eyes had not reached her hands; the code had not permitted it. She stood with her back to the duelling ground and the stain drying upon it, and she did not sit, for the code prescribed no rest after the law was satisfied. She did not think of the man's name, because she had never learned it and the accounting had not required it. She merely stood at the crossroads, exact and unsoftened, with the weight of the eleventh upon her, and waited for whatever came next without hoping that it would be different. The code made no promise of difference, and she did not add to the requirements.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I don't sit either. I stand there until the sun has dried the stain to something duller, something that looks less like a heart and more like dirt. Then I walk away. My hands don't stop shaking until I reach the inn.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stood at the crossroads until the shadow of the marker reached the far edge of the road. The light changed from gold to grey, and the air cooled. The code did not instruct her when to depart, only that she must render the accounting and yield the ground. She had done both. She turned toward the town, for the body required shelter, and to deny the body its needs would be to impair the instrument that the code might require of her tomorrow.

The inn stood at the near end of the street. She entered. The common room was warm and loud with voices that had nothing to do with the duelling ground. She went to the keeper and asked for water, speaking the words with the same precision she had brought to the accounting. The keeper poured it. She drank it slowly, neither rushing nor savoring. Then she found a place against the far wall where she could see the door, and she stood there with her hands at her sides, steady still, her eyes fixed upon nothing in particular. She did not sit. She had not sat since the accounting began, and she did not add to the requirements by permitting herself rest that the code had not prescribed. She merely stood, with the weight of the eleventh upon her, and waited without hoping for anything to arrive.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I find her leaning against the wall, still standing. I don't sit either. "Water," I say to the keeper, and my voice sounds normal again. I take the cup and stand near her, not looking at her directly. "They're talking about it already. The witnesses."
