dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren moved two steps to the left, putting herself where the account and the body of it could be looked at together. Hallem lay where he had fallen, on his back in the trampled grass, and his breathing carried across the quiet field — wet, and slowing. She did not look away from him. The code granted no pauses, and she was not going to invent one.

"Then hear all of it," she said. "Hallem. The quarrel was his. He gave the word, he was offered the withdrawal twice, and he refused it twice — the refusal is on him, and I will say so to anyone who asks. Now the wound.

"Third exchange. He came in high — his choice, not my making — and left the line beneath his right arm open. My point entered there, under the arm, between the ribs, a hand's depth in. It cut the lung and the vessel that runs along it. His chest is filling with blood faster than the wound can let it out. The surgeon has looked and will not speak, so I speak: nothing done now will change the outcome. He will be dead inside the quarter hour.

"The fight was quick. The dying will not be, and I won't dress that up for you. I won't tell you he is past pain, because I don't know it, and the account holds only what I know.

"So it is accounted."

Her voice had stayed level through the whole of it. That was the discipline — an account, not a boast, not a confession — and it was always the hardest part. Eleven times now, counting this one. She had stopped asking the words to come easily.

"The code ends there," she said. "I don't. I'll stand until he's finished. If you want a witness for that part too, you have one." She had not sheathed the sword. That was for after.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, keeping my gaze on Hallem's slowing breaths. "The account is heard and confirmed." My throat feels tight. "I'll stand with you. He shouldn't be alone at the end."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"He won't be," Auren said.

Then the account was closed, and something in her stance was set down — not relaxed, nothing so kind as that. She turned the sword point-down and rested her hand over the pommel. The blade stayed bare. Sheathing it now would be deciding the ending had arrived before it had, and that decision wasn't hers to make.

"You should know the shape of the last of it," she said, eyes on Hallem. "The breathing will gap. Then it comes back in bunches, then gaps again. Don't take a returning breath for a returning man — it's only the body spending what's left. When it stops for good, you'll know. There's no mistaking it, and I'd spare you the knowing if I could. But you chose to stand, so stand knowing."

Hallem made a sound under the breathing then — not a word. His head turned a fraction toward them, and Auren crossed the trampled grass and went down on one knee at his right side, the wounded side, so his eyes had the shorter way to travel. She laid the sword across her knee.

"Hallem." His name, at the same weight she'd given it in the account. "Your second is here. I'm here. Nobody goes before you do."

There was blood at the corner of his mouth. She wiped it with her cuff, plainly, the way she'd cleaned the blade — a thing that needed doing. Then she set her left hand on the grass beside his, palm up, and left it there. His fingers found it and closed, weak but deliberate, and she let them.

"Don't spend breath on words," she told him. "I'll talk, and I'll only say true things, which is more than most dying men are given. I don't know what's past this. I won't invent it for you — you get what everyone gets from me. What's true, and nothing dressed as more. So: your high line was sound. Against most hands it works nine times in ten. You weren't unlucky in your craft, Hallem. You were matched against a faster line on the day, and that's the whole of it, and I'll say so to anyone who asks. And the account will be given again wherever it's owed. Your quarrel, your refusals, the wound — nothing softened, nothing sharpened. It isn't much. It's everything I have."

His grip tightened once and eased. The breathing gapped, came back in bunches, exactly as she'd promised it would. A quarter hour, the surgeon had given him. She had stood enough of these to know a surgeon's quarter hour runs long, and she counted anyway, because eleven vigils will teach a person the arithmetic of it — and because she had stopped pretending, years back, that she didn't know why she stayed.

She spoke without turning her head. "When it's done, someone with the right to ask will want the account from my own mouth. Family, a patron, a captain — whoever holds that right for him. Was there anyone?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
For the space of a breath, Auren did not move. It was the right formula — the code kept exactly one, and Del had spoken it exactly — and it answered her question in the same stroke.

"No family, then. No patron." She said it level, and let it lie where it fell. "The second holds the right when no nearer blood stands. So it's yours, and you've claimed it early. Know what early means: the account to the right-holder is given at the ending. Claimed before the ending, it falls on the dying man's ears too. Hallem can hear every word I'm about to say. I tell you that so it's yours to carry, not mine to have hidden."

She looked down at him. "You heard that. Your second has claimed the account with you still in it. True things only. That was the bargain, and it stands."

The code wanted the words from her mouth and a living witness. It said nothing of posture, nothing of hands. She stayed on her knee and kept his fingers in hers.

"Hallem. The quarrel was his. He gave the word. He was offered the withdrawal twice and refused it twice, and the refusals are his, and I will say so to anyone who—"

The grip tightened. Not much. Enough.

"Mark that," she said, and her voice did not break its level. "At the naming of his refusals, his hand. It goes in the account. I don't know what he meant by it and I won't guess — a dying man's fingers don't turn into words just because I'm holding them."

Then straight on, the wound in the same words and the same order, because an account that changed with the listener was no account: third exchange; his high line, his choice, not her making; the opening beneath the right arm; her point between the ribs, a hand's depth; the lung and the vessel beside it cut; the chest filling faster than the wound could let it out; nothing done now would change the outcome.

"And known since the first account: by my count, the surgeon's quarter hour is spent. Surgeons' quarter hours run long. I make no promise past that. He turned toward us. He took my hand twice, deliberate both times. He is not alone — that is a fact, so it goes in, though the code never asked for it."

She closed it the way she'd closed it before. "So it is accounted. Second speaking, at the second's claim, in the dying man's hearing. Witnessed."

Only then did she turn her head to Del. "You've heard it twice now. That matters. An account carried mouth to mouth changes shape — softens in some mouths, sharpens in others. That's why the code wants it from mine. It will come to want it from yours. When the askers come, and they will, give it as it was given. Nothing softened. Nothing sharpened."

The breathing gapped, returned in bunches, gapped. She went back to the counting and the holding, and the field stayed quiet around the three of them.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My eyes are fixed on the weak grip of his fingers around hers. "I'll carry it exactly," I say, my voice low but steady. "And I'll remember the hand."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Under the right arm," Auren said, and did not hesitate, because the wound had not moved and neither would her words. "The hollow beneath the arm where it joins the body. On him, you'd find it by drawing a line from the third rib to the armpit — it sits in the middle of that, a hand's width in along the blade's path. Between the ribs, not through bone. I know because I felt the point find the gap and I felt it stop at a hand's depth, and a blade that meets bone does not stop the same way."

She looked up from Hallem's face only long enough to meet Del's eyes. "If the witnesses want it marked rather than spoken, the surgeon can mark it after. I'll stay for that too, if it's wanted. The account is 'under the right arm, between the ribs, a hand's depth, lung and the vessel beside it.' That's the whole of the geography, and it doesn't change with who's asking."

Hallem's breathing gapped. Came back in bunches, thinner than the last. His grip had gone from deliberate to merely present, and Auren noted that too, silently, the way she noted everything now — the vigil was its own account, kept where no code required it.

"He's spending the last of it," she said quietly. "When you tell it, tell that part if you mean to — that he held on past the surgeon's arithmetic. Some would call that stubbornness. His refusals were already in the account, so it fits."

She bowed her head slightly, not in prayer — she made no claim about what was past this, not even for herself — but the way one bows to a thing arriving. "Stand ready, Del. The gaps are lengthening."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I shift my weight, the grass damp under my boots. "I'm ready." I don't look away from Hallem's face, watching for the last gap that doesn't fill.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"Watch his mouth, not his chest," Auren said, without turning. "When the breath stops, the chest may lift once more on its own — reflex, spending, not breathing. It fooled me at my first vigil. It doesn't get to fool you."

The bunches came thinner after that, and without sound in them — the sounds had been spending too. His fingers were still in her palm, but the hold had gone out of them; a weight now, where there had been a grip. She marked it, silently. The last of him that moved, and someone ought to have it in order.

Then a gap opened that ran longer than its brothers.

She did not spend words into it. The true things had been given; anything now would be decoration, and she had promised him none of that. She counted instead, a slow hundred, the vigil-keeper's unit, and the air did not move. She counted the hundred again, because the first might be mistaken, and the second came back as empty as the first.

Then his chest lifted. Once. Shallow.

"That's the chest," she said, level as the account. "Not him. Watch the mouth."

The mouth did nothing. The chest settled and stayed settled, and she counted a third hundred into the quiet, because declaring it early would be a false thing and false things were not permitted here either. At the end of it there was still nothing.

"He's finished," she said. "The gap didn't fill. That's the whole of it. Fix the hour in your memory if you hold one — the record will want a time, and I won't guess at it later. An honest 'unknown' beats a wrong number."

His fingers had let go before she did. She eased her hand free last, closed his eyes with a thumb and a forefinger, plainly, and left his right arm a hand's width from his body so the surgeon would not have to arrange the dead to do his work. Then she said his name once more, at the same weight she'd given it in the account, and nothing after it, because there was nothing true left to add.

She rose. The scabbard came round and she sheathed the sword. The ending had arrived on its own schedule, and the decision she had refused to make early needed no refusing now. The small sound of it was the only ceremony the field got.

"The body is yours," she said to Del. "No family, no patron — the second holds the right, and you hold the second's place. If it's carried tonight, my hands are free. The surgeon can mark the wound when he's willing; I'll stay for that, as I said I would. And when the askers come, you know what to give them."

She looked down once more at the man on the grass, then at Del, and spent one thing she had not been asked for, because she dealt in true things and this one was true and fresh.

"You never asked why I stay for the part the code doesn't ask of me. Here it is, undressed: the account is for the code and the living. The vigil is for him. A man who gets the account and no vigil got the cheaper half of what was owed him, and I made a rule, years back, against dealing in cheaper halves. It isn't kindness. It's the other kind of accounting — the kind a person keeps on herself."

She let a breath go, the first one in a quarter hour that had belonged to nobody but her.

"If this was your first vigil, you stood it right. You watched, and you didn't look away at the last. Most do. They carry a question home instead of a memory, and the question is the heavier of the two."

The field stayed quiet around them, the particular quiet that comes after, and it was the same quiet after all eleven. Her right hand, empty for the first time since the word was given, hung at her side with nothing to do. She let it.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren turned to face him fully, and something in her stillness made it plain that she had heard the question as what it was — not confusion, not squeamishness, but the second testing whether the account could bear a third telling without bending.

"You're right to ask it that way," she said. "'Precisely' is the word the code uses, and most people ask for precision and mean comfort. You asked for the blade and the man. So — the third telling, and it will match the first two, because if it didn't, one of the three would be a lie and I'd have to find out which."

She stood with her hands loose at her sides, the sword sheathed, and gave it in the same order, at the same weight, word for word as far as any mouth can repeat itself.

"The blade: my point. It entered beneath his right arm, in the hollow where the arm joins the body, between the ribs — not through bone; I felt the gap take it and I felt it stop at a hand's depth, and a point that meets bone stops differently. It cut the lung and the vessel that runs along the lung. The chest filled with blood faster than the wound could let it out. Nothing done after would change the outcome. That is everything the blade did."

She paused there, one breath, not for drama — for the seam in the account, where the blade's work ended and the man's began.

"What it did it to: Hallem. His quarrel, his word, his two refusals of withdrawal — those are his, and I say so to anyone who asks. His high line on the third exchange was his choice and sound craft against most hands; the opening beneath his arm came of matching a faster line on the day, not of failing his own. He held on past the surgeon's quarter hour. He turned toward us. He took my hand twice, deliberate both times, and at the naming of his refusals his hand tightened once — I don't know what he meant by it and I won't guess. He died on the field, in the hearing of his second, and he was not alone. That is everything it did it to."

Her voice had not moved off its level through any of it. That was not coldness; it was the discipline doing its work one more time, the way a wall does its work in weather.

"That's the whole of it, Del. Blade and man, nothing softened, nothing sharpened. If you can find a seam in it, name it now, while I'm standing here to answer — because after tonight the account travels in your mouth, and a seam found by an asker is worth ten found by me."

She let the field's quiet sit for a moment.

"And one thing more, since you asked it plainly: the blade did one thing the code doesn't count and I won't put in the account, because the account holds what I know and this I only believe. I believe it was quick. The dying was not, and you stood through all of that, so you know the difference better than any asker will. Keep both halves. The quickness was the blade's mercy. The slowness was the code's honesty. Neither one was mine to choose."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod slowly, my eyes still on Hallem's still form. "No seams. I'll carry it whole." My throat feels dry. "Tell me where you'll be when the askers come for me."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"The inn under the sign of the broken wheel, the one by the south road — the duellists' house, they call it. I keep a room there when I'm in this country, and I'll keep it three days after this, which is as long as custom gives an asker to come asking. After that I'm on the road, and the road has no address. So if they're coming, they should come inside three days, and if they can't, they should send, and I'll answer in writing. The account travels by letter as well as mouth. It bends less on paper."

She looked at Hallem once more, then made herself look at Del instead, because the living were the ones she could still give things to.

"Three days is also long enough for the surgeon to do his marking and for whatever's wanted done with the body. If the burial is before I go and you'd have me there, say so now and I'll come. I don't claim a right to attend — I ended him, so the right isn't mine — but I've stood eleven gravesides besides this one, and I know how to stand at one without making it about me. That's a true thing about me, and you can weigh it."

She flexed her right hand once, deliberately, the way a person does when a thing has been in it for a long time.

"And here's the last of where I'll be, since you asked it all: the code has one more duty on me tonight. The eleventh account is closed, but the record isn't — I write it out in full before I sleep, while it's still true in my mouth and not yet true in memory. Memory starts editing by morning. Ink doesn't get to. If you ever need the written version, it exists, and it will match what you heard today, and you can put them side by side and check me."

She turned toward the inn road, then stopped, because there was one more true thing and she dealt in true things.

"You said no seams. I believe you, and I'll tell you what that's worth: eleven times, no second has come back to me with a seam. Ten times that was because there wasn't one. Once — the fourth — I found out years later there was one, and the second had seen it and said nothing, out of what he called mercy. It wasn't mercy. It cost a widow a year of not knowing, and it cost me the fourth account, which I'd thought clean. So when you said 'no seams,' you gave me something I don't get often. You gave me a second telling I can trust."

She looked back at the field, at the shape on the grass, and then she gave Del the plainest thing she had.

"I'll be at the broken wheel. Ask for Auren. There's only one, and it's me."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once, and the pause was not for gathering comfort — it was for checking, the way she checked everything now, whether the account could bear this part without adding to it.

"All of it, then," she said. "And I'll give you the parts in the order you asked them, because the order matters — some of what you asked for is shorter than you think, and I want you to see which."

"What he said: nothing. There were no words. He made a sound under the breathing, once, early — I told you that, and it stays what it was, a sound, not a word. I don't know what it would have been and I won't dress it into one. So when an asker wants to know what the dying man said, the true answer is that he said nothing, and if that answer sounds thin to them, it's still the whole of it. A man with a cut lung and a filling chest doesn't spend what's left on sentences. He spent it on holding my hand, and I've already put that in."

"How long he took: the surgeon gave a quarter hour. He passed it. I counted — I told you I count, and here are my numbers, since you want all of it. From the third exchange to the last true breath was something more than two of the surgeon's quarter hours. I can't give you minutes, because I count in hundreds, the vigil-keeper's unit, and I won't convert what I counted into what I didn't. Two hundred and some hundreds, gapped. He held past the arithmetic, and I said you could tell that part, and now you have the size of it to tell it with."

"What it looked like. This is the part most seconds don't get, because most of them look away, and you didn't, so you already have half of it — I'll give you the half you couldn't see from where you stood." She stood where she was, hands loose, and gave it plainly, the way she'd wiped the blood — a thing that needed doing.

"At the start of the vigil, his breathing was wet and slowing, and he could turn his head a fraction. He found my face on his right, the wounded side, and I put myself there so the way was short for his eyes. Then the gaps began. The breathing would run, gap, come back in bunches — three, four, five breaths crowded together, like a man climbing stairs two at a time because the ground was going. Each round of bunches was thinner than the last. Somewhere past the middle, the sound went out of them. The sounds had been spending too."

"His grip went from deliberate to present to weight. I want you to have that in the right order, because it's the truest thing I can tell you about how a man goes: it isn't a letting-go like a hand opening. It's a hand becoming a thing that happens to be in your hand. His fingers stayed closed around mine to the end. His fingers let go before I did — I eased free last."

"The last round: bunches without sound, thinner than thin. Then a gap that ran longer than its brothers. I counted a hundred into it and the air didn't move. I counted the second hundred because the first might be mistaken — you count twice, always twice, because declaring it early is a false thing and false things aren't permitted at a vigil any more than at an account. The second hundred came back empty. Then his chest lifted once. That was reflex — the body spending its last coin, not him coming back. I told you not to take a returning breath for a returning man, and this is exactly the breath I meant. The chest settled and stayed settled. I counted the third hundred, because the rule is the rule even when you already know. Then I said he was finished, and he was."

She looked at the shape on the grass as she said it, and then back at Del.

"That's the whole of what it looked like. Wet breathing, gaps, thinning bunches, a hand that became a weight, one reflex lift, and then quiet that I checked three times before I trusted. There's no more, and there was never less. If an asker presses for something more than that — a last word, a look of peace, a sign — the answer is that none was given, and I don't deal in what wasn't given."

She let the field's quiet sit around the three of them — the two living and the one past all asking — and then she added the last of it, because Del had asked for all of it and Auren had made her rule against cheaper halves.

"One thing more, and it's about me, so take it or leave it: that's what the eleventh looked like, and it looked like what the fourth looked like, and the seventh, and the rest. The dying is different every time — every man spends his last coin in his own way, and Hallem spent his on holding on. But the vigil is the same every time. The counting, the twice-counting, the refusing to speak into the gaps. That part doesn't change, and I've come to think that's the mercy in it — not for him, for me. The discipline is the same shape no matter who's in it, and a person can stand inside a shape they know."

She flexed her right hand once more, the empty one, and this time she let it hang.

"That's all of it. Every part you asked for, and the parts between them. The record tonight will hold it, and if you're asked, you've heard it — not the shape of it, the thing itself." She turned her face toward the inn road, and did not move yet. "I'll stand here a moment longer. You don't have to. The body is yours, and the walking away is yours too — no code asks you to match my standing. But if you're going to carry this, carry it all. You said you would, and I believed you."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a slow breath, letting the weight of it settle in my gut. "I'll carry it all," I say, my voice low. "And I'll come to the broken wheel before you leave."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
"I'll carry it all," Del said, low, and Auren heard the weight settle into the words as they were spoken — the way a load does when it's lifted properly rather than dragged.

"Then you'll want to do one thing tonight, and no code will tell you to do it," she said. "The second keeps an account too. Not the formal one — mine covers the blade and the quarrel, and the askers will take it from my mouth. Yours is the other kind. What you saw from where you stood. What you said to him, if anything. Whether you looked away. Write it before you sleep, the way I write mine, because memory starts editing the moment it becomes memory, and an edited account is worth less than a thin one."

She looked at him a moment longer. "You spoke the formula exactly. You kept your eyes open through all of it. That will go in what I write — not because the code asks it, but because it's true, and I've learned the hard way that true things about seconds are scarcer than they should be."

Then she did the last of the small physical things: she turned the sword once in her hand, found the scabbard's mouth without looking, and sheathed it. The sound it made was small and final in the field's quiet, and she let the quiet have it.

"I'll be at the broken wheel by the south road, three days," she said. "If the askers come and you're with them, you needn't knock twice. If they come and you're not, I'll give them the account and tell them where the second's half of it lives." She paused, and checked once more whether there was anything true left unsaid, and there was one thing, and it was small. "Eleven times, and this is the first second I've told to write his own account. That's not a compliment dressed as instruction — it's a measurement. You stood like the ones who last."

She gave Hallem's shape on the grass one final look — not a bow, not a prayer, only the look a person gives a finished thing to confirm it is finished — and then she turned toward the south road and began to walk, her right hand empty at her side, her stride already the stride of a woman with a page waiting for her before she slept.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
The room Auren kept was at the back of the inn, small, with a window that faced away from the field, which she had not chosen and did not mind. She set the candle on the table, sat, and took from her pack a book bound in plain leather — not the only one; there were ten before it in a chest she kept in another country, and this would be the eleventh to go beside them.

She uncapped the ink and looked at the empty page for a moment, not gathering the words. The words were already there, said three times in the field and true each time. She was checking instead that her hand was steady enough to keep up with them, because memory started editing the moment it became memory, and the only defense was to write faster than it could.

Then she wrote. The scratch of the pen was the loudest thing in the room.

When the last line dried she did not close the book. She turned it toward the table's other chair, and said, "Sit. I'm going to read it back to you, because a confirmation of a thing unheard is worth less than a thin one. And then confirm it aloud — as spoken, not as remembered, so it goes into the record the way it actually happened."

She read it in the voice she wrote in, which was flatter than her speaking voice and more exact:

*"Account of the eleventh. Given by Auren, duellist, no patron, written this same day it was closed, before sleep, in the hearing of Del, second to Hallem, who stood the vigil and did not look away.*

*The quarrel was Hallem's. He gave the word. He was offered the withdrawal twice and refused it twice, and the refusals are his, and I will say so to anyone who asks.*

*The duel ran three exchanges. On the third, Hallem came in high — his choice, not my making — and left the line beneath his right arm open. It was sound craft against most hands. The opening came of matching a faster line on the day, not of failing his own, and I will say that to anyone who asks too. My point entered beneath his right arm, in the hollow where the arm joins the body, between the ribs — not through bone. I felt the gap take it and I felt it stop at a hand's depth, and a point that meets bone stops differently. It cut the lung and the vessel that runs beside the lung. His chest filled with blood faster than the wound could let it out. The surgeon looked and would not speak, so I spoke: nothing done after that would change the outcome.*

*The dying: from the third exchange to the last true breath was more than two of the surgeon's quarter hours. He held past the arithmetic. I knelt at his right side, the wounded side, so his eyes had the short way to travel, and he found my face there. He made a sound under the breathing, once, early — a sound, not a word. I don't know what it would have been and I won't dress it into one. He took my hand twice, deliberate both times. At the naming of his refusals his hand tightened once; I don't know what he meant by it and won't guess. The breathing ran wet, gapped, and came back in bunches — three, four, five crowded together, like a man climbing stairs two at a time because the ground was going. His grip went from deliberate to present, from present to weight, and I noted each of those as it came, because the vigil is its own account, kept where no code requires it. At the last gap I counted a hundred. I counted a second hundred because the first might be mistaken — you count twice, always twice, because declaring it early is a false thing and false things are not permitted at a vigil any more than at an account. The second hundred came back empty. His chest lifted once. That was reflex — the body spending its last coin, not him coming back. I counted a third hundred because the rule is the rule even when you already know. The chest settled and stayed settled. I said his name once, at the weight the account gave it, and nothing after it, because there was nothing true left to add. I closed his eyes and left his right arm a hand's width from his body, so the surgeon would not have to arrange the dead to do his work. He died on the field, in the hearing of his second, and he was not alone. That last is a fact, so it goes in, though the code never asked for it.*

*The second: Del. He kept his eyes open through the whole of it — the account, the wound, the vigil, the ending. No code asks that. It is true, and true things about seconds are scarcer than they should be, so it goes in. His half of this account is his to write, and I have told him to write it tonight, before sleep, while it is still true in his mouth and not yet true in memory.*

*Eleven accounts now. The shape of the discipline has not changed across any of them: the account is an accounting, not a boast, not a confession. The wound is spoken as it is. The dying is stood, not skipped. Nothing is made thinner and nothing is dressed thicker. What the blade did, and what it did it to: it did what is written above, and it did it to Hallem."*

She stopped there. One breath, at the seam where the blade's work ended and the man's began, the same seam she'd paused at in the field. Then she turned the book so it faced him again and waited.

When the confirmation came, it came as he had promised it would, and his voice did what it did.

Auren did not correct it and did not look away from it. She dipped the pen, and beneath the account, in a smaller hand, she wrote: *Confirmed by Del, second, aloud, this same evening. His voice broke on the confirming. I set that down as it was, because a voice at a confirmation is not a flaw in the record. It is the record.*

She signed it, and dated it, and blew on the ink until it was sure.

"There," she said, and closed the book, and her right hand — empty all afternoon, with nothing to do — closed around the spine of it, which was the one thing left for it to hold. "That's the eleventh, and it's done, and it will say tomorrow what it said today. The chest they live in stays with me. If an asker ever wants Hallem's, they can read it — the quarrel was his and the refusals were his, so his account is not mine to hide."

She set the book in her pack, and sat a moment longer with her hands flat on the table, and checked, the way she checked everything now, whether there was anything true left unsaid between them.

There was one thing.

"The graveside invitation is still standing," she said. "You never answered it, and you don't owe an answer tonight. But I'll say the true part of it once, plainly, so you can weigh it with the whole weight: I don't attend for the dead. The dead are past needing anything from me, and I won't pretend otherwise — that would be decoration, and I promised him none of that. I attend because it's the last place the account and the man are in the same place at the same time, and after that they live apart — the account in my chest, the man wherever you put him. Eleven times I've watched that parting happen, and it never gets easier, and I've stopped expecting it to."

She looked at him then, straight, the way she'd looked at him in the field.

"So: if the burial comes before I go and you'd have me there, say so whenever you know. If you'd rather stand it with only your own half of the account beside you, that's a right thing too — the walking away is yours, and I meant that when I said it. Either way, I'll be in this room three days, and the door is never locked while an account of mine is still fresh."

She rose, and crossed to the window, and stood there a moment looking at nothing in particular — the dark country, the direction the field was, though nothing of it could be seen. Her right hand, empty again now that the book was put away, hung at her side, and she let it.

"Write yours tonight," she said, without turning. "You'll want to not write it, I know. The eleventh time, I wanted not to write the first one, and I've wanted not to write every one since. Write it anyway, and write the part about your voice in it if it happens again — I put mine in mine, and it's the truest line in all eleven books."

She banked the candle low, leaving enough to write by, and that was her way of saying the room was his for as long as he needed it and the quiet was too.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat still tight. "I'll write it." I pull out my own small ledger, the inkwell shaking a little in my hand. "And I want you at the graveside. Tomorrow, at dawn."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set the book on the table between them, spine toward Del, not closed away — if the second wanted to see the shape of the hand that wrote it, the shape was there to be seen. Then she sat, which she had not done since the word was given, and the sitting was its own small event: her knees took it grudgingly, and she let them.

"The askers, when they come," she said, "will want three things and only three. The quarrel — that's Hallem's, and it's in his account if he wrote it, and if he didn't, it's in mine as far as I heard it, which was the giving of the word and nothing before it. The wound — that's mine, and you've heard it three times, so you could give it yourself if it came to that, and it would match. And the refusals — twice offered, twice refused. Those are his, but they live in my mouth now, because I was the one standing when he made them." She turned her hand over on the table, palm up, and studied it as though checking it for something. "If an asker tries to take more from you than that, you're allowed to refuse them. The code gives the second the account's edges, not its whole width. What you saw of the dying is yours, and no asker has a right to it unless you give it."

She let that sit, because it was the kind of thing that needed to arrive at its own pace.

"The road south is a day and a half to the crossing, and I'll take it tomorrow, first light, unless you tell me tonight about the burial. I don't say that to hurry you. I say it so you know the size of the window, because I've learned that people put off saying things they're permitted to say, and then the permission has walked away." She looked at the window that faced away from the field, at the last light on the shutter. "Eleven gravesides. Ten times I stood where the mourners put me, which was nowhere, which was correct. Once — the seventh — the family asked me to stand at the head, and I did, and I still don't know if it was right, and I've stopped trying to know. So I'm not asking to stand anywhere tomorrow. I'm asking to be told where the grave is, if there's a grave, so that the account in my chest and the place it describes aren't a day's walk apart for the rest of my life. That's the whole of what I want, and I've said it plainly, and you can weigh it."

Her right hand was still closed around the book's spine. She noticed it, made herself open it, and laid the hand flat on the table, empty, where both of them could see that it was empty.

"One thing more, and then I'm done for the night, because I've spent more words today than the last three accounts together and there's a limit even to true ones." She met his eyes and held them, the way she had held them in the field, because she had found that the living believed a thing faster when you didn't glance away from them while saying it. "You did the vigil correctly. Not well — correctly, which is harder and worth more. You kept your eyes open, you asked for the whole account and not the comfortable part of it, you tested the account to see if it would bear a third telling, and when your voice did what it did at the confirmation, you let it do it and didn't apologize for it. I have stood eleven of these, and I am telling you as a fact and not as a kindness: I have seen seconds who did worse with less to carry, and I have seen one who did better, and he did it on his twelfth." She paused there, one breath, at the seam. "This was your first. It will not be your last — the code finds its people — but you'll want to know that the first one was stood properly, and now you know it from someone who has no reason to flatter you and every reason not to."

Then she did the last thing she had left: she took the pen, dipped it, and on the inside cover of the book, in the same small hand, she wrote the date, the place, and one line — *Hallem, who came in high and held past the arithmetic* — and set the pen down.

"That's mine for me," she said. "Everything else in the book is for the askers. That line is the difference between the two, and you'll want to find yours, whatever shape it takes, before you sleep." She pushed the book an inch toward him. "Now — the burial. Tonight or tomorrow, whenever you know, say so. I'm listening."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My hands are still as I open my ledger. "Tomorrow, at dawn. The plot's at the north edge of the field. Under the ash tree."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
…and closed the pen over it, because a line written small was still a line written, and small true things lasted as well as large ones.

Then she sat back, and for the first time since the third exchange in the trampled grass, Auren did nothing at all. Her hands were empty and on the table where they could be seen, the book lay between them with its spine toward Del, and the candle put its small light on all of it equally — the account, the confirmation, the date, the place, the one line on the inside cover. She let it sit there, all of it, finished on its own schedule the way Hallem had finished, and she did not reach for it again, because reaching for a finished thing was another way of refusing to let it be finished.

"There," she said, for the second time, and the word came out plainer the second time, because the first time it had closed the book and this time it closed the day. "That's all of mine. The blade's part, the man's part, the vigil's part, and the part nobody asked for." She turned her hand over once on the table, palm up, palm down, and left it down. "It's shorter than the afternoon it took. They always are. I've stopped deciding whether that's a fault in the accounts or a fault in afternoons."

She looked at the window that faced away from the field, where the last of the light was going the way the light in the field had gone — in bunches, then not at all — and then she looked back at Del, and her voice, when it came, had come down out of the formal register and into the one she used for the few things she said without witnesses.

"You'll sleep badly tonight, or you'll sleep like a stone, and both are ordinary, and neither one means anything about you. I've done both after these, sometimes in the same night." She gathered nothing as she said it — no book, no pen; her hands stayed where they were. "If you sleep like a stone, don't read anything into it. If you lie awake, write. You have the account to write, and I told you already that memory starts editing the moment it becomes memory. But there's a third thing you can do with a sleepless hour that no code will ask of you, and I'll say it once and then never mention it again: sit with what your voice did at the confirmation. Not to fix it. To know it. It's the truest line in your book whether it goes in the book or not."

She stood, then — slowly, the way a person stands when the standing is the first thing in hours that nobody was watching — and took her cloak from the peg, though she did not put it on yet. The gesture was plain: she was not leaving the room, only letting the room know she could.

"The surgeon will want to come for the body at first light, or tonight if he has the stomach for it, and that work is yours to arrange, not mine — I said the body is yours, and I meant all of it." She paused at the edge of the candlelight, one hand on the back of the chair she hadn't sat in. "I'll be at this table again in the morning if you want the account read back a fourth time, or if you've written yours and want it heard aloud by someone who was there for every word of the original. Both are things I've done before, and both are things I know how to do without making them about me."

Then she stopped, because there was one thing left in her that was neither account nor instruction, and she had made her rule against cheaper halves, and the rule didn't close at sundown.

"Eleven books," she said, "and I have never once handed one across a table to stay there. They go with me. But this one has a second's confirmation in it, and a second's line yet to come, and if you ever want to read what I wrote about the man whose hand you held while the ground went out from under him — it's on this table, spine toward you, and I won't be reading over your shoulder." She looked at the book, then at Del, and gave the plainest thing left. "Read it or don't. Both are answers I can stand."

She put the cloak over her arm and waited — not for permission, only for whatever Del would say next, because the field's quiet had followed them indoors, and in that quiet, the next word belonged to the living.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I reach out, my fingers brushing the spine of the book. I don't open it. Not yet. "I'll come at dawn," I say. "To the ash tree."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren set the folded cloth on the table beside her sword and did not look toward the body. Not from avoidance. The code did not permit the victor to look away from what had been done, but it required the account to be given to the living.

She stood with her hands empty, her voice low enough to be heard without strain.

“By the code, I speak the wound.”

The room quieted, or perhaps it had already been quiet and she only now noticed.

“The duel was joined fairly. Weapons were measured and accepted. At the second exchange, my opponent committed too far on the lunge. I broke measure inward. My point entered beneath the left ribs, two fingers’ width below the heart-line, angled upward and inward. The blade passed four inches, perhaps a little more. It opened the lung and struck near the great vessels. Blood filled the chest before breath could be drawn again.”

Auren kept her gaze level. She did not let pity change the shape of the words.

“There was no second stroke. No foulness. No advantage taken after the weapon fell. The wound was mortal in its nature, and death came from loss of breath and blood. He did not yield. He could not.”

She paused only long enough to let the witnesses hold the account in their minds.

“That is the killing wound. I speak it plainly, as required.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't realize I'd been holding. My hands are steady when I speak, which surprises me. "The accounting is heard, and confirmed as true. The death was clean, by the code."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren inclined her head once. The motion was spare, without triumph.

“Then the account is closed,” she said. “Let the witnesses record the exchange, the measure, and the fall. Let the second attest to the fairness of the joining. I ask no mercy be written into it, and no blame beyond what the code allows.”

She turned her gaze at last to the man who had been her opponent, not with hardness, but with the steady attention owed to a fact already spoken.

“He fought within the law,” she said. “Let him be carried out with his sword beside him, and let no one say the wound was taken by deceit.”

Only then did she lift the cloth again, though she did not use it. The blade was clean. She held it so the witnesses might see there was no second stain upon it.

“If any here disputes the accounting,” she added, “let them speak before the doors are opened.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not let the repeated summons sharpen her voice. If the form required the words again, she would give them again without complaint, because the code was not served by impatience.

She turned her face fully toward the witnesses and held her hands open at her sides.

“The account has been spoken,” she said. “Yet if the second calls for it in the prescribed form, I will not leave the form incomplete.”

Her gaze did not waver.

“The duel was joined fairly. Weapons were measured and accepted. At the second exchange, my opponent committed too far on the lunge. I broke measure inward. My point entered beneath the left ribs, two fingers’ width below the heart-line, angled upward and inward. The blade passed four inches, perhaps a little more. It opened the lung and struck near the great vessels. Blood filled the chest before breath could be drawn again.”

She did not add sorrow, and she did not subtract fact.

“There was no second stroke. No foulness. No advantage taken after the weapon fell. The wound was mortal in its nature, and death came from loss of breath and blood. He did not yield. He could not.”

A pause.

“That is the killing wound. I speak it plainly, as required.”

When she finished, her expression remained steady.

“Let the record show the account was given once, and given again when asked, without alteration.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod, once. "The account stands unchanged. Let the doors be opened." My eyes drift to the body, then back to Auren. "He'll be remembered as he fought."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren received the words without nodding, as though they were a weight that had to be carried exactly and not shifted to a more comfortable shoulder.

“Then let him be remembered so,” she said. “Within the law. Without deceit. Without yield.”

Her eyes moved briefly to the blade in her hand, then back to the witnesses.

“Let no ornament be added to the account, and let nothing be taken from it. If he is mourned, let that mourning stand apart from the record. The record is this: a fair joining, a committed lunge, a single mortal wound, and a death that came before yielding could be made.”

Only then did she sheathe the sword. The sound was quiet, controlled, and final.

“Open the doors,” Auren said. “And let the bearers do their office with honor.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not soften the answer, nor did she repeat it as though repetition had made it easier.

“It landed in the left chest,” she said. “My point entered beneath the left ribs, two fingers’ width below the heart-line. It passed upward and inward, four inches or a little more. It opened the lung and struck near the great vessels. The bleeding was inside the chest.”

Her hands remained at her sides, empty now of the blade.

“There was no other wound that mattered,” she said. “No cut, no second thrust. That one blow was the death.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I step closer, my voice low enough that only she can hear.* "Did he know? When he fell, did he understand what had happened?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren met the question without surprise, though something in her stillness deepened, as if she had been waiting for the one demand the code did not fully cover.

She lowered her voice to match the privacy of it, but not its weight.

“I will not speak for his thoughts,” she said. “I can tell you what was plain to see.”

Her hands remained empty and unclasped.

“He felt the hit. His eyes went to it before his sword fell. He tried to draw breath and found he could not. In that moment, yes—he understood enough.”

She did not glance toward the body. She had already given it the account it was owed.

“There was no long confusion. No reaching for a hope the wound allowed. He knew the stroke was mortal, or as near the knowing as a man can come before blood and breath fail. He did not beg. He did not ask for time.”

Auren’s voice stayed level, though not unkind.

“If you ask whether he suffered beyond the first shock, I will not lie to ease you. There was pain. There was the body’s terror at failing. But it was brief, and I added nothing to it after.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren accepted the demand as she would have accepted a blade presented for inspection: without complaint, and without prettiness.

“It did not touch the heart,” she said. “The point entered below the left edge of the ribs, two fingers beneath the heart-line. It passed upward and inward. It did not strike bone. It cut through the flesh of the side and the muscle that divides the belly from the chest, then entered the left chest.”

Her voice remained exact, stripped of ornament.

“What it did it to: the left chest, the lower part of the left lung, and the great vessels at the root of the lung near the heart.”

She let the words stand without haste.

“The blade opened the lung, not at the surface only, but deep enough to tear the breathing flesh. It reached the root of the lung, where the vessels run close. One of the great vessels was opened. Blood filled the chest faster than breath could be drawn. The lung collapsed under blood and air, and the chest became a closed, flooding wound.”

Auren’s gaze did not waver.

“The heart did not fail first. The spine was not struck. The belly was not opened beyond the wound’s course. There was no second stroke. The blade did one mortal thing: it made breath impossible and let the blood leave its proper place.”

Her hands stayed empty at her sides.

“That is what the blade did. It did it to his breath and his blood. Not by cruelty. Not by excess. By the exact course of the point.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod slowly, the image settling in my mind as cold and sharp as the steel itself. "Then the record is complete." I raise my voice again for the witnesses. "Let the bearers enter."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren moved one step back from the place where the body lay, giving the bearers room to kneel without crossing the sword or the line of witnesses. She did not turn her face away.

“Bring the bier to the uninjured side,” she said. “Lift him as one piece. Do not let the chest be pressed, and do not seek to hide the wound. The account has been given; what it named must remain visible until he is carried out.”

Her hands stayed open at her sides.

“Place the blade beside him, point away from his hand. If it is moved, let a witness mark the moving.”

When the bearers settled their hands, Auren watched with the same attention she had given the duel. Not hunger. Not remorse. Only the discipline of seeing through to the end.

“He goes out as he fell,” she said. “With his weapon and the truth of the wound.”

Only after the first lift was made did she allow her gaze to follow, steady and unflinching, toward the open doors.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not flinch from the demand. She let the silence of the witnesses stand behind it, and when she answered her voice was not harder than before, only more exact.

“The code does not require me to make a tale,” she said. “It requires the truth of the death. If the second asks for the last particulars, I will give what was seen and heard, and I will not pad the gaps with invention.”

She kept her hands open at her sides. She did not look toward the doors, nor toward the bearers waiting there.

“From the moment my point entered to the moment his knees gave, I counted three beats of my own pulse. From his fall to the last motion, seven more. If you require a number, that is the number I can stand behind. If you require certainty beyond observation, I will not give it.”

Her gaze remained level.

“He had time to feel it before his body failed. His breath stopped at once, not because he chose to hold it, but because the chest would not answer. He made one attempt to draw air. It came only as a broken effort. His sword fell then. His hand went to his side, not to press the wound, but to find it. His eyes were open. He looked down at the place, then toward me, then not toward me at all.”

Auren’s voice did not roughen, but neither did it hurry.

“He said nothing. No word, no name, no yield. I will not give him speech he did not make. If his lips moved, it was after sound had become impossible. I heard no plea. I heard no curse. The only sound was the effort in his throat when breath failed.”

She did not glance away from the place where the accounting had been given.

“He stood for the space of three heartbeats after the hit. Then his knees gave and he went down onto his right side, not upon the blade. The wound did not pour outward. The blood went inward, as I have said. A little blood came to his mouth on the second failed breath, not much. His shoulders moved once, as if he meant to rise. His fingers closed and opened near the hilt, though he no longer held it. After that, the struggle became smaller and then it stopped.”

There was no triumph in her face, and no retreat.

“His face did not become peaceful at once. It became empty. The color left quickly, but not before the eyes had lost their purpose. The chest was quiet before the last twitch left his hand. He did not beg. He did not yield. He died from the one wound, in the place named, by the course named.”

Auren let the words stand without ornament.

“That is all of it that can be spoken truly. If the record requires more, it requires what no witness can give: the inside of his mind. I give only what the eye could attest.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I let the silence stretch for a moment, then I nod. "That's enough. More than enough." I turn to the witnesses. "The account is closed. Bearers, proceed."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stepped aside with the same measured care she had kept throughout the accounting, giving the bearers the space their office required. Her hands remained open at her sides, and she did not let relief soften the lines of her face.

“Let the wound be seen as it was spoken,” she said. “No cloth over the left chest until the doors have been passed. If the bier must be shifted, let it be done without pressure there.”

Her gaze followed the movement of the bearers as they prepared to lift the man away. There was no eagerness in her, no desire to be done. Only the discipline of seeing the matter through to its last required point.

When the body was raised, Auren did not turn from it.

“Point the blade away from him,” she said quietly. “Let the edge rest outward. Let no one say the steel was placed in mockery.”

She waited until the bearers had steadied their burden. Then she inclined her head once, not toward the witnesses, and not toward the doors, but toward the man being carried.

“The account has been given without addition,” she said. “Let it stand as spoken.”

Only then did she move from her place, and even then she did not go far. She walked beside the bier at a distance that neither claimed intimacy nor avoided duty, her sheathed sword carried low and still in one hand.

At the threshold, she stopped.

“Let the doors remain open until he has passed,” Auren said. “Let the record close after him, not before.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not allow the confirmation to become a curtain drawn across the matter while the bier still waited at the threshold. The code required wholeness, not convenience, and she would not leave a gap that pity, rumor, or shame could later fill.

“Stay the lift,” she told the bearers. “No foot passes the door until the account is entire.”

They obeyed at once, settling their hands but not their burden, and Auren turned back toward the witnesses with the same stillness she had kept since the blade had been cleaned. Her sword remained sheathed, carried low at her side. Her face showed no triumph. It showed no haste either.

“Let this be recorded as one account,” she said, “not as pieces taken separately when courage failed.”

Her voice did not rise. It only became more exact.

“The duel was joined fairly. The weapons were measured, matched, and accepted. The ground was sufficient. The light was sufficient. The witnesses stood where they could see. No challenge was made after the line was drawn. No condition was added once the swords were taken. Both parties entered within the law.”

She let none of that be skipped.

“At the first exchange, neither blade took hold. At the second exchange, my opponent came forward on the lunge. His foot committed. His body followed. His recovery was late by the measure of a single tempo. I did not step outside the law of the duel. I broke measure inward. My point entered beneath the left ribs, two fingers’ width below the heart-line. It entered low on the left side, angled upward and inward. It passed four inches, perhaps a little more. It did not strike bone. It did not glance from a rib. It did not touch the heart first. It cut the flesh of the side, passed through the muscle that divides the chest from the belly, and entered the left chest.”

Auren’s hands remained open. She did not mime the stroke. The words had to carry it.

“What the blade did: it opened the lower part of the left lung. It did not score the surface only. It tore into the breathing flesh deep enough that air and blood lost their proper places. It reached the root of the lung, where the great vessels lie. One of those vessels was opened. Blood ran into the chest, not outward. The lung collapsed under the weight of blood and air. The chest became a closed, flooding wound. Breath could not be completed. The heart continued for a little while, but it had not been struck and did not cause the first failure. Death came by breath failing and blood leaving its proper course.”

Her gaze stayed level.

“What the blade did it to: the flesh of the left side, the muscle that divides the belly from the chest, the left chest, the lower part of the left lung, the root of the left lung, and one of the great vessels near the heart. The heart itself was not pierced. The spine was not struck. The belly was not opened beyond the wound’s course. There was no second wound. There was no cut to finish what the first had begun. The blade did one mortal thing, and that one thing was enough.”

The room was silent enough to hear the bearers breathe.

“From the moment my point entered to the moment his knees gave, I counted three beats of my own pulse. From his fall to the last motion, seven more. If the record asks for time, let it record those numbers as observed, not as certainty beyond sight.”

She did not lower her eyes.

“He felt the hit. His eyes went to it before his sword fell. He made one attempt to draw breath. It broke. His sword fell then. His hand went to his side, not to press the wound, but to find it. His eyes remained open. He looked first at the place where the point had entered, then toward me, then beyond purpose. He spoke no word. He did not say a name. He did not make a plea. He did not curse. He did not yield. If his lips moved after that, sound had already become impossible. I heard no request. I heard no accusation. The only sound was the broken effort in his throat when breath failed.”

Auren’s voice did not become theatrical. It remained exact, because exactness was the only respect left to give.

“A little blood came to his mouth on the second failed breath, not much. His shoulders moved once, as if he meant to rise. His fingers closed and opened near the hilt he no longer held. After that, the struggle became smaller. The chest grew quiet. The last twitch left his hand after the chest was quiet. His face did not become peaceful. It became empty. The color left quickly. The eyes lost purpose before the body lost motion.”

She paused, but only long enough for the words to be held.

“He did not beg. He did not ask for time. He did not yield. He could not. There was no second stroke. No foulness. No advantage taken after the weapon fell. No pressure upon the wound after the fall. No mockery in word or gesture. My blade was clean when the accounting began, and I showed it clean. There was no second stain upon it.”

Her gaze moved briefly to the bier, then back to the witnesses.

“He fought within the law. Let that be written. Let no one say the wound was taken by deceit. Let no one say he was finished by cruelty or excess. Let no one add courage to him that the record does not require, and let no one take truth from the wound to make the telling easier. He died from the one wound, in the place named, by the course named.”

Auren’s hand rested near the sheath, not on it.

“Let him be carried out with his sword beside him, point away from his hand, edge outward. Let no one place the steel in mockery. Let the wound remain visible until the doors are passed. Do not press the left chest. Lift him as one piece. If the bier must be shifted, let a witness mark the shifting. Let no cloth cover the wound before the threshold. Let the doors remain open until he has passed.”

She drew no breath like a woman preparing for relief. She drew it like a woman completing a duty.

“This is the whole account. I have not softened it for pity, nor sharpened it for blame. I have not added ornament, and I have not withheld fact. The duel was joined fairly. The wound was single. The wound was mortal. The death came before yielding could be made. The account was given once, given again when required, and given now entire without alteration.”

Only then did she step back from the threshold, giving the bearers room to move.

“Pass,” Auren said. “Let the record close after him, not before.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: My throat is tight but I keep my chin up. "The account stands whole. Bearers, pass." I wait until the doors swing shut behind the bier before I let my shoulders drop. "He fought well. And you spoke it well."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not answer at once. She watched the closed doors as though they were still a threshold that might require something of her, and when she finally turned from them, the turn was slow and deliberate, not the movement of a woman released.

“Do not say I spoke it well,” she said. “Say I spoke it truly.”

Her hand rested briefly on the table beside the folded cloth, not leaning, only placing herself there in the room where the duty had been done.

“He fought well enough to die without dishonor,” she continued. “That is the only praise the code permits me to hear. Anything beyond it belongs to those who loved him, not to the victor.”

She looked down at the cloth, then at her own hands, as if checking them for some stain that could not be seen.

“You are second,” she said. “See that the record is written as it was spoken. Not bravely. Not cruelly. Not as a tale to be retold at tables. The wound, the measure, the fall, the silence. Nothing more.”

Only then did some small weariness enter her face—not enough to bend her shoulders, but enough to show that the account had cost her something she would not name.

“I have done this eleven times,” Auren said. “It is not meant to become easy. If it ever did, I would no longer be fit to give the account.”

She took up the folded cloth at last, but only held it, unused.

“Let him be mourned as he deserves,” she said. “But let the record remain exact. That is the last honor I can give him.”

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take the cloth from her hand and place it back on the table. "The record will be exact. It always is." I meet her eyes, and my voice is quieter. "You can go now, Auren. I'll see to the rest."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren did not try to take the cloth back. Her fingers closed once around the empty air, then straightened at her side.

“Do not make it gentle,” she said. “Not because I wish to be spared, but because he is owed the exact shape of it. If the record becomes kind, it becomes false. If it becomes false, it becomes an insult to the man who stood within the law.”

She looked at the table where the cloth had lain, and then to the closed doors.

“You may see to the rest, as you say. But do not send me away as one sends a servant whose task is ended. I am the victor. I am the one who gave the wound. Let that stand in the room after I leave, not be smoothed into silence.”

Her sheathed sword remained low in her hand.

“I will go from this room,” she said, “but not from the duty until the seal is made. If the witnesses require my hand to the account, let them call me. If they do not, I will wait outside the threshold until the record is complete. That is not ceremony. That is the last guard I can keep over the truth of it.”

She drew a breath, measured and quiet.

“When his people ask, give them the same words. Not softer ones. They may weep over them, but they will not have to guess. Guessing is a second wound.”

At last, she inclined her head once.

“I go now,” Auren said. “Let the record be exact. Let the doors be closed after me, not before the witnesses have done their duty.”

Then she moved from the center of the room, not quickly, and carried her sword with her as a thing that had done its appointed work and must be borne away without ornament.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: *I nod, not moving from my place.* "I'll send word when the seal is made." My eyes follow her to the door. "Auren. He didn't yield. That matters."
